text: Machine learning systems encounter difficulties in learning predictors that remain robust under distribution shifts. These systems can achieve nearly perfect accuracy on i.i.d. data drawn from the training distribution, even when regularization is applied to prevent overfitting. However, their performance can decline to below-chance levels when there are even slight differences between the testing and training distributions \citep{goodfellow2015explaining,geirhos2020shortcut}. The field of Domain Generalization (DG) \cite{ganin2016domainadversarial, li2018domain} addresses this issue by proposing robust methods that ensure strong test performance on distributions that differ from but are systematically related to the training distribution \citep{mansour2019robust}. Invariant Risk Minimization (IRM) \citep{arjovsky2019invariant} is one of several recently successful approaches to Multi-Source Domain Generalization \citep{zhao2020multisource}, which encourages models to learn predictors with invariant performance across different ``domains'' or ``environments'' \citep{peters2015causal, heinzedeml2018invariant}. Given $n$ different training environments, these models extract a set of predictors from the feature space such that the conditional distribution of the outcomes given the predictors remains invariant across all training environments. Consequently, these predictors can generalize effectively to all test out-of-distribution (OOD) environments that share this invariance. Building on philosophical work that characterizes causation as invariance \citep{cartwright2003two, mitchell2000dimensions}, existing invariance-based DG methods have been interpreted as a weak form of causal discovery, where the returned predictors are the causal factors underlying the phenomena we aim to predict. Fairness is often characterized by robustness to changes in ``sensitive attributes'' \cite{arjovsky2019invariant}, particularly in the context of toxicity classification. Consider an automated moderation system used by an online news platform to determine which comments on a news article are toxic to online discourse and should be censored. The performance of a fair system should not be influenced by characteristics such as whether the comment pertains to issues related to race, gender, or other politically sensitive topics. Alternative definitions of distributive fairness differ in how the system's predictions should remain invariant to changes in the sensitive attribute. For example, statistical definitions such as Demographic Parity require that some conditional distribution of predictions given the sensitive attribute remains invariant to the sensitive attribute \citep{hardt2016equality}, while causal definitions such as counterfactual fairness \citep{kusner2018counterfactual} require that each individual's prediction remains invariant to counterfactual changes in that individual's sensitive attribute. There are numerous ethical and legal criticisms directed at systems that predict based on sensitive group membership \citep{barocas2016big}. Moreover, over-reliance on sensitive information could decrease robustness when the predictive performance of this information spuriously depends on the environmental context in which it is used. For instance, discussions about non-Caucasian racial identities may be highly predictive of comment toxicity on white supremacist internet forums, where members routinely make discriminatory remarks about ethnic minorities. However, on other internet forums that are more welcoming of diversity, the association between racial identity mention and toxicity would likely be far weaker. This brittleness of sensitive information has been identified as a key challenge that Perspective API, a Google-backed internet comment toxicity classifier, faced during implementation in real-world contexts \citep{borkan2019nuanced, jigsawmedium}, and has also been observed to cause bias in sentiment analysis \citep{kiritchenko2018examining} and facial detection \citep{buolamwini18a} tasks. Fair models, then, can potentially be constructed by learning predictors whose performance remains invariant across a variety of different environments. In this work, we empirically demonstrate that Domain Generalization can be used to build fair machine learning systems by constructing models that are invariant to spurious correlations involving the sensitive attribute. Specifically, we evaluate the performance of IRM on a fair internet comment toxicity classification task derived from the Civil Comments Dataset. In this task, the model must generalize from biased training environments exhibiting a strong but spurious correlation between the mention of a particular demographic identity and toxicity to a test environment where this correlation is reversed. \footnote{\url{https://github.com/adragnar/irm-toxicity-classification}} Our contributions are as follows: \begin{itemize} \item We find that IRM outperforms ERM in both generalization accuracy and group fairness on this dataset, highlighting the alignment of robustness and fairness for the type of data bias studied; \item We investigate the reason for this performance improvement via ablation studies: while sensitive information is marginally predictive, IRM exploits variation in this predictive power across environments to find an invariant (and thus more fair) solution; \item Examination of the IRM solution reveals that comment length is used as an invariant feature. While predicting from comment length may be more fair than predicting from sensitive group membership, IRM has still not found a truly ``causal'' feature. This highlights both a key limitation of the IRM approach of treating invariance as a proxy for causality, and the importance of environment diversity as an inductive bias for this method. \end{itemize}

text: Reconfiguration problems encompass a broad category of problems where a sequence of steps is required to transform one object into another. In this paper, we examine the problem of reconfiguring a collection of modular robots in a lattice using certain predefined moves. Numerous variants of this problem have been explored in both the robotics and computational geometry fields. In this paper, we investigate the reconfiguration problem for (edge-)connected configurations of hexagons and squares. As required for many applications, we ensure that (edge-)connectivity is preserved at all times, adhering to the so-called \emph{single backbone condition}~\cite{Dumitrescu-Suzuki-Yamashita-2004}). The permitted moves are pivots: a module can rotate around vertices shared with other modules, and at the conclusion of a move, the pivoting module must occupy a lattice cell. The interiors of two modules must never intersect. Hexagons have only two types of pivoting moves, as shown in Figure~\ref{fig:hex_moves}. In a \emph{restricted} move, a module $a$ adjacent to a module $s$ pivots around a vertex $v$ shared by $a$ and $s$, ending the pivoting move in the other cell that has $v$ on the boundary. The \emph{restricted model} of pivoting permits only this move. In a \emph{monkey} move, a module $a$ adjacent to a module $s$ begins pivoting around a vertex $v$ shared by $a$ and $s$, similar to the restricted move, but halfway through the rotation, another vertex $w$ of $a$ coincides with the vertex of a module $s'$. Then $a$ continues the move pivoting around $w$ in the same direction (clockwise or counterclockwise) as before until reaching a cell adjacent to~$s'$. The \emph{monkey model} of pivoting includes both the restricted move and the monkey move. Informally, the monkey move allows a module to continue pivoting in the same direction when a restricted move is not feasible. Further insights into the differences between both hexagonal models are presented in Section~\ref{sec:models}. In the square grid, two modules that share a vertex might not share an edge. Consequently, for square modules, there is a greater variety of pivoting moves. The three different sets of moves are illustrated in Figure~\ref{fig:square_moves}. The \emph{restricted model} includes only restricted moves, the \emph{leapfrog model} includes both restricted and leapfrog moves, and the \emph{monkey model} includes all moves. \ifabstract Section~\ref{sec_proto} contains a discussion of which of the above models have been actually implemented in practice. \fi } \later{ \iffull\paragraph*{Prototypes.} \fi \ifabstract

text: Automatic Speech Recognition (ASR) involves the automatic identification of speech. Speech Commands Recognition (SCR) is a subset of ASR where the system identifies brief spoken commands. This technology is crucial for enabling machines to comprehend human instructions. Potential applications include smartphones with virtual assistants, robots that execute spoken instructions, and smart home devices like Amazon Echo and Google Home. Such applications are increasingly influencing human-machine interactions. There are also numerous applications for this technology in both healthcare and education, such as for individuals who are blind or disabled \cite{1998Single-surgeonThoracoscopicSurgeryWith,2014EducationalSystemForThe}. Since many of these applications depend on compact devices with limited computational resources, fast and lightweight implementations are essential for real-time operation \cite{2018FPGAImplementationOfConvolutional}. Traditional SCR methods focus on extracting discriminative features from raw speech. Frequency domain features, such as the fast Fourier transform, are among the most commonly used to convert time-domain speech into frequency space \cite{1989Speaker-independentPhoneRecognitionUsing,2013TechniquesForFeatureExtraction}. After feature extraction, an acoustic model like the hidden Markov model (HMM) was traditionally used to represent sequences of words or phonemes \cite{2014SpeechAndLanguageProcessing.}. The combination of neural networks and HMM-based methods has been employed for over two decades \cite{2012ConnectionistSpeechRecognition:A,1986TheTRACEModelOf}. Recently, deep learning-based methods have surpassed traditional machine learning techniques in performance accuracy across various applications \cite{2012DeepNeuralNetworksFor,2015DeepLearning,2016DeepLearning}. Neural networks such as long short-term memory (LSTM) have improved the accuracy of natural language processing systems beyond conventional methods \cite{1999LearningToForget:Continual,2016LSTM:ASearchSpace}. Additionally, neural network-based methods have dominated the entire SCR field and are recognized as the state-of-the-art by the speech recognition community \cite{2014Small-footprintKeywordSpottingUsing,2017HelloEdge:KeywordSpotting,2018DeepResidualLearningFor,2019TemporalConvolutionForReal-time}. Meanwhile, various neural network architectures like convolutional neural networks (CNNs), LSTMs, and gated recurrent units (GRUs) have been effectively applied to SCR \cite{2017HelloEdge:KeywordSpotting,2018DeepResidualLearningFor,2019TemporalConvolutionForReal-time}. Direct application of CNNs on raw audio has been investigated in \cite{2018SpeakerRecognitionFromRaw,2018InterpretableConvolutionalFiltersWith,2018End-to-endSpeechRecognitionFrom}. However, the limited computational and memory capacities of embedded devices remain significant challenges to fully leveraging the advantages of highly accurate complex deep networks. To address the computational complexity on embedded devices, two general strategies are typically employed. One approach is to compress state-of-the-art deep models to lower computational costs without significantly compromising performance accuracy \cite{2019AnOptimizedRecurrentUnit,2020Small-FootprintOpen-VocabularyKeywordSpotting}. Alternatively, more efficient deep networks and methods can be used from the outset to achieve higher accuracy with reduced computational costs \cite{2019OperationalNeuralNetworks,2020Self-OrganizedOperationalNeuralNetworks}. The second approach is particularly important when training examples are limited or input signals are of low quality or resolution. By adopting either strategy, one can implement an effective classifier on energy-constrained embedded devices. Numerous studies focus on compressing complex networks or designing lightweight networks from the start. Progressive operational perceptrons (POPs) \cite{2017ProgressiveOperationalPerceptrons} aim to generalize conventional multilayer perceptrons (MLPs) using generalized operational perceptrons (GOPs). GOPs employ a unique set of operators to mimic the synaptic connections of biological neurons, allowing them to better capture the hidden semantics of data. PyGOP \cite{2019PyGOP:APythonLibrary} is a library for implementing GOPs on both CPU and GPU. The authors in \cite{2020ProgressiveOperationalPerceptronsWith} accelerate the learning process in POPs by utilizing memory and information from previously learned layers. The concept of biologically inspired neurons is further explored in \cite{2019HeterogeneousMultilayerGeneralizedOperational}, where each neuron in the network can have its own set of operators, resulting in a compact network. In \cite{2018ImprovingEfficiencyInConvolutional}, a generic neural network layer structure using a multi-linear projection is proposed, which requires significantly less memory compared to traditional CNNs while achieving superior performance. The authors in \cite{2017HelloEdge:KeywordSpotting} employed deep networks with dilated convolutions to attain high accuracy with fewer parameters. SincNet Kernels \cite{2018InterpretableConvolutionalFiltersWith} in the first convolutional layer of a CNN is another method to reduce the CNN by decreasing the number of learnable parameters. This technique is applied for speaker recognition in \cite{2018SpeakerRecognitionFromRaw} and later for phoneme recognition \cite{2018InterpretableConvolutionalFiltersWith}. Depth-wise separable convolutions (DSCconvs) were initially introduced in the image processing domain \cite{2017Xception:DeepLearningWith,2017Mobilenets:EfficientConvolutionalNeural} and later applied in SCR, keyword spotting \cite{2017HelloEdge:KeywordSpotting}, and machine translation \cite{2017DepthwiseSeparableConvolutionsFor} to reduce computational demands. In this paper, we propose a novel network layer to improve speech command recognition using a lightweight network. We achieve this by employing a new combination of self-organized operational neural networks (SelfONNs) \cite{2020Self-OrganizedOperationalNeuralNetworks} and quadratic forms kernels \cite{2017Non-linearConvolutionFiltersFor}. Experiments on the Google Speech Commands (GSC) \cite{2018SpeechCommands:ADataset} and synthetic speech commands (SSC) datasets\footnote{\url{https://kaggle.com/jbuchner/synthetic-speech-commands-dataset}} demonstrate the effectiveness of the proposed approach for recognizing speech commands, particularly in lightweight networks. To our knowledge, we are the first to propose combining SelfONNs and quadratic kernels to create a new network layer type to enhance the performance of a lightweight CNN. We are also the first to apply the concepts of SelfONN and quadratic kernels to the task of SCR. In the following sections, we present the most relevant work in Section~II. The proposed quadratic SelfONN approach for SCR is introduced in Section~III, and the experimental results are discussed in Section~IV. Finally, the paper concludes in Section~V.

text: The prevalence of robotic surgery has risen in recent years. Robotic surgical consoles, such as the da Vinci\textsuperscript{\textregistered} Surgical System~\cite{guthart2000intuitive} developed by Intuitive Surgical Inc. (Sunnyvale, CA), are being utilized instead of traditional surgical instruments like laparoscopes, with the objective of enhancing surgical quality and patient outcomes. These consoles fundamentally alter the nature of the surgeon's interaction with the patient. Investigating human surgical performance in this context is therefore an exciting research area that is essential for advancing our understanding of surgeon-robot interaction and improving patient outcomes. The comprehensive and precise surgical data available in various modes, such as videos and kinematics, can be employed to achieve a holistic understanding of the surgery and to study human surgical performance closely and accurately. \\ Much recent research in this field has concentrated on task-specific, supervised learning from a single modality. We contend that this approach has several limitations. Firstly, a task-specific learning paradigm (such as supervised skill detection, for instance) facilitates a very narrow understanding of the overall surgical process, providing limited insight beyond the specific training task. Additionally, supervised learning creates a reliance on expert annotations that are costly to obtain, subjective, and potentially erroneous. Finally, disregarding multiple modalities of information (such as video and kinematics) can hinder the learning of generalizable, feature-rich representations. \\ We propose that robotic surgery can be decomposed into a sequence of gestures or surgemes \cite{varadarajan2009data}. Consequently, it is feasible to model a surgery similarly to language models \cite{mikolov2013distributed, devlin2018bert} using the vocabulary of the surgemes. In this study, we introduce a self-supervised learning algorithm that learns task-agnostic surgical gesture representations from two modalities (namely, video and kinematics) that can generalize effectively across multiple tasks. \\ Our contributions in this paper are as follows: 1) we present a deep-learning-based architecture to learn self-supervised surgical gesture representations from video and kinematics, 2) we quantitatively demonstrate the utility of our representations across multiple tasks by achieving state-of-the-art accuracy in gesture recognition and high accuracy in skill recognition, 3) we qualitatively demonstrate the rich information encapsulated in our representations by visualizing our representations forming semantically meaningful clusters.

text: Human-Object Interaction (HOI) recognition has garnered substantial interest due to its critical role in scene understanding. The objective of HOI recognition is to extract multiple \textit{$<$verb, object$>$} pairs (\textit{e}.\textit{g}., ``hold, apple'') from an image. Image-level HOI classification presents challenges for two primary reasons. Firstly, the datasets \cite{hico15,vg17} exhibit a long-tailed distribution and significant class imbalance. Secondly, each image contains multiple labels, and the locations of the HOIs are not specified. Recent studies predominantly focus on utilizing object and keypoint detection while neglecting the classifier. We identify that the classifier plays a crucial role in both HOI classification and detection. A fundamental difference between HOI recognition and traditional image classification is that HOI classes are combinations of verbs and objects, resulting in a stronger semantic relationship between classes. For instance, in the HICO \cite{hico15} dataset, the average number of classes sharing the same verb is 5.1, and the average number sharing the same object category is 7.5. However, the effective utilization of such semantic cues remains underexplored in current methods. Some approaches \cite{liao2020ppdm,uniondet20,sgg-imp17,atl21,scg20} classify objects and verbs separately. This strategy significantly reduces the number of classes to predict but is susceptible to polysemy, as the same verb may have different meanings in various HOIs (\textit{e}.\textit{g}., ``{\em make}, pizza'', ``{\em make}, vase''). As a progression, we employ language models to generate text embeddings of HOI classes and use these to initialize the weight vectors in the linear classification layer. This method, termed \textit{Language Embedding Initialization}, demonstrates superior performance compared to the commonly used Random Initialization techniques \cite{xavier10,kaiminginit15}, especially in few-shot scenarios. The rationale is that the weight vectors in the linear classifier can be considered as proxies (feature centers) for each class \cite{circleloss20,normface17}. By using language embeddings for weight initialization, the initial positions of proxies in the vector space are determined by their semantic structure rather than being random. This setup facilitates the multi-label training process, as the vision feature from the backbone is guided to converge towards the semantic feature center, where HOIs that frequently co-occur in an image are also closely positioned (see \cref{fig:2_bert}). Moreover, language embeddings offer appropriate weight initialization for few-shot classes, where the weight vectors in the classifier cannot be effectively learned with limited samples. Previous studies \cite{transfer16,pairwise18} employ {\it weighted} sigmoid cross-entropy loss \cite{wbce15} to address the positive/negative imbalance per class. While this approach is superior to cross-entropy loss, it is less effective when the class imbalance is extreme (20.1\% of the classes in HICO have $\leq$ 5 positive samples). We introduce a novel loss function called Log-Sum-Exp Sign (\textit{LSE-Sign}) loss to enhance multi-label learning in long-tailed datasets. The loss function is designed such that its gradient form is a softmax function of losses from all classes. The softmax function amplifies the loss from poorly classified classes and reduces the loss from well-classified classes. This concept aids multi-label learning and dynamically balances the loss across all classes. It is important to note that the LSE-Sign loss differs from focal loss \cite{lin2017focal} in two aspects: 1) it considers the {\em relative} difficulty among all classes, whereas focal loss operates on each class individually, and 2) focal loss requires tuning two hyper-parameters. Although a detection-free baseline using ImageNet-1K pre-trained ViT-B/32 as the backbone suffers a significant performance drop compared to detection-assisted state-of-the-art methods (from 47.1 to 37.8 mAP), Language Embedding Initialization with BERT successfully raises it to 50.6 mAP. The approach is applicable to other types of language models, including SimCSE \cite{simcse21} and CLIP \cite{clip21}. LSE-Sign loss yields an average improvement of 3.1 mAP across eight experiments (\cref{tab:bce_vs_sign}). Building on these findings, we surpass existing detection-assisted methods \cite{pairwise18,pastanet20,hake19} by a significant margin. With a ResNet101 backbone, our method achieves 53.6 mAP, exceeding the state-of-the-art \cite{hake19} that utilizes both object and human keypoint detections by 6.5 mAP. With a ViT-B/16 backbone, our method achieves 65.6 mAP. On few-shot subsets, we achieve 52.7 mAP on 1-shot and 56.9 mAP on 5-shot classes. At the instance level, we separate the HOI detection task into localization and regional HOI classification. The advantage of being detection-free allows us to apply the classification model to a regional human-object box pair generated by any off-the-shelf detector. Using a vision transformer backbone, we convert bounding boxes into an attention mask so that the CLS token can only focus on the region of interest. Without additional training under instance-level supervision, it achieves state-of-the-art (SOTA) performance (32.35 mAP) on the HICO-DET dataset, surpassing the SOTA \cite{cdn21} trained on HICO-DET.

text: Pretraining large neural networks with a language modeling objective has resulted in substantial advancements across NLP \citep[][\emph{i.a.}]{peters2018deep,howard2018universal,radford2018improving,devlin2018bert,raffel2019exploring,brown2020language}. Further enhancements are often achievable by selecting a pretraining objective that more closely aligns with the downstream task of interest. Examples include casing prediction for named entity recognition \citep{Mayhew_Nitish_Roth_2020}, gap sentence generation for summarization \citep{zhang2019pegasus}, and sentence unshuffling for discourse representations \citep{lee2020slm}. Although such methods can significantly decrease the amount of training data needed, they generally still perform poorly when only a few examples are available for the downstream task, which is a common situation for many real-world applications of NLP. In these few-shot scenarios, however, substantial improvements are possible by reversing the adaptation process: Instead of making pretraining more similar to a downstream task, we can reformulate the downstream task to resemble the pretraining objective more closely. For masked language models \citep[e.g.,][]{devlin2018bert,lewis2019bart}, one such reformulation technique involves converting inputs into cloze questions by appending a text snippet that includes some form of task description, often as a short prompt \citep{radford2018language,schick2020exploiting}. Besides aligning pretraining and finetuning more closely, this approach offers the significant advantage of allowing users to \emph{explain} a task to a pretrained model, thereby facilitating the model's comprehension of the task. This is demonstrated in Figure~\ref{figure:motivational-example}, where a pretrained language model receives the same input with different instructions and adjusts its output accordingly. The concept of providing task descriptions is effective even in an unsupervised setting \citep{radford2018language} or when examples are simply given as additional context \citep{brown2020language}; however, it reaches its full potential when combined with gradient-based training on a small number of labeled examples \citep{schick2020just}. Unfortunately, current methods for this are restricted to text \emph{classification} tasks \citep{schick2020exploiting}. Inspired by their success, we explore whether the underlying concept can also be applied to more complex text-to-text tasks that require the \emph{generation} of text sequences from an input text, such as abstractive summarization. We introduce \textsc{genPet}{}, a novel method based on \textsc{Pet}{} \citep{schick2020exploiting}, which facilitates the finetuning of generative language models using both instructions and labeled examples. We demonstrate that \textsc{genPet}{} is a highly data-efficient method that enables us to finetune a pretrained \textsc{Pegasus}{} model \citep{zhang2019pegasus} with as few as 10 or 100 training examples. We assess our approach on a diverse set of six English headline generation and text summarization tasks in both zero-shot and few-shot settings and show that \textsc{Pegasus}{} trained with \textsc{genPet}{} significantly surpasses regular finetuning. In summary, our contributions are as follows: \begin{itemize}[topsep=0.5em] 	\setlength\itemsep{-0.1em} 	\item We introduce \textsc{genPet}{}, a finetuning procedure for generative language models that achieves excellent data efficiency by utilizing both textual instructions and training examples. 	\item We demonstrate that training \textsc{Pegasus}{} with \textsc{genPet}{} surpasses standard finetuning across a wide range of tasks and training set sizes. 	\item We analyze the factors contributing to \textsc{genPet}{}'s strong performance and quantify the impact of all its components. \end{itemize}

text: News curation involves the intricate task of selecting and prioritizing information based on certain relevance criteria, while considering constraints of time and space. Traditionally managed by editorial teams at newspapers and other media outlets, this curation is increasingly executed by machine learning (ML) systems that assess content relevance~\cite{allcott2017social,eslami_i_2015}. Consequently, complex and opaque ML systems now influence the news consumption of billions of users. A Pew Research Center study revealed that approximately half of U.S. adults using Facebook (53\%) believe they do not understand why specific posts appear in their news feeds~\cite{pew_facebook_feed_2019}. This prompts us to investigate how users perceive news recommendations and whether they can differentiate between trustworthy and untrustworthy ML recommendations. We also explore whether untrustworthy news stories, such as fake news, gain credibility in a trustworthy context, for example, when an ML system predicts five stories, where four are credible news stories and one is a fake news story. We define fake news as "fabricated information that imitates news media content in form but not in organizational process or intent"~\cite{lazer2018science}. Examining trust and fake news within the framework of algorithmic news curation is crucial, as such algorithms are integral to social media platforms like Facebook, which serve as primary channels for fake news dissemination~\cite{allcott2017social}. Research into trust in news and the tendency of individuals to believe rumors has a long-standing history~\cite{allport1947psychology,allport1945wartime}. Our focus is on trust in a news recommender system, which relates to the work of O'Donovan et al. and Massa and Bhattacharjee \cite{massa2004using,o2005trust}. Unlike their focus on trust in individual items, we concentrate on trust in the ML system and its recommendations. The study's design reflects how users engage with machine learning systems. Participants evaluate their trust in the recommendations of a machine learning system, specifically rating groups of news stories. Participants were informed that they were interacting with an ML system, meaning they were not merely rating the content. We emphasize trust because falling for fake news is not merely an error. Fake news is crafted to deceive by imitating news media content. Our setting aligns with human-in-the-loop and active machine learning, where users engage with a live system that they enhance through their actions \cite{rubens2015active,amershi2014power,Kulesza:2015:PED:2678025.2701399}. In such settings, improving a news curation algorithm by rating individual items would demand significant time and effort from users. Therefore, we explore explicitly rating ML recommendations as a whole to gather feedback. Examining how ML systems and their recommendations are perceived by users is crucial for those implementing algorithmic news curation and those aiming to enable users to identify algorithmic bias in practice. This is pertinent for all human-computer interaction designers who wish to facilitate user interaction with machine learning systems. This investigation is also relevant for ML practitioners seeking user feedback on their systems' quality or those aiming to crowdsource training data collection for their machine learning models \cite{Gulla:2017:ADN:3106426.3109436,ozgobek,Russakovsky2015}. In our experiment, participants engaged with a basic algorithmic news curation system that provided them with news recommendations akin to a collaborative filtering system~\cite{Resnick:1994:GOA:192844.192905,herlocker2000explaining}. We conducted a between-subjects study with two phases. Our participants were recruited from a vocational school. They all possessed a technical background and were briefed on the types of errors that ML systems might make unexpectedly. In the first phase, participants rated their trust in various news stories. This produced a pool of news stories with trust ratings from our participants. Participants rated different subsets of news stories, meaning each story in our study was rated by some users while others did not see it. In the second phase, the algorithmic news curation system combined unseen news stories for each user based on the median trust rating of each story. This implies that a story's trust rating is based on the intersubjective agreement of the participants who rated it in the first phase. This allowed us to examine how trust in individual stories affects trust in groups of news stories predicted by an ML system. We vary the number of trustworthy and untrustworthy news stories in the recommendations to study their impact on trust ratings using an 11-point scale. Our primary objective is to understand the trust ratings of ML output as a function of the trust in individual news items for a machine learning system. In summary, this paper addresses the following three research questions: \begin{itemize} \item Can users provide trust ratings for news recommendations of a machine learning system~(RQ1)? \item Do users distinguish trustworthy ML recommendations from untrustworthy ML recommendations~(RQ2)? \item Do users distinguish trustworthy ML recommendations from recommendations that include one individual untrustworthy news story~(RQ3)? \end{itemize} We discovered that users are capable of providing nuanced ratings of machine learning recommendations. In their trust ratings, they differentiate between trustworthy and untrustworthy ML recommendations, provided all stories in the output are either trustworthy or untrustworthy. However, participants are unable to distinguish trustworthy news recommendations from those that include one fake news story, even though they can differentiate other ML recommendations from trustworthy ones.

text: Statistical power is defined as the probability of rejecting a null hypothesis. Therefore, it is essential in detecting an effect of interest in any study. Traditionally, the most straightforward and effective method to enhance power is to increase the study's sample size, as it has the most significant impact on what the researcher can control \cite{cohen1992things}. However, practical considerations arise when increasing the sample size. In studies of rare diseases, the total population may be small, difficult to locate, and even more challenging to engage, such as in early- and late-stage neuro-genetic syndromes \cite{button2013power, szucs2017empirical}. Additionally, there may be access or funding constraints when attempting to increase the number of participants a researcher aims to recruit. In this article, we empirically demonstrate that adjusting the model parameters (\emph{i.e.}, weights) can significantly alter the study's power. Consequently, modifying model parameters can transform the study from moderately powered to well-powered research, even with a constant sample size. For the remainder of the article, we define well-powered research as having a power greater than \textit{0.8}. Fig.~\ref{fig:model-param-power} illustrates that even with a fixed sample size, power can vary considerably due to changes in model parameters. In Fig.~\ref{fig:power-grad}, we calculate power \textit{gradients} by examining the directional difference between clusters derived by KMeans, where the power and the squared L2-norm of the model parameters serve as the point coordinates. Thus, constructing such a manifold, as depicted in Fig.~\ref{fig:power-grad}, can greatly assist researchers in identifying regions of high power. Providing access to these plots is therefore a straightforward method of reducing the \textit{ideal} sample size without compromising power. However, as outlined in Algorithm~\ref{algo:power}, computing power even once necessitates \textit{200-1000} simulations. Moreover, the manifold parameter space, which includes model weights, sample size, and additional hyperparameter options, is vast. For example, for a model with seven predictors, with 11 options per predictor and 11 choices for $N$, the parameter space is $11^{7 + 1}$. Computation for this extensive space could potentially take days. Thus, in this work, we explore \textit{more economical} alternatives to simulating the entire power manifold. We present three distinct contributions: \begin{itemize} \item We develop a neural network-based method to predict power over a high-dimensional manifold for both classification and regression tasks. This approach achieves significant performance with only 10\% of the training data. \item We introduce four baselines for alternatively predicting power and evaluate all our methods on three models: regression, logistic, and Repeated Measures ANOVA. \item To utilize the transfer of knowledge from one model's power manifold to another, we first illustrate the intuition behind such a transfer. Subsequently, we demonstrate that such a transfer can achieve the same or improved results in every instance. We organize the remainder of the article as follows. We first review the relevant literature and outline the background information necessary to develop our algorithm. We provide pseudocodes for the core and auxiliary algorithms in this section. Next, we present our empirical results, highlight the major successes, and discuss the limitations. Finally, we also suggest potential future research directions. \end{itemize}

text: Simultaneous Localization And Mapping (SLAM) techniques generate navigational maps that allow robots to autonomously explore an environment, while emerging Semantic Mapping techniques incorporate semantic information about locations and objects within the environment. Semantic mapping allows robots to navigate based on the semantics of a location rather than merely geometric poses, thereby enabling the robot to reason about locations using automated planning or semantic interpretations of natural language commands \cite{thomason2020jointly}. Semantic maps are particularly advantageous for consumer-oriented robotic applications, such as assisting visitors in navigating an unfamiliar building \cite{Yedidsion_multi_robot} or retrieving objects \cite{Jiang_Walker_Hart_Stone_2019}. Manually labeling map semantics can be laborious or impractical for extensive maps. This study concentrates on the autonomous semantic labeling of a mapped environment. Buildings frequently contain signage that annotates important semantics for the benefit of human occupants, such as placards indicating office numbers. Previous research employed handcrafted detectors to identify door placards, register their location on a map, and transcribe their labels~\cite{Hart}~\cite{Case}. These methods necessitate either constructing a map before scanning for placards or having a human guide the robot during the scanning process. A contribution of this work is the simultaneous exploration of a new environment and registration of placards without human intervention through an enhanced Frontier Exploration algorithm, termed Interruptable Frontier Exploration (IFE). Interruptable Frontier Exploration allows the robot to explore its environment while an object detector searches for door placards. This process is termed \emph{passive observation}. Upon detecting a sign, the exploration is paused, and the robot conducts an \emph{active observation}, wherein it moves to an optimal position to segment, transcribe, and register the sign's location on the robot's map. To demonstrate IFE's performance, we compare it against a method that calculates a robot motion trajectory to scan for placards along previously discovered wall sections~\cite{Case}. We refer to this procedure as Wall-Scanning Discovery (WD). IFE requires significantly less time than WD by conducting fewer active scans and not needing a complete map before scanning for placards.

text: Recommender systems are essential in the rapidly evolving Internet era, aiming to predict the items users are most likely to find interesting. Collaborative filtering is an effective and widely adopted method in recommendation, dedicated to capturing latent user and item features from historical interactions. Early studies such as Matrix Factorization (MF)~\cite{koren2009matrix} decompose a rating matrix into user and item embeddings to capture implicit semantics. As the number of users and items has grown rapidly in recent years, more deep learning models have been proposed based on collaborative filtering to characterize diverse user preferences across a large number of items. For instance, ~\cite{berg2017graph} and~\cite{wang2019neural} construct user-item graphs to incorporate the multi-hop relationships of interactions. ~\cite{liang2018variational} and~\cite{li2017collaborative} introduce a variational auto-encoder framework into the model to infer the representation as a Gaussian distribution. 	 	Sequential recommendation is a significant component of recommender systems. It models user behaviors as a sequence of items rather than a set of items. Markov Chain (MC)~\cite{cheng2013you} is a classic method that models short-term item transitions and predicts the next item a user might prefer. Factorized personalized Markov chain (FPMC)~\cite{rendle2010factorizing} combines the Markov chain with traditional matrix factorization to model user preferences. With the advancement of deep learning networks, Recurrent Neural Networks (RNNs) have achieved success in sequential recommendation. For instance, Long Short-Term Memory (LSTM)~\cite{zhu2017next} is a common RNN variant that enhances the model’s ability to maintain sequential information through memory cells. GRU4Rec~\cite{chen2018sequential} applies Gated Recurrent Units (GRU) to session-based recommendation by introducing session-parallel mini-batches. RNN-based methods encounter the challenge of maintaining long-range information. Recently, self-attention networks have been applied to sequential recommendations to capture both long-term and short-term dependencies. SASRec and BERT4Rec achieve good prediction results using attention mechanisms. SASRec~\cite{kang2018self} can capture long-term dependencies by considering the influential weights of an entire historical sequence. BERT4Rec~\cite{sun2019bert4rec} employs a deep bidirectional self-attention network with Cloze tasks to enhance the efficiency of a transformer model. 	 	These prior works model user intentions with historical sequential interactions, overlooking dynamic underlying relationships between items. The edges linking pairwise items contain abundant semantic information about why and how users select one item after another. These underlying factors relate to real-world concepts, with one particular factor often playing a dominant role in a single situation. For example, consider two users interacting with six items, as shown in Figure~\ref{intro}. The link graph indicates that item 2 is adjacent to all the other five items. However, these edges are intuitively motivated by different factors. Item 2 is linked to items 1 and 4 because they share the same color, while it is linked to 5 and 6 because they have short sleeves. Item 3 is connected to item 2 because it can be used as a T-shirt jacket. These different factors illustrate the intention transformation of user behaviors and reveal the shared features of pairwise items. Therefore, recognizing and distinguishing the underlying item-link factors can enhance the expressive capacity of models, and disentangled representation learning~\cite{locatello2019challenging} is a common method proposed to achieve this goal. 	 	Disentangled representation learning has gained significant popularity in various fields such as Computer Vision~\cite{hsieh2018learning, mu2021disentangled}, and it has been applied to recommender systems recently. The general aim of disentangled representation learning is to separate distinct and informative factors from the variations in data, where each unit corresponds to a single concept in the real world. A single change in one factor will lead to a change in the relevant unit. Many models have demonstrated the ability to learn disentangled representations and have been applied to fulfill practical tasks. For example, by learning a disentangled representation of a face image, we can obtain independent representations of different facial features. We can then identify whether a person in a picture has bangs, is wearing glasses, is smiling, and so on. Furthermore, we can modify these features directionally by altering the values of the corresponding dimensions of these features. Therefore, learning disentangled representations can enhance the interpretability and controllability of models. 	 	The most prominent networks for learning disentangled representations are $\beta$-VAE and InfoGAN. $\beta$-VAE~\cite{higgins2016beta} introduces a coefficient hyperparameter $\beta$ to the KL-divergence term in the objective of a variational auto-encoder to encourage more factorized latent representations. This additional hyperparameter exerts significant pressure on the posterior distribution to match the factorized prior distribution~\cite{burgess2018understanding}. InfoGAN~\cite{chen2016infogan} maximizes the mutual information between a fixed small subset of the GAN’s noise variables and observations. In the context of recommender systems, Macrid-VAE~\cite{ma2019learning} infers high-level concepts of user intentions at the macro level and applies VAE to enhance disentanglement at the micro level. The authors also propose a self-supervised seq2seq training strategy for sequential recommendation~\cite{ma2020disentangled}, which compares user intentions between sub-sequences generated by an intention-disentangled encoder. DGCF~\cite{wang2020disentangled} devises intent-aware interaction graphs to distinguish user intentions over different items, focusing on user-item relationships. However, these studies do not consider item-link relationship patterns and fail to distinguish different user intentions behind sequences. Consequently, the sequential model becomes sensitive to noisy data and is difficult to interpret. 	 	In this paper, we propose an \textbf{E}dge-Enhanced \textbf{G}lobal \textbf{D}isentangled \textbf{G}raph \textbf{N}eural \textbf{N}etwork (EGD-GNN) model to capture item-link information. We model item representations and user intentions from both global and local levels. At the global level, we construct a global item-link graph over all sequences, with each item-pair in the sequences represented as an edge in the graph. Figure~\ref{intro} illustrates an example of constructing a global graph over two sequences. We employ the channel-aware mechanism to decompose edges into several channels, where each channel corresponds to an influential factor. The channels extract features specific to one of the disentangled factors from the neighbors and jointly aggregate different factors to the target item. At the local level, we model disentangled user-intention representation over the current sequence. We first infer the latent variation as a Gaussian distribution to enforce disentanglement from the statistical perspective of a variational auto-encoder. Then we use the channel-aware mechanism and aggregate item information through the edge channels from former items in the sequence. The aggregated item representation is used to express the current user intention. We conduct experiments based on our proposed method on three real-world datasets and compare the prediction results with state-of-the-art baselines. Results show that the EGD-GNN model not only outperforms previous works in prediction tasks but also compels the system to find good disentangled representations. text: \IEEEPARstart{W}{ith} the growing complexity of Information Technology (IT) operational environments, organizations have developed a need to maintain robust IT systems while simultaneously reducing operational costs, ticket volume, and enhancing customer satisfaction. IT operations are managed through an Incident, Problem, and Change (IPC) ticketing system, where an issue is recorded as an IT Service Desk ticket~\cite{Jan2015}. In this paper, these challenges are addressed by leveraging both structured and unstructured ticket information provided by the Service Desk (SD). Cognitive computing provides a means to transform and expand IT Services Delivery by removing the necessity for repeated training of service delivery skills. The system's learning capability serves as a key differentiator, enabling cognitive solutions to continuously improve through ongoing interactions and adapt to evolving needs. Moreover, service quality can be enhanced by preventing errors of omission and achieving faster problem resolution through automated understanding and reasoning of the most valid solutions. Although the human element is significantly reduced in effort, it will continue to play a crucial supervisory role to ensure seamless user interaction. Overall, cognitive computing transformation offers an unparalleled client experience and business competitiveness with operational efficiency and agility that have not been achievable until now. The SD receives tickets automatically generated by various device monitoring systems, and SD agents also manually create tickets in response to user requests. Currently, several analytical tools in the marketplace provide reports based solely on the structured data attributes of historical ticket records. Some of these tools have query capabilities to also identify the most frequently occurring keywords or specified patterns in the unstructured attributes of the tickets. These reports are then analyzed by specialized IT professionals to address the most predominant topics identified. While these tools offer benefits, they have limitations such as processing large data volumes, inability to uncover obvious and hidden issues, segregate noise from text, and extract user sentiments related to key topics from Customer Satisfaction (CSat) surveys and social media data. Existing literature surveys estimate that 80\% of information resides in unstructured data \cite{Rosu2012}. The proposed approach offers a solution that addresses all the aforementioned limitations. A key differentiator of the proposed approach is its ability to extract meaning from fragmented sentences in the unstructured ticket descriptions. Typically, this unstructured text appears in multiple languages, which are detected using language identification and normalized into a common language, English, through machine translation techniques. Conversely, due to varying language proficiency levels among the globally sourced pool of agents, the grammar quality also varies. To establish a common baseline for analytics application, this solution first translates all non-English text into English using statistical translation models. The choice of a statistical model over a grammar-based one is necessitated by the grammar quality of the input text. The statistical translation model introduces an additional layer of complexity for a cognitive system. The system has enabled numerous clients to uncover patterns and trends for identifying contributing causes and prescribing precautions swiftly, using data from hundreds of thousands of SD tickets. Typically, such analyses would have taken SD support teams weeks or even months. Consequently, identifying contributing causes allows support teams to utilize log analytics for root cause analysis. Additionally, this enables the team to adopt a proactive approach to identifying opportunities to optimize IT operations and enhance client satisfaction by demonstrating the following outcomes: \begin{itemize} \item Identification of contributing causes and actionable precautions from problem descriptions and resolutions. \item Transparency to pervasive issues otherwise concealed within volumes of unstructured data in tickets across different categories. \item Identification of emerging problems, trends, and automated change point detection. \item Identification of patterns that enable IT support teams to leverage real-time machine and data analytics for rapid root cause identification. \item Identification of self-service and automation opportunities, transforming operations from reactive to proactive. \item Transparency to pervasive issues otherwise hidden within volumes of unstructured text not captured in ticket categories. \item Sentiment analysis of CSat survey comments to identify potential future dissatisfiers. \item Correlation of social media and CSat sentiments with IT and application issues to enhance client experience. \item Predictive analytics for improving resolution times by re-prioritizing and routing tickets. \item Identification of skills and knowledge gaps derived from analyzing first-time resolution of failures, resolution times, and agent performance differences. \end{itemize} The paper is organized as follows. Section \ref{sec:Methodology} provides an overview of the cognitive computing platform components and the methodology of the overall system. Section \ref{sec:Algorithms} outlines the key algorithms developed for this system. Section \ref{sec:Applications} describes various applications and use cases, while the results of various experiments are presented in Section \ref{sec:Results}. The paper concludes in Section \ref{sec:Conclusion}.

text: Recommender systems assist users in easily locating their preferred items from a vast array of candidates. Typically, recommender models, such as collaborative filtering~\cite{koren2009matrix} and DeepFM~\cite{10.5555/3172077.3172127}, utilize users' historical behaviors to infer their preferences for future recommendations. Recommender systems that rely solely on exploitation models often experience closed-loop effects~\cite{jadidinejad2020using}: users predominantly interact with items recommended by the system, which further reinforces users' profiles with the items they engage with as suggested by the deployed model. Consequently, over time, the system becomes biased toward a narrow set of interests for each user, continually recommending a limited range of items to the same user. Contextual multi-armed bandit algorithms, such as LinUCB~\cite{li2010contextual}, are traditional methods that use side information to achieve a balance between exploration and exploitation, thereby mitigating the closed-loop effect. Items are considered as arms, and the recommender model acts as an agent. Essentially, in each round, the agent selects one arm with the highest potential from $K$ arm candidates and then receives a reward based on user-item interaction. The objective is to maximize the cumulative reward over $T$ rounds. However, these algorithms assume that $K$ is small, making it feasible to enumerate all arm candidates' scores and select the best one. This assumption holds true for certain scenarios where the candidates are naturally limited, such as homepage breaking news ranking, ads creative ranking, and online model selection. In the context of general recommender systems, to fully explore users' potential interests and genuinely alleviate the closed-loop effect, the arm candidates encompass the entire item repository, which typically contains millions or even billions of items. Classical bandit methods become impractical due to the high computational cost of evaluating each arm. To address this challenge, we initially propose a generic hierarchical contextual bandit~ (\textbf{HCB}) algorithm to efficiently explore users' interests in large-scale recommendation scenarios. Tree structures are commonly used to partition the search space to reduce computational costs~\cite{jain2016extreme,prabhu2014fastxml,zhu2018learning,zhuo2020learning}. {HCB} employs a tree structure as the index for coarse-to-fine retrieval. For instance, in an e-commerce scenario, \textsl{``Apparel > Clothing > Women's Clothing > Dresses''} represents a path from general apparel to women's dresses. Instead of utilizing the category taxonomy of items, we apply a bottom-up clustering method on item embeddings to organize items into a hierarchy tree, where each node contains a group of semantically similar items. Consequently, the number of items associated with each node on the hierarchy tree can be balanced, and users' collaborative behaviors (such as co-click relations) can be encoded to form the hierarchy tree. {HCB} leverages the hierarchical information and transforms the interest exploration problem into a series of decision-making problems. Starting from the root of the tree, at each non-leaf node, {HCB} executes a bandit algorithm among the child arms to select a child node until a leaf node is reached. Subsequently, another bandit algorithm is responsible for recommending an item from the leaf node to the user and collecting her feedback as a reward. The reward is back-propagated along the path to adjust the estimation of users' interest toward the hierarchy tree. The process of {HCB} resembles a depth-first search (DFS) approach. However, selecting a path in this DFS manner may introduce new uncertainties, particularly for a deep tree. Firstly, if the selection of the parent node is erroneous, all subsequent choices will be affected, which we term \textsl{error propagation}. Secondly, since user interests are typically diverse, it is possible that the user is interested in multiple child nodes located in different parts of the tree. Therefore, we further propose a progressive {HCB} (\textbf{pHCB}) algorithm to reduce uncertainties and enhance the recommendation capacity. Similar to the breadth-first search (BFS) process, {pHCB} explores items in an adaptive top-down manner. On one hand, it gradually maintains a limited number of nodes as a receptive field. If a node has been explored multiple times and the user's interest in this node has been confirmed, the node's child nodes will be added to the receptive field while the current node will be removed. On the other hand, {pHCB} learns user interests from different perspectives by executing a bandit algorithm with visible nodes in the receptive field as arms. Consequently, {pHCB} avoids greedily selecting only one node at each level, thereby improving {HCB}. To summarize, we make the following contributions: \squishlist \item We emphasize the importance of exploring users' interests across the entire item space to genuinely alleviate the closed-loop effect in personalized recommender systems. To our knowledge, this is the first attempt to implement CB models on millions of items. \item We propose two simple yet effective algorithms, namely {HCB} and {pHCB}, to efficiently explore users' potential interests through a hierarchical item tree. \item We conduct experiments on two large-scale recommendation datasets. The results demonstrate the superiority of {HCB} and {pHCB} over baseline methods, as well as their flexibility to integrate with various exploration methods such as LinUCB, Thompson Sampling, and $\epsilon$-greedy. Additionally, we design an experiment to verify that, thanks to the exploration mechanism, both {HCB} and {pHCB} can effectively mitigate the closed-loop effects in recommender systems and develop better user profiles in the long term. \squishend

Using the hierarchical information, HB transforms the interest exploration problem into a series of decision problems. Starting from the root of the tree, HB executes the multi-armed bandit algorithm on the non-leaf nodes to select the child nodes until the leaves. Then HB recommends the leaf node to the user and collects the reward. The process of HB is similar to a depth-first search. However, selecting a path in this DFS manner may lead to new uncertainties, especially for a deep tree. The reward is back-propagated along the path to adjust the estimation of the user's interest towards the tree. This paper introduces a hybridized hierarchical clustering (pHCB) algorithm to reduce the uncertainty and improve the recommendation capacity. The first is that if the parent node is incorrect, all nodes in the tree are affected, which we call "error propagation." The second is that the users' interests are generally diverse, so that the users are interested in many child nodes located at different depths of the tree. Like the breadth-first search (BFS) process, pHCB explores items in an adaptive top-down manner. On the one hand, it gradually keeps a limited number of nodes in its receptive field. If a node has been explored several times and the interest of the user has been confirmed, the child nodes of that node are added to the receptive field, while the node itself is removed. In summary, we make the following contributions: We emphasize the importance of exploring the entire item space to truly reduce the closed-loop effect in a personal recommender system. On the other hand, pHCB learns the interests of the user from various perspectives by executing the bandit learning method with visible nodes as arms, thus avoiding the greedy selection of one node at each level and improving the HCB. This is the first time to implement the CB model on millions of items. We also conduct experiments on two large-scale recommendation datasets. In addition, we design experiments to verify that, thanks to the exploration mechanism, both HCB and pHCB can effectively mitigate the closed-loop effects in recommender systems and develop better user profiles in the long run. The results demonstrate the superiority of HCB and pHCB over the reference methods and their flexibility to integrate with various exploration methods such as LinUCB, Thompson Sampling, and -greedy.

text: In this paper, we examine an evolutionary robotic system where both robot morphologies (bodies) and controllers (brains) evolve concurrently. Reproduction in this system necessitates the creation and assembly of a new body and brain to form the robot offspring. In the case of asexual reproduction, a single parent suffices, and the new body and brain are generated through random variation (mutation). For sexual reproduction (crossover), the bodies and brains of the parents must be recombined, resulting in an offspring composed of the resultant body, driven by the resultant brain. Regardless of the specific reproduction method, it generally cannot be assumed that the newly created body and brain will be well-matched. Although the parents may have well-matched bodies and brains, recombination and mutation are stochastic processes that can rearrange the parental genomes such that the resulting body and brain do not form a compatible combination. Consequently, the joint evolution of morphologies and controllers inherently presents a potential body-brain mismatch. This issue was initially identified by \citep{Eiben2013} and was recently revisited in \citep{Eiben2020}. The proposed solution involves the incorporation of learning. In the context of the robotic life cycle, this involves extending the straightforward two stages: the Morphogenesis Stage before 'birth' (when the robotic phenotype is constructed according to the genotype instructions) and the Operational Stage after 'birth' (when the robot performs its task(s) and attempts to reproduce). The third stage is the so-called Infancy Stage, which follows Morphogenesis, during which the 'newborn' robot learns to optimize the control of the inherited body and realizes its maximum potential. The term Infancy is not merely metaphorical; it also signifies an important detail: during this stage, the robot is not fertile, meaning it is not eligible for reproduction. Algorithmically, this implies that the fitness of a new robot is only assessed after the Infancy period, allowing the robot to undergo the (fitness-based) mate selection process only after learning is complete. This three-stage system architecture, termed The Triangle of Life, was described in 2013, but there are currently very few studies on the functioning of such systems. One reason is that there are generally few papers on the joint evolution of morphology and controller, as most work in evolutionary robotics focuses on the evolution of brains within a fixed body. Additionally, the computational costs can be prohibitive or at least discouraging. To illustrate the severity of this issue, note that the infant learning process is essentially a generate-and-test search process through the space of all possible controller configurations. Such a search algorithm must generate several new brains and test them all within the given body. This results in several additional fitness evaluations\footnote{For simplicity, we refer to all tests as fitness evaluations here.} for each newborn robot. Providing newborn robots with a learning budget of $N$ new controllers to be generated and tested during the Infancy stage implies that the total number of fitness evaluations will be $N$ times higher than evolving without learning. Of course, an appropriate value for $N$ depends on the system and the application at hand, but a few hundred or a few thousand learning trials are common in the literature. The primary objective of this research is to explore the effects of learning in morphologically evolving robots. To this end, we establish a system where (simulated) modular robots can reproduce and create offspring that inherit the parents’ morphologies and controllers. Thus, in our system, both bodies and brains are inheritable and therefore evolvable. Additionally, we make the brains not only evolvable but also learnable. We accomplish this by implementing a generic learning algorithm to optimize the inherited brain on any possible robot body. This system will be evaluated by assigning it a problem to solve: developing robots for the task of targeted locomotion. This task will be interfaced with the evolutionary system through an appropriate fitness function that quantifies a robot's ability to move towards a pre-specified target. Applying mate selection and survivor selection mechanisms based on this notion of fitness will drive evolution towards robots whose body and brain are well-suited for the given task. To investigate the effects of learning, we will conduct the robot evolution process in two versions: one purely evolutionary and one combining evolution and learning. In the first version, the brain of a robot child is inherited from its parents, and its fitness is determined directly after 'birth'. In the second version, the inherited brain of a robot child serves as the starting point for a learning algorithm, and the robot's fitness will be based on its performance using the learned brain. Based on these experiments, we address the issues of efficacy, efficiency, and the evolved morphologies. Regarding efficacy and efficiency, the main question is how the two algorithm variants compare in terms of the highest achieved performance and the time required to achieve the best performance. Our underlying hypothesis is that in a real-world application, learning provides a relatively fast and cost-effective means of reducing the number of slow and expensive evolutionary steps. Specifically, we can distinguish between learning trials and evolutionary trials. An evolutionary trial involves producing, activating, and testing a new robot, including the manufacturing of its body, while a learning trial entails producing, activating, and testing a new controller in a given robot. Since controllers are digital entities (i.e., lines of code), learning trials require significantly less time, effort, and material resources than evolutionary trials \citep{Eiben2021}. For example, if manufacturing a new robot takes 12 hours, computing and installing a new controller to be tested takes 10 seconds, and one fitness evaluation lasts one minute, then 1,000 evolutionary trials require approximately 501 days, while 1,000 learning trials cost less than one day. Our corresponding research questions are as follows. {\textbf{Research Question 1:}} How much 'savings' (in terms of evolutionary trials) can we achieve by incorporating infant learning as defined by the Triangle of Life architecture? The answer to this question will indicate whether it is preferable to allocate all allowable fitness evaluations to evolutionary trials (creation of a new robot with a new body and brain) or to divide them between evolutionary trials and learning trials (creation of a new brain in an existing body). Regarding the morphologies, we will consider quantifiable morphological traits, such as size and symmetry, and compare the trends during the evolutionary process as well as the morphologies in the final populations. {\textbf{Research Question 2:}} Will the inclusion of learning result in different evolved morphologies? Intuitively, one might expect no differences because learning is a process that only affects the brains, not the bodies. However, in the precursor to our current study, we recently found that incorporating learning can lead to different morphologies \citep{Miras2020}. Additionally, we investigate the evolution of {\it morphological intelligence}, defined by the learning potential of a given body. The idea is to withhold judgment about a newborn body and not assess it as-is immediately after birth with a semi-incidental controller, but to evaluate it as-it-can-be with a controller customized for that body through learning. Technically, we quantify morphological intelligence by what we call the {\it learning delta}, the performance difference between the inherited and the learned brain. Our definition and that of \citep{Gupta2021} are similar in spirit but differ in details. Specifically, \citep{Gupta2021} define morphological intelligence by the ability to learn novel tasks, whereas the notion based on \citep{Miras2020} relates it to the given task. {\textbf{Research Question 3:}} How does the morphological intelligence (measured by the learning delta) evolve over successive generations?

text: Document retrieval involves identifying relevant documents within a large collection to address specific queries. This task is significant in its own right and serves as a fundamental component in solving numerous natural language processing~(NLP) challenges, such as open domain question answering~\citep{chen2017reading} or fact-checking~\citep{thorne2018fever}. Traditionally, retrieval systems, or retrievers, utilize lexical similarities to align queries with documents, employing methods like TF-IDF or BM25 weighting~\citep{robertson2009probabilistic}. These methods, which rely on near-exact token matches between queries and documents, are hindered by the lexical gap and do not generalize effectively~\citep{berger2000bridging}. In contrast, neural network-based approaches enable learning beyond lexical similarities, achieving state-of-the-art results on question answering benchmarks, such as MS~MARCO~\citep{nguyen2016ms} or NaturalQuestions~\citep{kwiatkowski2019natural}. The impressive retrieval performance of neural networks has been feasible in domains and applications where extensive training datasets are accessible. For retrieval, constructing these datasets necessitates manually linking queries to relevant documents in the collection. This task becomes impractical when the collection comprises millions or billions of elements, leading to many situations where only a few in-domain examples, if any, are available. A potential solution is to train a dense retriever on a large retrieval dataset like MS~MARCO and then apply it to new domains, a scenario known as \emph{zero-shot}. Unfortunately, in this scenario, dense retrievers are frequently surpassed by classical methods based on term-frequency, which do not require supervision~\citep{thakur2021beir}. Furthermore, large annotated datasets are generally unavailable in languages other than English. Consequently, using extensive collections of supervised data is unsuitable for training multilingual retrieval systems. An intuitive alternative to transfer learning is unsupervised learning, prompting the question: \emph{is it feasible to train dense retrievers without supervision and achieve performance comparable to BM25?} Training dense retrievers without supervision can be accomplished by employing an auxiliary task that approximates retrieval. Given a document, one can generate a synthetic query and then train the network to retrieve the original document, among many others, given the query. The inverse Cloze task (ICT), introduced by \citet{lee2019latent} for pre-training retrievers, uses a specific sentence as a query and predicts the surrounding context. While this approach shows promising results as pre-training~\citep{chang2020pre,sachan2021endtoend}, it still falls short of BM25 when used as a zero-shot retriever. ICT is closely related to contrastive learning~\citep{wu2018unsupervised}, which has been extensively applied in computer vision~\citep{chen2020simple,he2020momentum}. Notably, computer vision models trained with the latest contrastive learning techniques have produced features well-suited for retrieval~\citep{caron2021emerging}. We thus propose to reassess how effectively contrastive learning can train dense retrievers without supervision. In this paper, we present the following contributions. First, we demonstrate that contrastive learning can produce strong unsupervised retrievers: our model achieves Recall@100 results that are competitive with BM25 on most of the BEIR benchmark. Second, in a few-shot setting, we show that our model benefits from a few training examples and achieves better results than transferring models from large datasets such as MS~MARCO. Third, when employed as a pre-training method before fine-tuning on MS~MARCO, our technique results in strong performance on the BEIR benchmark. We conduct ablations to justify our design choices and show that cropping outperforms the inverse Cloze task. Finally, we train a multilingual dense retriever using contrastive learning and demonstrate that it achieves state-of-the-art performance. Code and pre-trained models are accessible here: \url{https://github.com/facebookresearch/contriever}.

The task is important in itself, and forms a fundamental component of solving a number of natural language processing (NLP) tasks, such as open-domain question answering and fact-checking (p.chen et al., Reading, Reading, et al.). The solution is to use a dense search engine such as MARCO to search the new domains. However, the impressive performance of neural networks is only possible for those domains and applications where a large number of training data is available. On the other hand, neural networks can learn to learn beyond lexical similarity and have achieved state-of-the-art results in question answering competitions like MS-MARCO[Nguyen, 2016] and Natural Questions[Kwiatkowski, 2019]. Nevertheless, large annotated corpora are not available for languages other than English. This is impractical when the corpus consists of millions or billions of documents, and this leads to the situation where only a few examples of documents in the new domain are available, and this is what we call zero-shot learning. text: In recent years, there has been a significant increase in misinformation (along with related phenomena like disinformation and fake news), which can inflict substantial societal harm. Such adverse effects include, but are not limited to, influencing voting behavior in elections, healthcare decisions during pandemics, or stock market prices\footnote{e.g., the GameStop incident in 2021: \url{https://reut.rs/3ra7stz }}. The proliferation of misinformation has also led to extensive research, particularly in natural language processing (NLP), focused on the automatic fact-checking of claims \cite{fever,popat2018declare,multifc,hanselowski2019richly,wadden2020fact,xfact,covidfact}. Despite significant advancements, the task remains highly challenging. For instance, recent performance metrics on key datasets for natural claims show an F1 score of less than 50\%~\cite{Atanasova2020GeneratingFC,multifc,xfact}. Further examination of the data reveals that certain claims are significantly more difficult to fact-check than others, an issue that has not been extensively explored. {\bf Table~\ref{tab:taxonomy-examples}} presents several claims that were fact-checked by Politifact\footnote{\url{https://www.politifact.com}}. When comparing claims 3 and 5, claim 3 can be easily verified through a simple search that leads to a major media news article. Conversely, claim 5 lacks direct sources (i.e., written evidence, online or otherwise). Indeed, when historians were eventually consulted, they indicated that this claim remained uncertain. These examples demonstrate a wide range of difficulty levels in verifying different claims. In this study, we conduct an initial investigation into why certain claims are more challenging to fact-check than others, based on a manual analysis of claims from Politifact\footnote{\url{https://www.politifact.com/}} used in automated fact-checking datasets \cite{liar,liarplus,multifc}. This analysis allows us to identify five distinct factors contributing to claim difficulty: claim ambiguity, source support, source readability, source trustworthiness, and inference. Incorporating claim difficulty into fact-checking has implications for conceptual understanding, practical application, and research. Conceptually, although previous work has considered whether a claim is check-worthy \cite{checkthat2020,nakov2021clef}, a claim may be deemed check-worthy yet still be extremely difficult or impossible to fact-check. This has practical implications for fact-checking, where human resources are limited and must be strategically allocated, and for designing datasets for automated fact-checking, where including extremely difficult claims may not yield useful insights for comparing different algorithms. Furthermore, automated prediction of claim difficulty could assist fact-checking organizations in resource allocation, yet we are unaware of any research on this prediction task. While predicting claim difficulty appears to be a novel concept in the context of fact-checking, the importance of modeling and predicting the difficulty of different task instances is already acknowledged in other fields, such as machine translation \cite{Mishra2013AutomaticallyPS,Li2015DetectingCS}, syntactic parsing \cite{Garrette2013LearningAP}, or search engine switching behaviors \cite{white2009characterizing}, among others. From this perspective, we propose that instance difficulty prediction can provide similar benefits to fact-checking.
