text: Modern commercial buildings are intricate cyber-physical systems. They are increasingly outfitted with sensors and actuators, ranging from surveillance cameras and card readers for security and access control, to thermostats and air-quality sensors integrated into the Heating, Ventilation, and Air Conditioning (HVAC) system, which regulates the indoor environment while ensuring occupant comfort~\cite{Haggerty13,ardakanian2018}. These buildings represent significant financial investments, and their security management is even more critical than that of older buildings. Reasoning about and managing access to these buildings necessitate distinct access policies for various user types. For instance, as a standard practice, long-term building occupants such as employees who work in the building receive access privileges to their offices and shared spaces, based on their organizational roles; conversely, facilities-management personnel typically have access to more restricted areas where equipment is installed and to the Building Management System (BMS), which allows them to monitor and control equipment settings. Occupants may access sensing and control devices, such as light switches and thermostats, in the spaces to which they have physical access, even though these devices may affect building areas beyond the room in which they are physically located; for example, a thermostat in a room can determine the temperature setpoint of multiple adjacent rooms. Finally, visitors generally have limited access and are often required to be escorted by building occupants to the meeting rooms where their business occurs; they might control equipment in these rooms, but only for the duration of their meeting. In large commercial buildings, this approach entails substantial administrative overhead and exposes the building infrastructure to various security threats. Ideally, an automated solution is necessary to efficiently manage the access privileges of a building's occupants. Traditional role-based access-control models used in existing access control systems are cumbersome, as they require the specification of all roles and their relative authority, which is challenging in large buildings occupied by multiple organizations, each with its own distinct role hierarchy~\cite{Bindra19}. In this paper, we propose a methodology for managing building access control inspired by the concept of \emph{airline boarding passes} and the workflows surrounding them. At any given time, the airport is used by numerous airlines that manage their own flights at their respective gates and are responsible for issuing boarding passes to their passengers. Boarding passes become available shortly before passengers travel, enabling passengers to go through security, access their gate, and board their plane at the appropriate time. Each boarding pass is associated with an individual traveler and is valid only for a short period before the flight departure. During this period, security personnel can scan and verify the boarding pass. This methodology is intended to be implemented independently of any pre-existing access control delegation strategies, yet still coexist with already implemented access control systems. Our methodology can flexibly and securely manage building access privileges for long-term occupants and short-term visitors alike, addressing the challenges and risks mentioned above. We establish a set of services for {\em fine-grained} decentralized management of individuals' access privileges within a commercial building. We use the term fine-grained to mean (a) person-centric instead of role-based, (b) tailored to different space/system granularities, and (c) spanning multiple timescales. The underlying intuition for this work is that {\em if a person is authorized to have physical access to a particular location in a building, then they also have access and opportunity to manipulate the sensors and control points in this space.} This is because, in most cases, there is no additional access control beyond placing the equipment behind a locked door. Also, by implication, {\em if a person should not have access to some control points, they should not be authorized to access the space where this equipment is located.} Our methodology relies on blockchain smart contracts to describe, grant, audit, and revoke fine-grained permissions for building occupants and visitors in a decentralized manner~\cite{andersen2018democratizing}. The smart contracts are specified through a process that leverages information compiled from the BOT~\cite{Rasmussen17} and Brick~\cite{balaji2016brick} models of the building's spatial structure, equipment, and their relations. This information enables our methodology to grant an individual just the right access privileges to allow them to reach their destination within the building. We implement this intuition in the form of smart contracts, through which space-access privileges are granted to (and revoked from) individuals using an API that can be invoked by different software applications. The underlying \emph{access-control service} is responsible for accepting or rejecting individual access requests based on the currently valid smart contracts and their implications regarding access to sensors and actuators. We illustrate the proposed method through a typical use case in the context of a real building and argue that it can significantly reduce the administrative overhead while providing fine-grained, auditable access control. The rest of this paper is organized as follows. Section~\ref{sec:background} provides an overview of the context surrounding our work. Section~\ref{sec:method} describes in detail our methodology for smart-building access control using a graph model for reasoning and blockchain smart contracts for managing access. Section~\ref{sec:implement} examines the implementation of the proposed work along with use cases in which the proposed solution can greatly enhance the authorization and access control procedures in a real building. Section~\ref{sec:perform} evaluates the performance of the proposed solution in terms of throughput and delay. Section~\ref{sec:system} presents practical considerations for using blockchain-based access control. Section~\ref{sec:related} discusses related work on authorization and access-control solutions developed for the built environment. The paper concludes with an overview of the key contributions of our work and our plans for future work in Section~\ref{sec:conclusion}.

text: Few-shot learning, which aims to classify instances from unseen classes with only a few training examples, has experienced rapid progress in recent years. To swiftly adapt to novel classes, there has been significant emphasis on the meta-learning (or learning-to-learn) paradigm \cite{ren2018meta,snell2017prototypical,vinyals2016matching}. Meta-learning approaches have popularized the structuring of training data into {\em episodes}, thereby simulating the tasks that will be encountered during inference. Nonetheless, despite the improvements achieved, several recent image classification studies \cite{boudiaf2020transductive,chen2018closer,dhillon2019baseline,GuoECCV20-DS,tian2020rethinking,zikolaplacian} have noted that meta-learning may have limited generalization capacity beyond the standard 1- or 5-shot classification benchmarks. For example, in more realistic settings with domain shifts, simple classification baselines can outperform much more complex meta-learning methods \cite{chen2018closer,GuoECCV20-DS}. Deep-learning based semantic segmentation has generally benefited from methodological advances in image classification. Few-shot segmentation, which has recently gained popularity \cite{gairola2020simpropnet,wei2019fss,liu2020crnet,nguyen2019feature,rakelly2018conditional,pfenet,wangfew,wang2019panet,rpmm,yang2020new,zhang2019canet,zhang2020sg}, is no exception. In this context, a deep segmentation model is initially pre-trained on {\em base} classes. Then, model generalization is evaluated over few-shot {\em tasks} and novel classes not seen during base training. Each task includes an unlabeled test image, referred to as the {\em query}, along with a few labeled images (the {\em support} set). Recent literature in few-shot segmentation follows the learning-to-learn paradigm, with substantial research efforts focused on designing specialized architectures and episodic-training schemes for base training. However, i) episodic training itself implicitly assumes that testing tasks have a structure (e.g., the number of support shots) similar to the tasks used at the meta-training stage; and ii) base and novel classes are often assumed to be sampled from the same dataset. In practice, these assumptions may restrict the applicability of existing few-shot segmentation methods in realistic scenarios \cite{cao2019theoretical,chen2018closer}. Indeed, our experiments were consistent with findings in few-shot classification when extending beyond the standard settings and benchmarks. Specifically, we observed a saturation in performance among state-of-the-art methods \cite{cao2019theoretical} when increasing the number of labeled samples (See Table \ref{tab:n_shots_aggreg}). Additionally, in alignment with very recent observations in image classification \cite{chen2018closer}, existing meta-learning methods are less competitive in cross-domain scenarios (See Table \ref{tab:COCO2PASCAL_results_partial}). This raises questions about the viability of the current few-shot segmentation benchmarks and datasets, and motivates reconsidering the relevance of the meta-learning paradigm, which has become the \textit{de facto} choice in the few-shot segmentation literature. \subsection*{Contributions} In this work, we abandon meta-learning and reconsider a simple cross-entropy supervision during training on the base classes for feature extraction. Additionally, we propose a \textit{transductive} inference that better utilizes the support-set supervision than existing methods. Our contributions are summarized as follows: \begin{itemize} \item We introduce a new transductive inference--\textit{RePRI} (Region Proportion Regularized Inference)--for a given few-shot segmentation task. RePRI optimizes a loss integrating three complementary terms: \textit{i)} a standard cross-entropy on the labeled pixels of the support images; \textit{ii)} the entropy of the posteriors on the query pixels of the test image; and \textit{iii)} a global KL divergence regularizer based on the proportion of the predicted foreground pixels within the test image. RePRI can be applied on top of any trained feature extractor and uses exactly the same information as standard inductive methods for a given few-shot segmentation task. \item Although we employ a basic cross-entropy training on the base classes, without complex meta-learning schemes, RePRI achieves highly competitive performances on the standard few-shot segmentation benchmarks, PASCAL-5$^i$ and COCO-20$^i$, with gains of approximately $5\%$ and $6\%$ over the state-of-the-art in the 5- and 10-shot scenarios, respectively. \item We introduce a more realistic setting where, in addition to the usual shift on classes between training and testing data distributions, a shift in the images' feature distribution is also introduced. Our method achieves the best performances in this scenario. \item We demonstrate that precise region-proportion information on the query object substantially improves the results, with an average gain of 13\% on both datasets. While assuming the availability of such information is not realistic, we show that inexact estimates can still lead to significant improvements, opening a very promising direction for future research. \end{itemize}

text: Developing and evaluating recommenders to enhance business objectives are central concerns in e-commerce machine learning. A significant gap between the business and machine learning domains is that target metrics, such as gross merchandise value (GMV), are challenging to interpret as concrete learning objectives. Although several surrogate losses and evaluation metrics have demonstrated particular empirical success \cite{shani2011evaluating,herlocker2004evaluating}, online experimentation remains the primary method for assessing a candidate recommender's real-world performance. Specifically, there is widespread agreement on the various biases present in the collected historical data \cite{chen2020bias}, which can lead to the "feedback-loop effect" if empirical metrics are used without adjustment \cite{gilotte2018offline}. Recently, there has been a wave of innovations in refining online A/B testing and correcting offline evaluation methods \cite{yin2019identification,lee2018winner,xie2018false,gilotte2018offline}. However, these methods still fall short in certain applications where either the problem's complexity outweighs their potential benefits, or their assumptions are unmet. Since our work primarily discusses e-commerce recommendations, we assume an online shopping context throughout the paper. On the A/B testing side, there is a growing demand for interleaving the tested recommenders and targeted customers due to increasing interests in personalization \cite{schuth2015predicting}. The process of gathering sufficient observations and drawing inferences with adequate power is often slow and costly (in addition to the complexity of defining the buckets in advance), as the number of combinations can grow exponentially. Regarding recent advancements in offline A/B testing \cite{gilotte2018offline}, although some unbiasedness and optimality results have been theoretically demonstrated, real-world performance still relies on fundamental causal assumptions \cite{imbens2015causal}, such as unconfounding, overlapping, and identifiability, which are rarely satisfied in practice \cite{xu2020adversarial}. We emphasize that both online and offline testing play irreplaceable roles despite their limitations; however, the current challenges motivate us to explore more efficient solutions that can better utilize the randomized design of traffic. The production scenario motivating our work is selecting from several candidate recommenders that have shown comparable performances in offline evaluation. Through segment analysis, we find each recommender more favorable to specific customer groups, but definitive conclusions cannot be drawn due to exposure and selection bias in the historical data. In other words, while it is safe to launch each candidate online, randomized experiments are still needed to explore each candidate's real-world performance for different customer groups. We aim to design the experiment by considering customer features (e.g., their segmentation information) to minimize the cost of trying suboptimal recommenders on a customer group. Note that our goal diverges from traditional controlled experiments because we prioritize minimizing the cost over drawing rigorous inferences. Subsequently, we characterize our mission as a recommender-wise exploration-exploitation problem, a novel application to the best of our knowledge. Before proceeding, we illustrate the fundamental differences between our problem and learning the ensembles of recommenders \cite{jahrer2010combining}. Business metrics, such as GMV, are random variables that depend on the recommended content and the distributions governing customers' decision-making. Even if we have access to these distributions, we cannot know in advance the conditional distribution given the recommended content. Therefore, the problem cannot be accurately described by any fixed objective for learning the recommender ensembles. In our case, the exploration-exploitation strategy can be viewed as a sequential game between the developer and the customers. In each round $t=1,\ldots,n$, where the role of $n$ will be clarified later, the developer selects a recommender $a_t \in \{1,\ldots,k\}$ that generates the content $c_t$, e.g., top-k recommendations, according to the front-end request $r_t$, e.g., customer id, user features, page type, etc. Then the customer reveals the \textsl{reward} $y_t$, such as click or not-click. The problem setting resembles that of the \textsl{multi-armed bandits (MAB)} by considering each recommender as the \emph{action} (\emph{arm}). The front-end request $r_t$, along with the recommended content $c_t = a_t(x_t)$, can be considered the \emph{context}. Clearly, the context is informative of the reward because clicking depends on how well the content matches the request. On the other hand, a (randomized) experiment design can be characterized by a distribution $\pi$ over the candidate recommenders, i.e., $0 < \pi_t(a) < 1$, $\sum_{i=1}^k \pi_t(i)=1$ for $i=1,\ldots,n$. We note that a formal difference between our setting and classical \emph{contextual bandit} is that the context here depends on the candidate actions. Nevertheless, its impact becomes negligible if choosing the best set of contents is still equivalent to selecting the optimal action. Consequently, the goal of finding the optimal experimentation can be readily converted to optimizing $\pi_t$, which aligns with the bandit problems. The intuition is that by optimizing $\pi_t$, we refine the estimation of the structures between context and reward, e.g., via supervised learning, at a low exploration cost. The critical concern of conducting exploration in e-commerce, perhaps more concerning than in other domains, is that irrelevant recommendations can severely harm user experience and stickiness, which directly relates to GMV. Therefore, it is crucial to leverage problem-specific information, both the contextual structures and prior knowledge, to further design the randomized strategy for higher efficiency. We use the following toy example to illustrate our argument. \begin{example} Suppose there are six items in total, and the front-end request consists of a uni-variate user feature $r_t \in \mathbb{R}$. The reward mechanism is given by the linear model: \[ Y_t = \theta_1 \cdot I_1 \times X_t + \ldots + \theta_6 \cdot I_6 \times X_t; \] where $I_j$ is the indicator variable for whether item $j$ is recommended. Consider the top-3 recommendation from four candidate recommenders as follows (in the format of one-hot encoding): \\ \begin{equation} \begin{split} a_1(r_t) = [1, 1, 1, 0, 0, 0]; \\ a_2(r_t) = [0, 0, 0, 1, 1, 1]; \\ a_3(r_t) = [0, 0, 1, 0, 1, 1]; \\ a_4(r_t) = [0, 0, 0, 1, 1, 1]. \\ \end{split} \end{equation} If each recommender is explored with equal probability, the role of $a_1$ is underrated since it is the only recommender that provides information about $\theta_1$ and $\theta_2$. Also, $a_2$ and $a_4$ yield the same outputs, so their exploration probability should be halved. Similarly, the information provided by $S_3$ can be recovered by $S_1$ and $S_4$ (or $S_2$) combined, indicating a linear dependency structure we may leverage. \end{example} The example is representative of real-world scenarios, where the one-hot encodings and user features may simply be replaced by pre-trained embeddings. Thus far, we have provided an intuitive understanding of the benefits of well-designed online experiments. In Section \ref{sec:background}, we introduce the notations and the formal background of bandit problems. We then summarize the relevant literature in Section \ref{sec:related}. In Section \ref{sec:method}, we present our optimal design methods and describe the corresponding online infrastructure. Both the simulation studies and real-world deployment analysis are provided in Section \ref{sec:experiment}. We summarize the major contributions as follows. \begin{itemize} \item We propose a novel setting for online recommender selection through the lens of exploration-exploitation. \item We present an optimal experimental approach and describe the infrastructure and implementation. \item We provide both open-source simulation studies and real-world deployment results to demonstrate the efficiency of the approaches studied. \end{itemize}

text: Semantic Segmentation aims to perform dense prediction by labeling each pixel in an image according to the class it represents. Transformer-based vision networks \cite{vit,deit} have surpassed Convolutional Neural Networks in the image classification task \cite{imagenet}. Recently, transformer backbones have demonstrated remarkable performance when applied to downstream tasks such as semantic segmentation \cite{beit, fapn, swin-T}. Most architectural designs in vision transformers address the problem in one of two ways: (i) Utilize an existing pretrained backbone as an encoder and adapt it to downstream tasks using standard decoders like Semantic FPN \cite{sem-fpn} or UperNet \cite{upernet}; OR (ii) develop a new encoder-decoder network where the encoder is pretrained on ImageNet for semantic segmentation. Both approaches, as previously mentioned, involve finetuning the encoder backbone for the segmentation task. Finetuning on a large-scale dataset assists early attention layers in integrating local information at lower layers of the transformers \cite{vit-cnn}. However, it may still fail to capture the semantic context during finetuning due to the relatively smaller dataset size and a change in the number and nature of semantic classes from classification to segmentation. Hierarchical vision transformers \cite{segformer,swin-T} address the issue with progressive downsampling of features across stages, yet they still lack the semantic context of the image. Liu et al. \cite{swin-T} introduced the Swin Transformer, which builds hierarchical feature maps, making it suitable as a general-purpose backbone for major downstream vision tasks. \cite{twins} proposed using two types of attention: globally sub-sampled and locally sub-sampled, on top of PVT \cite{pvt} and CPVT \cite{cpvt} for effective segmentation. Xie et al. \cite{segformer} further refined the hierarchical transformer encoder by eliminating positional encoding, thus enhancing robustness to different resolutions typically encountered in segmentation tasks. These works modified the encoders to improve their performance for downstream tasks like segmentation and achieved notable success. However, they did not focus on capturing the semantic-level contextual information of the entire image. A deficiency in semantic contextual information results in sub-optimal segmentation performance, particularly for small objects that merge with the boundaries of larger categories, leading to incorrect predictions. Recently, \cite{segmenter} attempted to address this issue by designing a pure transformer-based decoder that jointly processes the patch and class embedding. Nonetheless, it does not perform effectively for small variants and fails with hierarchical architectures, resulting in sub-optimal performance when used with major transformer backbones like Swin \cite{swin-T} and Twins \cite{twins} transformers. Jin et al. in \cite{isnet} proposed ISNet to model image-level contextual information along with semantic-level contextual information by introducing the SLCM and ILCM modules in the decoder structure. However, there remains a limitation: ISNet is a CNN-based method and focuses solely on the decoder part of the network, leaving the encoder unchanged. To address the aforementioned issues, we propose the SeMask framework, which incorporates semantic information into hierarchical vision transformer architectures and enhances the global feature information captured by the transformers with semantic context. Existing frameworks design the architecture as an encoder-decoder structure with transformers pretrained on ImageNet \cite{imagenet} serving as the encoders and employing a specialized decoder for semantic segmentation. In contrast to directly using hierarchical transformers as a backbone, we insert a Semantic Layer after the Transformer Layer at each stage in the backbone, resulting in the SeMask version of the backbone as illustrated in \cref{fig:intro}. We employ a lightweight semantic decoder to accumulate the semantic maps from all stages, and a standard decoder like Semantic-FPN \cite{sem-fpn} for the main per-pixel prediction. The added semantic modeling alongside feature modeling throughout the encoder enhances the performance of the semantic segmentation task. In \cref{sec:experiments}, we integrate the proposed SeMask block into the Swin Transformer \cite{swin-T} and Mix Transformer \cite{segformer} backbones. Our experimental results demonstrate significant improvement in semantic segmentation for both backbones on two different datasets. To summarize, our contributions are threefold: \begin{itemize} \item To the best of our knowledge, we are the first to examine the effect of adding semantic context to pretrained transformer backbones for the semantic segmentation task. Furthermore, we introduce a SeMask Block that can be integrated into any existing hierarchical vision transformer. We provide empirical evidence by incorporating SeMask into Swin-transformer~\cite{swin-T} and Mix-Transformer~\cite{segformer}, achieving considerable performance improvement. \item We also propose using a simple semantic decoder for aggregating the semantic priors from different stages of the encoder. The semantic priors receive supervision from the ground truth using a per-pixel cross-entropy loss. \item Lastly, we provide an in-depth analysis of the SeMask Block's effect on two different datasets: ADE20K and Cityscapes. We achieve new state-of-the-art performance on the ADE20K dataset and an improvement exceeding $3\%$ on the Cityscapes dataset. \end{itemize}

text: Image captioning, which seeks to automatically describe the visual content of an unlabeled image with a sentence, is under active investigation~\cite{showandtell2015,bottomup2017,aoanet2019}. As a subfield, cross-lingual image captioning, which involves generating captions for a given image in a target language other than English, is garnering increasing interest in both the multimedia and computer vision domains~\cite{icmr16-ch-cap,WeiyuLan2017,Jiuxiang2018,2019Improving,2019Unpaired,gao2020unsupervised}. Earlier studies in this area focus on developing innovative algorithms that effectively train image captioning models for the target language using existing English datasets such as Flickr8k \cite{2015Framing}, Flickr30k \cite{2014From}, and MS-COCO \cite{mscoco2014}. For example, in \cite{icmr16-ch-cap}, Li \emph{et al.~} employ machine translation to automatically convert English captions of Flickr8k into Chinese and then train a Show-Tell model~\cite{showandtell2015} on the translated dataset. Noting that machine-translated sentences can sometimes be unreadable, Lan \emph{et al.~} \cite{WeiyuLan2017} introduce fluency-guided learning, where the significance of a training sentence is weighted by its fluency score as estimated by a deep language model. Song \emph{et al.~} \cite{2019Unpaired} enhance \cite{WeiyuLan2017} by incorporating self-supervised rewards concerning both fluency and visual relevance. Although this training process requires only a minimal (or even zero) amount of data in the target language, a comprehensive evaluation of the resulting models typically demands thousands of test images with manually written captions, known as \textit{references}, in the same language. Even with the aid of an interactive annotation system~\cite{icmr20-icap}, months of human labor are necessary to re-annotate a medium-sized test set for each target language. In this paper, we contribute to cross-lingual image captioning by introducing a novel approach to its evaluation. Specifically, we make a bold attempt to eliminate the necessity of references in the target languages. We propose three metrics that enable us to distinguish between models with good and poor performance when a test image is provided with just one reference in English. This requirement is valid, as prior work on cross-lingual image captioning is primarily conducted on established English datasets. Our main conclusions are two-fold: \begin{itemize} 	\item To our knowledge, this is the first study to evaluate image captioning models in a cross-lingual context without needing any reference in the target language. To achieve this, we propose three metrics, \emph{i.e.,~} WMDRel, CLinRel, and CMedRel, which evaluate the semantic relevance of auto-generated captions concerning the image content in various ways. 	\item We have conducted numerous experiments to assess the effectiveness of the three proposed metrics. Considering the different combinations of image captioning networks, \emph{i.e.,~} Show-Tell~\cite{showandtell2015}, Up-Down~\cite{bottomup2017}, and AoANet~\cite{aoanet2019}, and datasets, \emph{i.e.,~} COCO-CN~\cite{cococn2019} and VATEX~\cite{2019VATEX}, we construct a set of eight Chinese models for ranking. The combination of WMDRel, CLinRel, and CMedRel achieves a Spearman’s rank correlation of 0.952 with the sum of the four standard metrics, \emph{i.e.,~} BLEU-4, METEOR, ROUGE-L, and CIDEr. When no reference in the source language is provided, CMedRel alone has a Spearman correlation of 0.881 with CIDEr. \end{itemize}

text: In recent years, the medical imaging community has experienced a rapid surge in image processing methods based on Deep Learning (DL). These innovative techniques have demonstrated remarkable performance in numerous tasks, including Multiple Sclerosis (MS) lesion segmentation. Some automated algorithms have even achieved human-level performance under controlled evaluation conditions (see \cite{carass2017longitudinal}). Unlike the over-controlled conditions where most DL approaches have been validated, real-world data exhibit significant diversity. Consequently, the clinical application of MS lesion segmentation based on DL remains limited, primarily due to their inadequate generalization on new data from medical sites not included during training (unseen domains). This lack of generalization in DL methods can be attributed to several factors, such as the chosen solution during optimization, the diversity of the training dataset, or the generality of the extracted features. DL is founded on the assumption that training and test data are independent but originate from the same distribution. This assumption is often violated in medical imaging data, especially for Magnetic Resonance Imaging (MRI), where acquisition protocols, MRI scanners, patient populations, and software processing may vary depending on the clinical center or cohort. As a result of these data distribution differences (covariate shift), a performance decline is observed between the training data (source domain) and the test data derived from different distributions (target domain). This phenomenon is known as domain shift. An intuitive approach to mitigate this issue is to train on a broader and more heterogeneous dataset (as demonstrated by \cite{maartensson2020reliability}). However, this requires a large dataset annotated by experts, which is rarely available and laborious to produce. Some address this phenomenon by employing extensive data augmentation (such as \cite{zhang2020generalizing}). Others utilize a few available labeled images from the target domain to reduce the covariate shift, such as few-shot and one-shot learning strategies (see \cite{snell2017prototypical,valverde2019one}). Moreover, DL necessitates the tuning of a large number of parameters relative to the number of training data samples. Consequently, it typically converges to one of many possible local minima rather than the theoretical best parameter configuration that leads to the global minimum. Therefore, the model's generalization ability depends on the selected solution. The selection of the best generalizing local minimum remains an open question. On one hand, some studies have proposed selecting it using the local characteristics (\textit{e.g.}, flatness) of the loss function (see \cite{keskar2016large, wu2017towards}). On the other hand, an alternative strategy involves combining several local minima to enhance the method's generalization capability. This can be achieved by averaging several local minima of one model (\textit{e.g.}, snapshot ensemble \cite{huang2017snapshot}) or by combining outputs of different models trained independently (\textit{e.g.}, classical ensemble \cite{zhang2019multiple} and spatially distributed networks \cite{coupe2020assemblynet, huo20193d}). Unlike traditional methods that use handcrafted features, Convolutional Neural Networks (CNNs) automatically extract the most suitable set of features for a particular task. Although this strategy is highly efficient in extracting relevant features for a specific source domain, this set of features may not generalize well to the target domain. Some studies have proposed learning invariant features that are common across different source domains \cite{motiian2017unified,muandet2013domain,yang2013multi}. They attempted to apply regularization to learn an abstract representation of the specific computer vision task (\textit{i.e.}, similar to how humans understand high-level concepts). Indeed, the extraction of generalizing features lies between the freedom of the optimization process to find the optimal combination from data and the constraints used to minimize domain bias. The successful deployment of DL-based methods for MS lesion segmentation requires generalization capabilities that can ensure high performance for unseen domains. First, such methods should guarantee the convergence of the DL model to generalizing minima. Second, the training process should anticipate the reduction of the covariate shift. Moreover, the method should be enforced to learn MS lesion generalizing features from the source domain to effectively delineate lesions despite the target domain distribution. Finally, this solution should not require additional annotation when processing unseen domains. Recently, numerous studies have been proposed for MS lesion segmentation using CNNs.\\ First, \cite{brosch2016deep} proposed a deep 3D encoder-decoder network, with joint training of the encoder and the decoder. The authors used shortcut connections between the two interconnected pathways to integrate high and low-level features. This pioneering work demonstrated the high potential of deep learning for MS lesion segmentation.\\ \cite{valverde2017improving} proposed a cascade of two patch-wise 3D CNNs, consisting of a first sensitive network to reveal possible lesion candidates followed by a second network to reduce misclassified voxels. This cascade allows refined segmentation but uses a small receptive field that prevents capturing the global context. Later, the authors \cite{valverde2019one} improved their method by proposing a one-shot domain adaptation model that uses transfer learning and partial fine-tuning. However, this domain adaptation requires a labeled example from the new domain. Moreover, such strategies lead to different versions of the method after each adaptation, resulting in discrepancies in the segmentation. \\ \cite{hashemi2018asymmetric} addressed the problem of data imbalance (\textit{i.e.}, the under-sampling of the lesion class) by using an asymmetric similarity loss function based on the Tversky index to train a 3D CNN that performed better than Dice or cross-entropy measures. This result suggests that further work should be done on selecting an adequate loss function. Although the proposed loss can be tuned for the optimal trade-off between precision and recall in a particular domain, the generalization to unseen domains must be demonstrated.\\ \cite{zhang2019multiple} employed a fully convolutional densely connected network for MS lesion segmentation. They stacked adjacent 2D slices of different modalities with a channel-wise concatenation before forwarding this stack through a 2D CNN. The final segmentation is based on a majority vote along different orientations. While this method showed competitive performance in a well-controlled challenge, the stacking using only the two directly adjacent slices provides limited insight into the 3D nature of the data. Moreover, 2D features may not be considered as generalizing features when processing 3D volumes, which can result in limited generalization of the method.\\ \cite{aslani2019multi} proposed an end-to-end encoder-decoder 2D network with multiple downsampling branches, one for each input modality, and a decoder part where features from the different modalities are combined at multiple scales. This separation in encoder branches allows the model to encode information efficiently from each modality before combining them at a later stage. However, this 2D approach does not combine features based on axial, coronal, and sagittal orientations, which may significantly reduce its generalization on 3D images.\\ \cite{feng2019self} addressed MRI modality unavailability during segmentation by introducing sequence dropout. This is an important consideration since the availability of all modalities is not always guaranteed between datasets, which can greatly reduce the generalization capacity of a method. This framework randomly drops specific MRI sequences during training to learn the intrinsic information of each sequence. This technique demonstrated that it can produce acceptable segmentation even in the absence of one or two modalities. Nonetheless, it is less efficient than other state-of-the-art methods when all modalities are available (will be detailed in section \ref{same domain val}).\\ \cite{aslani2020scanner} addressed the problem of generalization to new domains by integrating a regularization network into the traditional encoder-decoder network. The regularizer penalizes the network when it learns features that allow the prediction of MRI scanning sites. However, \cite{li2018domain} have argued that such strategies suffer from overfitting, as the obtained representation may generalize well for all source domains but poorly for unknown target domains. All the cited MS methods (\cite{brosch2016deep,valverde2017improving,feng2019self,hashemi2018asymmetric,zhang2019multiple,aslani2019multi,feng2019self}) focused on obtaining accurate segmentation within the same domain evaluation. However, the use of out-of-domain datasets is essential to ensure a robust evaluation of a method's generalization capabilities. This issue is currently a hot topic (see \cite{maartensson2020reliability}, and \cite{bron2020cross}) and an important recommendation from the clinical world (see \cite{omoumi2021buy}). Experiments using training and testing images derived from the same domain are known to be biased [\cite{omoumi2021buy}] and do not ensure generalization. Therefore, a model used in clinical conditions should produce accurate segmentation for new domain images without the need for retraining with expert segmentation on the new domain. In this paper, we propose DeepLesionBrain (DLB), a novel method for MS lesion segmentation robust to domain shift, validated on out-of-domain testing (cross-dataset testing).\\ First, we utilize a large group of compact 3D CNNs spatially distributed over the brain with overlapping receptive fields between regions. By associating a distinct network with each region of the brain, the spatially distributed networks (see \cite{coupe2020assemblynet, huo20193d}) strategy simplifies the MS lesion segmentation from a single complex task on the whole brain to multiple simpler sub-tasks on each region. Moreover, the overlapping regions ensure consistent and stable consensus. Studies have highlighted that such a consensus-based strategy aids in the convergence towards generalizing minima (see \cite{breiman2001random,izmailov2018averaging,olson2018modern}). Moreover, applied to brain segmentation, this strategy demonstrated good generalization on unseen domains (\textit{e.g.}, child's brain or patients with Alzheimer's disease) when trained on healthy adult brains [\cite{coupe2020assemblynet}]. \\ Second, DLB is trained with a novel Image Quality Data Augmentation (IQDA) method, which mimics real-world data diversity by adding realistic alterations to the training images. As shown in the works of \cite{zhang2020does}, such a type of regularization technique aims to reduce covariate shift. IQDA proposes specific augmentations that constrain task learning to be independent of source data acquisition resolution, data contrast, or data quality. Consequently, the proposed augmentation strategy enables domain shift robustness. \\ Third, to ensure good feature generalization, we focus on the feature learning strategy. We consider that a generalizing model should learn two types of features: first, global and generic features, and second, local and specific features. Therefore, we propose Hierarchical Specialization Learning (HSL) to efficiently extract those features in two steps. In the first step, a single network (the generic network) is trained on all brain regions. In the second step, each network of the spatially distributed networks is initialized with the generic network weights and specialized for a specific region of the brain. \\ Finally, we propose a method using only two modalities (T1w and FLAIR) to ensure its compatibility with a large number of datasets. Most of the methods (\cite{feng2019self,brosch2016deep,valverde2017improving,zhang2019multiple}) optimize their segmentation using T1w, FLAIR, PD, and T2 modalities. However, in clinical conditions, not all these sequences are always available. Therefore, we focused our work on developing a robust approach using only two modalities.

text: Anomaly Detection (AD) in remote sensing data analysis has been and will remain a significant research topic for various applications~\cite{Stein02,Keshava04}. An anomaly decision is determined by analyzing the difference between the pixel under test (PUT) and the background. Numerous anomaly detectors have been proposed in the literature under several assumptions: 1) the selection of the background region and its distribution, 2) the method of calculating the distance between the PUT and the background statistics, and 3) the definition of the decision threshold or test statistic \cite{Matteoli2010}. Among the diverse range of AD methods, the Reed-Xiaoli (RX) is extensively used due to its simplicity, effective practical results, and efficiency in operational settings~\cite{Stein02,Keshava04}. The RX algorithm, which is arguably the most well-known AD method for hyperspectral images, is based on the assumption of a multivariate Gaussian distributed background and employs the Mahalanobis distance between the PUT and the background~\cite{Reed90tassp}. Regarding the background region, there are two primary approaches. In the global approach, the entire image is defined as the background, while in the local approach, pixels surrounding the PUT are defined as the background using a sliding window or a segmentation-based approach~\cite{Molero13jstars,Zhao15rs}. Additionally, potential anomalies can be censored to prevent degradation of the background statistics~\cite{Nar17dsp}. Although RX is computationally efficient and performs well for simple backgrounds (mostly linear), it cannot handle more complex, nonlinear, and/or non-Gaussian backgrounds. To address its limitations, more advanced techniques such as kernel methods can be employed to manage non-Gaussian distributed data~\cite{CampsValls09wiley,Kwon07,Longbotham14}. However, kernel RX is a computationally intensive method because it involves matrix inversion proportional to the sample count, e.g., for more than a thousand pixels. Conversely, the covariance matrix in RX has a fixed size proportional to the spectral dimension of the image, e.g., around ten for multispectral images and around a hundred for hyperspectral images. Since AD is typically the initial step in further recognition tasks, execution time is as important as, or even more critical than, detection accuracy \cite{Chen14taes}. Moreover, processor capacity (CPU or GPU), memory storage, and execution budget may be limited in operational applications \cite{Molero13jstars}. In \cite{Zhao16rs}, a fast recursive kernel RX method was recently introduced, which processes data in a causal manner. Although this method is rapid, threshold estimation for target decision is challenging because the detection result depends on the location of the PUT in the image. In this study, we propose an alternative approach to accelerate the kernel RX method while maintaining its accuracy: we suggest approximating the kernel function with random Fourier features~\cite{Rahimi07nips} to project data into a nonlinear feature space where a standard, cost-effective, and efficient linear RX method can be readily applied. Previous applications of the randomized approach in remote sensing have addressed classification and regression problems~\cite{Valero15igarss,Perez17rks}. The proposed randomized RX approach can significantly reduce execution time and memory storage compared to its kernel RX counterpart, while preserving nearly the same detection accuracy. We provide empirical evidence in both synthetic and real-world remote sensing target detection problems. The remainder of the paper is organized as follows. First, section \ref{sec:randomized_GRX} briefly reviews the proposed method used in this study. Then, section \ref{sec:experiments} presents the performance of the randomized RX method. Finally, we conclude in section \ref{sec:conclusion} with some remarks and prospective future work.

text: We introduce a Deep Interaction Prediction Network (\textsc{DIPN}\xspace) designed to learn object interactions from examples and utilize the trained network to accurately predict object poses following an arbitrary push action (Fig.~\ref{fig:intro}). To showcase its effectiveness, we integrate \textsc{DIPN}\xspace with a deep Grasp Network (\textsc{GN}\xspace) to tackle challenging clutter removal manipulation tasks. When given a choice between grasp and push actions, the goal is to clear all objects from the scene or workspace using the fewest possible actions. During each iteration of push/pick selection (Fig.~\ref{fig:system-architecture}), the system analyzes the scene and samples numerous candidate grasp and push actions. Grasps are immediately evaluated by \textsc{GN}\xspace, while for each candidate push action, \textsc{DIPN}\xspace produces an image representing the predicted result. Essentially, \textsc{DIPN}\xspace "imagines" the scene's outcome if the robot performs a specific push. The predicted future images are also evaluated by \textsc{GN}\xspace, and the action with the highest expected score, whether a push or a grasp, is executed. Our comprehensive evaluation indicates that \textsc{DIPN}\xspace can accurately predict object poses after a push action involving collisions, achieving less than $10\%$ average single object pose error in terms of IoU (Intersection-over-Union), which is a notable improvement over the compared baselines. Push predictions by \textsc{DIPN}\xspace produce clear synthetic images that \textsc{GN}\xspace can use to assess grasp actions in future states. Combined with \textsc{GN}\xspace, our complete pipeline achieves a $34\%$ higher completion rate, a $20.9\%$ higher grasp success rate, and a $30.4\%$ higher action efficiency compared to~\cite{zeng2018learning} in challenging clutter removal scenarios. Additionally, experiments indicate that \textsc{DIPN}\xspace can learn from randomly generated scenarios, with the learned policy maintaining high performance levels on challenging tasks involving previously unseen objects. Notably, \textsc{DIPN+GN}\xspace performs even better on real robotic hardware than in the simulation environment where it was developed.

text: Inertial navigation is an ongoing effort to estimate the states ({\it i.e.,} \; position and orientation) of a moving entity ({\it e.g.,}\; pedestrian) using only IMUs affixed to it. An IMU sensor, typically a combination of accelerometers and gyroscopes, is crucial in a wide array of applications from mobile devices to autonomous systems due to its excellent energy efficiency, portability, and adaptability \cite{lymberopoulos2015realistic}. However, traditional Newtonian-based inertial navigation methods not only exhibit poor performance but also impose unrealistic constraints that are unsuitable for everyday scenarios. For instance, strap-down inertial navigation systems (SINS) may yield incorrect sensor positions by performing double integration of IMU measurements, due to exponential error propagation through integration \cite{titterton2004strapdown}. Step-based pedestrian dead reckoning (PDR) methods can mitigate this accumulated error by utilizing prior knowledge of human walking patterns to predict trajectories \cite{tian2015enhanced}. Nevertheless, an IMU must be attached to a foot for the zero-velocity update \cite{foxlin2005pedestrian} or the subject must walk forward to maintain a constant motion direction in the body frame \cite{brajdic2013walk}. Additionally, inertial sensors are frequently combined with other sensors and models using the Extended Kalman Filter \cite{bloesch2015robust} to enhance estimation accuracy, where typical sensors include WiFi \cite{ahmetovic2016navcog}, Bluetooth \cite{li2017indoor}, LiDAR \cite{zhang2014loam}, or camera sensors \cite{leutenegger2015keyframe}. Nonetheless, these integrations with additional sensors introduce new challenges regarding instrument installation, energy efficiency, and data privacy. For example, Visual-Inertial Odometry (VIO) heavily relies on environmental factors such as lighting conditions, signal quality, and blurring effects \cite{usenko2016direct}. Recently, an increasing number of data-driven approaches such as IONet \cite{chen2018ionet}, RoNIN \cite{herath2020ronin}, and IDOL \cite{sun2021idol} have shown their ability to use well-trained neural networks to derive accurate estimates from IMU measurements, achieving competitive performance compared to the aforementioned methods. However, significant challenges persist when applying neural network techniques to IMU measurements: 1) most existing data-driven methods utilize sequence-based models ({\it e.g.,}\; LSTM \cite{LSTM}) to learn temporal correlations but fail to capture spatial relationships between multivariate time-series. 2) There is limited research exploring rich {\it contextual} information among IMU measurements in spatial and temporal dimensions for inertial feature representation. 3) Typically, uncertainties of IMU measurements and model outputs are assumed to be a fixed covariance matrix in these purely black-box neural inertial models, which leads to significant inaccuracies and reduced robustness as they can vary dramatically and unexpectedly in nature. In response to the aforementioned observations and concerns, a novel robust contextual Transformer network is proposed to regress velocity and predict trajectory from IMU measurements. Specifically, CTIN extends the concepts of ResNet-18 \cite{he2016deep} and Transformer \cite{vaswani2017attention} to exploit spatial and longer temporal information among IMU observations and then employs the attention technique to integrate this information for inertial navigation. The principal contributions of this paper are summarized as follows: \begin{itemize} \item Extending ResNet-18 with attention mechanisms to explore and encode spatial information of IMU samples. \item Proposing a novel self-attention mechanism to extract contextual features of IMU measurements. \item Implementing Multi-Task learning with novel loss functions to enhance learning efficiency and reduce model uncertainty. \item Comprehensive qualitative and quantitative comparisons with existing baselines demonstrate that CTIN surpasses state-of-the-art models. \item Providing a new IMU dataset with ground-truth trajectories under natural human motions for future reference. \item To our knowledge, CTIN is the first Transformer-based model for inertial navigation. \end{itemize} The remainder of this paper is organized as follows. Section \ref{sec: background} provides background on inertial navigation and the attention mechanism. Section \ref{sec: model} reviews the architecture and workflow of CTIN. The evaluation and related work are discussed in Section \ref{sec: evaluation} and Section \ref{sec: related_work}. Section \ref{sec: conclusion} presents the conclusion and future work.

text: Solving math word problems (MWPs) presents distinct challenges in comprehending natural-language problems and executing arithmetic reasoning over quantities using commonsense knowledge. As illustrated in \autoref{fig:example}, a typical MWP includes a brief narrative that describes a real-world scenario and poses a question regarding an unknown quantity. To resolve the MWP in \autoref{fig:example}, a machine must extract essential quantities from the text, such as "100 kilometers" and "2 hours," and comprehend their interrelationships. General mathematical knowledge, such as "distance = velocity $\times$ time," is then applied to compute the solution. Recently, researchers have concentrated on solving MWPs using neural-symbolic models~\cite{Ling2017ProgramIB, wang-etal-2017-deep, Huang2018NeuralMW, Wang2018TranslatingMW, Xie2019AGT}. These models typically comprise a neural perception module (\emph{i.e.}, Seq2Seq or Seq2Tree) that converts the problem text into a solution expression or tree, and a symbolic module that executes the expression to produce the final answer. Training these models necessitates full supervision of the solution expressions. However, these fully-supervised methods have three limitations. First, current MWP datasets provide only one solution per problem, despite the existence of multiple solutions that offer different approaches to solving the same problem. For example, the problem in \autoref{fig:example} can be solved by ``$(100/2) \times (2+3.5)$'' if the speed is calculated first and then multiplied by the total time; alternatively, it can be solved using ``$100 + 100/2 \times 3.5$'' by summing the distances of the journey's first and second parts. Models trained with full supervision on current datasets are compelled to fit the provided solution and cannot generate diverse solutions. Second, annotating the expressions for MWPs is labor-intensive. However, a significant number of MWPs with their final answers can be easily mined from the internet (\emph{e.g.}, online forums). Efficiently utilizing these partially-labeled data without expression supervision remains an unresolved issue. Third, current supervised learning methods suffer from a train-test discrepancy. Fully-supervised learning methods optimize expression accuracy rather than answer accuracy. However, the model is evaluated based on answer accuracy on the test set, resulting in an inherent performance gap. To address these challenges, we propose solving MWPs with \textit{weak supervision}, requiring only the problem texts and final answers. By directly optimizing answer accuracy instead of expression accuracy, learning with weak supervision naturally resolves the train-test discrepancy. Our model includes a tree-structured neural model similar to \citet{Xie2019AGT} to generate the solution tree and a symbolic execution module to compute the answer. However, the symbolic execution module for arithmetic expressions is non-differentiable concerning answer accuracy, making it impractical to use back-propagation for gradient computation. A straightforward approach is to employ policy gradient methods like REINFORCE~\cite{williams1992simple} to train the neural model. Policy gradient methods explore the solution space and update the policy based on generated solutions that happen to yield the correct answer. Since the solution space is vast and incorrect solutions are discarded with zero reward, these methods often converge slowly or fail to converge. To enhance the efficiency of weakly-supervised learning, we introduce a novel \textit{fixing} mechanism to learn from incorrect predictions, inspired by the human capacity to learn from failures through abductive reasoning~\cite{magnani2009abductive,Zhou2018AbductiveLT}. The fixing mechanism propagates the error from the root node to the leaf nodes in the solution tree, identifying the most probable \textit{fix} that can produce the desired answer. The corrected solution tree is subsequently used as a pseudo label to train the neural model. \autoref{fig:framework} illustrates how the fixing mechanism rectifies the incorrect solution tree by tracing the error in a top-down manner. Moreover, we design two practical techniques to efficiently traverse the solution space and identify possible solutions. First, we observe a positive correlation between the number of quantities in the text and the size of the solution tree (the number of leaf nodes in the tree), and propose a \textit{tree regularization} technique based on this observation to constrain the range of possible tree sizes and reduce the solution space. Second, we implement a \textit{memory buffer} to track and store the discovered fixes for each problem using the fixing mechanism. All solutions in the memory buffer are used as pseudo labels to train the model, encouraging the generation of more diverse solutions for a single problem. In summary, by integrating the fixing mechanism and the aforementioned two techniques, the proposed \textbf{learning-by-fixing} (LBF) method incorporates an exploration stage and a learning stage in each iteration, as depicted in \autoref{fig:framework}. We utilize the fixing mechanism and tree regularization to correct incorrect answers in the exploration stage and generate fixed expressions as pseudo labels. In the learning stage, we train the neural model using these pseudo labels. We conduct extensive experiments on the Math23K dataset~\cite{wang-etal-2017-deep}. The proposed LBF method significantly surpasses the reinforcement learning baselines in weakly-supervised learning and achieves comparable performance with several fully-supervised methods. Additionally, our proposed method attains significantly higher answer accuracies for all the top-3/5 answers compared to fully-supervised methods, demonstrating its advantage in generating diverse solutions. The ablative experiments also confirm the effectiveness of the designed algorithms, including the fixing mechanism, tree regularization, and memory buffer.

text: The aim of pattern mining is to identify a concise set of significant patterns that collectively represent a substantial portion of a dataset and are easily interpretable and reusable. Pattern mining actually includes a wide range of algorithms in knowledge discovery and data mining focused on dataset analysis \citep{aggarwal2014frequent5interesting}. Current methods in pattern mining focus on identifying an interesting \textit{pattern set} rather than merely a collection of individually interesting patterns, where the quality of patterns is assessed with respect to both the dataset and other patterns. A common theoretical foundation for pattern set mining is the Minimum Description Length principle (MDL)~\citep{grunwald2007minimum}, which is applicable to various types of patterns, such as itemsets~\citep{vreeken2011krimp}, patterns of arbitrary shapes in two-dimensional data~\citep{faas2020vouw}, sequences~\citep{hinrichs2017characterising}, graphs~\citep{bariatti2020graphmdl}, etc. Despite recent progress in pattern mining, algorithms for mining numerical data seem to be inadequately explored. Currently, one of the most prevalent methods for mining numerical pattern sets involves applying itemset mining to binarized datasets. This will be elaborated upon below, but first, we would like to mention an alternative to numeric pattern mining, namely ``clustering.'' In recent years, clustering algorithms have been extensively developed, resulting in many diverse and efficient methods \citep{Jain10,CraenendonckDB17,Jeantet0G20}. However, there exists a significant conceptual distinction between pattern mining and clustering. In pattern mining, the \textit{description} is prioritized, whereas in clustering, the emphasis is on \textit{object similarity}. In other words, numerical pattern mining is more concerned with describing a group of objects in terms of a set of attributes related to these objects, while clustering is more focused on identifying these groups of objects based on their commonalities as measured by a similarity or distance metric. The former involves certain requirements for interpretability, meaning the resulting patterns should define a region in the ``attribute space'' that is easy to interpret. Conversely, in clustering, the emphasis is on groups of objects or instances. The clusters may be constrained to specific shapes, such as spheres in \textsc{K-means} or \textsc{DBSCAN}, but the similarity of objects remains the most critical characteristic of clusters. For instance, clustering techniques like agglomerative single-linkage clustering in a multidimensional space might yield clusters of very complex shapes. Typically, these shapes are not a primary concern, although they are a significant focus in numerical pattern mining. Therefore, in this paper, we propose an MDL-based approach to numerical pattern set mining called \textsc{Mint} for ``Mining INTeresting Numerical Pattern Sets.'' \textsc{Mint} computes numerical patterns as $m$-dimensional hyper-rectangles, which are products of $m$ intervals, where the intervals correspond to the attributes and their values. The primary advantages of the \textsc{Mint} approach are that (i) \textsc{Mint} does not require prior exploration of the pattern space, as candidates for optimal patterns are computed dynamically, (ii) the total number of explored patterns is at most cubic (and at most quadratic in each iteration) in the number of objects with distinct descriptions considered as vectors of attribute values, (iii) \textsc{Mint} is based on MDL and produces a small set of non-redundant informative patterns. Furthermore, a series of experiments demonstrates that \textsc{Mint} is efficient and generates sets of high-quality patterns: the patterns delineate meaningful groups of objects with quite precise boundaries. Indeed, the \textsc{Mint} algorithm can mine numerical patterns on both small and large datasets, and it is often more efficient and reliable than its competitors \textsc{Slim} and \textsc{RealKrimp}. The proposed encoding scheme is based on prequential plug-in codes, which possess better theoretical properties than the codes used in \textsc{Slim}, \textsc{RealKrimp}, and an MDL-based method for discretization called \textsc{IPD}. The paper is organized as follows. In Section~\ref{sec:related_work}, we discuss the state-of-the-art algorithms in itemset pattern mining for numerical data. Section~\ref{sec:basics} introduces the main concepts used in the paper, while Section~\ref{sec:method} describes the foundations of the proposed method. Subsequently, Section~\ref{sec:experiments} presents the experiments conducted to illustrate the effectiveness and strengths of \textsc{Mint}. Finally, Section~\ref{sec:conclusion} concludes the paper with a discussion on the potential of \textsc{Mint} and some directions for future research.

text: \noindent In recent years, significant research has focused on employing deep learning models within computer-aided diagnostic (CAD) systems. These models have demonstrated promising diagnostic outcomes across various clinical fields, including fundoscopy \cite{asiri2019deep}, dermatology \cite{liu2020deep,esteva2017dermatologist}, and pulmonary disease diagnosis \cite{shoeibi2020automated,rajpurkar2017chexnet,gabruseva2020deep}. Given the global shortage of radiologists and the increasing issue of burnout \cite{wuni2020opportunities,ali2015diagnostic, kumamaru2018global,zha2018prevalence,rimmer2017radiologist}, developing deep learning systems for chest radiography addresses a natural need. The task of chest radiography is particularly suited to supervised learning, as large quantities of chest radiographs and their corresponding diagnostic labels are available as training data for deep learning models. Chest radiograph data has been aggregated into benchmark datasets for various diseases \cite{wang2017chestx,johnson2019mimic}, including the most recent addition of COVID-19 \cite{wang2020covid}. Deep learning models have achieved expert-level performance on these benchmark datasets \cite{rajpurkar2018deep,seyyed2020chexclusion}. Nonetheless, recent findings indicate that even the highest-performing deep learning models can be vulnerable to adversarial attacks \cite{finlayson2019adversarial,han2020deep}. \citet{finlayson2018adversarial} argue that the substantial costs in the medical industry, along with the reliance of pharmaceutical device and drug approvals on disease prevalence, may incentivize manipulation of disease detection systems. The primary contributions of this paper are as follows: \begin{enumerate} \item We conduct an in-depth exploration of backdoor attacks in medical imaging, focusing on chest radiography within the context of multi-label classification. Recognizing that multiple diseases can be detected simultaneously in a chest radiograph, we propose an evaluation framework for multi-label classification tasks. To our knowledge, this is the first instance where attention has been directed towards backdoor attacks in the context of multi-label classification. \item We demonstrate how the trigger appears in both low-level and high-level features learned by the model using Gradient-weighted Class Activation Mapping (Grad-CAM), a weakly-supervised explainability technique \cite{selvaraju2017grad}. By illustrating how explainability can be employed to detect the presence of a backdoor, we highlight the importance of explainability in assessing model robustness. \end{enumerate}

text: The PlatON network offers a platform for distributed transactions and computations~\cite{PlatON}. The network utilizes the Giskard consensus protocol~\cite{Giskard} to achieve consensus among participating nodes on which transaction blocks to incorporate into a distributed ledger (blockchain). The protocol is designed to tolerate up to one third of all participating nodes being Byzantine, meaning they may act adversarially~\cite{Byzantine}. In this paper, we provide a detailed specification of Giskard. Unlike the protocol documentation~\cite{Giskard}, which provides an overview and describes its general behavior, our objective is to specify the protocol in sufficient detail to guide implementation and formal verification. To achieve this, we offer definitions of both the protocol execution semantics and significant protocol properties, and we present proofs of its three primary safety properties based on these definitions. As our emphasis is on protocol safety, we omit discussion of higher-level features of Giskard and only provide a brief background; further context and motivation are available in the official documentation~\cite{Giskard}.

Correspondence to \email{alex@openai.com}, \email{prafulla@openai.com}, \email{aramesh@openai.com}} Images, including illustrations, paintings, and photographs, can often be described with text but typically require specialized skills and significant time to create. Consequently, a tool that can generate realistic images from natural language would enable humans to produce rich and varied visual content with exceptional ease. The capability to edit images using natural language also facilitates iterative refinement and precise control, both crucial for practical applications. Recent text-conditional image models can synthesize images from free-form text prompts and can combine unrelated objects in semantically plausible manners \citep{attngan,dmgan,dfgan,dalle,xmcgan}. However, they are not yet capable of producing photorealistic images that fully capture the details of their corresponding text prompts. Conversely, unconditional image models can generate photorealistic images \cite{biggan,stylegan,stylegan2,vqvae2}, sometimes with such fidelity that humans cannot distinguish them from real images \cite{zhou2019hype}. In this area of research, diffusion models \cite{dickstein,scorematching} have emerged as a promising class of generative models, achieving leading sample quality on various image generation benchmarks \citep{ddpm,sotapaper,cascaded}. To attain photorealism in the class-conditional setting, \citet{sotapaper} enhanced diffusion models with \textit{classifier guidance}, a technique that enables diffusion models to condition on a classifier's labels. The classifier is initially trained on noised images, and during the diffusion sampling process, gradients from the classifier guide the sample towards the label. \citet{uncond} achieved comparable results without a separately trained classifier by employing \textit{classifier-free guidance}, a guidance method that interpolates between predictions from a diffusion model with and without labels. Inspired by the ability of guided diffusion models to produce photorealistic samples and the capacity of text-to-image models to manage free-form prompts, we apply guided diffusion to the task of text-conditional image synthesis. Initially, we train a 3.5 billion parameter diffusion model that employs a text encoder to condition on natural language descriptions. Subsequently, we compare two methods for guiding diffusion models towards text prompts: CLIP guidance and classifier-free guidance. Through human and automated evaluations, we determine that classifier-free guidance results in higher-quality images. We observe that samples from our model generated with classifier-free guidance are both photorealistic and exhibit a broad range of world knowledge. When assessed by human judges, our samples are preferred over those from DALL-E \citep{dalle} 87% of the time for photorealism and 69% of the time for caption similarity. While our model can render a wide range of text prompts in a zero-shot manner, it may struggle to produce realistic images for complex prompts. Therefore, we equip our model with editing capabilities in addition to zero-shot generation, allowing humans to iteratively refine model samples until they align with more complex prompts. Specifically, we fine-tune our model to perform image inpainting, demonstrating its ability to make realistic edits to existing images using natural language prompts. The edits produced by the model align with the style and lighting of the surrounding context, including realistic shadows and reflections. Future applications of these models could potentially assist humans in creating compelling custom images with unprecedented speed and ease. We note that our resulting model can significantly reduce the effort needed to create convincing disinformation or Deepfakes. To prevent these use cases while supporting future research, we release a smaller diffusion model and a noised CLIP model trained on filtered datasets. We name our system GLIDE{}, which stands for \textbf{G}uided \textbf{L}anguage to \textbf{I}mage \textbf{D}iffusion for Generation and \textbf{E}diting. We refer to our smaller filtered model as GLIDE{} (filtered).

text: \noindent In recent years, there has been a rapid advancement in online recruitment platforms. With the growing volume of online recruitment data, numerous studies related to interviews have emerged, such as person-job (or talent-job) fit~\cite{shen2018joint, qin2018enhancing,luo2019resumegan, bian2019domain} and the automatic analysis of asynchronous video interviews (AVIs)~\cite{hemamou2019hirenet, hemamou2019slices,suen2019tensorflow}, which aim to facilitate automated job recommendations and candidate evaluations. Among these studies, person-job fit is framed as a supervised text matching problem. Given a set of labeled data (i.e., person-job match records), it seeks to predict the matching label between candidate resumes and job descriptions. Recently, deep learning has improved person-job fit methods by training more effective text matching or text representation models~\cite{xu2017measuring, jiang2019semantic}. AVI involves determining whether a candidate is suitable for hiring by evaluating their responses to interview questions. In AVIs, an interview is typically viewed as a sequence of questions and answers containing significant social signals. To evaluate candidates more comprehensively, AVI models extract features from video (or images), text, and voice during the question-answering process. In this study, we focus on scoring multiple QA pairs, extracting only text modality features, and defining this task as assessing candidates' competency rather than determining their employability. Based on the anatomy of human interviewers' evaluation processes, the solutions consist of two stages: (1) analyzing and evaluating individual QA pairs one by one to obtain the evaluation status, and (2) grading the candidate's competency based on the evaluation status of multiple QA pairs. For the first stage, existing methods often use text matching or attentional text matching algorithms to evaluate QA pairs~\cite{hemamou2019hirenet, suen2019tensorflow}, which input the concatenated representation of the question and answer into the subsequent classifier. As is well known, questions in asynchronous video interviews are not confined to specific domains. This means candidates can respond to questions based on their work or study experiences. Consequently, candidates' answers will vary, making it challenging to accurately evaluate answers solely through text matching. Intuitively, it is more reasonable to evaluate QA pairs through the semantic interaction between questions and answers. A significant challenge in this area is how to uncover the latent relationships between each question and answer. Graph neural networks (GNNs, ~\cite{dai2016discriminative, yao2019graph, ghosal2019dialoguegcn}) can learn effective node representations by encoding local graph structures and node attributes. Due to their model compactness and inductive learning capability, GNNs are widely employed in modeling relational data~\cite{battaglia2018relational, schlichtkrull2018modeling, pan2020semantic} and logical reasoning~\cite{luo2019improving, jiang2020reasoning}. Recently, ~\citet{zhang2020efficient} proposed a GNN variant, named ExpressGNN, to achieve a balance between representation power and model simplicity in probabilistic logic reasoning.~\citet{ghosal2019dialoguegcn} developed the DialogeGCN to address context propagation issues in RNN-based methods. Specifically, they utilize self and inter-speaker dependencies of interlocutors to model conversational context for emotion recognition. Inspired by~\cite{ghosal2019dialoguegcn}, we introduce a sentence-level relational GCN to represent the internal temporal and QA interaction dependencies during the question-answering process. For the second stage of grading the candidate, based on the representation of QA pairs, existing methods~\cite{hemamou2019hirenet,hemamou2019slices} tend to encode question-answer pairs as a sequence directly. However, such approaches result in insufficient interaction between the semantic information of question and answer pairs. Therefore, it is challenging to ensure the rationality and explainability of the evaluation. To address this issue, in the first stage, we introduce a semantic-level graph attention network (GAT) to model the interaction states of each QA session. To this end, we propose a Hierarchical Reasoning Graph Neural Network (HRGNN) for the automatic scoring of answer transcriptions (ASAT) in job interviews. Specifically, the proposed sentence-level relational graph convolutional neural network (RGCN) is used to capture the contextual dependency, and the semantic-level Reasoning graph attention network (RGAT) is applied to acquire the latent interaction states. The contributions of our work can be summarized as follows: \begin{itemize} \item We propose a relational graph neural network to address the lack of QA interaction in previous assessment methods. Specifically, the relation of internal temporal dependency in each question/answer aids in context understanding. Additionally, the relation of QA interaction dependency can establish the latent semantic interaction of question-to-answer and answer-to-question. \item To our knowledge, we are the first to construct a hierarchical graph neural network for ASAT to model the relation between sentences in the question and its homologous answer, and interact and infer at the semantic level. Although we only evaluate candidates' competence based on textual features, it significantly enhances the rationality and accuracy of the evaluation. \item Our model outperforms all existing benchmark approaches on a Chinese real-world dataset. Ablation studies and experimental results with 10 random seeds demonstrate the effectiveness and stability of our models. \end{itemize}
