text: With advancements in intelligent technologies, individual robots have become increasingly powerful. Consequently, a growing number of autonomous robots are being utilized to replace human labor in providing various services, such as floor cleaning, surveillance using \emph{unmanned aerial vehicles} (UAVs), surgical procedures with surgical robots, and manufacturing with mechanical arms \cite{2020-liu}. Conversely, the number of latency-sensitive and computation-intensive tasks performed by robots has significantly risen. For example, to mitigate the spread of COVID-19, UAVs are tasked with monitoring social distancing among individuals \cite{20-chamola}, and search-and-rescue operations are promptly executed following natural disasters. To address these challenges, \emph{multi-robot cooperation} (MRC) systems have garnered significant attention in recent years \cite{18-ismail}. However, the battery limitations, restricted sensing capabilities, and computational capacity of individual robots present challenges in task completion \cite{18-bedi}. \emph{Mobile edge computing} (MEC) technology has emerged as a promising solution for enabling task offloading via wireless communication, which aligns well with the MRC framework. On one hand, multiple robots must collaborate to complete tasks within strict time constraints. On the other hand, efficient communication and task allocation are crucial for ensuring effective cooperation among robots. Therefore, this paper examines a MEC-based MRC system where an intelligent \emph{master robot} (MR) serving as an edge server directs multiple \emph{slave robots} (SRs) to execute time-critical and computation-intensive tasks while minimizing and balancing the robots' energy consumption. \subsection{Related Works} \subsubsection{Robot Cooperation Networks} In recent years, \emph{Artificial intelligence} (AI) applications have been extensively and effectively employed to enhance the information processing capabilities of robots due to their proficiency in handling large datasets with high accuracy \cite{20-khan}. Nevertheless, the implementation of AI technology results in significant computational workloads \cite{17-kim}. In \cite{19-Alsamhi}, \emph{Machine learning} (ML) has been utilized to enhance the quality of connectivity and efficient data collection by robots. However, this work does not address cooperation among robots. To expedite time-critical robotic applications such as AI applications and robot navigation using \emph{Simultaneous Localization And Mapping} (SLAM) technology, numerous studies have focused on three areas \cite{18-ismail}: different robot types, control architectures, and communication technologies. In the robotics field, Boston Dynamics has transformed perceptions of robotic capabilities \cite{19-guizzo}. However, with limited resources, a single robot cannot complete large-scale, low-latency tasks. For instance, extensive environmental sensing and surveillance is a typical robotic application. To achieve precise sensing and timely monitoring, robots must gather sufficient data, communicate with each other, and compute cooperatively in an efficient manner. The MRC system leverages cooperation to overcome the resource limitations of individual robots. Initially, the introduction of controlled mobility has expanded the applications of sparse sensing as discussed in \cite{13-Mostofi}, which can be utilized for energy-efficient and non-redundant sensing in MRC networks. Secondly, the primary advantage of such systems is that robots can share their collected information and resource management strategies with others through advanced wireless communication technologies. Thus, effective wireless communication among robots is crucial for facilitating cooperation within MRC systems. In \cite{19-chen}, to achieve ultra-reliability and ultra-low latency, $p$-persistent real-time ALOHA has been proposed as the multiple access protocol for ad-hoc based MRC systems. With advancements in wireless communication technologies, cloud robots have gained particular attention \cite{15-kehoe}. In \cite{14-roazielo}, to reduce computational workload, a visual SLAM robotic system has been proposed using a distributed framework where the cloud server handles map optimization and storage information. However, the data transmission latency associated with cloud computing is intolerable. Therefore, to reduce latency, the critical issue is to establish a communication paradigm that facilitates cooperation among robots in the MRC system. MEC, emerging as a key technology of 5G, has become a viable solution for edge-enabled applications \cite{19-liu}. In the next subsection, we detail the latest developments in MEC technology. \subsubsection{Mobile edge computing} As a promising technology combining communication and computation offloading, MEC extends computation, communication, and storage resources to the network edge. It has an interdisciplinary nature between computation offloading and wireless communication, playing a crucial role in reducing energy consumption and latency \cite{20-Hai}. Therefore, MEC is a natural choice to support cooperation among robots, providing efficient communications and effective task assignment among robots. In \cite{15-chen}, to minimize task implementation latency and energy consumption, the authors investigated a computing resource allocation scheme for mobile users and MEC servers. In \cite{17-wang}, by jointly considering computation offloading, resource allocation, and content caching strategy, an \emph{Alternating Direction Method of Multipliers} (ADMM)-based algorithm was proposed to maximize the revenue of the \emph{MEC system operator} (MSO). In \cite{17-you}, an energy-efficient task offloading scheme for multiple devices was proposed. To address network congestion and long latency in cloud computing, a collaborative cloud and edge computing resource management algorithm was devised in \cite{19-ren}. \subsubsection{MEC based Cooperative Communication} As a vital technology enabling cooperation among robots via the mobile edge server, it has been extensively studied to conserve computational resources of users in conventional wireless communication systems. When multiple edge servers serve multiple users, centralized and distributed methods have been proposed to address the optimal task offloading problem in \cite{18-you} and \cite{16-chen}, respectively. Additionally, a joint offloading and trajectory design scheme has been studied to minimize the maximum delay in a MEC-based UAV system \cite{18-hu}. These studies considered a cooperative MEC system, but the users in these systems were not robots, so they did not account for the unique characteristics of robotic systems, such as environmental interaction capabilities. \subsection{Our Contributions} This paper details a MEC-based MRC system designed to execute computation-intensive and time-critical tasks while minimizing robot energy consumption to extend operational time. In the scenario studied, the intelligent MR is modeled as an edge server to decide on the duration of environment sensing, the amount of data collected by each SR, and the data offloaded from each SR. The mobile SRs primarily handle environment sensing and data collection. Subsequently, they can offload a portion of tasks to the MR to conserve energy during data processing. Two resource management strategies are proposed to minimize and balance energy consumption among SRs, ensuring timely task completion. The difference lies in considering the remaining energy at the SRs to ensure local data processing without offloading in the second scheme. Thus, it is more robust to unreliable wireless communication environments than the first scheme, but may consume more energy. The main contributions of the paper are summarized as follows. \begin{enumerate} 	\item[$\bullet$] An implementation framework for computation-intensive and time-critical tasks in MEC-based MRC systems is proposed. The task implementation process is divided into three stages. In the first stage, the SRs focus on environment sensing and data collection. In the second stage, the SRs may offload a portion of data to the MR and process the remaining data locally. In the third stage, the MR processes the data and may also upload a portion of data to the \emph{base station} (BS). The MR decides on the time allocated for sensing, data offloading, and the power scheme at the SRs at the start of task implementation. 	\item[$\bullet$] Two resource management and offloading strategies are developed to ensure timely task completion while minimizing robot energy consumption. In the first scheme, SR energy consumption is minimized and balanced to extend MRC system operation time. In the second scheme, SR remaining energy is considered to adapt to variable wireless communication environments. Consequently, each SR may process its entire collected data locally without offloading to the MR. Thus, it is more robust than the first scheme but may incur higher energy costs. 	\item[$\bullet$] Simulation results are presented to verify the effectiveness of the proposed schemes, and the robustness of the MRC system is also analyzed. \end{enumerate} The remainder of this paper is organized as follows. Section~\ref{System model} introduces the MEC-based MRC system model. Section~\ref{Problem} presents the framework and the corresponding problem formulation. Two resource management strategies are developed in Section~\ref{Optimal} and Section~\ref{suboptimal}, respectively. Numerical results are provided to verify the proposed schemes in Section~\ref{simulation}. The paper concludes in Section~\ref{CONCLUSION}.

text: Interactive media experiences provide individual audience members with media tailored to their specific context, knowledge, or needs. Unlike traditional media, where a single version of the content seeks to engage all audience members, interactive media varies either the information presented or its presentation form. The information used to determine this variation can be sourced from (1) users interacting with the content during consumption; (2) collecting it from the user at the beginning of the experience (thus enabling a more passive consumption mode); (3) an existing user profile; or (4) a combination of these. This paper focuses on the first source. The interactive nature of these experiences renders them more complex than traditional media forms. Consequently, it is crucial for production teams to monitor their success to identify and address content issues and learn how to enhance the user experience in future productions. A crucial metric for success is the level of audience engagement with the experience. However, user engagement is a complex, multifaceted phenomenon \cite{attfield2011towards}, and as media is typically consumed by a geographically distributed audience, in varying contexts and on different devices, accurate measurement poses both practical and methodological challenges. Interaction data have been utilized in some domains as an unobtrusive and scalable method of monitoring engagement \cite{attfield2011towards,lehmann2012models,doherty2018engagement}; our research aims to determine if it can also be applied in this domain. Given that interactive media experiences involve more interaction with the content than traditional media, is it feasible to monitor these interactions and use them to infer engagement? The study explores and introduces new methods of data collection and analysis techniques that broadcasters could employ to better understand their audiences and how engaged they were with the content; we are not evaluating an experience but exploring whether interaction data might be beneficial for measuring engagement. An additional motivation for measuring engagement through interaction data is the potential for near real-time monitoring of engagement. This capability would not only allow for retrospective analysis to improve future work but could also enable real-time content adaptation. For instance, audience members who appear highly engaged might be offered supplementary material, while those with lower engagement levels might receive a shorter or simpler conclusion to the content. Designing successful interventions of this nature is clearly challenging but could significantly enhance the user experience and is only feasible if engagement can be monitored in real-time. Interaction data have been successfully employed in other domains, such as online news \cite{lagun2016understanding,grinberg2018identifying,lu2018between,constantinides2018framework} and search \cite{diriye2012leaving,kim2014modeling,zhuang2017understanding}. It has also been used to derive user behaviors as proxies for engagement \cite{barbieri2016improving,arapakis2016predicting} and satisfaction \cite{chuklin2016incorporating,mehrotra2017user}. As techniques and measures for engagement remain untested in this domain, we study a production-quality and nationally released interactive TV show where the audience controls the presentation and their path through the story. We collected ground truth engagement metrics and user interactions (code and data are available: \cite{jonathan_carlton_2021_5137806}) from the live and in-the-wild interactive TV show to address the question: \begin{itemize} \item[\textit{(RQ)}] What behaviors can we infer from interaction metrics that aid in understanding how engaged an audience member is with an interactive media experience? \end{itemize} We extracted a range of metrics and examined how these relate to the engagement levels reported by audience members. To understand the relationships between metrics and engagement levels, we trained an interpretable model to predict engagement and derive feature importance using internal weights and a model-agnostic interpretation technique. We found that temporal metrics—the time between events and the time an audience member takes to complete the story—effectively distinguish and are strongly associated with engagement levels. Our findings demonstrate the utility of interaction data for providing media creators with insights into audience engagement and show that it can be directly inferred from the data alone. Overall, we make the following contributions: \begin{itemize} \item We confirm a link between user engagement and interaction metrics collected from an interactive media experience; \item We demonstrate the feasibility of predicting engagement levels from user interactions; \item We establish, more broadly, the utility of collecting and analyzing user interactions from interactive media experiences and the potential insights about user engagement that can be leveraged to inform the creative process. \end{itemize} The remainder of the paper is structured as follows: Section \ref{sec:background} discusses related work. Section \ref{sec:methods} describes the study, and Section \ref{sec:results} presents the results. Section \ref{sec:discussion} discusses and contextualizes the findings, and Section \ref{sec:conclusion} draws conclusions and considers future work.

text: \noindent Logos are fundamental elements of brand identity, and recognizing logos allows for statistical analysis of a brand's exposure and influence across numerous images/videos (\citeauthor{gao2014brand} \citeyear{gao2014brand}). Due to the design features of logos, which often favor simple symbols or text (\citeauthor{ad2012logo}\citeyear{ad2012logo}), logos lack rich information for representation; moreover, different logos may vary only by a character or a stroke, making it challenging to learn discriminative deep features. Logo recognition typically involves two steps: locating the bounding box and identifying the logo. Traditional logo recognition employs a closed-set approach, with popular frameworks including Faster R-CNN (\citeauthor{ren2015faster} \citeyear{ren2015faster}), SSD (\citeauthor{liu2016ssd} \citeyear{liu2016ssd}), and YOLOv3 (\citeauthor{redmon2018yolov3} \citeyear{redmon2018yolov3}), among others. However, the closed-set approach is more data-intensive and cannot recognize logos absent from the training set. To address this issue, open-set methods have been proposed (\citeauthor{tuzko2017open} \citeyear{tuzko2017open}; \citeauthor{bastan2019large} \citeyear{bastan2019large}; \citeauthor{fehervari2019scalable} \citeyear{fehervari2019scalable}), which involve two stages: detecting the logo box using a class-agnostic binary detector and identifying the detected box via classifier or retrieval. The binary detection stage can directly utilize the output from detection frameworks like Faster R-CNN and YOLOv3. The identification stage can employ metric learning to assess the distance of nonlinear data, facilitating the comparison of complex data within the embedding space. In practical applications, we observed that setting a low threshold allows the class-agnostic binary detector to easily detect logo-like regions, but it becomes challenging to determine if it is a logo and to which class it belongs, i.e., to effectively map logos in the embedding space with similar classes clustered and distinct classes separated. Consequently, we assert that the primary challenge lies in the second stage of logo recognition, which is our main focus in this study. The limitations of existing public logo datasets (Tab. \ref{table:1}) include: 1) a limited number of logo classes, inadequately reflecting real-world logo recognition challenges (\citeauthor{romberg2011scalable} \citeyear{romberg2011scalable}; \citeauthor{neumann2002integration} \citeyear{neumann2002integration}); 2) logos are often dominant in images due to web crawling, reducing scene complexity (\citeauthor{wang2020logodet} \citeyear{wang2020logodet}; \citeauthor{su2018open} \citeyear{su2018open}; \citeauthor{tuzko2017open} \citeyear{tuzko2017open}); 3) image-level annotation (\citeauthor{su2018scalable} \citeyear{su2018scalable}), which is unsuitable for logo recognition tasks. Therefore, we introduced Makeup216, which offers the following advantages: 1) it focuses on the makeup sector, necessitating stronger recognition algorithms due to minimal differences between logos; 2) it is sourced from real-world settings, where logos appear on actual products rather than posters, introducing various complexities such as blur, occlusion, mirror reflection, and non-rigid deformation; 3) it has the largest number of objects per image among all datasets. The benefits of Makeup216 significantly enhance the feasibility of logo recognition models. We discovered that pure logos have a limited field of view and insufficient information for recognition, which can easily result in incorrect retrieval, as illustrated in Fig. \ref{figure:1}(a), where the top-1 recalled logos are incorrect but exhibit high similarity. However, considering more external regions provides a broader perspective and contextual information. The products behind logos and the adjacent texts/symbols can aid in verification and prevent false recall, as demonstrated in Fig. \ref{figure:1}(b). Based on this insight, we propose a novel logo recognition framework incorporating an adversarial attention representation (AAR) module to utilize the marginal background. This framework clarifies its subject while retaining auxiliary information for more accurate judgment. The issues in Fig. \ref{figure:1}(a) are resolved within our proposed framework, which will be detailed in the experimental section. To evaluate the noise resistance of the logo recognition model, we developed a distractor set for Makeup216 inspired by the image retrieval dataset (\citeauthor{radenovic2018revisiting}\citeyear{radenovic2018revisiting}), and thus established two evaluation protocols: one without distractor samples and another with distractor samples. The proposed framework demonstrated superior performance when faced with distractor samples. The main contributions of this work are as follows: \begin{enumerate} \item A dataset focused on the makeup field is introduced. The diversity of logos and scene complexity make it a challenging dataset for logo recognition; a novel set of evaluation protocols is also developed to reflect the robustness of the logo recognition model. Both the Makeup216 dataset and the protocols will be publicly accessible. \item An adversarial attention representation (AAR) framework for logo recognition is proposed. This framework fully leverages marginal auxiliary information to enhance the representation of pure logos. The AAR framework identifies what should be emphasized and what can serve as a supplement for improved accuracy. \item Our framework establishes a baseline for logo recognition, and extensive experiments on Makeup216 and LogoDet-3k demonstrate that it achieves state-of-the-art performance. \end{enumerate}

text: Lexical semantic change has recently attracted interest at the intersection of natural language processing and historical linguistics\footnote{see \url{https://languagechange.org/}}, leading to the proposal of several datasets for various languages \cite{schlechtweg2020semeval2020}. This study is conducted within the framework of DIACR-Ita \cite{diacrita_evalita2020} at EVALITA 2020 \cite{Evalita2020}, which defines the task for the Italian language in a completely unsupervised manner. From DIACR-Ita, we received 18 target words\footnote{'egemonizzare', 'lucciola', 'campanello', 'trasferibile', 'brama', 'polisportiva', 'palmare', 'processare', 'pilotato', 'cappuccio', 'pacchetto', 'ape', 'unico', 'discriminatorio', 'rampante', 'campionato', 'tac', 'piovra'}, along with two temporally specific and preprocessed Italian corpora, namely \textit{T0} and \textit{T1}, which contain part-of-speech tagging and lemmatization details. We introduce two perspectives to address the problem, concerning how we represent target words and assess the lexical-semantic change across datasets. (1) employs the POS distribution of target words as a representation and utilizes an ensemble of distance measures for estimation. (2) uses the similarities of target words' neighbors as a representation and applies one (of two proposed) similarity measures for estimation. The subsequent three sections detail the previous works, modeling, and results we achieved using these approaches. Following this, section \ref{discussion_section} (Discussion) focuses on examining the second approach to demonstrate the influence of the $k$ parameter in similarity measures and the discriminatory performance of our embedding-based model.

text: \IEEEPARstart{A}{irborne} optical sectioning (AOS) \cite{Kurmi2018,Kurmi2019TAOS,Kurmi2019Sensor,Bimber2019IEEECGA,Kurmi2020GeoScience, David2020} is an effective aerial synthetic aperture imaging technique for revealing artifacts that are otherwise obscured by dense forests and remain invisible in individual images. For applications such as search and rescue (SAR) \cite{Kurmi2019TAOS} and wildlife observation \cite{David2020}, AOS captures the fractional heat signal emitted from hidden targets as an unstructured thermal light-field recorded with a camera drone (Fig.~\ref{fig:Fig0CameraPose}). Capturing over a broad synthetic aperture area (30–100 m diameter) supports optical sectioning through image integration \cite{Kurmi2018}. \vspace{-1.5em} The integral images (representing the signal of a wide-aperture sensor measurement) are computed by registering and averaging all individual image recordings based on the drone's three-dimensional poses and a defined synthetic focal plane. RGB images in the visible waveband (Sony Alpha 6000 RGB camera) are acquired for estimating the drone's pose, while thermal images (Flir Vue Pro; 7.5-13.5 $\mu m$ spectral band) are used for integration. Individual image recordings (both thermal and RGB) are stored on the camera's internal memory cards and downloaded for further processing after flights. After integration, targets at the focal plane will appear clear and sharp, while occluders at greater distances will be significantly blurred and disappear. Consequently, shifting focus by adjusting the focal plane interactively or automatically \cite{Kurmi2020GeoScience} towards its optimal position and orientation near the ground allows optical slicing through the forest and the discovery and inspection of concealed targets, such as human bodies or animals. AOS requires precise measurements of the drone's pose for each captured thermal image. Currently, it is implemented by applying state-of-the-art computer vision algorithms using a general-purpose structure-from-motion and multi-view stereo pipeline \cite{schonberger2016sfm,schoenberger2016mvs} to the high-resolution RGB images. However, a recent study \cite{Chin2018} has demonstrated that primarily estimating or fitting a model to data with outliers is an NP-hard problem. Thus, pose estimation remains error-prone, and resulting mis-registrations of individual recordings lead to defocus in AOS integral images. Note that, due to their low resolution, high noise level, low contrast, and poor texture of natural scenes, thermal images do not provide usable image features for reliable pose estimation. Various approaches for correcting the remaining pose errors have been proposed, such as optimizations by imposing structural constraints \cite{Li2018,Ovechkin2018,Hsiao2018}, utilizing localized depth maps \cite{Shin2018,Shamwell2019}, or fusing different sensors \cite{Mur-Artal2017,Qin2018}. In this article, we present an alternative approach for reducing remaining pose errors by considering the underlying optimization as a focusing problem instead of solving the Perspective-n-Point (PnP) problem \cite{Chin2018}. PnP solutions \cite{Li2018,Ovechkin2018,Hsiao2018,Shin2018,Shamwell2019,Mur-Artal2017,Qin2018} require robust feature detection, which is challenging in low-resolution thermal images and infeasible in the presence of strong occlusions. Thus, we address the focusing problem by optimizing 3 or 6 pose parameters per image using simple gray level variance (GLV) \cite{Firestone1991} (which does not rely on any image features) as an error metric. We have already demonstrated in \cite{Kurmi2020GeoScience} that GLV is invariant to occlusion and is therefore (in contrast to traditional gradient-, Laplacian-, and wavelet-based metrics reviewed in \cite{Pertuz2013}) an ideal visibility metric for AOS thermal integral images. Figure \ref{fig:Fig1Completeresult} illustrates AOS results when the synthetic focal plane is globally optimized as presented in \cite{Kurmi2020GeoScience} (focal plane), and the improved results when our new pose error reduction approach is applied to either 6D (brute force) or 3D (ours) pose parameters. For the latter, resulting integral images reveal more details as they are better focused and have a higher contrast. In the following sections, we will discuss the effects of errors in different pose parameters and various integration strategies leading to our final optimization approach with reduced parameter search space and early stopping. We will demonstrate that our approach improves the quality of integral images (compared to state-of-the-art pose estimation methods) while also being significantly faster and more efficient than the brute force optimization of all pose parameters. \vspace{-0.8em}

In order to obtain a correct image, it is necessary to know exactly where the drone is with respect to each captured picture. Objects in the focus plane, which can be automatically or interactively moved to the optimum position and orientation in the ground plane, make the forest cut into optical slices, and allow the discovery and inspection of hidden objects such as human beings and animals. Objects in the focus plane are sharp and clear, and objects in the background are greatly blurred and fade into the background. “In order to estimate the positions and orientations of the optical elements, the current state-of-the-art is to apply state-of-the-art computer vision methods to a general-purpose structure-from-motion and multi-view stereo pipeline (Schönberger, 2016; Schönberger, 2016). But as a recent study (Chin, 2018) has shown, merely estimating or fitting the model to data with outliers is an NP-hard problem. This means that the estimation of the positions and orientations is erroneous, and this means that the relative position of the images in the acoustic holograms is also erroneous. To compensate for the low resolution, high noise, low contrast, and lack of texture of natural scenes, thermal images cannot provide reliable features for pose estimation. Various methods have been proposed to correct for the remaining pose errors, including the application of geometric constraints (Li, Ovechkin and Hsiao, 2018), the use of local depth information (Shin and Shamwell, 2018), and the combination of information from different sensors (Mur-Artal, 2017 and Qin, 2018). In this paper, we propose an alternative method for reducing the remaining pose errors, which conceives the fundamental problem as a focus problem, rather than solving it as a Perspective-N-Point (PNN) problem. We address this problem by solving three or six poses per image using the simple gray-level variance (GLV) as an error metric. It has been demonstrated (Li, Ovechkin, Hsiao, Shin, Shamwell, Mur-Artal, Qin, 2018) that the gray-level variance (GLV, cf. Firestone, 1991) metric, which does not rely on the features of the image, is invariant to occlusion and, unlike traditional gradient-based, Laplacian-based and wavelet-based metrics (cf. Pertuz, 2013), is an ideal visibility metric for a spectral array. Our results demonstrate that our method greatly improves the quality of the overall image (compared to the best state-of-the-art methods) and is also significantly faster and more accurate than direct optimization of all the pose parameters. text: Traditionally, recommendation algorithms have been designed to optimize the accuracy of the recommendations provided to users. Nonetheless, as highlighted by other researchers, additional significant attributes of recommendations must be taken into account, such as diversity, serendipity, novelty~\cite{Vargas:2011:RRN:2043932.2043955,ge2010beyond,castells2011novelty}, and fairness \cite{yao2017beyond}. These attributes can substantially influence the utility of the recommendations for all system stakeholders \cite{abdollahpourimultistakeholder2020}. In this paper, we address the issue of \textit{popularity bias}, which is the inclination of recommender systems to disproportionately favor a small group of popular items in their recommendations, beyond what their popularity would justify, while disadvantaging items outside this group, even when these items are favored by a considerable number of interested users~\cite{park2008long,steck2011item,jannach2015recommenders}. Consider the distributions depicted in Figure \ref{amplify_item_groups}. These four plots compare item popularity with recommendation popularity for four well-known recommendation algorithms (\textit{RankALS} \cite{takacs2012alternating}, \textit{Biased Matrix Factorization (Biased-MF)} \cite{koren2009matrix}, \textit{User-based Collaborative Filtering (User-CF)} \cite{aggarwal2016neighborhood}, and \textit{Item-based Collaborative Filtering (Item-CF)} \cite{sarwar2001item}) using the MovieLens 1M \cite{movielens} dataset (See section \ref{data_section} for more details on this dataset). The x-axis represents the rank of each item when sorted from most to least popular. The black curve illustrates the cumulative frequency of ratings for different items at a given rank. As observed, a few highly ranked items dominate the entire rating history. For example, only 111 items (less than 3\%) account for more than 20\% of the ratings. In many consumer taste domains, where recommender systems are frequently used, a similarly skewed distribution of user interest is evident. A music catalog might contain artists whose songs have been played millions of times (Beyonc\'{e}, Ed Sheeran) and others whose songs have a much smaller audience (such as Iranian musician Kayhan Kalhor). These few popular items are termed the \textit{short-head} (denoted by $H$ in the plots) in the literature, occupying roughly 20\% of the ratings according to the Pareto Principle \cite{sanders1987pareto}. The remaining items in a long-tail distribution are typically divided into two other parts \cite{celma2008hits}: Tail items ($T$) are the larger number of less popular items that collectively account for roughly 20\% of the ratings\footnote{Tail items may also include new items that have yet to find their audience and will eventually become popular. Thus, popularity bias is related to the well-known item cold-start problem in recommendation.}, and \textit{Mid} items ($M$) consist of a larger number of items in between that collectively receive around 60\% of the ratings. These three item groups are shown at the top of each plot, categorizing the items based on their popularity into the most popular items ($H$), items with medium popularity ($M$), and less popular items ($T$). The blue curves in each plot illustrate the presence of popularity bias across the four algorithms. In the most extreme case (\textit{Item-CF}), almost no item beyond rank 111 is recommended. The head of the distribution, comprising less than 3\% of the total items, accounts for nearly 100\% of the recommendations provided to users. In \textit{User-CF}, this figure is 99\%. The other algorithms perform only slightly better in this respect, with the \textit{H} items constituting more than 64\% and 74\% of the recommendations in \textit{RankALS} and \textit{Biased-MF}, respectively. These plots illustrate the manifestation of popularity bias in recommendations. Users' rating profiles demonstrate skewed popularity distributions, and recommendation algorithms tend to amplify this bias, resulting in a ``rich get richer'' dynamic. However, we contend that this aggregate view of recommendation frequency provides an incomplete picture of the impact of popularity bias: our objective is to offer a more nuanced perspective informed by recent work in multistakeholder recommendation \cite{abdollahpourimultistakeholder2020}. The authors in \cite{abdollahpourimultistakeholder2020} differentiate among the primary stakeholders in recommender systems: 1) users (those who receive the recommendations) and 2) suppliers (those who provide or are otherwise associated with the recommended items). Popularity bias affects both of these stakeholders, as illustrated in Figure ~\ref{amplify_user_groups} (impact on users) and ~\ref{amplify_supplier_groups} (impact on suppliers). The first plot in Figure ~\ref{amplify_user_groups} displays the ratio of rated items for the three item groups $H$, $M$, and $T$ in the profiles of various users in the MovieLens 1M dataset. The interest of each user in the three item groups is measured, and users are sorted from the highest interest in popular items to the lowest, based on the ratio of different item groups in their profile. Users are initially sorted based on interest in $H$ items; if there is a tie, interest in $M$ is considered, and if a tie persists, interest in $T$ is compared. Sorted users are divided into three equal-sized bins $G=\{G_1, G_2, G_3\}$, ranging from most popularity-focused ($G_1$) to least ($G_3$). The y-axis indicates the proportion of each user's profile devoted to different item groups. The narrow blue band shows the proportion of each user's profile that consists of popular items ($H$), and its monotone decrease reflects the ranking of users. Note, however, that all user groups, even $G_1$, have rated many items from the \textit{Mid} (green) and \textit{Tail} (red) parts of the distribution, which is logical: there are only a few truly popular movies, and even the most blockbuster-focused viewer will eventually exhaust them. Other plots in Figure~\ref{amplify_user_groups} also depict users ordered by their popularity interest, but now the y-axis shows the proportion of recommended items delivered by different algorithms\footnote{The plots are ``banded'' because recommendation lists are of size 10, and there are only 10 possible ratio values for each item group.}. The difference from the original user profiles in rating data is stark, especially in the case of \textit{Item-CF} and \textit{User-CF}, where the users' profiles are rich in diverse item groups, but the generated recommendations are much less so. \textit{Tail} items do not appear at all, as evidenced by the red line at the bottom of the plots. In \textit{Item-CF}, almost 100\% of the recommendations are from the \textit{Head} category, even for users with the most niche-oriented profiles. The ``head-focused'' $G_1$ users receive recommendations that are not well-aligned with their interests in terms of item popularity, but the $G_3$ ``tail-focused'' users are poorly served, receiving a steady stream of popular movies in which they are less interested, with none of their long-tail interests addressed. Thus, we observe that popularity bias has a differential impact across the user base: all are affected, but some much more severely than others. Multistakeholder recommendation broadens our perspective of those impacted by recommendations to also include \textit{suppliers}, individuals or entities associated with the recommended items. In this paper, we have considered the director of each movie as the supplier for that movie. Figure~\ref{amplify_supplier_groups} examines popularity bias from the supplier-side of the recommendation interaction: the directors whose movies are being recommended. The plots here are comparable to Figure~\ref{amplify_item_groups}, but here we examine the popularity of movie directors in the data, also finding a skewed distribution indicating that movies from a few popular directors account for a large portion of the ratings. Similar to item groups, we have defined three supplier groups based on their popularity $S=\{S_1, S_2, S_3\}$: $S_1$ represents a few popular suppliers whose items account for 20\% of the ratings, $S_2$ are a larger number of suppliers with medium popularity whose items account for around 60\% of the ratings, and $S_3$ are the less popular suppliers whose items receive 20\% of the ratings\footnote{The popularity distribution of items and suppliers exhibits a strong long-tail shape. Therefore, to create groups with different popularity values, we cannot force the groups to have equal sizes, as this would result in groups with medium and extreme popularity having very similar average popularity.}. Examining the results returned by the recommendation algorithms, we observe that popularity bias also affects the suppliers in the recommendation interaction. Notably, in \textit{Item-CF}, movies from just 3 popular directors in $S_1$ (less than 0.4\%) account for 50\% of the recommendations produced, while items from $S_3$ are never recommended. This pattern is repeated across the other algorithms. This analysis demonstrates that popularity bias is a multistakeholder phenomenon, affecting entities on different sides of the recommender system (sometimes quite severely), and that any evaluation of the system's performance must consider the perspectives of different stakeholders. In this paper, we propose an algorithmic approach based on the novel concept of \textit{popularity calibration} that offers a comprehensive solution to the problem of popularity bias by addressing the needs of multiple stakeholders. A recommendation list is considered calibrated based on popularity when the range of items it covers matches the user's profile in terms of item popularity. For example, if a user has 20\% $H$ items, 40\% $M$ items, and 40\% $T$ items in her profile, we consider the recommendations to be calibrated when the ratio of each item group in the recommended list aligns with the aforementioned ratios. We demonstrate that our approach, while providing more calibrated recommendations for users, also results in fairer recommendations from the suppliers' perspective. It is important to note that calibrating recommendations in terms of popularity does not necessarily ensure that the recommended items will match users' overall preferences. For instance, a documentary movie and a film noir movie might both be non-popular, but a user might be interested in one while disliking the other. Nonetheless, the popularity calibration method we propose in this paper does not aim to calibrate recommendation lists in terms of content but rather solely based on the popularity of the items. Our contributions are as follows: \begin{itemize} \item We characterize popularity bias in multistakeholder terms as a problem impacting the entire recommendation ecosystem, and introduce metrics for quantifying its impact. \item We show that some of the existing metrics in the literature to evaluate popularity bias mitigation often hide important information about how a certain algorithm controls popularity bias for different stakeholders. \item We demonstrate the weaknesses of state-of-the-art re-ranking algorithms when examined from a multistakeholder perspective. \item We propose a new simple, yet effective, algorithm for enhancing popularity calibration using re-ranking, a method that can be applied to the output of any recommendation algorithm. \item Using music and movie datasets, we show that our method outperforms state-of-the-art baselines in mitigating the impact of popularity bias when the needs of multiple stakeholders are considered. \end{itemize}

text: Reinforcement learning for control has demonstrated significant success across a wide range of challenging sensory-motor control tasks, such as agile drone flight~\cite{Kaufmann2018drone,Kaufmann2020drone,Loquercio2021drone}, deformable object manipulation~\cite{Wu2019deformable}, and quadruped locomotion~\cite{Hwangbo2019agile,Miki2022wild,Lee2020terrain,margonlis2022rapid}. Compared to classical model-predictive control methods, reinforcement learning-based approaches allow for the utilization of more realistic forward dynamics models in the form of a physics simulator. Advances in rigid-body simulator technologies~\cite{Todorov2012mujoco, Makoviychuk2021Isaac} enable reinforcement learning algorithms to overcome their prohibitively high sample complexity by initially training in simulation and subsequently deploying directly on the physical robot. Nonetheless, discrepancies still exist between what the controller encounters in the simulator and in the physical environment, known as the \textit{sim-to-real gap}. Specifically, the challenge of developing visuomotor control policies that remain robust under changing perceptual conditions during deployment remains unresolved. Consider the illustration in Figure~\ref{fig:out-of-distribution}. A common strategy to address domain shift is to expose the agent to a wide range of data during training, with the expectation that the training distribution will adequately cover what the agent will encounter in the real world. When the simulator is extensible, domain randomization can be employed to generate more diverse training data~\cite{tobin2017domain,active-domain-randomization}. Alternatively, data augmentation techniques can be used to enhance existing data~\cite{yarats2021drqv2,hansen2020deployment}. Both strategies aim to create visual features that are invariant to perceptual changes unrelated to the task. However, achieving such invariance is not without cost. Additional training prolongs the wall-clock duration of the training process, while domain randomization necessitates manual tuning~\cite{Andrychowicz2020dexterous} and assumes that the policy network has sufficient capacity to manage the expanded input distribution. This added complexity can adversely impact model and policy performance~\cite{laskin2020reinforcement,hansen2020deployment}. Furthermore, there is an underlying assumption that one must have a rough idea of the types of perceptual shifts that might occur during deployment. Failures can occur when the target domain is unknown \textit{a priori} and falls \textit{out-of-distribution}, leading to a malfunctioning robot that cannot self-correct (see Figure~\ref{fig:out-of-distribution}). Unlike previous approaches that achieve invariance by memorizing what is irrelevant to the task during training, we consider a more challenging yet realistic scenario where the specifics of the deployment are not known beforehand. This necessitates that the agent truly generalize \textit{out-of-distribution}, without prior knowledge of the target environment. We further assume that reward supervision is unavailable, rendering fine-tuning via reinforcement learning infeasible. While this may seem an impossible task, it implicitly assumes that the \textit{same task} for which the agent was optimized during training remains well-defined in the target domain. This implies that the agent retains \textit{some} understanding of \textit{what it knows} despite the sudden emergence of numerous unknowns that are not essential for the task at hand. Without additional assumptions or loss of generality, this \textit{out-of-distribution} generalization problem can be framed as \textit{unsupervised policy adaptation} between two MDPs that share the same latent dynamics and reward structure, but with distinct pixel observations (See Figure~\ref{fig:graphicalmodels}). In this paper, we explore methods to enhance generalization under this challenging scenario. Instead of combating domain shift by embedding perceptual invariance directly into the network during training, we demonstrate a method to achieve feature invariance at deployment by leveraging the fact that the task of interest remains unchanged, thus the agent's internal experiences should also remain consistent. We gather latent features during training as examples of what the agent \textit{knows} about the task. In the target domain (see Figure~\ref{fig:latent-alignment}), the new latents deviate from these prior distributions. Our objective in unsupervised policy adaptation is to align the distribution of these latent features on the target domain with those observed during training. This unsupervised learning objective, termed \textit{latent alignment}, does not require paired image data between the source and target, and can be applied to any agent without imposing specific training requirements. To differentiate our approach from prior works that aim to achieve generalization by embedding invariances into the policy during training, we refer to our method as \textbf{\underline I}nvariance through \textbf{\underline L}atent \textbf{\underline A}lignment (\textbf{ILA}).

text: Ground-truth labels for health data are challenging and costly to obtain. A common source of missing labels is the lack of access to labelers (e.g., physicians) and patients not reporting symptoms. Consequently, many healthcare datasets are partially or entirely unlabelled, with larger prospective studies often having relatively fewer labels. This trade-off between study size and accuracy is particularly pronounced in healthcare, although it appears in most real-world studies across various domains. We aim to learn from person-generated activity time-series data with significantly imbalanced or missing labels. Since ground-truth labels are essential for supervised learning, we must explore alternative approaches to leverage the extensive information within the unlabelled data. One possible method to address this need is transfer learning, where a model is initially trained on a different but similar population to the final task. However, upon closer examination, implementing this in practice is challenging. Firstly, study design critically influences the signals that link the observed data to the output labels. It is unrealistic to expect access to a different dataset created with the same study design. Secondly, when studying a rare disease, its low prevalence makes it difficult to find a large, separate initial training set. Thus, transfer learning alone does not meet all our requirements. Self-supervised learning enables the learning of representations without predefined labels. Although the theoretical foundations of these methods are yet to be fully articulated, their empirical performance has been widely documented. This is most notable in natural language processing \cite{brown2020language} and other syntactic tasks such as programming \cite{chen2021evaluating}, as well as in image classification \cite{dosovitskiy2020image}. The classification of these models is debated, with some researchers \cite{bommasani2021foundation} referring to pre-trained, self-supervised, meta-learning models as \emph{Foundation Models}. A fundamental concept of self-supervised learning is that the objective is defined as a function of the data itself. However, selecting an optimal self-supervised objective task is complex. In this study, we examine and compare three objective tasks and assess their performance on influenza-like illness (ILI) prediction with a lab-validated ground-truth. We draw inspiration from natural language processing, where next-word prediction is a task that facilitates the learning of rich representations \cite{brown2020language}. Our end-to-end transformer models initially learn through self-supervision to predict next-day activity levels using activity data from the preceding ten days in a large population. These models are subsequently fine-tuned on the ILI prediction task and evaluated on a small dataset with laboratory-confirmed ILI labels. Final evaluation on an ILI prediction task in a held-out testing set indicates that performance is contingent on the self-supervision task.

Adversarial examples represent a significant security vulnerability for classifiers. Specifically, given a classifier $f$ and a test input $\mathbf{x}$, an attacker can craft a subtle perturbation $\delta$ such that $f(x)
eq f(x+\delta)$. The perturbation $\delta$ is termed an \emph{adversarial perturbation}, while the input $x+\delta$ is referred to as an \emph{adversarial example}. Numerous \emph{empirical} defenses~\citep{goodfellow2014explaining,na2017cascade,metzen2017detecting,svoboda2018peernets,buckman2018thermometer,ma2018characterizing,guo2018countering,dhillon2018stochastic,xie2018mitigating,song2018pixeldefend} have been developed to counter adversarial examples over recent years. However, these empirical defenses are often quickly circumvented by strong adaptive adversaries~\citep{carlini2017adversarial,athalye2018obfuscated,uesato2018adversarial,athalye2018robustness}. To resolve this ongoing challenge, numerous \emph{certified} defenses~\citep{scheibler2015towards,carlini2017provably,ehlers2017formal,katz2017reluplex,cheng2017maximum,lomuscio2017approach,fischetti2018deep,bunel2018unified,wong2017provable,wong2018scaling,raghunathan2018certified,raghunathan2018semidefinite,dvijotham2018training,dvijotham2018dual,gehr2018ai2,mirman2018differentiable,singh2018fast,weng2018towards,zhang2018efficient,gowal2018effectiveness,wang2018formal,lecuyer2018certified,li2018second,cohen2019certified,lee2019stratified,salman2019provably,wang2020certifying,jia2020certified,zhai2020macer} have been proposed. Specifically, a classifier $f$ is considered certifiably robust for an input $\mathbf{x}$ if it consistently predicts the same top-1 label (i.e., $f(x)=f(x+\delta)$) when the adversarial perturbation $\delta$ is constrained, for example, when the $\ell_p$-norm of $\delta$ is below a certain threshold. This threshold is also known as the \emph{certified radius}. In this study, we concentrate on $\ell_0$-norm adversarial perturbation, which allows arbitrary manipulation of some features of a test input and can be executed in the physical world. However, most existing certified defenses emphasize top-1 predictions. In numerous applications, top-$k$ predictions, which provide the $k$ most probable labels, are more pertinent. For example, when a classifier is used as a cloud service (also known as \emph{machine learning as a service})~\citep{Google_Cloud_Vision,microsoft_demo,amazon_demo,clarifai_demo}, top-$k$ labels for a test input are frequently provided to a customer for better-informed decisions; in recommender systems and web searches, top-$k$ items/webpages are suggested to a user. Despite the significance and relevance of top-$k$ predictions, their certified robustness against adversarial perturbations remains largely unexplored. An exception is the recent work by~\cite{jia2020certified}, which established a tight $\ell_2$-norm certified robustness for top-$k$ predictions. This $\ell_2$-norm certified robustness can be converted to $\ell_0$-norm certified robustness by utilizing the inequality between $\ell_0$-norm and $\ell_2$-norm. However, the $\ell_0$-norm certified robustness derived from such conversions is not optimal. \myparatight{Our work} We aim to establish $\ell_0$-norm certified robustness for top-$k$ predictions. Our method is based on \emph{randomized smoothing}~\citep{cao2017mitigating,liu2018towards,lecuyer2018certified,li2018second,cohen2019certified,lee2019stratified,jia2020certified,levine2019robustness}, which can construct a certifiably robust classifier from any base classifier by randomizing the input. We employ randomized smoothing because it is applicable to {any} classifier and scalable to large neural networks. Specifically, we utilize a randomized smoothing technique called \emph{randomized ablation}~\citep{levine2019robustness}, which achieves state-of-the-art $\ell_{0}$-norm certified robustness for top-1 predictions. Unlike other randomized smoothing methods~\citep{cao2017mitigating,lecuyer2018certified,li2018second,cohen2019certified} that randomize an input by adding \emph{additive} noise (e.g., Gaussian, Laplacian, or discrete noise) to it, randomized ablation randomizes an input by subsampling its features. Specifically, given an arbitrary classifier (referred to as \emph{base classifier}) and a test input $\mathbf{x}$, randomized ablation generates an \emph{ablated input} by retaining some randomly selected features in $\mathbf{x}$ and setting the remaining features to a special value, such as the median of the feature value, mean of the feature value, or a special symbol. When the test input is an image, the features are the image's pixels. Then, we feed the ablated input to the base classifier. Since the ablated input is random, the output of the base classifier is also random. Specifically, we denote by $p_j$ the probability that the base classifier outputs a label $j$ for the random ablated input. The original randomized ablation method constructs a \emph{smoothed classifier} that outputs the label with the highest label probability $p_j$ for a test input $\mathbf{x}$. In our study, the smoothed classifier returns the $k$ labels with the highest label probabilities for $\mathbf{x}$. Our primary theoretical contribution is an almost tight $\ell_0$-norm certified robustness guarantee for top-$k$ predictions for the smoothed classifier constructed by randomized ablation. Specifically, we first derive an $\ell_0$-norm certified robustness guarantee for top-$k$ predictions for the smoothed classifier. Our findings demonstrate that a label $l$ is provably among the top-$k$ labels predicted by the smoothed classifier for a test input $\mathbf{x}$ when the attacker arbitrarily perturbs at most $r_{l}$ features of $\mathbf{x}$, where $r_{l}$ is the $\ell_0$-norm {certified radius}. Furthermore, we prove that our certified radius is \emph{tight} when $k=1$ and \emph{almost tight} when $k>1$. Specifically, if no assumptions on the base classifier are made, it is impossible to derive a certified radius larger than $r_{l}+\mathbb{I}(k
eq 1)$. In other words, when an attacker manipulates at least $r_l+1+\mathbb{I}(k
eq 1)$ features of a test input, there exists a base classifier from which the smoothed classifier's top-$k$ predicted labels do not include $l$ or there are ties. Our work has several technical distinctions from~\citet{levine2019robustness}. First, we derive the $\ell_0$-norm certified radius for top-$k$ predictions for randomized ablation, whereas \citet{levine2019robustness} only derived the certified radius for top-1 predictions. Second, our certified radius is equal to or greater than that in \citet{levine2019robustness} for top-1 predictions, as we utilize the discrete nature of the label probabilities to derive our certified radius. Third, we prove the (almost) tightness of the certified radius, while \citet{levine2019robustness} did not. Our work also has several technical distinctions from~\citet{jia2020certified}, which derived a tight $\ell_2$-norm certified radius for top-$k$ predictions for randomized smoothing with Gaussian additive noise. Since they add additive Gaussian noise to a test input, the space of randomized inputs is continuous. However, our space of ablated inputs is discrete, as we randomize a test input by subsampling its features. Consequently, Jia et al. and our work employ substantially different techniques to derive the $\ell_2$/$\ell_0$-norm certified radii and prove their (almost) tightness. Specifically, when deriving the $\ell_2$/$\ell_0$-norm certified radii, our work needs to construct different regions in the discrete space of ablated inputs to apply the Neyman-Pearson Lemma~\citep{neyman1933ix}. When proving the (almost) tightness, we use a completely different approach from Jia et al.. First, Jia et al. rely on the Intermediate Value Theorem, which is not applicable to our discrete data. Second, since Gaussian noise is not uniform, Jia et al. need to prove the results via Mathematical Induction. However, Mathematical Induction is unnecessary in our case because the ablated inputs that can be derived from an input are uniformly distributed in the space of ablated inputs. We evaluate our method on CIFAR10 and ImageNet. Our results indicate that our method significantly outperforms the state-of-the-art for top-$k$ predictions. For example, our method achieves a certified top-3 accuracy of 69.2\% on ImageNet when an attacker arbitrarily perturbs 5 pixels of a test image. Under the same conditions,~\citet{jia2020certified} achieves a certified top-3 accuracy of only 9.0\% when converting their $\ell_2$-norm certified robustness to $\ell_0$-norm certified robustness. Our contributions can be summarized as follows:  egin{itemize} \item We derive an $\ell_0$-norm certified radius for top-$k$ predictions for randomized ablation. \item We prove that our certified radius is tight when $k=1$ and almost tight when $k>1$. \item We empirically evaluate our method on CIFAR10 and ImageNet. \end{itemize}

text: The individualization-refinement (IR) framework is a general backtracking method used by algorithms that solve problems related to the computation of symmetries of combinatorial objects~\cite{McKay201494}. These problems include algorithms for computing automorphism groups, isomorphism solvers, canonical labeling tools used for computing normal forms, and more recently, some machine learning computations in convolutional neural networks~\cite{DBLP:conf/ijcai/AbboudCGL21,DBLP:conf/aaai/0001RFHLRG19}. Indeed, all competitive graph isomorphism/automorphism solvers, such as \textsc{nauty}/\textsc{Traces}~\cite{nautyTracesweb, McKay201494}, \textsc{bliss}~\cite{bliss:webpage, DBLP:conf/alenex/JunttilaK07}, \textsc{saucy}~\cite{saucy:webpage, Darga:2004:ESS:996566.996712}, \textsc{conauto}~\cite{conauto:webpage, DBLP:conf/wea/Lopez-PresaCA13}, and \textsc{dejavu}~\cite{dejavu:webpage, DBLP:conf/alenex/AndersS21}, operate within this framework. These tools alternate between color-refinement techniques (such as the 1-dimensional Weisfeiler-Leman algorithm) and backtracking steps. The latter involve artificial individualization of indistinguishable vertices, leading to recursive branching and ultimately forming a tree of recursive function calls, known as the IR-tree. By employing clever invariants and heuristics, these tools can prune large portions of the IR-tree. Given that the non-recursive work is quasi-linear, it has long been established that the number of nodes traversed in the IR-tree is the key factor determining the running time for all these tools (see, for instance, \cite[Theorem 9]{thesis} and \cite{DBLP:journals/corr/abs-0804-4881}). In fact, the running times of the various tools closely reflect this~\cite{McKay201494,DBLP:conf/alenex/AndersS21}. The variation in traversal strategies among the tools results in a different number of traversed nodes, leading to varying running times. However, explicit bounds that rigorously demonstrate asymptotic advantages of randomized traversals over deterministic ones have only recently been established~\cite{anders_et_al:LIPIcs.ICALP.2021.16}. To achieve this, a specific problem—a search problem in trees with symmetries—is defined, capturing the precise parameters within which IR-algorithms operate. While these results are quite general within an abstract model, the bounds proven in~\cite{anders_et_al:LIPIcs.ICALP.2021.16} apply to the search problem in arbitrary trees with symmetries, regardless of whether they originate from actual IR-computations. Granted, the extensive benchmark library of \textsc{Traces}{}~\cite{nautyTracesweb,McKay201494} demonstrates that IR-trees exhibit a wide variety of forms and shapes. However, to date, there have been no comprehensive results actually analyzing which trees can arise as an IR-tree. \xparagraph{Contribution.} In this paper, we investigate which trees qualify as IR-trees. Originating from a branching process, all IR-trees are rooted, and all inner vertices have at least two children. Such trees are termed irreducible (or series reduced). Despite the vast variety of IR-trees arising from benchmark libraries, not all irreducible trees are IR-trees. However, we can provide a complete, constructive characterization of IR-trees. \begin{theorem} An irreducible tree is an IR-tree if and only if there is no node with exactly two children, where precisely one is a leaf. \end{theorem} To prove the theorem, we first provide and justify necessary conditions for a tree to be an IR-tree. We then demonstrate that these conditions are indeed sufficient by providing graphs on which the execution of an IR-algorithm yields the desired tree. Our proof is constructive, meaning that we develop an algorithm with the following property: given a tree~$T$ satisfying the necessary conditions, the algorithm produces a graph whose IR-tree is~$T$. As described in our definition of IR-trees in Section~\ref{sec:ir}, the trees are naturally associated with a coloring of the vertices. This coloring is a crucial component related to the automorphism group structure of the graph. Our characterization also fully describes how color classes may be distributed in a given tree. It turns out there are several simple restrictions, particularly for vertices with precisely two children, but apart from that, all colorings can be realized, and any number of symmetries can be ensured (see Section~\ref{sec:graph:constr}). Our characterization provides a fundamental argument transferring the analysis of abstract tree traversal strategies performed in \cite{anders_et_al:LIPIcs.ICALP.2021.16} to backtracking trees of IR-algorithms on actual instances. Specifically, we may conclude that the abstract trees used for the lower bounds of probabilistic algorithms in \cite{anders_et_al:LIPIcs.ICALP.2021.16} indeed appear as IR-trees. Interestingly, however, the abstract trees used for the lower bounds of deterministic algorithms (Theorem~13, \cite{anders_et_al:LIPIcs.ICALP.2021.16}) are not IR-trees. In fact, these trees have nodes with two children, one child that is a leaf and another that is not. This violates the necessary conditions as outlined by Theorem~\ref{thm:sufficient}. Fortunately, it also immediately follows from our results that a slight modification can rectify this: by simply replacing the respective leaves with inner nodes that have two attached leaves, the trees become actual IR-trees, due to our characterization. Overall, we therefore prove that the lower bounds of \cite{anders_et_al:LIPIcs.ICALP.2021.16} hold true in the IR-paradigm. \xparagraph{Cell Selectors and Invariants.} Formally, the IR-paradigm allows for different design choices in some of its components. For most of these, competitive practical solvers actually make very similar choices: the refinement is always \emph{color refinement} and solvers commonly choose as their pruning invariant (essentially) the so-called \emph{quotient graph}. The way in which the actual implementations differ from color refinement and quotient graphs is usually only in minor details and done to achieve practical speed-ups. This only leads to a slightly weaker refinement and invariants in some specific cases. In this paper, we therefore comply with these common design choices. Many other design choices, such as \emph{how} IR-trees are traversed, have no effect on the characterization of the IR-trees themselves. There is, however, one integral design choice where competitive IR-solvers do indeed vary in a way that affects which trees are IR-trees, namely the so-called \emph{cell selectors}. We should emphasize that Theorem~\ref{thm:sufficient} only states that for the trees satisfying the necessary conditions, there is some cell selector for which the graph is an IR-tree. However, we can also say something about specific cell selectors. Considering the characterization for a \emph{given} cell selector, there are two possibilities: either fewer trees turn out to be IR-trees, or the same characterization applies. We can use our results to argue that for some cell selectors used in practice, our necessary conditions are sufficient, while for others, they are not (see Section~\ref{sec:conclusion} for a discussion). \xparagraph{Techniques.} Many properties of a graph, such as symmetries, are directly tied to properties of its IR-tree. When modeling a graph intended to produce a particular IR-tree, two major difficulties arise, roughly summarized as follows: \begin{enumerate} \item The effect of color refinement on the graph needs to be controlled. \item The shape of the IR-tree may dictate that symmetries must be simultaneously represented in distinct parts of the graph. \end{enumerate} We resolve these issues using various gadget constructions specifically crafted for this purpose. We introduce \emph{concealed edges}, which allow us to precisely control the point in time at which the IR-process can see a certain set of edges, thereby allowing color refinement to take effect (resolving issue (1)). By combining concealed edges with gadgets enforcing particular regular abelian automorphism groups, we can synchronize symmetries across multiple branches of the tree (resolving issue (2)). Here, as the main tool, we demonstrate the following. As an additional restriction, which stems from the structure of IR-trees, we consider only trees where all leaves can be mapped to the same number of other leaves via symmetries (i.e., under automorphisms, all \emph{leaf orbits} have the same size). We show that each such tree $T$ can be embedded into a graph $H_T$, such that~$H_T$ restricts the symmetries of~$T$ in a particular way. Intuitively, we retain just enough symmetries to allow leaves to be mapped to each other whenever this is possible in~$T$. We thereby effectively couple leaf orbits so that when fixing one leaf, all other leaves are fixed as well. More formally, we prove the following theorem. \begin{restatable}{theorem}{thmtwo} Let~$T$~be a colored tree in which all leaf orbits have the same size. There exists a graph~$H_T$~containing~$T$~as an automorphism invariant induced subgraph so that the action of~$\Aut(H_T)$~is faithful on~$T$~and semiregular on the set of leaves of~$T$. Moreover,~$\Aut(H_T)$~induces the same orbits on~$T$ as~$\Aut(T)$. \end{restatable} Again, we prove the theorem in a constructive manner. All steps can be easily converted into an algorithm that takes as input an admissible (i.e., compatible with our necessary conditions from Section \ref{sec:necessary_conditions}) colored tree $T$ and produces a graph and cell selector with IR-tree $T$.

text: Deep learning methodologies have provided solutions with remarkable performance for general classification problems when abundant annotated data are available for training. Given that, in real-world applications, specific data are often scarce, expensive to label, non-stationary, or streaming, both new and traditional learning strategies have been integrated into the domain of deep learning to address these challenges \cite{kemker2018measuring}. Consequently, areas such as transfer learning \cite{wang2018deep}, reinforcement learning \cite{Ren2018DeepRL}, and incremental learning \cite{he2020incremental,sahoo2018online,tao2020fewshot,perezrua2020incremental}, both supervised and unsupervised, have gained renewed interest. Incremental learning refers to a classifier's capacity to evolve by continuously incorporating information from new instances and/or new classes without the need for full retraining \cite{kemker2018measuring}. Presently, incremental and online machine learning are gaining increasing attention, particularly in the context of learning from real-time data streams \cite{he2020incremental,sahoo2018online}. Specifically, rehearsal-free continual learning methods have shown their capability to expand a classifier's class set by considering only labels from new classes, while mitigating the issue of catastrophic forgetting \cite{tao2020fewshot,perezrua2020incremental}. This is particularly important when computational resources do not permit full retraining, or when confidentiality concerns prevent access to old samples during class set expansion. Conversely, less progress has been achieved in continual learning for a set of non-stationary classes, especially in tasks involving unsupervised streaming data. A classic example of incremental learning application, involving unsupervised, non-stationary, and streaming data, is video-to-video face recognition (V2V-FR) in video surveillance \cite{huang2015cox}. Typically, video frames are captured with a wide range of individual poses, camera positions, resolutions, and lighting conditions, often exceeding the diversity found in datasets used to train deep networks (which generally focus on web-extracted images) \cite{guo2016mscleb1m}. Transfer learning to specific task domains in V2V-FR has proven challenging even for deep learning encoders \cite{gunther2016face,lopezlopez2019dataset}, as image quality factors remain crucial for performance \cite{guo2019survey}. Furthermore, since data are continuously received in a streaming manner, individual appearances may change when switching between different cameras, which may also operate under varying conditions over time \cite{ditzler2015learning,disabato2019learning}. Although, in theory, these issues can be resolved with additional labeling, addressing every possible variation in a training dataset is practically infeasible \cite{he2020incremental}. Therefore, a more efficient and scalable approach is required \cite{maltoni2019continous,tao2020fewshot,perezrua2020incremental}. In this context, what truly reflects the application environment and the changes occurring over time is the actual data \textbf{incrementally} extracted during system operation, and thus \textbf{without labels}. Another feature of real-world V2V-FR applications is their inherent open-set nature \cite{scheirer2013toward,gunther2017towards}. Consider, for instance, an airport video surveillance scenario aimed at tracking certain \emph{individuals of interest (IoI)} who have not been collaboratively enrolled in the system, such as those displaying suspicious behaviors, among a larger group of \emph{unknown} non-target identities, which should be identified as \emph{unknown} non-target identities. In this paper, we introduce a novel incremental learning system, the Open-Set Dynamic Ensembles of SVM \ref{fig:illustrate}. Utilizing a deep feature encoder as a foundation, the system can leverage operational data to enhance and refine the recognition of target identities in an unsupervised manner. Additionally, driven by real-world requirements, the system is designed to function in a completely open-set environment. Based on the capabilities of a deep feature encoder, trained for the general face recognition task, an incremental learning module, fed with streaming data, simultaneously predicts and updates classifiers while addressing catastrophic forgetting issues. The incremental module relies on dynamic ensembles of SVM classifiers, which, from a single SVM constructed from a few labeled video frames directly taken from the footage, can acquire and adapt to additional information by adding or removing classifiers from ensembles. It follows the self-training strategy \cite{yarowsky1995unsupervised}, where predictions also serve as pseudo-labels used to update and improve the classifiers. Adaptations, based on the modular nature of ensembles, involve either adding or removing classifiers. The contributions of this paper can be summarized as follows: \begin{itemize} \item An approach to unsupervised incremental learning designed to operate online with streaming data, where predictions also serve as pseudo-labels during operation. \item A strategy to address both catastrophic forgetting issues and the impact of incorrect pseudo-labels. \item An approach to instance-incremental learning in the open-set, which can be extended to address the class-incremental problem. \item A method for person re-identification based on facial features, not directly reliant on a reservoir of face images. \end{itemize} The remainder of the paper is organized as follows. First, in Sec.~\ref{sec:rel_work}, we conduct an extensive review of the existing literature related to the problem. Subsequently, we present the proposed approach in Sec.~\ref{sec:desvm} and a series of experiments to examine its behavior in Sec.~\ref{sec:experiments} and~\ref{sec:results}. Finally, in Sec.~\ref{sec:conclusion}, we discuss the conclusions drawn from this work.

text: Cancer is emerging as the leading cause of death and the most significant barrier to increasing life expectancy in numerous countries~\cite{world2020report}. Lung cancer, representing over 11\% of all new cases, is the second most prevalent cancer and ranks first in cancer-related mortality worldwide, accounting for 18\% of total cancer deaths~\cite{Sung2021}. The primary treatments for lung cancer include surgical resection, chemotherapy, radiotherapy, and immunotherapy. Many of these treatments, along with successful diagnosis using bronchoscopy or computed tomography (CT)-guided biopsy, rely on accurately locating and often delineating (segmenting) the tumor from normal tissue in preoperative images, typically CT scans. Manual segmentation of lesions or tumors from preoperative CT scans is a labor-intensive and tedious task for oncologists, radiologists, and pulmonologists, potentially causing treatment delays and reducing survival rates, especially in clinics with limited resources. Furthermore, the quality of manual localization and segmentation depends on prior knowledge and clinical expertise. Even with established guidelines and standards, tumor segmentation is often subject to high inter- and intraobserver variability. Conversely, automatic segmentation techniques have the potential to deliver efficient, consistent, and more accurate outcomes. Automatic methods can reduce the time required to interpret images, allowing experts to allocate their limited time to optimize planning and treatment strategies. Historically, methods such as thresholding~\cite{UZELALTINBULAT2017}, region growing~\cite{Adams1994,Dehmeshki2008}, and graph cuts~\cite{GU2013692} were frequently proposed for segmenting lung tumors from CT images. These algorithms are suitable as semi-automatic methods but are inadequate for localizing lung tumors. Recent advancements in deep learning have enabled the automation of tasks that were previously performed only by trained experts~\cite{ramanto2019,kim2019}. Progress in hardware has facilitated the development of larger and more complex models, but much of the improvement is attributed to access to large amounts of annotated data. Today, particularly following the introduction of the U-Net~\cite{ronneberger2015} architecture, deep learning methods have become predominant in the field of medical image segmentation~\cite{Du2020}. However, convolutional neural networks (CNNs) require significant memory, especially for 3D volumes. Consequently, it is common to train networks using 2D or 2.5D input images~\cite{carvalho}, where the model evaluates one slice at a time, groups of slices, or 3D patches, and then applies a sliding window approach across the CT volume. Patching the 3D volume incurs a loss of perception, prompting the proposal of more efficient multi-scale 3D CNN architectures that allow for larger input volumes~\cite{Jiang2018}. An alternative approach is to perform segmentation in multiple steps, either using various algorithms or a cascade of CNNs~\cite{Hossain2019,isensee,carvalho,gan2021}. To address the issue of insufficient training data, unsupervised methods such as supervoxel have been proposed~\cite{Hansen2021}. To achieve faster convergence and more accurate results, multi-modality methods that incorporate magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) or positron emission tomography (PET) scans in addition to CT have been suggested~\cite{fu2021,Jiang2019,Jiang2019_2}. Neural network architectures capable of utilizing multiple annotation types have also been proposed~\cite{Wang2019,Mlynarski2019}. A more recent strategy to address the lack of training data is the teacher-student design, inspired by the concept of knowledge distillation~\cite{phuong19,furlanello18,hinton2015}. The teacher generates pseudo-annotations from suboptimal annotations to expand the dataset size for training the student. The teacher-student pattern can be applied to any type of network architecture and does not impose constraints on other hyperparameters or external configurations. A teacher-student design can be utilized in various ways, from leveraging unlabeled data~\cite{caron2021,Xie2020,Li2020}, to exploiting multiple modalities~\cite{Jiang2019,Jiang2019_2,Li2020}, and to employing datasets with different annotation types~\cite{sun2020,Zhang2021}. Our approach differs from the previously mentioned methods applied to lung tumor segmentation by utilizing annotations of varying supervision on the same modality, specifically CT images. Since CT scanning is less invasive for the patient than other modalities, our goal is to efficiently segment tumors from CT-only examinations. Our method is inspired by Sun \textit{et al.}~\cite{sun2020}, which demonstrates promising results using a teacher-student framework to segment liver and liver lesions with semantic and bounding box annotations. To the best of our knowledge, we are the first to implement a similar teacher-student framework for CT images to perform semantic segmentation of lung tumors. Our study indicates that even with a small dataset of semantic annotations, a student can achieve state-of-the-art performance given a sufficiently large pseudo-annotated dataset to learn from.
