text: While robot learning has achieved considerable progress, most algorithms are developed for robots operating independently. In reality, interaction with humans and other learning agents is unavoidable. Such interaction poses a substantial challenge for robot learning: other agents will \textit{update} their behavior in reaction to the robot, thereby continuously altering the robot's learning environment. For instance, consider an autonomous vehicle learning to modulate the speed of nearby human-driven cars to safely slow them down in the presence of traffic or construction. Initially, when you encounter this autonomous vehicle, you intend to act cautiously: as the autonomous vehicle decelerates, you also slow down. However, when it slows without an obvious reason, your strategy shifts: during your next interaction with this autonomous vehicle, you pass it without hesitation. The autonomous vehicle --- which initially believed it had learned the correct policy to slow your car --- is left perplexed and thwarted by your altered behavior! To effectively \textit{co-adapt} with other agents, the robot must predict how these agents' behaviors will evolve and model how its own actions impact the hidden intentions of others. Previous studies on these interactions make limiting assumptions about the other agents: treating them as stationary~\cite{davison1998predicting,stone2000defining,mealing2015opponent,albrecht2015hba,grover2018learning}, assuming a shared learning process among agents~\cite{foerster2016learning,lowe2017multi,foerster2018counterfactual}, directly accessing the underlying intentions and actions of other agents~\cite{albrecht2015hba,he2016opponent,hernandez2017efficiently, grover2018learning, foerster2018learning, everett2018learning}, or simplifying the intention space using hand-crafted features~\cite{kelley2008understanding,bandyopadhyay2013intention,bai2015intention,sadigh2016information,basu2019active, losey2019robots}. In contrast, we concentrate on general scenarios where the ego agent (e.g., a robot) repeatedly interacts with non-stationary, independently-controlled, and partially-observable agents. Humans seamlessly manage these situations daily (e.g., driving, walking) without explicitly modeling every low-level detail of each other's policy \cite{rubinstein1998modeling}. Inspired by human behavior, we acknowledge that: \begin{center} \vspace{-0.5em} \emph{The ego agent observes only the low-level actions of another agent, but --- similar to human-human interaction --- it is often adequate to maintain a high-level policy representation. We term this representation the \emph{latent strategy}, and recognize that latent strategies can evolve over time.} \vspace{-0.5em} \end{center} Learning the other agent's strategy enables the robot to \textit{anticipate} their responses during the current interaction. Additionally, modeling how the latent strategy evolves over time --- i.e., the \textit{latent dynamics} --- allows the robot to predict how its own actions will \textit{influence} the other agent's future intentions (see Fig.~\ref{fig:front}). Overall, we utilize latent representations of the other agent's policy to contribute the following towards learning in non-stationary multi-agent interaction: \textbf{Learning Latent Representations.} We propose an RL-based framework for multi-agent interaction that learns both latent strategies and policies for responding to these strategies. Our framework implicitly models how another agent's strategy evolves in response to the ego agent's actions. \textbf{Influencing Other Agents.} Ego agents using our proposed approach are encouraged to intentionally modify their policy to influence the latent strategies of other agents, especially when certain strategies are more conducive to co-adaptation than others. \textbf{Testing in Multi-Agent Settings.} We evaluate our approach against state-of-the-art methods across four simulated environments and a real robot experiment, where two $7$-DoF robot arms play air hockey. Our approach surpasses the alternatives and also learns to influence the other agent.

text: Automatic language identification is a complex problem, and distinguishing between closely related languages remains a primary challenge for state-of-the-art language identification systems~\cite{DSL2014}. Language technology for Scandinavian languages is in an early stage of development (e.g.~\newcite{kirkedal2019lacunae}). A significant issue is obtaining sufficient text to train large language models. High-quality language identification is essential for this data acquisition, yet leading models frequently confuse similar Nordic languages. This paper introduces a machine learning approach for automatic language identification among six closely related Nordic languages: Danish, Swedish, Norwegian (Nynorsk), Norwegian (Bokmål), Faroese, and Icelandic. This study investigates various methods for extracting features from a corpus of raw text data comprising Wikipedia summaries in the respective languages and assesses the performance of selected machine learning models. Specifically, we will compare the performance of traditional machine learning models such as Logistic Regression, Naive Bayes, Support Vector Machine, and K-Nearest Neighbors with more modern neural network approaches like Multilayer Perceptrons (MLP) and Convolutional Neural Networks (CNNs). After evaluating these models on the Wikipedia dataset, we will proceed to assess the best models on a dataset from a different domain to examine how well the models generalize when classifying sentences from an alternative domain.

text: In numerous environments, such as warehouses, factories, or homes, robots share their workspace with humans or other robots. Although obstacle occupancy in these settings is largely fixed or static, small areas within these environments may experience changes in occupancy during operation. We classify such environments as \emph{semi-structured}. Furthermore, in these applications, robots frequently perform repetitive tasks and require rapid and reliable motion planning capabilities. Consider the scenario depicted in Fig.~\ref{fig:cover}. The robot must grasp the bowl while avoiding the pitchers, table, and walls. Most of the environment (e.g., table, walls, free space above the table, etc.) can be presumed known, and since the task is repetitive, some information from previous planning queries can be reused to expedite planning. Commonly used algorithms like RRTs~\cite{lavalle1998rapidly,kuffner2000rrt} neither exploit the difference between static and movable obstacles nor leverage the repetitive nature of planning problems to accelerate planning. Roadmap-based methods such as Probabilistic Roadmaps (PRMs)~\cite{kavraki1996probabilistic} are either restricted to fully static environments or incur significant overheads in repair operations needed to manage movable obstacles. Enhancements to PRM have reduced costly collision checks~\cite{kavraki2000path}, addressed dynamic environments~\cite{leven2002framework,yang2017hdrm}, and captured repetitive motions~\cite{lehner2018repetition}, but their performance can still vary significantly depending on a planning query. Instead of preprocessing collision information offline, another class of planners utilizes previous experiences to accelerate search~\cite{Phillips-RSS-12,berenson2012robot,coleman2015experience}. However, these planners experience performance degradation when past information becomes invalid due to environmental changes. Consequently, these methods cannot provide fixed-time planning guarantees. Provably fixed-time planners were recently introduced in~\cite{islam2019provable,islam2020provably} for applications involving repetitive tasks. Given a start state, a goal region, and a known model of the environment, they precompute a compressed set of paths that can be used online to plan to any goal within the goal region in constant or bounded time. These methods have been previously applied to mail-sorting~\cite{islam2019provable} and for grasping objects moving along a conveyor belt~\cite{islam2020provably}. While our approach APP is inspired by these works, we concentrate on enabling online obstacle avoidance by explicitly considering movable obstacles during the preprocessing phase using the alternative paths planning approach. We extend these methods to manage movable obstacles while still ensuring provably fixed-time planning through the \emph{Alternative Paths Planner (APP)}. The central idea is to generate multiple alternative paths for each planning problem, ensuring that for any configuration of movable obstacles, one path is guaranteed to be traversable. Our approach to achieve this involves enforcing that these paths are \emph{disjoint}: they are sufficiently separated so that no single obstacle configuration can intersect two paths simultaneously. Managing $n$ movable obstacles requires generating at most $n+1$ fully disjoint paths. However, if the necessary number of disjoint paths cannot be identified for the given problem, we find additional partially overlapping paths (that do not meet the disjointness criterion) to provide the same guarantee. APP can be applied to performance-critical real-world scenarios such as mail-sorting, conveyor-belt picking, and shelving. For situations with multiple movable obstacles, we demonstrate microsecond-scale path-lookup times and achieve a 100\% success rate. We present experimental results from three domains, compare with state-of-the-art existing approaches, and validate our approach with a real-world case study.

text: Relational databases store a significant portion of global data and are generally accessed using structured query languages such as SQL. A natural language interface to these databases (NLIDB) could greatly enhance data accessibility by enabling users to retrieve and utilize information without programming skills. With the release of large-scale datasets \cite{wikisql,DBLP:conf/acl/RadevKZZFRS18,spider}, this task has attracted considerable attention and has been extensively studied in recent years. Previous research has mainly concentrated on converting grammatical, complete sentences into queries. However, an internal user survey of the search service in a major customer relationship management (CRM) platform\footnote{\url{https://www.salesforce.com/}} revealed that users often communicate in a colloquial manner, ranging from using only keywords (``player 42'') to very short phrases (``show player 42'') to complete sentences (``Who is the player who wears Jersey 42?''). Besides style variation, users omitting content words for brevity can make their queries ambiguous. This could make the task unsolvable even for models familiar with the NLS style of text. For instance, in Figure \ref{fig:example}, without the word ``Jersey'', it is unclear which column's value (\texttt{Id} or \texttt{Jersey}) should be 42. In this study, we demonstrate that Text2SQL systems trained solely on complete sentences find it challenging to adapt to the noisy keyword/short phrasal style of queries. To address this, we propose various data augmentation strategies inspired by our user search patterns and style. \hide{ \todo{We have enough space, can you show 2-3 examples in this figure? No need to use a boxed layout, you can show a table. Also please use .pdf to save the figure, which has higher resolution.} } To resolve the induced ambiguity, a potential solution is to leverage the table content by allowing the model to scan the table for different terms present in the query and use that information to disambiguate (If the token ``42'' was only found in the \texttt{Jersey} column, then \texttt{Jersey} must be the column equal to 42). Although effective, this approach could become prohibitively expensive (in terms of inference time or memory required) on large tables, as the model would need to search the entire table content for each query. We hypothesize that in most instances, the model requires only samples from the table content, not the exact rows matching tokens in the NLS query, to disambiguate columns. For example, if the \texttt{Id} column contained alphanumeric IDs, \texttt{Player} and \texttt{Nationality} contained strings, and \texttt{Jersey} contained two-digit numbers, then \texttt{Jersey} must be the column equal to 42. Sampling reduces the need for a full table scan for each query. The samples for each column could be generated offline and remain constant across queries or be periodically updated (to reflect potential distribution shifts in the table or user queries), allowing for adaptation and personalization without retraining the model. In summary, our contributions are as follows: \begin{enumerate} \itemsep0em \item We enhance the well-formed WikiSQL dataset with synthetic search-style queries to adapt to short, colloquial input. \item We propose new models that incorporate table content in a BERT encoder through two sampling strategies to address ambiguous queries. \item We conduct an in-depth qualitative and quantitative (accuracy, inference time, memory) analysis to demonstrate the effectiveness of each content sampling strategy. \item We develop a dataset of 400 queries to benchmark the performance of Text-to-SQL models in this context. \end{enumerate} \hide{ \begin{enumerate} \item augmenting well-formed text with synthetic data to ensure robustness over NLS style questions \item incorporating table content to a BERT model via two sampling strategies to handle ambiguous questions \item an in-depth qualitative and quantitative (accuracy, inference time, memory) analysis showcasing the efficacy of both content sampling strategies \item a curated dataset to benchmark performance on short, ambiguous questions. \end{enumerate} } In addition to adapting to NLS style queries, \textsc{ColloQL}\xspace also achieves state-of-the-art performance on the original WikiSQL~\cite{wikisql} dataset, surpassing all baselines that do not use execution-guided decoding. Our work builds on SQLova \cite{sqlova}, but our methods are applicable to other approaches\footnote{Our code and annotated data can be found at \\ \url{https://github.com/karthikradhakrishnan96/ColloQL}.}.

Currently, there exists a significant gap between the operational mechanisms of neural retrieval models on full text and the relevance labels that inform learning, evaluation, and analysis. These labels, as seen in the TREC Deep Learning Track 2019 (TREC-DL) \cite{trec2019overview}, encompass an entire document, often consisting of thousands of tokens. For traditional models that reduce document statistics to a bag of words, this level of label granularity is adequate. However, newly developed neural ranking models function at a more detailed level. They construct their score hierarchically from interactions among all words to produce a single score for the entire document \cite{Hofstaetter2020_sigir,zheng2019rltm,yilmaz2019}. Consequently, the task of neural retrieval models evolves into a combination of document-level relevance and word-level question answering or information extraction. The models must simultaneously identify relevant information spans and, based on these, make a scoring decision applicable to ranking numerous candidate documents. A significant challenge in their development and evaluation is the absence of datasets that adequately cover both sub-tasks. Existing datasets either emphasize retrieval results with dense judgments across ranked lists \cite{trec2019overview,hashemi2020antique}, or question answer selections in individual candidate texts that can be retrospectively converted to retrieval collections, resulting in incomplete retrieval judgments \cite{rajpurkar2016squad}. In this work, we introduce FiRA: a novel dataset of 	extbf{Fi}ne-grained 	extbf{R}elevance 	extbf{A}nnotations featuring word-level relevance selections and passage-level graded relevance labels for all pertinent documents of the TREC 2019 Deep Learning Document dataset. We divided the documents into snippets and presented query \& document snippet pairs to annotators. Figure ef{fig:fira-screenshot} illustrates an example of an annotated document-snippet. We ensure high quality by employing at least 3-way majority voting for each candidate and continuously monitoring quality parameters during our annotation campaign, such as the time spent per annotation. Additionally, by requiring annotators to select relevant text spans, we decrease the likelihood of false-positive retrieval relevance labels. Our annotation campaign was conducted with 87 computer science students using a custom annotation tool, which facilitates a seamless workflow between selecting relevance labels and relevant text spans. text: Deep reinforcement learning (RL) has achieved remarkable success across a broad range of tasks, including video game playing~\cite{dqn1, dqn2, starcraft2, a3c, a2c, ga3c, kf, pic, Jain19, JainECCV2020} and robotic control~\cite{Levine15, Gu17, Luo19}. However, a significant challenge is the lengthy training time, which limits the scalability of deep RL to more complex tasks. To mitigate the often excessive training duration, RL frameworks strive for two main properties: (1) High throughput, which ensures the framework collects data at very high rates, and (2) High sample efficiency, which ensures the framework learns the desired policy with less data. To achieve both, synchronous and asynchronous parallel actor-learners have been developed to accelerate RL training~\cite{a3c, a2c, impala, ga3c, seed_rl, ddppo, rlpyt, iswitch}. State-of-the-art synchronous methods, such as synchronous advantage actor critic (A2C)~\cite{a3c, a2c} and related algorithms~\cite{ppo, trpo, acktr}, are favored for their \emph{data efficiency}, \emph{training stability}, \emph{full determinism}, and \emph{reproducibility}. However, synchronous methods experience idle time since all actors must complete experience collection before updating trainable parameters. This issue is particularly problematic when the time for an environment step varies significantly. Consequently, existing synchronous methods do not scale well to environments where step time varies significantly due to computationally intensive 3D-rendering and (physics) simulation. \input{flow_time_fig} Conversely, asynchronous methods, such as asynchronous advantage actor-critic on a GPU (GA3C)~\cite{ga3c} and importance weighted actor-learner architectures (IMPALA)~\cite{impala}, achieve high throughput. However, these methods face a stale-policy issue~\cite{ga3c, impala} because learning and data collection occur asynchronously. The policy used to collect data (behavior policy) lags several updates behind the latest policy (target policy) used for parameter updates. This delay results in noisy gradients and thus reduces data efficiency. Consequently, asynchronous methods trade training stability for throughput. We demonstrate that this trade-off is unnecessary and propose High-Throughput Synchronous RL (HTS-RL), a technique that achieves both high throughput and high training stability. HTS-RL can be applied to many off-the-shelf deep RL algorithms, such as A2C, proximal policy optimization (PPO)~\cite{ppo}, and actor-critic using Kronecker-factored trust region (ACKTR)~\cite{acktr}. HTS-RL is particularly well-suited for environments with large step time variance: It performs concurrent learning and data collection, significantly increasing throughput. Additionally, actors interact with environment replicas asynchronously. This asynchronous interaction reduces idle time. Lastly, by performing batched synchronization, HTS-RL ensures that the lag between target and behavior policy equals one. Due to this constant latency, HTS-RL employs a 'one step delayed-gradient' update, which has the same convergence rate as a non-delayed version. As a result, HTS-RL retains the benefits of synchronous RL, \ie, \emph{data efficiency}, \emph{training stability}, \emph{full determinism}, and \emph{reproducibility}, while achieving speedups, especially in environments where step time varies. We demonstrate that HTS-RL enables speedup of A2C and PPO on Atari environments~\cite{gym, atari} and the Google Research Football environment (GFootball)~\cite{gfootball}. Following the evaluation protocol of~\citet{Henderson17} and~\citet{Colas18}, we compare to the state-of-the-art asynchronous method, IMPALA~\cite{impala}: our approach achieves {$3.7\times$} higher average episode reward on Atari games and {$43\%$} higher average game scores in the GFootball environment. When compared with synchronous A2C and PPO, our approach achieves a $2-6\times$ speedup. Code is available at~\url{https://github.com/IouJenLiu/HTS-RL}.

text: The containment of the Covid-19 pandemic has necessitated the mobilization of the most extensive global public health response in decades \cite{fisher2020global}. Consequently, a broad array of new digital health strategies has been rapidly implemented at scale \cite{fagherazzi2020digital}; while this swift deployment has been essential due to the urgency of the situation, it remains crucial to responsibly evaluate the implications of these strategies \cite{ienca2020responsible}. This paper focuses on the privacy implications of digital contact tracing smartphone applications \cite{ferretti2020quantifying}, also referred to as exposure notification apps \cite{Apple_Google}. It is well-established that the Covid-19 virus can be transmitted presymptomatically and asymptomatically \cite{Asymptomatic_transmission_1}, presenting a significant challenge for containment since infected individuals can spread the virus without showing symptoms. However, by identifying recent contacts of diagnosed individuals and encouraging them to isolate, contact tracing can reduce the reproductive number. Initially, contact-tracing efforts were manual; healthcare professionals gathered information about recent contacts from patients and informed those contacts about their high-risk status and the subsequent steps to follow \cite{Manual_contact_tracing}. Naturally, there are certain limitations to this, including patients' inability to report contacts with strangers and the discomfort they may experience when disclosing information about contact identities and times to healthcare professionals \cite{Disclosure_discomfort}. On a larger scale, if infection rates continue to rise, the volume of patients may make manual contact tracing impractical \cite{ferretti2020quantifying}. It is in this context that automated digital contact tracing/exposure notification apps become relevant \cite{kleinman2020digital, Apple_Google, Pan_European, bay2020bluetrace}, as they offer the potential to notify end-users of possible exposure to Covid-19 while reducing the manual labor required. By definition, contact tracing apps are intended to track colocation (though typically not the precise location) of app users, which raises significant privacy concerns \cite{bengio2020need}. Therefore, a major focus in the design of contact tracing protocols is on privacy \cite{levine1988contact, cho2020contact, raskar2020apps, rivest2020pact, trieu2020epione, troncoso2020decentralized}. Many efforts to characterize and ensure the privacy of contact-tracing apps have concentrated on the specific mechanisms they employ \cite{Mechanism_Privacy_1, MSB}; an ideal algorithm from a privacy-maximalist perspective would leak no information to any party other than what is necessary to inform the end-user of an exposure. Indeed, the Google-Apple Exposure Notification framework \cite{Apple_Google}, which is currently the predominant protocol adopted by many national tracing apps, is designed to disclose only the minimal information necessary to inform the end-user of exposure, along with some metadata about the individual exposure(s). This provides nearly no data to third parties (including, unfortunately, public health officials), but it offers a strong guarantee of user privacy protection against all but their contacts. The security analyses for these mechanisms are generally based on concealing everything except the result of the query (in this case, determining the exposure(s)), typically by employing cryptography. However, the result of the query itself reveals information; indeed, in any digital contact tracing app without robust validation of user identities—which is challenging when user privacy must be protected—it is possible using only logarithmically many identities for a user or another institution (such as a business) to infer details about their own exposure events. By combining that information with a record of other information about their contacts, this enables the revelation of the infection status of any of their contacts (or possibly customers) using the exposure notification system \cite{Inherent_limitations}. This privacy leak is independent of the algorithm used and is instead `inherent' to digital contact tracing, as it merely requires making repeated valid queries to the contact tracing system. Fortunately, there is substantial work in the scientific literature that has addressed controlling the leakage of information from the output of database queries, and we can conceptualize contact tracing as a form of distributed database query on the part of the end-user. By utilizing results from the differential privacy and statistical database privacy literature \cite{differential_privacy}, we may aim to protect against information leakage due to the query's output. Unfortunately, there is often a trade-off between utility and privacy, and there is a minimum threshold of added noise required to ensure any particular level of privacy, which may decrease the accuracy of contact tracing. In this paper, we reinterpret the problem of contact tracing as a special case of two other database query settings. First, a contact-tracing app needs to determine which of a user's contacts have been exposed to alert them; this can be viewed as a query for the ones in a binary database containing COVID statuses of the user's contacts. Alternatively, users of a contact-tracing app can be considered as nodes in a simple graph, with edges representing contact events with diagnosed users. In this context, alerting the user can be seen as recommending one node to another, similar to social recommendation algorithms \cite{social_recommendation_survey}. We thus translate two results from the mathematical privacy literature to inherent limitations of contact-tracing apps. The first, from statistical databases \cite{dinur_nissim}, is a lower bound on the error of queries for the number of diagnosed contacts in subsets of a user's contact database below which an adversary can almost completely reconstruct the database. The second, from graph-based social recommendation algorithms \cite{GRS}, is an explicit trade-off between the (differential) privacy and accuracy of alerting some target user about their high-risk contacts. We carefully adapt the settings of these results in their original forms to the setting of a contact-tracing app, which will allow us to deduce the conditions under which they apply to contact-tracing. We then use these conditions to restate the results as inherent privacy/accuracy trade-offs for digital contact tracing. Finally, we use specific numerical examples as the basis for a discussion of the results.

dipper_dipper: Introduction: The containment of the Covid-59 pandemic prompted the largest public health response the world has seen in many decades, and this was accomplished by rapid and widespread deployment of new digital health strategies. This rapid deployment was essential to the urgency of the situation, but it is also important to critically examine the implications of these strategies. Contact tracing began with manual methods, the health care staff collecting information on the patient's recent contacts and informing them of their high-risk status and the necessary steps to take. Of course, there are certain limitations, such as the inability to report contacts with strangers, and the discomfort they may feel when they have to report information about the identities and times of their contact with health care professionals (see reference: Discomfort in disclosure). Given that Covid-19 can be transmitted before and during the period of pre-symptoms, it is a serious challenge for containment to contain the infection in people who do not yet have any symptoms. Considering the increase in the rate of infection, a high number of cases would result in a huge workload for contact tracing (see cite: ferretti20quantifying). By their very nature, contact tracing apps are intended to track the co-location (but not the exact location) of their users, which raises serious privacy concerns. In this context, the importance of digital contact tracing and notification systems becomes greater (see cite: Kleinman20digital, apple_goose, pan-European, bay20bluetrace), as they can alert users to the possible risk of contact with CoVid while reducing the workload. The main concern in the design of contact-tracing protocols is to preserve their privacy. The security analysis of such mechanisms is based on concealing everything except the result of the request (in this case, the determination of the contact), usually by encryption. This privacy leak is independent of the particular protocol used, and is instead inherent in digital contact tracing, as it is only possible to find out more by repeating valid queries. The Google-Apple Exposure Notification Protocol, the protocol used by many national contact tracing applications, is designed to reveal only the minimum of information necessary to inform the end-user of a potential exposure, along with some meta-information about the individual exposures. This barely gives any information to third parties (unfortunately also to public health authorities), but ensures strong guarantees of privacy protection for users from everyone except their contacts. However, the result of the search itself also reveals information; in fact, any digital contact tracing app without a strong verification of the users’ identities — which is a problem if privacy is to be protected — can find out for a business or other organization with only a logarithmic number of identities about the details of their own exposure events. By combining that information with other information about their contacts, they can find out the infectivity of all their contacts (or possibly all their customers) by using the notification system. Unfortunately, there is a trade-off between utility and privacy, and there is a minimum level of noise which must be guaranteed for any particular level of privacy, which can have a negative effect on the accuracy of contact tracing. The problem of tracing contacts is interpreted here as a special case of two other query settings. First, a contact tracing application must know which of the contacts of the contact to be notified are uncovered, and this is seen as a query for the ones in a set of bits representing the contacts’ uncovered statuses. Fortunately, there are already extensive results in the scientific literature that deal with controlling the leakage of information from the result of a query, and we can regard contact tracing as a form of distributed query of the end-user, and we can exploit differential privacy and statistical privacy results to protect ourselves against the information leakage that the query will cause. We therefore translate two results from the mathematical literature on privacy into inherent limits of contact tracing applications. The first, from statistical databases, see dinur_nissim, is an error bound on a query for the number of contacted nodes in a subset of a contact database, under which an adversary can almost perfectly re-build the entire contact database. Second, a contact tracing application must be able to determine which of a contact's contacts have been exposed, in order to warn them; this is a search for the ones in a data set containing the COVID status of the contact's contacts. We will carefully translate these results from their original context into the setting of a contact-tracing application, thereby enabling us to infer the conditions under which they apply to contact-tracing. We will then use these conditions to restate these results as inherent trade-offs between privacy and accuracy in digital contact-tracing. In this context, alerting the user is akin to recommending one node to another, as in social recommendation algorithms [social_recommendation_survey]. Having discussed the numerical calculation, we will finally take a few numerical examples to elucidate the matter.

text: Over recent decades, multi-class classification has been applied across various domains, such as image recognition~\cite{krizhevsky2009cifar,deng2009imagenet, geusebroek2005amsterdam,Hsu02multisvm} and natural language processing~\cite{lang1995newsweeder,DBLP:journals/corr/abs-2005-14165,DBLP:journals/corr/abs-1801-06146}, among others. Loss functions have been crucial in the context of multi-class classification~\cite{DBLP:journals/corr/JanochaC17,kornblith2021why}. In the field of machine learning (ML), the classical loss functions most commonly referenced are the cross-entropy (CE) loss and the Crammer-Singer (CS) Loss, also known as the SVM loss. Prior to the advent of deep learning, the CS loss was extensively studied and employed for developing linear or kernelized models~\cite{10.5555/944790.944813}. However, in the era of deep learning, the CE loss appears to have surpassed the CS loss in practical applications~\cite{he2016deep}. One explanation is that the CE loss is consistent for multi-class classification (i.e., it yields a Bayes optimal classifier with an infinite number of samples), whereas the CS loss is generally inconsistent unless under a rare condition where the maximum conditional probability of a class label given the input exceeds $0.5$~\cite{10.5555/1005332.1044701}, which may hold for simple tasks like MNIST classification but is unlikely for complex tasks such as ImageNet classification~\cite{DBLP:journals/corr/abs-2006-07159,tsipras2020imagenet}. Nonetheless, the CE loss has been shown to be susceptible to label noise~\cite{ghosh2017robust,wang2019symmetric}. Consequently, efforts have been directed towards enhancing the robustness of the CE loss to make it noise-tolerant. A sufficient condition for a loss function to be noise-tolerant is known as the symmetric property~\cite{ghosh2017robust}, which means that the sum of losses over all possible class labels for a given data point remains constant. Based on the symmetric property, several variants of the CE loss have been introduced to incorporate the noise-tolerance property. However, a symmetric loss alone is often insufficient to achieve satisfactory performance in practice due to slow convergence~\cite{zhang2018generalized,ma2020normalized}. Therefore, a loss that interpolates between the CE loss and a symmetric loss typically achieves superior performance on real-world noisy datasets~\cite{wang2019symmetric,zhang2018generalized,englesson2021generalized,ma2020normalized}, such as on the WebVision data with 20\% noisy data~\cite{DBLP:journals/corr/abs-1708-02862}. These existing findings can be interpreted in terms of the degree of uncertainty in the provided label information. If the label information of an instance is certain (e.g., MNIST data), then the CS loss is a suitable choice~\cite{DBLP:journals/corr/Tang13}; if the label information is slightly uncertain (e.g., ImageNet Data), then the CE loss is preferable; if the label information is highly uncertain (e.g., WebVision data), then a loss that interpolates between the CE loss and a symmetric loss is optimal. While parameter tuning (e.g., the weights for combining the CE loss and a symmetric loss) can achieve dataset adaptivity, an unresolved issue remains: "\textit{Can we define a loss to achieve instance adaptivity, i.e., adaptivity to the uncertainty degree of label information for each instance?}" To address this issue, this paper proposes capturing the uncertainty in the label information of each instance using the distributionally robust optimization (DRO) framework. For any instance, we assign each class label a distributional weight and define the loss in the worst-case scenario of the distributional weights, properly regularized by a function, termed as label distributionally robust (LDR) losses. The advantages of employing the DRO framework to model the uncertainty of the given label information include: (i) it offers a unified framework for many existing loss functions, including the CE loss, the CS loss, and some of their variants, such as the top-$k$ SVM loss. (ii) it encompasses an intriguing family of losses by selecting the regularization function of the distributional weights as Kullback-Leibler (KL) divergence, referred to as LDR-KL loss for multi-class classification. The LDR-KL loss is closely associated with the temperature-scaled CE loss, which has been widely used in other contexts~\cite{HinVin15Distilling,chen2020simple}, where the temperature corresponds to the regularization parameter of the distributional weights. Thus, our theoretical analysis of the LDR-KL loss can potentially provide insights into using the temperature-scaled CE loss in various contexts. (iii) The LDR-KL loss can interpolate between the CS loss (at one end), the (margin-aware) CE loss (in between), and a symmetric loss (at the other end) by varying the regularization parameter, thereby offering greater flexibility for adapting to the noisy degree of given label information. Our contributions are the following: \begin{itemize}[noitemsep,topsep=0pt,parsep=0pt,partopsep=0pt] \item We establish a strong consistency of the LDR-KL loss, namely All-$k$ consistency, which is top-$k$ consistency (corresponding to the Bayes optimal top-$k$ error) for all $k\geq 1$, and a sufficient condition for the general family of LDR losses to be All-$k$ consistent. \item We demonstrate that an extreme case of the LDR-KL loss satisfies the symmetric property, rendering it tolerant to label noise. Additionally, we establish a negative result that a non-negative symmetric loss function cannot achieve top-$k$ consistency for $k=1$ and $k=2$ simultaneously. Therefore, we conclude that existing top-$1$ consistent symmetric losses cannot be All-$k$ consistent. \item We propose an adaptive LDR-KL loss, which enables us to automatically learn the personalized temperature parameter of each instance, adapting to its own noisy degree. We develop an efficient algorithm for empirical risk minimization based on the adaptive LDR-KL loss without incurring significant additional computational burden. \item We conduct extensive experiments on multiple datasets under different noisy label settings and demonstrate the stable and competitive performance of the proposed adaptive LDR-KL loss in all settings. \end{itemize}

text: A fully automated system capable of synthesizing realistic 3D human bodies that approach and grasp a target object in 3D space would be valuable across various domains, such as robotics, animation, and computer vision. Although significant progress has been made in synthesizing realistic hand--object interactions, most existing studies focus solely on hand pose synthesis without considering full-body movements~\cite{GRAB:2020, GrapingField:3DV:2020, jiang2021graspTTA}. Conversely, whole-body motion synthesis~\cite{holden2016deep, martinez2017human, hernandez2019human, MOJO} often overlooks the presence of objects within the scene. The task of modeling and synthesizing realistic whole-body grasping motions is challenging and remains unresolved for several reasons. Firstly, whole-body grasping motions involve both full-body dynamics and intricate finger movements~\cite{GRAB:2020}, and the high dimensional degrees of freedom complicate the synthesis of grasping motions. Secondly, a whole-body grasping sequence involves complex and frequent body--scene and hand--object contacts, which are difficult to synthesize in a perceptually realistic manner. For instance, the hand's surface should naturally conform to the object, and the whole-body motion should avoid foot-skating artifacts. Thirdly, given only an initial pose and a target object in 3D space, there are infinitely many ways for a person to approach and grasp the object. The diversity of plausible grasping motions is further increased by the wide potential variation in object shape and pose. Developing an effective generative model to capture this diversity and synthesize diverse realistic motions for grasping various 3D objects remains an open question. To tackle these challenges, we introduce \textbf{SAGA} (\textbf{S}toch\textbf{A}stic whole-body \textbf{G}rasping with cont\textbf{A}ct), a novel framework for generating whole-body grasping motions that can synthesize stochastic movements of a 3D human body approaching and grasping 3D objects. Our solution comprises two components: (1) a novel 3D body generator that synthesizes diverse static whole-body grasping end poses, and (2) a novel human motion generator that creates diverse and plausible motions between specified start and end poses. We present two key insights for both components. First, rather than directly using parametric body models (e.g., SMPL~\cite{SMPL-X:2019}) to represent 3D bodies, we utilize the markers-based representation~\cite{MOJO}, which captures 3D human shape and pose information with a set of sparse markers on the human body surface. As shown in~\cite{MOJO}, the markers-based representation is more accessible for neural networks to learn than the latent parameters of parametric body models, resulting in more realistic motion. We demonstrate that the markers-based representation is particularly advantageous over latent body parameters for learning whole-body grasping, as error accumulation along the kinematic chain significantly affects the physical plausibility of generated hand grasps, leading to severe hand--object interpenetration. Second, {\it contact} is central to our pipeline. As the human moves in 3D space and grasps a 3D object, physical contact is crucial for modeling realistic motions and interactions. For both components of our method, we learn contact representations from data and use them to guide interaction synthesis, significantly enhancing the realism of the generated motion. For static grasping pose generation, we constructed a multi-task conditional variational autoencoder (CVAE) to jointly learn whole-body marker positions and fine-grained marker--object contact labels. During inference, given a target object in 3D space, our model jointly generates a diverse set of consistent full-body marker locations and the contact labels on both the body markers and the object surface. A contact-aware pose optimization module further reconstructs a parametric body mesh from the predicted markers while explicitly enforcing hand--object contact by leveraging the predicted contact labels. Next, given the generated static whole-body grasping pose as the end pose and an initial pose as a start pose, we propose a novel generative motion infilling network to capture motion uncertainty and generate diverse motions in between. We design a CVAE-based architecture to generate both diverse in-between motion trajectories and diverse in-between local pose articulations. Additionally, contacts between feet and the ground are also predicted as a multi-task learning objective to enforce better foot-ground interaction. Furthermore, by leveraging the predicted human--object contacts, we design a contact-aware motion optimization module to produce realistic grasp-oriented whole-body motions from the generated marker sequences. By utilizing the GRAB~\cite{GRAB:2020} and AMASS~\cite{AMASS:ICCV:2019} datasets to train our generative models, our method can successfully generate realistic and diverse whole-body grasping motion sequences for approaching and grasping a variety of 3D objects. \myparagraph{Contributions.} In summary, we present (1) a novel generative framework to synthesize diverse and realistic whole-body motions for approaching and grasping various unseen objects by 3D humans with different body shapes, (2) a novel multi-task learning model to jointly learn static whole-body grasping poses and body--object interactions, (3) a novel generative motion infilling model capable of stochastically infilling both global trajectories and local pose articulations, resulting in diverse and realistic full-body motions between a start pose and an end pose. We conduct extensive experiments to validate our technical contributions. Experimental results demonstrate both the efficacy of our complete pipeline and the superiority of each component compared to existing solutions.

text: We examine a problem introduced by Feige, Gamarnik, Neeman, Rácz, and Tetali \cite{feige2020finding}, which involves identifying a large clique in a random graph $G\sim G(n,\frac{1}{2})$, where the graph $G$ can be accessed through queries to its adjacency matrix entries. The problem's input is a random graph $G(V,E)$ with $n$ vertices, where for each distinct vertex pair $\{u,v\}$, $(u,v)\in E$ occurs independently with probability $\frac{1}{2}$. To simplify terminology, we sometimes refer to a pair $\{u,v\}$ of distinct vertices as an edge, regardless of whether $(u,v)\in E$, but if $(u,v)\in E$, we call it a positive edge, and if $(u,v)\not\in E$, we call it a negative edge. The algorithm's objective is to find a clique (a complete subgraph) in $G$ that is as large as possible. The algorithm can access $G$ through queries to the adjacency matrix of $G$, querying an edge $\{u,v\}$ and receiving its status, whether positive or negative. These queries can be viewed as queries to a random oracle, where for each new query (not previously asked), the oracle responds positively with probability $\frac{1}{2}$ and negatively with probability $\frac{1}{2}$, independently of prior answers. The algorithm's limiting resource is the total number of queries $q$, while the algorithm's running time may be unbounded (e.g., exponential in $n$). The sequence of queries made by the algorithm can be adaptive, meaning the choice of the next query depends on answers to previous queries. The results of the $q$ queries induce a graph $G'(V,E')$, where the edges of $G'$ are those queried and received a positive answer. Since the algorithm is not restricted in computation time, it can identify the maximum clique in $G'$. Thus, the querying process aims to produce a graph $G'$ where the maximum clique is as large as possible. We denote this maximum clique by $K$ and its size by $k$. Note that for any nontrivial algorithm (where $k > 1$), $K$ (and similarly $k$) is a random variable that depends on the input graph $G$. Thus, for a given algorithm, we consider $k$ as the median size of the clique found by the algorithm. For reasons that will become apparent later, if $k$ is even, our results are somewhat simpler to express. Therefore, we assume that $k$ is even (this has a negligible effect on the results, a difference of at most~1 in the size of the clique found). We use $\delta$ as a parameter indicating the allowed number of queries, where $q = n^{\delta}$. (Sometimes $\delta$ is interpreted as requiring $q = O(n^{\delta})$. This has a negligible effect on the results.) Thus, our aim is to maximize $k$ (as a function of $n$ and $\delta$), such that there is an algorithm making at most $n^\delta$ queries, for which with probability at least $\frac{1}{2}$ over the choice of $G\sim G(n,\frac{1}{2})$, the graph $G'$ contains a clique $K$ of size $k$. We consider only $\delta\geq 1$, as for smaller $\delta$, the number of non-isolated vertices in $G'$ will be $n'<n$, and a similar problem can be solved with $n'$ instead of $n$. For $\delta=2$, the entire graph may be queried. The maximum clique size in a graph $G\sim G(n,\frac{1}{2})$ is with high probability (w.h.p.) approximately (ignoring low order terms) $2\log n$ (see \cite{matula1972employee}). Therefore, the maximum clique size in $G'$ satisfies w.h.p. $k\leq 2\log n + \Theta(1)$ for every $1\leq\delta<2$. Conversely, a clique of (expected) size $\log n$ can be found using approximately {$2n$} queries as follows. Initialize the sets $K=\emptyset$, $T=V(G)$. While $T$ is not empty, repeat the following: \begin{enumerate} \item Choose an arbitrary $t\in T$, and update $K\leftarrow K\cup \{t\}$. \item Query all pairs $\{\{t,t'\}\mid t'\in T\setminus\{t\}\}$. \item Remove $t$ and all its non-neighbors from $T$. \end{enumerate} The size of $T$ decreases by a factor of $2$ in each iteration (in expectation), resulting in roughly $\log n$ iterations, and the total expected number of queries is {$2n$}. After the final iteration, the set $K$ is a clique of expected size $\log n$. Therefore, the values of $k$ of interest range between $\log n$ and $2\log n$. In all computations, we will disregard terms of order $o(\log n)$ in the size of $k$. Thus, we can state the problem we aim to solve as follows: Maximize $\alpha$ for which a clique of size $k\ge \alpha\log n - o(\log n)$ can be found using a sequence of at most $n^\delta$ queries. Note that $\alpha$ is a function of $\delta$ which satisfies $1\leq\alpha\leq 2$. We provide a more formal definition of the value $\alpha$ we seek to determine. \begin{definition} Let $1\leq\delta<2$, $\alpha\leq 2$. A deterministic algorithm $\mathcal{A}$, which makes a sequence of at most $n^\delta$ adaptive queries (based on oracle answers), will be called a $(\delta,\alpha)$-algorithm if for every sufficiently large $n$, with probability at least $\frac{1}{2}$, the graph $G'$ (induced on edges discovered by the algorithm) contains a clique of size $k\ge \alpha\log n - o(\log n)$. \end{definition} \begin{definition} Let $1\leq\delta<2$. $\alpha_{*}(\delta)$ is defined as the supremum over $\alpha$ such that there exists a $(\delta,\alpha)$-algorithm. Note that $1\leq \alpha_{*}(\delta)\leq 2$. \end{definition} \begin{remark} Since we do not limit the time complexity of algorithms, if $G'$ contains at least one clique of size $k$, $\mathcal{A}$ can be assumed to find such a clique $K$ (e.g., by using exhaustive search), and to return it. \end{remark} A comprehensive solution to the stated problem is to determine the exact value of $\alpha_{*}(\delta)$ for every $1\leq \delta<2$. Lower bounds on $\alpha_{*}(\delta)$ are demonstrated by algorithms that find cliques of size $\alpha\log n$ (for $\alpha>1$). Such algorithms were presented in \cite{feige2020finding}, and can be found in Section \ref{algos_sec}. The presented algorithms are also suitable for a slightly different problem setting, where the algorithm's adaptiveness is restricted to a constant number of rounds. The upper bounds we will present in this paper will be for this restricted setting. In this setting, the algorithm may use a constant number $l$ of rounds, where in each round it may query at most $n^\delta$ edge queries simultaneously, and the oracle answers all of them. This means that the algorithm may choose queries in round $i$ based on answers given in previous rounds, but not on those given for queries in round $i$. Denote by $q_i$ the number of queries in round $i$. The pattern of queries in the first round gives us the queries graph $Q_1$ with $n$ vertices and $q_1$ edges. Similarly, the pattern of queries in any other round $i$ (that may depend on the answers to queries of previous rounds) gives us the queries graph $Q_i$ with $n$ vertices and $q_i$ edges. Note that the edges of $Q_i$ consist of all pairs queried in round $i$, and not only positive ones. We denote by $Q_{\leq i}$ the queries graph which includes all queries up to round $i$, i.e., $E(Q_{\leq i})=\bigcup_{j\leq i} E(Q_j)$. (Note that we use the term 'up to' in the meaning of 'up to and including'). We modify definitions \ref{def_org_1} and \ref{def_org_2} to comply with the restricted setting. \begin{definition} Let $l\in\mathbb{N}$, $1\leq\delta<2$, $\alpha\leq 2$. A deterministic algorithm $\mathcal{A}$, which makes $l$ rounds of queries with at most $n^\delta$ queries in each round, will be called a $(\delta,l,\alpha)$-algorithm if for every sufficiently large $n$, with probability at least $\frac{1}{2}$, $G'$ contains a clique of size $k\ge \alpha\log n - o(\log n)$. \end{definition} \begin{definition} Let $l\in\mathbb{N}$, $1\leq\delta<2$. $\alpha_{*}(\delta,l)$ is defined as the supremum over $\alpha$ such that there exists a $(\delta,l,\alpha)$-algorithm. \end{definition} These definitions can be extended to the case where the number of queries may not be the same in all rounds. In general, we may assume that in round $i$, the algorithm is restricted to $q_i=n^{\delta_i}$ queries for some $0<\delta_i<2$. This leads to similar definitions of a $((\delta_1,\dots,\delta_l),l,\alpha)$-algorithm and $\alpha_{*}((\delta_1,\dots,\delta_l),l)$ (see definitions in Section \ref{sec_two_rounds_large_delta}). Note that for every $l\in \mathbb{N}$, denoting $\delta\coloneqq \max_i \delta_i$ we have: \[\alpha_{*}((\delta_1,\dots,\delta_l),l)\leq \alpha_{*}(\delta,l)\leq \alpha_{*}(\delta)\] \subsection{Previous results} The problem of bounding $\alpha_{*}(\delta)$ and $\alpha_{*}(\delta,l)$ was studied by Feige, Gamarnik, Neeman, Rácz, and Tetali \cite{feige2020finding}. They established the following results regarding $\alpha_{*}(\delta,l)$: \begin{enumerate} \item For every $1\leq \delta<2$, $\alpha_{*}(\delta,1)=\delta$. \item For every $1\leq\delta\leq\frac{6}{5}$, $\alpha_{*}(\delta,2)\geq\frac{4\delta}{3}$, and for every $\frac{6}{5}\leq\delta<2$, $\alpha_{*}(\delta,2)\geq 1+\frac{\delta}{2}$. \item For every $1\leq \delta<2$, $\alpha_{*}(\delta,3)\geq1+\frac{\delta}{2}$. \item For $\delta=1$ and every $l\in\mathbb{N}$, $\alpha_{*}(1,l)\leq 2^{1-\frac{1}{2^l-1}}$. This gives: $\alpha_{*}(1,2)\leq 1.588$, $\alpha_{*}(1,3)\leq 1.812$ and so on. \item For every $1\leq\delta<2$ and $l\in\mathbb{N}$, $\alpha_{*}(\delta,l)\leq 2-\delta\left(\frac{2-\delta}{2}\right)^l$. \end{enumerate} An upper bound on $\alpha_{*}(\delta)$ was proved by Alweiss, Ben Hamida, He, and Moreira \cite{alweiss2021subgraph}. They demonstrated that for every $1\leq\delta<2$: \[\alpha_{*}(\delta)\leq 1+\sqrt{1-\frac{(2-\delta)^2}{2}}\] For example, for $\delta=1$ this gives $\alpha_{*}(1)\leq 1+\sqrt{\frac{1}{2}}\sim 1.707$. Since $\alpha_{*}(\delta,l)\leq \alpha_{*}(\delta)$, this result also improves the upper bound on $\alpha_{*}(\delta,l)$ for every $l\geq 3$.

text: Sparsification is a fundamental concept for reducing the size of a large graph $G$ while preserving its essential properties. Notable examples include spanners \cite{Chew89}, which approximately maintain distances up to a multiplicative factor, and cut and spectral sparsifiers \cite{BK96,ST04}, which preserve the cuts and Laplacian spectrum of the graph up to a $(1+\varepsilon)$ factor. These \emph{edge sparsifiers} enable the reduction of problems on dense graphs to sparse graphs, with an approximation factor introduced by the sparsification. Conversely, several methods, such as elimination-based Laplacian solvers \cite{KLPSS16}, necessitate \emph{vertex sparsification}, which involves reducing the number of vertices in the graph. In this study, we focus on the concept of vertex sparsification known as \emph{cut sparsification}, as introduced by \cite{HKNR98,Moitra09,LM10}. In this problem, we are provided with a graph $G$ and a set of \emph{terminals} $\mathcal{T} \subseteq V(G)$. Our objective is to construct a smaller graph $G'$ that approximates the value of all cuts in $G$ between terminals up to a multiplicative factor $q$, termed the \emph{quality} of the sparsifier. Specifically, we aim to construct a graph $G'$ that includes the terminals $\mathcal{T}$ among its vertices, such that for any subset $S \subseteq \mathcal{T}$, the minimum cut in $G$ (and $G'$) between $S$ and its complement $\mathcal{T} \backslash S$ differs by at most the multiplicative approximation $q$. Desirable attributes of an algorithm for producing vertex sparsifiers include achieving a quality $q$ close to $1$, while ensuring that the constructed graph $G'$ has few vertices, ideally nearly linear in the number of terminals, denoted as $k = |\mathcal{T}|$. Furthermore, for practical applications, we desire the runtime of the vertex sparsification algorithm to be polynomial or even linear in the size of the original graph $G$. Previous research has achieved various subsets of these properties. In the scenario where the sparsifier $G'$ has a vertex set exactly $\mathcal{T}$, an upper bound quality $q = O(\log k / \log\log k)$ was achieved \cite{Moitra09,LM10,CLLM10,EGKRTT14}, and a polynomial runtime was obtained by \cite{MM10}. In the case where the quality $q = 1$, upper bounds of $2^{2^k}$ \cite{HKNR98,KR14} and lower bounds of $2^{\Omega(k)}$ \cite{KR13} were achieved. Additionally, \cite{KW12} achieved a bound of size $O(Z^3)$ for quality $q = 1$ in polynomial time for graphs with integer capacities, where $Z$ is the total degree of all terminals. Despite this, it remains unknown whether quality $q = 1+\varepsilon$ sparsifiers with $\O({\mathrm{poly}}(k/\varepsilon))$ vertices exist except in special cases \cite{AGK14,ADKKP16}. In this paper, we present a vertex sparsification algorithm for $c$-edge connectivity, a thresholded version of cut sparsification, which maintains all cuts of size at most $c$ exactly, has a size linear in the number of terminals and polynomial in $c$, and runs in polynomial time for all $c$ (\cref{thm:main}). This concept, termed a \emph{connectivity-$c$ mimicking network}, was introduced in \cite{CDL21} to explore dynamic connectivity problems and parameterized complexity, leading to the first fully dynamic online algorithm for $c$-connectivities with nearly constant update time for constant $c$ \cite{JS20}. Specifically, we define that graph $G'$ is a connectivity-$c$ mimicking network for $G$ with terminals $\mathcal{T}$ if all cuts between terminals in $G$ with at most $c$ edges are preserved exactly in $G'$. The previous algorithm by \cite{CDL21}, which constructs a connectivity-$c$ mimicking network with $O(kc^4)$ edges, does not run in polynomial time due to its reliance on a well-linked decomposition concept from \cite{Chu12}, which requires an exact solution to a restricted version of the sparsest cut problem. Consequently, the algorithm's runtime depended exponentially on $c$. Our primary contribution is to leverage the matroid-based cut covering lemmas from \cite{KW12}, combined with a weaker notion of a well-linked decomposition. Specifically, we avoid performing a full well-linked decomposition and instead partition the graph $G$ into segments whose ``expansion'' concerning terminals is not too small, akin to an expander decomposition. text: Reinforcement learning has demonstrated significant success in addressing numerous challenging problems. Noteworthy contributions include DQN~\cite{mnih2015human}, AlphaGo~\cite{silver2016mastering}, and OpenAI Five~\cite{berner2019dota}. Nonetheless, these achievements often require a substantial number of interactions with the environment. For instance, AlphaZero~\cite{silver2017mastering} necessitates playing 21 million games during training. In contrast, a professional human player can play approximately 5 games daily, implying it would take a human player 11,500 years to accumulate the same level of experience. While sample complexity may be less problematic for RL algorithms applied in simulations and games, it becomes crucial for real-world applications such as robotic manipulation, healthcare, and advertisement recommendation systems, where high performance with low sample complexity is essential for feasibility. Significant advancements in sample-efficient RL have been made in recent years~\cite{chua2018deep, deisenroth2011pilco, srinivas2020curl, laskin2020reinforcement, kostrikov2020image, schwarzerdata, kaiser2019model}. Among these, model-based methods have gained considerable attention, as they utilize both real environment data and "imagined data" from the model to train the policy, enhancing sample efficiency~\cite{chua2018deep,deisenroth2011pilco}. However, most successes have been achieved in state-based environments. In image-based environments, certain model-based methods like MuZero~\cite{schrittwieser2020mastering} and Dreamer V2~\cite{hafner2020mastering} attain superhuman performance but lack sample efficiency; other methods like SimPLe~\cite{kaiser2019model} are quite efficient but yield lower performance (0.144 human normalized median scores). Recently, data-augmented and self-supervised methods applied to model-free approaches have achieved greater success in the data-efficient domain~\cite{schwarzerdata}. However, they still fall short of reaching human-level performance. Thus, to enhance sample efficiency while maintaining superior performance, we identify three essential components for a model-based visual RL agent: a self-supervised environment model, a mechanism to mitigate model compounding error, and a method to address the off-policy issue. In this study, we introduce EfficientZero, a model-based RL algorithm that attains high performance with limited data. Our method builds upon MuZero, incorporating three key modifications: (1) employing self-supervised learning to develop a temporally consistent environment model, (2) learning the \textit{value prefix} in an end-to-end fashion to help reduce the model's compounding error, and (3) using the learned model to adjust off-policy value targets. As depicted in Figure \ref{fig:compare}, our model achieves state-of-the-art performance on the widely used Atari~\cite{bellemare2013arcade} 100k benchmark and attains superhuman performance with only 2 hours of real-time gameplay. Specifically, our model achieves 194.3\% mean human normalized performance and 109.0\% median human normalized performance. For comparison, DQN~\cite{mnih2015human} achieves 220\% mean human normalized performance and 96\% median human normalized performance, requiring 500 times more data (200 million frames). To further validate the effectiveness of EfficientZero, we conduct experiments on simulated robotics environments from the DeepMind Control (DMControl) suite. It achieves state-of-the-art performance, surpassing the state SAC, which directly learns from the ground truth states. Our sample-efficient and high-performance algorithm paves the way for greater impact on numerous real-world challenges.

text: Over the years, \ac{NBR} has garnered significant interest from researchers \citep{fpmc,dream,bai2018attribute}. Baskets, which are sets of items purchased or consumed together, are common in many real-world services, with e-commerce and grocery shopping being notable examples~\citep{hao, raeder}. Given a sequence of baskets that a user has previously purchased or consumed, the objective of a \ac{NBR} system is to predict the basket of items the user will likely want to purchase or consume next. Within a basket, items lack temporal order and hold equal importance. A primary distinction between \ac{NBR} and session-based or sequential item recommendations is that \ac{NBR} systems must handle multiple items within a single set. Consequently, models designed for item-based recommendation are unsuitable for basket-based recommendation, leading to the development of specialized \ac{NBR} methods~\citep{tifuknn, recency, dream, beacon, intnet, clea, sets2sets, sun2020timestamp2}. \subsection{Types of recommendation methods} Over the years, a diverse array of recommendation methods has been developed. \emph{Frequency-based} methods remain significant as they can capture global statistics regarding item popularity; this is true for both item-based and \ac{NBR} scenarios. Similarly, \emph{nearest neighbor-based} methods have been employed for both item-based and basket-based recommendation scenarios. Recently, deep learning techniques have been developed to tackle sequential item recommendation problems, leveraging the ability of deep learning-based methods to capture hidden relations and automatically learn representations~\citep{batmaz-2019-deep}. Recent years have also seen proposals to address various aspects of the \ac{NBR} task using deep learning-based methods, such as item-to-item relations~\citep{beacon}, cross-basket relations~\citep{dnntsp}, and noise within a basket~\citep{clea}. Recent analyses suggest that deep learning-based approaches may not be optimal for all recommendation tasks and under all conditions~\citep{jannach-2020-why}. For generating a personalized ranked list of items, linear models and nearest neighbor-based approaches outperform deep learning-based methods~\citep{dacrema-2021-troubling}. In sequential recommendation problems, deep learning-based methods may be surpassed by simple nearest neighbor or graph-based baselines~\citep{dacrema-2019-are}. What about the task of \acl{NBR}? Here, the retrieval unit --- a basket -- is more complex than in the recommendation scenarios considered in~\citep{dacrema-2019-are,dacrema-2021-troubling,jannach-2020-why}, with intricate dependencies between items and baskets over time, thus creating potential for sophisticated representation learning-based approaches to \ac{NBR} to achieve performance improvements. In this paper, we examine the field more closely to determine if this is indeed the case. \subsection{A new analysis perspective} We identify significant gaps and issues in the \ac{NBR} literature. These include weak or absent baselines, the use of different datasets across papers, and non-standard metrics. We assess the performance of three families of state-of-the-art \ac{NBR} models (frequency-based, nearest neighbor-based, and deep learning-based) on three benchmark datasets, finding that no \ac{NBR} method consistently outperforms all others across all settings. Given these findings, we advocate for a more comprehensive analysis of the successes and failures of \ac{NBR} methods. As illustrated in Figure~\ref{fig:re-nbr}, baskets recommended in a \ac{NBR} scenario comprise \emph{repeat items} (items previously consumed by the user in earlier baskets) and \emph{explore items} (items new to the user). The novelty of recommended items has been previously studied, and related metrics have been proposed~\citep{epc-epd}, but novelty-oriented metrics are not specific to \ac{NBR} and focus solely on evaluating the novelty of the recommendation list. To enhance our understanding of the relative performance of \ac{NBR} models, particularly concerning repeat and explore items, we introduce a set of task-specific metrics for \ac{NBR}. Our newly proposed metrics help us discern which types of items are present in the recommended basket and evaluate the performance of \ac{NBR} models when suggesting new versus already-purchased items. \subsection{Main findings} Armed with our newly proposed metrics for \ac{NBR}, we conduct our large-scale comparison of \ac{NBR} models again and arrive at the following key findings: \begin{itemize} \item No \ac{NBR} method consistently surpasses all others across various datasets. \item All published methods exhibit a strong bias towards either repetition or exploration compared to the ground truth, which could negatively impact long-term engagement. \item There exists a substantial \ac{NBR} performance gap between repetition and exploration; recommending repeat items is considerably easier. \item In many scenarios, deep learning-based \ac{NBR} methods are outperformed by frequency-based baselines that populate a basket with the most frequent items in a user's history, potentially supplemented with items most frequent across all users. \item A bias towards repeat items accounts for most of the performance improvements of recently published methods, even though many complex modules or strategies specifically target explore items. \item We propose a new protocol for evaluating \ac{NBR} methods, including a new frequency-based \ac{NBR} baseline and new metrics to assess the potential performance improvements of \ac{NBR} methods. \item Existing \acs{NBR} methods have varying treatment effects on user performance and item exposure for users with different repetition ratios and items with different frequencies, respectively. \end{itemize} \noindent% Overall, our work illuminates the state-of-the-art of \ac{NBR}, offers suggestions to enhance our evaluation methodology for \ac{NBR}, aids in understanding the reasons behind performance differences, and provides insights to guide the design of future \ac{NBR} models.

text: With the increasing complexity of machine learning models, particularly in recommendation systems, effectively and efficiently managing abundant input features has become a critical issue. In online recommendation systems within an industrial context, models are frequently trained on billion-scale sparse features using one-hot encoding~\cite{cheng2016wide,zhou2018din,DBLP:conf/cikm/ShengZZDDLYLZDZ21}. Each feature can also be considered as a unique ID, which is often transformed into a low-dimensional embedding before being input into the model. A straightforward approach to handling large-scale input is to treat each feature independently. Using this approach, a DNN can be trained directly to estimate CTR based on the combination (e.g., concatenation) of features, where feature interaction depends on the implicit modeling of fully connected layers. However, features such as ``candidate item'' and ``user click history'' in recommendation systems are highly interrelated~\cite{zhou2018din,zhou2019dien}, indicating the presence of co-occurrence information. A well-known example is the ``Beer and Nappies'' story. Such feature interaction aids in more accurately estimating CTR. As demonstrated in Fig.\ref{fig:coaction}, if feature interaction is not considered, the effects of features A and B on the final label (click or not in CTR prediction) are modeled independently, as depicted by the blue lines. Feature interaction, shown by the grey line, explicitly connects the correlations of the feature pair (A, B) to the target label, providing more valuable information for the learning objective. We will explore this topic further in Sec. \ref{sec:revisit}. To model feature interaction, the simplest method is to use the cartesian product. Given two features A and B, once features A and B are selected, the co-occurrence <A, B> is treated as a new feature and input into the model. Since the co-occurrence information is directly provided as additional input, the training process becomes easier. Although the cartesian product is straightforward and effective, it has significant drawbacks, such as a large parameter volume and feature space, and poor generalization ability. Unlike the cartesian product, which introduces additional input information, several research efforts have focused on modeling feature interaction through careful combinations of input features. Typical examples include factorization-based methods~\cite{rendle2010factorization,qu2016product,WangFFW2017DCN,lian2018xdeepfm,xiao2017attentional,song2019autoint}, which emphasize both low- and/or high-order feature interactions by directly combining feature embeddings in latent vector space with various operators. As these methods consider feature interaction from the model perspective and the operators are well-designed, they are generally more deployment-friendly compared to the cartesian product. However, they still have some notable limitations. Unfortunately, the shallow structures of some factorization-based methods \cite{juan2016field,WangFFW2017DCN} restrict their representational power. More importantly, the embeddings generated by their operators are responsible for representation learning and feature interaction modeling simultaneously, which may impede the training process. Additionally, CAN differentiates the parameter space for representation learning and feature interaction modeling to prevent mutual interference during training. The main contributions of this work are summarized as follows: \begin{itemize}[leftmargin=*] \item We examine the effectiveness of the cartesian product and highlight the potential of implicit feature interaction modeling. Inspired by the independent coding of the cartesian product, we design a new feature interaction paradigm that achieves comparable performance to the cartesian product while consuming significantly fewer resources. \item We introduce the Co-Action Network (CAN) to model feature interaction among raw features at the input stage. Each feature ID in CAN is assigned to an individual micro-MLP to model the interaction with other features. text: {\bf Motivation}. Stack Overflow\footnote{https://stackoverflow.com/} is among the most prominent platforms for posing and responding to questions related to software development. Since its inception in 2008, the site has been extensively utilized by both professional developers and enthusiastic programmers to exchange and enhance their knowledge. As of September 2019, Stack Overflow has amassed over 10.9 million users and 18.1 million questions. The site's volume continues to expand with more than 150,000 new questions being added each month\footnote{https://data.stackexchange.com/}. The swift expansion of the Stack Overflow website poses challenges in managing its content and maintaining its appeal. Given its vast dataset (in terms of questions), manual management is prohibitively expensive and exhausting for the site's moderators \cite{moder2019, workload2019}. Consequently, there is an urgent need for automated methods to facilitate effective content management on the site. This necessity has captured the interest of various researchers in recent years \cite{Ashton2012, anton2014, Sebastian2019}. Despite several existing studies on Stack Overflow, only a few focus on the automated management and cleaning of its data. Additionally, most prior works concentrate on identifying and filtering low-quality or duplicate questions \cite{Muhammad2016, denzil2013, Denzil14}. In this study, we propose that it is reasonable to discard even high-quality questions once they no longer align with users' collective information needs, for instance, if the question pertains to an outdated software version or library. Retaining these irrelevant questions increases the cost of data storage and retrieval while offering minimal value. Furthermore, the presence of unnecessary information can negatively impact user experience, potentially leading to user dissatisfaction and attrition from the platform. We introduce the concept of "forgetting" such unattractive questions, allowing them to fade from users' perception similarly to how irrelevant memories are forgotten. As an initial step, this work addresses the problem of identifying quality-yet-irrelevant content on Stack Overflow by examining the early detection of questions that were once frequently encountered but will diminish in importance over time. Specifically, these are questions that were frequently asked and (1) recently viewed by many users with similar issues, but (2) will garner only limited views in the future. We term these as \emph{forgotten questions}. An example of a forgotten question is illustrated in Figure \ref{fig:ForgottenExample}. This question was created in 2008 and was highly viewed until late 2017. Notably, it received 710 views in the last six months of 2017. However, it attracted only a few views in the recent six months. {\bf Research Objectives}. Our analysis indicates that questions are not forgotten quickly, but rather gradually. Typically, it takes years for a highly viewed question to become forgotten. Moreover, predictions for the distant future are neither accurate nor practical. Therefore, we concentrate on questions that are in the process of being forgotten in the near future. Specifically, given a question that has been highly viewed recently, we aim to predict whether its view count will significantly decline in the upcoming period. For example, in the case shown in Figure \ref{fig:ForgottenExample}, at the time point 12/2017, when the question was highly viewed, instead of predicting if the question will be forgotten after two years, we aim to predict if its view count will decrease in the next three or six months. Our work is inspired by the concept of managed forgetting~\cite{claudia2018}: items of diminishing importance are de-emphasized to enhance focus on significant matters, akin to the role of forgetting in human cognitive processes~\cite{David2007}. Specifically, we aim to explore factors suggested by prior literature and general intuition that might influence the process of high-quality questions being forgotten on Stack Overflow. Additionally, we develop a framework for the early detection of such questions. This forgetting management framework can serve as a valuable tool to guide moderators in paying more attention and taking further actions regarding unnecessary content. It also aids in highlighting more important information to users and fostering user engagement. For instance, experienced developers would be more interested in recently highly viewed questions and are motivated to engage with them. Consequently, this helps improve the ranking of these questions by search engines and facilitates users in finding the information they currently need. It is crucial to highlight that our problem differs from and complements other content-driven studies such as \cite{Haoxiang2019}, which investigates questions' answers to detect obsolete content within questions. Such content may either be incorrect at the time of creation or become incorrect in the near future. In contrast, the forgetting of questions can be triggered by various reasons, with becoming incorrect or outdated being just one among them. {\bf Contributions}. We summarize our main contributions in this work as follows. \begin{itemize} \item We present the first study on forgetting management on Stack Overflow. We demonstrate that the forgetting process is prevalent among high-quality questions, albeit at a relatively slow pace. \item We explore a broad range of factors that may influence questions being forgotten and assess their potential as predictors for questions being forgotten. \item We evaluate the performance of several prediction models in identifying questions that are being forgotten. We identify certain categories where the questions being forgotten are more predictable, although the prediction task is generally challenging. We also demonstrate the predictive power of different feature groups and analyze their relative importance in these models. \end{itemize} The remainder of the paper is organized as follows: Section 2 discusses related work. Section 3 provides a description of the Stack Overflow dataset used and our study of forgotten questions. We then conduct experiments using a machine learning framework to predict forgotten questions on Stack Overflow in Section 4. We discuss some factors that can influence our forgetting prediction task in Section 5. Finally, we summarize our main contributions and discuss some promising directions for future work in Section 6.
