text: A prevalent method for generating explanations in automated planning has been to frame the issue as one of model reconciliation~\cite{chakraborti2017plan}. This approach allows for a balance between producing explanations that update the user's environmental model and choosing explicable action sequences that require no additional explanation. Central to this approach is an accurate user model, which is impractical in numerous applications. An alternative perspective is to consider explanations within the broader context of interaction. Humans utilize a diverse array of communicative channels during interactions, generating both conscious and subconscious responses, and employing various behavioral heuristics. To communicate effectively, an interaction agent must be capable of detecting and interpreting these signals or, ideally, anticipating them. With this context in mind, we are preparing a user study to observe human behavior and responses in a joint task interaction with a plan-based agent. While we anticipate that this study will confirm and expand upon previous research on joint task interaction, our primary focus is on understanding how concepts related to plan-based agents (e.g., plan generation, agent intention) can inform the agent's behavior. We have identified plan-based agent behaviors that interact with key elements of joint task interaction (e.g., uncertainty and knowledge differences). These behaviors have been employed to define two alternative agents: a reactive agent, which represents an initial interaction scenario, such as when little is known about the human's preferences and possibly the environment; and a partially predictive agent, which represents a more informed agent that provides information in advance and seeks to proactively mitigate user uncertainty. By collecting both objective and subjective data from humans interacting with these agents, we aim to better understand how such agents could be designed to be more acceptable to humans. As part of this work, we have developed a web-based user study that we are currently preparing to launch. The website facilitates a joint task interaction, where the human user must complete a task with the assistance of an instruction/explanation-providing virtual agent. In this paper, we present the objectives of our user study, the scenarios that participants will encounter, and the questions we are exploring. We also describe the agents to be compared in the study and the aspects of joint task interaction they allow us to examine. Although we do not yet have results from users, we present an empirical analysis to compare the strategies and explanations generated by each type of agent. We first provide an overview of the joint task setting and the necessary planning background. We discuss aspects of plan-based agent behavior relevant to joint task interactions and then use these to define two alternative agents. We present our intended user study, an empirical analysis, related work, and finally conclude.

Another way of considering explanations is to take them in the context of human interactions. In the course of their interactions, humans use a wide range of channels, conscious and unconscious responses, and many different strategies. To communicate effectively, the agent of interaction must be capable of detecting and interpreting these signals, or better yet, anticipating them. We are preparing a study to observe the human behavior and responses in a joint task with a plan-based agent. We expect this study to confirm and extend the previous research on joint task interaction, but our main goal is to understand how the concepts of plan-based agents (plan generation, agent intention) influence the agent's behavior. We have identified some plan-based agent behaviors that are connected to the key elements of joint task interaction (such as uncertainty and difference of knowledge). We have modeled these behaviours as two agents, a reactive agent which represents an initial situation, for example when little is known of the preferences of the human or of the environment; and a partially anticipatory agent which represents a more informed agent which tries to reduce the uncertainty of the human. We are developing a web-based experiment which we are preparing to launch. The system consists of a web site, which enables the human participant to perform a task with the help of an assisting agent. In this paper, we present the aims of our study, the tasks the participants are confronted with, the questions we are addressing, and the two agents which are to be compared in the experiment and which afford us an examination of the different aspects of task sharing. The first thing we do is a survey of the task and the necessary planning background. We then discuss relevant aspects of plan-based agent behavior relevant to joint task interaction and use them to define two alternative agents. Although we have no yet have any results from the users, we give an empirical analysis of the strategies and explanations generated by the two types of agents. In the following sections we present the study of the end-users, our empirical analysis, the work of others and our conclusions.

text: \IEEEPARstart{C}ivil drones have been a prominent topic for the past decade. This interest is notably shared among industry, academia, business, and civil society. In May 2021, Morgan Stanley issued a long-term forecast \cite{MS} predicting that by 2050 (three decades from now), the total market for urban air mobility (including delivery, air taxis, and patrolling drones, among others) will reach \$9 trillion (5-6\% of the projected global GDP) or even \$19 trillion (11-12\% of the projected global GDP) in the "bull case". Major technology companies such as Amazon, Google, and Uber have initiated projects focused on drones. Aircraft manufacturers are designing air taxis. Academia is also highly engaged in this field: currently, approximately 300,000 research documents are available in Scopus as a result of a keyword search string including "drone" and its synonyms like Unmanned Aerial Vehicle (UAV), Unmanned Aerial System (UAS), Unmanned Aircraft, and Remotely Piloted Aircraft Systems (RPAS). Even when the focus is limited to wireless communication, the interest remains substantial and is well encapsulated in several tutorial and survey papers \cite{vin_tut,Vin_safe} based on hundreds of selected research articles. Despite the enthusiasm of various stakeholders, drones are not yet part of our daily lives. The consensus among industry and academia is that regulatory and certification constraints are the primary barriers. For instance, even though articles \cite{vin_tut,Vin_safe} are technical, they emphasize this issue. Furthermore, the authors of \cite{MS} assert that \textit{the regulatory requirements for aviation are among the most underestimated risks}. Indeed, in 2021, Morgan Stanley reduced their market size estimate by 30% compared to their previous Blue paper released in 2018. One of the main reasons cited was "near-term hurdles related to regulation and certification." Conversely, we do not believe that regulatory bodies are acting with ill intent. We understand that managing and regulating technological innovation is a complex task involving many stakeholders: from civil society to security agencies, from university researchers to influential and resourceful companies. Partly, the restrictive policies address public concerns due to relatively low trust in the technology. Moreover, unmanned aviation is a novel field with numerous uncertainties and knowledge gaps. Since academic researchers are often public servants, we should strive to close these relevant gaps and address public concerns. By undertaking this task, we will aid policymakers while promoting balanced and harmonious technological development. Thus, the initial step is to identify the relevant problems and then solve them appropriately. The existence of 300,000 published research items indicates that academia is adept at identifying problems; however, the absence of drones in everyday life suggests that the problems are not always pertinent. This article aims to take a broader view of drone technology and evaluate the issues that are significant for all major stakeholders involved in technological development. This work builds on the accomplishments of Technology Assessment (TA). TA is an interdisciplinary research field that aims to provide knowledge for better-informed and well-considered decisions regarding new technologies \cite{gw09}. It offers information that could assist stakeholders (policymakers, citizens, engineers, etc.) in developing their strategies and courses of action \cite{TA_toolkit_98}. TA can also be applied to specific technical products, processes, services, and systems \cite{gw09}. It is utilized by various agencies and commissions of the European Union, the U.S. Government Accountability Office, and national research councils. In countries such as China, New Zealand, Italy, and Canada, TA is widely employed in sensitive areas like healthcare. In this article, we employ TA to identify pertinent problems and evaluate the current solutions aimed at addressing those problems. Through this, we will highlight relevant research directions for the wireless communications community. Additionally, by using TA, we provide tools for selecting an appropriate research and development project scope and framework to enhance project efficiency while considering the project's nature, technology readiness, and other relevant factors.

text: The COVID-19 pandemic has accelerated the widespread adoption of telehealth \cite{Wosik2020}, resulting in more than a 100\% increase in virtual urgent care visits and over a 4000\% rise in virtual non-urgent care visits \cite{telemedicine}. Typically, a virtual visit begins with the patient explaining their reason for the encounter/visit (RFE) \cite{who}. Subsequently, based on the RFE, an automated history-taking algorithm collects additional details, including information about the presenting symptoms, and ultimately directs the patient to a chat (video or text) with healthcare practitioners. This paper concentrates on an intermediate implicit step of identifying symptoms in the patient's RFE, as it forms the foundation for automated history taking. It is important to note that this is related to the task of medical named entity recognition, where the objective has been to extract symptoms from clinical text in electronic health records (see \cite{Baumel18} and references therein). In contrast, we focus on recognizing medical entities from patient text, as patient text (RFEs) is less standardized and often expresses symptoms in a colloquial manner. Figure ~\ref{fig:ml4hp} provides examples of RFEs from the dataset utilized in our study. Developing a model for medical symptom recognition presents several challenges: \begin{enumerate} \item \textbf{Access}: Since there is no publicly available dataset, any new telehealth platform aiming to develop its machine learning solution will need to begin with a small set of labeled data points and rapidly expand the scope. This also implies that as the number of labeled data points increases, the system may need to identify new symptoms that were previously unknown. \item \textbf{Multilabel distribution}: A given RFE may contain multiple symptoms, and \emph{all} symptoms must be extracted to enable accurate automated history taking. \item \textbf{Long-tailed distribution}: Some symptoms are common, while multiple symptoms tend to co-occur. This implicitly creates asymmetry and a long tail in the data distribution (Figure~\ref{fig:ml4hp}). This is further complicated by the distribution of the patient population on the telehealth platform. \end{enumerate} In light of these challenges, this work proposes a new active learning algorithm for efficiently gathering data labels. The main intuition for our algorithm is as follows: RFEs form distinct clusters that are medically grounded by underlying health conditions. Thus, the proposed algorithm selects informative examples by inducing clusterings in the latent space of unlabeled examples and choosing those that maximally cover that clustering. By finding the right balance between selecting points close to cluster centroids and points far from labeled RFEs, we can overcome the problem of long tail distribution. Our experiments demonstrate that our model surpasses the state-of-the-art in multi-label classification tasks and can address long-tailed distribution in our dataset. Ablation studies and qualitative analyses provide further insights into the benefits of our approach. \subsection*{Generalizable Insights about Machine Learning in the Context of Healthcare} In recent years, deep learning has been applied to various applications in healthcare. A primary characteristic of using deep learning for healthcare is addressing the lack of large annotated data. It is typically costly and time-consuming to collect a large labeled dataset, as annotations must be provided by healthcare professionals, and datasets cannot be easily shared between institutions when dealing with sensitive and high-risk data. On the other hand, deep models usually require large datasets to perform accurately and robustly. Consequently, many AI applications in healthcare remain inaccessible, and significant real-world impacts are delayed. Most prior work on active learning focuses on classification when the dataset is balanced. However, in many healthcare applications, the dataset exhibits a long-tailed distribution, and the task is to identify all the correct labels (rather than a single correct class). Similarly, previous active learning strategies typically assume that only one label is valid per data point. In our paper, we demonstrate the importance of ``multilabel'' classification—a data point can have multiple correct labels. Equally importantly, for each data point, correctly identifying all labels and not missing any is crucial for the subsequent task of history taking. In this work, we propose a new algorithm for actively selecting the most informative examples to label for the multi-label classification task. Our method leverages the latent space of the machine learning model to overcome the long-tailed distribution of data and to select a diverse set of data points covering a wide range of inputs.

text: Facilitating autonomous robots to address a variety of complex manipulation tasks has been a significant challenge for many years. Recently, deep reinforcement learning (DRL) methods have made substantial progress in designing robot manipulation behaviors that are challenging to engineer manually~\cite{kalashnikov2018qtopt, openai2019learning,openai2019solving,kalashnikov2021mtopt}. However, current DRL models struggle with long-horizon tasks due to the exploration challenge, as the robot must explore an excessively large space of potential behaviors to complete a task. To alleviate the exploration burden, previous DRL research has developed several temporal abstraction frameworks to leverage the hierarchical structure of manipulation tasks~\cite{coreyes18sectar,nachum2018hiro,bacon2016optioncritic,eysenbach2019sorb}. These approaches learn low-level controllers, often referred to as \textit{skills} or \textit{options}, alongside high-level controllers through trial-and-error. While they have shown better scalability than standard DRL methods, they frequently encounter high sample complexity, lack of interpretability, and fragile generalization. Meanwhile, extensive research in robotics over the years has produced a comprehensive set of functional modules specialized in specific robot behaviors, such as grasping~\cite{bohg2014graspsurvey} and motion planning~\cite{karaman2011rrtstar,ijspeert2013dmps}. These pre-constructed functional modules, termed \emph{behavior primitives}, demonstrate a high level of robustness and reusability for achieving particular manipulation objectives, like picking up objects with the end-effector and guiding the robot to a target configuration via a collision-free path. Despite their specialization, it remains challenging for DRL algorithms to utilize them as foundational elements to construct complex tasks. The difficulty primarily arises because these behavior primitives are inherently \textit{heterogeneous}. They accept non-uniform parameters as input, function at different temporal resolutions, and display varied behaviors. This necessitates an algorithm capable of reasoning about the temporal decomposition of a complex task and adaptively composing these behavior primitives as needed. Various hierarchical modeling strategies in robotics have employed behavior modules as foundational components. Notably, task-and-motion planning~\cite{kaelbling2011hpn, garrett2020tamp, wang2021comptamp} and neural programming~\cite{xu2018neural, huang2019neural} methods have utilized primitives like motion planners and pick-and-place controllers to model manipulation tasks in a compositional manner. These approaches require well-defined domain knowledge for task planning or substantial human supervision to train a high-level controller with accurate task decomposition. These assumptions constrain the scalability of these methods in practical tasks. In this study, we present MAPLE~(\textbf{Ma}nipulation \textbf{P}rimitive-augmented reinforcement \textbf{Le}arning), a comprehensive DRL algorithm that leverages a collection of pre-built behavior primitives to address long-horizon manipulation tasks. To tackle the exploration challenge faced by DRL algorithms, our approach employs a library of high-level behavior primitives (such as grasping or pushing objects) alongside low-level motor actions to autonomously learn a hierarchical policy (see \cref{fig:overview}). Our algorithm treats each behavior primitive as an implementation-agnostic controller that generates a temporally extended behavior. At a specific state, our DRL policy calls upon a behavior primitive (or an atomic motor action) and configures it with input parameters. For instance, the input parameters for a 6-DoF grasping module might be the pre-grasp end-effector pose. The chosen primitive interprets the input parameters and performs one or a sequence of motor actions to execute its specialized behavior. By incorporating behavior primitives into DRL algorithms, MAPLE~mitigates a significant portion of the complexity in manipulation planning, while allowing a general reinforcement learning algorithm the flexibility to uncover the compositional structure of tasks without extensive domain knowledge. Additionally, by retaining low-level motor actions, MAPLE~can depend on these actions for task stages where the finite library of behavior primitives cannot adequately express a desired behavior. We perform a comprehensive set of experiments on a collection of eight manipulation tasks with varying complexities in the robosuite simulation framework~\cite{robosuite2020}. We compare our method to conventional DRL approaches~\cite{haarnoja2018sac} that rely solely on low-level motor actions, hierarchical DRL methods that learn options~\cite{zhang2019dac,nachum2018hiro,chitnis2020schema}, or open-loop task schemas~\cite{chitnis2020schema}. MAPLE~achieves a $70\%$ improvement in task success rate compared to using only atomic actions, emerging as the sole method that consistently solved all single-arm tasks in the standard robosuite benchmark. We also develop a data-driven metric to quantitatively assess the compositionality of manipulation tasks based on the available primitives, providing new insights into the challenges and opportunities of compositional modeling for realistic manipulation tasks. We emphasize three contributions of this work: 1) We create a novel method that enhances standard DRL algorithms with pre-defined behavior primitives to alleviate the exploration burden; 2) We demonstrate the effectiveness of our method in solving diverse manipulation tasks and quantitatively analyze the compositional structure of these tasks; and 3) We illustrate that the modularity and abstraction provided by the behavior primitives facilitate knowledge transfer of the learned policies to new task variants and physical hardware.

Recent deep reinforcement learning methods have had great success in learning robot behaviours that are difficult to design by hand [Kalashnikov2018QTOP, OpenAI 2019 Learning, OpenAI 2019 Solving, Kalashnikov 21 mTOP]. However, the current DRL methods struggle with long-term tasks due to the exploration problem, where the robot has to explore too many potential actions to accomplish the task. Moreover, a large amount of robot research has yielded a large number of pre-built functions specialized in specific robot behavior, such as grasping (cf. Bohg, 2014, grasp-surv), motion planning (cf. Karaman, 2011rrt-star, cf. Ijspeert, 2013), etc. While these functions have shown better scalability than standard DRL methods, they often suffer from high sample complexity, lack of interpretability, and fragile generalization. To relieve this exploration burden, past DRL research has developed several temporal abstraction frameworks to exploit the hierarchical structure of the manipulation task. These preconstructed functions, called ‘behaviour primitives’ (emphasis added), have proven very robust and re-usable for achieving certain manipulation goals such as grasping objects with the end-effector, or guiding the robot to a target configuration along a collision-free path. Despite their specialisation, they remain a challenge for DRL-algorithms to use as the foundation for more complex tasks. This is especially difficult because the primitives are inherently heterogeneous; they accept input with different characteristics, have different temporal resolutions, and behave differently. The hierarchical modeling of robots has been the basis of many of its modeling strategies, including the task-and-motion planning strategy (Kaelbling, 2009, Garrett, 2020, Wang, 2021). Both task-and-motion planning and neural-network based modeling (Kaelbling, 2011, Garrett, 2020, Wang, 2021) have used primitives like motion planners and pick-and-place controllers to model manipulation tasks compositionally. The need to compose the primitives into a suitable hierarchy requires an algorithm that is capable of reasoning about the temporal decomposition of a complex task and composing the behavior primitives accordingly. In order to overcome the exploration problem of DRL methods, we propose to use a library of high-level primitives of action (grasp and push of objects) and a library of low-level actions to learn a hierarchical policy. These methods require for a task planning well-defined domain knowledge or a high-level controller that has been carefully supervised. At each state, our DRL policy calls a primitive action or a solitary motor command and passes on to it the required inputs. The inputs for a six-degree-of-freedom grasping-mode could include the end-effector position before grasping. These assumptions limit the scalability of these methods for practical tasks. Each behavior primitive is thus conceived as an implementation-independent controller which performs a sequence of motor actions. The selected primitive receives the inputs, carries out one or several motor actions in order to perform its specialized behavior. By introducing behavior primitives into DRL, MAPLE has been able to simplify the planning of a simple grasp, and has thus been able to reduce the complexity of the task of learning a simple grasp without a large amount of prior knowledge of the domain. We compare our method with conventional DRL approaches (cited in, Haarnoja, 2018sac) that rely only on low-level motor actions, with hierarchical DRL methods that learn options (cited in, Nachum, 2018hiro, Chitnis, 2020schema, and Chitnis,, and open-loop task schemas (cited in, Chitnis, ). We make three main contributions to the field: Firstly, we have developed a novel method to augment standard DRL algorithms with pre-defined action primitives, which reduce the exploration burden; Secondly, we have shown the effectiveness of our method in solving a variety of tasks, and quantified the compositional structure of these tasks; and thirdly, we have shown that the modularity and abstraction of the action primitives enables learned policies to be transferred to new task variants and physical hardware. We achieve a 70 per cent improvement over using only atomic actions. We have developed a data-driven metric to determine the compositionality of the task based on the primitives available. It provides a new way of evaluating the challenges and opportunities in modelling the compositionality of realistic tasks.

text: \input{images/figure1} Natural language processing (NLP) systems are available for only a small fraction of the world's more than 6,000 living languages, primarily due to the lack of resources necessary for training and evaluating models. Technological advancements are predominantly focused on languages with readily available data, leaving most other languages neglected~\cite{joshi2020state}. This issue is particularly pronounced for endangered languages, which face extinction risks due to declining numbers of native speakers and younger generations adopting other languages. For the majority of endangered languages, obtaining \emph{any} data is a significant challenge. In numerous instances, natural language text in these languages does exist. However, it is often inaccessible in machine-readable formats, such as paper books, scanned images, and unstructured web pages. These include publications from local publishers within communities speaking endangered languages, such as educational or cultural materials. Additionally, linguists documenting these languages often produce data like word lists and interlinear glosses, frequently in the form of handwritten notes. Examples from such scanned documents are illustrated in~\autoref{fig:dataset_example}. Digitizing textual data from these sources will not only facilitate NLP for endangered languages but also support linguistic documentation, preservation, and accessibility initiatives. In this study, we develop a benchmark dataset and propose a set of methods to extract data from these resources, concentrating on scanned images of paper books containing endangered language text. Typically, this type of digitization necessitates an optical character recognition (OCR) system. However, the extensive textual data and transcribed images required to train state-of-the-art OCR models from the ground up are unavailable in the context of endangered languages. Instead, we focus on \emph{post-correcting} the output of an off-the-shelf OCR tool capable of handling various scripts. We demonstrate that targeted post-correction methods can substantially enhance performance on endangered languages. Although OCR post-correction is a relatively well-explored area, most existing methods depend on significant resources in the target language, including a substantial amount of textual data to train a language model~\cite{schnober-etal-2016-still,dong-smith-2018-multi,8978127} or to generate synthetic data~\cite{krishna-etal-2018-upcycle}. While these resources are readily available for high-resource languages, they are severely limited for endangered languages, hindering the direct application of existing post-correction methods in our context. As an alternative, we introduce a method that builds on previous models for OCR post-correction, implementing three improvements tailored to the data-scarce setting. First, we employ a \textbf{multi-source model} to incorporate information from the high-resource translations commonly found in endangered language books. These translations are usually in the region's \textit{lingua franca} (e.g., \autoref{fig:dataset_example} (a,b,c)) or the primary language of the documentary linguist (e.g., \autoref{fig:dataset_example} (d) from \citet{shangaji-elar}). Next, we introduce \textbf{structural biases} to facilitate learning from limited data. Finally, we incorporate \textbf{pretraining methods} to leverage the small amount of unannotated data available in endangered languages. \medskip \noindent We summarize our main contributions as follows: \begin{itemize}[leftmargin=*, itemsep=3pt] \item A benchmark dataset for OCR post-correction on three critically endangered languages: Ainu, Griko, and Yakkha. \item A systematic analysis of a general-purpose OCR system, showing that it is not robust in the data-scarce setting of endangered languages. \item An OCR post-correction method that adapts the standard neural encoder-decoder framework to the highly under-resourced endangered language setting, reducing both the character error rate and the word error rate by 34\% compared to a state-of-the-art general-purpose OCR system. \end{itemize}

text: Driving in a real-world environment, characterized by constantly changing dynamics and the presence of other actors (i.e., non-player characters or NPCs), is inherently a hazardous task. Each actor within the environment can substantially affect the driving decisions of the Ego actor\footnote{The actor being tested and controlled by the tester.} and restrict the available options for navigation and safety planning. In extreme situations, these actors, whether intentionally or unintentionally, can impede the Ego actor's ability to complete the task safely. Thus, every actor in the environment poses a potential risk to the Ego actor. In this paper, we define the risk posed by an actor by estimating its influence on the decision-making process of the Ego actor within a given environment. Clearly, the risk is then a function of: \begin{enumerate*}[label=(\roman*)] \item the environment (i.e., driving scenario), and \item the uncertainty associated with predicting the future trajectories of the Ego actor. \end{enumerate*} \textbf{Driving scenario.} A driving scenario specifies the initial position of the Ego actor and the trajectories of NPCs. With each additional NPC on the road, the safe trajectories available to the Ego actor (i.e., the navigable space) can be significantly constrained. Similarly, certain locations in the environment are riskier than others, as the navigable space may vary greatly from one location to another (e.g., driving in construction zones). This reduction in safe trajectories is analogous to risk because it necessitates more vigilant driving and reduces the fallback options available to the Ego agent in unforeseen situations. This is illustrated in \cref{fig:motivation}(a). \textbf{Uncertainty.} Risk increases if the Ego actor cannot accurately predict the future trajectory of the NPCs. The accuracy of predictions decreases due to unclear intentions or sudden changes in the intentions of other participants in the driving environment (e.g., a pedestrian suddenly stops or runs, emergency braking, or vehicle breakdowns), measurement noise (e.g., due to adverse weather), or imperfections in ML/AI models (e.g., a pedestrian is not detected). This is illustrated in \cref{fig:motivation}(b). It is important to note that human drivers implicitly and continuously evaluate the risk associated with both the driving scenario and the uncertainties in the actions of other actors to drive safely. Accidents occur when human drivers fail to assess the risk, which can happen when (i) driving under the influence or while distracted, (ii) drivers are less than fully skilled, and (iii) expectations are mismatched because an actor violated traffic rules or made sudden actions (e.g., braking). It is unsurprising that the risk is amplified in the case of AI/ML-operated actors due to aleatoric and epistemic noise. Therefore, it is critically important to develop methods and models to quantify and characterize this risk at runtime, not only to ensure safety (by minimizing risk) but also to understand and identify situations where risk is irreducible, thereby preparing the passenger for an imminent collision via emergency braking or deploying airbags. In this paper, we demonstrate the practical significance of a risk metric and its importance for ensuring safety. The key contributions of this work lie in defining a novel risk metric and demonstrating the use of the proposed metric to quantify the relative risk associated with each actor in a real-world driving scenario. Although this paper focuses solely on self-driving cars as a use case, our framework is general and can be applied to other autonomous systems such as aerial vehicles or ML-driven computer systems. \textbf{Related work.} There are primarily two lines of research associated with defensive driving: (i) identifying a safe distance from other actors assuming everyone adheres to the "duty-of-care" policies, and (ii) identifying out-of-training-distribution (OOD) scenarios to plan for the worst-case to avoid collisions. \textit{Duty-of-care approaches} such as Safety Force Field (SFF)~\cite{SafetyForceField} and Responsibility-Sensitive Safety (RSS)~\cite{shalev2017formal} aim to estimate the safe distance from other actors, assuming that everyone follows road rules. Additionally, the goal is to identify the responsible party in the event of a safety hazard. \textit{OOD} models such as \cite{pmlr-v119-filos20a} aim to identify driving scenarios where the Ego actor's future trajectory (i.e., plan) exhibits significant variance. Such variance can be characterized using an ensemble of models or diverse data. Under high variance, the Ego actor opts for the most pessimistic plan to avoid collisions. For example, in \cite{pmlr-v119-filos20a}, the Ego actor's plan is generated using a Bayesian imitative model, and the variance of the imitation prior relative to the model posterior is used as a proxy for identifying distribution shifts. Upon detecting a distribution shift, the Ego actor can plan for either the worst-case model or the average model. Finally, in another line of research~\cite{Philion_2020_CVPR}, authors quantify the impact of uncertainty on driving performance but do not quantify the quality of the generated plan in terms of safety. In contrast, our objective is to (i) assign risk associated with an actor or a driving scenario by characterizing its negative influence on the degree of freedom of the Ego actor's navigational choices, and (ii) quantify the risk associated with the current plan and proactively mitigate safety hazards. This allows us to identify interesting driving scenarios in offline mode and to select the safest plan to help the Ego actor drive defensively.

text: Knowledge graphs~(KGs), which represent facts using semantic graph structures, have been applied to various artificial intelligence tasks, such as recommendation~\cite{leiconversational,2021Learning}, dialogue generation~\cite{moon-etal-2019-opendialkg,leiinteractive}, and question answering~\cite{ChristmannRASW19,zhu2021retrieving}. In KGs, facts are represented as triples, \texttt{(head~entity, relation, tail~entity)}, where the head entity is connected to the tail entity through the relation. As new knowledge continuously emerges, the issue of KG incompleteness has sparked significant research interest in the link prediction task, which involves predicting missing links in KGs~\cite{simple}. Mainstream link prediction models~\cite{bordes2013translating,Dettmers2018Convolutional} learn embeddings for entities and relations, then use a scoring function to assess the validity of triples. However, we contend that using embedding learning in mainstream link prediction models leads to two primary issues: \begin{itemize}[leftmargin=*] \item[\small$\bullet$] \textit{Unbalanced relation distribution.} As illustrated in Figure~\ref{fig:intro}, the relation distribution in a standard KG learning resource~(i.e., FB15K-237~\cite{toutanova-chen-2015-observed}) is notably unbalanced. For instance, the frequencies of the relations \texttt{/film/film/language} and \texttt{/film/film/edited} differ significantly. Mainstream link prediction models assume sufficient training instances for all relations and pay little attention to few-shot relations, overlooking the fact that few-shot relation learning can greatly affect learning performance. \item[\small$\bullet$] \textit{Existence of unseen relations.} Real-world KGs are typically open and rapidly evolving, resulting in numerous zero-shot relations not present in standard learning resources, such as the relation {\texttt{/film/film/sequel}} in Figure~\ref{fig:intro}. Mainstream link prediction models cannot handle unseen relations, as there are no training instances to learn their embeddings. This limitation may hinder the application of these models in downstream tasks. \end{itemize} Recently, some efforts have been made to address these issues. \citet{Xiongoneshot}, \citet{shi2018open}, and \citet{ChenMeta} employed meta-learning or metric-based approaches to train on limited samples and quickly learn new few-shot relations. These studies show potential in few-shot relation learning, but they struggle with unbalanced relation distributions, mainly due to the high time cost of training numerous relations. More recently, \citet{DBLP:journals/corr/abs-1907-08937} and \citet{Qin2020GenerativeAZ} predicted unseen relations by extracting information from textual descriptions. They successfully completed the unseen relation prediction task, but these models are unsuitable for link prediction tasks, as textual descriptions are often noisy and cannot connect seen and unseen relations. Ideally, a link prediction model should jointly learn many-, few-, and zero-shot relations. Regarding joint relation learning, we observed that semantic correlations, which indicate the similarities of relations in semantics, can bridge the learning of many-, few-, and zero-shot relations. Consider Figure~\ref{fig:intro} as an example. The many-shot relation ``\texttt{/film/film/language}'', few-shot relation ``\texttt{/film/film/edited}'', and zero-shot relation ``\texttt{/film/film/sequel}'' all pertain to ``\texttt{film}''. Assuming that semantically similar relations should be close in embedding space~\cite{yang2014embedding}, it is logical to use semantic correlations, like the one in this example, to achieve joint relation learning. Inspired by this, we propose a \textbf{G}eneralized \textbf{R}elation \textbf{L}earning framework (abbreviated as GRL) based on learning semantic correlations. GRL can be integrated into a mainstream link prediction model to make it (1) insensitive to unbalanced relation distributions and (2) capable of learning zero-shot relations. Specifically, GRL is integrated into a link prediction model after the embedding learning phase. To optimize relation embedding, GRL extracts rich semantic correlations using an attention mechanism, combines different relations, and minimizes the classification-aware loss to embed these semantic correlations in the relation embeddings. This approach enhances the proximity of semantically similar relations in vector space and the distinction of dissimilar relations. Consequently, few-shot relations can acquire knowledge from semantically similar many-shot relations; for zero-shot relations, their most semantically similar relation can also be predicted. In our experiments, we enhance two base models (DistMult~\cite{yang2014embedding} and ConvE~\cite{Dettmers2018Convolutional}) by incorporating the proposed GRL framework across all relation classes, i.e., many, few, and zero-shot relations. Our work represents a significant step towards a comprehensive understanding of KGs and a generalized solution for relation learning in the link prediction task. Our contributions are as follows: \begin{itemize}[leftmargin=*] \item[\small$\bullet$] We carefully address two major issues with the embedding learning used by mainstream link prediction models and emphasize the need for jointly learning many-, few-, and zero-shot relations. \item[\small$\bullet$] We propose the GRL framework by leveraging rich semantic correlations between relations to make link prediction models insensitive to unbalanced relation distributions and capable of learning zero-shot relations. \item[\small$\bullet$] We conduct experiments on six benchmarks to evaluate the link prediction capability of GRL, demonstrating that GRL enables base link prediction models to perform effectively across many-, few-, and zero-shot relations. \end{itemize}

text: Trajectory planning for autonomous agents frequently employs a receding time horizon. When functioning in environments with other agents, such as in autonomous driving, these plans must consider a predicted future and incorporate properties like collision-avoidance by utilizing predictions of other agents' future actions. A challenge of this approach is that the resulting motion plans of the "ego" vehicle cannot account for the responses of other agents to its own decisions. A classic example of this issue is an autonomous vehicle's inability to merge into dense traffic because it cannot anticipate that other agents will yield space. Game-theoretic motion planners address these reactions by integrating planning and prediction. Specifically, they represent the intentions of other agents in the environment as optimization problems that each agent attempts to solve, producing an equilibrium solution. This equilibrium comprises a set of interacting trajectories for all agents; the ego agent can then adhere to its own equilibrium trajectory. A significant limitation of game-theoretic planning is its assumption that the intentions of other agents are known to the ego and that the agents behave rationally concerning those intentions. In practice, beyond the scope of game-theoretic planning, these objectives and intents can be estimated in real-time and planned for as contingencies \cite{hardy2013contingency}. In this paper, we tackle this challenge within the context of game-theoretic planning and introduce a multi-hypothesis framework that addresses this uncertainty and related coupling. Specifically, our approach assumes the ego agent maintains a discrete set of hypotheses about the intentions of other agents. These hypotheses have associated probabilities and model uncertainties regarding intentions such as possible lane changes, typical speeds, aversion to acceleration, etc. Given uncertainty of this kind, we propose creating distinct optimization problems for each agent, which, when optimized, produce trajectories that qualitatively represent the different hypotheses. Replicas of each agent (one for each hypothesis) are generated and assigned to the corresponding optimization problem. We present a novel method of formulating the resulting dynamic game that enables the ego agent to consider interactions with the replica agents based on the probability of their corresponding hypothesis. This formulation is crucial for reasoning about collision-avoidance constraints in a probabilistic manner. Modeling the problem in this manner results in a pragmatic approach to this general class of motion-planning problems that autonomous vehicles must address. Our method generates interactive trajectories among multiple agents while explicitly considering uncertainty about others' intentions. We anticipate that our method will facilitate more practical applications of game-theoretic planning for autonomous vehicles. This paper is organized as follows. \cref{sec:related_work} examines other methods for multi-agent planning, including game-theoretic methods and methods utilizing derivatives of rational choice models, which consider the uncertainty of other agents. \cref{sec:preliminaries} reviews concepts related to game-theoretic planning necessary to formalize our method, which is detailed in \cref{sec:methods}. In \cref{sec:results}, we provide empirical results of our method on various realistic driving scenarios, and finally, we offer concluding remarks in \cref{sec:conclusion}.

text: Recognizing multi-party speech from an arbitrary number of speakers with naturally occurring speech overlap in a far-field environment is a challenging research problem that has been extensively studied for years \cite{Hain2007_AMI,fox13b_interspeech,Liu2016_SWC2,Barker_2018}. This issue is commonly referred to as the ``cocktail party problem.'' Solving this problem is crucial for advancing speech technology and establishing the foundation for natural human-device voice interactions. In such interactions, the speech agent on a smart device is expected to navigate through multi-party conversations and provide the necessary support. To enable real-time human-device interactions, the \ac{ASR} system must deliver transcripts in a streaming manner for all speakers in the conversation. For enhanced privacy protection, the \ac{ASR} system design should support local operation on the device only, implying that the model must be lightweight and resilient to acoustic front-end limitations. All these factors underscore the importance of streaming speech recognition for an arbitrary number of speakers with potential speech overlaps using a single distant microphone. Traditionally, multi-speaker \ac{ASR} was approached with cascaded modules such as speech separation and speech recognition \cite{Isik_2016, Menne_2019, Settle_2018, von_Neumann_2020, Neumann_2020}. Due to system complexity and technical limitations in some modules, such systems are more suitable for offline applications where the complete audio recording is available before the transcription task begins. In recent years, research progress has been made in training joint models that directly optimize multi-speaker ASR performance \cite{Yu_2017_icassp, Yu_2017_interspeech, Qian_2018, Seki_2018, Chang_2019, Tripathi_2020}. Recently, \cite{k2020serialized} proposed joint multi-speaker speech recognition and speaker change detection for any number of speakers via \ac{SOT}, demonstrating its effectiveness on a simulated multi-speaker test set of LibriSpeechMix. Subsequently, \cite{kanda2021largescale} showed that \ac{SOT} is also effective on a real multi-speaker meeting corpus, and subsequent works \cite{kanda2020joint, kanda2021slt, kanda2021endtoend, kanda2021comparative} extended \ac{SOT} into speaker-attributed ASR capable of transcribing ``who spoke what'' in multi-speaker conversations with one integrated model. In parallel, recent research has also begun to focus on maintaining the same performance under streaming conditions. Two conceptually similar streaming multi-speaker ASR models based on a \ac{RNN-T} \cite{graves2012sequence}, namely \ac{MS-RNN-T} \cite{SklyarPiunovaLiu_streaming_rnnt_icassp2021} and \ac{SURT} \cite{Lu2021}, were concurrently proposed to enable time-synchronous decoding of partially overlapping speech, and \cite{Lu2021} was later extended with speaker identification in \cite{lu2021streaming}. \cite{SklyarPiunovaLiu_streaming_rnnt_icassp2021} conducted evaluations of \ac{MS-RNN-T} on single-speaker LibriSpeech and two-speaker LibriSpeechMix. It demonstrated that \ac{MS-RNN-T} achieves comparable performance with offline multi-speaker ASR systems on two-speaker test data and also enhances the system's robustness on the noisy single-speaker test-other partition of LibriSpeech. This work builds on \cite{SklyarPiunovaLiu_streaming_rnnt_icassp2021}, with the following contributions. First, we demonstrate the advantage of on-the-fly overlapping speech simulation over fixed pre-simulated data for training, resulting in a new low \ac{WER} on the two-speaker partition of LibriSpeechMix with a streamable model architecture. Second, we address the primary limitation of \ac{MS-RNN-T}, namely the strict restriction on the maximum number of speakers in the audio. Assuming there are up to two speakers overlapping at a time, the proposed \ac{MT-RNN-T} model can recognize speech from an arbitrary number of speakers. Additionally, we take the first step towards streaming rich transcription of multi-party speech by introducing segmentation tags. Lastly, we conduct an in-depth performance analysis using proposed evaluation metrics, \ac{ORC} WER and turn counting accuracy, and discuss potential future work.

text: \vspace{-0.2cm} Embedding models have been foundational algorithms for numerous machine learning applications such as Information Retrieval (IR)~\citep{croft2010search,baeza1999modern} and Natural Language Processing (NLP)~\citep{word2vec, glove, attention, bert) over the past decade. These models are evolved derivatives of low-rank approximation and Matrix Factorization techniques that were prevalent in recommendation systems before the advent of Deep Learning (DL). The main objective of embedding models is to map a straightforward and intuitive representation of an input into an abstract low-dimensional dense vector space. This mapping facilitates two primary functions: 1) customizing the vectors for specific downstream applications and 2) pre-processing and storing documents or products as vectors, thus enhancing the efficiency of the retrieval process (commonly involving matrix multiplication followed by sorting, which are well-suited to modern hardware such as GPUs). In addition to computational benefits, embedding models capture the semantic relationships between queries and products. A pertinent example is product prediction for services like Amazon. A user-entered query must be matched against millions of products, and the optimal search results must be displayed in a fraction of a second. With basic product data, it would be challenging to determine that products with 'aqua' in their titles are relevant to the query 'water'. Instead, by projecting all products into a dense low-dimensional vector space, a query can also be projected into the same space, allowing an inner product computation with all product vectors (typically a dot product). Products with the highest inner product can then be displayed. These projections can be trained to encapsulate semantic information and can be continuously updated to reflect temporal changes in customer preferences. To our knowledge, embedding models are the most widely used in the industry, especially for product and advertisement recommendations (Amazon's DSSM~\citep{dssm}, Facebook's DLRM~\citep{dlrm}). However, the scale of these problems has dramatically increased in recent years, prompting research into extreme classification tasks where the number of classes reaches several million. Consequently, methods such as Tree-based Models~\citep{prabhu2014fastxml,Pfastre,agrawal2013multi} and Sparse-linear Models~\citep{weston2013label,pdsparse,ppdsparse} have emerged as strong alternatives. Notably, Tree-based models are significantly faster to train and evaluate compared to other methods. Nevertheless, most real Information Retrieval systems have dynamically changing output classes, and all extreme classification models struggle to generalize to new classes with limited training data (\emph{e.g.}, new products being added to the catalog daily). This has led to the resurgence of embedding models for large-scale Extreme Classification~\citep{bi2013efficient,annexml,sleec,chen2012feature}. {\bf Our Contributions:} In this paper, we present a novel, unique, and compelling argument that sparse high-dimensional embeddings are superior to their dense low-dimensional counterparts. In this context, we make two intriguing design choices: 1) We design the label embeddings (\emph{e.g.}, products in the catalog) to be high-dimensional, super-sparse, and orthogonal vectors. 2) We keep the label embeddings fixed throughout the training process and learn only the input embeddings (one-sided learning), unlike typical dense models where both input and label embeddings are learned. As we employ a combination of {\bf S}parse, {\bf O}rthogonal, {\bf L}earned, and {\bf R}andom embeddings, we code-name our method {\bf SOLAR}. We provide a theoretical foundation for SOLAR by demonstrating that one-sided and two-sided learning are mathematically equivalent. Our choices result in a four-fold advantage over previous methods: \begin{itemize}[leftmargin=*,nosep,nolistsep] \itemsep0em \item {\bf Matrix Multiplication to Inverted-Index Lookup:} Sparse high-dimensional embeddings can retrieve a subset of labels using a simple inverted-index~\citep{croft2010search} lookup, limiting computation and sorting to those labels. This significantly improves inference speed. \item {\bf Load-balanced Inverted Index:} By enforcing the label embeddings to be near-orthogonal and equally sparse (and keeping them fixed), we ensure that all buckets in an inverted index are equally filled, and we sample approximately the same number of labels for each input. This eliminates the well-known imbalanced buckets issue where we sub-sample nearly all labels for popular inputs, thereby impairing inference speed. \item {\bf Learning to Hash:} An Inverted-Index can be viewed as a hash table where all output classes are hashed into a few buckets~\citep{kulis2009learning, wang2017survey}. By fixing the label buckets and learning to map inputs to the corresponding label buckets, we perform a 'partial learning to hash' task in hindsight (further details in Appendix A). \item {\bf Zero-communication:} Our unique construction of label embeddings allows for distributed training over multiple GPUs with zero communication. Thus, we can train on a 1.67 M book recommendation dataset and the three largest extreme classification datasets, outperforming the respective baselines on all four in both precision and speed. \end{itemize} \vspace{-0.5cm}

text: In the knowledge economy, substantial volumes of data are gathered to aid decision-making, policy analytics, and service delivery, among other purposes. Nevertheless, the usability of these data is limited by the disclosure risks associated with data processing in general and data sharing in particular. Anonymisation is one of the key tools employed to mitigate this risk. The Anonymisation Decision-Making Framework (ADF) operationalises the processes of functional anonymisation \cite{elliot2018functional}. This concept originated from the work of the \textit{data environment analysis service} \cite{elliot2010data}, a support system for the 2011 UK census that concentrated on data confidentiality and disclosure control \cite{willenborg2012elements,duncan2011concepts,hundepool2012SDC}, particularly focusing on re-identification risk assessment \cite{chen1998, skinner1998estimating,skinner2002measure}. The fundamental principle of this concept is that disclosure risk does not reside in the data themselves but in the relationship between the data and their environment. Mackey and Elliot define the data environment as "the set of formal and informal structures, processes, mechanisms, and agents that either: (i) act on data; (ii) provide interpretable context for those data; or (iii) define, control, and/or interact with those data" \cite{mackey2013understanding}. Data environments exist in various forms. Examples include the open data environment, an end-user license management data environment, and restricted access secure data environments, among others. Despite this diversity, the ADF framework presumes that all data environments can be characterized by four descriptive features: other data, agents, infrastructure, and governance. It follows from the preceding discussion that to apply the appropriate anonymisation processes, one must consider both the data and their environment. Elliot et al. \cite{elliot2020anonymisation} developed the ADF to operationalise precisely such a process. The ADF emphasizes that suitable anonymisation decisions for a particular set of data are only feasible by considering the relationship between the data and their environment(s), which they term the \textit{data situation}.\\ \vspace{-12pt} \textbf{\textit{Problem statement}.} \textit{Data situations are frequently dynamic, as data transition between environments for both processing and use. Therefore, understanding contextual risk and managing that risk through anonymisation necessitates an awareness of, and the ability to map, the data flows between environments.} Currently, capturing and mapping \textit{data situations} for analysis within the ADF framework is performed manually, which is labor-intensive and prone to errors. To automate this mapping, we propose the use of data provenance—a concept already informally mentioned in the ADF. By integrating provenance with the ADF, we will be able to track data flows and identify both existing and proposed upstream and downstream data situations. We note that data provenance has already been applied in modeling similar issues such as situation awareness and decision-making \cite{baclawski2017framework}, control of direct and indirect data flows \cite{rong2020provenance}, and big data security and privacy \cite{gao2020big}. W3C PROV is a standard for provenance interoperability and for representing the origins of data and how it has been processed \cite{PROV-DM15,missier2013w3c}. PROV provides an abstract data model that includes agents, entities, activities, and relationship properties, which enables the representation of the provenance of data and systems. A crucial aspect of linking provenance to the ADF is the representation of data environments. In the W3C PROV data model, two constructs, \textit{bundles} and \textit{namespaces}, might be considered potential candidates for such representation. In this paper, we assess the potential value of both these solutions. We also explore how the elements of PROV (i.e., Entity, Bundle, Agent, Activity) could be employed to represent data environment features (agents, other data, infrastructure, governance). We observe that there are limitations to representing data environments in this manner and suggest some modifications that would enable the full capture of the desired features. The contributions of this work are as follows: \vspace{-12pt} \begin{enumerate} \item We outline—using an ADF use case—the requirements for provenance in the representation of data environments (in section \ref{sec:usecase}). \item Based on these requirements, we propose four different approaches to apply and extend W3C PROV to enable the representation of data environments for machine-enabled reasoning (in section \ref{sec:impl}). \item We then analyze the four approaches (in section \ref{sec:analysis}) \end{enumerate}

text: The primary objective of this research is to develop a system for maintaining an \emph{audit trail} within the knowledge representation (KR) framework based on graph hierarchies as introduced in \cite{harmer2020knowledge}. This system aims to document the history of primarily small, localized updates to a large knowledge corpus represented by graphs and graph hierarchies, where storing the entire corpus at each historical point is impractical. The requirement for transformations to be reversible in our practical application context does not limit the operations available for updating a corpus; instead, it introduces a manageable overhead for storing additional information that enables the reversal of applied transformations. Additionally, we devise mechanisms for maintaining multiple corpus versions, which is essential for accommodating different knowledge versions that correspond to varying viewpoints of knowledge curators or inherent knowledge conflicts (e.g., conflicting experimental results, alternative hypotheses). The primary use cases for audit trails in KRs based on graph hierarchies include version control for updates in schema-aware graph databases as presented in \cite{bonifati2019schema} and updates to knowledge corpora provided by the bio-curation framework KAMI \cite{harmer2019bio}. An audit trail system with the desired capabilities relies heavily on: (1) the existence of an \emph{efficient semantic representation of object transformations} (or deltas), which eliminates the need to store the object's state at each point in its transformation history; (2) the \emph{reversibility of transformations}, ensuring that any sequence of transformations can be undone; and (3) the existence of reliable means for \emph{composing a pair of successive transformations}, which allows for efficient storage and switching between different versions of the same object. In this study, we define the three aforementioned components concerning both individual objects (Section \ref{s:preliminaries}), such as graphs, and hierarchies of objects (Section \ref{s:rulehierarchy}), and discuss how these components can be utilized to construct an efficient audit trail (Section \ref{s:audit}). We introduce a mathematical framework for constructing a traceable history of transformations based on the sesqui-pushout (SqPO) approach \cite{corradini2006sesqui}, which operates on individual objects and hierarchies of objects from suitably structured categories. A transparent audit trail provides insight into the history of object transformations and allows for reverting to any point within this history. This feature is particularly valuable when attempting to correct an erroneous transformation. Furthermore, such an audit trail facilitates the efficient accommodation of multiple versions of the same object, which may arise, for example, from inconsistent transformations. \subsection*{Related work} SqPO rewriting generalizes the double (DPO) and single (SPO) pushout approaches to graph transformation, allowing for the cloning of graph elements in addition to the familiar operations of adding, deleting, and merging graph elements. Although the reversibility of SqPO rewriting has been previously explored \cite{danos2014reversible}, the composition of consecutive (and not necessarily sequentially independent) SqPO rewrites has been less thoroughly developed. The construction of such compositions has been provided for the DPO approach (see D-concurrent productions in \cite{ehrig1991parallelism}) and for specific cases of the SqPO approach (where rules are linear \cite{behr2019sesqui} and where the right-hand side of the first applied rule is precisely the left-hand side of the second rule \cite{lowe2015polymorphic}). In this work, we present such a construction for two consecutive applications of general SqPO rules, where the first must be reversible. This was inspired by \cite{ehrig1991parallelism} and adapted to SqPO rewriting. For the composition to be well-defined, we require the underlying category to possess a structure that allows for well-behaved generalized unions of objects (more formally, we require our category to be adhesive \cite{lack2005adhesive}). The concept of rule hierarchy and the question of the reversibility and composition of hierarchy rewrites represent a novel direction that extends SqPO rewriting from individual objects to hierarchies of objects \cite{harmer2020knowledge}. Our primary application of interest, a transformation audit trail, closely relates to the version control systems (VCSs) used in software development. While such systems typically manage different versions of software source code (represented by text files), our audit trail provides similar control for different versions of a graph or a graph hierarchy. Like VCSs, the transformation audit trail avoids maintaining the state of an object at every transformation by retaining only its current state along with a compact representation of its transformation history. Additionally, by employing a mechanism akin to \emph{delta compression} in VCSs, such audit trails enable the maintenance of multiple versions of the same object and facilitate switching between these versions. The versioning of diagrams expressing object-oriented data models in the field of model-driven engineering is closely related to audit trails for graph transformations because such model diagrams can be viewed as graphs with attributes. However, work in this domain \cite{schneider2004coobra, barmpis2015towards} typically considers the operations of adding and deleting graph elements (including attributes) to express changes to the data model, but largely omits those of cloning and merging, as these operations are challenging to interpret in the context of data modeling, whereas these operations are highly relevant in the context of KR. There is an extensive body of work on versioning for database systems \cite{salzberg1999comparison}, including graph databases\footnote{Versioning for the Neo4j database \url{https://github.com/h-omer/neo4j-versioner-core}} \cite{castelltort2013representing, khurana2013efficient}. Such systems are typically divided into snapshot- and delta-based classes (also known as copy and log), where the former stores snapshots of the entire database at different points in the revision history, while the latter preserves the transformation log. In this context, our system falls into a rather hybrid category: while the audit trail stores representations of transformations (logs), these logs themselves consist of subgraphs, i.e., graph patterns affected as a result of transformation. A different classification of versioning systems for graph databases divides them into those that provide the revision history from the perspective of individual nodes and edges (or relationships) and those that use the graph perspective \cite{castelltort2013representing}. While existing tools, such as \texttt{neo4j-versioner-core} or the one presented in \cite{castelltort2013representing}, primarily address versioning from the perspective of individual elements, our framework allows for versioning of the entire graph and even the hierarchy of graphs. Moreover, as with model versioning, existing database versioning techniques do not permit recording the operations of cloning and merging graph elements.

text: Recently, there has been significant progress in deep-learning-based methods for point cloud generation and completion, utilizing the autoencoder architecture. Techniques such as PointNet \cite{qi2016pointnet}, PointNet++ \cite{qi2017pointnetplusplus}, DGCNN \cite{dgcnn}, and Point Transformer \cite{zhao2020point} have thoroughly investigated encoders to achieve improved point cloud representations. Numerous methods also focus on the design of decoders. For instance, \cite{Fan_2017_CVPR, achlioptas2017latent_pc, yuan2018pcn, Yang_Wu_Zhang_Jin_2021} employ fully connected layers to produce coarse outputs. Studies such as \cite{Yang_2018_CVPR, groueix2018, liu2019morphing, Wen_2020_CVPR} transform 2D squares into 3D surfaces. As illustrated in Figure \ref{fig:introduction}(a), fully connected layers and folding operations are two prevalent techniques for converting latent features into point clouds. However, these methods do not thoroughly investigate the transformation concerning point constraints, network parameters, data flow, and convergence speed. As depicted in the upper airplane of Figure \ref{fig:introduction}(b), point clouds generated by the FC-based method often exhibit outliers and uneven surfaces. This occurs because the generated points do not share parameters, meaning each point has limited available parameters. When expanded to multiple branches, the resulting point clouds lack self-clustering properties. Self-clustering implies that points generated by each branch cluster together, reflecting an object's locality. text: \begin{wrapfigure}{r}{0.45\textwidth} \vspace{-40pt} \begin{center} \end{center} \vspace{-0.5cm} \caption{Quantization intervals utilized in the proposed method and prior works.} \vspace{-0.7cm} \end{wrapfigure} Recently, Federated Learning (FL)~\cite{mcmahan2017fl_google} has become a leading approach to address the significant demands on data privacy and computational resources. It enables numerous edge devices, referred to as workers, to collaboratively train a model without sharing private data. Due to FL's effectiveness, it has been extensively adopted in various practical applications, such as keyboard prediction~\cite{hard2018keyboard_prediction_fl, yang2018applied_keyboard} and privacy-sensitive services~\cite{sheller2018multi_institutional,sheller2018multi_brain_fl,pokhrel2020fl_block_chain}. However, during FL model training, model weights and gradients are frequently transmitted between the server and workers. As model complexity increases, communication costs inevitably become the primary bottleneck of FL systems. To address this issue, numerous studies have attempted to apply quantization to model weights~\cite{yu2019double_quantization,tang2019doublesqueeze} or gradients~\cite{wen2017terngrad,alistarh2017qsgd} to reduce the size of model update messages. Although these studies have made significant progress, they often struggle to train models with performance comparable to float-based non-compressed training when heavy compression is applied. Additionally, we observe that low-bit quantization may impair other widely used techniques (e.g., gradient sparsification~\cite{aji2017sparse_top_k,strom2015scalable_top_k}), which restricts further cost reductions. In this work, we introduce a novel quantization method based on the cosine function, which is simple yet effective for quantizing model weights and gradients for round-trip compression. Inspired by the key observation that gradients and model weights with larger magnitudes are more informative~\cite{han2015deep_compression,lin2018deep_gradient_compression,aji2017sparse_top_k}, we utilize the non-linearity of cosine functions to minimize quantization errors of extreme values, whereas most prior works~\cite{alistarh2017qsgd,han2015deep_compression} pursue an opposite objective, as illustrated in Fig.~\ref{fig:teaser}. Moreover, our method has low time/space complexity, requires \textit{no} additional training, and incurs minimal additional cost, making it particularly advantageous for federated learning systems, as edge devices often have limited hardware resources. We conduct extensive experiments under various scenarios on CIFAR-10 for image classification and the BraTS 2019 dataset for 3D volume segmentation. Our contributions are summarized as follows: (a) As the primary contribution, we propose a \textit{simple-yet-effective} cosine-based quantization scheme. It better preserves model performance, has low time/space complexity, and requires no additional training, making it applicable to a wide range of distributed learning problems. (b) Our proposed quantization can be used to compress model weights and gradients, thereby reducing overall communication costs in federated learning. (c) Our method is flexible and compatible with many existing useful techniques, such as gradient sparsification. By combining our quantization with other techniques, our system can achieve model performance similar to float-based non-compressed training at very high compression ratios, which is challenging for other quantization methods to achieve.

text: Numerous scenarios in software transformation and security necessitate the analysis or manipulation of a given program binary. The most typical situation arises when the source code of the binary is unavailable. Even when the source code is available, we might lack the toolchain or environment required to compile the transformed source, or we might be interested in analyses dependent on the actual machine code in the binary, such as the amount of padding around functions or buffers. In these contexts, the initial step of the analysis often involves \emph{disassembling} the binary, which is the process of converting its machine code into assembly code. The examination of \emph{disassembly} and the associated tool \emph{disassemblers} dates back to at least 1980~\cite{Horspool+Marovac:1980:AnApproach}. Recently, the precision of many disassemblers is nearing or even surpassing $99\percent$ on numerous real-world binaries—see, e.g.,~\cite{Andriesse+etal:2016:in-depth} and~\cite{Flores-Montoya+Schulte:2020:ddisasm}. Unfortunately, due to well-documented issues in binary analysis such as indirect jump resolution and function start identification, the proverbial "last $1$\percent" remains a challenge in disassembly. In response, our community has continued to develop innovative disassembly algorithms, with new research and enhancements appearing frequently—see, e.g.,~\cite{Flores-Montoya+Schulte:2020:ddisasm}, \cite{Miller+etal:2019:probabilistic}, and new versions of various existing disassemblers. Comparing highly accurate disassemblers is challenging for two reasons. First, since different disassemblers may have distinct weaknesses, a small alteration to the set of binaries used for evaluation can significantly change their accuracy ranking. Unfortunately, to date, publications in the disassembly literature tend to utilize different target sets; see, e.g., ~\cite{Andriesse+etal:2016:in-depth} vs. \cite{Flores-Montoya+Schulte:2020:ddisasm}. Second, as the accuracy of current disassemblers exceeds $99\percent$ on many binaries, we require nearly $100\percent$-accurate ground truth to rank the disassemblers reliably. However, as this paper will demonstrate, while previous research often did not elaborate on their ground truth generation methods, our own experience indicates that generating accurate ground truth is complex and not easily reproducible without a detailed description. For these reasons, we believe it is time for our community to begin standardizing a set of community-accepted binaries for benchmarking disassemblers on their accuracy and, for practical purposes, their execution time and memory usage. To facilitate this process, this paper introduces a preliminary version of our ongoing disassembly benchmark suite. We will discuss the design of our suite from two perspectives: (a) the set of binaries included, and (b) our method for generating accurate disassembly ground truth on the instructions in these binaries. Regarding aspect (a), we believe an effective disassembly benchmark suite should possess the following characteristics: \begin{enumerate*}[(i)] \item The included binaries should be \emph{diverse} in size, type (e.g., editor vs. web server), compilers used, and optimization settings applied. Achieving this would allow the binaries to better reflect the complexities in real-world binaries. \item The number of included binaries should be \emph{moderate}, meaning sufficiently large but not excessive. This would ensure the feasibility of evaluating disassemblers over every included binary, whose number increases multiplicatively with the number of included compilers and optimization settings in each included ISA-OS pair. \end{enumerate*} Currently, our benchmark suite is organized by a concept of "project names," which includes an open-source project and a specific version (e.g., \verb!openssh-7.1p2!). For each project name, we specify a particular target binary within (e.g., \verb!sshd!) and the set of ISA-OS pairs (e.g., \{x86-Linux, x64-Linux\}) that we include when building this project. Additionally, for each ISA-OS pair, we specify the list of compiler-version pairs and the list of optimization settings we include during the build, which will be detailed in~\S\ref{sec:current-benchmark}. To encourage adoption, we maintain our benchmark suite openly on GitHub (\url{https://github.com/pangine/disasm-benchmark}), hoping it will evolve over time similarly to the SPEC CPU benchmark~\cite{misc:speccpu} due to community contributions and future research. Regarding aspect (b), while one might assume that generating disassembly ground truth is merely a matter of having the compiler save the generated assembly code (e.g., \verb!gcc -S!), we find this to be an oversimplification in practice. First, even assuming we have all the generated assembly files, the assembly statements (instructions/directives) in these files do \emph{not} provide a complete description of the machine code in the binary, as some assembly statements allow multiple machine code encodings. Second, during the development of our current benchmark suite, we identified numerous corner cases that needed to be addressed when collecting the generated assembly files, extracting information from them, and representing such information. In~\S\ref{sec:gt}, we will discuss these challenges and our solutions to them. Finally, using our ongoing benchmark suite and our (already mature) ground truth generator and disassembler evaluator, we will present in~\S\ref{sec:eval} our findings on four prominent open-source disassemblers: BAP~\cite{misc:bap}, Ghidra~\cite{misc:ghidra}, Radare2~\cite{misc:radaretwo}, and ROSE~\cite{misc:rose}. Our findings largely align with~\cite{Andriesse+etal:2016:in-depth}: (i) function start identification remains a significant issue that hinders accurate disassembly, and (ii) linear-sweep disassembly~\cite{Schwarz+etal:2002:Disassembly} can be \emph{incidentally} highly accurate, although it cannot guarantee perfect accuracy and thus cannot be relied upon as a long-term solution. In summary, our contributions in this work are: \begin{enumerate*} \item We propose beginning to standardize a set of binaries from diverse projects compiled with multiple compilers and optimization settings for disassembler evaluation and present our work-in-progress suite as a starting point for community discussion. \item We developed a new system based on a widely-supported compiler toolchain feature known as "listing files" to generate accurate disassembly ground truth. We also developed support programs to evaluate four prominent open-source disassemblers against our ground truth and present our findings. \item We open-source all our code and data to enable future studies and to encourage community adoption of and contribution to our system and our benchmark suite. \end{enumerate*}
