text: Phishing websites represent a significant social-engineering threat, with their numbers having markedly increased in recent years~\cite{phishincreasing:2020,data-breach:2020}. To mitigate these attacks, the security community has made sustained efforts through automated tools that employ advanced machine learning~\cite{sahingoz2019machine,rao2019detection,hassanpour2018phishing,abdelhamid2017phishing}, deep learning~\cite{yang2019phishing,yi2018web,hassanpour2018phishing}, rule-based~\cite{moghimi2016new,sonowal2020phidma,tan2016phishwho,shirazi2018kn0w}, and heuristic~\cite{nguyen2013detecting,babagoli2019heuristic,jeeva2016intelligent,sreedharan2016systems} techniques. However, phishing websites are inherently elusive, frequently adapting to exploit various loopholes and adversarial strategies to evade detection by automated tools~\cite{liang2016cracking,rajivan2018creative,royremains,aleroud2020bypassing}. Consequently, domain hosting services, antiphishing tools, and web browsers often rely on one or more phishing feeds or blocklists, which are curated knowledge bases containing a frequently updated list of phishing URLs, added either manually or through a combination of automated discovery, manual reporting, and human verification. As Oest et al.~\cite{oest2020phishtime} have noted, phishing feeds are \textit{reactive} by nature, with a significant delay between the emergence of a website and its subsequent reporting. Nonetheless, these feeds typically undergo some form of manual evaluation, ideally rendering them less error-prone than automated detection systems. In this study, we examine phishing reports shared on Twitter~\cite{twitter:2021}, the widely used micro-blogging platform. To our knowledge, this is the first study to evaluate this resource as a substantial knowledge base for identifying new phishing websites, and throughout this paper, we focus on assessing its effectiveness and comparing its characteristics and performance with two other popular open-source phishing feeds—PhishTank and OpenPhish. Specifically, this paper: (i) Assesses the reliability and volume of information shared by these phishing reports and how they compare to two other open-source phishing feeds. (ii) Being hosted on Twitter, these reports can also be visibly interacted with by other users on the platform, a feature unavailable in the other two phishing feeds we study. We thus evaluate the frequency of these interactions, including those from domain registrars and organizations targeted by the reported phishing URLs, and examine the impacts of these interactions on the detection/removal of the reported URLs. (iii) We also analyze the aftermath of sharing these reports, i.e., how long the URLs remain active after being reported, as well as how quickly anti-phishing tools detect them. Both are factors that can protect the user from inadvertently accessing the threat. We collected and analyzed over 16k tweets containing 11k unique URLs from June 21 to August 17, 2021. Using a combination of automated and manual investigations, we repeatedly tracked various properties extracted from these posts, including checking the activity of these URLs, anti-phishing tool detection, information shared by these posts (such as relevant hashtags, images, etc.), true positive rate (percentage of URLs that are legitimate phishing attacks), and interactions with other users (likes, comments, and replies). We also compared the relevant statistics with two other phishing feeds—PhishTank and OpenPhish. In Section~\ref{datacollection}, we outline how we collected the phishing reports from Twitter and characterize them based on the domains they are hosted on. In Section~\ref{driveby}, we discuss several drive-by download URLs also reported by these accounts, a feature absent from the other two feeds. In Section~\ref{comparison}, we evaluate the information shared by these phishing reports (\ref{content-shared-by-reporters}), as well as by PhishTank (\ref{phishtank-share}) and OpenPhish (\ref{openphish-share}). We focus on the information shared by these reports (such as screenshots, IP addresses, names of targeted registrars/organizations, labeling of threats, etc.), as well as their reliability and validity in Section~\ref{validity-url}. Our sole goal in this section is to evaluate how the information shared by phishing reports on Twitter compares with the offerings from PhishTank and OpenPhish, which is later summarized in \textbf{Table~\ref{functionality}}. Unlike the two other phishing feeds, which usually do not allow user interaction, in Section~\ref{phishing-report-interactions}, we find the volume of interactions (favorites/retweets/comments) that these reports receive on Twitter, and whether interaction from the targeted domain/organization impacts how quickly these reported websites are removed. We also qualitatively explore the nature of these interactions (Fig~\ref{fig:interaction}) and determine the technological proficiency of users who typically interact with these reports (\ref{followers}). Finally, in Section~\ref{activity-website}, we determine how long these URLs remain active after being reported and how the rate (and pace) of removal compares with URLs posted on PhishTank and OpenPhish (Section~\ref{comparison}). We also check for the coverage of the phishing URLs by anti-phishing engines~\ref{virustotal-coverage}. Our main findings can be summarized as follows: \begin{enumerate} \item Twitter is a viable candidate for use as a knowledge base for phishing reports. Over three months, users consistently shared over 16.4k such reports covering 11.1k unique URLs hosted by 203 unique registrars and targeting 146 different organizations. Unlike PhishTank and OpenPhish, these accounts also reported URLs distributing drive-by downloads (7\%). \item The majority of URL reports from Twitter contained more information compared to PhishTank and OpenPhish, which can assist domain registrars and anti-phishing tools in expediting the threat identification process. \item The URLs shared in these reports have a high true positive rate (87\%), with only one account contributing to the majority (11\%) of the false positives in our dataset. \item These reports receive very low engagement, with only 13.8\% of the posts receiving at least one comment. The domain registrars and organizations targeted by the reported URLs (referred to as \textit{targets} henceforth) contributed to only 4\% of these comments. However, when they did respond to these reports, the URLs became inactive more quickly compared to URLs that do not receive such interaction. Moreover, only 10.2\% of the targets follow at least one such phishing report account, indicating that they are either unaware of these reporting accounts or do not consider them a credible source. \item 31\% of these reported URLs remain active even after a week of their first appearance in our dataset. Moreover, anti-phishing tools consistently have lower detection rates for at least 27\% of the URLs when compared to URLs appearing in other phishing feeds. \end{enumerate} Thus, our evaluation indicates that phishing reports shared on Twitter are a reliable and efficient source for conveying information regarding new phishing websites. Relying on these reports can help domain registrars and anti-phishing tools expedite the process of identifying newer phishing threats. Additionally, based on the volume of information shared by these reports, it proves to be a valuable resource for researchers in building detailed ground truth datasets with less effort and more efficiency compared to other open phishing feeds like PhishTank and OpenPhish. We explore our findings in greater detail from the proceeding section onwards.

text: Image classification is a well-established yet crucial task with numerous applications, including autonomous driving, industrial automation, medical diagnosis, and biometric identification~\cite{autonomous_driving, industrial_automation, medical_diagnosis, biometric_identification}. Supervised learning (SL) techniques have been widely employed to address this task due to their effectiveness~\cite{VGG, ResNet}. A well-known limitation of SL is the necessity for a substantial amount of training data for each class to be identified. Unfortunately, in many real-world situations, gathering training data for certain classes is challenging (e.g., endangered species and newly discovered species such as COVID-19 variants). When there are \textit{unseen} classes for which training data is unavailable, SL-based models tend to be biased towards the \textit{seen} classes, hindering the identification of the unseen classes. Recently, to address this limitation, a method has been proposed to train a classifier using manually annotated attributes (e.g., color, size, and shape; see Fig.~\ref{fig:CUB})~\cite{zsl_proposal, gzsl_intro}. The central concept of this method, known as generalized zero-shot learning (GZSL), is to learn the relationship between images and attributes from seen classes and then apply the trained model to identify unseen classes. In~\cite{ALE}, for instance, a method to identify unseen classes by assessing the compatibility between image features and attributes has been proposed. In~\cite{CVAE-GZSL}, a network that synthesizes image features from attributes has been used to generate training data for unseen classes. For extracting image features, a network trained on classification tasks (e.g., ResNet~\cite{ResNet}) is commonly used. A potential limitation of this extraction method is that the image feature may include attribute-irrelevant information (e.g., human fingers in Fig.~\ref{fig:CUB}), which can interfere with learning the relationship between the image and the attribute~\cite{DLFZRL, RFF-GZSL, Disentangled-VAE}. In this paper, we introduce a novel GZSL technique that eliminates interference caused by attribute-irrelevant information. The core idea of the proposed method is to extract the \textit{semantic feature}, which contains attribute-related information, from the image feature and then utilize it to learn the relationship between the image and the attribute. To extract the semantic feature, we employ a modified autoencoder comprising two encoders, namely, \textit{semantic} and \textit{residual} encoders (see Fig.~\ref{fig:SD}). In essence, the semantic encoder captures all attribute-related information in the image feature, while the residual encoder captures attribute-irrelevant information. In a conventional autoencoder, only reconstruction loss (the difference between the input and the reconstructed input) is used for training. In our approach, to ensure the semantic encoder captures only attribute-related information, we introduce two novel loss functions in addition to the reconstruction loss. First, we apply a mutual information (MI)-based loss to maximize (minimize) MI between the semantic (residual) encoder output and the attribute. Since MI measures the dependency between two random variables, using the MI-based loss allows us to encourage the semantic encoder to capture attribute-related information while discouraging the residual encoder from capturing any attribute-related information. Consequently, all attribute-related information is captured solely by the semantic encoder. Second, we employ a similarity-based loss to prevent the semantic encoder from capturing attribute-irrelevant information. For instance, when a bird image includes human fingers (see Fig.~\ref{fig:CUB}), we aim to exclude features related to the finger from the semantic encoder output. To achieve this, we maximize the similarity between the semantic encoder outputs of images belonging to the same class (e.g., bird images). Since attribute-irrelevant features are present in only a few image samples (e.g., human fingers in a few bird images), maximizing the similarity between semantic encoder outputs of the same class allows us to remove attribute-irrelevant information from the semantic encoder output. Through extensive experiments using various benchmark datasets (AwA1, AwA2, CUB, and SUN), we demonstrate that the proposed approach significantly outperforms traditional GZSL techniques. For instance, for the AwA2 and CUB datasets, our model achieves a 2\% improvement in GZSL classification accuracy over state-of-the-art techniques.

text: Clique finding is a well-explored subject within the graph community, with numerous intriguing practical applications in community detection \cite{6249683, palla2005uncovering, 7117352, fang2019efficient} and social network analysis \cite{4811845, rossi2015parallel}. Recently, the data mining community has integrated clique finding into deep learning classifiers to improve recommender systems in social networks \cite{dietrec, movierec}. Clique finding is extensively utilized in bioinformatics, where researchers employ graph models to identify variants in gene sequences \cite{variant}, efficiently cluster related genes in a database \cite{database}, and conduct protein structure analysis \cite{ppi}. The rapid increase in social media users and the vast size of genomic data have heightened the demand for high-performance systems capable of analyzing these large networks to count or enumerate their k-cliques. Clique finding is just one problem within Graph Pattern Mining (GPM). Motifs represent other general graph patterns that capture researchers' interest in this domain. Several GPM frameworks have been developed to count recurring instances of specified patterns within the search graph. These include Pangolin \cite{chen2020pangolin}, Peregrine \cite{jamshidi2020peregrine}, Arabesque \cite{teixeira2015arabesque}, Fractal \cite{dias2019fractal}, among others. The mentioned frameworks employ more generalized algorithms and offer their own APIs for counting instances of arbitrary, user-defined patterns. Conversely, there are algorithms specifically designed for counting k-cliques, such as kClist \cite{danisch2018listing}, Pivoter \cite{jain2020power}, and Arb-Count \cite{shi2021parallel}. Being custom-designed for a specific problem, these algorithms typically outperform the general-purpose GPM frameworks. KClist~\cite{danisch2018listing} is the current leading clique counting algorithm, known for its algorithmic efficiency and significant performance over previous work. However, when applied to large graphs, it exhibits limited parallel scalability, particularly for smaller clique sizes. We conduct a detailed analysis of kClist and identify scaling bottlenecks in both its primary phases: ordering and counting. The ordering phase directs the graph to prevent redundant counting of the same cliques in the subsequent counting phase. KClist employs a core ordering~\cite{matula1983smallest} to minimize the maximum degree, achieving the greatest reduction in algorithmic work during the counting phase. As the ordering phase consumes a significant portion of execution time and computing a core ordering is inherently sequential, it restricts scalability according to Amdahl's Law. The parallel speedup of kClist's counting phase quickly plateaus, with observed speedups as low as 5$\times$ on 24 cores for certain graphs. We find the counting phase is generally constrained by memory due to poor locality and the substantial volume of memory traffic. We introduce CITRON (Clique Counting with Traffic Reducing Optimizations), a high-performance clique counting algorithm. Due to its superior parallel scalability, it significantly outperforms kClist, particularly for smaller clique sizes. We determine that a core ordering is unnecessary, and a parallelizable ordering like a degree ordering not only significantly accelerates the ordering phase but also results in minimal slowdowns in the counting phase in practice. We enhance the counting phase with our novel subgraph construction approach, which substantially reduces memory accesses and improves their spatial locality. We assess CITRON on a collection of real-world graphs and compare it to kClist and other previous works. For counting triangles, we achieve speedups of $18.16 - 208.27\times$ (Geometric Mean: $102.436\times$) in the ordering phase and speedups of $1.1-2.6\times$ (Geometric Mean: $1.798\times$) in the counting phase, resulting in overall speedups of $14.37-39.37\times$ (Geometric Mean: $18.517\times$) over kClist. We have recently learned of ArbCount \cite{shi2021parallel}, which outperforms our method as shown in Table \ref{table:3}. However, we believe the analysis provided in this paper will be beneficial for those seeking to understand the performance characteristics of k-clique counting.

text: With the widespread use of mobile and edge devices, federated learning~\cite{konevcny2016federatedlearning, mcmahan2017communication} has emerged as a framework for training machine learning models across geographically distributed and heterogeneous devices. In federated learning, a central server interacts with numerous clients. The central server collaborates with the clients to train a machine learning model using the clients' local data. Federated learning is frequently modeled as a distributed optimization problem~\cite{konevcny2016federatedoptimization, konevcny2016federatedlearning, mcmahan2017communication, kairouz2019advances, wang2021field}. Let ${\mathcal{D}}$ represent the entire dataset distributed across all $N$ clients/devices/workers/machines, where each client $i$ possesses a local dataset ${\mathcal{D}}_i$. The objective is to solve the following optimization problem without sharing the local datasets with the central server: \begin{align} \min_{{\bm{x}}\in\mathbb{R}^d}\left\{ f({\bm{x}}; {\mathcal{D}}) := \frac{1}{N}\sum_{i=1}^N f({\bm{x}}; {\mathcal{D}}_i)\right\}, \end{align} where $f({\bm{x}}; {\mathcal{D}}_i) := \mathbb{E}_{d_i\sim{\mathcal{D}}_i} f({\bm{x}}; d_i)$. Here, ${\bm{x}} \in \mathbb{R}^d$ is the model, and $f({\bm{x}}; {\mathcal{D}})$, $f({\bm{x}}; {\mathcal{D}}_i)$, and $f({\bm{x}}; d_{i})$ denote the loss function of the model ${\bm{x}}$ on the entire dataset ${\mathcal{D}}$, the local dataset ${\mathcal{D}}_i$, and a random data sample $d_{i}$, respectively. \subsection{Communication efficiency} Communication between the central server and the clients is a primary bottleneck for federated learning applications, particularly when the number of clients is large, clients such as mobile phones have limited bandwidth, and/or the machine learning model has numerous parameters. Therefore, it is essential to design federated learning algorithms that minimize the overall communication cost, considering both \emph{the number of communication rounds} and \emph{the communication cost per communication round} to achieve the desired accuracy. Based on these two factors, there are two approaches for communication-efficient federated learning: 1) \emph{local methods}: in each communication round, clients perform multiple local update steps before communicating with the central server, aiming to reduce the number of communication rounds; 2) \emph{compressed methods}: clients send compressed communication messages to the central server, intending to lower the communication cost per communication round. Both categories have garnered significant attention. For local methods, a few examples include \algname{FedAvg}~\cite{mcmahan2017communication}, \algname{Local-SVRG}~\cite{gorbunov2020local}, \algname{SCAFFOLD}~\cite{karimireddy2020scaffold}, and \algname{FedPAGE}~\cite{zhao2021fedpage}. Conversely, numerous compressed methods have been proposed, including but not limited to \cite{alistarh2017qsgd, khirirat2018distributed, mishchenko2019distributed, horvath2019stochastic, li2020acceleration, li2020unified, gorbunov2021marina, condat2021murana, li2021canita, richtarik20223pc, li2022soteriafl, zhao2022beer}. In particular, the current state-of-the-art guarantees in convex and nonconvex settings are provided by \algname{CANITA}~\cite{li2021canita} and \algname{MARINA}~\cite{gorbunov2021marina}, respectively. In this paper, we concentrate on compression to improve communication efficiency. See \Cref{sec:compression} for further discussions. \subsection{Methods with variance reduction} Variance reduction, or \emph{data-variance} reduction, is a well-explored technique in standard/centralized finite-sum optimization, aiming to achieve a faster convergence rate. Numerous optimization algorithms employ the variance reduction technique, including \algname{SVRG}~\cite{johnson2013accelerating,reddi2016stochastic}, \algname{SAGA}~\cite{defazio2014saga}, \algname{SCSG}~\cite{lei2017less}, \algname{SARAH}~\cite{nguyen2017sarah}, \algname{SPIDER}~\cite{fang2018spider}, \algname{SSRGD}~\cite{li2019ssrgd,li2022simple}, and \algname{PAGE}~\cite{li2021page,li2021short}. These algorithms typically compute stochastic gradients using a subset of data samples (to achieve better convergence results) and periodically compute the full gradient using all data samples (to reduce data-variance). For instance, the convergence result for standard gradient descent (\algname{GD}) (which always computes full gradients) is $O(N/\epsilon^2)$ in the nonconvex setting, while the variance-reduced methods \algname{SARAH/SPIDER/PAGE} achieve a significantly better result of $O(\sqrt{N}/\epsilon^2)$. In the federated learning context, we decompose the \emph{data-variance} into two components: the \emph{client-variance} and the clients' \emph{local-variance}. The \emph{client-variance} captures the dissimilarity of data stored on different heterogeneous clients, i.e., the variance induced by different datasets ${\mathcal{D}}_i$ (see problem \eqref{eq:prob}), which is the variance encountered by the central server. The \emph{local-variance} or \emph{local-data-variance} is induced by the local data samples stored on each client, and it is the data-variance faced by the local clients if they compute local \emph{stochastic gradients} instead of local \emph{full gradients}. We emphasize that the \emph{client-variance} is the primary challenge for federated learning due to data heterogeneity, and even if one can compute the local \emph{full gradients} using the entire local dataset ${\mathcal{D}}_i$ on each client (i.e., eliminate the \emph{local-variance}), the \emph{client-variance} faced by the central server remains. Moreover, directly applying variance reduction algorithms like \algname{SVRG/PAGE} in federated learning has the following drawbacks: (1) These variance-reduced methods typically require periodic computation of the full gradient using all data samples (to reduce data-variance), which necessitates communication with all clients periodically in the federated learning context. However, federated learning applications often involve numerous clients; for example, Google Keyboard (Gboard)~\cite{hard2018federated,ramaswamy2019federated} involves billions of mobile phones, making it impractical to communicate with all clients in a communication round to reduce the \emph{client-variance}. (2) These variance-reduced algorithms do not utilize communication compression to further reduce the communication cost. Conversely, existing communication compression algorithms typically require communication with all clients in each communication round (see Tables~\ref{tab:results}). Among the compressed algorithms that support partial participation (PP) (do not require communication with all clients in each round), previous methods either need to communicate with all clients (FP) using uncompressed messages periodically (\algname{PP-MARINA}~\cite{gorbunov2021marina}), or do not benefit from the faster convergence rate of variance reduction (\algname{FedGLOMO}~\cite{das2020improved}, \algname{EF21-PP}~\cite{fatkhullin2021ef21}). Thus, we consider the following natural and important question: \begin{quote} 	\centering \emph{Can we incorporate client-variance reduction with communication compression\\ in the federated learning setting?} \end{quote} \subsection{Our contributions} In this paper, we develop the {\sf\footnotesize COFIG}\xspace and {\sf\footnotesize FRECON}\xspace algorithms for federated learning. Both algorithms support communication compression and fully partial participation, achieving the first/faster convergence using the client-variance reduction technique (see \Cref{tab:results}) under \emph{any heterogeneity}. Specifically, we summarize our main contributions as follows: \begin{enumerate} \item We design the {\sf\footnotesize COFIG}\xspace algorithm, which, to our knowledge, is the \emph{first} algorithm that supports \emph{partial participation} and communication compression for the \emph{general} non-strongly convex federated learning setting (see the convex column in \Cref{tab:results}). For the nonconvex setting, {\sf\footnotesize COFIG}\xspace successfully supports communication compression and fully partial participation (PP) (unlike \algname{PP-MARINA}) and benefits from the convergence speedup (unlike \algname{FedGLOMO} and \algname{EF21-PP}) by employing client-variance reduction (see the nonconvex column in \Cref{tab:results}). Additionally, {\sf\footnotesize COFIG}\xspace also supports the client's local-variance (\Cref{ass:bounded-variance}) and PP simultaneously, which is more practical than other compressed algorithms such as \algname{FedGLOMO} and \algname{PP-MARINA} in federated learning. \item For the nonconvex setting, we further develop a new {\sf\footnotesize FRECON}\xspace algorithm based on {\sf\footnotesize COFIG}\xspace, which can converge significantly faster than {\sf\footnotesize COFIG}\xspace (see the nonconvex column in \Cref{tab:results}). Specifically, {\sf\footnotesize FRECON}\xspace converges within $O((1+\omega)\sqrt{N}/(S\epsilon^2))$ communication rounds, matching the convergence result of \algname{PP-MARINA}. However, {\sf\footnotesize FRECON}\xspace supports fully partial participation with a subset of clients and is thus more practical than \algname{PP-MARINA}, which requires periodic full participation (FP) with uncompressed messages. Note that periodic FP necessitates periodic synchronization of all clients/devices in federated learning, which is usually impossible or unaffordable. \end{enumerate}

text: Recently, modern voice-controlled devices equipped with virtual assistants such as Alexa, Siri, and Google Assistant have become integral to various aspects of daily life, ranging from playing music to driving. Spoken Language Understanding (SLU) models, which interpret the semantic meaning of a user's spoken utterance, serve as the AI core of these devices. The SLU task is typically divided into two sub-tasks: intent classification (IC), which determines the intent of a user's utterance, and slot filling (SF), which extracts semantic components from the utterance. Consider an annotated utterance from the ATIS dataset \cite{atis}: \begin{quote} \textbf{city}~~~~~~ [$_{\bf{O}}$~where] [$_{\bf{O}}$~is] [$_{\bf{B-airport\_code}}$~MCO] \end{quote} The SF sub-task should classify "where" and "is" as ${\bf{O}}$ (i.e., Other), and "MCO" as ${\bf{B-airport\_code}}$, while the IC sub-task should identify \textbf{city} as the intent. Current state-of-the-art SLU models are predominantly DNN-based joint models for the two sub-tasks \cite{Liu2016AttentionBasedRN,do19,chen19}. These models generally employ two separate decoders to identify slot and intent labels on top of a shared encoder. As in many other NLP domains, the BERT encoder-decoder architecture has demonstrated its strong capability in capturing contextual information from data sources to enhance SLU performance \cite{chen19}. For typical SLU applications, the BERT encoder is initially pre-trained on a vast amount of unlabeled texts and subsequently fine-tuned on SLU training data. Given the rapid global expansion of the voice-controlled device market, there is an increasing demand for rapid language expansion in SLU models. Multilingual technology, which enables the development of a single model for multiple languages and facilitates knowledge transfer from one language's data resource to others, is currently one of the most effective solutions to meet this growing demand. Traditionally, an SLU model is trained on supervised monolingual data, resulting in a virtual assistant that can typically use only one language during a session. Conversely, a multilingual SLU model trained on supervised multilingual data can enable a virtual assistant to converse in multiple languages within a single session. Furthermore, from a development standpoint, multilingual modeling not only reduces the number of models that need to be built but also decreases the requirement for supervised data by transferring knowledge across languages. However, as languages differ in various aspects, from lexicon to syntax, the cross-language knowledge transfer capabilities of current multilingual techniques may still be limited. This raises questions about: i) what constitutes an ideal cross-language knowledge transfer; ii) what defines a naive cross-language knowledge transfer; and iii) the extent to which a multilingual model can transfer knowledge across languages. As one of the most successful recent multilingual techniques, multilingual BERT (mBERT) \cite{mBERT} is increasingly used in natural language processing models in both zero-shot\footnote{The model is trained in one language and tested on another.} and multilingual\footnote{The model is trained on multiple languages.} contexts \cite{wu-dredze-2019-beto,multiatis++}. Since mBERT is trained without any cross-lingual objectives and does not utilize aligned data, its strong cross-lingual capabilities are unexpected and have prompted research aimed at understanding the reasons behind its success \cite{pires2019multilingual}. In this paper, however, we focus on exploring the extent to which it can blur language boundaries in the \textit{multilingual} SLU context by comparing its ability to transfer knowledge across languages with both ideal and naive scenarios. Additionally, as mBERT is pre-trained for general purposes, we are also interested in enhancing its multilingual capabilities for the specific application of multilingual SLU. Our contribution in this paper is two-fold: \textit{First}, through extensive experiments with bilingual and trilingual SLU models, we demonstrate that although mBERT is significantly effective in blurring language boundaries even among distant language groups, there remains a gap to achieving ideal multilingual performance. \textit{Second}, we propose a novel adversarial model architecture to learn language-shared and language-specific representations on top of mBERT representations when fine-tuning on SLU data. The experimental results demonstrate that our proposed approach can reduce the gap to ideal multilingual performance.

text: In recent years, micro-blogging has emerged as a source of current and topical news. Twitter\footnote{www.twitter.com} is among the most popular micro-blogging services, bringing together millions of users and allowing them to publish and exchange short messages, known as \emph{tweets}. Since 2006, Twitter was a pioneer in providing APIs for accessing public data\footnote{https://developer.twitter.com/en.html}, enabling applications to retrieve tweets using specific keywords. However, there is no control over the retrieved tweets, which are not always relevant. Obtaining relevant responses necessitates multiple calls and filtering of the retrieved results. Several research studies aim to search for relevant tweets based on a given query~\cite{gabielkov2014sampling,gouriten2014scalable,li2013towards,safran2012improving}. Researchers have attempted to enhance methods using features such as hashtags, retweets, and mentions to retrieve the most relevant tweets from Twitter. For instance, a basic and straightforward method involves finding the frequency of a single word query across different Twitter features\cite{nazi2015walk}. Researchers have also attempted to use external information from sources like Wikipedia to enrich a query by identifying the most similar words to find the most related results to the given query \cite{guisado2016enrich}. In this paper, we utilized various external resources such as \textit{Wordnet}, \textit{Wordnik}, \textit{DBPedia}, and \textit{New York Times(NYT)} to compile the most comprehensive set of keywords similar to the original query keywords. We also developed a smart crawling algorithm based on tweet features to identify the most relevant tweets as early as possible, surpassing Twitter's limitations. Specifically, we introduce a new crawling algorithm called \textbf{Smart Twitter Crawling} (STiC) by considering two aspects: (i) Enriching the original query using external sources, and (ii) crawling the Twitter graph using a DFS search based on new scoring to reach the best nodes (tweets) related to the targeted topic. To assess the relevance of a tweet, the algorithm assigns a score by considering its content, hashtags, and the user associated with it, such as posting, replying, being mentioned, or retweeting. Based on this score, we can select highly related tweets in each iteration and continue by adding the related valuable tweets. Various experiments were conducted on tweets collected for different types of query keywords to evaluate the precision of the STiC algorithm. Our approach, compared to a simple BFS search, increased the precision of related retrieved tweets by up to 86% for some queries. Additionally, in terms of the number of retrieved results, we achieved significant improvement compared to the simple BFS model. In this paper, we first present related work in Section~\ref{sec:relatedwork}. Then, we detail our smart Twitter crawling approach, including query enrichment and Twitter graph crawling, in Section~\ref{sec:approach}. In Section~\ref{sec:experiments}, we present and discuss our results using different queries. Finally, in Section~\ref{sec:conclusion}, we provide our conclusions and perspectives.

text: Clinicians currently allocate more time to documenting information in electronic health records (EHRs) than to interacting with patients, and the inefficiency of EHRs is suggested to be a primary factor contributing to physician stress and burnout \citep{carayon15, gardner_burnout}. Physicians prefer using natural language and free-text for documentation instead of restrictive structured forms \citep{khorana}, yet clinicians have adapted to time-consuming note-writing by employing overloaded acronyms and jargon \citep{md_readability}. For instance, consider this sentence from an actual Emergency Department (ED) clinical note: \texttt{pt w/ h/o MS}. While \texttt{MS} might mean \texttt{mitral stenosis} to a cardiologist, it can also signify \texttt{multiple sclerosis} to other specialists. To a layperson, the clinical note may be unintelligible unless acronyms are expanded: \texttt{patient with a history of multiple sclerosis}. As a result, medical documentation is frequently noisy, ambiguous, and incomplete. The absence of structure in notes further impedes understandability for patients, other physicians, and machines \citep{Aljabri2018, patient_engagement, Koch-Weser_language2009}. The information within EHR notes remains largely untapped and currently cannot be easily utilized for downstream medical care or for machine learning models that depend on structured data. \paragraph{Statement of Contributions} We propose a method termed \emph{contextual autocomplete}, which efficiently captures clinical concepts at the point-of-care through learned suggestions. To achieve this, we construct a hierarchical language model for clinical concepts that can function in the noisy domain of ED notes. Our model is intended for deployment in a live hospital environment, with inputs limited to the triage information and previous medical notes available to a doctor \emph{before} a note is written. While these constraints make it impractical to construct a generative language model, we generalize to the task of \emph{autocompletion}, where we offer multiple suggestions for the next clinical concept to document, allowing the clinician to select the correct option. Since all suggestions are mapped to standardized clinical vocabularies, we can simultaneously impose structure on notes as they are being written, disambiguate between concepts, and expedite documentation for clinicians in real-world hospital settings. \paragraph{Clinical Relevance} We introduce contextual autocompletion as the foundation of an intelligent EHR in Figure \ref{typing_readability}. The contextual autocompletion tool reduces the amount of text a clinician must type by suggesting relevant terms using a learned context. Tagged terms uniquely identify clinical concepts and can be linked with pertinent information from the medical record. Furthermore, these terms can facilitate widespread improvements in documentation and decrease the overall cognitive load on doctors. Once a term is tagged, it can be automatically inserted in multiple locations within the clinical note to minimize the amount of redundant information a clinician types-- for instance, a tagged condition in an earlier part of a note can be automatically appended to the Past Medical History section that appears later on, as shown in the right panel of Figure \ref{typing_readability}. This alleviates the ``death by a thousand clicks" phenomenon that EHRs suffer from \citep{schulte_fry_2019}. Additionally, live-tagging clinical concepts can provide immediate benefits to physicians in the form of decision support; the captured structured data can then be used to develop smarter EHR interfaces that enable contextual information retrieval about disease history and lab trends, without ever leaving the note interface. Finally, tagging clinical concepts with our system allows for the translation of acronyms and domain-specific language to common names. By normalizing key clinical concepts from notes to a universal vocabulary (the Unified Medical Language System, or UMLS), notes written using our system are semi-structured and parseable. \FloatBarrier \paragraph{Generalizable Insights about Machine Learning in the Context of Healthcare} Previous research in clinical concept extraction attempts to retrospectively recover concepts from notes, but these methods often struggle to disambiguate between similar concepts and suffer due to a lack of labeled data \citep{mcn}. Even for a human expert, it is challenging to reliably disambiguate between concepts when the clinical intention is unclear. Developing a tool that allows clinicians to document terms on-the-fly not only reduces the documentation burden but also curates large-scale prospective datasets of labeled clinical concepts (e.g., conditions, symptoms, labs, and medications) in notes. These labels can be utilized to design robust medical knowledge graphs, develop better clinical entity extraction models, learn longitudinal patterns within disease history, and even build contextual representations of concepts. Learning relationships between clinical concepts, for example, can inform and fill gaps in existing medical ontologies \citep{umls_missingness}. Additionally, this work demonstrates the power of combining varying noisy and potentially incomplete sources of a patient's medical record to create a context for the current clinical setting that allows us to accurately predict concepts relevant to a new medical event. \FloatBarrier

text: Hand dexterity is crucial for everyday human activities, necessitating intricate and precise control of finger movements. While most animals demonstrate detailed motor controls for movement and many possess basic manipulation skills, the functionality and efficiency of human dexterity are unmatched, granting humans the unique capability to perform highly sophisticated tasks with ease. Consequently, developing similarly intelligent control strategies for robotic hands has been regarded as a significant goal in autonomous robot research. Nevertheless, it presents an exceptionally challenging problem due to its high-dimensional action space and complex, intermittent hand-object interactions. Reinforcement learning (RL) has gained popularity for addressing sensorimotor control tasks due to its ability to discover behaviors without extensive manual engineering~\cite{heess2017emergence,levine2016end}. Previous studies have also shown that with large-scale computation, RL policies can acquire effective skills to control dexterous hands from purely simulated experiences and execute complex tasks in the real world, such as in-hand rotation~\cite{andrychowicz2020learning} and solving a Rubik's Cube~\cite{akkaya2019solving}. However, the manipulation policies developed by these methods typically focus on a single predetermined object, rendering them impractical for real-world applications. Given the innumerable objects a robot might encounter in reality, it is impractical to develop a separate system for each one. Thus, it is essential for a policy to demonstrate strong robustness to object variations, ideally in a zero-shot manner, as humans do. Nonetheless, generalization to entirely unseen and geometrically diverse objects for dexterous manipulation policies has been underexplored in the community, primarily due to the erroneous belief that such generalization is beyond the reach of current RL algorithms. In this work, we demonstrate that with simple modifications, existing RL algorithms can generate strong and generalizable policies for a robotic hand with high degrees of freedom. First, we show that contrary to the prevalent belief in the community, a multi-task jointly-trained policy does not necessarily result in decreased performance compared to training on each task individually. Indeed, we demonstrate that in the context of dexterous manipulation, a multi-task policy can be a \textit{generalist} that matches the performance of single-task \textit{specialist} policies. Second, we illustrate that with an appropriate representation that can meaningfully associate the tasks, such a multi-task policy can even surpass the single-task \textit{specialists} on completely unseen objects, where the \textit{specialists} are trained on those objects. Furthermore, we reveal a linear scaling effect of improved generalization when trained on more objects, indicating the potential for future enhancement. We hope that our work can serve as a crucial step towards developing a general-purpose controller for dexterous hands. text: The modeling and rendering of humans is essential for enabling applications in sports visualization, telepresence, shopping, and various other fields. Although extensive research has been conducted using calibrated data, such as multiview laboratory setups \cite{shysheya2019textured, liu2019neural, liu2020neural}, synthesizing a person solely from "in the wild" data remains challenging. Approaches for 3D reconstruction necessitate training on synthetic ground truth meshes or 3D scans \cite{saito2019pifu, saito2020pifuhd, alldieck2019tex2shape, huang2020arch, lazova2019360, zhu2020reconstructing}, while image-to-image translation methods are limited to 2D synthesis \cite{chan2019everybody, wang2018video}. Our method addresses both challenges by reconstructing a volumetric representation of a person that can be animated and rendered in any pose from any viewpoint. We use as input a video of the person engaged in unconstrained activities, such as playing tennis or dancing. The key insight is that frames from a sufficiently long video (ranging from minutes to hours) provide extensive information about the person's appearance in various poses and viewpoints, even if each pose appears only once and from a single direction. A significant contribution of our paper is the design of a representation and a corresponding deep network that enable generalization to arbitrary poses and views based on these images. Our contributions include a representation of a person as an $RGB\alpha$ volume that can be reposed using a set of volumetric motion weights (adapting the work of~\cite{lombardi2019neural}), the design of a deep network that, after optimization over the video data, generates the person-specific volumes, a set of losses crafted to align the output with both the pixel values and the qualitative appearance of the input frames, and finally, a system that integrates these components to fit unconstrained videos and produce reposable, free-viewpoint renderings of the person. We demonstrate results on diverse video inputs, surpassing related methods and enabling applications such as motion re-targeting and bullet-time rendering. Our approach has certain limitations. We assume the subject's appearance is not view-dependent (lacking specular reflection) and, more importantly, that the appearance does not change with pose. This latter assumption implies that the results are most accurate to the original when the lighting is relatively diffuse and the shape, such as clothing, does not significantly alter during movement. Additionally, the resolution of results is constrained by the voxel grid and the inherent challenges of registering to, and accurately recovering body poses from, images in the wild. Despite these limitations, we present convincing results across various sequences that, while not physically exact, appear plausible.

text: Autoencoders are a robust class of Neural Networks capable of achieving compact data representations and are frequently employed as a denoising technique \cite{autoencoders}. In line with this concept, Quantum Autoencoders (QAEs) have recently appeared as a potential approach to address the severe quantum noise issue, which is prevalent in quantum computations on actual devices. In this paper, we concentrate on QAEs as introduced in \cite{bondarenko2019quantum}, which facilitate nearly perfect reconstruction of Greenberger–Horne–Zeilinger (GHZ) states affected by random bit-flips and minor unitary noise. An $m$-qubit GHZ state is defined as \begin{align} \frac{1}{\sqrt{2}}( \ket{0}^{\bigotimes m}+\ket{1}^{\bigotimes m}). \end{align} Examining GHZ states is particularly significant as they display long-range entanglement and are utilized in a broad array of applications. \medskip Notably, the circuit depth of the QAEs examined in this paper is quite shallow (for example, the QAE denoising 3-qubit GHZ states requires only 4 qubits), making them straightforward to implement on currently available quantum devices. These QAEs are based on the Quantum Neural Networks (QNNs) architecture outlined in \cite{beer2019efficient}, and are trained using an unsupervised learning approach \cite{sents2019unsupervised}. Although \cite{beer2019efficient} already offers a Matlab implementation of QNNs \cite{deepqnn}, we opt to implement the QAEs within a purely quantum framework, utilizing the Qiskit \cite{qiskit} library. In this research, we propose a comprehensive quantum (circuit) encoding of all algorithmic steps related to QAEs training and testing. Additionally, we discuss crucial implementation and training specifics along with extensive results of the QAEs. Finally, we conduct a detailed mathematical analysis of noise effects in Quantum Secret Sharing (QSS) and demonstrate methods to mitigate it. Thus, this work encompasses both theoretical and experimental dimensions of QAEs. \medskip This paper is structured as follows. Section \ref{Implementation} covers the theoretical foundation concerning the implementation and training of QAEs on quantum circuits. Section \ref{Results} provides numerical results regarding the QAEs' performance in denoising corrupted states exposed to various types of noise. Ultimately, in section \ref{QSS} we explore an application of QAEs in QSS and illustrate their importance in that context.

text: Environmental sound offers valuable insights into the physical environment. For instance, upon hearing: \emph{joyful laughing, a playful scream, and a splash;} one can not only visualize the specific objects or actions that might have created the audio scene but also infer plausible higher-level scenarios, such as a child rapidly descending a water slide at a water park and splashing into the water (see Figure~\ref{fig:image_pivot_idea}). Machines that can parse, represent, and describe such environmental sounds have practical potential. For instance, the National Association of the Deaf's captioning guide suggests that accessible audio caption generation systems should extend beyond speech recognition (i.e., identifying speakers and transcribing their spoken content) to provide textual descriptions of all sound effects, such as ``a large group of people talking excitedly at a party,'' to convey the complete information contained in the audio.\footnote{{\href{https://www.nad.org/resources/technology/captioning-for-access/what-is-captioning/}{nad.org's captioning guide}}; \citet{gernsbacher2015video} discusses the advantages of video captions beyond d/Deaf users.} The prevailing approach to studying \emph{machine hearing}~\citep{lyon2010machine} has involved human-annotated audio-text data, where the text consists of either free-form audio descriptions (e.g., ``the sound of heavy rain'') or tagsets~\citep{US8K,audioset,audiocaps,audiocaps-clotho}. However, existing supervised audio-text resources are limited. While some audio-text co-occurrences can be derived from audio-tag co-occurrences~\citep{freesound} or video captioning data~\citep{rohrbach2015dataset,MSR-VTT,oncescu2021queryd}, they are either insufficiently related to environmental sound or limited in scale and coverage. In this paper, we explore large-scale audio-text alignment without paired audio-text (AT) data. Drawing inspiration from pivot-based models for unsupervised machine translation~\citep{wu2007pivot,pivot-comparison-mt}, we introduce \merlotfont{vip-AnT}\xspace, short for \modelnamelong. \merlotfont{vip-AnT}\xspace employs images as a pivot modality to link audio and text. This mirrors our motivating example: when hearing a sound, humans can visually \emph{imagine} the related situation and literally \emph{describe} it. Pivoting is practically feasible because there is an abundance of image-text (VT) and video-audio (VA) co-occurrences available online, which can be used to train bimodal correspondence models (see Figure~\ref{fig:keyidea}). By implicitly connecting audio and text through the combination of VT and VA models, we facilitate a \emph{zero-resource} link between audio and text, enabling \merlotfont{vip-AnT}\xspace to infer audio-text connections without having explicitly observed these modalities together. We assess performance on zero-shot audio-text retrieval and zero-shot audio classification. On the Clotho caption retrieval task~\citep{audiocaps-clotho}, without any parallel AT data, \merlotfont{vip-AnT}\xspace exceeds the supervised state of the art by 2.2\% R@1; on zero-shot audio classification tasks, it sets new state-of-the-art results, achieving 57.1\% accuracy on ESC50~\citep{ESC50} and 44.7\% accuracy on US8K~\citep{US8K}. We also demonstrate that the zero-resource pivoting AT model \merlotfont{vip-AnT}\xspace can be enhanced by: \begin{enumerate}[wide=0\parindent,noitemsep \item[(1)] \emph{Unsupervised curation:} where noisy AT pairs are explicitly extracted from the pivoting model and used as additional training data (e.g., +5.7\% on ESC50 and +9.3\% on US8K); and \item[(2)] \emph{Few-shot curation:} where a limited number of human-annotated audio caption pairs are provided during training (e.g., a few hundred pairs increase the zero-shot audio classification accuracy by 8\% on US8K). \end{enumerate} However, for ESC-50, based on the empirical scaling relationship we identify, approximately $2^{21} \approx 2\text{M}$ aligned audio-text pairs would be necessary for the zero-shot model to achieve human parity on ESC50 under our configuration, which is significantly more than the largest currently available audio-text corpus of~\citet{audiocaps}. \begin{comment} Altogether, \yanpeng{this just duplicates the above para, maybe turn the above para into takeways?}: \begin{itemize}[wide=0\parindent,noitemsep] \item[(1)] We introduce \merlotfont{vip-AnT}\xspace, a tri-modal pivoting model that learns robust audio-text alignment without using any parallel audio-text pairs. \item[(2)] We examine scenarios with minimal audio-text supervision and find that even un-aligned audio-text pairs are beneficial. \item[(3)] We explore empirical scaling laws for \merlotfont{vip-AnT}\xspace and find that bridging the gap between zero-shot performance and supervised performance (e.g., on audio classification) would require an extremely large number of aligned audio-text pairs.\yanpeng{this finding is a bit strange, maybe it is because most of the newly added training samples have already been there in the training data.} \end{itemize} We believe that, by introducing the first tri-modal pivoting model and conducting comprehensive model analyses, our work will inspire future research on learning audio-text connections with minimal supervision. \end{comment}

text: The introduction of large pre-trained language models such as BERT~\cite{bert} has significantly impacted Natural Language Processing and Information Retrieval. These models have demonstrated a robust capacity to adapt to various tasks through simple fine-tuning. Early in 2019, \textit{Nogueira and Cho}~\cite{passage_ranking} achieved state-of-the-art results—by a substantial margin—on the MS MARCO passage re-ranking task, establishing a foundation for LM-based neural ranking models. Due to stringent efficiency requirements, these models were initially employed as re-rankers in a two-stage ranking pipeline, where first-stage retrieval—or candidate generation—is performed using bag-of-words models (e.g., BM25) that utilize inverted indexes. Although BOW models remain strong baselines~\cite{neural_hype}, they are affected by the longstanding vocabulary mismatch problem, where relevant documents may not contain terms present in the query. Consequently, there have been efforts to replace standard BOW approaches with learned (neural) rankers. Designing such models presents several challenges regarding efficiency and scalability; thus, there is a need for methods where most computations can be performed offline and online inference is rapid. Dense retrieval with approximate nearest neighbors search has demonstrated impressive results~\cite{xiong2021approximate,qu-etal-2021-rocketqa,lin-etal-2021-batch,Hofstaetter2021_tasb_dense_retrieval}, but it can still benefit from BOW models (e.g., by integrating both types of signals) due to the lack of explicit term matching. Consequently, there has been increasing interest in learning \emph{sparse representations} for queries and documents~\cite{snrm, dai2019contextaware,nogueira2019document,zhao2020sparta,sparterm2020,gao-etal-2021-coil,10.1145/3404835.3463030,10.1145/3404835.3463098}. By doing so, models can inherit desirable properties of BOW models such as exact-match of (possibly latent) terms, efficiency of inverted indexes, and interpretability. Moreover, by modeling implicit or explicit (latent, contextualized) \emph{expansion} mechanisms—similar to standard expansion models in IR—these models can mitigate the vocabulary mismatch. In this paper, we build upon the SPLADE model~\cite{10.1145/3404835.3463098} and propose several improvements/modifications that enhance effectiveness or efficiency: \begin{enumerate*} \item by simply altering the SPLADE pooling mechanism, we achieve a significant increase in effectiveness; \item concurrently, we propose an extension of the model without query expansion. This model is inherently more efficient, as all computations can be pre-computed and indexed offline, while still delivering competitive results; \item finally, we employ distillation techniques~\cite{hofstatter2020improving} to enhance SPLADE performance, achieving results close to state-of-the-art on the MS MARCO passage ranking task as well as the BEIR zero-shot evaluation benchmark~\cite{beir_2021}. \end{enumerate*}

text: Data sets and statistics concerning groups of individuals are increasingly collected and disseminated, serving as inputs for numerous optimization and learning algorithms. In many instances, the released data include sensitive information, the privacy of which is strictly governed by regulations. For instance, in the United States, census data is regulated under Title 13 \cite{Title13}, which mandates that no individual can be identified from any data release by the Census Bureau. In Europe, data releases are governed by the General Data Protection Regulation \cite{GDPR}, which addresses the control and transfer of personal data. Consequently, statistical agencies release data and statistics that preserve privacy and comply with these regulations. \emph{Differential Privacy} \cite{Dwork:06} is particularly relevant for achieving this objective. Differential privacy is a formal privacy framework that limits the disclosure risk for any individual involved in a computation. It is regarded as the de facto standard for privacy protection and has been adopted by various corporations \cite{erlingsson2014rappor,apple} and governmental agencies \cite{abowd2018us}. In data-release tasks, differentially private algorithms typically add carefully calibrated noise to the data before its release. However, while this process ensures privacy, it also impacts the accuracy of the released data. Specifically, the added noise often results in data sets that violate the consistency constraints of the application domain. For instance, in census statistics, the count of individuals satisfying a property must be consistent across a geographical hierarchy, such as national, state, and county levels. The addition of independent noise, however, cannot guarantee the consistency of these constraints. To address this limitation, differentially private outputs can be \emph{post-processed} using data-independent functions that transform the noisy data to align with the domain constraints. The post-processing step is assured to maintain differential privacy. Furthermore, when the feasible region is convex, a widely adopted class of post-processing functions, known as \emph{projections}, is guaranteed to enhance accuracy. Post-processing has been successfully applied in various applications, including census data \cite{abowd2018us}, energy systems \cite{fioretto:TSG20}, and mobility \cite{xi:15}. However, the impact of post-processing on the noise distribution is not well understood: It is often suggested that it may introduce bias and/or increase variance. Figure \ref{fig:bias} illustrates this aspect in a census data-release problem, described later in the paper. It shows the distribution of the Laplacian residual $\tilde{\bm{x}} - \bm{x}$, where $\bm{x}$ represents the true data and $\tilde{\bm{x}}$ the noisy data, obtained by applying Laplacian noise to $\bm{x}$, as well as the post-processed residual $\hat{\bm{x}} - \bm{x}$, where $\hat{\bm{x}}$ is the projection of $\tilde{\bm{x}}$ onto the feasible region. The results are presented for two counties, and, as observed, the post-processing introduces significant bias in their associated privacy-preserving data. The primary contribution of this paper is to initiate an understanding of the properties of post-processing. Motivated by census applications, it examines the behavior of two widely adopted classes of post-processing functions, referred to as \emph{projections}, for domains where the feasibility space is defined by linear equations. The two classes differ by the presence of non-negativity constraints. The paper demonstrates that, in the absence of non-negativity constraints, the projection does not introduce bias. When projections include non-negativity constraints, the paper provides an upper bound on the bias, offering insights into the types of problems for which the bias will be significant. Finally, the paper offers a detailed analysis of an important sub-problem used to satisfy hierarchical constraints in data-release tasks: It fully characterizes the residual distribution of the post-processed data, shows that it converges towards the Laplace distribution, and provides insights into the effect of projections on the variance of the post-processed data, which may have significant implications for group fairness.

text: This study addresses a perimeter defense problem within a conical environment where a single mobile vehicle aims to intercept mobile intruders before they enter a designated region (the perimeter). This situation occurs when a UAV is tasked with tagging (or relaying critical information to) the intruders (targets) before they reach a specific area of interest. The intruders are introduced at the boundary of the environment and move radially inward at a constant speed toward the perimeter. The vehicle, possessing a finite capture radius, moves with a bounded speed (exceeding that of the intruders) with the objective of \textit{capturing} as many intruders as possible before they reach the perimeter. This is an online problem because the number and arrival location of intruders are progressively revealed over time. Most previous studies in perimeter defense have either concentrated on determining optimal strategies for a limited number of agents or considered a stochastic arrival process for the intruders~\cite{von2020multiple,macharet2020adaptive,ShivamDVR2019}. Although these studies offer valuable insights, they essentially overlook the \emph{worst-case performance} where the intruders might coordinate their actions to overwhelm the defense \cite{von2021turret}. In this research, we employ a competitive analysis technique~\cite{sleator1985amortized} to evaluate online vehicle motion planning algorithms. In competitive analysis, we assess the performance of an online algorithm, $A$, using the concept of \emph{competitive ratio}, which is the ratio of an optimal offline algorithm's performance to algorithm $A$'s performance for a worst-case input instance. Algorithm $A$ is $c$-competitive if its competitive ratio does not exceed $c$, meaning its performance is assured to be within a factor, $c$, of the optimal for all input instances. In this study, the performance of an algorithm, whether online or offline, is measured by the fraction of intruders captured. A related research area is vehicle routing with new inputs arriving over time. Introduced on graphs in~\cite{psaraftis1988dynamic}, a typical approach requires that the vehicle routes be re-planned as new information becomes available over time. We refer the reader to \cite{bullo2011dynamic} and the references therein for a review of this literature. In most vehicle routing problems, the input (known as \emph{demands}) is static, and thus, the problem is to find the shortest route through the demands to minimize (maximize) the cost (reward); examples of such metrics include the total service time or the number of inputs \emph{serviced}. In perimeter defense scenarios, the input (intruders) is not static. Instead, they are moving towards a specified region, making this problem more challenging than the former. In our previous works, we introduced perimeter defense problems in circular and rectangular environments with stochastically generated input, \cite{ShivamDVR2019,Smith2009translating}. The key distinction of our current work from these past works is the characterization of \emph{competitiveness} for the worst-case inputs, as opposed to the average-case. Perimeter defense problems were initially introduced for a single vehicle and a single intruder in~\cite{isaacs1965differential}. Since then, perimeter defense has been predominantly formulated as a pursuit-evasion differential game. The multiplayer setting for the same has been extensively studied as a reach-avoid game in which the aim is to design control policies for the intruders and the defenders \cite{chen2016multiplayer,garcia2019strategies,davydov2020pursuer}. A typical approach requires computing solutions to the Hamilton-Jacobi-Bellman-Isaacs equation, which is generally only suitable for low-dimensional state spaces and in simple environments \cite{margellos2011hamilton,chen2014path}. Recent works include \cite{yan2019matchingbased, shishika2019perimeter,velhal2021decentralized,lee2021guarding}. Authors in \cite{yan2019matchingbased} propose a receding horizon strategy based on maximum matching, \cite{ shishika2019perimeter,velhal2021decentralized} consider a scenario wherein the defenders are constrained to be on the perimeter and \cite{lee2021guarding} extends the reach-avoid game to $n$-dimensional Euclidean spaces. Previously, we introduced a perimeter defense problem for linear environments based on the use of competitive analysis \cite{bajaj2021competitive}. The key distinction of our current work from the past work is the geometry of the environment which yields novel results in terms of optimally placing the vehicle, the role of capture radius, and additional conditions to guarantee competitiveness of the algorithms. The general contribution of this paper is that we consider a conical environment of unit radius and angle $2\theta$ in which an arbitrary number of intruders are released at the circumference of the environment at arbitrary time instances. Upon release, the intruders move radially inwards with fixed speed $v<1$ with the aim of reaching a conical perimeter of radius $\rho<1$ and angle $2\theta$. A single vehicle having a finite capture radius $r$, moves with maximum speed of unity with an aim to capture the intruders. Our main contributions are as follows. We first establish two necessary conditions in the parameter space for achieving a $c$-competitive algorithm with a finite $c$. Specifically, we characterize the parameter regime in which no online algorithm is $c$-competitive and a parameter regime in which no algorithm can be better than $2$-competitive. Next, we design and analyze three classes of algorithms and establish their competitiveness. Specifically, we identify parameter regimes in which the first two algorithms are provably $1$ and $2$-competitive, respectively, and the third algorithm has a finite competitive ratio that varies with the problem parameters ($r,\rho,\theta$). This paper is organized as follows. In section \ref{sec:Problem}, we formally describe our problem and define the competitive ratio for online algorithms. Section \ref{sec:Fundamental_limits} establishes two necessary conditions; first on achieving a finite competitive ratio and second on achieving at best a competitive ratio of $2$. In section \ref{sec:Algorithms}, we design and analyze three algorithms and establish their competitive ratios, section \ref{sec:Results} provides additional insights through numerous parameter space plots and finally, section \ref{sec:Conclusion} summarizes this work and outlines directions for future works.

The intruders are introduced at the edge of the environment and are directed radially towards the perimeter, at a constant speed. The vehicle, with a finite radius of capture, moves with a limited speed (faster than the intruders) with the aim of intercepting as many intruders as possible before they reach the perimeter. Former studies of the perimeter defence problem either dealt with the determination of the best strategy for a limited number of agents, or assumed the process of arrival of the intruders to be random (cf. : V.20, p. 580, M.609, D.2090). These studies give valuable insights, but they ignore the “em-pi-stressed” performance, in which the intruders might be able to coordinate their actions to overwhelm the defense. The performance of an algorithm, whether it is on-line or off-line, is measured by the percentage of intruders it captures. In this research we apply the competitive analysis technique of Sleator [1985amortized] to the performance evaluation of on-line vehicle planning algorithms. A given routing is c-competitive if its competitive ratio is less than c, which means that its performance is guaranteed to be within a factor of c of the best performance on all instances. In most vehicle routing problems, the inputs (called the demands) are given in a static way, and so the problem is to find the shortest route through the demands to minimize (maximize) the cost (reward); an example of this metric is the total service time and the number of demands satisfied. In the routing of vehicles, the inputs (called the demands) are given as static, and so the problem is to find the shortest route through the demands so as to minimize (maximize) the cost; an example of this metric is the total service time and the number of demands satisfied. Perimeter defense problems were first introduced for a single vehicle and a single intruder in cite idscs1965differential. They were later formulated with a single vehicle and a single intruder in cite idscs1965differential. The perimeter defense problem has been described on graphs in Bullo (1997), to which the reader is referred for a review of the literature. The main difference between the present work and previous works is the characterization of the competitiveness of worst-case inputs, as opposed to average-case inputs. Since then, the perimeter defense has been mainly formulated as a differential game. The usual procedure consists of solving the Jacobi-Bellman-Isaacs equation, which is only feasible in low-dimensional states spaces and simple environments. The problem of the perimeter defense of a linear region has already been addressed in previous works, citing Yan, Matching-based, Shishika, Perimeter, Velhal, Decentralized, and Lei, Guarding. For example, recent works include cite: Chen, Multiplayer, 2016, Garcia, 2019, Strategies, Davydov, 2020, Pursuit Strategies. The multiplayer setting for this problem has been extensively studied as a reach-avoid game, where the goal is to design control policies for the intruders and the defenders: cite: Chen, Multiplayer, Garcia, 2019, Strategies, Davydov, 2020, Pursuit Strategies. The authors of [Yan.2019.matchingbased] suggest a strategy based on maximum matching, [Shishika.2019perimeter, Velhal.2021 decentralized] consider the case when the defenders are constrained to the perimeter, and [Lee.2012.guarding] extends the reach-avoid game to n-dimensional Euclidean spaces. The main difference between our work and the previous ones is the geometry of the environment, which provides new results on the best placement of the vehicles, the role of the capture radius, and additional conditions to ensure the success of the algorithms. This paper takes as its object a conical environment of radius 1 and apex 2 theta, in which a random number of intruders are released at random times at the circumference of the environment. At the instant of their release, these intruders begin to move radially inward at a constant speed v1, with the aim of reaching the conical perimeter of radius 1 and apex 2 theta. A single vehicle with a finite capture radius r and a maximum speed 1.0 tries to capture these intruders. This paper is organized as follows. The main contributions of this paper are as follows: First, we establish two necessary conditions for the implementation of a finite c-best-c coding in the parameter space; Second, we establish two necessary conditions in the parameter space for the implementation of an n-competitive, finite n-competitive, n-competitive and n-best-c-competitive, finite n-competitive, n-competitive and n-best-c-competitive, finite n-competitive, and n-best-c-competitive coding system with a finite n. Then, in the section titled “The Problem”, we state the problem formally and define the competitive ratio for online algorithms. First, we design and analyze three classes of algorithms, and prove their competitiveness. Specifically, we identify the parameter regimes where the first two classes of algorithms are provably $e_1$- and $e_2$-competitive, and where the third class of algorithms has a finite competitive ratio that varies with the problem parameters r and. In the section Algorithms we design and analyze three different strategies, and determine their competitive ratios. In the section Results we obtain additional insights by presenting a series of plots in the parameter space. Finally, in the section Conclusions we summarize our work and give some hints at further research.

text: Semi-VOS involves tracking an object of interest throughout all video frames, given the ground truth mask of the initial frame. VOS assigns each pixel to either the background or the tracked object. This task has extensive applicability in various real-world scenarios, such as autonomous driving, surveillance, video editing, and the emerging class of augmented reality/mixed reality devices. VOS is challenging because it must differentiate the target object from other similar objects in the scene, even as the target's appearance evolves over time and through occlusions. Numerous methods have been proposed for solving video object segmentation, including online learning~\cite{robinson2020learning, maninis2018video}, mask propagation~\cite{lin2020flow, cheng2017segflow}, and template matching~\cite{wang2019fast, oh2019video}. A common theme among most of these previous methods is utilizing information from earlier frames—either just the first frame, some previous frames (with the first and last being popular choices), or all previous frames—to produce a high-quality segmentation mask. In this work, we pose a different question:\\ \textbf{Q: Can we use temporal information to identify when the object's appearance and position remain unchanged across frames?}\\ The motivation for this is to bypass much of the costly computation required to generate a high-quality mask for the current frame if it is nearly identical to the mask computed for the previous frame. Instead, we can generate the current frame's mask using an inexpensive model that makes minor adjustments to the previous frame's features. As illustrated in Fig.~\ref{fig:teaserIntro2}(a), for a significant portion of the frames in the popular DAVIS and YouTube-VOS datasets, object masks closely resemble those of the previous frames (73.3\% of consecutive frames in the DAVIS 17 dataset have an IoU greater than 0.7). We build on this observation by developing an inexpensive temporal matching module to rapidly assess the similarity between the current frame and the previous frame. We use this similarity to control the computation of a high-quality mask for the current frame—if the similarity is high, we reuse previous features with minor refinements and avoid the costly mask generation step. This enables us to bypass the majority of computations for the current frame without sacrificing accuracy. Our approach complements existing video object segmentation methods, and to demonstrate its generality, we integrate our proposal into multiple prior video object segmentation models—FRTM~\cite{robinson2020learning} and TTVOS~\cite{park2020ttvos}. To our knowledge, we are the first to propose dynamically skipping the computation of segmentation masks based on object movement. We believe this is a significant contribution that will allow high-quality video object segmentation models to operate on mobile devices in real time with minimal battery consumption. We make the following contributions in this paper: \begin{itemize} \item We advocate for leveraging temporal information to skip mask generation for frames with minimal or no movement. \item We develop a general framework to bypass mask computation, consisting of sub-networks to estimate movement across frames, dynamic selection between processing the full network or reusing the previous frame's features for mask generation, and a novel loss function to train this dynamic architecture. \item We evaluate our approach on multiple video object segmentation models (FRTM, TTVOS) and several challenging datasets (DAVIS 16, DAVIS 17, Youtube-VOS), demonstrating that we can save up to $47.5\%$ of computation and increase FPS by $1.45\times$ with minimal accuracy impact on DAVIS 16 (within approximately 0.4\% of the baseline). \end{itemize}
