text: Query attribute value extraction involves the dual task of identifying named entities in search queries as varied surface form attribute values and converting them into a canonical form to address issues of misspellings and abbreviations. These two sub-tasks are commonly referred to as named entity recognition (NER)~\cite{chiu2016named} and attribute value normalization (AVN)~\cite{putthividhya2011bootstrapped}. Figure~\ref{fig:framework} demonstrates the ideal process for query attribute value extraction. When a user inputs the query ``{\it MK tote for womans}'', we first employ a NER model to detect the entity type ``brand'' for ``{\it MK}'', ``product type'' for ``{\it tote}'', and ``audience'' for ``{\it womans}''. These identified named entities are in the informal surface form of attribute values. However, such informal forms do not align with the products indexed using canonical form attribute values in a formal written style. Specifically, ``{\it MK}'' is an abbreviation for the brand ``{\it Michael Kors}'', ``{\it tote}'' is a hyponym of the product type ``{\it handbag}'', and ``{\it womans}'' contains a spelling error. This misalignment creates significant challenges for the product search engine to retrieve the relevant product items that users actually prefer. Therefore, the AVN module is crucial for transforming each attribute value's surface form into its canonical form, such as converting ``{\it MK}'' to ``{\it Michael Kors}'', ``{\it tote}'' to ``{\it handbag}'', and ``{\it womans}'' to ``{\it women}''. In the E-commerce sector, extracting these attribute values from queries is essential for a wide range of product search applications, including product retrieval~\cite{cheng2020end}, ranking~\cite{wen2019building}, and query rewriting~\cite{guisado2016enrich}. Regrettably, existing studies focus solely on extracting surface form attribute values using NER while neglecting the transformation to canonical forms, which is impractical in real-world scenarios~\cite{kozareva2016recognizing, cheng2020end,wen2019building,cowan2015named}. To address this gap, this paper introduces a unified query attribute value extraction system encompassing both phases. By leveraging large-scale weakly-labeled behavior data to reduce supervision costs, we further enhance extraction performance. In the initial NER stage, recent advancements in deep learning models (e.g., Bi-LSTM+CRF) have shown promising results~\cite{huang2015bidirectional,raganato2017neural}. However, these models heavily depend on extensive labeled data, where manual labeling for token-level labels is notably expensive and labor-intensive. To mitigate this issue in E-commerce, previous studies \cite{kozareva2016recognizing,cheng2020end,wen2019building} have utilized large-scale behavior data from the product side as weak supervision for queries based on simple string match strategies. Nonetheless, these weakly-supervised labels contain substantial noise due to partial or incomplete token labels based on exact string matching. For instance, as illustrated in Table~\ref{tab:ws_example} case\#1, when using the attribute values of the top-clicked product ``{LG 32-inch television}'', i.e., ``brand'' for ``{\it LG}'', ``size'' for ``{\it 32-inch}'', ``product type'' for ``{\it television}'' as weak supervision to match the query ``{\it lg smart tv 32}'', it only generates the label ``brand'' for ``{\it lg}'', omitting valuable information for the unannotated tokens. Consequently, weak supervision-based methods~\cite{shang2018learning,cheng2020end} often perform poorly, and their performance may degrade further when powerful pre-trained language models (PLMs) (e.g., BERT~\cite{devlin2019bert}) are introduced, as PLMs are more susceptible to fitting noise. To tackle this issue, we propose a more reliable approach that incorporates some strongly-labeled human-annotated data to reduce noise in the weak labels from distant supervision. This allows the NER model to be enhanced by effectively utilizing both large-scale weakly-labeled behavior data and strongly-labeled human-annotated data. Regarding the second AVN phase, customers often use diverse surface forms to refer to each attribute value in search queries due to misspellings, spelling variants, or abbreviations. This situation frequently arises in user queries and product titles in e-commerce. For instance, eBay has reported that 20\% of product titles in the clothing and shoes category involve such surface form brand~\cite{putthividhya2011bootstrapped}. Therefore, normalizing these surface form attribute values derived from NER signals to a single normalized attribute value is crucial. This aspect is typically overlooked by existing studies~\cite{kozareva2016recognizing, cheng2020end,wen2019building,cowan2015named}. To reduce human annotation efforts, weakly-labeled behavior data can also aid AVN. For example, the query ``{\it MK tote for womans}'' mentioning the brand ``{\it MK}'' results in clicks on product items associated with the brand ``{\it Michael Kors}''. We can reasonably infer a strong connection between the surface form value ``{\it MK}'' and the canonical form value ``{\it Michael Kors}'' if this association occurs in numerous queries. Inspired by these observations, we propose a unified \textbf{QUE}ry \textbf{A}ttribute Value Extraction in E\textbf{CO}mmerce (\textbf{QUEACO}) framework that effectively utilizes large-scale weakly-labeled behavior data for both query NER and AVN. For query NER, QUEACO employs strongly-labeled data to denoise weakly-labeled data through a novel teacher-student network, where a teacher network trained on strongly-labeled data generates pseudo-labels to refine weakly-labeled data for instructing a student network. Unlike traditional teacher-student networks that can only produce pseudo-labels from a fixed teacher, our pseudo-labeling process from the teacher is continuously and dynamically adapted based on feedback from the student's performance on strongly-labeled data. This encourages the teacher network to generate improved pseudo-labels to instruct the student, thereby minimizing error propagation from noisy weak labels. For query AVN, we utilize weakly-labeled query-to-attribute behavior data and QUEACO NER predictions to model the associations between surface form and canonical form attribute values. Consequently, surface form attribute values from queries can be normalized to the most relevant canonical form attribute values from the products. Empirically, extensive experiments on a real-world large-scale E-commerce dataset demonstrate that QUEACO NER significantly outperforms state-of-the-art semi-supervised and weakly-supervised methods. Furthermore, we qualitatively demonstrate the effectiveness and necessity of QUEACO AVN. Our contributions can be summarized as follows: (1) To the best of our knowledge, our work is the first to propose a unified query attribute value extraction system in E-commerce, encompassing both query NER and AVN. QUEACO can automatically identify product-related attributes from user queries and convert them into canonical forms by leveraging weak supervision from large-scale behavior data; (2) Our QUEACO NER is also the first to efficiently utilize both human-annotated strongly-labeled data and large-scale weakly-labeled data from the query-product click graph. Moreover, the proposed QUEACO NER model significantly outperforms existing state-of-the-art baselines; (3) We propose the QUEACO AVN module that uses aggregated query-to-attribute behavioral data to establish connections among queries, surface form attribute values, and canonical form values. The proposed QUEACO AVN module effectively normalizes surface form values with spelling errors, spelling variants, and abbreviation issues.

text: The objective of manipulation is to achieve a specific arrangement of objects, often involving a desired set of contacts among them. In structured settings, this desired contact can be attained with a specific robot pose; however, in less-structured environments, the necessary robot pose may differ. A robot capable of reliably detecting contact modes can enhance autonomy, for instance, by employing online contact detection to switch the controller \cite{bledt2018} or to provide a reward signal to a learning process \cite{vecerik2018}. We define a {\it contact mode} as a constraint on the generalized position of the robot and environment $q$, specifically $\phi_i(q) = 0$ for the $i^{\mathrm{th}}$ mode. In robotics, this is often treated as an infinitely rigid kinematic constraint, either removed or enforced with impulses in time-stepping methods \cite{stewart2000}. In this context, we consider a compliant contact model where forces are evaluated over position $q$ \cite{castro2020, minniti2021a}. Contact can also be represented with an inequality $\phi_i(q) \geq 0$ to describe the non-penetration of rigid bodies \cite{posa2014, stewart2000}, but we distinguish contact conditions into discrete contact modes using equality constraints \cite{minniti2021a}. Contact mode can be utilized for task representation and planning. Offline contact models lack robustness to variations in environmental objects \cite{rosell2000}, which can be enhanced through online contact detection. text: Consider a weighted tree $T$. The tree metric induced by $T$, denoted as $M_T$, is defined as the complete graph on the vertices of $T$, where the weight of each edge $(u, v)$ corresponds to the weight of the path connecting $u$ and $v$ in $T$. For $t \ge 1$, a $t$-spanner for a metric $(V, d)$ is a subgraph $H$ of the complete graph on $V$ such that every pair of distinct points $u, v \in V$ is connected by a path in $H$ with a total weight of at most $t \cdot d(u, v)$. These paths are referred to as $t$-spanner paths. A $t$-spanner is said to have diameter $\Lambda$ if every pair of points is connected by a $t$-spanner path consisting of at most $\Lambda$ edges. Typically, $t$-spanners are constructed to be sparse, often containing a linear number of edges. The lightness of a graph is defined as the ratio of its weight to that of its minimum spanning tree. Solomon and Elkin \cite{tree-spanner} define a 1-spanner for tree metrics. For a weighted tree with $n$ vertices and a maximum degree of $\Delta$, the 1-spanner has $O(n)$ edges, a diameter of $O(\log n)$, lightness of $O(\log n)$, and a maximum degree bounded by $\Delta + O(1)$. Although this tree metric 1-spanner is an interesting construction on its own, it has been utilized in a series of papers as a tool to reduce the diameter of various Euclidean and doubling metric spanner constructions \cite{short-thin-lanky,doubling-spanner,optimal-euclidean-spanners,tree-spanner,partitions-to-covers}. Once a spanner is constructed, efficiently finding these short paths becomes crucial. A local routing algorithm for a weighted graph $G$ is a method that allows a message to be sent from any vertex in $G$ to a specified destination vertex. The successor for each vertex $u$ on the path followed by the routing algorithm must be determined using only the knowledge of the destination vertex, the neighborhood of $u$, and possibly some additional information stored at $u$. The efficiency of a routing algorithm is evaluated by the distance a message must travel through the network to reach its destination, as well as the storage requirements for each vertex. There is extensive research on local routing algorithms in the literature. The challenge of designing an effective local routing algorithm clearly depends on the properties of the underlying network. Some researchers have developed algorithms for very general classes of networks. For instance, the algorithm by Chan et al. \cite{heirarchical-routing-in-doubling-metrics} is applicable to any network, although its quality is influenced by the induced doubling dimension. Many researchers have concentrated on highly efficient algorithms for specific network classes. For example, there is a body of research on routing algorithms for various classes of planar graphs \cite{convex-subdivisions,routing-in-delaunay}. Support for efficient local routing algorithms is a desirable characteristic in a spanner, and in some recent studies, researchers have designed spanners that simultaneously support efficient local routing along with other properties. See, for instance, the work of Ashvinkumar et al. \cite{local-routing-in-sparse-and-light}. There seems to be limited research in the literature on designing spanners that achieve both support for local routing and low diameter. Given a spanner with diameter $\Lambda$, it is natural to require that a local routing algorithm on this spanner matches this diameter, i.e., the algorithm should be guaranteed to terminate after at most $\Lambda$ hops. Abraham and Malkhi \cite{compact-routing-in-euclidean-metrics} provide a construction, for any $\epsilon > 0$, of a $(1+\epsilon)$-spanner for points in two-dimensional Euclidean space with an associated routing algorithm. The diameter of the routing algorithm is $O(\log D)$ with high probability, where $D$ is the ratio of the largest to the smallest inter-point distances. The routing algorithm has a routing ratio of $O(\log n)$, with high probability, for $n$ points on a uniform grid. In this paper, we demonstrate that the 1-spanner construction by Solomon and Elkin \cite{tree-spanner} supports a local routing algorithm with a worst-case diameter of $O(\log n)$. In Section~\ref{app:doubling}, we show that this routing algorithm can be adapted to a class of doubling metric $(1+\epsilon)$-spanners, which utilize the 1-spanner construction to achieve low diameter while maintaining low weight and low degree.

text: A text index constructed on a string $T$ of length~$n$ is a data structure designed to resolve the following queries for a given pattern~$P$ of length~$m$: \begin{description} \crampedItems \item[\functionname{exists}(P)]: does the pattern~$P$ appear in $T$? \item[\functionname{count}(P)]: how many times does the pattern~$P$ appear in $T$? \item[\functionname{locate}(P)]: at which positions does the pattern~$P$ appear in $T$? \end{description} The responses are a boolean, a numerical value, and a list of starting positions in the text, respectively. The $\functionname{locate}(P)$ query is the most comprehensive, as the size of its returned set equals the return value of $\functionname{count}(P)$, while $\functionname{count}(P) > 0$ is a boolean condition equivalent to $\functionname{exists}(P)$. A notable example of such a text index is the FM-index~\cite{ferragina00fmindex}. It comprises a wavelet tree~\cite{grossi03wavelet} constructed on the BWT~\cite{burrows94bwt} of the text, and can resolve $\functionname{count}(P)$ in time proportional to the length of $P$ multiplied by the operational cost of the wavelet tree, which can be logarithmic in the alphabet size and up to constant~\cite{belazzougui14index}. Given that the BWT consists of $r$ maximal character runs, this data structure can be represented by two additional bit vectors~\cite[Thm.~3]{makinen05rle} of length~$n$ in $r \lg \sigma + \oh{r \lg \sigma} + \Oh{n}$ bits of space. This space can be further minimized with Huffman-shaped wavelet trees by utilizing the zeroth order empirical entropy on the string composed of the distinct letters of the runs in the BWT\@. For $\functionname{locate}$, the indexes based on the BWT are enhanced by sampling the suffix array~\cite{manber93sa}, which requires $n \lg n$ bits in its plain form. In the following, we do not consider $\functionname{locate}$ since this enhancement can be applied orthogonally to our proposed data structure and is reserved for future work. Although current methods achieve \Oh{m} time for $\functionname{count}(P)$ with $|P| = m$, they involve $\Oh{m}$ queries to the underlying wavelet tree data structure, which is executed with a constant number of random accesses. Regrettably, these random accesses render the FM-index relatively slow in practice. The BWT constructed on a grammar-compressed string enables matching non-terminals in a single backward search step, thus allowing us to \emph{bypass multiple characters} in one step. As a result, we spend less time on the cache-unfriendly wavelet tree, but more time on extracting the grammar symbols stored in cache-friendly arrays. Our experiments indicate that this additional work is justified by the reduced use of the wavelet tree in terms of time performance. Regarding space, the grammar captures compressibility more effectively than the run-length compression of the BWT built on the plain text. Here, we exploit certain properties of the GCIS (grammar compression by induced suffix sorting) grammar~\cite{nunes18grammar}, which have been identified by~\citet{akagi21grammar} and \citet{diaz21lms} for determining non-terminals of the text matching parts of the pattern. \paragraph{Our Contribution} In summary, our contribution is that combining the BWT with a specific grammar-based compression method potentially achieves better compression than the plain RLBWT, while simultaneously reducing memory accesses for count queries (heuristically). This comes at the cost of additional computation for constructing the grammar of the text during construction and of the pattern during a query. \subsection*{Related Work} Significant research effort has been devoted to analyzing and improving \functionname{count}{} of the BWT (e.g., \cite{makinen05rle} and the references therein) and the sampling of the suffix array (e.g.,~\cite{gagie18bwt} and the references therein). Another research direction involves grammar indexes, which typically enhance a grammar for \functionname{locate}{} queries. Although computing the smallest grammar is NP-complete~\cite{charikar05grammar}, there are grammars with a size of \Oh{r \log(n/r)}~\cite{gagie18bwt}, and some grammars are empirically much smaller than the RLBWT in practice. However, most indexes have a quadratic dependency on the pattern length for \functionname{locate}{}~\cite{claude12grammarindex,claude21grammarcompressed}, and cannot provide improved query times independent of the number of pattern occurrences, when considering only \functionname{count}{}. A recent exception is the grammar index of \citet{christiansen21optimaltime}, which achieves \Oh{m + \log^{2+\epsilon} n} time for \functionname{count}{} with a space of $\Oh{\gamma \log(n/\gamma)}$, where $\gamma$ is the size of the smallest string attractor~\cite{kempa18stringattractors} of the input text. However, this approach appears to be rather impractical, and to date, no one has attempted to implement it. Related to our work are the grammar indexes of \citet{akagi21grammar} and \citet{diaz21lms}, which are also based on the GCIS grammar, with the latter based on results of \citet{christiansen21optimaltime}. They also employ similar techniques for extracting non-terminals from the pattern grammar, for which they can be certain that these appear in the text grammar. However, they need to invoke \functionname{locate}{} for computing \functionname{count}{}, and thus their time complexity depends on the number of pattern occurrences. We are not aware of a combination of the BWT with grammar techniques, except for construction. Here, \citet{karkkainen12bwt} examined the construction of the BWT on a grammar-compressed input. They applied a grammar compression merging frequent bigrams similar to Re-Pair~\cite{larsson99repair}, and empirically improved the computation of the BWT as well as the reconstruction of the text from the BWT\@. With a similar objective, \citet{diazdominguez21grammar,diaz21grammar} computed the extended BWT~\cite{mantaci07ebwt}, a BWT variant for multiple texts, from the GCIS grammar.

text: The quantum community has achieved substantial progress in creating algorithms that promise speedup compared to their classical equivalents. Nonetheless, the integration of these algorithms into quantum circuits remains unresolved. Numerous groups employ machine learning \cite{cincio2018learning, fosel2021quantum}, genetic algorithms \cite{lee07,rasconi2019an}, and linear algebra methods \cite{re:amy:phds,nam2018automated} to design circuits that either exactly or approximately implement quantum primitives essential for many quantum algorithms. Researchers are also devising optimization techniques to effectively map logical circuits onto physical quantum devices \cite{itoko2020optimization,zulehner2018an}. In this study, we address the challenge of extending the SWAP test to accommodate an arbitrary number of overlapping states. Two-state SWAP tests are valuable primitives in quantum computing that utilize controlled-swap (CSWAP) gates and an ancillary qubit to estimate the inner product $|\langle \phi, \psi\rangle|^{2}$ between two pure quantum states $\phi$ and $\psi$ \cite{kopczyk2018quantum}, as well as to compute the overlap $\mathtt{Tr}(\rho \sigma)$ of two mixed states $\rho$ and $\sigma$ \cite{garcia2013swap}. When $\rho=\sigma$, a SWAP test assesses the purity of the quantum state $\sigma$ \cite{garcia2013swap}. For two $q$-qubit states $\phi,\psi$, the cost of computing $|\langle \phi, \psi\rangle|^{2}$ on a classical computer increases exponentially with $q$, whereas the depth of the SWAP test circuit on a quantum device increases linearly with $q$ \cite{garcia2013swap}, resulting in an exponential speedup that provides a quantum advantage if error correction/mitigation is feasible. The SWAP test is utilized in various applications that require state overlap estimation. It has been applied in quantum state characterization, such as measuring entanglement and indistinguishability \cite{Foulds2021, garcia2013swap}. It is beneficial for benchmarking a quantum computer by tracking the decoherence occurring within a circuit. It also serves as a crucial component in hybrid quantum machine learning algorithms. For example, in quantum supervised learning \cite{kopczyk2018quantum,ciliberto2018quantum,havlicek2019supervised} and particularly in quantum support vector machines (SVM) \cite{rebentrost2014quantum, rudolph2020generation}, it is employed to measure pairwise distances during cluster assignment. Although the issue of enhancing the SWAP test for two high-dimensional states has been explored in several studies \cite{cincio2018learning, garcia2013swap}, until now, except for a 3-state model presented in \cite{Hai-Rui, Galvao2019}, SWAP tests have only been implemented between two quantum states at a time \cite{kathuria2020implementation}. We investigate how to generalize the SWAP test to $m$ arbitrary pure quantum states $\ket{\phi_{1}...\phi_{m}}$ and compute $|\langle \phi_{i}, \phi_{j}\rangle|^{2}$ for all pairs $i\neq j$ using a maximum of $O(\log{m})$ measurements. Our method utilizes a pairing unitary $\mathcal{U}_{m}$ composed of $O(m)$ CSWAP gates controlled by $O(\log{m})$ ancillary qubits. The pairing operator applied to $m$ state registers produces a superposition state where all pairs $(\phi_{i}, \phi_{j})$ appear with positive probability on the first two state registers and are labeled with a basis state formed by the ancillaries. By applying a standard two-state SWAP test to the resulting superposition state, measurement on the ancillary qubits aligns the probability of an ancillary basis state with the state overlap this ancillary basis state is designated to label. Initially, we construct a unitary $\mathcal{U}_{4}$ for a 4-state input with three ancillaries and three CSWAP gates. We assert that the resulting circuit is optimal concerning the number of CSWAP gates when limiting the number of measurements to four. Subsequently, we use our 4-state circuit as a foundational element to develop a recursive algorithm capable of generating an $m$-state circuit for which all overlaps $|\langle \phi_{i}, \phi_{j}\rangle|^{2}$ are measured on $O(\log{m})$ ancillary qubits. We provide a formal analysis of its complexity and demonstrate that the resulting circuit depends on $c_m=O(m)$ CSWAP gates and $d_m=O(\log m)$ ancillaries. Given that our estimates of state overlaps are probabilistic, we must repeat our experiment to achieve an estimate of each state overlap with a mean squared error below a certain precision $\epsilon$. We model these repeated experiments by assuming access to an oracle that constructs the states $\ket{\phi_{1}}, ..., \ket{\phi_{m}}$. We argue that for arbitrary $m$, the constraint to limit the number of measurements to $O(\log m)$ is essential to ensure a polynomial number of oracle calls. Numerically, we implement a genetic procedure to explore how to optimally apply CSWAP gates to maximize the number of pairs that appear on the first two registers of a quantum circuit. Our optimization procedure is motivated by the fact that genetic algorithms are well-suited for optimization problems with complex parameter and energy landscapes. Genetic algorithms have been applied in various fields including scheduling, building design, and trajectory optimization \cite{Hart, Yu}. They have also been successful in automating classical circuit design \cite{aly} and more recently, in designing quantum circuits \cite{Potocek}. For $m=8$ input states and six measurements, we demonstrate empirically that a genetic algorithm does not find circuits with fewer than nine CSWAP gates, which is the number of CSWAP gates we use in our recursive construction (see \ref{circuit: U3}). \begin{figure}[t] \centering \tikzset{every picture/.style={scale=3}}

text: With the swift advancement of radiological imaging technologies, the production of ophthalmic images has increased significantly. There are three prevalent ophthalmic image modalities: (1) \textbf{Slit Lamp.} The slit lamp technique \cite{cheung2011validity} is typically employed to examine both the anterior and posterior segments of the human eye, including the eyelid, sclera, conjunctiva, iris, crystalline lens, and cornea. (2) \textbf{Retinal Fundus.} The retinal fundus image is a crucial eye imaging modality used to diagnose various ocular diseases \cite{fu2018joint,fu2018disc} by capturing the eye's inner lining and structures at the back of the eye. (3) \textbf{ASOCT.} Anterior Segment Optical Coherence Tomography (ASOCT) is utilized for the visualization and evaluation of anterior segment ocular features, such as the tear film, cornea, conjunctiva, sclera, rectus muscles, anterior chamber angle structures, and lens \cite{hirnschall2017prediction}. In recent decades, driven by advancements in pattern recognition and computer vision techniques, particularly deep learning methods \cite{litjens2017survey}, ophthalmic image processing has become increasingly vital in aiding disease diagnosis and assessment. However, the objective interpretation of ophthalmic images is challenged by high inter-observer variability and limited reproducibility. To address the discrepancies in expert interpretation, prior cases with similar disease manifestations can be presented to form a reference-based assessment using Content-Based Image Retrieval (CBIR). CBIR is employed to retrieve user-required images by indexing and mining visual features of image content (\textit{e.g.}, color, shape, texture) from extensive image databases \cite{zhou2017recent}. Unlike classification and grading tasks that provide direct diagnostic results, the objective of ophthalmic CBIR is to enhance diagnosis with evidence-based support. To better assist in assessment, CBIR requires a substantial number of cases, necessitating a retrieval algorithm that is both scalable and precise. To this end, hashing methods for CBIR emerge as a promising solution by representing a high-dimensional image as a compact hash-code due to their storage efficiency and processing speed \cite{conjeti2017deep,wu2019deep}. Recently, deep learning-based hashing methods have been extensively applied in medical image retrieval, such as deep multiple instances hashing for tumor assessment \cite{conjeti2017deep}, deep residual hashing for chest X-ray images \cite{conjeti2017hashing}, and order-sensitive deep hashing methods for multi-morbidity medical image retrieval \cite{chen2018order}, among others. However, existing deep hashing methods do not fully leverage the deep network's learning capacity to capture the features of salient regions effectively. The information from salient regions often serves as the primary clue for clinical diagnosis. Particularly in ophthalmology, different grades or classes of ophthalmic images may exhibit similar overall characteristics but possess subtle differences that can be distinguished by analyzing salient regions. As illustrated in Fig.\ref{fig1}, the ophthalmic images (A) and (B) are derived from ASOCT, a non-invasive high-resolution anterior segment imaging technique. Both (A) and (B) represent cataract cases with similar overall characteristics, but there are two types of salient regions that differentiate them: over-bright regions (blue) and over-dark regions (blue). Cataract grading heavily relies on detecting and observing these salient regions, so the representation of salient regions should be specifically considered in ophthalmic image retrieval. Furthermore, as depicted in Fig. \ref{fig1}, a retinal fundus image (C) contains three symptoms that can be diagnosed based on different salient regions (green rectangle). The pathological myopic eye is often characterized by a leopard fundus, the diagnosis of Diabetic Retinopathy (DR) can depend on the spatial information of the macula, and the large optic cup and abnormalities in the Retinal Nerve Fiber Layer (RNFL) are typical symptoms of glaucoma. The information from these salient regions should be captured and encoded into the hash-code to differentiate fundus images in the retrieval task. Inspired by the attention mechanism in deep networks \cite{woo2018cbam,chen2017sca}, we propose a novel end-to-end network, named Attention-based Saliency Hashing (ASH), to effectively mine salient regions of ophthalmic images and enhance the discriminative capability of the hash-code by exploiting these regions. To thoroughly mine salient regions and effectively increase their representation in the hashing space, we employ a spatial-attention module to focus on capturing the information of salient regions across the entire ophthalmic image. For similarity preservation, using input image pairs with shared weights, we apply the siamese structure \cite{bertinetto2016fully} to learn the pairwise loss in the objective function. The pairwise distance in the hashing space should be smaller if the input image pairs are similar, and larger otherwise. The main contributions of this paper are summarized as follows: \begin{itemize} \item[1)] Different grades or classes of ophthalmic images may exhibit similar overall characteristics but have subtle differences that can be distinguished by analyzing salient regions. To address this, we propose a novel end-to-end network, named Attention-based Saliency Hashing (ASH), for ophthalmic image retrieval. \item[2)] With the aid of a spatial-attention module, by focusing on salient regions throughout the entire ophthalmic image in an end-to-end manner, our ASH can enhance the representation of salient regions to maximize the discriminative capability of the hash-code. \item[3)] Experiments on two different modalities of ophthalmic image datasets demonstrate that our ASH can significantly improve accuracy while maintaining fair efficiency compared to state-of-the-art deep hashing methods. \end{itemize} The remainder of this paper is organized as follows: Section \uppercase\expandafter{\romannumeral2} introduces related works. Section \uppercase\expandafter{\romannumeral3} describes our methodology in detail. Section \uppercase\expandafter{\romannumeral4} extensively evaluates the proposed method on two ophthalmic image datasets. Section \uppercase\expandafter{\romannumeral5} provides concluding remarks.

text: Robots are increasingly operating in crowded environments and moving alongside humans. This is evident with service robots in airports, hotels, and restaurants, delivery robots on sidewalks, mobile robots in warehouses, and autonomous vehicles. For these robots to be deployed safely, it is essential for humans nearby to comprehend their navigation intentions. Historically, HRI researchers have concentrated on arm movement intentions \cite{gielniak2011generating,kwon2018expressing}, examining eye gaze \cite{moon2014meet,admoni2017social} and other non-verbal methods \cite{saunderson2019robots} for stationary robots to more effectively communicate such intentions. Recently, however, HRI researchers have also started investigating the externalization or visualization of robotic navigation intentions (e.g., path plans) \cite{coovert2014spatial,szafir2015communicating,chadalavada2015s,watanabe2015communicating,chadalavada2020bi,blenk2021lane}, to enhance the comprehensibility of robot navigation behaviors, thereby improving trust and acceptance. One approach to conveying navigation intentions is through directional projections \cite{coovert2014spatial,chadalavada2015s,watanabe2015communicating,chadalavada2020bi}, such as arrow projections \cite{coovert2014spatial,chadalavada2020bi}, where the robot uses a projector to display directional cues indicating its intended movement direction. These cues may appear as lines \cite{chadalavada2015s}, gradient bands \cite{watanabe2015communicating}, or arrows \cite{coovert2014spatial,chadalavada2020bi}. In contrast to head-mounted see-through augmented reality \cite{williams2018virtual,williams2018augmented}, projector-based augmented reality does not require participants to wear specialized hardware, allowing visualizations to be viewed by multiple observers simultaneously, thereby enhancing usability in group, team, or crowd settings~\cite{chen2019crowd,sebo2020robots,oliveira2021human}. As discussed in Section~\ref{sec:related_work}, several human-subjects studies \cite{coovert2014spatial,chadalavada2015s,watanabe2015communicating,chadalavada2020bi} have demonstrated the effectiveness of this method \cite{watanabe2015communicating,chadalavada2020bi}. In this study, we present a practical solution for robotic arrow projections, detail the implementation of this solution, and provide access to the corresponding code. Additionally, we specify a particular robot and off-the-shelf projector that we have successfully utilized, along with a summary of a comprehensive user study to offer further empirical evidence. For the implementation, we employed the widely used Robot Operating System (ROS) \cite{quigley2009ros} and its visualization tool, rviz \cite{gossow2011interactive}, for rendering the arrows. Utilizing ROS rendered the implementation robot-agnostic, as most robots used in research and development are compatible with ROS \cite{rosshowcase}. Even non-ROS frameworks \cite{kramer2007development,elkady2012robotics}, and cognitive architectures, such as DIARC~\cite{scheutz2019overview}, generally include bridges to ROS. Using rviz as the rendering engine eliminates the necessity for practitioners and researchers to learn a tool outside of the ROS ecosystem, such as Unity. Furthermore, rviz features a GUI and does not require any computer graphics programming. Given the extensive applications of arrow projection across various robots and its demonstrated effectiveness and efficiency, we believe our work is highly pertinent and advantageous to the HRI community. The readily available implementation with detailed documentation also enables researchers to concentrate on other intriguing and emerging issues in social navigation, such as human navigation modeling \cite{guy2010modeling,ratsamee2013social,ferrer2014proactive,che2018avoiding} and robot navigation that adheres to social or moral norms \cite{banisetty2021implicit,banisetty2021socially}. We welcome GitHub issues for inquiries and pull requests.

text: Multi-agent motion planning encompasses a broad spectrum of practical applications, yet it remains notoriously challenging. Navigating a single robot from an initial position to a target location while avoiding collisions with obstacles is exceedingly difficult due to the presence of complex obstacles, high-dimensional state spaces, nonlinear, nonholonomic dynamics, actuation constraints, and disturbances. Furthermore, when such complex robotic systems interact within a shared environment, the complexity of the problem exceeds the capabilities of most current methods. In this paper, we introduce the \underline{S}calable and \underline{S}afe \underline{M}ulti-agent \underline{M}otion (S2M2) planner, an innovative multi-agent motion planner capable of rapidly and effectively generating provably safe plans for agent models with high-dimensional nonlinear dynamics and bounded disturbances in continuous time and space. Rather than directly planning dynamically feasible trajectories, which is computationally prohibitive, S2M2 employs a separation-of-concerns strategy: Initially, we design piecewise linear (PWL) paths $S_i$ for each dynamic agent $\mathcal{A}_i$ to follow, acknowledging that agents cannot precisely adhere to these PWL paths. However, we demonstrate that with suitable tracking controllers, the actual trajectories of each agent under disturbances can converge to $S_i$ with guaranteed bounds on spatial tracking error. Importantly, we show that this error bound can be pre-computed for any qualified PWL path. The key to S2M2's high efficiency is our ability to formulate the problem of finding PWL paths for a single agent as a Mixed Integer-Linear Program (MILP), which can be efficiently solved using standard MILP solvers. To prevent inter-agent collisions, we integrate our single-agent motion planner with the priority-based search~\cite{ma2019searching}, which explores the space of priority orderings through systematic search. When priorities are assigned, lower-priority agents replan their paths while considering higher-priority agents as moving obstacles. Combined with the MILP-based path planner and guaranteed tracking controller, S2M2 efficiently finds plans that are provably safe and robust to disturbances during execution. Furthermore, by planning paths for multiple agents on a continuous map over continuous time, our method discovers high-quality solutions with low flowtime (i.e., the makespan sum of all single-agent plans). Consider an example involving two disc-shaped vehicles making u-turns, as depicted in Figure~\ref{fig:uturn}. Given the partially known initial locations and bounded disturbances, we first calculate the spatial error bound for tracking a path segment, which is a line, and then consider this error along with the agent shape to determine the possible swept area of the path segment. The swept area of agent $\mathcal{A}_1$ during its second segment $(p_{12}, p_{13})$ is shown in light blue. We also determine the minimum duration for each segment such that the agent has sufficient time to adjust its position after turning, which is $3$ seconds in our example. When our single-agent motion planner designs such paths for the agents, the obstacles are expanded with respect to the spatial tracking error and the agent shape, as shown in light red. The planner also enforces that each segment respects the minimum segment duration. As observed, when passing through the corridor, both agents decelerate and use this $3$ seconds to adjust their trajectories. After passing the corridor, agent $\mathcal{A}_2$ accelerates to its maximum speed to reach its goal location. When potential collisions are identified, some agents are assigned higher priorities and are thus treated as moving obstacles for others. In our example, agent $\mathcal{A}_1$ is given higher priority and therefore passes the corridor before agent $\mathcal{A}_2$. We evaluate the performance of S2M2 against ECBS-CT \cite{cohen2019optimal} and MAPF/C+POST \cite{honig2018trajectory} in 2D and 3D scenarios with ground vehicles and quadrotors, respectively. Results indicate that S2M2 surpasses both planners in terms of solution quality, achieving a $15\sim70\%$ reduction for most instances. Additionally, S2M2 requires significantly less time for pre-processing and also demonstrates competitive runtime performance compared to the other two planners.

Consequently, in our example, agent A-1 is given priority, and, consequently, passes through the corridor before agent A-2. Then, after having passed the corridor, agent A2 accelerates at full speed towards its goal. But S2M2 was able to carry out the preprocessing much faster, and its runtime performance was similar to that of the other two planners.

text: The task of identifying the most significant directions or \emph{principal components} of a matrix from noisy observations is a fundamental issue in both mathematical statistics and its applications \cite{Rao-1964-PCA,Johnstone-2001-LargestEigenvaluePCA,Ringner-2008-PCA,AW-2010-PCA}. The theoretical asymptotic behavior of this problem has been extensively studied through the analysis of idealized \emph{spiked matrix models}. The initial models, introduced by Johnstone \cite{Johnstone-2001-LargestEigenvaluePCA}, involved Gaussian observations from a covariance matrix altered by a rank-one ``spike,'' but the simpler \emph{Wigner spiked matrix model} captures much of the same phenomenology. We examine the following two probability distributions $\PP$ and $\QQ$ over $n \times n$ symmetric matrices. \begin{itemize} \item Under $\QQ = \QQ_n$, observe $\bW \in \RR^{n \times n}_{\sym}$ drawn from the \emph{Gaussian orthogonal ensemble (GOE)}, where $W_{ii} \sim \sN(0, \frac{1}{n})$ and $W_{ij} = W_{ji} \sim \sN(0, \frac{2}{n})$ for $i < j$, with all $\frac{n(n + 1)}{2}$ entries distributed independently. We also denote this distribution as $\QQ = \GOE(n)$. \item Under $\PP = \PP_n$, first draw $\bu \sim \Unif(\mathbb{S}^{n - 1})$ for $\mathbb{S}^{n - 1} \subset \RR^n$ as the unit sphere, and then observe $\bW = \bW_0 + \beta \bu\bu^{\top}$ for $\bW_0 \sim \GOE(n)$ and some fixed $\beta > 0$, which remains constant as $n \to \infty$. \end{itemize} Two natural statistical questions arise: (1) \emph{detection} or \emph{testing}, where we observe $\bW$ drawn from either $\PP$ or $\QQ$ and must determine the source distribution, and (2) \emph{recovery} or \emph{estimation}, where we observe $\bW \sim \PP$ and aim to produce an accurate estimate of $\bu$. In either scenario, the associated optimization problem of computing the largest eigenvalue is naturally considered: \begin{equation} \lambda_{\max}(\bW) \colonequals \max_{\|\bx\|_2 = 1} \bx^{\top} \bW \bx. \end{equation} For recovery, computing the maximizer $\bx^{\star}$ (the top eigenvector of $\bW$) serves as the maximum likelihood estimation of $\bu$. For detection, computing and thresholding $\lambda_{\max}(\bW)$ itself is a natural and often effective strategy. The optimal value and optimizer of $\lambda_{\max}(\bW)$ can be approximated (to any desired accuracy) in time $\poly(n)$, thus these correspond to efficient algorithms for recovery and detection, respectively. Moreover, these algorithms are essentially \emph{optimal}: almost whenever\footnote{Except in the critical case $\beta = 1$, where thresholding $\lambda_{\max}(\bW)$ does not distinguish $\PP$ from $\QQ$, but this can be achieved by employing more sophisticated statistics \cite{OJ-2020-TestingSpikedModels}.} it is possible to distinguish $\PP$ from $\QQ$ with high probability,\footnote{A sequence of events $A_n$ occurs \emph{with high probability} under a sequence of probability measures $\PP_n$ if $\lim_{n \to \infty} \PP_n[A_n] = 1$.} thresholding $\lambda_{\max}(\bW)$ accomplishes this; whenever it is possible to estimate $\bu$ non-trivially, the optimizer $\bx^{\star}$ achieves this. \begin{proposition}[\cite{FP-2007-LargestEigenvalueWigner,CDMF-2009-DeformedWigner,MRZ-2015-LimitationsSpectral,BMVVX-2018-InfoTheoretic}] Let $\bW \sim \PP$ with parameter $\beta \ge 0$ (note that setting $\beta = 0$ results in $\PP = \QQ$), and let $\bu$ be the spike vector. Let $\bx^{\star}(\bW)$ be the optimizer of $\lambda_{\max}(\bW)$, the top eigenvector of $\bW$ scaled to unit norm. Then, we have almost surely \begin{align} \lim_{n \to \infty} \lambda_{\max}(\bW) &= \left\{\begin{array}{ll} 2 & \text{if } 0 \leq \beta \leq 1, \\ \beta + \beta^{-1} > 2 \, \, \, \, \, \, & \text{if } \beta > 1, \end{array} \right. \\ \lim_{n \to \infty} |\la \bx^{\star}(\bW), \bu \ra| &= \left\{\begin{array}{ll} 0 & \text{if } 0 \leq \beta \leq 1, \\ \sqrt{1 - \beta^{-2}} > 0 & \text{if } \beta > 1. \end{array}\right. \end{align} Moreover, if $0 \le \beta < 1$, then there is no function of $\bW$ that with high probability correctly identifies whether $\bW$ is drawn from $\PP$ or $\QQ$, and if $0 \le \beta \leq 1$, then there is no unit vector-valued function of $\bW$ that has an inner product with $\bx$ asymptotically bounded away from zero with high probability when $\bW \sim \PP$. \end{proposition} \noindent The behavior of $\lambda_{\max}(\bW)$ is established by \cite{FP-2007-LargestEigenvalueWigner}, while the behavior of $|\langle \bx^{\star}(\bW), \bu \rangle|$ is determined by \cite{CDMF-2009-DeformedWigner} (both building on the foundational results of \cite{BBAP-2005-LargestEigenvalueSampleCovariance}). The impossibility of ``detection'' or of determining whether $\bW$ is drawn from $\PP$ or $\QQ$ with high probability is demonstrated by \cite{MRZ-2015-LimitationsSpectral} by establishing \emph{contiguity} of these two sequences of probability measures. Finally, \cite{BMVVX-2018-InfoTheoretic} show that this contiguity implies the impossibility of estimating $\bu$ with positive correlation. More refined models arise from selecting more structured distributions of $\bu$. This corresponds to extracting principal components under some prior knowledge of their structure. One natural example was introduced by \cite{MR-2015-NonNegative}, where $\bu$ is chosen uniformly from the positive orthant of $\mathbb{S}^{n - 1}$ instead of the entire sphere, resulting in the problem of \emph{non-negative PCA}. Here, the null model $\QQ$ remains as above, while $\PP$ is replaced with $\PP^+$ defined as follows: \begin{itemize} \item Under $\PP^+$, first draw $\bv \sim \Unif(\mathbb{S}^{n - 1})$, let $\bu$ have entries $u_i = |v_i|$, and then observe $\bW = \bW_0 + \beta \bu\bu^{\top}$ for $\bW_0 \sim \GOE(n)$ and some fixed $\beta > 0$. \end{itemize} Following the classical PCA case, we might hope to address detection and recovery by solving the optimization problem \begin{equation} \lambda^{+}(\bW) \colonequals \max_{\substack{\|\bx\|_2 = 1 \\ \bx \geq 0}} \bx^\top \bW \bx, \end{equation} where $\bx \geq 0$ means $x_i \geq 0$ for each $i \in [n]$. However, a crucial difference between classical PCA and non-negative PCA arises: unlike $\lambda_{\max}(\bW)$ and the associated optimizer, it is $\mathsf{NP}$-hard to compute $\lambda^+(\bW)$ for general $\bW$ \cite{KP-2002-CopositiveProgramming}. Therefore, non-negative PCA presents a more significant algorithmic challenge. Nonetheless, using an approximate message-passing (AMP) algorithm \cite{MR-2015-NonNegative} demonstrated that it is possible to solve this problem essentially to optimality for random inputs from $\QQ$ or $\PP^+$. We now focus solely on the ``null'' case $\bW \sim \QQ = \GOE(n)$. \begin{proposition}[Part of Theorem 2 and Proposition 4.5 of \cite{MR-2015-NonNegative}] Almost surely for $\bW \sim \GOE(n)$, \begin{equation} \lim_{n \to \infty} \lambda^+(\bW) = \sqrt{2}. \end{equation} Moreover, for any $\varepsilon > 0$, there exists an algorithm that runs in time $\poly(n)$ (with runtime also depending on $\varepsilon$) and computes $\bx \in \mathbb{S}^{n - 1}$ with $\bx \geq 0$ that has $\bx^{\top}\bW \bx \geq \sqrt{2} - \varepsilon$ with high probability. \end{proposition} \noindent This same algorithm is also effective for detection between $\QQ$ and $\PP^+$ and recovery under $\PP^+$. \begin{remark} One can verify that various simpler algorithms do not yield a solution of the same quality. For instance, if $\bv$ is the top eigenvector of $\bW$, then one simple algorithm is to take $\bv^+$ with entries $v^+_i = \max(0, v_i)$ and return $\bx = \bv^+ / \|\bv^+\|$. However, computing heuristically, we have \begin{equation} \bx^{\top}\bW \bx \approx \frac{1}{\|\bv^+\|^2} \cdot 2 \langle \bv, \bv^+ \rangle^2 \approx 2 \cdot 2 \cdot \left(\frac{1}{2}\right)^2 = 1, \end{equation} indicating that this choice of $\bx$ is inferior to that produced by AMP. \end{remark} In this paper, we explore an alternative to AMP, also suggested in \cite{MR-2015-NonNegative}, where we replace the intractable optimization problem $\lambda^+(\bW)$ with the following tractable convex relaxation, a natural \emph{semidefinite program (SDP)}: \begin{equation} \SDP(\bW) \colonequals \max_{\substack{\bX \succeq 0 \\ \bX \geq 0 \\ \Tr(\bX) = 1}} \la \bX, \bW \ra \geq \lambda^+(\bW). \end{equation} In \cite{MR-2015-NonNegative}, numerical experiments are presented suggesting that this SDP is effective in recovering $\bx$ under $\PP^+$, with the restriction of the top eigenvector of the optimizer $\bX^{\star}$ to only positive entries providing a comparable estimate of $\bu$ to the AMP algorithm (see their Section 5.3). In Section~\ref{sec:finite-size}, we present analogous experiments for $\bW \sim \GOE(n)$ and note that in this case, the SDP is often \emph{tight}, with the optimizer $\bX^{\star}$ being rank one within numerical tolerances. While the SDP is much slower than AMP, its apparent efficacy is nevertheless intriguing, suggesting that the algorithmic tractability of non-negative PCA might be unified with other situations where SDP relaxations of maximum likelihood estimation are tight \cite{BKS-2014-TightnessMLESDP}. Furthermore, the SDP offers some advantages over AMP: it algorithmically \emph{proves} (or \emph{certifies}) an upper bound on the value of $\lambda^+(\bW)$, and it may also exhibit robustness properties that SDPs have been shown to possess in other contexts~\cite{FK-2001-SemirandomGraphProblems,MPW-2016-RobustReconstruction,RTJM-2016-SDPRobustness}. The problem of determining the asymptotic behavior of the SDP as $n \to \infty$ under $\bW \sim \GOE(n)$ was also posed explicitly as Open Problem~9.5 in the lecture notes \cite{Bandeira-2015-TenLectures} of one of the authors. We therefore address the following two questions concerning this SDP and related algorithmic approaches when $\bW \sim \GOE(n)$. The first concerns this specific semidefinite program: \begin{enumerate} \item[1.] When $\bW \sim \GOE(n)$, does $\SDP(\bW) \to \sqrt{2}$ in probability as $n \to \infty$? \end{enumerate} As we will see, the answer in the limit $n \to \infty$, in surprising contrast to the experiments of~\cite{MR-2015-NonNegative} for small $n$, is \emph{no}. In fact, we instead have $\SDP(\bW) \to \lambda_{\max}(\bW) \approx 2$ as $n \to \infty$. We then inquire whether any remotely efficient algorithm that \emph{certifies} upper bounds on $\lambda^+(\bW)$ can improve upon this. \begin{enumerate} \item[2.] Does there exist an algorithm that runs in time $\exp(O(n^{1 - \eta}))$ for some fixed $\eta > 0$ and computes $c: \RR^{n \times n}_{\sym} \to \RR$ with the following two properties? \begin{itemize} \item For \emph{all} $\bW \in \RR^{n \times n}_{\sym}$, we have $c(\bW) \geq \lambda^+(\bW)$. \item When $\bW \sim \GOE(n)$, we have $c(\bW) \leq 2 - \varepsilon$ with high probability for some fixed $\varepsilon > 0$. \end{itemize} \end{enumerate} We provide rigorous evidence, based on the \emph{low-degree polynomial method}, that even the answer to this much broader question again is \emph{no}. \subsection{Organization} The remainder of the paper is organized as follows. In Section~\ref{sec:sdp}, we state and prove a lower bound on $\SDP(\bW)$ when $\bW \sim \GOE(n)$. In Section~\ref{sec:low-deg}, we state and prove a \emph{reduction} from a certain hypothesis testing problem to the problem of certifying bounds on $\lambda^+(\bW)$, and review evidence from prior work that this hypothesis testing problem is computationally hard. Finally, in Section~\ref{sec:finite-size}, we present the results of larger numerical experiments that capture the departure from the ``tight regime'' where the optimizer of $\SDP$ has rank one, a striking example of the difference between theoretical asymptotics and computations tractable at ``laptop scale'' for semidefinite programming.

text: The task of approximating the distribution of a target value $y$ given an input $x$ is fundamental to supervised learning tasks. When trained with standard losses such as Mean Square Error for regression or Cross-Entropy for classification, supervised methods are recognized for approximating the expected conditional distribution of the target given the input, specifically $\langle y|x \rangle$ \cite{bishop_mixture_1994}. This approach is typical when the target distribution is unimodal, and minor variations in the target value are primarily due to random noise. However, when the target distribution in a regression problem is not unimodal, most machine learning methods inadequately represent it by predicting an average value. text: From delivery drones to autonomous electric vertical take-off and landing (eVTOL) passenger aircraft, contemporary unmanned aircraft systems (UAS) can efficiently execute a wide range of tasks, including goods delivery, surveillance, public safety, weather monitoring, disaster relief, search and rescue, traffic monitoring, videography, and air transportation \citep{balakrishnan2018blueprint,kopardekar2016unmanned}. Urban air mobility (UAM) is anticipated to occur in urban environments near buildings or airports. Therefore, it is expected that UAS will utilize onboard detect and avoid systems to evade other traffic, adverse weather, terrain, and both man-made and natural obstacles without continuous human oversight \citep{kopardekar2016unmanned}. Numerous mathematical models for aircraft conflict resolution have been introduced in the literature. Research efforts can be categorized into centralized algorithms and decentralized algorithms. Centralized techniques can be based on semidefinite programming \citep{frazzoli2001resolution}, nonlinear programming \citep{raghunathan2004dynamic,enright1992discrete}, mixed-integer linear programming \citep{schouwenaars2001mixed,richards2002aircraft,pallottino2002conflict,vela2009mixed}, mixed-integer quadratic programming \citep{mellinger2012mixed}, sequential convex programming \citep{augugliaro2012generation,morgan2014model}, second-order cone programming \citep{acikmese2007convex}, evolutionary techniques \citep{delahaye2010aircraft,cobano2011path}, and particle swarm optimization \citep{pontani2010particle}. These centralized techniques often aim for the global optimum for all aircraft. However, as the number of aircraft increases, the computational cost of these methods typically scales exponentially. Among decentralized methods, the conflict resolution problem can also be formulated as a Markov Decision Process (MDP). Reinforcement Learning (RL) has been demonstrated to be an effective solution for aircraft traffic management, but it predominantly employs traditional algorithms \citep{sun2019reinforcement}. The next-generation airborne collision avoidance system (ACAS X) frames the collision avoidance systems (CAS) problem as a partially observable Markov Decision Process (POMDP) and has been extended to unmanned aircraft, known as ACAS Xu \citep{kochenderfer2012next}. Both ACAS X and ACAS Xu utilize Dynamic Programming (DP) to compute the expected cost of each action \citep{manfredi2016introduction, owen2019acas}. \cite{chryssanthacopoulos2012decomposition} combined decomposition methods and DP for optimized collision avoidance with multiple threats. Traditional RL algorithms necessitate a fine discretization scheme of state space and finite action space. Discretization can potentially reduce safety by introducing discretization errors and cannot provide flexible maneuver guidance for UAS. Additionally, discretizing large airspace implies a high computational demand and can be time-consuming. Tree search-based algorithms \citep{yang2018autonomous,yang2020scalable} are also applied to CAS problems using MDP formulation, which does not involve state discretization. However, they typically require significant onboard computation time to handle the continuous state space. The extensive and continuous state and action spaces pose a challenge for conflict resolution problems using reinforcement learning. Recently, Deep Reinforcement Learning (DRL) has been explored to address this challenge by employing the deep neural network to approximate the cost and the optimal policy functions. The development of DRL algorithms, such as Policy Gradient \citep{sutton2000policy}, Deep Q-Networks (DQN) \citep{mnih2013playing}, Double DQN \citep{van2016deep}, Dueling DQN \citep{wang2015dueling}, Deep Deterministic Policy Gradient (DDPG) \citep{lillicrap2015continuous}, Asynchronous Advantage Actor-Critic (A3C) \citep{mnih2016asynchronous}, and Proximal Policy Optimization (PPO) \citep{ppo2} has enhanced the potential of automation. \cite{li2019optimizing} utilized DQN to compute corrections for an existing collision avoidance approach to accommodate dense airspace. In \cite{yang2019real}, the feasibility of using algorithms based on DQN in UAV obstacle avoidance is validated. \cite{wulfeuav} concluded that DQN can surpass value iteration both in terms of evaluation performance and solution speed when addressing a UAV collision avoidance problem. The performance of the agent in avoiding single up to multiple aircraft using the DQN algorithm is examined in \cite{keong2019reinforcement}. \cite{brittain2020deep} proposed a novel deep multi-agent reinforcement learning framework based on PPO to identify and resolve conflicts among a variable number of aircraft in a high-density, stochastic, and dynamic sector in en-route airspace. The aforementioned DRL work is in continuous state and discrete action space. There has been limited progress on employing DRL to address UAS conflict resolution with continuous control. \cite{pham2019machine} proposed a method inspired by Deep Q-learning and Deep Deterministic Policy Gradient algorithms, which can resolve conflicts with a success rate of over 81\% in the presence of traffic and varying degrees of uncertainties. \cite{ma2018saliency} developed a generic framework that integrates an autonomous obstacle detection module and an actor-critic based reinforcement learning (RL) module to develop reactive obstacle avoidance behavior for a UAV. Experiments in \cite{ppo2} test PPO on a collection of benchmark tasks, including simulated robotic locomotion and Atari game playing, and demonstrate that PPO outperforms other online policy gradient methods. PPO seems to offer a favorable balance between sample complexity, simplicity, and wall-time. Thus, a PPO-based conflict resolution model is highly valuable for UAS traffic management, which is the primary motivation of this study. To the best of the authors' knowledge, this is the first study to develop a DRL approach based on the PPO algorithm to enable UAS to navigate successfully in continuous state and action spaces. The advantage of computing in continuous space is that there is no need to discretize the state space or smooth results for postprocessing. The proposed model with the optimal policy after offline training can be employed for UAS real-time online trajectory planning. The main contributions of this paper are as follows: \begin{itemize} \setlength\itemsep{0em} \item A PPO-based framework has been proposed for UAS to avoid both static and dynamic obstacles in continuous state and action spaces. \item A novel scenario state representation and reward function are developed, effectively mapping the environment to maneuvers. The trained model can generate continuous heading angle commands and speed commands. \item We have evaluated the effectiveness of the proposed learning framework in environments with static obstacles, environments with static obstacles and UAS position uncertainty, and deterministic and stochastic environments with dynamic obstacles. Results indicate that the proposed model can provide accurate and robust guidance and resolve conflicts with a success rate of over 99\%. \end{itemize} The remainder of this paper is organized as follows. \cref{background} describes the backgrounds of Markov Decision Process and Deep Reinforcement Learning. \cref{mdp} presents the model formulation using Markov Decision Process for UAS conflict resolution in continuous action space. In \cref{result}, the numerical experiments are presented to demonstrate the capability of the proposed approach to enable the UAS to learn to avoid conflict. \cref{Conclusion} concludes this paper.

text: Frequently-Asked-Questions (FAQ) consist of question-answer pairs that are either manually compiled or automatically extracted from pertinent documents. FAQs offer users a centralized source for the most pertinent or frequently sought information regarding a product or service, facilitating prompt customer assistance for general inquiries. \vspace*{1mm} {\bf Motivation.} FAQ retrieval systems offer a natural language interface for querying an FAQ collection, and are thus increasingly popular among large-scale service companies for disseminating information to customers. These systems provide dual benefits: (i) automation of customer service tasks, such as intelligent chatbots~\cite{massaro2018,yan2016} and automated email responses~\cite{karan2018,malik2007}, and (ii) enable effective access to internal FAQ documents for customer service agents, thereby enhancing quality and efficiency. Furthermore, with the emergence of personal assistants (such as XiaoIce, Siri, Alexa, Google Assistant, etc.), these "virtual agents" can answer questions and help users complete routine tasks through an additional channel to FAQs, hotlines, and forums, facilitating natural interaction with users~\cite{lommatzsch2019,por2020}. \vspace*{1mm} {\bf Challenges.} FAQ retrieval presents challenges, primarily due to the brevity of question-answer texts, which complicates bridging the {\em lexical and semantic gap} between a user query and the FAQ questions because of the short span with limited context~\cite{karan2018,lee2008}. Moreover, accurately interpreting user questions can be challenging due to informal expressions, domain-specific language, abbreviations, and mismatches between formal and colloquial terms~\cite{lommatzsch2019}. For instance, consider the questions {\small{\tt ``How can I seal a hole in the gas tank of my car?''}} and {\small{\tt ``How to patch a leak in the fuel compartment of my van?''}} which are semantically similar but show low lexical overlap and formal-colloquial mismatch. Additionally, FAQ retrieval systems must handle both keyword-based and {\em short span} "natural language" questions. Given their predominantly "customer-centric" nature, such systems typically require higher precision and interpretability compared to traditional information retrieval methods. \vspace*{1mm} {\bf Problem Statement.} The task of {\em FAQ Retrieval} involves efficiently ranking (based on relevance) the question-answer pairs of a collection in response to a user query. In essence, these retrieval engines aim to discern the underlying {\em intent} of users and retrieve the most pertinent answers containing the correct information~\cite{kothari2009}. Formally, consider a pre-curated collection (or repository) of question-answer $(Q, A)$ pairs constituting the FAQ $= \{(Q_1, A_1), \cdots, (Q_n, A_n)\}$, where $Q_i$ denotes a domain-related question, and $A_i$ represents the corresponding answer. Given a user query $q$, the task is to return an ordered list of FAQ $(Q, A)$ pairs, $\{(Q_1^q, A_1^q), \cdots, (Q_k^q, A_k^q)\}$, demonstrating high semantic and intent similarity with respect to the input user query $q$. \vspace*{1mm} {\bf Contributions.} This study introduces {\em TI-S2S}, a novel keyword-based supervised learning framework for efficient FAQ retrieval. Our approach employs a {\em sequence-to-sequence} model to generate representative labels for user questions to compute query-question similarity. Moreover, a variant incorporating "candidates" identified using a deep learning architecture to guide the retrieval process is demonstrated to further enhance performance. We demonstrate that our proposed framework effectively captures: (i) the domain-specificity of the application, (ii) characteristic words and/or concepts to differentiate between questions, and (iii) semantic similarity for retrieving relevant QA pairs from the FAQ collection. Experiments on a public FAQ dataset show our framework surpasses existing techniques in terms of accuracy and robustness to limited training data. Consequently, it implicitly considers both {\em document redundancy} and {\em query redundancy}~\cite{karan2018}.

The brevity of the question-answer text poses a challenge, because it makes it difficult to bridge the lexical and semantic gap between a question and an answer in such a short and limited context. A question like: “How do I repair a hole in the gas tank of my car?” or “How do I fix a leak in the gas tank of my car?” is not easy to interpret, due to the slang, jargon, abbreviations, and jarring between the colloquial and the idiomatic. "The task of the 'FAQ retrieval' consists in ranking the question-answer pairs in a collection in order of their relevance to a given question. But since FAQ retrieval systems must cope with both keywords and natural language questions which are often not only semantically close but also lexically distant, and often mismatched between the formal and the informal, they usually demand a higher precision and a higher degree of interpretability than are required by the methods of information retrieval. The set of the FAQs is a collection of question-answer (Q-A) pairs, where Q_i denotes a domain-related question and A_i the corresponding answer. Given a question q, the task is to return an ordered list of FAQs as a sequence of pairs, where “Q_1q, A_1q”,... “Q_n, A_n”, where “Q_i” denotes a domain-related question and “A_i” the corresponding answer. Essentially, the goal of these systems is to infer the underlying "intention" of the users and retrieve the most appropriate and relevant answers with the correct information. This paper introduces a new supervised learning framework, named TI-S2S, for efficient question-answering. It uses a sequence-to-sequence model to generate representative labels of questions to calculate similarity. Moreover, a variant that makes use of "candidates" identified by a deep learning architecture to guide the retrieval process is shown to further improve performance. The system demonstrates that it captures: i) the application-related nature of the question, ii) characteristic words or concepts that distinguish the question from other questions, and iii) semantic similarity to find relevant Q-A pairs from the collection of questions. This system thus implicitly considers the redundancy of the document and the question. The results of an experiment on a public set of questions show that the system has greater accuracy and is more robust than existing methods when it comes to the accuracy of its answers.

From G. Hinton's Turing Award-winning work on 	extit{backpropagation} in 1986 \cite{Rumelhart1986LearningRB} to contemporary optimizers standardized in widely used deep learning libraries such as Google's TensorFlow \cite{Abadi2016TensorFlowAS} and Facebook's PyTorch \cite{NEURIPS2019_9015}, the 	extit{gradient} is integral to the learning process of most deep learning models. For instance, in the task of image classification, the gradient guides the image classifier in adjusting its parameters to minimize the errors (i.e., the 	extit{loss function}) between the predictions and the actual class labels. As the model iteratively updates its parameters in the opposite direction of the gradient on various training samples, the loss function decreases progressively, enhancing the prediction accuracy of the learning model. However, the fundamental role of the gradient in deep learning is accompanied by its potential risks. As illustrated in Fig. ef{fig:intro_grad}, in a typical face recognition system, a batch of training images is first input into the neural network classifier. The classifier then predicts the labels, computes the average loss function, and employs back-propagation to calculate the gradient as the parameter derivative of the average loss. Since the gradient is explicitly derived from the data inputs and labels, it is plausible for an attacker to anticipate that the gradient could reveal sensitive information about the original training data. With the rise of novel distributed learning paradigms \cite{yang2019FL,Chen2020NebulaAS}, several research efforts have begun exploring the feasibility of inferring data properties \cite{Melis2019ExploitingUF}, membership \cite{Melis2019ExploitingUF, Nasr2019ComprehensivePA}, class representatives \cite{Hitaj2017DeepMU, Wang2019BeyondIC}, or data inputs \cite{Zhu2019DeepLF, Zhao2020iDLGID, Geiping2020InvertingG} from the gradient potentially exposed to a man-in-the-middle attacker or an honest-but-curious server \cite{Lyu2020,Kairouz2021AdvancesAO}. Despite the feasibility of privacy attacks via the gradient, most prior attacks encounter a common yet ambiguous performance bottleneck concerning the privacy leakage of their proposed methods. For instance, Melis et al. \cite{Melis2019ExploitingUF} report that the precision of sensitive word inference from the gradient decreases by over $30\%$ when the batch size increases by $8	imes$. Nasr et al. \cite{Nasr2019ComprehensivePA} observe that a shallower neural network model tends to leak less membership information. Zhu et al. \cite{Zhu2019DeepLF} note that the iterations required to reverse engineer a training batch from its average gradient increase by $10	imes$ when the batch size grows from $1$ to $8$, while the proposed attack is more prone to failure with a shallow neural network. In summary, the information leakage from the gradient appears to decrease with a larger training batch and a shallower neural network model. However, does this phenomenon have a common root cause intertwined with the underlying mechanism of deep learning? To our knowledge, the existing literature provides little insight into this fundamental question. 
oindent	extbf{Our Work.} We address the above question by examining the mechanism of 	extit{data reconstruction attack} \cite{Zhu2019DeepLF, Zhao2020iDLGID, Geiping2020InvertingG}, an emerging privacy threat that exploits the leaked average gradient of a deep learning model to reverse engineer the corresponding training batch. As depicted in the right part of Fig. ef{fig:intro_grad}, data reconstruction attack aims to reconstruct the training samples from the corresponding gradient, posing significant threats to the confidentiality of private training data. As one of the earliest data reconstruction attacks, Zhu et al. \cite{Zhu2019DeepLF} propose a learning-based approach to restore the training batch, treating the unknown training batch as learnable variables (i.e., 	extit{dummy data}). By minimizing the L2 distance between the gradient computed on the dummy data and the ground-truth gradient (i.e., 	extit{gradient matching}), they surprisingly find that reconstruction is possible when the batch size is no larger than $8$ on CIFAR-100 \cite{Krizhevsky2009LearningML}, although the reconstruction quality can be unstable across different trials and relatively small victim models. Subsequent works \cite{Zhao2020iDLGID,Geiping2020InvertingG} introduce technical refinements to the learning-based framework in \cite{Zhu2019DeepLF}, with similar bottlenecks observed in data reconstruction. However, due to their limited interpretability, none of the previous works have successfully characterized 	extit{why, when, and how data reconstruction from the gradient is feasible}, which, from our perspective, could be a crucial entry point to understanding and enhancing the privacy properties of the gradient. To explore the security boundary of data reconstruction from the gradient, we present the first analytical study of data reconstruction attacks on the family of fully-connected neural networks (FCNs) with rectified linear units (ReLUs \cite{Goodfellow-et-al-2016}), a fundamental neural network architecture commonly used for demonstrating novel attack and defense insights \cite{Jagielski2020HighAA,Tramr2016StealingML,Rolnick2020ReverseengineeringDR}. As arguably the most popular activation function in deep learning practices \cite{Goodfellow-et-al-2016}, a ReLU allows nonnegative inputs to pass through unaltered while blocking negative inputs. This distinctive gate-like behavior of ReLU enables each input sample to maintain its own set of 	extit{activation paths} as its 	extit{activation pattern} \cite{Montfar2014OnTN, Laurent2018TheMS}. We develop deterministic algorithms that decode the hidden information in the average gradient to ascertain the activation patterns of each sample, a crucial step to simplify the otherwise highly nonlinear gradient-matching problem to a linear equation system regarding the inputs to facilitate further analytical studies. By examining the conditions under which the activation patterns can be reconstructed from the gradient, we primarily make the following key contributions: 
oindent	extbf{(1) Neuron Exclusivity State Analysis.} For the first time, we identify the 	extit{neuron exclusivity state}, indexed by the number of 	extit{	extbf{Ex}clusively 	extbf{A}ctivated 	extbf{N}eurons} (ExANs, i.e., a ReLU activated by only one sample in a batch during a forward pass), as critical to the feasibility of data reconstruction attack. Specifically, we delineate the following boundary conditions for the neuron exclusivity state of a training batch under attack. 
oindent	extbf{(2) Boundary of Insecure Exclusivity States.} We identify the condition of 	extit{sufficient exclusivity}, i.e., when each sample in a batch has at least $2$ ExANs at the last ReLU layer and $1$ at the other layers, as a strong indicator of insecure neuron exclusivity states (Section ef{sec:atk_case_a}). Specifically, we demonstrate that a deterministic attack algorithm with guaranteed reconstruction accuracy (Theorem ef{col:optim_bound_mult}) can be devised for any training batch meeting the sufficient exclusivity condition. Evaluation on $5$ real-world scenarios encompassing medical, face recognition, and visual datasets and a diverse set of FCNs of varied depth and width shows that our attack consistently surpasses previous attacks by a significant margin in terms of reconstruction recognizability and achieves $100\%$ label inference accuracy (Section ef{sec:evaluation}). Additionally, we extend our attack algorithm to classifiers based on convolutional neural networks (CNNs) by integrating analytical and optimization-based techniques. 
oindent	extbf{(3) Boundary of Secure Exclusivity States.} By analyzing the remaining exclusivity state space, we further identify the 	extit{lack of exclusivity} condition, i.e., when each sample has $0$ ExAN at the first ReLU layer, as an indicator of the impossibility of unique reconstruction (Section ef{sec:def_case_b}). For these states, we prove that there always exist infinitely many artifact batches that yield exactly the same gradient as the victim's ground-truth batch, and derive the lower bound for the largest distance between an artifact batch and the ground-truth batch (Theorem ef{thm:impossible_reconstr}). This finding inspires us to devise an exclusivity reduction strategy, which replaces the first ReLU layer with a linear layer, to enhance the privacy of any batch of training samples when its size exceeds the number of neurons in the first layer, with minimal impact on model performance. For the completeness of our study, we also present preliminary experimental results in Section ef{sec:discussion} to empirically analyze the performance of data reconstruction on the remaining states.

text: Capturing users' preferences from their historical data is crucial for generating effective recommendations, as both users' preferences and items' characteristics are dynamic. Additionally, users' preferences are highly context-dependent (e.g., an individual is likely to be interested in purchasing a keyboard after buying a desktop). Thus, sequential recommendation seeks to predict the next set of items that users are likely to prefer by leveraging their historical data. Numerous algorithms have been developed to better comprehend users' sequential histories~\cite{SASRec, BERT4Rec, hidasi2018recurrent, CASER, M3, rendle2010factorizing, DIN, TRANSREC}. Despite their strong performance, most of these algorithms overlook the timestamp values of interactions. Although recent studies such as TiSASRec~\cite{TISASRec} have successfully integrated time information, their approach to using time was restricted to a single embedding scheme. Given that timestamp values contain abundant information, it would be advantageous to explore various forms of temporal embeddings that can fully extract diverse patterns, along with model architectures that can effectively utilize such diversity. In this paper, we propose \textbf{MEANTIME} (\textbf{M}ixtur\textbf{E} of \textbf{A}tte\textbf{NTI}on mechanisms with \textbf{M}ulti-temporal \textbf{E}mbeddings), which introduces multiple temporal embeddings to more effectively encode both absolute and relative positions of a user-item interaction in a sequence. Additionally, we employ multiple self-attention heads that process each positional embedding separately. This is advantageous because each head can function as an expert focusing on a specific pattern of user behaviors. Extensive experiments demonstrate that \textbf{MEANTIME} surpasses state-of-the-art algorithms on real-world datasets. Our contributions are as follows: \begin{itemize} \item We propose diversifying the embedding schemes used to encode the positions of user-item interactions in a sequence. This is achieved by applying multiple kernels to the positions/values of timestamps in a sequence to generate unique embedding matrices. \item We also introduce a novel model architecture that operates multiple self-attention heads concurrently, where each head specializes in extracting specific patterns from users' behaviors by utilizing one of the positional embeddings we propose above. \item We conducted extensive experiments to demonstrate the effectiveness of our method on real-world datasets. We also provide a comprehensive ablation study that aids in understanding the impact of various components in our model. \end{itemize}
