text: Although deep neural networks (DNNs) have achieved success in numerous computer vision and pattern recognition tasks, several limitations have hindered their broader application. For instance, due to the substantial computational cost associated with training and inference, deploying large DNN models on devices with limited computational resources is challenging \cite{wu2018deep}. The lack of interpretability renders DNNs unsuitable for real-world tasks where explainability in decision-making is essential. Since DNNs essentially stack basic computational units—a perceptron—it is reasonable to question whether substituting this atomic unit with alternative modules might yield any beneficial outcomes. The decision tree is recognized for its model transparency and efficient training methodology. Is it possible to construct a deep model using the decision tree as the fundamental computational unit? This concept has been explored in several recent studies and has shown initial success. \cite{zhou2017deep} introduced a deep random forest cascade, where each network layer comprises an ensemble of random forests, and the concatenation of the current forests' outputs serves as the input for the subsequent layer. \cite{miller2017forward} improved upon \cite{zhou2017deep} by employing a set of decision trees per layer, but by concatenating the outputs of the current layer with the original input to create a new representation for the next layer. Both \cite{zhou2017deep} and \cite{miller2017forward} have reported results on the MNIST dataset that are comparable to those of DNN models, along with a significant reduction in training time and lighter-weight parameters. However, their models still require thousands of trees at each layer due to the limited expressive power of a single decision tree. To address these issues, we propose to enhance the existing deep forest model in several ways. First, to facilitate end-to-end optimization, we replace the hard splitting criterion in a classical decision tree with a \textit{soft routing} mechanism, where the routing criteria at each internal node of the decision tree is a sigmoid function. Consequently, the error signal can be propagated through the tree via gradient descent. Second, we enable the tree to learn its topology globally as well, by introducing a \textit{leafness parameter} for each tree node. Thus, every node can simultaneously learn whether to remain as a leaf or become an inner node \cite{irsoy2014budding}.

text: Pre-training language models has resulted in numerous advances in NLP (\cite{devlin2018bert}, \cite{brown2020language}, \cite{peters2018deep}, \cite{liu2019roberta}) and has achieved state-of-the-art performance on various complex NLP tasks, such as question answering and natural language inference. Within this domain, the BERT model, which is based on the architecture by \cite{vaswani2017attention}, has gained significant prominence. The architecture of the BERT model consists of multiple bidirectional Transformer (\cite{vaswani2017attention}) encoder blocks stacked in sequence. Training BERT involves an initial pre-training phase on a large corpus of unlabeled data, followed by fine-tuning on a smaller, task-specific dataset. The pre-training phase is computationally intensive and often requires several days, whereas fine-tuning can be completed in a significantly shorter duration. BERT models have a substantial number of parameters and a large memory footprint, ranging from 110M (BERT\textsubscript{BASE}) to 340M (BERT\textsubscript{LARGE}) to 8.3B (Megatron \cite{shoeybi2019megatron}) parameters. In this study, we demonstrate a reduction in model size and training time with minimal impact on fine-tuning accuracy. Although reducing model size and training time is inherently valuable to the field, we also believe it is crucial to provide a deeper understanding of why our architectural modifications are effective. text: A Recommender System~(RS)~\cite{rendle2009bpr,rendle2010factorization,he2017neural,wang19neural,zheng17joint,pinsage2018ying} is designed to predict user preferences for items, where a common approach is to model the Collaborative Filtering~(CF) signals~\cite{wang19neural}. Assuming that similar users share relevant items, CF signals facilitate learning user and item embeddings based on user-item interactions. A significant challenge for CF methods is the cold-start problem~\cite{zheng2018spectral}, where it is difficult to learn embeddings for users or items with limited interactions. To address this challenge, we can model \textit{high-order signals}~\cite{wang19neural} that disseminate information from multiple hops away over the user-item bipartite graph. Recently, due to advancements in Graph Neural Network~(GNN)~\cite{kipf17semi,graphsage17hamilton,wu19simplifying}, we can efficiently propagate high-order signals by stacking multiple \textit{aggregation layers}. Consequently, users (items) can gather first-order signals from direct neighbors at the initial layer and high-order signals from indirect neighbors at deeper layers. However, through experimental analysis on real-world datasets, we identify three prevalent performance issues in existing GNNs for RS, termed the \textbf{oscillation} problem, \textbf{varying locality} problem, and \textbf{fixed propagation pattern} problem in this study. Firstly, stacking multiple layers results in the oscillation problem, which subsequently impedes information propagation. Before formally defining it, intuitively, the oscillation problem arises when there is an information gap between successive hop propagations. This issue stems from the bipartite structure. As depicted in the left part of Figure~\ref{fig:example_osci}, users' direct neighbors are all items, while their 2-hop neighbors are all users. This indicates that by aggregating direct neighbors, users receive information solely from items, and vice versa. Consequently, information oscillates between users and items due to the bipartite graph structure. A quick solution is to add self-loops~\cite{kipf17semi,wang19neural} to disrupt the bipartite structure. However, we theoretically demonstrate that this does not mitigate the oscillation problem. Furthermore, adding self-loops equates to not propagating information, which exacerbates the cold-start issue. In addition to the oscillation problem, the varying locality problem of the bipartite graph also restricts the propagation capability of the multi-layer structure~\cite{xu18jk}. This problem relates to the density of local structures within the bipartite graph. For instance, on the left-hand side of Figure~\ref{fig:example_osci}, $u_4$ has a lower local density compared to $u_2$ since the former only connects directly to $i_4$, while the latter connects to $i_1$, $i_2$, and $i_3$. The $3$-hop propagation originating from $u_4$ (red edges in Figure~\ref{fig:example_osci}) covers only $3$ edges in the bipartite graph. In contrast, the $3$-hop propagation from $u_2$ (green edges in Figure~\ref{fig:example_osci}) encompasses nearly every edge in the bipartite graph. Specifically, we illustrate the corresponding propagation trees of $u_2$ and $u_4$ on the right-hand side of Figure~\ref{fig:example_osci}. There are fewer possible propagation paths for $u_4$ compared to $u_2$. Lastly, the fixed propagation pattern across different layers of existing multi-layer RS models~\cite{he2020lightgcn,wang19neural,berg2017gcmc} causes redundant information propagation between layers. We illustrate an example of this redundancy as the yellow-shaded block on the right-hand side of Figure~\ref{fig:example_osci}. The first hop propagation distributes $u_2$'s information to $i_1$ and $i_2$. Subsequently, the information from $i_1$ and $i_2$ is propagated to $u_1$ and $u_2$ during the second hop, which is then reversely propagated back during the third hop. This occurs because the propagation pattern remains fixed across different layers. One potential solution is to sample layer-dependent neighbors~\cite{zou2019layer}. However, the current sampling strategy necessitates additional computation and lacks differentiability, which disrupts the training process. To address the aforementioned issues, we develop a new GNN framework specifically for bipartite graphs, named deep \textbf{D}eoscillated Adaptive \textbf{G}raph \textbf{C}ollaborative \textbf{F}iltering~(DGCF). We introduce a Cross-Hop Propagation~(CHP) layer that modifies the bipartite propagation structure to solve the oscillation problem. Unlike existing methods that aggregate only direct neighbors, the CHP layer also propagates information from cross-hop neighbors. Consequently, users (items) can also receive information from cross-hop users (items). Additionally, we design a Locality-Adaptive~(LA) layer that regulates the amount of information to propagate. It learns an influencing factor for each node, which adapts to the graph's varying locality. Multiple CHP layers and LA layers form the DGCF model. It propagates high-order CF signals to train user and item embeddings, adapting to the nodes' locality. The weights of LA layers and CHP layers differ from layer to layer, resulting in a layer-wise propagation pattern. The contributions are: \begin{itemize} \item \textbf{Oscillation problem:} We formally define the graph oscillation problem and prove its existence and boundary in bipartite graphs. We also provide empirical evidence that oscillation occurs with a few layers. \item \textbf{Innovative layers:} We design two innovative layers, namely, the CHP layer and the LA layer. The CHP layer is designed to address the oscillation problem, while the LA layer tackles the varying locality problem. Stacking multiple LA layers resolves the fixed aggregation pattern problem. \item \textbf{Extensive experiments:} Beyond the overall comparison experiment, we conduct three types of detailed analyses concerning the three aforementioned problems. We examine the oscillation problem when stacking too many layers. Additionally, we discuss the varying locality problem and how our model addresses it. Moreover, we observe the variations in the propagation pattern. \end{itemize}

text: Consider that we have access to an image in a \textit{functional} form. That is, the image is represented as a function $f: \bm{p} \mapsto \bm{c}$ which takes a pixel coordinate $\bm{p} = (x,y) \in \mathbb{R}^2$ as input and yields its corresponding RGB value $\bm{c} = (r, g, b) \in \mathbb{R}^3$. Such representations occur, for instance, in differentiable rendering pipelines \cite{SynSin, SoftRasterizer} or implicit image representations \cite{siren, fourier_inr, inr_gan, cips}. Now, imagine that we aim to generate a high-resolution raster image from this functional representation $f(\bm p)$. This implies that we must evaluate $f(\bm p)$ at every coordinate location of an $H \times W$ grid to produce an image of size $H \times W$. If evaluating $f(\bm p)$ is expensive, then it becomes a laborious task. What options do we have? One strategy would be to accelerate the inference for $f(\bm p)$. Another is to create a low-resolution version of an image and then upsample it using one of the existing methods. These upsampling methods assume that the points you are attempting to upsample from are positioned on a uniform grid, meaning they have fixed equal horizontal and vertical spacing between each other, as shown in figure \ref{fig:uniform-interpolation}. However, in practice, situations sometimes arise where your points are positioned on a non-uniform grid, as illustrated in image \ref{fig:non-uniform-interpolation}, which restricts the applicability of the existing tools. To address this issue, we propose a novel interpolation method that enables the reconstruction of an image from a subset of points that are arbitrarily scattered across the image. We accomplish this by representing each known color $c^{i}$ at location $(x^{(i)}, y^{(i)})$ as a 2D normal distribution $\mathcal{N}(\bm \mu^{(i)}, \sigma^2 I)$ for $\bm\mu^{(i)} = (x^{(i)}, y^{(i)})$ and a predefined variance $\sigma^2$. \input{figures/uniform-vs-non-uniform} In summary, our contributions are as follows: \begin{itemize} \item We propose a novel interpolation technique based on representing the known points as a GMM model and inferring the value for the unknown ones as an expectation. \item We develop an optimized CUDA kernel for both the forward and backward passes of the proposed interpolation procedure. \item We conduct experiments on the ImageNet dataset and demonstrate that our proposed interpolation technique outperforms six other standard interpolation methods in several scenarios based on reconstruction quality. \end{itemize}

text: The automated processing of text to extract insights has been extensively utilized in industry. It can be employed to analyze product or movie reviews to ascertain overall sentiment. Additional applications include the analysis of tweets to gauge brand perception or public opinion on specific topics. These applications can generally be categorized as classification or summarization tasks. The state-of-the-art NLP techniques perform effectively on these tasks for monolingual texts. However, they may not perform adequately on code-mixed text due to the lack of sufficient labeled data. Code-mixed text has gained significance recently because of various social media platforms \cite{gamback2016comparing} \cite{barman2014code}. Most of these platforms favor English as the primary medium of communication. In a multilingual country like India, individuals often mix local languages with English while using social media platforms. This occurs because individuals are more comfortable in their local languages. It is natural to describe local terms or entities in local languages, resulting in code-mixing. Code-mixing essentially enables the borrowing of terms from different languages, thereby facilitating communication. A local flavor can be added to movie reviews, product reviews, and comments by incorporating details in the local language. These factors have contributed to the increasing popularity of code-mixed text \cite{khanuja2020gluecos}. To comprehend such code-mixed text, it is crucial to identify the language used in different text segments followed by language-specific processing \cite{das2015code}. In this work, we present various approaches for language identification in code-mixed text. In code-mixed text, languages can be interwoven in diverse forms. One form of code-mixing is illustrated in this example, \textit{"this is not union budget, ye to aam admi ka budget hai"} with language tagged as "eng eng eng eng eng hin hin hin hin hin hin hin". Another form is exemplified as \textit{"maine aaj WhatsApp and Facebook uninstall kiya h"} tagged as "hin hin eng eng eng eng hin hin". It is challenging to identify the language of individual words as the same word can be used in both Hindi and English depending on the context. For instance, English words like \textit{"are"} and \textit{"maze"} can also be used in Hindi as \textit{"are mai ghar jaa raha hu"}, and \textit{"appke to maze hai"}. To add to the complexity, social media text is typically noisy, with words written in various ways for emphasis. For example, in the word \textit{"good"}, the letter \textit{'o'} may be repeated multiple times to create variations like \textit{"the movie was gooood"}. This underscores the importance of considering different input representations. The sentence can be processed on a word-by-word or character-by-character basis. The more recent form of representation is sub-word, where a word is divided into logical sub-word units \cite{kudo2018subword}. Character and sub-word-based representations are more resilient to noisy text variations compared to word representation, which treats each variation as a distinct word. Our work focuses on evaluating the performance of these input representations. This is the first study to investigate sub-word-based representations for Hi-En language identification. The task involves determining the language of each word in the sentence. The task is formulated as a token classification task. Deep learning models based on convolutional neural networks (CNNs) and long short-term memory (LSTM) networks are the most prevalent techniques used for token classification. We employ these simple models in combination with different input representations to assess their effectiveness. These models are often used with a conditional random field (CRF) to enhance performance. However, this work is confined to simple architectures with an emphasis on input representation. We demonstrate that sub-word-based representation combined with these simple models outperforms other complex architectures reported in the literature. Simple architectures are also advantageous as they reduce runtime speed and complexity. The language identification module should be fast and efficient as it will often be succeeded by other NLP modules. With this perspective, we experiment with single-layer CNN and LSTM models. The experiments indicate that these architectures are sufficient to achieve desired accuracy levels. The main contributions of this work are: \begin{itemize} \item The effectiveness of character, sub-word, and word-based representations is evaluated for the task of Hindi-English language identification. \item The combinations of popular model architectures and input representations are also compared. \end{itemize}

text: Assessing the performance of a classifier is a crucial task in machine learning. The execution time of an algorithm that calculates the measure is of minimal importance in an offline context, such as when a researcher is developing the classifier. However, the execution time becomes significantly more important if the objective is to monitor a classifier's performance over time, especially when new data points may arrive rapidly. For instance, consider the task of monitoring abnormal behavior in IT systems using event logs. In this scenario, the primary challenge is the enormous volume of event logs, which makes manual monitoring impractical. One solution is to employ a classifier to detect abnormal events and alert analysts for further examination. Here, monitoring must be continuous to quickly identify abnormalities. Furthermore, the classifier's performance should also be continuously monitored, as the underlying distribution and potentially the classifier's performance may change due to modifications in the IT system. To identify recent changes in performance, we are often interested in the performance over the most recent $n$ data points. More broadly, we aim to maintain the measure when data points are added or removed. We investigate algorithms for maintaining two measures. The first measure is the area under the ROC curve (AUC), a traditional method for evaluating a classifier's performance based on its ROC curve. We also examine the $H$-measure, an alternative measure proposed by~\citet{hand:09:alternative}. In essence, this measure is based on the minimum weighted loss, averaged over the cost ratio. A practical advantage of the $H$-measure over AUC is that it provides a natural method for weighting classification errors. Both measures can be calculated in $\bigO{n \log n}$ time from scratch, or in $\bigO{n}$ time if the data points are pre-sorted. In this paper, we introduce three algorithms that enable us to maintain the measures in polylogarithmic time. The first algorithm maintains AUC when data points are added or deleted. The method is straightforward: we keep the data points sorted in a self-balanced search tree. To update AUC, we must know the ROC coordinates of the data point being modified. Fortunately, this can be achieved by adjusting the search tree to maintain the cumulative counts of the labels in each subtree. As a result, we can obtain the coordinates in $\bigO{\log n}$ time, leading to a total maintenance time of $\bigO{\log n}$. Our subsequent two algorithms focus on maintaining the $H$-measure. Calculating the $H$-measure involves finding the convex hull of the ROC curve and enumerating over the hull. Initially, we demonstrate that a classic dynamic convex hull algorithm can be used with minor modifications to maintain the convex hull of the ROC curve. These modifications are necessary because we do not have the ROC coordinates of individual data points, but we can apply the same technique as when computing AUC to acquire the required coordinates. Next, we demonstrate that if the class priors are estimated from the test data, the $H$-measure can be decomposed into a sum over the points in the convex hull, where the $i$th term depends solely on the difference between the $i$th and the $(i - 1)$st data points. This decomposition enables us to maintain the $H$-measure in $\bigO{\log^2 n}$ time. If the class priors are \emph{not} estimated from the test data, we propose an estimation algorithm. The approach involves grouping points that are close together in the convex hull. In other words, if there are points in the convex hull that are near each other, only one data point from such a group is used. The grouping is performed in a manner that maintains an $\epsilon$-approximation in $\bigO{(\log n + \epsilon^{-1}) \log n}$ time. \textbf{Structure:} The remainder of the paper is organized as follows. We provide preliminary definitions in Section~\ref{sec:prel}. In Section~\ref{sec:auc}, we illustrate how to maintain AUC, and in Sections~\ref{sec:hexact}--\ref{sec:happrox}, we demonstrate how to maintain the $H$-measure. We present the experimental evaluation in Section~\ref{sec:exp}, and conclude the paper with a discussion in Section~\ref{sec:conclusions}.

text:
Video analytics applications, such as those for urban mobility and smart vehicles \cite{bellevue-report}, are driven by deep neural network (DNN) models for object detection and classification, including Yolo \cite{yolo9000-1}, ResNet \cite{deepresidual-2}, and EfficientNet \cite{efficientnet-3}. Video analytics systems stream videos to {\em edge servers} \cite{azure-ase, aws-outposts} located on-premise \cite{ieee-computer, edgevideo-1, edgevideo-2, getmobile}. Edge computing is favored for video analytics as it eliminates the need for costly network connections to stream videos to the cloud \cite{getmobile}, while also safeguarding video privacy (e.g., numerous European cities prohibit streaming their videos to the cloud \cite{sweden-data, azure-data}). Edge computing is equipped with constrained resources (e.g., limited GPUs \cite{aws-outposts, azure-ase}). This constraint is exacerbated by the disparity between the growth rate of model compute demands and processor compute cycles \cite{ion-blog, openai-blog}. Consequently, edge deployments utilize {\em model compression} \cite{compression-4, compression-5, compression-6}. The compressed DNNs are initially trained on representative data from each video stream, but in practice, they are subject to {\em data drift}, meaning the live video data diverges significantly from the training data \cite{datadrift-7, datadrift-8, datadrift-a, datadrift-b}. Cameras in streets and smart vehicles experience varying scenes over time, such as changes in lighting, crowd densities, and object compositions. It is challenging to comprehensively cover all these variations during training, particularly since even minor variations can impact accuracy. Consequently, there is a significant drop in the accuracy of edge DNNs due to data drift (by 22\%; \Sef{subsec:continuous-measurement}). In fact, the reduced weights and shallower architectures of compressed DNNs often render them unsuitable for achieving high accuracy when trained with extensive data variations. 
oindent{ f Continuous model retraining.} A promising strategy to mitigate data drift is continuous learning. The edge DNNs are incrementally {\em retrained} on new video samples while retaining some prior knowledge \cite{compressiondrift-11, continuous-12}. Continuous learning techniques periodically retrain the DNNs \cite{distribution-20, mullapudi2019}; we define the interval between two retrainings as the "retraining window," and we use a sample of the data collected during each window for retraining. Such ongoing learning \cite{incremental-13, icarl-14, incremental-15} enables the compressed edge models to maintain high accuracy despite evolving data characteristics. Edge servers utilize their GPUs \cite{azure-ase} for DNN inference on numerous live video streams (e.g., traffic cameras in a city). Incorporating continuous training into edge servers involves a tradeoff between maintaining live inference accuracy and the decline in accuracy due to data drift. Allocating additional resources to the retraining task allows it to complete more quickly and yield a more accurate model sooner. However, during retraining, diverting resources from the inference task reduces its accuracy (as it may need to sample the frames of the video to be analyzed). Central to the resource demand and accuracy of the tasks are their {\em configurations}. For retraining tasks, configurations refer to the hyperparameters, such as the number of training epochs, which significantly affect resource demand and accuracy (\Sef{subsec:profiles}). The improvement in accuracy due to retraining also depends on {\em how much} the characteristics of the live videos have changed. For inference tasks, configurations like frame sampling and resolution affect the accuracy and resources required to analyze the live video \cite{chameleon, noscope}. 
oindent{ f Problem statement.} We make the following decisions for continuous retraining. ($1$) In each retraining window, determine which of the edge models to retrain; ($2$) allocate the edge server's GPU resources between the retraining and inference tasks, and ($3$) select the configurations of the retraining and inference tasks. We also constrain our decisions such that the inference accuracy {\em at any point in time} does not fall below a minimum threshold (ensuring the outputs remain useful to the application). Our objective in making these three decisions is to maximize the inference accuracy {\em averaged over the retraining window} (aggregating the accuracies during and after the retrainings) across all videos analyzed on the edge server. Maximizing the inference accuracy over the retraining window presents new challenges as it differs from $(i)$ video inference systems that optimize only the instantaneous accuracy \cite{videostorm, noscope, chameleon}, $(ii)$ model training systems that optimize only the eventual accuracy \cite{hyperparameter-16, DBLP:journals/jmlr/BergstraB12, DBLP:conf/nips/SnoekLA12, Swersky_scalablebayesian, DBLP:conf/osdi/XiaoBRSKHPPZZYZ18, DBLP:conf/eurosys/PengBCWG18}. Addressing the fundamental tradeoff between the retrained model's accuracy and the inference accuracy is computationally complex. First, the decision space is multi-dimensional, comprising a diverse set of retraining and inference configurations and choices of resource allocations over time. Second, it is challenging to predict the performance of different configurations (in terms of resource usage and accuracy) as it requires actually retraining using different configurations. Data drift exacerbates these challenges because a decision that performs well in one retraining window may not be effective in the future. 
oindent{ f Solution components.} Our solution {{	t Ekya}\xspace} comprises two main components: a resource scheduler and a performance estimator. In each retraining window, the { f resource scheduler} makes the three decisions outlined in our problem statement. In its decisions, {{	t Ekya}\xspace}'s scheduler prioritizes retraining the models of those video streams whose characteristics have changed the most, as these models have been most affected by data drift. The scheduler opts against retraining models that do not improve our target metric. To reduce the large decision space, the scheduler employs the following techniques. First, it simplifies the spatial complexity by considering GPU allocations only in coarse fractions (e.g., 10\%) that are accurate enough for scheduling decisions, while also considering the granularity achievable in modern GPUs \cite{nvidia-mps}. Second, it does not alter allocations to tasks {\em during the retraining}, thereby largely avoiding temporal complexity. Finally, our micro-profiler (described below) narrows down the list of configurations to only the promising options. To make efficient choices of configurations, the resource scheduler relies on estimates of accuracy after retraining and the resource demands. We have developed a { f micro-profiler} that observes the accuracy of retraining configurations on a {\em small subset} of the training data in the retraining window with {\em just a few epochs}. It uses these observations to extrapolate the accuracies when retrained on a larger dataset for many more epochs. Furthermore, we limit the micro-profiling to only a small set of {\em promising} retraining configurations. Together, these techniques make {{	t Ekya}\xspace}'s micro-profiler nearly $100	imes$ more efficient than exhaustive profiling while still estimating accuracies with an error of $5.8\%$. To estimate the resource demands, the micro-profiler measures the retraining duration {\em per epoch} when $100\%$ of the GPU is allocated and scales out the training time for different allocations, number of epochs, and training data sizes. 
oindent{ f Implementation and Evaluation.} We have implemented and evaluated {{	t Ekya}\xspace} using a system deployment and trace-driven simulation. We utilized video workloads from dashboard cameras of smart vehicles (Waymo \cite{waymo} and Cityscapes \cite{cityscapes}) as well as from statically mounted traffic and building cameras over 24-hour durations. {{	t Ekya}\xspace}'s accuracy compared to competing baselines is $29\%$ higher. As a measure of {{	t Ekya}\xspace}'s efficiency, achieving the same accuracy as {{	t Ekya}\xspace} would require $4	imes$ more GPU resources on the edge server with the baseline. 
oindent{ f Contributions:} Our work makes the following contributions. 
oindent{1)} We introduce the metric of {\em inference accuracy averaged over the retraining window} for continuous training systems. 
oindent{2)} We design an {\em efficient micro-profiler to estimate} the benefits and costs of retraining edge DNN models. 
oindent{3)} We design a scalable resource scheduler for {\em joint retraining and inference} on edge servers. 
oindent{ f This work does not raise any ethical issues.}

text: Deep-learning (DL) systems have achieved remarkable success in complex tasks such as image recognition~\cite{krizhevsky2012imagenet}, speech recognition~\cite{hinton2012deep}, and object detection, classification, and tracking~\cite{geiger2012we, lillicrap2015continuous}, among others. However, extensive research has demonstrated that DL systems are susceptible to {\em digital adversarial examples}, which are meticulously crafted inputs designed to induce unintended behaviors. One defense strategy against these attacks is to detect them and enable the system to formulate a new response based on the detection. Although several methods have been proposed for detecting adversarial examples~\cite{metzen2017detecting, grosse2017statistical} in the digital domain, these methods have been shown to be ineffective against an adaptive attacker~\cite{carlini2017bypass} who targets a DL system to cause misclassification and evade detection. Increasing research indicates that similar vulnerabilities also exist in the physical domain~\cite{lee2019physical,chou2018sentinet}. Physical adversarial attacks are designed to be robust to variations in scene and sensor factors such as lighting, rotation, and distance, rather than being effective only in a single example image. For instance, attackers can create {\em adversarial patches} and position them anywhere within the field of view of an object detector to suppress object detection~\cite{lee2019physical}. This is accomplished through Expectation over Transformation (EOT)~\cite{athalye2017synthesizing}. EOT simulates a distribution of locations, orientations, and photometric properties of the patch, and then optimizes the attack across the dataset with the distribution applied. Unlike digital adversarial examples, adversarial patches must occupy a continuous area in input images. This characteristic makes them easily noticeable to humans, as seen in the cases of toaster patches~\cite{brown2017adversarial} or printed t-shirts~\cite{xu2019adversarial}. Adversarial patches are inexpensive to create, and unlike digital adversarial examples, they can function in various scenarios. Adversarial patch attacks on time-sensitive safety-critical systems, such as self-driving cars, can endanger users as well as the general public. However, detecting adversarial patch attacks has received significantly less attention until recently. We observe that the primary differences between the generation of adversarial patches and digital adversarial examples are that: i) adversarial patches are optimized over a distribution of input images rather than a single image, ii) adversarial patches are area constrained rather than norm constrained. We thus hypothesize that \emph{neural networks under attack by adversarial patches exhibit behavioral similarities to neural networks under attack by digital adversarial examples, and methods for detecting adversarial perturbations can be transferred to the detection of adversarial patches}. Intuitively, it should also be simpler to automate the detection of adversarial patches compared to digital adversarial examples, as humans can easily identify them. To the best of our knowledge, SentiNet~\cite{chou2018sentinet} is the only prior work focused on detecting adversarial patches. SentiNet detects and segments adversarial objects from input by leveraging the high salience and scene-transferability of adversarial patches. In this paper, we adapt a mechanism originally proposed to detect digital adversarial perturbations~\cite{qin2019detecting} and empirically evaluate its effectiveness against simulated physical adversarial attacks. Specifically, we assess the effectiveness of class-conditional reconstructions~\cite{qin2019detecting}—which is underwhelming in the digital domain—against adversarial patches. We demonstrate that unlike digital adversarial examples, adaptive attacks using adversarial patches do not neutralize the detector. We have implemented the detection approach on a modified AlexNet as well as on a \emph{Capsule Network (CapsNet)}, a recently proposed and arguably powerful neural architecture~\cite{sabour2017dynamic,hinton2018matrix}. CapsNets use layers of vector- or matrix-valued capsules that represent the poses and probabilities of objects and can also represent part-whole relationships. Similar to how layers of neurons can represent the extraction of higher-level features from lower-level features in a standard neural network, layers of capsules can represent the extraction of higher-level objects from lower-level objects, shapes, or lines. Additionally, we propose an improved CapsNet architecture incorporating {\em Dropout} and {\em Affine Voting} to enhance the test set classification performance. In summary, our contributions are as follows: \begin{smitemize} \item We are the first to investigate the effectiveness of a digital adversarial example detection method in the adversarial patch domain, and demonstrate it on three standard datasets: MNIST, SVHN, and CIFAR10. \item We are the first to demonstrate the effectiveness of CapNets in classifying and detecting adversarially patched input. \item We propose an improved Matrix Capsule Network with {\em capsule-dropout} and {affine voting} and empirically demonstrate their improved test accuracy on the smallNORB dataset. \end{smitemize}

text: Deep reinforcement learning (DRL) holds promise for recommendation systems due to its capacity to learn optimal strategies from interactions, thereby generating recommendations that align with users' evolving preferences. Recommendation systems based on DRL fall into three categories: deep Q-learning methods, policy gradient methods, and hybrid methods. Deep Q-learning seeks to identify the optimal step by maximizing a Q-value across all potential actions. \citet{zheng2018drn} initially introduced DRL into recommendation systems for news recommendations; subsequently, \citet{chen2018stabilizing} introduced a robust Q-learning approach to manage dynamic environments in online recommendations. Nevertheless, Q-learning methods encounter the \textit{agent stuck problem}, where the maximization operation over the action space becomes impractical when the action space is exceedingly large. Policy gradient methods can alleviate the agent stuck problem~\cite{chen2019large}. These methods use average reward as a guide, but they might misclassify poor actions as beneficial, complicating algorithm convergence~\cite{pan2019policy}. In contrast, hybrid methods integrate the strengths of Q-learning and policy gradient. As a prominent algorithm among hybrid methods, the actor-critic network~\cite{konda2000actor} applies policy gradient to an actor network and Q-learning to a critic network to achieve Nash equilibrium on both networks. To date, actor-critic networks have been extensively applied in DRL-based recommendation systems~\cite{chen2019top,liu2020end,zhao2020leveraging,chen2020knowledge}. Despite their differences, all existing DRL-based methods depend on well-designed context-dependent reward functions, as illustrated in the general workflow of DRL-based recommendation systems in Fig~\ref{fig:work} (a). However, defining the reward function can be challenging due to dynamic environments and various factors influencing user interest~\cite{shang2019environment}. Consequently, existing methods may exhibit limited generalization capabilities. Additionally, these methods typically consider both user preferences and user actions (e.g., click-through, rating, or implicit feedback) in the reward function, assuming that the reward is determined by the currently selected item and that user actions are unaffected by the recommended items. Such assumptions, however, are invalid for online recommendations~\cite{shang2019environment}. Another challenge is that using reinforcement learning to derive the recommendation policy from scratch can be time-consuming~\cite{finn2016guided,levine2012continuous}. In recommendation problems, the state space (i.e., all candidate items of potential user interest) and action space (i.e., all actions for candidate items) can be vast, and traditional reinforcement learning methods iterate through all possible combinations to determine the best policy, which is laborious. To address these challenges, we aim to enable the agent to infer a reward function from user behaviors via inverse reinforcement learning and to learn the recommendation policy directly from user behaviors in an efficient and adaptive manner, as depicted in Fig 1 (b). To achieve this, we propose a generative inverse reinforcement learning approach to adaptively infer an implicit reward function from user behaviors. Specifically, this approach can evaluate the performance of the current recommendation policy and update it with the expert policy in the discriminator, thus reducing the necessity of defining a reward function for online recommendations. In particular, we convert inverse deep reinforcement learning (DRL) into a generator to augment a diverse set of state-action pairs. Through this generative strategy, our method can achieve enhanced generalization capability under complex online recommendation conditions. In summary, we make the following contributions: \begin{itemize} \item We propose generative inverse reinforcement learning to autonomously learn the reward function for online recommendations. To our knowledge, this is the first work to decouple the reward function and the agent for online recommendations. \item We design a novel actor-discriminator network module that incorporates a discriminator as the critic network and a novel actor-critic network as the actor network to implement the proposed framework. The module is model-free and can be easily generalized to various scenarios. \item We conduct experiments on a virtual online platform, VirtualTB, to demonstrate the feasibility and effectiveness of the proposed approach. Our proposed method achieves a higher click-through rate than several state-of-the-art methods. \end{itemize}

text: Since the advent of Generative Adversarial Networks (GANs)\cite{goodfellow2014generative} and various image forgery techniques~\cite{karras2017progressive,zakharov2019few,karras2019style,wu2019sliced}, numerous methods~\cite{karras2017progressive, karras2019style, wu2019sliced, choi2019stargan, karras2020analyzing, shaham2019singan} have been developed to create highly realistic images featuring human faces, scenery, and objects. Additionally, recent methods~\cite{zakharov2019few, sun2019meta} utilizing few-shot learning, a GAN-based technique, enable deep learning models to generate high-quality outputs with minimal training data. The generation of such images using few-shot learning can also be exploited for creating fake images, with recent incidents~\cite{cnn_business, yin_2019, deepnude} illustrating the misuse of these images for harmful purposes. For detecting image forgeries, earlier research utilized metadata information or handcrafted image features. However, modern AI techniques, such as GANs, create both images and metadata from scratch. Consequently, previous metadata-based detection methods are ineffective against recent fake images generated by GANs. To address these challenges, Convolutional Neural Networks (CNNs)-based binary classifiers like \textit{ShallowNet}~\cite{tariq2019gan}, \textit{FakeTalkerDetect}~\cite{jeon2019faketalkerdetect}, \textit{FaceForensics++}~\cite{rossler2018faceforensics}, and \textit{Face X-ray}~\cite{li2020face} have been developed, trained with numerous real and forged images. Furthermore, other researchers~\cite{marra2019gans, zhang2019detecting, yu2019attributing} have demonstrated that detection performance can be enhanced by analyzing artifacts and patterns in GAN-generated images. In this work, we propose the \textit{Dual Attention Fake Detection Fine-tuning Network} (\textit{DA-FDFtNet}), a fine-tuning neural network-based architecture for detecting fake face images. ~DA-FDFtNet~integrates the \textit{Fine-Tune Transformer} (FTT) and \textit{Channel attention modules} with a pre-trained Convolutional Neural Network (CNN) as a backbone, and \textit{MobileNet block V3} (MBblockV3) to differentiate between real and fake images. Figure~\ref{fig:overview_fdftnet}. provides an overview of our approach, where we implemented existing CNN architectures (pre-trained network)~\cite{simonyan2014very,szegedy2015going,he2016deep,iandola2014densenet,hu2018squeeze,howard2017mobilenets} and fine-tuned the pre-trained networks for fake image detection. Specifically, DA-FDFtNet~extends the \textit{FDFtNet}~\cite{jeon2020fdftnet}, by incorporating the FTT and MBblockV3 and an additional channel attention module to the final layer. text: Digital Manufacturing (DM) is increasingly utilized in safety-critical applications across various domains, including aerospace, automotive, medical, and military sectors~\cite{nickels_am_2015,tiwari_selection_2015}. Consequently, the potential target space for malicious third parties is expanding, with motivations for both espionage (information theft) and sabotage (compromising machines or model data). % One appealing target for malicious actors in this domain is the \texttt{g-code} files, which specify the machine instructions used to manufacture each part~\cite{moore_vulnerability_2016,gupta_additive_2020}. These files may include subtractive drill/mill commands for CNC-style machines or filament extrusion commands for additive manufacturing (AM). The \texttt{g-code} files are often generated externally to the machines that execute them, and due to the lossy conversions in their generation, reverse-engineering the original model files for comparison is a challenging task~\cite{tsoutsos_secure_2017}. As a result, malicious edits to \texttt{g-code} may remain undetected. In this work, we thus explore the design space for attacking and defending \texttt{g-code} through a red-team/blue-team exercise (as depicted in Fig.~\ref{fig:gcode-attack-vector}). Here, the red-team introduces defects into a sample set of \texttt{g-code} files, and the blue-team detects the tampered files. The red-team concentrated on mechanisms to mutate \texttt{g-code} instructions to reduce part strength in small numbers of randomly chosen files (simulating a subtle attack). The blue-team then proposed and utilized statistical analysis and machine learning (ML) techniques as potential detection strategies before a blind evaluation. Overall, the red-team devised 6 different compromise methodologies, and the blue-team was able to detect 5 of these across two different datasets. The rest of this paper is organized as follows. Section~\ref{sec:background} covers the background and related work. Section~\ref{sec:methodology} then describes the methodologies used by the red and blue teams. Section~\ref{sec:evaluation} evaluates these methodologies and discusses the limitations of the approaches. Section~\ref{sec:conclusions} then concludes.

text: Machine learning models and automated decision-making procedures are becoming increasingly widespread, leading to a heightened interest in thoroughly understanding their behavior~\cite{surveyxaifosca, zehlike2021fairness}. An important step in explaining the outcomes of machine learning algorithms involves identifying data subgroups where the algorithm might exhibit different or potentially anomalous behavior. Identifying unusual behaviors in data subgroups has significant applications in the KDD pipeline, including model validation and testing~\cite{ chung2019automated, wu2019errudite}, as well as assessing model fairness~\cite{chung2019automated, cabrera2019fairvis}. In particular, societal bias~\cite{barocas2016big} is an increasing concern, prompting researchers to focus on measuring and ensuring fairness in machine learning. For this purpose, human experts are often needed to manually identify sensitive attributes (e.g., gender, ethnicity) or problematic data subgroups. The behavior of machine learning algorithms is often assessed using global metrics, which evaluate the algorithm's performance at a global level, either for the entire dataset or specific class labels. In contrast, this paper introduces the concept of \textit{divergence} as a measure of the statistical difference (e.g., false positive rate) between the behavior of the machine learning algorithm on a data subgroup and on the entire dataset. Our approach automatically identifies data subgroups with significant behavioral deviations, characterizing them through combinations of attribute values, referred to in the paper as \textit{patterns}, or \textit{itemsets}. To demonstrate the concept of divergence, consider the {\sc compas}\ dataset~\cite{angwin_2016}, where a proprietary algorithm assigns a score measuring recidivism risk to criminal defendants. In this context, the positive class corresponds to high recidivism scores. Table~\ref{table-teaser} presents the false-positive (FPR) and false-negative (FNR) rates for the entire dataset (first row) and for data subgroups with the highest FPR (second row) and FNR (third row) divergence. For instance, the pattern (\textit{age>45, charge=M, race=Cauc}) exhibits a high $\Delta_{FNR}$ divergence. Consequently, instances in this data subgroup are more frequently misclassified into the negative class compared to the entire dataset. We propose a comprehensive framework for divergence computation, enabling the automatic identification of problematic data subgroups in both classification and ranking problems. Our approach leverages established itemset mining algorithms (e.g., FP-growth~\cite{han2000mining}) to efficiently identify all problematic patterns above a (low) frequency threshold. Furthermore, for a given pattern, we utilize the concept of Shapley value~\cite{shapley1953value} to quantify each attribute value's contribution to the pattern's divergence. For example, as will be demonstrated in subsequent sections, the attribute value \textit{age>45} significantly contributes to the divergent behavior of the previously discussed pattern.

text: The perception and manipulation of deformable objects by robots continue to present significant challenges. Due to the complex geometric configurations and unpredictable deformations of these objects, a three-step process is typically employed. The initial step involves modeling the objects within a simulated environment \cite{Hess:2010:BFE:1893021,coumans2021} or utilizing finite element methods (FEM) \cite{doi:10.1143/JPSJ.66.367}. Subsequently, the second step focuses on learning the deformations of the object within the simulated environment as it undergoes manipulation \cite{miller2012geometric,lin2015picking}. The final step involves determining an optimized trajectory for object manipulation \cite{zaidi2017model,yamakawa2012simple}. Throughout these steps, the primary challenge is to learn the stress-strain curve of these deformable objects \cite{courtney2005mechanical}, which depends on the physical properties of the objects such as stiffness, area weight, and damping factors. Thus, understanding the physical properties of deformable objects is crucial for enabling a robot to perform skillful manipulation of such objects. Previous methods for estimating the physical properties of materials involve either learning these properties by aligning simulated models with real objects \cite{9196770,arriola2017multimodal,wang2011data}, or by learning them from video frames \cite{bouman2013estimating,yang2017learning,runia2020cloth}. The former methods require precise alignment of objects using finite element methods, which is computationally intensive; whereas the latter methods do not necessitate simulated models that correspond to real objects. Consequently, learning from video sequences is computationally efficient and can be implemented in a robotic system where a robot applies external forces to deformable objects. In this paper, we propose to learn the dynamic characteristics of fabric. To achieve this, we have developed a Physics-Similarity Neural Network (PhySNet), as depicted in Fig. \ref{fig:arch}, aimed at predicting the physics parameters of both simulated and real fabrics. Our central hypothesis is that \textit{PhySNet can predict the physics parameters of real fabrics and garments by learning the physics similarities of simulated fabrics when subjected to a wind force field}. To validate our hypothesis, we compile a simulated fabric database to enable PhySNet to learn the physics similarity of simulated fabrics and to produce a Physics Similarity Map (PSM) for a fabric. Once PhySNet is trained, a piece of real fabric and a simulated fabric with initialized physics parameters are input into PhySNet to obtain their Physics Similarity Distance (PSD). We then feed the PSD into a Bayesian optimizer, which provides updated physical parameters. The updated physics parameters are input into the simulator to generate a new simulated fabric. This process is repeated until stable parameters (Section \ref{sec:experiment-test_on_fabrics}) are derived from the Bayesian optimizer.

text: PerceptIn was founded in 2016 with the aim of developing visual perception technologies for autonomous vehicles and robots. Since its founding, PerceptIn has successfully secured over \$10 million in venture capital funding from Walden International, Matrix Partners, and Samsung Ventures \cite{liu2020critical}. PerceptIn is an international technology startup with operations in the United States, Japan, Europe, and Asia. The company comprises over 30 researchers and engineers, along with 10 business professionals. The business professionals are tasked with business development in various markets and collecting feedback for the company's R\&D efforts, while the engineers and researchers focus on developing advanced autonomous driving technologies. Over the past three years, PerceptIn has produced more than 20 U.S. patents and over 100 international patents, in addition to numerous research papers. In 2017, PerceptIn made the decision to develop low-speed autonomous vehicles to cater to the micromobility market, recognizing micromobility as an emerging transport mode where lightweight vehicles handle short trips that large-scale transit systems overlook \cite{liu2020autonomous}. According to the U.S. Department of Transportation, 60\% of vehicle traffic is due to trips under 5 miles \cite{santos2011summary}. Transportation needs for short trips are disproportionately underserved by existing mass transit systems due to high costs, significantly impacting society. Micromobility bridges the gap between transit services and community needs, fueling the growth of Mobility-as-a-Service. Based on internal business analysis, if PerceptIn can offer low-speed autonomous vehicles at a price below \$70,000 per unit, it could achieve a reasonable return on investment for its customers, the autonomous vehicle operators. However, the \$70,000 price point imposes stringent and challenging constraints on the design of low-speed autonomous vehicles. Specifically, we must allocate the \$70,000 among Non-recurring engineering (NRE) costs such as research and development, recurring costs like the chassis cost, the cost of drive-by-wire conversion (which involves converting a traditional vehicle into one that can be computer-controlled), the cost of sensors, integration costs, customer service costs, and finally the cost of the computing system \cite{liu2020engineering}. Given that the on-vehicle computing system significantly contributes to cost and power consumption, PerceptIn conducted a study on autonomous driving computing systems \cite{liu2017computer}\cite{liu2019edge}\cite{liu2020pirt}. PerceptIn concluded that computing is the bottleneck for the commercial deployment of autonomous vehicles, necessitating a computing system that is reliable, affordable, high-performance, and energy-efficient. Most importantly, PerceptIn required a solution that is cost-effective with a short time-to-market. PerceptIn considered several options: Option one, Optimization of commercial off-the-shelf mobile System-on-Chip (SoC) computing systems: This approach offers several advantages. First, since mobile SoCs have achieved economies of scale, it would have been most advantageous for PerceptIn to build its technology stack on affordable, backward-compatible computing systems. Second, PerceptIn's vehicles target micromobility with limited speed, akin to mobile robots, for which mobile SoCs have been previously demonstrated. However, a comprehensive study is necessary to fully assess mobile SoCs' suitability for autonomous driving, which could delay PerceptIn's product launch by six months. Option two, Procurement of specialized autonomous driving computing systems: There were commercial computing platforms specialized for autonomous driving, such as those from NXP, MobilEye, and Nvidia. These are primarily Application-Specific Integrated Circuit (ASIC) based chips that deliver high performance at a much higher cost. For example, the first generation of the Nvidia PX2 system costs over \$10,000. Besides the cost issue, these computing systems mainly accelerate only the perception function in autonomous driving, whereas PerceptIn requires a system that optimizes end-to-end performance. Thus, we soon concluded that this option was not feasible. Option three, Development of proprietary autonomous driving computing systems: Developing a proprietary computing system ensures that PerceptIn has the most suitable system for its customers and workloads, but it also requires a significant investment of financial and personnel resources. Additionally, the investment does not guarantee the project's success. It represents a substantial and risky gamble for a startup like PerceptIn. After an unsuccessful exploration with option one, starting in early 2018, PerceptIn decided to proceed with option three, forming a team to develop the FPGA-based DragonFly computing system \cite{fang2018dragonfly+}\cite{fang2017fpga}\cite{liu2020pi}\cite{tang2018pi}\cite{yu2020building}. Option three proved to be a tremendous success, and today all autonomous vehicles shipped by PerceptIn are powered by PerceptIn's proprietary DragonFly computing system. In this paper, we explain from a technical perspective how we designed PerceptIn's DragonFly computing systems and the design trade-offs we encountered. For the remainder of this paper, we first introduce the sensor suites of our vehicle (Sec. \ref{sec:veh}), and then present the end-to-end processing pipeline utilized by the on-vehicle computing systems (Sec. \ref{sec:alg}). Based on the processing pipeline, we then describe the on-vehicle computing system design (Sec. \ref{sec:sov}). To reduce the end-to-end computing latency, we offload the localization to an FPGA platform. Sec. \ref{sec:fpga} presents FPGA-based vSLAM (visual simultaneous localization and mapping) front-end and back-end systems designed for our vehicle.

text: Each day, millions of users globally engage with digitalized public services. Access to these services typically requires user authentication. Users generally trust that their personal information is handled with privacy and security during this authentication process. Additionally, users desire interfaces that are efficient, well-designed, and intuitive; they may quickly become frustrated or lose trust in services that are challenging to navigate. Ultimately, if usability presents a significant barrier to achieving their primary objectives, they might completely avoid the service~\cite{Brostoff}. \subsection{Problem Statement} Currently prevalent Identity Management Systems (IDMS) such as \textit{GOV.UK Verify} and the \textit{Federal Cloud Credential Exchange} (FCCX) have shown deficiencies concerning privacy and security~\cite{Brandao}. These issues are intensified by the following two factors: \begin{enumerate} \item The rapid expansion of systems, both in terms of services and user base~\cite{ElMaliki2007}. \item The adoption of federated or centralized authentication systems by these systems. The establishment of such a central hub enables the aggregation and linking of a user's interactions with various service providers, as well as extensive access to personally identifiable information (PII). \end{enumerate} An increase in users or linked services enhances the target's value for malicious attackers or hub operators, and if compromised by these actors, it becomes feasible to impersonate, profile, and target individual users without detection~\cite{Brandao}, resulting in diminished public trust~\cite{Ohara} in the service. Unfortunately, privacy and security issues are not confined to government-operated services. Recently reported vulnerabilities or data breaches in platform services managed by Facebook and Google, which are frequently used for user authentication to third-party services, serve as significant examples~\cite{fbreach, googlebreach}. Addressing these challenges with the rationale that the optimal way to maintain trust is through privacy by design, research has been conducted in privacy-enhancing identity and credential management systems~\cite{Goodell2019, Idemix, UPort, Chainspace, AnonCredLight}. Each of these systems individually addresses a subset of privacy and security issues, each possessing unique merits, privacy attributes, trade-offs, and limitations~\cite{Goodell2019}. However, the interaction between the specific advantages and limitations of these systems in the context of concrete use cases is not always well comprehended. Different use cases have distinct design requirements due to the specific needs of the system's stakeholders. Therefore, a thorough analysis is necessary to determine the specific considerations that system implementers and users must consider, comprehend, and address. Further research is also needed to evaluate the extent to which current privacy-enhancing identity and credential management systems can effectively compete with systems currently deployed and utilized by enterprises and governments. \subsection{Research Objectives} This chapter examines the feasibility and effectiveness of implementing privacy-enhancing identity management in large-scale public transport payment systems. To narrow the scope of the study, we explore the following three questions within the context of the protocol described by Goodell et al~\cite{Goodell2019}, referred to as the \textit{Distributed Digital Identity Architecture} (DigID): \begin{enumerate} \item How does the DigID address the primary privacy and security requirements of contemporary public transport payment systems compared to existing centralized solutions? \item What are the technical, operational, and user experience trade-offs when deploying DigID in a large-scale public transport network? \item To what extent can DigID satisfy or surpass the performance requirements of Transport for London's current payment infrastructure? \end{enumerate} We use London as a case study due to its scale, fare structure, and the availability of public data against which we can compare results. \subsection{Chapter Structure} The chapter proceeds as follows. The next section provides context for such a system and helps motivate their utility. Additionally, it introduces terminology and potential competing solutions. Section~\ref{overview} outlines the challenges in applying our proposed solution to Transport for London (TfL) and suggests possible extensions to address the limitations. Section~\ref{implementation} details the design-specific choices in the implementation. Section~\ref{results} describes the testing approach, Section~\ref{analysis} discusses the results, and Section~\ref{conclusion} offers an analysis, with a view toward future work.

text: In 2020, an estimated 276,480 women in the U.S. will be diagnosed with breast cancer, and 42,170 women will succumb to the disease \cite{Sieg20}. To inform management, most pathologists grade breast cancers using a standardized grading system \cite{Bloo51, Elst91}, which includes three features: 1) nuclear pleomorphism (or “atypia”), 2) degree of gland formation, and 3) mitotic count. The criteria for scoring mitotic count and gland formation are based on quantitative measures, whereas nuclear pleomorphism is assessed qualitatively by evaluating the nuclear morphology of the tumor microscopically on a scale from 1 to 3, indicating increasing deviation from normal epithelium. These three scores are combined to determine the final tumor grade. With the growing adoption of digital pathology, grading can now be performed on digitized histopathological images, providing similar agreement to assessments conducted via light microscopy \cite{Gint20}. Increasingly, pathologists can also be supported by Artificial Intelligence (AI) systems in routine practice \cite{Bera19, Niaz19, Bult20a, Rant20}. The most widely used AI technology for analyzing medical images is deep neural networks (deep learning; DL). Deep learning architectures consist of interconnected neurons that process an input image and perform a series of operations on the network's learnable weights to complete tasks such as classification, regression, and segmentation. These networks have achieved unprecedented success in various areas of computer vision \cite{Kriz12, Le13, Silv16, Devl18} and have led to recent advancements in digital pathology \cite{Jano16, Bejn17, Veta18, Nagp19, Bult20}. Specifically for breast cancer grading, automated mitosis detection was among the first applications of DL \cite{Cire13a, Veta15}, demonstrating its clinical and prognostic significance \cite{Tell18, Balk19, Balk19b}. Gland segmentation has been approached as a series of nuclei and gland detection tasks, as well as a segmentation task \cite{Nguy15, Lee18}, with extensions to clinical risk categories \cite{Buch16} using deep learning. Unlike gland formation and mitotic count, nuclear pleomorphism lacks a quantitative definition. Consequently, nuclear pleomorphism scoring is the least reproducible of the three grading components, limiting its utility \cite{Frie95, Meye05, Long05}. Research on automated nuclear pleomorphism scoring has been limited, involving techniques with manually crafted nuclear features \cite{Lu15, Gand19} combined with deep belief networks \cite{Maql16}, descriptor-based pixel-level image features \cite{Khan15}, or binary classification of high pleomorphism (score 3) using a simple convolutional neural network on small image patches \cite{Noel15}. Supervised DL requires ground-truth labels associated with images for training neural networks. Obtaining such labels is challenging for applications like pleomorphism scoring, which involves discrete classes and observer variability. Translating scores from multiple observers into a ground-truth label (e.g., based on majority or consensus) overlooks valuable information present in the distribution of individual expert scores. In this study, we propose a novel DL approach to nuclear pleomorphism scoring by treating it as a continuous score, rather than classifying it into three discrete categories. We reformulate the original three-category classification into a continuous spectrum of values ranging from the lowest to the most severe pleomorphism score. Our approach consists mainly of two components. The first component is an epithelial cell detection network developed previously \cite{Merc19}. This step aims to restrict the analysis to diagnostically relevant regions (i.e., invasive tumor) within a whole slide image. In the second step, a deep regression network predicts the continuous nuclear pleomorphism score for the tumor regions. Training this network does not require detailed manual annotations by pathologists, which is a key limiting factor in computational pathology. This work represents the first end-to-end fully automated nuclear pleomorphism scoring in breast cancer using DL. Furthermore, we translate a discrete classification into a continuous regression problem to retain valuable observer input, which has not been previously applied. The overview of our approach, \AI, outlining this two-stage process of nuclear pleomorphism scoring is presented in Figure \ref{fig:introduction:overview_inference}. To develop and validate our approach, we conducted two separate studies, resulting in two distinct data sets. The first study, referred to as the ROI-study, included $125$ tumor regions of interest (tumor ROIs) and an additional $79$ "normal appearing" epithelial regions of interest (normal ROIs) from $39$ whole slide images, carefully selected to encompass a wide variety of tumor morphology in breast cancer histopathology. We invited $10$ pathologists from $6$ countries to score nuclear pleomorphism on the tumor ROIs, each visually paired with a normal ROI from the same patient for the pathologists to use as a reference for scoring the degree of pleomorphism. We used the results of the ROI-study to train our \AI and to evaluate its performance compared to the panel of pathologists. In our automated approach, we used the averaged nuclear pleomorphism scores from the 10 pathologists as reference scores, representing their collective expertise rather than enforcing a discrete majority score. The \AI was trained on a wide range of tumor morphology, leveraging the reference scores to establish the concept of nuclear pleomorphism as a full spectrum of tumor morphology change. In the second study, referred to as the slide-study, $118$ whole slide images of breast cancer resection tissue sections were used to evaluate the trained \AI. The distribution of the slides mirrored the distribution of cases in routine clinical practice. For the slide-study, we invited $4$ pathologists to score nuclear pleomorphism of the slides, which were compared to our \AI for whole slide-level evaluation. More details on the ROI-study and slide-study are provided in Section \ref{sec:methodology}.

text: Pose transfer, which involves applying the desired pose of a source mesh to a target mesh, represents a promising yet challenging task in 3D computer vision with broad applicability across various industrial fields. However, existing methods ~\cite{NPT,LIMP,Unsupervised,AniFormer} perform well only within specific datasets of synthesized or known pose and shape spaces, and they fail to generalize to other unknown spaces with robust performance, significantly limiting further real-world applications. To achieve robust performance in unknown latent spaces and other domains, as illustrated in Fig.~\ref{fig:1}, we propose an innovative Transformer network aimed at generalized 3D mesh pose transfer. Specifically, we design a novel geometry-contrastive Transformer with geometrically structured encoders to enhance the identity mesh representation under the guidance of the pose mesh through their \emph{global geometric contrasts}. Locally, we introduce a new central geodesic contrastive loss to refine the geometric representation by considering the \emph{regional contrast of all the geodesic directions} of each vertex as back-propagation gradients. Additionally, we introduce a latent isometric regularization module to stabilize the unreliable performance in cross-dataset pose transfer challenges. Furthermore, we introduce a new 3D mesh dataset, SMG-3D, for quantitatively evaluating 3D pose transfer in unknown spaces. SMG-3D is based on spontaneous daily body gestures featuring more plausible and challenging body movements, distinct from those well-performed poses \cite{AMASS,DFAUST}. We employ a semi-synthetic approach to construct the dataset, providing necessary GT meshes for training and validation. Our SMG-3D dataset can be combined with other existing body mesh datasets for cross-dataset qualitative analysis. A natural question arises: why not simply use purely synthesized meshes for model training and evaluation? The concise answer is that models trained on purely synthesized meshes will not succeed in cross-dataset tasks. Indeed, while mesh synthesizing models like the SMPL series~\cite{SMPL, SMAL, SMPLX} can generate unlimited poses covering the entire latent space, or a large-scale dataset like AMASS \cite{AMASS} can mitigate inconsistencies with unknown dataset spaces, practical challenges remain. For instance, training a model on a small dataset like FAUST, with only 10 pose categories, requires over 26 hours to fully learn the latent space~\cite{LIMP}. Consequently, due to the immense variability of poses and movements, training the model with synthesized samples covering the entire pose space is impractical. It is preferable for a model to directly generalize to unknown latent spaces more efficiently. To address this, we propose the SMG-3D dataset to confront the cross-dataset learning challenge. It offers challenging latent distributions with natural and plausible body poses, including occlusions and self-contacts, rather than well-posed body movements like AMASS~\cite{AMASS}, which \textit{could advance research towards real-world scenarios one step further}. To summarize, our contributions are as follows: \begin{itemize}[leftmargin=*] \item A novel geometry-contrastive Transformer with positional embedding-free architectures achieving state-of-the-art performance on the challenging 3D pose transfer task. \item A straightforward and efficient central geodesic contrastive loss that enhances geometric learning by preserving the direction gradient of the 3D vertices. \item A challenging 3D human body mesh dataset (i.e., SMG-3D) offering unknown spaces of naturally plausible body poses with challenging occlusions and self-contacts for cross-dataset qualitative evaluation. \item A new latent isometric regularization module for adapting to challenging unknown spaces in cross-dataset tasks. \end{itemize}

text: Searcher struggle refers to the situation where a searcher "makes strenuous efforts in the face of difficulties"\footnote{\url{merriam-webster.com}} during a search process. During such moments, the user experiences negative emotions such as frustration, upset, or annoyance with the search activity. Detecting searcher struggle is crucial for Web search engines as it can prompt timely algorithm adjustments. Most current struggle detection methods are classifiers utilizing features that quantify user efforts~\cite{Li:2009:GAM:1571941.1571951,Jiang:2015:UPG:2684822.2685319}. This is because struggling behaviors are often indicated by excessive repetitions of user actions. For example, when searching for "curly hair dye," a user issued over twenty queries and still failed to find a satisfactory result. It is reasonable to infer that a high number of user efforts indicates user struggles. However, this assumption does not consistently align with real-world observations. One observation is that non-struggling search tasks may also involve numerous user-issued queries and clicks. For example, a user searched for "guy proposing ideas," and the log shows he browsed over 900 search results and bookmarked 27; the user reported enjoying the search throughout the session. Recent lab studies have raised similar concerns. Edwards and Kelly \cite{Edwards:2017:EFD:3077136.3080818} noted that while an increase in user effort might help predict searcher struggle, it can also indicate engagement or exploration. Without an effective mechanism, the distinguishing power of effort-based features diminishes, complicating the separation of negative experiences like struggle from positive experiences such as engagement, thereby hindering improvements in Web user experiences. This paper draws on psychology literature and proposes a new feature modulation method for struggle detection. Our work is inspired by Reversal Theory (RT)~\cite{gerrig2015psychology,apter2001motivation,personalitydynamics,APTER1984265,fourdomains}. RT is a "mode-based" psychological theory that challenges some fundamental assumptions in motivation and personality fields. Instead of assuming static personality traits, RT emphasizes the "complexity, changeability, and dynamics of human motivation and personality"~\cite{APTER1984265}. Its key insight is that people change in the flow of everyday life, and their personalities and motivations can reverse~\cite{personalitydynamics}. RT suggests counter-intuitive ideas, such as whether a user is conforming to rules or rebelling has little impact on their struggling behaviors, but whether they are engaged in a serious or playful task would matter. We conducted statistical hypothesis tests on these arguments and confirmed them using commercial search logs. Furthermore, RT posits that human motivations can be organized into a few dimensions, each consisting of two opposing states. Within one dimension, a person can reverse between the pair of states but can be active in only one at any given moment, which indeed suggests a bi-modal distribution instead of a single-modal distribution. We utilize this insight in this paper and propose a novel and effective feature modulation method for struggle detection. We propose to (1) select features relevant to the associated RT dimension, (2) moderate the selected features by reducing the bias between the two distributions in the bi-modal arousal model, and (3) send the modulated features to classifiers to determine if a search session contains struggling moments. Our method can be combined with any feature-based struggle detection method. We evaluate our approach using one-week-long search logs collected from both mobile and PC platforms. The experimental results demonstrate that our method is highly effective; it can significantly enhance a few top-performing methods by approximately 5\% in accuracy and about 9\% in positive precision.
