text: The release of the Bitcoin paper by~\cite{Satoshi2008} in 2008 has spurred interest in blockchains and smart contracts for the creation of innovative applications. There is a worldwide consensus regarding the potential of smart contracts in developing innovative applications across diverse sectors of industry and government~\cite{Hileman2017}. We concur with this perspective and believe that certain applications are effectively implemented using smart contracts deployed on-chain, such as those on the Ethereum~\cite{Ethereum2017}, Hyperledger Fabric~\cite{HyperledgerHome}, or Bitcoin~\cite{BitcoinHome} blockchains. However, we believe that the potential of on-chain smart contracts has been exaggerated. There are scenarios where employing on-blockchain smart contracts is excessive and others where they negatively impact the practicality or feasibility of the application~\cite{Morgen2018,Scriber2018,Valentina2018}. In such cases, developers should consider deploying smart contracts on Trusted Third Parties. It appears that the confusion arises from the novelty of the technology and the absence of a global consensus on the definitions of smart contracts and blockchains. Before proceeding with the discussion, we will present the definitions that will be used in the subsequent sections of this paper. \subsection{Blockchains} For software developers, a blockchain is middleware that incorporates built-in services useful for developing distributed applications without the need for a component (such as an authentication or database server) acting as central control. The key services that blockchains provide include indelible append-only storage, public-key-based access control for executing operations, public auditability of records, and notably, consensus services of a certain discipline (typically, eventual consensus). A wide range of applications can be developed based on blockchains; smart contracts are the most well-known but not the only one. At the implementation level, a blockchain can be described as a distributed data structure (also known as the ledger) consisting of an ordered, back-linked list (chain) of blocks. Blocks are appended to the list following an append-only model, and only when a group of nodes holding local replicas of the current blockchain state reach consensus on its next global state. The blocks typically store records of transactions executed by parties that do not necessarily trust each other, supporting the peer-to-peer execution model of the transactions. The transactions are operations intended to modify the current state of the blockchain and are not necessarily financial transactions. Building and maintaining a blockchain requires the integration of several technologies; consequently, different conceptual models have been proposed for modeling blockchains. For example, in~\cite{KenjiSaito2016}, a blockchain is viewed as a probabilistic state machine to highlight the probabilistic nature of the consensus algorithms used in blockchains. \subsection{Smart contracts} Intuitively, a smart contract is intended to be the digital equivalent of a traditional commercial contract written in a human language, such as English. By digital, we mean that the smart contract is a piece of computer code that can be executed to monitor or enforce the clauses specified in the conventional contract, programmatically at runtime. For instance, a financial contract for a loan agreement between a borrower and lender might specify that upon the borrower's request, the lender will advance GBP 100.00 to the borrower within five days of receiving the request. As an executable program, a smart contract is expected to be deployed on infrastructure that provides it with a runtime environment, including library support, facilities for managing the smart contract (initiate, stop, terminate, update, etc.), and databases for storing records of the inputs sent to the smart contracts and outputs produced by it. The primary responsibilities of the smart contract are i) to act as a contract monitor observing the interaction between the contracting parties; ii) to determine whether each operation (e.g., request loan, honor loan request, decline loan request, etc.) executed by the contracting parties is compliant or non-compliant with the terms specified in the contract and in accordance with the rights and obligations inherent in the contract, and iii) to produce a verdict. Note that in some existing smart contract applications, the declaration of the verdict is directly and intricately linked with an action (e.g., collect payment) that is executed when the verdict is contract compliant. However, we believe that for the sake of modularity, it is sensible to separate the two acts and focus on the verdict—the most fundamental operation that smart contracts need to perform. We consider the action as an arbitrary reaction that can be executed immediately or eventually by the smart contract itself or by a different component implemented in another software layer. In many applications, the action consists of allowing the execution of the contractual operation when it is declared contract compliant or preventing its execution when the operation is declared non-contract compliant by the smart contract. In this approach, the smart contract acts as a contract enforcer. The question that arises here is where to deploy the smart contract. \subsection{On--blockchain smart contracts} Smart contracts can be deployed on-chain. The term smart contract was introduced by Szabo in 1997~\cite{Szabo1997}, but it did not gain commercial interest until 2008 with the commercial success of Bitcoin as a cryptocurrency platform~\cite{Satoshi2008}. In Bitcoin~\cite{AndreasAntonopoulos2017}, smart contracts are implemented in an opcode stack-based script non-Turing complete language~\cite{BitcoinScript} and deployed on the Bitcoin blockchain. They were initially designed to mediate the execution of payment operations in BTCs (Bitcoin's cryptocurrency). Ethereum~\cite{AndreasAntonopoulos2018}, currently a leading blockchain platform, extends the concept of Bitcoin's smart contracts and implements a blockchain that supports smart contracts written in Turing-complete languages, such as Solidity~\cite{Solidity2017}. As demonstrated by numerous Bitcoin and Ethereum use cases, in several situations, smart contracts can be conveniently deployed on-chain, but it is essential to recognize that blockchains and smart contracts are two distinct technologies. Deploying smart contracts on-blockchain is just one of several deployment options. To understand this point, it is worth noting that smart contracts predate blockchains by several years. Research on smart contracts was initiated by Minsky in the mid-80s~\cite{Minsky1985} and continued by Marshall~\cite{Lindsay1993}. In early works, smart contracts were referred to as electronic contracts, executable contracts, digital contracts, and other similar terms. Given the widespread use of the term smart contract now, we will continue to use it throughout this document. \subsection{On--Trusted Third Parties smart contracts} Smart contracts can be deployed on--Trusted Third Parties (on--TTP). We define a TTP as an institution that, in addition to having the technical infrastructure for hosting smart contracts, has earned trust, reputation, and authority. E-commerce applications routinely utilize TTP services, examples include payment gateways, certification authorities, time-stamping services, custodian services, settlement services, and various brokerage services~\cite{Mainelli2015}. In smart contract applications, a TTP is logically positioned between the two business partners and is trusted to host and execute a single instance of the smart contract. The smart contract observes all operations executed by the partners and maintains undeniable records of them. Pioneering work on smart contracts~\cite{Minsky1985,Lindsay1993} primarily focused on on--TTP deployment. A strong assumption with a TTP--based deployment is that the TTP is trusted not to alter the contract code or misuse the sensitive data that the contractual parties expose to it. This issue can be addressed with the help of recently emerging trusted hardware technologies such as Intel SGX~\cite{VictorCostan2016} and ARM TrustZone~\cite{Sandro2019}. With this approach, the contract code can be deployed within the trusted environments that trusted hardware offers (called enclaves in SGX and trusted world in TrustZone). The trusted hardware prevents the TTP from altering the integrity of the contract code and examining sensitive data. \subsection{Contributions of this paper} Since the release of the Bitcoin paper~\cite{Satoshi2008}, smart contracts have been primarily discussed within the context and confines of blockchains to which they appear to be intrinsically linked. Consequently, the potential and practicality of smart contracts deployed on Trusted Third Parties (on--TTP) have been largely underestimated. The purpose and contribution of this paper are to restore balance. In pursuit of this objective, we discuss the advantages and disadvantages of using on--blockchain and on--TTP smart contracts. Our arguments are based on the following exercise. As developers, we were asked to advise on selecting a smart contract technology to implement a car insurance application. To provide a well-supported and defined recommendation, we conducted exploratory implementations (as opposed to fully developed) using on--chain and on--TTP smart contracts. In this paper, we share our experience and offer insights into the technical challenges we encountered. We have learned that some of these challenges are easier to address with on--TTP smart contracts than with on--chain smart contracts. We acknowledge that a significant disadvantage of an on--TTP smart contract is its reliance on a single TTP—a design feature considered undesirable and avoidable through the use of blockchains. However, we argue that in applications where the drawbacks of a TTP can be tolerated, on--TTP smart contracts might be a preferable alternative to their on--chain counterparts. The remainder of this paper is organized as follows. To initiate the discussion, Section~\ref{motivatingscenario} introduces the hypothetical use case of a car insurance application that we have been asked to implement as a smart contract application. Section~\ref{centralisedanddecentralised} explains that smart contracts can be implemented following either centralized or decentralized architectures. Section~\ref{onblockchainimplementation} discusses the experience we gained from implementing the car insurance application using an on--chain smart contract implemented in the Solidity language to be deployed on Ethereum. In Section~\ref{onTTPimplementation}, we include complementary arguments derived from implementing the example using an on--TTP smart contract. In Section~\ref{discussion}, we express our personal views on smart contracts and mention open research questions. To situate this article within a broader context, Section~\ref{relatedwork} provides a summary of pioneering articles on smart contracts and recent publications related to this article. Finally, we draw conclusions in Section~\ref{conclusions}.

text: In recent years, deep neural networks (DNNs) have achieved remarkable success across various domains of artificial intelligence, including computer vision~\cite{krizhevsky2012imagenet}, speech recognition~\cite{6296526}, and robotic control~\cite{levine2018learning}. Despite their outstanding performance, DNNs have been demonstrated to be susceptible to adversarial attacks that introduce imperceptible alterations to inputs~\cite{madry2017towards, goodfellow2014explaining,laidlaw2019functional, laidlaw2020perceptual, kang2019testing, dong2018boosting, carlini2017towards, chen2017ead, 7467366}. This vulnerability presents a significant challenge in security-critical applications such as autonomous driving and healthcare. To improve model robustness against adversarial attacks, numerous defense strategies have been proposed, including empirical~\cite{madry2017towards,zhang2019theoretically, papernot2016distillation,lin2020dual, singla2021skew, Kannan2018AdversarialLP, wang2019improving} and certifiable defenses~\cite{raghunathan2018certified,cohen2019certified, levine2020randomized, levine2019certifiably, sinha2017certifying, levine2021improved}. Adversarial training (AT)~\cite{madry2017towards} is regarded as one of the most effective algorithms for adversarial defenses. Numerous studies have aimed to enhance adversarial training by employing different loss functions, such as ALP~\cite{Kannan2018AdversarialLP}, TRADES~\cite{zhang2019theoretically}, and MART~\cite{wang2019improving}. However, these approaches typically train a single model without considering the synergy of a network ensemble. Moreover, most defense strategies concentrate on a single perturbation type, which may be susceptible to unseen perturbation types~\cite{tramer2019adversarial, maini2020adversarial}. For instance, models adversarially trained on $l_\infty$-bounded adversarial examples may be vulnerable to $l_1$ and $l_2$-bounded attacks. Knowledge distillation (KD)~\cite{hinton2015distilling} is a well-established technique for transferring knowledge from one model to another. Various forms of KD exist~\cite{wang2020knowledge}, including \textit{offline} KD, where teacher models are pretrained and the student learns from static teachers~\cite{hinton2015distilling}, and \textit{online} KD, where a group of student models learn from each other's predictions~\cite{zhang2018deep, guo2020online, song2018collaborative}. Several KD-based techniques have been proposed for adversarial defenses~\cite{papernot2016distillation, goldblum2019adversarially, arani2020adversarial, chen2021robust}. ~\cite{goldblum2019adversarially} illustrates that robustness can be transferred among models through KD, and~\cite{chen2021robust} demonstrates that KD can help alleviate robust overfitting. Table~\ref{tab:kd} outlines the differences among KD-based defenses. We contend that existing KD-based defenses are suboptimal in enhancing adversarial robustness. Defensive distillation (DD) trains a natural model with another natural model as the teacher, which fails to provide strong robustness since neither the teacher nor the student is adversarially trained, and it was compromised by~\cite{carlini2016defensive}. Adversarially robust distillation (ARD)~\cite{goldblum2019adversarially} trains a robust model with another robust model as the teacher to distill the robustness of a large network onto a smaller student, which depends on the availability of strong teacher models, and the student's improvement is constrained as the teacher remains fixed. Adversarial concurrent training (ACT)~\cite{arani2020adversarial} jointly trains a natural and a robust model in an online KD manner to align their feature spaces. However, since natural and robust models learn fundamentally different features~\cite{tsipras2018robustness}, aligning the feature space of a robust model with a natural model may lead to diminished robustness. In this paper, we introduce Mutual Adversarial Training (MAT), which enables models to share their adversarial robustness knowledge and instruct each other to become more robust. Unlike previous KD-based defenses, we simultaneously train a group of robust models, where each network learns not only from ground-truth labels as in standard AT but also from the soft labels of peer networks that encode peers’ knowledge for defending against adversarial attacks to achieve enhanced robustness. The architecture of MAT is depicted in Fig.~\ref{fig:mat}. MAT enhances model robustness through several mechanisms: 1) MAT inherits the advantages of KD, such as improving generalization~\cite{furlanello2018born} and mitigating robust overfitting~\cite{chen2021robust}. 2) \textit{MAT establishes a positive feedback loop for increasing model robustness}. Each network acts as a robust teacher, providing semantic-aware and discriminative soft labels to its peers. By learning from strong peers, a network becomes more robust, which in turn enhances the robustness of its peers. 3) \textit{MAT enables robust models to explore a broader space of adversarial samples and jointly discover more robust feature spaces and decision boundaries}. The adversarial examples of each model form a subspace of adversarial inputs~\cite{tramer2017space}, and the predictions of each model encode information about its decision boundary and adversarial subspace. In MAT, each model learns not only from its own adversarial examples but also receives information about peers' adversarial examples through the soft labels. Consequently, each model must consider a larger space of adversarial samples and identify a feature space and decision boundary that perform well on both its own adversarial examples and those of its peers, encouraging solutions that are more robust and generalizable. In summary, this paper proposes a novel KD-based adversarial training algorithm named MAT. MAT serves as a general framework for enhancing the adversarial robustness of any network without requiring strong teacher models. We further extend MAT to defend against multiple perturbation types (MAT-MP) by leveraging the transferability of adversarial robustness and propose several training strategies for training MAT-MP. Our extensive experiments demonstrate that MAT significantly improves the robustness of AT baselines and outperforms state-of-the-art methods for both single and multiple perturbations.

text: Android is increasingly becoming the most popular mobile operating system globally. Unfortunately, due to its prominence, it has also become the primary target platform for attackers. Adversaries exploit Android to deploy millions of malicious apps that deceive victims into disclosing their private data or executing harmful operations, such as monitoring users' activities, disseminating spam, or initiating unwanted advertisements. Concurrently, Android malware analysis, which encompasses malware detection and classification, has become an essential task for security researchers in both industry and academia. Consequently, numerous research studies have sought to identify Android malware~\cite{canfora2015effectiveness,gascon2013structural,li2018android,mclaughlin2017deep,hybroid}. Recently, a significant number of proposed approaches utilize the contextual information of Android applications to detect and classify Android malware, such as permissions and sensitive application programming interfaces (APIs). For instance, Li et al.~\cite{li2018android} introduced a classifier employing the factorization machine (FM) architecture, where they extract various Android app features (permissions, malicious APIs, etc.) from manifest files and source code. Similarly, Chen et al.~\cite{chen2018android} proposed a method that examines Android malware based on its static behavior, which involves the use of permissions, components, and sensitive API calls. Meanwhile, several studies also employ natural language processing (NLP)~\cite{kang2016n,xu2021detecting} based methods to detect Android malware, treating Android apps like documents and instructions in Android apps as words. For example, ~\cite{kang2016n} evaluates the effectiveness of uni-gram, bi-gram, and tri-gram with stacked generalization. Additionally, several existing studies rely on the Android network traffic pattern to identify legitimate and malicious behaviors~\cite{malik2016credroid,arora2014malware,zulkifli2018android,marin2020deepmal,wang2017malware,xu2021hawkeye,xu2020manis,xu2021falcon}. Most of these studies are based on manually indicated rules and develop rule-based classifiers for detecting Android malware, such as CICAndMal2017~\cite{lashkari2018toward}, which employs a third-party tool to extract nine features from the network PCAP (packet capture) file and detect malware using those specific features. Zulkifli et al.~\cite{zulkifli2018android} present a decision tree algorithm on network traffic as dynamic features of Android apps. Although the aforementioned methods provide the Android platform with an additional security layer, they have limitations. On one hand, for example, the contextual information of program code struggles against malware obfuscation techniques, such as ~\textit{identifier renaming}, ~\textit{string encryption}, ~\textit{dead-code insertion}, and ~\textit{instruction substitution}. These techniques alter the compiled code to evade detection easily. For instance, employing string encryption, the FM method in Li et al.~\cite{li2018android} would be affected because the system cannot extract the available permission information from the manifest file. Meanwhile, other NLP-based malware detection systems~\cite{kang2016n,xu2021detecting} are also affected by certain obfuscation techniques. On the other hand, for network traffic-based methods, the primary issue is the code coverage problem~\cite{tazaki2013direct}. As a type of dynamic feature-based method, network traffic represents only a small portion of code functionality. Most code functionalities do not require or generate network traffic. Moreover, most state-of-the-art network traffic-based malware detection systems are rule-based methods~\cite{malik2016credroid,arora2014malware,zulkifli2018android,marin2020deepmal,wang2017malware,hybroid}, which sophisticated attacks can easily evade since rule-based analysis depends on distinguishing expected versus anomalous behavior; these methods may struggle when malware is altered to conceal its footprints or behavior. Therefore, in this paper, we propose a hybrid pattern malware detection and categorization framework that integrates network and program code features. First, we transform the network packets into sequences of 2D gray images and employ a convolutional neural network (CNN) to pre-train the 2D gray images. We then utilize a bi-directional LSTM network to process the continuous network traffic and perform malware classification akin to the 2D image sequence classification task. Additionally, we develop an NLP-inspired method for the program code pattern based on the graph neural network (GNN). This method can detect obfuscated applications while maintaining excellent performance. In summary, we first design the \texttt{opcode2vec}, \texttt{function2vec}, and \texttt{graph2vec} components to represent instruction, function, and the entire program's information with vectors. text: Recent advancements in approaches based on end-to-end neural networks have demonstrated significant success across various sequence generation tasks, including machine translation~\cite{sutskever2014sequence,luong2015effective}, dialogue systems~\cite{vinyals2015neural,serban2016building}, textual summarization~\cite{rush2015neural,nallapati2016abstractive,see2017get}, image/video captioning~\cite{bahdanau2014neural,venugopalan2015sequence,pasunuru2017multi}, and question generation~\cite{du2017learning,du2018harvesting,zhang2019addressing}, among others. In all these tasks, cross-entropy loss optimization has been extensively utilized as a standard optimization method~\cite{sutskever2014sequence}, but it suffers from the issue of exposure bias~\cite{ranzato2015sequence} and fails to optimize for the non-differentiable automatic evaluation metrics that assess the quality of the generated sequence. The recent introduction of policy gradient-based reinforcement learning approaches addresses these issues in sequence generation tasks by directly optimizing the non-differentiable evaluation metrics~\cite{zaremba2015reinforcement,ranzato2015sequence,rennie2016self}. However, optimizing for a specific metric or reward through policy gradient-based approaches often results in improvements primarily in that specific metric, indicating that this approach may be exploiting the metrics~\cite{paulus2017deep}. The weighted average of multiple metrics or surrogate rewards has been investigated~\cite{liu2017improved}, but these methods must contend with determining the optimal scale balance across different metrics. Alternatively, one can optimize multiple metrics using a mixing ratio~\cite{pasunuru2018multi}, but this still requires careful tuning of the mixing ratio. Furthermore, all these reward approaches are static and do not vary during training, and not all metrics are important at every stage of training. Therefore, it may be beneficial to consider employing a dynamic combination of metrics, determining which rewards to use early versus later, or which rewards may be advantageous to revisit later in training, while considering the context of the complete history of rewards, the model’s current state, and the nature of the metric. To this end, we introduce a multi-armed bandit approach (which we designate as the DORB{} framework) where the arms of the bandit represent the choices of metrics we aim to optimize as rewards. In each round, the bandit selects the next possible metric to optimize based on its past performance history over these metrics, thereby enabling the automatic learning of an optimal curriculum of rewards. We investigate this approach in the context of exploration versus exploitation using the Exp3 algorithm~\cite{auer2002nonstochastic} with two novel approaches for bandit rewards: (1) Single Multi-reward Bandit (SM-Bandit); (2) Hierarchical Multi-reward Bandit (HM-Bandit). First, we introduce a reward scaling approach to maintain the metric rewards within the range $[0,1]$. Next, we present our SM-Bandit, where in each round, the bandit's reward is based on performance improvement from multiple sources. Here, we employ the average of all the scaled metric rewards from multiple sources as the final reward to the bandit. Finally, we introduce our HM-Bandit, which comprises a single first-level controller and $K$ second-level multi-armed bandits. The first-level controller aims to identify the under-performing reward metric, while the second-level bandits aim to activate the specific metric optimizer that will lead to a promising improvement in this specific metric. We validate the effectiveness of our approaches on two significant generation tasks: question generation and data-to-text generation (including an unseen-test transfer setup) using both automatic evaluation metrics and human evaluation. For question generation, we present results on the SQuAD QG dataset~\cite{du2017learning}, and for data-to-text NLG, we select the WebNLG dataset~\cite{gardent2017webnlg}. We demonstrate that our bandit-based approaches perform statistically significantly better (based on human evaluation) than robust single-reward based RL models as well as non-bandit based multi-reward methods such as the multi-task approach of~\newcite{pasunuru2018multi}. We further provide various interpretable analyses of our bandit progress and the learned rewards curriculum across different bandit approaches.

text: Object counting has gained increasing significance due to its diverse applications such as crowd surveillance, traffic monitoring, wildlife conservation, and inventory management. Most existing counting methods~\cite{zhang2016single, ma2019bayesian, biswas2017automatic} concentrate on a specific, single category. However, their performance declines drastically when applied to new categories. Additionally, collecting and labeling all categories for training is both challenging and expensive. Humans possess a generalization ability that enables them to learn and handle various vision tasks with minimal prior knowledge and experience. Inspired by this remarkable capability, we focus on this learning paradigm and design a network to efficiently recognize and count new categories given only a single example. We adopt the few-shot setting from ~\cite{ranjan2021learning} and adapt it for one-shot object counting. Specifically, the model receives an image with unseen novel categories and a supporting bounding box containing an example instance of the desired category as input, and then predicts the object count in the image. However, there are two primary challenges. \textbf{First}, the object counting task encompasses many different categories, and multiple categories may exist within the same image. Furthermore, in the few-shot setting, these categories do not overlap between training and inference. This necessitates that the model possess a strong ability to distinguish between features of different categories, while also effectively associating instances of the same category. \textbf{Second}, in one-shot counting, the model learns from only one supporting instance. The difficulty largely arises from the supporting sample potentially differing from other instances in aspects such as size and pose. Consequently, the model must be invariant to these variations without observing the commonalities across different instances. Therefore, in this paper, we propose an effective network named LaoNet for one-shot object counting. It comprises three main components: feature extraction, feature correlation, and the density regressor, as depicted in Figure~\ref{fig:network}. The feature correlation model and the feature extraction model are meticulously designed to address the aforementioned challenges. We propose the feature correlation based on Self-Attention and Correlative-Attention modules to learn intra-relations and inter-relations, respectively. The Self-Attention encourages the model to focus more on significant features and their correlations, enhancing the efficiency of information refinement. Previous few-shot counting methods~\cite{ranjan2021learning, yang2021class} typically utilize a convolution operation to match similarities between image features and supporting features. However, since the kernel is derived from supporting features with a default size and rotation angle, the convolution operation heavily relies on the quality of supporting features and the consistency of physical properties among different instances. In contrast, our designed feature correlation model benefits from two types of attention modules and addresses the aforementioned problem by considering all correlations. We further propose a Scale Aggregation mechanism in scale extraction to address scale variations among different categories and instances. By learning features from multiple subspaces, the model aggregates various scale information while maintaining spatial consistency. To summarize, our contribution is threefold. \begin{itemize} \item We design a novel network named LaoNet (A network by which you only need to Look At One instance) for one-shot object counting. By integrating Self-Attention and Correlative-Attention modules, LaoNet effectively exploits the correlation among novel category objects with high accuracy and efficiency. 	\item We propose a Scale Aggregation mechanism to extract more comprehensive features and integrate multi-scale information from the supporting box. 	 	\item The experimental results demonstrate that our model achieves state-of-the-art results with significant improvements on FSC-147~\cite{ranjan2021learning} and COCO~\cite{lin2014microsoft} datasets under the one-shot setting without fine-tuning. 	 	 \end{itemize}

text: Recommendation systems are now extensively utilized on online platforms such as Amazon \cite{amazon}, Google \cite{youtube_dnn,youtube1,NIS}, and Facebook~\cite{ebr}. Given the dynamic interactions between users and items, it is crucial to capture evolving user interests from users' historical records. To accurately represent user interests and make suitable recommendations, significant efforts have been devoted to studying sequential recommendation methods \cite{Caser,sasrec,GRU4Rec,SR-GNN}. Generally, the sequential recommendation task aims to characterize user representation from users' historical behaviors and predict the expected item accordingly. In light of the significant success of deep learning in modeling sequential dependencies and representation learning, numerous methods based on deep neural networks \citep*{r1} have been introduced to address this task. These include RNN-based frameworks~\cite{GRU4Rec,GRU4Rec+,STAMP}, various CNN blocks and structures~\cite{Caser,3D_CNN}, Graph Neural Networks (GNNs) \cite{SR-GNN,FGNN,GC-SAN}, and model variants \cite{sasrec,BERT4Rec,TiSASRec} that rely on the powerful multi-head self-attention \cite{atten}. Although these methods perform well, they may encounter issues with data sparsity \cite{Autoint,s3,sasrec} in sequential recommendations, particularly for models based on the multi-head self-attention mechanism, where only a single item prediction loss is used to optimize the entire model parameters to capture all possible correlations in input interaction sequences. To address this challenge, various self-supervised learning strategies have been introduced~\cite{yao2020self,CLRec}. Among these, the recently introduced contrastive learning (CL) objective~\cite{CL4SRec} has achieved very promising results. By combining effective data augmentation strategies and cooperating with the vanilla sequential prediction objective, the CL-based method can learn better sequence-level user representations and enhance the performance of sequential recommendations. However, the effectiveness of CL-based approaches depends on the correlated data augmentation methods, pretext tasks, efficient negative sampling, and hyper-parameter selection (e.g., the temperature in NCE and InfoNCE losses) \cite{jaiswal2021survey}. To mitigate these drawbacks, numerous efforts have been made to simplify contrastive learning. \cite{gao2021simcse} propose a very simple yet effective contrastive learning scheme that uses dropout noise as data augmentation to construct high-quality positive samples for sequence-level representation learning. Although this scheme is effective for unsupervised representation learning, adapting it to the sequential recommendation task still faces the dilemma where a higher proportion of the CL objective in model training leads to better representations that can easily distinguish positive and negative samples but might result in worse item prediction performance and vice versa. In other words, there is a noticeable gap between the discrimination of positive and negative samples and the task objective for the sequential recommendation. Thus, designing more training strategies to address the inherent issues of sequential recommendation models is key to obtaining better user representations, mainly for the item prediction task. text: Security researchers frequently identify significant security vulnerabilities in critical components, even those that have been extensively scrutinized and widely deployed. A promising trend in recent research involves the application of \textit{formal verification} techniques to substantial real-world systems. Such certified systems are accompanied by a machine-checkable proof that the implementation adheres to the specification of ``correctness''. For instance, Project Everest~\cite{everest} demonstrated the correctness of a complete HTTPS stack by not only constructing and verifying the TLS implementation but also the underlying toolchain. In this work, we focus on secure file systems. Previous verified file systems~\cite{fscq,yggdrasil,cogent} have demonstrated their correctness concerning crucial properties like guaranteed recovery from arbitrary crashes. However, none of these systems offer the features typically associated with {\em cryptographic} file systems, which generally employ cryptographic primitives to protect against integrity and/or confidentiality attacks, especially under the ``evil maid'' threat model~\cite{evil_maid}, where an attacker has temporary physical access to the target disk and can execute arbitrary read and write operations on the raw storage device. Our file system, IFSCQ, developed as an extension to FSCQ~\cite{fscq}, is the first file system that not only provides proven consistency guarantees against crash failures but also offers proven integrity guarantees against a compromised or malicious disk. At a high level, IFSCQ establishes a formal model of a malicious disk and proves that any compromise of data or metadata will be detected through cryptographic evidence. This is accomplished by constructing a traditional Merkle tree~\cite{merkle_tree} over every disk block. The root of the tree is stored in a modeled TPM (i.e., a small trusted storage where we can keep a limited number of Merkle tree root hashes), enabling us to store the majority of the Merkle tree on the potentially compromised disk while verifying its correctness each time it is re-read. As we will demonstrate later, integrating these integrity features into FSCQ required various modifications to FSCQ's core logic, but all our changes continued to satisfy FSCQ's proof obligations as well as the additional integrity properties we formalized and verified. We inherit the same trusted computing base (TCB) from FSCQ: we rely on the Coq proof system, Haskell compiler and runtime, and Linux FUSE (user-space file system support). Our objective was not to minimize the TCB but to verify that our cryptographic file system is ``correct'', both in terms of crash consistency and in detecting disk tampering. We note that many other research projects have explored how to verify an entire software stack~\cite{deepspec} or to generate C code with minimal runtime dependencies~\cite{cogent}. Such efforts would also be applicable to our work on IFSCQ if TCB minimization or full-stack verification were a goal. We note that the original FSCQ work is based on the design of the Unix Version~6 filesystem; it was not designed with modern optimizations. Instead, it was intended to be simple and to be extended for other purposes. Consequently, IFSCQ is similarly not intended to compete with modern production filesystems in terms of performance. It is meant to demonstrate the feasibility of applying formal verification to achieve important security properties. \vspace{1mm} \noindent\textbf{Threat model.} We assume that the hardware and operating system are trusted, but the disk may be malicious. We generalize the ``evil maid'' threat to a ``Byzantine disk,'' where adversaries can perform arbitrary writes at any time. Attacks could target specific file blocks, metadata blocks, or Merkle hash blocks, or they could roll back the entire state of the disk to a previously valid state. Therefore, we require some form of trusted ground truth to store and update the Merkle tree root. We adopt the term TPM (trusted platform module), which is included in many modern computers. We assume that our TPM provides us with a ``trusted boot'' facility, which most real TPMs support, but we diverge from real TPMs in several ways that we will describe later. \vspace{1mm} \noindent\textbf{Contributions.} Overall, we make the following contributions: \begin{itemize} \item The design and implementation of a certified file system with cryptographic integrity that is proven to be both crash-safe and capable of detecting data tampering. \item A formal model of malicious storage systems, along with desirable integrity properties a file system should provide against such attacks. \item A Merkle tree design that satisfies these integrity properties, capable of protecting all disk blocks (data blocks, inodes, and even unallocated blocks), while requiring only a small amount of trusted storage for root hashes. \item Evaluation results that demonstrate our system operates with reasonable overhead and defends against a variety of malicious attacks. \end{itemize} The remainder of the paper is organized as follows. Section~\ref{sec:background} provides the background necessary to understand our system. Section~\ref{sec:design} outlines the design of our system. Section~\ref{sec:proof} discusses our proof engineering. Section~\ref{sec:implementation} details our implementation. Section~\ref{sec:evaluation} presents our evaluation results. Section~\ref{sec:relatedwork} summarizes other related work. Section~\ref{sec:discussion} discusses potential improvements for IFSCQ, and Section~\ref{sec:conclusion} concludes.

text: Robots are increasingly functioning in environments requiring interaction with humans, such as in collaborative grasping~\cite{strabala2013toward,dragan2013legibility} and autonomous driving~\cite{montemerlo2008junior,levinson2011towards,sadigh2016planning,sadigh2016information}. Consequently, there is significant interest in developing planning and control algorithms for human-robot interaction. Ensuring the safety of such robots is crucial due to their potential to cause harm to humans~\cite{eder2014towards}. These challenges are particularly pronounced in scenarios like autonomous driving, where robots and humans may have divergent or conflicting objectives—such as a self-driving car executing an unprotected left turn~\cite{sadigh2016planning}. The primary challenge is defining safety for human-interactive robots. One could model the human as an adversary, but this approach is generally excessively conservative. An alternative strategy is to develop a model to predict human actions~\cite{ziebart2008maximum,fisac2018probabilistically,sadigh2019verifying} and ensure safety relative to this model. If the model accurately captures all human actions, then this approach guarantees safety. However, different humans may display markedly different behaviors~\cite{sadigh2016information}—for instance, individuals in a laboratory may behave differently than those on a street. Gathering data from all possible environments can be extremely challenging. If a behavior is not present in the training data, the model might not account for it. More fundamentally, even the most advanced machine learning models can make errors, potentially missing certain actions. Finally, \emph{responsibility sensitive safety (RSS)}~\cite{shalev2017formal} is an approach that manually specifies the range of permissible robot actions in various scenarios. Here, the designer of the robot controller is tasked with ensuring that permissible actions are exclusively safe actions. However, manually defining permissible robot actions for all potential scenarios is difficult, especially for robots in open-world environments. For example,~\cite{shalev2017formal} only formally defines permissible actions for a limited set of scenarios, such as lane changes. We propose an innovative approach to ensuring safety in human-interactive systems that considers all human behaviors within a certain bounded set. This involves two challenges: (i) defining the set of human behaviors, and (ii) ensuring safety concerning this set. We address these challenges as follows: \begin{itemize} \item {\bf Bounding human behavior via backup actions:} Instead of specifying the set of all actions the robot is \emph{allowed} to take (as in RSS), the designer specifies \emph{backup actions} that we assume the human always considers to prevent an accident (e.g., braking while steering in a particular direction). Specifically, we assume the human may take any action generally, but that they will take these actions when necessary to ensure safety. \item {\bf Ensuring safety via abstract interpretation:} We employ \emph{abstract interpretation}~\cite{cousot1977abstract} to conservatively overapproximate the system's reachable set for the aforementioned model of human behavior, and then ensure safety with respect to this overapproximation. \end{itemize} Initially, our concept of backup actions embodies the notion that we reasonably expect the human to undertake a limited range of evasive maneuvers to avoid an accident—e.g., if the robot gradually slows to a stop, we might expect the human to also decelerate to avoid a rear-end collision.\footnote{We do not assume the human will take evasive maneuvers such as swerving to avoid an accident (though they may do so if it is safe). Additionally, we assume a reasonable amount of time for them to brake and come to a stop.} If the robot is on a highway, coming to a stop is more hazardous, so we may require the robot to pull over to the shoulder before stopping. Similarly, we may require the robot to avoid stopping in an intersection. Specifying backup actions provides a means to define safety; we refer to this safety constraint as \emph{safety modulo fault}.\footnote{The term ``fault'' is used merely to indicate that safety disregards cases where the human does not act according to our model, not to attribute an accident to the human driver. The controller designer is responsible for designing the backup actions to achieve a reasonable notion of safety.} At a high level, to implement our framework, the designer of the robot controller must design the following: \begin{itemize} \item \textbf{Robot backup action:} An action the human anticipates the robot might take to ensure safety—e.g., braking without changing direction. It should be selected based on intuition regarding what actions the human driver expects the robot to take (e.g., based on traffic rules). \item \textbf{Human backup action set:} A set of actions that includes \emph{at least one} action the human considers taking to ensure safety—e.g., braking while steering in a particular direction. It should be chosen based on intuition about safety maneuvers the human driver considers taking. \end{itemize} In particular, while RSS requires the control designer to specify the set of \emph{all} actions the robot is allowed to take, we only require the designer to specify actions they believe the human considers taking to avoid an accident. Next, we propose an algorithm for ensuring safety modulo fault. Our algorithm builds on \emph{shielding}~\cite{akametalu2014reachability,alshiekh2018safe,wabersich2018linear,li2019robust}; specifically, rather than designing a specific controller, our algorithm takes as input an arbitrary controller designed to achieve the goal, and then combines it with a backup controller in a manner that attempts to use the given controller as often as possible while ensuring safety modulo fault. At a high level, it accomplishes this by using on-the-fly verification based on abstract interpretation to determine whether it is safe modulo fault to use the given controller; if so, it uses the given controller, but otherwise, it employs a backup controller. Finally, we empirically evaluate our approach in a simulation, including both scenarios where the humans are simulated and scenarios where the human is controlled by a real person via keyboard inputs. We demonstrate that our MPS modulo fault algorithm enables the robot to avoid accidents with both real and simulated humans, even when combined with a na\"{i}ve controller that completely ignores the humans. Figure~\ref{fig:overview} illustrates how our algorithm ensures safety while interacting with a human driver without being excessively cautious. It assumes that the human will at least slightly brake to avoid an accident (left). If it still cannot guarantee safety, then it allows the human to proceed first (right).

text: The Gaussian mechanism serves as a fundamental tool for numerous differentially private learning algorithms \cite{song2013stochastic, bassily2014private, abadi2016deep}. Although it is straightforward for mathematical reasoning and privacy accounting analyses, its continuous nature poses several practical challenges. For instance, it cannot be precisely represented on finite computers, which makes it susceptible to numerical errors that may compromise its privacy guarantees \cite{mironov2012significance}. Additionally, it is unsuitable for distributed learning environments that employ cryptographic multi-party computation techniques involving modular arithmetic, such as secure aggregation \cite{secagg, bell2020secagg}. To mitigate these issues, the binomial and (distributed) discrete Gaussian mechanisms have been recently proposed \cite{DworkKMMN06, agarwal2018cpsgd, CanonneKS20, ddg}. Unfortunately, each has its own limitations: the binomial mechanism can result in infinite privacy loss with a non-zero probability, and the discrete Gaussian: (a) lacks closure under summation (i.e., the sum of discrete Gaussians is not a discrete Gaussian), complicating analysis in distributed contexts and resulting in inferior performance compared to the continuous Gaussian in highly distributed, low-noise scenarios~\cite{ddg}; (b) requires a sampling algorithm not included in mainstream machine learning or data analysis software packages, making it challenging for engineers to implement in production settings (naïve implementations may lead to severe privacy errors). \textbf{Our contributions}\hspace{0.5em} To address these limitations, we propose and examine the multi-dimensional Skellam mechanism, which is based on adding noise distributed as the difference of two independent Poisson random variables. The Skellam noise is closed under summation (i.e., sums of Skellam random variables are also Skellam distributed) and can be easily sampled, as efficient Poisson samplers are widely available in numerical software packages. Its discrete nature also allows it to integrate well with cryptographic protocols and can result in communication savings. To evaluate the privacy guarantees of the Skellam mechanism and compare it with other mechanisms, we conduct a numerical evaluation of the privacy loss random variable and establish a sharp bound on the R\'enyi divergence between two shifted Skellam distributions. Our detailed analysis demonstrates that for a multi-dimensional query function with $\ell_1$ sensitivity $\Delta_1$ and $\ell_2$ sensitivity $\Delta_2$, the Skellam mechanism with variance $\mu$ achieves $(\alpha, \varepsilon(\alpha))$ R\'enyi differential privacy (RDP) \cite{mironov2017renyi} for $\varepsilon(\alpha) \leq \frac{\alpha \Delta_{2}}{2 \mu}+\min \left(\frac{(2\alpha - 1) \Delta_{2}+6 \Delta_1}{4 \mu^2}, \frac{ 3\Delta_1}{2 \mu}\right)$ (see Theorem \ref{thm:mainSK}). This indicates that the RDP guarantees are at most $1 + O\left(1/{\mu}\right)$ times worse than those of the Gaussian mechanism. To assess the Skellam mechanism's practical performance, we examine a differentially private and communication-constrained federated learning (FL) setting \cite{kairouz2019advances} where noise is locally added to the $d$-dimensional discretized client updates, which are then securely summed via a cryptographic protocol, such as secure aggregation (SecAgg) \cite{bell2020secagg, secagg}. We present a comprehensive algorithm that appropriately discretizes the data and applies the Skellam mechanism along with modular arithmetic to limit the data range and communication costs before implementing SecAgg. We demonstrate on distributed mean estimation and two benchmark FL datasets, Federated EMNIST~\cite{caldas2018leaf} and Stack Overflow~\cite{tffauthors2019}, that our method can achieve performance comparable to the continuous Gaussian baseline under stringent privacy and communication constraints, despite using generic RDP amplification via sampling~\cite{zhu2019poission} for our method and the exact RDP analysis for the subsampled Gaussian mechanism~\cite{mironov2019r}. Our method is implemented in TensorFlow Privacy~\cite{tf-privacy} and TensorFlow Federated~\cite{ingerman2019tff} and will be made open-source.\footnote{\url{https://github.com/google-research/federated/tree/master/distributed_dp}} Although we primarily focus on FL applications, the Skellam mechanism can also be applied in other learning and analytics contexts, including centralized settings. \textbf{Related work}\hspace{0.5em} The Skellam mechanism was initially introduced in the context of computational differential privacy from lattice-based cryptography~\cite{valovich2017computational} and private Bayesian inference~\cite{schein2019locally}. However, the privacy analyses in previous work do not readily extend to the multi-dimensional case, and they provide direct bounds for pure or approximate DP, which makes only advanced composition theorems~\cite{kairouz2015composition, dwork2010boosting} directly applicable in learning settings where the mechanism is applied repeatedly. For instance, the guarantees from~\cite{valovich2017computational} result in poor accuracy-privacy trade-offs, as shown in Fig.~\ref{fig:accounting-composition}. Moreover, we demonstrate in Section \ref{sec:skellam-pld} that extending the direct privacy analysis to the multi-dimensional setting is complex because the worst-case neighboring dataset pair is unknown in this scenario. For these reasons, our precise privacy analysis via a sharp RDP bound makes the Skellam mechanism practical for learning applications for the first time. These guarantees (almost) align with those of the Gaussian mechanism and enable the use of generic RDP amplification via subsampling methods \cite{zhu2019poission}. The mechanisms most similar to Skellam are the binomial \cite{agarwal2018cpsgd, DworkKMMN06} and the discrete Gaussian mechanisms \cite{CanonneKS20, ddg}. The binomial mechanism can (asymptotically) match the continuous Gaussian mechanism (when appropriately scaled). However, it does not achieve R\'enyi or zero-concentrated DP \cite{mironov2017renyi, BunS16} and has a privacy loss that can be infinite with a non-zero probability, leading to severe privacy failures. The discrete Gaussian mechanism provides R\'enyi DP and can be applied to distributed settings~\cite{ddg}, but it requires a sampling algorithm that is not yet available in data analysis software packages, despite being explored in the lattice-based cryptography community (e.g.,~\cite{roy2013high, dwarakanath2014sampling, rossi2019simple}). The discrete Gaussian is also not closed under summation, and the divergence can be substantial in highly distributed low-noise settings (e.g., quantile estimation~\cite{andrew2019differentially} and federated analytics~\cite{fedanalytics}), which causes privacy degradation. See the end of Section~\ref{sec:applying-skellam} for further discussion.

text: Considering that machine learning has reached superhuman performance in image classification~\citep{Ciresan_Schmidhuber_12,Krizhevsky_Hinton_12} and games \citep{Mnih_Hassabis_15,Silver_Hassabis_16}, it prompts the question of why similar outcomes are not observed in robotics. There are multiple reasons for this discrepancy. Firstly, learning to operate in the physical world is exponentially more challenging. Although the data needed by contemporary (deep) learning algorithms could be collected directly on a real robot~\citep{Levine_Quillen_16}, this approach is prohibitively costly in terms of time and resources for scaling. Alternatively, data can be produced in simulation more quickly, affordably, safely, and with unparalleled diversity. In this process, we must address the inevitable approximation errors that arise when modeling reality. These errors, commonly termed the \enquote*{reality gap}, stem from neglecting physical phenomena, inaccurate parameter estimation, or the discretized numerical integration in standard solvers. Exacerbating this problem, {state-of-the-art}\xspace (deep) learning techniques are recognized as being fragile \citep{Szegedy_Fergus_13,Goodfellow_Szegedy_14,Huang_Abbeel_17}, meaning they are sensitive to changes in their input domains. Moreover, the learner may exploit the simulator, overfitting to features that do not exist in the real world. For instance, \citet{Baker_Mordatch_20} observed that agents learned to exploit the physics engine to gain an unforeseen advantage. While this exploitation is an intriguing finding for studies conducted entirely in simulation, it is highly undesirable in {sim-to-real}\xspace scenarios. At best, the reality gap results in a performance decline, leading to a lower success rate or diminished tracking accuracy. More commonly, the learned policy is not transferable to the robot due to unknown physical effects. One challenging effect to model is friction, which often results in its underestimation in simulation, potentially causing motor commands that are insufficient to move the robot. Another cause of failure is parameter estimation errors, which can rapidly lead to unstable system dynamics. This situation is particularly hazardous for both the human and the robot. For these reasons, bridging the reality gap is a critical step to enable robots to learn from simulated experiences. There is a consensus that merely enhancing the simulator's accuracy will not bridge this gap~\citep{Hofner_White_20}. Examining breakthroughs in machine learning, we observe that deep models combined with large and diverse datasets result in improved generalization~\citep{Russakovsky_etal_2015,Radford_etal_2019}. In a similar vein, a technique known as domain randomization has recently gained traction (Figure~\ref{fig_sota_collage_sim2real}). The common feature of such methods is the perturbation of simulator parameters, state observations, or applied actions. Typical quantities to randomize include the inertia and geometry of bodies, the parameters of the friction and contact models, potential delays in actuation, motor efficiency coefficients, levels of sensor noise, as well as visual properties such as colors, illumination, camera position and orientation, or additional image artifacts (e.g., glare). Domain randomization can be viewed as a regularization technique that prevents the learner from overfitting to specific simulation instances. From a Bayesian perspective, the distribution over simulators can be interpreted as a representation of uncertainty. In this paper, we first present the necessary terminology and mathematical foundations for the problem (Section~\ref{sec_sota_mdp}). Next, we review early methods for learning from randomized simulations, outline the practical requirements, and describe measures for {sim-to-real}\xspace transferability (Section~\ref{sec_sota_simtoreal_foundations}). Subsequently, we explore the connections between research on {sim-to-real}\xspace transfer and related fields (Section~\ref{sec_sota_related_fields}). Moreover, we propose a taxonomy for domain randomization and classify the current state of the art (Section~\ref{sec_sota_domain_randomization}). Finally, we conclude and suggest potential future research directions (Section~\ref{sec_sota_discussion_and_outlook}). For those interested in gaining a deeper understanding of robot policy learning and policy search, we recommend these surveys:~\citet{Kober_Peters_13}, \citet{Deisenroth_Peters_13}, and \citet{Chatzilygeroudis_Mouret_20}.

text: Machine learning (ML) is increasingly employed to make predictions using privacy-sensitive data. In recent years, major technology companies such as Google and Amazon have started offering machine learning as a service to the public via their cloud platforms. While these systems can provide novel and intriguing insights across various fields, machine learning models trained on sensitive data also create a lucrative attack surface for adversaries. In a Membership Inference Attack (MIA)~\cite{shokri2016membership, yeom2017privacy}, an adversary seeks to identify the data used to train an ML model (i.e., its members). Successful MIAs breach individual privacy and pose a significant threat to unprotected ML models~\cite{shokri2016membership}. Differentially private (DP) mechanisms can be integrated into an ML model during the training process \cite{chaudhuri_differentially_nodate,Abadi_2016,beaulieujones2018privacypreserving, shokri2016membership, yeom2017privacy, yu2019differentially} to limit the influence a single data point has on the model's output. Training ML models with DP mechanisms is becoming more prevalent, with popular libraries such as TensorFlow~\cite{tensorflow} and PyTorch~\cite{pytorch} providing several DP training algorithms. Previous research has offered both experimental and theoretical evidence supporting DP training as a defense against MIAs~\cite{li2013membership,yeom2017privacy,jayaraman_evaluating_2019,shokri2016membership}. Yeom et al.~\cite{yeom2017privacy} demonstrate that DP training algorithms provide a \emph{theoretical upper bound} on the privacy leakage caused by MIAs. This bound, later refined by Erlingsson et al.~\cite{jayaraman2020revisiting}, offers robust protection for high DP levels (corresponding to small values of the DP parameter $\epsilon$), but rapidly weakens for large $\epsilon$. Nevertheless, empirical evaluations of MIAs against DP-trained models~\cite{jayaraman_evaluating_2019, jayaraman2020revisiting} indicate that large values of $\epsilon$, theoretically considered low-privacy settings, offer sufficient protection against MIAs in practice. Inspired by these findings, Murakonda and Shokri~\cite{murakonda2020ml} developed a tool for tuning $\epsilon$ based solely on the empirical performance of MIAs, thereby enhancing the model's utility at the cost of theoretical privacy guarantees. In summary, this body of literature suggests that applying DP mechanisms to ML models, even in significantly weakened privacy regimes, provides adequate protection against known MIAs. These studies on membership inference all follow a similar evaluation methodology where members and non-members are sampled independently from the same distribution. However, this underlying assumption does not always accurately represent real data~\cite{Mohammad2020, arjovsky2021distribution, pmlr-v97-recht19a, Martensson2020, nagarajan2021understanding, pmlr-v119-sagawa20a, sagawa2020distributionally}. Moreover, prior research has shown that data dependencies can lead to an overestimation of the privacy protection offered by DP~\cite{tschantz_sok_2020, kifer_no_2011, pufferfish, li2013membership, liu2016dependence}. Motivated by this, we conduct the first study of MIA performance on ML models trained with DP-SGD~\cite{Abadi_2016} \emph{under data dependencies}. We begin by examining the methodology from previous work on MIAs and identify the assumptions that support their theoretical findings~\cite{yeom2017privacy,jayaraman_evaluating_2019,nasr2021adversary}. Since there are no publicly known instances of MIAs against ML models in the wild, researchers are restricted to simulating attacks using theoretical games between the model owner and attacker, known as \emph{membership experiments}~\cite{yeom2017privacy}. We demonstrate that previous membership experiments assume independence between training samples, which may not represent many membership inference scenarios in practice. To address this, we propose a new membership experiment that relaxes the restrictive independence assumption. We show that previous DP-based bounds on the adversary's success do not hold in this more general setting. We emphasize that this does not imply that DP is broken or flawed. Rather, the guarantees of DP mechanisms no longer apply when defining membership inference with data dependencies. Intuitively, this is because DP mechanisms limit the effect that a \emph{single} sample has on the output. However, when training samples have dependencies, related samples can leak additional information about this single sample. Prior research has demonstrated the importance of studying MIA performance both theoretically and empirically~\cite{jayaraman_evaluating_2019, jayaraman2020revisiting}. Thus, we also examine the effect of data dependencies on the \emph{empirical performance} of MIAs under different instantiations of our membership experiment. Using six real-world datasets, we evaluate the performance of off-the-shelf attacks. These attacks have black-box query access to the target model and are given no additional background information about the data dependencies we consider. Using these attacks, we explore three different types of data dependencies. First, to examine the extent to which data dependencies can affect MIAs, we artificially divide a dataset into members and non-members using a clustering algorithm. Our results indicate that data dependencies can lead to perfect membership inference even in the presence of DP training. Second, we investigate the effects of an explicit bias in an attribute of the training set. Specifically, we create a gender and an education bias in the training set, and observe that MIA performance typically increases as the training set bias becomes more pronounced. Finally, we consider MIA performance on various real-world examples of data dependencies that occur during data collection. For instance, we study the effect of all members being from a specific health region (or hospital) and non-members from all other regions. We also examine the performance of MIAs when members and non-members originate from the same source (the US Census) but are curated by different researchers. In all of our evaluations with statistical dependencies among training samples, we observe a significant increase in MIA performance compared to related work where all samples are Independent and Identically Distributed (IID)~\cite{shokri2016membership,jayaraman_evaluating_2019, jayaraman2020revisiting, yeom2017privacy,jagielski2020auditing, nasr2021adversary}. This demonstrates that the assumption of data independence among training samples underestimates the attack performance. Our empirical evaluation yields attack performance exceeding the bounds of DP, confirming that the currently known DP bounds do not apply once we consider dependent data, and thus DP mechanisms are not a comprehensive solution for membership inference. This underscores the importance of considering data dependencies in future MIA evaluations and urges new research to develop better defenses and more realistic theoretical bounds on MIA performance.

text: Confidence intervals are frequently used to summarize the underlying distribution and to indicate outlier behavior. In this paper, we examine the problem of computing confidence intervals for time series. \citet{korpela2014confidence} introduced a concept for computing confidence intervals: instead of calculating point-wise confidence intervals, they suggest computing confidence bands. More formally, given $n$ time series $T$, we aim to find $k$ time series $U \subseteq T$ that minimize the envelope area, specifically, the sum $\sum_i \pr{\max_{t \in U} t(i)} - \pr{\min_{t \in U} t(i)}$. As argued by \citet{korpela2014confidence}, the advantage of using confidence bands over point-wise confidence intervals is superior family-wise error control: if point-wise intervals are used, we can only assert that a time series \emph{at some fixed point} is an outlier and must apply a correction for multiple testing (such as Bonferroni correction) to assert with a certain probability that the \emph{entire} time series is normal. In this paper, we explore approximation algorithms for finding confidence bands. Although \citet{korpela2014confidence} demonstrated that finding the optimal confidence band is an \textbf{NP}-hard problem, they did not offer any approximation algorithms or inapproximability results. We will first demonstrate that despite being an \textbf{NP}-hard problem, it is solvable for \emph{some} $k$. We achieve this by considering a different problem, where instead of a hard constraint, we have an objective function that favors selecting time series as long as they do not excessively increase the envelope area. The objective depends on the parameter $\alpha$; larger $\alpha$ values permit more increase in the envelope area. We will demonstrate that this problem can be solved exactly in polynomial time and that each $\alpha$ corresponds to a specific value of $k$. We will show that there are at most $n + 1$ such bands, and that we can identify all of them in polynomial time by varying $\alpha$. Next, we present a simple algorithm for approximating confidence bands by relating the problem to the weighted $k$-\textsc{MinUnion}\xspace problem. We will provide a variant of an algorithm by~\citet{chlamtac2018densest} that offers a $\sqrt{n} + 1$ guarantee. We also argue that—under a certain conjecture—we cannot approximate the problem better than $\bigO{n^{1/4}}$. Finally, we examine a variant of the problem where, instead of minimizing the envelope area, we minimize the width of the envelope, which is the maximum difference between the envelope boundaries. We demonstrate that a simple algorithm can achieve a 2-approximation. This approximation provides an interesting contrast to the inapproximability results when minimizing the envelope area. Surprisingly, this guarantee is tight: we will also show that there is no polynomial-time algorithm with a smaller guarantee unless $\textbf{P}=\textbf{NP}$. The remainder of the paper is organized as follows. We formally define the optimization problems in Section~\ref{sec:prel}. We address the regularized band problem in Section~\ref{sec:reg}, approximate minimization of envelope area in Section~\ref{sec:sum}, and approximate minimization of envelope width in Section~\ref{sec:max}. Section~\ref{sec:related} is dedicated to related work. We present our experiments in Section~\ref{sec:exp} and conclude with a discussion in Section~\ref{sec:conclusions}.

text: As the use of autonomous robotic systems becomes more widespread, it is essential for the controllers that operate them to demonstrate the sophistication necessary for functioning in our everyday, unstructured environments. Recent advancements in reinforcement learning (RL), when combined with deep neural networks as function approximators, have yielded remarkable outcomes across various complex robotic control tasks, such as dexterous in-hand manipulation \cite{dexterous}, quadrupedal locomotion \cite{haarnoja2018learning}, and targeted throwing \cite{throwing}. However, the absence of \textit{safety} assurances in deep RL-based controllers restricts their applicability in real-world robotics \cite{Ibarz_2021}. This limitation arises from the opaque nature of neural network policies and their inability to consistently handle out-of-distribution states, especially when models trained in simulation are applied to real-world scenarios. Conversely, the classical robotics community has developed numerous controllers and algorithms for a variety of real-world physical systems (ranging from mobile robots to humanoids) that enable the reliable and safe deployment of robotic agents in real-world settings. These include classical feedback controllers \cite{maxwell1868governors}, trajectory generators \cite{ijspeert2008central}, and behavior trees \cite{colledanchise2016behavior}. This reliability is due to their explicit analytical derivation and established models, which provide control theoretic guarantees, making them suitable for real-world deployment. However, they can be significantly suboptimal for complex tasks due to limitations in analytical modeling and approximations. A promising future direction in robot control involves integrating the complementary strengths of these different control mechanisms to overcome their respective limitations. Such approaches are observed in neuroscience as the foundational control strategy employed by biological systems. The dual-process theory of decision-making \cite{dickinson2002role} suggests that multiple distinct neural controllers are involved in action selection within biological systems. \citet{lee2014neural} provide evidence supporting this theory based on the human brain, demonstrating the existence of an arbitration mechanism that determines the extent to which different neural controllers influence behaviors. The arbitrator selects based on specific performance measures exhibited by each controller, leveraging their respective strengths in a given state. We take inspiration from this observation and introduce Bayesian Controller Fusion (BCF), a hybrid control strategy that merges the strengths of deep RL and traditional handcrafted controllers (\textit{control priors}) for safe real-world deployment. We define the final policy as a Bayesian composition of these two controllers, where the output for each system reflects their respective \textit{epistemic} uncertainty in a given state, as depicted in Figure \ref{front}. This enables BCF to naturally arbitrate control between the two systems based on their confidence to act. This has significant implications during real-world deployment, where we benefit from the dexterity of the learned system in states it has generalized to, while relying on the risk-averse behaviors of the handcrafted system in out-of-distribution states for safe operation. Notably, our method learns to control a real robot in joint space to accomplish a given task with no on-robot time (\textit{zero-shot}), even if the learned policy is not perfectly transferable from simulation to the real world. We validate our approach on two continuous control robotic tasks involving reactive navigation on a mobile robot and a manipulability-maximizing reacher on a robotic arm. We demonstrate how BCF enables us to reliably transfer a simulation-trained policy to the real world while achieving significant performance enhancements from the RL component compared to the handcrafted system alone. We view this as a promising and practical pathway to enabling simulation-trained RL controllers to safely function in the real world.

text: With the increasing popularity of open-access academic article repositories, such as arXiv or bioRxiv, disseminating new research findings has become almost effortless. Through these services, the research community shares tens of thousands of scientific papers each month\footnote{\url{https://arxiv.org/stats/monthly_submissions}}. However, the unreviewed nature of these repositories and the large volume of new publications have made it nearly impossible to identify relevant work and stay updated with the latest findings. Scientific paper summarization, a subtask within automatic text summarization, seeks to assist researchers by automatically condensing articles into a concise, human-readable form containing only the most essential information. In recent years, abstractive summarization, an approach where models are trained to generate fluent summaries by paraphrasing the source article, has achieved significant progress. State-of-the-art methods utilize large, pre-trained models~\citep{raffel2019t5, lewis2020bart}, define task-specific pre-training strategies~\citep{zhang2019pegasus}, and scale to long input sequences~\citep{zhao2020seal, zaheer2020bigbird}. Available large-scale benchmark datasets, such as arXiv and PubMed~\citep{cohan2018discourse}, were automatically collected from online archives and repurpose paper abstracts as reference summaries. However, the current form of scientific paper summarization, where models are trained to generate paper abstracts, has two limitations: 1) abstracts often contain information that is not of primary importance, 2) the vast majority of scientific articles include human-written abstracts, rendering the generated summaries redundant. To address these limitations, we introduce the task of disentangled paper summarization. The objective of this new task is to generate two summaries simultaneously: one strictly focused on the summarized article's novelties and contributions, and the other introducing the context of the work and previous efforts. In this form, the generated summaries can cater to the needs of diverse audiences: senior researchers and field experts who can benefit from reading the summarized contributions, and newcomers who can quickly understand the intricacies of the addressed problems by reading the context summary and gain a perspective of the latest findings from the contribution summary. For this task, we introduce a new large-scale dataset by extending the S2ORC~\citep{lo2020s2orc} corpus of scientific papers, which spans multiple scientific domains and provides rich citation-related metadata. We organize and process the data, extending it with automatically generated contribution and context reference summaries to enable supervised model training. We also introduce three abstractive baseline approaches: 1) a unified, controllable model manipulated with descriptive control codes~\citep{fan2018controllable,keskar2019CTRL}, 2) a one-to-many sequence model with a branched decoder for multi-head generation~\citep{luong2016mtl, bansal2018mts}, and 3) an information-theoretic training strategy leveraging supervision derived from the citation metadata~\citep{peyrard2019simple}. To benchmark our models, we design a comprehensive automatic evaluation protocol that measures performance across three axes: relevance, novelty, and disentanglement. We thoroughly evaluate and analyze the baseline models and investigate the effects of the additional training objective on the model's behavior. To demonstrate the usefulness of the newly introduced task, we conducted a human study involving human annotators in a hypothetical paper-reviewing setting. The results indicate that disentangled summaries are more helpful in 79\% of cases compared to abstract-oriented outputs. Code, model checkpoints, and data preparation scripts introduced in this work are available at~\url{https://github.com/salesforce/disentangled-sum}.
