text: Advancements in deep neural networks over the past decade have enabled models to begin addressing new tasks that require information from multiple modalities. The intersection of language and vision represents a significant area of research, particularly in visual question answering (VQA) \cite{Agrawal2015VQAVQ, Gupta2017SurveyOV}, which involves answering questions about images (as reviewed in \cite{Wu2017VisualQA, Srivastava2019VisualQA}). However, models that aim to solve human tasks must look beyond semantic information in text and visuals to exhibit nuanced behavior: they must learn complex referential relationships with numerous cases and exceptions (e.g., `green' might indicate a plant is healthy, or a person is ill, inexperienced, envious, or recycling), or use one modality to transcend learned statistical biases in the other \cite{Agrawal2018DontJA, Cadne2019RUBiRU, Chen2020CounterfactualSS, goyal2017making, Ramakrishnan2018OvercomingLP} (e.g., when asked, "what color is the banana?", we understand that they are typically yellow, but the one in a specific image might be pink). Representing such interactions presents a significant challenge in deep learning, as it is not immediately clear how to optimally fuse feature tensors within a network. Early studies employed vector concatenation to project various features into a new joint feature space \cite{Zhou2015SimpleBF, Lu2016HierarchicalQC}. Inspired by an earlier vision-only two-factor framework \cite{Tenenbaum:2000:SSC:1121517.1121518}, VQA models have significantly improved by adopting a `pooled' bilinear representation (BLP) of vision and text features \cite{DBLP:journals/corr/GaoBZD15, DBLP:journals/corr/FukuiPYRDR16, DBLP:journals/corr/KongF16, DBLP:journals/corr/KimOKHZ16, DBLP:journals/corr/abs-1708-01471, ben2019block, Yu2018BeyondBG}. Research on BLP for VQA has concentrated on: developing more efficient and cost-effective bilinear representations \cite{DBLP:journals/corr/KongF16, DBLP:journals/corr/KimOKHZ16, DBLP:journals/corr/abs-1708-01471, ben2019block}, integrating BLP with attention mechanisms \cite{Kim2018BilinearAN, Yu2018BeyondBG, DBLP:journals/corr/abs-1708-01471}, and recently analyzing and categorizing BLP (as a "joint" representation) alongside other fusion techniques and models \cite{Baltruaitis2019MultimodalML, zhang2019multimodal, 8715409}. Despite successes in VQA, BLP techniques have not yet been widely applied to video-QA baselines \cite{MovieQA, pororoqa, jang-CVPR-2017, Fan_2019_ICCV, lei2018tvqa, Xu2017VideoQA}. In this paper, we begin to bridge this research gap by applying BLP techniques to the TVQA \cite{lei2018tvqa}, TGIF-QA \cite{jang-CVPR-2017}, Ego-VQA \cite{Fan_2019_ICCV}, and MSVD-QA \cite{Xu2017VideoQA} datasets. Our contributions include: \textbf{I)} Replacing concatenation with BLP techniques in the TVQA baseline model \cite{lei2018tvqa}, \textbf{II)} Experimenting with a modified version of the TVQA baseline to accommodate BLP, which we call the `dual-stream' model, \textbf{III)} Conducting experiments to replace concatenation with BLP in the recently proposed heterogeneous-memory-enhanced multimodal attention (HME) model \cite{Fan2019HeterogeneousME}, \textbf{IV)} Utilizing the TVQA dataset in our experiments on HME, \textbf{V)} Providing insights into the poor performance concerning recent multimodal fusion taxonomies \cite{Baltruaitis2019MultimodalML, zhang2019multimodal, 8715409}, \textbf{VI)} Conducting experiments on the TVQA baseline model augmented with deep canonical correlation analysis (DCCA) \cite{Andrew2013DeepCC} to contrast a `coordinated' representation with BLP's `joint' representation (as defined in \cite{8715409}), \textbf{VII)} Offering several additional best practices to consider when transitioning BLP from image-QA to video-QA, \textbf{VIII)} Providing an overview of how bilinear representations compare and contrast with current psychological vision and perception models \cite{Goodale1992SeparateVP, milner2006visual, milner2008two, goodale2014and, Milner2017HowDT}. Notoriously, inconclusive or negative experimental results often remain unpublished, a practice that has been widely criticized \cite{Mlinari2017DealingWT, Faschinger2019DoNH, Sandercock2012NegativeRW}. We aim to report our experimental results to expand the public experimental scope of multimodal fusion and encourage critical future research that may build on, contrast, and critique our findings and hypotheses.

text: The field of question answering has greatly benefited from advancements in deep learning, particularly through pre-trained language models (LM)~\cite{radford2019language,devlin2018bert}. Although question answering over single passages (reading comprehension datasets) and large-scale open-domain corpora (open-domain QA) has seen significant progress, the performance of QA over book stories (BookQA) remains lacking. For instance, in the most prominent benchmark in this area, NarrativeQA~\cite{kovcisky2018narrativeqa}, which was introduced three years ago, current state-of-the-art methods exhibit only slight improvements over the initial baselines. Several challenges in NarrativeQA hinder research progress. First, narrative stories introduce a writing style distinct from the formal texts like those in Wikipedia. Second, the extensive length of books exceeds the processing capabilities of neural models, making evidence identification from an entire book crucial. Third, NarrativeQA is a generative task, and many answers cannot be directly matched to the original books. Thus, generative QA models are necessary. Finally, and most importantly, the dataset lacks annotations for supporting evidence. While this offers a realistic setting similar to open-domain QA, combined with the generative nature of the answers, it complicates the inference of supporting evidence, unlike most extractive open-domain QA tasks. The demands for evidence identification and the absence of supporting evidence annotations render the BookQA task akin to open-domain QA. In this paper, we initially examine whether the strategies employed in state-of-the-art open-domain QA systems can be adapted to enhance BookQA, including: (1) the neural ranker-reader pipeline~\cite{wang2018r}, where a neural ranker selects relevant passages (evidence) based on a question from a large pool of candidates; (2) the application of pre-trained LMs as readers and rankers, such as GPT~\cite{radford2019language}, BERT~\cite{devlin2018bert}, and their subsequent developments; (3) the distantly supervised and unsupervised training methods~\cite{wang2018r,Lee_2019orqa,min2019discrete,guu2020realm,karpukhin2020dense} that enable rankers to learn effectively from noisy gold data. By training a ranker-reader framework on BookQA, we achieve a new state-of-the-art on NarrativeQA using both generative and extractive readers. Based on these results and our analysis, we observe the following: \noindent$\bullet$ Employing pre-trained LMs as the reader model, such as BERT and GPT, enhances NarrativeQA performance. With the same BM25 IR baseline, they achieve a 5-6\% improvement in Rouge-L over their non-pre-trained versions. \noindent$\bullet$ Our specifically designed distant supervision signals significantly enhance the neural ranker, although the improvement remains modest compared to the upper bound. Further analysis of the ranker module confirms the training difficulty, as the improvement from the pre-trained LM BERT is minimal in this context.

text: Drones hold significant promise for revolutionizing urban logistics services. By facilitating rapid, adaptable, and efficient delivery, they can help meet the swiftly increasing logistics and e-commerce demands of densely populated urban areas~\cite{chung2020optimization}. Additionally, they can decrease our dependence on conventional ground delivery services that exacerbate traffic congestion~\cite{HolguinETAL18}. Nevertheless, operating package delivery services solely reliant on drones may be impractical due to their restricted flight range and payload capacity~\cite{SudburyETAL16}. To address these constraints, we examine the problem of operating delivery drones in conjunction with ground vehicles by permitting drones to travel on ground vehicles to conserve energy and extend their effective flight range~\cite{choudhury2019dynamic,choudhury2021efficient}. Specifically, we concentrate on routing a team of drones and trucks over a shared road network, where drones can utilize trucks as transit in addition to flying. We conceptualize our scenario as a \emph{coordinated} extension of the Multi-Agent Path Finding (MAPF) problem~\cite{stern2019multi}, which necessitates computing start-goal routes for all agents while striving to minimize the total path cost incurred by the drones and trucks. The path cost may differ for the two types of agents and can represent the energy consumed or the operational expense. As in the traditional MAPF formulation, our problem setting requires compliance with inter-agent constraints, which in our case limits the maximum number of drones that can concurrently use a truck. It also necessitates considering the potential cost savings from coordinating trucks and drones to share trip segments. The feature of agents temporarily coordinating has not been explored by the MAPF community thus far (to the best of our knowledge) and renders our problem significantly more challenging than the already complex classical MAPF~\cite{yu2013structure, YuLaValle16}. Most state-of-the-art MAPF algorithms focus on avoiding inter-agent collisions rather than optimizing coordination~\cite{felner2017search,stern2019multi}. Our recent work developed a MAPF solver for routing drones over transit networks~\cite{choudhury2021efficient} but assumed the transit vehicles follow fixed and known routes and that drones were not required to fly over the road network. Another study considered MAPF problems with cooperation but only planned for predefined agent pairs to arrive at fixed meeting points~\cite{greshler2021cooperative}, rather than simultaneously traversing a route. The operations research community has examined optimizing drones with trucks, but their methods are only applicable to a few agents on small abstract routing graphs~\cite{agatz2012optimization}. \vspace{5pt} \noindent\textbf{Contributions.} We develop an effective algorithmic strategy for coordinated MAPF in the context of drones and ground trucks functioning in tandem. Our central idea is to \textit{decompose our overall intractable MAPF problem into two distinct MAPF sub-problems that we can solve sequentially} (\Cref{fig:approach}). In Stage 1, we determine truck routes that are likely to be beneficial as transit options for drones. In Stage 2, we fix the truck routes, construct a transit network based on them, and overlay this network on the road graph. We then compute drone routes over the composite road-and-transit network, where drones incur no cost on the segments where they use transit (subject to capacity constraints). As a post-processing step, we re-route trucks not used as transit to their shortest road network paths. We implement two variants of our approach that employ different MAPF solvers; the first utilizes Enhanced Conflict-Based Search~\cite{barer2014suboptimal} and the second employs Prioritized Planning~\cite{silver2005cooperative} for both stages. We evaluate our approach on a range of coordinated MAPF settings over the Manhattan road network, with nearly $4500$ vertices and $10000$ edges covering an area of nearly \SI{200}{\kilo\metre\squared}, and up to $20$ trucks and $80$ drones. Our experiments demonstrate that coordinating drones and trucks can save more than $50\%$ of total vehicle distance traveled compared to no coordination. \textit{We refer to the sum of truck path distance and drone flight distance as vehicle distance traveled}, since drones incur no energy cost when riding on a truck. For brevity and convenience, we will use this phrase hereafter, with some abuse of terminology. Our approach plans paths for all settings within at most $5$ minutes of computation time on commodity hardware. We anticipate that our approach could serve as a foundation in more complex problem settings where we also need to optimally allocate agents to tasks (i.e., package-delivery locations) and determine the order in which to execute them. For example, in a manner similar to our previous work~\cite{choudhury2021efficient}, we could employ a bi-level approach where the upper layer allocates jobs to the agents and a lower-level planner---a coordinated MAPF solver in our case---executes the allocation in a receding-horizon fashion. \vspace{5pt} \noindent\textbf{Layout.} In~\Cref{sec:related} we review prior related fundamental approaches and state-of-the-art applications. In~\Cref{sec:problem} we introduce basic notation and definitions and describe our problem setting of coordinated MAPF. In~\Cref{sec:approach} we describe our two-stage approach for coordinated MAPF in detail and discuss our extensive experimental results in~\Cref{sec:results}. We conclude by summarizing our work and outlining future research directions in~\Cref{sec:conclusion}.

text: In server systems, the Quality of Service (QoS) of a job is typically assessed by its response time, which is defined as the duration between the job's release and its completion. In job scheduling, the response time is also referred to as the flow time. Specifically, for any schedule $\mathcal{S}$, let $c_i(\mathcal{S})$ represent the completion time of job $J_i$ under $\mathcal{S}$, and let $r_i$ denote the release time of $J_i$. The flow time of a job $J_i$ under $\mathcal{S}$, denoted by $f_i(\mathcal{S})$, is defined as \[ f_i(\mathcal{S}) = c_i(\mathcal{S}) - r_i. \] Two primary QoS objectives for a server system are the average, or equivalently, $\ell_1$ norm, of job flow times, and the maximum, or $\ell_{\infty}$ norm, of job flow times. It is well-established that Shortest Remaining Processing Time (SRPT), which minimizes the average flow time, may result in some jobs experiencing long and unfair flow times (i.e., job starvation). Conversely, First-Come-First-Served (FCFS), which minimizes the maximum flow time~\cite{10.5555/314613.314715}, can adversely affect the average flow time. \begin{example} In Fig.~\ref{fig: ex1}, jobs $J_1$ and $J_2$ are released at time 1, each with processing times of 2. All other jobs $J_i$ are released at time $i$ and have unit processing times. Assume that under SRPT, $J_1$ is executed first. Consequently, $J_2$ experiences starvation, as it must wait until all other jobs are completed. Under FCFS, however, the flow time for each job is only $O(1)$. \end{example} \begin{example} Consider Fig.~\ref{fig: ex2}. Compared to Fig.~\ref{fig: ex1}, the processing times of $J_1$ and $J_2$ in Fig.~\ref{fig: ex2} are increased to $n$. Under FCFS, the flow time for each job is $\Theta(n)$, resulting in an average flow time of $\Theta(n)$. Under SRPT, however, the average flow time is only $O(1)$. \end{example} The conventional method to balance the $\ell_1$ norm and the $\ell_{\infty}$ norm of flow time is to minimize the $\ell_2$ norm of flow time~\cite{doi:10.1137/090772228,10.1145/2755573.2755581}. Specifically, the $\ell_2$ norm of flow time under schedule $\mathcal{S}$ is \[ \sqrt{f_1(\mathcal{S})^2 + f_2(\mathcal{S})^2 + \cdots + f_n(\mathcal{S})^2}, \] where $n$ is the number of jobs. In this paper, we aim to minimize the $\ell_2$ norm of flow time online on a single machine. For the online problem of minimizing the $\ell_2$ norm of flow time, only standard algorithms, including SRPT, Shortest Job First (SJF), Shortest Elapsed Time First (SETF), and Round Robin (RR), have been analyzed, assuming the machine is provided with extra speed~\cite{doi:10.1137/090772228,10.1145/2755573.2755581}. However, SRPT, SJF, and SETF can cause job starvation, while FCFS and RR may degrade the average flow time. These limitations exacerbate the $\ell_2$ norm of flow time (see Appendix~\ref{sec: cr}). For example, the scenarios depicted in Figs.~\ref{fig: ex1} and \ref{fig: ex2} illustrate that FCFS and SRPT are $\Omega(n^{1/2})$-competitive for minimizing the $\ell_2$ norm of flow time. In this paper, we employ FCFS to alleviate the starvation induced by SRPT. Our algorithm initially follows SRPT. If a job has been in the system for an extended period and its remaining processing time is sufficiently small, the job becomes a starving job. Specifically, a job $J_i$ becomes starving at time $t$ if \[ \frac{t-r_i}{\text{remaining processing time of } J_i} \geq \theta, \] where $\theta$ is termed the \textit{starvation threshold}. Whenever some jobs are starving, the algorithm processes the job that becomes starving first. We denote the algorithm as $BAL(\theta)$ when the starvation threshold is set to $\theta$. For instance, $BAL(0)$ is equivalent to FCFS, and $BAL(\infty)$ is equivalent to SRPT. \subsection{Our Result} Our analysis of $BAL(\theta)$'s competitive ratio indicates that $\theta = n^{\frac{2}{3}}$ is the optimal starvation threshold. Among all the previously mentioned standard scheduling algorithms, SRPT and FCFS achieve the best-known competitive ratio of $O(n^{\frac{1}{2}})$ for minimizing the $\ell_2$ norm of flow time (see Appendix~\ref{sec: cr}). We demonstrate that $BAL(n^{\frac{2}{3}})$, a hybrid of SRPT and FCFS, achieves a considerably better competitive ratio of $O(n^{\frac{1}{3}})$. In practice, we can only estimate $n$. For instance, job scheduling is typically crucial during peak hours, and the job arrival process is generally modeled as a Poisson process. Therefore, the product of the job arrival rate and the duration of peak hours would serve as a good estimate of $n$. Nonetheless, in this study, we do not make any assumptions about the job arrival process or the estimation method. Instead, we assume that an estimate $\tilde{n}$ of $n$ with bounded error is provided. The following theorem presents the competitive ratio of $BAL(\tilde{n}^{\frac{2}{3}})$. Specifically, if $\tilde{n} = \Theta(n)$, then $BAL(\tilde{n}^{\frac{2}{3}})$ is $O(n^{\frac{1}{3}})$-competitive. \begin{restatable}{theorem}{beat} Let $\tilde{n}$ be an estimate of $n$ such that $\beta n \leq \tilde{n} \leq \alpha n$ for some $\frac{1}{n} \leq \beta \leq 1$ and $\alpha \geq 1$. Then the competitive ratio of $BAL(\tilde{n}^{\frac{2}{3}})$ for minimizing the $\ell_2$ norm of flow time is $O\left(\tilde{n}^{\frac{1}{3}} + n^{\frac{1}{2}}/\tilde{n}^{\frac{1}{6}}\right) = O\left( n^{\frac{1}{3}} \left( \alpha^{\frac{1}{3}} + \beta^{\frac{-1}{6}} \right) \right)$. \end{restatable} Observe that if the predicted number of jobs $\tilde{n}$ overestimates the actual number $n$, $BAL(\tilde{n}^{\frac{2}{3}})$ achieves an $O(\tilde{n}^{\frac{1}{3}})$-competitive ratio, which corresponds to the usual competitive ratio of the algorithm, but expressed in terms of the predicted number of jobs rather than the actual count. Conversely, if the prediction underestimates the true count, the competitive ratio is $O(n^{\frac{1}{2}}/\tilde{n}^{\frac{1}{6}})$, which is no worse than that of standard algorithms without prediction. \subsection{Related Work} In their foundational work, Bansal and Pruhs introduced the online problem of minimizing the $\ell_p$ norm of flow time~\cite{doi:10.1137/090772228}. They demonstrated that SRPT and SJF are $(1+\epsilon)$-speed $O(\frac{1}{\epsilon})$-competitive and that SETF is $(1+\epsilon)$-speed $O(\frac{1}{\epsilon^{2+2/p}})$-competitive. The results have been extended to all symmetric norms of flow time~\cite{golovin_et_al:LIPIcs:2008:1753} and identical machines~\cite{10.1145/1007352.1007411,10.5555/2133036.2133046}. Moreover, Im et al. showed that RR is $O(1)$-speed $O(1)$-competitive for the $\ell_2$ norm of flow time~\cite{10.1145/2755573.2755581}. In~\cite{angelopoulos2019primal,doi:10.1137/120902288}, more general objective functions were considered. Specifically, for a job $J_i$ with flow time $f_i$, a cost $g_i(f_i)$ is incurred. The only restriction on $g_i$ is that $g_i$ must be non-decreasing. For this general cost minimization problem, there are $O(1)$-speed $O(1)$-competitive online algorithms~\cite{angelopoulos2019primal,doi:10.1137/120902288}. For the offline setting, Bansal and Pruhs initially proposed an $O((\log \log P)^{1/p})$-approximation algorithm using linear programming rounding, where $P$ is the ratio of the maximum to minimum job size~\cite{doi:10.1137/130911317}. text: Simultaneous Localization and Mapping (SLAM) has been a prominent research topic in robotics and computer vision for several decades~\cite{cadena2016past,thrun2007simultaneous}. It involves estimating a robot's current position using onboard sensory data, \emph{e.g.}, LiDAR (Light Detection and Ranging) sensors, cameras, and inertial measurement units (IMU). SLAM is particularly advantageous in environments with weak GPS signals, such as indoor, urban, and underwater settings. Consequently, it has become a crucial component in AR/VR~\cite{grasa2013visual}, autonomous driving~\cite{bresson2017simultaneous}, and robotics applications where GPS is unavailable~\cite{weiss2011monocular}. Among existing systems, visual SLAM \cite{fuentes2015visual} is notably significant because cameras are low-cost passive sensors, consuming less energy than active sensors like sonar or LiDAR. Autonomous mobile robots operating outdoors greatly benefit from the low power consumption of cameras during extended deployments. Visual SLAM systems are classified into \emph{feature-based} methods and \emph{direct} methods. Feature-based methods~\cite{klein2007parallel, mur2015orb} detect and match features across frames, estimating relative camera motion by minimizing reprojection error; whereas direct methods~\cite{engel2014lsd, engel2017direct} estimate camera motion by directly minimizing photometric error without relying on feature correspondences. Direct methods exhibit higher accuracy and robustness compared to feature-based methods, particularly in environments with poor texture (less-textured or repetitively-textured) \cite{forster2016svo}. Since feature detection and matching algorithms are computationally intensive, sparse direct methods have the potential to operate much faster (\emph{e.g.}, $\geq300$ FPS for SVO \cite{forster2016svo}). Additionally, visual SLAM systems can be divided into monocular and multi-camera systems. Monocular systems~\cite{klein2007parallel,engel2014lsd,mur2015orb,engel2017direct} cannot determine the metric \textit{scale} of the environment, unlike multi-camera systems. Multi-camera systems generally achieve higher accuracy and robustness; stereo systems~\cite{mur2017orb,engel2015large,wang2017stereo} are particularly favored for their simplicity and accessibility. Most existing stereo visual systems employ the standard \textit{stereo matching} algorithm~\cite{hartley2003multiple} to address the scale issue, which has two primary drawbacks. First, finding stereo correspondences by individually searching along the respective epipolar lines is computationally demanding. Secondly, selecting the correct point is challenging when multiple points resemble the query point, especially in repetitive textures (\emph{e.g.}, grass, sand). We address these two limitations in~\cite{mo2019extending}, where 3D points in the monocular system are projected into the second camera, and the scale issue is resolved by minimizing photometric error. We demonstrate that such direct \textit{scale optimization} is computationally efficient and more robust to repetitive textures in the visual scene. However, even with metric scale, the global camera pose inevitably deviates from the ground truth as the camera moves, due to the incremental accumulation of relative camera motions. The \textit{loop closure} introduces non-local pose constraints to optimize poses globally and address this issue. The conventional bag-of-word (BoW) approach detects loop closures by matching features from the current view to the history. However, the BoW approach is not directly applicable to direct SLAM systems since direct SLAM systems do not extract descriptors for features. Alternatively, we propose a \emph{LiDAR descriptor-based} place recognition method~\cite{mo2020fast} for urban driving scenarios. We assume the vehicle moves in the forward direction, allowing us to accumulate 3D points from the stereo direct SLAM system to simulate LiDAR scans, which are described by a LiDAR descriptor for place recognition. This significantly enhances loop closure detection efficiency and ensures higher accuracy and robustness. In this paper, we systematically integrate scale optimization and the LiDAR descriptor-based place recognition approach into a fully-direct stereo SLAM system called DSV-SLAM; we provide an open-source implementation at {{\tt \url{https://github.com/IRVLab/direct_stereo_slam}}}. We conduct comprehensive experiments to validate its state-of-the-art accuracy, superior computational efficiency, and robustness in visually challenging scenarios. DSV-SLAM demonstrates the feasibility of a complete SLAM system without feature detection or matching. In DSV-SLAM, we utilize the state-of-the-art Direct Sparse Odometry (DSO)~\cite{engel2017direct} to track camera poses and estimate 3D points. We then extend this to an efficient and accurate stereo visual odometry (VO) using scale optimization~\cite{mo2019extending}. Subsequently, we employ the LiDAR descriptor-based place recognition approach~\cite{mo2020fast} to efficiently detect loop closures. The relative poses of potential loop closures are estimated by direct alignment and optionally refined using the Iterative Closest Point (ICP) method~\cite{besl1992method}. Finally, we construct and optimize a pose graph to further enhance the global accuracy of SLAM. Figure~\ref{fig:kitti00} illustrates the estimated trajectory and reconstructed environment by DSV-SLAM on sequence $00$ of the KITTI dataset~\cite{geiger2012we}.

text: With the exponential advancement of Artificial Intelligence (AI) technologies, the application of AI methods in structural engineering has notably increased in recent years, similar to many other fields. Numerous studies have utilized Machine Learning (ML) models to predict structural responses, fragility parameters, or performance limit states of steel and concrete moment frames, steel braced frames, and reinforced concrete walls \cite{ML1, ML2}. Other research has employed ML models to estimate structural model parameters (e.g., shear strength, drift capacity) from experimental data \cite{ML4, ML5}. In the realm of image-based structural health monitoring, a substantial number of ML-based computer vision studies have been conducted to automatically detect damage from images \cite{ML7, ML8}. Additional studies have concentrated on AI-based damage detection, localization, and classification using sensors installed on structures \cite{ML10, ML11}. Natural hazards, including earthquakes, tsunamis, and hurricanes, have the potential to cause fatalities, injuries, and damage to buildings and other infrastructure. Post-hazard reconnaissance is therefore crucial for improving the understanding of built environment performance, expediting recovery, and making informed decisions regarding current and future hazards. Although ML-based methods have been applied in natural hazards reconnaissance, relatively few studies have investigated techniques from natural language processing (NLP). NLP techniques could significantly enhance the efficiency and accuracy of post-hazard reconnaissance evaluation. In one of the few NLP-related studies, \citet{ML13} trained a long short-term memory (LSTM) model to classify building damage using text-based natural language damage descriptions according to the green, yellow, and red tagging categories of ATC-20. Social media data, such as tweets, have been utilized in a few studies to train ML algorithms for identifying direct eyewitness messages during disasters \cite{twitter1} and to discern themes in social media behavior during hazards \cite{twitter2}. This paper explores two applications of NLP in the context of earthquake reconnaissance. The first is the automatic generation of reconnaissance reports, which are a crucial component of each field reconnaissance. Automatic report generation aims to reduce the time required to produce a report and to enhance the accuracy and richness of information by facilitating access to numerous identified resources that might otherwise be overlooked. The second application involves using social media and crowd-sourcing to extract information related to earthquake consequences and resilience, such as recovery time, which is challenging to obtain through other methods. Given that this represents a novel and unexplored application area of AI, the preliminary study conducted here is anticipated to initiate advancements in this domain. The subsequent sections of the paper are organized as follows: The automatic data collection approach used for both applications is detailed in Section \ref{sec:data}. The methodology and applications of automatic report generation and recovery time estimation are described in Sections \ref{sec:briefing} and \ref{sec:social-media}. Finally, concluding remarks and future directions are presented in the last section.

text: A primary challenge in machine learning is developing models that are dependable and secure in real-world applications. Beyond excelling on the training distribution, deployed models should be robust to distributional shifts, consistent in their predictions, resistant to adversarial attacks, calibrated in their uncertainty estimations, and capable of detecting anomalous inputs. Numerous previous studies have addressed each of these issues individually \cite{madry, hendrycks2019robustness, guo2017calibration, emmott2015meta}, yet they can also be collectively considered as various facets of ML Safety \cite{hendrycks2021unsolved}. Consequently, the aforementioned properties can be regarded as safety measures. Ideally, models deployed in practical environments would perform effectively across multiple safety measures. Unfortunately, prior research has demonstrated that optimizing for certain desirable properties often compromises others. For instance, adversarial training enhances adversarial robustness but diminishes classification performance \cite{tsipras2018robustness}. Similarly, ensuring consistent predictions on out-of-distribution (OOD) inputs appears to conflict with the improved detection of these inputs, an insight supported by recent research \cite{empiricalpaper} which shows that existing methods assist with some safety metrics but hinder others. This prompts the question of whether it is feasible to enhance all safety measures with a single model. While previous augmentation methods generate images that are distinct (e.g., translations) or more entropic (e.g., additive Gaussian noise), we propose that an important yet underexplored dimension is creating images that are more complex. Unlike entropy or descriptive difficulty, which is maximized by purely noisy distributions, structural complexity is often characterized by the level of organization \cite{lloyd2001measures}. A classic example of structurally complex objects is fractals, which have recently been shown to be beneficial for pretraining image classifiers \cite{kataoka2020pre, Nakashima2021CanVT}. Thus, an intriguing question is whether sources of structural complexity can be utilized to enhance safety through data augmentation techniques. We demonstrate that Pareto improvements are achievable with \textsc{PixMix}, a straightforward and effective data processing method that utilizes images with complex structures and significantly enhances all existing safety measures. \textsc{PixMix} involves a novel data processing pipeline that incorporates structurally complex "dreamlike" images. These dreamlike images include fractals and feature visualizations. We find that feature visualizations are an appropriate source of complexity, thus showing that they have applications beyond interpretability. In extensive experiments, we observe that \textsc{PixMix} delivers significant improvements across a wide array of existing safety measures, surpassing many previous methods. text: Due to the significant success of deep convolutional networks~\cite{he2016deep, chen2017deeplab, long2015fully}, object recognition tasks, such as object detection and instance segmentation, have made remarkable advancements over the past decade. Predominant methods adhere to the "backbone with head" framework~\cite{he2017mask, chen2019hybrid, lin2017focal, tian2019fcos}. The backbone network~\cite{he2016deep}, pretrained on ImageNet, extracts features from input images. Subsequently, these extracted features are input into the head network to produce predictions for various recognition tasks, \textit{i.e.}, classification, box regression, and mask segmentation. Most image/video instance segmentation~\cite{he2017mask, huang2019mask, yang2019video, cao2020sipmask} and object detection methods~\cite{lin2017focal, tian2019fcos} exhibit a similar design for the head network. Specifically, four consecutive $3\times3$ convolutions are typically stacked in the head network to refine coarse instance features (see Fig.~\ref{fig1}(a)) prior to the final prediction. Indeed, such an explicit refinement design enlarges the receptive field and enhances the semantic level. However, merely stacking weight-independent convolutions has certain limitations. The receptive field achieved remains restricted under the explicit setting since it has been demonstrated that the effective receptive field is generally much smaller than the theoretical receptive field. Additionally, this method tends to lose the original instance signal, resulting in degraded performance and a substantial parameter burden as the number of convolutions increases. A question may arise: is it feasible to substitute these stacked $3\times3$ convolutions with a lightweight module while maintaining promising performance? A straightforward solution is to make these four convolutions weight-sharing (see Fig.~\ref{fig1}(b)). To illustrate this, we first provide an empirical comparison with the weight-sharing strategy. We observe that the commonly used four weight-independent $3\times3$ convolutions are not essential in the head network. Conversely, the weight-sharing design can achieve competitive performance with fewer parameters. To prevent performance degradation in the weight-sharing network, a shortcut connection in ResNet~\cite{he2016deep} can be introduced (see Fig.~\ref{fig1}(c)). The shortcut path facilitates smooth gradient propagation and prevents the network from forgetting original instance features. While enhancing overall segmentation performance, the weight-sharing strategy remains constrained by a limited receptive field. Therefore, we investigate a new perspective: \textit{What if instance features are refined through a recursive network stacked with infinite blocks?} An intuitive idea is to stack the weight-sharing blocks infinitely. In this manner, we observe that the output of the refinement network will eventually converge to an equilibrium state as the number of blocks increases, which can be expressed as: \begin{eqnarray} H^{\ast}=F_{\theta}(H^{\ast};X), \end{eqnarray} where $F_{\theta}$ denotes the nonlinear transformation with parameters $\theta$. $H^{\ast}$ and $X$ represent the equilibrium instance feature and original coarse instance feature, respectively. Inspired by DEQ~\cite{bai2019deep, bai2020multiscale}, we introduce implicit feature refinement (IFR) to enhance feature representation via a simulated infinite-depth network, where the transformation $F_{\theta}$ is utilized to construct the implicit model. Based on Eq.~\ref{eq1}, we can address the instance feature refinement as a fixed-point iteration problem. For the explicit design of transformation $F_{\theta}$, we simply employ a single residual block with double residual connections to minimize the overall parameters of the mask head (see Fig.~\ref{fig1}(d)). For the forward computation, several black-box Root-Find solvers (\textit{e.g.}, Broyden method~\cite{bai2020multiscale}) can be used to solve the root $H^{\ast}$ of the equilibrium equation presented in Eq.~\ref{eq1}. For back-propagation, gradients are computed based on the equilibrium feature resolved. Unlike explicitly stacked convolutions, IFR offers several advantages: 1) It simulates an infinite-depth feature refinement network using only the parameters of a single residual block; 2) It generates equilibrium instance features with a large receptive field, which is advantageous for instance segmentation. It should be noted that IFR can be readily extended to the head network of most image/video instance segmentation frameworks, including both two-stage and one-stage approaches. Extensive experiments on the COCO benchmark~\cite{lin2014microsoft} demonstrate that our proposed IFR benefits most image instance segmentation frameworks. For instance, it enhances the segmentation AP by 1.0\% on Mask R-CNN~\cite{he2017mask} with a ResNet-50-FPN backbone. Furthermore, it is also robust and adaptable for video instance segmentation on the YouTube-VIS~\cite{yang2019video} benchmark, achieving notable improvements on state-of-the-art frameworks. Additionally, it can be applied to several one-stage object detectors with minor modifications. Our main contributions are summarized as: \begin{itemize} \item Empirical experiments are conducted to analyze the impact of multiple stacked convolutions on refining instance features. \item Implicit feature refinement (IFR), which requires only the parameters of a residual block, is proposed to produce high-level equilibrium instance features with a global receptive field through fixed-point iteration. \item A double residual network is further introduced to prevent performance degradation and ensure smooth gradient propagation. \item The proposed IFR is a general plug-and-play module that can be easily extended to most instance segmentation frameworks and serves as a strong alternative to explicitly stacked convolutions in the head network. \end{itemize}

text: The current advancements in machine learning have reached remarkable accuracy in numerous computer vision tasks by training models exclusively on images. Building on these achievements and enhancing 3D object comprehension holds significant potential to drive a broader spectrum of applications, including augmented reality, robotics, autonomy, and image retrieval. However, understanding objects in 3D remains a formidable challenge due to the scarcity of extensive real-world datasets compared to 2D tasks (e.g., ImageNet~\cite{Deng:2009jn}, COCO~\cite{Lin:2014vm}, and Open Images~\cite{Kuznetsova:2020ff}). To facilitate ongoing progress in 3D object understanding within the research community, it is crucial to release object-centric video datasets that capture more of an object's 3D structure while aligning with the data format used for many downstream vision tasks (i.e., video or camera streams), thereby supporting the training and evaluation of machine learning models. The object-centric perspective aligns with the way our brains perceive new objects. For instance, when a child learns the shape of a chair, they will move around and observe the chair from various angles to gather information. In other words, "We must also move in order to perceive"~\cite{Gibson:1979}\cite{Zamir:2018}. We introduce the Objectron dataset, which is a collection of short, object-centric video clips capturing a broad set of common objects from multiple angles. Each video clip is supplemented by augmented reality (AR) session metadata, including camera poses, sparse point-clouds, and surface planes. The dataset also includes manually annotated 3D bounding boxes for each object, detailing the object's position, orientation, and dimensions. The dataset comprises $14,819$ annotated video clips and $4M$ annotated images collected from a geographically diverse sample (covering ten countries across five continents). Figure~\ref{fig:example-seq} illustrates an example video from our dataset. The Objectron dataset offers several advantages over existing works: \begin{itemize} \item Videos provide multiple views of the same object, enabling numerous applications beyond 3D object detection, such as multi-view geometric understanding, view synthesis, and 3D shape reconstruction. \item The 3D bounding box remains present throughout the entire video and is temporally consistent, facilitating 3D tracking applications. \item Our dataset is collected in natural settings to enhance generalization for real-world scenarios, unlike datasets gathered in controlled environments ~\cite{Hinterstoisser:2012ik}\cite{Calli:2017cd}. \item Each instance's translation and size are recorded in metric scale, thanks to precise on-device AR tracking, and provide sparse point clouds in 3D, enabling sparse depth estimation techniques. The images are calibrated, and the camera parameters are provided, allowing for the recovery of the object's true scale. \item Our annotations are dense and continuous, unlike some previous works~\cite{Savarese:2007by} where viewpoints have been discretized into bins. \item Each object category includes hundreds of instances, collected from various locations across different countries in diverse lighting conditions. \end{itemize} We have performed experiments for 3D object detection tasks using our dataset. We proposed a novel method to compute the precise 3D IoU of oriented 3D bounding boxes. These experiments can serve as baselines for future research.

text: Since its invention in 1972, \gls{ct} has rapidly become an indispensable non-destructive technique for industrial inspection~\cite{de2014industrial}, medical diagnosis~\cite{maier2018medical}, and material sciences~\cite{withers2007x}. \gls{ct} exemplifies computational imaging, where a physical quantity is encoded in the measured data via an image formation model and subsequently reconstructed by inverting this forward model. In X-ray \gls{ct}, an image of the attenuation coefficient is reconstructed from projections obtained through a circular acquisition. Under orthographic projection, this model is represented by the Radon transform. Discretized measurements of the Radon transform are referred to as sinograms, and their inversion is well-explored. The most notable method is a direct inversion with a closed-form solution known as \gls{fbp}~\cite{maier2018medical}. For accurate reconstruction using \gls{fbp}, adequate angular sampling is necessary, as defined by the Crowther criterion~\cite{crowther1970reconstruction}, which is derived from the Shannon-Nyquist sampling theorem. If this criterion is not met, aliasing artifacts manifest as streak artifacts, significantly diminishing diagnostic quality. This scenario is termed \gls{svct} and occurs in numerous practical applications, such as motion compensation~\cite{enjilela2019cubic} or dose reduction~\cite{gao2014low,yu2009radiation}. Various methods have been proposed to address the ill-posedness of \gls{svct} by integrating prior knowledge into the reconstruction algorithm. Traditionally, \gls{ir} is employed to optimize a data-fidelity term combined with suitable priors~\cite{kudo2013image,zhu2013improved,vandeghinste2011split}. For instance, the widely used \gls{tv} prior assumes piece-wise constant objects for \gls{ct}~\cite{sidky2008image}. Recently, learning-based reconstruction algorithms have gained significant attention~\cite{adler2017solving}. Notable examples include \gls{cnn}-based models designed to eliminate artifacts in the reconstruction domain~\cite{kofler2018u} or unrolled networks that emulate the data-fidelity driven \gls{ir}~\cite{ongie2020deep}. A less conventional approach is to treat \gls{svct} as a super-resolution or inpainting problem, where the missing information is interpolated between the sparse projections. A sparse-view sinogram can be either inpainted or 1D-super-resolved. In either case, 1D-upsampling of a sinogram is more constrained than its 2D counterpart~\cite{katsaggelos2007super} of natural images, as the sinogram data vary smoothly along the angular dimension~\cite{helgason}. Other typical tomographic challenges with similar formulations include metal artifact removal and limited angle tomography, as illustrated in Fig.~\ref{fig:superres_vs_inpainting}. Sinogram inpainting has not received much attention compared to iterative methods. This is because capturing the complex representations of sinograms proves to be an extremely challenging task~\cite{li2012strategy,tovey2019directional,kostler2006adaptive}. However, the rapid advancement of deep learning now allows us to efficiently capture low-dimensional representations of data across various image domains. These technological developments encourage us to explore the potential of addressing \gls{svct} with learning-based super-resolution. Specifically, we contend and will demonstrate that image processing in the measurement domain is preferable to post-reconstruction processing. This is because sinogram-based methods prevent the formation of streak artifacts, which are challenging to remove using local processing techniques (e.g., CNNs) due to their widespread distribution over the image domain. In this study, we propose a two-step architecture that learns super-resolution in the sinogram domain and subsequently eliminates the remaining artifacts in the image domain. The core concept is depicted in Fig.~\ref{fig:abstract}. The following summarizes our principal contributions: \begin{itemize} \item A novel two-step reconstruction approach in both the measurement and image domains, ensuring maximum detail preservation compared to single-step networks. \item A new domain-specific, lightweight perceptual loss that surpasses the VGG-based perceptual loss~\cite{johnson2016perceptual} in terms of accuracy, memory, and time efficiency. \item Loss functions and submodules specifically designed for sinogram-domain tasks, along with an extensive ablation study analyzing the effectiveness of each proposed module. \item Demonstration of accurate reconstructions for high compression ratios, achieving a substantial performance gain (over $4$ dB PSNR) compared to state-of-the-art algorithms. \end{itemize}

The most notable method is the direct inversion with a closed-form solution known as the gls,fbp,cite,medical method. For an accurate reconstruction with the Gls-fbp technique, adequate angular sampling is required, as defined by the Crowther criterion, derived from the Shannon-Nyquist sampling theorem. If this criterion is not met, aliasing artifacts occur, which cause streak artifacts and significantly degrade diagnostic quality. This situation is referred to as the Gls-svct and occurs in many practical applications, such as motion compensation (see Enjilela, 2019, and Gao, 2014, low-dose (see Gao, 2014) or dose reduction (see Gao, 2014, low-dose). A variety of methods have been proposed to overcome the ill-posedness of the problem of GLST by integrating prior knowledge into the reconstruction process. For example, the widely used GLSTv prior, which assumes that the objects are piece-wise constant, was introduced in Sidky 2008. Recently, learning-based reconstruction approaches have attracted considerable attention. For instance, some models have been designed to remove artifacts from the reconstruction domain by introducing the concept of artifacts, and some have been developed to emulate the data-driven glsir, glssvct, glssvct, glssvct, glssvct, glssvct, cite, citeongie2020deep, glssvct, or a hybrid model of glsir, glsir, glsir, gls, or gls,glsgls,citekofler2018u. Other typical tomographic problems with similar formulations are metal artifact removal and restricted-angle tomography, as illustrated in Fig. 1. Either sparse-view sinograms can be inpainted or 1D superresolved. Either way, 1D upsampling of a sinogram is more constrained than the 2D superresolution of natural images, as the sinogram data vary smoothly along the angular dimension. Compared to iterative methods, in-painting has not received much attention. This is because capturing the complex representations of the sinograms proves to be an extremely difficult task [Li, 2012: strategy, Tovey, 2019: directional, Kostler, 2006: adaptive]. However, deep learning methods allow us to efficiently capture low-dimensional representations of data in various image domains. We maintain and will demonstrate that image processing in the acquisition domain is preferable to post-reconstruction processing. This is because sinogram-based methods prevent streak artifacts, which are difficult to remove using local processing methods (e.g., convolutional neural networks) because of their widespread distribution in the image domain. These technological developments encourage us to explore the potential for addressing the issue of glssvtir with learning-based super-resolution. At the beginning: A novel two-step architecture, learning super-resolution in the sinogram domain and subsequently removing artifacts in the image domain. The central idea is depicted in Fig. 1 [10]. - Item. A new domain-adapted, light-weight perceptual loss which surpasses the VGG-based perceptual loss in accuracy, memory and time efficiency. - Item. Loss functions and submodules specifically designed for the sinogram domain, together with an extensive ablation study which analyzes the effectiveness of each proposed module. - Item. Accurate reconstruction at high compression ratios, resulting in a performance gain of more than 12 dB of PSNR compared to state-of-the-art. Itemized End

text: Swarm intelligence has illuminated the collective behavior of autonomous entities governed by simple rules, such as ants, boids, and particles. This concept has been applied to groups of robots, and swarm robotics has garnered significant attention over the past two decades. Each autonomous component of the system is referred to as a robot, module, agent, process, or sensor, and various swarm robot systems have been explored, including the \emph{autonomous mobile robot system}~\cite{SY99}, the \emph{population protocol model}~\cite{AADFP04}, \emph{programmable particles}~\cite{DDGRSS14}, \emph{Kilobot}~\cite{RCN14}, and \emph{3D Catoms}~\cite{TPB19}. Dumitrescu et al. examined the \emph{metamorphic robotic system} (MRS), which consists of a collection of \emph{modules} on an infinite 2D square grid~\cite{DSY04a,DSY04b}. The modules are \emph{anonymous}, meaning they are indistinguishable from one another. They are also \emph{autonomous} and \emph{uniform}, implying that each module independently determines its movement using a shared algorithm. They are \emph{oblivious}, indicating that each module lacks memory of past actions. Consequently, each module determines its behavior by observing other modules in adjacent cells. Each module can execute a \emph{sliding} move to a side-adjacent cell and a \emph{rotation} by $90$ degrees around a cell. The modules must maintain \emph{connectivity}, defined by the side-adjacency of cells occupied by modules. The authors considered \emph{reconfiguration} of the MRS, which requires the MRS to transform from an initial shape to a specified final shape~\cite{DSY04a}. They demonstrated that any horizontally convex connected initial shape of an MRS can be converted to any convex final shape through a straight chain shape. Subsequently, Dumitrescu and Pach proved that any connected initial shape can be transformed into any connected final shape via a straight chain shape~\cite{DP06}. In essence, the MRS possesses the capability of "universal reconfiguration." Reconfiguration can induce dynamic behavior in the MRS. Dumitrescu et al. showed that the MRS can advance by repeatedly undergoing reconfiguration~\cite{DSY04b}. They presented a reconfiguration that achieves the fastest \emph{locomotion}. Doi et al. noted that the oblivious modules can utilize the MRS's shape as global memory, enabling the MRS to solve more complex problems as the number of modules increases. They explored \emph{search} in a finite 2D square grid, which requires the MRS to locate a target cell within a finite rectangular \emph{field}~\cite{DYKY18}. Each module lacks knowledge of the target cell's position or the initial configuration of the MRS. They demonstrated that the MRS can locate the target cell by sweeping each row of the field without prior knowledge. Specifically, if the modules agree on the cardinal directions (i.e., north, south, east, and west), three modules are both necessary and sufficient; otherwise, five modules are necessary and sufficient. Nakamura et al. examined \emph{evacuation} of the MRS from a finite rectangular field in the 2D square grid~\cite{NSY20}. There is a hole (i.e., two side-adjacent cells) on the field's wall, and the MRS must exit through it from any arbitrary initial position and shape. They showed that two modules are necessary and sufficient when the modules agree on the cardinal directions; otherwise, four modules are necessary and sufficient. In this paper, we examine the impact of common knowledge on search by the MRS in the 3D cubic grid. We consider the following three scenarios: $(i)$ modules equipped with a common \emph{compass} (i.e., they agree on the direction and orientation of $x$, $y$, and $z$ axes), $(ii)$ modules equipped with a common vertical axis (i.e., they agree on the direction and orientation of the $z$ axis), and $(iii)$ modules not equipped with a common compass (i.e., they have no agreement on directions and orientations). We demonstrate that three modules are necessary and sufficient when the modules have a common compass, and five modules are necessary and sufficient when the modules lack a common compass. The numbers of sufficient modules in the 3D cubic grid are identical to those in the 2D square grid~\cite{DYKY18} because the MRS has more states in the 3D cubic grid than in the 2D square grid. For the intermediate case with a common vertical axis, we demonstrate that four modules are necessary and sufficient. Thus, our results in the 3D cubic grid reveal a smooth trade-off between the computational power of the MRS and the common knowledge among modules, which previous results in the 2D square grid could not identify. We present search algorithms for these three settings and demonstrate the necessity by analyzing the state transition graph of the MRS. \noindent{\bf Related work.}~Reconfiguration of swarm robot systems has been discussed for the MRS~\cite{DP06,DSY04a}, autonomous mobile robots~\cite{FYOKY15,SY99}, and programmable particles~\cite{DGRSS15,DFSVY20}. Michail et al. considered the \emph{programmable matter system}, which is similar to the MRS, and investigated reconfiguration using only rotations and using both rotations and slidings~\cite{MSS19}. They demonstrated that the combination of rotations and slidings ensures universal reconfiguration, whereas rotations alone do not. They also presented an $\mathrm{O}(n^2)$-time reconfiguration algorithm using rotations and slidings. Almethen et al. considered reconfiguration by \emph{line-pushing}, where each module is equipped with the ability to push a line of modules~\cite{AMP20a}. They presented an $\mathrm{O}(n \log n)$-time universal reconfiguration algorithm that does not guarantee connectivity of intermediate shapes and an $\mathrm{O}(n \sqrt{n})$-time reconfiguration algorithm that transforms a diagonal line into a straight chain while preserving connectivity. The same authors later demonstrated that their programmable matter system possesses the capability of universal reconfiguration and an $\mathrm{O}(n \sqrt{n})$-time reconfiguration algorithm along with an $\Omega(n \log n)$ lower bound~\cite{AMP20b}.

text: A self-modifying code is a computer program that alters its instructions during execution while maintaining overall functionality. These alterations may be local (affecting a small section of code) or global (impacting the entire code), persistent (modifying the copy on disk) or non-persistent (temporary patching). The modification can occur at compile-time, link-time, during post-processing, or at runtime. The code responsible for the modification may be a separate process or integrated into the target code itself. Certain self-modifying codes can be categorized into specific cases as follows: \begin{enumerate} \item \textbf{Packers}: These are the most basic type. These codes contain the actual payload in a compressed and/or encrypted form. The executable blob is extracted from it and executed entirely in memory. \item \textbf{Obfuscators}: These tools take an executable file as input and generate another file as output. The output binary contains a different set of instructions while preserving overall behavior. The output binary does not include any additional functionality. \item \textbf{Self-injecting codes}: These programs insert extra code into their own process (or a forked child process) and execute it there. The injected code can run within the main thread (effectively terminating the old code without releasing associated memory and metadata) or in a newly created thread. \item \textbf{Self-debugging codes}: These programs attach themselves as a debugger or to a child copy of the same process. The debugger process can then control the debuggee process, including overwriting the executable code. An advantageous side effect is that dynamically debugging these programs becomes very challenging. \item \textbf{Self-healing codes}: These programs can detect patching (either in a file or in memory) and can restore the original state by reversing the patch. \end{enumerate} We will explore self-debugging code in detail and introduce another technique that enables our malware to operate in both forward execution mode (as all programs do) and reverse execution mode (where instructions are executed in reverse order). The malware exhibits different behavior in each direction. The malicious code is active only when execution occurs in the reverse direction, allowing it to evade various analysis attempts: \begin{enumerate} \item Tools like IDA Pro analyze the reverse-engineered assembly using a top-down approach. Since our code exhibits malicious behavior during bottom-up execution, the behavior is not immediately evident. \item Tools such as debuggers or sandboxes typically attach to processes using the same mechanisms employed in self-debugging. As a beneficial side effect, if such a tool is attached to our code, the self-debugging component fails to execute (since the OS permits only one process to act as a debugger for any given process), and the payload executes in a top-down manner, thereby concealing its malicious behavior. \end{enumerate}

text: For a robot to interact intelligently with its environment, it must swiftly and accurately ascertain the relative position and orientation of nearby robots, individuals, vehicles, and various other static and dynamic obstacles within the scene. Tasks that depend on such estimations are numerous, ranging from drone racing~\cite{spica2018realtime} to pedestrian avoidance~\cite{badue2019selfdrivingcarsurvey}, and are crucial for developing truly autonomous robots. Nevertheless, the capability to track the six Degree of Freedom (6DoF) relative pose of a dynamic object in real-time, using onboard sensing and computation, remains largely inaccessible to current robot perception frameworks. To address this gap, we introduce \textbf{M}onocular \textbf{S}equential \textbf{L}ightweight \textbf{R}otation \textbf{A}nd \textbf{P}osition \textbf{T}racking \textbf{O}n-\textbf{R}obots (MSL-RAPTOR), a lightweight, versatile robot perception module designed to track the 6DoF relative pose of a dynamic object using solely an onboard monocular camera. MSL-RAPTOR achieves performance comparable to state-of-the-art methods that rely on additional sensors (e.g., depth) and greater computational power. Current methods for 6DoF relative pose estimation from vision can be categorized into model-based, deep learning-based, and hybrid approaches. Model-based methods depend on matching an object's view to a database of templates or visual features. These approaches are constrained in scenes with low texture or changing conditions and are not applicable when prior 3D models of objects are unavailable \cite{schmidt2014dart,andriluka2010humantracking}. Deep learning techniques, such as PoseCNN~\cite{xiang2017posecnn} and LieNets~\cite{do2018lienets}, address these issues by directly estimating the relative pose from images, learning this inverse mapping from a substantial corpus of training data. Hybrid methods integrate elements of deep neural networks and model-based techniques. For instance, BB8~\cite{rad2017bb8}, SSD-6D~\cite{kehl2017ssd}, and SingleShotPose~\cite{tekin2018ssp} (SSP) utilize deep neural networks to estimate the 2D projections of the 3D bounding box surrounding the object. These projections are subsequently used to solve the Perspective-n-Point (PnP) problem to derive a pose estimate~\cite{lepetit2009epnp}. Another hybrid approach, NOCS~\cite{wang2019normalized}, estimates pose using pixel correspondences and depth data with category-level canonical representations. However, the aforementioned deep and hybrid methods overlook temporal correlations among multiple frames that could assist in object tracking. In contrast, 6-PACK~\cite{wang20196sixpack} exploits temporal consistency by learning to represent objects using keypoints matched between frames. Although these methods demonstrate impressive pose estimation performance, they are either too slow, too computationally intensive, or require excessive prior model knowledge to be practical for onboard relative pose perception in resource-constrained robots. These same constraints apply to numerous pose tracking methods developed for self-driving cars, where tracking methods constitute a crucial component of the system~\cite{badue2019selfdrivingcarsurvey}. These systems depend on the use of advanced sensors and/or computational capabilities to achieve real-time performance and often assume planar constraints since they exclusively deal with land-based objects (e.g., pedestrians, other vehicles), thus functioning only as SE(2) trackers with 3DoF (e.g.~\cite{cho2014multi, buyval2018realtime}). \textbf{Contribution.} Considering the requirements for onboard robotic perception, we propose MSL-RAPTOR, which aims to integrate the best features of deep learning-based and model-based perception paradigms. MSL-RAPTOR processes raw image data using a dual deep neural network architecture at the front-end to generate and track an angled 2D bounding box around an object in the scene. text: Video analytic systems have achieved widespread success across various fields, ranging from computationally intensive tasks like facial recognition for surveillance, to mobile applications such as object detection for mobile-based augmented reality (AR)~\cite{rohan2019convolutional, apicharttrisorn2019frugal, rao2017mobile}, and real-time systems like pedestrian and vehicle localization for autonomous driving~\cite{feng2020deep, arnold2019survey, li2019gs3d}. A fundamental capability shared by these applications is the detection of objects in videos. There is an increasing number of use cases for conducting such video object detection on {\em mobile devices}. These devices are progressively equipped with mobile GPUs, although they are significantly less powerful than those found in server-class machines. Nonetheless, there is a drive to perform video processing in (near) real-time on streaming content directly on the device itself\footnote{For convenience, we will often use the shorthand ``device" to refer to a ``mobile device".}. This is necessary, for instance, to enhance the user's immersive experience ({e.g.,}\xspace in AR/VR games) or to provide high-confidence outputs from streaming videos ({e.g.,}\xspace for pedestrian recognition in autonomous driving). A typical operational target is processing each frame in 33 ms, which corresponds to a video stream rate of 30 frames per second (FPS). We empirically find that state-of-the-art (SOTA) protocols (designed for servers) when executed on mobile platforms significantly exceed this latency threshold. For example, MEGA~\cite{chen2020memory}, regarded as a SOTA solution, requires 253.4 ms per frame on NVIDIA AGX Xavier, when utilizing all computing resources. In response, a range of efficient models and systems has been proposed to enhance their efficiency or performance on mobile devices~\cite{tan2020efficientdet, sandler2018mobilenetv2, jiang2020learning, zhu2018towards, chen2018optimizing, liu2016ssd, redmon2018yolov3, zhang2018single}. \begin{comment} The existing research primarily focuses on accuracy and may need to leverage server-class machines or cloud enterprises~\cite{wu2019sequence, chen2020memory, sabater2020robust, zhu2017flow, deng2019relation}. However, mobile applications typically face limited energy or computational resources while still requiring strict latency guarantees. To enhance the user's immersive experience ({e.g.,}\xspace in AR/VR games) or to provide high-confidence outputs from streaming videos ({e.g.,}\xspace for pedestrian recognition in autonomous driving), such tasks must be performed in near real-time under stringent latency requirements of 33 ms (30 FPS) or lower. Even with advancements in mobile GPU devices, these devices lack the computational power that server-class machines or cloud enterprises provide. In response, efficient models and systems have been proposed to enhance their efficiency or performance on mobile devices~\cite{tan2020efficientdet, sandler2018mobilenetv2}. \end{comment} Another strategy to make streaming analytics feasible on mobile devices is to employ both object detection and tracking, as embodied by the ``\textit{tracking-by-detection}'' technique~\cite{bae2014robust, muller2018trackingnet}. By interspersing multiple frames of tracking (which is less computationally intensive than detection) with each frame where object detection is performed, the overall performance can be accelerated. The tracking-by-detection technique reveals several adaptation strategies. This may involve selecting from a set of detectors and trackers and determining how to manage the trigger frequency between the detector and tracker. Empirically, we observe that the execution time of an object tracker is 10 times lower than that of an object detector. A careful selection of such adaptation strategies is essential to meet the real-time requirements for energy, latency, and accuracy, particularly on mobile devices. The stringent requirements on mobile devices during runtime reveal another challenge for streaming video analytics: \textit{how to adapt (at runtime) to the dynamic user requirements and available resources on the device?} To address this issue, several recent studies have considered multi-branch solutions~\cite{fang2018nestdnn, xu2020approxdet, xu2019approxnet, lee2021benchmarking}. Such solutions incorporate multiple execution kernels in a system and select the optimal one {\em during runtime} to meet the user's latency requirements. However, the omission of features that control energy consumption is a significant limitation of all these approaches. Furthermore, compared to recent studies on efficient convolutional neural network (CNN) architectures, there has been limited research and application of efficient object detection solutions on embedded devices, along with the issue of using outdated feature extractors. In real-world applications, the variability of video content, available resources on mobile devices, and manual control of the requirements make dynamic adaptations even more challenging. The broad range of energy, latency, and accuracy requirements necessitates that the system be adaptable to a variety of scenarios. Thus, the design must fulfill the following prerequisites: (1) designing an execution kernel that is both energy and latency efficient for the mobile device, (2) analyzing the energy consumption and latency performance of all execution branches on mobile devices, and (3) developing an adaptive scheduler to make decisions at runtime to simultaneously satisfy multiple requirements. However, to our knowledge, no previous work has incorporated all of these design innovations. Another aspect that has been overlooked to date is how these algorithms perform when there is resource contention on the device. Such resource contention can occur due to co-located applications running on the same device, a common scenario since these are multi-purpose devices. Hence, for instance, when video detection is in progress, another computationally intensive task such as speech recognition may also be executing on the device. No prior work has evaluated the latest video object detection systems under varying resource contention on leading GPU-enabled mobile devices. In this work, we introduce {\textsc{Virtuoso}}\xspace\footnote{Just as a \name is a person who possesses exceptional skill, expertise, or talent in a particular endeavor, we believe our system demonstrates such skill in configuring streaming video object detection on embedded or mobile devices.\xspace}, which is tailored for mobile devices under varying resource constraints, with additional efficiency knobs\footnote{We use the term ``efficiency knobs'' rather than the more common term ``tuning knobs'' as we are focusing on the performance metric of accuracy, normalized by latency or energy cost to achieve that accuracy, in other words, efficient accuracy.} for energy-aware adaptation. {\textsc{Virtuoso}}\xspace selects the most efficient baseline object detectors EfficientDet~\cite{tan2020efficientdet} and SSD~\cite{liu2016ssd}, enhances them by integrating object trackers, and provides 155 execution branches by exposing 8 efficiency knobs within one system. Furthermore, {\textsc{Virtuoso}}\xspace includes a scheduler that can select the optimal branch during runtime to satisfy the energy and latency requirements while maximizing accuracy. We also evaluated a total of 15 baseline models on 3 different embedded boards under 2 resource contention levels to better understand the energy, latency, and accuracy performance of the latest models for video object detection. We evaluate {\textsc{Virtuoso}}\xspace and the baselines using the ILSVRC 2015 VID datasets on 3 NVIDIA mobile GPUs of increasing compute capacity --- Jetson TX2, Xavier NX, and AGX Xavier, under 2 different power modes of AGX Xavier. On each board and under each power mode, {\textsc{Virtuoso}}\xspace is the best solution that can automatically choose the optimal branch to satisfy the energy and latency requirements and maximize accuracy performance. With the multi-branch execution kernel, {\textsc{Virtuoso}}\xspace can adapt its energy efficiency within a wide range (span of 89X) and also latency in a wide range (span of 128X). Such wide ranges of energy efficiency and latency can satisfy various scenarios at runtime to optimize the functionality of our video object detection system. Given a 1 J per frame energy requirement, {\textsc{Virtuoso}}\xspace can achieve 52.0\% accuracy, and given a 33.3 ms latency budget, {\textsc{Virtuoso}}\xspace can achieve 60.1\% accuracy on an AGX Xavier board. Additionally, when energy and latency do not have stringent limits, {\textsc{Virtuoso}}\xspace can achieve 63.9\% accuracy, which is more than 10\% higher than baseline models. \begin{comment} From the benchmark results, we learned some valuable lessons, including the following: tracking-by-detection is the most efficient way to decrease energy consumption for video object detection; accuracy is mostly determined by the selection of object detector as the tracker will use the detection results from the detector for its initialization; the majority of energy consumption comes from GPU module on mobile devices. \end{comment} In this paper, our contributions are as follows. \vspace{-3pt} \begin{enumerate}[leftmargin=1em] \item We present {\textsc{Virtuoso}}\xspace, the most energy-efficient and adaptive video object detection system for mobile devices. {\textsc{Virtuoso}}\xspace can dynamically adapt its runtime configurations based on the given user requirements. Our runtime scheduler solves the optimization problem for accuracy at any energy and latency level and thus can guarantee the Pareto optimal performance on resource-constrained devices. We are the only adaptive model performing this 3D (energy-latency-accuracy) tuning while handling resource contention. \item {\textsc{Virtuoso}}\xspace designs an efficient multi-branch execution kernel with a total of 8 different efficiency knobs, optimized for both energy efficiency and latency on mobiles. This provides {\textsc{Virtuoso}}\xspace with more flexibility to a wider range of available resources, a span of 89X energy adapting space when baseline models cannot, and 4.5X larger latency adapting space than the baseline FastAdapt~\cite{lee2021benchmarking}. {\textsc{Virtuoso}}\xspace can achieve 97\% lower energy consumption and up to 50 times faster execution time, compared to using the object detection kernel only. \item We evaluate our proposed systems and 15 baselines (including 3 latest video object detection solutions and our enhanced FRCNN~\cite{ren2015faster}, YOLO~\cite{redmon2018yolov3}, SSD~\cite{liu2016ssd}, and EfficientDet~\cite{tan2020efficientdet} for both energy and latency on the embedded devices) on 3 NVIDIA Jetson embedded devices and under different GPU resource availability, energy efficiency constraint, and latency constraints. Additionally, we also investigate and evaluate the impact of different device power modes, which has not been evaluated before. % % Different power modes allow several configurations with different CPU frequencies and number of CPU cores online. % We demonstrate accuracy superiority to baselines given any efficiency constraint. \end{enumerate} The rest of the paper is organized as follows. In Section.~\ref{sec:tech}, we present our overall design for {\textsc{Virtuoso}}\xspace and its key components, such as the dynamic scheduler and efficiency knobs for handling various user requirements for latency or energy consumption. In Section.~\ref{sec:implementations}, we present the multi-branch kernel design and implementation of {\textsc{Virtuoso}}\xspace, along with different runtime environments for evaluation. Section.~\ref{sec:evaluation} consists of two parts: First, we evaluate the overall performance of {\textsc{Virtuoso}}\xspace. Next, we evaluate {\textsc{Virtuoso}}\xspace and its multi-branch kernels against other baselines.
