Although the mobile GPU devices have been greatly improved, they still cannot compete with the computational power of the server-class machines or cloud clusters. Most of these systems rely on server-side computing or cloud computing, and the accuracy of these systems is the first consideration. The current research is mainly based on accuracy, and it may need to rely on the server or the cloud. Comment. Another strategy for making streaming analytic on mobile devices feasible is to combine object detection and tracking as is done in the “tracking-by-detection” technique. By interleaving several frames of tracking (which is less computation-intense than detection) with a frame of object detection, one can speed up the performance. Hence, to enhance the gaming experience (for example, in augmented reality or virtual reality) or to provide high-confidence outputs from streaming videos (for example, in the case of pedestrian recognition for driverless cars), these tasks must be performed in near-real time with a strict latency requirement of 33 ms or less. The technique of detection-tracking also gives rise to several adaptation strategies. This includes choosing among different trackers and varying the sensitivity of the two by varying the frequency of the epochs. Adaptation strategies are needed to meet real-time requirements for energy, latency, and accuracy, especially in mobile devices. In this paper we have tried to address the challenge of adapting at run-time to dynamically changing demands and available resources. We observe that the execution time of an object tracker is 10 times less than the execution time of an object detector. Recent studies have tried to address this challenge by considering multi-core solutions, such as Fang et al.’s NestDNN, Xu et al.’s Approach Detection, Xu et al.’s Approach Neural-Network, and Lee et al.’s Benchmarking. On the other hand, compared to the recent studies on efficient convolutional neural network architectures, the research and application of efficient object detection solutions on embedded devices have been lagging, and this is not to mention the problem of outdated feature extractors. In real applications, the variability of the contents of the videos, the limited resources of the mobile terminals, and the need for manual adjustment make dynamic adaptation even more difficult. Such solutions include multiple kernels in the system and select the best one during runtime to meet the end-user's needs. The wide variability of the energy, latency and accuracy requirements requires the system to be adaptable to a variety of applications. The omission of features regulating the consumption of energy is a major drawback of all these solutions. We know of no previous work which includes all these innovations. One thing that has not yet been studied is how these algorithms act when there is resource contention on the device. This resource contention can be caused by the presence of other applications running on the same device, which is common because they are multiple-function devices. Hence the design must meet the following requirements: (1) design an energy and latency-aware kernel for mobile devices, (2) analyze the energy consumption and the latency performance of all execution paths on mobile devices, and (3) design an adaptative scheduler to make runtime decisions that simultaneously satisfy multiple requirements. Until now no one has evaluated the performance of the most recent object-detection systems on the leading mobile devices with a GPU. For example, while a detection task is underway, another, more complex task such as a voice recognition task may be running on the same device. The Virtuoso X-space, which has been adapted to mobile devices under resource constraints, with extra energy-aware knobs for energy-aware adaptation. In summary, Virtuoso combines the most efficient object detection methods EfficientDet, cited in Tan et al. ’s paper, and SSD, cited in Liu’s paper, and enhances them with object trackers to provide 155 branch points, with eight efficiency controls available. Virtuoso also includes a scheduler, which, by considering the available inputs, chooses the best branch to optimize accuracy in real time. We also tested fifteen base models of the most recent object detection models on three different embedded platforms, under two resource contention conditions, to gain a better understanding of the energy, latency, and accuracy of the latest models of object detection. We have tested Virtuoso-Xspace and two of the best known solutions on three NVIDIA mobile devices with increasing computing power, the Jetson TX2, the Xavier NX and the AGX Xavier, the latter of which has two power modes. On each board and in each power mode, Virtuoso-Xspace is the best solution, which automatically chooses the appropriate branching strategy to satisfy the requirements of energy and latency, and to obtain the best accuracy. Virtuoso-Xspace is the only one, with a multi-branch kernel, which can adapt its energy consumption within a wide range (a ratio of 89) and its latency within a wide range (a ratio of 128). ... At 1 mJ per frame VirtuosoXspace achieves an accuracy of 52%, and with a delay of 33.3 ms VirtuosoXspace achieves an accuracy of 61% on the AGX-Xavier platform. With no limit on energy and delay, VirtuosoXspace achieves an accuracy of 63%, which is more than 10% higher than the previous model. text: Currently, information is produced in multiple formats, such as text, images, audio, video, etc. Consequently, for a query in one format (e.g., text), the pertinent information might exist in another format (e.g., image). Cross-modal Information Retrieval (IR) algorithms are being developed to address these search needs. \vspace{2mm} \noindent {\bf Need for Zero-shot Information Retrieval (ZSIR):} An IR task's train-test setup involves learning parameters for different classes or categories of queries. Traditional cross-modal retrieval methods require training data for all query classes to train the retrieval models. However, such methods may fail to retrieve data for queries from {\it new} or {\it unseen} classes. For example, consider a retrieval model trained on images and textual descriptions of various vehicle classes, such as `car', `motorbike', `aeroplane', etc. Now, if presented with a query `bus', the model should retrieve images and textual descriptions of buses (for which it has not been trained). This scenario aligns with the ``zero-shot'' setup~\cite{Larochelle:2008:ZLN:1620163.1620172,ZeroShotNIPS2009,ZeroShotNorouzi2013}, which focuses on recognizing new/unseen classes with limited training classes. Such scenarios are pertinent in any contemporary search system, where new events, hashtags, etc., emerge daily. Therefore, unlike the traditional IR evaluation setup, the zero-shot paradigm must be integrated into an IR setting. Specifically, zero-shot cross-media retrieval aims to achieve retrieval across multiple formats (e.g., retrieving images in response to a textual query) where there is no overlap between the query classes in training and test data. Zero-Shot IR (ZSIR) is particularly challenging as models must manage not only the different semantics across seen and unseen query classes but also the heterogeneous features of data across various formats. \vspace{2mm} \noindent {\bf Present work and differences with prior works:} Although extensive research has been conducted on general multimodal and cross-modal retrieval~\cite{cross-modal-ir-survey}, to our knowledge, only a few prior studies have explored cross-modal IR in a zero-shot setting~\cite{scottreed-cvpr16,ZSL_GAN_cvpr2018,ijcai2018-92,8643797,AgNet-TNNLS2019, CZHash-ICDM2020} (see Section~\ref{sec:related} and Section~\ref{sub:baselines} for details of these methods). Some of these earlier works assume additional information about class labels (e.g., a measure of semantic similarity between class labels), which may not always be available. In this paper, we propose a novel model for cross-modal IR in a zero-shot setting, based on Conditional Generative Adversarial Networks (GANs)~\cite{mirza-conditional14}, capable of retrieving {\it images} relevant to a given {\it textual} query. Our model, which we name {\bf \texttt{ZSCRGAN}{}} (Zero-Shot Cross-modal Retrieval GAN), relies solely on the textual data to perform the retrieval and {\it does not require additional information about class labels}. Although previous ZSIR models~\cite{ZSL_GAN_cvpr2018,ijcai2018-92,8643797} also utilize GANs, the primary novel contributions of the proposed model can be summarized as follows: (1)~We propose the \textbf{use of incorrect classes} to enable the generator to produce features unique to a specific class by distinguishing it from other classes. (2)~We develop a \textbf{Common Space Embedding Mapper (CSEM)} to map both the image embeddings and the text embeddings to a common space where retrieval can be executed. {\it This is the crucial step that allows our model to perform retrieval without relying on additional semantic information of class labels.} (3)~We develop an {\bf Expectation-Maximization (E-M) based method} for efficiently training the retrieval model, where the GAN and the CSEM are trained alternately. We demonstrate that this E-M setup enables better retrieval than jointly training the GAN and the CSEM. We conduct experiments on several benchmark datasets for zero-shot retrieval -- (1)~the Caltech-UCSD Birds dataset, (2)~the Oxford Flowers-102 dataset, (3)~the North America Birds (NAB) dataset, (4)~the Wikipedia dataset, and (5)~the Animals With Attribute (AWA) dataset. Our proposed \texttt{ZSCRGAN}{} significantly outperforms several strong and diverse baselines on all the datasets, including ZSIR models~\cite{scottreed-cvpr16,8643797,ZSL_GAN_cvpr2018}, state-of-the-art Zero-Shot classification models~\cite{verma-cvpr18,xian2018feature_gen} suitably adapted for the Text-to-Image retrieval setting, as well as state-of-the-art Zero-Shot Hashing models~\cite{AgNet-TNNLS2019, CZHash-ICDM2020,DCMH-AAAI17}. Additionally, note that our proposed model can be utilized not only with textual queries but also with other forms of queries such as attribute vectors, as demonstrated by its application on the AWA dataset. We make the implementation of \texttt{ZSCRGAN}{} publicly available at \url{https://github.com/ranarag/ZSCRGAN}.

text: Dense retrieval systems initially encode queries and documents into a dense embedding space and subsequently perform information retrieval by locating a query's nearest neighbors within this space~\cite{orqa, sentence-bert, dpr, ance}. With advancements in pre-trained language models~\cite{bert, lu2021less}, specialized training strategies~\cite{dpr, ance}, and efficient nearest neighbor search~\cite{faiss, scann}, dense retrieval systems have demonstrated effectiveness across various tasks, such as web search~\cite{msmarco}, open domain question answering~\cite{naturalquestions}, and zero-shot IR~\cite{beir}. Retrieval using dense, fully-learned representations has the potential to address fundamental challenges in sparse retrieval. For instance, vocabulary mismatch can be resolved \textit{if} the embeddings accurately capture the information need of a query and map it to pertinent documents. However, decades of IR research indicate that deducing a user's search intent from a brief and often ambiguous search query is difficult~\cite{croft2010search}. Even with advanced pre-trained language models, it is unrealistic to expect an encoder to perfectly embed the underlying information need from a few query terms. A common method to enhance query understanding in sparse retrieval systems is \textit{pseudo relevance feedback} (PRF)~\cite{croft2010search,PRF,rm12}, which utilizes the top retrieved documents from an initial search as supplementary information to enrich the query representation. Whether PRF information is employed through query expansion~\cite{PRF,trec2004} or query term reweighting~\cite{bendersky2011parameterized}, its effectiveness has been consistently observed across various search scenarios, making PRF a standard practice in many sparse retrieval systems. This work utilizes PRF information to enhance query representations in dense retrieval. Given the top retrieved documents from a dense retrieval model, e.g., ANCE~\cite{ance}, we develop a PRF query encoder, ANCE-PRF, which employs a BERT encoder~\cite{bert} to process the query and the PRF documents to refine the query representation. ANCE-PRF is trained end-to-end using relevance labels and learns to optimize the query embeddings using the rich information from PRF documents. It reuses the document index from ANCE to avoid duplicating index storage. In experiments on MS MARCO and TREC Deep Learning (DL) Track passage ranking benchmarks, ANCE-PRF consistently outperforms ANCE and several recent dense retrieval systems that utilize more sophisticated models and training strategies~\cite{ltre,mebert}. We also observe significant improvements on DL-HARD~\cite{dlhard} queries, a curated set designed to include complex search intents challenging for neural systems. To the best of our knowledge, ANCE-PRF ranks among the top-performing first-stage retrieval systems on the highly competitive MARCO passage ranking leaderboard. Our studies confirm that the advantages of ANCE-PRF lie in its ability to leverage the useful information from the PRF documents while disregarding the noise from irrelevant PRF documents. The PRF encoder allocates significantly more attention to terms from the relevant PRF documents compared to those from irrelevant documents. A case study reveals that the encoder focuses more on PRF terms that complement the query terms in representing search intents. These factors help ANCE-PRF learn better query embeddings that are closer to the relevant documents and improve the majority of testing queries.\footnote{Our code, checkpoints, and ranking results are open-sourced at \url{https://github.com/yuhongqian/ANCE-PRF}.}

text: Given the widespread presence and significance of smart devices in our daily lives, the capability to comprehend and operate User Interfaces (UIs) has become a crucial task for Artificial Intelligence. For example, a model capable of locating a UI component based on its description can be highly beneficial for voice interfaces, while a model that can predict the outcome of clicking a button can assist in page navigation. To effectively operate a UI, models must understand the user's tasks and intentions, as well as how to execute these tasks within the provided UI. However, understanding UIs is a challenging and relatively unexplored area. Firstly, there are numerous tasks associated with UI understanding. Typically, these tasks are cross-modal and cross-domain, such as clicking a button via voice command and retrieving an icon through a semantically similar one. Previous research in this area often focuses on a single task at a time. Training a distinct complex model for each task is inefficient for on-device model deployment. Furthermore, models may experience overfitting if the task-specific data is limited. Pre-training models on large-scale datasets to extract features has demonstrated significant effectiveness in multiple domains, such as ResNet \cite{he2016deep} in computer vision and BERT \cite{devlin2018bert} in natural language processing. There is no universal feature representation for user interfaces, and it remains uncertain whether a pre-trained feature extraction model can enhance multiple UI-related tasks. Secondly, the data source and format of UIs differ from natural image and language corpora. For instance, the View Hierarchy (VH) in mobile apps and the Document Object Model (DOM) in web pages are tree structures that represent the UI layout. The VH and DOM contain structural and semantic information about the UI, although they are not typically visible to users and include short phrases that provide hints about functionality. Effectively utilizing this domain-specific knowledge for general UI understanding remains an unresolved issue. Thirdly, understanding the functionality of UIs is more complex than learning about their appearance. It is common for UI elements with similar appearances to have very different semantic meanings, and vice versa. In the example in Figure \ref{fig:icon-semantic}, all the icons resemble each other (``houses''), yet they possess different functionalities that can only be interpreted with additional context. In this paper, we propose ActionBert, a pre-trained transformer-style \cite{vaswani2017attention} model that utilizes sequential user action information for UI understanding. Our primary insight is that the semantic meaning of a UI and the functionality of UI components can be captured through user actions, such as a sequence of clicks and their effects on the UI. This model leverages the representational power of transformer models and incorporates domain-specific information like VH and user actions to develop embeddings that reflect the functionality of different UI elements. To our knowledge, this is the first attempt to create a generic feature representation in this domain. Our main contributions in this paper are: \begin{itemize} \item To our knowledge, we are the first to combine the powerful transformer models with domain-specific knowledge, such as VH and user actions, to enhance machines' understanding of UIs. \item We introduce ActionBert, a transformer-style multi-modal model designed to capture the context and semantic meaning of UI elements by introducing new self-supervised pre-training tasks based on user actions and UI-specific features. \item We assess the proposed model on four types of UI downstream tasks, encompassing various real-life use cases. We demonstrate that the proposed model surpasses existing models across all tasks. \end{itemize}

For example, a model that can detect a button from its description is useful in voice-controlled systems, while a model that can predict the result of clicking a button is helpful in navigating the UI. Usually, these tasks are multi-modal and cross-domain, such as a button click by a voice command or an icon search by a semantically similar one. text: A growing challenge in NLP is long-form question-answering (LFQA), where a paragraph-length response is generated for an open-ended question. LFQA systems have the potential to become a primary method for people to learn about the world, yet they currently fall short of human performance \citep{hurdles}. Existing research typically concentrates on two fundamental components of the task: information retrieval and synthesis. In this study, we utilize existing solutions for these components: we delegate document retrieval to the Microsoft Bing Web Search API,\footnote{\url{https://www.microsoft.com/en-us/bing/apis/bing-web-search-api}} and employ unsupervised pre-training to achieve high-quality synthesis by fine-tuning GPT-3 \citep{gpt3}. Rather than attempting to enhance these components, we focus on integrating them using more reliable training objectives. Following \citet{summarization}, we employ human feedback to directly optimize answer quality, enabling us to achieve performance that is competitive with humans. We present two primary contributions: \begin{itemize} \item We develop a text-based web-browsing environment that a fine-tuned language model can engage with. This enables us to enhance both retrieval and synthesis in an end-to-end manner using general methods such as imitation learning and reinforcement learning. \item We produce answers \textit{with references}: passages extracted by the model from web pages during browsing. This is essential for allowing labelers to assess the factual accuracy of answers without undergoing a challenging and subjective independent research process. \end{itemize} Our models are primarily trained to answer questions from ELI5 \citep{eli5}, a dataset of questions sourced from the ``Explain Like I'm Five'' subreddit. We gather two additional types of data: \textit{demonstrations} of humans using our web-browsing environment to answer questions, and \textit{comparisons} between two model-generated answers to the same question (each with its own set of references). Answers are evaluated for their factual accuracy, coherence, and overall usefulness. We utilize this data in four principal ways: behavior cloning (i.e., supervised fine-tuning) using the demonstrations, reward modeling using the comparisons, reinforcement learning against the reward model, and rejection sampling against the reward model. Our most effective model employs a combination of behavior cloning and rejection sampling. We also find reinforcement learning to be beneficial when inference-time computational resources are more constrained. We assess our best model in three distinct ways. First, we compare our model's answers to those written by our human demonstrators on a held-out set of questions. Our model's answers are preferred 56\% of the time, indicating human-level proficiency in using the text-based browser. Second, we compare our model's answers (with references removed, for fairness) to the top-voted answer provided by the ELI5 dataset. Our model's answers are favored 69\% of the time. Third, we evaluate our model on TruthfulQA \citep{truthfulqa}, an adversarial dataset of short-form questions. Our model's answers are accurate 75\% of the time, and both accurate and informative 54\% of the time, surpassing our base model (GPT-3), though still not reaching human performance. The remainder of the paper is organized as follows: \begin{itemize} \item In Section \ref{section:environment}, we describe our text-based web-browsing environment and how our models interact with it. \item In Section \ref{section:methods}, we detail our data collection and training methods. \item In Section \ref{section:evaluation}, we assess our best-performing models (for different inference-time compute budgets) on ELI5 and TruthfulQA. \item In Section \ref{section:experiments}, we present experimental results comparing our various methods and how they scale with dataset size, parameter count, and inference-time compute. \item In Section \ref{section:discussion}, we discuss the implications of our findings for training models to answer questions truthfully, and broader impacts. \end{itemize}

dipper_dipper: Introduction. A growing challenge in NLP is to generate a paragraph-length response to an open-ended question. LFQ systems have the potential to become an important way in which people learn about the world, but currently they fall short of human performance. The work of others has been concentrated on the two main aspects of the task, information search and synthesis. The system we propose is concerned not with improving these two aspects but with the integration of these two aspects into a more reliable system. In the first step, we rely on an unsupervised learning for the retrieval of information based on the GPT3 method, and in the second step we directly optimize the quality of answers by the use of human feedback. We present two main contributions. First, we have developed a text-based web-browsing environment for a carefully trained language model which can be used for end-to-end learning. Second, we have produced answers to questions based on extracts from web pages as the model is navigating. Our models are primarily trained to answer questions from the ELI5 dataset, a collection of questions from the subreddit 'Explain Like I'm Five'. It is necessary to enable the labeler to determine the factual accuracy of answers without the difficult and subjective process of independently verifying them. We collect two types of data: human demonstrations, where human experts answer questions in our web browsing environment, and model comparisons, where we compare two model-generated answers to the same question, each with its own set of citations. We use these data in four main ways: re-learning (i.e., re-training), inference (i.e., learning from the citations), a posteriori learning (i.e., using past data to learn from the past) and for transfer learning. Answers are evaluated for their factual accuracy, coherence, and general usefulness. Our best model uses a combination of supervised fine-tuning (supervised learning) from demonstrations, modeling of rewards from comparisons, reinforcement learning from the reward model, and rejection sampling from the reward model. We test our best model in three ways. We also find that reinforcement learning can be advantageous when the resources of the inference engine are more limited. First, we compare the model's answers to the human demonstrators' answers to a set of questions. The second is to compare the model’s answers (with cites, to be fair) with the highest-rated answers from the ELI5 dataset. The model’s answers are preferred 66% of the time. text: Self-driving in complex and dynamic traffic scenarios presents significant challenges. Firstly, there are various road topologies and scenarios to consider, such as roundabouts, multi-lane streets, and intersections\cite{Chen2019DeepIL}. Secondly, the intricate and interdependent interactions among multiple road agents, including pedestrians, bicyclists, and vehicles, are difficult to model\cite{Chen2020RobotNI}. Additionally, compliance with various traffic rules, such as traffic lights, lane markings, and speed limits, is necessary. Traditional decision-making and planning methods are primarily rule-based and struggle to generalize to new scenarios. Consequently, they necessitate time-consuming and iterative manual tuning of rules and parameters to sustain performance\cite{Zeng2019EndToEndIN}. In recent years, deep learning has significantly advanced self-driving vehicle (SDV) technology as an alternative approach. The capability to \textit{learn and self-optimize} behavior from data reduces the need for labor-intensive engineering to model all potential scenarios, making deep driving models well-suited for self-driving in high-dimensional, nonlinear, and dynamic environments\cite{Cai2020ProbabilisticEV, Chen2019LearningBC,OhnBar2020LearningSD, codevilla2018end, codevilla2019exploring, Tai2019VisualbasedAD}. However, current learning-based models are not well-designed for scalable self-driving in a uniform framework. Specifically, most studies concentrate only on isolated tasks such as conditional urban driving\cite{OhnBar2020LearningSD, codevilla2018end, codevilla2019exploring,Chen2019LearningBC,Tai2019VisualbasedAD}, lane-following\cite{Xu2017EndtoEndLO}, lane-changing\cite{Wang2018ARL}, or collision avoidance\cite{Porav2018ImminentCM, Woo2020CollisionAF}. In summary, high-performance scalable driving models capable of handling extensive traffic scenarios remain elusive. To address this issue, this paper proposes a graph-based deep neural network, \textit{DiGNet} (driving in graphs), for scalable self-driving. Specifically, we employ graph attention networks (GAT)\cite{velickovic2018graph} to model the complex interactions among traffic agents, utilize semantic bird's-eye view (BEV) images to represent road topologies and traffic rules, and apply the variational auto-encoder (VAE)\cite{kingma2014autoencoding} to extract compact yet effective environmental features. The primary contributions of this paper are as follows: (1) We propose a specially designed network architecture for self-driving in generic traffic scenarios, which accounts for both driving contexts and the interactions among dynamic road agents. (2) We demonstrate the scalable and safe self-driving performance of the proposed method through extensive closed-loop evaluations in both familiar and unfamiliar urban, rural, and highway environments.

text: Neural Networks (NNs) are computational models consisting of one or more feature representation layers and a final linear learner. In recent years, deep NNs have significantly advanced the state-of-the-art performance in various real-world applications, such as image classification \cite{krizhevsky2012imagenet,he2016deep}, speech recognition \cite{hinton2012deep}, and natural language processing \cite{bahdanau2014neural}, among others. However, the theoretical understanding of these empirical successes in NNs remains limited. A primary conceptual challenge is the high non-convexity of these models, indicating that first-order algorithms like gradient descent (GD) or stochastic gradient descent (SGD) might converge to poor local stationary points. Nonetheless, it is observed in practice that with the aid of several techniques such as dropout \cite{SHKSS-dropout} and batch normalization \cite{ioffe15}, deep neural networks (DNNs) can be effectively trained from random initialization with consistent results. The solutions obtained through appropriate training procedures perform well and consistently. In other words, two distinct random initializations (using the same initialization and training strategy) generally produce models that yield similar predictions on test data. Thus, it can be concluded that proper neural network training results in similar solutions. This behavior is akin to that of convex optimization, rather than typical non-convex optimization problems that often become trapped in suboptimal local stationary solutions. Since solutions from different random initializations are similar and reproducible, it can also be hypothesized that with proper training, deep neural networks can achieve solutions near the global optimum. These empirical observations seem quite enigmatic, necessitating the development of new mathematical models for neural networks that can bridge the gap between non-convex and convex models for better understanding. Beyond the aforementioned empirical observations, practitioners also recognize that overparameterized neural networks (NNs) with numerous hidden units are easier to learn \cite{zhang2016understanding}. They attain better and more consistent performance. Related to this empirical observation, it was noted in the 1990s that neural networks with infinitely many hidden units are simpler to model and analyze theoretically \cite{Neal95-thesis,Williams97-nips}. In recent years, there have been substantial theoretical advancements in the analysis of overparameterized NNs with a vast number of hidden units approaching infinity. Notably, it has been demonstrated that such systems behave like convex systems under various restricted conditions. This provides theoretical justification for the empirical observations regarding the reproducibility of neural network training. { In this paper, we review some recently developed mathematical models for overparameterized NNs, focusing on the {\em neural tangent kernel} (NTK) view and the {\em mean field} (MF) view. Section~\ref{sec:2two-levelNN} introduces the basic formulation for two-layer NNs, and Section~\ref{sec:random} introduces a closely related learning model, random kitchen sinks \cite{rahimi2009weighted}. In Section \ref{sec:ntk}, we examine the NTK view for two-layer NNs, which demonstrates that a two-layer NN can be equivalently expressed as a linear model in the tangent space under certain specialized conditions. Section \ref{sec:meanfield} considers the MF view for two-layer NNs. In this view, a continuous two-layer NN is regarded as a learned distribution over the weights, leading to a more realistic mathematical model for analyzing practical behaviors of NNs. In Section \ref{sec:exp}, we compare the three models from the feature learning perspective. Section \ref{sec:deepnn} considers potential extensions on deep NNs for NTK and MFs. In Section \ref{sec:complexity}, we introduce some basic complexity results for NTK. Section \ref{sec:othermodel} reviews some other mathematical models. Finally, we conclude the paper and outline active research directions in Section \ref{sec:conclusion}.} \IEEEpubidadjcol

text: With the rapid increase in the number of scientific papers, it becomes increasingly difficult for researchers to identify papers worth reading from a vast body of literature for quick reviews or to stay updated with the latest advancements. When faced with an unfamiliar research topic, a user might attempt to read survey papers on the topic and consult the reference lists in these surveys for further details. However, a high-quality and current survey is not always available for every research topic. A user might also use academic search engines to locate related papers to read. Existing academic search engines typically retrieve a list of articles by calculating the semantic similarity between the user's query and each article individually, disregarding the prerequisite relationships among the search results. Therefore, it would be highly beneficial if we could retrieve a list of core papers with a reading order for a given query to provide users with a reading path. In this manner, a user can follow the generated reading path and quickly become acquainted with a new research field. In recent years, research on scientific paper analysis has garnered significant attention. However, most existing studies focus on citation recommendation~\cite{zhou2008learning, tang2009discriminative, he2010context, ren2014cluscite, sun2017recommendation}, which aims to recommend citations for a given text. Another category of research focuses on citation classification \cite{jurgens2016citation, teufel2006automatic, dong2011ensemble, zhao2019context, cohan2019structural, pride2020authoritative}, aiming to infer the author's intention for citing a paper. There are also studies on generating reading lists for users. \cite{jardine2014automatically} proposed ThemedPageRank to create reading lists by re-ranking topic-related papers. \cite{ekstrand2010automatically} developed a reading list for a given query set by exploring collaborative and content-based filtering techniques. However, these methods overlook the prerequisite relationships among the returned papers. \cite{gordon2017structured} designed a concept graph-based approach to generate structured reading lists, which considers the prerequisite concepts of the topic. However, this method heavily depends on the quality of the existing concept graph. Previous research on reading list generation primarily addresses the issue of "what to read" by producing a list of papers for a given research topic. However, to assist users unfamiliar with a research field, existing research omits two critical problems: "how to read" and "how to understand". For the first problem, we need to organize different research works in a structured manner, allowing a user to read the papers according to the paths in the structure and gain an understanding of how research on a specific topic has evolved over time. Note that simply organizing papers by publication date is insufficient, as the correlation between different research works is overlooked. For the second problem, we need to include some papers in our generated path that may not be directly related to the queried research topic but are quite helpful or essential for understanding the highly related papers in our generated list. Motivated by the above analysis, in this paper, we introduce a new task, {\em Reading Path Generation (RPG)}, which aims to automatically create a reading path for a given query. Our task is designed to assist researchers who are new to a field in conducting a quick survey by addressing the two problems mentioned above. Specifically, we aim to retrieve a list of papers that includes research works highly related to the given query, as well as prerequisite research works essential for understanding the highly related works. Furthermore, we organize these papers to form a reading path, considering both the chronological order and the correlation between different research works. We hope that by reading the retrieved papers according to the reading path, a user can easily understand each research work, quickly complete a survey, and form a comprehensive view of the research history of any topic. Due to the lack of benchmark datasets for evaluating Reading Path Generation, we further propose the {\em SurveyBank} dataset, which is specifically designed for our newly proposed task. We create SurveyBank without any human labeling based on two key insights. The first insight is that many existing high-quality survey papers are already available, each written by professional researchers and containing highly valuable information on how to form a survey about a research topic. Based on this observation, we use the key phrases extracted from survey titles as the inputs for the RPG task and reading paths inferred from surveys' reference lists as true labels. We initially collect $41,194$ surveys in the field of computer science from Google Scholar and S2ORC \cite{lo-etal-2020-s2orc}. Subsequently, $9,321$ high-quality surveys are selected to form SurveyBank, covering 10 topics in computer science, such as Artificial Intelligence, Computer Networks, and Databases. The second key insight is that the citation relationship between different papers reflects the coherence between them. Therefore, we construct a large-scale scientific citation graph with 6 million papers from S2ORC~\cite{lo-etal-2020-s2orc} in the field of computer science based on citation relationships, and this citation graph covers the reference lists of each survey. To the best of our knowledge, SurveyBank is currently the largest survey dataset. Last but not least, we also propose and implement a Real-time Reading Path Generation System (RePaGer), which takes key phrases as inputs and generates a reading path of papers for users to read. In RePaGer, we begin by retrieving top-$K$ articles, referred to as initial seed papers, from Google Scholar. We then re-allocate seeds by first capturing neighbors of initial seed papers as seed candidates and subsequently selecting articles with high co-occurrence. We infer that these newly selected seeds are more likely to be prerequisite concepts of a topic since multiple articles directly relevant to the topic cite them. Finally, we propose the Node-Edge Weighted Steiner Tree (NWST), a graph optimization-based approach, to identify a reading path with prerequisite chains for a given query. Our model not only considers the importance of each paper within the entire citation network but also accounts for the relationships among them. We conduct extensive evaluations based on the SurveyBank dataset and compare our proposed approach for Reading Path Generation with existing academic search engines and baseline methods. The evaluation results demonstrate that our approach outperforms other baselines and can generate insightful reading paths for different research topics.

(Ekstrand, 2010; Ekstrand, 2014; Ekstrand, 2016; Ekstrand, 2017; Ekstrand, 2018; Ekstrand, 2019; Ekstrand, 2018; Ekstrand, 2017; apropos; apropos; cohan, cohan, cohan, cohan, cohan, cohan, cohan, cohan, cohan, cohan, cohan, cohan, cohan, cohan, cohan, cohan, cohan, cohan, cohan, cohan, cohan, cohan, cohan, cohan, cohan, cohan, cohan, cohan, cohan, cohan, cohan, cohan, cohan, cohan, cohan, cohan, cohan, cohan, cohan, cohan, cohan, cohan, cohan, cohan, cohan, april, 2020, authority) ) However, this method is highly dependent on the quality of the existing concept network. In the previous generation of reading lists, the main problem has been what to read, and the solution has been to generate a list of papers in a given area of research. However, to help users unfamiliar with the research area, this research has two important problems: how to read, and how to understand. Note that simply sorting papers by date is not enough, because it does not consider the relationships between papers. First, organize different papers in a structural way so that the reader can read the papers in a certain order and understand the development of research in a certain field. Second, include in the generated path papers that may not be directly related to the topic but are useful or essential for understanding closely related papers. Since there is no evaluation dataset for RPG, we propose SurveyBank, which was created to support the task we are proposing. Having considered the above problems, we propose a new task, Reading Path Generation (RPG), the goal of which is to create a reading path for a given query. Specifically, we intend to provide a list of papers that are closely related to the given query and are prerequisite for understanding the closely related papers. Without human intervention, the SurveyBank relies on two insights. First, it arranges the retrieved papers in a reading path, taking into account both the chronology of the publication and the relationship between different studies. It is hoped that a reader, by reading the papers in this order, will quickly be able to grasp the nature of each research program, make a rapid survey, and obtain a quick and comprehensive overview of the research history on any topic. The first is that a large number of high-quality review papers already exist, each of which was written by professional authors and contains valuable information on how to write a review on a topic. Based on this observation, we used the titles of these papers as inputs for the RPG task, and the reading paths extracted from the references of these papers as real annotations. The second is that the degree of citation between two papers reflects the degree of similarity between them. In this paper we present a real-time reading path generation system, RePaGer, that takes a key phrase as input and provides a list of articles for the reader to read. In this paper we present a large-scale citation network of 6,000,000 articles in the field of computing, based on citation relations. This network covers the reference lists of each article. From these articles we collected 41,194 papers from Google Scholar and S2ORC. We filtered out 9,321 papers as good ones, and created Survey Bank, which is composed of ten topics in the field of computer science, such as artificial intelligence, networks, and databases. The RePaGer process starts by obtaining the first initial seeds from the Google Scholar, i.e. the top k articles. We assume that these newly selected seeds are more likely to be required concepts for a topic, since they are cited by many articles closely related to the topic. As far as we know, SurveyBank is the largest repository of papers. Finally, we propose a graph-based approach based on a Steiner tree to find a reading path with a chain of pre-requisites for a given query. We also conduct extensive evaluations of the SurveyBank dataset to compare our proposed method of generating reading paths with existing academic search engines and other methods. The evaluation shows that our approach outperforms the other methods and can generate a meaningful reading path for different research topics.

text: The study of 3D-aware image synthesis has garnered significant attention recently~\cite{graf, giraffe, pigan}. A novel approach involves integrating a Neural Radiance Field (NeRF)~\cite{nerf} into a Generative Adversarial Network (GAN)~\cite{gan}. Specifically, the generator based on a 2D Convolutional Neural Network (CNN) is substituted with a generative implicit function, which maps raw 3D coordinates to point-wise densities and colors, conditioned on the provided latent code. This implicit function encodes both the structure and texture of the output image within the 3D space. However, there are two issues with directly incorporating NeRF~\cite{nerf} into the generator. On one hand, the implicit function in NeRF generates color and density for each 3D point using a Multi-Layer Perceptron (MLP) network. With a highly localized receptive field, the MLP struggles to globally represent the underlying structure when synthesizing images. Thus, using only the 3D coordinates as inputs~\cite{graf, pigan, giraffe} is insufficiently expressive to guide the generator with the global structure. On the other hand, volume rendering computes the pixel values of the output image independently, necessitating the sampling of numerous points along the camera ray for each pixel. Consequently, the computational cost rises significantly as the image size increases. This may result in inadequate optimization during model training, leading to suboptimal performance in high-resolution image generation. Previous research has demonstrated that 2D GANs benefit from valid representations learned by the generator~\cite{interfacegan, higan, xu2021generative}. These generative representations describe a synthesis with \textit{high-level features}. For instance, Xu~\textit{et al.}~\cite{xu2021generative} confirm that a face synthesis model recognizes the landmark positions of the output face, while Yang~\textit{et al.}~\cite{higan} identify multi-level variation factors emerging from generating bedroom images. These representative features encode rich texture and structural information, thereby improving the synthesis quality~\cite{stylegan} and the controllability~\cite{interfacegan} of image GANs. In contrast, as previously mentioned, existing 3D-aware generative models directly render pixel values from coordinates~\cite{graf, pigan}, without learning explicit representations. In this work, we introduce a novel generative model, termed \textbf{VolumeGAN}, which achieves 3D-aware image synthesis by \textit{explicitly learning a structural and a textural representation}. Rather than using 3D coordinates as inputs, we generate a feature volume using a 3D convolutional network, which encodes the relationships between various spatial regions and compensates for the limited receptive field caused by the MLP in NeRF. With the feature volume modeling the underlying structure, we query a coordinate descriptor from the feature volume to describe the structural information for each 3D point. We then employ a NeRF-like model to create a feature field, using the coordinate descriptor combined with the raw coordinate as input. The feature field is further accumulated into a 2D feature map as the textural representation, followed by a CNN with a $1\times1$ kernel size to render the output image. In this manner, we separately model the structure and texture with the 3D feature volume and the 2D feature map, enabling disentangled control of shape and appearance. We assess our approach on various datasets and demonstrate its superior performance compared to existing alternatives. Regarding image quality, VolumeGAN achieves a substantially improved Fréchet Inception Distance (FID) score~\cite{fid}. For example, using the FFHQ dataset~\cite{stylegan} at $256\times256$ resolution, we enhance the FID from $36.7$ to $9.1$. We also enable 3D-aware image synthesis on the challenging indoor scene dataset, \textit{i.e.}, LSUN bedroom~\cite{lsun}. Our model also exhibits stable control of object pose and shows improved consistency across different viewpoints, benefiting from the learned structural representation (\textit{i.e.}, the feature volume). Furthermore, we conduct a detailed empirical study on the learned structural and textural representations and analyze the trade-off between image quality and the 3D property.

text: Data minimization is a fundamental principle of the European Union's Data Protection Regulation~\citep{regulation2016regulation}, as well as data protection laws in other regions: \begin{quote} "Personal data shall be: [...] adequate, relevant and limited to what is necessary in relation to the purposes for which they are processed (data minimisation)" \end{quote} This requirement acts as a guideline for processing data with respect. Recent empirical studies have demonstrated that it is feasible to replicate the performance of data-driven systems using substantially less data~\cite{biega2020dm, chow2013differential,vincent2019data, wen2018exploring}. These results stem from the diminishing returns observed in data collection across various applications and domains~\cite{hestness1712deep, krause2010utility,tae2020slice}. Recognizing that data limitation is achievable, legal guidelines suggest algorithmic techniques that could be integrated into minimization processes, such as feature selection~\cite{icoDataMinimizationTechniques} or the analysis of learning curves~\cite{norwegianAuthorityArtificial}. However, despite the availability of numerous algorithmic techniques that could be adapted to meet the minimization requirement, the data minimization principle has received limited attention from the computer science community thus far. As scholars have noted in efforts to revive discussion on the principle, a lack of concrete mathematical definitions and guidelines is a primary factor hindering adoption~\cite{finckreviving}. Indeed, qualitative research has revealed an absence of consistent data minimization standards or comprehension of the principle among software developers~\cite{senarath2018understanding}. Recent interpretations of data minimization suggest linking the purpose of data collection in data-driven systems to performance metrics, an interpretation known as \emph{performance-based data minimization}~\cite{finckreviving,biega2020dm}. Our work follows this interpretation, addressing the question of \emph{how to proactively satisfy the performance-based data minimization principle in machine learning with personal data}. \\ \textbf{Contributions.} In this study, we introduce FIDO, a Framework for Inhibiting Data Overcollection, and illustrate how ongoing personal data collection could be managed within the context of data minimization. FIDO's primary conceptual innovation is to \emph{adaptively learn an algorithm's performance curve} to accurately determine an \emph{appropriate data collection stopping point}. By directly modeling the performance curve, the framework remains adaptable to various underlying feature acquisition algorithms and definitions of performance. Experiments with multiple datasets in the recommender systems domain confirm this adaptability and demonstrate FIDO's capability to estimate algorithm performance with additional data accurately \emph{without} collecting more data. The core technical contribution of FIDO lies in its procedure for estimating performance curves, which builds on recent machine learning literature that identifies three distinct phases in the performance curves of learning algorithms: the small data phase, the power law phase, and the diminishing returns phase \cite{hestness1712deep}. We demonstrate that these performance phases can be observed in the context of user data collection and provide a method to model the data collection phases directly by adaptively learning a piecewise power law curve. Empirical experiments reveal that other methods for estimating performance curves systematically \emph{overestimate} the return on additional data. Modeling each phase directly allows FIDO to not only learn the performance curve more accurately as data is acquired but also meet practical constraints of data minimization. Finally, we explore issues related to user-level data minimization. We illustrate the impacts that algorithmic components such as active feature acquisition (a technique to intelligently select which feature values to acquire) may have on minimization outcomes. We find that active feature acquisition can result in unequal, concentrated data collection from a small group of users, as well as decreased minimization performance for evolving user communities or when sensitive features are excluded from initial data collection. We also find that user-specific performance curves are highly variable, where collecting more data can often lead to a \emph{decrease} in user-specific performance. This paper aims to provide a computational perspective on the GDPR's principle of data minimization, contributing insights to the ongoing discussions about the technical implementation of this core data protection principle, and to offer recommendations to practitioners and scholars moving forward.

text: The \textit{Security-Constrained Economic Dispatch} (SCED) serves as a crucial optimization model for Transmission System Operators (TSOs) to manage real-time energy markets while ensuring the reliable operation of power grids \cite{conejo2018power}. In the United States, TSOs such as MISO and PJM execute a SCED every five minutes, necessitating that the optimization problem be resolved in an even shorter timeframe, specifically well under a minute \cite{Chen2018_MarketClearingSoftware}. Security constraints, which ensure resilience against the failure of any single component, make SCED models particularly complex for large systems \cite{Chiang2015_SolvingSCOPF,Wang2016_SolvingCorrectiveSCOPF,velloso2021exact}, unless only a limited set of contingencies is considered. With the proliferation of distributed resources and increasing operational uncertainty, these computational bottlenecks are expected to become even more significant \cite{Chen2018_MarketClearingSoftware}. This paper is driven by the increasing proportion of renewable generation, particularly wind, in the MISO system, which necessitates risk-aware market-clearing algorithms. A specific challenge is the aspiration to conduct risk analysis in real time by solving numerous scenarios for load and renewable production \cite{werho2021_ScenarioGenerationWind}. However, systematically solving many SCED instances is impractical given the stringent constraints of real-time operations. To address this computational challenge, this paper proposes developing an optimization proxy for SCED, namely, a Machine Learning (ML) model capable of predicting an optimal solution for SCED within acceptable numerical tolerances and in milliseconds. It is crucial to clarify that the current objective is not to replace optimization-based market-clearing tools. Rather, the proposed optimization proxy offers operators an additional tool for risk assessment. This enables rapid evaluation of how the system would respond under various scenarios without the need to perform costly optimizations. Specifically, because these predictions are aggregated into risk metrics, minor prediction errors on individual instances are permissible. \subsection{Related Literature and Challenges} The integration of ML and optimization for power systems has garnered increasing attention in recent years. One research direction \cite{pan2019deepopf, fioretto2020predicting, chatzos2020high, lei2020data, chatzos2021spatial, velloso2020combining, zamzam2020learning, owerko2020optimal} employs ML models to predict an optimal solution to the Optimal Power Flow (OPF) problem. Pan et al. \cite{pan2019deepopf} train a Deep Neural Network (DNN) model to predict solutions to security-constrained DC-OPFs and report results on systems with no more than 300 buses. A common limitation of ML models, also noted in \cite{pan2019deepopf}, is that predictions are not guaranteed to meet the original problem's constraints. To address this limitation, recent efforts \cite{fioretto2020predicting, chatzos2020high} incorporate Lagrangian duality into the training of DNNs to capture the physical and operational constraints of AC-OPFs. A similar approach is adopted in Velloso et al. \cite{velloso2020combining} in the context of preventive security-constrained DC-OPF. Specifically, a DNN is trained using Lagrangian duality techniques and then employed as a proxy for the time-intensive master problem in a column-and-constraint generation algorithm. More recently, Chatzos et al. \cite{chatzos2021spatial} embed the Lagrangian duality framework in a two-stage learning process that utilizes a regional decomposition of the power network, facilitating more efficient distributed training. Another research direction involves integrating ML models within optimization algorithms to enhance runtime performance. For example, several papers (e.g., \cite{deka2019learning,misra2021learning,xavier2021learning, yang2020fast,guha2019machine}) attempt to identify active constraints to reduce problem complexity. In \cite{xavier2021learning}, the authors explore learning feasible solutions to the unit commitment problem. Venzke et al. \cite{venzke2020neural} employ a DNN model to learn the feasible region of a dynamic SCOPF and convert the resulting DNN into a mixed-integer linear program. Existing research papers in ML for power systems generally suffer from two limitations. Firstly, most papers present numerical results on small academic test systems, which are one to two orders of magnitude smaller than actual transmission systems. This is particularly concerning, as higher-dimensional data adversely affects the convergence and accuracy of machine-learning algorithms. Secondly, nearly all papers rely on artificially-generated data whose distribution does not reflect the variability observed in real operations. For instance, only changes in load are considered, typically without capturing spatio-temporal correlations. Other sources of uncertainty, such as renewable production, are not considered, nor is the variability of economic bids. Lastly, changes in commitment decisions throughout the day are rarely addressed, although they introduce non-trivial, combinatorial distribution shifts. \subsection{Contributions and Outline} To address these limitations, the paper proposes a novel ML pipeline that is rooted in the structure of real-world market operations. The approach leverages the TSO's advance knowledge of 1) commitment decisions and 2) day-ahead forecasts for load and renewable productions. Indeed, both are available by the time the day-ahead market has been executed. Additionally, the paper provides a comprehensive analysis of real-time market behavior, which informs a novel ML architecture to better capture the nature of actual operations. The proposed learning pipeline is illustrated in Figure~\ref{fig:learning_pipeline}. First, commitment decisions and day-ahead forecasts for load and renewable generation are collected following the clearing of the day-ahead market. Second, this information is used to generate a training dataset of SCED instances using classical data augmentation techniques. Third, specialized ML models are trained, ideally one for each hour of the operating day, thereby mitigating the combinatorial explosion of commitment decisions: each ML model only needs to consider one set of commitments and focus on load/renewable scenarios around the forecasts for that hour. Fourth, throughout the operating day, the trained models are employed in real time to evaluate a large number of scenarios. The entire data-generation and training process is completed in a few hours. The remainder of the paper is organized as follows. Section \ref{sec:opt_pipeline} describes the interaction between day-ahead and real-time markets in the MISO system and provides an overview of the real-time SCED for MISO. Section \ref{sec:methodology} examines the behavior of real-time market solutions, proposes a combined Classification-Then-Regression architecture, and presents the overall ML pipeline. Numerical experiments on a real-life system are reported in Section \ref{sec:results}.

The same approach was adopted in Velloso et al. (cite as Velloso2020Combining) in the context of security-constrained preventive OPF. Specifically, the neural network was trained using Lagrangian duality techniques, and then employed as a proxy for the master problem in a column generation approach. Another research direction is to integrate ML models in the framework of optimization methods to increase runtime performance. More recently, Chatzos et al. [2021] have embedded the Lagrangian duality framework in a two-stage learning process which, using a regional decomposition of the power network, enables more efficient distributed training. In, the authors explore the possibility of learning feasible solutions for the unit commitment problem. In, Venzke et al. show that, in contrast to other approaches, active constraints do not necessarily reduce the complexity of the problem. The available research on ML for power systems has two main shortcomings: firstly, most of the research papers show numerical results on small academic test systems, which are one to two orders of magnitude smaller than the actual power grid. Second, most of the papers apply a DNN model to learn the feasible region of a dynamic SCOP and then convert the resulting DNN into a mixed-integer linear program. Secondly, almost all papers use artificially derived data whose distribution does not reflect the variability of real operations. Only changes in load are considered, for example, usually without considering spatial and temporal correlations. This is particularly worrying since the number of dimensions affects the convergence and accuracy of machine-learning methods. These limitations are: * other sources of uncertainty such as renewable production * variability of economic bids * changes in commitment decisions * throughout the day * To address these limitations, this paper proposes a novel ML-based trading mechanism based on the operational structure of the real market. The approach uses the TSO's advance knowledge of 1) its own commitment decisions and 2) the day-ahead forecasts of demand and renewable production, which are both available by the time the daily auction has been completed. The proposed learning procedure is depicted in Figure: Learning_Pipeline. First, we collect the dispatch decisions and the day-ahead forecasts of load and of the generation of the wind farm from the clearing of the market day. Then, with the help of classical data augmentation methods, we create a training set of SCED instances. The entire process of data generation and learning takes only a few hours. Third, the specialized ML models are trained, ideally one for each hour of the operating day, which helps to avoid the combinatorial explosion of the commitment decisions, as each ML model is only concerned with one set of commitments, and thus focuses on the load-renewable scenarios around the forecasts for the respective hour. Finally, during the operation, the trained models are used to evaluate a large number of scenarios in real time. The rest of the paper is organized as follows. Section reference, section :optimization_pipeline describes the interplay between the day-ahead and real-time markets in the MISO system and provides an overview of the real-time SCED for MISO. Section reference, section: methodology describes the properties of real-time market solutions, proposes a combined classification-regression architecture, and presents the entire machine learning process. Reporting the numerical experiments with the real system in the section entitled RESULTS.

text: DNA sequencing is designed to assess the genetic composition of individuals. Without delving into the specifics of the various technologies, these processes ascertain (fragments of) the genetic sequence. Typically, the primary data analysis involves, among other steps: 1) alignment against a reference genome, such as GRCh38 for human samples, and 2) variant calling. The primary outcome is a list of variants, i.e., a set of differences unique to the measured individual (sample), often presented in a tabular file like the Variant Call Format~(VCF)~\cite{vcf}. These variants are employed in subsequent applications ranging from fundamental and association research studies to clinical diagnostics. It is beneficial to focus solely on differences (relative to a reference) since the genome is generally large~(approximately $3 \cdot 10^9$ nucleotides for humans), but the individual differences between two genomes are relatively small~(approximately $0.6\%$~\cite{variation}). When variants are linked to phenotypic traits, they are documented in the literature and stored with their annotations in (locus-specific) databases. Typically, the representation of the variant in VCF is refined to a more suitable format for reporting. For this purpose, many (domain-specific) languages exist. The most notable are: \begin{itemize} \item Recommendations of the Human Genome Variation Society~(HGVS)~\cite{hgvs}; \item SPDI~\cite{spdi}, the internal data model for variants used by the National Center for Biotechnology Information (NCBI); \item Variant Representation Specification~(VRS)~\cite{vrs}, developed by the Global Alliance for Genomic Health (GA4GH). \end{itemize} These languages strive to represent the observed differences in a manner that is comprehensible to humans and/or interpretable by machines, and while VCF is implicitly tied to the tools and configuration used in the primary data analysis, these representations are process-agnostic and universally interpretable. In the domain of variant recording, certain simplifications are common. First, small (local) variants on a single molecular sequence (part of the same haplotype) are recorded separately, as this is convenient when storing large numbers of variants in databases. Phasing information, i.e., whether small variants are part of the same haplotype, is often incomplete or missing. This is partly a direct result of the sequencing technology and partly because this information is removed. Second, in some representations (notably, HGVS), uncertainties may be expressed. Typically, the uncertainties pertain to the positioning of the variant within the reference genome, but the exact composition of larger insertions might also be unknown. Finally, unchanged regions may be implicit. During primary data analysis, particularly the alignment step, the sequence from the reference genome is assumed to be present even when direct evidence, such as coverage information from the sequencing process, is absent. For the remainder of this paper, we adopt a strict perspective on the nature of variants: \begin{enumerate} \item A variant consists of deletions, insertions, or a combination thereof with respect to a single molecular sequence. When these operations occur in combination, they are considered phased, in cis, or part of the same allele and can be documented as phase sets or allele descriptions. Many variant description languages have introduced higher-order operations like single nucleotide variants (SNV) (referred to as substitutions in HGVS), multi-nucleotide variants (deletion/insertions), duplications, transpositions, inversions, repeats, etc. We consider all of these notions to be special cases of the definition provided above. \item We consider only \emph{interpretable} variants, i.e., given a \emph{reference sequence}, there is a deterministic and unambiguous method of ``applying'' the variants such that the result is the (originally) measured \emph{observed sequence}, cf. the Unix~\texttt{diff} and \texttt{patch} utilities. \end{enumerate} \noindent As is already observed within the various variant representation languages, it is often feasible to have multiple representations describing the same observed sequence. These possibilities can arise from the choice of ``operator'', e.g., an SNV can also be represented by a deletion of one nucleotide followed by an insertion of one nucleotide. Another factor contributing to the number of possibilities is the structure of the reference sequence. Consider the reference sequence~\texttt{ATTTA} and the observed sequence~\texttt{ATTA}. One of the symbols~\texttt{T} is removed; specifying which one precisely yields a number~($3$) of possibilities. To determine a universally accepted representation of a variant, most variant representation languages employ a \emph{normalization} procedure. Normalization selects a \emph{canonical} representation from the set of possibilities. Unfortunately, this procedure is not standardized across the various languages, e.g., the $3'$-rule in HGVS vs. the $5'$-rule in VCF. Within a specific language, however, proper normalization resolves the issue of identifying \emph{equivalent} variant representations. The implications of using non-normalized variant representations have been reviewed in~\cite{variant_name, variant_calling, curation, litvar}. Solutions to this problem are presented in~\cite{unified, improved_vcf, vmc_spec, smash, plyranges, gql, ask2me, deletions}. Often dedicated tools~\cite{varsome, validator, mutalyzer, vde} are required to rigorously apply the proposed normalization procedure. Normalized variant representations can be textually compared using standard string matching. \noindent Arguably, the identification of equivalent variant representations, i.e., determining whether two variant descriptions result in the same observed sequence, is currently the most intriguing query in the variant domain, as it enables the grouping and matching of equivalent variants and their annotations. With the advent of long-read single-molecule sequencing technologies (provided by platforms such as those manufactured by Pacific Biosciences and Oxford Nanopore), which are capable of providing direct evidence of numerous small variants that are part of the same haplotype, a richer set of questions arises. For example, identification of suballeles, which is of interest in the fields of molecular microbiology (strain typing) and pharmacogenomics (star allele calling), can be achieved by determining whether the suballele of interest is contained within the observed allele. Minimal sequence-level alignments, informally defined as sequences of deletions/insertions that transform one string into another, having the shortest length possible, are used to define relations between given variants of the same reference sequence. Figure~\ref{fig:example} provides an example. In Section~\ref{sec:formal} we precisely define how the relations depend on the set of all alignments between the two sequences. In the example situation, the containment relation takes precedence over the overlap relation. In this paper, we explore the relations of variants in an exhaustive manner. In addition to the equivalence relation, we partition the domain of binary variant relations into Boolean relations: equivalence; containment, i.e., either a variant is fully contained in another or a variant fully contains another; overlap, i.e., two variants have (at least) one common element; and disjoint, i.e., no common elements. Because of this partitioning, exactly one of the aforementioned relations is true for every pair of variants. For determining the relation, we consider all (minimal) variant representations simultaneously.

text: The Tresillo is a rhythm originating from Africa, which was introduced to the Caribbean during the Atlantic Slave Trade era. Popularized in Cuba, this rhythm subsequently spread globally\cite{acquista2009tresillo, floyd1999black} and is present in numerous musical genres. \par While it serves as a primary rhythm independently, the Tresillo is also employed as a rhythmic pattern in other rhythms, such as the Reggaeton and Clave rhythms. Based on \cite{floyd1999black}, the Tresillo rhythm can be defined as follows (see Figure \ref{fig:tresillo}). The rhythm pattern comprises a dotted eighth note, followed by a sixteenth note, an eighth rest, and an eighth note, repeated twice within a 4/4 measure. By adding a beat on each quarter note, the Reggaeton rhythm is formed (see Figure \ref{fig:reggaeton}). Altering the second half of the measure to include an eighth rest, two eighth notes, and another eighth rest results in the basic Clave rhythm pattern (see Figure \ref{fig:clave}). The Tresillo rhythm is frequently utilized in Latin American music. However, the application of this "danceable Cuban Clave son"\cite{sethares2014geometry} is not confined to Latin American music, as it has also been incorporated into Western music's rhythm sections \cite{sethares2014geometry, biamonte2018rhythmic}. Recent popular examples include songs such as "Shape of You" by Ed Sheeran and "Cheap Thrills" by Sia, both of which topped the Billboard Charts. Further examination of the pop charts by the authors, through listening to the Billboard Charts, confirms the regular use of this rhythm in pop music. Although the use, evolution, and popularity of the Tresillo rhythm have been explored in qualitative studies \cite{acquista2009tresillo, sandroni2001tresillo, sethares2014geometry, biamonte2018rhythmic, floyd1999black}, its popularity has not been quantitatively analyzed before. In pursuit of a method to examine the use of this specific rhythm, we developed an approach to computationally represent the main rhythm of a pop song and the Tresillo rhythm, comparing both through various similarity measurements. Based on these similarity measures, a distinct temporal trend in Tresillo usage can be observed in the US Billboard Top 20 Charts over the past 20 years (1999-2019). \par This paper is structured as follows: First, the secondary literature from several relevant fields will be discussed. Subsequently, several assumptions necessary for conducting the presented analysis will be outlined in the problem statement section. The Data section will address the selected data sources and data format for the analysis. In the method section, the final data representation, proposed rhythm similarity measures, and evaluation metrics will be presented and explained. In the results section, the various rhythm similarity measures will be evaluated and compared. This section also includes a description and analysis of the temporal trend. The paper concludes with a discussion of the chosen methods and obtained results. Additionally, a possible interpretation of the results is presented. Finally, we propose potential extensions of the presented work.
