text: Legged robots exhibit remarkable versatility and can be applied across a broad spectrum of applications. However, achieving robust locomotion remains a complex issue that requires further exploration. Stability and safety are critical prerequisites for a robot to operate effectively in real-world environments. The question arises: despite the versatility of legged robots, why do they not yet match human capabilities? To realize the intended versatility, we explored the fundamental aspect of learning balance recovery strategies. Humans employ a variety of strategies (e.g., arm movements, ankle and hip adjustments, stepping, etc.) to regain balance following an external disturbance. They utilize past experiences to refine their methods. Furthermore, we examined existing biped robot locomotion frameworks. Although their stability has improved significantly, they are still not sufficiently stable and safe for use in everyday environments. Several stabilization approaches for biped robots have been proposed, which can be categorized into three major groups. In the remainder of this section, these categories will be introduced, and recent works in each category will be briefly reviewed. \subsection{Analytical Approaches} The fundamental concept behind approaches in this category involves using a dynamics model of the robot and designing a set of controllers (e.g., force controller~\cite{mason2016balancing}, hybrid position/force~\cite{faraji2019bipedal}, admittance controller~\cite{caron2020icra}) based on specific criteria to minimize tracking error. The Linear Inverted Pendulum~(LIP) is the most widely used model in the literature, abstracting the robot's overall dynamics as a single mass. It limits the vertical movement of the mass to provide a linear model, enabling a rapid solution for real-time implementations. This model has been studied and extended for decades to design and analyze legged robot locomotion~\cite{takenaka2009real,englsberger2015three}. Takaneka et al.~\cite{takenaka2009real} introduced the Divergent Component of Motion~(DCM) concept, which divides the LIP's dynamics into stable and unstable components, such that controlling the unstable component suffices to maintain stability. In~\cite{englsberger2015three}, DCM was extended to 3D, and several control approaches, including classical feedback controllers~\cite{morisawa2014biped}, Linear Quadratic Regulator~(LQR)-based methods~\cite{faraji2019bipedal,8967778}, and Model Predictive Control~(MPC)~\cite{brasseur2015robust}, have been proposed to formulate biped locomotion frameworks. All of these aim to compensate for tracking error by employing a combination of three strategies: manipulating the Ground Reaction Force~(GRF) and adjusting the position and timing of the next step. Recently, researchers have been exploring the relaxation of LIP assumptions (e.g., COM vertical motion and angular momentum), which introduces challenges associated with nonlinearities~\cite{caron2020icra, kajita2018biped, seyde2018inclusion}. \vspace{-2mm} \subsection{Machine Learning Approaches} Approaches in this category are designed to learn a feasible policy through interaction with the environment. Currently, Deep Reinforcement Learning~(DRL) has demonstrated its capability in solving complex locomotion and manipulation tasks, which typically involve high-dimensional continuous observation and action spaces~\cite{gu2017deep,abreu2019learning}. Data augmentation in DRL is commonly used to enhance optimization performance; however, in this work, we limit the focus to symmetry-oriented solutions. The process of generating symmetric data from actual samples is employed to improve various robotic tasks~\cite{lin2020robotics}, including the walking gait of different humanoid models~\cite{abdolhosseini2019learning} and quadruped robots~\cite{mishra2019augmenting} (with more than one plane of symmetry). Learning from scratch with DRL can result in highly efficient behaviors, even in asymmetrical configurations~\cite{Abreu2019runfaster}. Nonetheless, if not regulated through model constraints (e.g., symmetry, pattern generators), it can be difficult to produce human-like behaviors in a reasonable timeframe. \subsection{Hybrid Approaches: combining analytical and learning} Approaches in this category focus on integrating the potential of both aforementioned categories. To achieve this, learning algorithms can be combined with model-based gait pattern generators to predict parameters and learn residual dynamics (compensatory action), leading to impressively accurate behaviors~\cite{koryakovskiy2018model,ahn2020data}. These frameworks typically consist of a set of layers connected in hierarchical structures. Yang et al.~\cite{yang2018learning} developed a hierarchical framework to ensure the stability of a humanoid robot by learning motor skills. Their framework comprises two independent layers: the high-level layer generates a set of joint angles, and the low-level layer translates those angles into joint torques using a set of PD controllers. Their reward function consisted of six distinct terms, mostly related to traditional push recovery strategies, and was obtained by summing all terms with different weights. \subsection{Overview of the Proposed Framework and Contributions} This work concentrates on bipedal locomotion, which is the most challenging aspect of legged robots. Specifically, we aim to address the intriguing question of whether a learning algorithm can learn to control and modulate a model-based control policy, such as a gait pattern generator. Our contributions are as follows: \textbf{(i)} we developed a locomotion framework for humanoid robots that integrates both analytical control and machine learning. An overview of this system is depicted in Fig.~\ref{fig:Cover}. Specifically, we use an abstract dynamics model to analytically formulate a closed-loop biped locomotion and recovery strategies as a kernel, and combine it with a symmetry-enhanced optimization framework using Proximal Policy Optimization~(PPO)~\cite{schulman2017ppo} to learn residual dynamics. The learned policy adjusts a set of parameters of the pattern generator and generates compensatory actions as the residual dynamics to regain stability; \textbf{(ii)} we proposed a learning method where the data is only partially augmented, leveraging the symmetry to improve learning time and human-likeness without restricting asymmetric movements, thus broadening the range of possible behaviors. The remainder of this paper is structured as follows: In Section~\ref{sec:pattern}, the architecture of our fully parametric kernel pattern generator will be presented, and each module will be explained. Subsequently, in Section~\ref{sec:learningResidual}, our learning framework will be introduced, and we will explain how we augmented this framework with the kernel pattern generator to regulate kernel parameters and learn model-free skills~(generating compensatory joint positions). In Section~\ref{sec:simScenarios}, a set of simulation scenarios will be designed to validate the performance of the proposed framework. Subsequently, in Section~\ref{sec:simulations}, a series of simulations will be conducted to provide assessments and analyses regarding overall performance, optimized policy behavior, symmetry, and robustness. Finally, conclusions and future research directions are presented in Section~\ref{sec:conclusion}.

text: The objective of this paper is to examine the Parallel Drone Scheduling Traveling Salesman Problem (PDSTSP), which is defined as follows. We are provided with a complete undirected graph $G=(V, E)$ where the set of vertices is $V=\{0,1,...,n, n+1\}$ and the set of edges is $E=\{(i, j): i, j \in V, i < j\}$. Vertex 0 signifies the depot, while vertex $n+1$ is a duplicate of the depot vertex, introduced for modeling purposes. The other vertices represent the customer set $V_c$. At the depot, there is a truck and a set $D$ of $m$ drones available for delivery operations. A subset of \textit{drone-eligible} customers is denoted as $V_{d}\subseteq V_c$, whose distance from the depot and parcel weight are suitable for drone delivery. The set of customers that must be served by the truck is denoted by $V_{t}=V_c \setminus V_d$. The travel time for the truck from node $i$ to node $j$ is denoted as $t_{ij}$. The time a drone requires to service customer $i$ is denoted as $t'_i$, which is calculated by doubling the flight time from the depot to customer $i$. The PDSTSP involves constructing a set of routes for the truck and the fleet of drones such that: (i) each customer vertex is visited exactly once by either the truck or a drone; (ii) the truck route begins and ends at the depot; (iii) the drone performs round trips from the depot to serve several customers (one customer per trip); (iv) the total time to serve all customers and return all vehicles to the depot is minimized. The PDSTSP has garnered considerable attention in the literature since its initial introduction in \citet*{murray2015flying}. The authors propose a Mixed Integer Linear Programming (MILP) formulation to model the problem and develop a basic heuristic. This heuristic divides the customers into two subsets, one for the truck and another for the drones. Two subproblems, the TSP and the Parallel Machine Scheduling (PMS) problem, defined on two customer sets, are solved separately to construct the truck tour and drone tours, respectively. Additionally, an improvement step is conducted to reassign customers either to the drone set or to the truck to better balance the activities of the truck and drones. The solution approaches are tested on small instances with up to 20 customers. Numerous efforts have been made to efficiently solve larger PDSTSP instances. \citet*{mbiadou2018iterative} propose the first metaheuristic, known as the iterative two-step heuristic method. The first step constructs a customer sequence (also referred to as a giant or TSP tour) that visits all the customers. In the second step, dynamic programming is employed to divide the giant tour into a truck tour and a set of trips for the drones, creating a complete PDSTSP solution. The method is tested on newly generated instances with up to 229 customers. \citet*{dell2020matheuristic} subsequently propose a matheuristic that employs the same concept as found in \cite*{mbiadou2018iterative}. However, instead of dynamic programming, a MILP approach is used to manage the second step. The results indicate that the algorithm is slower but yields better solutions than the heuristic of \cite{mbiadou2018iterative}. A nature-inspired algorithm called Hybrid Ant Colony Optimization (HACO) is proposed in \citet*{Dinh2021}. The algorithm reuses the concept from \cite{mbiadou2018iterative} that represents a PDSTSP solution as a permutation of all customers. However, the authors propose a new dynamic programming approach with a controllable number of states while exploring a broader solution space to divide the giant tour into a complete PDSTSP solution. Several problem-specific components such as local search and solution construction also significantly enhance the algorithm's performance. When tested on benchmark instances from the literature, the HACO algorithm surpasses the two existing metaheuristics in terms of both execution time and solution quality. The most recent metaheuristic for the PDSTSP is a Ruin-and-Recreate algorithm called Slack Induction by String and Sweep Removals (SISSR) introduced in \cite{Nguyen2021}. By effectively exploiting PDSTSP solution characteristics, the metaheuristic introduces ``sufficient" flexibility to a solution through new removal operators during the ruin phase. This is expected to improve the potential for enhancing solutions later in the recreate phase. Also in \cite{Nguyen2021}, the authors introduce a new variant of the PDSTSP called PDSVRP, which allows multiple trucks and considers the objective of minimizing total transportation costs. \citet*{Raj2021} present a variant of the PDSVRP problem where they consider an objective function that minimizes the completion time for all vehicles to return to the depot. The authors propose three MILP formulations and develop a branch-and-price (BAP) algorithm and a BAP-based heuristic to solve the problem. They report that their exact methods can optimally solve all the small PDSTSP instances of \cite{murray2015flying} and three instances with 52 customers from \cite{mbiadou2018iterative}. Most recently, \citet*{MBIADOUSALEU2021} generalize the PDSTSP problem similarly to the PDSVRP. The problem is named the Parallel Drone Scheduling Multiple Traveling Salesman Problem. A hybrid Iterated Local Search is proposed. A MILP formulation and a straightforward branch-and-cut approach are also designed to solve small instances. As previously mentioned, most approaches proposed to solve the PDSTSP fall within the category of heuristic methods. To our knowledge, the results of exact algorithms for the problem are quite limited. Only optimal results obtained on small instances with no more than 20 customers and three instances with 52 customers are provided in \cite{murray2015flying, dell2020matheuristic, Raj2021}. Optimal solutions for 87 out of 90 benchmark instances with up to 229 customers created by \cite{mbiadou2018iterative} have never been reported. The primary motivation of this paper is to address this methodological gap by proposing a simple, yet efficient exact branch-and-cut (B\&C) algorithm for the PDSTSP. The experimental results on the currently largest problem instances of \cite{mbiadou2018iterative} demonstrate that the developed solution approach can solve all but two instances within a reasonable execution time. To provide more challenging instances for future testing of solution methods, we introduce a new set of instances with up to 600 customers. We report the results of the state-of-the-art algorithms obtained on these instances to further evaluate their performance. The remainder of the paper is structured as follows: Section \ref{sec-formulation} describes our MILP formulation along with several valid inequalities, upon which the branch-and-cut algorithm is proposed in Section \ref{sec-method}. Section \ref{sec-experiment} presents experimental results, and Section \ref{sec-conclusion} concludes our research.

The rest of the article is organized as follows: in Section "Formula" we present our MILP formulation with some valid inequalities, to which the branch-and-cut method is applied in Section "Methods". The results of experiments with the currently largest instances of the iterative method show that the developed solution method can solve all but two instances in a reasonable time. Section III gives a summary of the experimental results, and section IV the conclusion.

text: In global efforts to address climate change and transition to sustainable energy sources, there has been a notable increase in the development and advancement of wind power systems in recent years \cite{darwish_al-dabbagh_2020}. However, the complexity of the environments where wind turbines are deployed, particularly offshore, often results in irregular loads, operational inconsistencies, and failures in various electrical and mechanical sub-components within the turbine \cite{windenergy_journal}. Operations & Maintenance (O&M) is essential for addressing such issues through fault detection and diagnosis \cite{ATTOUI201411}, and currently accounts for up to one-third of the total cost of energy generation \cite{seyr_muskulus_2019}. Condition-based monitoring (CBM) \cite{STETCO2019620} is crucial in O&M, enabling the monitoring of operational changes and anomalies in the turbine and its sub-components. Over the past decade, there has been growing interest in using signal-processing techniques and physics-based modeling for CBM. Recently, the wind industry has seen the application of Artificial Intelligence (AI) techniques for data-driven decision-making in O&M, utilizing Supervisory Control & Data Acquisition (SCADA) data generated by various sensors in the turbine at regular intervals. Some applications of Explainable AI (XAI) models \cite{BARREDOARRIETA202082,8329419,app10093258} provide interpretations and reasoning behind predictions made by traditionally black-box AI models during decision support, such as identifying feature importances for SCADA parameters leading to faults \cite{windenergy_journal}. These techniques have been highly successful, particularly for anomaly prediction in turbine sub-components \cite{anomaly_paperhongshan,electronics9050751,Bo_2019}, wind resource assessment \cite{MURTHY20171320,DAI2017378}, and forecasting critical operational parameters \cite{CHEN2018414,RePEc:eee:appene:v:241:y:2019:i:c:p:229-244,RePEc:eee:energy:v:201:y:2020:i:c:s0360544220308008} with high accuracy, which can be vital for improving the utilization efficiency of wind energy \cite{LIU2020113324}. However, they fail to provide contextualized information (e.g., detailed descriptions of failures and maintenance reports to fix/prevent such inconsistencies), which is essential for achieving ambient intelligence during decision support. More importantly, these techniques do not offer a concrete foundation to serve as a generic basis for critical concepts in the wind industry, related to maintenance strategies and their relationship with other sources of heterogeneous information, such as SCADA data from sensors, alarm logs, images describing failures, and prognostic actions, etc. Knowledge bases (KBs) or knowledge graphs (KGs) play a crucial role in supporting effective and informed decision-making by interlinking heterogeneous entities (such as numerical data from sensors) with contextualized and semantic information \cite{amador-paper-kg}. KGs have been successfully used for optimal decision support in several safety-critical applications such as healthcare for clinical decision support \cite{health_semantic}, power systems for optimizing service processes \cite{Yuan_2018}, manufacturing for process safety management \cite{MAO2020107094}, finance for making business decisions \cite{kg_finance_yang}, etc. Given the multidisciplinary nature of wind farm construction and management, as well as the presence of multiple subsystems interacting with other subsystems and various external components, a systematic organization of knowledge in the wind industry can play a crucial role in assisting developers, designers, and researchers to utilize such domain-specific information for decision support \cite{wes-5-259-2020}. Compared to other disciplines, the wind industry has seen very limited application of KGs for explainable decision support. In early work in this area, Zhu et al. \cite{4470371} developed a wind power plant information model using the web ontology language (OWL) for systematic management of domain-specific information. The proposed ontology in the paper consists of conceptual information for wind power plant management with multiple classes based on different types of turbines, their functional parts, etc., embedded as semantic information with corresponding OWL descriptions. While the paper demonstrates the significant potential of graph databases for managing complex information in the wind industry through its conceptual overview, it does not provide a practical demonstration of the proposed ontology, including its use cases in real-world information management in the wind energy domain. Moreover, there is no mention of the applicability of the proposed ontology for O&M, particularly to facilitate decision support in real-world turbines. Küçük and Arslan \cite{KUCUK2014484} utilized web resources, specifically from Wikipedia, to develop a domain ontology for the wind energy sector. Their ontology is constructed semi-automatically and provides extensive coverage of the wind energy domain as a discipline, including terms like meteorological data, sub-components of the turbine, monitoring and control systems, etc. This can be useful for utilization in question-answering systems during information retrieval, where specific segments of natural language texts from the Wikipedia articles relevant to the end user can be accessed easily. While the semi-automatic construction of the ontology is less time-consuming and simpler, it cannot provide low-level details pertaining to the wind industry and O&M of turbines. Moreover, it lacks the ability to provide a coherent view of critical aspects in CBM, including the role of SCADA data for anomaly prediction and power forecasting, maintenance tasks for failures in the turbine and its sub-components, and more thorough and technically detailed descriptions for engineers & technicians beyond the Wikipedia articles. The role of the KG for utilization in real-world decision support systems is also not showcased in the paper. In another study, Quaeghebeur et al. \cite{wes-5-259-2020} proposed a graph database for the wind energy domain, consisting of a conceptual overview of several important terms and parameters in the wind energy sector, such as power curves, associated relationships between turbine sub-components, mathematical and statistical distributions for modeling vital parameters, etc. The KG for this study was developed from scratch by the authors and provides a foundational ontology for the wind turbine as a system with a specific focus on offshore wind power. Similar to Zhu et al. \cite{4470371}, their focus is on developing knowledge representations and structured information pertaining to the wind industry. The paper provides significant information and descriptions that can be queried from the KG, being particularly beneficial for education and training purposes. However, the proposed KG does not contain any description of different types of faults that occur in real-world turbines, varieties of alarms, and their relationship to turbine sub-components and maintenance action strategies to fix/prevent the failures. More importantly, it does not demonstrate the applicability of the KG for O&M, and its use cases for explainable decision support in real-world practical scenarios. As is evident, while these few existing studies have demonstrated the potential of utilizing KGs for systematically structuring conceptual information in the wind industry, they only serve as an endpoint \cite{amador-paper-kg} providing information for consultation without the ability to further reason over the data. Moreover, these ontologies need to be queried manually through specialized programming languages to extract relevant and meaningful information, which may not be easily accessible to turbine engineers & technicians. The existing studies clearly do not focus on the critical aspects of O&M and their utility in decision-making systems for tasks such as recommendations and predictions. We believe that the optimal utility of KGs for decision support in the wind industry can only be realized by integrating conceptual information on O&M with other heterogeneous data, such as SCADA parameters from sensors, alarm types, turbine sub-components, preventive/predictive/corrective maintenance action strategies, etc., and their associated relationships. In this paper, we propose the role of KGs for explainable decision support in the wind industry and their utility in real-world applications for O&M. We present a novel KG, \textit{XAI4Wind}, and manually develop the domain-specific ontology for O&M in the wind industry. The proposed KG currently contains 537 nodes and 1059 relationships (of 9 different types) and includes several types of heterogeneous data such as descriptions of various types of SCADA features, alarm types, turbine sub-components, and maintenance action strategies. To demonstrate use cases, we show that the KG can be queried interactively in Neo4j, and graph data science algorithms can be applied to generate novel insights during O&M. Notably, we utilize SCADA data from an operational turbine and demonstrate its interfacing with an Explainable AI (XAI) model. We illustrate the intrinsic role that the proposed KG can play in decision support during various failures predicted in the turbine by the XAI model, by providing thorough descriptions of fault conditions and maintenance actions required to fix/prevent the failures. Unlike existing studies, our proposed KG can be queried both manually (by querying through relevant syntactic commands in programming) and automatically (through its integration with the XAI model), thereby paving the way for autonomous decision-making for the wind energy sector, which can serve as a complementary resource to aid decisions by engineers & technicians. According to Futia and Vetrò \cite{info11020122}, the integration of KGs with XAI models can contribute to more comprehensive decisions through knowledge matching, cross-disciplinary, and interactive explanations. Figure ~\ref{intro_kgfig} describes the overview of our proposed KG and its applications, which are demonstrated in this paper. The different elements (SCADA data, XAI model, and model predictions) have mutual interaction and can also consult the KG independently for information querying/retrieval. We make the KG publicly available, and it can be further developed/expanded in the future as new terms, concepts, and maintenance action strategies emerge in the wind industry. We envisage that our work can serve as a foundation for encouraging future research in utilizing KGs for O&M in the wind industry, providing more value and utility to the conventionally opaque AI models to move closer to achieving human-level intelligence. The paper is organized as follows: Section ~\ref{data_sec} describes the datasets used for constructing the KG and demonstrating its application on an operational turbine. Section ~\ref{kg_databases} introduces KG databases and their basic concepts. The development of the proposed KG is described in Section ~\ref{dev_kg}. Section ~\ref{use_kg} discusses potential use cases of the KG in decision support. A brief discussion on the experimental results and the wider applicability of the KG to other turbines beyond the LDT is presented in Section ~\ref{discussion}. Finally, Section ~\ref{conclusion} concludes the paper and outlines the path for future work.

text: Video Retrieval is among the most significant and challenging issues in the digital realm today. It involves ranking videos within a database according to their relevance to user-submitted queries. Although most practical applications utilize video metadata to transform the problem into a straightforward page ranking issue, there exist extensive databases of videos lacking labeled metadata. User queries can take various forms. The most common form of input is textual input. One of the most widely accessible applications of text-to-video retrieval is Google's video search. However, its performance is largely dependent on the metadata of the videos within its search domain. Some research has been conducted in recent years on video retrieval using text queries, and performance in this area has improved over time. In this paper, we concentrate our efforts on video retrieval using image queries, an area with comparatively less research. There are also limitations in most methods proposed thus far, and numerous challenges must be addressed by any proposed method. The most significant of these challenges is devising an efficient method for storing the videos in the search database. Another major unresolved challenge is leveraging the temporal information present in video data. While image classification and object detection tasks in images have demonstrated significant success in recent years, merely searching for objects in video frames would fail to utilize the temporal information inherent in videos. In this paper, we introduce a novel approach to address this issue. Initially, we pre-process a video database to extract key features from the video frames. These features are clustered so that similar frames are grouped into the same cluster. We generate embeddings for these clusters by aggregating the embeddings of their constituent frames. To incorporate temporal information in videos, we model these clusters as nodes within a graph. Subsequently, the cluster embeddings are enhanced by incorporating information from neighboring clusters. These enhanced cluster embeddings are stored and utilized in our video ranking process. The proposed method was evaluated using the MSR-VTT dataset.

text: Future cellular communication systems are anticipated to further enhance the range of applications offered by 5G systems \cite{yazar6g}. They will offer a highly adaptable platform capable of delivering features such as integrated sensing, flexible multi-band usage, and smart, green, and secure communications. In next-generation cellular communication, \ac{AI}, integrated sensing, and communication are expected to be crucial enablers. \ac{V2X} or autonomous driving has garnered significant attention in recent years and is anticipated to be utilized in next-generation communication systems. For instance, the convergence of \ac{MEC} and blockchain technologies for a novel, robust, resilient, and reliable architecture for V2X communications is proposed in \cite{khan2021robust}. With recent industrial advancements from Google's Waymo, Baidu's Apollo, and Tesla's Autopilot technologies \cite{Cusumano}, full self-driving capabilities are feasible in the future. However, the foundational secure communication technologies supporting them remain in an early stage. In the realm of security, quantum computers are gradually being developed by several prominent \ac{IT} and cloud companies (Google, IBM, Honeywell, and Microsoft). In the long term, quantum computers are expected to achieve quantum superiority, and recent industrial efforts by Google have demonstrated that these claims are plausible \cite{arute2019quantum}. Devices and computers with quantum capabilities can swiftly address complex problems by executing numerous operations concurrently. Quantum-capable devices can also be employed to compromise security protocols established between network devices (such as \ac{TLS}, \ac{DTLS}, \ac{IPSec}, etc.), breach encryption schemes used in security protocols, and expose secure communications. In this context, algorithms resistant to quantum threats in security protocols operated between mobile network devices must be employed. Consequently, secure communication can be established within the mobile network. \ac{NIST} is currently addressing this issue and has organized a competition to select the most effective algorithm resistant to quantum attacks. Algorithms such as NTRU, Saber, and Kyber have already advanced to the final round of the \ac{NIST} competition \cite{NIST_comp}. After the \ac{NIST} competition concludes, one algorithm will be chosen as the standard \ac{QRSA} and implemented across all devices (similar to \ac{AES}/\ac{DES}, which resulted from previous \ac{NIST} competitions and are widely used today). Currently, existing encryption algorithms can be implemented in the software and hardware of mobile devices to ensure the operation of the security protocol. However, a significant challenge arises when implementing \glspl{QRSA}. This challenge is determining how to execute the computational processes within the algorithm. In examining existing \glspl{QRSA} such as NTRU, Saber, and Kyber, the computational load on the \ac{CPU} cores of devices for processing mathematical operations with very high-order polynomials is substantial. The computational processes for existing encryption algorithms such as \ac{AES}, \ac{ECC}, etc., are already in use, and the current hardware capabilities of devices can support these types of operations. However, for \glspl{QRSA}, we are dealing with very high-degree polynomials. Therefore, the computational resources required for \glspl{QRSA} on the devices are greater than those needed for the encryption algorithms already in use. For this reason, performing computations for a \ac{QRSA} based on high-order polynomials with the currently available software and hardware is very challenging. To address this issue, an efficient computation and orchestration framework is needed that is aware of the entire topological view of the mobile and \ac{V2X} network and can execute different computation methods for each \ac{QRSA}. To this end, the following contributions are made in this paper: \begin{itemize} \item We discuss key concepts and present the integration of post-quantum and mobile network connectivity through the \ac{SCO} framework with potential use cases. (Section \ref{Background} and \ref{frameworks}) \item We evaluate how post-quantum methods can be integrated into mobile networks via simulation analysis and discuss the evaluation results. (Section \ref{experiments}) \item From a standardization perspective, we describe current \glspl{SDO} efforts and their potential contributions to network management and orchestration and post-quantum technologies. (Section \ref{standardization}) \end{itemize}

text: In recommender systems, user-item interactions and their associated side information can be represented as a graph consisting of a set of objects (nodes) and their relationships (edges). Since these graphs inherently contain at least two distinct types of nodes, namely user $u$ and item $v$, they are classified as heterogeneous graphs (or heterographs). Owing to the significant expressive power of these graphs and the rapid advancement of graph-based methods~\cite{kipf2016gcn, schlichtkrull2018rgcn, wu2019simplifying, chen2020simple}, graph-based recommendation methods~\cite{wang2019ngcf, chen2020revisiting, he2020lightgcn, wang2018ripplenet, Wang2019kgcn, wang2019kgat, fan2019graph, Liu2020Hetero} have garnered increasing attention in recent years. To obtain more effective representations, some researchers attempt to leverage the structure of the interaction graph by propagating user and item embeddings across it. For instance, inspired by the graph convolutional network (GCN)~\cite{kipf2016gcn}, Wang \emph{et al.} proposed NGCF (neural graph collaborative filtering)~\cite{wang2019ngcf} to derive more effective embeddings. Subsequently, both LR-GCCF (linear residual graph convolutional collaborative filtering)~\cite{chen2020revisiting} and LightGCN~\cite{he2020lightgcn} discovered that eliminating certain components in standard GCN (such as non-linear activation and feature transformation) can enhance performance for collaborative filtering (CF). Despite achieving notable progress, existing graph-based representation learning methods still encounter the data sparsity issue, which is prevalent in real-world recommendations. Since the aforementioned methods are not specifically designed to tackle this problem, they may experience significant performance degradation when confronted with it. A typical solution to mitigate this issue is incorporating side information~\cite{GUO2017202}, which can increase indirect node connections or enrich node features. Recommendation-related textual information contains abundant side information, but most existing efforts~\cite{Wang2019kgcn, fan2019graph, wang2019kgat} that incorporate side information overlook it, thereby limiting their performance. To address the data sparsity issue, similar to HGNR (heterogeneous graph neural recommendation)~\cite{Liu2020Hetero}, based on the interaction graph (Figure~\ref{fig:graph}-(a)), we introduce description and comment nodes to construct our heterograph (Figure~\ref{fig:graph}-(b)). However, it is important to note that merely adding these nodes does not increase indirect connections between users and items. Nevertheless, the text nodes themselves contain abundant features, which are beneficial for adjusting the embeddings of users and items. Inspired by this, we employ advanced natural language processing (NLP) techniques to initialize the embeddings of text nodes, thereby integrating the semantics to enhance representation ability. Through node information propagation, the embeddings of users and items will incorporate textual knowledge, which can effectively help mitigate the data sparsity issue. HGNR employs standard GCN to learn embeddings on heterograph. In other words, it converts the heterogeneous learning process into a homogeneous one, which may result in unexpected information loss and performance degradation. By iteratively applying the GCN framework over different relations, RGCN (Relational Graph Convolutional Network) has been shown to effectively handle the highly multi-relational data characteristic on heterograph~\cite{schlichtkrull2018rgcn}. In light of this, applying RGCN to propagate information on heterograph is a more suitable choice. However, simply using the standard RGCN is not ideal, as distinguishing different relations requires the standard RGCN to have a larger parameter scale than the GCN on the same heterograph, complicating and reducing the efficiency of training the RGCN-based model. To resolve this issue, we propose a modified RGCN to propagate information on heterograph in this work. Firstly, it has been demonstrated in \cite{wu2019simplifying, he2020lightgcn} that feature transformation and non-linear activation of the standard GCN contribute minimally to CF performance. Similarly, we eliminate these two components to simplify RGCN and thereby enhance its performance and efficiency. Secondly, we adopt the weighted layer combination in LightGCN~\cite{he2020lightgcn} and the initial residual in GCNII~\cite{chen2020simple} to further refine RGCN for improved performance. The experimental results indicate that the aforementioned modifications on RGCN can significantly enhance recommendation performance. After obtaining efficient user and item embeddings through feature propagation of the modified RGCN, another crucial component of the recommender system is the matching function. Almost all existing graph-based representation learning methods use the inner product as the matching function~\cite{wang2019ngcf, he2020lightgcn, Wang2019kgcn, wang2019kgat}. However, in the heterographs we constructed, both the description and comment nodes contain rich semantics, and the simple linear inner product is inadequate for these complex features. To address the semantic features learned by GNN from heterographs, GraphRec~\cite{fan2019graph} concatenated latent factors of users and items and used an MLP (multi-layer perception) to predict ratings. Meanwhile, DeepCF~\cite{deng2019deepcf}, which applies an MLP neural network on the user-item interaction matrix, combines the strengths of neural representation learning and neural matching function learning to overcome their respective limitations. Inspired by GraphRec and DeepCF, we design a predictive network that integrates graph-based representation learning with neural matching function learning to better accommodate the semantics. Specifically, the combination of graph-based representation learning and neural matching function learning can capture the low-rank user-item relations and jointly learn the complex matching function. In summary, the main contributions of our work in this paper are as follows: \begin{itemize} \item We construct a heterograph and initialize the embeddings of text nodes using advanced NLP techniques to exploit the knowledge in the related textual information. Then, by employing a modified RGCN, the semantics in these text nodes can be propagated to derive the representations of users and items. \item Recognizing that the inner product is ineffective for complex semantics, we propose a predictive framework that combines graph-based representation learning with neural matching function learning for improved predictions. \item Extensive experiments are conducted on three benchmark datasets, and the results confirm the superior performance of our method over several baselines. \end{itemize} The remainder of this paper is organized as follows: Section~\ref{sec: relatedwork} discusses related work; Section~\ref{sec: method} details the proposed model; Section~\ref{sec: experiment} presents and analyzes the experimental results; Finally, Section~\ref{sec: conclusion} concludes this paper.

text: If autonomous vehicles are intended to function as traffic management systems \cite{wu2017flow}, it is essential for them to navigate safely around human-operated vehicles on highways and in urban areas. However, ensuring safe navigation is challenging due to the significant uncertainty present in real-world driving situations, which complicates the driving problem. Typically, Hamilton-Jacobi reachability analysis (HJI) is employed to identify safe strategies in the presence of unknown elements within a dynamical system \cite{bansal2017hamilton}. In prior research, a framework was developed \cite{fisac2018general} to safeguard a system against a single known source of uncertainty using Hamilton-Jacobi reachability, aiming to protect the system from the worst-case scenario. Nevertheless, in actual driving situations, it might be necessary to account for multiple sources of uncertainty. As illustrated in figures \ref{fig:sets} and \ref{fig:illustration}, extreme worst-case scenarios may not yield a viable safety strategy, and it could be that ensuring safety is unattainable. Therefore, in this study, we examine the reduction of conservativeness in Hamilton-Jacobi safety analysis by incorporating structure into some or all of the human models. Specifically, we explore a modeling approach concerning the second disturbance that leverages the structure of human behavior, enabling the application of differential game theory in more densely populated dynamic driving environments.

text: The NILC-Metrix set of metrics was developed through both funded projects involving multiple researchers and master's and doctoral projects at the Interinstitutional Center for Computational Linguistics --- NILC\footnote{\url{http://www.nilc.icmc.usp.br/}}, spanning from 2008 to 2021. Below, we summarise the motivation for creating this extensive set of metrics, the stages of its development, and the re-implementations of certain metrics to standardise the use of Natural Language Processing (NLP) tools. The initial impetus for developing a set of metrics for the automatic evaluation of textual complexity in BP originated from the PorSimples project, which focused on the Simplification of Portuguese Texts for Digital Inclusion and Accessibility \cite{candido-etal-2009-supporting,aluisio-gasperin-2010-fostering}. The PorSimples project targets individuals with low literacy who seek information from web texts but face challenges due to their rudimentary and basic literacy levels, as indicated by the functional literacy measure known as INAF\footnote{\url{https://ipm.org.br/inaf}}. In numerous projects reviewed in the literature, automatic text simplification is executed as a process that reduces the lexical and/or syntactic complexity of a text while attempting to maintain its meaning and information \cite{Carroll98practicalsimplification,Max2006,Shardlow2014}. However, certain simplification projects, such as the Terence project, require simplifications that enhance text comprehension both at the local level, aiding in establishing connections between adjacent sentences, and at the global level, assisting in constructing a mental representation of the text \cite{terence_2014}. Other initiatives, like the Newsela\footnote{\url{https://newsela.com/}} company, perform conceptual simplification, simplifying content as well as form \cite{xu-etal-2015-problems}. Newsela also incorporates elaborations in the text to clarify certain concepts or uses redundancies to highlight key parts of the text. Additionally, operations reduce and omit information unsuitable for a specific audience. Based on the aforementioned simplification projects, we recognised that textual complexity and simplification are closely linked in the NLP field. We also observed that the type of simplification employed in the Terence project aims to enhance text coherence, leading the authors to describe this simplification as occurring at the cognitive level. Newsela's simplification is the most comprehensive in terms of various operations, although it still lacks full automation (but see the advancements by \cite{alva-manchego-etal-2017-learning}). During the PorSimples project, we developed a system named \textbf{Facilita}, which adapts web content for readers with low literacy by employing lexical elaboration and named entity labeling \cite{Watanabe2010}, and the simplification system was named \textbf{Simplifica}. A distinctive feature of Simplifica was its two levels of simplification, termed natural and strong, designed to assist individuals literate at basic and rudimentary levels, respectively. To evaluate the textual complexity of the resulting text and determine whether the simplification objective was met, a multiclass predictor of textual complexity was constructed using traditional machine learning methods. This predictor necessitated the extraction of a set of metrics to evaluate text complexity and compute proxies to assess the cohesion and coherence of the simplifications supported by Simplifica's automatic rules. In this context, the Coh-Metrix-Port \cite{Scarton2010a,Scarton2010b,Scarton2010c} project was initiated. At NILC, prior to PorSimples, we conducted a readability study aimed at adapting the Flesch Index to BP \cite{fleschport1996}, based on a corpus designed to help identify the weights of the linear formula that evaluates word length and sentence length in texts from various genres and sources. The Flesch Index \cite{flesch1948} is premised on the theory that shorter words and sentences facilitate easier reading. Although practical, as it provides a numerical indication of text complexity that can be associated with educational levels, it does not specify which operations to perform on a text to achieve shorter sentence lengths, for instance. Furthermore, it can lead to errors, as brevity is not the sole characteristic of an easy-to-read text. One critique of the Flesch Index and other traditional readability formulas \cite{dalechall1948,gunning1952,fry1968,kincaidetal1975} is their frequent use as prescriptive guides for adapting instructional material, rather than as simple predictive tools for textual complexity \cite{crossley2008assessing}. These errors stem from a misunderstanding that traditional readability formulas were not designed to explain text difficulty, as they are not grounded in theories of text comprehension. Instead, these formulas were based on the statistical correlation of superficial text measures with its complexity level, previously determined by a linguist or education specialist, for example. Recognising the limitations of traditional readability formulas at the outset of the Coh-Metrix-Port project, we selected the Coh-Metrix project as the foundation for the metrics to be developed in PorSimples. Coh-Metrix computes computational cohesion and coherence metrics for both written and spoken texts \cite{Graesser2004,Coh-Metrix_2011,graesser2014coh} based on models of textual understanding and cognitive reading models \cite{kintsch1978toward,kintsch1973reading,kintsch1998comprehension} that elucidate: (i) how a reader engages with a text, (ii) the types of memories involved in reading, such as how excessive word use before the main verb negatively impacts sentence processing, (iii) the role of propositional content in speech \cite{kintsch1998comprehension}, indicating that enhancing text coherence improves comprehension \cite{crossley2007toward}, and (iv) how cohesion mechanisms, such as discourse markers and entity repetition, contribute to creating a coherent text. In summary, similar to the Coh-Metrix tool\footnote {\url{http://cohmetrix.com/}} for the English language, the textual complexity analysis planned in Coh-Metrix-Port employs a multilevel analysis framework. Coh-Metrix-Port offered 48 metrics grouped into 10 classes. However, one requirement was the use of open-source NLP tools. Consequently, many syntactic metrics were not implemented due to the lack of high-performing free parsers at the time. Subsequently, the AIC tool (Automatic Analysis of the Intelligibility of the Corpus) was developed \cite{maziero2008ferramenta} within the PorSimples project. AIC includes 39 metrics (most of which are syntactic) based on the Palavras parser \cite{bick2000palavras} (see details in Section 2). After PorSimples concluded in 2010, new metrics were added to the initial 48 of the Coh-Metrix-Port tool and the 39 of the AIC. This included 25 new metrics from the Coh-Metrix-Dementia \cite{CBMS_CMD_2015,Aluisio_Propor16}, developed in a master's dissertation. During the Coh-Metrix-Dementia implementation, the first re-implementation of Coh-Metrix-Port occurred to standardise interfaces and NLP tool usage. For instance, the nlpnet PoS tagger \cite{evaluating_2015} was established as the default tagger, as Coh-Metrix-Dementia incorporates the 48 metrics of Coh-Metrix-Port. In 2017, during a NILC student's PhD, a large lexical base with 26,874 BP words was automatically annotated with concreteness, age of acquisition, imageability, and subjective frequency (similar to familiarity) \cite{TSD2017}, facilitating the implementation of 24 psycholinguistic metrics. The technology transfer project titled \textit{Personalisation of Reading using Automatic Complexity Classification and Textual Adaptation tools} introduced 72 new metrics, many related to lexical and syntactic simplicity, to the already extensive set of metrics developed by NILC. Finally, the RastrOS project\footnote {\url{https://osf.io/9jxg3/?view_only=4f47843d12694f9faf4dd8fb23464ea9}} brought a new implementation to the 10 metrics based on semantic cohesion, via Latent Semantic Analysis (LSA) \cite{Landauer1997HowWC}, as well as for the calculation of lexical frequency metrics, now normalised. For training the LSA model with 300 dimensions, a large corpus of web documents, BrWaC \cite{wagner-filho-etal-2018-brwac}, was utilised. This same corpus, along with the corpus Brasileiro\footnote{\url{http://corpusbrasileiro.pucsp.br/}}, was used to calculate the lexical frequency metrics. NILC-Metrix is, therefore, the culmination of various research projects developed at NILC. Its metrics were revised (some rewritten, others discarded, and several updated with new NLP resources) and documented in detail between 2016 and 2017. This documentation is available on the project's website. The metrics can be accessed via a web interface\footnote {\url{http://fw.nilc.icmc.usp.br:23380/nilcmetrix}} and its code is publicly available for download\footnote{\url{https://github.com/nilc-nlp/nilcmetrix}}, under an AGPLv3 license. Two of the parsers used by the metrics, Palavras and LX-parser \cite{LXparser_SilvaBCR10}, need to be installed for the correct functioning of the metrics that depend on them; Palavras is a proprietary parser; LX-parser has a license that does not allow the parser to be distributed\footnote{\url{http://lxcenter.di.fc.ul.pt/tools/en/conteudo/LX-Parser_License.pdf}}. In this paper, we present NILC-Metrix in detail and demonstrate the tool's potential with three applications of its metrics: (i) an evaluation of texts heard and read by children, highlighting the differences between the subtitles of films and children's series from the Leg2Kids project\footnote{\url{http://www.nilc.icmc.usp.br/leg2kids/}} and informative texts written for children in Elementary School I and II, compiled during the Coh-Metrix-Port and Adapt2Kids project \cite{Hartmann_Aluisio_2020}; (ii) a new predictor of textual complexity for the corpus of original and simplified texts from the PorSimples project, comparing its results with the predictor developed in \cite{aluisio-etal-2010-readability}; and (iii) a predictor of textual complexity, using narrative transcripts from the Adole-Sendo project\footnote{\url{adole-sendo.info/}}. The remainder of this paper is organised as follows. Section 2 describes two tools developed during PorSimples that provided the foundation for NILC-Metrix. Section 3 presents the metrics, grouped into 14 classes, which is very similar to the organisation of the metrics used by Coh-Metrix v3.0, to facilitate comparative studies. Section 4 presents the corpora used in the NILC-Metrix applications and also the results of the three experiments with the metrics. Section 5 conducts a review analysing studies that utilised sets of metrics available in NILC-Metrix, across various research areas --- Natural Language Processing, Neuropsychological Language Tests, Education, Language, and Eye-tracking studies. Finally, Section 6 presents some concluding remarks and suggests future work.

text: This paper introduces a method for actively sampling individuals within a population to help mitigate the spread of pandemics such as COVID-19. Sampling algorithms are frequently employed in machine learning to acquire training data labels for classification ("active learning" \cite{AL-MJ, pz2006}) and in bandit algorithms \cite{bandit-wolpert} to explore complex search spaces through exploration and exploitation. The method we propose in this paper builds upon these concepts but applies them to the context of controlling the spread of an epidemic within a population. The literature on managing disease spread through active sampling concepts primarily originates from the public health field. There are two reasons this literature has considered sampling, although these are sometimes intertwined in the context of population surveillance \cite{lee2010principles}. The first reason is to estimate the actual incidence or spread of a disease, such as HIV, within a population. In estimating HIV incidence, methods such as population surveys and "sentinel surveillance" \cite{magnani2005review, fylkesnes_studying_1998} have proven useful. The population survey in a catchment area (i.e., where disease is likely) involves (stratified/cluster) random sampling and is generally considered the gold standard, although it is known to be costly \cite{lee2010principles}. In contrast, sentinel surveillance collects data from a subset of venues (the "sentinels," e.g., clinics) where individuals with the disease are likely to seek treatment. Recognizing that sensitive diseases like HIV may be prevalent in hard-to-reach populations who might remain undetected due to illegal or illicit activities (e.g., sex workers, drug users), the literature \cite{magnani2005review, goel2010assessing} has critically examined other techniques such as snowball sampling (beginning with a few seeds who have the disease and asking them to name others who might), respondent-driven sampling (similar to snowball, but with longer chains and fewer referrals per seed), and time-location sampling (e.g., sampling users at night in districts with brothels). With sensor data, newer forms of sampling are also emerging. It has been shown, for instance, that to quantify disease spread in livestock, sampling the nodes (physical locations) with the greatest movement can be effective \cite{dawson2015sampling}. The second reason for considering sampling strategies is to mitigate disease spread by proactively identifying individuals who need to be quarantined or tested. A common method for this in the public health literature is contact tracing \cite{PhysRevE.66.056115, eames2003contact, underwood_contact_2003}. The idea is to sample contacts of known infected individuals for the presence of disease, and, along with quarantine, this was the main mechanism used worldwide during the COVID-19 pandemic \cite{salathe2020covid, hellewell2020feasibility}. Traditionally, contact tracing is conducted through questionnaires, but newer automated contact tracing based on tracking cell phone proximities has also been proposed \cite{ferretti2020quantifying}. The SARS-CoV-2 pathogen and its transmission possess unique characteristics that render none of these sampling methodologies sufficient on their own. \begin{itemize} \item The potential for pre-symptomatic and asymptomatic spread eliminates pure sentinel-based strategies that would test only those reporting symptoms at clinics. For the same reason, contact tracing alone would be inadequate. This is because contact tracing targets only contacts of those known to have tested positive. Asymptomatic carriers may have also transmitted the disease to their contacts, but these will not be actively pursued by this strategy. Hence, random sampling is also beneficial. \item The pathogen has also been shown to persist on surfaces or in the air in specific locations for extended periods. Therefore, location-based sampling may also be advantageous. \item There is uncertainty regarding whether individuals develop long-lasting immunity. Consequently, sampling strategies may need to allow for re-testing the same individuals repeatedly. \item Information about how covariates influence contracting the disease and being affected by it is still evolving. For instance, while it is known that comorbidities and age affect outcomes, there is still uncertainty about whether this knowledge is complete. Moreover, how covariates might affect contracting the disease remains uncertain. In this context, covariate-based sampling strategies alone might be insufficient. Sampling strategies that target specific \emph{individuals} for testing are therefore crucial. \item The highly infectious nature of the pathogen and the extent of its worldwide spread have placed constraints on testing capacities, necessitating the prioritization of tests if they are to be effective in mitigating the spread. \end{itemize} The method presented in this paper addresses all five aspects noted above. This paper introduces dynamic active sampling strategies based on multi-armed bandit algorithms that can optimally integrate the different sampling ideas to generate real-time lists of whom to sample. Bandit algorithms are particularly adept at combining exploration with exploitation and have proven successful in many scenarios where this combination is crucial. This is the case with SARS-CoV-2, where exploration (random sampling) must be effectively combined with exploitation (contact tracing, location-based sampling) in a dynamic manner based on data. One of the key aspects of our work is that we identify specific individuals to test/sample, as opposed to criteria or covariate-based sampling strategies. Furthermore, our algorithm operates in a highly uncertain network environment. Specifically, the contacts between individuals are initially only partially observable and are revealed gradually based on individual sampling. The bandit algorithm therefore first employs the Thompson sampling strategy to balance between expansion into unobserved nodes to identify possible new hotspots and densification on the observed portion to utilize the knowledge gained for testing. If densification is chosen, an inner-level upper confidence bounding (UCB) policy is designed to balance between individuals with a higher probability of infection and those with greater information uncertainty. To quantify the closeness of individuals and the risk of infection, we construct a heterogeneous network embedding to encode social interactions by a continuous latent representation. To model how the sampling affects, and is in turn affected by, the underlying environment, we implement an agent-based model constructed from realistic data from New York City. Several recent COVID-19 studies have focused on the ability to predict and flatten the disease's spread by applying different intervention policies \cite{Keskinocak2020.07.22.20160036,Keskinocak2020.04.29.20084764, topirceanu2020centralized,atkeson2020will,ferguson2020report,chang2020modelling}. Among the policies examined were case isolation, home quarantine, social distancing, restrictions on air travel, and school closures and reopening. To assess the efficiency of these restrictions, most of these studies coupled S/I/R (susceptible/infected/recovered) diffusion modeling \cite{hethcote2000mathematics,cooper2020sir} with an Agent-Based Simulation Model (ABM) \cite{perez2009agent} of infectious spread under different restriction scenarios. Among these studies, an ABM of COVID-19 spread in New York City under different quarantine policies was offered by \cite{hoertel2020facing}. This model serves as a basis for the ABM developed in this work. Also, in contemporaneous work, \cite{grushka2020framework} present a framework that uses historical data to build a classifier that computes a "risk score," which forms the basis for determining how to combine exploration and exploitation. While the idea of using bandit-based algorithms for testing is important, the challenge lies in developing specific methods that address all the complexities noted previously. Our work presents a specific method that is adaptive, dynamic, and comprehensive. Along the lines of whom to sample for testing, there is a similar question of whom to vaccinate. For example, \cite{chen2020allocation} present adaptive and dynamic covariate-based policies for vaccination. Our framework allows vaccination to be incorporated into the background dynamics to test the effectiveness of combinational strategies such as smart testing with vaccination. We make the following significant contributions. First, we present a novel active sampling algorithm to effectively manage pandemics such as COVID-19 (to our knowledge, no methods in the literature have been developed for this problem yet). We develop a general multi-armed bandit framework for this problem that (a) can leverage information of different types such as individuals and locations, (b) can handle uncertainty in both the underlying disease dynamics and information, and (c) is designed to sample based on individuals rather than covariates. Second, we make several modeling contributions related to how bandit-based algorithms can function in this setting. Specifically, we construct a heterogeneous network to capture social relations, neighborhood similarity, and community membership, and demonstrate how this can drive a two-level active sampling strategy to sample individuals. The use of network embedding ideas within the heterogeneous network is novel. Third, we make important contributions to the literature on multi-armed bandits as well. Beyond classic bandit problems, there exists limited literature on active search on graphs, with the objective of finding as many target nodes as possible with some given property. Most existing work assumes that the complete network structure and underlying process is known beforehand. There is very little work on partially observed and dynamically changing networks and underlying (disease) dynamics. We model the partially observed scenarios within this framework and demonstrate how the network can be strategically expanded over time to support the active sampling strategy. \iffalse since we consider a scenario where the sampling is not independent of the environment, but itself affects the underlying mechanism. text: The objective of a regression model is to learn a mapping $f:\mathcal{X}\rightarrow\mathcal{Y}$ from a set of data points $(x_m,y_m)\in \mathcal{X}\times \mathcal{Y}, \ m=1,\ldots,M,$ such that $y_m\approx f(x_m)$, while mitigating overfitting \cite{wahba1990spline,gyorfi2006distribution,hastie2009overview}. Here, $\mathcal{X}$ represents the input domain and $\mathcal{Y}$ denotes the set of possible outcomes. A typical approach to achieve this task is to solve a minimization problem of the form \begin{equation} \min_{f\in \mathcal{F}} \left( \sum_{m=1}^M { E}\left(f(x_m),y_m\right) + \mathcal{R}(f)\right), \end{equation} where $\mathcal{F}$ is the search space, the convex loss function ${ E}:\mathcal{Y}\times\mathcal{Y}\rightarrow\mathbb{R}_{\geq 0}$ ensures the consistency of the learned mapping with the data points, and the regularization functional $\mathcal{R}:\mathcal{F}\rightarrow \mathbb{R}_{\geq 0}$ incorporates prior knowledge about the form of the mapping $f$, which is intended to reduce overfitting. \subsection{Nonparametric regression} In certain instances, the optimization can be conducted over an infinite-dimensional function space. A notable example is the class of reproducing-kernel Hilbert spaces (RKHS) $\mathcal{F}=\mathcal{H}(\mathbb{R}^d)$, $\mathcal{X}= \mathbb{R}^d$, $\mathcal{Y}=\mathbb{R}$ \cite{poggio1990networks,poggio1990regularization}, where the regression problem is expressed as \begin{equation} \min_{f\in \mathcal{H}(\mathbb{R}^d)} \left(\sum_{m=1}^M { E}\left(f(\boldsymbol{x}_m),y_m\right) + \lambda \|f\|_{\mathcal{H}}^2\right). \end{equation} The key result in RKHS theory is the kernel representer theorem \cite{kimeldorf1971some,scholkopf2001generalized}, which asserts that the unique solution of \eqref{Eq:RKHS} admits the kernel expansion \begin{equation} f(\cdot) = \sum_{m=1}^M a_m {\rm k}(\cdot,\boldsymbol{x}_m), \end{equation} where ${\rm k}:\mathbb{R}^d\times\mathbb{R}^d\rightarrow\mathbb{R}$ is the unique reproducing kernel of $\mathcal{H}(\mathbb{R}^d)$ and $a_m\in\mathbb{R},m=1,\ldots,M,$ are learnable parameters. The expansion \eqref{Eq:KernelExpansionL2} allows the infinite-dimensional problem~\eqref{Eq:RKHS} to be reformulated into a finite-dimensional one, enabling the use of standard computational tools of convex analysis to solve it. Many classical kernel-based methods are derived from this approach, including support-vector machines and radial-basis functions \cite{scholkopf2001learning,evgeniou2000regularization,steinwart2008support}. \subsection{Parametric regression} When \eqref{Eq:GeneralSupervisedLearning} cannot be reformulated as a finite-dimensional optimization problem, another prevalent method is to limit the search space $\Spc F$ to a subspace that allows a parametric representation. This method is employed in deep neural networks (DNNs), which have emerged as a significant tool in machine learning and data science in recent years \cite{LeCun2015,Goodfellow2016}. They surpass classical kernel-based methods in various image-processing tasks. Specifically, they have become state-of-the-art for image classification \cite{Krizhevsky2012}, inverse problems \cite{jin2017deep}, and image segmentation \cite{Ronneberger2015}. However, most published studies are empirical, and the exceptional performance of DNNs is not yet fully comprehended. Consequently, many recent studies aim to examine DNNs from a theoretical standpoint. Not surprisingly, {\it stability} and {\it interpretability}, which are fundamental principles in machine learning, are central to these studies. For instance, the stability of leading deep-learning-based methods has been significantly questioned in image classification \cite{moosavi2016deepfool,fawzi2017robustness} and image reconstruction \cite{antun2020instabilities}. Efforts have also been made to understand and interpret DNNs from various perspectives, such as rate-distortion theory \cite{macdonald2019rate,heiss2020distribution}). Nevertheless, the community is still far from achieving a comprehensive understanding, and these issues remain active research areas. \subsection{Our Contributions} In this paper, we propose two variational formulations for regressing one-dimensional data that prioritize ``stable'' and ``simple'' regression models. Similar to RKHS theory, these are nonparametric continuous-domain problems in the sense that $\mathcal{F}$ in \eqref{Eq:GeneralSupervisedLearning} is an infinite-dimensional function space. Motivated by the stability principle, we concentrate on developing regression schemes with controlled Lipschitz regularity. This is inspired by the observation that many analyses in deep learning require assumptions on the Lipschitz constant of the learned mapping \cite{arjovsky2017wasserstein,bora2017compressed,neyshabur2017exploring}. Similarly, when a trainable module is integrated into an iterative-reconstruction framework, the convergence rate of the overall scheme often depends on the Lipschitz constant of this module \cite{gupta2018cnn,zhang2017beyond,sun2020block,liu2020rare,wu2020simba,bohra2021learning}. In our first formulation, we employ the Lipschitz constant of the learned mapping as a regularization term. Specifically, we consider the minimization problem \begin{equation} \min_{f\in{\rm Lip}(\mathbb{R})} \left( \sum_{m=1}^M { E}\left(f(x_m),y_m\right) + \lambda L(f) \right), \end{equation} where ${\rm Lip}(\mathbb{R})$ is the space of Lipschitz-continuous real functions and $L(f)$ represents the Lipschitz constant of $f\in {\rm Lip}(\mathbb{R})$. In this formulation, one can control the Lipschitz regularity of the learned function implicitly by adjusting the regularization parameter $\lambda$. We establish a representer theorem that characterizes the solution set of \eqref{Eq:LipRegIntro}. Specifically, we demonstrate that the global minimum is achieved by a continuous and piecewise-linear (CPWL) mapping. Subsequently, motivated by the simplicity principle, we identify the mapping with the minimal number of linear regions. It is noteworthy that many previous studies examine problems similar to \eqref{Eq:LipRegIntro} in more general settings, typically using the Lipschitz constant of the $n$th derivative $\mathcal{R}(f)=L(f^{(n)})$ with $n \geq 0$ as the regularization term \cite{mcclure1975perfect,karlin1975interpolation,de1975small,micchelli1976optimal,de1976best,pinkus1988smoothest}. More recently, \cite{von2004distance} has investigated the classification problem over metric spaces and derived a parametric form for a solution of this problem. Our aim is to complement this intriguing line of research by focusing more on computational aspects of \eqref{Eq:LipRegIntro} ({\it e.g.}, finding the sparsest CPWL solution) and by providing a detailed analysis of the $n=0$ case, which is related to second-order total-variation minimization. In the second scenario, we explicitly control the Lipschitz constant of the learned mapping by imposing a hard constraint. Drawing inspiration from the theoretical insights of the first problem, we incorporate a second-order total-variation (TV) regularization term that is known to promote sparse CPWL functions \cite{unser2019Deepspline,debarre2020sparsest}. This leads to the minimization problem \begin{align} \min_{f\in{\rm BV}^{(2)}(\mathbb{R})} &\left( \sum_{m=1}^M { E}\left(f(x_m),y_m\right) + \lambda {\rm TV}^{(2)}(f) \right), \nonumber\\ &\text{s.t.} \quad L(f)\leq \overline{L}, \end{align} where ${\rm BV}^{(2)}(\mathbb{R})$ is the space of functions with bounded second-order TV and $\overline{L}$ is the user-defined upper bound for the desired Lipschitz regularity of the learned mapping. The interesting aspect of \eqref{Eq:LipCnstIntro} is that the simplicity and stability of the learned mapping can be adjusted by tuning the parameters $\lambda>0$ and $\overline{L}>0$, respectively. In this case as well, we prove a representer theorem which guarantees the existence of CPWL solutions. Again, we propose an algorithm to find the sparsest CPWL solution. \subsection{Connection to Neural Networks} Another significant motivation for this work is to further clarify the close connection between CPWL functions and neural networks. It is well established that the input-output mapping of any feed-forward DNN with linear spline ({\em e.g., } the rectified linear unit, also known as ReLU) activations is a CPWL function \cite{pascanu2013number,Montufar2014}. Moreover, any CPWL function can be represented {\it exactly} by a DNN with linear-spline activations \cite{arora2016understanding}. This establishes a direct link with spline theory, as first highlighted by Poggio {\it et al.} \cite{Poggio2015} and then further explored in various works \cite{unser2019Deepspline,balestriero2020mad,parhi2020role,parhi2021banach,parhi2021kinds}. For shallow networks, the connection with our framework becomes even more explicit. It is well known in the literature that the standard training ({\em i.e., } with weight decay) of a two-layer univariate ReLU network is equivalent to solving a TV-based variational problem such as~\eqref{Eq:LipCnstIntro} without the Lipschitz constraint \cite{savarese2019how, parhi2020role}. As we demonstrate, these results can be readily extended to prove the equivalence between the training of a Lipschitz-constrained two-layer univariate ReLU network and our formulation~\eqref{Eq:LipCnstIntro}. Our description of the solution set of Problem~\eqref{Eq:LipCnstIntro} thus provides insights into the training of Lipschitz-aware neural networks. \subsection{Outline} The paper is structured as follows: we review the necessary mathematical background in Section \ref{sec:prelim}. In Section \ref{sec:Proposals}, we introduce our supervised-learning formulations and state their corresponding representer theorems. We then propose our algorithms for finding the corresponding sparsest CPWL solution in Section \ref{sec:Algo}. Finally, we provide numerical illustrations and discussions in Section \ref{sec:Numerical}.

text: The ability to detect previously unseen novelties, or anomalies, is crucial for humans to become aware of new threats and opportunities. Examples include identifying novel behaviors in natural systems, detecting security threats, or identifying equipment malfunctions. While anomaly detection (AD) methods targeting images \cite{reiss2021panda,hendrycks2019using,tack2020csi} typically cover a wide range of data domains, video AD has predominantly concentrated on surveillance footage. In these videos \cite{luo2017revisit,mahadevan2010anomaly}, often captured by security cameras, normal walking behavior is typically classified as the normal class, while other behaviors (such as riding a bike or crowd gathering) are classified as anomalies. Recently, numerous new techniques have been proposed, advancing performance on these benchmarks \cite{georgescu2021anomaly,park2020learning}. However, other types of video anomalies largely remain outside the focus of current research. In this study, we investigate various types of anomalies and evaluate different methods to address them. Our research focuses on physical irregularities in the motion or trajectory of an object that have been largely neglected and introduces new benchmarks for video anomaly detection.
