text: Deep neural networks (DNNs) have demonstrated significant performance advancements across various fields. Identifying an appropriate DNN architecture is essential for deploying a DNN to a novel task and achieving superior performance. However, since the architecture is characterized by a combination of numerous hyperparameters (such as convolutional layer filter sizes and the presence of connections between certain layers), optimizing this combination demands substantial human effort and expert knowledge. Neural architecture search (NAS) has been explored as a promising method for automatically discovering sophisticated DNN architectures, thereby addressing the challenges of applying DNNs to previously unencountered tasks. Nevertheless, the substantial computational cost (in terms of time and space complexity) of NAS poses a limitation for its applications, particularly in commercial settings that do not utilize multiple high-spec GPUs. Consequently, reducing the computational cost of NAS represents a crucial research direction. One-shot NAS mitigates the time complexity of NAS by concurrently optimizing the architecture and the parameters (weights) in a single or a few training processes. It retains a comprehensive deep learning model with numerous layers and connections, referred to as the parent network, which can encapsulate all potential architectures within the search space as its sub-network. The parent network holds all the parameters needed by candidate architectures, which are shared among different architectures. The quality of an architecture is assessed using these shared parameters, significantly reducing the computational time for architecture search compared to traditional methods that require training parameters from scratch for each candidate architecture evaluation. From the perspective of GPU memory usage, one-shot NAS can be divided into dense propagation NAS (DP-NAS) and sparse propagation NAS (SP-NAS). DP-NAS necessitates loading the entire parent network into GPU memory to execute forward and/or backward propagation, whereas SP-NAS requires loading only a sub-network. DP-NAS is more prevalent due to the success of DARTS and its successors \cite{liu2018darts,xie2018snas,yao2020nasp}. However, its high memory usage restricts its search space. SP-NAS addresses this limitation and offers more flexible search spaces on a standard GPU with limited memory. Therefore, we concentrate on SP-NAS in this study. To further decrease the computational cost of one-shot SP-NAS, we introduce a novel one-shot SP-NAS, termed \emph{AdvantageNAS}. Although numerous factors influence the performance of NAS (such as performance estimation and search space) and achieving state-of-the-art (SOTA) performance may necessitate searching for the optimal combination of these factors, this study focuses on the search strategy. We stress that the aim of this study is not to obtain the SOTA architecture but to examine the efficiency of the search strategy. AdvantageNAS is a gradient-based SP-NAS.\footnote{The benefits of gradient-based approaches are as follows. Methods using evolutionary algorithms (e.g., \cite{real2017evo}) or progressive search techniques (e.g., \cite{liu2018pnas}) must define a mutation or expansion strategy based on the search space. Such manual preparations based on the search space are unnecessary in gradient-based methods. Another benefit of gradient-based methods is their ease of implementation in most modern deep learning frameworks, as they support automatic differentiation of deep neural networks.} This category of NAS includes ENAS \cite{pham2018enas}, ProxylessNAS \cite{cai2018proxylessnas}, PARSEC \cite{casale2019parsec}, and GDAS \cite{xuanyi2019gdas}. These methods introduce a family of parametric probability distributions from which an architecture is sampled, and the distribution parameter is updated with a gradient of the objective function estimated using the Monte Carlo method, which indirectly optimizes the architecture itself. As the gradient is estimated, reducing the variance of the gradient estimate intuitively enhances the search efficacy. Inspired by the actor-critic approach \cite{konda2000ac}, we incorporate the concept of \emph{advantage}, which has been introduced to address the well-known \emph{credit assignment} problem of policy gradients \cite{Minsky:1961:ire}. We analyze AdvantageNAS both theoretically and empirically. Empirical studies demonstrate that it performs effectively on various tasks with different search spaces, while theoretical studies ensure its performance on empirically unforeseen tasks. Theoretical studies are relatively rare in NAS research; however, they are crucial for exploring search strategies for NAS. Our contributions are summarized as follows: \begin{itemize} \item We introduce a novel SP-NAS, namely AdvantageNAS. Our analysis of a test scenario shows that the estimation variance of the gradient is reduced compared to REINFORCE \cite{Williams1992}, which serves as a baseline search strategy for ENAS. \item The theoretical investigation reveals that the estimated gradient in AdvantageNAS is an unbiased estimator of the gradient of the expected loss. From this unbiasedness, we deduce that AdvantageNAS monotonically improves the expected loss and thus converges. Furthermore, we confirm that reducing the gradient variance contributes to an improved lower bound of the loss improvement in each iteration. \item We compared AdvantageNAS with various gradient-based NAS methods in three different settings to demonstrate its efficacy on different search spaces. Our experiments were conducted on the same code base to compare the search strategies.\footnote{NAS approaches using different components such as search spaces and training protocols have been compared in the literature. However, it has been reported, e.g.,\ in \cite{Yang2020iclr}, that such differences in the components make it difficult to fairly compare the contributions of each component. Our code: \url{https://github.com/madoibito80/advantage-nas}.} The results indicated that AdvantageNAS converges more rapidly than existing SP-NAS approaches. \end{itemize}

The Wasserstein barycenter (WB) is a widely used technique in statistics and machine learning for summarizing data from multiple sources while preserving their intrinsic geometry~\cite{martial11}. The problem is formally defined as follows. Consider a collection of data represented by $k$ discrete probability distributions $\mu_1,\ldots,\mu_k$ on $\mathbb{R}^d$. Given non-negative weights $\lambda_1,\ldots,\lambda_k$ that sum to $1$, and a class $\mathbb{P}$ of probability distributions on $\mathbb{R}^d$, a Wasserstein barycenter under the $L_p$ objective for a parameter $p>0$ is a probability distribution $
u\in\mathbb{P}$ that minimizes  egin{equation} \sum_{i=1}^k\lambda_iW_p(\mu_i,
u)^p, \end{equation} where $W_p(\mu_i,
u)$ denotes the $p$-Wasserstein distance. The Wasserstein barycenter is a fundamental concept that encapsulates the geometric notion of centrality among point clouds, as it employs the optimal transport distance~\cite{bertsimas1997introduction} between multiple observed sets. Consequently, Wasserstein barycenters have been extensively applied in machine learning~\cite{srivastava2018scalable}, data sciences~\cite{ruschendorf2002n,elvander2020multi}, image processing~\cite{rubner1997earth}, computer graphics~\cite{pele2009fast}, and statistics~\cite{villani2008optimal}, with applications in constrained clustering~\cite{cuturi2014fast, ho2017multilevel}, Bayesian learning~\cite{srivastava2018scalable}, texture mixing~\cite{rabin2011wasserstein}, and shape interpolation~\cite{solomon2015convolutional}. Unfortunately, the problem is NP-hard to compute \cite{AltschulerB21, BorgwardtP21}, and many algorithms that approximate the Wasserstein barycenter experience significant running times, particularly for high-dimensional datasets~\cite{MuzellecC19}. Indeed, \cite{altschuler2021wasserstein} recently proposed an algorithm that computes the Wasserstein barycenter with a runtime that depends exponentially on the dimension, thus encountering the ``curse of dimensionality.'' To mitigate these computational challenges, we explore dimensionality reduction for computing the Wasserstein barycenter. Dimensionality reduction can enhance the performance of downstream algorithms on high-dimensional datasets in various contexts, as discussed in the survey~\cite{cunningham2015linear}. Specifically, for Wasserstein barycenters, dimensionality reduction offers several practical and theoretical advantages, including reduced storage requirements, faster computation of distances, and versatility: it can serve as a pre-processing tool and be integrated with \emph{any} algorithm for computing the Wasserstein barycenter. \subsection{Our Results} In this paper, we investigate dimensionality reduction techniques for computing a Wasserstein barycenter of discrete probability distributions. Our primary findings demonstrate that it is feasible to project the distributions into lower dimensions while provably maintaining the quality of the barycenter. A pivotal result in dimensionality reduction is the classical Johnson-Lindenstrauss (JL) lemma~\cite{johnson1984extensions}, which asserts that projecting a dataset of $N$ points into approximately $O(\log N)$ dimensions suffices to preserve all pairwise distances. Utilizing the JL lemma, we first demonstrate that we can assume the distributions reside in $O(\log(nk))$ dimensions, where $k$ is the number of input distributions for which we are computing the barycenter, $n$ is the size of the support of the barycenter, and each of the $k$ input distributions has support size $\poly(n)$. For $p=2$, there exists a closed form for the cost of any candidate barycenter in terms of the pairwise distances of the points in the input distributions. Thus, it is straightforward to observe that our bound results from the fact that there are $k \cdot \poly(n)$ total point masses in the union of all the distributions, and therefore, projecting them into a dimension of size $O(\log( k \poly(n))) = O(\log(nk))$ suffices to preserve all of their pairwise distances. However, for $p
eq 2$, a closed form for the optimal cost no longer exists, so preservation of all pairwise distances is insufficient. Instead, we employ a Lipschitz extension theorem, specifically the Kirszbraun theorem, which allows us to ``invert'' the dimensionality reduction map and argue the preservation of the cost of the Wasserstein barycenter under a general $L_p$ objective. For more details, see Section~ef{sec:log(nk) reduction}. 	extbf{Dimensionality reduction independent of $k$.} While the JL lemma is known to be tight~\cite{LarsenN16, LarsenN17}, it is possible to enhance its dimensionality guarantees for \emph{specific} problems, such as various formulations of clustering \cite{CohenEMMP15,BecchettiBC0S19,MakarychevMR19}. Indeed, our main result is that we can achieve a dimension bound \emph{beyond} the $O(\log(nk))$ bound that follows from the JL lemma and Kirszbraun theorem. We demonstrate that it suffices to project the support points onto $O(\log n)$ dimensions, which is \emph{independent} of the number of distributions $k$. In fact, we establish a stronger statement that projecting the points supported by the distributions onto $O(\log n)$ dimensions preserves the cost of the objective \eqref{eq:bary def} for \emph{any} distribution $
u$ supported on at most $n$ points (Theorem~ef{thm:jl:main}). The algorithmic application of this theorem is that one can take \emph{any} approximation algorithm or heuristic for computing the Wasserstein barycenter and combine it with dimensionality reduction. A simplification of our theorem is presented below, where we omit some parameters for clarity.  egin{theorem}[Theorem ef{thm:jl:main} Simplified] Let $\mu_1,\ldots,\mu_k$ be discrete probability distributions on $\mdef{\mathbb{R}}^d$ such that $|	extrm{supp}(\mu_i)| \le \poly(n)$ for all $i$. There exists a dimensionality reduction map $\pi:\mathbb{R}^d	o\mathbb{R}^m$ for $m=O(\log n)$ such that projection under $\pi$ preserves the cost of objective \eqref{eq:bary def} for any $
u$ supported on at most $n$ points. \end{theorem} The result is remarkable because the projected dimension is independent of the number of input distributions $k$, which could be significantly larger than $n$. text: Dhrupad is among the most ancient forms of North Indian classical vocal music. A typical Dhrupad concert setting includes a solo vocalist or a duo as the lead, accompanied by a pakhawaj player for percussion, with a tanpura providing the harmonic drone in the background\cite{bonnie_wade}. A Dhrupad performance extends for over an hour and features an elaborate, unaccompanied \textit{raga alap} followed by a composed piece, the \textit{bandish}, performed with the percussion instrument. The bandish is not only presented in its original form but also serves as a basis for further rhythmic improvisation (\textit{laykari}), where the vocalist sings the syllables of the bandish text at varying rhythmic densities and patterns \cite[chapter~10]{clayton}. Throughout, the pakhawaj accompaniment either plays a basic pattern (\textit{theka}) of the metric cycle (\textit{tala}), a rhythmic improvisation to match the vocalist’s improvisation, or a free solo improvisation while the vocalist presents lines of fixed composition or the refrain \cite[p.~111]{clayton}. \\ Figure~\ref{fig:concert_structure} illustrates the structure of a bandish performance from the vocalist's perspective. The intermediate refrain sections are the non-improvised parts where the artist sings a line of the bandish or a segment of it before returning to another phase of improvisation.\\ A primary distinction between Khyal and Dhrupad bandish performances is the interaction between the lead and accompanying percussion instrument. In Khyal, artists typically alternate improvising while the other maintains the basic rhythm or refrain, whereas in Dhrupad, there are also sections where both improvise simultaneously. A comprehensive segmentation of a Dhrupad bandish performance would thus involve providing rhythmic descriptions of both un-improvised and improvised sections for each - the vocals and the pakhawaj.\\ Several other levels of segmentation could be applied to this form of music. One could focus on identifying sections of un-improvised and improvised music. With the bandish text itself comprising sections positioned in different parts of an octave, each with a couple of lines, another level of segmentation could be based on which of these is being presented or improvised upon by the vocalist. While the former segmentation could be somewhat defined by changes in rhythmic attributes, the latter would rely more on melodic characteristics. Changes in timbral attributes, correlated with the nature of articulation accompanying the various rhythmic or melodic changes, could also assist with each type of segmentation.\\ The objective of this work is to develop automatic methods for the structural segmentation of the Dhrupad bandish concert based solely on the tempo and the relationships of the rhythmic densities of the individual instruments. Given that vocal onsets are notoriously difficult to detect (even in isolated vocals due to the diversity inherent to singing), we resort to alternative methods for directly estimating the local rhythmic density. Advances in deep learning have led to the creation of methods that treat the estimation of the predominant tempo from the raw audio spectral representation as a classification task \cite{schreiber-ismir18,schreiber-smc19,mtl-beat-tempo-19}. We investigate a similar approach for our task of estimating the changing surface tempo or rhythmic density across a concert audio. In light of the significant improvements reported in audio source separation in recent years, we also consider using source separation followed by tempo estimation for the constituent instruments (vocals and pakhawaj) to provide a more complete description of each section.\\ The principal new contributions of this work are as follows: (i) a dataset of tempo markings and rhythmic density-based structural segmentation annotations for Dhrupad bandish concerts, (ii) adapting a state-of-the-art tempo estimation method to the task of estimating local surface tempo or rhythmic density of the polyphonic mix, and (iii) employing source separation to extend this to each instrument (vocals and pakhawaj) to ultimately achieve a musically relevant segmentation of bandish concerts with section labels defined in terms of the rhythmic density inter-relationships.

text: The prediction of stock market returns and volatility has garnered significant interest from both academia and the financial sector. However, is it possible to predict stock market prices and volatility? Or at the very least, can predictions be made at certain specific times? Assessing sentiment derived from online platforms such as Twitter or financial news articles can be instrumental in developing trading strategies. Moreover, sentiment extracted from financial news may possess predictive capabilities that portfolio and risk managers can exploit. Our analysis yields results and conclusions that can be divided into three segments. Firstly, correlations between sentiment scores and stock market returns were statistically significant solely for our headline dataset. The findings reveal a statistically significant negative correlation between negative news and the closing price of the FTSE100 index (returns). The most substantial correlation between sentiment and volatility measures was observed in our tweets dataset, whereas no correlation or only weak correlation was identified in the headlines and news stories dataset. This can be attributed to the fact that tweets are often more timely and responsive to various events, while publishing articles requires more time, and the market operates under the principle ``Buy on rumors, sell on news.'' This paper is organized as follows. In Section \ref{sec:related}, we review related research. In Section \ref{sec:data}, we describe the data sources used to calculate sentiment scores: Thomson Reuters, RavenPack, and Twitter. In Section \ref{sec:correlation}, we perform a correlation analysis and Granger's causality test. In Section \ref{sec:lda}, we conduct further experiments to determine if topic modeling (or Latent Dirichlet Allocation) can be used to enhance the prediction accuracy of the next day's stock market directional volatility. In Sections \ref{sec:results} and \ref{sec:conclusion}, we present the results of the analysis and discuss future work.

text: A growing body of research has described tools, employed optimization techniques, or proposed new algorithms to assist in automating the design and/or fabrication of robots (e.g.,~\citep{Luck-RSS-17,Schulz17,HoovFearing08,pervan2018low,zhang2020abstractions}). Among these approaches, algorithms that aim to manage or minimize resources are particularly significant (for instance, see~\citep{censi17co}). Memory is a resource of particular interest to us, not because RAM is costly, but because reducing state requirements often reveals insights into the fundamental informational structure of specific robot tasks~(cf.~\citep{connell90,donald95information}). To this end, we focus on filter reduction, specifically targeting combinatorial filters of the type advocated by LaValle~\citep{lavalle10sensing}. These filters are discrete versions of the probabilistic estimators prevalent in modern robotics, and they provide particularly elegant solutions for certain practical tasks (e.g., see \citep{tovar2014combinatorial}). The minimization problem for combinatorial filters is straightforward to state and comprehend, but ongoing research on the topic~\citep{okane2013reduction,o2017concise,saberifar2017combinatorial,rahmani2018relationship,zhang20cover,rahmani2020integer} reveals that it involves complexities beyond initial appearances. To motivate filter minimization, consider the safari park with a vehicle rental service illustrated in Figure~\ref{fig:motivating_scenario}. The rental cars are each equipped with a compass and an intelligent gear shifting system. The compass measures the vehicle's heading before and after movement, e.g., `nw' indicates that the vehicle was heading north and then turned to face west. The intelligent gear shifting system uses the compass readings as input and automatically shifts gears to comply with the speed limit. There are three types of speed limits on roads: ($a$) between $15$ and $30$ (gray), ($b$) speeds below $30$ (brown), or ($c$) slower than $15$ (green). Each vehicle can operate with a low gear to drive at a maximum speed of $15$, and with a high gear to drive between speeds $15$ and $30$. A na\"ive gear shifting system that satisfies the speed limits is realized by a filter shown in Figure~\ref{fig:motivating_input}: each vertex represents a system state, each edge represents the state transition, with the label on the edges representing the compass readings. A vertex is colored gray if the system outputs high gear, colored green if it outputs low gear, or colored both colors if the system may use either gear (via, for instance, a nondeterministic choice). We aim to find a minimal filter, like the one shown in Figure~\ref{fig:motivating_minimal}, that achieves the desired behavior with the fewest states. A natural approach is to first construct a discrete state-transition system (such as in Figure~\ref{fig:motivating_input}) based on the problem description. Then, the subsequent step is to apply an algorithm capable of compressing it. Despite the apparent similarity of combinatorial filter minimization to the problem of state minimization of deterministic automata, with Myhill--Nerode's renowned and efficient reduction~\citep{hopcroft06introduction}, minimization of combinatorial filters is NP-complete~\citep{okane2013reduction}. One line of research examines filter minimization based on merger operations. These algorithms reduce filter minimization to a graph coloring instance~\citep{okane2013reduction,o2017concise,saberifar2017combinatorial} or integer linear programming~\citep{rahmani2020integer}. Saberifar et al.~\citep{saberifar2017combinatorial} investigated special cases, approximation, and parameterized complexity of filter minimization. Rahmani and O'Kane~\citep{rahmani2018relationship} demonstrated that the well-known concept of \emph{bisimulation} relation generally yields only sub-optimal solutions. They proposed three distinct integer linear programming formulations to search for the smallest equivalence relation~\citep{rahmani2020integer}. Recent work indicates that both merge and split operations are necessary to find a minimal filter~\citep{zhang20cover}. It formalizes the problem as a clique cover problem subject to the constraint that the output filter should be deterministic and must simulate the output of the input filter. However, both criteria involve constraints that are exponential in size, which is evidently computationally unattractive. In this paper, we propose a new, competitive formulation of the filter minimization problem with only a polynomial number of constraints, resulting in a concise nonlinear integer programming formulation. Since employing nonlinear constraints is generally computationally inefficient, we `flatten' these nonlinear constraints leading to (1) an integer linear programming and (2) a Boolean satisfaction formalism—both involve expressions of constraints that are of comparable size. Looking at the experimental results in depth, we observed that many constraints remain inactive during the iterative search for a minimal filter. To accelerate computation within the Boolean satisfaction formalism, we treat these constraints just-in-time: only introducing a constraint when we detect that some proposed variable assignment would violate it. Empirical results show that the speedup from this treatment can outweigh the overhead of detecting and dynamically introducing the constraints. After presenting the problem statement in Section~\ref{sec:prob}, we first formalize filter minimization as an integer nonlinear program in Section~\ref{sec:INP}. Based on that, we provide integer linear programming and Boolean satisfaction formulations in Section~\ref{sec:ILP_SAT}. Experimental results are presented in Section~\ref{sec:expr}.

text: Ranking search results that align with a user query is an essential aspect of information retrieval (IR) systems that support many popular websites. Typically, learning to rank (LTR) models are developed to evaluate and order the results, and they are trained using labels derived from user interactions with the results. Although pairwise or listwise loss functions are most frequently used in training LTR models, the scoring of results during inference is generally performed in a unilateral manner. This method of scoring results independently does not account for inter-document dependencies. However, research indicates that the perception of a search result is affected by other adjacent results \cite{agarwal2015constrained, neighbor_effect, wang2016beyond}. This behavior is particularly evident in domains such as e-commerce search, where users often compare and contrast options presented on a results page as part of their purchasing process. Modeling such dependencies is crucial within the top results (for example, results displayed on the first page), which users predominantly interact with. Furthermore, in numerous real-world applications, there is a need to ensure certain predetermined distributional criteria within results on a search results page. Managing the overall composition of results on the page is vital for user perception of a website and is often driven by business objectives or long-term goals aimed at objectives such as user retention. For instance, ensuring that the range of options available for a query is represented within the top results is a significant objective at eBay. Other examples of such business objectives include demonstrating diversity in e-commerce inventory, reducing bias in top results, or personalizing results. Therefore, the formation of an optimal set of top results (documents, or referred to as items in this paper) must consider any distributional criteria and inter-result dependencies, along with the individual quality of results. We refer to the top results for a search query, such as $k$ items shown on the first page as perceived by the user (where $k \ll n$, $n$ is the number of results in the recall), as the slate. In this paper, we introduce a novel approach and an architecture to generate an optimal slate. An optimal slate is conceptualized as one that maximizes the likelihood of meeting search needs while satisfying predetermined query-specific distributional criteria. We jointly optimize for traditional ranking metrics and the slate's adherence to distributional criteria, while modeling intra-slate dependencies. Various approaches have been proposed by researchers to produce a set-aware ranking towards slate optimization. Heuristic methods such as Maximal Marginal Relevance (MMR) \cite{MMR}, IA-Select \cite{IA-Select}, and xQuAD \cite{xQuAD} aim to incorporate diversity into a slate or minimize user dissatisfaction as users browse the returned results. These methods, however, tend to employ simpler heuristics that may lack the expressive capability of the more sophisticated models increasingly used to capture inter-document dependencies. More recent models adopt set-aware ranking architectures \cite{group_wise_ranking,seq2slate}. By modeling a representation of the candidate set of documents and scoring documents with awareness of the candidate set, these approaches aim to produce an optimal slate in a set-aware manner. For example, groupwise scoring functions (GSF) \cite{group_wise_ranking} propose multivariate scoring functions to jointly score documents, and Seq2Slate \cite{seq2slate} employs pointer networks to score documents sequentially. While these approaches are set-aware during inference, they are designed to optimize classic ranking metrics such as normalized discounted cumulative gain (nDCG). They do not explicitly model the additional distributional criteria, which is an important consideration in practice. To the best of our knowledge, there are no existing neural network-based methods directly addressing this specific problem observed in search and specifically e-commerce. To that end, we propose conditional sequential slate optimization (CSSO), a novel framework that aims to address the slate optimization problem. It incorporates a sequential decoding approach built upon a pointer network that, during sequential decoding, manages the composition of the slate according to predetermined distributional criteria, while jointly optimizing traditional ranking metrics such as nDCG. This approach treats the slate optimization problem as a re-ranking problem, where a \textit{base-ranker} produces a ranking based on a unilateral scoring of items, and the \textit{re-ranker} processes a set of $n$ ranked items to produce a slate of size $k$, where $k \ll n$. We express query-specific distributional criteria concerning the slate by means of representative or domain-specific features of the items being ranked. The hybrid optimization goal might lead to divergent optimization directions for each term as the model must balance among ranking quality and all aspects within the predetermined distributional criteria set. Furthermore, due to the existence of non-unique solutions and the non-convex nature of this problem, coupled with the non-differentiable nature of metrics like nDCG, it is challenging for traditional gradient-based methods to find an optimal slate. To tackle this novel and challenging problem, we employ Reinforcement Learning (RL) for the training of CSSO. RL provides a systematic way to search in the feature space while progressively improving the non-differentiable optimization goal with the aid of the policy gradient method. Simultaneously, with the exploration strategy in RL, the learned model is able to generalize better than traditional supervised methods by efficiently learning the meaningful features from the rollouts. In the training, we utilize items’ click-through data from IR systems as implicit relevance labels. Within the RL paradigm, a state is represented \textit{jointly} by the current items on the slate, the distance from the predetermined distribution, and the encoded candidate set. An action is equivalent to the item selection process in each step of decoding, and reward is determined based on the slate composition after the decoding process by considering both ranking quality and adherence to distributional criteria. The optimization problem, thus well-defined, can be solved by policy gradient in the finite horizon with length $k$, and we adopt a baseline model to reduce the variance in training. The key contributions of our work can be summarized as follows: \begin{itemize} \item A framework to jointly optimize a slate for document relevance as well as adherence to a predetermined distribution, thus attempting to address an industry pain point of re-ranking to personalize, mitigate bias, or introduce diversity in results. \item An enhancement to pointer network to include a conditional structure that facilitates representing slate composition during the decoding phase. \end{itemize} In experiments performed on public and proprietary e-commerce datasets, CSSO produces results with comparable ranking metrics and better distribution conformity when compared with state-of-the-art (SOTA) slate optimization methods. On Yahoo \cite{yahoo_dataset} and Web30k \cite{LETOR} datasets with additional simulation for imitating users’ real-world behaviors, we demonstrate that both nDCG and GAP (distribution conformity metric which will be defined in the sections that follow) can be simultaneously optimized in the ranking task. Experiments on datasets from eBay.com search sessions show a significant improvement in GAP metrics and comparable ranking metrics to the production ranker. In general, CSSO performs well with respect to both nDCG and GAP. We view CSSO as a practical approach to solve a very relevant industry problem of optimizing a slate for relevance and slate composition based on business objectives. We envision that the approach can be applied to solve problems such as ensuring diversity, mitigating bias, and adhering to business objectives across search and recommendation systems in various web domains including e-commerce, online media, and web search.

text: The availability of computational resources has been increasing exponentially since at least the 1970s, and all indications suggest that this trend will persist, making these resources more affordable and accessible well into the foreseeable future. Researchers have been able to exploit the substantial computational resources available to enhance the control of robotic systems, with advancements in computational capacity and algorithmic development continually unlocking new domains. A promising development in this area is model-free reinforcement learning, a branch of machine learning that enables an agent to interact with its environment and independently learn to optimize a reward measure. The potential here is to enable researchers to address problems in systems that are difficult to model or for which the user lacks a solution. Recent examples in robotics include controlling a 47 DOF humanoid to navigate various obstacles \cite{heess_emergence_2017}, dexterously manipulating objects with a 24 DOF robotic hand \cite{openai_learning_2018}, and enabling a physical quadruped robot to run \cite{hwangbo_learning_2019} and recover from falls \cite{lee_robust_2019}. In this paper, we investigate legged locomotion. This class of problems is notoriously challenging, making reinforcement learning a popular tool for addressing it. We contend that hand-designed, model-based control still represents the state of the art (as exemplified by Boston Dynamics), but reinforcement learning has proven to be a productive approach. There are instances where learned policies outperform hand-designed ones \cite{hwangbo_learning_2019}, and there is strong reason to believe that these learning methods will continue to improve in terms of performance gains and ease of use. However, these algorithms have a significant drawback in that they are largely black boxes. It remains an open challenge to determine precisely what an RL agent has learned. If all that is known is that an agent achieved a very high reward, it is unclear how to ensure that the system is safe and sensible across all regions of the state space it will encounter during its operation. Additionally, we cannot necessarily make assertions about the stability or robustness properties of the system. Recent work \citep{Taleledeep} has employed mesh-based tools to investigate precisely these issues. However, the utility of any mesh-based tool to accurately discretize a state space is constrained by the curse of dimensionality. In practice, these methods can only handle relatively high-dimensional systems if the growth of the reachable space is significantly smaller than the exponential growth of the full state space in which the system is embedded. To extend these methods to higher-dimensional systems, we need to find ways to prevent the volume of visited states from expanding proportionately. One way to quantify this growth rate is by using one of the several notions of "fractional dimensions" from fractal geometry. In this work, we introduce an efficient meshing algorithm, which we refer to as box meshing. We demonstrate that this approach makes it feasible to calculate the so-called mesh dimension in the context of reinforcement learning. We also propose using other notions of fractional dimension from the literature as a proxy for the property of interest. We then demonstrate that reinforcement learning agents can be trained to reduce these measures by post-processing their reward function. We present the results of this training and conclude with a brief analysis of the resulting structure for selected policies.

text: Recent advancements in deep neural networks (DNNs) have led to breakthroughs in numerous fields, including computer vision and speech recognition. The capabilities of DNNs inspire boundless imagination among researchers. Numerous significant and intriguing studies on DNNs have emerged. There are various types of DNNs, such as convolutional neural networks (e.g., LeNet \cite{45_lecun1998gradient}, AlexNet \cite{33_krizhevsky2012imagenet}, ResNet \cite{42_he2016deep}) and recurrent neural networks (e.g., LSTM \cite{46_olah2015understanding}). With the rapid advancement of DNNs, an increasing number of researchers are focusing on the security of DNNs. Specifically, generating adversarial examples and defending against adversarial attacks are essential techniques in DNN security. The vulnerability of DNNs \cite{2_szegedy2013intriguing} has garnered significant attention since its discovery. Numerous studies in the literature focus on this topic. These studies can be broadly divided into two categories: adversarial attacks \cite{2_szegedy2013intriguing,6_goodfellow2014explaining,7_kurakin2016adversarial,8_papernot2016limitations,9_moosavi2016deepfool,10_carlini2017towards,11_chen2017zoo,12_moosavi2017universal,13_su2019one,14_zhao2017generating,15_tabacof2016adversarial} and adversarial defenses \cite{2_szegedy2013intriguing,24_madry2017towards,43_tramer2017ensemble,44_papernot2016distillation,50_huang2015learning,51_cheng2020cat,52_song2018improving,53_zhang2019theoretically}. Adversarial attack methods aim to create adversarial examples capable of deceiving DNNs. Furthermore, these adversarial examples are typically imperceptible to humans. Conversely, adversarial defenses enhance the robustness of DNNs against adversarial examples. Adversarial attacks and defenses resemble a zero-sum game. Many studies adhere to the definition of adversarial examples as being very similar to original natural images yet capable of deceiving DNNs \cite{2_szegedy2013intriguing}. Under this definition, an adversarial example is imperceptible to humans (referred to as an imperceptible adversarial example). However, there are alternative forms of adversarial examples. For instance, some research involves adding patches to the original image to deceive DNNs \cite{16_brown2017adversarial,17_liu2018dpatch,18_karmon2018lavan,19_lee2019physical}. These are termed adversarial patches, which can deceive DNNs despite being noticeable to humans. Additionally, adversarial noise images deliberately manipulated by humans can deceive DNNs \cite{4_nguyen2015deep}. Although these noise images hold no meaning for humans, DNNs still classify them with high confidence into a specific class (referred to as unrecognizable adversarial examples). It is noteworthy that the aforementioned works primarily focus on image perturbations designed to induce incorrect class labels. Consequently, Sabour et al. \cite{55_DBLP:journals/corr/SabourCFF15} focus on the hidden layers of DNN representations and propose a method to construct an adversarial example that is perceptually similar to one image but whose hidden layer representation closely resembles a different image from another class. Their work raises questions about DNN representation and the interpretation of adversarial examples. Further study is warranted on how adversarial disturbances are represented in the hidden layer and whether hidden layer information can be utilized to develop stronger adversarial defense strategies. Building on the aforementioned studies, this paper analyzes the characteristics of different types of adversarial examples. We observe that whether the sample is an imperceptible adversarial example, an adversarial patch, or an unrecognizable adversarial example, there is uncertainty (correct or incorrect) in the machine's prediction results. However, for humans, as long as the disturbance does not alter the original objective reality, human judgment is generally accurate. We emphasize the significant difference between human vision and DNNs in recognizing images. Humans recognize images in pixel space, whereas machines do so in a specialized space (hidden layer), which can be considered a machine's "vision" space. Therefore, we propose the hypothesis that, without altering the objective reality, the impact of adversarial disturbances on prediction results depends on whether the original characteristic semantics are altered during the hidden layer propagation process. Based on this hypothesis, we propose a defense mechanism that incorporates hidden layer representation to enhance the adversarial robustness of the model. Our defense strategy compresses input information and filters out much of it, including adversarial perturbations. In fact, the proposed defense method can be regarded as an activation function, which operates in the neural network's hidden layer and contributes to improving the model's adversarial robustness. We also theoretically validate the effectiveness of the defense in a simple case. Additionally, we provide a specific defensive function and empirically verify the effectiveness of our defense mechanism. It is noteworthy that our defensive model achieves state-of-the-art performance. Finally, we discuss how to construct imperceptible adversarial examples, adversarial patches, and unrecognizable adversarial examples using hidden layer representation. The contributions are listed as follows: \begin{enumerate} 	\item We examine the characteristics of different types of adversarial examples (imperceptible adversarial examples, adversarial patches, and unrecognizable adversarial examples) and propose the hypothesis that the representation of adversarial perturbations in the hidden layer differs significantly from that of clean examples. 	\item Based on this hypothesis, we propose an effective and efficient defense method to enhance the model's adversarial robustness. The proposed defense strategy compresses input information and filters out much of it, including adversarial perturbations. This defense strategy is also regarded as an activation function, and we theoretically demonstrate its effectiveness. 	\item By incorporating hidden layer representation, we present three types of adversarial attacks to generate imperceptible adversarial examples, unrecognizable adversarial examples, and adversarial patches, as illustrated in Fig. \ref{overview_123}. 	\item Our defense method, which achieves state-of-the-art performance, attains $97.09\%$ accuracy under CW on MNIST, $89.03\%$ accuracy under CW on CIFAR10, and $64.38\%$ under CW on ImageNet. \end{enumerate} In the remainder of this paper, Section \ref{section2} introduces related work in the literature. In Section \ref{section3}, we discuss three types of adversarial examples and propose a hypothesis. In Section \ref{section4}, we propose a defense strategy and a specific defense function (activation function). In Section \ref{section5}, incorporating hidden layer representation, we introduce three adversarial attacks to generate three types of adversarial examples, respectively. In Section \ref{experiment}, we conduct extensive experiments and confirm the effectiveness of our methods. Finally, Section \ref{conclusion} concludes the paper.

text: In contemporary times, cyber-attacks are typically executed by skilled hackers and are characterized by hybrid TTPs (Tactics, Techniques, and Procedures) and prolonged adversarial behaviors. Consequently, detecting them using traditional intrusion detection methods is highly challenging\cite{2018A,2020Preparing}, as these methods generally focus on short-term behaviors and overlook the system's rich contextual information. To address this issue, we examine numerous existing studies and determine that provenance data represent the optimal approach for cyber-attack detection\cite{2018Provenance,2017Applying,2020UNICORN}. Provenance data describe system entities (e.g., processes, files, sockets) and the interactions between these entities, which are typically represented as system events (e.g., read, write, fork). Firstly, provenance data can illustrate how system entities interact with one another and provide extensive contextual information for each entity\cite{2015Trustworthy}. Secondly, provenance data can link causally related events even when these events are separated by significant time intervals\cite{2020UNICORN}. Provenance data are generally collected through OS audit logs (e.g., Linux Auditd\cite{LINUXAuditd}, Windows ETW\cite{ETW}). To execute the cyber-attack detection task using provenance data, most existing works model the provenance data as a directed acyclic graph (termed a provenance graph), where nodes represent system entities and edges denote system events. Figure 1 illustrates an example of a provenance graph. Subsequently, most existing studies (e.g., SLEUTH\cite{2018SLEUTH}, HOLMES\cite{2019HOLMES}, CONAN\cite{0CONAN}) attempt to detect cyber-attacks by manually crafting a variety of rules based on threat knowledge (e.g., kill chain\cite{2015Technical}, ATT\&CK\cite{ATT&CK}). Although rule-based detection strategies are efficient and have achieved state-of-the-art performance, they still possess the following limitations. Firstly, designing rules is an extremely challenging task, as it necessitates specialized domain knowledge of cyber-attack strategies, operating systems, and computer networks. Secondly, rules lack generalization capability, as they are crafted within specific macro environments (e.g., cyber-attack strategies, network environment). They quickly become outdated and require adjustment or even redesign when the macro environment changes. Thirdly, rules are constrained by human experience and cannot handle complex and latent patterns. Conversely, learning-based techniques have long been applied to cybersecurity tasks such as intrusion detection\cite{2018A,2020Preparing}, malware detection\cite{2017Malware,2020Enhancing}, and fraud detection\cite{2018Online,2020Interleaved}. Compared to rule-based techniques, learning-based techniques offer the following advantages. Firstly, learning-based techniques (particularly deep learning techniques) can extract latent patterns and construct detection models from the training dataset with minimal domain knowledge. Secondly, the detection model can adapt to new macro environments by retraining or fine-tuning in an automated manner. Since provenance data are represented as provenance graphs, we utilize GNN (Graph Neural Network)\cite{2019Comprehensive} to construct the cyber-attack detection model. However, due to the complexity of cyber-attacks and system provenance, constructing a cyber-attack detection model based on GNN remains a challenging task. Firstly, provenance graphs generated from OS audit logs are intricate. A provenance graph comprises multiple types of nodes (e.g., processes, files, sockets) and multiple types of edges (e.g., read, write, and create). Additionally, a node or an edge can be characterized by supplementary attributes (e.g., a file can be described by attributes such as source, file extension, and sensitivity level). text: \vspace{-2mm} Our physical world is inherently three-dimensional, where the complete form and dynamics of objects are present and persist within 3D space. Nonetheless, most visual predictive models currently employed in robotics, which forecast the motion of objects under an applied action, are restricted to predicting only 2D motion (i.e., optical flow) from partial observations, such as predicting the 2D flow of pixels \citep{vijayanarasimhan2017sfm,dosovitskiy2015flownet}, or predicting the 3D scene flow of visible points from a partial point cloud \citep{byravan2017se3,byravan2018se3}. Unfortunately, modeling the motion of only visible surfaces often results in data degradation, where objects fade and vanish from the representation as they become occluded. This limitation causes predictive models to underperform in cluttered environments, where objects frequently appear, disappear, and then reappear in view as the robot manipulates them. In this study, we explore the advantages of learning a complete and enduring 3D scene representation for visual predictive modeling. We introduce \textbf{3D Dynamic Scene Representation\xspace (DSR)}: a 3D volumetric scene representation that simultaneously discovers, tracks, and reconstructs novel objects while predicting their motion under robotic interactions. Specifically, the representation captures three object properties, all of which have long been considered essential to human scene understanding~\cite{spelke2007core}. \begin{itemize} \vspace{-2mm} \item[\textbullet] \textbf{{Permanence}:} visual information is integrated into a persistent 3D representation. This ensures that as objects disappear from view due to occlusion, they remain within the representation. This capability allows for more accurate predictions of object motion when moved by other objects in occlusion or when they gradually reappear in view. \item[\textbullet] \textbf{Amodal completeness:} from partial observations of the scene, DSR infers the complete 3D occupancy of each object, including regions not directly observed. This feature enables it to predict the rigid body motion of the entire object rather than just visible surfaces. \item[\textbullet] \textbf{Spatiotemporal continuity:} the representation identifies individual object instances and tracks their identity over time. \item[\textbullet] \textbf{Interpretability:} DSR explicitly models object instances, geometry, and motion, facilitating its use for high-level reasoning in robotic applications. \vspace{-2mm} \end{itemize} To learn this scene representation, we introduce DSR-Net\xspace, a 3D recurrent neural network comprising two main components: 1) a scene encoder that encodes visual observations (i.e., depth images) into a volumetric 3D scene representation, and 2) a motion prediction network that takes the 3D scene representation and an action to be performed by the robot to predict volumetric scene flow. The scene flow is then employed to spatially warp the current scene representation before integrating it with the 3D scene representation of the subsequent time step. The warping operation allows the network to aggregate information over time in a spatially coherent manner. DSR-Net\xspace is trained end-to-end in simulation and subsequently tested in the real world with a robotic manipulator on a tabletop setup. Our experimental results demonstrate that our system achieves state-of-the-art performance in predicting the rigid body motion of novel objects under robot interaction in unstructured cluttered environments. The contributions of our paper are three-fold. First, we introduce a novel 3D dynamic scene representation (DSR) that captures object permanence, amodal completeness, and continuity—desirable properties as part of a perception stack for downstream robot manipulation tasks. Second, we propose DSR-Net\xspace, an end-to-end framework that learns such 3D representations via 3D convolutions. Third, we develop a new benchmark dataset with over 80,000 simulated interactions and 1,500 real-world interactions for learning and evaluating dynamic 3D scene representations. Our experiments in both simulation and the real world demonstrate that DSR-Net\xspace achieves state-of-the-art performance in predicting 3D scene dynamics. Furthermore, it enables more accurate action planning in manipulation tasks such as planar pushing. Please find additional results and videos in the supplementary material.

text: Accurate box estimation is crucial for the success of a tracker. Early tracking methods typically address this issue through multi-scale search~\cite{SiameseFC,ECO,DRT,unveiling} or a sampling-then-regression approach~\cite{SINT,MDNet}, which are often imprecise and significantly constrain tracker performance. To achieve more robust and precise tracking outcomes, numerous state-of-the-art trackers~\cite{SPM,CascadedSiameseRPN,ATOM,DiMP} employ a multi-stage tracking approach, introducing additional stages to enhance box estimation accuracy. These trackers initially locate the target coarsely and subsequently refine the initial result in subsequent stages to achieve more precise box predictions. Nonetheless, even state-of-the-art trackers can further improve box estimation. An oracle experiment supports this view. We configure the tracker's search region to always center on the ground truth, ensuring that performance is primarily influenced by box estimation capability. Table~\ref{tab:oracle} demonstrates that under this oracle setting, the AUC scores of state-of-the-art trackers remain far from ideal, indicating unsatisfactory box estimation, despite some methods (\emph{e.g.}, ATOM~\cite{ATOM}, DiMP~\cite{DiMP}) incorporating built-in box estimation modules. In contrast, with a perfectly centered search region, the proposed Alpha-Refine significantly outperforms, illustrating Alpha-Refine's excellence in box estimation. Furthermore, most refinement methods in existing trackers~\cite{SPM,CascadedSiameseRPN,ATOM,DiMP} exhibit limited transferability, as their training is intertwined with other components. Additional retraining is necessary when these refinement modules are applied to new base trackers. In contrast, Alpha-Refine is independently trained and can be seamlessly integrated into any existing tracker in a plug-and-play manner, without requiring additional training or modifications to the base tracker. In this study, we investigate and compare a range of design options. Specifically, we evaluate various feature fusion modules and prediction heads. We also examine the use of an auxiliary mask head, which incorporates pixel-level supervision during training. We determine that extracting and preserving precise spatial information is essential for accurate box estimation. Consequently, we ultimately employ pixel-wise correlation and a key-point style prediction head to better preserve and utilize detailed spatial information. Additionally, an auxiliary mask head is incorporated, encouraging the network to extract more detailed spatial information, resulting in more accurate box estimation. Moreover, if the mask head is retained during inference, Alpha-Refine enables base trackers to predict the object's mask, accommodating scenarios where a mask is necessary. The design options will be discussed in Section~\ref{sec:method} and validated in Section~\ref{sec:experiment}. To validate the effectiveness of our Alpha-Refine module, we select six well-known base trackers: ECO~\cite{ECO}, RT-MDNet~\cite{RTMDNet}, SiamRPNpp~\cite{SiamRPNplus}, ATOM~\cite{ATOM}, DiMP~\cite{DiMP}, and DiMPsuper~\cite{DiMP}, across several tracking benchmarks, including LaSOT~\cite{LaSOT}, GOT-10K~\cite{GOT10K}, TrackingNet~\cite{Trackingnet}, and VOT2020~\cite{VOT2020}. As illustrated in Fig.~\ref{LaSOT_Improvement}, experimental results indicate that our proposed refinement module significantly enhances the performance of base trackers. Compared to its competitors (\emph{i.e.}, IoU-Net~\cite{ATOM,DiMP} and SiamMask~\cite{SiamMask}), Alpha-Refine also achieves superior performance by a substantial margin. The proposed Alpha-Refine method results in a series of enhanced trackers, among which ARSiamRPN (Alpha-Refine enhanced SiamRPNpp) and ARDiMP50 (Alpha-Refine enhanced DiMP50) offer a favorable efficiency-precision balance, while ARDiMPsuper (Alpha-Refine enhanced DiMPsuper) attains state-of-the-art performance at real-time speeds across multiple benchmarks.

text: Learned index structures have gained prominence as an alternative to traditional database indexes in recent years, following the demonstration of their potential by Kraska et al. \cite{originalLearnedIndex}. The core concept of learned indexes is to conceptualize the index as a model that predicts the position of a specific key within the dataset. A primary advantage of this type of index is the reduced index size, which can result in a memory footprint reduction by orders of magnitude, as the trained model or model hierarchy in the index occupies less space than storing the actual data. Additionally, these indexes exchange increased computational demands for fewer memory accesses, potentially enhancing performance if the computation cycles are less costly compared to memory access latency. However, for such an index to be accurate in its predictions, the index model must be trained on the target dataset before deployment, which constrains the index's dynamic capabilities. Several proposals have been made \cite{histtree, alex, pgmindex, fittingtree, shifttable, radixspline, learnedMultiDim} for learned index structures since the initial proposal by Kraska et al. \cite{originalLearnedIndex}. These proposals and initial benchmarking efforts \cite{benchmarkingTUMMIT, benchmarkingSOSD} already compare learned indexes to index structures that do not rely on learned models. However, these comparisons primarily focus on higher-level metrics such as throughput (requests completed per second), latency (average time to complete a request), index size, and scalability concerning the number of threads used, among others. While these metrics are crucial and necessary to assess the overall benefits and drawbacks of learned index structures, they represent only one aspect, particularly for main-memory-optimized index structures. These metrics alone do not provide a comprehensive understanding of how learned indexes utilize the micro-architectural resources of a processor (e.g., utilization of front-end resources and various levels of the cache hierarchy). In this paper, our aim is to illuminate this other aspect. To accomplish our objective, we focus on the learned index ALEX \cite{alex}, which is among the first learned indexes specifically designed to facilitate efficient updates and inserts. We conduct a micro-architectural analysis of ALEX, comparing its behavior to two index structures that do not utilize learned models: ART \cite{artpaper, artcode}, a trie-based index structure, and B+tree \cite{btreecode}, a tree-based index structure. The reason for selecting these two structures for comparison is that ALEX has already been compared against them in the original paper \cite{alex} and in other studies \cite{benchmarkingTUMMIT, histtree}. This allows our results to be cross-verified. We develop a benchmark driver \footnote{Will be made available once the paper is accepted.} that generates YCSB-like \cite{ycsbpaper} workloads. Using this driver, we produce four workloads with varying read-write intensities and two datasets of different sizes. We then report the breakdown of execution cycles into various micro-architectural components following Intel's Top-down Micro-architecture Analysis Method (TMAM) \cite{tmam}. Our study reveals the following: \begin{list}{\labelitemi}{\leftmargin=1.5em} \item{Similar to ART and B+Tree, ALEX spends the majority of its execution cycles in memory-bound stalls due to long-latency data stalls from the last-level cache. Unlike ART and B+Tree, ALEX generally exhibits fewer stalls and spends fewer cycles per instruction across different workload patterns.} \item{Conversely, inserts to the right-end of the tree (\textit{out-of-bound} keys) cause an order of magnitude increase in the per-request instruction footprint of ALEX, whereas the impact on ART and B+Tree is not substantial, due to model re-training. The instruction-level parallelism for such instructions, however, is quite high. Consequently, this increase in instruction footprint does not significantly affect the overall execution time for ALEX.} \end{list} The remainder of the paper is organized as follows. First, \Cref{background} reviews related work and provides a brief overview of the index structures used in this study as well as the micro-architecture of a processor. Then, \Cref{setup} describes the experimental setup and methodology, and \Cref{results} presents and discusses the results of the analysis. Finally, \Cref{conclusion} concludes with a summary of our findings and outlines directions for future research.

text: Over the past decade, advancements in hardware have made multicore parallel machines commonplace. Although various programming paradigms and tools facilitate parallelism in multicore machines, the paradigm based on \defn{nested parallelism} with a \defn{randomized work-stealing (RWS) scheduler} is undoubtedly the most prevalent and widely adopted. The nested parallelism model and its variants are supported by most parallel programming languages (e.g., Cilk, TBB, TPL, X10, Java Fork-join, and OpenMP), are introduced in textbooks (e.g., Cormen, Leiserson, Rivest, and Stein~\cite{CLRS}), and are utilized in numerous research papers (for example: \cite{agrawal2014batching,blelloch2010low,BCGRCK08,BG04,Blelloch1998,blelloch1999pipelining,BlellochFiGi11,BST12,Cole17,BBFGGMS16,dinh2016extending,chowdhury2017provably,blelloch2018geometry,dhulipala2020semi,BBFGGMS18,Dhulipala2018,blelloch2020randomized,gu2021parallel,blelloch2016justjoin,sun2018pam,sun2019parallel,ptreedb}). At a high level, this model allows an algorithm to recursively and dynamically generate (\emph{fork}) parallel tasks, which are executed on $P$ processors by a dynamic scheduler. This nested (binary) fork-join provides an effective abstraction for shared-memory parallelism. For the user (algorithm designer or programmer), it is a straightforward extension of the classic programming model with additional keywords for task creation (e.g., \op{fork}) and synchronization (e.g., \op{join}) between tasks. The \defn{randomized work-stealing (RWS) scheduler} is essential in this framework. It automatically and dynamically maps a nested parallel algorithm to the hardware efficiently in both theory and practice. In this paper, we explore two significant topics related to the RWS scheduler. First, we present a \defn{new, simplified, and classroom-ready version of analysis for the RWS scheduler}, which we believe is more comprehensible than existing versions. Second, we offer some \defn{new analyses for parallel cache complexity} for nested-parallel algorithms based on the RWS scheduler. We provide a list of nearly optimal bounds in \Cref{table:intro}, with further discussions to follow. Our first contribution is a simplified analysis of the RWS scheduler. The theoretical efficiency of the RWS scheduler was initially demonstrated by Blumofe and Leiserson~\cite{blumofe1999scheduling}, and has since been analyzed in various contexts (for example: \cite{Acar02,itpa,muller2016latency,acar2013scheduling,BBFGGMS16,singer2019proactive,Acar2016tapp,singer2020scheduling,arora2001thread}). Although these analyses often consider more complex scenarios (e.g., including external I/Os), they are quite intricate. To our knowledge, the details of these proofs are covered in very few courses on parallelism, and RWS is typically treated as a black box. Therefore, we focus on bounding the number of steals of the RWS scheduler, aiming to determine the simplest analysis for the RWS scheduler that is most comprehensible in an educational context. This paper introduces a simplified analysis in \Cref{sec:rws}. Unlike most existing analyses, our version does not depend on defining a potential function for a substructure of the computation, which we believe enhances understanding. Our analysis is inspired by a recent study~\cite{itpa} that is similar to~\cite{agrawal2008adaptive,suksompong2014bounds}. Our analysis differs from~\cite{itpa} in two respects. First, unlike~\cite{itpa}, we do not assume all processors operate in lock-steps (the PRAM setting). Instead, we assume a highly asynchronous setting, which is more realistic for modern parallel machines. Second, we separate the mathematical calculations from the details of the RWS algorithm, which may be beneficial for classroom instruction. Our second and primary contribution of this paper concerns the parallel cache complexity for algorithms using the RWS scheduler. On contemporary machines, memory access costs often dominate the execution time of most combinatorial algorithms. To address this, Aggarwal and Vitter~\cite{AggarwalV88} initially formalized the external-memory model to capture the I/O cost of an algorithm, which was refined by Frigo et al.~\cite{Frigo99} as the ideal-cache model. The cost measure is termed \emph{I/O complexity}~\cite{AggarwalV88} (denoted as $Q_1$) or \emph{cache complexity}~\cite{Frigo99} when specifying the communication cost between the cache and the main memory. While this model has been highly successful in the algorithm and database communities, few results have extended it to the parallel (distributed cache) setting, which we summarize in \Cref{sec:cachebound}. Among these, Acar, Blelloch, and Blumofe~\cite{Acar02} first defined and demonstrated that the parallel cache complexity $Q_P$ is at most $Q_1+O(PDM/B)$, where $P$, $D$, $M$, and $B$ represent the number of processors, span (also known as depth, the longest critical path of dependencies), cache size, and cache block size, respectively (definitions in \Cref{sec:prelim}). However, this bound is pessimistic and often too loose. Frigo and Strumpen~\cite{frigo2009cache} and subsequent work by Cole and Ramachandran~\cite{cole2013analysis,cole2012revisiting} demonstrated tighter parallel cache complexity for many cache-oblivious algorithms summarized in \Cref{table:intro}. However, the bounds involve a polynomial overhead\footnote{Such overhead is typically $n^{a}$, where $a$ is a constant and $1/2\le a<1$.} on the input size when the span is polynomial relative to the input size. Such overhead can easily dominate the cache bound when applied to real-world input sizes, as discussed in the caption of \Cref{table:intro}. Closing this gap remained an open question. In this paper, we significantly narrow this gap for a variety of algorithms. The polynomial overhead in previous analyses~\cite{Acar02,frigo2009cache,cole2013analysis,cole2012revisiting} arises from the high span of these algorithms (a polynomial of the algorithm's span appears in the bound). The key insight in our analysis is to decouple such polynomial correlation between the algorithm's span and the overhead for parallel cache complexity. Our new analysis is inspired by the abstraction of \kdgrid{} recently proposed by Blelloch and Gu~\cite{BG2020}, which was previously used to demonstrate sequential cache bounds. We extend this idea for analyzing parallel cache complexity. Our analysis directly examines the ``real'' dependencies in the computation structure of these algorithms, rather than those induced by parallelism. Specifically, the core of our analysis is the \emph{recurrences} of these algorithms. Consequently, the parallel dependency of the computation (the algorithm's span) does not appear in the analysis. This approach helps us avoid the complexity of delving into the details of the scheduling algorithms in the analysis, and the analysis is no more complex than solving recurrences. To achieve this, we define the \dacrecur{}, which effectively models the recurrence patterns of many classic algorithms, and present a general theorem, \Cref{thm:recur}, to solve these recurrences. By applying these results, we achieve the new bounds in \Cref{table:intro}. The parallel overheads are polylogarithmic instead of polynomial relative to the input size, compared to the lower bounds by~\cite{ballard2014communication,BG2020}. We believe the methodology is of independent interest and could be useful in analyzing other parallel or sequential algorithms. We leave this as future work. The contributions of this paper are as follows. \begin{enumerate} \item We present a new analysis for the randomized work-stealing scheduler, which avoids using potential functions and is very straightforward. \item We propose the \dacrecur{} and a general theorem (\Cref{thm:recur}) for solving it, applicable to solving the parallel cache complexity for many classic parallel algorithms. \item We demonstrate new cache complexity bounds for various algorithms, shown in \Cref{table:intro}, which significantly improve existing results and are very close to the lower bounds (only a polylogarithmic overhead). \end{enumerate} \input{table-main} \hide{

We have two differences from I.T.P.A., namely: (1) we do not assume that all the processors execute in lock-step, as I.T.P.A. does; (2) we do not assume that the communication channels are symmetrical, as they do in I.T.P.A. Second, we separate the mathematical calculation from the RWS steps, which might be useful in teaching. In modern systems, memory accesses often dominate the time taken by most combinatorial algorithms. Instead, we assume an extremely asynchronous setting, which is more realistic in terms of modern parallel machines. The second and principal contribution of this paper is the parallel complexity of algorithms with the RWS scheduler. To model this situation, Aggarwal and Vitter formulated the external memory model to capture the I/O cost of an algorithm, which Frigo and others refined into the ideal cache model. “This model has been a great success in the communities of algorithms and data bases, but only a few results have been obtained to extend it to the parallel (distributed cache) setting, and which we summarise in ‘Cachebound’. Acar, Blelloch and Blumofe (reference “Acar02”) first defined and proved that the parallel complexity of the distributed cache complexity Q_P is at most Q_1+O(P/D) where P, D, M and B are the number of nodes, the span, the longest critical path of dependencies, the size of the cache and the size of the memory block, respectively. The main insight of our analysis is to decouple the correlation between the granularity of the involved algorithms and the overhead of parallel cache complexity. The main insight of the previous analysis (see, for example, Acar ’02, Frgo ’09, Cole ’13 analysis, and Cole ’12 revisiting) is that the polynomial overhead of the involved algorithms translates into the granularity of the inputs (a polynomial of the granularity appears in the bound). The new analysis is inspired by the kd-grid abstraction recently introduced by Blelloch and Guecitre (BG 2020) and previously used to prove sequential cache bounds. We extend this idea to analyze the cache complexity of parallel programs. In this paper, we significantly narrow the gap for a large number of granularities. In fact, the heart of our analysis is the recurrences of these rules. This approach allows us to avoid the complexity of analyzing the details of the schedules, and the analysis itself is no more complex than solving recurrences. The contributions of this paper are as follows. After defining a data structure dacrecur, which represents the recurrence relation of many classic algorithms, we prove a general result thm:recur, which proves that the recurrences can be solved by a general result thm:recur. text: When healthcare professionals (HCPs) utilize a treatment search engine to identify treatment options for their patients, they must develop a certain level of trust in the system. Although accuracy, performance, and design are crucial for establishing such trust, additional measures may be necessary to achieve a level where HCPs are confident enough to use the system in critical situations, such as when a patient's life may be at risk. A search engine typically provides a ranked list of related items in response to a specific query. However, the absence of explanations may result in users' distrust, as they may not comprehend the underlying rationale for retrieving an item in response to a query. In the medical field, where the imperative to avoid errors is significant, incorrectly attributing the cause of a mistake could have fatal consequences. Consequently, without the capacity to interpret the model, HCPs' trust in the model diminishes and they may ultimately refrain from using the model's outputs \cite{pu2006trust}. Furthermore, due to compliance regulations, most search engines in the medical domain provide unordered lists of related items in response to a query, complicating users' efforts to identify or differentiate the most pertinent items for their needs. For example, treatment search engines like clinicaltrials.gov do not offer relevance-based ranking of documents, partly because ranking treatment options that meet criteria may be subject to favoritism, which is strictly prohibited for clinical trials \cite{Clinical58:online}. Additionally, for an effective and comprehensive search, ordering based on status/date/title may not always be the most practical for end users, as it tends to separate similar results. One potential solution to provide explanations is to employ contemporary explainable methods. One category of such methods offers only global explanations, allowing us to evaluate the search engine as a whole, but failing to provide adequate explanations for each individual query \cite{dam2018explainable}. Another option is to employ methods for local explainability, such as LIME \cite{das2020opportunities} and SHAP \cite{lundberg2017unified}, which explain how or why a specific result is provided. However, these methods are designed for machine learning problems, such as classification and regression, rather than for explaining search engine results. When local explanations were applied to explain search results, they were either based on a single feature from the documents, like word prominence \cite{verma2019lirme}, or not applicable to clinical trials since they rely on user reviews for each document \cite{catherine2017explainable} (which are unavailable for clinical trials). Another significant challenge is providing HCPs with user-friendly, reliable, and easy-to-understand explanations. A major limitation of current explainability techniques, such as LIME \cite{das2020opportunities}, is that they tend to assist users with technical backgrounds in interpreting the system. HCPs are not universally expected to understand the detailed workings of a complex retrieval model. Therefore, HCPs require explanations that are high-level and intuitive, without necessarily reflecting the exact inner workings of retrieval models. This presents an opportunity to construct explanation models that are not sensitive to minor changes in the search engine model. For instance, with a treatment search engine, we might provide a local explanation such as “the queried disease is mentioned in the retrieved clinical trial’s title,” and as long as the retrieval model uses this as a feature, we are employing a generic explanation method, allowing us to develop the search engine and explanation module relatively independently in practice. In this paper, we develop an explainability method that offers tailored explanations to medical practitioners for retrieved items. To achieve this, meaningful features from clinical trials are extracted from various data sources, and user preferences are elicited using a crowdsourcing-based methodology. We then propose a method to translate preferences into the importance level of features. Based on the importance levels of features, tailored explanations are generated for each specific query, for which we develop a sentence template to present them to users. Additionally, we introduce explainability scores, which are used to order retrieved items. The results indicate that employing local explainability in clinical search engines enhances HCPs' trust, search experience, and satisfaction with result ordering.
