text: Semantic segmentation aims to partition an image into segments associated with semantic categories. Despite significant advancements~\cite{FCN,Deeplab,Deeplabv3Plus,pspnet,ocrnet,segformer}, current semantic segmentation models are predominantly trained in a supervised fashion with a fixed set of predefined semantic categories, often necessitating hundreds of samples per class. In contrast, humans can identify at least 30,000 basic categories~\cite{biederman1987recognition,fu2017recent} and recognize novel categories from a few \textit{high-level descriptions}. Achieving human-level capability to recognize objects and scenes in images remains a fundamental objective in computer vision. Recent studies on zero-shot semantic segmentation (ZS3)~\cite{spnet,ZS3Net} have indeed progressed towards this ultimate objective. Following fully supervised semantic segmentation models~\cite{FCN,Deeplabv3Plus,Deeplab} and zero-shot classification models~\cite{lampert2013attribute,zhang2016zero,jayaraman2014zero,rohrbach2011evaluating,akata2015evaluation}, these studies conceptualize zero-shot semantic segmentation as a \textit{pixel-level zero-shot classification problem}. Although these studies have shown promising outcomes, two primary issues remain unresolved: (1) They typically transfer knowledge from seen to unseen classes using \textit{language} models~\cite{spnet,ZS3Net,fasttext} pre-trained solely on text, which limits their effectiveness on vision tasks. While large-scale pre-trained \textit{vision-language} models (e.g., CLIP~\cite{clip} and ALIGN~\cite{align}) have shown potential in \textit{image-level} vision tasks, their efficient integration into the \textit{pixel-level} ZS3 problem remains unexplored. (2) They usually establish correlations between \textit{pixel-level} visual features and semantic features for knowledge transfer, which is \textit{unnatural} since humans typically use \textit{words or texts} to describe \textit{objects/segments} instead of \textit{pixels} in images. As depicted in Fig.~\ref{fig:confusion}, it is unsurprising that \textit{pixel-level} classification exhibits low accuracy on \textit{unseen classes}, thereby degrading the final segmentation quality. This phenomenon is particularly evident when the number of unseen categories is large (see Fig.~\ref{fig:visadeinfercoco}). An intuitive observation is that, given an image for semantic segmentation, humans can initially \textit{group pixels into segments} and subsequently conduct a \textit{segment-level semantic labeling} process. For instance, a child can easily group the pixels of an object, even if he/she does not know the object's name. Therefore, we propose that {\em a human-like zero-shot semantic segmentation procedure should be divided into two sub-tasks}: \begin{itemize} \item[-] A {\em class-agnostic grouping} to cluster pixels into segments. This task is essentially a classical image partition/grouping problem~\cite{DDMCMC,NormalizeCUT,supervisedeval}, which can be revitalized through deep learning-based methods~\cite{maskformer,KNet,panopticsegformer}. \item[-] A {\em segment-level zero-shot classification} to assign semantic labels, either seen or unseen, to segments. \end{itemize} Since the grouping task does not involve semantic categories, a grouping model trained on seen classes can be readily transferred to unseen classes. The segment-level zero-shot classification is robust for unseen classes and offers a flexible means to incorporate pre-trained large-scale vision-language models~\cite{clip} into the ZS3 problem. To realize the decoupling concept, we introduce a straightforward yet effective {\em zero-shot semantic segmentation model with transformer}, named ZegFormer, which employs a transformer decoder to produce \textit{segment-level} embeddings, as illustrated in Fig.~\ref{fig:pipeline}. This is followed by a \textit{mask projection} for \textit{class-agnostic grouping} (CAG) and a \textit{semantic projection} for \textit{segment-level zero-shot classification} (s-ZSC). The \textit{mask projection} converts each \textit{segment-level} embedding into a mask embedding, which can be used to derive a binary mask prediction via a dot product with a high-resolution feature map. The \textit{semantic projection} creates correspondences between \textit{segment-level} embeddings and semantic features of a pre-trained \textit{text encoder} for s-ZSC. While the aforementioned steps can constitute an independent approach for ZS3, the model trained on a small dataset struggles to achieve strong generalization. Thanks to the decoupling formulation, it is also adaptable to use an \textit{image encoder} of a vision-language model to generate image embeddings for zero-shot segment classification. We empirically find that the segment classification scores with image embeddings and s-ZSC are complementary. We combine them to obtain the final classification scores for segments. The proposed ZegFormer model has been thoroughly evaluated through experiments and has demonstrated superiority on various commonly-used benchmarks for ZS3. It surpasses state-of-the-art methods by \textbf{22 points} in terms of mIoU for unseen classes on the PASCAL VOC~\cite{voc}, and by \textbf{3 points} on the COCO-Stuff~\cite{coco-stuff}. Based on the challenging ADE20k-Full dataset~\cite{ade20k}, we also establish a new ZS3 benchmark with {\bf 275 unseen classes}, which is significantly larger than those in PASCAL-VOC ($5$ unseen classes) and COCO-Stuff ($15$ unseen classes). On the ADE20k-Full ZS3 benchmark, our performance is comparable to MaskFormer~\cite{maskformer}, a fully supervised semantic segmentation model. Our contributions in this paper are three-fold: \begin{itemize} 	\item We introduce a new formulation for the ZS3 task by dividing it into two sub-tasks, {\em a class-agnostic grouping} and {\em a segment-level zero-shot classification}, which offers a more natural and flexible approach to integrate pre-trained large-scale vision-language models into ZS3. 	\item With this new formulation, we present a simple and effective ZegFormer model for ZS3, which employs a transformer decoder to generate \textit{segment-level} embeddings for grouping and zero-shot classification. To our knowledge, the proposed ZegFormer is the first model to fully leverage the pre-trained large-scale vision-language model (\eg CLIP~\cite{clip}) for ZS3. 	\item We achieved state-of-the-art results on standard benchmarks for ZS3. The ablation and visualization analyses demonstrate that the decoupling formulation significantly outperforms pixel-level zero-shot classification. \end{itemize}

text: Despite recent advancements in autonomous driving, HD maps remain crucial in modern systems as they offer detailed information on road infrastructure, enabling applications such as motion planning and enhanced perception. However, accurately determining the vehicle's pose within the map is essential for utilizing HD maps. To address this localization task, high-precision systems typically use RTK-GNSS systems integrated with IMUs or vehicle odometry in a probabilistic fusion scheme~\cite{jo2011interacting,schreiber2016vehicle}. Nevertheless, the high cost of equipment and limitations in dense urban environments restrict these methods to research and data generation. Consequently, most deployed autonomous vehicles use an HD map that stores information about environmental elements like lane topology, traffic signs, and traffic lights for localization. With this information available, landmark-based localization has garnered interest. These methods involve a perception module to extract necessary features from sensor readings and continuously match them to available map elements to constrain the vehicle pose~\cite{caselitz2016monocular,cattaneo2019cmrnet}. Supported by extensive research and advances in deep learning, perception modules in modern systems typically include a convolutional neural network (CNN) to extract necessary features from the environment~\cite{poggenhans2018precise},~\cite{pauls2020monocular}. Although state-of-the-art CNN architectures can provide a comprehensive understanding of the environment using sensors such as cameras~\cite{porzi2019seamless,mohan2021efficientps} and LiDARs~\cite{sirohi2021efficientlps}, most CNNs cannot provide a reliable confidence estimate or tend to be overconfident in their predictions. This can undermine a localization algorithm's robustness and accuracy. The task of uncertainty estimation with deep learning extends standard neural network-based methods to additionally predict the associated uncertainty or confidence in the predictions. Popular uncertainty estimation methods primarily use sampling-based techniques~\cite{gal2016dropout}, which are computationally and time-intensive. While research on sampling-free methods is gaining traction, current approaches focus on predicting uncertainties for a single task like classification~\cite{sensoy2018evidential} or regression~\cite{amini2019deep}. In contrast, an overall perception system for autonomous vehicles involves various tasks, such as segmentation and detection. In this paper, we aim to address the localization problem in challenging urban scenarios using a low-cost sensor setup and extremely sparse HD maps containing only lane borders and traffic lights. We introduce a novel monocular camera-based localization system that leverages the uncertainty estimations of our proposed multi-task perception module. The perception module simultaneously predicts the uncertainties associated with the semantics of the lane and the bounding box parameters of the traffic lights in a single pass. The main contributions of this paper are: 1) a novel pose graph localization system robust in challenging scenarios by exploiting predicted uncertainties, 2) a multi-task uncertainty-aware perception module capable of simultaneously predicting semantic and regression uncertainties in a sampling-free manner, 3) a novel association-free and differentiable cost map generation module guided by prediction uncertainties. We demonstrate the performance improvement by incorporating uncertainties into our localization method by evaluating it on the challenging Lyft 5 dataset~\cite{kesten2019lyft}.

text: Deep Packet Inspection (DPI) middleboxes are extensively utilized as components of contemporary network security infrastructures \cite{xu2016survey}. They are stateful, meaning they not only examine individual packets but also reassemble them to establish stateful connections defined by a network protocol (e.g., TCP), following a predefined state machine. To achieve this, they (for simplicity, referred to as DPIs) must incorporate a custom network protocol implementation, which is often simplified compared to its counterpart on endpoint platforms (e.g., the OS kernel) due to limited computational resources, excessive overhead, and occasionally the necessity to maintain generality amidst ambiguous network protocol specifications. \point{Adversarial Packets} Since the inception of DPI, numerous attacks have been devised to bypass them. These attacks exploit the differences between the DPI's and the OS-level network protocol implementations to craft subtle yet potent packets that trigger entirely different behaviors on the DPI and at the endpoint (e.g., server). For instance, such a packet may be crafted to cause the DPI to ignore it, while it still reaches and is accepted by the server. Such packets can potentially carry malicious payloads and still evade DPI detection (as their contents would not be inspected at all). Even more concerning, previous research indicates that in some cases, using just one such packet could cause the DPI to cease monitoring the associated connection, thereby allowing subsequent packets in the connection to pass through without raising alarms. \point{Automated Discovery of Evasion Packets} In recent years, as network protocol stacks have become increasingly complex with newly added features \cite{ramaiah2010improving}, a growing number of vendor-specific implementations, and continually evolving specifications, there has been an increase in research \cite{li2017lib, bock2019geneva, wang2020symtcp} on automating the discovery of \textit{adversarial packets} as described above, to evade DPIs. By employing principled search \cite{li2017lib}, genetic mutation \cite{bock2019geneva}, or symbolic execution \cite{wang2020symtcp}, a wide variety of adversarial packets can be identified with minimal manual intervention. While this advances the understanding of attackers, it presents a significant challenge from the defense perspective. As protocol stacks evolve and become more intricate, the potential discrepancies that may be uncovered with automation can theoretically increase, making it impractical to manually analyze these subtle implementation issues and patch all of them in the codebase; additionally, it is challenging to generate new hardcoded DPI policies to keep pace with new discrepancies that may arise given the rapid evolution of implementations and protocol standards. \point{Existing Defenses} Given its complexity, only a few limited countermeasures have been proposed against adversarial packets. Notably, \cite{kreibich2001network}, Kreibich et al., apply \textit{traffic normalization} to mitigate the threats of adversarial packets. Specifically, a so-called traffic normalizer is proposed, which acts as a network forwarding element preceding DPI middleboxes and alters/drops the packets passing through the latter according to a predefined set of rules. These rules are manually curated to describe the "normal traffic" (e.g., the IP header length field must never be smaller or greater than the actual header length). Unfortunately, this countermeasure cannot scale in the presence of automation—the achievable search space of all possible adversarial packets can become large enough to make timely manual curation impractical. Moreover, the ever-evolving protocol standards introduce false alarms—a previously correct rule can later cause incorrect decisions (e.g., normal packets being dropped) due to updated implementations. It is also noteworthy that as a normalizer, or more generally a \textit{traffic shaper}, \cite{kreibich2001network} provides no detection capability; rather, it blindly alters the traffic stream. \point{Our Approach} Our objective in this paper is to design a practical defense to effectively detect evasion attempts on DPI middleboxes. Instead of relying on extensive manual curation/analysis, we propose a novel, fully automated (with minimal feature engineering) Machine Learning (ML)-based approach called \textsc{$\text{CLAP}$}\xspace (\textbf{C}ontext \textbf{L}earning based \textbf{A}dversarial \textbf{P}rotection). \textsc{$\text{CLAP}$}\xspace learns the benign (what we call) \textit{context} from only normal traffic traces (i.e., unsupervised) and uses this learning to detect adversarial packets. In other words, \textsc{$\text{CLAP}$}\xspace determines whether the context of the unseen packets "fits" in the associated connection or not. Specifically, the context of a packet is composed of two types of sub-contexts to describe the aforementioned "fitness" of a given packet: \squishlist \item \textbf{Inter-packet context}, which captures the inter-relationships among different packets in the connection in terms of how their header fields change/evolve over the trace; these changes generally relate to the transitioning of states for a stateful network protocol (e.g., TCP); \item \textbf{Intra-packet context}, which captures the inter-relationships among different header fields in a given packet (in terms of the combinations of their values). \squishend By learning the joint distribution (i.e., the \textit{packet context}) of the two (sub-)contexts from benign traffic, \textsc{$\text{CLAP}$}\xspace automatically identifies violations thereof, caused by adversarial packets. \point{Motivating Example} To illustrate the intuition behind how \textsc{$\text{CLAP}$}\xspace operates, we present a concrete attack and its detection with \textsc{$\text{CLAP}$}\xspace. Bad-Checksum-RST is an attack that has been reported in \cite{wang2020symtcp, bock2019geneva} and shown to be effective against the Great Firewall (GFW), a state-of-the-art DPI-based censorship system. It injects an ill-formed RST packet with a corrupted TCP checksum value after the three-way handshake. Since common endhost TCP implementations perform rigorous checksum verification but the GFW does not, this injected RST packet is dropped by the endhost but not by the GFW. As a result, upon seeing an RST packet, the GFW would disengage its monitoring of the connection, while communications between the two endhosts would be allowed to continue. By learning the benign context from a large set of clean network traces, \textsc{$\text{CLAP}$}\xspace understands what requirements (inter- and intra-packet contexts) must be satisfied by a packet at its position in the connection (e.g., can it be an RST and if so, should its checksum be correct?); then, \textsc{$\text{CLAP}$}\xspace checks whether the packet conforms (fits in) to a benign packet context. In this case, the RST packet with a bad checksum value that appears after the three-way handshake is identified as violating both the inter- (RST should not occur at this point) and intra-packet (checksum of RST packet should be correct) contexts (based on training) and thus, the evasion attempt is detected. \point{Contributions} In summary, our contributions in this paper are: \begin{enumerate} \item We are the first to propose a fully automated unsupervised learning approach to detect adversarial packets crafted to evade DPI middleboxes. \item Our evaluations on 73 state-of-the-art DPI evasion attacks over realistic backbone traffic captures show that by only learning from benign traffic, \textsc{$\text{CLAP}$}\xspace achieves an overall detection AUC-ROC of over \underline{\textbf{0.963}}\xspace, with an average EER of only \underline{\textbf{0.061}}\xspace (the two most commonly used evaluation metrics for ML-based IDSs \cite{mirsky2018kitsune,aqil2017jaal,marin2018rawpower,marin2019deepsec}). \item Our evaluations demonstrate that beyond detection, \textsc{$\text{CLAP}$}\xspace achieves an average Top-5 localization accuracy (identifying a sequence of five packets most likely to contain the attack vector) of \underline{\textbf{94.6\%}}\xspace (Top-3 of \underline{\textbf{91.0\%}}\xspace). \item Our performance analysis indicates that our pipeline can process over 2,100 packets per second on a single CPU core, with linear scalability. \item We will open source both our implementation of \textsc{$\text{CLAP}$}\xspace and the used datasets at https://github.com/seclab-ucr/CLAP to enable reproducibility and future extensions. \end{enumerate}

text: Recently, there has been a resurgence of interest in contrastive learning (CL) \cite{DBLP:conf/nips/KhoslaTWSTIMLK20,jaiswal2021survey,liu2020self} within the field of deep representation learning. Owing to its capability to extract general features from large volumes of unlabeled data and to regularize representations in a self-supervised manner, CL has driven significant advancements across various research domains \cite{you2020graph,wujc2021self,chen2020simple,gao2021simcse}. Since CL does not require data annotation, it naturally addresses the data sparsity challenge in recommender systems \cite{sarwar2001sparsity,hao2021pre}. A growing number of recent studies \cite{wujc2021self,yu2021self,xia2020self,zhou2020s,zhou2021contrastive,yu2021socially} have aimed to leverage CL to enhance recommendation performance, demonstrating notable improvements. A common approach \cite{wujc2021self} to applying CL in recommendation involves first augmenting the user-item bipartite graph with structural perturbations (e.g., stochastic edge/node dropout at a certain ratio), and then maximizing the consistency of representations under different views learned via a graph encoder. In this context, the CL task serves as an auxiliary task and is optimized jointly with the recommendation task (Fig. \ref{figure:gcl}). \par Despite the promising results achieved by CL, the underlying reasons for the performance improvements remain unclear. Intuitively, we hypothesize that contrasting different graph augmentations can capture the essential information present in the original user-item interactions by randomly eliminating redundancy and impurity through edge/node dropout. Unexpectedly, several recent studies \cite{yu2021socially,zhou2021selfcf,DBLP:conf/sigir/LeeKJPY21} have indicated that even extremely sparse graph augmentations (with an edge dropout rate of 0.9) in CL can yield desirable performance gains. This phenomenon is quite puzzling and counter-intuitive because a high dropout rate would lead to a substantial loss of raw information and a highly skewed graph structure. This naturally raises an important question: \textit{Do we really need graph augmentations when integrating CL with recommendation?} \par To address this question, we first conduct experiments with and without graph augmentations to compare performance. The results reveal that in the absence of graph augmentations, the performance is still comparable to that with graph augmentations. We then examine the embedding space learned by non-CL and CL-based recommendation methods. By visualizing the distributions of the representations and relating them to their performances, we find that the CL loss, rather than the graph augmentation, is what truly influences recommendation performance. Optimizing the contrastive loss InfoNCE \cite{oord2018representation} results in more evenly distributed user/item representations, regardless of whether graph augmentations are applied, which implicitly helps mitigate the popularity bias \cite{chen2020bias}. Meanwhile, although not as effective as anticipated, graph augmentations are not entirely useless, as properly perturbed versions of the original graph aid in learning representations invariant to disturbance factors \cite{bachman2019learning,chen2020simple}. However, generating hand-crafted graph augmentations necessitates constant reconstruction of the graph adjacency matrix during training, which is quite time-consuming. Additionally, dropping a critical edge/node (e.g., a cut edge) may divide a connected graph into several disconnected components, risking that the augmented graph and the original graph share little learnable invariance. Given these drawbacks, a subsequent question arises: \textit{Are there more effective and efficient augmentation approaches?} \par In this paper, we provide an affirmative answer to this question. Building on our finding that the uniformity of the representation distribution is crucial, we develop a graph-augmentation-free CL method where the uniformity is more controllable. Technically, we adhere to the graph CL framework depicted in Fig. \ref{figure:gcl}, but we eliminate the dropout-based graph augmentation and instead introduce random uniform noises to the original representations for representation-level data augmentation. Imposing different random noises generates variance between contrastive views, while the learnable invariance is preserved due to the controlled magnitude. Compared to graph augmentation, the noise version directly regularizes the embedding space towards a more even distribution, which is easy to implement and significantly more efficient. \par The major contributions of this paper are summarized as follows: \begin{itemize}[leftmargin=*] 	\item We experimentally elucidate why CL can enhance recommendation performance and demonstrate that the InfoNCE loss, rather than graph augmentation, is the decisive factor. 	\item We propose a simple yet effective graph-augmentation-free CL method for recommendation that can regulate uniformity in a smooth manner. It serves as an ideal alternative to cumbersome graph augmentation-based CL methods. 	\item We conduct a comprehensive experimental study on three benchmark datasets, showing that the proposed method has distinct advantages over its graph augmentation-based counterparts in terms of recommendation accuracy and model training efficiency. \end{itemize}

text: The current state of data privacy can be described as the post-privacy era due to the unforeseen consequences of the big data revolution. The well-known Cambridge Analytica scandal \cite{berghel2018malice} exemplifies how re-identification can be accomplished by cross-analyzing large datasets containing private information. The technological revolution that has led us to post-privacy has not been halted by privacy regulations such as the General Data Protection Regulation (GDPR). We are now experiencing another (r)evolution that could restore data privacy—blockchain. In 2018, the European Union implemented the GDPR \cite{EUdataregulations2018}, which governs the collection, processing, and protection of personal data, including protected health information (PHI). Article 4(15) of the EU GDPR defines data concerning health as: “personal data related to the physical or mental health of a natural person, including the provision of healthcare services, which reveal information about his or her health status.” The Health Insurance Portability and Accountability Act (HIPPA) is fundamental to U.S. healthcare law and primarily addresses privacy rights and access rather than ownership of patient data \cite{annas2003hipaa}. In this context, each state has ownership of its citizens' patient data, which is regulated by the respective state law. With 50 states, there are 50 different laws, court cases, and interpretations regarding the ownership of patient data. New Hampshire is the only state that has enacted legislation stating that patient data ownership belongs to the patient. How GDPR will interact and align with U.S. state laws is yet to be determined. Blockchain, initially introduced with the launch of Bitcoin in 2008, has become more diluted in its definition, and there is currently no fixed, universally accepted definition of the term blockchain. To clarify its use in this research, we have defined Blockchain as a distributed, decentralized, and tamper-proof ledger without any centralized control. Blockchain technology and other Distributed Ledger Technologies (DLT) could enhance our data privacy and empower individuals with control and access over their data, including health data. The aim of this study is twofold: (i) to analyze the various designs of blockchain and examine GDPR compliance for different components in established or proposed blockchain applications in the healthcare sector and, (ii) to offer future researchers guidance on how to comply with GDPR when designing blockchain applications within the healthcare domain. The remainder of this paper is organized as follows: \textbf{Section II} provides a brief introduction to blockchain technology and outlines previous work addressing blockchain compliance with GDPR; \textbf{Section III} presents the research approach; \textbf{Section IV} describes four blockchain applications in healthcare identified through the literature; \textbf{Section V} presents our results and analysis; \textbf{Section VI} provides a discussion and conclusion to the work, and offers recommendations for future work.

text: The reliable detection of encrypted data fragments is a crucial primitive with numerous applications in security and digital forensics. For example, ransomware detection algorithms utilize estimates of the randomness in write-operations' data to swiftly identify signs of malicious encryption processes~\cite{kirda_redemption,mehnaz_rwguard,continella_shieldfs:_2016,kirda_unveil}. During digital forensic analysis of hard drives and phones, it is often essential to identify encrypted archives~\cite{conti_automated_2010}. Additionally, encryption detection is extensively employed in network protocol analysis~\cite{de_carli_botnet_2017,dorfinger_real-time_2010}. A common method to tackle this issue is to estimate the Shannon entropy of the sequence of interest using the Maximum Likelihood Estimator (MLE): $\hat{H}_{MLE}$. This method exploits the observation that the distribution of byte values in an encrypted stream closely resembles a uniform distribution; thus, high entropy serves as a proxy for randomness. This estimator is advantageous due to its simplicity and computational efficiency. Since non-encrypted digital data is presumed to have low byte-level entropy, the estimator is expected to effectively distinguish between non-encrypted and encrypted content. Although this method is still widely used (e.g.,~\cite{kirda_redemption,mehnaz_rwguard,continella_shieldfs:_2016,kirda_unveil}), several studies have pointed out its limitations. Modern applications often compress data before storage and transmission. Notable examples include the zip compressed file format and HTTP compression~\cite{http-rfc} (both utilizing the DEFLATE algorithm). As compression eliminates recurring patterns in data, compressed streams tend to display high Shannon entropy. Consequently, compressed data exhibit $\hat{H}_{MLE}$ values that are similar to and often overlap with those of encrypted data. In theory, compressed content can be identified using suitable parsers. However, many security-related applications, such as ransomware detection, traffic analysis, and digital forensics, typically do not have access to complete file information but rather operate at the level of \textit{fragments} of data. In these scenarios, the metadata required by parsers is absent or incomplete~\cite{park_data_2008}. In light of this issue, several studies have explored alternative tests to differentiate between encrypted and compressed content~\cite{malhotra_detection_2007,wang_using_2011,foresti_efficient_2016,lipmaa_data_2017,hahn2018detecting,casino_hedge_2019,choudhury_empirical_2020}. While these studies have the potential to be beneficial, there has been limited assessment of their performance on a standardized dataset. As a result, there is no clear understanding of how these methods: (i) perform across various compressed file formats and sizes, and (ii) compare to one another. The potential negative consequences are substantial: employing ineffective techniques for identifying encrypted content can undermine the efficacy of ransomware detectors~\cite{gaspari2019}, and significantly restrict the capability of forensic tools. Our research compares select state-of-the-art methods on a large dataset comprising different data types and fragment sizes. We discover that, while more advantageous than entropy estimates, current methods fail to consistently achieve high accuracy. To address this, we introduce \textsc{EnCoD} (\textbf{En}cryption/\textbf{Co}mpression \textbf{D}istinguisher), a novel neural network-based method. Our evaluation demonstrates that \textsc{EnCoD} surpasses existing methods for most considered file types, across all considered fragment sizes. \textsc{EnCoD} can classify data fragments as small as $512B$ with $86\%$ accuracy, increasing to up to $~94\%$ for purely compressed data (i.e., zip, gzip) and up to $100\%$ for compressed application data fragments (e.g., pdf, jpeg, mp3) for $8KB$ fragment sizes. Overall, this paper makes the following contributions: \begin{itemize} \item We review and categorize the existing literature on distinguishing compressed and encrypted data fragments. \item We systematically evaluate and compare state-of-the-art methods on a large, standardized dataset that includes a variety of fragment formats and sizes. \item We propose a new neural-network-based method, which outperforms current state-of-the-art tests in distinguishing encrypted from compressed content for most considered formats, across all considered fragment sizes. \item We propose a new multi-class classifier that can accurately label a fragment as encrypted data, general-purpose compressed data (zip/gzip/rar), or one of multiple application-specific compressed data (png, jpeg, pdf, mp3). \item We thoroughly discuss the implications of our findings in terms of the applicability of the evaluated methods. \end{itemize}

We show that EnCoD can classify data fragments as small as 5128 bytes with 86.6% accuracy, which increases to 94.7% for purely compressed data (i.e. zip, gzip) and 97.6% for compressed application data (e.g. pdf, jpeg, mp3) for fragments as large as 8kB. item We propose a new multiclass classifier which can accurately label a fragment as encrypted data, general-purpose compressed data (zip/gzp/rar), or one of many application-specific compressed data (png, jpeg, pdf, mp3). We propose a new neural-network based method which outperforms the current state-of-the-art in recognizing encrypted from compressed content for most of the considered formats, at all of the considered fragment sizes. dipper_dipper: The reliable detection of encrypted data fragments is a key primitive with many applications in security and digital forensics. In digital forensic analysis of hard disks and mobile devices it is often necessary to detect encrypted archives. For example, ransomware detection algorithms exploit an estimate of the degree of randomness in the write-operation data in order to quickly recognize signs of malicious encryption processes (for example, kirda_redemption, mehnaz_rwguard, continella_shieldfs:_2016, kirda_unveil). As well, encryption detection is widely used in network protocol analysis. In this case, a common approach to this problem is to estimate the Shannon entropy of the sequence of interest using the maximum likelihood estimator H_hat=H_ln(S). This method is based on the observation that the distribution of byte values in an encrypted stream closely resembles the uniform distribution, and that a high entropy is a proxy for randomness. The advantage of the estimator is simplicity and efficiency. Since the entropy of non-encrypted digital data is expected to be low, the estimator should distinguish encrypted and non-encrypted data. However, although this method is still widely used (e.g. Kirda_Redemption, Mehnaz_RWGuard, Continella_ShieldFS:_2016, Kirda_Unveil), several studies have pointed out its limitations. Streams that have been compressed before being stored or transmitted have a high Shannon entropy. Modern applications compress data before storing or transmitting them. Notable examples of compression are the ZIP compressed file format and the compression of the HTTP protocol (both based on the DEFLATE compression method). Compressed data have H-MLE values similar to and often identical with those of encrypted data. In theory, it is possible to detect compressed content with suitable parsers. However, many security applications, such as ransomware detection, traffic analysis, and digital forensics, generally do not have access to complete files, and operate at the level of text fragments. In view of this problem, several studies have developed alternative ways to detect encrypted and compressed content. Some of these studies are cited below. References: Malhotra Detection 2007, Wang Using 2011, Foresti Efficient 2016, Lipmaa Data 2017, Hahn Detection 2018, Casino Hedge 2019, Choudhury Hedging 2019, Choudhury Empirical 2020. There is very little work on the performance of these methods on a standardized dataset. Our research compares the performance of several current state-of-the-art methods on a large set of different data fragments and types of encryption. The absence of such work is not insignificant, as ineffective methods for identifying encrypted data can seriously weaken the effectiveness of ransomware-detection tools and reduce the capabilities of forensic tools. We review and classify the existing literature on the distinction between encrypted and compressed fragments. We introduce EnCoD (Encryption/Compression Distinguisher), a novel method based on neural networks, to overcome this difficulty. The results of our evaluations show that EnCoD outperforms the best of the existing methods for most of the considered file formats and at all the tested fragment sizes. We show that EnCoD can correctly classify fragments as small as 5100 bytes with an accuracy of 86.6%, which increases to 94.7% for purely compressed data (e.g. zip, gzip) and 97.6% for compressed applications (e.g. tar, gz). We systematically compare the accuracy of the most advanced methods on a large and standardized data set of different fragments of different sizes and formats. We propose a new neural network-based method which outperforms the current state-of-the-art in recognizing encrypted from compressed content for most of the considered formats, at all the considered fragment sizes. We propose a new multiclass classifier which can accurately classify a fragment as encrypted data, general purpose compressed data (.gz,.Z, RAR), or one of many application-specific compressed data (.PNG,.JPEG,.PDF,.JPEG,.mp3) for fragments as small as 8 kB. CHAPTER XXV—END-ITM

text: The brain is among the most intricate and enigmatic tissues, governing the movement, perception, and emotions of animals, including humans. Nevertheless, the detailed brain structure of most animals remains largely undiscovered due to its immense complexity. Our research is centered on connectomics, which seeks to resolve the comprehensive connectivity graphs in animal brains to elucidate the underlying mechanisms of intelligence and inspire improved treatments for neurological diseases. Recently, with advancements in modern electron microscopy (EM) techniques, neuroscientists have been gathering petabytes of volumetric images at {\em nanometer} resolution, facilitating the analysis of detailed neuronal connectivities and subcellular structures such as synapses and mitochondria~\cite{kasthuri2015saturated,xu2020connectome,shapson2021connectomic}. Segmenting cellular and subcellular structures from microscopy images is typically the initial step before structural~\cite{talwar2020topological} and functional~\cite{shapson2021connectomic} analysis. Computationally, segmentation tasks can generally be divided into two categories: {\em semantic} segmentation, which assigns each pixel a class label, and {\em instance} segmentation, which also assigns each pixel an object index in addition to the class label. Currently, deep learning has become the {\em de facto} approach for both semantic segmentation~\cite{chen2017deeplab} and instance segmentation~\cite{he2017mask,ronneberger2015u}, achieving state-of-the-art performance on most natural-scene and biomedical image datasets without relying on hand-crafted features. However, several challenges arise when applying these automated approaches to the segmentation of large-scale connectomics datasets. First, existing open-source segmentation packages are typically designed for standard benchmark datasets, meaning that adapting these tools to new data with different scales and formats requires significant time for hardware adjustments and data pre-processing. Second, implementing specialized network architectures or different learning objectives for new tasks is often cumbersome in existing frameworks. Another challenge is that most packages, despite their good performance on segmentation tasks, lack comprehensive tutorials and documentation, which increases the learning burden for researchers with limited programming experience. To address these challenges, we introduce {\em PyTorch Connectomics} (PyTC), an open-source deep-learning framework for the semantic and instance segmentation of volumetric microscopy images. PyTC is built on the state-of-the-art deep learning library PyTorch~\cite{NEURIPS2019_9015} and benefits from its flexibility and simplicity in neural network implementation. Our framework is not tailored to a specific imaging modality, data scale, or model architecture but is versatile for various datasets and segmentation tasks, setting us apart from previous works like flood-filling networks (FFN)~\cite{januszewski2018high} for neuron segmentation, StarDist~\cite{weigert2020star} for nuclei segmentation, and CleftNet~\cite{liu2021cleftnet} that focus solely on synapses. Similar to nnU-Net~\cite{isensee2021nnu}, we identify a set of components such as data loaders, image augmentations, and optimizers that require minimal adaptation across different datasets and tasks. However, nnU-Net is limited to semantic segmentation, whereas our framework can handle both semantic and instance segmentation. Furthermore, our framework is significantly more customizable than nnU-Net, allowing us to address unique challenges in different datasets and tasks, which helps us achieve notably better performance (\eg, synaptic cleft segmentation). Several supported tasks of PyTC are illustrated in Figure~\ref{fig:teaser}. Specifically, we design PyTC by identifying the primary needs of connectomics researchers in various components of segmentation. For data loading, we manage large datasets by automatically dividing them into manageable chunks, compatible with parallel and distributed processing and easily adaptable to different hardware conditions. For modeling, researchers can customize 2D, 3D, or mixed architectures (for anisotropic images) and adjust the number of layers and kernels based on data complexity. The model can also learn multiple targets with multiple losses for each target, facilitating hybrid-representation learning to fully utilize annotations. Additionally, users can easily configure data-loading, model-building, optimization, and visualization by simply modifying a configuration file without coding. The design also ensures the reproducibility of experiments and is user-friendly for the development and maintenance of the package. Finally, we provide a detailed description of the design and usage of PyTC in our documentation and tutorials to expedite the learning process. In summary, we present the {\em PyTorch Connectomics} framework to address challenges in volumetric microscopy image segmentation by achieving scalability and flexibility in data processing, modeling, and learning. We are actively enhancing the framework with feedback from biomedical researchers and contributions from the open-source community. We are incorporating recent machine learning techniques such as semi-supervised and self-supervised learning to effectively utilize vast unlabelled data, which can better support experts in connectomics research.

text: Evaluating the brain's structure is essential for comprehending its normal and pathological functions. Recent advancements in electron microscopy (EM) facilitate three-dimensional (3D) imaging of tissue spanning hundreds of micrometers with nanometer-scale resolution, offering novel opportunities to investigate brain ultrastructure \cite{Phelps2021ReconstructionMicroscopy, Nahirney2021}. Quantitative analysis of 3D-EM data, such as assessing the morphology of ultrastructures, spatial distribution, or cellular connectivity, necessitates the instance segmentation of individual ultrastructural elements \cite{Abdollahzadeh2021DeepACSONMicroscopy, Kleinnijenhuis2020AMicroscopy, Yuan2021HIVE-Net:Images}. Manually performing this segmentation is laborious, if not impractical, due to the vast size and immense number of components in typical 3D-EM data. For instance, manually labeling 215 neurites in a volume of 500 million voxels took 1500 hours \cite{Berning2015}, and \revised{we estimated that manually segmenting axons in a white matter EM with 300 million voxels, each measuring $15 \times 15 \times 50 nm^3$, would take 2400 hours} \cite{Abdollahzadeh2019AutomatedMatter}. Consequently, analyzing 3D-EM data of brain tissue necessitates developing advanced software tools that enable neuroscientists to automatically visualize, segment, and extract the geometric and topological characteristics of brain ultrastructures. Several software tools exist for analyzing 3D-EM data, including open-source packages such as Microscopy Image Browser (MIB) \cite{Belevich2016}, DeepMIB \cite{Belevich2021DeepMIB:Segmentation}, Knossos \cite{Knossos}, \revised{webKnossos \cite{Boergens2017WebKnossos:Connectomics}}, AxonSeg \cite{Zaimi2016AxonSeg:Analysis}, AxonDeepSeg \cite{Zaimi2018AxonDeepSeg:Networks}, TrackEM2 \cite{Cardona2012}, CATMAID \cite{Saalfeld2009}, \revised{VAST \cite{Berger2018VASTStacks}, NeuroMorph \cite{Jorstad2018NeuroMorph:Connectivity}}, SegEM \cite{Berning2015}, Ilastik \cite{ilastik}, or MyelTracer \cite{Kaiser2021Myeltracer:Quantification}, and proprietary software like Amira (Thermofisher Scientific$^{ TM }$, MA, \url{www.thermofisher.com/amira-avizo}) or Imaris (Oxford Instruments, Abingdon, UK, \url{www.imaris.oxinst.com}). Table \ref{tbl:software} summarizes the primary features of the \revised{open source} software packages. However, the segmentation tools in these packages are primarily designed for manual or semi-automatic segmentation, making them highly labor-intensive for users. The supervised learning-based segmentation methods in these packages, such as those in DeepMIB \cite{Belevich2021DeepMIB:Segmentation} or AxonDeepSeg \cite{Zaimi2018AxonDeepSeg:Networks}, generally require manually annotated training data, which can be challenging and tedious to create. Furthermore, although some packages offer excellent visualization capabilities, they are not optimized for interactive correction, proofreading, and validation of automatic segmentations. In this context, we developed a \textbf{G}raphical user interface for \textbf{A}utomati\textbf{C} \textbf{S}egmentation of ax\textbf{ON}s, named gACSON, for analyzing axonal morphology in large 3D-EM datasets of the brain. The \revised{Matlab-based} gACSON builds upon our previous pipelines ACSON \cite{Abdollahzadeh2019AutomatedMatter} and DeepACSON \cite{Abdollahzadeh2021DeepACSONMicroscopy} for 3D-EM segmentation and morphometrics, offering an intuitive graphical user interface (GUI) and additional segmentation algorithms for myelin and the intra-axonal space of myelinated axons. The software facilitates automatic unsupervised segmentation without requiring manually annotated training data. While ACSON and DeepACSON are automated segmentation pipelines, gACSON is an interactive tool, providing user-friendly options to review and correct segmentations. \revised{It} also enables segmentation of a subset of all myelinated axons, allowing users to avoid waiting for the segmentation of all myelinated axons to complete. More importantly, \revised{the software} offers instance segmentation of myelin that associates myelin sheaths with the corresponding intra-axonal space instance. This feature distinguishes \revised{the new tool} from our existing ACSON and DeepACSON pipelines \cite{Abdollahzadeh2019AutomatedMatter}. With the software, users can visualize and review the segmented ultrastructure or amend the results of an automated segmentation by providing a dynamic environment for interactive merge or split operations on the segmented components. Like the ACSON and DeepACSON pipelines, gACSON extracts morphological parameters of segmented myelinated axons, such as axonal diameter or eccentricity, but extends the morphological parameters to measure myelin thickness and g-ratio by enabling instance segmentation of myelin. Moreover, visualization, segmentation evaluation, or correction of automatic segmentation results is not restricted to EM but can be applied to other biomedical imaging modalities, such as light microscopy images. The structure of this paper is as follows: Sections \ref{seg_pip} and \ref{morph_pip} present the gACSON segmentation and morphometry pipelines, respectively. Section \ref{visualization} introduces the GUI, including the parameter settings and tools for proofreading and correcting the automatic segmentation and evaluating the accuracy of the segmentation results. In Section 3, we demonstrate the application of the software to segment a new dataset of six serial block-face scanning electron microscopy (SBEM) volumes of the rat somatosensory cortex. We further make these volumes and segmentations publicly available.

text: Recent advancements in Supervised Re-Identification (re-ID) have resulted in outstanding performance on commonly utilized public re-ID datasets (\cite{ye2021deep,ni2021adaptive}). However, performance experiences a notable decline when re-ID models are evaluated across datasets, i.e., on images from a target context distinct from the training context. In this practical scenario, to avoid the expensive manual annotation of new target datasets, Unsupervised Domain Adaptation (UDA) has garnered interest among machine learning and computer vision researchers. The objective of UDA is to transfer valuable knowledge from a re-ID model in a source domain to a target domain, without any additional identity (ID) labels in the target domain. Unsupervised Domain Adaptive re-ID (UDA re-ID) methods have been developed to address the open-set nature of re-ID, where test-time classes differ from those encountered during training. An initial line of research in UDA re-ID explored \emph{Domain Translation}. This category of approaches seeks to bridge the gap between source and target domains in the image space using style-transfer generative models (\cite{wei2018person, deng2018image, peng2019cross, zhong2018generalizing, qi2019novel}) or by constraining the feature space to learn a domain-invariant discriminative representation (\cite{chang2019disjoint, li2018adaptation, li2019cross, lin2018multi, mekhazni2020unsupervised}). Nevertheless, Domain Translation-based approaches are unable to learn target-specific discriminative features, thereby limiting the re-ID performance achieved on the target domain.\\ Recent UDA re-ID approaches extensively rely on the utilization of \emph{pseudo-labels} for the target domain data (\cite{song2020unsupervised, zhang2019self, jin2020global, tang2019unsupervised, zhai2020ad, zou2020joint, yang2019asymmetric, chendeep, ge2020mutual, zhai2020multiple, zhao2020unsupervised, zou2020joint,peng2020unsupervised, Zhang_2021_CVPR, Yang_2021_CVPR}). Indeed, learning with these target pseudo-labeled samples can result in a more identity-discriminative representation in the target domain. For this purpose, researchers have devised a wide array of Pseudo-Labeling frameworks, based on a diverse range of modeling choices. Consequently, various directions have been pursued to enhance pseudo-label-based UDA re-ID approaches: some studies focus on improving the predicted pseudo-labels (\cite{jiattention,zhai2020ad, tang2019unsupervised, zou2020joint, Chen_2021_CVPR, Zheng_2021_CVPR, zheng2021online, Zhang_2021_CVPR}), while others aim to mitigate the impact of pseudo-label errors during training (\cite{ge2020mutual, zhao2020unsupervised, zhai2020multiple, jin2020global, liu2020domain, fu2019self, Xuan_2021_CVPR,lin2020unsupervised, Yang_2021_CVPR, lin2020unsupervised, Yang_2021_CVPR, feng2021complementary, ge2020self}). These Pseudo-Labeling practices, integrated into specific Pseudo-Labeling methods, have been experimentally shown to enhance performance. However, there is no comprehensive theoretical framework that can justify these practices, highlight the conditions for their effectiveness, and explain how they improve performance.\\ Moreover, some of these practices are not unanimously agreed upon among Pseudo-Labeling UDA re-ID researchers: the most common example is leveraging (\cite{dub2020, ge2020self, Isobe_2021_ICCV, dubourvieux2021improving}) or alternatively discarding (\cite{zhang2019self, zhai2020ad}) the available ground-truth labeled source data to optimize the model jointly with the pseudo-labeled target data. It is noteworthy that the majority of Pseudo-Labeling UDA re-ID approaches do not utilize the available source training set (\cite{zhang2019self, zhai2020ad, song2020unsupervised, jin2020global, tang2019unsupervised, zhai2020ad, zou2020joint, yang2019asymmetric, chendeep}) after gaining access to target pseudo-labels. However, some recent studies (\cite{dub2020, ge2020self, dubourvieux2021improving, Isobe_2021_ICCV}) have experimentally demonstrated that the source data, when continuously used alongside the target pseudo-labeled data, can enhance re-ID performance on the target domain. Can the source data contribute to improving the cross-dataset re-ID performance of any Pseudo-Labeling approach? Are there specific conditions under which any Pseudo-Labeling UDA re-ID method can benefit from the source data after accessing target pseudo-labels? These questions remain unanswered.\\ We believe the absence of general insight into these key UDA re-ID questions is due to the predominance of empirically-oriented works in UDA re-ID. Therefore, this work aims to address these questions with a general theoretical framework and to highlight best practices for designing an effective Pseudo-Labeling UDA re-ID method. text: This paper presents a policy learning approach that utilizes task-and-motion planning (TAMP) to train robot manipulation policies for tasks with extended horizons. Contemporary policy learning techniques can address robotic control tasks using complex sensory inputs~\cite{Finn16, trpo, rubiks}, but their success has predominantly been confined to tasks with short horizons. Learning policies capable of executing long sequences of manipulation actions remains an unresolved challenge~\cite{oneshothier, subpol}. In contrast, TAMP methods can efficiently solve problems requiring numerous abstract actions while satisfying complex geometric constraints in high-dimensional configuration spaces~\cite{hiertamp, extendtamp}. However, their use is often restricted to controlled environments because TAMP methods require reliable world state tracking and time allocation for planning~\cite{garretttamp, householdmarathon}. To address these issues, two research directions have emerged. The first employs machine learning to identify policies or heuristics that reduce planning time~\cite{feasibletamp, scorespace, guidetamp, gripsqp, mctstamp, chitnis2016guided}. This broadens the applicability of TAMP but still depends on explicit state estimation. The second approach involves learning policies that mimic the output of TAMP solvers. These methods decrease reliance on state estimation by, for example, learning predictors to ground the logical state~\cite{dpdl} or training recurrent models to predict task plan feasibility~\cite{geomlearn}. These learned policies operate directly on perceptual data and do not require hand-coded state estimation. However, TAMP solvers define a highly non-linear mapping from observations to controls, complicating imitation. Additionally, the computational resources needed for planning limit the availability of training data for learning. In this paper, we build on both approaches. Drawing inspiration from guided expert imitation~\cite{GPS, grp}, we train feed-forward policies to imitate TAMP. Our key insight is that \citet{tamp2014}'s modular TAMP framework supports a distributed TAMP architecture that: 1) is optimized for throughput (as opposed to low latency, which is the typical focus in TAMP research); 2) trains policies to imitate the planner output; and 3) employs these policies to amortize planning across problems, thereby reducing computational costs. This creates a virtuous cycle where learning accelerates planning, and faster planning provides more supervision. We propose a policy architecture that leverages the TAMP domain definition to enhance learning performance. Task plans from our system supervise a task-level model that learns to predict a parameterized action. This output selects from and parameterizes a set of control networks, one for each action schema. We demonstrate that this architecture can execute manipulation skills in high-dimensional environments from complex sensory input. Consequently, our system integrates task and motion planning into a single feed-forward policy. The contributions of this work are as follows: 1) we present a design for a distributed, asynchronous, high-throughput task and motion planning system that uses policy learning to expedite planning; 2) we propose a hierarchical policy architecture that leverages the TAMP problem specification; and 3) we implement and evaluate this method to demonstrate its ability to learn to achieve multiple goals over (comparatively) long horizons with high-dimensional sensory data and action spaces. In a 2D pick-place task, we train policies that accurately place 3 objects onto targets 83\% of the time from RGB images. In the RoboSuite~\cite{robosuite2020} pick-place benchmark, we train policies for 7-DoF joint control that place 4 objects $88\%$ of the time from object pose vectors. In the multitask RoboDesk benchmark, our learned policy achieves an average success rate of 79\% across 9 diverse tasks with 7-DoF joint control from RGB images.

text: It is well-established and comprehended that humans can link voices and faces due to the shared structure of the neuro-cognitive pathways for these modalities~\cite{kamachi2003putting,belin2004thinking}. Recently, Nagrani et al.~\cite{nagrani2018seeing,nagrani2018learnable,nagrani2017voxceleb} introduced the face-voice association task to the vision community by creating a large-scale audio-visual dataset, which includes the faces and voices of $1,251$ celebrities. Since then, the face-voice association task has attracted considerable research interest~\cite{horiguchi2018face,kim2018learning,nagrani2018learnable,nagrani2018seeing,nawaz2019deep,wen2021seeking,wen2018disjoint}. Additionally, we are observing the development of new audio-visual datasets to explore this emerging task. For instance, Nawaz et al.~\cite{nawaz2021cross} introduced a Multilingual Audio-Visual (\textit{MAV-Celeb}) dataset to examine the influence of language on the face-voice association task; it includes video and audio recordings of various celebrities speaking multiple languages. Most existing studies ~\cite{kim2018learning,nagrani2018seeing,nagrani2018learnable,nawaz2021cross} address face-voice association as a cross-modal biometric task. The two main challenges in devising an effective method for this task involve learning a common yet discriminative embedding space, where instances from both modalities are adequately aligned and instances of semantically similar identities are proximate. Typically, separate networks for face and voice modalities are used to obtain the respective feature embeddings, and contrastive or triplet loss formulations are employed to construct this embedding space. Although these loss formulations demonstrate some effectiveness in this task, they are restrictive in the following ways. First, they require tuning a margin hyperparameter, which is challenging as the distances between instances can vary significantly during training. Secondly, the run-time training complexity for contrastive and triplet losses is $\mathcal{O} (n^2)$ and $\mathcal{O} (n^3)$, respectively, where $n$ represents the number of available instances for a modality. Finally, to address the high run-time training complexity challenge, various carefully designed negative mining strategies are employed, which are both time-intensive and performance-sensitive. A few methods, such as \cite{nawaz2019deep}, have attempted to replace the contrastive/triplet loss formulations by employing auxiliary identity centroids~\cite{wen2016discriminative}. The training process alternates between two steps: 1) clustering embeddings around their identity centroids and pushing embeddings away from all other identity centroids, and 2) updating these centroids using the mini-batch instances. Such centroid-based losses are used alongside traditional classification loss (i.e., softmax cross-entropy (CE)). However, their coexistence is unintuitive and ineffective because the former promotes margins in Euclidean space, whereas the latter implicitly achieves separability in the angular domain. In this work, we hypothesize that an enriched unified feature representation, integrating complementary cues from both modalities, along with an effective yet efficient supervision formulation, is essential for realizing a discriminative joint embedding space for improved face-voice association. To this end, we propose a lightweight, plug-and-play mechanism that leverages the best of both modalities through fusion and semantically aligns fused embeddings with their identity labels via orthogonality constraints. We instantiate our proposed mechanism in the two-stream pipeline, which provides face and voice embeddings, and the resulting overall framework is an effective and efficient approach for face-voice matching and verification tasks. We summarize our key contributions as follows. 1) We propose to harness the complementary features from both modalities in forming enriched feature embeddings that are consistent with the semantics of identity, thereby enabling improved identity recognition. 2) We propose to impose orthogonality constraints on the fused embeddings. These constraints are not only coherent with the angular characteristic of the commonly employed classification loss but are also very efficient as they operate directly on mini-batches. 3) Experimental results on the large-scale VoxCeleb \cite{nagrani2017voxceleb} demonstrate the effectiveness of our method on both face-voice verification and matching tasks. Furthermore, we observe that our method performs favorably against existing state-of-the-art methods. 4) We conduct a thorough ablation study to analyze the impact of different components.

text: Edge-aware filters are among the most frequently utilized image processing operators across a broad spectrum of computational photography applications. Also referred to as \emph{edge-preserving smoothing} operators, they are a crucial component in numerous image manipulation algorithms, including tonemapping, image abstraction, detail enhancement, and texture removal. The widespread use of these operators can be attributed to their apparent ability to detect significant, structure-defining edges in an image and to treat them differently from other image details and discontinuities. In the last decade, a significant number of edge-preserving smoothing operators have been introduced in the literature, with some specifically designed for particular tasks, such as texture removal or multiscale detail manipulation, while others lack a clearly stated objective. We provide several specific examples in Section \ref{sec-smoothing-operators}. These operators vary in several respects, such as their visual style, internal algorithmic approach (e.g., local versus global operators), the number and range of parameters (ranging from at least one to many), and runtime complexity (from seconds to minutes). Such differences may not be immediately evident to a user who is only casually acquainted with these methods, making the task of selecting the appropriate operator for a specific purpose (or a specific image), as well as determining its parameters, quite challenging. When introducing a new filter, researchers typically provide side-by-side visual comparisons of images processed by existing operators. For such a comparison to be meaningful, an image should be processed by the different operators to an \emph{equivalent degree}. However, each operator is controlled by its own parameter(s), and there is no established consistent mapping between the parameters of different operators. This is further complicated by the fact that even for a single method, the visual effect of its parameters on the result is often input-dependent, and the relationship between its parameters may vary at different smoothing levels. Consequently, in practice, the parameters for each of the compared methods are chosen subjectively by the authors, typically through trial-and-error. The decision of which methods to compare is also complex. Ideally, one would like to include in the comparison methods that are related in their approach to the proposed one, along with those representing entirely different approaches. It is also important to consider the primary intended application for which the competing methods were originally designed. Finally, a common benchmark should be used for all comparisons, but, in practice, no established benchmark exists; furthermore, it is not uncommon to see cases where a different image is selected to compare the proposed method to each of the existing competitors. In this paper, we propose a new methodology for evaluating and comparing edge-preserving smoothing operators in a more meaningful, objective, and quantitative manner. We propose a mechanism for achieving roughly equivalent smoothing degrees by different operators, effectively establishing a mapping between their main governing parameters on a per-image basis. Having established such a mapping, we can quantitatively measure various characteristics of different operators. This provides several insights into the operators' behavior and enables more meaningful comparisons, both visually and quantitatively. Finally, we can cluster the different operators based on the similarity of their effect, using strictly empirical observations. Our observations on innate method behavior suggest specific recommendations for both developers and end-users of such operators. The remainder of this paper is organized as follows: Section~\ref{sec-background} reviews existing approaches for comparing tonemapping operators and several previous comparative surveys of edge-preserving filters. Section~\ref{sec-methods} first briefly lists the filters we chose to demonstrate our methodology for comparing and evaluating smoothing operators, and then introduces the methodology itself. Section~\ref{sec-results} demonstrates the use of our methodology on the selected set of operators. Section~\ref{sec-conclusions} provides a concluding discussion and offers some ideas for future research.

text: Machine learning systems often face challenges in developing predictors that remain robust under distributional shifts. While these systems can achieve near-perfect accuracy on i.i.d data from the training distribution, even when regularization is applied to mitigate overfitting, their performance can plummet to below chance when tested on data with even minor discrepancies from the training set \citep{goodfellow2015explaining,geirhos2020shortcut}. The Domain Generalization (DG) field \cite{ganin2016domainadversarial, li2018domain} tackles this issue by creating methods designed to maintain high test performance on distributions that, although different, are systematically linked to the training distribution \citep{mansour2019robust}. Among the recent successful strategies in Multi-Source Domain Generalization \citep{zhao2020multisource} is Invariant Risk Minimization (IRM) \citep{arjovsky2019invariant}, which promotes the learning of predictors with consistent performance across multiple ``domains'' or ``environments'' \citep{peters2015causal, heinzedeml2018invariant}. For $n$ distinct training environments, these models derive a set of predictors from the feature space such that the conditional distribution of outcomes given these predictors remains stable across all training environments. This invariance allows these predictors to generalize effectively to any out-of-distribution (OOD) test environments sharing the same invariant properties. Drawing from philosophical work that defines causation as invariance \citep{cartwright2003two, mitchell2000dimensions}, current invariance-based DG methods are seen as a weak form of causal discovery, where the resulting predictors are considered the causal factors underlying the phenomena of interest. Fairness is often defined in terms of robustness to variations in ``sensitive attributes'' \cite{arjovsky2019invariant}, particularly in contexts like toxicity classification. Consider an automated moderation system used by an online news platform to filter out toxic comments. A fair system's performance should remain unaffected by whether a comment pertains to subjects like race, gender, or other politically sensitive topics. Different fairness definitions vary in how they require predictions to remain invariant to changes in sensitive attributes. For instance, statistical fairness definitions such as Demographic Parity demand that some conditional distribution of predictions, given the sensitive attribute, remains unchanged \citep{hardt2016equality}. In contrast, causal definitions like counterfactual fairness \citep{kusner2018counterfactual} require that each individual's prediction remains invariant to hypothetical changes in their sensitive attribute. Ethical and legal critiques often target systems that base predictions on sensitive group membership \citep{barocas2016big}. Moreover, heavy reliance on sensitive information can undermine robustness if this information's predictive performance is context-dependent. For example, discussions about non-Caucasian identities might strongly predict comment toxicity on forums with white supremacist ideologies, where members frequently make biased remarks about minorities. Conversely, on forums that embrace diversity, the link between racial identity mentions and toxicity would likely be weaker. This sensitivity issue was identified as a significant challenge for Perspective API, a Google-supported toxicity classifier, during its real-world deployment \citep{borkan2019nuanced, jigsawmedium}, and similar biases have been noted in sentiment analysis \citep{kiritchenko2018examining} and facial detection \citep{buolamwini18a} tasks. Thus, fair models might be developed by learning predictors that maintain consistent performance across diverse environments. In this study, we empirically show that Domain Generalization can be employed to create fair machine learning models by designing systems that are invariant to spurious correlations involving sensitive attributes. Specifically, we evaluate the performance of IRM on a fair internet comment toxicity classification task derived from the Civil Comments Dataset. The task requires the model to generalize from biased training environments, where there is a strong but misleading correlation between the mention of a demographic identity and toxicity, to a test environment where this correlation is reversed. \footnote{\url{https://github.com/adragnar/irm-toxicity-classification}} Our contributions are as follows: \begin{itemize} \item We demonstrate that IRM surpasses ERM in both generalization accuracy and group fairness on this dataset, emphasizing the synergy between robustness and fairness in the context of data bias explored; \item Through ablation studies, we investigate the reasons behind this performance enhancement: although sensitive information is only marginally predictive, IRM leverages the variation in this predictive power across environments to identify an invariant (and thus fairer) solution; \item Analysis of the IRM solution indicates that comment length is employed as an invariant feature. While using comment length may be fairer than relying on sensitive group membership, IRM has yet to identify a genuinely ``causal'' feature. This underscores a key limitation of the IRM approach, which treats invariance as a stand-in for causality, and highlights the significance of environmental diversity as an inductive bias for this technique. \end{itemize}

text: Reconfiguration problems are a broad class of challenges where the objective is to devise a series of transformations to convert one object into another. This paper focuses on the challenge of reconfiguring a set of modular robots arranged in a lattice through predetermined moves. Various forms of this problem have been explored extensively within both the robotics and computational geometry fields. Herein, we investigate the reconfiguration problem for configurations of hexagons and squares that are (edge-)connected. A critical requirement for numerous applications is maintaining (edge-)connectivity throughout the process, adhering to the \emph{single backbone condition}~\cite{Dumitrescu-Suzuki-Yamashita-2004}. The permissible moves are pivots, where a module rotates around vertices it shares with other modules, ensuring that the pivoting module concludes its move within a lattice cell. It is imperative that the interiors of two modules do not intersect. Hexagons permit only two types of pivoting moves, as depicted in Figure~\ref{fig:hex_moves}. During a \emph{restricted} move, a module $a$, adjacent to module $s$, pivots around a vertex $v$ shared by both $a$ and $s$, and completes the move in the adjacent cell sharing vertex $v$. The \emph{restricted model} permits only this type of move. Conversely, in a \emph{monkey} move, module $a$, also adjacent to $s$, begins pivoting around vertex $v$ as in the restricted move. Midway through, another vertex $w$ of $a$ aligns with a vertex of another module $s'$. The module $a$ continues its pivot around $w$, maintaining the same rotational direction, either clockwise or counterclockwise, until it occupies a cell next to $s'$. The \emph{monkey model} encompasses both restricted and monkey moves. Essentially, the monkey move enables a module to persist in its pivoting direction when a restricted move is unfeasible. Section~\ref{sec:models} delves into the distinctions between these hexagonal models. In the square grid, two modules sharing a vertex do not necessarily share an edge, resulting in a wider array of pivoting moves for square modules. The three distinct sets of moves are illustrated in Figure~\ref{fig:square_moves}. The \emph{restricted model} is limited to restricted moves, the \emph{leapfrog model} incorporates both restricted and leapfrog moves, and the \emph{monkey model} includes all possible moves. \ifabstract Section~\ref{sec_proto} provides an overview of which models have been practically implemented. \fi } \later{ \iffull\paragraph*{Prototypes.} \fi \ifabstract
