text: Automatic Speech Recognition (ASR) involves the automated detection and understanding of spoken language. Within ASR, Speech Commands Recognition (SCR) focuses on identifying brief spoken instructions, enabling machines to interpret human commands. This technology is pivotal in applications such as mobile assistants on smartphones, robots that respond to verbal instructions, and smart home devices like Amazon Echo and Google Home. These applications are reshaping human-machine interaction significantly. Furthermore, SCR has numerous applications in fields such as medicine and education, particularly benefiting individuals who are blind or have disabilities \cite{1998Single-surgeonThoracoscopicSurgeryWith,2014EducationalSystemForThe}. Given that many of these applications operate on compact devices with limited processing capabilities, there is a critical need for implementations that are both fast and efficient to ensure real-time performance \cite{2018FPGAImplementationOfConvolutional}. Traditional SCR methodologies typically involve extracting distinctive features from raw audio. Among the most common are frequency domain features like the fast Fourier transform, which translate time-domain speech into frequency space \cite{1989Speaker-independentPhoneRecognitionUsing,2013TechniquesForFeatureExtraction}. Following feature extraction, classical acoustic models such as the hidden Markov model (HMM) are employed to represent sequences of phonemes or words \cite{2014SpeechAndLanguageProcessing.}. For over two decades, combinations of neural networks with HMM-based approaches have been utilized \cite{2012ConnectionistSpeechRecognition:A,1986TheTRACEModelOf}. In recent years, deep learning techniques have surpassed traditional machine learning methods in terms of performance accuracy across various applications \cite{2012DeepNeuralNetworksFor,2015DeepLearning,2016DeepLearning}. Neural networks, particularly long short-term memory (LSTM) networks, have significantly improved the accuracy of natural language processing systems compared to conventional approaches \cite{1999LearningToForget:Continual,2016LSTM:ASearchSpace}. The dominance of neural network-based approaches in SCR has established them as the state-of-the-art within the speech recognition community \cite{2014Small-footprintKeywordSpottingUsing,2017HelloEdge:KeywordSpotting,2018DeepResidualLearningFor,2019TemporalConvolutionForReal-time}. Concurrently, various neural network architectures, including convolutional neural networks (CNNs), LSTMs, and gated recurrent units (GRUs), have been effectively applied to SCR \cite{2017HelloEdge:KeywordSpotting,2018DeepResidualLearningFor,2019TemporalConvolutionForReal-time}. Direct application of CNNs to raw audio data has been investigated in studies such as \cite{2018SpeakerRecognitionFromRaw,2018InterpretableConvolutionalFiltersWith,2018End-to-endSpeechRecognitionFrom}. However, the limited computational and memory resources of embedded devices still pose significant challenges in fully harnessing the advanced capabilities of complex deep networks. To address the computational constraints of embedded devices, two main strategies are typically adopted. One approach involves compressing state-of-the-art deep models to reduce computational demands without significantly compromising accuracy \cite{2019AnOptimizedRecurrentUnit,2020Small-FootprintOpen-VocabularyKeywordSpotting}. Alternatively, more efficient deep networks and methodologies can be developed from the outset to achieve high accuracy with lower computational overhead \cite{2019OperationalNeuralNetworks,2020Self-OrganizedOperationalNeuralNetworks}. This latter strategy is particularly crucial when training data is limited or when input signals are of low quality or resolution. By employing either strategy, it is feasible to implement an effective classifier on energy-constrained embedded devices. Numerous studies have concentrated on either simplifying complex networks or designing lightweight networks from scratch. Progressive operational perceptrons (POPs) \cite{2017ProgressiveOperationalPerceptrons} aim to extend traditional multilayer perceptrons (MLPs) through generalized operational perceptrons (GOPs). GOPs utilize a unique set of operators that emulate the synaptic connections of biological neurons, enhancing their ability to learn the hidden semantics of data. The PyGOP library \cite{2019PyGOP:APythonLibrary} facilitates the implementation of GOPs on both CPU and GPU platforms. In \cite{2020ProgressiveOperationalPerceptronsWith}, the learning process in POPs is accelerated by leveraging memory and information from previously learned layers. Further exploration of biologically inspired neurons is presented in \cite{2019HeterogeneousMultilayerGeneralizedOperational}, where each neuron in the network can employ its unique set of operators, resulting in a more compact network. A novel neural network layer structure utilizing multi-linear projection is introduced in \cite{2018ImprovingEfficiencyInConvolutional}, requiring significantly less memory than traditional CNNs while delivering superior performance. The study in \cite{2017HelloEdge:KeywordSpotting} employs deep networks with dilated convolutions to achieve high accuracy with fewer parameters. SincNet Kernels \cite{2018InterpretableConvolutionalFiltersWith}, applied at the first convolutional layer of a CNN, offer another method to reduce the number of learnable parameters, as demonstrated in speaker recognition \cite{2018SpeakerRecognitionFromRaw} and phoneme recognition \cite{2018InterpretableConvolutionalFiltersWith}. Depth-wise separable convolutions (DSCconvs), initially introduced in image processing \cite{2017Xception:DeepLearningWith,2017Mobilenets:EfficientConvolutionalNeural}, have also been applied to SCR, keyword spotting \cite{2017HelloEdge:KeywordSpotting}, and machine translation \cite{2017DepthwiseSeparableConvolutionsFor} to decrease computational demands. In this paper, we introduce a novel network layer designed to improve the recognition of speech commands using a lightweight network. This is achieved through a unique integration of self-organized operational neural networks (SelfONNs) \cite{2020Self-OrganizedOperationalNeuralNetworks} and quadratic form kernels \cite{2017Non-linearConvolutionFiltersFor}. Experiments conducted on the Google Speech Commands (GSC) \cite{2018SpeechCommands:ADataset} and synthetic speech commands (SSC) datasets\footnote{\url{https://kaggle.com/jbuchner/synthetic-speech-commands-dataset}} demonstrate the efficacy of our proposed method, particularly in lightweight network settings. To our knowledge, this is the first instance of combining SelfONNs with quadratic kernels to create a new network layer that enhances the performance of a lightweight CNN. Additionally, this study pioneers the application of SelfONN and quadratic kernels in the context of SCR. The remainder of this paper is structured as follows: Section~II reviews the most pertinent related work. Section~III details the proposed quadratic SelfONN approach for SCR. Section~IV discusses the experimental results. Finally, conclusions are presented in Section~V.

text: In recent years, the prevalence of robotic surgery has notably increased. Systems like the da Vinci\textsuperscript{\textregistered} Surgical System~\cite{guthart2000intuitive}, created by Intuitive Surgical Inc. (Sunnyvale, CA), are replacing traditional surgical instruments such as laparoscopes, with the objective of enhancing both surgical quality and patient outcomes. These robotic consoles fundamentally transform the nature of the surgeon's interaction with the patient. Consequently, investigating human surgical performance in this context is a compelling research area, essential for deepening our understanding of surgeon-robot dynamics and improving patient care. The diverse and precise surgical data available, encompassing modalities like videos and kinematics, offers a comprehensive view of surgeries and facilitates an accurate analysis of human surgical performance. Recent studies in this field have predominantly concentrated on task-specific, supervised learning using a single modality. We contend that this strategy has notable limitations. Primarily, a task-specific learning model, such as supervised skill detection, provides a limited perspective of the entire surgical process, offering minimal insights beyond the specific task it is trained on. Additionally, supervised learning relies heavily on expert annotations, which are costly, subjective, and prone to errors. Moreover, neglecting the integration of multiple information modalities, such as video and kinematics, hinders the development of versatile, feature-rich representations. We propose that robotic surgeries can be decomposed into a sequence of gestures or surgemes \cite{varadarajan2009data}, allowing us to model surgeries akin to language models \cite{mikolov2013distributed, devlin2018bert} based on the vocabulary of surgemes. This paper introduces a self-supervised learning algorithm designed to acquire task-agnostic surgical gesture representations from two modalities—video and kinematics—that can effectively generalize across various tasks. Our contributions in this paper are threefold: 1) we present a deep learning-based architecture that facilitates the self-supervised learning of surgical gesture representations from video and kinematics, 2) we quantitatively validate the effectiveness of our representations across multiple tasks by achieving state-of-the-art accuracy in gesture recognition and high accuracy in skill recognition, 3) we qualitatively exhibit the richness of information encapsulated in our representations by showcasing how they form semantically meaningful clusters.

text: The domain of Human-Object Interaction (HOI) recognition has garnered substantial attention due to its pivotal role in scene comprehension. The objective of HOI recognition is to extract multiple \textit{$<$verb, object$>$} pairs (e.g., ``hold, apple'') from an image. Classifying HOIs at the image level presents challenges for two primary reasons. Firstly, datasets such as \cite{hico15,vg17} exhibit a long-tailed distribution with significant class imbalance. Secondly, images contain multiple labels, and the exact locations of the HOIs are not specified. Recent research has predominantly focused on utilizing object and keypoint detection, often neglecting the classifier's importance. Our findings highlight that the classifier is indeed crucial for both HOI classification and detection tasks. A key difference between HOI recognition and standard image classification lies in the composition of HOI classes, which are verb-object combinations, leading to stronger semantic links between classes. For instance, in the HICO dataset \cite{hico15}, the average number of classes sharing a verb is 5.1, while those sharing an object category average 7.5. Despite this, existing methods have yet to fully exploit these semantic cues. Some studies \cite{liao2020ppdm,uniondet20,sgg-imp17,atl21,scg20} treat verbs and objects as independent classification tasks. This approach simplifies the prediction process by reducing the number of classes but risks issues with polysemy, where a verb might have different meanings in different contexts (e.g., ``{\em make}, pizza'' versus ``{\em make}, vase''). To advance this field, we employ language models to create text embeddings for HOI classes, which are then used to initialize the weight vectors in the linear classification layer. This method, termed \textit{Language Embedding Initialization}, demonstrates improved performance over traditional Random Initialization techniques \cite{xavier10,kaiminginit15}, especially in scenarios with limited examples. The underlying principle is that the weight vectors in a linear classifier act as proxies or feature centers for each class \cite{circleloss20,normface17}. By initializing these weights with language embeddings, the initial proxy positions in the vector space are semantically informed rather than arbitrary. This setup facilitates the multi-label training process by guiding the vision features from the backbone toward the semantic feature center, where frequently co-occurring HOIs are also closely situated (refer to \cref{fig:2_bert}). Moreover, language embeddings offer effective weight initialization for few-shot classes, where the classifier's weight vectors cannot be adequately learned with minimal samples. Previous research \cite{transfer16,pairwise18} has utilized {\it weighted} sigmoid cross-entropy loss \cite{wbce15} to address the class imbalance in positive/negative samples. While this approach surpasses standard cross-entropy loss, it struggles with extremely imbalanced classes (20.1\% of HICO classes have $\leq$ 5 positive samples). We introduce a novel loss function, Log-Sum-Exp Sign (\textit{LSE-Sign}) loss, to enhance multi-label learning in long-tailed datasets. This loss function is crafted such that its gradient is a softmax function of losses across all classes, emphasizing poorly classified classes while diminishing losses from well-classified ones. This dynamic balancing fosters multi-label learning. Notably, LSE-Sign loss differs from focal loss \cite{lin2017focal} in two aspects: it considers the {\em relative} difficulty among all classes, unlike focal loss which operates on each class individually, and it does not require tuning multiple hyper-parameters. Despite the significant performance drop of a detection-free baseline using ImageNet-1K pre-trained ViT-B/32 as the backbone compared to detection-assisted state-of-the-art methods (from 47.1 to 37.8 mAP), Language Embedding Initialization with BERT elevates it to 50.6 mAP. This strategy extends to other language models like SimCSE \cite{simcse21} and CLIP \cite{clip21}. LSE-Sign loss yields an average improvement of 3.1 mAP across eight experiments (\cref{tab:bce_vs_sign}). Building on these insights, our approach surpasses existing detection-assisted methods \cite{pairwise18,pastanet20,hake19} by a significant margin. Employing a ResNet101 backbone, our method achieves 53.6 mAP, outperforming the state-of-the-art \cite{hake19} that relies on both object and human keypoint detections by 6.5 mAP. With a ViT-B/16 backbone, our method reaches 65.6 mAP. On few-shot subsets, our results are 52.7 mAP on 1-shot and 56.9 mAP on 5-shot classes. At the instance level, we separate the HOI detection task into localization and regional HOI classification. The benefit of a detection-free approach allows us to apply the classification model to any regional human-object box pair generated by off-the-shelf detectors. Using a vision transformer backbone, we convert bounding boxes into an attention mask, ensuring that the CLS token focuses solely on the region of interest. Without additional instance-level training, our method achieves state-of-the-art (SOTA) performance (32.35 mAP) on the HICO-DET dataset, surpassing the SOTA \cite{cdn21} trained specifically on HICO-DET.

text: The pretraining of large neural networks using a language modeling objective has revolutionized NLP, delivering substantial advancements \citep[][\emph{inter alia}]{peters2018deep,howard2018universal,radford2018improving,devlin2018bert,raffel2019exploring,brown2020language}. Enhancements can often be achieved by selecting a pretraining objective that aligns more closely with the specific downstream task. For instance, casing prediction benefits named entity recognition \citep{Mayhew_Nitish_Roth_2020}, gap sentence generation aids summarization \citep{zhang2019pegasus}, and sentence unshuffling supports discourse representations \citep{lee2020slm}. Although these strategies can significantly cut down the volume of training data needed, they generally struggle when only a few examples are available for the downstream task—a frequent situation in many practical NLP applications. In these few-shot scenarios, however, notable improvements can be made by reversing the adaptation process: rather than aligning pretraining with the downstream task, we can reframe the downstream task to resemble the pretraining objective. For masked language models \citep[e.g.,][]{devlin2018bert,lewis2019bart}, this can be achieved by transforming inputs into cloze questions through the addition of a text snippet containing a task description, often in the form of a concise prompt \citep{radford2018language,schick2020exploiting}. This strategy not only harmonizes pretraining and finetuning but also allows users to \emph{convey} a task to a pretrained model, enhancing the model's comprehension of the task. Figure~\ref{figure:motivational-example} exemplifies this, showing how a pretrained language model adjusts its output when given the same input with varying instructions. Providing task descriptions proves effective even in an unsupervised context \citep{radford2018language} or when examples are presented as additional context \citep{brown2020language}; however, its full potential is realized when combined with gradient-based training on a limited number of labeled examples \citep{schick2020just}. Unfortunately, existing methodologies are restricted to text \emph{classification} tasks \citep{schick2020exploiting}. Motivated by their success, we explore the transferability of this concept to more complex text-to-text tasks that necessitate the \emph{generation} of text sequences from input text, such as abstractive summarization. We propose \textsc{genPet}{}, an innovative approach inspired by \textsc{Pet}{} \citep{schick2020exploiting}, which facilitates the finetuning of generative language models using both instructions and labeled examples. Our findings demonstrate that \textsc{genPet}{} is a data-efficient method that allows for the finetuning of a pretrained \textsc{Pegasus}{} model \citep{zhang2019pegasus} with as few as 10 or 100 training instances. We assess our method across six diverse English headline generation and text summarization tasks in both zero-shot and few-shot settings, showing that \textsc{Pegasus}{} trained with \textsc{genPet}{} significantly surpasses conventional finetuning. text: The task of news curation involves the intricate process of selecting and prioritizing information based on specific relevance criteria, all while contending with constraints of time and space. Traditionally managed by editorial teams within newspapers and media organizations, this responsibility is increasingly being assumed by machine learning (ML) systems, which evaluate content relevance~\cite{allcott2017social,eslami_i_2015}. Consequently, these sophisticated and often opaque ML systems are shaping the news consumption habits of billions worldwide. A study by the Pew Research Center highlights that approximately 53\% of U.S. adults using Facebook feel they do not comprehend the criteria for post inclusion in their news feeds~\cite{pew_facebook_feed_2019}. This observation propels our inquiry into how users perceive news recommendations and their ability to discern between reliable and unreliable ML recommendations. We also explore if untrustworthy news content, such as fake news, gains credibility when presented alongside trustworthy information—such as when an ML system predicts a mix of four credible stories and one fake news story. We define fake news as "fabricated information that mirrors the form of news media content but lacks the corresponding organizational process or intent"~\cite{lazer2018science}. Understanding trust and the propagation of fake news within algorithmic news curation is crucial, given that these algorithms are integral to social media platforms like Facebook, which serve as significant conduits for fake news dissemination~\cite{allcott2017social}. The study of trust in news and the tendency of individuals to believe rumors has a storied history~\cite{allport1947psychology,allport1945wartime}. Our focus is on trust in a news recommender system, drawing connections to the work of O'Donovan et al. and Massa and Bhattacharjee \cite{massa2004using,o2005trust}. However, our emphasis diverges from theirs by concentrating on trust in the ML system and its recommendations rather than in the individual items. The study's design reflects user interaction with machine learning systems, where participants evaluate their trust in the system's recommendations by rating groups of news stories. Participants were informed that their interaction was with an ML system, rather than merely assessing content. Trust is a focal point because falling for fake news is not simply a blunder; fake news is crafted to deceive by imitating legitimate news media content. Our approach aligns with human-in-the-loop and active machine learning paradigms, where users engage with a dynamic system that they enhance through their actions \cite{rubens2015active,amershi2014power,Kulesza:2015:PED:2678025.2701399}. In such contexts, improving a news curation algorithm by assessing individual items would demand significant time and effort from users. Therefore, we investigate the strategy of explicitly rating ML recommendations as a whole to collect feedback. Examining user perceptions of ML systems and their recommendations is vital for those employing algorithmic news curation and for those aiming to empower users to recognize algorithmic bias. This is pertinent for human-computer interaction designers who seek to facilitate user interaction with machine learning systems. Furthermore, this investigation is significant for ML practitioners interested in gathering user feedback on system quality or those looking to crowdsource training data for their models \cite{Gulla:2017:ADN:3106426.3109436,ozgobek,Russakovsky2015}. In our experiment, participants engaged with a straightforward algorithmic news curation system that provided news recommendations akin to a collaborative filtering system~\cite{Resnick:1994:GOA:192844.192905,herlocker2000explaining}. We executed a between-subjects study encompassing two phases. Our participants were recruited from a vocational school, all possessing a technical background and briefed on the potential for ML systems to err unexpectedly. In the initial phase, participants assessed their trust in various news stories, generating a pool of stories with trust ratings. Different subsets of news stories were rated by participants, meaning each story was evaluated by some users while others did not encounter it. In the subsequent phase, the algorithmic news curation system assembled unseen news stories for each user based on the median trust rating of each story. This implies that a story's trust rating is derived from the collective agreement of the participants who rated it in the first phase. This setup allowed us to explore how trust in individual stories affects trust in groups of news stories predicted by an ML system. By varying the proportion of trustworthy and untrustworthy news stories in the recommendations, we examined their impact on trust ratings using an 11-point scale. Our primary objective is to comprehend how the trust ratings of ML outputs relate to the trustworthiness of individual news items within a machine learning framework. In summary, this paper addresses the following research questions: \begin{itemize} \item Can users assess trust in news recommendations made by a machine learning system~(RQ1)? \item Are users capable of differentiating between trustworthy and untrustworthy ML recommendations~(RQ2)? \item Can users distinguish trustworthy ML recommendations from those containing a single untrustworthy news story~(RQ3)? \end{itemize} Our findings reveal that users can provide nuanced ratings for machine learning recommendations. They can discern between trustworthy and untrustworthy ML recommendations when all stories are either trustworthy or untrustworthy. However, participants struggle to identify trustworthy recommendations when they include a single fake news story, despite being able to differentiate other ML recommendations from trustworthy ones.

text: Statistical power represents the likelihood of correctly rejecting a null hypothesis, making it essential for detecting hypothesized effects in research. Traditionally, the most straightforward method to enhance power is by increasing the sample size, as it is the most controllable factor for researchers and has a substantial impact \cite{cohen1992things}. However, practical challenges arise when attempting to expand the sample size. For instance, in studies of rare diseases, the target population may be inherently small, hard to identify, and even more difficult to involve, such as in early- and late-stage neuro-genetic syndromes \cite{button2013power, szucs2017empirical}. Additionally, logistical or financial constraints may limit the ability to recruit more participants. In this study, we demonstrate empirically that adjusting model parameters (\emph{i.e.}, weights) can significantly influence the power of a study. Consequently, modifying these parameters can transform a moderately powered study into one that is well-powered, even with a fixed sample size. Throughout this paper, we define well-powered research as having a power greater than \textit{0.8}. Fig.~\ref{fig:model-param-power} illustrates how power can vary substantially with changes in model parameters, even when the sample size remains constant. In Fig.~\ref{fig:power-grad}, we calculate power \textit{gradients} by examining the directional differences between clusters identified by KMeans, using power and the squared L2-norm of the model parameters as coordinates. The generation of such a manifold, as depicted in Fig.~\ref{fig:power-grad}, can greatly assist researchers in pinpointing regions of high power. Providing access to these visualizations offers a straightforward means to reduce the \textit{ideal} sample size without compromising power. However, as outlined in Algorithm~\ref{algo:power}, even a single computation of power necessitates \textit{200-1000} simulations. Moreover, the manifold parameter space, which includes model weights, sample size, and additional hyperparameters, is vast. For example, a model with seven predictors, each with 11 options, and 11 choices for the $N$, results in a parameter space of $11^{7 + 1}$. Exploring this extensive space could require several days. Therefore, this work explores more \textit{cost-effective} alternatives to simulating the entire power manifold. Our contributions are as follows: \begin{itemize} \item We introduce a neural network-based method to predict power across a high-dimensional manifold for both classification and regression tasks. This method achieves notable performance using just 10\% of the training data. \item We establish four baseline methods for predicting power and evaluate all our approaches using three models: regression, logistic, and Repeated Measures ANOVA. \item To facilitate knowledge transfer from the power manifold of one model to another, we first elucidate the rationale behind such a transfer. Subsequently, we demonstrate that this approach can yield equivalent or improved results in every scenario. \end{itemize} The remainder of the article is structured as follows. We begin by reviewing relevant literature and providing the foundational information necessary for developing our algorithm, including pseudocodes for both core and auxiliary algorithms. We then present our empirical findings, highlight key successes, and discuss limitations. Finally, we suggest directions for future research.

text: Simultaneous Localization And Mapping (SLAM) methodologies empower robots to autonomously navigate by constructing navigational maps, while emerging Semantic Mapping techniques enrich these maps with semantic data about locations and objects. This semantic enhancement allows robots to navigate using the meaning of locations rather than just their geometric coordinates, facilitating reasoning about spaces through automated planning or interpreting natural language commands \cite{thomason2020jointly}. Semantic maps are especially advantageous in consumer-oriented robotic applications, such as assisting visitors in navigating unfamiliar buildings \cite{Yedidsion_multi_robot} or retrieving objects \cite{Jiang_Walker_Hart_Stone_2019}. However, manually annotating semantic information on extensive maps is often cumbersome or impractical. This study is dedicated to the autonomous semantic labeling of mapped environments. Buildings frequently contain signage that provides essential semantic information for human users, such as office number placards. Previous research employed custom-built detectors to identify these door placards, map their locations, and transcribe their labels~\cite{Hart}~\cite{Case}. These approaches either necessitate creating a map before searching for placards or require human guidance during the scanning process. A key contribution of this work is facilitating simultaneous exploration of new environments and registration of placards without human intervention, utilizing an enhanced Frontier Exploration algorithm known as Interruptable Frontier Exploration (IFE). Interruptable Frontier Exploration enables the robot to explore its surroundings while an object detector identifies door placards. This is termed \emph{passive observation}. Upon detecting a sign, exploration is paused, and the robot conducts an \emph{active observation}; it maneuvers to an optimal vantage point to segment, transcribe, and log the sign's location on the map. To evaluate the efficacy of IFE, we compare it with a method that determines a robot's motion path to scan for placards along previously-mapped wall sections~\cite{Case}. This method is referred to as Wall-Scanning Discovery (WD). IFE is notably more time-efficient than WD, as it requires fewer active scans and does not necessitate a complete map before placard detection.

text: Recommender systems have become indispensable in today's rapidly evolving digital landscape, striving to suggest items that users are most likely to appreciate. A prevalent and effective method in this domain is collaborative filtering, which seeks to uncover latent features of users and items through their past interactions. Earlier techniques, such as Matrix Factorization (MF)~\cite{koren2009matrix}, break down a rating matrix into user and item embeddings to capture hidden semantics. With the exponential growth in the number of users and items, deep learning models have been increasingly developed on top of collaborative filtering to better represent diverse user preferences across vast item collections. For instance, ~\cite{berg2017graph} and~\cite{wang2019neural} construct user-item graphs to incorporate multi-hop interaction relationships, while~\cite{liang2018variational} and~\cite{li2017collaborative} employ a variational auto-encoder framework to derive representations as Gaussian distributions. Sequential recommendation is a crucial segment of recommender systems, where user interactions are modeled as sequences rather than sets of items. The Markov Chain (MC)~\cite{cheng2013you} is a traditional approach that captures short-term item transitions to forecast the next likely item a user might enjoy. The Factorized Personalized Markov Chain (FPMC)~\cite{rendle2010factorizing} synergizes the Markov chain and conventional matrix factorization to model user preferences. With advancements in deep learning, Recurrent Neural Networks (RNNs) have shown promise in sequential recommendation tasks. Long Short-Term Memory (LSTM)~\cite{zhu2017next}, a variant of RNN, enhances the model's ability to retain sequential information using memory cells. GRU4Rec~\cite{chen2018sequential} leverages Gated Recurrent Units (GRU) for session-based recommendations by employing session-parallel mini-batches. However, RNN-based methods struggle with long-range dependencies, prompting the adoption of self-attention networks in sequential recommendations to capture both long-term and short-term dependencies. SASRec and BERT4Rec achieve commendable prediction results using attention mechanisms. SASRec~\cite{kang2018self} effectively captures long-term dependencies by considering the weighted influence of an entire historical sequence, while BERT4Rec~\cite{sun2019bert4rec} utilizes a deep bidirectional self-attention network with Cloze tasks to boost transformer model efficiency. Previous research predominantly models user intentions through historical sequential interactions, often overlooking the dynamic underlying relationships between items. The connections between item pairs are rich in semantic information, elucidating why and how users transition between items. These underlying factors relate to real-world concepts, with specific factors often dominating in particular situations. Consider two users interacting with six items, as illustrated in Figure~\ref{intro}. The link graph reveals that item 2 is connected to all other items, though these connections are driven by different factors. For instance, item 2 links to items 1 and 4 due to shared color, while it connects to items 5 and 6 because of short sleeves. Item 3 connects to item 2 as it can serve as a T-shirt jacket. These factors illuminate the transformation of user behaviors and highlight shared features of item pairs. Therefore, identifying and distinguishing these underlying item-link factors can enhance model expressiveness, and disentangled representation learning~\cite{locatello2019challenging} is a widely adopted method to achieve this. Disentangled representation learning has gained traction across various domains, including Computer Vision~\cite{hsieh2018learning, mu2021disentangled}, and has recently been applied to recommender systems. Its primary goal is to isolate distinct and informative factors from data variations, with each unit linked to a specific real-world concept. Altering one factor results in changes to the corresponding unit. Numerous models have demonstrated the capability to learn disentangled representations and have been applied to practical tasks. For example, by disentangling a face image, independent representations of various facial features can be obtained, enabling the identification of attributes such as bangs, glasses, or smiles. Furthermore, these features can be modified directionally by adjusting the relevant dimensional values. Thus, learning disentangled representations enhances model interpretability and controllability. The foremost networks for learning disentangled representations are $\beta$-VAE and InfoGAN. $\beta$-VAE~\cite{higgins2016beta} introduces a coefficient hyperparameter $\beta$ to the KL-divergence term in the variational auto-encoder objective, promoting more factorized latent representations. This hyperparameter exerts significant pressure on the posterior distribution to align with the factorized prior distribution~\cite{burgess2018understanding}. InfoGAN~\cite{chen2016infogan} maximizes mutual information between a fixed small subset of GAN's noise variables and observations. In the realm of recommender systems, Macrid-VAE~\cite{ma2019learning} infers high-level user intention concepts at the macro level and utilizes VAE to enhance micro-level disentanglement. The authors also propose a self-supervised seq2seq training strategy for sequential recommendation~\cite{ma2020disentangled}, comparing user intentions across sub-sequences generated by an intention-disentangled encoder. DGCF~\cite{wang2020disentangled} designs intent-aware interaction graphs to differentiate user intentions across items, focusing on user-item relationships. However, these studies overlook item-link relationship patterns and fail to distinguish varied user intentions behind sequences, rendering the sequential model susceptible to noise and challenging to interpret. In this work, we introduce an \textbf{E}dge-Enhanced \textbf{G}lobal \textbf{D}isentangled \textbf{G}raph \textbf{N}eural \textbf{N}etwork (EGD-GNN) model to capture item-link information. Our approach models item representations and user intentions at both global and local levels. Globally, we construct an item-link graph encompassing all sequences, with each item pair represented as an edge. Figure~\ref{intro} illustrates the creation of a global graph over two sequences. We employ a channel-aware mechanism to decompose edges into multiple channels, each corresponding to an influential factor. These channels extract features specific to one disentangled factor from neighbors and collectively aggregate different factors to the target item. Locally, we model disentangled user-intention representation within the current sequence. We first infer latent variation as a Gaussian distribution to enforce disentanglement from the variational auto-encoder's statistical perspective. Subsequently, we utilize the channel-aware mechanism to aggregate item information through edge channels from preceding items in the sequence. The aggregated item representation expresses the current user intention. We validate our method on three real-world datasets, comparing prediction results with state-of-the-art baselines. Results indicate that the EGD-GNN model not only excels in prediction tasks but also compels the system to discover robust disentangled representations. The primary contributions of this paper are as follows: \begin{itemize} \item To our knowledge, this is the first study to explore disentangled representation at both global and local levels to learn factorized underlying factors of item relationships. \item We introduce a disentangled graph neural network to infer the factors behind item pairs that drive user intentions. We apply the GNN model to both the global graph and local sequences to learn item link patterns and leverage the variational auto-encoder for its statistical advantages. \item Our model is evaluated on three real-world datasets, and experimental results demonstrate its ability to achieve an effective disentangled representation over sequences to reflect user intentions. \end{itemize} The remainder of this paper is structured as follows. Section~\ref{related} reviews related works pertinent to our study. Section~\ref{preliminary} outlines the problem formulation, model definitions, and essential preliminaries. In Section~\ref{methodology}, we detail our proposed model. Section~\ref{experiment} presents and visualizes experimental results, validating our model's efficacy. Finally, Section~\ref{conclusion} concludes the paper and suggests future research directions.

text: \IEEEPARstart{W}{ith} the growing intricacies of Information Technology (IT) operational environments, organizations face the challenge of maintaining robust IT systems while simultaneously cutting operational costs, reducing ticket volume, and enhancing customer satisfaction. IT operations are managed through an Incident, Problem, and Change (IPC) ticketing system, where issues are logged as IT Service Desk tickets~\cite{Jan2015}. This paper addresses these challenges by leveraging both structured and unstructured ticket information provided by the Service Desk (SD). Cognitive computing offers a transformative approach to IT Services Delivery by minimizing the necessity for repetitive training of service delivery skills. The system's learning capability distinguishes cognitive solutions, enabling them to continuously improve through ongoing interactions and adapt to evolving needs. Furthermore, service quality can be enhanced by preventing errors of omission and resolving issues more swiftly through automated understanding and reasoning to identify the most effective solutions. Although human effort is significantly reduced, the human element remains crucial in a supervisory capacity to ensure seamless user interaction. In essence, cognitive computing transformation delivers an unparalleled client experience and enhances business competitiveness with operational efficiency and agility previously unattainable. The SD receives tickets both automatically from various device monitoring systems and manually from user requests. Numerous analytical tools available today generate reports based solely on structured data attributes from historical ticket records. Some of these tools also offer query capabilities to identify frequently occurring keywords or specific patterns within the unstructured ticket attributes. IT professionals then analyze these reports to address the most prevalent topics. While these tools offer advantages, they have limitations, such as processing vast data volumes, identifying obvious and hidden issues, filtering noise from text, and extracting user sentiments from Customer Satisfaction (CSat) surveys and social media. Surveys in the literature estimate that 80\% of information is contained in unstructured data \cite{Rosu2012}. The proposed solution addresses all these limitations. A distinctive feature of the proposed approach is its ability to extract meaning from fragmented sentences within unstructured ticket descriptions. Typically, this unstructured text appears in multiple languages, which are detected using language identification and normalized to a common language, English, using machine translation techniques. Due to varying language proficiency levels among the globally sourced agents, grammar quality also varies. To establish a common baseline for analytics application, this solution initially translates all non-English text into English using statistical translation models. The choice of a statistical model over a grammar-based one is driven by the input text's grammar quality. The statistical translation model introduces an additional layer of complexity for a cognitive system. This system has enabled numerous clients to swiftly uncover patterns and trends, identifying contributing causes and prescribing precautions using data from hundreds of thousands of SD tickets. Such analyses, which would have taken SD support teams weeks or months, can now be performed promptly. Identifying contributing causes allows support teams to utilize log analytics for root cause analysis. Moreover, this empowers the team to proactively identify opportunities for optimizing IT operations and enhancing client satisfaction by demonstrating the following outcomes: \begin{itemize} \item Extraction of contributing causes and actionable precautions from problem descriptions and resolutions. \item Revealing pervasive issues that are otherwise obscured by volumes of unstructured data in tickets across various categories. \item Detection of emerging problems, trends, and automated change points. \item Identification of patterns enabling IT support teams to leverage real-time machine and data analytics for rapid root cause discovery. \item Recognition of self-service and automation opportunities, transforming operations from reactive to proactive. \item Transparency to pervasive issues hidden behind extensive unstructured text not captured in ticket categories. \item Sentiment analysis of CSat survey comments to identify potential future dissatisfiers. \item Correlation of social media and CSat sentiments with IT and application issues to enhance client experience. \item Predictive analytics for improving resolution times through re-prioritization and ticket routing. \item Identification of skills and knowledge gaps derived from analyzing first-time failure resolutions, resolution times, and agent performance differences. \end{itemize} The paper is structured as follows: Section \ref{sec:Methodology} provides an overview of the cognitive computing platform components and overall system methodology. Section \ref{sec:Algorithms} details the key algorithms developed for this system. Section \ref{sec:Applications} explores various applications and use-cases, while Section \ref{sec:Results} presents the outcomes of various experiments. The paper concludes in Section \ref{sec:Conclusion}.

text: Recommender systems are designed to assist users in discovering preferred items from a vast array of options. Models like collaborative filtering~\cite{koren2009matrix} and DeepFM~\cite{10.5555/3172077.3172127} typically utilize users' past behaviors to predict future preferences. However, systems relying solely on exploitation models often encounter closed-loop effects~\cite{jadidinejad2020using}, where users primarily engage with the recommended items, reinforcing their profiles with these interactions. Consequently, over time, the system becomes predisposed to a narrow set of interests, repeatedly suggesting a limited selection of items to the same user. To counteract this, contextual multi-armed bandit algorithms, such as LinUCB~\cite{li2010contextual}, employ side information to balance exploration and exploitation, thus mitigating the closed-loop phenomenon. In these algorithms, items are conceptualized as arms, and the recommender model functions as an agent. In each iteration, the agent selects the arm with the highest potential from $K$ candidates, receiving a reward based on user-item interaction, aiming to maximize cumulative rewards over $T$ rounds. These algorithms assume a small $K$, making it feasible to evaluate all arm candidates' scores and select the best. This assumption holds in contexts where candidate pools are naturally limited, such as ranking breaking news on a homepage, ad creatives, or online model selection. However, in broader recommender systems, where the aim is to thoroughly explore user interests and genuinely alleviate closed-loop effects, the arms encompass the entire item repository, often containing millions or billions of items. Classical bandit approaches become impractical due to the prohibitive computational cost of evaluating every arm. To tackle this challenge, we introduce a generic hierarchical contextual bandit (\textbf{HCB}) algorithm to effectively explore user interests in large-scale recommendation environments. Tree structures are frequently used to partition search spaces and reduce computational overhead~\cite{jain2016extreme,prabhu2014fastxml,zhu2018learning,zhuo2020learning}. {HCB} employs a tree structure for coarse-to-fine retrieval, such as navigating from \textsl{``Apparel > Clothing > Women's Clothing > Dresses''} in e-commerce scenarios. Rather than relying on item category taxonomies, we apply a bottom-up clustering approach on item embeddings to form a hierarchy tree, grouping semantically similar items at each node. This method balances the number of items per node and encodes users' collaborative behaviors (e.g., co-click relations) to construct the hierarchy tree. {HCB} utilizes the hierarchical structure to transform interest exploration into a sequence of decision-making tasks. Starting at the tree's root, {HCB} applies a bandit algorithm at each non-leaf node among child arms to select a child node until a leaf node is reached. Subsequently, another bandit algorithm recommends an item from the leaf node, collecting user feedback as a reward. This reward is back-propagated along the path to refine the estimation of users' interests within the hierarchy. The {HCB} process resembles a depth-first search (DFS) strategy. However, this path selection approach can introduce new uncertainties, particularly in deep trees. If a parent node selection is erroneous, it can influence all subsequent choices, a phenomenon we term \textsl{error propagation}. Additionally, given the diversity of user interests, a user may be interested in multiple child nodes across different tree sections. To address these issues, we propose a progressive {HCB} (\textbf{pHCB}) algorithm to reduce uncertainties and enhance recommendation capabilities. Analogous to breadth-first search (BFS), {pHCB} explores items adaptively from top to bottom. It maintains a limited number of nodes as a receptive field. If a node is repeatedly explored and user interest is confirmed, its children are added to the receptive field while the current node is removed. Simultaneously, {pHCB} learns diverse user interests by applying a bandit algorithm with visible nodes in the receptive field as arms. Consequently, {pHCB} avoids the pitfall of selecting only one node per level, thereby improving {HCB}. In summary, our contributions are as follows: \squishlist \item We emphasize the necessity of exploring the entire item space to genuinely mitigate the closed-loop effect in personalized recommender systems. To our knowledge, this is the first effort to apply CB models to millions of items. \item We propose two straightforward yet effective algorithms, {HCB} and {pHCB}, for efficiently exploring users' potential interests through a hierarchical item tree. \item We conduct experiments on two large-scale recommendation datasets, demonstrating the superiority of {HCB} and {pHCB} over baseline models, as well as their flexibility to integrate with various exploration methods like LinUCB, Thompson Sampling, and $\epsilon$-greedy. Furthermore, we design an experiment to confirm that both {HCB} and {pHCB} effectively alleviate closed-loop effects in recommender systems, leading to improved long-term user profiles. \squishend

text: This paper delves into an evolutionary robotic system where both the physical structures (morphologies) and the control systems (brains) of robots are evolved in tandem. In such a system, reproduction involves generating a new body and brain, which are then combined to create a robot offspring. For asexual reproduction, a single parent suffices, and the offspring's body and brain arise through random mutations. In contrast, sexual reproduction (crossover) necessitates the recombination of the parents' bodies and brains, resulting in an offspring with a hybrid body and brain. Regardless of the reproduction method, it is generally uncertain whether the newly formed body and brain will be compatible. Even if the parental bodies and brains are well-matched, the stochastic nature of recombination and mutation can disrupt the parental genomes, potentially leading to a mismatch between the resulting body and brain. This inherent issue of body-brain mismatch in joint evolution of morphologies and controllers was initially identified by \citep{Eiben2013} and revisited in \citep{Eiben2020}. To address this, learning is introduced as a solution. In the robotic life cycle, this introduces a third stage beyond the traditional two: the Morphogenesis Stage (before 'birth', where the robot is constructed according to its genotype) and the Operational Stage (after 'birth', where the robot performs tasks and attempts reproduction). The new stage, termed the Infancy Stage, occurs post-Morphogenesis, where the 'newborn' robot learns to optimize its inherited body control to realize its full potential. The term Infancy is not merely metaphorical; it signifies that during this stage, the robot is not yet fertile and cannot reproduce. Algorithmically, this means the robot's fitness is assessed only after the Infancy period, allowing it to participate in the mate selection process based on fitness only after learning is complete. The concept of this three-stage architecture, known as The Triangle of Life, was introduced in 2013, yet it has seen limited exploration in practice. This is partly due to the scarcity of research on the simultaneous evolution of morphology and controllers, as most evolutionary robotics studies focus on brain evolution within a static body framework. Additionally, the computational demands can be significant, if not daunting. To illustrate, the infant learning process is essentially a generate-and-test search through all possible controller configurations. This search requires generating and testing multiple new brains within a given body, resulting in numerous additional fitness evaluations\footnote{For simplicity, all tests are referred to as fitness evaluations.} for each newborn robot. Allocating a learning budget of $N$ new controllers during the Infancy stage implies that the total number of fitness evaluations will be $N$ times higher than without learning. The appropriate value for $N$ varies by system and application, but literature commonly cites several hundred to a few thousand learning trials. The primary aim of this research is to explore the impact of learning in robots undergoing morphological evolution. We establish a system where (simulated) modular robots can reproduce, passing on morphologies and controllers to their offspring. Thus, both bodies and brains in our system are inheritable and evolvable. Furthermore, we enhance the brains' evolvability by making them learnable, implementing a generic learning algorithm to optimize the inherited brain for any robot body. We will test this system by assigning it the task of developing robots for targeted locomotion. This task will be integrated into the evolutionary system using a fitness function that measures a robot's ability to reach a predefined target. Evolution will be driven by mate selection and survivor selection mechanisms based on this fitness measure, steering the development towards robots with bodies and brains well-suited for the task. To assess the learning effects, we will conduct the robot evolution process in two scenarios: one purely evolutionary and another combining evolution with learning. In the first scenario, a robot child's brain is directly inherited from its parents, and its fitness is evaluated immediately after 'birth'. In the second scenario, the inherited brain serves as a starting point for a learning algorithm, and the robot's fitness is determined by its performance with the learned brain. Our experiments will address efficacy, efficiency, and evolved morphologies. Regarding efficacy and efficiency, we will compare the two algorithm variants in terms of peak performance and the time required to reach the best performance. We hypothesize that learning provides a relatively fast and cost-effective means of reducing the number of slow and costly evolutionary steps in real-world applications. Specifically, we differentiate between learning trials and evolutionary trials. An evolutionary trial involves creating, activating, and testing a new robot, including its body construction, whereas a learning trial involves creating, activating, and testing a new controller on an existing robot. Since controllers are digital (i.e., lines of code), learning trials demand considerably less time, effort, and resources than evolutionary trials \citep{Eiben2021}. For instance, if manufacturing a new robot takes 12 hours, computing and installing a new controller takes 10 seconds, and a fitness evaluation lasts one minute, then 1,000 evolutionary trials would require approximately 501 days, whereas 1,000 learning trials would take less than a day. Our research questions are as follows. {\textbf{Research Question 1:}} How much 'savings' (in terms of evolutionary trials) can be achieved by incorporating infant learning as defined by the Triangle of Life architecture? The response to this question will clarify if it is more beneficial to allocate all fitness evaluations to evolutionary trials (creating a new robot with a new body and brain) or to divide them between evolutionary and learning trials (creating a new brain for an existing body). Regarding morphologies, we will examine quantifiable traits such as size and symmetry, comparing trends throughout the evolutionary process and in the final populations. {\textbf{Research Question 2:}} Does the inclusion of learning result in different evolved morphologies? Intuitively, one might expect no differences since learning affects only the brains, not the bodies. However, our preliminary study suggests that learning can indeed lead to different morphologies \citep{Miras2020}. Additionally, we explore the evolution of {\it morphological intelligence}, defined by a body's learning potential. The concept is to delay judgment of a newborn body, evaluating it not as it is immediately after birth with a semi-random controller, but as it can be with a controller tailored to it through learning. Technically, we quantify morphological intelligence using the {\it learning delta}, the performance gap between the inherited and learned brain. Our definition aligns in spirit with that of \citep{Gupta2021}, though differing in details. Specifically, \citep{Gupta2021} defines morphological intelligence by the ability to learn novel tasks, while \citep{Miras2020} ties it to the given task. {\textbf{Research Question 3:}} How does morphological intelligence (measured by the learning delta) evolve over successive generations?

text: The task of document retrieval involves identifying relevant documents from a vast collection to address specific queries. This task is crucial on its own and serves as a foundational element in solving numerous natural language processing~(NLP) challenges, including open domain question answering~\citep{chen2017reading} and fact-checking~\citep{thorne2018fever}. Traditionally, retrieval systems, known as retrievers, have relied on lexical similarity to align queries with documents, employing techniques like TF-IDF or BM25 weighting~\citep{robertson2009probabilistic}. These methods depend on nearly exact token matches between queries and documents, which limits their ability to bridge the lexical gap and hampers generalization~\citep{berger2000bridging}. In contrast, neural network-based approaches transcend lexical similarities, achieving state-of-the-art outcomes on question answering datasets such as MS~MARCO~\citep{nguyen2016ms} and NaturalQuestions~\citep{kwiatkowski2019natural}. Neural networks have demonstrated impressive retrieval capabilities in domains with extensive training datasets. For retrieval tasks, these datasets require manual pairing of queries with relevant documents, a daunting task when collections encompass millions or billions of items. This leads to scenarios where few, if any, in-domain examples are available. A viable approach is to train a dense retriever on a large dataset like MS~MARCO and apply it to novel domains, a process known as \emph{zero-shot} learning. However, in this context, dense retrievers often lag behind traditional term-frequency-based methods, which operate without supervision~\citep{thakur2021beir}. Furthermore, large annotated datasets are typically unavailable in languages other than English, making supervised data collections unsuitable for training multilingual retrieval systems. An intuitive alternative to transfer learning is unsupervised learning, prompting the question: \emph{Can dense retrievers be trained without supervision to rival BM25's performance?} Unsupervised training of dense retrievers can be realized through an auxiliary task that simulates retrieval. By generating a synthetic query from a document, the network can be trained to retrieve the original document among many, based on the query. The inverse Cloze task (ICT), introduced by \citet{lee2019latent} for retriever pre-training, uses a sentence as a query to predict its surrounding context. Although promising for pre-training~\citep{chang2020pre,sachan2021endtoend}, this method still falls short of BM25 in zero-shot retrieval scenarios. ICT shares a strong connection with contrastive learning~\citep{wu2018unsupervised}, extensively utilized in computer vision~\citep{chen2020simple,he2020momentum}. Notably, vision models trained with advanced contrastive learning techniques have produced features highly effective for retrieval~\citep{caron2021emerging}. Consequently, we aim to explore the potential of contrastive learning in training unsupervised dense retrievers. This paper presents several key contributions. Firstly, we demonstrate that contrastive learning can produce robust unsupervised retrievers, with our model achieving Recall@100 results comparable to BM25 across most of the BEIR benchmark. Secondly, in a few-shot scenario, our model shows significant improvement with minimal training examples, surpassing models transferred from large datasets like MS~MARCO. Thirdly, when employed as a pre-training approach prior to fine-tuning on MS~MARCO, our method achieves notable performance on the BEIR benchmark. We conduct ablations to justify our design choices, revealing that cropping is more effective than the inverse Cloze task. Finally, we develop a multilingual dense retriever using contrastive learning, achieving state-of-the-art results. The code and pre-trained models can be accessed at: \url{https://github.com/facebookresearch/contriever}.

text: In recent years, there has been a notable increase in the spread of misinformation, along with related issues like disinformation and fake news, which pose significant threats to society. Such harmful information can sway electoral choices, influence healthcare decisions during crises, or impact financial markets\footnote{e.g., the GameStop incident in 2021: \url{https://reut.rs/3ra7stz }}. This surge in misinformation has spurred extensive research, particularly in the field of natural language processing (NLP), focusing on the automatic verification of claims \cite{fever,popat2018declare,multifc,hanselowski2019richly,wadden2020fact,xfact,covidfact}. Despite considerable advancements, the task remains formidable. For instance, the latest performance metrics on key datasets for natural claims are below 50\% F1~\cite{Atanasova2020GeneratingFC,multifc,xfact}. A closer examination of the data indicates that certain claims present greater challenges for fact-checking, a topic that has not been thoroughly explored. {\bf Table~\ref{tab:taxonomy-examples}} presents several claims evaluated by Politifact\footnote{\url{https://www.politifact.com}}. Comparing claims 3 and 5, claim 3 can be easily verified through a simple search that yields a major media news article. Conversely, claim 5 lacks direct sources (i.e., written or online evidence). Even historians, when consulted, acknowledged the claim's ultimate uncertainty. These examples demonstrate the wide range of difficulties encountered in fact-checking various claims. In this study, we conduct an initial exploration into why some claims are inherently more challenging to fact-check than others, using a manual analysis of claims from Politifact\footnote{\url{https://www.politifact.com/}} featured in automated fact-checking datasets \cite{liar,liarplus,multifc}. This analysis identifies five distinct factors influencing claim difficulty: claim ambiguity, source support, source readability, source trustworthiness, and inference. Considering claim difficulty in the fact-checking process has implications on conceptual, practical, and research fronts. Conceptually, while earlier studies have assessed if a claim is worth checking \cite{checkthat2020,nakov2021clef}, a claim may be deemed check-worthy yet remain extremely challenging or impossible to verify. This affects practical fact-checking, where human resources are limited and require careful allocation, and influences dataset design for automated fact-checking, where including overly difficult claims might not yield valuable insights for comparing different algorithms. Moreover, predicting the difficulty of claims automatically could aid fact-checking organizations in resource management, though we are not aware of any existing research on this prediction task. Although predicting claim difficulty is a novel concept in fact-checking, the importance of modeling and predicting task instance difficulty is acknowledged in other domains, such as machine translation \cite{Mishra2013AutomaticallyPS,Li2015DetectingCS}, syntactic parsing \cite{Garrette2013LearningAP}, and user behavior in search engines \cite{white2009characterizing}, among others. From this standpoint, we propose that predicting instance difficulty could provide similar benefits to the field of fact-checking.

text: In contemporary times, commercial buildings have evolved into intricate cyber-physical systems. They are increasingly equipped with a variety of sensors and actuators, ranging from surveillance cameras and card readers for security and access control, to thermostats and air-quality sensors integrated into the Heating, Ventilation, and Air Conditioning (HVAC) systems, which are pivotal in regulating the indoor environment and ensuring occupant comfort~\cite{Haggerty13,ardakanian2018}. These structures represent significant financial investments, making their security management even more crucial compared to older edifices. Managing access to these buildings necessitates the implementation of distinct access policies tailored to various user types. Typically, long-term occupants, such as employees, are granted access to their offices and shared facilities according to their organizational roles. Conversely, facilities-management personnel usually have access to more restricted areas where equipment is located, as well as to the Building Management System (BMS), which allows them to oversee and adjust equipment settings. Occupants can interact with sensing and control devices like light switches and thermostats in the spaces they can physically access, although these devices might affect areas beyond their immediate vicinity; for instance, a thermostat in one room might set the temperature for multiple neighboring rooms. Visitors generally have restricted access, requiring an escort by building occupants to meeting rooms for their business engagements, where they might control equipment but only for the meeting's duration. In expansive commercial buildings, this system results in considerable administrative burden and exposes the infrastructure to various security vulnerabilities. An automated solution is ideally necessary to effectively manage the access privileges of building occupants. Traditional role-based access-control models, commonly used in current systems, are cumbersome because they demand the specification of all roles and their relative authority, posing a challenge in large buildings housing multiple organizations, each with distinct role hierarchies~\cite{Bindra19}. This paper introduces a methodology for managing building access control inspired by the concept of \emph{airline boarding passes} and the procedures surrounding them. Airports are utilized by numerous airlines, each managing its own flights at specific gates and responsible for issuing boarding passes to passengers. These passes become available shortly before travel, enabling passengers to clear security, access their gate, and board their plane at the appropriate time. Each boarding pass is linked to an individual traveler and is valid only shortly before flight departure, allowing security personnel to scan and verify it. Our proposed methodology can be implemented independently of existing access control delegation strategies while coexisting with current systems. Our approach offers a flexible and secure means of managing access privileges for both long-term occupants and short-term visitors, addressing the aforementioned challenges and risks. We establish a suite of services for the {\em fine-grained} decentralized management of access privileges within a commercial building. By fine-grained, we refer to a system that is (a) person-centric rather than role-based, (b) adaptable to various space/system granularities, and (c) applicable across multiple timescales. The underlying premise is that {\em if an individual is authorized to physically access a specific location in a building, they should also have the capability to interact with the sensors and control points there.} This is primarily because equipment is typically secured only by being placed behind locked doors. Conversely, {\em if someone is not permitted to access certain control points, they should not be allowed entry to the space housing the equipment.} Our methodology utilizes blockchain smart contracts to define, grant, audit, and revoke fine-grained permissions for building occupants and visitors in a decentralized manner~\cite{andersen2018democratizing}. These smart contracts are crafted using information derived from the BOT~\cite{Rasmussen17} and Brick~\cite{balaji2016brick} models, which describe the building's spatial structure, equipment, and their interrelations. This data enables our methodology to assign the precise access privileges necessary for individuals to reach their intended destinations within the building. Smart contracts implement this concept by granting and revoking space-access privileges to individuals through an API that can be called by various software applications. The underlying \emph{access-control service} evaluates individual access requests, accepting or rejecting them based on the active smart contracts and their implications for sensor and actuator access. We demonstrate our method with a typical use case in a real building context and argue that it can significantly reduce administrative overhead while providing detailed, auditable access control. The remainder of this paper is organized as follows. Section~\ref{sec:background} offers an overview of the context surrounding our work. Section~\ref{sec:method} details our methodology for smart-building access control using a graph model for reasoning and blockchain smart contracts for access management. Section~\ref{sec:implement} explores the implementation of our proposed work alongside use cases where the solution can greatly enhance authorization and access control procedures in real buildings. Section~\ref{sec:perform} assesses the performance of our solution in terms of throughput and delay. Section~\ref{sec:system} discusses practical considerations for utilizing blockchain-based access control. Section~\ref{sec:related} reviews related work on authorization and access-control solutions designed for the built environment. The paper concludes with a summary of our key contributions and future work plans in Section~\ref{sec:conclusion}.

text: Few-shot learning, which targets the classification of instances from previously unseen classes with only a few training samples, has experienced significant advancements in recent years. To facilitate rapid adaptation to new classes, there has been a notable emphasis on the meta-learning paradigm, also known as learning-to-learn \cite{ren2018meta,snell2017prototypical,vinyals2016matching}. Meta-learning methods have highlighted the importance of organizing training data into {\em episodes}, which mimic the tasks encountered during inference. Despite these advancements, recent studies in image classification \cite{boudiaf2020transductive,chen2018closer,dhillon2019baseline,GuoECCV20-DS,tian2020rethinking,zikolaplacian} suggest that meta-learning may not generalize well beyond standard 1- or 5-shot classification benchmarks. For example, in more realistic scenarios involving domain shifts, simple classification baselines can outperform complex meta-learning strategies \cite{chen2018closer,GuoECCV20-DS}. Deep learning-based semantic segmentation has generally benefited from methodological innovations in image classification, and few-shot segmentation, which has recently gained traction \cite{gairola2020simpropnet,wei2019fss,liu2020crnet,nguyen2019feature,rakelly2018conditional,pfenet,wangfew,wang2019panet,rpmm,yang2020new,zhang2019canet,zhang2020sg}, follows this trend. In few-shot segmentation, a deep segmentation model is initially trained on {\em base} classes. The model's ability to generalize is then evaluated on few-shot {\em tasks} involving novel classes not seen during base training. Each task consists of an unlabeled test image, termed the {\em query}, accompanied by a few labeled images known as the {\em support} set. Current research in few-shot segmentation aligns with the learning-to-learn paradigm, focusing heavily on developing specialized architectures and episodic-training strategies for base training. However, i) episodic training presumes that test tasks share a similar structure (e.g., number of support shots) with those used during meta-training; and ii) it is often assumed that base and novel classes originate from the same dataset. In practice, these assumptions may restrict the practical application of current few-shot segmentation approaches in real-world scenarios \cite{cao2019theoretical,chen2018closer}. Our experiments corroborate findings from few-shot classification, revealing performance saturation among leading methods when increasing the number of labeled samples (See Table \ref{tab:n_shots_aggreg}). Furthermore, echoing recent insights in image classification \cite{chen2018closer}, existing meta-learning approaches are less effective in cross-domain scenarios (See Table \ref{tab:COCO2PASCAL_results_partial}). This raises questions about the effectiveness of current few-shot segmentation benchmarks and datasets, prompting a reevaluation of the meta-learning paradigm, which has become the \textit{de facto} standard in few-shot segmentation literature. \subsection*{Contributions} In this study, we set aside the meta-learning framework and revisit a straightforward cross-entropy supervision approach during base class training for feature extraction. Additionally, we introduce a \textit{transductive} inference method that more effectively utilizes support-set supervision than existing techniques. Our key contributions are as follows: \begin{itemize} \item We propose a novel transductive inference method, \textit{RePRI} (Region Proportion Regularized Inference), for few-shot segmentation tasks. RePRI optimizes a loss that combines three complementary components: \textit{i)} a standard cross-entropy on labeled pixels of support images; \textit{ii)} the entropy of the posteriors on query pixels of the test image; and \textit{iii)} a global KL divergence regularizer based on the proportion of predicted foreground pixels in the test image. RePRI can be applied to any trained feature extractor, utilizing the same information as standard inductive methods for a given few-shot segmentation task. \item Despite employing a basic cross-entropy training on base classes without complex meta-learning schemes, RePRI achieves highly competitive results on standard few-shot segmentation benchmarks, PASCAL-5$^i$ and COCO-20$^i$, with improvements of approximately $5\%$ and $6\%$ over the state-of-the-art in 5- and 10-shot scenarios, respectively. \item We propose a more realistic scenario where, in addition to the typical class shift between training and testing data distributions, there is also a shift in the images' feature distribution. Our method achieves superior performance in this setting. \item We demonstrate that precise region-proportion information on the query object significantly enhances results, with an average gain of 13\% on both datasets. While assuming access to such precise information may be unrealistic, we show that even approximate estimates can lead to substantial improvements, suggesting a promising avenue for future research. \end{itemize}
