text: In the realm of e-commerce machine learning, developing and evaluating recommenders to achieve business objectives is a central endeavor. A significant challenge arises from the disconnect between business metrics, such as gross merchandise value (GMV), and their interpretation as concrete learning goals. Although some surrogate losses and evaluation metrics have demonstrated empirical success \cite{shani2011evaluating,herlocker2004evaluating}, online experimentation remains a primary method for assessing a recommender's performance in real-world scenarios. There is widespread recognition of various biases present in historical data \cite{chen2020bias}, which can lead to the "feedback-loop effect" if empirical metrics are applied without adjustments \cite{gilotte2018offline}. Recent advances have focused on improving online A/B testing and refining offline evaluation methods \cite{yin2019identification,lee2018winner,xie2018false,gilotte2018offline}. However, these advancements often fall short in specific contexts where the complexity of the problem overshadows their benefits, or their assumptions are unmet. Our work centers on e-commerce recommendations, and we assume an online shopping environment throughout this paper. On the A/B testing front, there is a rising interest in interleaving tested recommenders with targeted customers due to increasing personalization demands \cite{schuth2015predicting}. Collecting sufficient observations and making inferences with adequate power is often time-consuming and expensive, especially given the exponential growth in combination possibilities and the need for predefined bucket definitions. Regarding recent offline A/B testing advancements \cite{gilotte2018offline}, while certain unbiasedness and optimality results have been theoretically established, practical performance still hinges on fundamental causal assumptions \cite{imbens2015causal}, such as unconfounding, overlapping, and identifiability, which are seldom met in practice \cite{xu2020adversarial}. We emphasize that despite their limitations, both online and offline testing are indispensable. Nonetheless, current challenges encourage us to seek more efficient solutions that better exploit the randomized design of traffic. Our production scenario involves selecting from several candidate recommenders that have displayed similar performances in offline evaluations. Segment analysis reveals that each recommender is more favorable to specific customer groups, yet conclusions are hindered by exposure and selection biases in historical data. While it is feasible to launch each candidate online, randomized experiments are still necessary to explore each candidate's real-world performance across different customer groups. Our experimental design aims to incorporate customer features, such as segmentation information, to minimize the cost of deploying suboptimal recommenders to a customer group. Unlike traditional controlled experiments, our primary concern is cost minimization rather than rigorous inference. We frame our task as a recommender-wise exploration-exploitation problem, a novel application to our knowledge. Before proceeding, we highlight the fundamental differences between our problem and learning recommender ensembles \cite{jahrer2010combining}. Business metrics like GMV are random variables influenced by both the recommended content and the distributions governing customer decision-making. Even with access to these distributions, the conditional distribution given the recommended content remains unknown. Thus, the problem cannot be adequately captured by any fixed objective for learning recommender ensembles. In our scenario, the exploration-exploitation strategy resembles a sequential game between the developer and the customers. During each round $t=1,\ldots,n$, where $n$ will be clarified later, the developer selects a recommender $a_t \in \{1,\ldots,k\}$ to generate content $c_t$, such as top-k recommendations, based on the front-end request $r_t$, which includes customer id, user features, page type, etc. Subsequently, the customer reveals the \textsl{reward} $y_t$, such as a click or non-click. This setting parallels the \textsl{multi-armed bandits (MAB)} framework, viewing each recommender as an \emph{action} (\emph{arm}). The front-end request $r_t$, along with the recommended content $c_t = a_t(x_t)$, serves as the \emph{context}. The context is informative of the reward, as clicking depends on how well the content aligns with the request. Additionally, a (randomized) experiment design can be represented by a distribution $\pi$ over the candidate recommenders, i.e., $0 < \pi_t(a) < 1$, $\sum_{i=1}^k \pi_t(i)=1$ for $i=1,\ldots,n$. We note a formal distinction from classical \emph{contextual bandit} settings, where the context here is influenced by candidate actions. However, this impact diminishes if selecting the best content set equates to choosing the optimal action. Consequently, finding the optimal experimentation can be translated into optimizing $\pi_t$, aligning with bandit problems. Optimizing $\pi_t$ allows us to refine the estimation of the structures between context and reward, e.g., through supervised learning, at a low exploration cost. In e-commerce, the critical challenge of exploration, perhaps more severe than in other domains, is that irrelevant recommendations can significantly damage user experience and retention, directly impacting GMV. Thus, leveraging problem-specific information, including contextual structures and prior knowledge, is crucial for designing a more efficient randomized strategy. We illustrate our argument with the following toy example. \begin{example} Consider a scenario with six items, where the front-end request involves a univariate user feature $r_t \in \mathbb{R}$. The reward mechanism follows a linear model: \[ Y_t = \theta_1 \cdot I_1 \times X_t + \ldots + \theta_6 \cdot I_6 \times X_t; \] where $I_j$ indicates whether item $j$ is recommended. Examine the top-3 recommendations from four candidate recommenders as follows (in one-hot encoding): \\ \begin{equation} \begin{split} a_1(r_t) = [1, 1, 1, 0, 0, 0]; \\ a_2(r_t) = [0, 0, 0, 1, 1, 1]; \\ a_3(r_t) = [0, 0, 1, 0, 1, 1]; \\ a_4(r_t) = [0, 0, 0, 1, 1, 1]. \\ \end{split} \end{equation} If each recommender is explored with equal probability, $a_1$ is undervalued since it uniquely provides information about $\theta_1$ and $\theta_2$. Also, since $a_2$ and $a_4$ yield identical outputs, their exploration probability should be halved. Similarly, the information from $S_3$ can be reconstructed by combining $S_1$ and $S_4$ (or $S_2$), indicating a linear dependency structure that can be exploited. \end{example} This example typifies real-world scenarios, where one-hot encodings and user features can be replaced with pre-trained embeddings. We have thus far provided an intuitive grasp of the benefits of well-designed online experiments. In Section \ref{sec:background}, we introduce the notations and formal background of bandit problems. We then review the relevant literature in Section \ref{sec:related}. In Section \ref{sec:method}, we detail our optimal design methods and describe the corresponding online infrastructure. Section \ref{sec:experiment} presents both simulation studies and real-world deployment analyses. Our major contributions are summarized as follows: \begin{itemize} \item We propose a novel framework for online recommender selection through the lens of exploration-exploitation. \item We introduce an optimal experimental approach and outline the infrastructure and implementation. \item We offer open-source simulation studies and real-world deployment results to demonstrate the efficacy of the studied approaches. \end{itemize}

text: Semantic Segmentation involves the task of assigning a class label to each pixel in an image, effectively creating a dense prediction map. Recent advances in vision networks, particularly those based on transformers \cite{vit,deit}, have surpassed the performance of Convolutional Neural Networks in image classification tasks \cite{imagenet}. In contemporary research, transformer architectures have demonstrated exceptional performance when adapted to secondary tasks like semantic segmentation \cite{beit, fapn, swin-T}. Vision transformers typically tackle architectural design through two primary strategies: (i) Utilizing an existing pretrained backbone as an encoder and adapting it for downstream tasks with established decoders like Semantic FPN \cite{sem-fpn} or UperNet \cite{upernet}; or (ii) Developing a novel encoder-decoder architecture where the encoder is pretrained on ImageNet specifically for semantic segmentation. Both approaches involve finetuning the encoder on the segmentation task. Finetuning from a large-scale dataset aids the initial attention layers in capturing local details at the lower layers of transformers \cite{vit-cnn}. Nevertheless, this process often fails to fully leverage semantic context during finetuning due to the dataset's limited size and the altered nature and number of semantic classes from classification to segmentation tasks. Hierarchical vision transformers \cite{segformer,swin-T} address this by progressively downsampling features across stages, yet they still miss capturing the semantic context of the image. Liu et al. \cite{swin-T} introduced the Swin Transformer, which constructs hierarchical feature maps, making it suitable as a versatile backbone for major vision tasks. In \cite{twins}, a dual attention mechanism—global and local—was proposed on top of PVT \cite{pvt} and CPVT \cite{cpvt} to enhance segmentation efficiency. Xie et al. \cite{segformer} further refined the hierarchical transformer encoder by eliminating positional encoding, thereby enhancing its robustness across varying resolutions typical in segmentation tasks. Despite these advancements, these methods did not adequately capture the semantic-level contextual information of entire images. The absence of such semantic context often results in subpar segmentation, particularly for small objects that get misclassified due to merging with larger category boundaries. Recently, \cite{segmenter} attempted to address this by designing a pure transformer-based decoder that jointly processes patch and class embeddings. However, it struggles with small variants and hierarchical architectures, leading to suboptimal performance when integrated with major transformer backbones like Swin \cite{swin-T} and Twins \cite{twins} transformers. In \cite{isnet}, Jin et al. proposed ISNet to model both image-level and semantic-level contextual information by introducing SLCM and ILCM modules within the decoder. However, ISNet, being CNN-based, focuses solely on the decoder, leaving the encoder unchanged. To overcome these challenges, we propose the SeMask framework, which integrates semantic information into hierarchical vision transformer architectures and enhances the global feature information captured by transformers with semantic context. Existing frameworks typically adopt an encoder-decoder architecture with ImageNet-pretrained transformers \cite{imagenet} as encoders and specialized decoders for semantic segmentation. In contrast, we introduce a Semantic Layer after each Transformer Layer within the backbone, creating the SeMask version of the backbone, as depicted in \cref{fig:intro}. A lightweight semantic decoder aggregates semantic maps from all stages, while a standard decoder like Semantic-FPN \cite{sem-fpn} handles per-pixel predictions. This semantic modeling, combined with feature modeling throughout the encoder, enhances semantic segmentation performance. In \cref{sec:experiments}, we incorporate the SeMask block into the Swin Transformer \cite{swin-T} and Mix Transformer \cite{segformer} backbones. Our experiments demonstrate notable improvements in semantic segmentation across two datasets. In summary, our contributions are threefold: \begin{itemize} \item We are the first to explore the impact of integrating semantic context into pretrained transformer backbones for semantic segmentation. We introduce the SeMask Block, which can be seamlessly integrated into any existing hierarchical vision transformer. Empirical evidence shows significant performance gains when SeMask is applied to Swin-transformer~\cite{swin-T} and Mix-Transformer~\cite{segformer}. \item We propose a straightforward semantic decoder to aggregate semantic priors from various encoder stages. These semantic priors are supervised using a per-pixel cross-entropy loss. \item Lastly, we conduct a comprehensive analysis of the SeMask Block's impact on two datasets: ADE20K and Cityscapes. We achieve state-of-the-art performance on the ADE20K dataset and a performance improvement exceeding $3\%$ on the Cityscapes dataset. \end{itemize}

text: The field of image captioning, which seeks to generate descriptive sentences for unlabeled images, is undergoing extensive research~\cite{showandtell2015,bottomup2017,aoanet2019}. Within this domain, cross-lingual image captioning—capable of generating captions in languages other than English—is gaining substantial interest in the fields of multimedia and computer vision~\cite{icmr16-ch-cap,WeiyuLan2017,Jiuxiang2018,2019Improving,2019Unpaired,gao2020unsupervised}. Earlier studies have focused on developing novel algorithms to train image captioning models for non-English languages using English datasets such as Flickr8k \cite{2015Framing}, Flickr30k \cite{2014From}, and MS-COCO \cite{mscoco2014}. For example, in \cite{icmr16-ch-cap}, Li \emph{et al.~} employ machine translation to convert English captions from Flickr8k into Chinese and then train a Show-Tell model~\cite{showandtell2015} using these translated captions. Recognizing that machine-translated sentences often lack readability, Lan \emph{et al.~} \cite{WeiyuLan2017} introduce a fluency-guided learning approach, which assigns importance to training sentences based on fluency scores generated by a deep language model. Building on this, Song \emph{et al.~} \cite{2019Unpaired} enhance the approach by incorporating self-supervised rewards that consider both fluency and visual relevance. Although this training method can operate with minimal or even no data in the target language, evaluating the resulting models on a large scale typically demands thousands of test images with manually crafted captions, or \textit{references}, in the target language. Even with the assistance of an interactive annotation system~\cite{icmr20-icap}, re-annotating a medium-sized test set for each target language requires months of human effort. This paper introduces a novel evaluation method for cross-lingual image captioning. Specifically, we challenge the necessity of target language references by proposing three metrics that differentiate between high and low-performing models using only a single English reference per test image. This assumption is reasonable, given that previous cross-lingual image captioning studies predominantly utilize established English datasets. Our primary findings are as follows: \begin{itemize} 	\item As far as we know, this is the first work to evaluate cross-lingual image captioning models without needing references in the target language. We introduce three metrics—WMDRel, CLinRel, and CMedRel—that assess the semantic alignment of auto-generated captions with image content in diverse ways. 	\item We conducted extensive experiments to test the effectiveness of these proposed metrics. Using combinations of image captioning architectures, such as Show-Tell~\cite{showandtell2015}, Up-Down~\cite{bottomup2017}, and AoANet~\cite{aoanet2019}, along with datasets like COCO-CN~\cite{cococn2019} and VATEX~\cite{2019VATEX}, we created eight Chinese models for ranking. The combined use of WMDRel, CLinRel, and CMedRel shows a Spearman’s rank correlation of 0.952 with the sum of four standard metrics: BLEU-4, METEOR, ROUGE-L, and CIDEr. When no source language reference is available, CMedRel alone achieves a Spearman correlation of 0.881 with CIDEr. \end{itemize}

text: The field of medical imaging has recently experienced a surge in the development of image processing techniques leveraging Deep Learning (DL), achieving impressive results across various applications, notably in the segmentation of Multiple Sclerosis (MS) lesions. Certain automated algorithms have even attained performance levels comparable to human experts under controlled evaluation settings \cite{carass2017longitudinal}. However, while many DL methods have been validated in such controlled environments, real-world data present significant variability. This diversity limits the clinical adoption of DL-based MS lesion segmentation due to inadequate generalization to data from medical sites not included in the training phase (unseen domains). The poor generalization of DL models can be attributed to factors like the chosen optimization solution, the heterogeneity of the training dataset, or the generality of the extracted features. DL models operate under the assumption that training and test datasets are independent yet drawn from the same distribution. This assumption often fails in medical imaging, particularly in Magnetic Resonance Imaging (MRI), where variations in acquisition protocols, MRI scanners, patient demographics, and software processing differ across clinical centers or cohorts. Such discrepancies in data distribution, known as covariate shift, lead to a performance drop when transitioning from training data (source domain) to test data from different distributions (target domain), a phenomenon termed domain shift. To mitigate this issue, one intuitive approach is training on a more extensive and diverse dataset \cite{maartensson2020reliability}. However, this necessitates a large, expertly annotated dataset, which is often unavailable and labor-intensive to produce. Some approaches address this by implementing extensive data augmentation \cite{zhang2020generalizing}, while others utilize few available labeled images from the target domain to minimize covariate shift, employing strategies like few-shot and one-shot learning \cite{snell2017prototypical,valverde2019one}. Moreover, DL models require tuning numerous parameters relative to the number of training samples, typically converging to one of many possible local minima rather than the theoretical global minimum. Thus, the model's generalization capability hinges on selecting the most suitable local minimum. Identifying the best generalizing local minimum remains unresolved. Some research suggests using local characteristics, such as the flatness of the loss function \cite{keskar2016large, wu2017towards}, while others propose combining multiple local minima to enhance generalization. This can be achieved by averaging several local minima within a model, as in snapshot ensembles \cite{huang2017snapshot}, or by integrating outputs from independently trained models, as seen in classical ensembles \cite{zhang2019multiple} and spatially distributed networks \cite{coupe2020assemblynet, huo20193d}. In contrast to traditional methods relying on handcrafted features, Convolutional Neural Networks (CNNs) autonomously extract the most pertinent features for a given task. While this approach efficiently derives relevant features for a specific source domain, these features may not generalize well to the target domain. Some studies propose learning invariant features that span different source domains \cite{motiian2017unified,muandet2013domain,yang2013multi}, aiming to apply regularization to learn an abstract representation of the task, akin to human comprehension of high-level concepts. The extraction of generalizing features balances the optimization process's freedom to find optimal data combinations and the constraints used to minimize domain bias. For DL-based MS lesion segmentation to succeed, generalization capabilities ensuring high performance on unseen domains are crucial. Such methods must guide the DL model to generalizing minima and anticipate covariate shift reduction during training. Furthermore, they should enforce the learning of MS lesion generalizing features from the source domain to accurately delineate lesions across target domain distributions, without necessitating additional annotation for unseen domains. Recently, numerous studies have explored MS lesion segmentation using CNNs. \cite{brosch2016deep} introduced a deep 3D encoder-decoder network with joint training of the encoder and decoder, utilizing shortcut connections to integrate high and low-level features. This pioneering work highlighted the potential of deep learning in MS lesion segmentation. \cite{valverde2017improving} presented a cascade of two patch-wise 3D CNNs, initially identifying potential lesions and subsequently reducing misclassified voxels. This approach allows refined segmentation but is limited by a small receptive field that hinders global context capture. Later, \cite{valverde2019one} enhanced their method with a one-shot domain adaptation model using transfer learning and partial fine-tuning, though requiring a labeled example from the new domain and leading to segmentation inconsistencies post-adaptation. \cite{hashemi2018asymmetric} addressed data imbalance by employing an asymmetric similarity loss function based on the Tversky index to train a 3D CNN, outperforming Dice or cross-entropy measures. While the proposed loss can be optimized for precision-recall trade-offs in specific domains, its generalization to unseen domains remains unproven. \cite{zhang2019multiple} utilized a fully convolutional densely connected network for MS lesion segmentation, stacking adjacent 2D slices of different modalities before processing through a 2D CNN. The final segmentation relies on a majority vote across orientations, but the limited insight into the 3D nature of data restricts generalization. \cite{aslani2019multi} proposed an end-to-end encoder-decoder 2D network with multiple downsampling branches for each input modality, combining features at multiple scales. However, this 2D approach lacks integration of axial, coronal, and sagittal features, potentially reducing generalization on 3D images. \cite{feng2019self} addressed MRI modality unavailability by introducing sequence dropout, a key consideration given the variability in modality availability across datasets. This framework randomly omits MRI sequences during training to learn intrinsic sequence information, achieving acceptable segmentation without all modalities but underperforming compared to state-of-the-art methods when all modalities are present (detailed in section \ref{same domain val}). \cite{aslani2020scanner} tackled generalization to new domains by incorporating a regularization network into the traditional encoder-decoder framework, penalizing the network for learning features that predict MRI scanning sites. However, \cite{li2018domain} noted that such strategies may overfit, generalizing well for source domains but poorly for unknown target domains. The aforementioned MS methods \cite{brosch2016deep,valverde2017improving,feng2019self,hashemi2018asymmetric,zhang2019multiple,aslani2019multi,feng2019self} primarily focus on achieving accurate segmentation within the same domain evaluation. However, employing out-of-domain datasets is crucial for evaluating a method's generalization capabilities. This topic is currently of significant interest \cite{maartensson2020reliability,bron2020cross} and a key recommendation from the clinical community \cite{omoumi2021buy}. Evaluations using same-domain training and testing images are known to be biased \cite{omoumi2021buy} and do not guarantee generalization. Therefore, models intended for clinical use must accurately segment new domain images without requiring retraining with expert segmentation in the new domain. In this paper, we introduce DeepLesionBrain (DLB), a novel method for MS lesion segmentation that is resilient to domain shift, validated through out-of-domain testing (cross-dataset testing). Initially, we deploy a large ensemble of compact 3D CNNs spatially distributed across the brain, with overlapping receptive fields between regions. By assigning a unique network to each brain region, the spatially distributed networks approach \cite{coupe2020assemblynet, huo20193d} simplifies MS lesion segmentation from a complex whole-brain task to multiple simpler regional sub-tasks. The overlapping regions facilitate consistent and stable consensus, with studies indicating that such consensus-based strategies aid in converging towards generalizing minima \cite{breiman2001random,izmailov2018averaging,olson2018modern}. Applied to brain segmentation, this strategy has demonstrated good generalization on unseen domains (e.g., child's brain or patients with Alzheimer's disease) when trained on healthy adult brains \cite{coupe2020assemblynet}. Furthermore, DLB is trained using a novel Image Quality Data Augmentation (IQDA) method, simulating real-world data diversity by introducing realistic alterations to training images. As evidenced by \cite{zhang2020does}, this regularization technique aims to reduce covariate shift. IQDA proposes specific augmentations that decouple task learning from source data acquisition resolution, contrast, or quality, thereby enhancing domain shift robustness. To ensure effective feature generalization, we emphasize feature learning strategies. A generalizing model should acquire both global, generic features and local, specific features. Hence, we propose Hierarchical Specialization Learning (HSL) to extract these features efficiently in two stages. Initially, a single network (the generic network) is trained on all brain regions. Subsequently, each network within the spatially distributed networks is initialized with the generic network's weights and specialized for a specific brain region. Lastly, we propose a method utilizing only two modalities (T1w and FLAIR) to ensure broad dataset compatibility. Most approaches \cite{feng2019self,brosch2016deep,valverde2017improving,zhang2019multiple} optimize segmentation using T1w, FLAIR, PD, and T2 modalities. However, in clinical settings, not all sequences are consistently available. Our work focuses on developing a robust approach using only two modalities.

These studies try to make the deep learning model go into a generalized minimum, to avoid a covariance shift during training, and to make the learned features applicable to the distribution of the unknown target domain, without having to use additional annotation for the unknown domain. text: Anomaly Detection (AD) in the realm of remote sensing data analysis stands as a pivotal research domain for a multitude of applications~\cite{Stein02,Keshava04}. The determination of anomalies is achieved by evaluating the variance between the pixel under test (PUT) and its surrounding background. Numerous anomaly detection methods have been introduced in the literature, each based on distinct assumptions: 1) the selection of the background region and its distribution, 2) the methodology for computing the distance between the PUT and the background statistics, and 3) the criteria for defining the decision threshold or test statistic \cite{Matteoli2010}. Among the extensive array of AD techniques, the Reed-Xiaoli (RX) algorithm is particularly favored for its straightforwardness, effective results, and operational efficiency~\cite{Stein02,Keshava04}. The RX algorithm, arguably the most recognized AD technique for hyperspectral imagery, presumes a multivariate Gaussian distribution for the background and employs the Mahalanobis distance to compare the PUT with the background~\cite{Reed90tassp}. Regarding the background region, two principal methodologies exist. The global approach considers the entire image as the background, whereas the local approach defines the background as the pixels surrounding the PUT, using either a sliding window or a segmentation-based strategy~\cite{Molero13jstars,Zhao15rs}. Additionally, potential anomalies may be censored to avoid compromising the background statistics~\cite{Nar17dsp}. Although RX is efficient computationally and performs well with simple, mainly linear backgrounds, it struggles with more intricate, nonlinear, or non-Gaussian backgrounds. Advanced techniques, such as kernel methods, can address these limitations by managing non-Gaussian distributed data~\cite{CampsValls09wiley,Kwon07,Longbotham14}. However, kernel RX is computationally intensive due to the necessity of inverting matrices proportional to the sample size, often exceeding a thousand pixels. Conversely, the covariance matrix in the RX method has a fixed size, correlating with the spectral dimension of the image, typically around ten for multispectral and around a hundred for hyperspectral images. Given that AD generally precedes further recognition tasks, the execution time is equally, if not more, critical than detection accuracy \cite{Chen14taes}. Moreover, operational applications may face constraints in processor capacity (CPU or GPU), memory storage, and execution budget \cite{Molero13jstars}. A recent development in \cite{Zhao16rs} introduced a fast recursive kernel RX method that processes data in a causal manner. Despite its speed, estimating the threshold for target decision remains challenging because detection outcomes depend on the PUT's location within the image. In this paper, we introduce an innovative approach to accelerate the kernel RX method without compromising its accuracy. Our strategy involves approximating the kernel function using random Fourier features~\cite{Rahimi07nips}, thereby projecting data into a nonlinear feature space where a standard, cost-effective, and efficient linear RX method can be applied. The randomized approach has previously been utilized in remote sensing for classification and regression tasks~\cite{Valero15igarss,Perez17rks}. The proposed randomized RX method substantially reduces execution time and memory requirements compared to the kernel RX method, while maintaining nearly identical detection accuracy. We provide empirical evidence from both synthetic and real-world remote sensing target detection scenarios. The structure of the paper is as follows. Section \ref{sec:randomized_GRX} offers a concise overview of the method proposed in this study. Section \ref{sec:experiments} details the performance of the randomized RX method. Finally, section \ref{sec:conclusion} concludes with observations and potential directions for future research.

text: We introduce a novel Deep Interaction Prediction Network (\textsc{DIPN}\xspace) designed to learn object interactions from examples, enabling precise prediction of object poses following arbitrary push actions (see Fig.~\ref{fig:intro}). To highlight its utility, we integrate \textsc{DIPN}\xspace with a deep Grasp Network (\textsc{GN}\xspace) to tackle complex tasks involving clutter removal. The primary goal is to clear all objects from a given scene or workspace using the fewest possible actions, choosing between grasp and push options. During each cycle of push/pick decision-making (illustrated in Fig.~\ref{fig:system-architecture}), the system assesses the scene and generates numerous candidate grasp and push actions. While \textsc{GN}\xspace instantly evaluates and scores grasp actions, \textsc{DIPN}\xspace produces images depicting the predicted effects of each potential push, effectively "visualizing" the scene's evolution if a particular push is executed. These predicted images are then scored by \textsc{GN}\xspace, and the action—whether a push or a grasp—yielding the highest anticipated score is performed. Our extensive evaluations reveal that \textsc{DIPN}\xspace can predict post-push object poses with collisions with remarkable accuracy, achieving an average single object pose error of less than $10\%$ in terms of Intersection-over-Union (IoU), significantly outperforming existing baselines. The push predictions generated by \textsc{DIPN}\xspace create clear synthetic images that facilitate \textsc{GN}\xspace in evaluating future grasp actions. In combination with \textsc{GN}\xspace, our pipeline enhances completion rates by $34\%$, grasp success rates by $20.9\%$, and action efficiency by $30.4\%$ compared to the approach in~\cite{zeng2018learning} in demanding clutter removal tasks. Additionally, our experiments indicate that \textsc{DIPN}\xspace effectively learns from randomly generated scenarios, with the policy maintaining high performance levels on challenging tasks involving novel objects. Notably, the \textsc{DIPN+GN}\xspace system demonstrates superior performance on real robotic hardware compared to its development environment in simulation.

text: Inertial navigation remains a persistent challenge focused on determining the states, such as position and orientation, of moving entities like pedestrians, using solely IMUs attached to them. Typically comprising accelerometers and gyroscopes, an IMU sensor is integral to numerous applications ranging from mobile technology to autonomous systems, valued for its energy efficiency, portability, and adaptability \cite{lymberopoulos2015realistic}. However, traditional Newtonian-based inertial navigation techniques not only perform inadequately but also impose impractical constraints unsuitable for everyday applications. For instance, strap-down inertial navigation systems (SINS) may inaccurately determine sensor positions due to exponential error growth during double integration of IMU data \cite{titterton2004strapdown}. Step-based pedestrian dead reckoning (PDR) methods mitigate this error by utilizing prior knowledge of human gait to anticipate trajectories \cite{tian2015enhanced}. Nevertheless, these methods require the IMU to be foot-mounted for zero-velocity updates \cite{foxlin2005pedestrian} or necessitate consistent forward walking to maintain a steady motion direction in the body frame \cite{brajdic2013walk}. Furthermore, integrating inertial sensors with supplementary sensors and models via the Extended Kalman Filter \cite{bloesch2015robust} enhances estimation accuracy. Typical auxiliary sensors include WiFi \cite{ahmetovic2016navcog}, Bluetooth \cite{li2017indoor}, LiDAR \cite{zhang2014loam}, or cameras \cite{leutenegger2015keyframe}. Yet, these integrations introduce new challenges regarding sensor setup, energy consumption, and data privacy. For example, Visual-Inertial Odometry (VIO) is heavily influenced by environmental conditions like lighting, signal quality, and blur \cite{usenko2016direct}. Recently, data-driven methods such as IONet \cite{chen2018ionet}, RoNIN \cite{herath2020ronin}, and IDOL \cite{sun2021idol} have emerged, leveraging neural networks to derive precise estimates from IMU data, often surpassing traditional techniques. Despite their promise, significant challenges persist in applying neural networks to IMU data: 1) Most data-driven models use sequence-based architectures (e.g., LSTM \cite{LSTM}) to capture temporal correlations but overlook spatial relationships in multivariate time-series. 2) There is scant research on leveraging the rich spatial and temporal contextual information in IMU data for feature representation. 3) These neural inertial models often assume a fixed covariance matrix for IMU data and model output uncertainties, leading to inaccuracies and reduced robustness due to natural fluctuations. Addressing these challenges, we introduce a novel robust contextual Transformer network designed to regress velocity and predict trajectories from IMU data. Specifically, CTIN builds upon the concepts of ResNet-18 \cite{he2016deep} and Transformer \cite{vaswani2017attention} to harness spatial and extended temporal information from IMU readings, employing attention mechanisms to integrate this data for inertial navigation. The primary contributions of this paper include: \begin{itemize} \item Extending ResNet-18 with attention mechanisms to explore and encode the spatial properties of IMU data. \item Introducing a novel self-attention mechanism to extract contextual features from IMU measurements. \item Utilizing Multi-Task learning with innovative loss functions to enhance learning efficiency and minimize model uncertainty. \item Comprehensive qualitative and quantitative evaluations demonstrate CTIN's superiority over existing state-of-the-art models. \item Providing a new IMU dataset featuring ground-truth trajectories under natural human movements for future research. \item To our knowledge, CTIN represents the first Transformer-based model dedicated to inertial navigation. \end{itemize} The remainder of this paper is structured as follows. Section \ref{sec: background} provides background information on inertial navigation and attention mechanisms. Section \ref{sec: model} outlines the architecture and workflow of CTIN. Evaluation and related work are discussed in Section \ref{sec: evaluation} and Section \ref{sec: related_work}, respectively. Finally, Section \ref{sec: conclusion} presents conclusions and future directions.

text: Addressing math word problems (MWPs) presents distinct challenges in interpreting natural language and executing arithmetic reasoning with quantities and commonsense knowledge. As illustrated in \autoref{fig:example}, a typical MWP involves a brief narrative that describes a real-world scenario and poses a question about an unknown quantity. To solve the problem depicted in \autoref{fig:example}, a machine must identify key numerical values from the text, such as "100 kilometers" and "2 hours," and discern their interrelationships. Utilizing fundamental mathematical principles like "distance = velocity $\times$ time," the solution can then be computed. Recent research has concentrated on employing neural-symbolic models to solve MWPs~\cite{Ling2017ProgramIB, wang-etal-2017-deep, Huang2018NeuralMW, Wang2018TranslatingMW, Xie2019AGT}. These models typically integrate a neural perception module (e.g., Seq2Seq or Seq2Tree) that translates the problem text into a solution expression or tree, alongside a symbolic module that executes the expression to derive the final answer. Training these models necessitates complete supervision of the solution expressions. Nevertheless, fully-supervised methodologies exhibit three primary limitations. Firstly, existing MWP datasets provide only a single solution per problem, despite the existence of multiple valid solutions that offer different solution pathways. For example, the problem in \autoref{fig:example} can be resolved through ``$(100/2) \times (2+3.5)$'' by initially determining the speed and then multiplying by the total time; alternatively, it can be tackled using ``$100 + 100/2 \times 3.5$'' by summing the distances of the journey's segments. Models trained under full supervision are constrained to fit the provided solution, limiting their ability to generate diverse solutions. Secondly, annotating expressions for MWPs is labor-intensive, while a wealth of MWPs with final answers can be easily sourced from the internet (e.g., online forums). Efficiently leveraging these partially-labeled data without expression supervision remains a challenge. Thirdly, current supervised learning strategies experience a train-test mismatch. Fully-supervised learning optimizes for expression accuracy rather than answer accuracy, yet models are evaluated based on answer accuracy during testing, leading to a performance gap. To tackle these challenges, we propose solving MWPs through \textit{weak supervision}, which requires only problem texts and final answers. By focusing on optimizing answer accuracy instead of expression accuracy, weak supervision naturally mitigates the train-test discrepancy. Our approach employs a tree-structured neural model akin to \citet{Xie2019AGT} for generating the solution tree, complemented by a symbolic execution module for answer computation. However, the symbolic execution module is non-differentiable concerning answer accuracy, precluding gradient computation via back-propagation. A straightforward solution is to apply policy gradient techniques such as REINFORCE~\cite{williams1992simple} to train the neural model. Policy gradient methods explore the solution space, updating the policy based on solutions that yield the correct answer. Given the vast solution space and the zero reward for incorrect solutions, these methods often converge slowly or fail altogether. To enhance the efficiency of weakly-supervised learning, we introduce an innovative \textit{fixing} mechanism inspired by humans' ability to learn from errors through abductive reasoning~\cite{magnani2009abductive,Zhou2018AbductiveLT}. This mechanism propagates errors from the root to the leaf nodes in the solution tree to identify the most likely \textit{fix} that produces the correct answer. The corrected solution tree serves as a pseudo label for training the neural model. \autoref{fig:framework} illustrates how the fixing mechanism rectifies an incorrect solution tree by tracing the error in a top-down approach. Moreover, we propose two practical strategies for efficiently exploring the solution space and identifying potential solutions. First, we observe a correlation between the number of quantities in the text and the solution tree's size (i.e., the number of leaf nodes) and introduce a \textit{tree regularization} technique to constrain possible tree sizes, thereby reducing the solution space. Second, we implement a \textit{memory buffer} to track and store discovered fixes for each problem using the fixing mechanism. Solutions stored in the memory buffer serve as pseudo labels to train the model, promoting the generation of diverse solutions for a single problem. In summary, by integrating the fixing mechanism with these two strategies, the proposed \textbf{learning-by-fixing} (LBF) method encompasses an exploration and a learning phase in each iteration, as depicted in \autoref{fig:framework}. During the exploration phase, we utilize the fixing mechanism and tree regularization to amend incorrect answers and generate fixed expressions as pseudo labels. In the learning phase, the neural model is trained using these pseudo labels. We perform extensive experiments on the Math23K dataset~\cite{wang-etal-2017-deep}. The LBF method significantly surpasses reinforcement learning baselines in weakly-supervised settings and achieves performance comparable to several fully-supervised approaches. Additionally, our method demonstrates superior answer accuracy for the top-3/5 answers compared to fully-supervised methods, highlighting its strength in producing diverse solutions. Ablation studies further confirm the effectiveness of our designed algorithms, including the fixing mechanism, tree regularization, and memory buffer.

text: The aim of pattern mining is to identify a concise set of intriguing patterns that collectively represent a substantial portion of a dataset, offering interpretability and reusability. Pattern mining encompasses a wide array of algorithms within the domain of knowledge discovery and data mining, focusing on dataset analysis \citep{aggarwal2014frequent5interesting}. Current methodologies in pattern mining prioritize the discovery of an interesting \textit{pattern set} over individual patterns, assessing pattern quality in relation to both the dataset and other patterns. A frequent theoretical foundation for pattern set mining is the Minimum Description Length principle (MDL)~\citep{grunwald2007minimum}, applicable to various pattern types, such as itemsets~\citep{vreeken2011krimp}, arbitrary-shaped patterns in 2D data~\citep{faas2020vouw}, sequences~\citep{hinrichs2017characterising}, and graphs~\citep{bariatti2020graphmdl}. Despite recent progress in pattern mining, algorithms tailored for numerical data mining remain underexplored. Typically, numerical pattern sets are mined by applying itemset mining to binarized datasets. This approach will be further elaborated upon later; however, it is important to mention that clustering represents an alternative approach to numeric pattern mining. Over recent years, clustering algorithms have seen substantial development, resulting in numerous effective methodologies \citep{Jain10,CraenendonckDB17,Jeantet0G20}. However, a fundamental conceptual distinction exists between pattern mining and clustering. Pattern mining prioritizes \textit{description}, whereas clustering emphasizes \textit{object similarity}. Essentially, numerical pattern mining focuses on describing groups of objects through their attributes, while clustering identifies these groups based on shared characteristics, measured via similarity or distance. The former requires interpretability, meaning patterns should delineate an easily interpretable region within the "attribute space." Conversely, clustering targets groups of objects or instances, often constrained by shape, such as spheres in \textsc{K-means} or \textsc{DBSCAN}, yet prioritizes object similarity as a defining cluster feature. For instance, agglomerative single-linkage clustering in multidimensional spaces may yield clusters with complex shapes, which are typically overlooked in clustering but are crucial in numerical pattern mining. In response, this paper introduces \textsc{Mint}, an MDL-based approach for mining numerical pattern sets, standing for "Mining INTeresting Numerical Pattern Sets." \textsc{Mint} identifies numerical patterns as $m$-dimensional hyper-rectangles, products of $m$ intervals, linked to attributes and their corresponding values. The primary advantages of \textsc{Mint} include: (i) the ability to compute candidate optimal patterns dynamically without prior exploration of the pattern space, (ii) a maximum cubic exploration of patterns, with at most quadratic exploration per iteration, based on the number of objects with distinct attribute value vectors, and (iii) reliance on MDL, producing a concise set of non-redundant, informative patterns. Moreover, experimental results demonstrate \textsc{Mint}'s efficiency and its ability to generate high-quality pattern sets, delineating meaningful object groups with precise boundaries. The \textsc{Mint} algorithm effectively mines numerical patterns across both small and large datasets, often outperforming competitors like \textsc{Slim} and \textsc{RealKrimp}. The encoding scheme employed is based on prequential plug-in codes, which offer superior theoretical properties compared to the codes used in \textsc{Slim}, \textsc{RealKrimp}, and the MDL-based discretization method \textsc{IPD}. The structure of this paper is as follows. Section~\ref{sec:related_work} reviews state-of-the-art algorithms for itemset pattern mining in numerical data contexts. Section~\ref{sec:basics} outlines the foundational concepts utilized throughout the paper, while Section~\ref{sec:method} details the proposed method's core principles. Section~\ref{sec:experiments} presents experiments that highlight \textsc{Mint}'s effectiveness and advantages. Finally, Section~\ref{sec:conclusion} offers concluding remarks on \textsc{Mint}'s potential and suggests avenues for future research.

text: \noindent In the past few years, significant research efforts have been dedicated to integrating deep learning models into computer-aided diagnostic (CAD) systems. These models have demonstrated remarkable diagnostic capabilities across various clinical fields, including fundoscopy \cite{asiri2019deep}, dermatology \cite{liu2020deep,esteva2017dermatologist}, and the diagnosis of pulmonary diseases \cite{shoeibi2020automated,rajpurkar2017chexnet,gabruseva2020deep}. The global shortage of radiologists and the rising issue of burnout \cite{wuni2020opportunities,ali2015diagnostic, kumamaru2018global,zha2018prevalence,rimmer2017radiologist} have naturally led to the development of deep learning systems tailored for chest radiography. This area is particularly amenable to supervised learning due to the availability of extensive datasets of chest radiographs paired with diagnostic labels, which serve as valuable training data for deep learning models. Comprehensive datasets of chest radiographs have been assembled to serve as benchmarks for diagnosing various diseases \cite{wang2017chestx,johnson2019mimic}, with recent additions including COVID-19 \cite{wang2020covid}. In these benchmark datasets, deep learning models have demonstrated performance on par with human experts \cite{rajpurkar2018deep,seyyed2020chexclusion}. Nonetheless, recent findings indicate that even top-performing deep learning models can be vulnerable to adversarial attacks \cite{finlayson2019adversarial,han2020deep}. \citet{finlayson2018adversarial} argue that the substantial costs associated with the medical sector, coupled with the reliance on disease prevalence for pharmaceutical device and drug approvals, may incentivize the manipulation of disease detection systems. The primary contributions of this paper are outlined as follows: \begin{enumerate} \item We conduct an in-depth investigation of backdoor attacks within the realm of medical imaging, concentrating on chest radiography in a multi-label classification setting. Recognizing that a chest radiograph can simultaneously indicate multiple diseases, we introduce an evaluation framework tailored for multi-label classification tasks. To our knowledge, this is the inaugural study addressing backdoor attacks in the context of multi-label classification. \item We demonstrate the manifestation of the trigger in both low-level and high-level features learned by the model using Gradient-weighted Class Activation Mapping (Grad-CAM), a technique for weakly-supervised explainability \cite{selvaraju2017grad}. By illustrating how explainability can uncover the presence of a backdoor, we highlight the critical role of explainability in assessing model robustness. \end{enumerate}

text: The PlatON network facilitates a platform designed for handling distributed transactions and computations~\cite{PlatON}. At the core of its functionality is the Giskard consensus protocol~\cite{Giskard}, which ensures agreement among the network's nodes about which transaction blocks should be appended to the blockchain. This protocol is robust enough to handle scenarios where up to one-third of the participating nodes exhibit Byzantine behavior, meaning they may act maliciously~\cite{Byzantine}. This paper offers a comprehensive specification of the Giskard protocol. Unlike the existing protocol documentation~\cite{Giskard}, which provides a general overview and describes its operational dynamics, our objective is to detail the protocol thoroughly enough to aid in both implementation and formal verification. We achieve this by defining the semantics of protocol execution and outlining significant protocol properties, alongside presenting proofs for its three fundamental safety properties based on these definitions. Our primary concern is the safety of the protocol; therefore, we omit discussions on Giskard's higher-level features, offering only a succinct background. For further context and motivation, readers are referred to the official documentation~\cite{Giskard}.

text: \xdef\@thefnmark{}\@footnotetext{$^*$Equal contribution. Correspondence to \email{alex@openai.com}, \email{prafulla@openai.com}, \email{aramesh@openai.com}} Visual content, encompassing illustrations, paintings, and photographs, can often be succinctly described through text, yet crafting them typically demands specialized expertise and significant time investment. Consequently, a tool that can generate realistic images from natural language inputs would enable individuals to effortlessly create diverse and rich visual content. Moreover, the capacity to refine images through natural language facilitates iterative improvements and precise control, essential for practical applications. Contemporary text-conditional image models have advanced to the point where they can generate images from free-form textual prompts, effectively integrating unrelated elements in semantically coherent ways \citep{attngan,dmgan,dfgan,dalle,xmcgan}. Nonetheless, these models still struggle to produce photorealistic images that fully embody their textual descriptions. Conversely, unconditional image models have demonstrated the ability to create photorealistic images \cite{biggan,stylegan,stylegan2,vqvae2}, sometimes with such realism that they are indistinguishable from genuine images by human observers \cite{zhou2019hype}. Within this research domain, diffusion models \cite{dickstein,scorematching} have emerged as a leading class of generative models, delivering state-of-the-art results on various image generation benchmarks \citep{ddpm,sotapaper,cascaded}. To attain photorealism in class-conditional settings, \citet{sotapaper} enhanced diffusion models with \textit{classifier guidance}, a method that allows these models to be conditioned on classifier labels. Initially, the classifier is trained on noisy images, and during the sampling phase, gradients from the classifier guide the sample towards the label. \citet{uncond} achieved comparable outcomes without the need for a separately trained classifier by employing \textit{classifier-free guidance}, which interpolates predictions from a diffusion model with and without labels. Inspired by the potential of guided diffusion models to produce photorealistic samples and the capability of text-to-image models to interpret free-form prompts, we leverage guided diffusion for text-conditional image synthesis. We begin by training a diffusion model with 3.5 billion parameters that employs a text encoder for conditioning on natural language descriptions. Subsequently, we evaluate two methods for guiding diffusion models in response to text prompts: CLIP guidance and classifier-free guidance. Through human and automated assessments, we determine that classifier-free guidance generates superior-quality images. Our findings indicate that images produced by our model using classifier-free guidance are not only photorealistic but also encompass a broad spectrum of world knowledge. Human evaluators prefer our samples over those from DALL-E \citep{dalle} 87\% of the time for photorealism and 69\% of the time for alignment with captions. Although our model can adeptly handle a wide range of text prompts in a zero-shot manner, it occasionally struggles with generating realistic images for more complex prompts. To address this, we equip our model with editing capabilities alongside zero-shot generation, allowing users to iteratively refine samples to better match intricate prompts. In particular, we fine-tune our model for image inpainting, demonstrating its ability to make realistic edits to existing images based on natural language commands. The edits seamlessly integrate with the surrounding context, maintaining consistent style and lighting, including realistic shadows and reflections. Future developments of these models could significantly enhance human capabilities in crafting custom images with remarkable speed and simplicity. We recognize that our model's efficiency in producing convincing disinformation or Deepfakes poses a risk. To mitigate this while supporting future research, we release a smaller diffusion model and a noised CLIP model trained on curated datasets. We have named our system GLIDE{}, an acronym for \textbf{G}uided \textbf{L}anguage to \textbf{I}mage \textbf{D}iffusion for Generation and \textbf{E}diting. Our smaller, curated model is referred to as GLIDE{} (filtered).

However, it still hasn't been able to produce a photorealistic image that is completely faithful to its textual description. Moreover, the ability to refine images through natural language allows iterative improvements and precise control, both essential to practical applications. Text-conditional image models have now reached a point where they can generate images from free-form textual prompts, combining in a semantically coherent way unrelated elements in a meaningful way. Unlike class-conditional generative models, however, unconditional generative models have demonstrated their ability to create photorealistic images, e.g., biggan, stylegan, stylegan2, vqvae2 (with some models so realistic that they are indistinguishable from the real images by human observers, e.g., zhou2019hype). To attain photorealism in class-conditional settings, the sotapaper method enhanced diffusion models with classifier guidance, a method that allows these models to be conditioned on the classifier labels. Inspired by the potential of guided diffusion models to produce photorealistic samples, and the capability of text-to-image models to interpret free-form inputs, we exploit guided diffusion for text-conditional image synthesis. Initially, the classifier is trained on noisy images, and during the sampling phase, gradients from the classifier guide the sample towards the label. In contrast, cittext uncond obtained comparable results without the need for a separately trained classifier, by using the ‘textit-classifier-free guidance’, which is an interpolation between the predictions of a diffusion model with and without a label. Having trained a diffusion model with a total of 3.5 billion parameters that conditions on natural language descriptions, we then compare two ways of guiding diffusion models: CLIP guidance and classifier-free guidance. Both human and machine evaluators conclude that classifier-free guidance produces images of higher quality. Although our model is capable of generating images from a wide range of zero-shot text prompts, it sometimes struggles to produce realistic images for more complex prompts. Our findings suggest that images produced by our model under classifier-free guidance are not only photorealistic but also encompass a broad spectrum of world knowledge. These edits integrate smoothly with the surroundings, maintaining a consistent style, lighting, shadows, and reflections. In order to overcome these difficulties, our model provides editing capabilities alongside zero-shot generation, allowing iterative refinement of samples to better match complex prompts. We acknowledge that our model's efficiency in producing convincing disinformation or deepfakes is a potential risk. In order to mitigate this risk while enabling further research, we release a smaller version of our model and a noised CLIP model, both trained on curated datasets. text: \noindent The landscape of online recruitment platforms has evolved significantly in recent years. With the burgeoning volume of recruitment data available online, numerous studies have emerged focusing on areas such as person-job (or talent-job) fit~\cite{shen2018joint, qin2018enhancing, luo2019resumegan, bian2019domain} and the automated analysis of asynchronous video interviews (AVIs)~\cite{hemamou2019hirenet, hemamou2019slices, suen2019tensorflow}. These studies aim to facilitate automated job recommendations and candidate evaluations. In particular, the person-job fit is approached as a supervised text matching problem, where the goal is to predict the matching label between candidate resumes and job descriptions using a set of labeled data (i.e., person-job match records). Recent advancements in deep learning have further refined these methods by developing more effective text matching and text representation models~\cite{xu2017measuring, jiang2019semantic}. AVIs, on the other hand, focus on assessing a candidate's suitability for a position by analyzing their responses to interview questions. In AVIs, interviews are typically viewed as sequences of questions and answers rich in social signals. To provide a comprehensive evaluation of candidates, AVI models extract features from video (or image), text, and voice during the question-answering process. Our work concentrates on scoring multiple QA pairs, where we extract features solely from the text modality and define the task as assessing candidate competency rather than determining employability. The evaluation process mirrors the approach of human interviewers and consists of two stages: (1) analyzing and evaluating each QA pair individually to derive an evaluation status, and (2) assessing the candidate's overall competency based on the evaluation statuses of multiple QA pairs. In the first stage, prevalent methods utilize text matching or attentional text matching algorithms for evaluating QA pairs~\cite{hemamou2019hirenet, suen2019tensorflow}, where the concatenated representation of a question and its answer is fed into a classifier. As is well-known, questions in asynchronous video interviews are not confined to specific domains, allowing candidates to respond based on their work or study experiences. Consequently, the diversity in candidates' answers poses challenges for accurate evaluation through mere text matching. A more intuitive approach involves assessing QA pairs through the semantic interplay between questions and answers. The primary challenge here is uncovering the hidden relationships between each question and its corresponding answer. Graph neural networks (GNNs, ~\cite{dai2016discriminative, yao2019graph, ghosal2019dialoguegcn}) are adept at learning effective node representations by encoding local graph structures and node attributes. Due to their compact model structure and inductive learning capabilities, GNNs are extensively utilized in modeling relational data~\cite{battaglia2018relational, schlichtkrull2018modeling, pan2020semantic} and logical reasoning~\cite{luo2019improving, jiang2020reasoning}. Recently, ~\citet{zhang2020efficient} introduced a GNN variant, ExpressGNN, which achieves a balance between representational power and model simplicity in probabilistic logic reasoning. Similarly, ~\citet{ghosal2019dialoguegcn} developed DialogueGCN to tackle context propagation challenges inherent in RNN-based methods, leveraging self and inter-speaker dependencies to model conversational context for emotion recognition. Drawing inspiration from~\cite{ghosal2019dialoguegcn}, we propose a sentence-level relational GCN to capture internal temporal and QA interaction dependencies during question answering. In the second stage, when grading a candidate based on QA pair representations, existing methods~\cite{hemamou2019hirenet, hemamou2019slices} often encode question-answer pairs as a direct sequence. However, such approaches may result in inadequate interaction between the semantic content of question and answer pairs, compromising the rationality and explainability of the evaluation. To address this, we introduce a semantic-level graph attention network (GAT) in the first stage to model the interaction dynamics of each QA session. To this end, we propose a Hierarchical Reasoning Graph Neural Network (HRGNN) for the automatic scoring of answer transcriptions (ASAT) in job interviews. Specifically, the sentence-level relational graph convolutional neural network (RGCN) is employed to capture contextual dependencies, while the semantic-level Reasoning graph attention network (RGAT) is utilized to discern latent interaction states. The contributions of our work are summarized as follows: \begin{itemize} \item We introduce a relational graph neural network to address the lack of QA interaction in previous assessment methods. The internal temporal dependency within each question/answer enhances context comprehension, and the QA interaction dependency reveals latent semantic interactions from question-to-answer and answer-to-question. \item To our knowledge, we are pioneers in constructing a hierarchical graph neural network for ASAT to model sentence relations within questions and their corresponding answers, facilitating semantic-level interaction and inference. While our evaluation focuses solely on textual features, it significantly enhances the rationality and accuracy of the assessment. \item Our model surpasses all existing benchmark approaches on a real-world Chinese dataset. Ablation studies and experiments with 10 random seeds demonstrate the effectiveness and stability of our models. \end{itemize}

text: The advent of intelligent technologies has significantly enhanced the capabilities of individual robots, resulting in their widespread deployment to replace human labor in various tasks such as floor cleaning, surveillance with \emph{unmanned aerial vehicles} (UAVs), robotic surgeries, and manufacturing processes using mechanical arms \cite{2020-liu}. Consequently, there has been a substantial increase in latency-sensitive and computation-intensive tasks performed by robots. For example, UAVs are utilized to monitor social distancing during the COVID-19 pandemic \cite{20-chamola}, and search-and-rescue operations are executed promptly following natural disasters. To address these complexities, \emph{multi-robot cooperation} (MRC) systems have garnered significant interest recently \cite{18-ismail}. Nevertheless, individual robots face challenges due to limited battery life, sensing capabilities, and computational power \cite{18-bedi}. \emph{Mobile edge computing} (MEC) has emerged as a viable solution, facilitating task offloading through wireless communication, which aligns seamlessly with the MRC framework. On one side, multiple robots must collaborate to complete tasks within stringent time constraints. On the other, efficient communication and task distribution are crucial for effective robot cooperation. In this paper, we explore a MEC-based MRC system where an intelligent \emph{master robot} (MR), functioning as an edge server, coordinates multiple \emph{slave robots} (SRs) to execute time-sensitive and computation-heavy tasks while optimizing and balancing energy consumption among the robots. \subsection{Related Works} \subsubsection{Robot Cooperation Networks} In recent years, \emph{Artificial intelligence} (AI) has been widely applied to enhance robots' information processing capabilities, thanks to its proficiency in handling large datasets with high precision \cite{20-khan}. However, the integration of AI technology significantly increases computational demands \cite{17-kim}. In \cite{19-Alsamhi}, \emph{Machine learning} (ML) was employed to enhance robotic connectivity and data collection efficiency, though inter-robot cooperation was not addressed in this study. To accelerate time-sensitive robotic applications like AI-driven tasks and robot navigation using \emph{Simultaneous Localization And Mapping} (SLAM), research has focused on three primary areas \cite{18-ismail}: diverse robot types, control architectures, and communication technologies. Boston Dynamics, for instance, has transformed perceptions of robotic capabilities \cite{19-guizzo}. Yet, a single robot, constrained by limited resources, cannot manage extensive, low-latency operations. For example, comprehensive environmental sensing and monitoring require efficient data collection, inter-robot communication, and cooperative computation. The MRC system leverages collaboration to mitigate the resource limitations of individual robots. Initially, controlled mobility has expanded applications for sparse sensing \cite{13-Mostofi}, which can be utilized for energy-efficient and non-redundant sensing in MRC networks. Furthermore, a key advantage of these systems is the ability of robots to share collected information and resource management strategies through advanced wireless communication technologies, making effective wireless communication a critical component in facilitating inter-robot cooperation within MRC systems. In \cite{19-chen}, $p$-persistent real-time ALOHA was proposed as a multiple access protocol for ad-hoc based MRC systems to achieve ultra-reliability and ultra-low latency. Cloud robots have gained notable attention with advancements in wireless communication technologies \cite{15-kehoe}. In \cite{14-roazielo}, a visual SLAM robotic system was introduced to alleviate computational loads by employing a distributed framework where the cloud server manages map optimization and storage. However, the latency associated with cloud computing remains a significant drawback. Thus, establishing a communication paradigm to enhance robot cooperation in MRC systems is crucial for reducing latency. As a pivotal 5G technology, MEC has emerged as a feasible solution for edge-enabled applications \cite{19-liu}. The subsequent subsection delves into recent MEC technology advancements. \subsubsection{Mobile edge computing} MEC, a promising technology for communication and computation offloading, extends resources for computation, communication, and storage to the network edge. Its interdisciplinary nature, bridging computation offloading and wireless communication, plays a vital role in reducing energy consumption and latency \cite{20-Hai}. Consequently, MEC is a natural fit for supporting robot cooperation, facilitating efficient inter-robot communication and task allocation. In \cite{15-chen}, a resource allocation scheme for mobile users and MEC servers was explored to minimize task execution latency and energy consumption. Furthermore, \cite{17-wang} introduced an \emph{Alternating Direction Method of Multipliers} (ADMM)-based algorithm, optimizing computation offloading, resource allocation, and content caching to maximize \emph{MEC system operator} (MSO) revenue. In \cite{17-you}, an energy-efficient task offloading strategy for multiple devices was proposed. To address network congestion and high latency in cloud computing, a collaborative cloud and edge resource management algorithm was developed in \cite{19-ren}. \subsubsection{MEC based Cooperative Communication} As a crucial technology for enabling robot cooperation via mobile edge servers, MEC has been extensively studied to conserve computational resources in conventional wireless communication systems. For scenarios where multiple edge servers cater to numerous users, centralized and distributed methods have been proposed to tackle the optimal task offloading problem in \cite{18-you} and \cite{16-chen}, respectively. Additionally, a joint offloading and trajectory design scheme was investigated to minimize the sum of maximum delays in a MEC-based UAV system \cite{18-hu}. While these studies considered cooperative MEC systems, they did not account for the unique characteristics of robotic systems, such as environmental interaction capabilities. \subsection{Our Contributions} This paper presents a MEC-based MRC system designed to execute computation-intensive and time-sensitive tasks while minimizing robot energy consumption to extend operational time. In the proposed scenario, the intelligent MR is modeled as an edge server responsible for deciding the duration of environmental sensing, the volume of data collected by each SR, and the data offloaded from each SR. The mobile SRs primarily handle environmental sensing and data collection, offloading certain tasks to the MR to conserve energy during data processing. We propose two resource management strategies aimed at minimizing and balancing energy consumption among SRs, ensuring timely task completion. The second strategy considers the SRs' remaining energy to allow local data processing without offloading, making it more robust to unreliable wireless communication environments than the first strategy, albeit with potentially higher energy costs. The primary contributions of this paper are outlined as follows: \begin{enumerate} 	\item[$\bullet$] We propose an implementation framework for computation-intensive and time-critical tasks within MEC-based MRC systems, dividing the task execution process into three stages. Initially, SRs focus on environmental sensing and data collection. Subsequently, SRs may offload some data to the MR while processing the remainder locally. Finally, the MR processes the data and may upload a portion to the \emph{base station} (BS). At the onset of task execution, the MR determines the time allocation for sensing, data offloading, and the power scheme at the SRs. 	\item[$\bullet$] Two resource management and offloading strategies are developed to ensure timely task completion while minimizing robot energy consumption. The first strategy focuses on minimizing and balancing SR energy consumption to enhance MRC system operational time. The second strategy incorporates SRs' remaining energy to adapt to variable wireless communication conditions, allowing SRs to process all collected data locally without offloading to the MR. This approach is more resilient than the first strategy but may incur higher energy costs. 	\item[$\bullet$] Simulation results are provided to validate the proposed schemes' effectiveness and analyze the MRC system's robustness. \end{enumerate} The paper is structured as follows. Section~\ref{System model} introduces the MEC-based MRC system model. Section~\ref{Problem} outlines the framework and corresponding problem formulation. Two resource management strategies are detailed in Sections~\ref{Optimal} and \ref{suboptimal}, respectively. Section~\ref{simulation} presents numerical results to validate the proposed schemes. The paper concludes in Section~\ref{CONCLUSION}.

text: Interactive media experiences offer a personalized approach, delivering content tailored to the unique context, knowledge, or needs of each audience member. Unlike traditional media, which presents a single version of content to engage all viewers, interactive media can vary both the information and its presentation. This variation is determined by factors such as: (1) user interaction with the content during consumption, (2) data collected from the user at the beginning of the experience, enabling a more passive consumption mode, (3) pre-existing user profiles, or (4) a combination of these methods. Our focus in this paper is primarily on user interaction during content consumption. The complexity of interactive experiences surpasses that of traditional media, necessitating that production teams evaluate their success to identify and correct content issues and enhance future user experiences. A primary indicator of success is the level of audience engagement with the experience. However, measuring user engagement is challenging due to its complex and multifaceted nature \cite{attfield2011towards}, especially since media is consumed by audiences dispersed across various contexts and devices. This situation presents both practical and methodological challenges for accurate measurement. Interaction data has been employed in some fields as a scalable and unobtrusive means of monitoring engagement \cite{attfield2011towards,lehmann2012models,doherty2018engagement}; our research seeks to determine whether such data can be effective in this domain. Given the increased interactivity inherent in interactive media, can we monitor these interactions to infer engagement levels? This study investigates new methods for gathering information and analytical techniques that broadcasters could utilize to gain deeper insights into audience engagement with their content. We are not evaluating a specific experience but rather exploring the potential utility of interaction data in measuring engagement. Another compelling reason for measuring engagement through interaction data is the potential for near real-time monitoring. This capability would facilitate not only retrospective analysis for future improvements but also enable dynamic content adaptation. For instance, highly engaged audience members might receive additional material, while those less engaged could be presented with a simplified or abbreviated conclusion. Designing such interventions is undoubtedly challenging but could significantly enhance user experience, contingent on the ability to monitor engagement in real-time. Interaction data has proven successful in domains such as online news \cite{lagun2016understanding,grinberg2018identifying,lu2018between,constantinides2018framework} and search \cite{diriye2012leaving,kim2014modeling,zhuang2017understanding}. It has also been used to infer user behaviors as proxies for engagement \cite{barbieri2016improving,arapakis2016predicting} and satisfaction \cite{chuklin2016incorporating,mehrotra2017user}. Since engagement metrics and techniques remain untested in this domain, we examine a nationally released, production-quality interactive TV show where audiences control the presentation and navigate the story. We collected ground truth engagement metrics alongside user interactions (code and data are available: \cite{jonathan_carlton_2021_5137806}) from this live, in-the-wild interactive TV show to address the question: \begin{itemize} \item[\textit{(RQ)}] What behaviors can be deduced from interaction metrics that illuminate audience engagement with an interactive media experience? \end{itemize} We extracted various metrics and analyzed their relationship with audience-reported engagement levels. To elucidate these relationships, we trained an interpretable model to predict engagement and determine feature importance using internal weights and a model-agnostic interpretation technique. Our results indicate that temporal metrics—such as the time between events and the duration taken by an audience member to complete the story—are effective in distinguishing and are strongly correlated with engagement levels. Our findings underscore the value of interaction data in providing media creators with insights into audience engagement, demonstrating that engagement can be directly inferred from the data. Our contributions are as follows: \begin{itemize} \item We establish a connection between user engagement and interaction metrics gathered from an interactive media experience; \item We show the feasibility of predicting engagement levels based on user interactions; \item We broadly validate the usefulness of collecting and analyzing user interactions from interactive media experiences, highlighting the potential insights into user engagement that can be integrated into the creative process. \end{itemize} The remainder of the paper is organized as follows: Section \ref{sec:background} reviews related work. Section \ref{sec:methods} outlines the study, and Section \ref{sec:results} presents the findings. Section \ref{sec:discussion} contextualizes the results, and Section \ref{sec:conclusion} concludes with reflections on future work.
