text: \noindent Logos serve as fundamental elements of brand identity, and their recognition allows for statistical analysis of a brand's visibility and impact across numerous images and videos (\citeauthor{gao2014brand} \citeyear{gao2014brand}). Logos are typically designed with simplicity, often utilizing minimalistic symbols or text (\citeauthor{ad2012logo}\citeyear{ad2012logo}). This design choice implies that logos contain limited information, and subtle variations, such as a single character or stroke, can make it challenging to develop discriminative deep learning features. Logo recognition generally involves two main steps: determining the bounding box and identifying the logo itself. Traditional approaches to logo recognition employ a closed-set methodology, with prevalent frameworks including Faster R-CNN (\citeauthor{ren2015faster} \citeyear{ren2015faster}), SSD (\citeauthor{liu2016ssd} \citeyear{liu2016ssd}), and YOLOv3 (\citeauthor{redmon2018yolov3} \citeyear{redmon2018yolov3}). Nonetheless, closed-set methods require extensive data and fail to recognize logos absent from the training dataset. To address these limitations, open-set methods have been developed (\citeauthor{tuzko2017open} \citeyear{tuzko2017open}; \citeauthor{bastan2019large} \citeyear{bastan2019large}; \citeauthor{fehervari2019scalable} \citeyear{fehervari2019scalable}). These methods involve two stages: detecting logo boxes using a class-agnostic binary detector and subsequently identifying the logos with a classifier or retrieval system. The binary detection phase can leverage outputs from frameworks like Faster R-CNN and YOLOv3. In the identification phase, metric learning can be employed to assess nonlinear data distances, facilitating more straightforward comparisons within the embedding space. Additionally, we develop a novel set of evaluation protocols to assess the robustness of logo recognition models. Both the Makeup216 dataset and the evaluation protocols will be made publicly accessible. \item We propose an adversarial attention representation (AAR) framework for logo recognition. This framework effectively utilizes marginal auxiliary information to enhance the representation of pure logos. The AAR distinguishes between primary focus areas and supplementary information to improve accuracy. \item Our framework establishes a baseline for logo recognition, and extensive experiments on Makeup216 and LogoDet-3k demonstrate its state-of-the-art performance. \end{enumerate}

text: The study of lexical semantic change has recently sparked interest at the crossroads of natural language processing and historical linguistics\footnote{see \url{https://languagechange.org/}}. Consequently, various datasets have been introduced to cater to different languages \cite{schlechtweg2020semeval2020}. This research is situated within the framework of DIACR-Ita \cite{diacrita_evalita2020} at EVALITA 2020 \cite{Evalita2020}, which challenges participants to address the Italian language task using a completely unsupervised approach. Within DIACR-Ita, we were provided with 18 target words\footnote{'egemonizzare', 'lucciola', 'campanello', 'trasferibile', 'brama', 'polisportiva', 'palmare', 'processare', 'pilotato', 'cappuccio', 'pacchetto', 'ape', 'unico', 'discriminatorio', 'rampante', 'campionato', 'tac', 'piovra'}, along with two temporally distinct and preprocessed Italian corpora, labeled \textit{T0} and \textit{T1}, which incorporate part-of-speech tagging and lemmatization data. Our approach to addressing the problem is twofold, focusing on the representation of target words and the estimation of lexical-semantic change across datasets. The first method relies on the POS distribution of target words as its representation and utilizes an ensemble of distance measures for estimation. The second approach employs the similarities of neighboring words as the representation, applying one of two proposed similarity measures for estimation. The subsequent sections provide a detailed account of prior research, the modeling strategies employed, and the results achieved through these methods. Following this, section \ref{discussion_section} (Discussion) delves into an analysis of the second approach, highlighting the influence of the $k$ parameter on similarity measures and evaluating the discriminatory capabilities of our embedding-based model.

text: \IEEEPARstart{A}{irborne} optical sectioning (AOS) \cite{Kurmi2018,Kurmi2019TAOS,Kurmi2019Sensor,Bimber2019IEEECGA,Kurmi2020GeoScience, David2020} is a powerful aerial synthetic aperture imaging method that uncovers artifacts hidden beneath dense forest canopies, which remain undetectable in individual photographs. In applications such as search and rescue (SAR) \cite{Kurmi2019TAOS} and wildlife monitoring \cite{David2020}, AOS captures the subtle thermal signals emitted by obscured objects. This is achieved through an unstructured thermal light-field recorded by a drone-mounted camera (Fig.~\ref{fig:Fig0CameraPose}). By spanning a broad synthetic aperture area, ranging from 30 to 100 meters in diameter, AOS facilitates optical sectioning through image integration \cite{Kurmi2018}. \vspace{-1.5em} Integral images, which represent the signals captured by a wide-aperture sensor, are generated by aligning and averaging all individual image captures according to the drone's three-dimensional positions and a predetermined synthetic focal plane. For estimating the drone's position, RGB images are taken using a Sony Alpha 6000 camera, while thermal images, captured in the 7.5-13.5 $\mu m$ spectral band with a Flir Vue Pro camera, are used for integration. Both thermal and RGB images are stored on the cameras' internal memory cards and retrieved post-flight for subsequent processing. Upon integration, targets located at the focal plane emerge with clarity and sharpness, whereas occluders at varying distances become significantly blurred and disappear. This allows the focal plane to be adjusted interactively or automatically \cite{Kurmi2020GeoScience} to its optimal position and orientation near the ground, enabling optical slicing through the forest and facilitating the detection and examination of hidden targets like human bodies or animals. Accurate measurement of the drone's pose for each thermal image captured is crucial for AOS. Current implementations employ advanced computer vision algorithms, leveraging general-purpose structure-from-motion and multi-view stereo pipelines \cite{schonberger2016sfm,schoenberger2016mvs} applied to high-resolution RGB images. However, recent research \cite{Chin2018} indicates that estimating or fitting models to data with outliers is an NP-hard issue, making pose estimation prone to errors. These inaccuracies can lead to misalignment in single recordings, resulting in defocused AOS integral images. Due to their low resolution, high noise, low contrast, and poor texture, thermal images do not provide reliable features for effective pose estimation. Several methods have been proposed to correct residual pose errors, including optimizations that impose structural constraints \cite{Li2018,Ovechkin2018,Hsiao2018}, utilize localized depth maps \cite{Shin2018,Shamwell2019}, or integrate multiple sensors \cite{Mur-Artal2017,Qin2018}. This paper introduces an alternative method for minimizing residual pose errors by framing the problem as one of focusing rather than tackling the Perspective-n-Point (PnP) problem \cite{Chin2018}. PnP solutions \cite{Li2018,Ovechkin2018,Hsiao2018,Shin2018,Shamwell2019,Mur-Artal2017,Qin2018} necessitate robust feature detection, which is challenging in low-resolution thermal images and impractical under significant occlusions. Instead, we address the focusing challenge by optimizing 3 or 6 pose parameters per image, employing simple gray level variance (GLV) \cite{Firestone1991} as an error metric. This approach does not depend on any image features. As demonstrated in \cite{Kurmi2020GeoScience}, GLV is unaffected by occlusion and serves as an ideal visibility metric for AOS thermal integral images, unlike traditional gradient-, Laplacian-, and wavelet-based metrics reviewed in \cite{Pertuz2013}. Figure \ref{fig:Fig1Completeresult} showcases AOS outcomes when the synthetic focal plane is globally optimized as described in \cite{Kurmi2020GeoScience} (focal plane) and the enhanced results achieved with our novel pose error reduction technique applied to either 6D (brute force) or 3D (our method) pose parameters. With our method, the resulting integral images exhibit greater detail, improved focus, and higher contrast. In subsequent sections, we will explore the effects of errors in various pose parameters and the integration strategies that culminate in our final optimization approach, which features a reduced parameter search space and early stopping. We will demonstrate that our approach not only enhances the quality of integral images compared to leading pose estimation techniques but also significantly accelerates the process, offering greater efficiency than the exhaustive optimization of all pose parameters. \vspace{-0.8em}

text: In the early days, recommendation algorithms prioritized maximizing the precision of recommendations delivered to users. However, as noted by other scholars, several additional aspects of recommendations, such as diversity, serendipity, novelty~\cite{Vargas:2011:RRN:2043932.2043955,ge2010beyond,castells2011novelty}, and fairness \cite{yao2017beyond}, are equally crucial. These elements significantly influence the utility of recommendations for all involved parties \cite{abdollahpourimultistakeholder2020}. This paper addresses the issue of \textit{popularity bias}, where recommender systems disproportionately favor a small subset of popular items, often beyond what their actual popularity justifies, while neglecting items outside this subset, even if they are preferred by a substantial number of users~\cite{park2008long,steck2011item,jannach2015recommenders}. Consider the distributions depicted in Figure \ref{amplify_item_groups}. These graphs illustrate the contrast between item popularity and recommendation popularity across four well-established recommendation algorithms (\textit{RankALS} \cite{takacs2012alternating}, \textit{Biased Matrix Factorization (Biased-MF)} \cite{koren2009matrix}, \textit{User-based Collaborative Filtering (User-CF)} \cite{aggarwal2016neighborhood}, and \textit{Item-based Collaborative Filtering (Item-CF)} \cite{sarwar2001item}) using the MovieLens 1M \cite{movielens} dataset (see Section \ref{data_section} for more details). The x-axis ranks items from most to least popular. The black curve represents the cumulative frequency of ratings for items at each rank. Notably, a small number of top-ranked items dominate the rating history. For example, a mere 111 items (fewer than 3\%) account for over 20\% of the ratings. This skewed distribution of user interest is prevalent in many consumer domains where recommender systems are utilized. In a music catalog, for instance, some artists have songs played millions of times (e.g., Beyonc\'{e}, Ed Sheeran), while others have a smaller following (like Iranian musician Kayhan Kalhor). These popular items, termed the \textit{short-head} (denoted by $H$ in the plots), occupy about 20\% of the ratings, as per the Pareto Principle \cite{sanders1987pareto}. Items in a long-tail distribution are further divided into two categories \cite{celma2008hits}: Tail items ($T$) are numerous but less popular, collectively making up about 20\% of the ratings\footnote{Tail items may also include new items yet to gain popularity, linking popularity bias to the well-known item cold-start problem in recommendations.}, and \textit{Mid} items ($M$) are more numerous, receiving around 60\% of the ratings collectively. Each plot partitions items into the most popular ($H$), medium popularity ($M$), and less popular ($T$) categories. The blue curves in each plot illustrate the prevalence of popularity bias across the four algorithms. In the most extreme case (\textit{Item-CF}), items beyond rank 111 are scarcely recommended. The head of the distribution, constituting under 3\% of total items, accounts for nearly 100\% of user recommendations. For \textit{User-CF}, this figure is 99%. The other algorithms perform slightly better, with \textit{H} items comprising over 64\% and 74\% of recommendations in \textit{RankALS} and \textit{Biased-MF}, respectively. These plots reveal the extent of popularity bias in recommendations. Users' rating profiles show skewed popularity distributions, and recommendation algorithms tend to exacerbate this bias, creating a "rich get richer" scenario. However, this aggregate view of recommendation frequency offers an incomplete picture of popularity bias's impact. Our aim is to provide a more nuanced perspective, informed by recent work in multistakeholder recommendation \cite{abdollahpourimultistakeholder2020}. In \cite{abdollahpourimultistakeholder2020}, authors differentiate between key stakeholders in recommender systems: 1) users (recipients of recommendations) and 2) suppliers (providers or supporters of recommended items). Popularity bias affects both stakeholder groups, as seen in Figures ~\ref{amplify_user_groups} (impact on users) and ~\ref{amplify_supplier_groups} (impact on suppliers). The first plot in Figure ~\ref{amplify_user_groups} depicts the ratio of rated items for the three item groups $H$, $M$, and $T$ in different users' profiles from the MovieLens 1M dataset. Each user's interest in these item groups is assessed, and users are sorted based on their preference for popular items, from highest to lowest, by the ratio of different item groups in their profile. Users are first sorted by interest in $H$ items, then $M$ if tied, and finally $T$ if still tied. Sorted users are divided into three equal-sized bins $G=\{G_1, G_2, G_3\}$, from most popularity-focused ($G_1$) to least ($G_3$). The y-axis shows the proportion of each user's profile dedicated to different item groups. The narrow blue band indicates the proportion of each user's profile consisting of popular items ($H$), with its monotone decrease reflecting user ranking. Notably, all user groups, even $G_1$, have rated many items from the \textit{Mid} (green) and \textit{Tail} (red) sections of the distribution. This is logical, as there are only a few truly popular movies, and even the most blockbuster-focused viewer will eventually exhaust them. Other plots in Figure~\ref{amplify_user_groups} also order users by their interest in popularity, but now the y-axis shows the proportion of recommended items delivered by different algorithms\footnote{The plots are "banded" because recommendation lists are of size 10, allowing only 10 possible ratio values for each item group.}. The difference with original user profiles in rating data is stark, notably in \textit{Item-CF} and \textit{User-CF}, where users' profiles are rich in diverse item groups, yet the recommendations are not. \textit{Tail} items are absent, as indicated by the red line at the bottom of the plots. In \textit{Item-CF}, nearly 100\% of recommendations are from the \textit{Head} category, even for users with niche-oriented profiles. The "head-focused" $G_1$ users receive recommendations poorly matched to their interests in terms of item popularity, while $G_3$ "tail-focused" users are underserved, receiving an unvaried selection of popular movies with none of their long-tail interests addressed. This highlights that popularity bias differentially affects users: all are impacted, but some more severely than others. Multistakeholder recommendation broadens our understanding of those affected by recommendations to include \textit{suppliers}, individuals or entities behind the recommended items. In this study, we consider each movie's director as its supplier. Figure~\ref{amplify_supplier_groups} explores popularity bias from the supplier perspective: the directors whose movies are recommended. These plots are comparable to Figure~\ref{amplify_item_groups}, but here we examine the popularity of movie directors in the data, revealing a skewed distribution where movies from a few popular directors dominate ratings. Like item groups, we define three supplier groups based on popularity $S=\{S_1, S_2, S_3\}$: $S_1$ represents a few popular suppliers whose items account for 20\% of ratings, $S_2$ includes more suppliers with medium popularity whose items constitute around 60\% of ratings, and $S_3$ consists of less popular suppliers whose items receive 20\% of ratings\footnote{The popularity distribution of items and suppliers has a pronounced long-tail shape. Thus, to form groups with distinct popularity values, groups cannot be forced to have equal sizes, as this would result in groups with similar average popularity.}. Examining the recommendation algorithms' results, we observe that popularity bias also impacts suppliers in the recommendation interaction. Notably, in \textit{Item-CF}, movies from just 3 popular directors in $S_1$ (less than 0.4\%) account for 50\% of recommendations, while items from $S_3$ are never recommended. This pattern recurs across other algorithms. This analysis underscores that popularity bias is a multistakeholder phenomenon, affecting entities on different sides of the recommender system (sometimes quite severely), and any evaluation of the system's performance must consider the perspectives of diverse stakeholders. In this paper, we propose an algorithmic solution grounded in the novel concept of \textit{popularity calibration}, offering a comprehensive remedy for popularity bias by addressing multiple stakeholders' needs. A recommendation list is considered calibrated based on popularity when the range of items it covers aligns with the user's profile in terms of item popularity. For instance, if a user's profile comprises 20\% $H$ items, 40\% $M$ items, and 40\% $T$ items, recommendations are deemed calibrated when the ratio of each item group in the recommended list matches these proportions. We demonstrate that our approach not only yields more calibrated recommendations for users but also ensures fairer recommendations from the suppliers' perspective. It is important to note that calibrating recommendations by popularity does not inherently ensure alignment with users' overall preferences. For example, a user might like one non-popular documentary but dislike another non-popular film noir. Nonetheless, the popularity calibration method we propose does not aim to align recommendation lists by content but solely by item popularity. Our contributions are as follows: \begin{itemize} \item We conceptualize popularity bias in multistakeholder terms as an issue affecting the entire recommendation ecosystem and introduce metrics to quantify its impact. \item We reveal that some existing metrics for evaluating popularity bias mitigation often obscure crucial information about how certain algorithms manage popularity bias for different stakeholders. \item We expose the shortcomings of state-of-the-art re-ranking algorithms when viewed through a multistakeholder lens. \item We propose a new, straightforward, yet effective algorithm for enhancing popularity calibration through re-ranking, applicable to the output of any recommendation algorithm. \item Using music and movie datasets, we demonstrate that our method surpasses state-of-the-art baselines in mitigating popularity bias when considering multiple stakeholders' needs. \end{itemize}

text: Reinforcement learning has demonstrated remarkable success across a broad spectrum of complex sensory-motor control tasks, such as agile drone navigation~\cite{Kaufmann2018drone,Kaufmann2020drone,Loquercio2021drone}, manipulation of deformable objects~\cite{Wu2019deformable}, and quadrupedal locomotion~\cite{Hwangbo2019agile,Miki2022wild,Lee2020terrain,margonlis2022rapid}. Unlike traditional model-predictive control methods, reinforcement learning approaches can utilize more realistic forward dynamics models through physics simulators. Advances in rigid-body simulation technologies~\cite{Todorov2012mujoco, Makoviychuk2021Isaac} have enabled reinforcement learning algorithms to mitigate their high sample complexity by initially training in simulation before transitioning to real-world deployment. However, a \textit{sim-to-real gap} persists, characterized by discrepancies between the simulated and physical environments. A particularly challenging issue is developing visuomotor control policies that maintain robustness amidst changing perceptual conditions during deployment. Figure~\ref{fig:out-of-distribution} illustrates this challenge. A typical strategy to address domain shift involves exposing the agent to diverse data during training, aiming for the training distribution to sufficiently cover the agent's real-world experiences. When simulators are flexible, domain randomization can be employed to create varied training datasets~\cite{tobin2017domain,active-domain-randomization}. Alternatively, data augmentation can enhance existing datasets~\cite{yarats2021drqv2,hansen2020deployment}. Both strategies strive to generate visual features invariant to task-irrelevant perceptual changes. Nonetheless, achieving such invariance imposes costs: additional training time and manual tuning for domain randomization~\cite{Andrychowicz2020dexterous}, and the need for policy networks with adequate capacity to manage an expanded input distribution. These complexities might degrade model and policy performance~\cite{laskin2020reinforcement,hansen2020deployment}. Moreover, these methods often presuppose prior knowledge of potential perceptual shifts during deployment. If the target domain is unknown \textit{a priori} and falls \textit{out-of-distribution}, the robot may fail to adapt, resulting in ineffective operation (see Figure~\ref{fig:out-of-distribution}). Distinct from previous methods that achieve invariance by memorizing task-irrelevant details during training, we explore a more demanding yet realistic scenario where deployment specifics are not predetermined. This scenario necessitates true \textit{out-of-distribution} generalization without prior environmental knowledge. We further assume the absence of reward supervision, precluding fine-tuning via reinforcement learning. Although this seems daunting, it implicitly assumes that the \textit{same task} optimized during training remains applicable in the target domain. Thus, the agent retains an understanding of \textit{what it knows}, despite encountering numerous unknowns irrelevant to the task. Without additional assumptions or loss of generality, this \textit{out-of-distribution} generalization can be framed as \textit{unsupervised policy adaptation} between two MDPs sharing the same latent dynamics and reward structure, but differing in pixel observations (See Figure~\ref{fig:graphicalmodels}). In this study, we explore strategies to enhance generalization in this challenging context. Instead of embedding perceptual invariance into the network during training to counter domain shift, we propose achieving feature invariance at deployment by leveraging the constancy of the task. Consequently, the agent's internal experiences should remain consistent. We utilize latent features collected during training as representations of the agent's task knowledge. On the target domain (see Figure~\ref{fig:latent-alignment}), these new latent features diverge from their previous distributions. Our goal in unsupervised policy adaptation is to align the distribution of these latent features on the target domain with those from training. This unsupervised learning objective, termed \textit{latent alignment}, does not necessitate paired image data between source and target and is applicable to any agent without specific training constraints. To distinguish our approach from prior methods that embed invariances during training, we introduce it as \textbf{\underline I}nvariance through \textbf{\underline L}atent \textbf{\underline A}lignment (\textbf{ILA}).

text: Acquiring ground-truth labels for health data presents significant challenges and incurs substantial costs. Common obstacles include the unavailability of labelers, such as physicians, and patients failing to report symptoms, leading to missing labels. Consequently, healthcare datasets often remain partially or entirely unlabeled, with larger prospective studies frequently experiencing a relative scarcity of labels. This compromise between study size and accuracy is notably pronounced in healthcare, though it is a common issue across various research fields. Our focus is on harnessing person-generated activity time-series data characterized by heavily imbalanced or missing labels. Since supervised learning necessitates ground-truth labels, alternative methods must be explored to leverage the extensive information embedded in unlabeled data. One promising approach is transfer learning, where a model is initially trained on a different yet similar population to that of the target task. However, implementing this in practice is fraught with difficulties. Firstly, the design of a study significantly influences the signals linking observed data to output labels, making it unrealistic to expect access to another dataset developed with an identical study design. Secondly, when investigating a rare disease, the low prevalence poses a challenge in assembling a large, distinct initial training set. Thus, transfer learning alone does not fully meet our requirements. Self-supervised learning offers a framework for learning data representations without explicit labels. While the theoretical underpinnings of these methods are still emerging, their empirical success is well-documented, particularly in fields like natural language processing \cite{brown2020language}, programming tasks \cite{chen2021evaluating}, and image classification \cite{dosovitskiy2020image}. The classification of these models is a topic of debate, with some researchers \cite{bommasani2021foundation} categorizing pre-trained, self-supervised, meta-learning models as \emph{Foundation Models}. A fundamental aspect of self-supervised learning is that the objective is defined as a function of the data itself. However, determining the most effective self-supervised objective task is complex. In this study, we analyze and compare three objective tasks, assessing their efficacy in predicting influenza-like illness (ILI) using lab-validated ground-truth data. Drawing inspiration from natural language processing, where next-word prediction facilitates the learning of rich representations \cite{brown2020language}, our end-to-end transformer models initially employ self-supervision to predict next-day activity levels based on activity data from the preceding ten days in a large cohort. These models are subsequently fine-tuned for the ILI prediction task and evaluated against a small dataset with laboratory-confirmed ILI labels. The ultimate assessment on a held-out testing set for the ILI prediction task demonstrates that the choice of self-supervision task significantly influences performance.

Adversarial examples represent a significant security threat to classifiers. For a given classifier $f$ and a test input $\mathbf{x}$, an attacker can design a subtle perturbation $\delta$ that is nearly invisible to humans, yet causes the classifier to misclassify, such that $f(x)
eq f(x+\delta)$. This perturbation $\delta$ is termed an \emph{adversarial perturbation}, and the resulting input $x+\delta$ is known as an \emph{adversarial example}. Numerous \emph{empirical} defenses have been proposed over recent years to counter adversarial examples~\citep{goodfellow2014explaining,na2017cascade,metzen2017detecting,svoboda2018peernets,buckman2018thermometer,ma2018characterizing,guo2018countering,dhillon2018stochastic,xie2018mitigating,song2018pixeldefend}. Nevertheless, these defenses are often quickly undermined by sophisticated adaptive adversaries~\citep{carlini2017adversarial,athalye2018obfuscated,uesato2018adversarial,athalye2018robustness}. To break this cycle, several \emph{certified} defenses have been introduced~\citep{scheibler2015towards,carlini2017provably,ehlers2017formal,katz2017reluplex,cheng2017maximum,lomuscio2017approach,fischetti2018deep,bunel2018unified,wong2017provable,wong2018scaling,raghunathan2018certified,raghunathan2018semidefinite,dvijotham2018training,dvijotham2018dual,gehr2018ai2,mirman2018differentiable,singh2018fast,weng2018towards,zhang2018efficient,gowal2018effectiveness,wang2018formal,lecuyer2018certified,li2018second,cohen2019certified,lee2019stratified,salman2019provably,wang2020certifying,jia2020certified,zhai2020macer}. A classifier $f$ is considered certifiably robust for an input $\mathbf{x}$ if it can be proven to consistently predict the same top-1 label (i.e., $f(x)=f(x+\delta)$) when the adversarial perturbation $\delta$ is constrained, such as when its $\ell_p$-norm is below a certain threshold, referred to as the \emph{certified radius}. Our focus in this study is on $\ell_0$-norm adversarial perturbations, which involve altering specific features of a test input and can be implemented physically. Despite the prevalence of certified defenses, most concentrate on top-1 predictions. In many scenarios, top-$k$ predictions, which provide the $k$ most probable labels, are more applicable. For example, in cloud-based classifier services (\emph{machine learning as a service})~\citep{Google_Cloud_Vision,microsoft_demo,amazon_demo,clarifai_demo}, top-$k$ labels are often returned to users for better decision-making; similarly, in recommendation systems and search engines, top-$k$ items or webpages are suggested to users. Yet, the certified robustness of top-$k$ predictions against adversarial perturbations remains largely unexamined. An exception is the work by~\cite{jia2020certified}, which established a precise $\ell_2$-norm certified robustness for top-$k$ predictions. This $\ell_2$-norm robustness can be adapted to $\ell_0$-norm through the inequality between these norms, but the resulting $\ell_0$-norm robustness is not optimal. \myparatight{Our work} Our objective is to establish $\ell_0$-norm certified robustness for top-$k$ predictions. Our method employs \emph{randomized smoothing}~\citep{cao2017mitigating,liu2018towards,lecuyer2018certified,li2018second,cohen2019certified,lee2019stratified,jia2020certified,levine2019robustness}, which can transform any base classifier into a certifiably robust one by randomizing the input. We choose randomized smoothing for its versatility with any classifier and its scalability to large neural networks. Specifically, we utilize \emph{randomized ablation}~\citep{levine2019robustness}, which provides state-of-the-art $\ell_{0}$-norm certified robustness for top-1 predictions. Unlike other methods~\citep{cao2017mitigating,lecuyer2018certified,li2018second,cohen2019certified} that add \emph{additive} noise (e.g., Gaussian, Laplacian) to inputs, randomized ablation modifies inputs by subsampling their features. For a given classifier (the \emph{base classifier}) and test input $\mathbf{x}$, randomized ablation creates an \emph{ablated input} by keeping some randomly chosen features of $\mathbf{x}$ and assigning a special value (e.g., median, mean, or a distinct symbol) to the rest. In image data, features correspond to pixels. The ablated input is then processed by the base classifier, resulting in a probabilistic output. We denote $p_j$ as the likelihood that the base classifier assigns label $j$ to the random ablated input. The original randomized ablation method forms a \emph{smoothed classifier} that selects the label with the highest probability $p_j$ for $\mathbf{x}$. In our adaptation, the smoothed classifier outputs the $k$ labels with the highest probabilities for $\mathbf{x}$. Our principal theoretical achievement is an almost exact $\ell_0$-norm certified robustness assurance for top-$k$ predictions using the smoothed classifier from randomized ablation. We initially establish an $\ell_0$-norm certified robustness for top-$k$ predictions with the smoothed classifier. Our findings confirm that a label $l$ is guaranteed to be among the top-$k$ labels predicted by the smoothed classifier for $\mathbf{x}$, provided the adversary alters no more than $r_{l}$ features of $\mathbf{x}$, where $r_{l}$ is the $\ell_0$-norm \emph{certified radius}. Furthermore, we demonstrate that our certified radius is \emph{tight} for $k=1$ and \emph{nearly tight} for $k>1$. Specifically, without assumptions on the base classifier, deriving a certified radius greater than $r_{l}+\mathbb{I}(k
eq 1)$ is infeasible. This implies that if an attacker changes at least $r_l+1+\mathbb{I}(k
eq 1)$ features of a test input, there could exist a base classifier such that the smoothed classifier's top-$k$ predictions exclude $l$ or result in ties. Our study diverges technically from~\citet{levine2019robustness} in several ways. Firstly, we derive the $\ell_0$-norm certified radius for top-$k$ predictions using randomized ablation, whereas \citet{levine2019robustness} only addressed top-1 predictions. Secondly, our certified radius matches or exceeds that of \citet{levine2019robustness} for top-1 predictions, as we utilize the discrete nature of label probabilities in our derivation. Thirdly, we establish the (almost) tightness of the certified radius, a claim not made by \citet{levine2019robustness}. Our work also contrasts with~\citet{jia2020certified}, which provided a tight $\ell_2$-norm certified radius for top-$k$ predictions using Gaussian noise in randomized smoothing. Their use of continuous Gaussian noise contrasts with our discrete ablation approach, requiring different methodologies to derive and validate the $\ell_2$/$\ell_0$-norm certified radii. Specifically, we devise distinct regions in the discrete space of ablated inputs to apply the Neyman-Pearson Lemma~\citep{neyman1933ix}. In proving (almost) tightness, our method diverges from Jia et al., who employed the Intermediate Value Theorem, unsuitable for our discrete context, and relied on Mathematical Induction, which is unnecessary for our uniformly distributed ablated inputs. We validate our method on CIFAR10 and ImageNet datasets, demonstrating significant improvements over current methods for top-$k$ predictions. For example, our approach achieves a certified top-3 accuracy of 69.2\% on ImageNet when an adversary modifies 5 pixels of a test image, compared to only 9.0\% certified top-3 accuracy by~\citet{jia2020certified} when converting their $\ell_2$-norm robustness to $\ell_0$-norm. In summary, our contributions include:  egin{itemize} \item Deriving an $\ell_0$-norm certified radius for top-$k$ predictions using randomized ablation. \item Proving the tightness of our certified radius for $k=1$ and its near-tightness for $k>1$. \item Empirically validating our approach on CIFAR10 and ImageNet. \end{itemize}

Unlike other methods (e.g. Lecuyer, Cohen, Cohen-Gross, Cohen-Gross2, LeCuyer, 2018) which add additive noise to the inputs (e.g. Gaussian, Laplacian), randomized ablation modifies the inputs by removing their features. Then we will establish the minimum L0-norm-based robustness assurance guarantee for the top-k prediction using the smooth classifier. Random ablation first creates a smooth classifier that chooses the label pj with the highest probability for x. Then we subject the random ablated input to the basic classifier, which then gives the probability that the random ablated input will be assigned pj. Our main theoretical achievement is the nearly exact assurance of elliptic-norm certification of robustness of predictions made by the smoothed classifier under randomized ablation. In our adaptation, the smoothed classifier predicts the k labels with the highest probabilities for a feature. We show that a label $l$ is guaranteed to be among the top k labels predicted by the smoothed classifier for a feature $x$ if the adversary modifies no more than $r l$ features of $x$, where $r l$ is the certified radius of the smoothed classifier. This paper diverges in many ways from the Robustness study. First, we compute the ell_0 norm certified radius for all top-k predictions, while the Robustness paper considers only the top-k predictions. Moreover, we show that our certified radius is tight for k = 1 and almost tight for k > 1 without making any assumptions on the smoothed classifier. Secondly, the certified radius of our method matches or exceeds that of citet-levine.robustness for the first prediction, because we use the discrete nature of the probabilities of labeling in our derivation. Thirdly, we prove the tightness of the certified radius, which was not claimed in citet-levine.robustness. This implies that if the attacker changes at least $r_l+1+I$ features of the test example, there exists a base classifier such that the top-k predictions of the smoothed classifier either exclude r_l or result in a tie. In our proof of the (almost) tightness of the bound, our method differs from Jia et al., who employed the intermediate value theorem, which is inappropriate for the discrete context, and relied on mathematical induction, which is not necessary for our uniformly distributed ablated inputs. We invent discrete regions in the space of ablated inputs, in which we apply the Neyman–Pearson lemma. “In summary, our main contribution is a method of elliptic-norm certified radius of ablation for top-k learning, with a random ablation. We have tested this method on the CIFAR10 and ImageNet datasets, demonstrating significant improvements over existing methods in top-k learning. For example, when an adversary modifies five pixels of the test image, our method achieves a certified top-3 accuracy of 69.2% on ImageNet, whereas the cited Jia20 only achieved a certified top-3 accuracy of 0.9 on ImageNet, after converting their robustness to elliptic norm robustness. text: The individualization-refinement (IR) framework serves as a versatile backtracking method utilized by algorithms that tackle problems related to the symmetries of combinatorial structures~\cite{McKay201494}. This encompasses algorithms for computing automorphism groups, solving isomorphism problems, generating canonical labels for normal forms, and more recently, applications in machine learning within convolutional neural networks~\cite{DBLP:conf/ijcai/AbboudCGL21,DBLP:conf/aaai/0001RFHLRG19}. Indeed, all leading graph isomorphism/automorphism solvers, including \textsc{nauty}/\textsc{Traces}~\cite{nautyTracesweb, McKay201494}, \textsc{bliss}~\cite{bliss:webpage, DBLP:conf/alenex/JunttilaK07}, \textsc{saucy}~\cite{saucy:webpage, Darga:2004:ESS:996566.996712}, \textsc{conauto}~\cite{conauto:webpage, DBLP:conf/wea/Lopez-PresaCA13}, and \textsc{dejavu}~\cite{dejavu:webpage, DBLP:conf/alenex/AndersS21}, are built upon this framework. These tools integrate color-refinement strategies, like the 1-dimensional Weisfeiler-Leman algorithm, with backtracking operations that artificially individualize indistinguishable vertices, leading to recursive branching and forming what is known as the IR-tree. By employing sophisticated invariants and heuristics, these tools efficiently prune large sections of the IR-tree. Given that the non-recursive operations are nearly linear in complexity, it has been established that the number of nodes traversed within the IR-tree primarily dictates the execution time of these tools (refer to \cite[Theorem 9]{thesis} and \cite{DBLP:journals/corr/abs-0804-4881}). Consequently, the running times of these tools closely correlate with this factor~\cite{McKay201494,DBLP:conf/alenex/AndersS21}. Variability in traversal strategies among the tools results in differing numbers of traversed nodes and hence varying execution times. However, only recently have explicit bounds been derived that demonstrate the asymptotic benefits of randomized traversals over deterministic ones~\cite{anders_et_al:LIPIcs.ICALP.2021.16}. To this end, a specific problem, namely a search problem in trees with symmetries, has been defined, encapsulating the parameters within which IR-algorithms operate. While these findings are broadly applicable within an abstract model, the bounds established in~\cite{anders_et_al:LIPIcs.ICALP.2021.16} pertain to search problems in arbitrary trees with symmetries, irrespective of their origin from actual IR-computations. Although the extensive benchmark library of \textsc{Traces}{}~\cite{nautyTracesweb,McKay201494} demonstrates a wide array of IR-tree forms, there has been a lack of comprehensive analysis on which specific trees can manifest as IR-trees. \xparagraph{Contribution.} This paper investigates the nature of IR-trees. Originating from a branching process, all IR-trees are rooted with each internal vertex having at least two children, classifying them as irreducible (or series reduced) trees. Despite the diversity of IR-trees observed in benchmark libraries, not every irreducible tree qualifies as an IR-tree. Nevertheless, we provide a complete, constructive characterization of IR-trees. \begin{theorem} An irreducible tree qualifies as an IR-tree if and only if no node exists with exactly two children, where only one is a leaf. \end{theorem} To establish this theorem, we first outline necessary conditions for a tree to be considered an IR-tree and justify these conditions. We then demonstrate their sufficiency by constructing graphs that, when processed by an IR-algorithm, yield the specified tree. Our proof is constructive, providing an algorithm with the capability to generate a graph whose IR-tree matches a given tree~$T$, provided~$T$ satisfies the necessary conditions. As detailed in Section~\ref{sec:ir}, IR-trees naturally align with a vertex coloring scheme, which is intrinsically linked to the graph's automorphism group structure. Our characterization thoroughly delineates how color classes may be distributed within a tree. There exist several simple restrictions, particularly for vertices with exactly two children; however, beyond these constraints, any coloring can be realized, and any number of symmetries can be assured (refer to Section~\ref{sec:graph:constr}). Our characterization offers a foundational argument that translates the analysis of abstract tree traversal strategies from \cite{anders_et_al:LIPIcs.ICALP.2021.16} to the backtracking trees of IR-algorithms applied to actual instances. Specifically, we conclude that the abstract trees used for lower bounds of probabilistic algorithms in \cite{anders_et_al:LIPIcs.ICALP.2021.16} do indeed manifest as IR-trees. Interestingly, the abstract trees employed for lower bounds of deterministic algorithms (Theorem~13, \cite{anders_et_al:LIPIcs.ICALP.2021.16}) do not qualify as IR-trees. These trees feature nodes with two children, one of which is a leaf while the other is not, violating the necessary conditions outlined in Theorem~\ref{thm:sufficient}. Fortunately, our results imply that a minor modification can rectify this: by replacing the respective leaves with internal nodes each having two leaves, the trees transform into genuine IR-trees, as per our characterization. Consequently, we validate that the lower bounds from \cite{anders_et_al:LIPIcs.ICALP.2021.16} are applicable within the IR-framework. \xparagraph{Cell Selectors and Invariants.} The IR-framework allows for various design choices within its components. In practice, most competitive solvers make similar choices: the refinement is typically \emph{color refinement}, and the pruning invariant is often the \emph{quotient graph}. The differences in implementation from color refinement and quotient graphs are generally minor and aimed at enhancing practical performance, resulting in slightly weaker refinement and invariants in specific scenarios. In this study, we align with these prevalent design choices. Several other design choices, such as the method of traversing IR-trees, do not influence the characterization of IR-trees themselves. However, one critical design choice that does impact which trees qualify as IR-trees is the selection of \emph{cell selectors}. It is important to note that Theorem~\ref{thm:sufficient} states that for trees meeting the necessary conditions, there exists some cell selector for which the graph is an IR-tree. We can further discuss specific cell selectors. For a given cell selector, there are two outcomes: either fewer trees qualify as IR-trees, or the same characterization applies. Our findings allow us to argue that for certain cell selectors used in practice, our necessary conditions are indeed sufficient, whereas for others they are not (see Section~\ref{sec:conclusion} for further discussion). \xparagraph{Techniques.} Numerous graph properties, such as symmetries, are directly associated with the properties of its IR-tree. When modeling a graph intended to produce a specific IR-tree, two major challenges arise: \begin{enumerate} \item Controlling the impact of color refinement on the graph. \item Ensuring that the IR-tree's structure accommodates simultaneous representation of symmetries in different graph sections. \end{enumerate} We address these challenges through specialized gadget constructions. We introduce \emph{concealed edges}, which enable precise control over when the IR-process recognizes certain edges, allowing color refinement to take effect (addressing issue (1)). By integrating concealed edges with gadgets that enforce specific regular abelian automorphism groups, we synchronize symmetries across various tree branches (addressing issue (2)). Our main tool involves the following concept. As an additional constraint derived from IR-tree structures, we focus on trees where all leaves can be mapped to the same number of other leaves through symmetries (i.e., all \emph{leaf orbits} under automorphisms have identical sizes). We demonstrate that each such tree $T$ can be embedded into a graph $H_T$, where~$H_T$ restricts $T$'s symmetries in a specific manner. Intuitively, we maintain just enough symmetries to allow leaves to be mapped to each other whenever feasible in~$T$. This effectively couples leaf orbits so that fixing one leaf results in the fixation of all others. Formally, we establish the following theorem. \begin{restatable}{theorem}{thmtwo} Let~$T$~be a colored tree in which all leaf orbits have the same size. There exists a graph~$H_T$~containing~$T$~as an automorphism invariant induced subgraph such that the action of~$\Aut(H_T)$~is faithful on~$T$~and semiregular on the set of leaves of~$T$. Moreover,~$\Aut(H_T)$~induces the same orbits on~$T$ as~$\Aut(T)$. \end{restatable} We prove this theorem constructively, allowing each step to be translated into an algorithm that takes an admissible (i.e., compatible with our necessary conditions from Section \ref{sec:necessary_conditions}) colored tree $T$ and generates a graph and cell selector with IR-tree $T$.

text: Deep Learning methodologies have achieved remarkable success in addressing general classification challenges, particularly when ample annotated datasets are available for training. However, in practical scenarios, data can often be limited, expensive to annotate, non-stationary, or continuously streaming. To tackle these real-world constraints, both novel and traditional learning strategies have been integrated into the field of Deep Learning \cite{kemker2018measuring}. Consequently, areas such as transfer learning \cite{wang2018deep}, reinforcement learning \cite{Ren2018DeepRL}, and both supervised and unsupervised incremental learning \cite{he2020incremental,sahoo2018online,tao2020fewshot,perezrua2020incremental} have gained renewed interest. Incremental learning refers to a classifier's capacity to evolve by assimilating information from new instances or classes continuously, without the need for complete retraining \cite{kemker2018measuring}. This approach is increasingly gaining traction, especially in scenarios involving real-time data streams \cite{he2020incremental,sahoo2018online}. Notably, rehearsal-free continual learning methods have shown promise in expanding a classifier's class set using only new class labels, while mitigating the issue of catastrophic forgetting \cite{tao2020fewshot,perezrua2020incremental}. This is particularly advantageous when computational resources are insufficient for full retraining, or when privacy concerns restrict access to previous samples during class set expansion. Despite these advances, progress in continual learning with non-stationary classes, particularly for unsupervised streaming data tasks, remains limited. An illustrative application of incremental learning in the context of unsupervised, non-stationary, and streaming data is video-to-video face recognition (V2V-FR) in surveillance systems \cite{huang2015cox}. Video frames often capture individuals under varying poses, camera angles, resolutions, and lighting conditions, exceeding the diversity found in datasets typically used to train deep networks, which usually focus on web-sourced images \cite{guo2016mscleb1m}. Transfer learning for V2V-FR tasks poses challenges even for deep learning encoders due to the significant impact of image quality on performance \cite{gunther2016face,lopezlopez2019dataset,guo2019survey}. Additionally, as data is continuously streamed, individual appearances may vary across different camera setups, which can operate under changing conditions over time \cite{ditzler2015learning,disabato2019learning}. Although theoretically, these challenges could be addressed through extensive labeling, in practice, it is infeasible to account for every possible variation in a training dataset \cite{he2020incremental}. Therefore, a more efficient and scalable solution is required \cite{maltoni2019continous,tao2020fewshot,perezrua2020incremental}. The true context of application and the evolving changes over time are best represented by the actual data \textbf{incrementally} gathered during system operation, which typically lacks labels. Another key aspect of real-world V2V-FR applications is their inherently open-set nature \cite{scheirer2013toward,gunther2017towards}. Consider, for instance, an airport surveillance system designed to track certain \emph{individuals of interest (IoI)} who have not been pre-enrolled in the system, such as those exhibiting suspicious behavior, among a broader group of \emph{unknown} non-target identities, which should be recognized as \emph{unknown}. In this work, we introduce an innovative incremental learning framework named Open-Set Dynamic Ensembles of SVM \ref{fig:illustrate}. Utilizing a deep feature encoder as its foundation, the system leverages operational data to enhance the recognition of target identities in an unsupervised manner. Moreover, it is specifically crafted to function in a fully open-set environment. Built upon the capabilities of a deep feature encoder trained for general face recognition, the incremental learning component processes stream data to concurrently predict and update classifiers while addressing catastrophic forgetting. This module employs dynamic ensembles of SVM classifiers, starting with a single SVM constructed from a few labeled video frames directly sourced from surveillance footage. It can adapt by incorporating or discarding classifiers within the ensembles. Adopting a self-training approach \cite{yarowsky1995unsupervised}, predictions serve as pseudo-labels to refine and enhance the classifiers. The modular nature of the ensembles allows for adaptations through the addition or removal of classifiers. The main contributions of this paper are summarized as follows: \begin{itemize} \item An unsupervised incremental learning approach designed for online operation with streaming data, where predictions also serve as pseudo-labels. \item A strategy to mitigate both catastrophic forgetting and errors arising from incorrect pseudo-labels. \item An instance-incremental learning method for open-set scenarios, extendable to address class-incremental challenges. \item A face-based person re-identification technique that does not rely on a reservoir of face images. \end{itemize} The remainder of this paper is structured as follows. Section~\ref{sec:rel_work} provides a comprehensive review of the relevant literature. Subsequently, Section~\ref{sec:desvm} presents our proposed approach, followed by experimental evaluations in Sections~\ref{sec:experiments} and~\ref{sec:results}. Finally, Section~\ref{sec:conclusion} offers concluding reflections on our findings.

text: Cancer has emerged as the foremost cause of mortality and a critical barrier to extending life expectancy across numerous nations~\cite{world2020report}. Lung cancer, representing over 11\% of all newly diagnosed cases, ranks as the second most common cancer and leads in cancer-related deaths globally, contributing to 18\% of all cancer fatalities~\cite{Sung2021}. The primary treatments for lung cancer encompass surgical resection, chemotherapy, radiotherapy, and immunotherapy. These interventions, alongside successful diagnoses through bronchoscopy or CT-guided biopsy, necessitate precise tumor localization and often require delineation (segmentation) from surrounding healthy tissue in preoperative CT images. The manual segmentation of lesions or tumors from preoperative CT scans is an arduous and time-consuming task for oncologists, radiologists, and pulmonologists, potentially causing treatment delays and reducing survival rates, especially in resource-limited settings. Furthermore, the effectiveness of manual localization and segmentation is contingent upon the practitioner's prior knowledge and clinical experience. Despite established guidelines and standards, tumor segmentation is susceptible to significant inter- and intraobserver variability. In contrast, automatic segmentation techniques offer the promise of delivering efficient, consistent, and more precise results. These automated methods can reduce the time required for image analysis, allowing experts to allocate their limited time more effectively to planning and optimizing treatments. Historically, techniques such as thresholding~\cite{UZELALTINBULAT2017}, region growing~\cite{Adams1994,Dehmeshki2008}, and graph cuts~\cite{GU2013692} have been proposed for segmenting lung tumors from CT images. While these algorithms are suitable as semi-automatic methods, they fall short in effectively localizing lung tumors. Recent breakthroughs in deep learning have enabled the automation of tasks previously reliant on skilled professionals~\cite{ramanto2019,kim2019}. Although advancements in hardware have facilitated the development of larger and more complex models, much of the progress is attributed to the availability of extensive annotated datasets. Currently, deep learning methods, particularly following the introduction of the U-Net architecture~\cite{ronneberger2015}, have become predominant in medical image segmentation~\cite{Du2020}. However, convolutional neural networks (CNNs) are memory-intensive, especially when dealing with 3D volumes. Consequently, models are often trained using 2D or 2.5D input images~\cite{carvalho}, processing one slice, chunks of slices, or 3D patches at a time, and applied in a sliding window fashion across the CT volume. This patching approach can result in a loss of perception, prompting the development of more efficient multi-scale 3D CNN architectures that accommodate larger input volumes~\cite{Jiang2018}. Alternatively, segmentation can be performed in multiple stages, employing either multiple algorithms or a cascade of CNNs~\cite{Hossain2019,isensee,carvalho,gan2021}. To address the challenge of insufficient training data, unsupervised methods such as supervoxel approaches have been proposed~\cite{Hansen2021}. Multi-modality strategies that incorporate MRI or PET scans alongside CT have been suggested to expedite convergence and enhance accuracy~\cite{fu2021,Jiang2019,Jiang2019_2}. Additionally, neural network architectures capable of utilizing various annotation types have been explored~\cite{Wang2019,Mlynarski2019}. A more recent tactic to mitigate the lack of training data is the teacher-student paradigm, drawing inspiration from knowledge distillation~\cite{phuong19,furlanello18,hinton2015}. In this framework, the teacher generates pseudo-annotations from suboptimal annotations to expand the training dataset for the student. The teacher-student model can be applied to any network architecture and does not impose constraints on other hyperparameters or external settings. This design can be utilized in diverse ways, from leveraging unlabeled data~\cite{caron2021,Xie2020,Li2020}, to exploiting multiple modalities~\cite{Jiang2019,Jiang2019_2,Li2020}, and employing datasets with varied annotation types~\cite{sun2020,Zhang2021}. Our approach diverges from previously applied methods in lung tumor segmentation by leveraging annotations of varying supervision levels within the same modality, specifically CT images. Given that CT scanning is less invasive than other modalities, our goal is to effectively segment tumors using CT-only examinations. Our methodology is inspired by Sun \textit{et al.}~\cite{sun2020}, which demonstrated promising results using a teacher-student framework to segment liver and liver lesions with semantic and bounding box annotations. To the best of our knowledge, we are pioneering the application of a similar teacher-student framework for semantic segmentation of lung tumors in CT images. Our findings suggest that even with a limited dataset of semantic annotations, a student can achieve state-of-the-art performance if trained on an adequately large pseudo-annotated dataset.

text: While robot learning has progressed remarkably, most algorithms are tailored for robots operating independently. In real-world scenarios, however, interaction with humans and other learning entities is unavoidable. This interaction poses a substantial challenge: the behaviors of these other agents will \textit{adapt} in response to the robot, continuously altering the learning environment. Consider an autonomous vehicle learning to modulate the speed of nearby human-driven cars to ensure safety when there is traffic or construction ahead. Initially, encountering this autonomous car, your instinct is to proceed with caution: as it decelerates, you follow suit. But if it slows down without a clear reason, your approach shifts: in future encounters, you might pass it without hesitation. The autonomous car, which believed it had mastered the policy to regulate your speed, finds itself perplexed by your altered behavior! To effectively \textit{co-adapt} with other agents, a robot must predict how these agents' behaviors will evolve and understand how its own actions influence their hidden intentions. Previous studies on such interactions often impose limiting assumptions about other agents: assuming they are stationary~\cite{davison1998predicting,stone2000defining,mealing2015opponent,albrecht2015hba,grover2018learning}, using a shared learning process among agents~\cite{foerster2016learning,lowe2017multi,foerster2018counterfactual}, having direct access to other agents' intentions and actions~\cite{albrecht2015hba,he2016opponent,hernandez2017efficiently, grover2018learning, foerster2018learning, everett2018learning}, or simplifying intention spaces with manually crafted features~\cite{kelley2008understanding,bandyopadhyay2013intention,bai2015intention,sadigh2016information,basu2019active, losey2019robots}. In contrast, our focus is on general scenarios where the ego agent (e.g., a robot) engages repeatedly with non-stationary, independently-controlled, and partially-observable agents. Humans navigate such situations daily (e.g., driving, walking) without modeling every detail of others' policies \cite{rubinstein1998modeling}. Drawing inspiration from human behavior, we note that: \begin{center} \vspace{-0.5em} \emph{The ego agent observes only the low-level actions of another agent, but --- akin to human-human interactions --- a high-level policy representation often suffices. We term this as the \emph{latent strategy}, acknowledging that these strategies can evolve over time.} \vspace{-0.5em} \end{center} By learning the strategy of another agent, the robot can \textit{predict} their responses during interactions. Additionally, understanding how the latent strategy evolves over time --- the \textit{latent dynamics} --- allows the robot to foresee how its own actions will \textit{impact} the future intentions of the other agent (see Fig.~\ref{fig:front}). We utilize latent representations of the other agent's policy to advance learning in non-stationary multi-agent interactions through the following contributions: \textbf{Learning Latent Representations.} We present a reinforcement learning (RL) framework for multi-agent interaction that acquires both latent strategies and responsive policies. This framework inherently models how another agent's strategy shifts in reaction to the ego agent's actions. \textbf{Influencing Other Agents.} The ego agents employing our approach are incentivized to deliberately modify their policy to affect the latent strategies of other agents, especially when certain strategies are more conducive to co-adaptation. \textbf{Testing in Multi-Agent Settings.} We evaluate our methodology against leading techniques in four simulated environments and a real-world robot experiment involving two $7$-DoF robot arms playing air hockey. Our approach surpasses existing methods and successfully learns to influence the other agent.

text: The task of automatic language identification poses significant challenges, particularly when distinguishing between languages that share close similarities. This issue represents a primary obstacle for contemporary language identification systems~\cite{DSL2014}. Scandinavian languages, in particular, face a developmental stage in language technology (e.g.~\newcite{kirkedal2019lacunae}). A significant challenge is the scarcity of sufficient textual data necessary for training extensive language models. Accurate language identification is crucial for sourcing such data, yet even advanced models frequently struggle to differentiate among similar Nordic languages. In this paper, we introduce a machine learning methodology aimed at automatically identifying six closely-related Nordic languages: Danish, Swedish, Norwegian (Nynorsk), Norwegian (Bokmål), Faroese, and Icelandic. We investigate various techniques for feature extraction from a corpus comprising raw text data, specifically Wikipedia summaries in the respective languages, and assess the performance of several machine learning models. Specifically, we will evaluate the effectiveness of traditional machine learning models, including Logistic Regression, Naive Bayes, Support Vector Machine, and K Nearest Neighbors, against modern neural network approaches like Multilayer Perceptrons (MLP) and Convolutional Neural Networks (CNNs). Following the evaluation on the Wikipedia dataset, we will extend our analysis to test the top-performing models on data from a different domain, aiming to determine the models' ability to generalize when classifying sentences from varied contexts.
dipper: The task of automatic language identification presents great challenges, especially when distinguishing languages that are very similar to each other. This is a significant obstacle for modern language identification systems (cf. e.g. cite DSL 2014). In this paper, we present a new machine learning methodology that is capable of recognizing six closely related Nordic languages: Danish, Swedish, Norwegian Nynorsk, Norwegian Bokml and Icelandic. The training of such language models requires a lot of data, and even very advanced language models have difficulties recognizing these languages. Using the summaries of the various language versions of Wikipedia, we examine the feature extraction methods, which are mainly based on the morphology of the words and phrases in the texts. The performance of various learning models on the data set is compared, especially the conventional models of support vector machines, naive Bayes, support vector machines, k-nearest neighbors, as well as modern models of neural networks, such as multilayer perceptron (MLP) and convolutional neural networks (CNN).

text: Robots frequently operate in shared environments like warehouses, factories, and homes, where they coexist with humans or other robots. In these settings, while most obstacles remain static, certain small areas may experience changes in occupancy during operations. Such environments are termed \emph{semi-structured}. Within these applications, robots typically execute repetitive tasks, necessitating fast and dependable motion planning capabilities. Consider the scenario depicted in Fig.~\ref{fig:cover}. Here, the robot's task is to grasp a bowl while maneuvering around pitchers, a table, and walls. Much of the environment, such as the table, walls, and open space above the table, can be considered known. Given the repetitive nature of the task, information from earlier planning queries can be reused to expedite the planning process. Widely adopted algorithms like RRTs~\cite{lavalle1998rapidly,kuffner2000rrt} do not leverage the distinction between static and movable obstacles, nor do they exploit the repetitive nature of planning tasks to enhance planning speed. Roadmap-based techniques, such as Probabilistic Roadmaps (PRMs)~\cite{kavraki1996probabilistic}, are typically confined to fully static environments or face significant overhead from repair operations needed to manage movable obstacles. While enhancements to PRMs have reduced costly collision checks~\cite{kavraki2000path}, adapted to dynamic settings~\cite{leven2002framework,yang2017hdrm}, and captured repetitive motions~\cite{lehner2018repetition}, their performance still varies widely based on the planning query. Instead of offline preprocessing of collision information, another group of planners utilizes past experiences to accelerate search~\cite{Phillips-RSS-12,berenson2012robot,coleman2015experience}. However, these planners suffer performance declines when environmental changes render previous information obsolete, and thus cannot guarantee fixed-time planning. Recently, planners with provably fixed-time performance were introduced in~\cite{islam2019provable,islam2020provably} for tasks involving repetitive actions. These planners precompute a compact set of paths from a start state to a goal region, allowing any goal within the region to be reached in constant or bounded time. Such methods have been applied to tasks like mail-sorting~\cite{islam2019provable} and grasping objects on conveyor belts~\cite{islam2020provably}. While our approach, APP, is inspired by these works, we emphasize online obstacle avoidance by explicitly considering movable obstacles during preprocessing through the alternative paths planning approach. We advance these methodologies to accommodate movable obstacles while maintaining provably fixed-time planning using the \emph{Alternative Paths Planner (APP)}. The central concept involves generating multiple alternative paths for each planning problem, ensuring that at least one path remains navigable regardless of the arrangement of movable obstacles. This is achieved by ensuring that paths are \emph{disjoint}, meaning they are sufficiently separated so that no single obstacle configuration can block more than one path simultaneously. For $n$ movable obstacles, it suffices to create at most $n+1$ fully disjoint paths. If the problem constraints prevent finding the necessary number of disjoint paths, we generate additional partially overlapping paths to maintain the guarantee. APP is applicable to performance-critical real-world scenarios such as mail-sorting, conveyor-belt picking, and shelving. In environments with multiple movable obstacles, we demonstrate path-lookup times in the microsecond range and achieve a 100\% success rate. We present experimental results across three domains, benchmark against existing state-of-the-art methods, and validate our approach with a real-world case study.

We advance these methods to include movable obstacles while maintaining provably fixed-time planning using the em>Alternative Paths Planner (APP)/em>. These methods have been applied to tasks such as mail sorting and grasping objects on a conveyor belt. Our approach, APP, is inspired by these works, but it emphasizes obstacle avoidance by explicitly considering movable obstacles during the preprocessing phase, in the alternative paths planning approach. The basic concept is to make the paths alternative, to provide for at least one alternative, regardless of the arrangement of the movable obstacles. In case of n movable obstacles, it is sufficient to create at most n + 1 paths. This is achieved by ensuring that the paths are disjoint, which means sufficiently far apart so that no obstacle configuration can block more than one path simultaneously. APP is applicable to real-world performance-critical tasks such as mail sorting, picking from conveyor belts and shelf stocking. Even in environments with multiple movable obstacles, we have demonstrated path-finding times in the microsecond range, with a guarantee of one hundred percent success. When the constraints of the problem prevent the necessary number of disjoint paths from being found, we generate extra partially overlapping paths to ensure the guarantee. We present experimental results from three domains and we compare our approach to the state-of-the-art methods. We also demonstrate the effectiveness of our approach on a real-world case study.

text: Relational databases are repositories for a substantial portion of global data, typically accessed through structured query languages such as SQL. Implementing a natural language interface to these databases (NLIDB) would greatly enhance data accessibility, empowering users to extract and utilize information without requiring programming skills. The introduction of extensive datasets \cite{wikisql,DBLP:conf/acl/RadevKZZFRS18,spider} has heightened interest in this area, leading to extensive research in recent years. Historically, research has concentrated on converting grammatically correct, complete sentences into queries. However, an internal survey conducted on the search service of a prominent customer relationship management (CRM) platform\footnote{\url{https://www.salesforce.com/}} highlighted that users often communicate in an informal style. This communication ranges from using mere keywords (e.g., "player 42") to brief phrases (e.g., "show player 42") and complete sentences (e.g., "Who is the player who wears Jersey 42?"). Beyond stylistic variations, users often omit content words for brevity, which can introduce ambiguity, potentially rendering questions unsolvable even for models familiar with natural language style (NLS) text. For instance, as depicted in Figure \ref{fig:example}, omitting the word "Jersey" makes it unclear whether the value 42 should correspond to the \texttt{Id} or \texttt{Jersey} column. This study demonstrates that Text2SQL systems, when trained solely on complete sentences, struggle with the noisy, keyword-driven, or short phrasal question styles. To address this, we propose various data augmentation techniques inspired by our users' search behaviors and communication styles. \hide{ \todo{We have enough space, can you show 2-3 examples in this figure? No need to use a boxed layout, you can show a table. Also please use .pdf to save the figure, which has higher resolution.} } To manage the resultant ambiguity, one promising approach is to leverage the table content, enabling the model to examine the table for terms present in the question and use that to clarify ambiguities. For instance, if the token "42" appears exclusively in the \texttt{Jersey} column, then it should be associated with \texttt{Jersey}. While effective, this method can become prohibitively resource-intensive, especially in terms of inference time or memory usage, when applied to large tables, as the model must search the entire table content for each query. We propose that, generally, the model requires only samples from the table content rather than exact matching rows to resolve column ambiguities. For example, if the \texttt{Id} column consists of alphanumeric IDs, while \texttt{Player} and \texttt{Nationality} contain strings, and \texttt{Jersey} features two-digit numbers, then it follows that \texttt{Jersey} should equate to 42. Sampling reduces the necessity for exhaustive table scans for each query. These samples can be generated offline for each column and remain static across different questions or be periodically updated to adjust for potential shifts in table distribution or user queries, facilitating adaptation and personalization without necessitating model retraining. In summary, our contributions include: \begin{enumerate} \itemsep0em \item Enhancing the WikiSQL dataset with synthetic search-style questions to accommodate concise, informal input. \item Developing novel models that integrate table content into a BERT encoder through two sampling strategies to address ambiguous questions. \item Conducting comprehensive qualitative and quantitative analyses (accuracy, inference time, memory) to evaluate the effectiveness of each content sampling strategy. \item Creating a dataset of 400 questions to evaluate the performance of Text-to-SQL models in this context. \end{enumerate} \hide{ \begin{enumerate} \item augmenting well-formed text with synthetic data to ensure robustness over NLS style questions \item incorporating table content to a BERT model via two sampling strategies to handle ambiguous questions \item an in-depth qualitative and quantitative (accuracy, inference time, memory) analysis showcasing the efficacy of both content sampling strategies \item a curated dataset to benchmark performance on short, ambiguous questions. \end{enumerate} } Beyond adapting to NLS-style queries, \textsc{ColloQL}\xspace also achieves leading performance on the original WikiSQL~\cite{wikisql} dataset, surpassing all non-execution guided decoding baselines. Our work builds upon SQLova \cite{sqlova}, yet our methodologies are applicable to other frameworks\footnote{Our code and annotated data are accessible at \\ \url{https://github.com/karthikradhakrishnan96/ColloQL}.}.
