There is a notable gap between how neural retrieval models process full text and the relevance labels used for learning, evaluation, and analysis. In datasets like the TREC Deep Learning Track 2019 (TREC-DL) \cite{trec2019overview}, relevance labels apply to entire documents, which can contain thousands of tokens. Traditional models, which reduce document information to a bag of words, find this level of granularity adequate. However, newer neural ranking models work at a finer level, building document scores from the interaction of individual words \cite{Hofstaetter2020_sigir,zheng2019rltm,yilmaz2019}. This evolution shifts the focus of neural retrieval models towards integrating document-level relevance with word-level tasks such as question answering or information extraction. These models must identify relevant information spans and use them to rank numerous candidate documents. A significant challenge in their development and evaluation is the absence of datasets that effectively address both these tasks. Existing datasets either emphasize retrieval results with dense judgments across ranked lists \cite{trec2019overview,hashemi2020antique} or focus on question-answer selections in single texts, which can be retrofitted into retrieval collections but result in incomplete judgments \cite{rajpurkar2016squad}. In this paper, we introduce FiRA, a dataset featuring 	extbf{Fi}ne-grained 	extbf{R}elevance 	extbf{A}nnotations with word-level relevance selections and passage-level graded relevance labels for all relevant documents in the TREC 2019 Deep Learning Document dataset. We divided the documents into snippets and presented query \& document snippet pairs to annotators. Figure ef{fig:fira-screenshot} illustrates an example of an annotated document-snippet. We ensured high-quality annotations by employing at least 3-way majority voting for each candidate and continuously monitoring quality parameters, such as the time spent per annotation, throughout our annotation campaign. Additionally, by requiring annotators to select relevant text spans, we minimized the chance of false-positive retrieval relevance labels. Our annotation process involved 87 computer science students using a custom tool designed for a smooth workflow between selecting relevance labels and identifying relevant text spans. The FiRA dataset comprises 
umprint{24199} query \& document-snippet pairs from all 
umprint{1990} relevant documents for the 
umprint{43} TREC-DL queries. We chose to extend the TREC-DL document ranking test collection, using the ranked retrieval data as a foundation because: 1) it allows us to focus our annotation efforts, as fine-grained annotations are resource-intensive, and 2) it enables comparison between our non-expert annotators and TREC's expert annotators. FiRA is model-agnostic, incorporating the complete set of TREC annotations. FiRA opens up several possibilities:  egin{itemize} \item 	extbf{Training:} FiRA can be utilized for standalone and multi-task retrieval \& QA fine-tuning. Its density and coverage over query-document pairs support granular fine-tuning using word-level loss functions. \item 	extbf{Evaluation:} FiRA enhances TREC-DL evaluation with more detailed relevance labels and the capability to assess answer passages extracted from full documents. Combined with labeled non-relevant documents from TREC-DL, FiRA facilitates the evaluation of rankings and answer selections. \item 	extbf{Analysis:} Neural document ranking models that generate relevance scores for complete documents can be deeply analyzed, particularly their partial results and attention regions, using FiRA. \end{itemize} The subjective nature of relevance tasks is a well-discussed topic in IR research \cite{borlund2003concept}. When dealing with human-annotated datasets, understanding the noise and uncertainty introduced by varying human judgments is crucial. To address this, we employed 3-way majority voting in our data collection. Additionally, we provide a quantitative analysis of the following question with FiRA:  egin{itemize} \item[	extbf{RQ1}] How much subjectivity is present in our fine-grained relevance annotations? \end{itemize} To investigate this, we selected 10 pairs for annotation by all participants, allowing us to study subjectivity with a dense distribution that minimizes outliers. We discovered that on a 2-level-graded relevance scale, our annotators showed strong agreement, whereas subjectivity increased on the 4-level-graded relevance and text selections. We leveraged our dataset for an in-depth examination of positional bias in relevance across a document and within individual snippets. By presenting snippets to annotators in random order, we aimed to eliminate attention bias towards the beginning and answer the following research question:  egin{itemize} \item[	extbf{RQ2}] Is there a position-based relevance bias in long documents? \end{itemize} Our FiRA annotations reveal a higher probability of finding relevant answers at the start of documents, although a significant number of relevant snippets are also located later in the text. Moreover, we analyzed annotator behavior concerning relevant word selection within a single snippet. An assessment of the MSMARCO-QA \cite{msmarco16} dataset indicated a strong bias towards the beginning of snippets. Using FiRA, we addressed the question:  egin{itemize} \item[	extbf{RQ3}] Are annotators biased towards the beginning of a snippet? \end{itemize} We established a control group and a treatment group, in which the first and second halves of texts were rotated. Neither group exhibited a starting position bias. In fact, the rotation group highlighted the importance of context around relevant span selection, as split sentences were less frequently chosen. To demonstrate FiRA's utility, we used the fine-grained judgments to evaluate the performance of the state-of-the-art TKL neural document re-ranking model \cite{Hofstaetter2020_sigir}, leveraging TKL's interpretability functions. The TKL model identifies the three regions of 30 words each used to compute the document score.  egin{itemize} \item[	extbf{RQ4}] How many of FiRA's relevant spans does the TKL model utilize to compute the document score? \end{itemize} We observed that the TKL model trained on TREC-DL data \cite{trec2019overview} disproportionately emphasizes the beginning of documents as a ranking signal. The insights gained through FiRA can guide the development of the next generation of neural document ranking models. Our FiRA dataset, including raw annotations, documentation, and all associated helper scripts, is freely accessible at: \ 	extit{\url{https://github.com/sebastian-hofstaetter/fira-trec-19-dataset}}

text: Deep reinforcement learning (RL) has demonstrated remarkable success across a diverse array of tasks, such as mastering video games~\cite{dqn1, dqn2, starcraft2, a3c, a2c, ga3c, kf, pic, Jain19, JainECCV2020} and controlling robotic systems~\cite{Levine15, Gu17, Luo19}. Despite these achievements, the extensive training duration remains a significant barrier to scaling deep RL to more intricate tasks. To mitigate the often prohibitive training times, RL frameworks strive for two critical attributes: (1) High throughput, which ensures rapid data collection, and (2) High sample efficiency, which facilitates learning the desired policy with minimal data. To fulfill these criteria, both synchronous and asynchronous parallel actor-learner architectures have been devised to expedite RL training~\cite{a3c, a2c, impala, ga3c, seed_rl, ddppo, rlpyt, iswitch}. Contemporary synchronous methods, like the synchronous advantage actor-critic (A2C)~\cite{a3c, a2c} and similar algorithms~\cite{ppo, trpo, acktr}, are favored for their \emph{data efficiency}, \emph{training stability}, \emph{full determinism}, and \emph{reproducibility}. However, these methods are hampered by idle periods, as all actors must complete experience collection before updating trainable parameters. This inefficiency is exacerbated when the duration of environment steps varies greatly. Consequently, current synchronous methods struggle to scale in environments where step times fluctuate due to computationally intensive tasks like 3D rendering and physics simulations. \input{flow_time_fig} Conversely, asynchronous methods, such as asynchronous advantage actor-critic on a GPU (GA3C)~\cite{ga3c} and importance weighted actor-learner architectures (IMPALA)~\cite{impala}, achieve high throughput. However, these approaches encounter the stale-policy issue~\cite{ga3c, impala}, as learning and data collection occur asynchronously. The behavior policy used for data collection lags several updates behind the target policy employed for parameter updates, leading to noisy gradients and reduced data efficiency. Thus, asynchronous methods often sacrifice training stability for increased throughput. We demonstrate that this trade-off is unnecessary by introducing High-Throughput Synchronous RL (HTS-RL), a technique that achieves both high throughput and training stability. HTS-RL is compatible with numerous off-the-shelf deep RL algorithms, such as A2C, proximal policy optimization (PPO)~\cite{ppo}, and actor-critic using Kronecker-factored trust region (ACKTR)~\cite{acktr}. HTS-RL is particularly well-suited for environments with significant step time variance: it conducts learning and data collection concurrently, which markedly enhances throughput. Additionally, actors engage with environment replicas asynchronously, reducing idle time. By employing batched synchronization, HTS-RL ensures the lag between target and behavior policy is limited to one. This consistent latency allows HTS-RL to employ a 'one step delayed-gradient' update, maintaining the same convergence rate as a non-delayed version. Consequently, HTS-RL preserves the benefits of synchronous RL, namely \emph{data efficiency}, \emph{training stability}, \emph{full determinism}, and \emph{reproducibility}, while achieving significant speedups, especially in environments with variable step times. We demonstrate that HTS-RL accelerates A2C and PPO in Atari environments~\cite{gym, atari} and the Google Research Football environment (GFootball)~\cite{gfootball}. Adhering to the evaluation protocol of~\citet{Henderson17} and~\citet{Colas18}, we compare our method to the state-of-the-art asynchronous approach, IMPALA~\cite{impala}. Our approach achieves {$3.7\times$} higher average episode rewards on Atari games and {$43\%$} higher average game scores in the GFootball environment. Compared to synchronous A2C and PPO, our approach realizes a $2-6\times$ speedup. The code is accessible at~\url{https://github.com/IouJenLiu/HTS-RL}.

text: The Covid-19 pandemic has necessitated an unprecedented global mobilization of public health resources \cite{fisher2020global}. To address this crisis, a plethora of digital health strategies have been rapidly implemented on a large scale \cite{fagherazzi2020digital}. While such swift deployment is essential due to the pressing nature of the pandemic, it remains crucial to thoroughly evaluate the implications of these strategies \cite{ienca2020responsible}. This paper specifically examines the privacy concerns associated with digital contact tracing smartphone applications, also referred to as exposure notification apps \cite{ferretti2020quantifying, Apple_Google}. The transmission of the Covid-19 virus, even by individuals who are presymptomatic or asymptomatic, presents a significant challenge for containment efforts, as these individuals can spread the virus unknowingly \cite{Asymptomatic_transmission_1}. Contact tracing aims to mitigate this issue by identifying and isolating recent contacts of diagnosed individuals, thereby reducing the virus's reproductive number. Initially, contact tracing was conducted manually, with healthcare workers gathering information from patients about their recent contacts and notifying those contacts of their potential exposure and necessary precautions \cite{Manual_contact_tracing}. However, this method has limitations, such as patients' inability to report encounters with strangers and the discomfort associated with disclosing contact details to healthcare providers \cite{Disclosure_discomfort}. As infection rates rise, the sheer volume of cases may render manual tracing unmanageable \cite{ferretti2020quantifying}. This is where automated digital contact tracing or exposure notification apps become valuable \cite{kleinman2020digital, Apple_Google, Pan_European, bay2020bluetrace}, as they can alert users of potential Covid-19 exposure while significantly reducing the manual effort involved. Contact tracing apps, by design, monitor the proximity of users rather than their precise locations, which introduces notable privacy concerns \cite{bengio2020need}. Consequently, privacy has become a central consideration in the development of contact tracing protocols \cite{levine1988contact, cho2020contact, raskar2020apps, rivest2020pact, trieu2020epione, troncoso2020decentralized}. Efforts to ensure the privacy of these apps have largely focused on the specific mechanisms employed \cite{Mechanism_Privacy_1, MSB}. Ideally, from a privacy-centric perspective, an algorithm should divulge no information beyond what is necessary to inform the end-user of potential exposure. The Google-Apple Exposure Notification framework \cite{Apple_Google}, widely adopted by numerous national tracing apps, is structured to disclose only the essential details to notify the user of exposure, along with some metadata about the exposure event(s). This framework ensures minimal data sharing with third parties, including public health authorities, thereby offering robust user privacy protection against all but their direct contacts. Security analyses of these mechanisms typically focus on concealing all information except the exposure determination, often through cryptographic means. However, the result of the query itself can leak information. In digital contact tracing apps that lack stringent user identity validation—a challenge given the need to protect user privacy—an individual or entity (e.g., a business) can use a limited number of identities to deduce details about their exposure events. By correlating this data with other contact information, it becomes possible to ascertain the infection status of contacts or customers using the exposure notification system \cite{Inherent_limitations}. This privacy breach is independent of the algorithm used and is an inherent aspect of digital contact tracing, as it merely requires making multiple legitimate queries to the system. Fortunately, extensive research exists on controlling information leakage from database query outputs, which can be applied to contact tracing viewed as a distributed database query by the end-user. By leveraging insights from differential privacy and statistical database privacy fields \cite{differential_privacy}, we aim to mitigate information leakage due to query outputs. However, achieving a balance between utility and privacy often entails a trade-off, with a requisite minimum noise addition to ensure a certain level of privacy, potentially impacting the accuracy of contact tracing. In this paper, we reframe the contact tracing problem as a specific instance of two other database query scenarios. First, a contact tracing app queries which contacts of a user are exposed, akin to querying a binary database of the user's contacts' Covid statuses. Alternatively, users can be conceptualized as nodes in a graph, with edges representing contact events with diagnosed users. In this framework, alerting a user parallels recommending one node to another, similar to social recommendation algorithms \cite{social_recommendation_survey}. We adapt two key results from mathematical privacy literature to elucidate inherent limitations of contact-tracing apps. The first, from statistical databases \cite{dinur_nissim}, provides a lower bound on query error for diagnosed contacts in a user's contact database, below which an adversary could nearly reconstruct the database. The second, from graph-based social recommendation algorithms \cite{GRS}, outlines a trade-off between differential privacy and the accuracy of alerting users about high-risk contacts. We tailor these results to the context of contact tracing, allowing us to identify conditions under which they apply. We then reinterpret these conditions as inherent privacy-accuracy trade-offs for digital contact tracing. Finally, we discuss these findings using specific numerical examples.

text: Over recent decades, multi-class classification has found applications across diverse fields such as image recognition~\cite{krizhevsky2009cifar,deng2009imagenet, geusebroek2005amsterdam,Hsu02multisvm} and natural language processing~\cite{lang1995newsweeder,DBLP:journals/corr/abs-2005-14165,DBLP:journals/corr/abs-1801-06146}. A critical component in this domain is the role of loss functions~\cite{DBLP:journals/corr/JanochaC17,kornblith2021why}. In the realm of machine learning (ML), traditional loss functions such as the cross-entropy (CE) loss and the Crammer-Singer (CS) Loss, also known as the SVM loss, have been pivotal. Prior to the advent of deep learning, the CS loss was extensively researched and applied for constructing linear or kernelized models~\cite{10.5555/944790.944813}. However, with the rise of deep learning, the CE loss has largely eclipsed the CS loss in practical applications~\cite{he2016deep}. This preference arises because the CE loss ensures consistency in multi-class classification, meaning it can achieve a Bayes optimal classifier with an infinite sample size. Conversely, the CS loss lacks this consistency unless the maximum conditional probability of a class label given the input exceeds $0.5$~\cite{10.5555/1005332.1044701}, a scenario plausible for straightforward tasks like MNIST classification but improbable for complex challenges like ImageNet classification~\cite{DBLP:journals/corr/abs-2006-07159,tsipras2020imagenet}. Nonetheless, the CE loss is susceptible to label noise~\cite{ghosh2017robust,wang2019symmetric}. Consequently, efforts have been made to enhance the noise tolerance of the CE loss. A necessary condition for a loss function to resist noise is known as the symmetric property~\cite{ghosh2017robust}, where the aggregate loss across all potential class labels for a data point remains constant. In line with this property, various CE loss variants have been developed to incorporate noise tolerance. However, relying solely on a symmetric loss often results in suboptimal performance due to slow convergence~\cite{zhang2018generalized,ma2020normalized}. Hence, a hybrid loss that balances the CE loss with a symmetric loss frequently yields superior results on real-world datasets with noise~\cite{wang2019symmetric,zhang2018generalized,englesson2021generalized,ma2020normalized}, such as the WebVision dataset with 20\% noise~\cite{DBLP:journals/corr/abs-1708-02862}. These observations can be understood through the lens of label information uncertainty. When label information is certain (e.g., MNIST data), the CS loss is suitable~\cite{DBLP:journals/corr/Tang13}; for slightly uncertain label information (e.g., ImageNet data), the CE loss is preferable; for highly uncertain labels (e.g., WebVision data), a loss that interpolates between the CE and a symmetric loss is optimal. Although parameter tuning (e.g., adjusting weights between the CE and symmetric loss) can adapt to dataset-specific characteristics, a pertinent question remains: "\textit{Is it possible to define a loss that adapts to the uncertainty level of label information for each instance?}" To tackle this question, we propose utilizing the distributionally robust optimization (DRO) framework to capture the uncertainty in label information for each instance. For any given instance, we assign a distributional weight to each class label and define the loss considering the worst-case scenario of these weights, regularized by a specific function, termed as label distributionally robust (LDR) losses. The DRO framework offers several advantages for modeling label information uncertainty: (i) It provides a unified framework encompassing various existing loss functions, including the CE loss, the CS loss, and their variants such as the top-$k$ SVM loss. (ii) By selecting Kullback-Leibler (KL) divergence as the regularization function for distributional weights, it introduces an intriguing family of losses known as LDR-KL loss for multi-class classification. The LDR-KL loss closely relates to the temperature-scaled CE loss, widely applied in other contexts~\cite{HinVin15Distilling,chen2020simple}, where the temperature corresponds to the regularization parameter of the distributional weights. Consequently, our theoretical insights into the LDR-KL loss may inform the use of temperature-scaled CE loss across different scenarios. (iii) By varying the regularization parameter, the LDR-KL loss can interpolate between the CS loss, the margin-aware CE loss, and a symmetric loss, offering greater adaptability to the noise level of label information. Our contributions are as follows: \begin{itemize}[noitemsep,topsep=0pt,parsep=0pt,partopsep=0pt] \item We establish the strong consistency of the LDR-KL loss, termed All-$k$ consistency, which corresponds to top-$k$ consistency (aligning with the Bayes optimal top-$k$ error) for all $k\geq 1$, and provide a sufficient condition for the general family of LDR losses to achieve All-$k$ consistency. \item We demonstrate that an extreme case of the LDR-KL loss upholds the symmetric property, rendering it resistant to label noise. Additionally, we present a negative result showing that a non-negative symmetric loss function cannot simultaneously achieve top-$k$ consistency for $k=1$ and $k=2$. Thus, we conclude that existing top-$1$ consistent symmetric losses cannot be All-$k$ consistent. \item We introduce an adaptive LDR-KL loss, enabling the automatic learning of a personalized temperature parameter for each instance, tailored to its noise level. We devise an efficient algorithm for empirical risk minimization based on the adaptive LDR-KL loss without imposing significant additional computational demands. \item We conduct comprehensive experiments across various datasets under different noisy label conditions, demonstrating the stable and competitive performance of the proposed adaptive LDR-KL loss across all scenarios. \end{itemize}

text: The development of a fully automated system capable of generating realistic 3D human bodies that approach and grasp objects in a 3D space holds significant potential across various domains, such as robotics, animation, and computer vision. Despite notable advancements in synthesizing realistic hand-object interactions, current research predominantly centers on hand pose synthesis, often overlooking the integration of full-body movements~\cite{GRAB:2020, GrapingField:3DV:2020, jiang2021graspTTA}. Conversely, whole-body motion synthesis~\cite{holden2016deep, martinez2017human, hernandez2019human, MOJO} tends to disregard the presence of objects within the scene. The task of modeling and synthesizing realistic whole-body grasping motions remains challenging and unresolved, primarily due to several factors. First, these motions demand the coordination of full-body dynamics alongside intricate finger movements~\cite{GRAB:2020}, where the high dimensionality complicates the synthesis process. Second, the complexity of synthesizing realistic body-scene and hand-object contacts is heightened by the need for perceptual realism. For instance, the hand should naturally conform to the object's surface, and foot-skating artifacts must be avoided in whole-body motion. Third, given a starting pose and a target object in 3D space, there are countless potential approaches to grasp the object. The diversity of feasible grasping motions is further complicated by the variability in object shape and orientation, posing a significant challenge in designing a generative model capable of capturing this diversity to synthesize realistic motions for grasping various 3D objects. To tackle these challenges, we introduce \textbf{SAGA} (\textbf{S}toch\textbf{A}stic whole-body \textbf{G}rasping with cont\textbf{A}ct), an innovative framework for generating whole-body grasping motions that can stochastically create 3D human body movements approaching and grasping 3D objects. Our approach is comprised of two main components: (1) a novel 3D body generator that produces diverse static whole-body grasping end poses, and (2) a novel human motion generator that fabricates diverse and plausible motions between specified start and end poses. We offer two pivotal insights for these components. Firstly, rather than employing parametric body models (e.g., SMPL~\cite{SMPL-X:2019}) to represent 3D bodies, we utilize a markers-based representation~\cite{MOJO}, which captures 3D human shape and pose information using sparse markers on the body surface. As shown in~\cite{MOJO}, this representation is more accessible for neural networks to learn compared to parametric body model parameters, resulting in more realistic motion. The markers-based approach is particularly beneficial for learning whole-body grasping, as errors accumulating along the kinematic chain significantly affect the physical plausibility of generated hand grasps, leading to problematic hand-object interpenetration. Secondly, the concept of {\it contact} is central to our methodology. As humans navigate 3D space and interact with objects, physical contact is crucial for modeling realistic motions and interactions. Both components of our method incorporate learned contact representations from data to guide interaction synthesis, thereby enhancing the realism of the generated motion. For static grasping pose generation, we constructed a multi-task conditional variational autoencoder (CVAE) to simultaneously learn whole-body marker positions and detailed marker-object contact labels. During inference, given a target object in 3D space, our model generates a diverse array of consistent full-body marker locations and contact labels on both the body markers and the object surface. A contact-aware pose optimization module then reconstructs a parametric body mesh from the predicted markers, enforcing hand-object contact using the predicted contact labels. Subsequently, with the generated static whole-body grasping pose as the end pose and an initial pose as the start pose, we propose a novel generative motion infilling network to capture motion uncertainty and generate diverse motions in between. We design a CVAE-based architecture to produce both diverse in-between motion trajectories and diverse in-between local pose articulations. Additionally, contacts between feet and ground are predicted as part of a multi-task learning objective to ensure improved foot-ground interaction. Furthermore, utilizing the predicted human-object contacts, we develop a contact-aware motion optimization module to create realistic grasp-oriented whole-body motions from the generated marker sequences. By leveraging the GRAB~\cite{GRAB:2020} and AMASS~\cite{AMASS:ICCV:2019} datasets for training our generative models, our method effectively generates realistic and varied whole-body grasping motion sequences for approaching and grasping a wide range of 3D objects. \myparagraph{Contributions.} In summary, our contributions include (1) a novel generative framework to synthesize diverse and realistic whole-body motions for 3D humans approaching and grasping a variety of unseen objects, accommodating various body shapes, (2) a novel multi-task learning model to jointly learn static whole-body grasping poses and body-object interactions, and (3) a novel generative motion infilling model that stochastically infills both global trajectories and local pose articulations, producing diverse and realistic full-body motions between a start and an end pose. We conduct extensive experiments to validate our technical contributions. The experimental results confirm both the effectiveness of our complete pipeline and the superiority of each component over existing solutions.

On the other hand, whole-body motion synthesis (cite, holden, 2016, martinez, 2017, hernandez, 2019, MOJO) tends to ignore the presence of objects in the scene. The task of modelling and synthesising realistic grasping actions is difficult and unresolved primarily because of several factors. First, these actions involve the combination of full-body dynamics and complex finger movements, where the high dimensionality complicates the synthesis process. Second, the complexity of the synthesis of body-part-object and hand-part-object contacts is increased by the need for perceptual realism. Thirdly, given a starting pose and a target object in 3D space, there are countless ways to approach the object. This diversity of feasible grasps is further complicated by the variability of the shape and orientation of the object, which makes it very difficult to design a generative model that can reproduce this diversity and can generate realistic grasping motions of different 3D objects. For example, the hand must naturally conform to the surface of the object and the foot must avoid skating in a whole-body motion. To meet these challenges, we introduce SAGA (Stochastic whole-body Grasping with Contingency), an innovative framework for generating whole-body grasping motions, which can stochastically create 3D human body movements approaching and grasping 3D objects. Our approach is based on two main components: a novel 3D body generator which can produce diverse static poses of the body grasping an object, and a novel human motion generator which can produce diverse and plausible movements between the specified start and end poses. We provide two key insights into these components. Moreover, this system has a number of other advantages over previous work. For instance, instead of using a parametric body model (such as SMPL), we use a marker-based representation which captures human shape and pose by placing markers at different locations on the body surface. As shown in MOJO, this representation is more accessible to neural networks, and thus leads to more realistic motion. Secondly, the concept of ‘contact’ is central to our methodology. As humans move through the 3D space and interact with objects, physical contact is essential to the modeling of realistic motion and interaction. Both components of our method use the learned representations of contact to guide the synthesis of interactions, thereby increasing the realism of the generated motion. In order to generate the static grasping pose, we use a conditional variational auto-encoder to simultaneously learn the position of the body markers and the contact information on the object. When we are given a target object in the 3D space, the model predicts a large number of consistent whole-body marker positions, as well as detailed contact information on both the body markers and the object surface. A contact-aware pose-generation module then reconstructs a body-mesh from the predicted markers, and uses the contact information to optimize the pose. In addition, we design a multi-objective learning objective that predicts the contact of the feet with the ground, to obtain a better foot-ground interaction. Then, with the generated static grasping pose as the end pose, and the initial pose as the start pose, we propose a new generative motion infilling network, which takes into account the uncertainty of motion and generates diverse motions in between. Contributions. We use the GRAB and AMASS data for training our generative models, and our method can effectively generate realistic and varied whole-body grasping motions for approaching and grasping various 3D objects. Using the predicted human-object contacts, we develop a contact-aware motion-planning module to generate realistic whole-body grasping motions from the generated marker sequences. We conducted extensive experiments to validate our technical contributions, and the experimental results showed the effectiveness of our entire system and the superiority of each individual component over existing methods. In brief, we provide a novel framework for generating realistic whole-body movements of 3D human figures grasping a wide range of unknown objects, accommodating different body shapes; a novel multi-task learning model to learn both static poses and the interaction between the body and the object; and a novel motion-infilling model to produce realistic whole-body movements from a start pose to a goal pose.

text: We delve into a problem first introduced by Feige, Gamarnik, Neeman, Rácz, and Tetali \cite{feige2020finding}, which involves identifying a substantial clique in a random graph $G\sim G(n,\frac{1}{2})$. This graph $G$ can be explored through queries to its adjacency matrix. The problem's input is a random graph $G(V,E)$ on $n$ vertices, where each pair $\{u,v\}$ of distinct vertices forms an edge $(u,v)\in E$ independently with probability $\frac{1}{2}$. For simplicity, we refer to any pair $\{u,v\}$ as an edge, regardless of its presence in $E$, labeling it a positive edge if $(u,v)\in E$ and a negative edge if $(u,v)\not\in E$. The algorithm's objective is to locate the largest possible clique (a complete subgraph) within $G$. The algorithm can interrogate $G$ through its adjacency matrix, querying an edge $\{u,v\}$ to determine its status as positive or negative. These queries can be conceptualized as interactions with a random oracle, where each new query yields a positive response with probability $\frac{1}{2}$ and a negative one with the same probability, independently of prior responses. The algorithm's primary constraint is the total number of queries $q$, while its computational time may be unbounded (e.g., exponential in $n$). The sequence of queries can be adaptive, allowing the selection of the next query based on previous responses. The $q$ queries result in a graph $G'(V,E')$, where the edges of $G'$ are those queried and confirmed as positive. Given that the algorithm's computation time is unrestricted, it can identify the maximum clique in $G'$. Therefore, the querying process aims to construct a graph $G'$ where the maximum clique is as large as possible. We denote this maximum clique by $K$ and its size by $k$. For any meaningful algorithm (where $k > 1$), $K$ (and thus $k$) is a random variable dependent on the input graph $G$. For a given algorithm, we consider $k$ as the median size of the clique found. Our results are more straightforward to express when $k$ is even, so we assume $k$ is even (this assumption affects the results negligibly, with a difference of at most 1 in the clique size found). We use $\delta$ as a parameter representing the permitted number of queries, where $q = n^{\delta}$. (Occasionally, $\delta$ is interpreted such that $q = O(n^{\delta})$, which has a negligible impact on the results.) Our aim is to maximize $k$ (as a function of $n$ and $\delta$), ensuring an algorithm that makes at most $n^\delta$ queries can, with probability at least $\frac{1}{2}$ over the choice of $G\sim G(n,\frac{1}{2})$, find a clique $K$ of size $k$ in $G'$. We restrict our consideration to $\delta\geq 1$, as for smaller $\delta$, the number of non-isolated vertices in $G'$ becomes $n'<n$, allowing a similar problem to be solved with $n'$ instead of $n$. For $\delta=2$, the entire graph may be queried. The maximum clique in a graph $G\sim G(n,\frac{1}{2})$ is, with high probability (w.h.p.), approximately of size $2\log n$ (ignoring lower-order terms) \cite{matula1972employee}. Thus, w.h.p., the maximum clique size in $G'$ satisfies $k\leq 2\log n + \Theta(1)$ for every $1\leq\delta<2$. Conversely, a clique of expected size $\log n$ can be found using roughly $2n$ queries as follows. Start with sets $K=\emptyset$ and $T=V(G)$. While $T$ is non-empty, repeat: \begin{enumerate} \item Select any $t\in T$, and update $K\leftarrow K\cup \{t\}$. \item Query all pairs $\{\{t,t'\}\mid t'\in T\setminus\{t\}\}$. \item Remove $t$ and its non-neighbors from $T$. \end{enumerate} The size of $T$ decreases by a factor of 2 in each iteration (on average), resulting in about $\log n$ iterations, with the total expected number of queries being $2n$. After the final iteration, $K$ forms a clique of expected size $\log n$. Therefore, the values of $k$ of interest range between $\log n$ and $2\log n$. In all calculations, we disregard terms of order $o(\log n)$ in $k$'s size. Thus, our problem can be articulated as follows: Maximize $\alpha$ such that a clique of size $k\ge \alpha\log n - o(\log n)$ can be found using at most $n^\delta$ queries. Note that $\alpha$ is a function of $\delta$ satisfying $1\leq\alpha\leq 2$. We formally define the value $\alpha$ we seek. \begin{definition} For $1\leq\delta<2$, $\alpha\leq 2$, a deterministic algorithm $\mathcal{A}$ that performs a sequence of at most $n^\delta$ adaptive queries (based on oracle responses) is termed a $(\delta,\alpha)$-algorithm if for every sufficiently large $n$, with probability at least $\frac{1}{2}$, the graph $G'$ (formed by edges discovered by the algorithm) contains a clique of size $k\ge \alpha\log n - o(\log n)$. \end{definition} \begin{definition} For $1\leq\delta<2$, $\alpha_{*}(\delta)$ is defined as the supremum over $\alpha$ for which a $(\delta,\alpha)$-algorithm exists. Note that $1\leq \alpha_{*}(\delta)\leq 2$. \end{definition} \begin{remark} Since algorithm time complexity is not restricted, if $G'$ includes at least one clique of size $k$, $\mathcal{A}$ is assumed to locate and return such a clique $K$ (e.g., via exhaustive search). \end{remark} A comprehensive solution to the problem requires determining the exact value of $\alpha_{*}(\delta)$ for every $1\leq \delta<2$. Lower bounds on $\alpha_{*}(\delta)$ are established by algorithms that find cliques of size $\alpha\log n$ (for $\alpha>1$). Such algorithms were introduced in \cite{feige2020finding} and are detailed in Section \ref{algos_sec}. The algorithms presented are also applicable to a slightly different problem setting, where the algorithm's adaptiveness is limited to a constant number of rounds. The upper bounds we present in this paper pertain to this restricted setting. In this framework, the algorithm may utilize a constant number $l$ of rounds, with at most $n^\delta$ edge queries per round, and the oracle responds to all simultaneously. This allows the algorithm to select queries for round $i$ based on responses from previous rounds, but not on those in the same round. Denote by $q_i$ the number of queries in round $i$. The first round's query pattern forms the query graph $Q_1$ with $n$ vertices and $q_1$ edges. Similarly, any other round $i$ (dependent on previous rounds' responses) forms the query graph $Q_i$ with $n$ vertices and $q_i$ edges. Note that $Q_i$'s edges include all pairs queried in round $i$, not just positive ones. We denote by $Q_{\leq i}$ the query graph including all queries up to round $i$, i.e., $E(Q_{\leq i})=\bigcup_{j\leq i} E(Q_j)$. (Here, 'up to' includes 'up to and including'). We adjust definitions \ref{def_org_1} and \ref{def_org_2} for this restricted setting. \begin{definition} For $l\in\mathbb{N}$, $1\leq\delta<2$, $\alpha\leq 2$, a deterministic algorithm $\mathcal{A}$ that performs $l$ rounds of queries with at most $n^\delta$ queries each round is termed a $(\delta,l,\alpha)$-algorithm if for every sufficiently large $n$, with probability at least $\frac{1}{2}$, $G'$ contains a clique of size $k\ge \alpha\log n - o(\log n)$. \end{definition} \begin{definition} For $l\in\mathbb{N}$, $1\leq\delta<2$, $\alpha_{*}(\delta,l)$ is defined as the supremum over $\alpha$ for which a $(\delta,l,\alpha)$-algorithm exists. \end{definition} These definitions can be extended to scenarios where the number of queries varies across rounds. Generally, we assume that in round $i$, the algorithm is restricted to $q_i=n^{\delta_i}$ queries for some $0<\delta_i<2$. This leads to analogous definitions of a $((\delta_1,\dots,\delta_l),l,\alpha)$-algorithm and $\alpha_{*}((\delta_1,\dots,\delta_l),l)$ (see definitions in Section \ref{sec_two_rounds_large_delta}). For every $l\in \mathbb{N}$, with $\delta\coloneqq \max_i \delta_i$, we have: \[\alpha_{*}((\delta_1,\dots,\delta_l),l)\leq \alpha_{*}(\delta,l)\leq \alpha_{*}(\delta)\] \subsection{Previous results} The task of determining bounds for $\alpha_{*}(\delta)$ and $\alpha_{*}(\delta,l)$ was explored by Feige, Gamarnik, Neeman, Rácz, and Tetali \cite{feige2020finding}. They established the following results for $\alpha_{*}(\delta,l)$: \begin{enumerate} \item For every $1\leq \delta<2$, $\alpha_{*}(\delta,1)=\delta$. \item For $1\leq\delta\leq\frac{6}{5}$, $\alpha_{*}(\delta,2)\geq\frac{4\delta}{3}$, and for $\frac{6}{5}\leq\delta<2$, $\alpha_{*}(\delta,2)\geq 1+\frac{\delta}{2}$. \item For every $1\leq \delta<2$, $\alpha_{*}(\delta,3)\geq1+\frac{\delta}{2}$. \item For $\delta=1$ and any $l\in\mathbb{N}$, $\alpha_{*}(1,l)\leq 2^{1-\frac{1}{2^l-1}}$. This implies: $\alpha_{*}(1,2)\leq 1.588$, $\alpha_{*}(1,3)\leq 1.812$, etc. \item For every $1\leq\delta<2$ and $l\in\mathbb{N}$, $\alpha_{*}(\delta,l)\leq 2-\delta\left(\frac{2-\delta}{2}\right)^l$. \end{enumerate} An upper bound on $\alpha_{*}(\delta)$ was proven by Alweiss, Ben Hamida, He, and Moreira \cite{alweiss2021subgraph}. They demonstrated that for every $1\leq\delta<2$: \[\alpha_{*}(\delta)\leq 1+\sqrt{1-\frac{(2-\delta)^2}{2}}\] For instance, for $\delta=1$, this yields $\alpha_{*}(1)\leq 1+\sqrt{\frac{1}{2}}\sim 1.707$. Since $\alpha_{*}(\delta,l)\leq \alpha_{*}(\delta)$, this result also enhances the upper bound on $\alpha_{*}(\delta,l)$ for every $l\geq 3$.

text: Sparsification is a critical concept in graph theory that involves reducing the size of a large graph $G$ while preserving its essential properties. Notable examples include spanners \cite{Chew89}, which maintain approximate distances within a multiplicative factor, and cut and spectral sparsifiers \cite{BK96,ST04}, which preserve the graph's cuts and Laplacian spectrum up to a $(1+\varepsilon)$ factor. These \emph{edge sparsifiers} enable the transformation of dense graph problems into sparse ones, albeit with an approximation factor due to sparsification. Conversely, certain techniques, such as elimination-based Laplacian solvers \cite{KLPSS16}, necessitate \emph{vertex sparsification}, which involves reducing the graph's vertex count. In this study, we focus on \emph{cut sparsification}, a form of vertex sparsification introduced by \cite{HKNR98,Moitra09,LM10}. Given a graph $G$ and a set of \emph{terminals} $\mathcal{T} \subseteq V(G)$, the objective is to construct a smaller graph $G'$ that approximates the value of all cuts in $G$ between terminals up to a multiplicative factor $q$, known as the \emph{quality} of the sparsifier. Specifically, $G'$ should include the terminals $\mathcal{T}$ among its vertices, ensuring that for any subset $S \subseteq \mathcal{T}$, the minimum cut in $G$ and $G'$ between $S$ and its complement $\mathcal{T} \backslash S$ differ by at most the factor $q$. An ideal algorithm for vertex sparsifiers aims to achieve a quality $q$ near 1 while ensuring that the constructed graph $G'$ contains few vertices, ideally nearly linear in the number of terminals, denoted as $k = |\mathcal{T}|$. Additionally, for practical applications, the runtime of the vertex sparsification algorithm should be polynomial or even linear in the size of the original graph $G$. Previous research has achieved different combinations of these properties. When the sparsifier $G'$ has a vertex set exactly $\mathcal{T}$, an upper bound quality $q = O(\log k / \log\log k)$ has been attained \cite{Moitra09,LM10,CLLM10,EGKRTT14}, with a polynomial runtime achieved by \cite{MM10}. For quality $q = 1$, upper bounds of $2^{2^k}$ \cite{HKNR98,KR14} and lower bounds of $2^{\Omega(k)}$ \cite{KR13} have been established. Furthermore, \cite{KW12} obtained a bound of size $O(Z^3)$ for quality $q = 1$ in polynomial time for graphs with integer capacities, where $Z$ represents the total degree of all terminals. However, it remains uncertain whether quality $q = 1+\varepsilon$ sparsifiers with $\O({\mathrm{poly}}(k/\varepsilon))$ vertices exist except in specific cases \cite{AGK14,ADKKP16}. In this paper, we introduce a vertex sparsification algorithm for $c$-edge connectivity, a thresholded version of cut sparsification, which preserves all cuts of size at most $c$ exactly, has a size linear in the number of terminals and polynomial in $c$, and executes in polynomial time for any $c$ (\cref{thm:main}). This concept, termed a \emph{connectivity-$c$ mimicking network}, was introduced in \cite{CDL21} to explore dynamic connectivity problems and parameterized complexity, leading to the first fully dynamic online algorithm for $c$-connectivities with nearly constant update time for constant $c$ \cite{JS20}. Specifically, a graph $G'$ is considered a connectivity-$c$ mimicking network for $G$ with terminals $\mathcal{T}$ if all cuts between terminals in $G$ with at most $c$ edges are preserved exactly in $G'$. The previous algorithm from \cite{CDL21} for constructing a connectivity-$c$ mimicking network with $O(kc^4)$ edges does not run in polynomial time due to its reliance on a well-linked decomposition from \cite{Chu12}, which requires an exact solution to a restricted sparsest cut problem. Consequently, the algorithm's runtime scales exponentially with $c$. Our primary contribution involves leveraging the matroid-based cut covering lemmas from \cite{KW12} and integrating them with a weaker notion of a well-linked decomposition. Specifically, we avoid a complete well-linked decomposition and instead partition the graph $G$ into segments whose ``expansion'' relative to terminals is not minimal, resembling an expander decomposition. Our key lemma (\cref{lemma:expanderc}), utilizing matroid theory and representative sets from \cite{KW12}, provides a direct bound on the size of a connectivity-$c$ mimicking network for these expander-like segments based on expansion. We then unify the connectivity-$c$ mimicking networks of the segments to form a connectivity-$c$ mimicking network for the original graph. This approach allows us to employ approximate sparsest cut algorithms (\cref{thm:sparsecut} \cite{ALN05}), which operate in polynomial time. Unfortunately, achieving a $O(m {\mathrm{poly}}(c))$ runtime remains elusive due to the costly linear algebra required to identify independent sets in matroids. However, we are optimistic that a $O(m {\mathrm{poly}}(c))$ runtime is feasible and could have broader applications in enhancing data structures for connectivity and flows, as discussed in \cref{subsec:future}. \subsection{Our Results} Our principal result demonstrates that, given a graph $G$ with $k$ terminals $\mathcal{T}$, a connectivity-$c$ mimicking network with $\O(kc^3)$ edges can be constructed in polynomial time. \begin{theorem} For any edge-capacitated graph $G$ with $n$ vertices and a set $\mathcal{T}$ of $k$ terminals, there exists an algorithm that constructs a connectivity-$c$ mimicking network $H$ of $G$ with $O(kc^3\log^{3/2}n\log\log n)$ edges in time $n^{O(1)}$. \end{theorem} Without requiring a polynomial time algorithm, we can slightly enhance the size. Notably, the mimicking networks we create are all minors of $G$, as shown by Theorem 1.1 in \cite{CDL21} and the subsequent commentary, indicating these networks can be constructed in $O(m(c\log n)^{O(c)})$ time, which is super-polynomial for $c \ge \log n$. \begin{theorem} For any edge-capacitated graph $G$ with $n$ vertices and a set $\mathcal{T}$ of $k$ terminals, there exists a connectivity-$c$ mimicking network $H$ of $G$ with $O(kc^3)$ edges. \end{theorem} These findings surpass Theorem 1.1 in \cite{CDL21} for any $c \ge \log n$, as the runtime there depended on $c^{O(c)}$, which is super-polynomial for $c \ge \log n$. This improvement enhances the runtime for survivable network design on low treewidth graphs, as indicated by Theorem 6.3 of \cite{CDL21}. For further details, see Section 6.2 of \cite{CDL21}. \begin{corollary} An algorithm exists that precisely solves {\sf Subset $c$-EC} on an input graph $G$ with $n$ vertices in time $n \exp\left(O(c^3\mathrm{tw}(G)\log(\mathrm{tw}(G)c)\right)$, where $\mathrm{tw}(G)$ represents the treewidth of $G$. \end{corollary} \subsection{Related work} Our work synthesizes concepts from various fields, encompassing cut sparsification and mimicking networks, matroid theory and polynomial kernelization, as well as sparsest cut and expander decompositions. \paragraph{Cut sparsification and mimicking networks.} Without additional vertices, the best known bounds are $O(\log k / \log \log k)$ \cite{CLLM10,MM10} and $\Omega(\sqrt{\log k} / \log\log k)$ \cite{MM10}. \cite{Chu12} offers an algorithm that constructs an $O(1)$-quality sparsifier with $O(Z^3)$ edges in time ${\mathrm{poly}}(n) \cdot 2^Z$, and \cite{KW12} provides a polynomial time algorithm for a quality-$1$ sparsifier with $O(Z^3)$ edges using matroid theory. The general existence of $(1+\varepsilon)$-quality cut sparsifiers with at most $\O({\mathrm{poly}}(k/\varepsilon))$ edges remains unresolved. A different line of inquiry focuses on \emph{mimicking networks}, i.e., quality-$1$ cut sparsifiers, with size dependent solely on the number of terminals $k$. Here, upper bounds of $2^{2^k}$ \cite{HKNR98,KRTV12} and lower bounds of $2^{\Omega(k)}$ \cite{KR14} are documented. For planar graphs, an upper bound of $O(k^22^{2k})$ \cite{KR13} and a lower bound of $2^{\Omega(k)}$ \cite{KPZ17} are known. Furthermore, \cite{CSWZ00} provides an upper bound of $O(k \cdot 2^{2^{\mathrm{tw}(G)}})$ for bounded treewidth graphs, along with more precise results for a small number of terminals. \paragraph{Sparsest cut and expansion.} The conductance of a graph is a fundamental measure that has been thoroughly researched. Cheeger's inequality \cite{Cheeger70} links conductance to the graph's spectrum, leading to significant interest in efficiently approximating conductance and the related sparsest cut problem. A $O(\log n)$ approximation was introduced by \cite{LR99}, followed by approximation ratios of $O(\sqrt{\log n})$ for the uniform case \cite{ARV09} and $O(\sqrt{\log n}\log\log n)$ for the nonuniform case \cite{ALN05}. Further efforts have aimed at enhancing the efficiency of these algorithms \cite{AHK04,Sherman09}. The sparsest cut problem is closely related to the concept of \emph{expander decomposition}, which involves partitioning a graph so that all segments are expanders. Significant progress has been made towards achieving linear time algorithms for expander decompositions \cite{ST04,NS17,SW19,CGL20}, with many approaches based on the cut-matching game \cite{KRV06}. Both the cut-matching game \cite{RST14} and expander decompositions \cite{KLOS14,CGP18,KPSW19,CDL21} have been extensively utilized in graph algorithms. \paragraph{Polynomial kernelization and parametrization.} Kernelization in parameterized algorithms aims to efficiently reduce problem size to a function of a parameter $k$, while preserving essential properties. For instance, if $k$ is the number of terminals in a graph $G$, one may inquire whether $G$ can be reduced to a size polynomial in $k$ while maintaining all terminal cuts exactly. \cite{KW12}, employing tools from matroid theory and representative sets \cite{Lovasz77,Marx09}, demonstrates polynomial kernels for several problems. Recently, \cite{W20} achieved an improved kernelization size for multiway-cut using a combination of graph partitioning and representative sets, akin to the approach of this work. \subsection{Future directions} Several promising avenues for future exploration exist. \paragraph{Improved algorithm runtime.} Refining the algorithm to construct connectivity-$c$ mimicking networks of size $\O(kc^3)$ in $\O(m \cdot {\mathrm{poly}}(c))$ time could unlock numerous applications. Specifically, such an advancement might enable the development of algorithms for fully dynamic online $c$-connectivity, building on the work of \cite{JS20}, with an update time of $\O({\mathrm{poly}}(c))$ per iteration. Conversely, the query time in \cite{JS20} scales exponentially with $c$, at least $(c\log n)^c$. Moreover, this could extend to fully dynamic $(1+\varepsilon)$-approximate maxflow algorithms in unweighted graphs. One potential pathway to achieve a nearly linear construction runtime $\O(m \cdot {\mathrm{poly}}(c))$ is to reinterpret the concepts of representative sets on the direct sum matroids from \cref{lemma:expanderc} combinatorially, in terms of matching, flows, and cuts. This might allow constructing the representative set via a maximum flow routine on the appropriate graph, rather than performing linear algebra over matroid representations. \paragraph{Optimal $c$ dependence in sparsifier size.} Determining the optimal dependence on $c$ in the size of the connectivity-$c$ mimicking network is an intriguing challenge. We have only established a lower bound of $2kc$, and a lower bound of $\Omega(kc)$ when all terminals have degree 1. We suspect an upper bound of $O(kc^2)$ or even $O(kc)$ is feasible. \paragraph{Application towards $(1+\varepsilon)$-quality cut sparsification.} Extending the ideas of this work to construct $(1+\varepsilon)$-quality cut sparsifiers with at most $\O(k/{\mathrm{poly}}(\varepsilon))$ edges would be an exciting development. A plausible strategy involves selecting a slightly super-constant $c = C\log n/\varepsilon^2$, identifying a set of edges $F$ covering all cuts of size at most $c$ between terminals, and applying a uniform sampling procedure \cite{BK96,ADKKP16} to the remaining edges. However, this approach appears challenging due to the presence of numerous potential minimum cuts between a fixed terminal partition.

text: Reinforcement learning (RL) has seen remarkable achievements across a range of complex challenges. Pioneering efforts such as DQN~\cite{mnih2015human}, AlphaGo~\cite{silver2016mastering}, and OpenAI Five~\cite{berner2019dota} exemplify this success. Nonetheless, these advancements often require substantial interaction with the environment. For instance, AlphaZero~\cite{silver2017mastering} necessitates 21 million games during training. In stark contrast, a skilled human player, averaging 5 games daily, would need approximately 11,500 years to amass equivalent experience. While sample complexity may not pose significant hurdles in simulations and gaming applications, it becomes a critical factor when RL algorithms are applied to real-world scenarios such as robotic manipulation, healthcare, and advertisement recommendation systems, where balancing high performance with low sample complexity is crucial for practical deployment. Significant strides have been made in enhancing sample efficiency in RL over recent years~\cite{chua2018deep, deisenroth2011pilco, srinivas2020curl, laskin2020reinforcement, kostrikov2020image, schwarzerdata, kaiser2019model}. Model-based approaches have garnered particular interest because they leverage both real-world data and "imagined data" generated by the model to train policies, thus optimizing sample efficiency~\cite{chua2018deep,deisenroth2011pilco}. However, these methods have largely thrived in state-based environments. In image-based settings, while some model-based techniques like MuZero~\cite{schrittwieser2020mastering} and Dreamer V2~\cite{hafner2020mastering} achieve exceptional performance, they are not sample efficient. Conversely, methods such as SimPLe~\cite{kaiser2019model} demonstrate efficiency but fall short in performance, with only 0.144 human normalized median scores. Recently, data-augmented and self-supervised strategies applied to model-free methods have shown promise in data efficiency~\cite{schwarzerdata}, yet they still lag behind human-level expectations. To enhance sample efficiency while maintaining high performance, we identify three critical components for a model-based visual RL agent: a self-supervised environment model, a strategy to mitigate model compounding errors, and a technique to address off-policy issues. In this paper, we introduce EfficientZero, a model-based RL algorithm designed to deliver superior performance with constrained data usage. Our approach extends MuZero with three pivotal modifications: (1) employing self-supervised learning to develop a temporally consistent environment model, (2) end-to-end learning of the \textit{value prefix}, which helps reduce model compounding errors, and (3) utilizing the learned model to adjust off-policy value targets. As depicted in Figure \ref{fig:compare}, our model achieves state-of-the-art results on the Atari~\cite{bellemare2013arcade} 100k benchmark, reaching super-human performance with merely 2 hours of real-time gameplay. Specifically, our model attains 194.3\% mean human normalized performance and 109.0\% median human normalized performance. For comparison, DQN~\cite{mnih2015human} achieves 220\% mean and 96\% median human normalized performance, but requires 500 times more data (200 million frames). To further demonstrate EfficientZero's effectiveness, we conduct experiments in simulated robotics environments within the DeepMind Control (DMControl) suite, achieving state-of-the-art results and surpassing SAC, which learns directly from ground truth states. Our algorithm's sample efficiency and high performance pave the way for broader impacts on various real-world applications.

text: The field of \ac{NBR} has garnered significant attention from researchers over time \citep{fpmc,dream,bai2018attribute}. Baskets, which are collections of items bought or consumed simultaneously, are ubiquitous in various real-world applications, such as e-commerce and grocery shopping~\citep{hao, raeder}. The primary objective of a \ac{NBR} system is to predict the next basket of items a user might wish to purchase or consume, based on their historical sequence of baskets. Unlike session-based or sequential item recommendations, where order matters, in a basket, all items are unordered and equally significant. Consequently, \ac{NBR} systems must handle multiple items within a set, distinguishing them from item-based recommendation models, which are not suitable for basket-based recommendation. This has led to the development of specialized \ac{NBR} methodologies~\citep{tifuknn, recency, dream, beacon, intnet, clea, sets2sets, sun2020timestamp2}. \subsection{Types of recommendation methods} The evolution of recommendation methods over the years has introduced a diverse array of approaches. \emph{Frequency-based} methods remain influential as they effectively capture global item popularity statistics, applicable to both item-based and \ac{NBR} contexts. Similarly, \emph{nearest neighbor-based} techniques have been staples in both item and basket recommendation scenarios. Recent advancements have seen deep learning techniques being applied to sequential item recommendation, leveraging their ability to uncover latent relationships and automatically learn representations~\citep{batmaz-2019-deep}. Deep learning has also been employed to tackle various facets of the \ac{NBR} challenge, such as item-to-item interactions~\citep{beacon}, cross-basket relationships~\citep{dnntsp}, and noise within baskets~\citep{clea}. Recent evaluations suggest that deep learning approaches may not universally excel across all recommendation tasks or conditions~\citep{jannach-2020-why}. For tasks requiring the generation of a personalized ranked list of items, linear models and nearest neighbor-based strategies often outperform deep learning methods~\citep{dacrema-2021-troubling}. In sequential recommendation contexts, simpler nearest neighbor or graph-based baselines can surpass deep learning models~\citep{dacrema-2019-are}. Regarding \acl{NBR}, the retrieval unit—a basket—presents a more intricate challenge than those considered in previous studies~\citep{dacrema-2019-are,dacrema-2021-troubling,jannach-2020-why}, due to the complex dependencies between items and baskets over time. This complexity suggests a potential for advanced representation learning-based solutions to enhance \ac{NBR} performance. This paper aims to investigate whether this potential is realized. \subsection{A new analysis perspective} In reviewing the \ac{NBR} literature, we identify significant shortcomings, such as inadequate or absent baselines, inconsistent datasets across studies, and non-standard metrics. We assess the performance of three leading \ac{NBR} model families—frequency-based, nearest neighbor-based, and deep learning-based—across three benchmark datasets, discovering that no single method consistently outperforms the others in all contexts. In light of these findings, we advocate for a more comprehensive analysis of the strengths and weaknesses of \ac{NBR} methods. As illustrated in Figure~\ref{fig:re-nbr}, baskets recommended in a \ac{NBR} context include \emph{repeat items} (previously consumed by the user) and \emph{explore items} (new to the user). Although the novelty of recommended items has been explored and related metrics have been proposed~\citep{epc-epd}, these metrics are not specific to \ac{NBR} and focus solely on recommendation novelty. To enhance our understanding of \ac{NBR} model performance, particularly regarding repeat and explore items, we introduce a set of task-specific metrics. These new metrics help identify item types in recommended baskets and evaluate \ac{NBR} models' effectiveness in suggesting new versus previously purchased items. \subsection{Main findings} Utilizing our newly proposed \ac{NBR} metrics, we conduct an extensive comparison of \ac{NBR} models, leading to several key insights: \begin{itemize} \item No single \ac{NBR} method consistently surpasses all others across various datasets. \item Published methods exhibit a strong bias towards either repetition or exploration compared to actual user behavior, potentially affecting long-term engagement. \item There is a notable performance disparity between repetition and exploration in \ac{NBR}; recommending repeat items is substantially easier. \item In many scenarios, frequency-based baselines outperform deep learning-based \ac{NBR} methods by populating baskets with the most frequently purchased items in a user's history, supplemented by items popular among all users. \item Recent methods' performance gains are largely attributable to a bias towards repeat items, despite complex modules or strategies targeting explore items. \item We propose a new evaluation protocol for \ac{NBR} methods, including a novel frequency-based baseline and metrics to assess potential performance improvements. \item Current \acs{NBR} methods impact user performance and item exposure differently based on users' repetition ratios and item frequencies. \end{itemize} \noindent% In summary, our research illuminates the current state of \ac{NBR}, offers recommendations for refining evaluation methodologies, elucidates performance disparities, and provides insights to guide the development of future \ac{NBR} models.

Later, in a review of the literature on aclNBR, we found several shortcomings, including the lack of proper controls, the inconsistent data and metrics used in studies, and the lack of standardization of approaches. In the figure above, the baskets recommended in the NBR context include both repeated items (those already bought by the customer) and new ones. In short, our research reveals the current state of NBR and makes recommendations for improving evaluation methodology, explains the differences in performance, and provides insights to guide the development of future NBR models. text: The increasing intricacy of machine learning models, particularly in recommendation systems, has underscored the importance of managing abundant input features both effectively and efficiently. In industrial contexts, online recommendation systems frequently train models on billions of sparse features encoded as one-hot vectors~\cite{cheng2016wide,zhou2018din,DBLP:conf/cikm/ShengZZDDLYLZDZ21}. Each feature can be interpreted as a distinct ID, which is typically transformed into a low-dimensional embedding before being incorporated into the model. A straightforward approach to handling these large-scale inputs is to treat each feature in isolation. Under this method, a DNN is trained to predict CTR by combining features, often through concatenation, where the interaction among features is implicitly captured by the fully connected layers. Nonetheless, certain features, such as "candidate item" and "user click history," exhibit significant interdependencies~\cite{zhou2018din,zhou2019dien}, exemplified by the classic "Beer and Nappies" scenario. Such feature interactions can enhance the accuracy of CTR predictions. As depicted in Fig.\ref{fig:coaction}, neglecting feature interactions results in the independent modeling of the influences of features A and B on the final label (click or not in CTR prediction), as represented by the blue lines. The grey line depicts feature interaction, explicitly linking the correlation between feature pair (A, B) and the target label, thereby providing more valuable information for the learning objective. A deeper exploration of this topic will be presented in Sec. \ref{sec:revisit}. To capture feature interactions, the simplest method involves using the cartesian product. When two features, A and B, are selected, their co-occurrence <A, B> is treated as a new feature and introduced into the model. This direct inclusion of co-occurrence data simplifies the training process. Although the cartesian product is straightforward and effective, it suffers from significant drawbacks, such as an enormous parameter volume and feature space, as well as limited generalization ability. In contrast to the cartesian product, which introduces supplementary input information, various research efforts have focused on modeling feature interactions through strategic combinations of input features. Notable examples include factorization-based methods~\cite{rendle2010factorization,qu2016product,WangFFW2017DCN,lian2018xdeepfm,xiao2017attentional,song2019autoint}, which emphasize both low- and high-order feature interactions by directly combining feature embeddings in latent vector spaces using various operators. These methods, which approach feature interaction from a model perspective with well-crafted operators, are generally more deployment-friendly than the cartesian product. However, they also have notable limitations. The shallow structures of some factorization-based methods \cite{juan2016field,WangFFW2017DCN} restrict their expressive power. More importantly, the embeddings generated by these operators are tasked with both representation learning and feature interaction modeling, potentially complicating the training process. This dual responsibility can diminish the memory capacity for feature interactions, thereby reducing the model's overall effectiveness. \author{Weijie Bian$\dagger$, Kailun Wu$\dagger$, Lejian Ren$\dagger$, Qi Pi$\dagger$, Yujing Zhang$\dagger$, Can Xiao$\dagger$} \author{Xiang-Rong Sheng$\dagger$, Yong-Nan Zhu$\dagger$, Zhangming Chan$\dagger$, Na Mou$\dagger$, Xinchen Luo$\dagger$} \author{Shiming Xiang$\ddagger$, Guorui Zhou$\dagger$, Xiaoqiang Zhu$\dagger$, Hongbo Deng$\dagger$} \authornote{Hongbo Deng is the corresponding author (dhb167148@alibaba-inc.com).} \affiliation{% \institution{$\dagger$Alibaba Group\qquad \qquad \qquad$\ddagger$Institute of Automation, Chinese Academy of Sciences} \city{Beijing} \country{China} } \email{{weijie.bwj,kailun.wukailun,lejian.rlj,dhb167148}@alibaba-inc.com} To address these challenges, we introduce the \textbf{C}o-\textbf{A}ction \textbf{N}etwork (\textbf{CAN}), designed to effectively capture feature interactions and leverage the mutual and shared information between different feature pairs. Specifically, for each feature pair, the embeddings from one side (induction feature) are used to form an MLP, which is then applied to the other side (feed feature) within the co-action unit. This approach to feature interaction modeling significantly reduces the additional parameter requirement from $O(N^2 \times D)$ to $O(N\times (D' + D))$ ($N$ represents the number of features, while $D$ and $D'$ are the dimensions of parameters used in the co-action unit, with $D < D' \ll N$) compared to the cartesian product. Furthermore, CAN enhances non-linear modeling capabilities and fitting potential by employing MLPs in the co-action unit, surpassing traditional factorization-based methods. Moreover, CAN separates the parameter spaces for representation learning and feature interaction modeling, preventing mutual interference during training. Multi-order enhancement and multi-level independence are also utilized to boost CAN's expressive capacity. The primary contributions of this research are as follows: \begin{itemize}[leftmargin=*] \item We critically examine the efficacy of the cartesian product and highlight the potential of implicit feature interaction modeling. Inspired by the independent coding of the cartesian product, we propose a novel feature interaction paradigm that achieves comparable performance with significantly reduced resource consumption. \item We introduce the Co-Action Network (CAN) to model feature interactions among raw features at the input stage. In CAN, each feature ID is assigned to a unique micro-MLP to model interactions with other features. This design enhances the expressive capability of feature interaction modeling while maintaining a limited parameter count. The individual micro-MLP exhibits greater expressive power than standard operators used in factorization-based methods. \item We perform extensive experiments on both public and industrial datasets. The consistent superiority of CAN in modeling feature interactions compared to state-of-the-art competitors is validated. Deploying CAN leads to a 12\% increase in CTR and an 8\% rise in RPM in Alibaba's display advertisement system. \end{itemize}

text: {\bf Motivation}. Stack Overflow\footnote{https://stackoverflow.com/} stands as a premier platform for users to pose and answer inquiries related to software development. Since its inception in 2008, it has become a vital resource for both seasoned software developers and passionate programmers to exchange and enhance their expertise. By September 2019, the platform had amassed over 10.9 million users and hosted 18.1 million questions. The site continues to expand, with more than 150,000 new questions being posted monthly\footnote{https://data.stackexchange.com/}. The swift expansion of Stack Overflow presents significant challenges in content management and maintaining user engagement. Due to the vast volume of data (specifically questions), manual oversight is both costly and taxing for site moderators \cite{moder2019, workload2019}. Consequently, there is a pressing demand for automated solutions to streamline content management. This necessity has garnered the interest of various researchers in recent years \cite{Ashton2012, anton2014, Sebastian2019}. Although several studies have explored Stack Overflow, only a few have focused on automating the management and cleansing of its data. Most prior research primarily targets the identification and filtering of low-quality or duplicate questions \cite{Muhammad2016, denzil2013, Denzil14}. In our study, we assert that even high-quality questions should be discarded when they no longer align with users' collective information needs, such as when a question pertains to an outdated software version or library. Retaining such irrelevant questions not only escalates the costs of data storage and retrieval but also offers minimal value. Moreover, the presence of superfluous information can degrade user experience, potentially leading to user dissatisfaction and attrition from the platform. We introduce the concept of "forgetting" these less appealing questions, allowing them to gradually fade from users' awareness, akin to how irrelevant memories are naturally forgotten. As an initial step, this work tackles the challenge of pinpointing quality content on Stack Overflow that, while once frequently accessed, has diminished in relevance over time. Specifically, these are questions that were once commonly posed and (1) recently garnered significant attention from users encountering similar issues but (2) are expected to attract minimal interest in the future. We label these as \emph{forgotten questions}. Figure \ref{fig:ForgottenExample} illustrates an example of such a question, originally posted in 2008 and widely viewed until late 2017, accumulating 710 views in the last six months of 2017. However, it has received scant views in the recent half-year period. {\bf Research Objectives}. Our analysis reveals that the process of questions becoming forgotten is gradual, often taking years for a popular question to fade into obscurity. Moreover, predicting outcomes far into the future proves inaccurate and impractical. Thus, our focus is on questions currently in the process of being forgotten in the near term. Specifically, for a question that has recently been highly viewed, we aim to forecast whether its view count will significantly decline in the upcoming period. For example, referring to the case in Figure \ref{fig:ForgottenExample}, at the time point 12/2017 when the question was frequently accessed, instead of predicting its obsolescence after two years, we aim to anticipate a decrease in its views over the next 3 to 6 months. Our work is inspired by the concept of managed forgetting~\cite{claudia2018}, where items of diminishing importance are de-emphasized to enhance focus on significant matters, mirroring the function of forgetting in human cognition~\cite{David2007}. We specifically seek to investigate factors highlighted by previous research and general intuition that might influence the process of high-quality questions being forgotten on Stack Overflow. Additionally, we develop a framework for the early detection of such questions. This forgetting management framework serves as a valuable tool for moderators, guiding them to prioritize and address unnecessary content. It also aids in elevating important information for users, thus fostering user engagement. For instance, experienced developers are likely to be more interested in recently popular questions, prompting interactions that enhance these questions' search engine rankings, thereby facilitating users' access to current information. It is crucial to note that our problem is distinct from and complements other content-focused studies like \cite{Haoxiang2019}, which analyze question answers to identify obsolete content. Such content may be incorrect from its inception or become outdated in the near future. In contrast, the forgetting of questions can arise from various causes, with becoming incorrect or outdated being just one factor. {\bf Contributions}. We encapsulate our primary contributions as follows: \begin{itemize} \item We conduct the inaugural study on forgetting management in Stack Overflow, demonstrating that the forgetting phenomenon is widespread among high-quality questions, albeit at a slow rate. \item We explore an extensive array of factors that could influence the forgetting of questions and evaluate their effectiveness as predictors for this phenomenon. \item We assess the performance of several predictive models in identifying questions that are being forgotten. We pinpoint certain categories where forgotten questions are more predictable, even though the overall prediction task remains challenging. We also highlight the predictive power of different feature groups and analyze their relative importance in these models. \end{itemize} The remainder of the paper is structured as follows: Section 2 reviews related work. Section 3 details the Stack Overflow dataset used and our study of forgotten questions. In Section 4, we perform experiments using a machine learning framework to forecast forgotten questions on Stack Overflow. Section 5 discusses factors that might impact our forgetting prediction task. Finally, Section 6 encapsulates our main contributions and suggests promising avenues for future research.
