text: The generation of explanations in automated planning has often been approached through the lens of model reconciliation~\cite{chakraborti2017plan}. This methodology strives to strike a balance between crafting explanations that update the user's understanding of the system and choosing action sequences that are inherently comprehensible, thus requiring no further clarification. However, a significant limitation of this approach is its reliance on an accurate model of the user, which is frequently impractical in real-world scenarios. An alternative perspective is to consider explanations as part of a broader interactive dialogue. In human interactions, communication channels are diverse, encompassing both deliberate and automatic responses, as well as various behavioral heuristics. For an interaction agent to communicate effectively, it must be adept at recognizing and interpreting these signals or, ideally, predicting them. With this framework in mind, we are designing a user study to observe human behavior and responses during a collaborative task with a plan-based agent. While we anticipate that our study will corroborate and expand upon previous research on joint task interaction, our primary aim is to explore how concepts integral to plan-based agents, such as plan generation and agent intention, can be leveraged to guide the agent's conduct. We have pinpointed specific behaviors of plan-based agents that engage with critical elements of joint task interaction, such as uncertainty and knowledge disparities. These behaviors have informed the creation of two distinct agents: a reactive agent, which embodies an initial interaction scenario where there is limited knowledge about the human's preferences and possibly the environment; and a partially predictive agent, which acts as a more knowledgeable entity that preemptively provides information and seeks to reduce user uncertainty. By collecting both quantitative and qualitative data from human interactions with these agents, we aim to deepen our understanding of how such agents can be designed to be more human-friendly. As a component of this research, we have developed a web-based user study, which we are currently preparing for deployment. The platform facilitates a joint task interaction, wherein the human participant is tasked with completing an activity with the assistance of a virtual agent that offers instructions and explanations. This paper outlines the objectives of our user study, the scenarios that participants will encounter, and the research questions we aim to address. We also describe the agents to be compared in the study and the facets of joint task interaction they enable us to investigate. Although user results are not yet available, we provide an empirical analysis to compare the strategies and explanations generated by each type of agent. We begin by providing an overview of the joint task setting and the essential planning background. Subsequently, we discuss aspects of plan-based agent behavior pertinent to joint task interactions and utilize these insights to define two alternative agents. We then detail our proposed user study, present an empirical analysis, review related work, and conclude the paper.

text: \IEEEPARstart{C}ivil drones have captivated attention for over ten years, drawing interest from industry, academia, business sectors, and civil society alike. In May 2021, Morgan Stanley projected a substantial future for urban air mobility, suggesting that by 2050, the market could expand to \$9 trillion (equating to 5-6\% of the anticipated global GDP) or potentially reach \$19 trillion (11-12\% of the projected global GDP) in an optimistic scenario \cite{MS}. Major technology companies such as Amazon, Google, and Uber are actively developing drone-related projects, and aircraft manufacturers are venturing into air taxi design. Academic circles are equally engaged, with approximately 300,000 research documents indexed in Scopus, stemming from keyword searches involving "drone" and its synonyms like Unmanned Aerial Vehicle (UAV), Unmanned Aerial System (UAS), Unmanned Aircraft, and Remotely Piloted Aircraft Systems (RPAS). Even when focusing specifically on wireless communication, the level of interest remains high, as highlighted in several tutorial and survey papers \cite{vin_tut,Vin_safe}, which synthesize findings from numerous research articles. Despite the widespread enthusiasm across different sectors, drones have yet to become a staple of daily life. Both industry and academia largely agree that regulatory and certification barriers are significant hurdles. This challenge is noted in technical articles \cite{vin_tut,Vin_safe}, and the authors of \cite{MS} emphasize that \textit{regulatory requirements for aviation are among the most underestimated risks}. Notably, in 2021, Morgan Stanley adjusted their market size forecast downward by 30% compared to their 2018 Blue paper, citing "near-term hurdles related to regulation and certification" as a primary reason. Conversely, it is not our stance that regulatory bodies act with ill intent. We acknowledge the complexity of governing technological advancements, involving a diverse array of stakeholders—from civil society and security agencies to academic researchers and powerful corporations. The restrictive policies partly respond to public concerns about the technology's reliability. Additionally, unmanned aviation is a nascent field with numerous uncertainties and knowledge gaps. As academic researchers, often serving the public interest, it is our responsibility to bridge these knowledge gaps and address public apprehensions. By doing so, we can assist policymakers and foster balanced technological progress. Therefore, identifying pertinent issues is crucial before devising appropriate solutions. While academia excels at problem identification, as evidenced by 300,000 research publications, the lack of widespread drone integration suggests that not all identified problems are pertinent. This article seeks to provide a comprehensive examination of drone technology, evaluating issues that matter to all key stakeholders in technological development. This study builds on the foundations of Technology Assessment (TA), an interdisciplinary field aimed at delivering insights for well-informed decision-making regarding new technologies \cite{gw09}. TA offers valuable information to stakeholders, including policymakers, citizens, and engineers, aiding in strategy and action plan development \cite{TA_toolkit_98}. It can be applied to specific technical products, processes, services, and systems \cite{gw09}, and is utilized by various agencies and commissions within the European Union, the U.S. Government Accountability Office, and national research councils. Countries such as China, New Zealand, Italy, and Canada employ TA extensively in sensitive domains like healthcare. In this article, we leverage TA to pinpoint critical issues and evaluate existing solutions aimed at resolving these challenges. Through this approach, we highlight pertinent research directions for the wireless communications community. Additionally, TA provides methodologies for defining the scope and framework of research and development projects, enhancing project efficiency by considering factors such as project nature and technology readiness.

text: The COVID-19 pandemic has significantly accelerated the use of telehealth services \cite{Wosik2020}, resulting in an over 100\% rise in virtual urgent care visits and an astonishing more than 4000\% surge in virtual non-urgent care visits \cite{telemedicine}. Typically, a virtual consultation begins with the patient articulating the reason for their visit (RFE) \cite{who}. Subsequently, an automated history-taking algorithm gathers additional details about the symptoms presented, after which the patient is connected to a healthcare provider through video or text chat. This paper delves into an essential intermediate step: detecting symptoms within the patient's RFE, a crucial element for automated history taking. This task is akin to medical named entity recognition, which aims to extract symptoms from clinical texts in electronic health records (see \cite{Baumel18} and related works). However, our focus is on recognizing medical entities from patient-generated text, as RFEs tend to be less standardized and often describe symptoms in everyday language. Figure ~\ref{fig:ml4hp} illustrates sample RFEs from the dataset utilized in our study. Developing a model for recognizing medical symptoms involves several challenges: \begin{enumerate} \item \textbf{Access}: Due to the lack of publicly available datasets, any new telehealth platform aiming to develop a machine learning solution must begin with a limited set of labeled data and rapidly expand its dataset. As more data points are labeled, the system must adapt to identify newly emerging symptoms. \item \textbf{Multilabel distribution}: RFEs may contain multiple symptoms, and it is crucial to extract \emph{all} of them to ensure accurate automated history taking. \item \textbf{Long-tailed distribution}: While some symptoms are prevalent, others co-occur less frequently, creating an asymmetric, long-tailed data distribution (Figure~\ref{fig:ml4hp}). This complexity is further compounded by the diverse patient demographics using the telehealth platform. \end{enumerate} In response to these challenges, we introduce a novel active learning algorithm designed to efficiently gather data labels. The core idea of our approach is that RFEs form distinct clusters reflective of underlying health conditions. Our algorithm strategically selects informative examples by clustering unlabeled data points in a latent space and choosing those that best represent each cluster. By balancing the selection of points near cluster centroids with those distant from already labeled RFEs, we address the issue of long-tailed distribution. Our experimental results demonstrate that our model surpasses current state-of-the-art methods in multi-label classification tasks and effectively manages the long-tailed distribution present in our dataset. Further insights into the benefits of our approach are provided through ablation studies and qualitative analyses. \subsection*{Generalizable Insights about Machine Learning in the Context of Healthcare} In recent years, deep learning has been increasingly applied across various healthcare domains. A significant challenge in employing deep learning for healthcare applications is the scarcity of large annotated datasets. Collecting such datasets is often costly and time-consuming since annotations must be provided by healthcare experts, and sharing datasets between institutions is challenging due to the sensitive nature of the data. Conversely, deep learning models typically require extensive datasets to achieve high accuracy and robustness. Consequently, many AI applications in healthcare remain inaccessible, delaying their potential real-world impact. Previous active learning research has predominantly focused on classification tasks with balanced datasets. However, in numerous healthcare applications, datasets exhibit a long-tailed distribution, necessitating the identification of all relevant labels rather than a single correct class. Additionally, traditional active learning strategies generally assume a single valid label per data point. Our research emphasizes the critical importance of "multilabel" classification, where multiple correct labels may exist for a single data point. Accurately identifying all labels for each data point is crucial for the subsequent history-taking process. We propose a novel algorithm that actively selects the most informative examples for labeling in multi-label classification tasks. Our method leverages the machine learning model's latent space to address the long-tailed data distribution and to select a diverse set of data points, thereby encompassing a broad spectrum of inputs.

text: The quest to enable autonomous robots to tackle a wide range of intricate manipulation tasks has been a formidable challenge for many years. Recently, deep reinforcement learning (DRL) methods have achieved significant progress in crafting robotic manipulation behaviors that are traditionally challenging to engineer by hand~\cite{kalashnikov2018qtopt, openai2019learning,openai2019solving,kalashnikov2021mtopt}. Despite these advancements, the most advanced DRL models struggle with tasks that require long-term planning due to the exploration problem—robots must navigate an overwhelmingly large array of potential behaviors to complete a task. To alleviate this exploration burden, previous DRL research has proposed various frameworks for temporal abstraction that leverage the hierarchical nature of manipulation tasks~\cite{coreyes18sectar,nachum2018hiro,bacon2016optioncritic,eysenbach2019sorb}. These frameworks typically involve learning low-level controllers, referred to as \textit{skills} or \textit{options}, alongside high-level controllers through trial-and-error. While these methods offer improved scalability compared to basic DRL methods, they often encounter issues such as high sample complexity, poor interpretability, and fragile generalization. Simultaneously, decades of research in robotics have produced a comprehensive array of functional modules tailored for specific robotic behaviors, such as grasping~\cite{bohg2014graspsurvey} and motion planning~\cite{karaman2011rrtstar,ijspeert2013dmps}. These pre-existing functional modules, which we term \emph{behavior primitives}, are highly robust and reusable for achieving certain manipulation objectives, like picking up objects with an end-effector or navigating a robot to a target position via a collision-free path. Despite their specialized capabilities, integrating these behavior primitives as foundational elements for complex task construction in DRL algorithms remains a challenge. This difficulty arises mainly because these behavior primitives are inherently \textit{heterogeneous}. They require diverse input parameters, function at different temporal scales, and exhibit unique behaviors, necessitating an algorithm capable of decomposing a complex task into temporal segments and adaptively composing these behavior primitives. Numerous hierarchical modeling techniques in robotics have employed behavior modules as foundational components. Notably, task-and-motion planning~\cite{kaelbling2011hpn, garrett2020tamp, wang2021comptamp} and neural programming~\cite{xu2018neural, huang2019neural} approaches have utilized primitives like motion planners and pick-and-place controllers to model manipulation tasks in a compositional manner. These methods often rely on precise domain knowledge for task planning or require substantial human oversight to train a high-level controller with accurate task decomposition, which constrains their scalability in real-world tasks. In this study, we present MAPLE~(\textbf{Ma}nipulation \textbf{P}rimitive-augmented reinforcement \textbf{Le}arning), a versatile DRL algorithm that leverages a set of pre-configured behavior primitives to address long-horizon manipulation tasks. To tackle the exploration challenges inherent in DRL algorithms, our approach employs a library of high-level behavior primitives (like grasping or object pushing) alongside low-level motor actions to autonomously develop a hierarchical policy (refer to \cref{fig:overview}). Our algorithm conceptualizes each behavior primitive as a controller that is agnostic to its implementation but capable of generating temporally extended behaviors. At any given state, our DRL policy selects a behavior primitive (or an atomic motor action) and configures it with input parameters. For instance, the input parameters for a 6-DoF grasping module might include the pre-grasp end-effector pose. The chosen primitive then interprets these parameters and executes one or several motor actions to fulfill its designated behavior. By integrating behavior primitives into DRL frameworks, MAPLE mitigates a significant portion of the complexity in manipulation planning while allowing a generic reinforcement learning algorithm the freedom to uncover the compositional structure of tasks without extensive domain expertise. Additionally, by maintaining low-level motor actions, MAPLE can resort to these actions for task phases where the finite set of behavior primitives cannot adequately express the desired behavior. We conduct comprehensive experiments on a collection of eight manipulation tasks with varying complexity levels within the robosuite simulation environment~\cite{robosuite2020}. We compare our approach with standard DRL techniques~\cite{haarnoja2018sac} that rely solely on low-level motor actions, hierarchical DRL methods that learn options~\cite{zhang2019dac,nachum2018hiro,chitnis2020schema}, or open-loop task schemas~\cite{chitnis2020schema}. MAPLE achieves a $70\%$ improvement in task success rate compared to using only atomic actions and is the only method consistently solving all single-arm tasks in the standard robosuite benchmark. We also introduce a data-driven metric to quantitatively assess the compositionality of manipulation tasks based on the available primitives, providing fresh insights into the challenges and potential of compositional modeling for realistic manipulation tasks. Our work offers three primary contributions: 1) We propose an innovative method that enhances standard DRL algorithms with predefined behavior primitives to ease the exploration burden; 2) We demonstrate the efficacy of our approach in addressing diverse manipulation tasks and quantitatively examine the compositional structure of these tasks; and 3) We illustrate that the modularity and abstraction provided by behavior primitives facilitate the transfer of learned policies to new task variations and physical hardware.

In this study, we present MAPLE (Manipulation via Premia-augmented Reinforcement Learning), a flexible reinforcement learning method which uses a set of pre-defined behavior primitives to solve long-term manipulation tasks. Notably, task and motion planning, e.g., kaelbling2011hpn, garrett2020tamp, wang2020comptamp, and neural-program approaches, e.g., xu2018neural, huang2019neural, and a large amount of human guidance to train a high-level controller with an accurate task decomposition, which limits their scalability in the real world. Our approach consists of a library of high-level behavior primitives (such as grasping or pushing objects) and lower-level motor actions that can be used to form a hierarchical policy (see the overview in Fig. 3). Our DRL policy selects a behavior primitive or an atomic action for a given state, and imposes on it the required inputs. Our behavior primitives are conceived as controllers, agnostic to their implementation, and capable of generating temporally extended behaviors. text: \input{images/figure1} Natural language processing (NLP) systems have been developed for only a small subset of the world's more than 6,000 living languages. The primary barrier is the scarcity of resources necessary for training and evaluating models. Technological advancements tend to focus on languages with abundant data, leaving many others, particularly endangered languages, neglected~\cite{joshi2020state}. Endangered languages face the threat of extinction due to a declining number of native speakers and younger generations adopting other languages. For these languages, obtaining \emph{any} form of data is a significant challenge. While text in these languages may exist, it is often inaccessible in non-machine-readable formats such as paper books, scanned images, and unstructured web pages. These include publications from local presses within communities speaking endangered languages, encompassing educational and cultural materials. Additionally, linguists working on these languages produce data like word lists and interlinear glosses, frequently recorded as handwritten notes. Some examples from scanned documents are illustrated in~\autoref{fig:dataset_example}. Converting this textual data into digital form can facilitate NLP applications for endangered languages and support efforts in linguistic documentation, preservation, and accessibility. In this study, we develop a benchmark dataset and introduce a series of methods to extract data from these sources, with a focus on scanned images of paper books containing endangered language text. Typically, this digitization process involves optical character recognition (OCR) systems. However, the large volumes of text and transcribed images required to train advanced OCR models from scratch are not available for endangered languages. Therefore, we concentrate on \emph{post-correcting} the results of an existing OCR tool that supports multiple scripts. We demonstrate that specialized post-correction techniques can substantially enhance performance for endangered languages. Although OCR post-correction has been extensively researched, most current approaches depend on significant resources in the target language, including ample text data for training a language model~\cite{schnober-etal-2016-still,dong-smith-2018-multi,8978127} or creating synthetic data~\cite{krishna-etal-2018-upcycle}. While such resources are readily available for high-resource languages, they are severely limited for endangered languages, making it impractical to directly apply existing post-correction methods in our context. To address this, we propose a method building on previous OCR post-correction models with three enhancements suited to a data-scarce environment. First, we employ a \textbf{multi-source model} to leverage information from high-resource translations commonly found in endangered language books. These translations are typically in the regional \textit{lingua franca} (e.g., \autoref{fig:dataset_example} (a,b,c)) or the primary language of the documenting linguist (e.g., \autoref{fig:dataset_example} (d) from \citet{shangaji-elar}). Next, we introduce \textbf{structural biases} to facilitate learning from limited data. Finally, we incorporate \textbf{pretraining methods} to exploit the minimal unannotated data available in endangered languages. \medskip \noindent We summarize our main contributions as follows: \begin{itemize}[leftmargin=*, itemsep=3pt] \item We present a benchmark dataset for OCR post-correction in three critically endangered languages: Ainu, Griko, and Yakkha. \item We conduct a systematic evaluation of a general-purpose OCR system, revealing its lack of robustness in the data-scarce context of endangered languages. \item We propose an OCR post-correction method that adapts the standard neural encoder-decoder framework to the highly under-resourced setting of endangered languages, achieving a 34\% reduction in both character error rate and word error rate compared to a state-of-the-art general-purpose OCR system. \end{itemize}

text: Navigating real-world driving environments, which are dynamic and populated by various entities such as non-player characters (NPCs), inherently involves risk. Each entity within this environment can substantially impact the driving decisions of the Ego actor\footnote{The actor being tested and controlled by the experimenter.}, potentially constraining their available options for navigation and safety strategies. In certain instances, these entities may inadvertently or deliberately obstruct the Ego actor's ability to safely execute their task. Consequently, every entity presents a potential risk to the Ego actor. This paper aims to define the risk posed by an entity by evaluating its impact on the decision-making process of the Ego actor within a specific environment. The risk, therefore, is contingent on two primary factors: \begin{enumerate*}[label=(\roman*)] \item the characteristics of the environment (i.e., driving scenario), and \item the uncertainty involved in predicting the Ego actor's future trajectories. \end{enumerate*} \textbf{Driving scenario.} The driving scenario includes the initial positioning of the Ego actor and the paths of NPCs. With each additional NPC, the safe paths available to the Ego actor (i.e., the navigable space) can become significantly limited. Furthermore, some locations within the environment are inherently riskier than others due to variations in navigable space, such as areas under construction. This reduction in safe paths correlates with increased risk, necessitating heightened attention and reducing fallback options for the Ego actor in unexpected situations, as depicted in \cref{fig:motivation}(a). \textbf{Uncertainty.} The risk escalates when the Ego actor cannot accurately predict the future movements of NPCs. Prediction accuracy diminishes due to unclear intentions or sudden changes in the behavior of other participants (e.g., pedestrians abruptly stopping or running, emergency braking, or vehicle breakdowns), measurement inaccuracies (e.g., adverse weather conditions), or flaws in ML/AI models (e.g., failure to detect a pedestrian). This is illustrated in \cref{fig:motivation}(b). It is important to recognize that human drivers instinctively and continuously evaluate the risks associated with both the driving scenario and the uncertainties in other actors' actions to maintain safety. Accidents occur when drivers fail to adequately assess these risks, which can happen due to distractions, insufficient driving skills, or unexpected actions by other actors that violate traffic rules or involve sudden maneuvers (e.g., abrupt braking). The presence of aleatoric and epistemic noise amplifies these risks for AI/ML-driven actors. Therefore, it is crucial to develop methodologies and models that can quantify and characterize these risks in real-time. This not only ensures safety by minimizing risk but also helps identify situations where risk is unavoidable, allowing preparations such as emergency braking or airbag deployment to protect passengers during imminent collisions. In this paper, we highlight the practical significance of a risk metric and its role in ensuring safety. Our main contributions include the introduction of a novel risk metric and demonstrating its application in quantifying the relative risk associated with each actor in a real-world driving scenario. While this paper focuses on self-driving cars as a use case, our framework is versatile and can be extended to other autonomous systems, such as aerial vehicles or AI-driven computer systems. \textbf{Related work.} Research related to defensive driving primarily focuses on two areas: (i) determining safe distances from other entities based on adherence to "duty-of-care" policies, and (ii) identifying out-of-training-distribution (OOD) scenarios to plan for worst-case collision avoidance. \textit{Duty-of-care approaches}, like the Safety Force Field (SFF)~\cite{SafetyForceField} and Responsibility-Sensitive Safety (RSS)~\cite{shalev2017formal}, aim to estimate safe distances assuming all entities comply with traffic rules. Additionally, these approaches seek to identify responsible parties in safety incidents. \textit{OOD} models, such as those in \cite{pmlr-v119-filos20a}, focus on identifying driving scenarios where the Ego actor's future trajectory exhibits significant variance, which can be assessed using model ensembles or diverse data. In high-variance situations, the Ego actor opts for the most conservative plan to avoid collisions. For instance, in \cite{pmlr-v119-filos20a}, the Ego actor's plan is generated using a Bayesian imitative model, with the imitation prior's variance relative to the model posterior serving as a proxy for detecting distribution shifts. Upon detecting a shift, the Ego actor can choose between a worst-case or average model plan. Another research direction~\cite{Philion_2020_CVPR} quantifies the impact of uncertainty on driving performance but does not assess the safety quality of the generated plan. In contrast, our objective is to (i) assign risk to an actor or driving scenario by evaluating its adverse impact on the Ego actor's navigational freedom, and (ii) quantify the risk associated with the current plan to proactively address safety hazards. This approach enables the identification of intriguing driving scenarios in offline mode and the selection of the safest plan to assist the Ego actor in defensive driving.

text: Knowledge graphs (KGs) are semantic structures that encapsulate facts in a graph format, and they have been effectively utilized in numerous AI tasks such as recommendation systems~\cite{leiconversational,2021Learning}, dialogue generation~\cite{moon-etal-2019-opendialkg,leiinteractive}, and question answering~\cite{ChristmannRASW19,zhu2021retrieving}. In these graphs, facts are represented as triples, \texttt{(head~entity, relation, tail~entity)}, signifying a connection from the head entity to the tail entity through a specific relation. As knowledge continuously evolves, KGs often face incompleteness, sparking significant interest in the link prediction task, which aims to infer missing connections within KGs~\cite{simple}. Predominant link prediction models~\cite{bordes2013translating,Dettmers2018Convolutional} typically learn embeddings for entities and relations, employing a scoring function to evaluate triple validity. However, we contend that embedding methods in mainstream link prediction models encounter two primary challenges: \begin{itemize}[leftmargin=*] \item[\small$\bullet$] \textit{Unbalanced relation distribution.} As illustrated in Figure~\ref{fig:intro}, the distribution of relations in common KG datasets, such as FB15K-237~\cite{toutanova-chen-2015-observed}, is notably skewed. For instance, the occurrences of relations like \texttt{/film/film/language} and \texttt{/film/film/edited} vary significantly. Mainstream models presume ample training data for all relations, often neglecting few-shot relations, which can severely impact learning performance. \item[\small$\bullet$] \textit{Existence of unseen relations.} Real-world KGs are dynamic and rapidly expanding, leading to numerous zero-shot relations absent in standard datasets, such as \texttt{/film/film/sequel} in Figure~\ref{fig:intro}. These unseen relations challenge mainstream models, which lack training samples to derive their embeddings, potentially limiting their application in downstream tasks. \end{itemize} Recent research efforts have begun tackling these issues. Approaches by \citet{Xiongoneshot}, \citet{shi2018open}, and \citet{ChenMeta} employ meta-learning or metric-based strategies to train with limited samples, facilitating rapid learning on new few-shot relations. Although promising for few-shot learning, these methods struggle with unbalanced relation distributions due to the extensive time required to train numerous relations. More recent works by \citet{DBLP:journals/corr/abs-1907-08937} and \citet{Qin2020GenerativeAZ} address unseen relations by leveraging information from textual descriptions, successfully completing prediction tasks for these relations. However, these models are unsuitable for link prediction tasks, as textual descriptions can be noisy and fail to connect seen and unseen relations effectively. Ideally, a link prediction model should seamlessly integrate learning across many-, few-, and zero-shot relations. In the context of joint relation learning, semantic correlations—indicating relational similarities—can bridge the learning of various relation types. For example, in Figure~\ref{fig:intro}, the many-shot relation \texttt{/film/film/language}, the few-shot relation \texttt{/film/film/edited}, and the zero-shot relation \texttt{/film/film/sequel} all pertain to "film." Assuming semantically similar relations should cluster in embedding space~\cite{yang2014embedding}, exploiting such correlations can facilitate joint relation learning. Inspired by this, we introduce a \textbf{G}eneralized \textbf{R}elation \textbf{L}earning (GRL) framework, designed to learn semantic correlations. GRL can be integrated into mainstream link prediction models, enhancing their resilience to unbalanced distributions and enabling zero-shot relation learning. Specifically, GRL is incorporated into a link prediction model post-embedding learning. It optimizes relation embeddings by extracting rich semantic correlations through an attention mechanism, merging different relations, and minimizing classification-aware loss to embed these correlations implicitly. This approach enhances the proximity of similar relations in vector space while distinguishing dissimilar ones, allowing few-shot relations to learn from semantically similar many-shot relations and enabling predictions for zero-shot relations. In our experiments, we enhance two base models, DistMult~\cite{yang2014embedding} and ConvE~\cite{Dettmers2018Convolutional}, by implementing the GRL framework across all relation categories. Our work advances a comprehensive understanding of KGs and offers a generalized solution for relation learning in link prediction tasks. Our contributions are summarized as follows: \begin{itemize}[leftmargin=*] \item[\small$\bullet$] We address two critical issues in embedding learning for mainstream link prediction models, emphasizing the importance of joint learning for many-, few-, and zero-shot relations. \item[\small$\bullet$] We propose the GRL framework, leveraging rich semantic correlations to make link prediction models robust to unbalanced distributions and capable of zero-shot relation learning. \item[\small$\bullet$] We conduct experiments on six benchmarks to assess GRL's link prediction effectiveness, demonstrating that GRL enables base models to excel across many-, few-, and zero-shot relations. \end{itemize}

text: In the realm of autonomous agents, trajectory planning frequently employs a receding time horizon approach. This is particularly crucial in environments where multiple agents interact, such as in autonomous driving scenarios. Here, plans must not only anticipate future states but also incorporate collision-avoidance strategies by predicting the future actions of other agents. A significant challenge arises because the resulting motion plans of the "ego" vehicle do not account for how other agents might react to its movements. A classic problem illustrating this is an autonomous vehicle's difficulty in merging into heavy traffic due to its inability to predict that other drivers might create space. Game-theoretic motion planners address this issue by integrating planning and prediction. They represent the intentions of other agents as optimization problems each agent seeks to solve, culminating in an equilibrium solution. This equilibrium comprises a network of interdependent trajectories for all agents, allowing the ego agent to adhere to its equilibrium path. However, a major limitation of game-theoretic planning is its reliance on the assumption that the ego agent is aware of other agents' intentions and that these agents act rationally according to these intentions. In real-world scenarios, outside strict game-theoretic contexts, these intentions can be estimated in real-time and planned for as potential contingencies \cite{hardy2013contingency}. This paper tackles this issue within the framework of game-theoretic planning by introducing a multi-hypothesis approach that incorporates this uncertainty and the resulting interdependencies. Specifically, our method presumes that the ego agent maintains a discrete set of hypotheses about the intentions of other agents, each associated with a probability. These hypotheses capture uncertainties such as potential lane changes, typical speeds, and aversion to acceleration. To handle such uncertainties, we propose formulating distinct optimization problems for each agent. When solved, these problems yield trajectories that qualitatively reflect the various hypotheses. We create replicas of each agent, corresponding to each hypothesis, and assign them to the appropriate optimization problem. We propose an innovative formulation of the resulting dynamic game, enabling the ego agent to consider interactions with replica agents based on the probability of their respective hypotheses. This approach is pivotal in addressing collision-avoidance constraints from a probabilistic perspective. This modeling strategy provides a practical solution to this category of motion-planning challenges faced by autonomous vehicles. Our method generates interactive trajectories among multiple agents while explicitly considering the uncertainty in others' intentions. We anticipate that our approach will facilitate more effective application of game-theoretic planning in autonomous vehicle contexts. The structure of this paper is as follows. \cref{sec:related_work} explores alternative multi-agent planning methods, including game-theoretic approaches and those utilizing rational choice model derivatives that account for agent uncertainty. \cref{sec:preliminaries} reviews game-theoretic planning concepts essential for formalizing our method, which is detailed in \cref{sec:methods}. In \cref{sec:results}, we present empirical evaluations of our method across various realistic driving scenarios, concluding with final observations in \cref{sec:conclusion}.

text: The task of recognizing speech from multiple speakers, particularly when their voices overlap naturally in far-field environments, has long posed a significant challenge in research \cite{Hain2007_AMI,fox13b_interspeech,Liu2016_SWC2,Barker_2018}. This issue, often termed the "cocktail party problem," is crucial for advancing speech technology and establishing seamless human-device voice interactions. In these interactions, smart devices' speech agents must adeptly manage multi-party dialogues to offer necessary assistance. To facilitate real-time interaction, the \ac{ASR} system must be capable of streaming transcriptions for all speakers involved. Furthermore, to enhance privacy, these systems should operate locally on the device, necessitating models that are both lightweight and resilient to acoustic limitations. These considerations underscore the need for streaming speech recognition systems that can handle an arbitrary number of speakers with overlapping speech using only a single distant microphone. Historically, multi-speaker \ac{ASR} employed a series of modules, such as speech separation followed by recognition \cite{Isik_2016, Menne_2019, Settle_2018, von_Neumann_2020, Neumann_2020}. However, due to their complexity and certain technical constraints, these systems are better suited for offline use, where the complete audio is available prior to transcription. Recent advancements have focused on training unified models that directly enhance multi-speaker ASR performance \cite{Yu_2017_icassp, Yu_2017_interspeech, Qian_2018, Seki_2018, Chang_2019, Tripathi_2020}. A notable development by \cite{k2020serialized} introduced a joint approach for multi-speaker speech recognition and speaker change detection using \ac{SOT}, demonstrating its efficacy on simulated multi-speaker datasets like LibriSpeechMix. Subsequent research by \cite{kanda2021largescale} validated \ac{SOT}'s effectiveness on real-world multi-speaker meeting corpora, and further studies \cite{kanda2020joint, kanda2021slt, kanda2021endtoend, kanda2021comparative} expanded \ac{SOT} into speaker-attributed ASR, enabling comprehensive transcription of "who spoke what" using a single model. Concurrently, research has shifted towards maintaining performance under streaming conditions. Two similar streaming multi-speaker ASR models, \ac{MS-RNN-T} \cite{SklyarPiunovaLiu_streaming_rnnt_icassp2021} and \ac{SURT} \cite{Lu2021}, built on \ac{RNN-T} \cite{graves2012sequence}, were developed to support time-synchronous decoding of overlapping speech. The model in \cite{Lu2021} was later enhanced with speaker identification \cite{lu2021streaming}. \cite{SklyarPiunovaLiu_streaming_rnnt_icassp2021} evaluated \ac{MS-RNN-T} on single-speaker LibriSpeech and two-speaker LibriSpeechMix, showing it matches offline multi-speaker ASR systems' performance on two-speaker tests and boosts system robustness for noisy single-speaker test partitions in LibriSpeech. Building on \cite{SklyarPiunovaLiu_streaming_rnnt_icassp2021}, this paper presents several contributions. Firstly, we demonstrate the benefits of dynamically simulating overlapping speech during training over using fixed pre-simulated data, achieving a new low \ac{WER} on the two-speaker LibriSpeechMix partition with a streamable model. Secondly, we tackle the primary limitation of \ac{MS-RNN-T}, which is its fixed speaker count constraint. By assuming up to two overlapping speakers at any time, the proposed \ac{MT-RNN-T} model can recognize speech from any number of speakers. Additionally, we take initial steps towards streaming comprehensive transcriptions of multi-party conversations by introducing segmentation tags. Lastly, we provide an in-depth performance analysis using new evaluation metrics, \ac{ORC} WER and turn counting accuracy, while discussing potential avenues for future research.

text: \vspace{-0.2cm} Over the past decade, embedding models have become foundational algorithms in various machine learning domains, including Information Retrieval (IR)~\citep{croft2010search,baeza1999modern} and Natural Language Processing (NLP)~\citep{word2vec, glove, attention, bert}. These models have evolved from low-rank approximation and Matrix Factorization techniques which previously led the field of recommendation systems before the rise of Deep Learning (DL). The main goal of embedding models is to transform inputs into a simplified, intuitive representation within an abstract low-dimensional dense vector space. This transformation serves two key purposes: 1) customizing vectors for specific downstream tasks, and 2) enabling efficient pre-processing and storage of documents or products as vectors, thereby streamlining the retrieval process through operations like matrix multiplication and sorting—tasks that are well-suited for modern hardware such as GPUs. Beyond computational efficiency, embedding models excel at capturing semantic relationships between queries and products. Consider the example of a product search service like Amazon. When a user enters a query, it must be matched against millions of products, with the best results displayed almost instantaneously. With raw product data, it would be challenging to determine that products with 'aqua' in their titles are relevant to the query 'water'. By projecting products into a dense low-dimensional vector space, both the query and products can be represented in the same space, allowing for inner product calculations (typically a dot product) with all product vectors. Products with the highest inner product values can then be displayed. These projections are designed to encapsulate semantic information and can be continuously updated to reflect changes in customer preferences over time. Embedding models are widely used in the industry, particularly for product and advertisement recommendations, as evidenced by systems like Amazon's DSSM~\citep{dssm} and Facebook's DLRM~\citep{dlrm}. Nonetheless, the scale of these challenges has dramatically increased in recent years, leading to research in extreme classification tasks where the number of classes can reach several million. Consequently, alternative approaches such as Tree-based Models~\citep{prabhu2014fastxml,Pfastre,agrawal2013multi} and Sparse-linear Models~\citep{weston2013label,pdsparse,ppdsparse} have gained traction. Notably, Tree-based models offer faster training and evaluation compared to other methods. However, most real-world Information Retrieval systems face dynamically changing output classes, and extreme classification models struggle to generalize to new classes with limited training data (\emph{e.g.}, new products added daily). This has led to a renewed interest in embedding models for large-scale Extreme Classification~\citep{bi2013efficient,annexml,sleec,chen2012feature}. {\bf Our Contributions:} This paper presents a novel and compelling argument that sparse high-dimensional embeddings surpass their dense low-dimensional counterparts. We introduce two innovative design choices: 1) We configure the label embeddings (\emph{e.g.}, products in the catalog) to be high-dimensional, super-sparse, and orthogonal vectors. 2) We maintain fixed label embeddings throughout the training process, focusing solely on learning the input embeddings (one-sided learning), unlike traditional dense models where both input and label embeddings are learned. By employing a combination of {\bf S}parse, {\bf O}rthogonal, {\bf L}earned, and {\bf R}andom embeddings, we dub our method {\bf SOLAR}. We establish a theoretical foundation for SOLAR, demonstrating the mathematical equivalence of one-sided and two-sided learning. Our approach offers four distinct advantages over previous methods: \begin{itemize}[leftmargin=*,nosep,nolistsep] \itemsep0em \item {\bf Matrix Multiplication to Inverted-Index Lookup:} Sparse high-dimensional embeddings allow for the retrieval of a subset of labels through a simple inverted-index~\citep{croft2010search} lookup, limiting computation and sorting to those labels, thereby significantly enhancing inference speed. \item {\bf Load-balanced Inverted Index:} By ensuring label embeddings are near-orthogonal and equally sparse, and keeping them fixed, we achieve equal distribution across all buckets in an inverted index, sampling a similar number of labels for each input. This addresses the common issue of imbalanced buckets where popular inputs lead to subsampling nearly all labels, compromising inference speed. \item {\bf Learning to Hash:} An Inverted-Index functions as a hash table where output classes are hashed into a few buckets~\citep{kulis2009learning, wang2017survey}. By fixing label buckets and learning to map inputs to these buckets, we effectively perform a 'partial learning to hash' task (further details in Appendix A). \item {\bf Zero-communication:} Our unique label embedding design facilitates distributed training across multiple GPUs without requiring communication. This capability allows us to train on a 1.67 M book recommendation dataset and the three largest extreme classification datasets, outperforming respective baselines in both precision and speed. \end{itemize} \vspace{-0.5cm}

text: In today's knowledge-driven economy, vast quantities of data are amassed to facilitate decision-making, policy analysis, service provision, and more. Nevertheless, the utility of such data is often limited by the potential for disclosure risks during data processing, especially when data is shared. Anonymisation is a key strategy employed to mitigate these risks. The Anonymisation Decision-Making Framework (ADF) implements the processes of functional anonymisation \cite{elliot2018functional}. This framework emerged from the work of the \textit{data environment analysis service} \cite{elliot2010data}, a support system designed for the 2011 UK census, which concentrated on data confidentiality and disclosure control \cite{willenborg2012elements,duncan2011concepts,hundepool2012SDC}, with a particular focus on re-identification risk assessment \cite{chen1998, skinner1998estimating,skinner2002measure}. The core premise is that disclosure risk is not inherent in the data itself but rather in the interaction between the data and the surrounding environment. Mackey and Elliot describe the data environment as "the set of formal and informal structures, processes, mechanisms, and agents that either: (i) act on data; (ii) provide interpretable context for those data; or (iii) define, control, and/or interact with those data" \cite{mackey2013understanding}. Data environments can vary widely, including open data environments, end-user license management environments, and secure data environments with restricted access, among others. Despite this diversity, the ADF framework posits that all data environments can be characterized by four fundamental features: other data, agents, infrastructure, and governance. Consequently, to apply effective anonymisation processes, it is crucial to consider both the data and their environmental context. Elliot et al. \cite{elliot2020anonymisation} developed the ADF to operationalise such considerations. The ADF underscores that appropriate anonymisation decisions for any dataset can only be made by examining the relationship between the data and its environment, referred to as the \textit{data situation}.\\ \vspace{-12pt} \textbf{\textit{Problem statement}.} \textit{Data situations are frequently dynamic, as data transition between environments for processing and usage. Thus, comprehending contextual risk and managing it through anonymisation necessitates an understanding of, and ability to map, the data flows between environments.} Currently, the manual process of capturing and mapping \textit{data situations} for analysis within the ADF framework is labor-intensive and susceptible to errors. To automate this mapping, we propose leveraging data provenance—a concept informally referenced in the ADF. By integrating provenance with the ADF, we can track data flows and identify both existing and proposed upstream and downstream data situations. Notably, data provenance has been utilized in modeling similar challenges, such as situation awareness and decision-making \cite{baclawski2017framework}, controlling direct and indirect data flows \cite{rong2020provenance}, and ensuring big data security and privacy \cite{gao2020big}. W3C PROV is a standard for provenance interoperability, detailing the origins of data and its processing history \cite{PROV-DM15,missier2013w3c}. PROV provides an abstract data model encompassing agents, entities, activities, and relationship properties, enabling the representation of data and system provenance. A crucial aspect of linking provenance to the ADF is representing data environments. Within the W3C PROV data model, the constructs \textit{bundles} and \textit{namespaces} may serve as potential candidates for this representation. This paper explores the viability of these solutions and considers how PROV elements (i.e., Entity, Bundle, Agent, Activity) could represent data environment features (agents, other data, infrastructure, governance). We acknowledge limitations in representing data environments this way and propose modifications to fully capture the desired features. The contributions of this work are as follows: \vspace{-12pt} \begin{enumerate} \item We detail—using an ADF use case—the requirements for provenance in representing data environments (in section \ref{sec:usecase}). \item Based on these requirements, we propose four distinct approaches to apply and extend W3C PROV for representing data environments to enable machine-enabled reasoning (in section \ref{sec:impl}). \item We subsequently analyze these four approaches (in section \ref{sec:analysis}). \end{enumerate}

text: This study aims to develop a system capable of maintaining an \emph{audit trail} for the knowledge representation (KR) framework, which is structured around graph hierarchies as introduced in \cite{harmer2020knowledge}. The system is intended to chronicle the evolution of a vast knowledge corpus, represented by graphs and their hierarchies, through primarily small, localized updates, without the impracticality of storing the entire corpus at each historical juncture. While the transformations required for our application need to be reversible, this does not limit the range of operations available for updating the corpus. Instead, it introduces a manageable overhead for storing supplementary data that facilitates the reversal of transformations. Additionally, we propose mechanisms for sustaining multiple corpus versions, which is vital for capturing diverse knowledge perspectives or inherent conflicts, such as contradictory experimental findings or alternative hypotheses. Key applications of audit trails in KR based on graph hierarchies include version control for schema-aware graph database updates as discussed in \cite{bonifati2019schema}, and modifications to knowledge corpora within the bio-curation framework KAMI \cite{harmer2019bio}. The envisioned audit trail system hinges on several core components: (1) the \emph{efficient semantic representation of object transformations} (or deltas), which eliminates the need to store the object's state at each transformation stage; (2) the \emph{reversibility of transformations}, ensuring any transformation sequence can be undone; and (3) robust methods for \emph{composing successive transformations}, enabling efficient storage and navigation between different object versions. This paper delineates these components as they pertain to individual objects (Section \ref{s:preliminaries}), such as graphs, and to hierarchies of objects (Section \ref{s:rulehierarchy}), and explores their application in constructing an effective audit trail (Section \ref{s:audit}). We introduce a mathematical framework for documenting transformation histories through the sesqui-pushout (SqPO) approach \cite{corradini2006sesqui}, which operates on individual objects and object hierarchies within suitably structured categories. A clear audit trail offers visibility into the transformation history and facilitates reverting to any point within it, a feature invaluable for correcting erroneous transformations. Furthermore, such a trail supports the efficient management of multiple object versions, which may emerge from inconsistent transformations. \subsection*{Related work} SqPO rewriting extends the double (DPO) and single (SPO) pushout methods for graph transformation by incorporating graph element cloning alongside the more conventional operations of addition, deletion, and merging. Although the reversibility of SqPO rewriting has been explored \cite{danos2014reversible}, the composition of consecutive SqPO rewrites, which may not be sequentially independent, is less developed. Compositions have been constructed for the DPO approach (see D-concurrent productions in \cite{ehrig1991parallelism}) and for specific SqPO cases (where rules are linear \cite{behr2019sesqui} and where the right-hand side of the first rule matches the left-hand side of the second \cite{lowe2015polymorphic}). This paper presents a construction for two consecutive applications of general SqPO rules, requiring the first to be reversible, drawing inspiration from \cite{ehrig1991parallelism} and adapting it to SqPO rewriting. To ensure well-defined compositions, the underlying category must support well-behaved generalized unions of objects, necessitating an adhesive category structure \cite{lack2005adhesive}. The concept of rule hierarchy and the exploration of hierarchy rewrite reversibility and composition represent a novel extension of SqPO rewriting from individual objects to object hierarchies \cite{harmer2020knowledge}. Our primary interest lies in a transformation audit trail akin to version control systems (VCSs) used in software development. While VCSs typically manage software source code versions (represented as text files), our audit trail provides similar control over graph or graph hierarchy versions. Like VCSs, the transformation audit trail avoids recording the object's state at each transformation by maintaining only the current state along with a compact transformation history. Through a mechanism resembling \emph{delta compression} in VCSs, these audit trails facilitate the management of multiple object versions and transitions between them. Versioning in model-driven engineering, particularly for diagrams representing object-oriented data models, relates closely to graph transformation audit trails, as such diagrams can be viewed as graphs with attributes. However, work in this area \cite{schneider2004coobra, barmpis2015towards} typically focuses on adding and deleting graph elements, including attributes, to reflect data model changes, often neglecting cloning and merging operations, which are challenging to interpret in data modeling but are of significant interest in KR. Extensive research exists on database system versioning \cite{salzberg1999comparison}, including graph databases\footnote{Versioning for the Neo4j database \url{https://github.com/h-omer/neo4j-versioner-core}} \cite{castelltort2013representing, khurana2013efficient}. These systems are generally categorized into snapshot-based and delta-based classes (also known as copy and log), with the former storing complete database snapshots at various revision points, and the latter preserving transformation logs. Our system occupies a hybrid category: while the audit trail retains transformation representations (logs), these logs comprise subgraphs or graph patterns impacted by transformations. Another classification of graph database versioning systems distinguishes between those offering revision histories from the perspective of individual nodes and edges (or relationships), and those adopting a graph-centric view \cite{castelltort2013representing}. Existing tools, such as \texttt{neo4j-versioner-core} or the one in \cite{castelltort2013representing}, primarily address versioning from the standpoint of individual elements. In contrast, our framework supports versioning of entire graphs and graph hierarchies. Moreover, similar to model versioning, current database versioning techniques lack the capability to document cloning and merging operations of graph elements.

text: In recent years, deep learning methods for point cloud generation and completion have advanced significantly, particularly those leveraging autoencoder architectures. Various approaches, including PointNet \cite{qi2016pointnet}, PointNet++ \cite{qi2017pointnetplusplus}, DGCNN \cite{dgcnn}, and Point Transformer \cite{zhao2020point}, have focused intensively on refining encoders to achieve superior point cloud representations. Concurrently, considerable research has been dedicated to optimizing decoder designs. For instance, works such as \cite{Fan_2017_CVPR, achlioptas2017latent_pc, yuan2018pcn, Yang_Wu_Zhang_Jin_2021} employ fully connected layers to produce coarse outputs, while \cite{Yang_2018_CVPR, groueix2018, liu2019morphing, Wen_2020_CVPR} transform 2D planes into 3D surfaces. As depicted in Figure \ref{fig:introduction}(a), both fully connected layers and folding operations are prevalent techniques for converting latent features into point clouds. Nonetheless, these methods fall short in thoroughly exploring the transformation concerning point constraints, network parameters, data flow, and convergence speed. As illustrated by the upper airplane in Figure \ref{fig:introduction}(b), point clouds generated via FC-based techniques often exhibit outliers and uneven surfaces. This issue arises because the generated points lack shared parameters, resulting in limited available parameters for each point. When scaled to multiple branches, the resulting point clouds lack self-clustering properties. Self-clustering refers to the tendency of points generated by each branch to coalesce, reflecting an object's locality. The lower airplane in Figure \ref{fig:introduction}(b) exemplifies a self-clustered point cloud. The absence of a centripetal constraint allows each generated point excessive freedom, leading to this problem. In contrast, folding-based methods utilize significantly fewer parameters and employ grid priors to constrain generated points on a smooth 2-manifold, allowing for expansion to multiple branches. However, these methods suffer from slow convergence speeds, as deforming a 2D square into diverse 3D surfaces using limited parameters is challenging. Additionally, 3D objects often feature non-smooth surfaces, which folding operations struggle to accommodate, given that the generated surfaces originate from smooth 2-manifolds. text: \begin{wrapfigure}{r}{0.45\textwidth} \vspace{-40pt} \begin{center} \end{center} \vspace{-0.5cm} \caption{Quantization intervals utilized in the proposed method and prior works.} \vspace{-0.7cm} \end{wrapfigure} Federated Learning (FL)~\cite{mcmahan2017fl_google} has recently gained traction as a leading strategy to address the substantial requirements for data privacy and computational efficiency. This approach enables numerous edge devices, referred to as workers, to collaboratively train a model without the need to exchange private data. Due to its effectiveness, FL has been integrated into various real-world applications, including keyboard prediction~\cite{hard2018keyboard_prediction_fl, yang2018applied_keyboard} and services that prioritize privacy~\cite{sheller2018multi_institutional,sheller2018multi_brain_fl,pokhrel2020fl_block_chain}. Nevertheless, the repeated transmission of model weights and gradients between the server and workers during FL model training poses a significant challenge. As models become more complex, communication costs quickly emerge as a critical bottleneck in FL systems. To mitigate this issue, numerous studies have explored quantization techniques for model weights~\cite{yu2019double_quantization,tang2019doublesqueeze} or gradients~\cite{wen2017terngrad,alistarh2017qsgd} to decrease the size of model update messages. Despite the advancements achieved by these methods, they often struggle to maintain model performance comparable to non-compressed, floating-point training when subjected to heavy compression. Moreover, low-bit quantization can negatively impact other prevalent techniques, such as gradient sparsification~\cite{aji2017sparse_top_k,strom2015scalable_top_k}, thereby restricting further cost reduction. In our study, we introduce an innovative quantization approach based on the cosine function, which efficiently quantizes model weights and gradients for round-trip compression. Drawing from the observation that gradients and model weights with higher magnitudes carry more information~\cite{han2015deep_compression,lin2018deep_gradient_compression,aji2017sparse_top_k}, we exploit the non-linear properties of cosine functions to minimize quantization errors for extreme values. This contrasts with the objectives of most previous works~\cite{alistarh2017qsgd,han2015deep_compression}, as illustrated in Fig.~\ref{fig:teaser}. Our method is characterized by low time and space complexity, requires no additional training, and incurs minimal extra cost, making it particularly advantageous for federated learning systems, where edge devices often have limited hardware capabilities. We performed comprehensive experiments across various scenarios using the CIFAR-10 dataset for image classification and the BraTS 2019 dataset for 3D volume segmentation. Our contributions are summarized as follows: (a) Our primary contribution is the introduction of a \textit{simple-yet-effective} cosine-based quantization scheme. This approach effectively maintains model performance, exhibits low time and space complexity, and necessitates no extra training, making it suitable for a wide range of distributed learning challenges. (b) Our quantization technique can compress model weights and gradients, thereby reducing overall communication costs in federated learning. (c) Our method is versatile and compatible with many existing techniques, such as gradient sparsification. By integrating our quantization with other methods, our system can achieve model performance comparable to non-compressed floating-point training at high compression ratios, a feat that other quantization techniques find challenging to replicate.

text: In various contexts of software transformation and security, it is often essential to examine or manipulate a program's binary. This necessity is particularly evident when the source code is unavailable. Even when the source code is accessible, the absence of the appropriate toolchain or environment for compiling the altered source, or a specific interest in analyses reliant on the machine code, such as assessing padding around functions or buffers, might still lead to working directly with binaries. Typically, the initial phase of such analysis involves \emph{disassembling} the binary, a process that converts machine code into assembly language. The exploration of \emph{disassembly} and the development of \emph{disassemblers} can be traced back to at least 1980~\cite{Horspool+Marovac:1980:AnApproach}. Recently, many disassemblers have achieved or surpassed $99\percent$ accuracy on numerous real-world binaries, as noted in works like~\cite{Andriesse+etal:2016:in-depth} and~\cite{Flores-Montoya+Schulte:2020:ddisasm}. Nevertheless, challenges such as resolving indirect jumps and identifying function starts persist, complicating the achievement of the elusive ``last $1$\percent'' in disassembly accuracy. Consequently, the community continues to innovate, with frequent advancements and new methodologies emerging—see, for instance,~\cite{Flores-Montoya+Schulte:2020:ddisasm}, \cite{Miller+etal:2019:probabilistic}, and updates to existing disassemblers. Assessing highly precise disassemblers poses significant challenges. Firstly, because different disassemblers may have distinct vulnerabilities, even minor alterations in the binary set used for evaluation can markedly alter their accuracy rankings. Unfortunately, the literature on disassembly often employs varied target sets; for example, see~\cite{Andriesse+etal:2016:in-depth} compared to \cite{Flores-Montoya+Schulte:2020:ddisasm}. Secondly, given that current disassemblers often exceed $99\percent$ accuracy, having a nearly $100\percent$ accurate ground truth is crucial for reliable ranking. However, as this paper will demonstrate, while earlier studies have not extensively documented their methods for generating ground truth, our experience indicates that creating accurate ground truth is complex and difficult to replicate without detailed guidance. Considering these issues, we believe it is crucial for the community to establish a standardized set of binaries for benchmarking disassembler accuracy, as well as their performance in terms of runtime and memory usage. To facilitate this effort, this paper introduces the initial version of our evolving disassembly benchmark suite. We will examine the design of our suite from two perspectives: (a) the selection of binaries included, and (b) the methodology for generating accurate disassembly ground truth for the instructions within these binaries. For aspect (a), an effective disassembly benchmark suite should possess the following characteristics: \begin{enumerate*}[(i)] \item The binaries should exhibit \emph{diversity} in terms of size, type (e.g., editor versus web server), compilers utilized, and optimization settings applied. This diversity helps the suite better reflect the complexities found in real-world binaries. \item The suite should contain a \emph{moderate} number of binaries, sufficient to provide comprehensive evaluation but not so large as to be impractical. This balance ensures the feasibility of assessing disassemblers across all included binaries, considering the multiplicative growth in the number of compilers and optimization settings for each ISA-OS pair. \end{enumerate*} Currently, our benchmark suite is organized by "project names," each representing an open-source project and a specific version (e.g., \verb!openssh-7.1p2!). For each project name, we identify a specific target binary (e.g., \verb!sshd!) and the set of ISA-OS pairs (e.g., \{x86-Linux, x64-Linux\}) included in the build. Additionally, for each ISA-OS pair, we define the list of compiler-version pairs and optimization settings used, as detailed in~\S\ref{sec:current-benchmark}. To promote adoption, we openly maintain our benchmark suite on GitHub (\url{https://github.com/pangine/disasm-benchmark}), hoping it will evolve with community input and future research, akin to the evolution of the SPEC CPU benchmark~\cite{misc:speccpu}. Regarding aspect (b), while one might assume that generating disassembly ground truth merely involves saving compiler-generated assembly code (e.g., \verb!gcc -S!), this assumption oversimplifies the reality. Even with all assembly files available, they do not fully describe the machine code in the binary, as some assembly statements can be encoded in multiple ways. Furthermore, during the development of our benchmark suite, we encountered numerous edge cases that required careful handling when collecting, extracting, and representing assembly information. In~\S\ref{sec:gt}, we will explore these challenges and our approaches to addressing them. Finally, leveraging our evolving benchmark suite and our mature ground truth generator and disassembler evaluator, we present in~\S\ref{sec:eval} our analyses of four notable open-source disassemblers: BAP~\cite{misc:bap}, Ghidra~\cite{misc:ghidra}, Radare2~\cite{misc:radaretwo}, and ROSE~\cite{misc:rose}. Our findings are largely consistent with~\cite{Andriesse+etal:2016:in-depth}: (i) function start identification remains a significant obstacle to accurate disassembly, and (ii) linear-sweep disassembly~\cite{Schwarz+etal:2002:Disassembly} can achieve high accuracy by chance but lacks the potential for guaranteed perfect accuracy, making it unreliable as a long-term solution. In conclusion, our contributions in this work are: \begin{enumerate*} \item We advocate for the establishment of a standardized set of binaries from diverse projects, compiled with various compilers and optimization settings, to evaluate disassemblers, and present our evolving suite as a basis for community dialogue. \item We have developed a novel system utilizing a widely-supported compiler toolchain feature known as "listing files" to generate precise disassembly ground truth. Additionally, we have created support programs to evaluate four leading open-source disassemblers against our ground truth, and we share our findings. \item We have open-sourced all our code and data to facilitate future research and encourage community adoption and contributions to our system and benchmark suite. \end{enumerate*}

text: Phishing websites represent a significant social-engineering threat, with their prevalence having surged in recent years~\cite{phishincreasing:2020,data-breach:2020}. In response, the security community has developed a range of automated tools employing advanced machine learning~\cite{sahingoz2019machine,rao2019detection,hassanpour2018phishing,abdelhamid2017phishing}, deep learning~\cite{yang2019phishing,yi2018web,hassanpour2018phishing}, rule-based~\cite{moghimi2016new,sonowal2020phidma,tan2016phishwho,shirazi2018kn0w}, and heuristic~\cite{nguyen2013detecting,babagoli2019heuristic,jeeva2016intelligent,sreedharan2016systems} techniques to combat these attacks. However, phishing sites are notoriously adaptable, often exploiting vulnerabilities and using adversarial strategies to evade detection by automated systems~\cite{liang2016cracking,rajivan2018creative,royremains,aleroud2020bypassing}. Consequently, domain hosting services, antiphishing tools, and web browsers frequently depend on one or more phishing feeds or blocklists. These are curated databases that are regularly updated with phishing URLs, added either manually or through a mix of automated discovery, manual reporting, and human verification. As Oest et al.~\cite{oest2020phishtime} highlight, phishing feeds are inherently \textit{reactive}, with a notable delay between the emergence of a phishing site and its subsequent reporting. Nevertheless, these feeds typically undergo some degree of manual assessment, ideally making them less prone to errors than fully automated systems. In this study, we explore phishing reports disseminated on Twitter~\cite{twitter:2021}, a widely used micro-blogging platform. To our knowledge, this is the first comprehensive analysis of Twitter as a potent knowledge base for detecting new phishing sites. Throughout this paper, we assess its effectiveness and compare its features and performance against two other popular open-source phishing feeds: PhishTank and OpenPhish. Specifically, this paper: (i) Investigates the reliability and volume of information shared through these phishing reports, comparing them to two other open-source phishing feeds. (ii) Examines the unique aspect of Twitter-hosted reports, which allow user interaction—a feature absent in the other two feeds. We analyze the frequency of these interactions, including those from domain registrars and organizations targeted by the reported phishing URLs, and assess their impact on the detection and removal of these URLs. We collected and scrutinized over 16k tweets containing 11k unique URLs between June 21 and August 17, 2021. However, when they did respond, the URLs became inactive more swiftly than those without such interaction. text: Image classification is a foundational task with significant relevance across numerous fields, including autonomous driving, industrial automation, medical diagnosis, and biometric identification~\cite{autonomous_driving, industrial_automation, medical_diagnosis, biometric_identification}. Supervised learning (SL) methods have been widely adopted due to their effectiveness in tackling this task~\cite{VGG, ResNet}. However, a notable limitation of SL is its demand for extensive training data for each class to be recognized. In many real-world situations, gathering such data for specific classes—like endangered species or newly emerging variants such as COVID-19—is challenging. When classes are \textit{unseen} and lack training data, SL models tend to favor \textit{seen} classes, hindering the recognition of the unseen ones. To address this limitation, a method leveraging manually annotated attributes (e.g., color, size, and shape; refer to Fig.~\ref{fig:CUB}) for classifier training has emerged~\cite{zsl_proposal, gzsl_intro}. This approach, known as generalized zero-shot learning (GZSL), involves learning the correlation between images and attributes from seen classes, enabling the model to identify unseen classes. For instance, in~\cite{ALE}, a strategy was introduced to identify unseen classes by evaluating the compatibility between image features and attributes. Meanwhile,~\cite{CVAE-GZSL} employed a network to synthesize image features from attributes, thereby generating training data for unseen classes. Typically, image feature extraction relies on networks trained for classification tasks (e.g., ResNet~\cite{ResNet}). A potential issue with this method is that the extracted features may include information irrelevant to the attributes (e.g., human fingers in Fig.~\ref{fig:CUB}), complicating the learning of image-attribute relationships~\cite{DLFZRL, RFF-GZSL, Disentangled-VAE}. In this paper, we introduce a novel GZSL method designed to eliminate the interference from attribute-irrelevant information. Our approach focuses on extracting a \textit{semantic feature}, which encapsulates only attribute-related information, from the image feature to facilitate learning the image-attribute relationship. To achieve this, we employ a modified autoencoder architecture featuring two encoders: the \textit{semantic} and \textit{residual} encoders (illustrated in Fig.~\ref{fig:SD}). Essentially, the semantic encoder isolates attribute-related information, while the residual encoder captures attribute-irrelevant details. Traditional autoencoders utilize only reconstruction loss (the discrepancy between the input and its reconstruction) for training. Our method introduces two innovative loss functions in addition to reconstruction loss to ensure the semantic encoder exclusively captures attribute-related information. Firstly, we apply a mutual information (MI)-based loss to maximize (minimize) the MI between the semantic (residual) encoder output and the attribute. MI quantifies the dependency between two random variables, so by employing MI-based loss, we encourage the semantic encoder to focus on attribute-related information while preventing the residual encoder from capturing such information. Consequently, the semantic encoder captures all attribute-related information. Secondly, we implement a similarity-based loss to prevent the semantic encoder from including attribute-irrelevant information. For instance, if a bird image includes human fingers (see Fig.~\ref{fig:CUB}), we aim to exclude finger-related features from the semantic encoder output. To achieve this, we enhance the similarity between semantic encoder outputs of images belonging to the same class (e.g., bird images). Since attribute-irrelevant features appear in only a few samples (e.g., human fingers in some bird images), maximizing similarity within the same class helps eliminate attribute-irrelevant information from the semantic encoder output. Extensive experiments conducted on various benchmark datasets (AwA1, AwA2, CUB, and SUN) reveal that our proposed method significantly surpasses conventional GZSL techniques. For instance, on the AwA2 and CUB datasets, our model achieves a 2\% improvement in GZSL classification accuracy compared to state-of-the-art methods.
