text: A text index constructed on a string $T$ of length $n$ serves as a data structure capable of efficiently resolving several types of queries for a given pattern $P$ of length $m$: \begin{description} \crampedItems \item[\functionname{exists}(P)]: Does the pattern $P$ appear within $T$? \item[\functionname{count}(P)]: How many times is the pattern $P$ found in $T$? \item[\functionname{locate}(P)]: Where exactly does the pattern $P$ occur in $T$? \end{description} The responses to these queries are a boolean for existence, a numerical count, and a list of starting indices in the text, respectively. The $\functionname{locate}(P)$ query is the most informative, as the size of its output corresponds to the result of $\functionname{count}(P)$, and a positive count directly confirms the pattern's existence, equivalent to $\functionname{exists}(P)$. A notable instance of such a text index is the FM-index~\cite{ferragina00fmindex}. This index utilizes a wavelet tree~\cite{grossi03wavelet} constructed on the Burrows-Wheeler Transform (BWT)~\cite{burrows94bwt} of the text. It can resolve $\functionname{count}(P)$ queries in time proportional to $m$, multiplied by the operational cost of the wavelet tree, which is typically logarithmic in terms of alphabet size and can be constant~\cite{belazzougui14index}. Given that the BWT comprises $r$ maximal character runs, this data structure can be represented using two supplementary bit vectors~\cite[Thm.~3]{makinen05rle}, occupying $r \lg \sigma + \oh{r \lg \sigma} + \Oh{n}$ bits of space. This space requirement can be optimized further by employing Huffman-shaped wavelet trees, leveraging the zeroth order empirical entropy of the string formed by the distinct letters of the BWT runs. For $\functionname{locate}$ queries, BWT-based indexes are enhanced by sampling the suffix array~\cite{manber93sa}, which, in its uncompressed form, demands $n \lg n$ bits. In this paper, we do not delve into $\functionname{locate}$ queries, as their augmentation is orthogonal to our proposed data structure and is reserved for future exploration. Current methods achieve $\Oh{m}$ time complexity for $\functionname{count}(P)$, with $|P| = m$, involving $\Oh{m}$ queries to the underlying wavelet tree structure, executed through a constant number of random accesses. These random accesses, however, render the FM-index less efficient in practice. By utilizing a BWT constructed on a grammar-compressed string, we can match non-terminals in a single backward search step, effectively allowing us to \emph{bypass multiple characters} in one move. As a result, we spend less time on the wavelet tree, which is not cache-friendly, and more on extracting grammar symbols from cache-friendly arrays. Our experiments indicate that this trade-off is beneficial in terms of time performance, reducing the reliance on the wavelet tree. Regarding space, the grammar captures compressibility more effectively than the run-length compression of the BWT on plain text. We exploit specific features of the GCIS (grammar compression by induced suffix sorting) grammar~\cite{nunes18grammar}, as identified by~\citet{akagi21grammar} and \citet{diaz21lms}, to identify non-terminals in the text that match portions of the pattern. \paragraph{Our Contribution} In summary, our contribution lies in demonstrating that combining the BWT with a particular grammar-based compression technique can achieve superior compression compared to the plain RLBWT, while also reducing memory accesses for count queries (heuristically). This improvement comes at the cost of additional computation required to construct the grammar for both the text and the pattern during a query. \subsection*{Related Work} Significant research has been devoted to analyzing and enhancing the \functionname{count}{} operation of the BWT (e.g., \cite{makinen05rle} and references therein) and the suffix array sampling (e.g.,~\cite{gagie18bwt} and references therein). Another research avenue involves grammar indexes, which typically augment a grammar for \functionname{locate}{} queries. Although determining the smallest grammar is NP-complete~\cite{charikar05grammar}, there exist grammars with a size of \Oh{r \log(n/r)}~\cite{gagie18bwt}, and empirically, some grammars are notably smaller than the RLBWT in practice. However, most indexes exhibit a quadratic dependency on the pattern length for \functionname{locate}{}~\cite{claude12grammarindex,claude21grammarcompressed}, and they fail to improve query times independently of the pattern's occurrence count when only \functionname{count}{} is considered. A novel exception is the grammar index by \citet{christiansen21optimaltime}, achieving \Oh{m + \log^{2+\epsilon} n} time for \functionname{count}{}, with a space complexity of $\Oh{\gamma \log(n/\gamma)}$, where $\gamma$ denotes the size of the smallest string attractor~\cite{kempa18stringattractors} of the input text. This approach, however, appears impractical, and no implementation has been attempted thus far. Related to our work are the grammar indexes of \citet{akagi21grammar} and \citet{diaz21lms}, also based on the GCIS grammar, with the latter building on the findings of \citet{christiansen21optimaltime}. They employ similar strategies for extracting non-terminals from the pattern grammar, ensuring their presence in the text grammar. However, they rely on \functionname{locate}{} to compute \functionname{count}{}, making their time complexity dependent on the pattern's occurrence frequency. We are not aware of any prior work combining the BWT with grammar techniques, except in the context of construction. In this regard, \citet{karkkainen12bwt} explored constructing the BWT on grammar-compressed input. They applied a grammar compression method that merges frequent bigrams akin to Re-Pair~\cite{larsson99repair}, showing empirical improvements in BWT computation and text reconstruction from the BWT. With a similar aim, \citet{diazdominguez21grammar,diaz21grammar} computed the extended BWT~\cite{mantaci07ebwt}, a BWT variant for multiple texts, from the GCIS grammar.

Their effectiveness depends on the data distribution at deployment corresponding to that at training, which is often not the case. This paper tackles the problem of predicting, analyzing, and mitigating risks of failure in classifier systems. To make machine learning trustworthy, it is important to develop models and tools that can detect and understand the sources of uncertainty. Unfortunately, many systems fail without warning, keeping a high confidence in their predictions, despite the underlying problems, [nguyen-2015-deep, jiang-2014-trust, goodfellow-2014-explaining]. For example, if the introspection component suggests that there is a high probability of error in the ML system's output, the system could defer the decision to a human expert in order to avoid adverse consequences. We aim to generate uncertainty scores for predictions, which will (a) predict inputs likely to cause system failure, (b) identify the uncertainty type contributing to the risk, and (c) take suitable mitigation actions. By combining different uncertainty scores, a system can enhance its robustness in handling challenging new data points. The usual method for judging the trustworthiness of machine learning predictions is to calculate a confidence score based on the expected value of a prediction, such as the maximum class probability (MCP) in neural ML and the distance from the decision boundary in SVMs. When dealing with many out-of-distribution points, acquiring more training samples and retraining the system could be a solution. The main challenge is to decide on the appropriate action for a specific condition. text: The field of quantum computing has witnessed remarkable progress in formulating algorithms that promise significant speed advantages over classical methods. Yet, translating these algorithms into functional quantum circuits remains a challenging task. Various research groups have turned to machine learning techniques \cite{cincio2018learning, fosel2021quantum}, genetic algorithms \cite{lee07,rasconi2019an}, and linear algebra methods \cite{re:amy:phds,nam2018automated} to design circuits that precisely or approximately implement quantum primitives vital for numerous quantum algorithms. Additionally, efforts are underway to develop optimization strategies that effectively map logical circuits onto physical quantum hardware \cite{itoko2020optimization,zulehner2018an}. Our research focuses on extending the SWAP test to handle an arbitrary number of overlapping states. The SWAP test for two states is a fundamental tool in quantum computing, utilizing controlled-swap (CSWAP) gates and an ancillary qubit to determine the inner product $|\langle \phi, \psi\rangle|^{2}$ between two quantum states $\phi$ and $\psi$ \cite{kopczyk2018quantum}, as well as to assess the overlap $\mathtt{Tr}(\rho \sigma)$ between two mixed states $\rho$ and $\sigma$ \cite{garcia2013swap}. When $\rho$ equals $\sigma$, the test evaluates the purity of the quantum state $\sigma$ \cite{garcia2013swap}. For two $q$-qubit states $\phi,\psi$, the computational cost of calculating $|\langle \phi, \psi\rangle|^{2}$ classically scales exponentially with $q$, whereas the SWAP test circuit's depth on a quantum system increases linearly with $q$ \cite{garcia2013swap}, offering an exponential speedup and quantum advantage if error correction or mitigation is feasible. The SWAP test is integral to various applications requiring state overlap estimation. It is employed in quantum state characterization, such as measuring entanglement and indistinguishability \cite{Foulds2021, garcia2013swap}. It serves as a benchmarking tool on quantum computers by tracking decoherence through a circuit and is a crucial component in hybrid quantum machine learning algorithms. For example, in quantum supervised learning \cite{kopczyk2018quantum,ciliberto2018quantum,havlicek2019supervised}, particularly in quantum support vector machines (SVM) \cite{rebentrost2014quantum, rudolph2020generation}, it measures pairwise distances during cluster assignment. While enhancements to the SWAP test for two high-dimensional states have been explored \cite{cincio2018learning, garcia2013swap}, implementations have traditionally been limited to two quantum states at a time, except for a 3-state model found in \cite{Hai-Rui, Galvao2019} \cite{kathuria2020implementation}. We investigate the generalization of the SWAP test to $m$ arbitrary pure quantum states $\ket{\phi_{1}...\phi_{m}}$, enabling the computation of $|\langle \phi_{i}, \phi_{j}\rangle|^{2}$ for all distinct pairs $i\neq j$ with at most $O(\log{m})$ measurements. Our method employs a pairing unitary $\mathcal{U}_{m}$, composed of $O(m)$ CSWAP gates, controlled by $O(\log{m})$ ancillary qubits. This pairing operator, when applied to $m$ state registers, yields a superposition state where every pair $(\phi_{i}, \phi_{j})$ appears with positive probability on the first two state registers, labeled by an ancillary basis state. By applying a standard two-state SWAP test to this superposition, the measurement on the ancillary qubits correlates the probability of an ancillary basis state with the state overlap it labels. Initially, we design a unitary $\mathcal{U}_{4}$ for a 4-state input using three ancillaries and three CSWAP gates, demonstrating that this circuit is optimal in terms of CSWAP gate usage when restricting measurements to four. Subsequently, we leverage our 4-state circuit as a foundation to create a recursive algorithm that constructs an $m$-state circuit, allowing all overlaps $|\langle \phi_{i}, \phi_{j}\rangle|^{2}$ to be measured on $O(\log{m})$ ancillary qubits. We provide a detailed complexity analysis, showing that the resulting circuit employs $c_m=O(m)$ CSWAP gates and $d_m=O(\log m)$ ancillaries. Given that our overlap estimates are probabilistic, repeated experiments are necessary to achieve an estimate of each state overlap with a mean squared error below a specified precision $\epsilon$. We model these repeated trials by assuming access to an oracle capable of constructing the states $\ket{\phi_{1}}, ..., \ket{\phi_{m}}$. We argue that, for arbitrary $m$, the limitation on the number of measurements to $O(\log m)$ is crucial to ensure a polynomial number of oracle calls. Numerically, we implement a genetic algorithm to determine the optimal application of CSWAP gates, maximizing the number of pairs appearing on the first two registers of a quantum circuit. This optimization is inspired by the suitability of genetic algorithms for complex optimization problems involving intricate parameter and energy landscapes. Genetic algorithms are widely used in various fields, including scheduling, building design, and trajectory optimization \cite{Hart, Yu}. They have also been effective in automating classical circuit design \cite{aly} and, more recently, in quantum circuit design \cite{Potocek}. For $m=8$ input states and six measurements, our empirical results show that a genetic algorithm does not discover circuits with fewer than nine CSWAP gates, which matches the number of CSWAP gates used in our recursive construction (see \ref{circuit: U3}). \begin{figure}[t] \centering \tikzset{every picture/.style={scale=3}}

text: The swift advancement of radiological imaging technologies has led to a surge in the production of ophthalmic images. There are three primary modalities in ophthalmic imaging: (1) \textbf{Slit Lamp.} This technique \cite{cheung2011validity} is predominantly employed to examine both the anterior and posterior segments of the eye, covering structures such as the eyelid, sclera, conjunctiva, iris, crystalline lens, and cornea. (2) \textbf{Retinal Fundus.} Retinal fundus imaging is crucial for diagnosing various ocular conditions \cite{fu2018joint,fu2018disc} as it captures the eye's interior lining and the back structures. (3) \textbf{ASOCT.} Anterior Segment Optical Coherence Tomography (ASOCT) facilitates the visualization and evaluation of anterior segment ocular features, including the tear film, cornea, conjunctiva, sclera, rectus muscles, anterior chamber angle structures, and lens \cite{hirnschall2017prediction}. Over recent decades, propelled by advancements in pattern recognition and computer vision, particularly deep learning \cite{litjens2017survey}, the processing of ophthalmic images has become increasingly pivotal in aiding disease diagnosis and assessment. However, the objective interpretation of these images often suffers from high inter-observer variability and limited reproducibility. To address this inconsistency, prior cases with similar disease characteristics can be used as references through Content-Based Image Retrieval (CBIR). CBIR facilitates the retrieval of user-specific images by indexing and analyzing visual features such as color, shape, and texture from extensive image databases \cite{zhou2017recent}. Unlike direct classification and grading tasks that provide diagnostic outcomes, ophthalmic CBIR enhances diagnosis through evidence-based support. For effective assessment, CBIR requires a substantial number of cases, necessitating a retrieval algorithm that is both scalable and accurate. Hashing methods have emerged as a promising solution for CBIR, representing high-dimensional images with compact hash-codes due to their efficient storage and processing capabilities \cite{conjeti2017deep,wu2019deep}. In recent times, deep learning-based hashing techniques have been extensively employed for medical image retrieval, including deep multiple instance hashing for tumor evaluation \cite{conjeti2017deep}, deep residual hashing for chest X-ray analysis \cite{conjeti2017hashing}, and order-sensitive deep hashing for multi-morbidity medical image retrieval \cite{chen2018order}. Nonetheless, current deep hashing approaches do not fully harness the deep network's ability to precisely capture features of salient regions, which are often crucial for clinical diagnosis. In ophthalmology, images of different grades or classes may appear similar overall but exhibit subtle differences discernible through salient region analysis. As illustrated in Fig.\ref{fig1}, ophthalmic images (A) and (B) derived from ASOCT, a non-invasive high-resolution anterior segment imaging technique, are both cataract cases with similar appearances. However, they can be distinguished by two types of salient regions: over-bright areas (blue) and over-dark areas (blue). Cataract grading heavily relies on identifying and observing these salient regions, necessitating their representation in ophthalmic image retrieval. Furthermore, as depicted in Fig. \ref{fig1}, a retinal fundus image (C) displays three symptoms diagnosable through distinct salient regions (green rectangle). A pathological myopic eye is often identified by a leopard fundus. Diabetic Retinopathy (DR) diagnosis can depend on the spatial configuration of the macula, while glaucoma is typically characterized by a large optic cup and abnormalities in the Retinal Nerve Fiber Layer (RNFL). The information from these salient regions must be encoded into the hash-code to effectively differentiate fundus images in retrieval tasks. Drawing inspiration from the attention mechanism in deep networks \cite{woo2018cbam,chen2017sca}, we introduce a novel end-to-end network called Attention-based Saliency Hashing (ASH). This network is designed to enhance the discriminative power of the hash-code by leveraging salient regions. To thoroughly mine these regions and amplify their representation in the hashing space, we employ a spatial-attention module that targets the capture of salient region information across the entire ophthalmic image. For maintaining similarity, we utilize the siamese structure \cite{bertinetto2016fully} with input image pairs sharing weights to learn pairwise loss in the objective function. In the hashing space, the pairwise distance should be minimized for similar image pairs and maximized otherwise. The primary contributions of this paper are as follows: \begin{itemize} \item[1)] Ophthalmic images of different grades or classes may exhibit similar overall appearances but can be differentiated through salient region analysis. To address this, we propose the novel end-to-end network, Attention-based Saliency Hashing (ASH), for ophthalmic image retrieval. \item[2)] Utilizing a spatial-attention module, our ASH focuses on salient regions in a comprehensive manner, enhancing the representation of these regions to maximize the hash-code's discriminative potential. \item[3)] Experiments conducted on two different ophthalmic image datasets demonstrate that our ASH significantly improves accuracy while maintaining efficiency, compared to leading deep hashing methods. \end{itemize} The remainder of this paper is organized as follows: Section \uppercase\expandafter{\romannumeral2} reviews related works. Section \uppercase\expandafter{\romannumeral3} provides a detailed description of our methodology. Section \uppercase\expandafter{\romannumeral4} offers a comprehensive evaluation of the proposed method on two ophthalmic image datasets. Section \uppercase\expandafter{\romannumeral5} concludes the paper.

text: Robots are increasingly becoming a common sight in crowded environments, moving seamlessly alongside humans. This trend includes service robots in airports, hotels, and restaurants, delivery robots traversing sidewalks, mobile robots operating in warehouses, and autonomous vehicles. To ensure the safe deployment of these robots, it is crucial for the surrounding people to comprehend the robots' navigation intentions. Historically, Human-Robot Interaction (HRI) researchers have concentrated on understanding arm movement intentions \cite{gielniak2011generating,kwon2018expressing}, examining eye gaze \cite{moon2014meet,admoni2017social}, and other non-verbal communication methods \cite{saunderson2019robots} for stationary robots. However, there is a growing interest in the field to explore how robotic navigation intentions, such as path plans, can be externalized or visualized \cite{coovert2014spatial,szafir2015communicating,chadalavada2015s,watanabe2015communicating,chadalavada2020bi,blenk2021lane}. This shift aims to enhance the clarity of robots' navigation behaviors, thereby fostering trust and acceptance. One approach to convey navigation intentions involves using directional projections \cite{coovert2014spatial,chadalavada2015s,watanabe2015communicating,chadalavada2020bi}, including arrow projections \cite{coovert2014spatial,chadalavada2020bi}. In this method, a robot utilizes a projector to cast directional cues that signal its intended path. These cues can manifest as lines \cite{chadalavada2015s}, gradient bands \cite{watanabe2015communicating}, or arrows \cite{coovert2014spatial,chadalavada2020bi}. Unlike head-mounted see-through augmented reality systems \cite{williams2018virtual,williams2018augmented}, projector-based augmented reality does not necessitate special hardware for observers, enabling multiple viewers to perceive the visualizations simultaneously. This feature enhances usability in group, team, or crowd scenarios~\cite{chen2019crowd,sebo2020robots,oliveira2021human}. As elaborated in Section~\ref{sec:related_work}, several human-subject studies \cite{coovert2014spatial,chadalavada2015s,watanabe2015communicating,chadalavada2020bi} have demonstrated the effectiveness of this technique \cite{watanabe2015communicating,chadalavada2020bi}. In this paper, we present a practical solution for implementing robotic arrow projections, detailing the implementation process and providing access to the code. We also specify the particular robot and off-the-shelf projector we employed successfully, along with a comprehensive summary of a large-scale user study that offers further empirical support. For the implementation, we utilized the widely-used Robot Operating System (ROS) \cite{quigley2009ros} and its visualization tool, rviz \cite{gossow2011interactive}, to render the arrows. The use of ROS ensures the implementation is compatible with various robots, as many research and development robots support ROS \cite{rosshowcase}. Even systems not based on ROS \cite{kramer2007development,elkady2012robotics}, as well as cognitive architectures like DIARC~\cite{scheutz2019overview}, often include ROS bridges. By using rviz as the rendering engine, practitioners and researchers can remain within the ROS ecosystem, avoiding the need to learn external tools like Unity. Additionally, rviz offers a graphical user interface and does not require knowledge of computer graphics programming. Considering the broad applicability of arrow projection across different robotic platforms and its demonstrated effectiveness, our work is poised to significantly benefit the HRI community. The readily accessible implementation, accompanied by detailed documentation, allows researchers to concentrate on other intriguing and emerging topics within social navigation, such as human navigation modeling \cite{guy2010modeling,ratsamee2013social,ferrer2014proactive,che2018avoiding} and robot navigation that adheres to social or moral norms \cite{banisetty2021implicit,banisetty2021socially}. We invite feedback in the form of GitHub issues and encourage pull requests for further collaboration.

text: Motion planning for multiple agents, while critical for numerous practical applications, presents significant challenges. Even guiding a single robot from a starting point to a destination while avoiding collisions with obstacles is daunting. This complexity arises from factors such as intricate obstacles, high-dimensional state spaces, nonlinear and nonholonomic dynamics, actuation constraints, and disturbances. When multiple robots interact within a shared space, the complexity escalates beyond the reach of many current methodologies. In this study, we introduce the \underline{S}calable and \underline{S}afe \underline{M}ulti-agent \underline{M}otion (S2M2) planner—a cutting-edge solution for multi-agent motion planning. S2M2 is capable of rapidly and effectively generating plans that are provably safe for agent models characterized by high-dimensional nonlinear dynamics and bounded disturbances in continuous time and space. Instead of directly computing dynamically feasible trajectories, which is computationally prohibitive, S2M2 employs a separation-of-concerns strategy. Initially, we construct piecewise linear (PWL) paths $S_i$ for each dynamic agent $\mathcal{A}_i$, acknowledging that exact adherence to these paths is unattainable. Nevertheless, we demonstrate that with suitable tracking controllers, agents' actual trajectories, even under disturbances, can converge to $S_i$ with guaranteed spatial tracking error bounds. Crucially, these error bounds can be pre-determined for any valid PWL path. The core of S2M2's efficiency lies in framing the task of identifying PWL paths for a single agent as a Mixed Integer-Linear Program (MILP), solvable efficiently with existing MILP solvers. To prevent inter-agent collisions, we integrate our single-agent motion planner with a priority-based search method~\cite{ma2019searching}, which systematically explores priority orderings. When priorities are set, agents with lower priority adjust their paths, treating higher-priority agents as dynamic obstacles. Coupled with the MILP-based path planner and reliable tracking controller, S2M2 can efficiently devise plans that are robust to disturbances and provably safe during execution. Furthermore, by planning paths for multiple agents on a continuous map and over continuous time, our approach yields high-quality solutions with reduced flowtime, defined as the makespan sum of all individual agent plans. Consider, for instance, two disc-shaped vehicles executing u-turns, illustrated in Figure~\ref{fig:uturn}. With partially known initial positions and bounded disturbances, we initially calculate the spatial error bound for tracking a linear path segment. This error, combined with the agent's shape, helps determine the potential swept area of the path segment. The swept area for agent $\mathcal{A}_1$ during its second segment $(p_{12}, p_{13})$ is depicted in light blue. We also determine the minimum duration for each segment, ensuring the agent has adequate time to realign after a turn, which is $3$ seconds in our scenario. As our single-agent motion planner designs such paths, obstacles are expanded considering the spatial tracking error and agent shape, highlighted in light red. The planner enforces a minimum segment duration constraint. Notably, as the agents navigate the corridor, they decelerate, utilizing these $3$ seconds to adjust their paths. Once through the corridor, agent $\mathcal{A}_2$ accelerates towards its target. In cases of potential collisions, some agents are prioritized and treated as moving obstacles for others. In our scenario, agent $\mathcal{A}_1$ is given precedence, allowing it to traverse the corridor before agent $\mathcal{A}_2$. We evaluate S2M2 against ECBS-CT \cite{cohen2019optimal} and MAPF/C+POST \cite{honig2018trajectory} in both 2D and 3D environments involving ground vehicles and quadrotors. The results indicate that S2M2 surpasses both planners in solution quality, achieving a $15\sim70\%$ improvement in most cases. Additionally, S2M2 significantly reduces preprocessing time and exhibits competitive runtime performance compared to the other planners.

text: The challenge of extracting the principal components of a matrix from noisy data is a pivotal issue in mathematical statistics and its applications \cite{Rao-1964-PCA,Johnstone-2001-LargestEigenvaluePCA,Ringner-2008-PCA,AW-2010-PCA}. This problem has been extensively explored through the lens of \emph{spiked matrix models}, which offer theoretical insights into the asymptotic behavior of such tasks. Johnstone's seminal work \cite{Johnstone-2001-LargestEigenvaluePCA} introduced models with Gaussian observations influenced by a rank-one perturbation, or "spike," on the covariance matrix. A simpler yet equally illustrative model, the \emph{Wigner spiked matrix model}, also captures these phenomena effectively. We define two probability distributions $\PP$ and $\QQ$ on $n \times n$ symmetric matrices as follows: \begin{itemize} \item Under $\QQ = \QQ_n$, the matrix $\bW \in \RR^{n \times n}_{\sym}$ is drawn from the \emph{Gaussian orthogonal ensemble (GOE)}, where $W_{ii} \sim \sN(0, \frac{1}{n})$ and $W_{ij} = W_{ji} \sim \sN(0, \frac{2}{n})$ for $i < j$. These entries are independent, totaling $\frac{n(n + 1)}{2}$. We denote this distribution as $\QQ = \GOE(n)$. \item Under $\PP = \PP_n$, we first sample $\bu \sim \Unif(\mathbb{S}^{n - 1})$, where $\mathbb{S}^{n - 1} \subset \RR^n$ represents the unit sphere. Subsequently, we observe $\bW = \bW_0 + \beta \bu\bu^{\top}$, where $\bW_0 \sim \GOE(n)$ and $\beta > 0$ is constant as $n \to \infty$. \end{itemize} This framework leads to two primary statistical inquiries: (1) \emph{detection} or \emph{testing}, which involves determining whether $\bW$ originates from $\PP$ or $\QQ$, and (2) \emph{recovery} or \emph{estimation}, which entails estimating $\bu$ given that $\bW \sim \PP$. Both scenarios naturally involve the optimization problem of finding the largest eigenvalue: \begin{equation} \lambda_{\max}(\bW) \colonequals \max_{\|\bx\|_2 = 1} \bx^{\top} \bW \bx. \end{equation} For recovery, identifying the maximizer $\bx^{\star}$ (the top eigenvector) provides a maximum likelihood estimate for $\bu$. In detection, thresholding $\lambda_{\max}(\bW)$ is a straightforward and often effective method. The optimal value and corresponding optimizer of $\lambda_{\max}(\bW)$ can be approximated with arbitrary precision in polynomial time $\poly(n)$, indicating efficient algorithms for both recovery and detection. These algorithms are nearly \emph{optimal}: except for the critical case $\beta = 1$, where $\lambda_{\max}(\bW)$ fails to distinguish $\PP$ from $\QQ$, but more advanced statistics can succeed \cite{OJ-2020-TestingSpikedModels}. Generally, when distinguishing $\PP$ from $\QQ$ is feasible with high probability,\footnote{An event $A_n$ occurs \emph{with high probability} under probability measures $\PP_n$ if $\lim_{n \to \infty} \PP_n[A_n] = 1$.} thresholding $\lambda_{\max}(\bW)$ achieves this; similarly, the optimizer $\bx^{\star}$ succeeds when non-trivial estimation of $\bu$ is possible. \begin{proposition}[\cite{FP-2007-LargestEigenvalueWigner,CDMF-2009-DeformedWigner,MRZ-2015-LimitationsSpectral,BMVVX-2018-InfoTheoretic}] Consider $\bW \sim \PP$ with parameter $\beta \ge 0$ (where $\beta = 0$ implies $\PP = \QQ$), and let $\bu$ be the spike vector. Let $\bx^{\star}(\bW)$ denote the optimizer of $\lambda_{\max}(\bW)$, the top eigenvector of $\bW$ normalized to unit length. Then, almost surely, \begin{align} \lim_{n \to \infty} \lambda_{\max}(\bW) &= \left\{\begin{array}{ll} 2 & \text{if } 0 \leq \beta \leq 1, \\ \beta + \beta^{-1} > 2 \, \, \, \, \, \, & \text{if } \beta > 1, \end{array} \right. \\ \lim_{n \to \infty} |\la \bx^{\star}(\bW), \bu \ra| &= \left\{\begin{array}{ll} 0 & \text{if } 0 \leq \beta \leq 1, \\ \sqrt{1 - \beta^{-2}} > 0 & \text{if } \beta > 1. \end{array}\right. \end{align} Furthermore, if $0 \le \beta < 1$, no function of $\bW$ can reliably determine whether $\bW$ is from $\PP$ or $\QQ$ with high probability. Similarly, if $0 \le \beta \leq 1$, no unit vector-valued function of $\bW$ can maintain an inner product with $\bx$ that is asymptotically non-zero with high probability when $\bW \sim \PP$. \end{proposition} \noindent The behavior of $\lambda_{\max}(\bW)$ is elucidated by \cite{FP-2007-LargestEigenvalueWigner}, while \cite{CDMF-2009-DeformedWigner} address the behavior of $|\langle \bx^{\star}(\bW), \bu \rangle|$, building on foundational work by \cite{BBAP-2005-LargestEigenvalueSampleCovariance}. The impossibility of reliably distinguishing whether $\bW$ is drawn from $\PP$ or $\QQ$ is demonstrated by \cite{MRZ-2015-LimitationsSpectral} through establishing \emph{contiguity} between these probability measures. Additionally, \cite{BMVVX-2018-InfoTheoretic} show that this contiguity implies the futility of estimating $\bu$ with positive correlation. More sophisticated models arise from selecting more structured distributions for $\bu$, which corresponds to principal component extraction under known structural constraints. A notable example is provided by \cite{MR-2015-NonNegative}, where $\bu$ is sampled uniformly from the positive orthant of $\mathbb{S}^{n - 1}$, leading to the problem of \emph{non-negative PCA}. In this scenario, the null model $\QQ$ remains unchanged, but $\PP$ is replaced by $\PP^+$, defined as: \begin{itemize} \item Under $\PP^+$, first draw $\bv \sim \Unif(\mathbb{S}^{n - 1})$, set $u_i = |v_i|$, and observe $\bW = \bW_0 + \beta \bu\bu^{\top}$ with $\bW_0 \sim \GOE(n)$ and a fixed $\beta > 0$. \end{itemize} In parallel with classical PCA, one might attempt detection and recovery by solving the optimization problem: \begin{equation} \lambda^{+}(\bW) \colonequals \max_{\substack{\|\bx\|_2 = 1 \\ \bx \geq 0}} \bx^\top \bW \bx, \end{equation} where $\bx \geq 0$ implies $x_i \geq 0$ for all $i \in [n]$. However, unlike $\lambda_{\max}(\bW)$ and its optimizer, computing $\lambda^+(\bW)$ is $\mathsf{NP}$-hard for general $\bW$ \cite{KP-2002-CopositiveProgramming}, making non-negative PCA a more complex computational challenge. Despite this, \cite{MR-2015-NonNegative} demonstrated that an approximate message-passing (AMP) algorithm can effectively solve this problem for random inputs from $\QQ$ or $\PP^+$, achieving near-optimal results. Our focus now shifts to the ``null'' scenario where $\bW \sim \QQ = \GOE(n)$. \begin{proposition}[Part of Theorem 2 and Proposition 4.5 of \cite{MR-2015-NonNegative}] Almost surely, for $\bW \sim \GOE(n)$, \begin{equation} \lim_{n \to \infty} \lambda^+(\bW) = \sqrt{2}. \end{equation} Additionally, for any $\varepsilon > 0$, there exists an algorithm that operates in time $\poly(n)$ (with runtime dependent on $\varepsilon$) and computes $\bx \in \mathbb{S}^{n - 1}$ with $\bx \geq 0$, achieving $\bx^{\top}\bW \bx \geq \sqrt{2} - \varepsilon$ with high probability. \end{proposition} \noindent This algorithm is also effective for distinguishing between $\QQ$ and $\PP^+$ and for recovery under $\PP^+$. \begin{remark} Various simpler algorithms fail to achieve similar quality solutions. For instance, if $\bv$ is the top eigenvector of $\bW$, one might consider $\bv^+$ with entries $v^+_i = \max(0, v_i)$ and use $\bx = \bv^+ / \|\bv^+\|$. However, heuristic calculations yield \begin{equation} \bx^{\top}\bW \bx \approx \frac{1}{\|\bv^+\|^2} \cdot 2 \langle \bv, \bv^+ \rangle^2 \approx 2 \cdot 2 \cdot \left(\frac{1}{2}\right)^2 = 1, \end{equation} indicating this $\bx$ is inferior to AMP's output. \end{remark} This paper explores an alternative to AMP, as suggested in \cite{MR-2015-NonNegative}, by replacing the intractable $\lambda^+(\bW)$ with a tractable convex relaxation via a \emph{semidefinite program (SDP)}: \begin{equation} \SDP(\bW) \colonequals \max_{\substack{\bX \succeq 0 \\ \bX \geq 0 \\ \Tr(\bX) = 1}} \la \bX, \bW \ra \geq \lambda^+(\bW). \end{equation} Numerical experiments in \cite{MR-2015-NonNegative} suggest this SDP is effective for recovering $\bx$ under $\PP^+$, with the positive entries of the top eigenvector of the optimizer $\bX^{\star}$ providing a comparable estimate to AMP (see Section 5.3 of their work). In Section~\ref{sec:finite-size}, we conduct similar experiments for $\bW \sim \GOE(n)$, noting that the SDP is often \emph{tight}, with $\bX^{\star}$ being rank one within numerical precision. Although slower than AMP, the SDP's apparent efficacy hints at unifying the algorithmic tractability of non-negative PCA with other scenarios where SDP relaxations of maximum likelihood estimation are tight \cite{BKS-2014-TightnessMLESDP}. Moreover, the SDP has advantages over AMP: it can \emph{certify} an upper bound on $\lambda^+(\bW)$, and it might exhibit robustness properties seen in other contexts~\cite{FK-2001-SemirandomGraphProblems,MPW-2016-RobustReconstruction,RTJM-2016-SDPRobustness}. The asymptotic behavior of the SDP as $n \to \infty$ with $\bW \sim \GOE(n)$ was posed as Open Problem~9.5 in the lecture notes \cite{Bandeira-2015-TenLectures}. We thus investigate two questions regarding this SDP and related algorithmic strategies when $\bW \sim \GOE(n)$. The first question addresses the specific semidefinite program: \begin{enumerate} \item[1.] For $\bW \sim \GOE(n)$, does $\SDP(\bW) \to \sqrt{2}$ in probability as $n \to \infty$? \end{enumerate} Contrary to the experiments in~\cite{MR-2015-NonNegative} for small $n$, we find that the answer is \emph{no} in the asymptotic limit. Instead, $\SDP(\bW)$ approaches $\lambda_{\max}(\bW) \approx 2$ as $n \to \infty$. We then explore whether any efficient algorithm can \emph{certify} bounds on $\lambda^+(\bW)$ better than this. \begin{enumerate} \item[2.] Is there an algorithm running in time $\exp(O(n^{1 - \eta}))$ for some $\eta > 0$ that computes $c: \RR^{n \times n}_{\sym} \to \RR$ with the following properties? \begin{itemize} \item For all $\bW \in \RR^{n \times n}_{\sym}$, $c(\bW) \geq \lambda^+(\bW)$. \item For $\bW \sim \GOE(n)$, $c(\bW) \leq 2 - \varepsilon$ with high probability for some $\varepsilon > 0$. \end{itemize} \end{enumerate} We provide rigorous evidence, using the \emph{low-degree polynomial method}, that the answer to this broader question is again \emph{no}. \subsection{Organization} The remainder of this paper is structured as follows. Section~\ref{sec:sdp} presents and proves a lower bound on $\SDP(\bW)$ for $\bW \sim \GOE(n)$. In Section~\ref{sec:low-deg}, we introduce a \emph{reduction} from a hypothesis testing problem to the problem of certifying bounds on $\lambda^+(\bW)$ and review prior evidence suggesting the computational difficulty of this hypothesis testing problem. Finally, Section~\ref{sec:finite-size} details larger numerical experiments illustrating the deviation from the ``tight regime,'' where the SDP optimizer is rank one, highlighting the contrast between theoretical asymptotics and feasible computations for semidefinite programming at ``laptop scale.''

text: The task of approximating the distribution of a target variable $y$ given an input $x$ is fundamental to supervised learning. Supervised techniques, when trained with typical loss functions like Mean Square Error for regression or Cross-Entropy for classification, are designed to approximate the expected conditional distribution $\langle y|x \rangle$ \cite{bishop_mixture_1994}. This approach is effective when the target distribution is unimodal, with minor deviations in the target value primarily caused by random noise. However, in regression problems where the target distribution is multimodal, most machine learning methods struggle, often predicting an average value that does not accurately capture the distribution. In multimodal scenarios, a single input sample may correspond to multiple probable outcomes, necessitating the solution of a conditional density estimation problem. To tackle such challenges, the Mixture Density Network (MDN) \cite{bishop_mixture_1994} was introduced, capable of approximating complex conditional target distributions. MDNs have been applied in fields such as robotics \cite{choi_uncertainty_2018}, epidemiology \cite{davis_use_2020}, and finance \cite{schittenkopf_volatility_1998}. Although MDNs are typically designed for vectorial input data, many real-world problems involve relational data where structural aspects significantly influence possible outcomes, as seen in epidemiology \cite{opuszko_impact_2013}. Over the past two decades, substantial research has focused on adapting graph processing techniques (refer to surveys by \citet{bacciu_gentle_2020,wu_comprehensive_2020}). The objective is to derive optimal representations of structured samples for specific tasks using various neighborhood aggregation, graph coarsening, and information propagation methods. Applications such as drug design \cite{podda_deep_2020}, social network classification \cite{yang_revisiting_2016}, and natural language processing \cite{beck_graph--sequence_2018} benefit significantly from these adaptive methods for structured data. Our key contribution is the introduction of a hybrid approach, termed the Graph Mixture Density Network (\textsc{GMDN}{}), to address multimodal target distributions in machine learning models for graphs. This model generates a multimodal distribution conditioned on an input graph, applicable to the entire structure or its components. For example, given an observable input graph $x$, \textsc{GMDN}{} is trained to approximate the potentially multimodal distribution of the target variable $y$ through maximum likelihood estimation. The likelihood serves as the primary metric for optimizing density estimation tasks \cite{nowicki_estimation_2001}, indicating how well the model fits the empirical data distribution. Unlike traditional regression problems that predict a single output value \cite{bishop_mixture_1994}, \textsc{GMDN}{} enhances the capability of deep learning models for graphs by accommodating multimodal output distributions. We validate \textsc{GMDN} on a new benchmark application presented in this paper, involving extensive epidemiological simulations\footnote{\url{https://github.com/diningphil/graph-mixture-density-networks}} where both structural and multimodal factors are crucial for determining epidemic outcomes. The results demonstrate that \textsc{GMDN}{} significantly improves likelihood scores. Additionally, we assess our model on two real-world chemical graph regression tasks to illustrate how \textsc{GMDN}{} effectively captures uncertainty in output predictions, revealing multiple plausible chemical property values for a given molecular input.

text: The capabilities of modern unmanned aircraft systems (UAS) have expanded significantly, encompassing a wide range of applications from delivery drones to autonomous eVTOL passenger aircraft. These systems can efficiently execute tasks such as goods delivery, surveillance, public safety operations, weather monitoring, disaster relief, search and rescue, traffic monitoring, videography, and air transportation \citep{balakrishnan2018blueprint,kopardekar2016unmanned}. Urban air mobility (UAM) is anticipated to develop primarily around urban centers, often near buildings or airports. Consequently, it is expected that UAS will be equipped with onboard detect-and-avoid systems to autonomously navigate around other traffic, adverse weather, terrain, and both natural and artificial obstacles, minimizing the need for constant human oversight \citep{kopardekar2016unmanned}. Numerous mathematical models have been developed for aircraft conflict resolution. These models are generally categorized into centralized and decentralized algorithms. Centralized approaches include semidefinite programming \citep{frazzoli2001resolution}, nonlinear programming \citep{raghunathan2004dynamic,enright1992discrete}, mixed-integer linear programming \citep{schouwenaars2001mixed,richards2002aircraft,pallottino2002conflict,vela2009mixed}, mixed-integer quadratic programming \citep{mellinger2012mixed}, sequential convex programming \citep{augugliaro2012generation,morgan2014model}, second-order cone programming \citep{acikmese2007convex}, evolutionary techniques \citep{delahaye2010aircraft,cobano2011path}, and particle swarm optimization \citep{pontani2010particle}. These methods aim to find a global optimum for all aircraft involved, but their computational complexity tends to increase exponentially with the number of aircraft. On the other hand, decentralized methods often frame the conflict resolution problem as a Markov Decision Process (MDP). Reinforcement Learning (RL) has shown promise in aircraft traffic management, primarily through traditional algorithms \citep{sun2019reinforcement}. The next-generation airborne collision avoidance system (ACAS X) addresses the collision avoidance challenge as a partially observable Markov Decision Process (POMDP) and has been adapted for unmanned aircraft as ACAS Xu \citep{kochenderfer2012next}. Both ACAS X and ACAS Xu employ Dynamic Programming (DP) to evaluate the expected cost of actions \citep{manfredi2016introduction, owen2019acas}. \cite{chryssanthacopoulos2012decomposition} integrated decomposition methods with DP to enhance collision avoidance amidst multiple threats. Traditional RL algorithms necessitate fine discretization of state and action spaces, which can introduce discretization errors, potentially reducing safety and limiting maneuver flexibility for UAS. Additionally, discretizing extensive airspace demands significant computational resources and is often time-intensive. Tree search-based algorithms \citep{yang2018autonomous,yang2020scalable} have also been applied to CAS problems using MDP frameworks, avoiding state discretization but requiring substantial onboard computation time for continuous state spaces. The challenge of managing large and continuous state and action spaces in conflict resolution problems has spurred interest in Deep Reinforcement Learning (DRL), which leverages deep neural networks to approximate cost and optimal policy functions. Advances in DRL algorithms, such as Policy Gradient \citep{sutton2000policy}, Deep Q-Networks (DQN) \citep{mnih2013playing}, Double DQN \citep{van2016deep}, Dueling DQN \citep{wang2015dueling}, Deep Deterministic Policy Gradient (DDPG) \citep{lillicrap2015continuous}, Asynchronous Advantage Actor-Critic (A3C) \citep{mnih2016asynchronous}, and Proximal Policy Optimization (PPO) \citep{ppo2}, have expanded automation possibilities. \cite{li2019optimizing} applied DQN to refine an existing collision avoidance strategy in dense airspace. In \cite{yang2019real}, DQN-based algorithms were validated for UAV obstacle avoidance. \cite{wulfeuav} found that DQN outperforms value iteration in both performance and solution speed for UAV collision avoidance. The use of DQN to manage avoidance of multiple aircraft is explored in \cite{keong2019reinforcement}. \cite{brittain2020deep} introduced a deep multi-agent reinforcement learning framework using PPO to resolve aircraft conflicts in a high-density, dynamic airspace. The aforementioned DRL work operates within continuous state and discrete action spaces. Progress in applying DRL to UAS conflict resolution with continuous control remains limited. \cite{pham2019machine} devised a method inspired by Deep Q-learning and Deep Deterministic Policy Gradient algorithms, achieving a success rate exceeding 81\% amidst traffic and uncertainties. \cite{ma2018saliency} proposed a framework integrating an autonomous obstacle detection module with an actor-critic based reinforcement learning module to enable reactive obstacle avoidance for UAVs. Testing of PPO on benchmark tasks, including robotic locomotion and Atari games, demonstrated its superiority over other online policy gradient methods, highlighting PPO's balance between complexity, simplicity, and efficiency \citep{ppo2}. Consequently, a PPO-based conflict resolution model holds significant promise for UAS traffic management, motivating this study. To the best of the authors' knowledge, this study pioneers the development of a DRL approach based on the PPO algorithm, enabling UAS to navigate successfully in continuous state and action spaces. The advantage of continuous space calculations is the elimination of the need for state space discretization or postprocessing smoothing. The proposed model, once trained offline to determine the optimal policy, is applicable for real-time online trajectory planning for UAS. The primary contributions of this paper are as follows: \begin{itemize} \setlength\itemsep{0em} \item A PPO-based framework is introduced for UAS to avoid both static and dynamic obstacles in continuous state and action spaces. \item A novel scenario state representation and reward function are developed to effectively map environmental conditions to maneuvers, enabling the trained model to generate continuous heading and speed commands. \item The proposed learning framework's efficacy is tested in environments with static obstacles, static obstacles with UAS position uncertainty, and deterministic and stochastic environments with dynamic obstacles. Results demonstrate that the model provides precise and robust guidance, achieving a conflict resolution success rate exceeding 99\%. \end{itemize} The paper is structured as follows. \cref{background} provides an overview of Markov Decision Processes and Deep Reinforcement Learning. \cref{mdp} details the model formulation using a Markov Decision Process for UAS conflict resolution in continuous action space. Numerical experiments demonstrating the proposed approach's capability to teach UAS to avoid conflicts are presented in \cref{result}. Finally, \cref{Conclusion} concludes the paper.

text: Frequently-Asked-Questions (FAQ) consist of a set of question-answer pairs, either manually curated or automatically extracted from pertinent documents. These FAQs serve as a centralized resource, offering users immediate access to the most sought-after or pertinent information about a product or service, thereby facilitating swift customer support for general inquiries. \vspace*{1mm} {\bf Motivation.} FAQ retrieval systems offer a natural language interface for searching through an FAQ collection, gaining popularity among large service providers as a means to deliver information to customers. Such systems offer dual benefits: (i) they automate customer service tasks, such as through intelligent chatbots~\cite{massaro2018,yan2016} and automated email responses~\cite{karan2018,malik2007}, and (ii) they enable customer service agents to efficiently access internal FAQ documents, thereby enhancing service quality and efficiency. Moreover, with the rise of personal assistants like XiaoIce, Siri, Alexa, and Google Assistant, these "virtual agents" provide an additional avenue for users to obtain answers and perform routine tasks, complementing FAQs, hotlines, and forums, and fostering a more natural interaction with users~\cite{lommatzsch2019,por2020}. \vspace*{1mm} {\bf Challenges.} FAQ retrieval presents significant challenges, primarily due to the brevity of question-answer texts, which complicates bridging the {\em lexical and semantic gap} between user queries and FAQ questions because of their limited context~\cite{karan2018,lee2008}. Additionally, accurately interpreting user questions is often challenging due to informal language, domain-specific terminology, abbreviations, and mismatches between formal and colloquial terms~\cite{lommatzsch2019}. For instance, questions like {\small{\tt ``How can I seal a hole in the gas tank of my car?''}} and {\small{\tt ``How to patch a leak in the fuel compartment of my van?''}} are semantically similar but display minimal lexical overlap and formal-colloquial discrepancies. Furthermore, FAQ retrieval systems must adeptly manage both keyword-based and {\em short span} "natural language" questions. Given their primarily "customer-centric" nature, these systems require higher precision and interpretability than traditional information retrieval methods. \vspace*{1mm} {\bf Problem Statement.} The task of {\em FAQ Retrieval} involves efficiently ranking question-answer pairs by relevance in response to a user query. Essentially, these retrieval engines strive to discern the user's underlying {\em intent} and retrieve the most pertinent answers containing the correct information~\cite{kothari2009}. Consider a pre-arranged repository of question-answer $(Q, A)$ pairs that make up the FAQ $= \{(Q_1, A_1), \cdots, (Q_n, A_n)\}$, where $Q_i$ is a question related to the domain, and $A_i$ is its corresponding answer. Given a user query $q$, the objective is to produce an ordered list of FAQ $(Q, A)$ pairs, $\{(Q_1^q, A_1^q), \cdots, (Q_k^q, A_k^q)\}$, that exhibit high semantic and intent similarity to the input query $q$. \vspace*{1mm} {\bf Contributions.} This paper introduces {\em TI-S2S}, an innovative keyword-based supervised learning framework designed for efficient FAQ retrieval. Our approach utilizes a {\em sequence-to-sequence} model to generate representative labels for user questions, facilitating the computation of query-question similarity. Furthermore, a variant that incorporates "candidate" identification using a deep learning architecture is demonstrated to enhance performance. Our proposed framework effectively captures: (i) the domain-specificity of the application, (ii) distinctive words and concepts for differentiating questions, and (iii) semantic similarity for retrieving relevant QA pairs from the FAQ collection. Experiments conducted on a public FAQ dataset reveal that our framework surpasses existing methods in terms of accuracy and exhibits robustness even with limited training data. Consequently, it inherently considers both {\em document redundancy} and {\em query redundancy}~\cite{karan2018}.

The profound impact of G. Hinton's pioneering work on 	extit{backpropagation} in 1986 \cite{Rumelhart1986LearningRB} has been instrumental in the development of modern optimizers, now integral to deep learning libraries such as Google's Tensorflow \cite{Abadi2016TensorFlowAS} and Facebook's PyTorch \cite{NEURIPS2019_9015}. The 	extit{gradient} is central to the training of most deep learning models. For instance, in image classification, the gradient guides the model in adjusting its parameters to minimize the discrepancy (the 	extit{loss function}) between predicted outputs and actual class labels. By iteratively updating its parameters in the opposite direction of the gradient for various training samples, the model progressively reduces the loss function, thereby enhancing prediction accuracy. Nevertheless, the gradient's fundamental role in deep learning also poses a privacy risk. As depicted in Fig. ef{fig:intro_grad}, in a typical face recognition system, a batch of images is fed into a neural network classifier. The classifier predicts labels, computes the average loss, and uses backpropagation to derive the gradient, which is the derivative of the average loss with respect to the parameters. Given that the gradient is directly derived from the input data and labels, attackers might exploit this to extract sensitive information from the original training data. With the rise of distributed learning paradigms \cite{yang2019FL,Chen2020NebulaAS}, research has started to explore the potential of inferring data properties \cite{Melis2019ExploitingUF}, membership information \cite{Melis2019ExploitingUF, Nasr2019ComprehensivePA}, class representatives \cite{Hitaj2017DeepMU, Wang2019BeyondIC}, or even data inputs \cite{Zhu2019DeepLF, Zhao2020iDLGID, Geiping2020InvertingG} from gradients potentially exposed to a man-in-the-middle attacker or a curious server \cite{Lyu2020,Kairouz2021AdvancesAO}. Despite the potential for privacy breaches via gradients, previous attacks have encountered a common yet vague performance limitation in their privacy leakage strategies. For instance, Melis et al. \cite{Melis2019ExploitingUF} observed a reduction in the precision of sensitive word inference from gradients by over $30\%$ when batch size increased eightfold. Nasr et al. \cite{Nasr2019ComprehensivePA} noted that shallower neural networks tend to leak less membership information. Zhu et al. \cite{Zhu2019DeepLF} found that the number of iterations needed to reverse-engineer a training batch from its average gradient increased tenfold as the batch size grew from $1$ to $8$, and attacks were more likely to fail with shallower networks. This suggests that larger training batches and shallower models might mitigate information leakage from gradients. However, the underlying cause of this phenomenon remains unexplored in existing literature. 
oindent	extbf{Our Work.} We delve into this issue by examining the mechanics of 	extit{data reconstruction attacks} \cite{Zhu2019DeepLF, Zhao2020iDLGID, Geiping2020InvertingG}, a burgeoning privacy threat that leverages the leaked average gradient of a deep learning model to reverse-engineer the associated training batch. As illustrated in the right section of Fig. ef{fig:intro_grad}, these attacks aim to reconstruct training samples from the gradient, posing significant threats to the confidentiality of private data. Zhu et al. \cite{Zhu2019DeepLF} pioneered a learning-based method to restore training batches by treating unknown batches as learnable variables (i.e., 	extit{dummy data}). By minimizing the L2 distance between the gradient on dummy data and the actual gradient (i.e., 	extit{gradient matching}), they found reconstruction feasible when the batch size was no more than $8$ for CIFAR-100 \cite{Krizhevsky2009LearningML}, though the quality varied across trials and smaller models. Subsequent works \cite{Zhao2020iDLGID,Geiping2020InvertingG} introduced technical refinements to this framework, yet similar bottlenecks persisted. Due to their limited interpretability, previous studies have not adequately explained 	extit{why, when, and how data reconstruction from gradients is possible}, which could be crucial for understanding and enhancing gradient privacy. To delineate the security boundaries of data reconstruction from gradients, we conduct the first analytical study of such attacks on fully-connected neural networks (FCNs) with rectified linear units (ReLUs \cite{Goodfellow-et-al-2016}), a fundamental architecture frequently used to explore novel attack and defense strategies \cite{Jagielski2020HighAA,Tramr2016StealingML,Rolnick2020ReverseengineeringDR}. As the most prevalent activation function in deep learning \cite{Goodfellow-et-al-2016}, ReLU allows nonnegative inputs to pass through unchanged while blocking negative inputs. This distinctive gate-like behavior enables each input sample to possess its own set of 	extit{activation paths}, forming its 	extit{activation pattern} \cite{Montfar2014OnTN, Laurent2018TheMS}. We devise deterministic algorithms to decode hidden information in the average gradient, identifying each sample's activation patterns—a pivotal step that simplifies the nonlinear gradient-matching problem to a linear equation system concerning inputs, facilitating further analytical exploration. By examining conditions under which activation patterns can be reconstructed from gradients, we contribute the following insights: 
oindent	extbf{(1) Neuron Exclusivity State Analysis.} We introduce the concept of 	extit{neuron exclusivity state}, marked by the count of 	extit{	extbf{Ex}clusively 	extbf{A}ctivated 	extbf{N}eurons} (ExANs, i.e., ReLUs activated by only one sample in a batch during a forward pass), as critical to the feasibility of data reconstruction attacks. We define boundary conditions for neuron exclusivity states in a training batch under attack. 
oindent	extbf{(2) Boundary of Insecure Exclusivity States.} We identify the 	extit{sufficient exclusivity} condition, where each batch sample has at least $2$ ExANs at the last ReLU layer and $1$ at other layers, as a strong indicator of insecure neuron exclusivity states (Section ef{sec:atk_case_a}). We demonstrate that a deterministic attack algorithm with guaranteed reconstruction accuracy (Theorem ef{col:optim_bound_mult}) can be developed for any batch meeting the sufficient exclusivity condition. Evaluations across $5$ real-world scenarios, including medical, face recognition, and visual datasets, and a variety of FCNs of different depths and widths, show our attack significantly outperforms previous methods in reconstruction recognizability and achieves $100\%$ label inference accuracy (Section ef{sec:evaluation}). Additionally, we extend our attack strategy to convolutional neural networks (CNNs) by integrating analytical and optimization-based methods. 
oindent	extbf{(3) Boundary of Secure Exclusivity States.} By analyzing the remaining exclusivity state space, we define the 	extit{lack of exclusivity} condition, where each sample has $0$ ExAN at the first ReLU layer, as indicative of the impossibility of unique reconstruction (Section ef{sec:def_case_b}). For these states, we prove the existence of infinitely many artifact batches that produce identical gradients to the victim's ground-truth batch and establish a lower bound for the maximum distance between an artifact and the ground-truth batch (Theorem ef{thm:impossible_reconstr}). This finding motivates an exclusivity reduction strategy, replacing the first ReLU layer with a linear layer, to enhance the privacy of any training batch larger than the number of neurons in the first layer, with minimal impact on model performance. To complete our study, we present preliminary experimental results in Section ef{sec:discussion} to empirically assess data reconstruction performance across the remaining states.

text: Understanding users' preferences through their historical data is crucial for generating effective recommendations, as both user preferences and item characteristics are constantly evolving. Additionally, these preferences are highly context-dependent (e.g., purchasing a desktop may increase interest in buying a keyboard). Consequently, sequential recommendation systems aim to forecast the next items users might prefer by leveraging their historical interactions. Numerous algorithms have been developed to better interpret users' sequential histories~\cite{SASRec, BERT4Rec, hidasi2018recurrent, CASER, M3, rendle2010factorizing, DIN, TRANSREC}. Despite achieving impressive results, many of these approaches overlook the temporal aspect of interactions. Recent advancements like TiSASRec~\cite{TISASRec} have integrated time information, yet their approach is limited to a singular embedding strategy. Given the wealth of information contained in timestamps, it is advantageous to explore various temporal embeddings to fully capture diverse patterns and to develop model architectures that can utilize this diversity effectively. This paper introduces \textbf{MEANTIME} (\textbf{M}ixtur\textbf{E} of \textbf{A}tte\textbf{NTI}on mechanisms with \textbf{M}ulti-temporal \textbf{E}mbeddings), a novel approach that incorporates multiple temporal embeddings to more accurately represent both absolute and relative positions of user-item interactions within a sequence. We enhance this approach by using multiple self-attention heads, each processing a different positional embedding. This allows each head to act as a specialist, focusing on specific user behavior patterns. Comprehensive experiments demonstrate that \textbf{MEANTIME} surpasses current state-of-the-art algorithms on real-world datasets. Our main contributions include: \begin{itemize} \item We introduce a variety of embedding schemes to encode the positions of user-item interactions in sequences. This involves applying multiple kernels to the positions and timestamp values within a sequence to generate distinct embedding matrices. \item We propose an innovative model architecture that employs multiple self-attention heads concurrently. Each head is designed to specialize in extracting specific patterns from user behaviors by utilizing one of the positional embeddings we introduce. \item We conducted extensive experiments to validate our method's effectiveness on real-world datasets, alongside a detailed ablation study to elucidate the impact of different components within our model. \end{itemize}

text: Deep neural networks (DNNs) have achieved remarkable success across various tasks in computer vision and pattern recognition. However, several challenges hinder their broader application. One major issue is the considerable computational expense required for both training and inference, which complicates the deployment of large-scale DNN models on devices with constrained computational capabilities \cite{wu2018deep}. Additionally, the opacity of DNNs renders them unsuitable for scenarios where understanding the rationale behind decisions is essential. Given that DNNs essentially consist of repeated layers of basic computational units, or perceptrons, it is worth exploring whether substituting these units with alternative modules might yield unexpected benefits. Decision trees are renowned for their transparency and efficient training processes. This raises the question: can we construct a deep model that employs decision trees as its fundamental computational units? Recent research has investigated this concept, showing promising initial results. For instance, \cite{zhou2017deep} introduced a deep random forest cascade, where each layer comprises an ensemble of random forests, with the outputs of the current forests serving as inputs for the subsequent layer. Building on this, \cite{miller2017forward} enhanced the approach by incorporating a set of decision trees per layer, combining the current layer's outputs with the original input to generate a new representation for the next layer. Both studies \cite{zhou2017deep, miller2017forward} demonstrated performance on par with DNN models on the MNIST dataset, while achieving significant reductions in training time and lighter model parameters. Despite these advancements, their models still require thousands of trees per layer due to the limited expressive capacity of individual decision trees. In response to these challenges, we propose several enhancements to the existing deep forest model. Firstly, to enable end-to-end optimization, we introduce a \textit{soft routing} mechanism that replaces the traditional hard splitting criteria in decision trees. In this approach, the routing decisions at each internal node are determined by a sigmoid function, allowing for gradient descent to propagate error signals through the tree. Secondly, we introduce a \textit{leafness parameter} for each tree node, enabling the tree to globally learn its structure. This addition allows each node to dynamically determine whether it should function as a leaf or an internal node \cite{irsoy2014budding}.

text: The advent of language model pre-training has triggered numerous advancements in natural language processing (NLP) \cite{devlin2018bert, brown2020language, peters2018deep, liu2019roberta}, achieving state-of-the-art performance across various complex tasks such as question-answering and natural language inference. Within this domain, the BERT model, grounded in the architecture proposed by \cite{vaswani2017attention}, has gained significant attention. BERT's architecture is composed of multiple stacked bidirectional Transformer encoder blocks \cite{vaswani2017attention}. The training process involves an initial pre-training phase on a vast corpus of unlabeled data, followed by fine-tuning on a smaller, task-specific dataset. While pre-training is computationally intensive and may take several days, fine-tuning is relatively quicker. BERT models are characterized by a substantial number of parameters and memory requirements, ranging from 110 million in BERT\textsubscript{BASE} to 340 million in BERT\textsubscript{LARGE}, and up to 8.3 billion in Megatron \cite{shoeybi2019megatron}. In our study, we illustrate how reducing model size and training duration can be achieved with minimal impact on fine-tuning accuracy. Although the reduction in model size and training time is inherently valuable, we also aim to provide a comprehensive understanding of the efficacy of our architectural changes. Drawing parallels to the research conducted by \cite{clark2019does}, we employ probing linear classifiers and centered kernel alignment \cite{kornblith2019similarity} to elucidate the enhancements brought about by our modifications.

text: Recommender Systems~(RS)~\cite{rendle2009bpr,rendle2010factorization,he2017neural,wang19neural,zheng17joint,pinsage2018ying} are designed to predict user preferences for items, often utilizing Collaborative Filtering~(CF) signals~\cite{wang19neural}. These signals are based on the assumption that users with similar tastes will share common items, allowing the system to derive user and item embeddings from user-item interactions. A significant challenge in CF methods is the cold-start problem~\cite{zheng2018spectral}, where it becomes difficult to learn embeddings for users or items with limited interactions. To address this, high-order signals~\cite{wang19neural} are modeled to disseminate information across multiple hops in the user-item bipartite graph. The emergence of Graph Neural Networks~(GNN)~\cite{kipf17semi,graphsage17hamilton,wu19simplifying} facilitates the propagation of these high-order signals by employing multiple \textit{aggregation layers}. Consequently, users and items can gather first-order signals from immediate neighbors at initial layers and high-order signals from more distant neighbors at deeper layers. Nevertheless, through empirical analysis on real-world datasets, we identify three common performance issues in existing GNNs for RS, termed as the \textbf{oscillation} problem, \textbf{varying locality} problem, and \textbf{fixed propagation pattern} problem. The oscillation problem arises when stacking multiple layers, disrupting information propagation. Intuitively, this problem manifests as a gap in information flow between successive hops, primarily due to the bipartite graph structure. As depicted on the left side of Figure~\ref{fig:example_osci}, users' direct neighbors are exclusively items, while their 2-hop neighbors are all users. This results in users receiving information solely from items when aggregating direct neighbors, and vice versa, causing information to oscillate between users and items. Adding self-loops~\cite{kipf17semi,wang19neural} is a proposed solution to break the bipartite structure, yet we theoretically establish that it fails to mitigate the oscillation problem. Moreover, introducing self-loops effectively halts information propagation, further aggravating the cold-start issue. In addition to oscillation, the varying locality problem in the bipartite graph constrains the propagation capacity of multi-layer structures~\cite{xu18jk}. This issue pertains to the density of local structures within the bipartite graph. For instance, in Figure~\ref{fig:example_osci}, $u_4$ has a lower local density compared to $u_2$, as it is directly connected only to $i_4$, whereas $u_2$ connects to $i_1$, $i_2$, and $i_3$. The 3-hop propagation from $u_4$ (red edges in Figure~\ref{fig:example_osci}) spans only 3 edges, while $u_2$’s 3-hop propagation (green edges) nearly encompasses all edges in the graph. The propagation tree on the right side of Figure~\ref{fig:example_osci} shows that $u_4$ has fewer potential propagation paths than $u_2$. Lastly, the fixed propagation pattern across layers in existing multi-layer RS models~\cite{he2020lightgcn,wang19neural,berg2017gcmc} leads to redundant information transfer. An example of this redundancy is shown as the yellow-shaded block on the right side of Figure~\ref{fig:example_osci}. Initially, $u_2$'s information is spread to $i_1$ and $i_2$ in the first hop. This information then propagates to $u_1$ and $u_2$ in the second hop and is subsequently reversed in the third hop. This redundancy stems from the unchanging propagation pattern across layers. Sampling layer-dependent neighbors~\cite{zou2019layer} is a potential solution, though the current sampling strategies are computationally intensive and non-differentiable, complicating the training process. To address these challenges, we introduce a novel GNN framework tailored for bipartite graphs, called deep \textbf{D}eoscillated Adaptive \textbf{G}raph \textbf{C}ollaborative \textbf{F}iltering~(DGCF). We develop a Cross-Hop Propagation~(CHP) layer that modifies the bipartite propagation structure to resolve the oscillation problem. Unlike existing methods that focus solely on direct neighbors, the CHP layer also facilitates the transfer of information from cross-hop neighbors, enabling users and items to receive data from cross-hop counterparts. Additionally, we introduce a Locality-Adaptive~(LA) layer to regulate information flow, learning an influence factor for each node that adjusts to the graph's varying locality. The DGCF model is composed of multiple CHP and LA layers, enabling the adaptive propagation of high-order CF signals to optimize user and item embeddings. The weights of LA and CHP layers vary across layers, establishing a layer-wise propagation pattern. Our contributions include: \begin{itemize} \item \textbf{Oscillation problem:} We formally define and prove the existence and boundaries of the graph oscillation problem in bipartite graphs, providing empirical evidence of its occurrence with a limited number of layers. \item \textbf{Innovative layers:} We develop two novel layers, the CHP layer and the LA layer. The CHP layer is designed to tackle the oscillation problem, while the LA layer addresses the varying locality issue. The use of multiple LA layers solves the fixed aggregation pattern problem. \item \textbf{Extensive experiments:} Beyond overall comparisons, we conduct detailed analyses on the three identified problems. We examine the oscillation issue when excessive layers are stacked, explore the varying locality problem and our model's solution, and observe changes in the propagation pattern. \end{itemize}

text: Consider a scenario where an image is available in a \textit{functional} format. Specifically, the image is expressed as a function $f: \bm{p} \mapsto \bm{c}$, which accepts a pixel coordinate $\bm{p} = (x,y) \in \mathbb{R}^2$ and returns the corresponding RGB value $\bm{c} = (r, g, b) \in \mathbb{R}^3$. Such functional image representations are commonly found in differentiable rendering systems \cite{SynSin, SoftRasterizer} or implicit image representations \cite{siren, fourier_inr, inr_gan, cips}. Suppose we aim to create a high-resolution raster image from this functional form $f(\bm p)$. This requires evaluating $f(\bm p)$ at every point on an $H \times W$ grid to produce an image of the same dimensions. If the function $f(\bm p)$ is computationally expensive to evaluate, this process becomes laborious. What solutions are available? One strategy involves accelerating the inference process for $f(\bm p)$. Alternatively, we could generate a low-resolution image and subsequently upsample it using existing techniques. These upsampling techniques generally assume that the points being upsampled are arranged on a uniform grid, meaning they have consistent horizontal and vertical spacing, as shown in Figure \ref{fig:uniform-interpolation}. However, in real-world scenarios, points may be distributed on a non-uniform grid, as illustrated in Figure \ref{fig:non-uniform-interpolation}, which restricts the effectiveness of current tools. To address this challenge, we introduce a novel interpolation method that enables image reconstruction from a set of points scattered arbitrarily across the image. Our approach involves modeling each known color $c^{i}$ at a location $(x^{(i)}, y^{(i)})$ as a two-dimensional normal distribution $\mathcal{N}(\bm \mu^{(i)}, \sigma^2 I)$, where $\bm\mu^{(i)} = (x^{(i)}, y^{(i)})$ and $\sigma^2$ is a predefined variance. \input{figures/uniform-vs-non-uniform} In summary, our contributions include: \begin{itemize} \item Introducing a novel interpolation technique that models known points using a Gaussian Mixture Model (GMM) and infers unknown values as expectations. \item Developing an optimized CUDA kernel to efficiently handle both the forward and backward computations of the proposed interpolation method. \item Demonstrating through experiments on the ImageNet dataset that our interpolation technique surpasses six standard interpolation methods in several scenarios based on reconstruction quality. \end{itemize}
