text: The industry has extensively embraced automatic text processing to extract valuable insights. This technology is applied to analyze product or movie reviews to ascertain the overall sentiment. Additionally, it is used to assess tweets to gauge public perception of a brand or opinions on specific topics. Fundamentally, these applications involve tasks of classification or summarization. State-of-the-art NLP techniques excel in handling these tasks for texts in a single language. However, their performance diminishes when applied to code-mixed text due to the scarcity of labeled data. The relevance of code-mixed text has surged, especially on various social media platforms \cite{gamback2016comparing} \cite{barman2014code}. English often serves as the primary medium of communication on these platforms. In multilingual countries like India, users frequently blend their local languages with English on social media. This mixing occurs because individuals find it more comfortable to express certain terms or entities in their native languages, resulting in code-mixing. Code-mixing facilitates communication by borrowing terms from multiple languages. It adds a local flavor to movie reviews, product reviews, and comments by incorporating local language details. These dynamics have contributed to the rising popularity of code-mixed text \cite{khanuja2020gluecos}. To comprehend code-mixed text, it is crucial to identify the languages used in different segments of the text, followed by language-specific processing \cite{das2015code}. Our research explores various methods for language identification in code-mixed text. In such texts, languages can be interwoven in diverse patterns. Consider the example \textit{"this is not union budget, ye to aam admi ka budget hai"}, tagged as "eng eng eng eng eng hin hin hin hin hin hin hin". Another example is \textit{"maine aaj WhatsApp and Facebook uninstall kiya h"}, tagged as "hin hin eng eng eng eng hin hin". Identifying the language of individual words is challenging, as some words may be used in both Hindi and English depending on context. For instance, English words like \textit{"are"} and \textit{"maze"} appear in Hindi phrases such as \textit{"are mai ghar jaa raha hu"} and \textit{"appke to maze hai"}. The challenge intensifies with the inherent noisiness of social media text, where words are often stylized differently for emphasis. For example, the word \textit{"good"} might be elongated to \textit{"gooood"}. This necessitates diverse input representations. Sentences can be processed on a word-by-word or character-by-character basis. A more recent approach is sub-word representation, where words are decomposed into logical sub-word units \cite{kudo2018subword}. Character and sub-word representations are more resilient to text variations compared to word representations, which treat each variation as distinct. Our study primarily evaluates the performance of these input representations. Notably, this work is pioneering in exploring sub-word representations for Hindi-English language identification. The task involves determining the language of each word in a sentence, framed as a token classification task. Deep learning models, particularly convolutional neural networks (CNNs) and long short-term memory (LSTM) networks, are popular for token classification. We employ these models alongside various input representations to assess their effectiveness. These models are often paired with a conditional random field (CRF) to enhance performance. However, our focus remains on simple architectures and input representation. We demonstrate that sub-word-based representation, combined with these straightforward models, outperforms more complex architectures documented in the literature. Simpler architectures are advantageous as they reduce runtime and complexity. The language identification module must be efficient and swift, as it typically precedes other NLP modules. With this in mind, we experiment with single-layer CNN and LSTM models. Our experiments reveal that these architectures achieve the desired accuracy levels. The primary contributions of this work are: \begin{itemize} \item An evaluation of the effectiveness of character, sub-word, and word-based representations for Hindi-English language identification. \item A comparison of various combinations of popular model architectures and input representations. \end{itemize}

The state-of-the-art NLP techniques perform admirably in such tasks when applied to single-language texts, but their performance decreases when applied to code-mixed texts because of the scarcity of labeled data. In multilingual countries like India, users frequently mix local languages with English on social media. English is the most widely used medium of communication on these platforms. The relevance of code-mixed texts has increased, especially on social media. Code-mixing facilitates communication by borrowing terms from several languages. It also adds a local flavor to movie reviews, product reviews, and comments by using local slang. It is thus essential to be able to identify the language used in the different sections of the text, in order to be able to process it in the appropriate manner. The growing importance of such texts can be explained by the fact that they can be comprehended only by using the languages used in them. Our research is therefore concerned with various methods for language identification in mixed-language text. This kind of linguistic intertwining can take place in a variety of ways. For example, a text like “This is not the Union budget, it is the Aam Admi budget” is tagged “eng eng eng eng eng hin hin hin hin hin.” Another text like “Main aaj main WhatsApp and Facebook uninstall kiya hai,” is tagged “hin hin eng eng eng hin hin.” The difficulty is exacerbated by the noise and stylization in the text. For instance, English words such as “are” and “maze” appear in Hindi phrases like “are-i-am-ghar-i-am” and “textit-appke-tum-maze-hai”—and are sometimes stylized differently for emphasis. – It is therefore necessary to have different input representations. A sentence can be treated on a word-by-word or character-by-character basis. For example, the word “textit – good” could be elongated into “textit – gooood”. - Character and sub-word representations are more resistant to text variations compared to word representations, which treat each variation as a different word. A newer approach is sub-word representation, where words are decomposed into logical sub-word units. This work is a first step towards exploring sub-word representations for language identification. Deep learning models, particularly convolutional neural networks (CNNs) and long short-term memory (LSTM) networks, are popular for this task. The task is to determine the language of each word in a sentence. This task is formulated as a token classification task. These models are often combined with a conditional random field (CRF) to improve performance. Our emphasis is on simple architectures and input representations. We use these models in combination with various input representations to study their effectiveness. The language identification must be quick and efficient since it is usually the first of the NLP stages. Simpler architectures are advantageous in that they are simpler and require less time. We demonstrate that sub-word based models, combined with a simple architecture, outperform more complex architectures published in the literature. The major contributions of this work are: (i) to test the effectiveness of character, sub-word and word-based representations for the identification of the English-Hindi language pair. (ii) to test the single-layer neural network architectures. (iii) to test the accuracy of the model on the data set. An enumeration and comparison of the various combinations of the popular models and input representations.

text: Evaluating a classifier's effectiveness is essential in the realm of machine learning. While the algorithm's execution time for computing this evaluation is of minimal concern in offline scenarios, such as during the research phase of classifier development, it becomes significantly more important when performance monitoring is required in real-time, especially when data points are rapidly incoming. Consider the task of identifying irregular activities within IT systems using event logs. The sheer volume of these logs makes manual monitoring impractical. A feasible solution is deploying a classifier to detect anomalies and notify analysts for further examination. Continuous monitoring is crucial to swiftly identify irregularities. Additionally, the classifier's performance must be consistently tracked, as changes in the IT system can alter the data distribution and, consequently, the classifier's effectiveness. To detect recent performance shifts, interest often lies in assessing performance over the latest $n$ data points. More broadly, the goal is to uphold the performance measure amidst the addition or removal of data points. This study focuses on algorithms that maintain two performance measures. The first is the area under the ROC curve (AUC), a traditional method for evaluating classifier performance through its ROC curve. We also explore the $H$-measure, introduced by~\citet{hand:09:alternative}, which is based on the minimum weighted loss averaged over cost ratios. A notable advantage of the $H$-measure over AUC is its intuitive approach to weighting classification errors. Both measures can be freshly computed in $\bigO{n \log n}$ time, or in $\bigO{n}$ time if data points are pre-sorted. This paper introduces three algorithms enabling the maintenance of these measures in polylogarithmic time. The first algorithm addresses AUC maintenance with data point additions or deletions. The strategy involves keeping data points ordered within a self-balancing search tree. Updating the AUC requires knowing the ROC coordinates of the altered data point. This is achieved by adjusting the search tree to track cumulative label counts within each subtree, allowing coordinate retrieval in $\bigO{\log n}$ time, thus ensuring a total maintenance time of $\bigO{\log n}$. The subsequent two algorithms focus on the $H$-measure. Calculating the $H$-measure necessitates determining the ROC curve's convex hull and iterating over it. Initially, we demonstrate that a classical dynamic convex hull algorithm, with minor modifications, can sustain the ROC curve's convex hull. These modifications are necessary because individual data point ROC coordinates are unavailable; however, the same technique used for AUC computation can provide the required coordinates. We further illustrate that, by estimating class priors from test data, the $H$-measure can be decomposed into a sum over convex hull points, where the $i$th term relies solely on the difference between the $i$th and $(i - 1)$st data points. This decomposition allows the $H$-measure to be maintained in $\bigO{\log^2 n}$ time. If class priors are not derived from test data, we propose an estimation algorithm. This method involves grouping proximate points on the convex hull. Essentially, if points on the convex hull are near each other, only one point from the group is used. The grouping ensures an $\epsilon$-approximation in $\bigO{(\log n + \epsilon^{-1}) \log n}$ time. \textbf{Structure:} The remainder of the paper is structured as follows. Section~\ref{sec:prel} provides preliminary definitions. Section~\ref{sec:auc} details the maintenance of AUC, while Sections~\ref{sec:hexact}--\ref{sec:happrox} focus on maintaining the $H$-measure. The experimental evaluation is presented in Section~\ref{sec:exp}, and the paper concludes with a discussion in Section~\ref{sec:conclusions}.

Applications in video analytics, such as those used for urban mobility and intelligent vehicles \cite{bellevue-report}, are increasingly driven by deep neural network (DNN) models for tasks like object detection and classification. Prominent examples include Yolo \cite{yolo9000-1}, ResNet \cite{deepresidual-2}, and EfficientNet \cite{efficientnet-3}. Typically, these video analytics systems transmit video feeds to {\em edge servers} \cite{azure-ase, aws-outposts} situated on-site \cite{ieee-computer, edgevideo-1, edgevideo-2, getmobile}. Edge computing is favored for such analytics because it avoids the high costs associated with streaming videos to the cloud \cite{getmobile} and maintains video privacy, a requirement in many European cities that prohibit cloud streaming \cite{sweden-data, azure-data}. Edge computing resources are inherently limited, often equipped with less powerful GPUs \cite{aws-outposts, azure-ase}. This constraint is further exacerbated by the disparity between the rapid growth in model compute requirements and the slower advancements in processor capabilities \cite{ion-blog, openai-blog}. Consequently, edge systems depend on {\em model compression} techniques \cite{compression-4, compression-5, compression-6}. Initially, compressed DNNs are trained on representative samples from each video stream. However, in real-world scenarios, they face {\em data drift}, where the live video data significantly deviates from the training data \cite{datadrift-7, datadrift-8, datadrift-a, datadrift-b}. Street cameras and smart vehicles frequently encounter dynamic scenes with varying lighting, crowd densities, and object types. It is challenging to anticipate all these variations during training, and even minor changes can degrade accuracy. Consequently, edge DNNs experience a notable accuracy decline due to data drift, with reductions reaching 22\% (\Sef{subsec:continuous-measurement}). Moreover, the reduced parameters and simpler architectures of compressed DNNs often fail to maintain high accuracy when faced with extensive data variability. 
oindent{ f Continuous model retraining.} Addressing data drift effectively requires continuous learning. Edge DNNs are incrementally {\em retrained} on new video data while retaining previously acquired knowledge \cite{compressiondrift-11, continuous-12}. Continuous learning methods periodically update the DNNs \cite{distribution-20, mullapudi2019}; the interval between updates is termed the "retraining window," during which a sample of accumulated data is used for retraining. This ongoing adaptation \cite{incremental-13, icarl-14, incremental-15} enables compressed edge models to sustain high accuracy despite evolving data characteristics. Edge servers leverage their GPUs \cite{azure-ase} to perform DNN inference across multiple live video streams, such as those from city traffic cameras. Introducing continuous training on edge servers involves balancing the accuracy of live inference against the degradation caused by data drift. Allocating more resources to retraining expedites the process, yielding a more accurate model sooner. However, reallocating resources from inference to retraining can reduce inference accuracy, as it may necessitate frame sampling for analysis. The {\em configurations} of these tasks critically influence their resource demands and accuracy. For retraining tasks, configurations encompass hyperparameters like the number of training epochs, which significantly affect resource needs and performance (\Sef{subsec:profiles}). The improvement in accuracy from retraining also hinges on the extent of changes in live video characteristics. For inference tasks, configurations such as frame sampling and resolution determine the accuracy and resources required to process live video \cite{chameleon, noscope}. 
oindent{ f Problem statement.} We focus on the following decisions for continuous retraining: ($1$) determining which edge models to retrain during each window; ($2$) distributing the edge server's GPU resources between retraining and inference tasks; and ($3$) selecting configurations for both retraining and inference tasks. Our decisions are constrained to ensure that inference accuracy {\em at any given time} remains above a minimum threshold, ensuring the utility of outputs to applications. Our goal is to maximize the inference accuracy {\em averaged over the retraining window} (encompassing accuracies during and post-retraining) across all videos processed by the edge server. This objective introduces new challenges, differing from $(i)$ video inference systems that focus solely on instantaneous accuracy \cite{videostorm, noscope, chameleon}, and $(ii)$ model training systems that prioritize eventual accuracy \cite{hyperparameter-16, DBLP:journals/jmlr/BergstraB12, DBLP:conf/nips/SnoekLA12, Swersky_scalablebayesian, DBLP:conf/osdi/XiaoBRSKHPPZZYZ18, DBLP:conf/eurosys/PengBCWG18}. Addressing the core tradeoff between retrained model accuracy and inference accuracy is computationally intensive. Firstly, the decision space is multi-dimensional, encompassing various retraining and inference configurations and temporal resource allocation choices. Secondly, evaluating the performance of different configurations (in terms of resource use and accuracy) requires actual retraining with those configurations. Data drift compounds these challenges, as decisions effective in one retraining window may not be suitable in future windows. 
oindent{ f Solution components.} Our approach, {{	t Ekya}\xspace}, comprises two primary components: a resource scheduler and a performance estimator. Within each retraining window, the { f resource scheduler} executes the three decisions outlined in our problem statement. {{	t Ekya}\xspace}'s scheduler prioritizes retraining models for video streams that have undergone significant characteristic changes, as these are most impacted by data drift. The scheduler avoids retraining models that do not contribute to improving the target metric. To navigate the vast decision space, the scheduler employs several strategies. Firstly, it reduces spatial complexity by considering GPU allocations in coarse fractions (e.g., 10\%), which suffice for scheduling decisions while accommodating the granularity of modern GPUs \cite{nvidia-mps}. Secondly, it maintains constant job allocations {\em during retraining}, largely bypassing temporal complexity. Lastly, our micro-profiler (detailed below) narrows down the configuration options to only those that are promising. To make informed configuration choices, the resource scheduler relies on predictions of post-retraining accuracy and resource demands. We developed a { f micro-profiler} that assesses the accuracy of retraining configurations on a {\em small subset} of training data within the retraining window using {\em only a few epochs}. These observations are extrapolated to predict accuracies for larger datasets over more epochs. Additionally, micro-profiling is limited to a select group of {\em promising} retraining configurations. Collectively, these techniques make {{	t Ekya}\xspace}'s micro-profiler nearly $100	imes$ more efficient than exhaustive profiling, achieving accuracy estimates with a $5.8\%$ error margin. To estimate resource demands, the micro-profiler measures retraining time {\em per epoch} when $100\%$ of the GPU is used, and extrapolates the training duration for varying allocations, epoch counts, and data sizes. 
oindent{ f Implementation and Evaluation.} We have implemented and tested {{	t Ekya}\xspace} through system deployment and trace-driven simulations. Our evaluation utilized video workloads from smart car dashboard cameras (Waymo \cite{waymo} and Cityscapes \cite{cityscapes}) as well as stationary traffic and building cameras over 24-hour periods. {{	t Ekya}\xspace} achieved $29\%$ higher accuracy compared to alternative baselines. Notably, matching {{	t Ekya}\xspace}'s accuracy would require $4	imes$ more GPU resources on the edge server using the baseline approach. 
oindent{ f Contributions:} Our research offers the following contributions. 
oindent{1)} We propose the metric of {\em inference accuracy averaged over the retraining window} for continuous training systems. 
oindent{2)} We develop an {\em efficient micro-profiler to estimate} the benefits and costs of retraining edge DNN models. 
oindent{3)} We create a scalable resource scheduler for {\em joint retraining and inference} on edge servers. 
oindent{ f This work does not raise any ethical issues.}

The use of a single GPU in the edge server to run deep learning on multiple live video streams, such as traffic lights, and allocate more resources to the retraining process to accelerate the retraining process, resulting in a more accurate model earlier. The continuous adaptation of the compressed model is able to maintain high accuracy even when the data changes. These tasks are greatly influenced by the "configuration" of the task, which is greatly influenced by the resource requirements and accuracy of the task. For the training task, the configuration is mainly hyper-parameters such as the number of epochs, which greatly affect the resource requirements and the performance of the task (see Section S.2). The accuracy of the retraining task depends on the amount of change in the live characteristics. For the inference task, the frame resolution and accuracy, and the accuracy and resource requirements of the live processing task depend on the degree of change in the live characteristics. The accuracy improvements obtained from the retraining task depend on the degree of change in the live characteristics. Our goal is to optimize the average accuracy of the inference task during the retraining window over all the videos handled by the edge server. This is an expensive task of balancing the accuracy of the model and the accuracy of inference. The main task is to balance the trade-off between the accuracy of the retrained model and the accuracy of inference. We focus on the following continuous retraining decisions: which edge models to retrain in each window, how to allocate the GPU resources of the edge server to retraining and inference, and how to set the configurations of retraining and inference. We make sure that the inference accuracy is always above a minimum threshold, which guarantees the usefulness of inference output for applications. This goal presents new challenges that distinguish it from: (i) the design of inference systems for videos, which focus on the sole accuracy of the resulting inference (cite hyperparameter-16, dblp:journals/jmlr/BergstraB12, dblp:conf/nips/SnoekLA12, sw_scaled_bayesian, dblp:conf/emsys/PengBCWG18, sw_resource-economy-policy, dblp:conf/osdi/XiaoBRSKHPPZ18, dblp:conf/ems/PengBCWG18). To compare the performance of different configurations (in terms of resource use and accuracy), retraining is necessary. Secondly, drifting data makes it difficult to compare the performance of different configurations over time, as the best decision for one retraining window may not be valid in the next. Inside the retraining windows, the resource scheduler takes the three decisions mentioned in the problem statement. To navigate this huge decision space, the scheduler uses several strategies. Ekyaxspace's scheduler puts the highest priority on retraining the models for the data streams that have changed the most, since these are the ones most affected by data drift. The resource scheduler relies on predictions of accuracy and resource requirements to make informed choices about the best possible combinations. text: Deep-learning (DL) systems have achieved remarkable success in tackling complex tasks such as image recognition~\cite{krizhevsky2012imagenet}, speech recognition~\cite{hinton2012deep}, and various object-related tasks like detection, classification, and tracking~\cite{geiger2012we, lillicrap2015continuous}. Nevertheless, extensive research has revealed that DL systems are susceptible to {\em digital adversarial examples}, which are meticulously crafted inputs designed to induce unintended behaviors. A viable defense against such attacks is to detect them, thereby allowing the system to adapt its actions accordingly. Although numerous techniques have been proposed for identifying adversarial examples in the digital realm~\cite{metzen2017detecting, grosse2017statistical}, these approaches often falter against an adaptive adversary~\cite{carlini2017bypass} who aims to mislead a DL system into misclassification while evading detection. Recent studies indicate that similar vulnerabilities are present in the physical domain~\cite{lee2019physical,chou2018sentinet}. Physical adversarial attacks are designed to withstand variations in environmental and sensor conditions, such as lighting, rotation, and distance, rather than being effective solely in a single image instance. For instance, attackers can engineer {\em adversarial patches} and strategically position them within an object detector's field of view to inhibit object detection~\cite{lee2019physical}. This is accomplished using the Expectation over Transformation (EOT) method~\cite{athalye2017synthesizing}, which simulates a range of locations, orientations, and photometric characteristics for the patch, optimizing the attack across a dataset with these distributions. Unlike digital adversarial examples, adversarial patches must occupy a contiguous area in input images, making them readily noticeable to humans, as seen with toaster patches~\cite{brown2017adversarial} or printed t-shirts~\cite{xu2019adversarial}. These patches are cost-effective to create and function in diverse scenarios. Adversarial patch attacks pose significant risks to time-sensitive, safety-critical systems like self-driving cars, endangering both users and the public. Yet, the detection of such attacks has only recently garnered attention. We observe that the primary distinctions between generating adversarial patches and digital adversarial examples are: i) adversarial patches are optimized across a distribution of input images instead of a single image, and ii) they are constrained by area rather than norm. Consequently, we propose the hypothesis that \emph{neural networks under attack by adversarial patches exhibit behaviors similar to those under attack by digital adversarial examples, allowing methods for detecting adversarial perturbations to be adapted for identifying adversarial patches}. Intuitively, automating the detection of adversarial patches should be more straightforward than for digital adversarial examples, given that humans can easily identify them. To our knowledge, SentiNet~\cite{chou2018sentinet} is the sole prior work focused on detecting adversarial patches. SentiNet identifies and segments adversarial objects from inputs by exploiting the high salience and scene-transferability of adversarial patches. In this paper, we adapt a mechanism initially devised to detect digital adversarial perturbations~\cite{qin2019detecting} and empirically assess its performance against simulated physical adversarial attacks. Specifically, we evaluate the effectiveness of class-conditional reconstructions~\cite{qin2019detecting}—which underperform in the digital domain—against adversarial patches. We demonstrate that, unlike digital adversarial examples, adaptive attacks using adversarial patches do not compromise the detector. Our detection approach has been implemented on a modified AlexNet and a \emph{Capsule Network (CapsNet)}, a recently proposed and potentially powerful neural architecture~\cite{sabour2017dynamic,hinton2018matrix}. CapsNets employ layers of vector- or matrix-valued capsules that represent object poses and probabilities, as well as part-whole relationships. Similar to how neuron layers in a standard neural network extract higher-level features from lower-level ones, capsule layers extract higher-level objects from lower-level components, shapes, or lines. Additionally, we propose an enhanced CapsNet architecture incorporating {\em Dropout} and {\em Affine Voting} to improve classification performance on test datasets. In summary, our contributions are as follows: \begin{smitemize} \item We are the first to investigate the applicability of a digital adversarial example detection method in the adversarial patch domain, demonstrating its effectiveness on three standard datasets: MNIST, SVHN, and CIFAR10. \item We are the first to establish the capability of CapNets in classifying and detecting inputs with adversarial patches. \item We propose an improved Matrix Capsule Network featuring {\em capsule-dropout} and {affine voting}, and empirically demonstrate their enhanced test accuracy on the smallNORB dataset. \end{smitemize}

text: Deep reinforcement learning (DRL) holds great potential for enhancing recommendation systems by learning optimal strategies through interactions, thereby generating recommendations that align with users' evolving preferences. DRL-based recommendation systems are generally categorized into three types: deep Q-learning methods, policy gradient methods, and hybrid methods. Deep Q-learning focuses on identifying the optimal action by maximizing a Q-value across all possible actions. \citet{zheng2018drn} were pioneers in integrating DRL into recommendation systems for news, followed by \citet{chen2018stabilizing}, who introduced a robust Q-learning approach to manage dynamic environments in online recommendations. However, Q-learning methods encounter the \textit{agent stuck problem}, where the requirement to maximize over a vast action space becomes impractical. Policy gradient methods offer a solution to the agent stuck problem~\cite{chen2019large}. These methods use average reward as a guiding principle, yet they may mistakenly classify poor actions as beneficial, complicating convergence~\cite{pan2019policy}. Hybrid methods, in contrast, leverage the strengths of both Q-learning and policy gradient approaches. Among these, the actor-critic network~\cite{konda2000actor} is particularly popular, employing policy gradient on an actor network and Q-learning on a critic network to achieve a Nash equilibrium. This approach has seen extensive application in DRL-based recommendation systems~\cite{chen2019top,liu2020end,zhao2020leveraging,chen2020knowledge}. Despite their differences, all current DRL-based methods depend on carefully crafted, context-sensitive reward functions, as illustrated in Fig~\ref{fig:work} (a). However, defining such reward functions is often challenging due to the dynamic nature of environments and multiple factors influencing user interests~\cite{shang2019environment}. Consequently, these methods may exhibit limited generalization capabilities. Moreover, they typically incorporate both user preferences and actions (e.g., clicks, ratings, or implicit feedback) into the reward function, assuming that the reward is solely determined by the selected item and that user actions remain unaffected by the recommended items. This assumption does not hold in online recommendation contexts~\cite{shang2019environment}. Another significant challenge lies in the time-intensive process of using reinforcement learning to derive recommendation policies from scratch~\cite{finn2016guided,levine2012continuous}. Given the vast state space (i.e., potential items of interest to users) and action space (i.e., possible actions for these items), traditional reinforcement learning methods must explore all possible combinations to determine the optimal policy, a process that is often cumbersome. To address these challenges, we aim to enable the agent to deduce a reward function from user behaviors using inverse reinforcement learning, thereby learning the recommendation policy directly from user interactions in a more efficient and adaptive manner, as depicted in Fig 1 (b). We propose a generative inverse reinforcement learning approach to adaptively infer an implicit reward function from user behaviors. This method evaluates the performance of the current recommendation policy and updates it with the expert policy in the discriminator, reducing the necessity of defining a reward function for online recommendations. Specifically, we reformulate inverse deep reinforcement learning (DRL) into a generator to enhance the diversity of state-action pairs. This generative approach improves generalization ability under complex online recommendation scenarios. In summary, our contributions are as follows: \begin{itemize} \item We introduce generative inverse reinforcement learning to autonomously derive reward functions for online recommendations. To our knowledge, this is the first attempt to decouple the reward function from the agent in online recommendation systems. \item We develop an innovative actor-discriminator network module, featuring a discriminator as the critic network and a new actor-critic network as the actor network, to implement the proposed framework. This module is model-free and easily adaptable to various scenarios. \item We validate the feasibility and effectiveness of our approach through experiments on a virtual online platform, VirtualTB, where our method achieves a higher click-through rate compared to several state-of-the-art techniques. \end{itemize}

text: The advent of Generative Adversarial Networks (GANs)~\cite{goodfellow2014generative} and diverse image manipulation techniques~\cite{karras2017progressive,zakharov2019few,karras2019style,wu2019sliced} has enabled the creation of remarkably lifelike images, including human faces, scenery, and objects. Recently, methods utilizing few-shot learning~\cite{zakharov2019few, sun2019meta}, a GAN-based technique, have empowered deep learning models to generate high-quality outputs using minimal training data. This capability can be harnessed to fabricate fake images, as evidenced by recent incidents~\cite{cnn_business, yin_2019, deepnude} where such images were used with malicious intent. Traditionally, image forgery detection relied on metadata or handcrafted image features. However, modern AI techniques, including GANs, generate both images and their metadata from scratch, rendering previous metadata-based detection methods ineffective against GAN-generated images. To tackle these challenges, CNN-based binary classifiers like \textit{ShallowNet}~\cite{tariq2019gan}, \textit{FakeTalkerDetect}~\cite{jeon2019faketalkerdetect}, \textit{FaceForensics++}~\cite{rossler2018faceforensics}, and \textit{Face X-ray}~\cite{li2020face} have been developed, trained on extensive datasets of authentic versus forged images. Additionally, research~\cite{marra2019gans, zhang2019detecting, yu2019attributing} has demonstrated that analyzing artifacts and patterns in GAN images can enhance detection performance. In this paper, we introduce the \textit{Dual Attention Fake Detection Fine-tuning Network} (\textit{DA-FDFtNet}), a refined neural network architecture tailored for detecting fake face images. \textit{DA-FDFtNet} integrates the \textit{Fine-Tune Transformer} (FTT) and \textit{Channel attention modules} with a pre-trained Convolutional Neural Network (CNN) as its foundation, along with \textit{MobileNet block V3} (MBblockV3) to differentiate between real and fraudulent images. Figure~\ref{fig:overview_fdftnet} illustrates our approach, which employs existing CNN architectures (pre-trained networks)~\cite{simonyan2014very,szegedy2015going,he2016deep,iandola2014densenet,hu2018squeeze,howard2017mobilenets} and fine-tunes them for detecting fake images. Notably, \textit{DA-FDFtNet} expands upon \textit{FDFtNet}~\cite{jeon2020fdftnet} by implementing FTT and MBblockV3 along with an additional channel attention module at the final layer. Specifically, FTT utilizes self-attention for diverse feature extraction from images, while MBblockV3 employs various convolution and structural techniques to extract features, and the channel attention module captures feature dependencies across spatial and channel dimensions. To address the constraints of small datasets, we applied diverse data augmentation techniques to refine the baseline model and enhance performance across various fake image types. Our experiments span four deepfake types (FaceSwap, DeepFakes, Face2Face, and NeuralTextures) and GAN-generated face images (StarGAN, PGGAN, StyleGAN, and StyleGAN2), demonstrating our method's efficacy across different domains. Our main contributions include: \begin{itemize} \item We introduce DA-FDFtNet, an advanced neural network-based fake image detector achieving 97.02\% accuracy, significantly improving baseline model accuracy by 1\% to 47%. \item We develop an innovative fine-tuning neural network classifier requiring minimal data for fine-tuning, easily integrable with popular CNN architectures. \item We conduct a comprehensive evaluation on eight different deepfake and GAN-generated fake image datasets, showcasing our approach's effectiveness across various domains. \end{itemize} The paper is structured as follows: Section 2 provides an overview of fake image detection methods and our novel approach. Section 3 details the dataset, baseline models, and the architecture of \textit{DA-FDFtNet}. Section 4 discusses the training specifics and presents our experimental results. Finally, Section 5 concludes the paper.

text: Digital Manufacturing (DM) has become increasingly prevalent in safety-critical sectors, including aerospace, automotive, medical, and military industries~\cite{nickels_am_2015,tiwari_selection_2015}. As a result, the landscape for potential attacks by malicious entities is expanding, driven by motives such as espionage (stealing information) and sabotage (disrupting machinery or data integrity). A particularly appealing target for these malicious actors is the \texttt{g-code} files, which contain the precise machine instructions required to produce each component~\cite{moore_vulnerability_2016,gupta_additive_2020}. In CNC-style machines, these files might include commands for subtractive drilling or milling, whereas in additive manufacturing (AM), they could specify filament extrusion. These \texttt{g-code} files are typically created outside the machines that execute them, and the conversion process involved is often lossy, making it challenging to reverse-engineer the original model files for verification~\cite{tsoutsos_secure_2017}. Consequently, alterations to \texttt{g-code} can easily go undetected. In this study, we explore the \emph{strategies for both attacking and defending} \texttt{g-code} within a red-team/blue-team framework, as illustrated in Fig.~\ref{fig:gcode-attack-vector}. In this scenario, the red-team introduces flaws into a sample set of \texttt{g-code} files, while the blue-team is tasked with identifying these altered files. The red-team concentrated on \emph{methods for altering} \texttt{g-code} instructions to weaken part strength in a few randomly selected files, simulating a covert attack. The blue-team then applied \emph{statistical analysis and machine learning (ML)} approaches as potential detection methods, leading up to a blind evaluation. In total, the red-team developed six distinct attack strategies, and the blue-team successfully identified five of these across two different datasets. The structure of this paper is as follows. Section~\ref{sec:background} presents the background and related literature. Section~\ref{sec:methodology} outlines the approaches employed by the red and blue teams. Section~\ref{sec:evaluation} assesses these approaches and discusses their limitations. Finally, Section~\ref{sec:conclusions} provides the conclusion.

text: The increasing ubiquity of machine learning models and automated decision-making systems has sparked significant interest in thoroughly understanding their behaviors~\cite{surveyxaifosca, zehlike2021fairness}. A crucial aspect of elucidating machine learning algorithm outcomes involves identifying data subgroups where the algorithm may exhibit distinct or potentially anomalous behaviors. Recognizing these unique subgroup behaviors is essential in the Knowledge Discovery and Data Mining (KDD) process, with applications spanning model validation and testing~\cite{chung2019automated, wu2019errudite} to assessing model fairness~\cite{chung2019automated, cabrera2019fairvis}. The issue of societal bias~\cite{barocas2016big} is becoming increasingly prominent, prompting researchers to focus on measuring and ensuring fairness in machine learning. To address these concerns, human experts often need to manually identify sensitive attributes, such as gender or ethnicity, or detect problematic data subgroups. Typically, the performance of machine learning algorithms is assessed using global metrics that evaluate the algorithm's effectiveness across the entire dataset or specific class labels. In contrast, this paper introduces the notion of \textit{divergence} as a metric to quantify statistical differences (e.g., false positive rate) between the algorithm's performance on a specific data subgroup versus the entire dataset. Our methodology automatically identifies data subgroups exhibiting significant behavioral deviations by characterizing them through combinations of attribute values, referred to as \textit{patterns} or \textit{itemsets} in this paper. To demonstrate the concept of divergence, consider the {\sc compas}\ dataset~\cite{angwin_2016}, where a proprietary algorithm assigns recidivism risk scores to criminal defendants. In this context, the positive class indicates high recidivism scores. Table~\ref{table-teaser} presents the false-positive (FPR) and false-negative (FNR) rates for the entire dataset (first row) alongside the data subgroups with the highest FPR (second row) and FNR (third row) divergence. For instance, the pattern (\textit{age>45, charge=M, race=Cauc}) exhibits a pronounced $\Delta_{FNR}$ divergence, indicating that instances within this subgroup are more frequently misclassified into the negative class compared to the overall dataset. We introduce a comprehensive framework for computing divergence, enabling the automatic detection of problematic data subgroups in both classification and ranking scenarios. Our approach leverages established itemset mining algorithms, such as FP-growth~\cite{han2000mining}, to efficiently identify all problematic patterns exceeding a minimal frequency threshold. Furthermore, for a given pattern, we utilize the Shapley value concept~\cite{shapley1953value} to assess the contribution of each attribute value to the pattern's divergence. For example, as will be detailed in subsequent sections, the attribute value \textit{age>45} is the primary contributor to the divergent behavior of the previously discussed pattern.

text: The perception and manipulation of deformable objects by robots present significant challenges. This complexity arises from the intricate geometric structures and unpredictable deformations of such objects. Typically, a three-step approach is employed to address these challenges. Initially, the objects are modeled within a simulated environment \cite{Hess:2010:BFE:1893021,coumans2021} or through finite element methods (FEM) \cite{doi:10.1143/JPSJ.66.367}. Subsequently, the second phase involves learning the deformations that occur as the object is manipulated in this simulated setting \cite{miller2012geometric,lin2015picking}. The final step focuses on devising an optimized trajectory for the manipulation process \cite{zaidi2017model,yamakawa2012simple}. A critical aspect of these steps is understanding the stress-strain relationship of the deformable objects \cite{courtney2005mechanical}, which is influenced by their physical attributes such as stiffness, area weight, and damping factors. Consequently, acquiring knowledge of these physical properties is essential for enabling robots to adeptly manipulate deformable objects. Historically, methods for estimating the physical properties of materials have involved either aligning simulated models with actual objects to learn these properties \cite{9196770,arriola2017multimodal,wang2011data} or extracting them from video frames \cite{bouman2013estimating,yang2017learning,runia2020cloth}. The first approach demands precise alignment through finite element methods, which is computationally demanding. In contrast, the latter approach bypasses the need for matching simulated models to real objects, making it computationally more efficient and suitable for robotic systems where robots exert external forces on deformable objects. In this study, we propose a novel approach to learning the dynamic characteristics of fabrics. We introduce the Physics-Similarity Neural Network (PhySNet), depicted in Fig. \ref{fig:arch}, designed to predict the physical parameters of both simulated and real fabrics. Our central hypothesis is that \textit{PhySNet can infer the physical parameters of real fabrics and garments by learning the physics similarities of simulated fabrics subjected to a wind force field}. To validate this hypothesis, we have developed a simulated fabric database that enables PhySNet to learn these physics similarities and generate a Physics Similarity Map (PSM) for a given fabric. Once PhySNet is trained, it processes a real fabric alongside a simulated fabric with initialized physical parameters to calculate their Physics Similarity Distance (PSD). This PSD is then fed into a Bayesian optimizer, which refines the physical parameters. The updated parameters are used to produce a new simulated fabric model. This cycle repeats until the Bayesian optimizer converges on stable parameters, as detailed in Section \ref{sec:experiment-test_on_fabrics}.

text: Founded in 2016, PerceptIn emerged with the mission to innovate visual perception technologies tailored for autonomous vehicles and robotics. Since its establishment, the company has successfully secured over \$10 million in venture capital from prominent investors such as Walden International, Matrix Partners, and Samsung Ventures \cite{liu2020critical}. Operating as a global technology startup, PerceptIn maintains a presence in the U.S., Japan, Europe, and Asia. The team comprises over 30 researchers and engineers alongside 10 business professionals. While the engineers and researchers focus on pioneering autonomous driving technologies, the business professionals are tasked with market development and feedback collection to inform the company's R\&D initiatives. Over the past three years, PerceptIn has amassed more than 20 U.S. patents and over 100 international ones, in addition to publishing numerous research papers. In 2017, PerceptIn embarked on a project to create low-speed autonomous vehicles targeting the burgeoning micromobility market. Micromobility refers to the use of lightweight vehicles for short-distance travel, a segment often overlooked by large-scale transit systems \cite{liu2020autonomous}. According to the U.S. Department of Transportation, trips under 5 miles account for 60\% of vehicle traffic \cite{santos2011summary}. The high costs associated with current mass transit systems inadequately address the transportation needs of short trips, significantly impacting society. By bridging transit services with community requirements, micromobility is propelling the growth of Mobility-as-a-Service. PerceptIn's internal analysis suggested that offering low-speed autonomous vehicles priced under \$70,000 per unit could yield a satisfactory return on investment for its customers, the autonomous vehicle operators. However, this pricing benchmark imposes stringent design constraints. The \$70,000 must be allocated across various cost components, including Non-recurring engineering (NRE) costs like R&D, recurring costs such as chassis, drive-by-wire conversion (i.e., adapting a traditional vehicle for computer control), sensor integration, customer service, and the computing system \cite{liu2020engineering}. Recognizing that the on-vehicle computing system significantly influences cost and power consumption, PerceptIn undertook an investigation into autonomous driving computing systems \cite{liu2017computer}\cite{liu2019edge}\cite{liu2020pirt}. The study concluded that computing represents a bottleneck in the commercial deployment of autonomous vehicles, necessitating a system that is reliable, cost-effective, high-performance, and energy-efficient. A solution that is both affordable and quick to market was paramount. PerceptIn considered several strategies: Option one involved optimizing existing commercial off-the-shelf mobile System-on-Chip (SoC) computing systems. This strategy offered advantages due to mobile SoCs' economies of scale, enabling the development of a technology stack on cost-effective, backward-compatible systems. Given that PerceptIn's vehicles operate at limited speeds akin to mobile robots, mobile SoCs had demonstrated potential in similar contexts. Nonetheless, a comprehensive study to assess mobile SoCs' suitability for autonomous driving could delay the product launch by six months. Option two considered procuring specialized autonomous driving computing systems from commercial platforms such as NXP, MobilEye, and Nvidia. These Application-Specific Integrated Circuit (ASIC)-based systems provide high performance but at a premium cost, with the first-generation Nvidia PX2 system exceeding \$10,000. Moreover, these systems primarily enhance perception functions, whereas PerceptIn required a solution optimizing end-to-end performance, rendering this option unfeasible. Option three entailed developing proprietary autonomous driving computing systems. This approach promised a system tailored to PerceptIn's specific needs and customer demands but required substantial financial and human resources, with no guaranteed success—a significant risk for a startup like PerceptIn. After an ineffective trial with option one, PerceptIn opted for option three in early 2018, assembling a team to create the FPGA-based DragonFly computing system \cite{fang2018dragonfly+}\cite{fang2017fpga}\cite{liu2020pi}\cite{tang2018pi}\cite{yu2020building}. This decision proved highly successful, as all PerceptIn's autonomous vehicles now operate with the proprietary DragonFly system. This paper delves into the technical design of PerceptIn's DragonFly computing systems and the trade-offs encountered. The remainder of this paper outlines the vehicle's sensor suites (Sec. \ref{sec:veh}), followed by the end-to-end processing pipeline facilitated by the on-vehicle computing systems (Sec. \ref{sec:alg}). Based on this pipeline, we detail the design of the on-vehicle computing system (Sec. \ref{sec:sov}). To minimize end-to-end computing latency, localization tasks are offloaded to an FPGA platform. Section \ref{sec:fpga} discusses the FPGA-based vSLAM (visual simultaneous localization and mapping) front-end and back-end systems developed for our vehicle.

text: Globally, millions engage daily with digitalized public services, necessitating user authentication for access. During this process, users expect their personal data to be handled with privacy and security. Moreover, they desire interfaces that are efficient, intuitive, and straightforward, as cumbersome or unclear services can lead to frustration and diminished trust. If usability becomes a significant hurdle, users might ultimately abandon the service altogether~\cite{Brostoff}. \subsection{Problem Statement} Widely adopted Identity Management Systems (IDMS) like \textit{GOV.UK Verify} and the \textit{Federal Cloud Credential Exchange} (FCCX) have exhibited notable privacy and security vulnerabilities~\cite{Brandao}. These issues are compounded by two primary factors: \begin{enumerate} \item The rapid expansion of these systems in both service offerings and user base~\cite{ElMaliki2007}. \item The shift towards federated or centralized authentication frameworks. Such centralization facilitates the aggregation and correlation of user interactions across various service providers, potentially exposing extensive personal identifiable information (PII). \end{enumerate} As systems grow and interconnect, they become increasingly attractive to malicious actors, who, if successful in breaching these systems, can impersonate, profile, and target users without detection~\cite{Brandao}, thereby eroding public confidence~\cite{Ohara}. These privacy and security challenges are not confined to government services alone. Recent data breaches involving platforms like Facebook and Google, which often authenticate users for third-party services, underscore the issue~\cite{fbreach, googlebreach}. To address these challenges, the principle of privacy by design has guided research into privacy-enhancing identity and credential management systems~\cite{Goodell2019, Idemix, UPort, Chainspace, AnonCredLight}. Each system tackles specific privacy and security issues, offering unique benefits, privacy features, trade-offs, and limitations~\cite{Goodell2019}. However, the interaction between these systems' strengths and weaknesses in practical use cases is not always clear. Different scenarios require varied design considerations based on stakeholder needs. Thus, a thorough analysis is necessary to identify and address the specific concerns of system implementers and users. Further investigation is needed to evaluate whether current privacy-enhancing systems can effectively compete with existing enterprise and government solutions. \subsection{Research Objectives} This chapter explores the practicality and impact of adopting privacy-enhancing identity management in extensive public transport payment systems. Focusing the study, we address three questions within the framework of the protocol by Goodell et al~\cite{Goodell2019}, termed the \textit{Distributed Digital Identity Architecture} (DigID): \begin{enumerate} \item In what ways does DigID fulfill the essential privacy and security criteria of contemporary public transport payment systems compared to existing centralized models? \item What are the technical, operational, and user experience considerations and compromises when deploying DigID in a large-scale public transport network? \item How effectively can DigID meet or surpass the performance benchmarks of Transport for London's current payment systems? \end{enumerate} London serves as a case study due to its extensive network, complex fare system, and the availability of public data for comparative analysis. \subsection{Chapter Structure} The chapter proceeds as follows. The next section sets the stage by contextualizing these systems and highlighting their significance, while also introducing relevant terminology and alternative solutions. Section~\ref{overview} outlines the challenges of implementing our proposed solution in Transport for London (TfL) and suggests potential enhancements to overcome these barriers. Section~\ref{implementation} delves into the specific design decisions made during implementation. Section~\ref{results} covers the testing methodology, Section~\ref{analysis} interprets the findings, and Section~\ref{conclusion} presents a discussion with insights for future research directions.

text: In 2020, it is expected that 276,480 women in the United States will receive a breast cancer diagnosis, with 42,170 fatalities anticipated from the disease \cite{Sieg20}. To assist in clinical decision-making, pathologists typically classify breast cancers using a standardized grading system \cite{Bloo51, Elst91}, which evaluates three specific features: 1) nuclear pleomorphism (also known as “atypia”), 2) the degree of gland formation, and 3) the mitotic count. While the criteria for assessing mitotic count and gland formation are quantitatively defined, nuclear pleomorphism is evaluated qualitatively by examining the microscopic nuclear morphology of the tumor. This assessment is conducted on a scale from 1 to 3, indicating increasing deviations from normal epithelial appearance. The overall tumor grade is determined by combining these three scores. With the advent of digital pathology, grading can also be performed on digitized histopathological images, offering comparable agreement to traditional light microscopy \cite{Gint20}. Moreover, pathologists are increasingly aided by Artificial Intelligence (AI) systems in routine evaluations \cite{Bera19, Niaz19, Bult20a, Rant20}. Deep neural networks, a subset of AI technologies, are predominantly utilized for the analysis of medical images. These deep learning (DL) architectures consist of interconnected neurons that process input images and apply a series of operations to the learnable network weights to perform tasks such as classification, regression, and segmentation. This technology has achieved remarkable success in various computer vision domains \cite{Kriz12, Le13, Silv16, Devl18} and has recently advanced digital pathology \cite{Jano16, Bejn17, Veta18, Nagp19, Bult20}. Specifically in breast cancer grading, automated mitosis detection was one of the pioneering applications of DL \cite{Cire13a, Veta15}, proving its clinical and prognostic significance \cite{Tell18, Balk19, Balk19b}. Gland segmentation has been approached as a series of nuclei and gland detection tasks, as well as a segmentation challenge \cite{Nguy15, Lee18}, with extensions to clinical risk categorization using deep learning \cite{Buch16}. Unlike gland formation and mitotic count, nuclear pleomorphism lacks a quantitative definition, rendering it the least reproducible component of the grading system, thus limiting its effectiveness \cite{Frie95, Meye05, Long05}. Efforts to automate nuclear pleomorphism scoring have been limited, primarily involving manually crafted nuclear features \cite{Lu15, Gand19}, deep belief networks \cite{Maql16}, descriptor-based pixel-level image features \cite{Khan15}, or binary classification of high pleomorphism (score 3) using simple convolutional neural networks on small image patches \cite{Noel15}. Supervised DL necessitates ground-truth labels for training neural networks. However, obtaining such labels is challenging for tasks like pleomorphism scoring, which involves discrete classes and observer variability. Translating multiple observers' scores into a single ground-truth label (e.g., by majority or consensus) overlooks valuable insights present in the variability of expert scores. In this study, we propose a novel DL approach to nuclear pleomorphism scoring, treating it as a continuous spectrum rather than discrete categories. We redefine the original three-category classification into a continuum of values, ranging from the lowest to the highest pleomorphism scores. Our methodology involves two primary components. The initial phase employs a previously developed epithelial cell detection network \cite{Merc19}, focusing the analysis on diagnostically relevant regions (i.e., invasive tumor) within a whole slide image. The subsequent phase utilizes a deep regression network to predict continuous nuclear pleomorphism scores within these tumor regions. Notably, this network's training does not require detailed manual annotations by pathologists, addressing a significant limitation in computational pathology. This work represents the first end-to-end, fully automated DL approach for nuclear pleomorphism scoring in breast cancer, converting a discrete classification into a continuous regression problem to retain critical observer input previously unexploited. Figure \ref{fig:introduction:overview_inference} presents an overview of our approach, \AI, detailing the two-stage process of nuclear pleomorphism scoring. To develop and validate our approach, we conducted two distinct studies, resulting in two separate datasets. The first study, termed the ROI-study, included $125$ tumor regions of interest (tumor ROIs) and $79$ "normal appearing" epithelial regions of interest (normal ROIs) from $39$ whole slide images. These were meticulously selected to encompass a diverse range of tumor morphologies in breast cancer histopathology. We enlisted $10$ pathologists from $6$ countries to score nuclear pleomorphism on the tumor ROIs, each paired with a normal ROI from the same patient to serve as a reference for pleomorphism scoring. The ROI-study results were used to train \AI and evaluate its performance against the pathologist panel. In our automated approach, the averaged nuclear pleomorphism scores from the 10 pathologists served as reference scores, capturing their collective expertise rather than enforcing a discrete majority score. \AI was trained on diverse tumor morphologies, utilizing the reference scores to conceptualize nuclear pleomorphism as a continuous spectrum of morphological change. The second study, referred to as the slide-study, involved $118$ whole slide images of breast cancer resection tissue sections used to evaluate the trained \AI. The slide distribution mirrored the case distribution in routine clinical practice. For the slide-study, $4$ pathologists were invited to score nuclear pleomorphism, with their assessments compared to \AI for whole slide-level evaluation. Further details on the ROI-study and slide-study are provided in Section \ref{sec:methodology}.

text: Pose transfer, which involves applying the pose of a source mesh to a target mesh, represents an intriguing yet complex task within the realm of 3D computer vision. This technique holds potential for numerous industrial applications. However, current methodologies~\cite{NPT,LIMP,Unsupervised,AniFormer} demonstrate efficacy only within the confines of predefined datasets characterized by known poses and shape spaces. These methods struggle to generalize effectively to unfamiliar spaces, thereby hindering their practical deployment in real-world scenarios. To address the challenge of achieving robust performance across unknown latent spaces and diverse domains, as illustrated in Fig.~\ref{fig:1}, we introduce an innovative Transformer network designed for generalized 3D mesh pose transfer. At the core of our approach is a geometry-contrastive Transformer featuring geometrically structured encoders. This design aims to refine the identity mesh representation by leveraging the \emph{global geometric contrasts} provided by the pose mesh. On a local scale, we propose a central geodesic contrastive loss to enhance geometric representation, focusing on the \emph{regional contrast of all geodesic directions} for each vertex, which are utilized as back-propagation gradients. Additionally, we incorporate a latent isometric regularization module to stabilize performance across different datasets, addressing the inconsistencies in pose transfer tasks. In conjunction with our model, we introduce the SMG-3D dataset, a novel 3D mesh dataset intended for the quantitative evaluation of 3D pose transfer in unknown spaces. SMG-3D captures everyday spontaneous body gestures, presenting more varied and challenging movements compared to well-established datasets~\cite{AMASS,DFAUST}. Constructed using a semi-synthetic approach, the dataset provides essential ground truth meshes for model training and validation. Furthermore, SMG-3D can be integrated with existing body mesh datasets to facilitate cross-dataset qualitative analyses. A pertinent question arises: why not rely solely on synthesized meshes for model training and evaluation? The succinct response is that models trained exclusively on synthetic meshes tend to underperform in cross-dataset tasks. Although mesh synthesis models like the SMPL series~\cite{SMPL, SMAL, SMPLX} can generate an extensive array of poses spanning the entire latent space, or large-scale datasets like AMASS~\cite{AMASS} can mitigate inconsistencies with unknown dataset spaces, practical limitations remain. For instance, training a model on the modestly sized FAUST dataset, which includes only 10 pose categories, requires over 26 hours~\cite{LIMP} to fully capture the latent space. The immense diversity of poses and movements renders it impractical to train models on synthesized samples that encompass the entire pose space. Therefore, a model capable of generalizing efficiently to unknown latent spaces is highly desirable. Our SMG-3D dataset addresses this cross-dataset learning challenge by offering a diverse range of natural and plausible body poses, complete with occlusions and self-contacts, as opposed to the well-posed movements found in AMASS~\cite{AMASS}. This advancement aims to bridge the gap between research and real-world applications. In summary, our contributions are as follows: \begin{itemize}[leftmargin=*] \item We introduce a novel geometry-contrastive Transformer devoid of positional embeddings, achieving state-of-the-art results in the challenging 3D pose transfer task. \item We propose a straightforward and effective central geodesic contrastive loss, enhancing geometric learning by preserving the directional gradients of 3D vertices. \item We provide a challenging 3D human body mesh dataset (SMG-3D) featuring unknown spaces with naturally plausible body poses, occlusions, and self-contacts for cross-dataset qualitative evaluation. \item We develop a new latent isometric regularization module to adapt to challenging unknown spaces in cross-dataset tasks. \end{itemize}

text: Searcher struggle refers to the scenario where a user encounters significant challenges during a search process, making intense efforts to overcome these difficulties\footnote{\url{merriam-webster.com}}. During such moments, users often experience negative emotions like frustration, annoyance, or distress due to the search activity. Identifying instances of searcher struggle is crucial for Web search engines, as it enables them to adjust their algorithms promptly. Predominantly, current methods for detecting struggle involve classifiers that utilize features quantifying user efforts~\cite{Li:2009:GAM:1571941.1571951,Jiang:2015:UPG:2684822.2685319}, as struggling behaviors typically manifest through frequent repetitions of user actions. For example, a user searching for "curly hair dye" might issue over twenty queries without achieving satisfactory results. It is a common assumption that a high volume of user efforts indicates struggle. Nevertheless, this assumption does not consistently reflect real-world scenarios. It is observed that tasks not involving struggle can also entail numerous queries and clicks. For example, a user searching for "guy proposing ideas" explored over 900 search results and bookmarked 27, yet reported enjoying the session. Recent laboratory studies echo these observations. Edwards and Kelly \cite{Edwards:2017:EFD:3077136.3080818} highlighted that while increased user effort might suggest struggle, it can equally indicate engagement or exploration. Without an effective mechanism to differentiate, the utility of effort-based features is reduced, complicating the task of distinguishing negative experiences like struggle from positive ones such as engagement, thus hindering improvements in Web user experiences. This study draws on psychological literature to introduce a novel feature modulation approach for detecting struggle. Our methodology is inspired by Reversal Theory (RT)~\cite{gerrig2015psychology,apter2001motivation,personalitydynamics,APTER1984265,fourdomains}, a "mode-based" psychological framework that challenges conventional beliefs in motivation and personality studies. RT emphasizes the "complexity, changeability, and dynamics of human motivation and personality"~\cite{APTER1984265}, proposing that individuals undergo changes in daily life, with personalities and motivations capable of reversal~\cite{personalitydynamics}. RT posits counter-intuitive ideas, such as the irrelevance of rule conformity or rebellion to struggling behaviors, while the nature of the task—serious or playful—holds significance. We validated these claims through statistical hypothesis tests on commercial search logs. Furthermore, RT organizes human motivations into several dimensions, each comprising two opposing states. Within a dimension, an individual can switch between states but only be active in one at any given time, indicating a bi-modal rather than a single-modal distribution. We harness this insight to propose a new feature modulation method for struggle detection. Our approach involves (1) selecting features pertinent to the RT dimension, (2) adjusting these features to reduce bias between the two distributions within the bi-modal arousal model, and (3) feeding the modulated features into classifiers to ascertain if a search session includes struggling moments. Our method can be integrated with any feature-based struggle detection approach. We tested its effectiveness using a week-long dataset of search logs from both mobile and PC platforms. The experimental outcomes demonstrate that our method significantly enhances several leading methods, achieving approximately 5\% improvement in accuracy and about 9\% increase in positive precision.

text: The release of the Bitcoin white paper by~\cite{Satoshi2008} in 2008 has spurred significant interest in blockchains and smart contracts as a foundation for innovative applications. There is a widespread recognition of the potential of smart contracts to revolutionize applications across diverse sectors, from industry to government~\cite{Hileman2017}. We concur with this perspective, recognizing the practicality of implementing certain applications through smart contracts deployed on platforms like Ethereum~\cite{Ethereum2017}, Hyperledger Fabric~\cite{HyperledgerHome}, or Bitcoin~\cite{BitcoinHome}. However, we believe that the capabilities of on--chain smart contracts are sometimes overstated. In some cases, their use may be excessive, or even counterproductive, rendering applications impractical or unfeasible~\cite{Morgen2018,Scriber2018,Valentina2018}. In such scenarios, developers should consider deploying smart contracts on Trusted Third Parties (TTP). The confusion likely stems from the novelty of the technology and the lack of a unified understanding of smart contracts and blockchains. Before delving deeper, we will clarify the definitions we adhere to throughout this paper. \subsection{Blockchains} For software developers, a blockchain functions as middleware, offering built-in services for creating distributed applications without a centralized control component, such as an authentication or database server. Key services provided by blockchains include immutable append-only storage, public-key-based access control for operations, public auditability of records, and consensus services, typically based on eventual consensus. Blockchains support a wide array of applications, with smart contracts being the most recognized, though not the sole option. Implementation-wise, a blockchain is a distributed data structure, or ledger, comprising an ordered, back-linked list (chain) of blocks. Blocks are appended following an append-only model, contingent on consensus among nodes holding local replicas of the blockchain's current state. These blocks typically store transaction records executed by parties without mutual trust, supporting the peer-to-peer transaction execution model. Transactions aim to alter the blockchain's current state and are not limited to financial transactions. Constructing and maintaining a blockchain necessitates integrating multiple technologies, leading to various conceptual models for blockchain representation. For example,~\cite{KenjiSaito2016} conceptualizes a blockchain as a probabilistic state machine, highlighting the probabilistic nature of consensus algorithms used. \subsection{Smart contracts} A smart contract can be envisioned as a digital analogue of a traditional commercial contract, typically written in a human language like English. By digital, we mean a piece of computer code that executes to monitor or enforce the clauses of a conventional contract programmatically at runtime. For instance, a financial contract between a borrower and lender might stipulate that the lender will advance GBP 100.00 to the borrower within five days upon request. As an executable program, a smart contract requires deployment on infrastructure providing a runtime environment, including library support, facilities for managing the smart contract (initiate, stop, terminate, update, etc.), and databases for recording inputs and outputs. The smart contract's primary roles are: i) to monitor interactions between contracting parties; ii) to assess whether each operation (e.g., request loan, honor loan request, decline loan request) complies with the contract terms and inherent rights and obligations; and iii) to render a verdict. In some applications, the verdict declaration is linked to an action (e.g., collect payment) executed upon contract compliance. However, for modularity, we advocate separating these acts, focusing on the verdict as the core operation smart contracts perform. The action is an arbitrary reaction, executed immediately or eventually by the smart contract itself or another component in a different software layer. Often, the action involves allowing or preventing the execution of a contractual operation based on compliance, positioning the smart contract as an enforcer. This raises the question of where to deploy the smart contract. \subsection{On--blockchain smart contracts} Smart contracts can be deployed on--chain. The term "smart contract" was introduced by Szabo in 1997~\cite{Szabo1997}, but it gained commercial traction in 2008 with Bitcoin's success as a cryptocurrency platform~\cite{Satoshi2008}. In Bitcoin~\cite{AndreasAntonopoulos2017}, smart contracts are implemented using an opcode stack-based script language that is non--Turing complete~\cite{BitcoinScript}, and they are deployed on the Bitcoin blockchain. Initially, they were designed to facilitate payment operations in BTC (Bitcoin's cryptocurrency). Ethereum~\cite{AndreasAntonopoulos2018}, a leading blockchain platform, expands on Bitcoin's concept, supporting smart contracts written in Turing--complete languages like Solidity~\cite{Solidity2017}. Numerous use cases in Bitcoin and Ethereum demonstrate that smart contracts can be effectively deployed on--chain; however, it is crucial to recognize that blockchains and smart contracts are distinct technologies. On--blockchain deployment is merely one of several options. Notably, smart contracts predate blockchains by several years. Early research on smart contracts was pioneered by Minsky in the mid--80s~\cite{Minsky1985} and continued by Marshall~\cite{Lindsay1993}, where they were referred to as electronic, executable, or digital contracts. Given the term's prevalence, we will continue using "smart contract" in this document. \subsection{On--Trusted Third Parties smart contracts} Smart contracts can also be deployed on Trusted Third Parties (on--TTP). We define a TTP as an institution equipped with the technical infrastructure for hosting smart contracts and possessing trust, reputation, and authority. E-commerce applications frequently utilize TTP services, such as payment gateways, certification authorities, time-stamping services, custodian services, settlement services, and various brokerage services~\cite{Mainelli2015}. In smart contract applications, a TTP is logically positioned between two business partners, trusted to host and execute a single instance of the smart contract. The smart contract monitors all operations executed by the partners and maintains undeniable records. Early work on smart contracts~\cite{Minsky1985,Lindsay1993} primarily focused on on--TTP deployment. A significant assumption with TTP-based deployment is the trust that the TTP will not alter the contract code or misuse the sensitive data exposed by contractual parties. This concern can be mitigated using emerging trusted hardware technologies like Intel SGX~\cite{VictorCostan2016} and ARM TrustZone~\cite{Sandro2019}. With these technologies, contract code can be deployed within trusted environments (enclaves in SGX and trusted world in TrustZone), preventing the TTP from compromising the contract code's integrity or accessing sensitive data. \subsection{Contributions of this paper} Since the Bitcoin paper's release~\cite{Satoshi2008}, discussions on smart contracts have primarily occurred within the blockchain context, to which they seem inherently linked. Consequently, the potential and practicality of smart contracts deployed on Trusted Third Parties (on--TTP) have been largely overlooked. This paper aims to redress this imbalance by examining the pros and cons of on--blockchain and on--TTP smart contracts. Our analysis stems from a practical exercise: as developers, we were tasked with advising on the appropriate smart contract technology for a car insurance application. To provide a well-informed recommendation, we conducted exploratory implementations (not fully developed) using both on--chain and on--TTP smart contracts. In this paper, we share our experiences and insights into the technical challenges encountered, noting that some were more easily addressed with on--TTP smart contracts. We acknowledge that a significant drawback of an on--TTP smart contract is its reliance on a single TTP—a design aspect deemed undesirable and avoidable through blockchains. Nonetheless, we argue that in scenarios where TTP-related issues are manageable, on--TTP smart contracts might offer a superior alternative to their on--chain counterparts. The remainder of this paper is organized as follows. Section~\ref{motivatingscenario} introduces the hypothetical use case of a car insurance application we were asked to implement as a smart contract application. Section~\ref{centralisedanddecentralised} explains how smart contracts can be implemented using either centralized or decentralized architectures. Section~\ref{onblockchainimplementation} discusses our experiences implementing the car insurance application with an on--chain smart contract in Solidity for deployment on Ethereum. In Section~\ref{onTTPimplementation}, we present complementary arguments from implementing the example using an on--TTP smart contract. Section~\ref{discussion} offers our personal views on smart contracts and highlights open research questions. To contextualize this article, Section~\ref{relatedwork} summarizes pioneering articles on smart contracts and recent related publications. We conclude in Section~\ref{conclusions}.
