text: The remarkable achievements of deep neural networks (DNNs) in diverse areas of artificial intelligence, such as computer vision~\cite{krizhevsky2012imagenet}, speech recognition~\cite{6296526}, and robotic control~\cite{levine2018learning}, have been well-documented in recent years. Despite their impressive capabilities, DNNs remain susceptible to adversarial attacks that involve subtle, often imperceptible, alterations to input data~\cite{madry2017towards, goodfellow2014explaining, laidlaw2019functional, laidlaw2020perceptual, kang2019testing, dong2018boosting, carlini2017towards, chen2017ead, 7467366}. This vulnerability presents a significant challenge in security-sensitive applications, including autonomous vehicles and medical diagnostics. To bolster model resilience against adversarial threats, numerous defense strategies have been introduced, encompassing both empirical approaches~\cite{madry2017towards,zhang2019theoretically, papernot2016distillation,lin2020dual, singla2021skew, Kannan2018AdversarialLP, wang2019improving} and certifiable defenses~\cite{raghunathan2018certified,cohen2019certified, levine2020randomized, levine2019certifiably, sinha2017certifying, levine2021improved}. Among these, adversarial training (AT)~\cite{madry2017towards} ranks as one of the most effective defense mechanisms. Various enhancements to adversarial training have been explored through different loss functions, including ALP~\cite{Kannan2018AdversarialLP}, TRADES~\cite{zhang2019theoretically}, and MART~\cite{wang2019improving}. However, these methods typically focus on training a single model without leveraging the potential synergy of multiple networks. Furthermore, many defenses are tailored to specific perturbation types, leaving models vulnerable to unfamiliar perturbations~\cite{tramer2019adversarial, maini2020adversarial}. For instance, models trained on $l_\infty$-bounded adversarial examples may not withstand $l_1$ and $l_2$-bounded attacks. Knowledge distillation (KD)~\cite{hinton2015distilling} is a prominent technique for transferring insights from one model to another. KD manifests in various forms~\cite{wang2020knowledge}, such as \textit{offline} KD, where student models learn from pre-trained static teachers~\cite{hinton2015distilling}, and \textit{online} KD, where a cohort of student models learn collaboratively from each other’s predictions~\cite{zhang2018deep, guo2020online, song2018collaborative}. Several KD-based techniques have been developed for adversarial defenses~\cite{papernot2016distillation, goldblum2019adversarially, arani2020adversarial, chen2021robust}. For example,~\cite{goldblum2019adversarially} illustrates the transferability of robustness through KD, while~\cite{chen2021robust} highlights KD's role in mitigating robust overfitting. Table~\ref{tab:kd} delineates the distinctions among KD-based defenses. We contend that existing KD-based defenses fall short in optimizing adversarial robustness. Defensive distillation (DD) employs a natural model as a teacher for another natural model, offering limited robustness since neither model undergoes adversarial training, as demonstrated by~\cite{carlini2016defensive}. Adversarially robust distillation (ARD)~\cite{goldblum2019adversarially} uses a robust model to impart robustness to a smaller student model, though its effectiveness hinges on the presence of strong teacher models, and the student’s improvement is constrained by the static teacher. Adversarial concurrent training (ACT)~\cite{arani2020adversarial} simultaneously trains a natural and a robust model in an online KD framework to align their feature spaces. However, due to the fundamentally different features learned by natural and robust models~\cite{tsipras2018robustness}, aligning their feature spaces could degrade robustness. In this study, we introduce Mutual Adversarial Training (MAT), a novel approach whereby models collaboratively enhance each other's adversarial robustness. Unlike prior KD-based defenses, MAT involves the concurrent training of multiple robust models. Each model not only learns from true labels, as in traditional AT, but also absorbs soft labels from peer networks, which encapsulate shared knowledge for countering adversarial attacks, thereby achieving heightened robustness. The MAT framework is depicted in Fig.~\ref{fig:mat}. MAT offers several advantages in enhancing model robustness: 1) It leverages KD benefits, such as improved generalization~\cite{furlanello2018born} and reduced robust overfitting~\cite{chen2021robust}. 2) \textit{MAT establishes a positive feedback loop for increasing robustness}. Each network acts as a robust teacher, providing peers with semantic-rich and discriminative soft labels. By learning from strong peers, a network becomes more robust, further enhancing its peers' robustness. 3) \textit{MAT enables robust models to explore a broader adversarial sample space, discovering more resilient feature spaces and decision boundaries collectively}. Each model's adversarial examples form a subspace of adversarial inputs~\cite{tramer2017space}, and their predictions reveal insights into their decision boundaries and adversarial subspaces. In MAT, models learn not only from their adversarial examples but also from peers' examples through soft labels, compelling them to consider a larger adversarial space and find feature spaces and decision boundaries that perform well across both their own and peers' adversarial examples, fostering more robust and generalizable solutions. In conclusion, we propose a new KD-based adversarial training algorithm, MAT, which serves as a comprehensive framework to enhance the adversarial robustness of any network without relying on strong teacher models. We extend MAT to defend against multiple perturbation types (MAT-MP) by leveraging the transferability of adversarial robustness and propose several strategies for training MAT-MP. Our extensive experiments demonstrate that MAT significantly boosts the robustness of AT baselines and surpasses state-of-the-art methods for both single and multiple perturbations.

text: Android has rapidly established itself as the world's leading mobile operating system. However, this popularity has also made it a prime target for cybercriminals. Attackers exploit Android by deploying millions of malicious applications designed to deceive users into disclosing personal information or engaging in harmful activities, such as monitoring user behavior, disseminating spam, or displaying intrusive ads. Consequently, the study of Android malware, encompassing detection and classification, has become a vital endeavor for security experts in both industry and academia. Numerous studies have emerged aiming to identify Android malware~\cite{canfora2015effectiveness,gascon2013structural,li2018android,mclaughlin2017deep,hybroid}. A significant number of recent methodologies utilize the contextual attributes of Android applications, such as permissions and sensitive APIs, to identify and categorize malware. For instance, Li et al.~\cite{li2018android} developed a classifier based on the factorization machine (FM) framework, extracting key features like permissions and malicious APIs from manifest files and source code. Similarly, Chen et al.~\cite{chen2018android} introduced a method that evaluates static behaviors of Android malware, focusing on permissions, components, and sensitive API calls. Additionally, natural language processing (NLP) techniques have been applied to malware detection, treating Android applications akin to documents, with app instructions analogous to words~\cite{kang2016n,xu2021detecting}. For example, the study in ~\cite{kang2016n} assesses uni-gram, bi-gram, and tri-gram models using stacked generalization. Moreover, several studies have focused on analyzing Android network traffic patterns to discern legitimate from malicious behavior~\cite{malik2016credroid,arora2014malware,zulkifli2018android,marin2020deepmal,wang2017malware,xu2021hawkeye,xu2020manis,xu2021falcon}. Many of these rely on manually defined rules to construct rule-based classifiers for malware detection, such as CICAndMal2017~\cite{lashkari2018toward}, which employs a third-party tool to extract nine features from network PCAP files for malware identification. Zulkifli et al.~\cite{zulkifli2018android} proposed a decision tree algorithm leveraging network traffic as dynamic features of Android apps. While these methods provide an additional security layer for Android, they have notable limitations. Contextual information from program code is vulnerable to obfuscation techniques like \textit{identifier renaming}, \textit{string encryption}, \textit{dead-code insertion}, and \textit{instruction substitution}, which alter the compiled code to evade detection. For instance, string encryption could compromise the FM approach of Li et al.~\cite{li2018android} by preventing the extraction of permissions from manifest files. Similarly, NLP-based malware detection systems~\cite{kang2016n,xu2021detecting} are susceptible to certain obfuscation strategies. Network traffic-based methods face the challenge of code coverage~\cite{tazaki2013direct}. Being a dynamic feature-based approach, network traffic reflects only a subset of code functionalities, as many do not involve or generate network traffic. Furthermore, the majority of state-of-the-art network traffic-based malware detection systems are rule-based~\cite{malik2016credroid,arora2014malware,zulkifli2018android,marin2020deepmal,wang2017malware,hybroid}, which can be easily circumvented by sophisticated attacks, as these methods depend on distinguishing expected from anomalous behavior; hence, they may falter when malware adapts to conceal its actions. In response, this paper introduces a hybrid pattern malware detection and categorization framework that integrates both network and program code features. Initially, network packets are transformed into sequences of 2D gray images, which are pre-trained using a convolutional neural network (CNN). Subsequently, a bi-directional LSTM network processes the continuous network traffic, performing malware classification akin to 2D image sequence classification. Furthermore, we propose an NLP-inspired method for program code pattern detection using a graph neural network (GNN), capable of identifying obfuscated applications while maintaining high performance. Specifically, we design the \texttt{opcode2vec}, \texttt{function2vec}, and \texttt{graph2vec} components to encapsulate instruction, function, and program-level information as vectors. After extracting features from both network traffic and program code, these vectors are input into a classifier trained to distinguish between benign and malicious applications. Ultimately, \textit{hybrid-Falcon}\xspace effectively identifies Android malware families, surpassing most existing frameworks with a detection accuracy of 97.16\% and a categorization accuracy of 88.32%. In this paper, we emphasize two key innovations: the use of a bi-directional LSTM for processing 2D image sequences and a graph-based malware detection approach employing natural language processing techniques for node representation. \bigskip \noindent In summary, we make the following main contributions: \begin{itemize} 	\item We introduce \textit{hybrid-Falcon}\xspace, a hybrid pattern Android malware detection and categorization framework that combines the network traffic and program code features. 	\item We design a bidirectional LSTM network to accomplish 2D gray images sequence classification, which takes the network packets (converted to 2D images) as input. 	\item We create and release a dataset, \textit{AndroNetMnist}\xspace, which includes 3,255,391 2D gray images in five categories (Benign, Adware, Ransomware, Scareware, and SMSmalware) for network traffic classification. 	\item We design and implement an NLP-inspired malware detection and categorization module for the program code that can process obfuscated programs. 	\item We evaluate the accuracy of our approach using real malicious and benign datasets. 	\item We release our work as an open-source project after the paper is accepted. \end{itemize}

text: The field of sequence generation has recently seen significant progress due to the development of end-to-end neural network methods. These have achieved notable success in tasks such as machine translation~\cite{sutskever2014sequence,luong2015effective}, dialogue systems~\cite{vinyals2015neural,serban2016building}, text summarization~\cite{rush2015neural,nallapati2016abstractive,see2017get}, image and video captioning~\cite{bahdanau2014neural,venugopalan2015sequence,pasunuru2017multi}, and question generation~\cite{du2017learning,du2018harvesting,zhang2019addressing}. Traditionally, these tasks rely on optimizing cross-entropy loss~\cite{sutskever2014sequence}, which, although standard, suffers from exposure bias~\cite{ranzato2015sequence} and fails to directly optimize the non-differentiable metrics used to evaluate sequence quality. The advent of reinforcement learning techniques, especially those based on policy gradients, has mitigated these issues by focusing directly on these evaluation metrics~\cite{zaremba2015reinforcement,ranzato2015sequence,rennie2016self}. While policy gradient methods can enhance performance on specific metrics, they often result in improvements limited to those metrics, indicating a tendency to exploit the metrics themselves~\cite{paulus2017deep}. Attempts to address this include using a weighted average of multiple metrics~\cite{liu2017improved}, which involves balancing different metric scales, or employing a mixing ratio for multi-metric optimization~\cite{pasunuru2018multi}, which requires careful tuning. However, these methods typically use static rewards that do not adapt throughout the training process, and the importance of metrics may vary at different training stages. A dynamic approach that adapts the choice of metrics and rewards throughout training, considering both the model's state and the historical context, could be more effective. In response, we introduce a multi-armed bandit framework, termed the DORB{} framework, where each arm represents a metric that can be optimized as a reward. The bandit selects metrics to optimize based on historical performance, facilitating the automatic development of an optimal reward curriculum. This approach is explored within the exploration-exploitation paradigm using the Exp3 algorithm~\cite{auer2002nonstochastic}, and we propose two novel reward strategies: (1) Single Multi-reward Bandit (SM-Bandit) and (2) Hierarchical Multi-reward Bandit (HM-Bandit). Initially, we propose a reward scaling technique to normalize metric rewards within the range $[0,1]$. text: The task of object counting has gained significant importance due to its diverse applications, including crowd surveillance, traffic monitoring, wildlife conservation, and inventory management. Most current counting approaches~\cite{zhang2016single, ma2019bayesian, biswas2017automatic} are tailored to specific, singular categories. Unfortunately, their effectiveness diminishes dramatically when applied to new categories. Furthermore, gathering and annotating data for all possible categories is both challenging and expensive. Humans possess a remarkable ability to generalize, enabling them to tackle various visual tasks with minimal prior knowledge and experience. Inspired by this capability, our work aims to design a network that can efficiently identify and count new categories using only a single example. We adopt and adapt the few-shot framework from ~\cite{ranjan2021learning} to develop a one-shot object counting model. This model processes an input image containing unseen novel categories alongside a supporting bounding box with an exemplar instance, subsequently predicting the object count in the image. However, two primary challenges arise. \textbf{First}, the object counting task encompasses numerous categories, with multiple categories potentially present in one image. In the few-shot setting, there is no overlap between the categories used for training and those for inference. Consequently, the model must excel in distinguishing features across different categories while effectively associating instances of the same category. \textbf{Second}, in one-shot counting, the model relies on a single supporting instance. The challenge is compounded by variations in size and pose among instances, necessitating that the model remain invariant to these differences without observing commonalities across instances. In response, we introduce LaoNet, an effective network for one-shot object counting. LaoNet comprises three core components: feature extraction, feature correlation, and a density regressor, as depicted in Figure~\ref{fig:network}. The feature correlation and feature extraction models are meticulously crafted to tackle the aforementioned challenges. Our feature correlation approach employs Self-Attention and Correlative-Attention modules to learn intra-relations and inter-relations, respectively. Self-Attention directs the model's focus toward critical features and their interconnections, enhancing information refinement efficiency. Prior few-shot counting techniques~\cite{ranjan2021learning, yang2021class} typically use convolution operations to match image and supporting features. However, since the kernel is derived from supporting features with fixed size and rotation, convolution heavily relies on the quality and consistency of supporting features across instances. Our feature correlation model, leveraging two types of attention modules, addresses this issue by considering all correlations. Additionally, we introduce a Scale Aggregation mechanism within scale extraction to handle scale variations across categories and instances. By learning from multiple subspaces, the model integrates diverse scale information while preserving spatial consistency. In summary, our contributions are threefold: \begin{itemize} \item We develop a novel network, LaoNet (Look At One instance), for one-shot object counting. By integrating Self-Attention and Correlative-Attention modules, LaoNet effectively captures correlations among novel category objects with high precision and efficiency. 	\item We introduce a Scale Aggregation mechanism to extract comprehensive features and merge multi-scale information from the supporting box. 	 	\item Our experimental results demonstrate that our model achieves state-of-the-art performance with notable improvements on the FSC-147~\cite{ranjan2021learning} and COCO~\cite{lin2014microsoft} datasets under the one-shot setting, without requiring fine-tuning. 	 \end{itemize}

text: In today's digital landscape, recommendation systems are integral to platforms like Amazon \cite{amazon}, Google \cite{youtube_dnn,youtube1,NIS}, and Facebook~\cite{ebr}. These systems must adeptly capture the changing preferences of users through their interaction history, a task that is crucial for making precise recommendations. Consequently, significant research has focused on developing sequential recommendation methods \cite{Caser,sasrec,GRU4Rec,SR-GNN}. The core objective of sequential recommendation is to derive user representations from historical behavior and predict subsequent items. Given the success of deep learning in modeling sequential dependencies, numerous deep neural network-based approaches \citep*{r1} have been advanced to tackle this challenge. These include RNN-based frameworks~\cite{GRU4Rec,GRU4Rec+,STAMP}, various CNN architectures~\cite{Caser,3D_CNN}, Graph Neural Networks (GNNs) \cite{SR-GNN,FGNN,GC-SAN}, and models utilizing multi-head self-attention \cite{sasrec,BERT4Rec,TiSASRec}. Despite their effectiveness, these models often struggle with data sparsity \cite{Autoint,s3,sasrec}, particularly those using multi-head self-attention, where a single item prediction loss is optimized to capture all potential interactions. To overcome these limitations, self-supervised learning strategies have been introduced~\cite{yao2020self,CLRec}. Among these, contrastive learning (CL) \cite{CL4SRec} has shown promising outcomes. By integrating data augmentation techniques with traditional sequential prediction objectives, CL-based methods can enhance sequence-level user representations and improve recommendation performance. However, the success of CL approaches depends heavily on data augmentation, pretext tasks, negative sampling strategies, and hyper-parameter settings like the temperature in NCE and InfoNCE losses \cite{jaiswal2021survey}. Efforts to simplify contrastive learning include the proposal by \cite{gao2021simcse}, which uses dropout noise for data augmentation, creating high-quality positive samples for sequence-level learning. While effective for unsupervised learning, applying this to sequential recommendations poses challenges: a stronger CL objective improves representation discrimination but can degrade item prediction accuracy, highlighting a gap between sample discrimination and sequential recommendation objectives. Thus, developing training strategies that address these issues is vital for enhancing user representations focused on item prediction. Inspired by recent findings that simple regularization on supervised task outputs can significantly boost performance~\cite{liang2021r}, we propose exploring consistency training for sequential recommendations. We introduce bidirectional KL divergence regularization in the output space to manage inconsistencies across forward passes with varying dropout. Unlike tasks in machine translation, summarization, and language understanding, we argue that output space regularization alone is insufficient for sequential recommendation's data sparsity. Therefore, we design a novel regularization objective for the representation space. Departing from previous methods using cosine \cite{gao2021simcse} and L2 \cite{ma2017dropout,zolna2018fraternal} distances, we propose regularizing the probability distribution of user representations. This allows us to apply bidirectional KL loss effectively to address representation inconsistency. Experiments on three public benchmarks and a new large-scale dataset demonstrate that our simple consistency training for sequential recommendation (CT4Rec) surpasses state-of-the-art contrastive learning methods by a significant margin. Further experiments confirm the ease of extending our consistency training to data-related scenarios. An Online A/B test also validates our method's effectiveness. Additionally, we extend our approach to the CTR prediction task, with experiments on two new industrial datasets further proving its efficacy. In summary, our contributions are as follows: \begin{itemize} \item We introduce a straightforward yet effective consistency training method for sequential recommendations, utilizing two bidirectional KL losses. This work is pioneering in examining consistency training from various angles with a unified objective for sequential recommendation. \item Our consistency training method is adaptable to other inconsistency scenarios and tasks, such as data augmentation and CTR prediction. \item Extensive experiments on four offline datasets demonstrate that our CT4Rec outperforms SOTA models based on contrastive learning, offering superior performance and faster convergence. An Online A/B test also shows substantial improvements over robust ensemble models. \end{itemize}

text: Even the most thoroughly examined and widely deployed critical components often contain severe security vulnerabilities, as consistently revealed by security researchers. Recently, a promising research direction has emerged, employing \textit{formal verification} techniques on substantial real-world systems. These verified systems provide a machine-checkable proof that their implementation adheres to the specified ``correctness''. For instance, Project Everest~\cite{everest} demonstrated the correctness of an entire HTTPS stack by not only constructing and verifying the TLS implementation but also validating the underlying toolchain. This paper focuses on secure file systems. Although previous verified file systems~\cite{fscq,yggdrasil,cogent} have established their correctness concerning crucial properties like recovery assurance from arbitrary crashes, they lack features typically associated with {\em cryptographic} file systems. Such systems employ cryptographic techniques to protect against integrity and confidentiality breaches, especially under the ``evil maid'' threat model~\cite{evil_maid}, where an attacker gains temporary physical access to the target disk, enabling arbitrary read and write operations on the raw storage device. Our file system, IFSCQ, extends FSCQ~\cite{fscq} and is the first to offer both proven consistency guarantees against crash failures and verified integrity assurances against a compromised or malicious disk. At its core, IFSCQ establishes a formal model of a malicious disk, proving that any data or metadata compromise will be detected through cryptographic evidence. This is accomplished by overlaying a traditional Merkle tree~\cite{merkle_tree} across each disk block. The tree's root is securely stored in a modeled TPM (trusted platform module), which serves as a small, trusted storage space for a few Merkle tree root hashes. This setup allows us to maintain the majority of the Merkle tree on the potentially compromised disk while ensuring its integrity upon each read operation. As we will detail later, integrating these integrity features into FSCQ necessitated various modifications to FSCQ's core logic, yet all changes adhered to FSCQ's proof obligations while incorporating the additional integrity properties we defined and verified. We maintain the same trusted computing base (TCB) as FSCQ, relying on the Coq proof system, Haskell compiler and runtime, and Linux FUSE (user-space file system support). Our aim was not to minimize the TCB but to ensure our cryptographic file system's ``correctness'' in terms of crash consistency and disk tampering detection. It's worth noting that other research endeavors have explored verifying entire software stacks~\cite{deepspec} or generating C code with minimal runtime dependencies~\cite{cogent}. Such approaches could be applied to IFSCQ if the goal were TCB minimization or full-stack verification. The original FSCQ was modeled after the Unix Version~6 filesystem, lacking modern optimizations. It was designed to be straightforward, with the intention of future extensions. Consequently, IFSCQ is not aimed at competing with contemporary production filesystems in performance. Instead, it serves to illustrate the feasibility of applying formal verification to critical security properties. \vspace{1mm} \noindent\textbf{Threat model.} We operate under the assumption that both the hardware and operating system are trustworthy, but the disk may be compromised. We expand the ``evil maid'' threat into a ``Byzantine disk'' scenario, where adversaries can perform arbitrary writes at any moment. Such attacks could target specific file blocks, metadata blocks, or Merkle hash blocks, or even revert the entire disk to a previously valid state. Therefore, a trusted reference point is necessary to store and update the Merkle tree root. We utilize the concept of a TPM (trusted platform module), common in modern computers, and assume it provides a ``trusted boot'' feature, which most real TPMs support, although our approach diverges from real TPMs in several ways, which we will discuss later. \vspace{1mm} \noindent\textbf{Contributions.} Our contributions are as follows: \begin{itemize} \item We present the design and implementation of a certified file system with cryptographic integrity, proven to be resilient against crashes and capable of detecting data tampering. \item We introduce a formal model for malicious storage systems and outline the integrity properties a file system should offer to counteract such threats. \item We propose a Merkle tree design that satisfies these integrity properties, protecting all disk blocks (including data, inodes, and unallocated blocks), while requiring minimal trusted storage for root hashes. \item We provide evaluation results demonstrating that our system operates with reasonable overhead and effectively defends against various malicious attacks. \end{itemize} The remainder of the paper is structured as follows. Section~\ref{sec:background} provides the necessary background to comprehend our system. Section~\ref{sec:design} details our system's design. Section~\ref{sec:proof} discusses our proof engineering efforts. Section~\ref{sec:implementation} outlines our implementation. Section~\ref{sec:evaluation} presents our evaluation findings. Section~\ref{sec:relatedwork} reviews related work. Section~\ref{sec:discussion} explores potential improvements for IFSCQ, and Section~\ref{sec:conclusion} concludes the paper.

text: Robots are increasingly being deployed in environments where interaction with humans is crucial, such as in collaborative tasks like grasping~\cite{strabala2013toward,dragan2013legibility} and autonomous driving~\cite{montemerlo2008junior,levinson2011towards,sadigh2016planning,sadigh2016information}. Consequently, there is significant interest in developing algorithms for planning and control that facilitate effective human-robot interaction. Ensuring the safety of these robots is of utmost importance, given their potential to cause harm to humans~\cite{eder2014towards}. This is especially critical in scenarios like autonomous driving, where the objectives of robots and humans might diverge or conflict, such as when a self-driving car executes an unprotected left turn~\cite{sadigh2016planning}. A primary challenge lies in defining safety for robots that interact with humans. One might consider modeling humans as adversaries, but this often results in overly conservative systems. Alternatively, a predictive model of human actions can be learned~\cite{ziebart2008maximum,fisac2018probabilistically,sadigh2019verifying}, ensuring safety in accordance with this model. This approach is effective if the model accurately captures all human actions. However, human behavior can vary widely~\cite{sadigh2016information}; for instance, individuals in a lab setting may behave differently than those on a street. Collecting comprehensive data from every possible scenario is a daunting task. If certain behaviors are absent from the training data, the model might fail to account for them. Moreover, even the most advanced machine learning models can make errors, potentially overlooking critical actions. Lastly, \emph{responsibility sensitive safety (RSS)}~\cite{shalev2017formal} involves manually defining acceptable robot actions in various scenarios. Here, the responsibility falls on the robot controller's designer to ensure that only safe actions are deemed acceptable. However, specifying acceptable actions for all conceivable scenarios is particularly challenging for robots in open-world environments. For example,~\cite{shalev2017formal} only formalizes acceptable actions for a limited set of scenarios, such as lane changes. We introduce a novel method to ensure safety in human-interactive systems by accounting for all human behaviors within a bounded set. This approach addresses two main challenges: (i) defining the set of human behaviors and (ii) ensuring safety concerning this set. Our solutions are as follows: \begin{itemize} \item {\bf Bounding human behavior via backup actions:} Instead of specifying all permissible robot actions (as in RSS), designers specify \emph{backup actions} that humans are believed to consider to avert accidents (e.g., braking while steering). We assume humans can take any action generally but will resort to these actions when necessary for safety. \item {\bf Ensuring safety via abstract interpretation:} We employ \emph{abstract interpretation}~\cite{cousot1977abstract} to conservatively overestimate the system's reachable set for the modeled human behavior and ensure safety based on this overapproximation. \end{itemize} Our concept of backup actions is grounded in the assumption that humans will undertake a limited range of evasive maneuvers to prevent accidents—such as slowing down to avoid rear-ending a stopping robot.\footnote{We do not assume humans will swerve to avoid accidents unless it is safe. A reasonable time frame is assumed for braking and stopping.} On highways, stopping might be hazardous, so the robot may need to pull over before stopping. Similarly, stopping at intersections should be avoided. Specifying backup actions helps define safety, termed \emph{safety modulo fault}.\footnote{The term "fault" implies that safety considerations exclude scenarios where human actions deviate from our model, not to assign blame for accidents. The controller designer is tasked with defining backup actions to achieve a reasonable safety standard.} To implement our framework, the robot controller's designer must focus on: \begin{itemize} \item \textbf{Robot backup action:} An action anticipated by humans to ensure safety—like braking without changing direction—should be based on intuition about human expectations of robot behavior (e.g., traffic rules). \item \textbf{Human backup action set:} A set of actions including \emph{at least one} that humans consider for safety—such as braking while steering—should be based on intuition about human safety maneuvers. \end{itemize} Unlike RSS, which requires specifying all permissible robot actions, our approach only requires specifying actions humans might consider to avoid accidents. We propose an algorithm to ensure safety modulo fault. Building on \emph{shielding} techniques~\cite{akametalu2014reachability,alshiekh2018safe,wabersich2018linear,li2019robust}, our algorithm integrates an arbitrary goal-oriented controller with a backup controller, maximizing the use of the former while ensuring safety modulo fault. This is achieved via on-the-fly verification using abstract interpretation to assess the safety of employing the given controller; if deemed safe, the controller is used; otherwise, the backup controller is deployed. Finally, we empirically validate our approach through simulations involving both human simulations and real human interactions via keyboard inputs. Our MPS modulo fault algorithm effectively prevents accidents with both real and simulated humans, even when paired with a simplistic controller that disregards human presence. Figure~\ref{fig:overview} illustrates our algorithm's capability to maintain safety in human interactions without excessive caution. It presumes that the human will apply minimal braking to prevent accidents (left). If safety cannot be assured, it allows the human to proceed first (right).

text: The Gaussian mechanism serves as a fundamental component in a wide array of differentially private learning algorithms \cite{song2013stochastic, bassily2014private, abadi2016deep}. Although it facilitates mathematical reasoning and privacy accounting, its continuous nature poses practical challenges. Specifically, it cannot be precisely represented on finite computational systems, leading to numerical inaccuracies that may compromise privacy guarantees \cite{mironov2012significance}. Additionally, it is unsuitable for distributed learning scenarios involving cryptographic multi-party computation with modular arithmetic, such as secure aggregation \cite{secagg, bell2020secagg}. To mitigate these issues, the binomial and (distributed) discrete Gaussian mechanisms have been proposed \cite{DworkKMMN06, agarwal2018cpsgd, CanonneKS20, ddg}. Nonetheless, these alternatives have limitations: the binomial mechanism can incur infinite privacy loss with a certain probability, and the discrete Gaussian mechanism: (a) lacks closure under summation, complicating its use in distributed environments and resulting in inferior performance compared to the continuous Gaussian in highly distributed, low-noise scenarios~\cite{ddg}; (b) requires a sampling algorithm absent from mainstream machine learning and data analysis software, posing challenges for practical implementation (naïve implementations risk severe privacy breaches). \textbf{Our contributions}\hspace{0.5em} To address these limitations, we propose and examine the multi-dimensional Skellam mechanism, which introduces noise through the difference of two independent Poisson random variables. The Skellam noise retains closure under summation, allowing sums of Skellam random variables to remain Skellam distributed, and is readily sampled using widely available efficient Poisson samplers in numerical software. Its discrete nature aligns well with cryptographic protocols and offers potential communication efficiencies. We conduct a numerical evaluation of the privacy loss random variable and establish a precise bound on the R\'enyi divergence between two shifted Skellam distributions to assess the Skellam mechanism's privacy guarantees and its comparison with other mechanisms. Our detailed analysis reveals that for a multi-dimensional query function with $\ell_1$ sensitivity $\Delta_1$ and $\ell_2$ sensitivity $\Delta_2$, the Skellam mechanism with variance $\mu$ achieves $(\alpha, \varepsilon(\alpha))$ R\'enyi differential privacy (RDP) \cite{mironov2017renyi} where $\varepsilon(\alpha) \leq \frac{\alpha \Delta_{2}}{2 \mu}+\min \left(\frac{(2\alpha - 1) \Delta_{2}+6 \Delta_1}{4 \mu^2}, \frac{ 3\Delta_1}{2 \mu}\right)$ (refer to Theorem \ref{thm:mainSK}). This indicates that the RDP guarantees are, at most, $1 + O\left(1/{\mu}\right)$ times less favorable than those provided by the Gaussian mechanism. To evaluate the Skellam mechanism's practical performance, we examine a differentially private and communication-constrained federated learning (FL) scenario \cite{kairouz2019advances} where noise is locally added to the $d$-dimensional discretized client updates, which are then securely aggregated via a cryptographic protocol like secure aggregation (SecAgg) \cite{bell2020secagg, secagg}. We present a comprehensive algorithm that discretizes data, applies the Skellam mechanism, and utilizes modular arithmetic to limit data range and communication costs before implementing SecAgg. Our experiments on distributed mean estimation and two benchmark FL datasets—Federated EMNIST~\cite{caldas2018leaf} and Stack Overflow~\cite{tffauthors2019}—demonstrate that our method can achieve performance comparable to the continuous Gaussian baseline under stringent privacy and communication constraints. This is despite employing generic RDP amplification through sampling~\cite{zhu2019poission} for our method and precise RDP analysis for the subsampled Gaussian mechanism~\cite{mironov2019r}. Our implementation is available in TensorFlow Privacy~\cite{tf-privacy} and TensorFlow Federated~\cite{ingerman2019tff} and will be open-sourced.\footnote{\url{https://github.com/google-research/federated/tree/master/distributed_dp}} Although our focus is on FL applications, the Skellam mechanism is applicable to other learning and analytics contexts, including centralized settings. \textbf{Related work}\hspace{0.5em} The Skellam mechanism was initially introduced in the realm of computational differential privacy from lattice-based cryptography~\cite{valovich2017computational} and private Bayesian inference~\cite{schein2019locally}. However, previous privacy analyses do not readily extend to multi-dimensional cases and provide direct bounds for pure or approximate DP, limiting the applicability of advanced composition theorems~\cite{kairouz2015composition, dwork2010boosting} in learning contexts where the mechanism is repeatedly applied. For instance, the guarantees from~\cite{valovich2017computational} result in suboptimal accuracy-privacy trade-offs, as illustrated in Fig.~\ref{fig:accounting-composition}. Additionally, as discussed in Section \ref{sec:skellam-pld}, extending direct privacy analysis to multi-dimensional settings is complex due to the unknown worst-case neighboring dataset pair. Consequently, our precise privacy analysis using a sharp RDP bound renders the Skellam mechanism practical for learning applications for the first time. These guarantees closely align with those of the Gaussian mechanism and enable the use of generic RDP amplification via subsampling methods \cite{zhu2019poission}. The mechanisms most similar to Skellam are the binomial \cite{agarwal2018cpsgd, DworkKMMN06} and discrete Gaussian mechanisms \cite{CanonneKS20, ddg}. While the binomial mechanism can asymptotically approximate the continuous Gaussian mechanism when properly scaled, it does not achieve R\'enyi or zero-concentrated DP \cite{mironov2017renyi, BunS16} and can result in infinite privacy loss with non-zero probability, risking severe privacy failures. The discrete Gaussian mechanism offers R\'enyi DP and is applicable to distributed settings~\cite{ddg}, yet it necessitates a sampling algorithm not yet integrated into data analysis software, despite exploration within the lattice-based cryptography community (e.g.,~\cite{roy2013high, dwarakanath2014sampling, rossi2019simple}). Furthermore, the discrete Gaussian is not closed under summation, and its divergence can be substantial in highly distributed low-noise settings (e.g., quantile estimation~\cite{andrew2019differentially} and federated analytics~\cite{fedanalytics}), leading to privacy deterioration. Further discussion is provided at the conclusion of Section~\ref{sec:applying-skellam}.

Skellam mechanism has been proposed for the purpose of calculating differential privacy, based on lattice cryptography, and for the purpose of private Bayesian inference, based on local private lattices. For the subsampled Gaussian mechanism, the analysis of the reduced disclosure is precise. For the Skellam mechanism, the analysis of the reduced disclosure is less precise. The most similar mechanism to Skellam’s is the binomial distribution of citations agarwal2018cpsgd, citation dworkkmmn06 and discrete Gaussian citation canonneks20. As an example, the analysis by Valovich and Kairouz produces suboptimal accuracy-privacy trade-offs, as shown in Fig. 3. The discrete Gaussian mechanism has zero-centered probability and is applicable to distributed settings [ddg], but it requires a sampling method which has not yet been integrated into the statistical analysis software, despite its application to lattice-based encryption (cf. Roy, ‘13 High, Dwarakanath, ‘14 Sampling, Rossi, ‘19 Simple). The guarantees provided by this mechanism are quite similar to those of the Gaussian mechanism, and it is possible to use generic RDP amplification methods, such as subsampling (zhu2019poission). Moreover, our precise privacy analysis using a sharp RDP bound makes the Skellam mechanism applicable for learning purposes for the first time. More details are given in the conclusion of this section. Moreover, the discrete Gaussian is not closed under summation and its divergence can be substantial in a highly distributed low-noise setting [Andrew2019differentially], or in federated analytics [Andrew2019federatedanalytics], which degrades privacy.

text: Despite the remarkable achievements of machine learning in fields such as image classification~\citep{Ciresan_Schmidhuber_12,Krizhevsky_Hinton_12} and gaming~\citep{Mnih_Hassabis_15,Silver_Hassabis_16}, these successes have not been mirrored in robotics. Several factors contribute to this discrepancy. Primarily, mastering actions in the physical realm is significantly more challenging. Although modern (deep) learning algorithms could theoretically gather the necessary data directly from physical robots~\citep{Levine_Quillen_16}, this approach is impractical due to its prohibitive time and resource demands. A more viable solution is to generate data through simulations, which are faster, cost-effective, safer, and offer unmatched diversity. However, this method introduces unavoidable approximation errors when modeling reality. Known as the \enquote*{reality gap}, these errors stem from neglecting certain physical phenomena, inaccuracies in parameter estimation, or the numerical integration discretization in typical solvers. Complicating matters further, current (deep) learning techniques are notoriously fragile~\citep{Szegedy_Fergus_13,Goodfellow_Szegedy_14,Huang_Abbeel_17}, being highly susceptible to variations in their input domains. Additionally, learners might exploit the simulator, overfitting to features absent in the real world. For instance, \citet{Baker_Mordatch_20} observed agents leveraging the physics engine for unexpected advantages. While this exploitation is intriguing within simulation-based studies, it is undesirable for {sim-to-real}\xspace applications. At best, the reality gap results in diminished performance, such as reduced success rates or tracking precision. More often, the policy learned is not applicable to the robot due to unaccounted physical effects. Friction, which is notoriously difficult to model, often leads to underestimation in simulations, causing motor commands to lack the necessary strength to mobilize the robot. Errors in parameter estimation can also destabilize system dynamics, posing risks to both humans and robots. Therefore, bridging the reality gap is crucial for enabling robots to benefit from simulated experiences. Merely enhancing simulator accuracy is insufficient to close this gap~\citep{Hofner_White_20}. Drawing parallels from machine learning advancements, we observe that deep models, when paired with extensive and varied datasets, achieve superior generalization~\citep{Russakovsky_etal_2015,Radford_etal_2019}. In a similar vein, domain randomization has emerged as a promising technique (Figure~\ref{fig_sota_collage_sim2real}). This approach involves perturbing simulator parameters, state observations, or actions. Commonly randomized elements include body inertia and geometry, friction and contact model parameters, actuation delays, motor efficiency coefficients, sensor noise levels, and visual attributes such as color, lighting, camera positioning, and image artifacts like glare. Domain randomization acts as a regularization method, preventing learners from overfitting to specific simulation instances. From a Bayesian standpoint, the distribution over simulators reflects uncertainty. In this paper, we begin by establishing the necessary terminology and mathematical principles (Section~\ref{sec_sota_mdp}). We then explore early methods for learning from randomized simulations, outline practical requirements, and discuss measures for {sim-to-real}\xspace transferability (Section~\ref{sec_sota_simtoreal_foundations}). Following this, we examine the links between {sim-to-real}\xspace transfer research and related domains (Section~\ref{sec_sota_related_fields}). We also propose a taxonomy for domain randomization and classify the current state of the art (Section~\ref{sec_sota_domain_randomization}). Finally, we offer conclusions and suggest potential future research avenues (Section~\ref{sec_sota_discussion_and_outlook}). For readers seeking foundational knowledge in robot policy learning and policy search, we recommend the surveys by~\citet{Kober_Peters_13}, \citet{Deisenroth_Peters_13}, and \citet{Chatzilygeroudis_Mouret_20}.

text: The application of machine learning (ML) to predict outcomes from privacy-sensitive data is on the rise. Major technology firms like Google and Amazon have recently started providing machine learning services to the public via their cloud platforms. While these systems can uncover novel insights across various domains, they also expose machine learning models trained on sensitive information to potential adversarial attacks. One such attack is the Membership Inference Attack (MIA)~\cite{shokri2016membership, yeom2017privacy}, where the adversary aims to ascertain whether specific data was part of the training set of an ML model. Successful MIAs can breach individual privacy and pose a considerable threat to inadequately protected ML models~\cite{shokri2016membership}. To mitigate such risks, differentially private (DP) mechanisms are incorporated during the ML model training process \cite{chaudhuri_differentially_nodate,Abadi_2016,beaulieujones2018privacypreserving, shokri2016membership, yeom2017privacy, yu2019differentially}, limiting the influence any single data point has on the model's output. The adoption of DP mechanisms in ML training is becoming widespread, with popular libraries like TensorFlow~\cite{tensorflow} and PyTorch~\cite{pytorch} offering several DP training algorithms. Research has provided both empirical and theoretical support for DP training as a defense against MIAs~\cite{li2013membership,yeom2017privacy,jayaraman_evaluating_2019,shokri2016membership}. Yeom et al.~\cite{yeom2017privacy} demonstrated that DP training algorithms provide a \emph{theoretical upper bound} on privacy leakage due to MIAs. This bound was later refined by Erlingsson et al.~\cite{jayaraman2020revisiting}, showing robust protection at high DP levels (small DP parameter $\epsilon$ values), but diminishing rapidly with larger $\epsilon$. Despite this, empirical evaluations of MIAs on DP-trained models~\cite{jayaraman_evaluating_2019, jayaraman2020revisiting} indicate that even large $\epsilon$ values, which theoretically imply low privacy, can effectively protect against MIAs in practical scenarios. Inspired by these insights, Murakonda and Shokri~\cite{murakonda2020ml} developed a tool to tune $\epsilon$ based on empirical MIA performance, enhancing model utility at the cost of theoretical privacy assurances. In essence, this research suggests that DP mechanisms can offer adequate protection against known MIAs, even under weakened privacy settings. The evaluation methodologies in these MIA studies typically assume that members and non-members are sampled independently from the same distribution. However, this assumption does not always align with real-world data scenarios~\cite{Mohammad2020, arjovsky2021distribution, pmlr-v97-recht19a, Martensson2020, nagarajan2021understanding, pmlr-v119-sagawa20a, sagawa2020distributionally}. Furthermore, prior research indicates that data dependencies can lead to an overestimation of the privacy protection offered by DP~\cite{tschantz_sok_2020, kifer_no_2011, pufferfish, li2013membership, liu2016dependence}. Motivated by this, we conduct a pioneering investigation into MIA performance on ML models trained with DP-SGD~\cite{Abadi_2016} \emph{considering data dependencies}. Our study begins by examining the methodologies from previous MIA research to uncover the assumptions underlying their theoretical conclusions~\cite{yeom2017privacy,jayaraman_evaluating_2019,nasr2021adversary}. Due to the absence of publicly documented MIAs on ML models in the wild, researchers simulate attacks via theoretical games between model owners and attackers, known as \emph{membership experiments}~\cite{yeom2017privacy}. We reveal that earlier membership experiments presume independence among training samples, which may not reflect many practical scenarios. To address this, we propose a new membership experiment that relaxes the stringent independence assumption. We demonstrate that the previously established DP-based bounds on adversary success fail to hold in this broader context. This does not imply that DP is flawed; rather, it highlights that DP guarantees do not apply when membership inference includes data dependencies. Intuitively, DP mechanisms limit the impact of a \emph{single} sample on the output, but when samples are interdependent, related samples can inadvertently reveal additional information about a single sample. Prior studies emphasize the necessity of exploring MIA performance both theoretically and empirically~\cite{jayaraman_evaluating_2019, jayaraman2020revisiting}. Consequently, we also examine how data dependencies affect the \emph{empirical performance} of MIAs under various configurations of our membership experiment. Utilizing six real-world datasets, we assess the effectiveness of standard attacks, which have black-box query access to the target model without any extra background on the data dependencies in question. Through these attacks, we explore three types of data dependencies. First, to assess the impact of data dependencies on MIAs, we artificially divide a dataset into members and non-members using a clustering algorithm. Our findings indicate that data dependencies can facilitate perfect membership inference even with DP training. Second, we explore how an explicit bias in a training set attribute influences outcomes. Specifically, we introduce gender and education biases in the training set, observing that MIA performance generally improves as biases become more pronounced. Lastly, we evaluate MIA performance on various real-world data dependencies encountered during data collection. For instance, we examine scenarios where all members belong to a specific health region (or hospital) while non-members are from other regions. We also assess MIA performance when members and non-members originate from the same source (the US Census) but are curated by different researchers. In all evaluations involving statistical dependencies among training samples, we observe a marked increase in MIA performance compared to related studies where samples are assumed to be Independent and Identically Distributed (IID)~\cite{shokri2016membership,jayaraman_evaluating_2019, jayaraman2020revisiting, yeom2017privacy,jagielski2020auditing, nasr2021adversary}. This indicates that assuming data independence among training samples underestimates attack efficacy. Our empirical analysis reveals attack performance exceeding the bounds of DP, confirming that the existing DP bounds are inapplicable once data dependencies are considered, and thus DP mechanisms are not a panacea for membership inference. This underscores the need to account for data dependencies in future MIA evaluations and calls for new research to develop improved defenses and more realistic theoretical bounds on MIA performance.

text: Confidence intervals serve as a fundamental tool for summarizing the underlying distribution and identifying outlier behavior. This paper delves into the challenge of determining confidence intervals specifically for time series data. \citet{korpela2014confidence} introduced an innovative approach for computing confidence intervals by advocating for confidence bands rather than point-wise intervals. Formally, given a set of $n$ time series $T$, the task is to identify $k$ time series $U \subseteq T$ that minimize the envelope area, expressed as the sum $\sum_i \pr{\max_{t \in U} t(i)} - \pr{\min_{t \in U} t(i)}$. The advantage of employing confidence bands, as highlighted by \citet{korpela2014confidence}, lies in superior family-wise error control: while point-wise intervals only allow for the identification of an outlier at a specific point, confidence bands facilitate a broader assertion about the normalcy of the entire time series without necessitating multiple testing corrections like the Bonferroni correction. Our focus in this paper is on exploring approximation algorithms for deriving confidence bands. Although \citet{korpela2014confidence} demonstrated the \textbf{NP}-hard nature of finding the optimal confidence band, they did not furnish any approximation algorithms or inapproximability results. We will demonstrate that despite the \textbf{NP}-hard classification, solutions exist for specific values of $k$. This is achieved by reframing the problem to prioritize an objective function that favors selecting time series which do not excessively expand the envelope area. The objective is influenced by the parameter $\alpha$, where higher $\alpha$ values permit greater increases in the envelope area. We will illustrate that this problem can be solved exactly in polynomial time, with each $\alpha$ correlating to a specific $k$ value. We will also establish that there are at most $n + 1$ such bands, all discoverable in polynomial time by adjusting $\alpha$. Subsequently, we introduce a straightforward algorithm to approximate confidence bands by linking the problem to the weighted $k$-\textsc{MinUnion}\xspace problem. We propose a variant of an algorithm by~\citet{chlamtac2018densest} that offers a $\sqrt{n} + 1$ guarantee. Moreover, we argue that, based on certain conjectures, the problem cannot be approximated better than $\bigO{n^{1/4}}$. Additionally, we explore a problem variant that focuses on minimizing the width of the envelope, defined as the maximum difference between the envelope boundaries. We demonstrate that a basic algorithm can achieve a 2-approximation. This finding provides a compelling contrast to the inapproximability outcomes when minimizing the envelope area. Notably, this guarantee is optimal: we will also show that no polynomial-time algorithm with a smaller guarantee exists unless $\textbf{P}=\textbf{NP}$. The structure of the paper is as follows. In Section~\ref{sec:prel}, we formally define the optimization problems. Section~\ref{sec:reg} addresses the solution to the regularized band problem. Section~\ref{sec:sum} focuses on the approximation of envelope area minimization, while Section~\ref{sec:max} deals with the approximation of envelope width minimization. Section~\ref{sec:related} reviews related work. Our experimental results are presented in Section~\ref{sec:exp}, and we conclude with a discussion in Section~\ref{sec:conclusions}.

text: The proliferation of autonomous robotic systems necessitates controllers that can adeptly navigate the complexities of our everyday, unstructured environments. Recent strides in reinforcement learning (RL), particularly when integrated with deep neural networks for function approximation, have demonstrated remarkable success in various intricate robotic control tasks. These tasks include dexterous in-hand manipulation \cite{dexterous}, quadrupedal locomotion \cite{haarnoja2018learning}, and precision throwing \cite{throwing}. However, a significant challenge remains: the absence of \textit{safety} assurances in deep RL-based controllers, which hampers their practical deployment in real-world robotics \cite{Ibarz_2021}. This issue stems from the opaque nature of neural network policies and their struggle to handle out-of-distribution states reliably, a problem especially evident when transitioning models trained in simulation to real-world applications. Conversely, the classical robotics field has developed numerous controllers and algorithms for diverse physical systems, ranging from mobile robots to humanoids, enabling the safe and reliable deployment of robotic agents in real-world scenarios. These solutions include classical feedback controllers \cite{maxwell1868governors}, trajectory generators \cite{ijspeert2008central}, and behavior trees \cite{colledanchise2016behavior}. Their success is largely due to their explicit analytical foundations and well-understood models, which provide control-theoretic guarantees, making them suitable for real-world use. Nonetheless, these approaches often fall short in terms of optimality when tackling complex tasks, due to constraints in analytical modeling and approximations. A promising avenue for advancing robot control lies in integrating the complementary strengths of these diverse control strategies to overcome their individual limitations. This concept finds parallels in neuroscience, where biological systems employ such strategies. According to the dual-process theory of decision-making \cite{dickinson2002role}, multiple neural controllers are implicated in action selection within biological systems. \citet{lee2014neural} provide evidence supporting this theory, highlighting an arbitration mechanism in the human brain that determines the influence of different neural controllers on behavior. This arbitrator evaluates specific performance metrics of each controller, leveraging their strengths in various states. Inspired by these insights, we introduce Bayesian Controller Fusion (BCF), a hybrid control strategy that merges the strengths of deep RL with traditional handcrafted controllers (\textit{control priors}) for safe deployment in real-world scenarios. We conceptualize the final policy as a Bayesian amalgamation of these two controllers, where each system's output reflects its \textit{epistemic} uncertainty in a given state, as illustrated in Figure \ref{front}. BCF facilitates the natural arbitration of control between the two systems, guided by their confidence in action. This approach is crucial for real-world deployment, allowing us to harness the dexterity of the learned system in states it has effectively generalized to, while relying on the risk-averse behaviors of the handcrafted system in out-of-distribution states for safety. Notably, our method enables learning to control a real robot in joint space to accomplish a task without requiring on-robot time (\textit{zero-shot}), despite potential imperfections in transferring the learned policy from simulation to reality. We validate our approach on two continuous control robotic tasks: reactive navigation on a mobile robot and a manipulability-maximizing reacher on a robotic arm. Our results demonstrate how BCF facilitates the reliable transfer of a simulation-trained policy to the real world, achieving significant performance gains from the RL component compared to using the handcrafted system alone. We regard this as a promising and practical path to enabling simulation-trained RL controllers to operate safely in real-world environments.

text: The rise of open-access repositories like arXiv and bioRxiv has simplified the process of sharing new research discoveries. Each month, these platforms facilitate the dissemination of tens of thousands of scientific papers by the research community\footnote{\url{https://arxiv.org/stats/monthly_submissions}}. However, the lack of peer review and the overwhelming volume of publications make it challenging to pinpoint relevant studies and stay updated with the latest advancements. Scientific paper summarization, a branch of automatic text summarization, seeks to aid researchers by distilling articles into concise, human-readable summaries that highlight only the most critical information. Recently, abstractive summarization has achieved remarkable advancements. This approach involves training models to create coherent summaries by rephrasing the source material. Cutting-edge techniques utilize large pre-trained models~\citep{raffel2019t5, lewis2020bart}, implement task-specific pre-training methods~\citep{zhang2019pegasus}, and handle extended input sequences~\citep{zhao2020seal, zaheer2020bigbird}. Large-scale benchmark datasets like arXiv and PubMed~\citep{cohan2018discourse} were compiled automatically from digital archives, using paper abstracts as reference summaries. Nonetheless, training models to generate paper abstracts presents two issues: 1) abstracts often include non-essential details, and 2) most scientific articles already feature human-composed abstracts, rendering generated summaries redundant. To overcome these limitations, we propose the task of disentangled paper summarization. This task involves generating two distinct summaries: one focused on the article's innovations and contributions, and the other on the context of the work and prior research. This dual-summary approach caters to varied audiences: experienced researchers and experts who benefit from the summarized contributions, and novices who can quickly grasp the problem's nuances through the context summary, gaining insights from the contribution summary. For this endeavor, we have developed a new extensive dataset by enhancing the S2ORC~\citep{lo2020s2orc} corpus of scientific papers, which encompasses diverse scientific fields and includes comprehensive citation-related metadata. We process and organize this data, enriching it with automatically created contribution and context reference summaries to support supervised model training. Additionally, we introduce three abstractive baseline methods: 1) a unified, controllable model guided by descriptive control codes~\citep{fan2018controllable,keskar2019CTRL}, 2) a one-to-many sequence model with a branched decoder for generating multiple outputs~\citep{luong2016mtl, bansal2018mts}, and 3) an information-theoretic training approach utilizing supervision derived from citation metadata~\citep{peyrard2019simple}. To evaluate our models, we establish a thorough automatic evaluation protocol assessing performance in terms of relevance, novelty, and disentanglement. We conduct an in-depth evaluation and analysis of the baseline models, exploring the impact of the additional training objective on model behavior. To demonstrate the utility of the newly proposed task, we performed a human study in a simulated paper-reviewing context with human annotators. The findings indicate that disentangled summaries are more beneficial in 79\% of cases compared to abstract-focused outputs. The code, model checkpoints, and data preparation scripts introduced in this study are accessible at~\url{https://github.com/salesforce/disentangled-sum}.

text: Over the past decade, significant progress in deep neural networks has enabled models to tackle new tasks that require integrating information from multiple modalities. A prominent research area within this domain is the intersection of language and vision, notably in visual question answering (VQA) \cite{Agrawal2015VQAVQ, Gupta2017SurveyOV}, which involves answering questions about images (see surveys \cite{Wu2017VisualQA, Srivastava2019VisualQA}). However, to effectively emulate human-like tasks, models must transcend mere semantic interpretation of text and visuals. They need to demonstrate sophisticated behaviors, such as understanding complex referential relationships that include numerous exceptions (e.g., 'green' could indicate a healthy plant, an ill person, inexperience, envy, or recycling). Moreover, models should leverage one modality to overcome learned biases in another \cite{Agrawal2018DontJA, Cadne2019RUBiRU, Chen2020CounterfactualSS, goyal2017making, Ramakrishnan2018OvercomingLP} (for instance, while bananas are typically yellow, a specific image might depict a pink banana). Capturing these intricate interactions presents a formidable challenge in deep learning, as optimal methods for fusing feature tensors within a network remain elusive. Initial approaches involved vector concatenation to map diverse features into a unified feature space \cite{Zhou2015SimpleBF, Lu2016HierarchicalQC}. Drawing inspiration from an earlier vision-only two-factor framework \cite{Tenenbaum:2000:SSC:1121517.1121518}, VQA models have significantly advanced by adopting a 'pooled' bilinear representation (BLP) of visual and textual features \cite{DBLP:journals/corr/GaoBZD15, DBLP:journals/corr/FukuiPYRDR16, DBLP:journals/corr/KongF16, DBLP:journals/corr/KimOKHZ16, DBLP:journals/corr/abs-1708-01471, ben2019block, Yu2018BeyondBG}. Research into BLP for VQA has concentrated on developing more efficient and cost-effective bilinear representations \cite{DBLP:journals/corr/KongF16, DBLP:journals/corr/KimOKHZ16, DBLP:journals/corr/abs-1708-01471, ben2019block}, integrating BLP with attention mechanisms \cite{Kim2018BilinearAN, Yu2018BeyondBG, DBLP:journals/corr/abs-1708-01471}, and recently analyzing and categorizing BLP as a "joint" representation alongside other fusion methods and models \cite{Baltruaitis2019MultimodalML, zhang2019multimodal, 8715409}. Despite their success in VQA, BLP techniques have not yet been extensively applied to video-QA baselines \cite{MovieQA, pororoqa, jang-CVPR-2017, Fan_2019_ICCV, lei2018tvqa, Xu2017VideoQA}. This paper seeks to bridge this gap by applying BLP techniques to datasets such as TVQA \cite{lei2018tvqa}, TGIF-QA \cite{jang-CVPR-2017}, Ego-VQA \cite{Fan_2019_ICCV}, and MSVD-QA \cite{Xu2017VideoQA}. Our contributions include: \textbf{I)} Replacing concatenation with BLP techniques in the TVQA baseline model \cite{lei2018tvqa}, \textbf{II)} Introducing a modified version of the TVQA baseline, called the 'dual-stream' model, to incorporate BLP, \textbf{III)} Conducting experiments to replace concatenation with BLP in the recently proposed heterogeneous-memory-enhanced multimodal attention (HME) model \cite{Fan2019HeterogeneousME}, \textbf{IV)} Utilizing the TVQA dataset for our experiments on HME, \textbf{V)} Providing insights into the suboptimal performance concerning recent multimodal fusion taxonomies \cite{Baltruaitis2019MultimodalML, zhang2019multimodal, 8715409}, \textbf{VI)} Performing experiments on the TVQA baseline model enhanced with deep canonical correlation analysis (DCCA) \cite{Andrew2013DeepCC} to contrast a 'co-ordinated' representation with BLP's 'joint' representation (as defined in \cite{8715409}), \textbf{VII)} Offering additional best practices for transitioning BLP from image-QA to video-QA, \textbf{VIII)} Presenting an overview of how bilinear representations align with contemporary psychological models of vision and perception \cite{Goodale1992SeparateVP, milner2006visual, milner2008two, goodale2014and, Milner2017HowDT}. Notoriously, inconclusive or negative experimental results often go unpublished, a practice that has been widely criticized \cite{Mlinari2017DealingWT, Faschinger2019DoNH, Sandercock2012NegativeRW}. We aim to report our experimental outcomes to broaden the public experimental landscape of multimodal fusion and to foster critical future research that can build upon, contrast, and critique our findings and hypotheses.

text: Recent advancements in deep learning, particularly the development of pre-trained language models (LMs)~\cite{radford2019language,devlin2018bert}, have significantly enhanced the field of question answering. This progress is evident in tasks such as single passage question answering (reading comprehension datasets) and large-scale open-domain corpora (open-domain QA). However, when it comes to question answering over book stories (BookQA), the performance remains subpar. A case in point is the NarrativeQA benchmark~\cite{kovcisky2018narrativeqa}, introduced three years ago, where the latest state-of-the-art methods show only slight gains over the initial baselines. NarrativeQA presents several challenges that hinder research advancements. Firstly, narrative stories introduce a unique writing style distinct from formal texts like Wikipedia. Secondly, the extensive length of book inputs exceeds the processing capacity of neural models, making it crucial to identify evidence across entire books. Thirdly, as NarrativeQA is a generative task, many answers do not have exact matches in the original texts, necessitating the use of generative QA models. Lastly, and most critically, the dataset lacks annotations for supporting evidence. Although this mirrors the realistic conditions of open-domain QA, it complicates the inference of supporting evidence, unlike most extractive open-domain QA tasks. The need for evidence identification and the absence of supporting evidence annotations render the BookQA task analogous to open-domain QA. This paper explores whether techniques from cutting-edge open-domain QA systems can be adapted to enhance BookQA. These include: (1) the neural ranker-reader pipeline~\cite{wang2018r}, where a neural ranker selects relevant passages (evidence) from a vast pool based on the question; (2) the application of pre-trained LMs such as GPT~\cite{radford2019language}, BERT~\cite{devlin2018bert}, and their successors as readers and rankers; (3) distantly supervised and unsupervised training methods~\cite{wang2018r,Lee_2019orqa,min2019discrete,guu2020realm,karpukhin2020dense} that enhance rankers' learning from noisy gold data. By implementing a ranker-reader framework for BookQA, we achieve a new state-of-the-art on NarrativeQA using both generative and extractive readers. Our findings and analysis indicate several key observations: \noindent$\bullet$ Employing pre-trained LMs as reader models, such as BERT and GPT, enhances NarrativeQA performance. With an identical BM25 IR baseline, these models yield a 5-6\% improvement in Rouge-L scores compared to their non-pre-trained counterparts. \noindent$\bullet$ Our specifically crafted distant supervision signals significantly enhance the neural ranker, although the improvement remains modest relative to the upper bound. Further examination of the ranker module reveals the challenges in training, as the gains from the pre-trained LM BERT are minimal.

text: Drones hold the potential to revolutionize urban logistics by providing rapid and adaptable delivery solutions, meeting the escalating demands of dense urban environments driven by logistics and e-commerce growth~\cite{chung2020optimization}. They offer an alternative to conventional ground delivery systems, which often exacerbate traffic congestion~\cite{HolguinETAL18}. Nonetheless, solely relying on drones for package delivery poses challenges due to their restricted flight range and limited payload capacity~\cite{SudburyETAL16}. To address these challenges, our research explores a hybrid delivery model where drones collaborate with ground vehicles, hitching rides to conserve energy and extend their operational range~\cite{choudhury2019dynamic,choudhury2021efficient}. Our focus is on optimizing the routing of drones and trucks over a shared road network, with drones utilizing trucks for transit in addition to flying. We conceptualize this as a \emph{coordinated} extension of the Multi-Agent Path Finding (MAPF) problem~\cite{stern2019multi}, which involves computing start-to-goal routes for all agents while minimizing the total path cost for both drones and trucks. The path cost varies between agent types, reflecting either energy consumption or operational costs. Similar to the classical MAPF, our problem requires adherence to inter-agent constraints, such as limiting the number of drones that can ride a truck simultaneously, and necessitates an analysis of the cost benefits of shared segments between trucks and drones. The concept of temporary coordination among agents is novel within the MAPF community (to our knowledge) and adds complexity to our problem beyond the already challenging classical MAPF~\cite{yu2013structure, YuLaValle16}. Current MAPF algorithms prioritize avoiding collisions over optimizing cooperation~\cite{felner2017search,stern2019multi}. Our recent work introduced a MAPF solver for drone routing over transit networks~\cite{choudhury2021efficient}, assuming fixed transit vehicle routes and no requirement for drones to navigate the road network. Another study addressed cooperative MAPF but only planned for predefined pairs of agents meeting at fixed points~\cite{greshler2021cooperative}, rather than concurrently traversing a route. The operations research field has explored optimizing drone-truck collaborations, but their methods are limited to a small number of agents on simplified routing graphs~\cite{agatz2012optimization}. \vspace{5pt} \noindent\textbf{Contributions.} We propose a novel algorithmic solution for coordinated MAPF involving drones and trucks operating together. Our primary innovation is to \textit{decompose the complex MAPF problem into two manageable MAPF sub-problems, which we solve sequentially} (\Cref{fig:approach}). In the first stage, we determine truck routes that are beneficial for drone transit. In the second stage, we fix these truck routes, construct a transit network based on them, and integrate this network with the road graph. We then calculate drone routes over this combined road-and-transit network, where drones incur no cost on transit segments, subject to capacity constraints. As a final step, we re-route trucks not utilized for transit along their shortest paths in the road network. We implement two variants of our approach using different MAPF solvers; one employs Enhanced Conflict-Based Search~\cite{barer2014suboptimal} and the other utilizes Prioritized Planning~\cite{silver2005cooperative} for both stages. We test our approach across various coordinated MAPF scenarios over the Manhattan road network, encompassing nearly $4500$ vertices and $10000$ edges over an area of approximately \SI{200}{\kilo\metre\squared}, with up to $20$ trucks and $80$ drones. Our findings indicate that coordinating drones and trucks can reduce total vehicle distance traveled by more than $50\%$ compared to non-coordinated scenarios. \textit{We define the vehicle distance traveled as the sum of truck path distance and drone flight distance}, noting that drones incur no energy cost while on a truck. For simplicity, we will use this term henceforth, acknowledging some terminological imprecision. Our approach computes paths for all scenarios within a maximum of $5$ minutes on standard hardware. We anticipate that our method could be foundational in more intricate problem settings, where optimal task allocation to agents (i.e., delivery locations) and task execution sequencing are required. For example, similar to our previous work~\cite{choudhury2021efficient}, we might employ a bi-level strategy where the upper level assigns jobs to agents and the lower-level planner—our coordinated MAPF solver—executes these assignments in a receding-horizon manner. \vspace{5pt} \noindent\textbf{Layout.} In~\Cref{sec:related}, we review foundational approaches and cutting-edge applications related to our work. In~\Cref{sec:problem}, we introduce the necessary notation and definitions and describe our coordinated MAPF problem setting. \Cref{sec:approach} details our two-stage coordinated MAPF approach, and our extensive experimental results are discussed in~\Cref{sec:results}. We conclude by summarizing our contributions and suggesting future research directions in~\Cref{sec:conclusion}.
