text: In server systems, the Quality of Service (QoS) for a job is typically quantified by its response time, defined as the duration from job release to its completion. In the context of job scheduling, this metric is also known as the flow time. For any given schedule $\mathcal{S}$, let $c_i(\mathcal{S})$ represent the completion time of job $J_i$ under $\mathcal{S}$, and $r_i$ be the release time of $J_i$. Consequently, the flow time of job $J_i$ under $\mathcal{S}$, noted as $f_i(\mathcal{S})$, is expressed as \[ f_i(\mathcal{S}) = c_i(\mathcal{S}) - r_i. \] Two primary QoS objectives in server systems are the average flow time, corresponding to the $\ell_1$ norm, and the maximum flow time, or the $\ell_{\infty}$ norm. It is well-documented that the Shortest Remaining Processing Time (SRPT) algorithm, which minimizes the average flow time, can result in extended and unfair flow times for certain jobs, leading to job starvation. Conversely, the First-Come-First-Served (FCFS) strategy minimizes the maximum flow time~\cite{10.5555/314613.314715} but can adversely affect the average flow time. \begin{example} In Fig.~\ref{fig: ex1}, jobs $J_1$ and $J_2$ are released at time 1, each requiring 2 units of processing time. All subsequent jobs $J_i$ are released at time $i$ and have unit processing times. Assuming SRPT is employed and $J_1$ is prioritized, $J_2$ experiences starvation as it waits for the completion of all other jobs. Under FCFS, however, each job's flow time is merely $O(1)$. \end{example} \begin{example} Refer to Fig.~\ref{fig: ex2}. Unlike Fig.~\ref{fig: ex1}, the processing times for $J_1$ and $J_2$ in Fig.~\ref{fig: ex2} are increased to $n$. In the FCFS scheme, each job's flow time becomes $\Theta(n)$, leading to an average flow time of $\Theta(n)$. Conversely, SRPT maintains an average flow time of only $O(1)$. \end{example} To balance the $\ell_1$ and $\ell_{\infty}$ norms of flow time, the standard approach involves minimizing the $\ell_2$ norm of flow time~\cite{doi:10.1137/090772228,10.1145/2755573.2755581}. Specifically, the $\ell_2$ norm of flow time under schedule $\mathcal{S}$ is given by \[ \sqrt{f_1(\mathcal{S})^2 + f_2(\mathcal{S})^2 + \cdots + f_n(\mathcal{S})^2}, \] where $n$ denotes the total number of jobs. This paper focuses on minimizing the $\ell_2$ norm of flow time in an online setting on a single machine. For the online problem of minimizing the $\ell_2$ norm of flow time, existing analyses have primarily focused on standard algorithms like SRPT, Shortest Job First (SJF), Shortest Elapsed Time First (SETF), and Round Robin (RR), assuming the machine operates at an enhanced speed~\cite{doi:10.1137/090772228,10.1145/2755573.2755581}. However, SRPT, SJF, and SETF can lead to job starvation, while FCFS and RR may compromise the average flow time. Such limitations negatively impact the $\ell_2$ norm of flow time (refer to Appendix~\ref{sec: cr}). The scenarios depicted in Figs.~\ref{fig: ex1} and \ref{fig: ex2} illustrate that both FCFS and SRPT are $\Omega(n^{1/2})$-competitive in minimizing the $\ell_2$ norm of flow time. In this paper, we propose using FCFS to alleviate the starvation issue inherent in SRPT. Our algorithm initially adheres to SRPT principles. However, if a job remains in the system for an extended period and its remaining processing time is sufficiently small, it becomes a starving job. Specifically, a job $J_i$ is considered starving at time $t$ if \[ \frac{t-r_i}{\text{remaining processing time of } J_i} \geq \theta, \] where $\theta$ is the \textit{starvation threshold}. When jobs are identified as starving, the algorithm prioritizes processing the first job that reached starvation. We denote the algorithm with a starvation threshold set to $\theta$ as $BAL(\theta)$. text: Over the past few decades, Simultaneous Localization and Mapping (SLAM) has emerged as a pivotal research area in robotics and computer vision~\cite{cadena2016past,thrun2007simultaneous}. This domain focuses on determining a robot's position in real-time using onboard sensory data such as LiDAR (Light Detection and Ranging) sensors, cameras, and inertial measurement units (IMU). SLAM proves particularly advantageous in environments where GPS signals are unreliable, including indoor, urban, and underwater settings. Consequently, it has become a critical component in augmented and virtual reality (AR/VR)~\cite{grasa2013visual}, autonomous vehicles~\cite{bresson2017simultaneous}, and robotics applications where GPS is unavailable~\cite{weiss2011monocular}. Among the various SLAM systems, visual SLAM~\cite{fuentes2015visual} garners significant attention due to the low cost and energy efficiency of cameras compared to active sensors like sonar or LiDAR. This energy efficiency is especially beneficial for autonomous mobile robots operating outdoors over extended periods. Visual SLAM techniques are generally categorized into \emph{feature-based} and \emph{direct} methods. Feature-based approaches~\cite{klein2007parallel, mur2015orb} involve detecting and matching features across frames and estimating camera motion by minimizing reprojection errors. In contrast, direct methods~\cite{engel2014lsd, engel2017direct} determine camera motion by minimizing photometric errors, bypassing the need for feature correspondences. Direct methods often exhibit superior accuracy and robustness in environments with poor or repetitive textures~\cite{forster2016svo}. Given the computational intensity of feature detection and matching, sparse direct methods can achieve higher processing speeds, such as $\geq300$ FPS in SVO~\cite{forster2016svo}. Visual SLAM systems are further divided into monocular and multi-camera systems. While monocular systems~\cite{klein2007parallel,engel2014lsd,mur2015orb,engel2017direct} cannot determine the absolute \textit{scale} of the environment, multi-camera systems can, often delivering improved accuracy and robustness. Stereo systems~\cite{mur2017orb,engel2015large,wang2017stereo} are particularly favored for their simplicity and availability. Most contemporary stereo visual systems address the scale problem using the conventional \textit{stereo matching} algorithm~\cite{hartley2003multiple}, which presents two primary challenges. First, determining stereo correspondences by searching along epipolar lines is computationally demanding. Second, selecting the correct match becomes difficult when textures are repetitive, such as in grassy or sandy landscapes. In~\cite{mo2019extending}, we address these issues by projecting 3D points from a monocular system into a second camera, resolving scale through photometric error minimization. This direct \textit{scale optimization} is shown to be both computationally efficient and more resilient to repetitive visual textures. Despite obtaining metric scale, the global camera pose tends to drift from the ground truth over time, as it is computed by incrementally accumulating relative motions. \textit{Loop closure} introduces non-local constraints to globally optimize poses, mitigating this drift. The traditional bag-of-words (BoW) method detects loop closures by matching current view features with historical ones. However, BoW is unsuitable for direct SLAM systems that do not extract feature descriptors. We propose a \emph{LiDAR descriptor-based} place recognition technique~\cite{mo2020fast} for urban driving, assuming the vehicle moves forward, allowing us to accumulate 3D points from stereo direct SLAM to simulate LiDAR scans. These are then described using a LiDAR descriptor for efficient place recognition, enhancing loop closure detection accuracy and robustness. This paper presents a comprehensive integration of scale optimization and LiDAR descriptor-based place recognition into a fully-direct stereo SLAM system, named DSV-SLAM. We provide an open-source release at {{\tt \url{https://github.com/IRVLab/direct_stereo_slam}}}. Through extensive experimentation, we validate its state-of-the-art accuracy, computational efficiency, and robustness in visually challenging environments. DSV-SLAM exemplifies the feasibility of a complete SLAM system without feature detection or matching. It employs Direct Sparse Odometry (DSO)~\cite{engel2017direct} for tracking camera poses and estimating 3D points, which is then extended to an accurate and efficient stereo visual odometry (VO) through scale optimization~\cite{mo2019extending}. Following this, the LiDAR descriptor-based place recognition method~\cite{mo2020fast} is utilized for effective loop closure detection. Potential loop closures' relative poses are estimated by direct alignment and optionally refined using the Iterative Closest Point (ICP) method~\cite{besl1992method}. A pose graph is then constructed and optimized to enhance global SLAM accuracy. Figure~\ref{fig:kitti00} depicts the estimated trajectory and environment reconstruction by DSV-SLAM on sequence $00$ of the KITTI dataset~\cite{geiger2012we}.

text: The rapid advancement of Artificial Intelligence (AI) technologies has significantly influenced structural engineering, mirroring trends in various other fields. Recent years have witnessed a notable rise in the application of AI methods within this domain. Numerous studies have leveraged Machine Learning (ML) models to forecast structural responses, assess fragility parameters, and determine performance limit states for structures such as steel and concrete moment frames, steel braced frames, and reinforced concrete walls \cite{ML1, ML2}. Additional research has utilized ML models to derive structural model parameters, like shear strength and drift capacity, from experimental data \cite{ML4, ML5}. In the realm of image-based structural health monitoring, a substantial body of work has focused on ML-driven computer vision techniques for the automatic detection of structural damage from images \cite{ML7, ML8}. Furthermore, some studies have concentrated on AI-driven damage detection, localization, and classification using sensors positioned on structures \cite{ML10, ML11}. Natural disasters, including earthquakes, tsunamis, and hurricanes, pose significant risks to human life and infrastructure, often resulting in fatalities, injuries, and damage to buildings. Conducting post-hazard reconnaissance is crucial for improving our understanding of how structures perform during such events, accelerating recovery efforts, and making informed decisions regarding both current and future hazards. While ML-based approaches have been applied in the context of natural hazard reconnaissance, the exploration of natural language processing (NLP) techniques remains relatively limited. NLP has the potential to greatly enhance the efficiency and precision of post-hazard evaluations. Among the few studies in this area, \citet{ML13} utilized a long short-term memory (LSTM) model to classify building damage based on text descriptions, categorizing them according to the ATC-20's green, yellow, and red tagging system. Additionally, social media platforms, such as Twitter, have been used in some studies to train ML algorithms for analyzing eyewitness accounts during disasters \cite{twitter1} and for identifying patterns in social media activity during such events \cite{twitter2}. This paper explores two NLP applications within the context of earthquake reconnaissance. The first application involves the automatic generation of reconnaissance reports, which are crucial for each field investigation. Automated report generation aims to reduce the time required to produce reports while enhancing their accuracy and comprehensiveness by providing access to numerous resources that might otherwise be overlooked. The second application focuses on utilizing social media and crowd-sourcing to gather information related to earthquake impacts and resilience, such as recovery time, which is challenging to obtain through other means. Given the novelty of this AI application area, the preliminary study presented herein is anticipated to pave the way for advancements in this field. The paper is structured as follows: Section \ref{sec:data} details the automatic data collection approach employed for both applications. Sections \ref{sec:briefing} and \ref{sec:social-media} discuss the methodologies and applications of automatic report generation and recovery time estimation, respectively. The final section provides concluding remarks and outlines future research directions.

text: The pursuit of developing machine learning models that are both reliable and safe in practical applications remains a significant challenge. Beyond excelling on the training distribution, models in deployment must be robust against distributional changes, maintain consistency in their predictions, withstand adversarial attacks, provide well-calibrated uncertainty estimates, and effectively identify anomalous inputs. While numerous studies have addressed these issues in isolation \cite{madry, hendrycks2019robustness, guo2017calibration, emmott2015meta}, they collectively contribute to the broader field of ML Safety \cite{hendrycks2021unsolved}. Thus, the aforementioned characteristics serve as critical safety measures. In an ideal scenario, models deployed in real-world environments would excel across multiple safety measures. However, existing research indicates that enhancing certain desired properties often compromises others. For example, adversarial training enhances adversarial robustness but simultaneously reduces classification accuracy \cite{tsipras2018robustness}. Likewise, ensuring consistent predictions on out-of-distribution (OOD) inputs appears to conflict with the improved detection of such inputs, as recent studies suggest \cite{empiricalpaper}. This observation prompts the inquiry into whether a single model can simultaneously enhance all safety measures. Traditional augmentation strategies have focused on generating images that differ in form (e.g., translations) or exhibit higher entropy (e.g., additive Gaussian noise). We propose that a less explored yet crucial dimension is the creation of images with increased complexity. Unlike entropy or descriptive difficulty, which peak with purely noisy distributions, structural complexity is often measured by the level of organization \cite{lloyd2001measures}. Fractals, a classic example of structurally complex objects, have recently shown promise in pretraining image classifiers \cite{kataoka2020pre, Nakashima2021CanVT}. This raises the intriguing possibility of utilizing structural complexity sources to enhance safety through data augmentation. We demonstrate that Pareto improvements are achievable with \textsc{PixMix}, a straightforward yet powerful data processing approach that utilizes images with intricate structures to significantly enhance all current safety measures. \textsc{PixMix} introduces a novel data processing pipeline incorporating structurally complex "dreamlike" images, including fractals and feature visualizations. Our findings indicate that feature visualizations serve as an effective complexity source, extending their utility beyond mere interpretability. Through comprehensive experimentation, we establish that \textsc{PixMix} delivers notable improvements across a wide spectrum of existing safety measures, surpassing many prior methods. The code is accessible at \href{https://github.com/andyzoujm/pixmix}{\texttt{github.com/andyzoujm/pixmix}}.

text: Deep convolutional networks have revolutionized object recognition tasks, such as detection and segmentation, achieving remarkable advancements over the past decade~\cite{he2016deep, chen2017deeplab, long2015fully}. The prevalent approach adheres to the "backbone with head" framework~\cite{he2017mask, chen2019hybrid, lin2017focal, tian2019fcos}, where a backbone network~\cite{he2016deep}, pretrained on ImageNet, extracts features from images. These features are subsequently processed by the head network to generate predictions for various tasks like classification, box regression, and mask segmentation. In both image and video instance segmentation~\cite{he2017mask, huang2019mask, yang2019video, cao2020sipmask}, as well as object detection~\cite{lin2017focal, tian2019fcos}, the head network typically utilizes a similar design. Specifically, it often employs four consecutive $3\times3$ convolutions to refine coarse instance features (refer to Fig.~\ref{fig1}(a)) before making final predictions. This explicit refinement strategy expands the receptive field and enhances semantic understanding. However, merely stacking independent convolutions has its drawbacks. The effective receptive field is often smaller than the theoretical one, and this approach can lose original instance signals, leading to performance degradation and increased parameter load as the number of convolutions grows. This poses a question: can these stacked $3\times3$ convolutions be replaced with a lightweight module without sacrificing performance? A straightforward approach is to implement weight-sharing across the four convolutions (see Fig.~\ref{fig1}(b)). Through empirical comparison, we observe that the commonly used independent $3\times3$ convolutions in the head network are not essential. The weight-sharing design achieves comparable performance with fewer parameters. To mitigate performance degradation in weight-sharing networks, integrating shortcut connections from ResNet~\cite{he2016deep} is beneficial (see Fig.~\ref{fig1}(c)). These shortcuts facilitate smooth gradient propagation and help retain original instance features, thus enhancing overall segmentation performance. However, the weight-sharing approach still faces limitations due to restricted receptive fields. This leads us to explore a novel direction: \textit{What if instance features are refined through a recursive network with infinite stacked blocks?} By infinitely stacking weight-sharing blocks, we find that the network's output converges to an equilibrium state as block numbers increase, represented by: \begin{eqnarray} H^{\ast}=F_{\theta}(H^{\ast};X), \end{eqnarray} where $F_{\theta}$ denotes the nonlinear transformation with parameters $\theta$, and $H^{\ast}$ and $X$ are the equilibrium and original coarse instance features, respectively. Drawing inspiration from DEQ~\cite{bai2019deep, bai2020multiscale}, we propose implicit feature refinement (IFR) to enhance feature representation by simulating an infinite-depth network, using the transformation $F_{\theta}$ to construct the implicit model. According to Eq.~\ref{eq1}, refining instance features is treated as a fixed-point iteration problem. For the explicit transformation $F_{\theta}$, a single residual block with dual residual connections is employed to minimize mask head parameters (see Fig.~\ref{fig1}(d)). In forward computation, black-box Root-Find solvers (\textit{e.g.}, Broyden method~\cite{bai2020multiscale}) are used to find the root $H^{\ast}$ of the equilibrium equation in Eq.~\ref{eq1}. During back-propagation, gradients are derived from the solved equilibrium feature. Unlike explicitly stacked convolutions, IFR offers several advantages: 1) It mimics an infinite-depth refinement network with only the parameters of a single residual block; 2) It generates equilibrium instance features with a large receptive field, beneficial for segmentation tasks. Notably, IFR can be seamlessly integrated into the head network of most image/video segmentation frameworks, applicable to both two-stage and one-stage methods. Extensive experiments on the COCO benchmark~\cite{lin2014microsoft} reveal that IFR significantly enhances most image instance segmentation frameworks. For instance, it boosts the segmentation AP by 1.0\% on Mask R-CNN~\cite{he2017mask} with a ResNet-50-FPN backbone. Additionally, it demonstrates robustness and flexibility in video instance segmentation on the YouTube-VIS~\cite{yang2019video} benchmark, yielding substantial improvements in state-of-the-art frameworks. It is also adaptable to various one-stage object detectors with minimal adjustments. Our main contributions are summarized as follows: \begin{itemize} \item Conducted empirical studies to assess the impact of multiple stacked convolutions on instance feature refinement. \item Proposed implicit feature refinement (IFR), which requires only a residual block's parameters, to generate high-level equilibrium instance features with a global receptive field through fixed-point iteration. \item Introduced a double residual network to prevent performance degradation and ensure smooth gradient propagation. \item Established IFR as a versatile plug-and-play module, easily extendable to most instance segmentation frameworks, serving as a robust alternative to explicitly stacked convolutions in the head network. \end{itemize}

text: Recent advancements in machine learning have led to remarkable performance in computer vision tasks by training models exclusively on images. Building on these achievements to enhance 3D object comprehension holds significant promise for a broader spectrum of applications, including augmented reality, robotics, autonomous systems, and image retrieval. However, mastering 3D object understanding remains challenging due to the scarcity of extensive real-world datasets, unlike the abundance available for 2D tasks, such as ImageNet~\cite{Deng:2009jn}, COCO~\cite{Lin:2014vm}, and Open Images~\cite{Kuznetsova:2020ff}. To support ongoing progress in 3D object understanding, there is a pressing need for the dissemination of object-centric video datasets. These datasets, which capture the 3D structure of objects more effectively and align with the data formats commonly used in downstream vision tasks (like video or camera streams), are crucial for training and evaluating machine learning models. This object-centric perspective aligns with human perception; for instance, when a child learns the shape of a chair, they naturally explore it from various angles to gather information. As Gibson noted, "We must also move in order to perceive"~\cite{Gibson:1979}\cite{Zamir:2018}. We introduce the Objectron dataset, a collection of brief, object-centric video clips that showcase a wide array of common objects from multiple perspectives. Each clip is supplemented with augmented reality (AR) session metadata, which includes camera poses, sparse point-clouds, and surface planes. Additionally, the dataset provides manually annotated 3D bounding boxes for each object, detailing the object’s position, orientation, and size. Comprising $14,819$ annotated video clips and $4M$ annotated images, the dataset was gathered from a geographically diverse sample spanning ten countries across five continents. Figure~\ref{fig:example-seq} presents an example video from our dataset. The Objectron dataset offers several advantages over existing datasets: \begin{itemize} \item The videos provide multiple perspectives of the same object, facilitating a wide range of applications beyond 3D object detection, such as multi-view geometric understanding, view synthesis, and 3D shape reconstruction. \item The inclusion of a 3D bounding box throughout the video ensures temporal consistency, supporting 3D tracking applications. \item Our dataset is collected in natural settings, enhancing its applicability to real-world scenarios, unlike datasets obtained in controlled environments~\cite{Hinterstoisser:2012ik}\cite{Calli:2017cd}. \item Thanks to precise on-device AR tracking, each instance's translation and size are recorded in metric scale, and sparse point clouds in 3D are provided, enabling sparse depth estimation techniques. The images are calibrated, and camera parameters are available, allowing for accurate recovery of the object's true scale. \item Our annotations are both dense and continuous, contrasting with previous work~\cite{Savarese:2007by} where viewpoints were discretized into bins. \item Each object category includes hundreds of instances, collected from various locations, across different countries, and under diverse lighting conditions. \end{itemize} We have performed experiments on 3D object detection tasks using our dataset. A novel method was proposed to accurately calculate the 3D IoU of oriented 3D bounding boxes, providing a baseline for future research endeavors.

text: Since its inception in 1972, \gls{ct} has rapidly become indispensable for various applications such as industrial inspection~\cite{de2014industrial}, medical diagnostics~\cite{maier2018medical}, and material sciences~\cite{withers2007x}. As a quintessential example of computational imaging, \gls{ct} involves encoding a physical quantity into measured data via an image formation model, which is subsequently reconstructed by inverting this model. In X-ray \gls{ct}, the task involves reconstructing an image of the attenuation coefficient from projections obtained through circular acquisition. This process, under orthographic projection, is mathematically represented by the Radon transform. The discretized measurements of the Radon transform are referred to as sinograms, and their inversion is a well-explored problem. Among the various techniques, the direct inversion method known as \gls{fbp} provides a closed-form solution~\cite{maier2018medical}. For accurate reconstruction using \gls{fbp}, adherence to the Crowther-criterion~\cite{crowther1970reconstruction}, which is derived from the Shannon-Nyquist sampling theorem, is essential. Failure to meet this criterion results in aliasing artifacts, commonly manifesting as streaks that significantly degrade diagnostic quality. This scenario is known as \gls{svct} and is prevalent in practical situations, particularly when addressing challenges such as motion compensation~\cite{enjilela2019cubic} or dose reduction~\cite{gao2014low,yu2009radiation}. To mitigate the ill-posed nature of \gls{svct}, several strategies have been developed that integrate prior knowledge into the reconstruction process. Traditional approaches involve \gls{ir}, which optimizes a data-fidelity term in conjunction with suitable priors~\cite{kudo2013image,zhu2013improved,vandeghinste2011split}. A widely used prior is \gls{tv}, which assumes the object being imaged is piece-wise constant~\cite{sidky2008image}. In recent years, learning-based reconstruction methods have gained significant traction~\cite{adler2017solving}. Notable examples include \gls{cnn}-based models designed to eliminate reconstruction artifacts~\cite{kofler2018u} and unrolled networks that emulate the data-fidelity-driven \gls{ir}~\cite{ongie2020deep}. An alternative perspective considers \gls{svct} as akin to a super-resolution or inpainting problem, where missing information is interpolated between sparse projections. In this context, a sparse-view sinogram can be approached through either inpainting or 1D super-resolution. This task is more constrained than the 2D upsampling of natural images~\cite{katsaggelos2007super}, as sinogram data exhibit smooth variations along the angular dimension~\cite{helgason}. Other tomographic challenges with similar formulations include metal artifact removal and limited angle tomography, as illustrated in Fig.~\ref{fig:superres_vs_inpainting}. Despite its potential, sinogram inpainting has not attracted as much attention as iterative methods, largely due to the difficulty of capturing the complex representations inherent in sinograms~\cite{li2012strategy,tovey2019directional,kostler2006adaptive}. However, the rapid advancements in deep learning now make it feasible to efficiently capture low-dimensional representations in various image domains. These technological strides inspire us to explore learning-based super-resolution as a solution for \gls{svct}. We propose that processing in the measurement domain is preferable to post-reconstruction processing. The core concept is depicted in Fig.~\ref{fig:abstract}. Our primary contributions are summarized as follows: \begin{itemize} \item We introduce a novel two-step reconstruction strategy that operates in both the measurement and image domains, ensuring superior detail preservation compared to single-step networks. \item We develop a domain-specific, lightweight perceptual loss that surpasses the VGG-based perceptual loss~\cite{johnson2016perceptual} in terms of accuracy, memory, and computational efficiency. \item We design loss functions and submodules specifically for tasks in the sinogram domain, and conduct an extensive ablation study to evaluate the effectiveness of each component. \item We demonstrate the ability to achieve accurate reconstructions at high compression ratios, with a notable performance improvement exceeding $4$ dB in PSNR compared to existing state-of-the-art methods. \end{itemize}

text: Swarm intelligence provides insights into the collective behaviors exhibited by autonomous entities following simple rules, such as ants, boids, and particles. This concept has been extended to groups of robots, leading to the field of swarm robotics, which has garnered significant interest over the past two decades. Within these systems, each autonomous unit is referred to as a robot, module, agent, process, or sensor. Various swarm robotic systems have been explored, including the \emph{autonomous mobile robot system}~\cite{SY99}, the \emph{population protocol model}~\cite{AADFP04}, \emph{programmable particles}~\cite{DDGRSS14}, \emph{Kilobot}~\cite{RCN14}, and \emph{3D Catoms}~\cite{TPB19}. Dumitrescu et al. introduced the \emph{metamorphic robotic system} (MRS), comprising a collection of \emph{modules} arranged on an infinite 2D square grid~\cite{DSY04a,DSY04b}. These modules are \emph{anonymous}, meaning they cannot be distinguished from one another. They are also \emph{autonomous} and \emph{uniform}, with each module independently determining its movements using a shared algorithm. Furthermore, they are \emph{oblivious}, lacking memory of past actions. Consequently, each module makes decisions based on its observations of neighboring modules. Modules can \emph{slide} to adjacent cells and \emph{rotate} by $90$ degrees around a cell. They must maintain \emph{connectivity}, defined by the side-adjacency of occupied cells. The authors explored \emph{reconfiguration} of the MRS, which involves transitioning from an initial shape to a specified final shape~\cite{DSY04a}. They demonstrated that any horizontally convex connected initial shape of an MRS can be transformed into any convex final shape via a straight chain shape. Subsequently, Dumitrescu and Pach proved that any connected initial shape can be reconfigured into any connected final shape through a straight chain shape~\cite{DP06}. This implies the MRS possesses "universal reconfiguration" capabilities. Reconfiguration enables dynamic behavior within the MRS. Dumitrescu et al. illustrated that the MRS can progress by continuously reconfiguring~\cite{DSY04b}, achieving the most efficient \emph{locomotion}. Doi et al. highlighted that oblivious modules can utilize the MRS's shape as a form of global memory, allowing the MRS to tackle more complex problems as the number of modules increases. They investigated \emph{search} on a finite 2D square grid, requiring the MRS to locate a target cell within a finite rectangular \emph{field}~\cite{DYKY18}. Each module lacks prior knowledge of the target cell's location or the MRS's initial configuration. They demonstrated that the MRS can discover the target cell by methodically sweeping each row of the field without any prior information. Specifically, if the modules share an understanding of cardinal directions (i.e., north, south, east, west), three modules are both necessary and sufficient; otherwise, five modules are required. Nakamura et al. examined the \emph{evacuation} of the MRS from a finite rectangular field on the 2D square grid~\cite{NSY20}. A hole (consisting of two side-adjacent cells) is located on the field's boundary, and the MRS must exit through it from any starting position and shape. They found that two modules suffice when the modules agree on cardinal directions, whereas four modules are needed otherwise. In this study, we explore the impact of shared knowledge on the MRS's search capabilities within a 3D cubic grid. We consider three scenarios: $(i)$ modules outfitted with a common \emph{compass} (i.e., consensus on the orientation of $x$, $y$, and $z$ axes), $(ii)$ modules with a common vertical axis (i.e., agreement on the $z$ axis orientation), and $(iii)$ modules without a common compass (i.e., no directional consensus). We establish that three modules suffice when equipped with a common compass, whereas five modules are required without one. The necessary module counts in the 3D cubic grid mirror those in the 2D square grid~\cite{DYKY18} due to the increased state space in the 3D environment. For the scenario with a common vertical axis, four modules are both necessary and sufficient. Our findings in the 3D cubic grid reveal a gradual trade-off between the MRS's computational power and the shared knowledge among modules, a nuance not captured in previous 2D grid studies. We present search algorithms for these configurations and demonstrate necessity through analysis of the MRS's state transition graph. \noindent{\bf Related work.}~Reconfiguration in swarm robotic systems has been extensively studied for the MRS~\cite{DP06,DSY04a}, autonomous mobile robots~\cite{FYOKY15,SY99}, and programmable particles~\cite{DGRSS15,DFSVY20}. Michail et al. examined the \emph{programmable matter system}, akin to the MRS, and explored reconfiguration using rotations alone and in combination with slidings~\cite{MSS19}. They concluded that the integration of rotations and slidings ensures universal reconfiguration, whereas rotations alone do not. They also proposed an $\mathrm{O}(n^2)$-time reconfiguration algorithm utilizing both rotations and slidings. Almethen et al. investigated reconfiguration via \emph{line-pushing}, where modules can push a line of other modules~\cite{AMP20a}. They introduced an $\mathrm{O}(n \log n)$-time universal reconfiguration algorithm that does not maintain connectivity of intermediate shapes and an $\mathrm{O}(n \sqrt{n})$-time algorithm that preserves connectivity while transforming a diagonal line into a straight chain. Subsequently, the same authors demonstrated that their programmable matter system possesses universal reconfiguration capabilities and provided an $\mathrm{O}(n \sqrt{n})$-time reconfiguration algorithm, along with an $\Omega(n \log n)$ lower bound~\cite{AMP20b}.

text: Self-modifying code refers to a type of program that alters its own instructions during execution while maintaining its intended functionality. These changes can be localized, affecting only a small portion of the code, or widespread, impacting the entire codebase. They can be enduring, by modifying the copy on disk, or temporary, through techniques like monkey patching. Modifications can occur at various stages, including compile-time, link-time, post-processing, or during runtime. The code responsible for these changes might operate as a separate entity or be integrated within the target program itself. Certain self-modifying codes can be categorized into specific types, such as: \begin{enumerate} \item \textbf{Packers}: These are the most straightforward. They encapsulate the actual payload in a compressed or encrypted format. The executable content is extracted and executed entirely in memory. \item \textbf{Obfuscators}: These tools transform an executable file into another with different instructions while retaining the original behavior. The resulting binary does not incorporate any new functionalities. \item \textbf{Self-injecting codes}: These programs insert additional code into their own process or a forked child process, executing it there. This injected code may run within the main thread, effectively replacing the existing code without freeing associated resources, or it may execute in a newly spawned thread. \item \textbf{Self-debugging codes}: These programs can attach themselves as a debugger to their process or a child copy. The debugger process can then control the debuggee, including overwriting executable code. This makes dynamic debugging of such programs particularly challenging. \item \textbf{Self-healing codes}: These programs can identify patches, whether in a file or memory, and restore the original state by undoing the patch. \end{enumerate} We will examine self-debugging code in depth and introduce an alternative method that enables malware to execute in both forward (standard) and reverse (instructions processed in reverse order) modes. The malware exhibits distinct behaviors depending on the execution direction. The malicious component activates exclusively during reverse execution, allowing it to evade various analysis techniques: \begin{enumerate} \item Tools like IDA Pro, which analyze reverse-engineered assembly in a top-down manner, will not immediately detect the malicious behavior since it manifests during bottom-up execution. \item Debuggers and sandboxes typically attach to processes using similar methods as self-debugging. Consequently, if such a tool attaches to our code, the self-debugging mechanism fails to operate (since the OS permits only one debugger per process), causing the payload to execute in a top-down manner and concealing its malicious nature. \end{enumerate}

text: For a robot to effectively engage with its surroundings, it must swiftly and precisely ascertain the position and orientation of nearby robots, people, vehicles, and various static and dynamic obstacles. This requirement spans applications from drone racing~\cite{spica2018realtime} to pedestrian avoidance~\cite{badue2019selfdrivingcarsurvey}, highlighting the necessity of such estimations for the development of truly autonomous robots. Despite this, the real-time tracking of a dynamic object's six Degree of Freedom (6DoF) relative pose using onboard sensors and computing resources remains mostly unattainable with current robotic perception systems. To address this gap, we introduce \textbf{M}onocular \textbf{S}equential \textbf{L}ightweight \textbf{R}otation \textbf{A}nd \textbf{P}osition \textbf{T}racking \textbf{O}n-\textbf{R}obots (MSL-RAPTOR), a versatile and efficient perception module tailored for tracking the 6DoF relative pose of dynamic objects using solely an onboard monocular camera. MSL-RAPTOR achieves performance comparable to state-of-the-art methods that rely on additional sensors (e.g., depth) and higher computational power. Current 6DoF relative pose estimation techniques using vision are categorized into model-based, deep learning-based, and hybrid methods. Model-based techniques typically involve matching an object's view against a database of templates or visual features, which proves challenging in environments with low texture or varying conditions and is impractical without pre-existing 3D models of objects~\cite{schmidt2014dart,andriluka2010humantracking}. Deep learning techniques, such as PoseCNN~\cite{xiang2017posecnn} and LieNets~\cite{do2018lienets}, address these issues by directly estimating relative pose from images through learning from extensive training datasets. Hybrid methods integrate aspects of both deep learning and model-based strategies. For instance, BB8~\cite{rad2017bb8}, SSD-6D~\cite{kehl2017ssd}, and SingleShotPose~\cite{tekin2018ssp} (SSP) employ deep neural networks to predict 2D projections of the 3D bounding box surrounding the object, which are then used to solve the Perspective-n-Point (PnP) problem for pose estimation~\cite{lepetit2009epnp}. Another hybrid approach, NOCS~\cite{wang2019normalized}, utilizes pixel correspondences and depth data with category-level canonical representations for pose estimation. However, these deep and hybrid methods often neglect the temporal correlations across multiple frames that could enhance object tracking. In contrast, 6-PACK~\cite{wang20196sixpack} exploits temporal consistency by learning to represent objects through keypoints that are matched across frames. Despite their impressive pose estimation capabilities, these methods tend to be either too slow, computationally intensive, or reliant on excessive prior model knowledge, making them unsuitable for practical onboard relative pose perception in resource-constrained robots. These limitations are also evident in numerous pose tracking techniques developed for self-driving vehicles, where tracking systems are a crucial component~\cite{badue2019selfdrivingcarsurvey}. These techniques typically depend on advanced sensors and computational resources to deliver real-time performance and often assume planar constraints, focusing solely on land-based objects (e.g., pedestrians, other vehicles), thus operating as SE(2) trackers with 3DoF~\cite{cho2014multi, buyval2018realtime}. \textbf{Contribution.} In light of the requirements for onboard robotic perception, we present MSL-RAPTOR, which integrates the strengths of deep learning-based and model-based perception paradigms. MSL-RAPTOR processes raw image data using a dual deep neural network architecture in the front-end to generate and track an angled 2D bounding box around an object. text: Video analytics systems have achieved significant success across diverse fields, from demanding tasks like facial recognition for surveillance to mobile applications such as object detection in augmented reality (AR) environments~\cite{rohan2019convolutional, apicharttrisorn2019frugal, rao2017mobile}, and real-time applications like pedestrian and vehicle localization in autonomous driving~\cite{feng2020deep, arnold2019survey, li2019gs3d}. A fundamental capability shared by these applications is video object detection. The demand for executing such tasks on {\em mobile devices} is on the rise. Despite being equipped with mobile GPUs, these devices lack the computational power of server-class machines. However, there is a pressing need to perform video processing in (near) real-time directly on the device\footnote{For convenience, we refer to a "mobile device" simply as "device".}. This necessity arises to enhance user experiences in applications such as AR/VR games or to ensure reliable outputs from streaming videos, like pedestrian recognition in autonomous vehicles. The target is to process each frame in 33 ms, aligning with a video stream rate of 30 frames per second (FPS). Our empirical investigations reveal that current state-of-the-art (SOTA) protocols, designed for servers, exceed this latency threshold when executed on mobile platforms. For instance, the MEGA~\cite{chen2020memory} solution, recognized as a SOTA, requires 253.4 ms per frame on an NVIDIA AGX Xavier, utilizing all available computing resources. In response, a variety of efficient models and systems have been put forth to enhance performance and efficiency on mobile devices~\cite{tan2020efficientdet, sandler2018mobilenetv2, jiang2020learning, zhu2018towards, chen2018optimizing, liu2016ssd, redmon2018yolov3, zhang2018single}. \begin{comment} The majority of existing research focuses on accuracy and often relies on server-class machines or cloud infrastructures~\cite{wu2019sequence, chen2020memory, sabater2020robust, zhu2017flow, deng2019relation}. However, mobile applications frequently face constraints in energy or computational resources while still demanding strict latency guarantees. To enhance user experiences in applications like AR/VR games or ensure reliable outputs from streaming videos, such tasks must be executed in near real-time, adhering to latency requirements of 33 ms (30 FPS) or less. Despite advances in mobile GPU technology, these devices cannot match the computational power of server-class machines or cloud enterprises. In response, efficient models and systems have been developed to optimize performance on mobile devices~\cite{tan2020efficientdet, sandler2018mobilenetv2}. \end{comment} An alternative strategy to enable streaming analytics on mobile devices involves combining object detection with tracking, embodied in the "tracking-by-detection" technique~\cite{bae2014robust, muller2018trackingnet}. By alternating between multiple frames of lightweight tracking and each frame of object detection, overall performance can be accelerated. This technique offers various adaptation strategies, including choosing among detectors and trackers and determining the trigger frequency between them. Our empirical findings show that the execution time for an object tracker is significantly lower, about 10 times less, than that for an object detector. Selecting the right adaptation strategies is crucial to meet real-time requirements for energy, latency, and accuracy, particularly on mobile devices. The stringent runtime requirements of mobile devices introduce a further challenge in streaming video analytics: \textit{how to dynamically adapt to changing user requirements and available resources on the device?} To tackle this issue, recent studies have explored multi-branch solutions~\cite{fang2018nestdnn, xu2020approxdet, xu2019approxnet, lee2021benchmarking}. These solutions incorporate multiple execution kernels within a system, selecting the optimal one {\em during runtime} to meet latency demands. However, they often overlook features that manage energy consumption. Moreover, compared to recent advances in efficient convolutional neural network (CNN) architectures, there is limited research on efficient object detection solutions for embedded devices, along with the challenge of outdated feature extractors. In real-world applications, the dynamic nature of video content, available resources on mobile devices, and manual control of requirements complicate adaptive processes. The broad spectrum of energy, latency, and accuracy requirements necessitates a system capable of adapting to various scenarios. Therefore, the design must meet these prerequisites: (1) creating an execution kernel that is both energy and latency-efficient for mobile devices, (2) analyzing the energy consumption and latency performance of all execution branches on mobile devices, and (3) developing an adaptive scheduler to make runtime decisions that satisfy multiple requirements simultaneously. To our knowledge, no prior work has encompassed all these design innovations. Another overlooked aspect is how these algorithms perform under resource contention on the device. Such contention can occur due to other applications running concurrently on the same device, a common scenario given the multi-purpose nature of these devices. For instance, during video detection, another demanding task like speech recognition might also be running. No previous research has assessed the performance of the latest video object detection systems under varying resource contention on leading GPU-enabled mobile devices. In this work, we introduce {\textsc{Virtuoso}}\xspace\footnote{Like a virtuoso, known for exceptional skill, we believe our system exhibits such proficiency in configuring streaming video object detection on embedded or mobile devices.\xspace}, which is tailored for mobile devices under varying resource constraints, with additional efficiency knobs\footnote{We prefer "efficiency knobs" over "tuning knobs" as we focus on the performance metric of accuracy, normalized by latency or energy cost to achieve that accuracy, emphasizing efficient accuracy.} for energy-aware adaptation. {\textsc{Virtuoso}}\xspace selects the most efficient baseline object detectors EfficientDet~\cite{tan2020efficientdet} and SSD~\cite{liu2016ssd}, enhances them by integrating object trackers, and offers 155 execution branches by exposing 8 efficiency knobs within one system. Additionally, {\textsc{Virtuoso}}\xspace features a scheduler capable of selecting the optimal branch during runtime to meet both energy and latency requirements while maximizing accuracy. We also evaluated a total of 15 baseline models on 3 different embedded boards under 2 resource contention levels to better understand the energy, latency, and accuracy performance of the latest models for video object detection. We evaluate {\textsc{Virtuoso}}\xspace and the baselines using the ILSVRC 2015 VID datasets on 3 NVIDIA mobile GPUs of increasing computational capacity — Jetson TX2, Xavier NX, and AGX Xavier, under 2 different power modes of AGX Xavier. On each board and under each power mode, {\textsc{Virtuoso}}\xspace emerges as the best solution, automatically selecting the optimal branch to meet energy and latency requirements while maximizing accuracy performance. With the multi-branch execution kernel, {\textsc{Virtuoso}}\xspace can adapt its energy efficiency over a broad range (span of 89X) and latency over a wide range (span of 128X). Such extensive ranges of energy efficiency and latency enable the system to accommodate various runtime scenarios, optimizing the functionality of our video object detection system. Given a 1 J per frame energy requirement, {\textsc{Virtuoso}}\xspace can achieve 52.0\% accuracy, and with a 33.3 ms latency budget, it can attain 60.1\% accuracy on an AGX Xavier board. Furthermore, when energy and latency constraints are relaxed, {\textsc{Virtuoso}}\xspace can achieve 63.9\% accuracy, exceeding baseline models by more than 10\%. \begin{comment} From the benchmark results, we gained several insights, including: tracking-by-detection is the most efficient method to reduce energy consumption for video object detection; accuracy is primarily determined by the choice of object detector since the tracker relies on detection results for initialization; the majority of energy consumption on mobile devices is attributed to the GPU module. \end{comment} In this paper, our contributions are as follows. \vspace{-3pt} \begin{enumerate}[leftmargin=1em] \item We introduce {\textsc{Virtuoso}}\xspace, an advanced, energy-efficient, and adaptive video object detection system for mobile devices. {\textsc{Virtuoso}}\xspace dynamically adjusts its runtime configurations based on user requirements. Our runtime scheduler addresses the optimization problem for accuracy at any energy and latency level, ensuring Pareto optimal performance on resource-constrained devices. We are the only adaptive model conducting this 3D (energy-latency-accuracy) tuning while managing resource contention. \item {\textsc{Virtuoso}}\xspace designs an efficient multi-branch execution kernel featuring 8 distinct efficiency knobs, optimized for both energy efficiency and latency on mobile devices. This flexibility allows {\textsc{Virtuoso}}\xspace to adapt to a wider range of available resources, offering an 89X energy adaptation space when baseline models cannot, and a 4.5X larger latency adaptation space than the baseline FastAdapt~\cite{lee2021benchmarking}. {\textsc{Virtuoso}}\xspace achieves up to 97\% lower energy consumption and executes up to 50 times faster compared to using the object detection kernel alone. \item We assess our proposed systems and 15 baselines (including 3 recent video object detection solutions and our enhanced FRCNN~\cite{ren2015faster}, YOLO~\cite{redmon2018yolov3}, SSD~\cite{liu2016ssd}, and EfficientDet~\cite{tan2020efficientdet} for both energy and latency on embedded devices) on 3 NVIDIA Jetson embedded devices under different GPU resource availability, energy efficiency constraints, and latency constraints. Additionally, we examine and evaluate the impact of different device power modes, which has not been previously explored. Different power modes facilitate various configurations with different CPU frequencies and numbers of CPU cores online. We demonstrate accuracy superiority over baselines under any efficiency constraint. \end{enumerate} The remainder of the paper is organized as follows. Section~\ref{sec:tech} presents our overall design for {\textsc{Virtuoso}}\xspace and its key components, such as the dynamic scheduler and efficiency knobs for handling various user requirements for latency or energy consumption. In Section~\ref{sec:implementations}, we detail the multi-branch kernel design and implementation of {\textsc{Virtuoso}}\xspace, along with different runtime environments for evaluation. Section~\ref{sec:evaluation} comprises two parts: first, we evaluate the overall performance of {\textsc{Virtuoso}}\xspace, and then we compare {\textsc{Virtuoso}}\xspace and its multi-branch kernels against other baselines.

In addition, the recent development of efficient convolutional neural network (CNN) architectures for embedded devices, and the difficulty of using the features of existing architectures, make it difficult to build an efficient object-detection solution for embedded devices. The wide range of energy, latency, and accuracy requirements requires a system that can adapt to different situations. The design must therefore satisfy the following prerequisites: a kernel which is both energy and latency efficient on mobile devices; an analysis of the energy consumption and latency of all execution branches on mobile devices; and an adaptive scheduler which, during run-time, makes decisions satisfying both requirements. To our knowledge, no work has hitherto embodied all these innovations. An ignored aspect of these algorithms is their behavior under resource contention on the device. A prior study has not yet analyzed the performance of the most recent object detection systems in a varying number of resources on the leading mobile devices equipped with a GPU. This resource competition may occur because other applications are simultaneously running on the same device, which is a common occurrence in multi-use devices. For example, during the detection of an object, another demanding task such as speech recognition can be performed. We present a system called 'Virtuoso' which selects the two most efficient object detectors, EfficientDet and SSD, and combines them with object trackers, to provide 155 permutations, by exposing eight efficiency knobs. It is based on a scheduler that can choose at runtime the best combination of resources, so as to minimize the energy cost and the delay, while achieving the best accuracy. It was tested on the ILSVRC-VID dataset, on three mobile platforms from NVIDIA with increasing performance: the Jetson TX2, the Xavier NX and the AGX Xavier, with two power modes for the latter. The multi-branch kernel of the Virtuoso X-space system makes it possible to vary the energy efficiency over a wide range (89x) and the latency over a wide range (32x). This wide range of energy efficiency and latency allows the system to accommodate various runtime situations, thus enhancing the performance of our visual object detection system. We also evaluated fifteen other models on three boards and two levels of resource contention to understand the energy, latency, and accuracy of the latest models for object detection in videos. We present Virtuoso, a new, energy-efficient and adaptable object detection system for mobile devices. For each scene and each power mode, Virtuoso X-space emerges as the best solution, as it automatically selects the best branch to match the energy and latency requirements, while maintaining accuracy of the model. From these results, we infer that the most efficient way to reduce energy consumption when object tracking is to use a tracker that is based on the results of a detection since trackers depend on the results of the object tracker to initialize themselves. text: In today's digital age, information is produced in various formats, such as text, images, audio, and video. Consequently, a query in one format, like text, might find its corresponding information in another format, such as an image. To address these diverse search needs, Cross-modal Information Retrieval (IR) algorithms are being developed. \vspace{2mm} \noindent {\bf Need for Zero-shot Information Retrieval (ZSIR):} In a typical IR task, parameters are learned for different query classes during the train-test process. Traditional cross-modal retrieval techniques necessitate training data for all query classes to develop the retrieval models. However, these techniques often fail when dealing with queries from {\it new} or {\it unseen} classes. Consider a scenario where a retrieval model is trained on images and textual descriptions of vehicles like `car', `motorbike', and `aeroplane'. If presented with a query for `bus', the model should retrieve relevant images and descriptions of buses, even though it hasn't been trained on that class. This scenario exemplifies the ``zero-shot'' framework~\cite{Larochelle:2008:ZLN:1620163.1620172,ZeroShotNIPS2009,ZeroShotNorouzi2013}, which aims to identify unseen classes based on limited training data. Such challenges are pertinent in contemporary search systems, where new phenomena, hashtags, and topics emerge frequently. Thus, integrating the zero-shot paradigm into an IR framework is crucial, diverging from traditional IR evaluations. Zero-shot cross-media retrieval seeks to facilitate retrieval across different formats (e.g., retrieving images in response to a text query) without any class overlap between training and testing datasets. Zero-Shot IR (ZSIR) is particularly demanding as it requires models to manage both the semantic discrepancies between seen and unseen query classes and the diverse data characteristics across formats. \vspace{2mm} \noindent {\bf Present work and differences with prior works:} Although substantial work exists on multimodal and cross-modal retrieval~\cite{cross-modal-ir-survey}, only a handful of studies have explored cross-modal IR within a zero-shot framework~\cite{scottreed-cvpr16,ZSL_GAN_cvpr2018,ijcai2018-92,8643797,AgNet-TNNLS2019, CZHash-ICDM2020} (refer to Section~\ref{sec:related} and Section~\ref{sub:baselines} for details). Some of these studies depend on additional class label information, such as semantic similarity measures, which may not always be accessible. In this paper, we introduce a novel model for zero-shot cross-modal IR utilizing Conditional Generative Adversarial Networks (GANs)~\cite{mirza-conditional14}, designed to retrieve {\it images} corresponding to a given {\it textual} query. Our model, termed {\bf \texttt{ZSCRGAN}{}} (Zero-Shot Cross-modal Retrieval GAN), operates solely on textual data for retrieval, eliminating the need for extra class label information. While previous ZSIR models~\cite{ZSL_GAN_cvpr2018,ijcai2018-92,8643797} also employ GANs, our model's primary innovations include: (1)~Introducing the \textbf{use of wrong classes} to guide the generator in creating features distinct to a particular class by differentiating it from others. (2)~Developing a \textbf{Common Space Embedding Mapper (CSEM)} that aligns both image and text embeddings into a shared space for retrieval. {\it This is a crucial step enabling our model to perform retrieval without relying on additional semantic class label information.} (3)~Proposing an {\bf Expectation-Maximization (E-M) based approach} to train the retrieval model efficiently, alternating between training the GAN and the CSEM. This E-M framework demonstrates superior retrieval performance compared to joint training of the GAN and CSEM. We conduct experiments on several benchmark datasets for zero-shot retrieval, including (1)~the Caltech-UCSD Birds dataset, (2)~the Oxford Flowers-102 dataset, (3)~the North America Birds (NAB) dataset, (4)~the Wikipedia dataset, and (5)~the Animals With Attribute (AWA) dataset. Our \texttt{ZSCRGAN}{} consistently surpasses a range of robust baselines across all datasets, including ZSIR models~\cite{scottreed-cvpr16,8643797,ZSL_GAN_cvpr2018}, cutting-edge Zero-Shot classification models~\cite{verma-cvpr18,xian2018feature_gen} adapted for Text-to-Image retrieval, and leading Zero-Shot Hashing models~\cite{AgNet-TNNLS2019, CZHash-ICDM2020,DCMH-AAAI17}. Additionally, our model is versatile, capable of handling not only textual queries but also other query types like attribute vectors, as shown in its application to the AWA dataset. We have made the \texttt{ZSCRGAN}{} implementation publicly accessible at \url{https://github.com/ranarag/ZSCRGAN}.

text: Dense retrieval systems are designed to transform queries and documents into a dense embedding space, where retrieval is executed by identifying the nearest neighbors to a query within this space~\cite{orqa, sentence-bert, dpr, ance}. The evolution of pre-trained language models~\cite{bert, lu2021less}, specialized training methodologies~\cite{dpr, ance}, and optimized nearest neighbor search techniques~\cite{faiss, scann} have significantly enhanced the performance of dense retrieval systems across various applications, such as web search~\cite{msmarco}, open domain question answering~\cite{naturalquestions}, and zero-shot information retrieval (IR)~\cite{beir}. Utilizing dense, fully-learned representations in retrieval can potentially tackle fundamental issues found in sparse retrieval systems. For instance, the problem of vocabulary mismatch might be mitigated \emph{if} embeddings can effectively encapsulate the information need underlying a query and relate it to pertinent documents. Nonetheless, extensive IR research highlights the difficulty of accurately deducing a user's search intent from brief and often ambiguous queries~\cite{croft2010search}. Even with advanced pre-trained language models, expecting an encoder to flawlessly capture the nuanced information need from limited query terms is impractical. A well-established method to enhance query comprehension in sparse retrieval systems is \emph{pseudo relevance feedback} (PRF)~\cite{croft2010search,PRF,rm12}. This method enriches the query representation by incorporating the top retrieved documents from an initial search. PRF's effectiveness is evident whether it is applied through query expansion~\cite{PRF,trec2004} or query term reweighting~\cite{bendersky2011parameterized}, making it a staple in many sparse retrieval systems. This study employs PRF information to refine query representations within dense retrieval frameworks. Using the top documents retrieved by a dense retrieval model like ANCE~\cite{ance}, we construct a PRF query encoder, ANCE-PRF. This encoder utilizes a BERT model~\cite{bert} to process both the query and PRF documents, enhancing the query representation. ANCE-PRF is trained in an end-to-end manner using relevance labels, optimizing query embeddings through the comprehensive information provided by PRF documents, while maintaining the document index from ANCE to avoid redundant index storage. In evaluations on MS MARCO and the TREC Deep Learning (DL) Track passage ranking benchmarks, ANCE-PRF consistently outperforms ANCE and several contemporary dense retrieval systems employing more complex models and training strategies~\cite{ltre,mebert}. Notably, significant improvements are observed on DL-HARD~\cite{dlhard} queries, which are curated to present complex search intents that pose challenges for neural systems. To our knowledge, ANCE-PRF ranks among the top-performing first-stage retrieval systems on the competitive MARCO passage ranking leaderboard. Our research indicates that ANCE-PRF's strengths lie in its capacity to harness beneficial information from PRF documents while filtering out irrelevant noise. The PRF encoder prioritizes terms from relevant PRF documents, allocating less attention to those from irrelevant sources. A case study reveals that the encoder focuses on PRF terms that complement query terms in representing search intents. This capability enables ANCE-PRF to develop superior query embeddings that align more closely with relevant documents, enhancing the performance of most test queries.\footnote{Our code, checkpoints, and ranking results are available at \url{https://github.com/yuhongqian/ANCE-PRF}.}

text: The ubiquity and significance of smart devices in our everyday lives have made the comprehension and operation of User Interfaces (UIs) a crucial task for Artificial Intelligence. For example, a model capable of identifying a UI component based on its description is invaluable for voice interfaces, while a model predicting the outcome of a button click can enhance page navigation. To adeptly manage a UI, models must grasp the user's objectives and intentions, as well as the methods to execute tasks within the given UI framework. Despite its importance, UI understanding remains a complex and underexplored domain. Firstly, UI understanding encompasses a variety of tasks, often spanning multiple modalities and domains, such as executing a button click via voice command or locating an icon by semantic similarity. Historically, research has focused on individual tasks in isolation. Developing separate, intricate models for each task is inefficient for deployment on devices. Additionally, models risk overfitting when task-specific data is scarce. Pre-training on extensive datasets to derive features has proven effective across numerous fields, as demonstrated by ResNet \cite{he2016deep} in computer vision and BERT \cite{devlin2018bert} in natural language processing. However, a universal feature representation for user interfaces is lacking, and the potential benefits of a pre-trained feature extraction model for diverse UI-related tasks remain uncertain. Secondly, the data sources and formats for UIs differ significantly from those of natural images and language corpora. For instance, the View Hierarchy (VH) in mobile applications and the Document Object Model (DOM) in web pages are tree structures that depict UI layouts. These structures contain both structural and semantic information about the UI, though they are not typically visible to users and include short phrases hinting at functionality. Leveraging this domain-specific knowledge for general UI understanding is an unresolved challenge. Thirdly, deciphering the functionality of UIs poses greater difficulty than understanding their appearance. UI elements with similar visual characteristics often have vastly different semantic meanings, and vice versa. As illustrated in Figure \ref{fig:icon-semantic}, icons may appear similar (e.g., "houses"), yet possess distinct functionalities that require additional contextual interpretation. In this study, we introduce ActionBert, a pre-trained transformer-style model \cite{vaswani2017attention} that utilizes sequential user action data for UI comprehension. Our primary insight is that user actions, such as a series of clicks and their subsequent effects on the UI, can encapsulate the semantic essence of a UI and the functionality of its components. The model capitalizes on the representational strength of transformer models, integrating domain-specific information like VH and user actions to develop embeddings that convey the functionality of various UI elements. To our knowledge, this represents the inaugural effort to establish a generic feature representation in this area. Our significant contributions include: \begin{itemize} \item We are pioneering the integration of potent transformer models with domain-specific insights, such as VH and user actions, to enhance machine comprehension of UIs. \item We introduce ActionBert, a multi-modal transformer-style model that captures the context and semantic significance of UI elements by implementing novel self-supervised pre-training tasks based on user actions and UI-specific characteristics. \item We assess the proposed model across four categories of UI downstream tasks, reflecting a range of practical applications. Our results demonstrate that the proposed model surpasses existing models in performance across all tasks. \end{itemize}

text: Robots are increasingly tasked with executing precise manipulation, navigation, and target tracking across diverse domains, from industrial automation to space missions. The integration of visual feedback is advantageous for tasks demanding fine manipulation, particularly when the robot's end-effector is proximal to the object of interest. Conversely, for tasks like guiding a quadcopter to land from a distance, visual feedback proves effective when the onboard camera can capture discernible image features. In scenarios where the object falls outside the camera's field of view (FOV), or when feature extraction is unreliable or suffers loss, learning-based motion generation techniques such as dynamic movement primitives (DMP) become essential for robot control. For instance, in wire harness assembly, the robot must guide the wire to the pin along a trajectory that avoids collisions with fixtures, even if the pin is not continuously visible to the camera mounted on the robot's end-effector. In such circumstances, a learned DMP can facilitate the wire's approach to the pin, setting the stage for visual feedback to take over \cite{Wirepinning}. Inspired by these scenarios and the need for stable transitions between learned and vision-based controllers, this paper introduces a novel approach that integrates DMP \cite{ijspeert2003learning} with Image-based Visual Servoing (IBVS) \cite{chaumette2006visual}. Our algorithm ensures stable transitions between DMP and IBVS controllers, enabling the robot to reach its target from an initial position, even without continuous visual feedback. This integrated system is termed the DMP-IBVS switched system. Numerous techniques have been devised to develop robot controllers that utilize visual feedback to maintain objects within the FOV (see, e.g., \cite{lopez2009homography,gans2011keeping,Salehi2021ICRA}). For instance, \cite{Wang2021SMC} presents a trajectory planning and tracking control strategy for mobile robots, employing a virtual-goal-guided rapidly exploring random tree (RRT) for planning and IBVS with FOV constraints for tracking. In \cite{Huang2021SMC}, a constrained IBVS approach is proposed for helicopter landings on moving platforms, utilizing control barrier functions to adhere to FOV constraints. Meanwhile, \cite{Ke2017SMC} develops a model predictive controller (MPC) for visual servoing of mobile robots, addressing visibility constraints and velocity limits in IBVS. Contrasting these methods, this paper focuses on a learning-based robot motion generation using DMP to produce control commands when visual feedback is absent, alongside a switching control law to transition to the IBVS controller when visual feedback becomes available. Arbitrary switching between stable subsystems can cause instability \cite{liberzon2003switching,liberzon1999basic}. In \cite{hespanha1999stability}, an average dwell time condition based on multiple Lyapunov functions is formulated to stabilize switched systems. The authors of \cite{daafouz2002stability} introduce a linear matrix inequality-based condition to verify the existence of a quadratic Lyapunov function for proving the asymptotic stability of switched discrete systems. LaSalle's invariance principle is extended to switched linear systems in \cite{hespanha2004uniform}, allowing for asymptotic stability deduction using multiple Lyapunov functions with negative semidefinite Lie derivatives. A comprehensive survey on switched linear system stability is presented in \cite{lin2009stability}, analyzing stabilizability issues. In \cite{branicky1998multiple}, multiple Lyapunov functions are proposed for Lyapunov stability analysis, and iterated function systems are used for Lagrange stability. Invariance-like results for nonautonomous nonlinear switched systems are developed in \cite{kamalapurkar2018invariance}. Output feedback systems and observers have been extensively studied in switched systems analysis. The method in \cite{Astolfi2020_tac} examines switching between locally and globally converging observers with asymptotic stability. A composite output feedback control law, switching between locally and globally asymptotically stable controllers, is derived in \cite{Prieur2011_tac}. Switched systems analysis has proven effective in addressing complex robotics challenges, such as visual servo control and vision-based trajectory tracking. For example, \cite{gans2007stable} introduces an asymptotically stable hybrid switched systems visual servo controller that transitions between IBVS and position-based visual servo control (PBVS) using multiple Lyapunov functions, enhancing stability regions. An estimator that alternates between state predictor and image-based observer for object localization is presented in \cite{parikh2016switched}, accommodating intermittent image feedback. Stability is ensured using a common Lyapunov function. In \cite{parikh2018target}, an estimator for moving target pose estimation is developed, leveraging intermittent measurements to learn the motion model. The observer-predictor framework in \cite{parikh2017switched,chen2019switched} addresses target and trajectory tracking with intermittent measurements, switching between a globally uniformly ultimately bounded (GUUB) and an unstable system. The switched error system is shown to be GUUB based on dwell time conditions. Image-based tracking approaches primarily switch systems to manage feature track losses, occlusions, and limited camera FOV. Switched systems analysis is also applied to target tracking with intermittent observations from stationary camera networks in \cite{harris2020target}. In \cite{zegers2019switched}, consensus protocols for distributed multi-agent systems are developed using switched systems analysis, where the leader intermittently informs followers. Switched systems application to biped locomotion is explored in \cite{veer2019switched}, proving the boundedness of input-to-state (ISS) stable switched systems with multiple equilibria. These results typically involve switching between globally or locally stable systems. Unlike previous switched systems approaches addressing feature track losses, occlusions in object tracking, localization, and IBVS-PBVS stability enhancements, this paper proposes a method that switches between image-based and learning-based control when image feedback is unavailable, due to factors like limited camera FOV, occlusions, or feature losses. Our new switched systems analysis accommodates transitions between locally stable (IBVS) and globally stable (DMP) modes, aiming to regulate the camera's pose relative to a target. When visual feedback is accessible, the IBVS controller generates camera accelerations; otherwise, DMP takes over. DMP functions as an online end-effector acceleration controller, trained using demonstration data from a pose regulation task. This approach is beneficial in robotic tasks where an eye-in-hand robot arm or ground robot with a mounted camera requires precision control through DMP and IBVS. The paper's technical contributions include: \begin{itemize} \item Development of a common state-space representation for analyzing the switched system stability of IBVS and DMP acceleration controllers. \item Introduction of a novel IBVS acceleration control law with closed-loop dynamics proven to be UUB when the initial state is near the goal state. \item Presentation of combined position and orientation DMPs with dynamics proven to be globally asymptotically stable. \item Analysis of the switching between locally stable IBVS and globally stable DMP using multiple Lyapunov functions, with switched system dynamics shown to converge to a bound, analytically derived. An algorithm ensuring stable switching between IBVS and DMP subsystems is also developed. \end{itemize} Building on our earlier work \cite{rotithor2020combining}, this paper delivers comprehensive stability analyses for DMP and IBVS systems, alongside a switching and stability analysis for the integrated system. Experimental results for a pose regulation task are demonstrated using the Baxter robot's eye-in-hand configuration, validating the switched system's performance amid image-feedback occlusions and comparing it to a DMP-only controller. The paper is structured as follows. Section \ref{sec:Coordinate-System} discusses the coordinate frames related to the robot base, camera, goal location, and their kinematics. Section \ref{sec:IBVS} introduces an IBVS acceleration controller with error dynamics proven to be uniformly ultimately bounded (UUB). Section \ref{sec:TaskSpace-Control} presents position and orientation DMPs with globally asymptotic stability of error dynamics. Section \ref{sec:Hybrid-System} proves the switched system's stability and develops an average dwell time condition. Section \ref{sec:Experiments} presents experimental results for the switched system. \textit{Notations:} The set of real numbers and integers is denoted by $\mathbb{R}$ and $\mathbb{Z}$, respectively.
