text: The field of natural language processing (NLP) faces a significant challenge with long-form question-answering (LFQA), where the goal is to generate detailed, paragraph-length responses to open-ended questions. Although LFQA systems hold promise as a primary means for individuals to acquire knowledge, they currently do not match human capabilities \citep{hurdles}. The prevalent research in this domain primarily addresses two essential components: information retrieval and synthesis. In our study, we capitalize on established solutions for these components by utilizing the Microsoft Bing Web Search API\footnote{\url{https://www.microsoft.com/en-us/bing/apis/bing-web-search-api}} for document retrieval and employing unsupervised pre-training to enhance synthesis through GPT-3 fine-tuning \citep{gpt3}. Rather than refining these individual elements, our focus is on integrating them with more reliable training objectives. Drawing on the work of \citet{summarization}, we employ human feedback to directly enhance answer quality, achieving performance levels that rival human outputs. Our research presents two primary contributions: \begin{itemize} \item We develop a text-based web-browsing environment that enables a fine-tuned language model to interact dynamically. This setup allows us to refine both retrieval and synthesis through holistic methods such as imitation learning and reinforcement learning. \item We produce answers \textit{with references}, which include passages selected by the model from web pages during browsing. This approach is vital for enabling evaluators to assess the factual accuracy of answers without resorting to the complex and subjective task of independent verification. \end{itemize} Our models are predominantly trained to address questions from the ELI5 dataset \citep{eli5}, which originates from the ``Explain Like I'm Five'' subreddit. In addition, we gather two supplementary types of data: \textit{demonstrations} of human interactions within our web-browsing environment to answer questions, and \textit{comparisons} between two model-generated answers to identical questions, each accompanied by distinct references. These answers are evaluated based on factual accuracy, coherence, and overall utility. We utilize this data through four principal approaches: behavior cloning (supervised fine-tuning) using demonstrations, reward modeling using comparisons, reinforcement learning with the reward model, and rejection sampling against the reward model. Our most successful model combines behavior cloning with rejection sampling. We also observe that reinforcement learning offers advantages when computational resources during inference are constrained. Our best model undergoes evaluation through three distinct methods. Initially, we compare the model's responses to those crafted by human demonstrators on a separate set of questions. Our model's responses are favored 56\% of the time, indicating human-level proficiency in using the text-based browser. Subsequently, we compare our model's answers (with references removed for impartiality) to the top-voted responses from the ELI5 dataset, with our model's answers being preferred 69\% of the time. Lastly, we assess our model using TruthfulQA \citep{truthfulqa}, an adversarial dataset of concise questions. Our model's answers are accurate 75\% of the time, and both accurate and informative 54\% of the time, surpassing the base model (GPT-3) but still falling short of human performance. The remainder of this paper is organized as follows: \begin{itemize} \item Section \ref{section:environment} details our text-based web-browsing environment and the interaction of our models with it. \item Section \ref{section:methods} delves into our data collection and training methodologies. \item Section \ref{section:evaluation} presents an evaluation of our top-performing models across various inference-time computational budgets on ELI5 and TruthfulQA. \item Section \ref{section:experiments} offers experimental results comparing our different methodologies and their scalability with respect to dataset size, parameter count, and inference-time computation. \item Section \ref{section:discussion} explores the implications of our findings for training models to answer questions truthfully and discusses broader impacts. \end{itemize}

text: Navigating self-driving vehicles through intricate and ever-changing traffic conditions presents significant challenges. The complexity arises from the need to accommodate a variety of road configurations and situations, such as roundabouts, multi-lane roads, and intersections\cite{Chen2019DeepIL}. Moreover, the intricate and interconnected interactions among diverse road users—including pedestrians, cyclists, and vehicles—pose substantial modeling difficulties\cite{Chen2020RobotNI}. Additionally, adherence to various traffic regulations, including signals, lane demarcations, and speed limits, is imperative. Traditional decision-making and planning methods predominantly rely on rule-based systems, which struggle to adapt to novel situations. Consequently, these methods necessitate labor-intensive and iterative fine-tuning of rules and parameters to sustain their effectiveness\cite{Zeng2019EndToEndIN}. In recent years, deep learning has emerged as a transformative approach in self-driving vehicle (SDV) technology. Its capacity to \textit{learn and optimize} behavior from data significantly reduces the engineering burden of modeling every conceivable scenario, making deep learning models particularly suited for tackling the complexities of high-dimensional, nonlinear, and dynamic environments\cite{Cai2020ProbabilisticEV, Chen2019LearningBC,OhnBar2020LearningSD, codevilla2018end, codevilla2019exploring, Tai2019VisualbasedAD}. Nonetheless, existing learning-based models are not yet optimized for scalable self-driving within a unified framework. Typically, research efforts focus on isolated tasks such as conditional urban driving\cite{OhnBar2020LearningSD, codevilla2018end, codevilla2019exploring,Chen2019LearningBC,Tai2019VisualbasedAD}, lane-following\cite{Xu2017EndtoEndLO}, lane-changing\cite{Wang2018ARL}, or collision avoidance\cite{Porav2018ImminentCM, Woo2020CollisionAF}. Consequently, achieving high-performance, scalable driving models capable of managing extensive traffic scenarios remains a challenge. To address this, we introduce a graph-based deep neural network, \textit{DiGNet} (driving in graphs), designed for scalable self-driving. Our approach leverages graph attention networks (GAT)\cite{velickovic2018graph} to capture the complex interactions among traffic participants, employs semantic bird's-eye view (BEV) images to represent road layouts and traffic regulations, and utilizes the variational auto-encoder (VAE)\cite{kingma2014autoencoding} to derive compact, effective environmental representations. The key contributions of this paper are as follows: (1) We present a novel network architecture tailored for self-driving in diverse traffic scenarios, integrating both contextual driving information and dynamic interactions among road agents. (2) We validate the scalability and safety of our proposed method through comprehensive closed-loop evaluations across both familiar and novel urban, rural, and highway settings.

text: Neural Networks (NNs) are computational architectures that consist of one or more layers for feature representation, culminating in a final linear learner. Over recent years, deep neural networks have significantly advanced the state-of-the-art in various practical applications, including image classification \cite{krizhevsky2012imagenet,he2016deep}, speech recognition \cite{hinton2012deep}, and natural language processing \cite{bahdanau2014neural}. Despite these empirical achievements, the theoretical understanding of neural networks remains limited. A primary challenge is the models' high degree of non-convexity, which implies that first-order algorithms like gradient descent (GD) or stochastic gradient descent (SGD) might converge to suboptimal local stationary points. Nonetheless, empirical evidence shows that with techniques like dropout \cite{SHKSS-dropout} and batch normalization \cite{ioffe15}, deep neural networks can be effectively trained from random starting points, yielding consistent outcomes. Properly trained models tend to produce similar predictions on test data, even when initialized differently. This suggests that effective training of neural networks results in similar solutions, akin to convex optimization problems, rather than typical non-convex ones that often get trapped in poor local optima. The reproducibility and similarity of solutions from different initializations hint at the possibility that well-trained deep neural networks can approximate globally optimal solutions. These phenomena are intriguing and necessitate the development of novel mathematical frameworks that can connect the dots between non-convex and convex models to enhance our understanding. Moreover, practitioners have observed that overparameterized neural networks, those with a large number of hidden units, are easier to train and deliver more consistent performance \cite{zhang2016understanding}. This aligns with earlier findings from the 1990s, which noted that neural networks with an infinite number of hidden units are more straightforward to model and analyze theoretically \cite{Neal95-thesis,Williams97-nips}. Recent years have witnessed substantial theoretical progress in analyzing overparameterized networks with a vast number of hidden units approaching infinity. Notably, such systems have been shown to behave like convex systems in certain restricted scenarios, offering theoretical backing for the empirical reproducibility of neural network training. In this paper, we explore some of the latest mathematical models developed for overparameterized neural networks, with a particular emphasis on the {\em neural tangent kernel} (NTK) perspective and the {\em mean field} (MF) perspective. Section~\ref{sec:2two-levelNN} outlines the basic formulation for two-layer neural networks, while Section~\ref{sec:random} discusses a related learning model known as random kitchen sinks \cite{rahimi2009weighted}. In Section \ref{sec:ntk}, we delve into the NTK perspective for two-layer networks, demonstrating how a two-layer neural network can be expressed as a linear model in the tangent space under specific conditions. Section \ref{sec:meanfield} examines the MF perspective for two-layer networks, where a continuous two-layer network is viewed as a distribution over the weights, leading to a more practical mathematical model for analyzing neural network behavior. Section \ref{sec:exp} compares the three models from the standpoint of feature learning. Section \ref{sec:deepnn} explores potential extensions of NTK and MF to deep neural networks. In Section \ref{sec:complexity}, we introduce fundamental complexity results for NTK. Section \ref{sec:othermodel} reviews additional mathematical models. Finally, Section \ref{sec:conclusion} concludes the paper and highlights active research areas. \IEEEpubidadjcol

text: In the midst of an ever-growing deluge of scientific publications, researchers face increasing difficulty in discerning which papers are worth their time, whether for a swift overview or to stay abreast of cutting-edge developments. When delving into an unfamiliar research area, individuals often resort to survey papers, consulting their reference lists for deeper insights. Unfortunately, high-caliber, up-to-date surveys are not always accessible for every research domain. Alternatively, researchers might turn to academic search engines to locate pertinent literature. However, these engines typically compile lists based on semantic similarity between a user's query and individual articles, neglecting the interdependencies among the results. Consequently, there is significant value in generating a curated list of fundamental papers, complete with a recommended reading sequence, to guide users along an educational trajectory. This approach allows users to efficiently familiarize themselves with new research landscapes. The field of scientific paper analysis has garnered considerable interest recently. Nonetheless, most studies have concentrated on citation recommendation~\cite{zhou2008learning, tang2009discriminative, he2010context, ren2014cluscite, sun2017recommendation}, which suggests citations for specific texts. Another line of research focuses on citation classification \cite{jurgens2016citation, teufel2006automatic, dong2011ensemble, zhao2019context, cohan2019structural, pride2020authoritative}, intending to decipher the motivations behind citing particular works. Additionally, some efforts aim to generate reading lists \cite{jardine2014automatically, ekstrand2010automatically}, though these often overlook the prerequisite relationships between papers. \cite{gordon2017structured} introduced a concept graph-based method to produce structured reading lists, incorporating prerequisite concepts, yet this approach heavily depends on the quality of pre-existing concept graphs. Traditional research on reading list generation primarily addresses the question of "what to read" by compiling paper lists for specific topics. However, for those unfamiliar with a field, two pivotal issues remain unresolved: "how to read" and "how to understand." Addressing the first requires organizing research works in a structured format, guiding users through a historical evolution of a topic. A mere chronological arrangement fails to capture the intricate correlations between studies. The second issue involves including papers that, while not directly linked to the query, are crucial for comprehending the primary literature. In light of these considerations, this paper introduces the task of {\em Reading Path Generation (RPG)}, which seeks to automatically construct a reading pathway tailored to a specific query. This task is crafted to assist newcomers in swiftly surveying a field by addressing the aforementioned challenges. Our goal is to retrieve a list of papers that encompasses both works closely related to the query and foundational studies essential for understanding them. These papers are then organized into a reading path that respects both chronological progression and inter-research correlations. By following this path, users can efficiently grasp each work, complete a comprehensive survey, and gain an overarching view of a topic's research history. Given the absence of benchmark datasets for evaluating Reading Path Generation, we introduce the {\em SurveyBank} dataset, tailored for our proposed task. SurveyBank is developed without human annotation, drawing on two key insights. Firstly, many existing high-quality surveys, authored by experts, provide valuable frameworks for constructing research overviews. We leverage key phrases from survey titles as RPG inputs, using reference lists as ground truth reading paths. Initially, we collected 41,194 computer science surveys from Google Scholar and S2ORC \cite{lo-etal-2020-s2orc}, selecting 9,321 high-quality surveys to form SurveyBank. This dataset spans 10 computer science topics, including Artificial Intelligence, Computer Networks, and Databases. Secondly, citation relationships reveal coherence among papers. Thus, we constructed a comprehensive scientific citation graph featuring 6 million papers from S2ORC~\cite{lo-etal-2020-s2orc}, encompassing survey reference lists. SurveyBank stands as the largest survey dataset known to date. Furthermore, we propose and implement a Real-time Reading Path Generation System (RePaGer) that takes key phrases as input and creates a reading path for users. In RePaGer, we begin by retrieving top-$K$ initial seed papers from Google Scholar. We then refine these seeds by identifying neighboring papers as candidates and selecting those with high co-occurrence. These selected seeds likely represent prerequisite concepts, as they are frequently cited by topic-relevant articles. We introduce the Node-Edge Weighted Steiner Tree (NWST), a graph optimization-based method, to identify reading paths with prerequisite chains for a given query. Our model evaluates both the significance of individual papers within the citation network and their interconnections. We conducted extensive evaluations using the SurveyBank dataset, comparing our Reading Path Generation approach against existing academic search engines and baseline methods. Results indicate that our method surpasses other baselines, effectively producing insightful reading paths across various research topics.

text: The field of 3D-aware image synthesis has gained significant traction recently~\cite{graf, giraffe, pigan}. A novel approach involves the fusion of a Neural Radiance Field (NeRF)~\cite{nerf} with a Generative Adversarial Network (GAN)~\cite{gan}. This method replaces the traditional 2D Convolutional Neural Network (CNN) generator with a generative implicit function, which transforms raw 3D coordinates into point-wise densities and colors, contingent on a latent code. This implicit function effectively encodes both the structural and textural aspects of the image within a 3D space. Despite its potential, directly utilizing NeRF~\cite{nerf} within the generator presents two main challenges. Firstly, NeRF's implicit function employs a Multi-Layer Perceptron (MLP) to determine color and density for each 3D point. The MLP's limited receptive field makes it challenging to globally represent the structure during image synthesis. Consequently, relying solely on 3D coordinates as inputs~\cite{graf, pigan, giraffe} lacks the expressiveness needed to guide the generator with comprehensive structural information. Secondly, volume rendering computes pixel values independently, necessitating extensive point sampling along each pixel's camera ray. This process escalates computational demands, particularly with larger image resolutions, potentially hindering model optimization and degrading high-resolution image generation performance. Previous research indicates that 2D GANs benefit from meaningful representations learned by the generator~\cite{interfacegan, higan, xu2021generative}. These generative representations encapsulate synthesis through \emph{high-level features}. For instance, Xu~\textit{et al.}~\cite{xu2021generative} demonstrate that a face synthesis model can recognize landmark positions on the generated face, while Yang~\textit{et al.}~\cite{higan} reveal multi-level variation factors when generating bedroom images. Such representative features enrich texture and structure information, thereby enhancing synthesis quality~\cite{stylegan} and image GANs' controllability~\cite{interfacegan}. In contrast, current 3D-aware generative models render pixel values directly from coordinates~\cite{graf, pigan}, without developing explicit representations. In this paper, we introduce a novel generative model named \textbf{VolumeGAN}, designed to achieve 3D-aware image synthesis by \emph{explicitly learning structural and textural representations}. Rather than using 3D coordinates as inputs, we construct a feature volume through a 3D convolutional network, which captures relationships across spatial regions, compensating for the MLP's limited receptive field in NeRF. This feature volume models the underlying structure, allowing us to extract a coordinate descriptor that conveys structural data for each 3D point. Subsequently, we employ a NeRF-like model to generate a feature field, using the coordinate descriptor alongside the raw coordinate as input. This feature field is then compiled into a 2D feature map representing texture, which a CNN with a $1\times1$ kernel size uses to render the final image. By separately modeling structure and texture with the 3D feature volume and the 2D feature map, we facilitate disentangled control over shape and appearance. We validate our model across diverse datasets, showcasing its superior performance compared to existing methods. VolumeGAN significantly enhances image quality, as evidenced by improved Fréchet Inception Distance (FID) scores~\cite{fid}. For example, with the FFHQ dataset~\cite{stylegan} at $256\times256$ resolution, we reduced the FID from $36.7$ to $9.1$. Our approach also enables 3D-aware image synthesis on challenging datasets like LSUN bedroom~\cite{lsun}. The model demonstrates stable control over object pose and maintains consistency across viewpoints, attributed to the learned structural representation (i.e., the feature volume). Additionally, we conduct a comprehensive empirical analysis of the learned structural and textural representations, exploring the balance between image quality and 3D properties.

text: Data minimisation stands as a fundamental tenet within the European Union's Data Protection Regulation~\citep{regulation2016regulation}, as well as in data protection statutes globally: \begin{quote} "Personal data shall be: [...] adequate, relevant and limited to what is necessary in relation to the purposes for which they are processed (data minimisation)" \end{quote} This principle acts as a directive for handling data with due care. Recent empirical studies have demonstrated that data-driven systems can achieve comparable performance with a substantially reduced dataset~\cite{biega2020dm, chow2013differential,vincent2019data, wen2018exploring}. These insights are attributed to the diminishing returns observed in data collection across various fields and applications~\cite{hestness1712deep, krause2010utility,tae2020slice}. Acknowledging the feasibility of data limitation, legal frameworks suggest incorporating algorithmic strategies into minimization processes, such as feature selection~\cite{icoDataMinimizationTechniques} or analyzing learning curves~\cite{norwegianAuthorityArtificial}. Despite the availability of numerous algorithmic methods that could be adapted to meet the minimization criteria, the data minimisation principle has been largely overlooked by the computer science community. Scholars have pointed out that the lack of precise mathematical definitions and guidelines significantly hampers its adoption~\cite{finckreviving}. Qualitative studies reveal an absence of consistent standards or a clear understanding of data minimization among software developers~\cite{senarath2018understanding}. Emerging interpretations of data minimization suggest linking the purpose of data collection in data-driven systems to performance metrics, a concept known as \emph{performance-based data minimization}~\cite{finckreviving,biega2020dm}. Our research aligns with this interpretation, exploring \emph{how to proactively fulfill the performance-based data minimization principle in machine learning with personal data}. \\ \textbf{Contributions.} This paper introduces FIDO, a Framework for Inhibiting Data Overcollection, showcasing an approach to personal data collection within the context of data minimization. The core idea of FIDO is to \emph{adaptively learn an algorithm's performance curve} to precisely identify an \emph{optimal stopping point for data collection}. By directly modeling the performance curve, the framework maintains versatility across various feature acquisition algorithms and performance definitions. Experiments conducted on diverse datasets in the recommender systems domain validate this adaptability and demonstrate FIDO's capability to accurately estimate algorithm performance based on additional data \emph{without} further data collection. The principal technical contribution of FIDO lies in its performance curve estimation method, which builds upon recent machine learning research identifying three distinct phases in learning algorithms' performance curves: the small data phase, the power law phase, and the diminishing returns phase \cite{hestness1712deep}. We show that these phases are evident in user data collection contexts and provide a technique to model these phases by adaptively learning a piecewise power law curve. Empirical results reveal that other methods for estimating performance curves tend to \emph{overestimate} the benefits of additional data. FIDO's direct modeling of each phase allows for a more accurate learning of the performance curve as data is gathered, addressing practical data minimization constraints. Furthermore, we delve into issues concerning user-level data minimization. We explore how algorithmic components like active feature acquisition (a strategy for selectively acquiring feature values) impact minimization outcomes. Our findings indicate that active feature acquisition can result in disproportionate data collection from a limited user group and reduced minimization efficiency for dynamic user communities or when sensitive features are omitted from initial data collection. Additionally, we observe significant variability in user-specific performance curves, where gathering more data can sometimes lead to a \emph{decline} in individual user performance. This paper aims to provide a computational perspective on the GDPR's data minimization principle, contributing valuable insights to ongoing discussions about the technical execution of this key data protection principle and offering recommendations for practitioners and researchers in the field.

text: The \textit{Security-Constrained Economic Dispatch} (SCED) serves as a crucial optimization framework for Transmission System Operators (TSOs) to manage real-time energy markets while ensuring the stable operation of power grids \cite{conejo2018power}. In the United States, TSOs such as MISO and PJM execute SCED every five minutes, requiring solutions to the optimization problem in less than a minute \cite{Chen2018_MarketClearingSoftware}. The complexity of SCED models, particularly for large systems, is heightened by security constraints that ensure resilience against the failure of any single component \cite{Chiang2015_SolvingSCOPF,Wang2016_SolvingCorrectiveSCOPF,velloso2021exact}, unless a limited set of contingencies is considered. As the penetration of distributed resources grows and operational uncertainties increase, these computational challenges are expected to intensify \cite{Chen2018_MarketClearingSoftware}. This study is driven by the increasing share of renewable energy, particularly wind, in the MISO network, necessitating market-clearing algorithms that incorporate risk awareness. A significant challenge is conducting real-time risk assessments by solving numerous scenarios for load and renewable output \cite{werho2021_ScenarioGenerationWind}. However, solving multiple SCED instances systematically is impractical under real-time constraints. To address this, we propose an optimization proxy for SCED—a Machine Learning (ML) model capable of predicting optimal SCED solutions within acceptable numerical tolerances and executing these predictions in milliseconds. It is crucial to clarify that the intention is not to replace existing optimization-based market-clearing tools. Instead, the proposed optimization proxy serves as an additional resource for operators to assess risks. This tool enables rapid evaluation of system behavior under various scenarios without incurring the high costs of traditional optimizations. Since these predictions are aggregated into risk metrics, minor prediction inaccuracies in individual cases are permissible. \subsection{Related Literature and Challenges} The integration of ML with optimization in power systems has garnered increasing interest in recent years. One area of research \cite{pan2019deepopf, fioretto2020predicting, chatzos2020high, lei2020data, chatzos2021spatial, velloso2020combining, zamzam2020learning, owerko2020optimal} involves using ML models to predict solutions to the Optimal Power Flow (OPF) problem. Pan et al. \cite{pan2019deepopf} developed a Deep Neural Network (DNN) model to predict solutions for security-constrained DC-OPFs, demonstrating results on systems with no more than 300 buses. A common issue with ML models, as noted in \cite{pan2019deepopf}, is their inability to guarantee adherence to the original problem's constraints. To address this, recent studies \cite{fioretto2020predicting, chatzos2020high} have incorporated Lagrangian duality into DNN training to capture the physical and operational constraints of AC-OPFs. A similar methodology is applied by Velloso et al. \cite{velloso2020combining} within preventive security-constrained DC-OPF, where a DNN trained with Lagrangian duality techniques is used as a proxy for the master problem in a column-and-constraint generation algorithm. More recently, Chatzos et al. \cite{chatzos2021spatial} have embedded the Lagrangian duality framework into a two-stage learning process that utilizes a regional decomposition of the power network, facilitating more efficient distributed training. Another research direction focuses on incorporating ML models into optimization algorithms to enhance runtime performance. Various studies (e.g., \cite{deka2019learning,misra2021learning,xavier2021learning, yang2020fast,guha2019machine}) aim to identify active constraints to simplify problem complexity. In \cite{xavier2021learning}, researchers explore learning feasible solutions to the unit commitment problem. Venzke et al. \cite{venzke2020neural} employ a DNN model to delineate the feasible region of a dynamic SCOPF and convert the resulting DNN into a mixed-integer linear program. Current ML research for power systems often faces two significant limitations. Firstly, most studies present numerical results on small academic test systems, which are significantly smaller than real transmission systems. This is concerning because higher-dimensional data negatively affects the convergence and accuracy of machine-learning algorithms. Secondly, many studies rely on artificially-generated data that fails to reflect the variability encountered in real operations. For example, they often consider only load changes, neglecting spatio-temporal correlations. Other uncertainties, such as renewable output and economic bid variability, are not accounted for. Lastly, variations in commitment decisions throughout the day, which introduce complex, combinatorial distribution shifts, are rarely addressed. \subsection{Contributions and Outline} To address these limitations, this paper introduces an innovative ML pipeline rooted in the structure of actual market operations. The approach capitalizes on the TSO's pre-existing knowledge of commitment decisions and day-ahead forecasts for load and renewable production, which are accessible once the day-ahead market is cleared. Additionally, the paper offers a comprehensive analysis of real-time market dynamics, informing a novel ML architecture that better reflects the realities of operational environments. The proposed learning pipeline is illustrated in Figure~\ref{fig:learning_pipeline}. Initially, commitment decisions and day-ahead forecasts for load and renewable generation are collected following the day-ahead market clearing. This data is then utilized to create a training dataset of SCED instances, employing classical data augmentation methods. Specialized ML models are subsequently trained, ideally one for each hour of the operational day, to mitigate the combinatorial complexity of commitment decisions. Each ML model focuses on a specific set of commitments and examines load/renewable scenarios around the hourly forecasts. During the operational day, these trained models are applied in real time to assess numerous scenarios. The entire data generation and training process is completed within a few hours. The remainder of the paper is structured as follows. Section \ref{sec:opt_pipeline} discusses the interaction between day-ahead and real-time markets in the MISO system and provides an overview of the real-time SCED for MISO. Section \ref{sec:methodology} examines the behavior of real-time market solutions, proposes a combined Classification-Then-Regression architecture, and outlines the overall ML pipeline. Numerical experiments conducted on a real-life system are presented in Section \ref{sec:results}.

text: The primary objective of DNA-sequencing is to ascertain the genetic composition of individuals. Although there are various technologies, the core process involves determining fragments of the genetic sequence. Typically, the initial data analysis includes several key steps: firstly, aligning the sequence against a reference genome, such as GRCh38 for human samples, and secondly, performing variant calling. The main output is a list of variants, which represents the unique differences for the individual sample, often formatted in a table like the Variant Call Format (VCF)~\cite{vcf}. These variants are pivotal for subsequent applications, which range from basic research and association studies to clinical diagnostics. Focusing on differences relative to a reference is beneficial due to the genome's vast size (approximately $3 \cdot 10^9$ nucleotides in humans), whereas the differences between individual genomes are comparatively minor (around $0.6\%$~\cite{variation}). When variants are linked to phenotypic traits, they are documented in scientific literature and stored with annotations in locus-specific databases. Typically, the VCF representation of a variant is refined into a format more suitable for reporting. Various domain-specific languages exist for this purpose, including: \begin{itemize} \item The Human Genome Variation Society's recommendations (HGVS)~\cite{hgvs}; \item SPDI~\cite{spdi}, used by the National Center for Biotechnology Information (NCBI) as their internal variant data model; \item The Variant Representation Specification (VRS)~\cite{vrs}, developed by the Global Alliance for Genomic Health (GA4GH). \end{itemize} These languages aim to represent observed differences in a format that is understandable by humans and/or interpretable by machines. Unlike VCF, which is closely tied to the tools and configurations used in primary data analysis, these representations are independent of specific processes and universally interpretable. In the field of variant recording, certain simplifications are frequently made. Firstly, small local variants on a single molecular sequence (part of the same haplotype) are documented separately, facilitating the storage of numerous variants in databases. Information regarding phasing—whether small variants belong to the same haplotype—is often incomplete or missing. This is partly due to limitations of sequencing technology and partly because this information is sometimes discarded. Secondly, in some representations (notably HGVS), uncertainties may be expressed. These uncertainties typically pertain to the variant's position within the reference genome, though the precise composition of larger insertions might also be unclear. Lastly, unchanged regions might be implied. During the alignment step of primary data analysis, it is assumed that the reference genome's sequence is present, even if direct evidence, such as coverage data from sequencing, is absent. For the remainder of this paper, we adopt a precise perspective on the nature of variants: \begin{enumerate} \item A variant is defined by deletions, insertions, or a combination thereof, relative to a single molecular sequence. When these operations occur together, they are considered phased, in cis, or part of the same allele, and can be described as phase sets or allele descriptions. Many variant description languages have introduced higher-order operations like single nucleotide variants (SNV) (termed substitutions in HGVS), multi-nucleotide variants (deletions/insertions), duplications, transpositions, inversions, repeats, etc. We view all these as specific instances of the aforementioned definition. \item We focus exclusively on \emph{interpretable} variants, meaning that given a \emph{reference sequence}, there exists a deterministic and clear method to ``apply'' the variants, resulting in the originally measured \emph{observed sequence}, akin to the Unix~\texttt{diff} and \texttt{patch} utilities. \end{enumerate} \noindent As noted in various variant representation languages, multiple representations often exist for the same observed sequence. These variations can arise from the choice of ``operator'', for instance, an SNV might also be depicted as a deletion of one nucleotide followed by an insertion of another. Another factor contributing to these variations is the structure of the reference sequence. Consider the reference sequence~\texttt{ATTTA} and the observed sequence~\texttt{ATTA}. Removing one of the \texttt{T} symbols offers several ($3$) possibilities. To establish a universally accepted variant representation, most variant representation languages utilize a \emph{normalization} procedure. Normalization selects a \emph{canonical} representation from the available options. Unfortunately, this procedure is not standardized across different languages, such as the $3'$-rule in HGVS versus the $5'$-rule in VCF. However, within a given language, proper normalization addresses the issue of identifying \emph{equivalent} variant representations. The implications of using non-normalized variant representations have been reviewed in~\cite{variant_name, variant_calling, curation, litvar}. Solutions to this problem are discussed in~\cite{unified, improved_vcf, vmc_spec, smash, plyranges, gql, ask2me, deletions}. Often, specialized tools~\cite{varsome, validator, mutalyzer, vde} are necessary to accurately implement the proposed normalization procedure. Once normalized, variant representations can be compared textually using standard string matching techniques. \noindent Identifying equivalent variant representations, i.e., determining if two variant descriptions lead to the same observed sequence, is arguably the most intriguing query in the variant domain. This capability facilitates grouping and matching equivalent variants and their annotations. text: Originating in Africa and transported to the Caribbean during the era of the Atlantic Slave Trade, the Tresillo rhythm gained widespread recognition in Cuba. From there, it proliferated globally, permeating various musical genres \cite{acquista2009tresillo, floyd1999black}. \par The Tresillo serves not only as a standalone rhythm but also as a foundational rhythmic pattern for other styles such as Reggaeton and Clave. Referencing \cite{floyd1999black}, the Tresillo rhythm can be defined as follows (see Figure \ref{fig:tresillo}). The rhythmic pattern is composed of a dotted eighth note, followed by a sixteenth note, an eighth rest, and an eighth note, repeated twice within a 4/4 measure. By incorporating a beat on each quarter note, the pattern transforms into the Reggaeton rhythm (see Figure \ref{fig:reggaeton}). Modifying the second half of the measure to an eighth rest, two eighth notes, and another eighth rest results in the basic Clave rhythm pattern (see Figure \ref{fig:clave}). Predominantly featured in Latin American music, the Tresillo rhythm, described as a "danceable Cuban Clave son" \cite{sethares2014geometry}, has transcended its origins to influence Western music as well \cite{sethares2014geometry, biamonte2018rhythmic}. Contemporary examples include chart-topping hits like Ed Sheeran's "Shape of You" and Sia's "Cheap Thrills." An examination of the Billboard Charts reveals the frequent incorporation of this rhythm in pop music. Although the Tresillo's use, evolution, and popularity have been qualitatively examined \cite{acquista2009tresillo, sandroni2001tresillo, sethares2014geometry, biamonte2018rhythmic, floyd1999black}, a quantitative analysis of its prevalence has yet to be conducted. To explore this rhythm's usage, we devised a computational approach to represent both the primary rhythm of a pop song and the Tresillo rhythm, employing various similarity measurements. These measurements reveal a distinct temporal trend in the prevalence of the Tresillo in the US Billboard Top 20 Charts over the past two decades (1999-2019). \par This paper is structured as follows: We begin with a discussion of relevant secondary literature spanning multiple fields. The problem statement section outlines the assumptions necessary for our analysis. The Data section details the selected data sources and formats. In the method section, we present and explain the final data representation, proposed rhythm similarity measures, and evaluation metrics. The results section evaluates and compares the different rhythm similarity measures and analyzes the observed time trend. We conclude with a discussion of the methods and findings, offering interpretations of the results and suggesting potential extensions for future work.

text: Legged robots exhibit remarkable versatility, making them suitable for a wide array of applications. However, the challenge of achieving robust locomotion remains a complex issue requiring further exploration. Ensuring {stability and safety} is crucial for robots operating in real-world environments. This raises the question: despite their versatility, why have legged robots not yet matched human capabilities? To realize the intended versatility, our research delves into the core aspect of learning balance recovery strategies. Humans employ a combination of strategies—such as arm, ankle, and hip movements, or stepping—to regain balance after disturbances, improving these techniques through experience. Additionally, we examined existing biped robot locomotion frameworks. Although significant progress has been made in enhancing their stability, they still fall short of the stability and safety needed for everyday environments. Various methods for stabilizing biped robots have been proposed, which can be grouped into three primary categories. This section will introduce these categories and briefly review recent advancements in each. \subsection{Analytical Approaches} Approaches in this category fundamentally rely on employing a dynamics model of the robot to design controllers, such as force controllers~\cite{mason2016balancing}, hybrid position/force~\cite{faraji2019bipedal}, and admittance controllers~\cite{caron2020icra}, aimed at minimizing tracking error based on specific criteria. The Linear Inverted Pendulum~(LIP) model is predominantly utilized in literature, simplifying the robot's overall dynamics to a single mass. By constraining vertical mass movement, a linear model is achieved, facilitating rapid real-time solutions. Over decades, this model has been extensively studied and expanded to design and analyze legged robot locomotion~\cite{takenaka2009real,englsberger2015three}. Takaneka et al.~\cite{takenaka2009real} introduced the Divergent Component of Motion~(DCM) concept, which divides the LIP's dynamics into stable and unstable components, focusing on controlling the unstable part to maintain stability. In~\cite{englsberger2015three}, DCM was extended to 3D, and various control strategies, including classical feedback controllers~\cite{morisawa2014biped}, Linear Quadratic Regulator~(LQR)-based methods~\cite{faraji2019bipedal,8967778}, and Model Predictive Control~(MPC)~\cite{brasseur2015robust}, were proposed for formulating biped locomotion frameworks. These strategies aim to compensate for tracking errors by manipulating the Ground Reaction Force~(GRF) and adjusting the position and timing of the next step. Recent research is exploring the relaxation of LIP assumptions, such as COM vertical motion and angular momentum, introducing challenges related to nonlinearities~\cite{caron2020icra, kajita2018biped, seyde2018inclusion}. \vspace{-2mm} \subsection{Machine Learning Approaches} This category focuses on developing feasible policies through environmental interaction. Presently, Deep Reinforcement Learning~(DRL) has demonstrated its effectiveness in addressing complex locomotion and manipulation tasks, typically characterized by high-dimensional continuous observation and action spaces~\cite{gu2017deep,abreu2019learning}. In DRL, data augmentation is commonly applied to enhance optimization performance. However, this work narrows its focus to symmetry-oriented solutions. By generating symmetric data from actual samples, various robotic tasks can be improved~\cite{lin2020robotics}, including the walking gait of humanoid models~\cite{abdolhosseini2019learning} and quadruped robots~\cite{mishra2019augmenting} with multiple planes of symmetry. While DRL can learn efficient behaviors from scratch, even in asymmetrical settings~\cite{Abreu2019runfaster}, achieving human-like behaviors within a reasonable timeframe can be challenging without model restrictions such as symmetry or pattern generators. \subsection{Hybrid Approaches: combining analytical and learning} This category aims to integrate the strengths of both analytical and learning approaches. By merging learning algorithms with model-based gait pattern generators, parameters can be predicted, and residual dynamics (compensatory actions) can be learned, resulting in highly accurate behaviors~\cite{koryakovskiy2018model,ahn2020data}. Such frameworks typically consist of interconnected hierarchical layers. Yang et al.~\cite{yang2018learning} developed a hierarchical framework to stabilize a humanoid robot by learning motor skills. This framework comprises two independent layers: the high-level layer generates joint angles, while the low-level layer translates these angles into joint torques using PD controllers. Their reward function, composed of six distinct terms related to traditional push recovery strategies, was derived by aggregating these terms with varying weights. \subsection{Overview of the Proposed Framework and Contributions} This study targets the intricate challenge of bipedal locomotion in legged robots. Specifically, we explore whether a learning algorithm can effectively control and adjust a model-based control policy, such as a gait pattern generator. Our contributions include: \textbf{(i)} the development of a locomotion framework for humanoid robots that integrates analytical control with machine learning. An overview of this system is shown in Fig.~\ref{fig:Cover}. We utilize an abstract dynamics model to analytically formulate closed-loop biped locomotion and recovery strategies as a core element, integrating it with a symmetry-enhanced optimization framework using Proximal Policy Optimization~(PPO)~\cite{schulman2017ppo} to learn residual dynamics. The learned policy modifies pattern generator parameters and produces compensatory actions as residual dynamics to restore stability; \textbf{(ii)} the proposal of a learning method where data is only partially augmented, employing symmetry to enhance learning speed and human-likeness without constraining asymmetric movements, thereby expanding the range of potential behaviors. The paper is organized as follows: Section~\ref{sec:pattern} presents the architecture of our fully parametric kernel pattern generator, detailing each module. Section~\ref{sec:learningResidual} introduces our learning framework, explaining its augmentation with the kernel pattern generator to regulate kernel parameters and learn model-free skills (generating compensatory joint positions). Section~\ref{sec:simScenarios} outlines simulation scenarios designed to validate the framework's performance. Section~\ref{sec:simulations} provides simulations for performance assessment, policy behavior optimization, symmetry, and robustness analysis. Finally, conclusions and future research directions are discussed in Section~\ref{sec:conclusion}.

text: This paper aims to explore the Parallel Drone Scheduling Traveling Salesman Problem (PDSTSP), which is defined as follows. Consider a complete undirected graph $G=(V, E)$ where the vertex set is $V=\{0,1,\ldots,n,n+1\}$ and the edge set is $E=\{(i, j): i, j \in V, i < j\}$. The depot is represented by vertex 0, while vertex $n+1$ serves as its duplicate for modeling purposes. The vertices between them represent the customers, denoted as $V_c$. At the depot, a truck and a fleet of $m$ drones, designated as set $D$, are available to handle deliveries. A subset of customers, $V_{d}\subseteq V_c$, is identified as \emph{drone-eligible}, meaning their distance from the depot and parcel weight make them suitable for delivery by drones. The remaining customers, who must be served by the truck, are denoted by $V_{t}=V_c \setminus V_d$. The truck's travel time between nodes $i$ and $j$ is represented by $t_{ij}$, while the time a drone requires to service customer $i$ is $t'_i$, calculated as twice the flying time from the depot to customer $i$. The PDSTSP involves designing routes for both the truck and drones such that: (i) each customer is visited exactly once by either the truck or a drone; (ii) the truck's route begins and concludes at the depot; (iii) drones make round trips from the depot to serve individual customers; and (iv) the total time to serve all customers and return all vehicles to the depot is minimized. Since its introduction by \citet*{murray2015flying}, the PDSTSP has garnered considerable attention in the literature. The authors introduced a Mixed Integer Linear Programming (MILP) model and a simple heuristic to tackle the problem. This heuristic segregates customers into two groups, one for truck delivery and another for drones. The truck tour and drone tours are constructed by separately solving two subproblems: the Traveling Salesman Problem (TSP) and the Parallel Machine Scheduling (PMS) problem, each defined over its respective customer set. An additional improvement step reallocates customers between the truck and drones to optimize their workloads. These methods were tested on small instances with a maximum of 20 customers. Efforts to address larger PDSTSP instances have been pursued. \citet*{mbiadou2018iterative} introduced the first metaheuristic, an iterative two-step method. Initially, a sequence visiting all customers (a giant or TSP tour) is constructed. This sequence is then divided into a truck tour and drone trips using dynamic programming, resulting in a complete PDSTSP solution. This approach was tested on newly created instances with up to 229 customers. Subsequently, \citet*{dell2020matheuristic} proposed a matheuristic that employs a similar strategy to \cite*{mbiadou2018iterative} but replaces dynamic programming with a MILP formulation for the second step. Although slower, this method yields superior solutions compared to the heuristic by \cite{mbiadou2018iterative}. A nature-inspired approach, Hybrid Ant Colony Optimization (HACO), was proposed by \citet*{Dinh2021}. This algorithm builds on the concept from \cite{mbiadou2018iterative}, representing a PDSTSP solution as a customer permutation. However, it introduces a novel dynamic programming method with a manageable number of states to explore a broader solution space, effectively splitting the giant tour into a complete PDSTSP solution. The algorithm incorporates problem-specific components like local search and solution construction, enhancing its performance. When tested on benchmark instances, HACO outperformed existing metaheuristics in both speed and solution quality. The latest metaheuristic, a Ruin-and-Recreate algorithm called Slack Induction by String and Sweep Removals (SISSR), was introduced by \cite{Nguyen2021}. This approach effectively utilizes PDSTSP solution characteristics by implementing new removal operators during the ruin phase, which creates opportunities for solution improvement in the recreate phase. Additionally, \cite{Nguyen2021} introduced a new PDSTSP variant, the PDSVRP, allowing multiple trucks and focusing on minimizing total transportation costs. In \citet*{Raj2021}, a PDSVRP variant is presented, targeting the minimization of the time taken for all vehicles to return to the depot. The authors developed three MILP formulations, alongside a branch-and-price (BAP) algorithm and a BAP-based heuristic to solve the problem. Their exact methods optimally solved all small PDSTSP instances from \cite{murray2015flying} and three instances with 52 customers from \cite{mbiadou2018iterative}. Recently, \citet*{MBIADOUSALEU2021} extended the PDSTSP in a manner akin to the PDSVRP, resulting in the Parallel Drone Scheduling Multiple Traveling Salesman Problem. They proposed a hybrid Iterated Local Search, a MILP formulation, and a basic branch-and-cut approach for small instances. As previously noted, the majority of PDSTSP solution methods are heuristic in nature. Exact algorithm results are scarce, with optimal solutions reported only for small instances with up to 20 customers and select instances with 52 customers in \cite{murray2015flying, dell2020matheuristic, Raj2021}. No optimal solutions have been reported for 87 out of 90 benchmark instances with up to 229 customers created by \cite{mbiadou2018iterative}. This paper seeks to address this gap by introducing a straightforward yet effective exact branch-and-cut (B\&C) algorithm for the PDSTSP. Our experiments on the largest instances from \cite{mbiadou2018iterative} demonstrate that our approach can solve all but two instances within reasonable time limits. Furthermore, we introduce a new set of instances with up to 600 customers to provide more challenging scenarios for future solution method testing. We also present results from state-of-the-art algorithms on these instances to further evaluate their performance. The remainder of this paper is organized as follows: Section \ref{sec-formulation} details our MILP formulation and the valid inequalities that form the basis of the branch-and-cut algorithm proposed in Section \ref{sec-method}. Section \ref{sec-experiment} presents the experimental findings, and Section \ref{sec-conclusion} wraps up our study.

text: Amidst global endeavors to combat climate change and shift towards sustainable energy, wind power systems have seen remarkable growth and innovation in recent years \cite{darwish_al-dabbagh_2020}. Nevertheless, the deployment of wind turbines, particularly in offshore environments, often results in irregular loads, operational inconsistencies, and failures in various electrical and mechanical components of the turbines \cite{windenergy_journal}. Operations & maintenance (O&M) becomes crucial in addressing these issues through fault detection and diagnosis \cite{ATTOUI201411}, accounting for nearly one-third of the total energy generation cost \cite{seyr_muskulus_2019}. Condition-based monitoring (CBM) \cite{STETCO2019620} is pivotal in O&M, enabling the detection of operational changes and anomalies in turbines and their components. Over the past decade, there has been increasing interest in leveraging signal-processing techniques and physics-based models for CBM. More recently, the wind industry has embraced Artificial Intelligence (AI) techniques for data-driven decision-making in O&M, utilizing Supervisory Control & Data Acquisition (SCADA) data collected by turbine sensors. Explainable AI (XAI) models \cite{BARREDOARRIETA202082,8329419,app10093258} have been applied to provide interpretations and reasoning behind the predictions of traditional black-box AI models, such as identifying SCADA parameters that lead to faults \cite{windenergy_journal}. These techniques have been highly successful in predicting anomalies in turbine components \cite{anomaly_paperhongshan,electronics9050751,Bo_2019}, assessing wind resources \cite{MURTHY20171320,DAI2017378}, and forecasting critical operational parameters \cite{CHEN2018414,RePEc:eee:appene:v:241:y:2019:i:c:p:229-244,RePEc:eee:energy:v:201:y:2020:i:c:s0360544220308008} with high accuracy, which is vital for improving wind energy utilization efficiency \cite{LIU2020113324}. However, they often lack contextual information, such as detailed failure descriptions and maintenance reports, which are essential for achieving ambient intelligence in decision support. Furthermore, these techniques do not provide a solid foundation for critical concepts in the wind industry, such as maintenance strategies and their relation to other heterogeneous information sources like SCADA data, alarm logs, and failure images. Knowledge bases (KBs) or knowledge graphs (KGs) are crucial for informed decision-making by linking heterogeneous entities (such as sensor data) with contextual and semantic information \cite{amador-paper-kg}. KGs have been effectively used in several safety-critical fields, including healthcare for clinical decision support \cite{health_semantic}, power systems for optimizing service processes \cite{Yuan_2018}, manufacturing for process safety management \cite{MAO2020107094}, and finance for business decision-making \cite{kg_finance_yang}. Given the multidisciplinary nature of wind farm construction and management, as well as the interaction of multiple subsystems with external components, a systematic organization of knowledge in the wind industry can significantly assist developers, designers, and researchers in utilizing domain-specific information for decision support \cite{wes-5-259-2020}. Despite their potential, the application of KGs in the wind industry for explainable decision support remains limited. An early work by Zhu et al. \cite{4470371} developed a wind power plant information model using the web ontology language (OWL) for systematic management of domain-specific information. The ontology includes conceptual information for wind power plant management with classes based on turbine types and functional parts, embedded as semantic information with OWL descriptions. While this work highlights the potential of graph databases for managing complex information in the wind industry, it lacks practical demonstrations of the ontology's use cases in real-world information management and its applicability to O&M for decision support in turbines. Küçük and Arslan \cite{KUCUK2014484} developed a domain ontology for wind energy using web resources, particularly Wikipedia. Their semi-automatically constructed ontology covers the wind energy domain, including meteorological data, turbine sub-components, and monitoring systems, useful for question-answering systems during information retrieval. However, it lacks detailed insights into the wind industry and O&M of turbines, including SCADA data's role in anomaly prediction and power forecasting, and comprehensive technical descriptions for engineers and technicians. The paper does not showcase the KG's role in real-world decision support systems. Quaeghebeur et al. \cite{wes-5-259-2020} proposed a graph database for the wind energy domain, offering a conceptual overview of key terms and parameters like power curves and relationships between turbine components. Developed from scratch, this KG provides a foundational ontology for wind turbines, focusing on offshore wind power. While it offers valuable educational and training resources, it lacks descriptions of real-world turbine faults, alarm types, and maintenance strategies for failure prevention. Moreover, it does not demonstrate the KG's applicability to O&M or its use in explainable decision support in practical scenarios. These studies, while promising in structuring conceptual information in the wind industry, serve mainly as endpoints \cite{amador-paper-kg} without enabling further reasoning over the data. Additionally, querying these ontologies requires specialized programming languages, which may not be easily accessible to turbine engineers and technicians. The studies do not focus on O&M's critical aspects or their utility in decision-making systems for recommendations and predictions. We argue that the optimal use of KGs for decision support in the wind industry can be achieved by integrating O&M conceptual information with heterogeneous data, such as SCADA parameters, alarm types, turbine components, and maintenance strategies, and their interrelationships. This paper proposes the use of KGs for explainable decision support in the wind industry and their utility in real-world O&M applications. We introduce a novel KG, \textit{XAI4Wind}, and manually develop a domain-specific ontology for O&M in the wind industry. The proposed KG comprises 537 nodes and 1059 relationships (across 9 types), encompassing various heterogeneous data, including SCADA features, alarm types, turbine components, and maintenance strategies. We demonstrate use cases by showing that the KG can be interactively queried in Neo4j, with graph data science algorithms applied to generate insights during O&M. We utilize SCADA data from an operational turbine, interfacing it with an Explainable AI (XAI) model. Our KG plays a crucial role in decision support during turbine failures predicted by the XAI model, offering detailed fault conditions and maintenance actions. Unlike existing studies, our KG can be queried manually (via relevant syntactic commands) and automatically (integrated with the XAI model), paving the way for autonomous decision-making in the wind energy sector, complementing engineers' and technicians' decisions. According to Futia and Vetrò \cite{info11020122}, integrating KGs with XAI models can enhance decision-making through knowledge matching and interactive explanations. Figure ~\ref{intro_kgfig} illustrates an overview of our proposed KG and its demonstrated applications. The elements (SCADA data, XAI model, and predictions) interact mutually and can independently consult the KG for information retrieval. We have made the KG publicly available, allowing for future expansion as new terms, concepts, and maintenance strategies emerge in the wind industry. We anticipate that our work will lay the foundation for future research in utilizing KGs for O&M in the wind industry, enhancing the value of traditionally opaque AI models and advancing towards human-level intelligence. The paper is structured as follows: Section ~\ref{data_sec} details the datasets used for constructing the KG and demonstrating its application on an operational turbine. Section ~\ref{kg_databases} introduces KG databases and fundamental concepts. The development of the proposed KG is outlined in Section ~\ref{dev_kg}. Section ~\ref{use_kg} explores potential KG use cases in decision support. Section ~\ref{discussion} presents a brief discussion on experimental results and the KG's broader applicability to other turbines beyond the LDT. Finally, Section ~\ref{conclusion} concludes the paper and outlines future work directions.

text: In the contemporary digital landscape, Video Retrieval stands out as both a prominent and complex issue. The task involves ranking videos within a database according to their relevance to user-generated queries. Although many practical solutions rely on video metadata to simplify this into a straightforward page ranking challenge, numerous video databases lack annotated metadata. User queries can manifest in various formats, with textual input being the most prevalent. A widely recognized application of text-to-video retrieval is Google’s video search, which relies heavily on the metadata of videos within its search scope. Recent research has explored video retrieval using text queries, and performance in this area has seen significant advancements over time. This paper shifts focus to video retrieval via image queries, an area with comparatively less research. Existing methods face several limitations and numerous challenges that must be addressed. The foremost challenge is devising an efficient strategy for storing videos in the search database. Another unresolved challenge is leveraging the temporal information inherent in video data. Although image classification and object detection have achieved remarkable success in recent years, merely identifying objects in video frames fails to capture the temporal dynamics present in videos. We introduce a novel approach to tackle this issue. Initially, we preprocess the video database to extract essential features from the video frames. These features are then clustered so that similar frames are grouped together. We create embeddings for these clusters by combining the embeddings of their individual frames. To incorporate temporal information, we represent these clusters as nodes in a graph. Subsequently, we enhance the cluster embeddings by integrating information from adjacent clusters. These enriched cluster embeddings are stored and utilized in our video ranking process. Our proposed method was evaluated using the MSR-VTT dataset.

text: The evolution of cellular communication systems is poised to significantly expand the range of applications beyond what current 5G systems offer \cite{yazar6g}. These future systems will serve as a versatile platform, capable of delivering advanced features such as integrated sensing, flexible multi-band operations, and smart, sustainable, and secure communications. In this context, \ac{AI}, integrated sensing, and communication are anticipated to be pivotal components. The domain of \ac{V2X} and autonomous driving, which has garnered substantial interest recently, is expected to play a crucial role in these next-generation systems. For instance, the integration of \ac{MEC} with blockchain technology to create a novel, robust, and resilient architecture for V2X communications is explored in \cite{khan2021robust}. Companies like Google with Waymo, Baidu with Apollo, and Tesla with Autopilot have made significant strides in autonomous driving technologies \cite{Cusumano}, suggesting a future where fully autonomous vehicles are feasible. Despite these advancements, the secure communication technologies that underpin these systems remain relatively undeveloped. In the realm of security, several prominent \ac{IT} and cloud companies, including Google, IBM, Honeywell, and Microsoft, are gradually developing quantum computers. Over time, quantum computers are expected to achieve quantum supremacy, a claim supported by Google's recent industrial advancements \cite{arute2019quantum}. Devices equipped with quantum capabilities can tackle complex problems rapidly by executing numerous operations simultaneously. These quantum-enabled devices can also potentially compromise existing security protocols (such as \ac{TLS}, \ac{DTLS}, \ac{IPSec}), disrupt encryption schemes, and jeopardize secure communications. Consequently, it is imperative to employ algorithms that are resistant to quantum threats within security protocols across mobile networks to ensure secure communication. \ac{NIST} is actively addressing this issue by organizing a competition to identify the most effective algorithm against quantum attacks. Algorithms like NTRU, Saber, and Kyber have advanced to the final stage of this competition \cite{NIST_comp}. Upon completion of the \ac{NIST} competition, a single algorithm will be chosen as the standard \ac{QRSA} and implemented universally across devices, similar to how \ac{AES}/\ac{DES} emerged from previous \ac{NIST} competitions and are widely utilized today. Currently, existing encryption algorithms can be deployed on mobile devices in both software and hardware to facilitate the functioning of security protocols. However, a significant challenge arises with the implementation of \glspl{QRSA}. This challenge involves determining the method for executing computational processes within the algorithm. Analysis of existing \glspl{QRSA}, such as NTRU, Saber, and Kyber, reveals that the computational load on device \ac{CPU} cores for processing high-order polynomials is substantial. While existing encryption algorithms like \ac{AES} and \ac{ECC} are well-supported by current hardware capabilities, \glspl{QRSA} demand more computational resources due to their reliance on high-degree polynomials. Therefore, performing computations for a \ac{QRSA} based on these polynomials is challenging with the current software and hardware infrastructure. Addressing this issue necessitates an efficient computational and orchestration framework that comprehensively understands the topology of the mobile and \ac{V2X} networks and can adapt different computational strategies for each \ac{QRSA}. This paper makes the following contributions: \begin{itemize} \item We explore fundamental concepts and demonstrate the integration of post-quantum technologies with mobile network connectivity through the \ac{SCO} framework, highlighting potential use cases. (Sections \ref{Background} and \ref{frameworks}) \item We assess the integration of post-quantum methods into mobile networks through simulation analysis and discuss the resulting evaluations. (Section \ref{experiments}) \item From a standardization viewpoint, we outline current \glspl{SDO} initiatives and their potential impact on network management, orchestration, and post-quantum technologies. (Section \ref{standardization}) \end{itemize}

text: Recommender systems often represent user-item interactions and associated side information through a graph, comprising nodes (objects) and edges (relationships). These graphs, containing at least two node types—users ($u$) and items ($v$)—are classified as heterogeneous graphs, or heterographs. The expressive power of such graphs, combined with the advancements in graph-based methodologies~\cite{kipf2016gcn, schlichtkrull2018rgcn, wu2019simplifying, chen2020simple}, has led to a surge in interest in graph-based recommendation techniques~\cite{wang2019ngcf, chen2020revisiting, he2020lightgcn, wang2018ripplenet, Wang2019kgcn, wang2019kgat, fan2019graph, Liu2020Hetero}. To enhance representation efficacy, researchers have explored leveraging the interaction graph's structure by transmitting user and item embeddings across it. For instance, Wang \emph{et al.} introduced NGCF (neural graph collaborative filtering)~\cite{wang2019ngcf), drawing inspiration from graph convolutional networks (GCN)~\cite{kipf2016gcn}. Subsequently, LR-GCCF (linear residual graph convolutional collaborative filtering)~\cite{chen2020revisiting} and LightGCN~\cite{he2020lightgcn} demonstrated that omitting certain standard GCN components, such as non-linear activation and feature transformation, could enhance collaborative filtering (CF) performance. Despite notable advancements, these graph-based representation learning methods encounter challenges with data sparsity, a prevalent issue in real-world scenarios. As these methods weren't explicitly designed to tackle data sparsity, they risk significant performance drops. A common strategy to mitigate this issue is the incorporation of side information~\cite{GUO2017202}, which can bolster indirect node connections or enrich node features. Though recommendation-related textual information is rich in side information, many existing approaches~\cite{Wang2019kgcn, fan2019graph, wang2019kgat} overlook it, constraining their effectiveness. To address data sparsity, akin to HGNR (heterogeneous graph neural recommendation)~\cite{Liu2020Hetero}, we extend the interaction graph (Figure~\ref{fig:graph}-(a)) by adding description and comment nodes to form our heterograph (Figure~\ref{fig:graph}-(b)). However, merely incorporating these nodes doesn't inherently boost indirect user-item connections. Nonetheless, the text nodes possess abundant features, beneficial for refining user and item embeddings. Motivated by this, we employ advanced natural language processing (NLP) techniques to initialize text node embeddings, thereby integrating semantics to strengthen representation capabilities. Through node information propagation, user and item embeddings will incorporate textual insights, effectively mitigating data sparsity challenges. HGNR employs standard GCN for embedding learning on heterographs, translating the heterogeneous learning into a homogeneous one, potentially causing information loss and performance decline. RGCN (Relational Graph Convolutional Network), however, adeptly handles the multi-relational nature of heterographs by iteratively applying the GCN framework across various relations~\cite{schlichtkrull2018rgcn}. Thus, leveraging RGCN for information propagation on heterographs is more advantageous. Yet, standard RGCN isn't ideal due to its larger parameter scale compared to GCN on the same heterograph, complicating and inefficiency in training RGCN-based models. To overcome this, we propose a modified RGCN for heterograph information propagation. Firstly, as shown in \cite{wu2019simplifying, he2020lightgcn}, feature transformation and non-linear activation in standard GCN contribute minimally to CF performance. Consequently, we eliminate these components to streamline RGCN, enhancing its efficiency and performance. Secondly, we integrate the weighted layer combination from LightGCN~\cite{he2020lightgcn} and the initial residual from GCNII~\cite{chen2020simple} to further refine RGCN. Experimental results confirm that these RGCN modifications significantly boost recommendation performance. Upon obtaining efficient user and item embeddings through the modified RGCN's feature propagation, the recommender system's crucial component is the matching function. Most graph-based representation learning methods employ the inner product as the matching function~\cite{wang2019ngcf, he2020lightgcn, Wang2019kgcn, wang2019kgat}. However, in our constructed heterographs, description and comment nodes carry substantial semantics, rendering the simple linear inner product inadequate for these intricate features. To address the semantic features derived from GNN in heterographs, GraphRec~\cite{fan2019graph} concatenated user and item latent factors, using an MLP (multi-layer perception) for rating predictions. Concurrently, DeepCF~\cite{deng2019deepcf}, which applies an MLP neural network on the user-item interaction matrix, merges neural representation learning and neural matching function learning to overcome their respective limitations. Drawing inspiration from GraphRec and DeepCF, we devise a predictive network that merges graph-based representation learning with neural matching function learning to align with the semantics. Specifically, this integration captures low-rank user-item relations and jointly learns the complex matching function. In conclusion, our work contributes the following: \begin{itemize} \item We construct a heterograph and initialize text node embeddings using advanced NLP techniques to harness knowledge from related textual information. By employing a modified RGCN, semantics from these text nodes are propagated to derive user and item representations. \item Recognizing the inner product's ineffectiveness for complex semantics, we introduce a predictive framework that combines graph-based representation learning with neural matching function learning for enhanced prediction accuracy. \item We conduct comprehensive experiments on three benchmark datasets, and the results demonstrate our method's superior performance compared to several baselines. \end{itemize} The paper's structure is as follows: Section~\ref{sec: relatedwork} reviews related work; Section~\ref{sec: method} elaborates on the proposed model; Section~\ref{sec: experiment} presents and examines the experimental findings; finally, Section~\ref{sec: conclusion} concludes the paper.

text: Atrial Fibrillation (AF) is a cardiac condition that often remains undiagnosed for extended periods unless a cardiologist examines the patient's ECG report. AF impacts approximately 1\% of the global population \cite{zoni2014epidemiology}, with an estimated 2.3 million cases in the United States alone. To facilitate early detection and reduce incidence rates, ECG signals can be scrutinized using sophisticated AI methodologies. Essentially, ECG signals represent time-series data that can be systematically analyzed to identify AF by detecting irregularities. Figure 1 illustrates a standard ECG signal, where the labels P, Q, R, S, and T denote various components of the heart, specifically the atria and ventricles, through which electrical impulses travel.\\ The wave pattern indicative of AF is marked by: \\ 1) The absence of P waves. \\ 2) Inconsistent intervals between R points throughout the signal.\\ These characteristics are evident in Figure 2, which displays an ECG signal indicative of AF. The primary challenges in diagnosing AF through ECG analysis include:\\ 1) ECG signals are prone to random variations and low-frequency noise, which can lead to inconsistent diagnostic outcomes \cite{wu2020study}.\\ 2) Manual interpretation of ECG signals is inherently subjective and vulnerable to observer discrepancies, as non-AF signals may also show irregular RR intervals and lack P waves \cite{nurmaini2020robust}.

text: The integration of autonomous vehicles into traffic management systems is contingent upon their ability to safely navigate alongside human-operated vehicles on both highways and urban roads \cite{wu2017flow}. Ensuring this safe navigation is challenging due to the significant uncertainties inherent in real-world driving conditions, which complicate the driving task. Hamilton-Jacobi reachability analysis (HJI) is a common approach to identifying safe strategies when dealing with the unknown elements of a dynamic system \cite{bansal2017hamilton}. Previous studies have developed frameworks utilizing Hamilton-Jacobi reachability to shield systems from a single, known source of uncertainty, aiming to safeguard against the most adverse scenarios \cite{fisac2018general}. Nonetheless, actual driving conditions often involve multiple sources of uncertainty. As illustrated in Figures \ref{fig:sets} and \ref{fig:illustration}, focusing solely on extreme worst-case scenarios may render the formulation of a viable safety strategy impractical, potentially leading to situations where ensuring safety is unattainable. In response, this research explores methods to reduce the conservativeness of Hamilton-Jacobi safety analysis by incorporating structural elements into some or all human behavior models. We specifically examine a modeling approach that addresses a secondary disturbance, leveraging the structured nature of human behavior. This allows for the application of differential game theory in more complex and dynamic driving environments.
