text: The NILC-Metrix suite of metrics was crafted through a collaboration of funded initiatives and academic projects, including master's and doctoral research, at the Interinstitutional Center for Computational Linguistics (NILC)\footnote{\url{http://www.nilc.icmc.usp.br/}}, spanning from 2008 to 2021. This section provides an overview of the motivations for creating this comprehensive set of metrics, the developmental stages, and the re-implementation efforts to standardize the application of Natural Language Processing (NLP) tools. The impetus to construct a metric system for evaluating the complexity of Brazilian Portuguese (BP) texts automatically originated from the PorSimples project, which focused on simplifying Portuguese texts to enhance digital inclusion and accessibility \cite{candido-etal-2009-supporting,aluisio-gasperin-2010-fostering}. PorSimples aimed to assist individuals with limited literacy who seek information from web texts but struggle due to their rudimentary and basic literacy levels, as indicated by the INAF functional literacy metric\footnote{\url{https://ipm.org.br/inaf}}. Automatic text simplification is frequently approached as a method to reduce the lexical and syntactic complexity of texts while maintaining their meaning and informational content \cite{Carroll98practicalsimplification,Max2006,Shardlow2014}. Nonetheless, certain projects, such as Terence, require simplifications that enhance text comprehension at both local and global levels, ensuring coherent mental representations \cite{terence_2014}. Other initiatives, like Newsela\footnote{\url{https://newsela.com/}}, also pursue conceptual simplification, modifying content and form \cite{xu-etal-2015-problems}. Newsela's approach includes elaborations to clarify concepts and uses redundancies to underscore key information, while omitting unsuitable content for specific audiences. These simplification projects underscore the close relationship between textual complexity and simplification in NLP. The Terence project, for example, emphasizes coherence improvements, characterizing its simplification as cognitive. Newsela's approach is comprehensive in its operations, albeit not fully automated (though advancements have been noted by \cite{alva-manchego-etal-2017-learning}). In the PorSimples project, we developed \textbf{Facilita}, a system for adapting web content for readers with low literacy through lexical elaboration and named entity labeling \cite{Watanabe2010}. The simplification system, \textbf{Simplifica}, offered two levels of simplification—natural and strong—to assist individuals with basic and rudimentary literacy. To evaluate the textual complexity of the output and verify the success of the simplification, a multiclass textual complexity predictor was constructed using traditional machine learning techniques. This predictor necessitated extracting a set of metrics to evaluate text complexity and compute proxies for cohesion and coherence in Simplifica's automated simplifications. Thus, the Coh-Metrix-Port project was initiated \cite{Scarton2010a,Scarton2010b,Scarton2010c}. Prior to PorSimples, NILC conducted a readability study to adapt the Flesch Index to BP \cite{fleschport1996}, utilizing a corpus to determine the linear formula weights that assess word and sentence length across various text genres and sources. The Flesch Index \cite{flesch1948} posits that shorter words and sentences enhance readability. Although practical as a numerical indicator of text complexity, it does not specify operations to achieve shorter sentences. Additionally, it may lead to misconceptions, as brevity is not the sole factor in readability. Traditional readability formulas \cite{dalechall1948,gunning1952,fry1968,kincaidetal1975} have been criticized for being prescriptive rather than predictive tools for textual complexity \cite{crossley2008assessing}. These errors stem from misunderstanding that such formulas, lacking text comprehension theories, correlate superficial text measures with complexity levels previously determined by experts. Recognizing the limitations of traditional readability formulas, the Coh-Metrix-Port project adopted the Coh-Metrix framework to develop metrics for PorSimples. Coh-Metrix evaluates computational cohesion and coherence in written and spoken texts \cite{Graesser2004,Coh-Metrix_2011,graesser2014coh}, grounded in textual understanding and cognitive reading models \cite{kintsch1978toward,kintsch1973reading,kintsch1998comprehension}, which elucidate: (i) reader-text interactions, (ii) memory types involved in reading, e.g., how excessive pre-verb word usage burdens working memory and hinders sentence processing, (iii) the propositional content's role in speech \cite{kintsch1998comprehension}, asserting that enhanced text coherence boosts comprehension \cite{crossley2007toward}, and (iv) how cohesion mechanisms, like discourse markers and entity repetition, contribute to coherence. In essence, Coh-Metrix-Port, akin to the English Coh-Metrix tool\footnote{\url{http://cohmetrix.com/}}, employs a multilevel analysis framework for textual complexity evaluation. Coh-Metrix-Port encompasses 48 metrics within 10 categories. However, a prerequisite was using open-source NLP tools, limiting the implementation of syntactic metrics due to the absence of high-performing free parsers at that time. Consequently, the AIC tool (Automatic Analysis of the Intelligibility of the Corpus) was developed \cite{maziero2008ferramenta} as part of PorSimples. AIC comprises 39 metrics (primarily syntactic) based on the Palavras parser \cite{bick2000palavras} (details in Section 2). Following PorSimples' conclusion in 2010, additional metrics were incorporated into the original 48 from Coh-Metrix-Port and 39 from AIC. This included 25 new metrics from Coh-Metrix-Dementia \cite{CBMS_CMD_2015,Aluisio_Propor16}, created during a master's thesis. During Coh-Metrix-Dementia's implementation, Coh-Metrix-Port underwent its first re-implementation to standardize interfaces and NLP tool usage. For instance, the nlpnet PoS tagger \cite{evaluating_2015} was established as the default, integrating Coh-Metrix-Port's 48 metrics. In 2017, a NILC PhD student developed a large lexical base with 26,874 BP words, annotated with concreteness, age of acquisition, imageability, and subjective frequency (akin to familiarity) \cite{TSD2017}, facilitating the introduction of 24 psycholinguistic metrics. The project \textit{Personalisation of Reading using Automatic Complexity Classification and Textual Adaptation tools} expanded the metric set by 72, many focusing on lexical and syntactic simplicity. The RastrOS project\footnote{\url{https://osf.io/9jxg3/?view_only=4f47843d12694f9faf4dd8fb23464ea9}} introduced a new implementation for 10 semantic cohesion metrics using Latent Semantic Analysis (LSA) \cite{Landauer1997HowWC}, alongside normalized lexical frequency metrics. The LSA model, with 300 dimensions, was trained on the BrWaC corpus \cite{wagner-filho-etal-2018-brwac}, which, along with the Brasileiro corpus\footnote{\url{http://corpusbrasileiro.pucsp.br/}}, was used for lexical frequency calculations. NILC-Metrix represents the culmination of numerous NILC research endeavors. Between 2016 and 2017, its metrics were rigorously revised (some rewritten, others discarded, and several updated with new NLP resources) and thoroughly documented, with the documentation accessible online. The metrics are available via a Web interface\footnote{\url{http://fw.nilc.icmc.usp.br:23380/nilcmetrix}} and the code can be downloaded\footnote{\url{https://github.com/nilc-nlp/nilcmetrix}}, licensed under AGPLv3. For proper functionality, two parsers, Palavras and LX-parser \cite{LXparser_SilvaBCR10}, must be installed; Palavras is proprietary, while LX-parser's license restricts distribution\footnote{\url{http://lxcenter.di.fc.ul.pt/tools/en/conteudo/LX-Parser_License.pdf}}. In this paper, we delve into the specifics of NILC-Metrix and demonstrate its capabilities through three metric applications: (i) analyzing texts heard and read by children, contrasting film and series subtitles from the Leg2Kids project\footnote{\url{http://www.nilc.icmc.usp.br/leg2kids/}} with informative texts for elementary school children, compiled during the Coh-Metrix-Port and Adapt2Kids project \cite{Hartmann_Aluisio_2020}; (ii) developing a new textual complexity predictor for PorSimples' original and simplified text corpus, compared to the predictor in \cite{aluisio-etal-2010-readability}; and (iii) creating a textual complexity predictor using narrative transcripts from the Adole-Sendo project\footnote{\url{adole-sendo.info/}}. The paper is structured as follows: Section 2 details two tools from PorSimples foundational to NILC-Metrix. Section 3 introduces the metrics, organized into 14 classes, mirroring Coh-Metrix v3.0 for comparative ease. Section 4 discusses the corpora used in NILC-Metrix applications and the results of three metric experiments. Section 5 reviews studies employing NILC-Metrix metrics across various fields—Natural Language Processing, Neuropsychological Language Tests, Education, Language, and Eye-tracking studies. Finally, Section 6 offers concluding insights and future work suggestions.

In short, Coh-Metrix-Port, which is similar to the English Coh-Metrix, uses the same multi-level analysis for the evaluation of textual complexity as does the English Coh-Metrix (url: cohmetrix.com). In the course of the development of the Coh-Metrix-Port in 2010, additional metrics were added to the forty-eight Coh-Metrix-Port metrics and the thirty-nine AIC metrics. A prerequisite for the latter was the use of open-source NLP tools, which precluded the implementation of syntactic metrics, for lack of efficient free parsers. In the course of implementing Coh-Metrix-Dementia, Coh-Metrix-Port was given its first reimplementation to standardize the use of its interfaces and the choice of NLP tools. Among other things, it made the NLPNetPOS tagger (NBN:POSTERIOR16) the default tagger, with its 48 coh-metrics. Consequently, the AIC tool was developed, based on the Parser Palavras de Bick (details in section 2). The project textit: Personalisation of Reading Using Automatic Com-plexity Classification and Textual Adaptation Tools developed from the project RastrOS, which reimplemented ten semantic metrics based on latent semantic analysis, together with lexical frequency metrics normalized for the number of words. It also included twenty-five new metrics from Coh-Metrix-Dementia, which were created during a master's thesis. The LSA model with 300 dimensions was trained on the BrWaC corpus, cited by Wagner-Filho et al., BrWaC, which, together with the Brasileiro corpus, cited by Brasileiro et al., was used to calculate the frequency of lexical units. The NILC-Metrix is the result of many NILC projects. During the years of 2016 and 2017, it was carefully revised (some rewritten, others discarded, and some with new NLP resources), and its documentation was made public. The source code is available on github, licensed under the AGPL-v3 license. In this paper we present the NILC-Metrix system and show its functioning in three metric applications: (i) comparing the texts heard and read by children, in the case of the texts heard and read by the Leg2Kids project, comparing the films and series of the project Leg2Kids with the informational texts for elementary school students, compiled by the Coh-Metrix-Port project and the Adapt2Kids project (cite: Hartmann_Aluisio_2020); (ii) developing a new predictor for the original and simplified texts of the Por Simples project, compared with the predictor of Aluisio et al. (2010); and (iii) creating a predictor for the text complexity from the narrative transcripts of the Adole-Sendo project. The article is divided as follows: Section 2 describes the two tools of the PorSimples system on which NILC-Metrix is based; Section 3 presents the metrics, classified into fourteen classes to facilitate comparison with Coh-Metrix V3.0; Section 4 deals with the corpora used in the NILC-Metrix application and the results of three experiments; Section 5 deals with studies involving the NILC-Metrix metrics in various fields: natural language processing, neuropsychological tests of language, instruction, language, and eye-tracking studies. For proper functioning of NILC-Metrix two parsers are required: the palavras parser and the LX-parser (reference: LXparser_SilvaBCR10). The palavras parser is proprietary, but the LXparser is proprietary, but the LXparser license does not permit the distribution of it. Section 6 ends with a few insights and some suggestions for further research.

text: In this paper, we introduce a novel approach for actively sampling individuals within a population to curtail the spread of pandemics like COVID-19. Sampling algorithms, often employed in machine learning for acquiring training data labels in classification tasks ("active learning" \cite{AL-MJ, pz2006}) and in bandit algorithms \cite{bandit-wolpert} for navigating complex search spaces, form the foundation of our method. We extend these concepts to the realm of epidemic control within populations. The application of active sampling ideas in managing disease spread is predominantly explored within public health literature. Two main motivations underpin this focus on sampling, often overlapping in the context of population surveillance \cite{lee2010principles}. Firstly, sampling is used to estimate the true incidence or spread of a disease, such as HIV, in a population. Techniques like population surveys and "sentinel surveillance" \cite{magnani2005review, fylkesnes_studying_1998} have proven effective. Population surveys in areas with likely disease presence employ (stratified/cluster) random sampling, considered the gold standard despite high costs \cite{lee2010principles}. Conversely, sentinel surveillance collects data from specific venues ("sentinels," such as clinics) frequented by those likely to seek treatment. Recognizing that sensitive diseases like HIV may be prevalent in hard-to-reach groups engaged in illegal activities (e.g., sex workers, drug users), the literature \cite{magnani2005review, goel2010assessing} has examined alternative methods like snowball sampling (starting with a few infected individuals who then identify others), respondent-driven sampling (similar to snowball, but with longer chains and fewer referrals), and time-location sampling (e.g., sampling individuals in nightlife districts). With advancements in sensor data, new sampling methods have emerged; for instance, sampling locations with high movement has been effective in quantifying disease spread in livestock \cite{dawson2015sampling}. Secondly, sampling strategies aim to mitigate disease spread by identifying individuals for quarantine or testing. A prevalent method in public health is contact-tracing \cite{PhysRevE.66.056115, eames2003contact, underwood_contact_2003}, which involves sampling contacts of known infected individuals to detect the presence of disease. This approach, coupled with quarantine, was a primary mechanism during the COVID-19 pandemic \cite{salathe2020covid, hellewell2020feasibility}. Traditionally conducted through questionnaires, contact tracing has evolved with proposals for automated systems using cell phone proximity data \cite{ferretti2020quantifying}. The SARS-Cov-2 virus presents unique challenges that render existing sampling methodologies inadequate on their own: \begin{itemize} \item Pre-symptomatic and asymptomatic transmission excludes reliance on sentinel-based strategies that test symptomatic clinic visitors. Similarly, contact tracing alone is insufficient, as it only tracks contacts of confirmed positive cases, missing asymptomatic carriers who may also spread the virus. Thus, random sampling is essential. \item The virus's ability to persist on surfaces or in the air at certain locations suggests the utility of location-based sampling. \item Uncertainty regarding long-term immunity necessitates sampling strategies that allow for repeated testing of individuals. \item The evolving understanding of covariates affecting disease contraction and impact requires sampling strategies that target specific individuals rather than relying solely on covariate-based approaches. \item The pathogen's high infectivity and global spread impose constraints on testing capacities, necessitating prioritized testing to effectively control the spread. \end{itemize} Our proposed method addresses these five facets by employing dynamic active sampling strategies based on multi-armed bandit algorithms, which optimally integrate various sampling methodologies to generate real-time sampling lists. Bandit algorithms excel in balancing exploration with exploitation, a crucial aspect for SARS-Cov-2, where random sampling (exploration) must be dynamically combined with contact-tracing and location-based sampling (exploitation) based on incoming data. A significant feature of our approach is its focus on identifying specific individuals for testing, rather than relying on criteria or covariate-based sampling. Our algorithm operates within a high-uncertainty network environment, where initial contact information between individuals is partially observable and gradually revealed through sampling. The bandit algorithm employs Thompson sampling to navigate the trade-off between exploring unobserved nodes to identify potential hotspots and densifying observed areas to leverage acquired knowledge for testing. If densification is chosen, an inner-level upper confidence bounding (UCB) policy balances testing individuals with higher infection probabilities against those with greater informational uncertainty. We construct a heterogeneous network embedding to represent social interactions in a continuous latent space, quantifying individual proximity and infection risk. To model the interaction between sampling and the underlying environment, we use an agent-based model informed by realistic New York City data. Recent COVID-19 studies have explored predicting and mitigating disease spread through various intervention policies \cite{Keskinocak2020.07.22.20160036,Keskinocak2020.04.29.20084764, topirceanu2020centralized,atkeson2020will,ferguson2020report,chang2020modelling}, including case isolation, home quarantine, social distancing, travel restrictions, and school closures. These studies often integrate S/I/R (susceptible/infected/recovered) diffusion modeling \cite{hethcote2000mathematics,cooper2020sir} with Agent-Based Models (ABM) \cite{perez2009agent} to simulate infectious spread under different scenarios. An ABM of COVID-19 spread in New York City under varying quarantine policies was developed by \cite{hoertel2020facing}, serving as a basis for our ABM. Concurrently, \cite{grushka2020framework} proposed a framework using historical data to build a classifier determining a "risk score" for combining exploration and exploitation. While bandit-based testing algorithms are crucial, developing methods that address all noted complexities is challenging. Our work presents an adaptive, dynamic, and comprehensive method. Beyond testing, similar questions arise regarding vaccination targets. For instance, \cite{chen2020allocation} propose adaptive, dynamic covariate-based vaccination policies. Our framework accommodates vaccination within its dynamics, enabling the evaluation of combinational strategies like smart testing combined with vaccination. Our contributions are as follows: We introduce an innovative active sampling algorithm for pandemic management, specifically targeting COVID-19, with no existing methods addressing this problem in the literature. We develop a general multi-armed bandit framework capable of leveraging diverse information types, handling uncertainty in both disease dynamics and information, and focusing on individual-based rather than covariate-based sampling. We also contribute to modeling how bandit algorithms function in this context, constructing a heterogeneous network to capture social relations, neighborhood similarity, and community membership, which drives a two-level active sampling strategy. The integration of network embedding ideas within this heterogeneous network is novel. Additionally, we contribute to multi-armed bandit literature, addressing active search on graphs with limited literature on partially observed and dynamically changing networks and underlying disease dynamics. We model these scenarios and demonstrate strategic network expansion over time to support active sampling. \iffalse since we consider a scenario where the sampling is not independent of the environment, but itself affects the underlying mechanism. While there are similarities to reinforcement learning, the state-action space is so large to render existing reinforcement learning paradigms intractable for this problem.There are two levels of exploration/ exploitation trade-offs. First, the network structure is partially observable and can only be revealed gradually based on individual sampling. Second, since we do not have full knowledge of the disease states of the entire population, the probability of infections is not known and needs to be learnt as we sample their contacts and observe their test results. \fi Before delving into the specifics, it's crucial to underscore the necessity of smart testing strategies, even when tests are inexpensive or vaccines are available, for several reasons: \begin{itemize} \item Tests are never entirely free; the infrastructure for testing (production, distribution, result management) incurs significant costs. \item In cases of active infections with substantial economic impact, policymakers may need to incentivize individuals to undergo testing, particularly asymptomatic ones, which might entail compensating for quarantine time if mandated. \item Certain individuals may have a higher likelihood of being asymptomatic carriers or pose a greater societal risk when infected. Smart testing can help identify these individuals. \item Pandemics like COVID-19 are likely to recur, and there's no guarantee that future tests will be affordable, especially in early stages where active testing is crucial. Our methodology is applicable to mitigating any pandemic's spread. \item We view vaccines as complementary to testing, and as demonstrated, active testing strategies remain crucial alongside vaccinations as part of a comprehensive pandemic eradication strategy. \end{itemize}

text: The primary aim of a regression model is to establish a function $f:\mathcal{X}\rightarrow\mathcal{Y}$ from a dataset consisting of pairs $(x_m,y_m)\in \mathcal{X}\times \mathcal{Y}, \ m=1,\ldots,M,$ ensuring that $y_m\approx f(x_m)$ while mitigating overfitting issues \cite{wahba1990spline,gyorfi2006distribution,hastie2009overview}. Here, $\mathcal{X}$ represents the input space, and $\mathcal{Y}$ denotes the range of possible outputs. A prevalent approach to achieve this involves solving the minimization problem given by \begin{equation} \min_{f\in \mathcal{F}} \left( \sum_{m=1}^M { E}\left(f(x_m),y_m\right) + \mathcal{R}(f)\right), \end{equation} where $\mathcal{F}$ denotes the search space, the convex loss function ${ E}:\mathcal{Y}\times\mathcal{Y}\rightarrow\mathbb{R}_{\geq 0}$ ensures the mapping's consistency with the data, and the regularization functional $\mathcal{R}:\mathcal{F}\rightarrow \mathbb{R}_{\geq 0}$ incorporates prior information about the form of $f$, aimed at reducing overfitting. \subsection{Nonparametric regression} In certain scenarios, the optimization is performed over an infinite-dimensional function space. A notable example is the family of reproducing-kernel Hilbert spaces (RKHS) $\mathcal{F}=\mathcal{H}(\mathbb{R}^d)$, with $\mathcal{X}= \mathbb{R}^d$ and $\mathcal{Y}=\mathbb{R}$ \cite{poggio1990networks,poggio1990regularization}. Here, the regression task is formulated as \begin{equation} \min_{f\in \mathcal{H}(\mathbb{R}^d)} \left(\sum_{m=1}^M { E}\left(f(\boldsymbol{x}_m),y_m\right) + \lambda \|f\|_{\mathcal{H}}^2\right). \end{equation} A cornerstone of RKHS theory is the kernel representer theorem \cite{kimeldorf1971some,scholkopf2001generalized}, which asserts that the unique solution to \eqref{Eq:RKHS} can be expressed as a kernel expansion \begin{equation} f(\cdot) = \sum_{m=1}^M a_m {\rm k}(\cdot,\boldsymbol{x}_m), \end{equation} where ${\rm k}:\mathbb{R}^d\times\mathbb{R}^d\rightarrow\mathbb{R}$ is the unique reproducing kernel of $\mathcal{H}(\mathbb{R}^d)$, and $a_m\in\mathbb{R},m=1,\ldots,M,$ are the parameters to be learned. This expansion \eqref{Eq:KernelExpansionL2} transforms the infinite-dimensional problem~\eqref{Eq:RKHS} into a finite-dimensional one, allowing the use of standard convex analysis tools to solve it. This approach underlies many classical kernel-based methods, including support-vector machines and radial-basis functions \cite{scholkopf2001learning,evgeniou2000regularization,steinwart2008support}. \subsection{Parametric regression} When \eqref{Eq:GeneralSupervisedLearning} cannot be transformed into a finite-dimensional optimization problem, another common strategy is to confine the search space $\Spc F$ to a subspace that can be parameterized. This is the approach taken by deep neural networks (DNNs), which have gained significant traction in machine learning and data science \cite{LeCun2015,Goodfellow2016}. DNNs have surpassed traditional kernel-based methods in numerous image-processing applications, becoming the benchmark for image classification \cite{Krizhevsky2012}, solving inverse problems \cite{jin2017deep}, and image segmentation \cite{Ronneberger2015}. Despite their empirical success, the superior performance of DNNs remains not fully understood. Consequently, recent research has increasingly focused on the theoretical study of DNNs. In these studies, {\it stability} and {\it interpretability}, essential principles in machine learning, are central themes. For instance, the stability of advanced deep-learning methods has faced significant challenges in image classification \cite{moosavi2016deepfool,fawzi2017robustness} and image reconstruction \cite{antun2020instabilities}. Various attempts have been made to interpret DNNs through different lenses, such as rate-distortion theory \cite{macdonald2019rate,heiss2020distribution}. However, these topics remain active research areas, and a comprehensive understanding is yet to be achieved. \subsection{Our Contributions} In this paper, we propose two variational frameworks for regressing one-dimensional data, emphasizing the development of ``stable'' and ``simple'' regression models. These frameworks, akin to RKHS theory, involve nonparametric continuous-domain problems where $\mathcal{F}$ in \eqref{Eq:GeneralSupervisedLearning} is an infinite-dimensional function space. Guided by the stability principle, our focus is on creating regression schemes with controlled Lipschitz regularity, a significant consideration given that many analyses in deep learning necessitate assumptions on the Lipschitz constant of the learned function \cite{arjovsky2017wasserstein,bora2017compressed,neyshabur2017exploring}. Moreover, when a trainable module is integrated into an iterative-reconstruction framework, the convergence rate of the entire scheme frequently depends on the Lipschitz constant of this module \cite{gupta2018cnn,zhang2017beyond,sun2020block,liu2020rare,wu2020simba,bohra2021learning}. Our first formulation incorporates the Lipschitz constant of the learned function as a regularization term, leading to the minimization problem \begin{equation} \min_{f\in{\rm Lip}(\mathbb{R})} \left( \sum_{m=1}^M { E}\left(f(x_m),y_m\right) + \lambda L(f) \right), \end{equation} where ${\rm Lip}(\mathbb{R})$ denotes the space of Lipschitz-continuous real functions and $L(f)$ represents the Lipschitz constant of $f\in {\rm Lip}(\mathbb{R})$. By adjusting the regularization parameter $\lambda$, one can implicitly manage the Lipschitz regularity of the learned function. We establish a representer theorem that delineates the solution set of \eqref{Eq:LipRegIntro}, demonstrating that the global minimum is achieved by a continuous and piecewise-linear (CPWL) mapping. Furthermore, inspired by the simplicity principle, we identify the mapping with the fewest linear regions. text: The ability to detect novel or anomalous events is crucial for humans to identify potential threats and opportunities. This capability is essential in various scenarios, such as identifying unusual patterns in natural systems, recognizing security threats, or detecting equipment failures. Although anomaly detection (AD) techniques for images \cite{reiss2021panda,hendrycks2019using,tack2020csi} cover a wide range of data domains, video AD has predominantly concentrated on surveillance footage. In these videos \cite{luo2017revisit,mahadevan2010anomaly}, typically captured by security cameras, normal pedestrian movement is often classified as the standard behavior, while activities like cycling or crowding are considered anomalies. Recent years have seen a surge in innovative methods that have enhanced performance on these benchmarks \cite{georgescu2021anomaly,park2020learning}. Despite this progress, other categories of video anomalies remain largely unexplored in current research. This study delves into various types of anomalies, evaluating diverse methodologies to address them. We focus on physical irregularities in the movement or path of an object, which have been significantly underrepresented, and introduce new benchmarks for video anomaly detection.

text: Deep neural networks (DNNs) have revolutionized performance across numerous fields. Selecting an optimal DNN architecture is crucial for adapting a DNN to new tasks and achieving superior results. However, the architecture's complexity, dictated by numerous hyperparameters such as convolutional layer filter sizes and inter-layer connections, demands significant human expertise and effort to optimize. Neural architecture search (NAS) emerges as a promising solution, automating the discovery of advanced DNN architectures and addressing the challenges in deploying DNNs to novel tasks. The substantial computational demands (in terms of both time and space) of NAS pose significant challenges, particularly for commercial applications without access to multiple high-performance GPUs. Thus, minimizing NAS's computational burden is a critical research focus. One-shot NAS addresses time complexity by concurrently optimizing both architecture and parameters (weights) in a single or limited number of training processes. This approach utilizes a comprehensive deep learning model, termed the parent network, which encompasses all potential architectures within the search space as sub-networks. The parent network retains all parameters needed by candidate architectures, sharing them across different architectures. This parameter sharing allows for architecture evaluation using shared parameters, significantly reducing computational time compared to traditional methods that require training parameters from scratch for each candidate. From a GPU memory perspective, one-shot NAS can be divided into dense propagation NAS (DP-NAS) and sparse propagation NAS (SP-NAS). DP-NAS necessitates loading the entire parent network into GPU memory for forward and/or backward propagation, while SP-NAS only requires loading a sub-network. DP-NAS is widely adopted due to the success of DARTS and its derivatives \cite{liu2018darts,xie2018snas,yao2020nasp}. However, its high memory usage restricts the search space. SP-NAS overcomes these limitations, enabling more versatile search spaces on GPUs with constrained memory. Therefore, this study concentrates on SP-NAS. To further alleviate the computational demands of one-shot SP-NAS, we introduce a novel method called \emph{AdvantageNAS}. While various factors, such as performance estimation and search space, impact NAS performance, and state-of-the-art (SOTA) results may require exploring optimal combinations of these factors, our study focuses on the search strategy. Our aim is not to achieve the SOTA architecture but to explore the search strategy's efficiency. AdvantageNAS is a gradient-based SP-NAS.\footnote{Gradient-based approaches offer several benefits. Unlike methods using evolutionary algorithms (e.g., \cite{real2017evo}) or progressive search techniques (e.g., \cite{liu2018pnas}), which require defining mutation or expansion strategies tailored to the search space, gradient-based methods avoid such manual preparations. Furthermore, these methods are easily implementable in most contemporary deep learning frameworks, thanks to their support for automatic differentiation of deep neural networks.} This NAS category includes ENAS \cite{pham2018enas}, ProxylessNAS \cite{cai2018proxylessnas}, PARSEC \cite{casale2019parsec}, and GDAS \cite{xuanyi2019gdas}. These techniques introduce a parametric probability distribution family from which architectures are sampled, updating the distribution parameter using the gradient of the objective function estimated via the Monte Carlo method, thereby indirectly optimizing the architecture. Intuitively, reducing the gradient estimate's variance enhances search efficiency. Drawing inspiration from the actor-critic approach \cite{konda2000ac}, we incorporate the concept of \emph{advantage}, which addresses the well-known \emph{credit assignment} issue in policy gradients \cite{Minsky:1961:ire}. We conduct both theoretical and empirical evaluations of AdvantageNAS. Empirical results demonstrate its effectiveness across various tasks with differing search spaces, while theoretical analyses assure its performance on tasks not previously encountered empirically. Although theoretical studies are relatively rare in NAS research, they are crucial for exploring NAS search strategies. Our contributions are as follows: \begin{itemize} \item We introduce AdvantageNAS, a novel SP-NAS. In a test scenario, we show that it reduces the gradient estimation variance compared to REINFORCE \cite{Williams1992}, a baseline search strategy for ENAS. \item Our theoretical analysis confirms that AdvantageNAS's estimated gradient is an unbiased estimator of the expected loss gradient. This unbiasedness suggests that AdvantageNAS consistently improves the expected loss, ensuring convergence. Additionally, reducing gradient variance enhances the lower bound of loss improvement in each iteration. \item We compared AdvantageNAS with various gradient-based NAS methods across three distinct settings to demonstrate its effectiveness on different search spaces. All experiments were conducted using the same code base to ensure fair comparison of search strategies.\footnote{The literature often compares NAS approaches using different components like search spaces and training protocols. However, as noted in \cite{Yang2020iclr}, such variations complicate fair comparisons of each component's contributions. Our code: \url{https://github.com/madoibito80/advantage-nas}.} The findings reveal that AdvantageNAS converges more swiftly than existing SP-NAS methods. \end{itemize}

The Wasserstein barycenter (WB) is a widely used tool in statistics and machine learning for integrating data from multiple origins while preserving their intrinsic geometric characteristics~\cite{martial11}. The problem is formulated as follows: consider $k$ discrete probability distributions $\mu_1,\ldots,\mu_k$ on $\mathbb{R}^d$. With non-negative weights $\lambda_1,\ldots,\lambda_k$ summing to $1$, and a class $\mathbb{P}$ of probability distributions on $\mathbb{R}^d$, a Wasserstein barycenter under the $L_p$ objective for some $p>0$ is a distribution $
u\in\mathbb{P}$ that minimizes  egin{equation} \sum_{i=1}^k\lambda_iW_p(\mu_i,
u)^p, \end{equation} where $W_p(\mu_i,
u)$ denotes the $p$-Wasserstein distance. The Wasserstein barycenter effectively encapsulates the geometric notion of centrality among data points by employing the optimal transport distance~\cite{bertsimas1997introduction} across several datasets. Consequently, Wasserstein barycenters have found extensive applications in machine learning~\cite{srivastava2018scalable}, data science~\cite{ruschendorf2002n,elvander2020multi}, image processing~\cite{rubner1997earth}, computer graphics~\cite{pele2009fast}, and statistics~\cite{villani2008optimal}, with uses in constrained clustering~\cite{cuturi2014fast, ho2017multilevel}, Bayesian learning~\cite{srivastava2018scalable}, texture mixing~\cite{rabin2011wasserstein}, and shape interpolation~\cite{solomon2015convolutional}. However, computing the Wasserstein barycenter is NP-hard \cite{AltschulerB21, BorgwardtP21}, and many approximation algorithms are hampered by significant computational demands, particularly in high-dimensional datasets~\cite{MuzellecC19}. Indeed, \cite{altschuler2021wasserstein} provides an algorithm with runtime exponentially dependent on the dimension, illustrating the "curse of dimensionality." To mitigate these computational challenges, we explore dimensionality reduction for Wasserstein barycenter computation. Dimensionality reduction can enhance the performance of algorithms on high-dimensional datasets across various contexts, as discussed in~\cite{cunningham2015linear}. Specifically for Wasserstein barycenters, dimensionality reduction offers practical and theoretical advantages, such as reduced storage requirements, faster distance computations, and flexibility: it can be a preprocessing step compatible with \emph{any} Wasserstein barycenter algorithm. \subsection{Our Results} This paper investigates dimensionality reduction techniques for computing the Wasserstein barycenter of discrete probability distributions. Our findings demonstrate that it is feasible to project distributions into lower dimensions while retaining the barycenter's quality. A cornerstone of dimensionality reduction is the Johnson-Lindenstrauss (JL) lemma~\cite{johnson1984extensions}, which asserts that projecting a dataset of $N$ points into approximately $O(\log N)$ dimensions suffices to preserve all pairwise distances. Applying the JL lemma, we first establish that the distributions can be assumed to reside in $O(\log(nk))$ dimensions, where $k$ is the number of input distributions, $n$ is the barycenter support size, and each input distribution has support size $\poly(n)$. For $p=2$, a closed form for the cost of any candidate barycenter exists, based on the pairwise distances within the input distributions. Thus, our bound stems from the presence of $k \cdot \poly(n)$ point masses across all distributions, and projecting them into $O(\log(nk))$ dimensions suffices to maintain pairwise distances. However, for $p
eq 2$, no closed form exists for the optimal cost, making distance preservation insufficient. Instead, we utilize a Lipschitz extension theorem, specifically the Kirszbraun theorem, to "invert" the dimensionality reduction map and argue for cost preservation under a general $L_p$ objective. Further details are in Section~ef{sec:log(nk) reduction}. 	extbf{Dimensionality reduction independent of $k$.} Although the JL lemma is known to be tight~\cite{LarsenN16, LarsenN17}, dimensionality guarantees can be improved for \emph{specific} problems, such as various clustering formulations \cite{CohenEMMP15,BecchettiBC0S19,MakarychevMR19}. Our main result shows that we can surpass the $O(\log(nk))$ bound from the JL lemma and Kirszbraun theorem. We demonstrate that projecting onto $O(\log n)$ dimensions suffices, independent of the number of distributions $k$. In fact, we prove a stronger result: projecting the distribution support points onto $O(\log n)$ dimensions preserves the cost of objective \eqref{eq:bary def} for \emph{any} distribution $
u$ supported on at most $n$ points (Theorem~ef{thm:jl:main}). This theorem implies that any approximation algorithm or heuristic for the Wasserstein barycenter can be combined with dimensionality reduction. Below is a simplified version of our theorem, omitting some parameters for clarity.  egin{theorem}[Theorem ef{thm:jl:main} Simplified] Let $\mu_1,\ldots,\mu_k$ be discrete probability distributions on $\mdef{\mathbb{R}}^d$ such that $|	extrm{supp}(\mu_i)| \le \poly(n)$ for all $i$. There exists a dimensionality reduction map $\pi:\mathbb{R}^d	o\mathbb{R}^m$ for $m=O(\log n)$ such that projection under $\pi$ preserves the cost of objective \eqref{eq:bary def} for any $
u$ supported on at most $n$ points. \end{theorem} This result is striking because the projected dimension is independent of the number of input distributions $k$, which could be much larger than $n$. Therefore, the random projection map $\pi$ cannot guarantee preserving most pairwise distances between the support points of the $k$ distributions. Our primary tool is a "robust" Lipschitz extension theorem from \cite{MakarychevMR19} for $k$-means clustering, adapted to the Wasserstein barycenter problem's geometry. 	extbf{Optimality of dimensionality reduction.} We complement our upper bound results by proving that the dimension bound of $\log n$ is \emph{tight} when using a random Gaussian matrix as the projection map. We also show that the JL lemma is tight for computing optimal transport between two distributions with support size $n$. Specifically, we present a lower bound indicating that $\Omega(\log n)$ dimensions are necessary for a random projection to preserve the optimal transport cost. Thus, our findings reveal a distinction between the geometries of the optimal transport and Wasserstein barycenter problems, as we surpass the JL bound in the latter. 	extbf{Hardness of approximation.} Additionally, we establish the NP-hardness of approximation for the Wasserstein barycenter problem. Specifically, it is NP-hard to find an approximate barycenter within a factor of $1.0013$ of the optimal cost if the barycenter's support size is restricted. This complements recent findings by \cite{AltschulerB21, BorgwardtP21} that computing sparse Wasserstein barycenters is NP-hard. 	extbf{Coresets for Wasserstein barycenters.} To further reduce dataset complexity, coresets can be employed to minimize the number of input points instead of the input dimension $d$. If the number of input distributions $k$ significantly exceeds the support size $n$, we demonstrate the existence of a weighted subset $C$ of approximately $\poly(n)$ distributions. Computing the optimal barycenter on $C$ is equivalent to doing so on the original input, with minimal approximation loss. Consequently, using subset $C$ can enhance efficiency in downstream algorithms involving Wasserstein barycenters. Moreover, the coreset approach is compatible with our dimensionality reduction techniques. Our methods allow simultaneous reduction of both the input distribution size $k$ and the data dimension $d$, while maintaining optimal clustering within a small approximation factor. In Supplementary Section ef{sec:sup_constrained}, we explore a connection between the Wasserstein barycenter problem and constrained low-rank problems, encompassing examples like singular value decomposition (SVD) and $k$-means clustering. Although this connection does not yield improved results, it categorizes the Wasserstein barycenter within a broader class of problems, potentially leading to future applications. 	extbf{Experiments.} Finally, we present experimental evaluations of our proposed methodology. Our findings suggest that dimensionality reduction can be combined with \emph{any} Wasserstein barycenter algorithm to retain the algorithm's approximation guarantees. Specifically, we showcase real high-dimensional datasets where solving the Wasserstein barycenter problem in reduced dimensions results in computational savings while maintaining solution quality. Experiments in Section ef{sec:experiments} demonstrate that on natural datasets, the dimension can be reduced by $1$-$2$ orders of magnitude with only a $5\%$ increase in solution cost. We also empirically evaluate our coreset construction, showing reduced error and fewer required samples compared to simple uniform sampling. \subsection{Related Work} The NP-hardness of computing sparse Wasserstein barycenters was established by \cite{AltschulerB21, BorgwardtP21}, leading most algorithmic efforts to focus on approximating Wasserstein barycenters within an additive $\varepsilon$ of the optimal cost. \cite{agueh2011barycenters} initially examined approximating Wasserstein barycenters under conditions where either (1) distributions $\mathbb{P}$ have discrete support on $\mathbb{R}$, (2) $k=2$, or (3) $\mu_i$ are multivariate Gaussians in $\mathbb{R}^d$. While there is ongoing research on barycenters of continuous distributions, e.g.,~\cite{alvarez2016fixed,chewi2020gradient}, our focus is on discrete input distributions. For these, the literature primarily categorizes based on barycenter support assumptions~\cite{altschuler2021wasserstein}. 	extbf{Fixed-support.} The "fixed-support approximation" algorithms assume the barycenter's support is among a predetermined set of points. These algorithms then solve a polynomial-size linear program associated with the set~\cite{cuturi2014fast,benamou2015iterative,carlier2015numerical,staib2017parallel,kroshnin2019complexity,lin2020fixed}. Unfortunately, the potential points often must form an $\varepsilon$-net over the entire space, leading to a size of $1/\varepsilon^d$, which is susceptible to the curse of dimensionality. Nevertheless, for constant dimensions, these algorithms typically run in $\poly(n,k,D/\varepsilon)$ time, where $D$ bounds the support diameters of input distributions. This is further enhanced by \cite{altschuler2021wasserstein}, achieving runtime $\poly(n,k,\log(D/\varepsilon))$. 	extbf{Free support.} Another algorithm class makes no assumptions about the optimal barycenter's support. These "free-support algorithms" optimize over the entire set of potential barycenters, which can number up to $n^k$. Consequently, these algorithms, e.g.,~\cite{cuturi2014fast,LuiseSPC19}, either have exponential runtime or rely on heuristics lacking theoretical guarantees. \cite{altschuler2021wasserstein} demonstrated how to explore the $n^k$ possible points in polynomial time for fixed $d$.

text: Dhrupad stands as one of the most ancient traditions in North Indian classical vocal music. Typically, a Dhrupad concert features a solo vocalist or a duo leading the performance, accompanied by a pakhawaj player providing percussion, while a tanpura delivers a continuous harmonic drone in the background\cite{bonnie_wade}. A Dhrupad recital, which extends over an hour, begins with an intricate, unaccompanied \textit{raga alap} and transitions into the \textit{bandish}, a composed piece performed with the percussion. The bandish serves both as a standalone piece and a foundation for rhythmic improvisation (\textit{laykari}), where the singer articulates the bandish syllables in varied rhythmic densities and configurations \cite[chapter~10]{clayton}. Throughout the performance, the pakhawaj player may execute a basic pattern (\textit{theka}) of the metric cycle (\textit{tala}), improvise rhythmically in response to the vocalist, or perform a free solo improvisation while the vocalist delivers lines of the fixed composition or refrain \cite[p.~111]{clayton}. \\ Figure~\ref{fig:concert_structure} illustrates the structural flow of a bandish performance from the vocalist's perspective. The intermediate refrain portions are the non-improvised segments where the singer performs a line or fragment of the bandish before returning to a phase of improvisation.\\ A notable distinction between Khyal and Dhrupad bandish performances lies in the interplay between the lead and accompanying percussion instruments. In Khyal, musicians typically alternate improvisations while the other maintains the basic rhythm or refrain. Conversely, in Dhrupad, there are instances where both the vocalist and percussionist improvise simultaneously. Therefore, a comprehensive segmentation of a Dhrupad bandish performance requires rhythmic descriptions of both un-improvised and improvised sections for each element—the vocals and the pakhawaj.\\ Several additional segmentation levels can be applied to this musical form. One level could focus on identifying un-improvised and improvised music sections. Given that the bandish text itself is structured with sections positioned at various octave points, each containing a few lines, another segmentation level could focus on which section the vocalist is presenting or improvising upon. While the former segmentation might be characterized by changes in rhythmic qualities, the latter would rely more on melodic features. Furthermore, variations in timbral attributes, linked to articulation styles accompanying rhythmic or melodic shifts, could assist in each type of segmentation.\\ The aim of this study is to devise automated methods for the structural segmentation of Dhrupad bandish concerts, relying solely on the tempo and rhythmic density relationships of the individual instruments. Recognizing the challenges in detecting vocal onsets—especially in isolated vocals due to the inherent diversity in singing—we explore alternative techniques for directly estimating local rhythmic density. We adopt a similar strategy for estimating the evolving surface tempo or rhythmic density throughout a concert audio. Given the notable advancements in audio source separation recently, we also investigate the application of source separation followed by tempo estimation for each instrument (vocals and pakhawaj) to provide a comprehensive description of each section.\\ The primary contributions of this research include: (i) compiling a dataset with tempo markings and rhythmic density-based structural segmentation annotations for Dhrupad bandish concerts, (ii) adapting a cutting-edge tempo estimation method to estimate local surface tempo or rhythmic density within the polyphonic mix, and (iii) employing source separation to extend this estimation to each instrument (vocals and pakhawaj), ultimately achieving a musically meaningful segmentation of bandish concerts with section labels defined by rhythmic density inter-relationships.

text: The prediction of stock market returns and volatility has garnered significant interest from both academic circles and the financial sector. A pertinent question arises: Is it feasible to forecast stock market prices and their volatility? Or, at the very least, can predictions be made at certain times? Extracting sentiment from online platforms like Twitter and financial news articles proves advantageous in formulating trading strategies. Moreover, sentiment derived from financial news may possess predictive capabilities that portfolio and risk managers can exploit. Our analysis yields conclusions that can be categorized into three distinct segments. Initially, we observed that correlations between sentiment scores and stock market returns were statistically significant exclusively within our headline dataset. Specifically, a statistically significant negative correlation was found between negative news and the closing price of the FTSE100 index (returns). The most pronounced correlation between sentiment and volatility metrics was evident in our tweets dataset, whereas the headlines and news stories dataset exhibited either no correlation or a weak one. This discrepancy can be attributed to the immediacy and reactivity of tweets to events, contrasting with the longer publication time for articles, aligning with the market adage, "Buy on rumors, sell on news." This paper is organized as follows. Section \ref{sec:related} delves into related research. In Section \ref{sec:data}, we outline the data sources employed for sentiment score computation, including Thomson Reuters, RavenPack, and Twitter. Section \ref{sec:correlation} presents a correlation analysis alongside Granger's causality test. In Section \ref{sec:lda}, we explore whether topic modeling, specifically Latent Dirichlet Allocation, can improve the accuracy of predicting the next day's stock market directional volatility. Finally, Sections \ref{sec:results} and \ref{sec:conclusion} detail our analytical findings and propose directions for future research.

text: The automation of robot design and fabrication has been significantly advanced by a growing body of research that introduces tools, optimizes methods, and proposes novel algorithms (e.g.,~\citep{Luck-RSS-17,Schulz17,HoovFearing08,pervan2018low,zhang2020abstractions}). Among these, algorithms that focus on resource management or minimization are of particular importance (see~\citep{censi17co}). Our interest lies specifically in memory, not due to its cost, but because reducing state requirements often reveals insights into the core informational structure of specific robotic tasks~(cf.~\citep{connell90,donald95information}). Consequently, we concentrate on filter reduction, specifically targeting combinatorial filters as introduced by LaValle~\citep{lavalle10sensing}. These filters are discrete counterparts to the probabilistic estimators prevalent in contemporary robotics, offering particularly elegant solutions for certain practical tasks (e.g., see \citep{tovar2014combinatorial}). Although the minimization of combinatorial filters is straightforward to articulate and comprehend, ongoing research~\citep{okane2013reduction,o2017concise,saberifar2017combinatorial,rahmani2018relationship,zhang20cover,rahmani2020integer} reveals its underlying complexity. To illustrate the concept of filter minimization, consider the scenario depicted in Figure~\ref{fig:motivating_scenario}, featuring a safari park with a vehicle rental service. Each rental car is equipped with a compass and an intelligent gear-shifting system. The compass records the vehicle's heading before and after movement, such as `nw' indicating a change from north to west. The gear system uses these compass readings to automatically shift gears, ensuring compliance with speed limits. The roads have three speed limit categories: ($a$) 15 to 30 (gray), ($b$) below 30 (brown), or ($c$) under 15 (green). Vehicles can travel at a maximum speed of 15 in low gear and between 15 and 30 in high gear. A basic gear-shifting system that adheres to these limits is represented by the filter in Figure~\ref{fig:motivating_input}. In this diagram, each vertex signifies a system state, each edge denotes a state transition, and the edge labels represent compass readings. A vertex is colored gray for high gear output, green for low gear, or both if either gear is permissible (via, for example, a nondeterministic choice). Our goal is to identify a minimal filter, such as the one in Figure~\ref{fig:motivating_minimal}, that achieves the desired behavior with the fewest states. The initial step involves constructing a discrete state-transition system (as shown in Figure~\ref{fig:motivating_input}) based on the problem description. The subsequent step is to apply an algorithm capable of compressing this system. Despite its apparent similarity to the state minimization problem in deterministic automata, addressed by the efficient Myhill--Nerode reduction~\citep{hopcroft06introduction}, combinatorial filter minimization is NP-complete~\citep{okane2013reduction}. Some research focuses on filter minimization through merger operations, reducing the problem to graph coloring~\citep{okane2013reduction,o2017concise,saberifar2017combinatorial} or integer linear programming~\citep{rahmani2020integer}. Saberifar et al.~\citep{saberifar2017combinatorial} explored special cases, approximations, and parameterized complexity in filter minimization. Rahmani and O'Kane~\citep{rahmani2018relationship} demonstrated that the traditional concept of \emph{bisimulation} often leads to sub-optimal solutions. They introduced three distinct integer linear programming formulations to find the smallest equivalence relation~\citep{rahmani2020integer}. Recent studies indicate that both merge and split operations are essential for obtaining a minimal filter~\citep{zhang20cover}. This approach frames the problem as a clique cover task, constrained by the requirement that the output filter must be deterministic and simulate the input filter's output. However, both criteria involve exponentially large constraints, posing significant computational challenges. In this paper, we introduce an alternative formulation of the filter minimization problem, characterized by a polynomial number of constraints and resulting in a concise nonlinear integer programming approach. Given the general inefficiency of nonlinear constraints, we transform these into (1) an integer linear programming and (2) a Boolean satisfaction framework—both featuring constraints of comparable size. \gobble{Unlike the one-time optimization approach of linear and nonlinear programming, Boolean satisfaction iteratively enumerates integer values of the objective. Considering the small domain of the objective for filter minimization and the efficiency of exploiting constraints in conjunctive normal form, Boolean satisfaction surpasses other methods in experiments.} Our detailed analysis of experimental results revealed that many constraints remain inactive during the iterative search for a minimal filter. To expedite computation within the Boolean satisfaction framework, we adopt a just-in-time approach for constraints: introducing them only when a proposed variable assignment would otherwise violate them. Empirical evidence suggests that the computational speedup from this method can outweigh the overhead associated with detecting and dynamically introducing constraints. Following the problem statement in Section~\ref{sec:prob}, we first formalize filter minimization as an integer nonlinear program in Section~\ref{sec:INP}. Building on this, we present integer linear programming and Boolean satisfaction formulations in Section~\ref{sec:ILP_SAT}. The experimental results are discussed in Section~\ref{sec:expr}.

text: In information retrieval (IR) systems, which are integral to numerous popular websites, ranking search results that align with user queries is paramount. Learning to rank (LTR) models typically manage the scoring and ordering of these results, trained using labels derived from user interactions. Although pairwise or listwise loss functions are prevalent in the training phase, the scoring during inference often occurs independently. This isolated scoring approach overlooks the interdependencies among documents. Research indicates that a search result's perception is affected by its neighboring results \cite{agarwal2015constrained, neighbor_effect, wang2016beyond}. This effect is particularly evident in e-commerce searches, where users frequently compare options on a results page during their shopping journey. Capturing these dependencies is crucial, especially for the top results, such as those on the first page, which receive the most user attention. Additionally, in many practical scenarios, there is a need to maintain specific distributional criteria within the results on a search page. The overall composition of these results significantly influences user perception and is often guided by business strategies or long-term goals like user retention. For example, at eBay, ensuring that the top results reflect the full range of available selections is a key objective. Other business goals might include promoting diversity, reducing bias, or personalizing results. Therefore, crafting an optimal set of top results (referred to as items in this context) necessitates accounting for both distributional criteria and inter-result dependencies, alongside individual result quality. We define the top results for a search query, such as $k$ items shown on the first page viewed by the user (where $k \ll n$, $n$ being the total number of results recalled), as the slate. This paper introduces a novel methodology and architecture to create an optimal slate. An optimal slate is envisioned as one that maximizes the likelihood of meeting search needs while adhering to specified distributional criteria for a query. Our approach simultaneously optimizes traditional ranking metrics and ensures the slate meets distributional criteria, while acknowledging intra-slate dependencies. Various methodologies have been explored to achieve slate optimization through set-aware ranking. Heuristic methods like Maximal Marginal Relevance (MMR) \cite{MMR}, IA-Select \cite{IA-Select}, and xQuAD \cite{xQuAD} strive to integrate diversity or minimize user dissatisfaction as they navigate the results. However, these methods often rely on simpler heuristics, lacking the sophistication of more advanced models designed to capture inter-document dependencies. Recent advancements have embraced set-aware ranking architectures \cite{group_wise_ranking,seq2slate}. By representing and scoring documents with awareness of the candidate set, these methods aim to produce an optimal slate. For instance, groupwise scoring functions (GSF) \cite{group_wise_ranking} propose multivariate scoring, while Seq2Slate \cite{seq2slate} employs pointer networks for sequential scoring. Although these methods are set-aware during inference, they primarily optimize traditional ranking metrics such as normalized discounted cumulative gain (nDCG) and do not explicitly account for additional distributional criteria, a crucial consideration in practice. To our knowledge, there are no neural network-based methods currently addressing this specific challenge, particularly in e-commerce search. To address this gap, we propose conditional sequential slate optimization (CSSO), a novel framework targeting the slate optimization problem. It employs a sequential decoding strategy built on pointer networks, managing slate composition according to predefined distributional criteria while optimizing traditional metrics like nDCG. This framework treats slate optimization as a re-ranking task, where a \textit{base-ranker} initially ranks items unilaterally, and a \textit{re-ranker} refines this to produce a slate of size $k$, where $k \ll n$. Query-specific distributional criteria are expressed through representative or domain-specific features of the items. The hybrid optimization goal can lead to conflicting optimization paths as the model must balance ranking quality with all aspects of the set distributional criteria. Additionally, the non-unique solutions, non-convex nature of the problem, and the non-differentiability of metrics like nDCG make it challenging for traditional gradient-based methods to find an optimal slate. To address this complex issue, we leverage Reinforcement Learning (RL) for training CSSO. RL offers a structured approach to explore the feature space while progressively refining the non-differentiable optimization goal using policy gradient methods. Moreover, RL's exploration strategy enables the model to generalize better than traditional supervised methods by effectively learning meaningful features from rollouts. During training, we use click-through data from IR systems as implicit relevance labels. Within the RL framework, a state is defined \textit{jointly} by the current slate items, the deviation from the predetermined distribution, and the encoded candidate set. An action corresponds to selecting an item at each decoding step, and the reward is based on the slate's composition post-decoding, considering both ranking quality and distributional criteria adherence. The optimization problem, thus well-defined, is addressed using policy gradient in a finite horizon of length $k$, with a baseline model employed to reduce training variance. The key contributions of our work include: \begin{itemize} \item A framework to jointly optimize a slate for document relevance and adherence to a predetermined distribution, addressing industry challenges in re-ranking for personalization, bias mitigation, or diversity enhancement. \item An enhancement to pointer networks, incorporating a conditional structure to represent slate composition during decoding. \end{itemize} In experiments conducted on both public and proprietary e-commerce datasets, CSSO achieves competitive ranking metrics and superior distribution conformity compared to state-of-the-art slate optimization methods. On Yahoo \cite{yahoo_dataset} and Web30k \cite{LETOR} datasets, with additional simulations to mimic real-world user behaviors, we demonstrate simultaneous optimization of nDCG and GAP (a distribution conformity metric defined in subsequent sections). Tests on eBay.com search session datasets show notable improvements in GAP metrics and comparable ranking metrics to the production ranker. Overall, CSSO excels in optimizing both nDCG and GAP. We regard CSSO as a practical solution to the industry-relevant problem of optimizing slates for relevance and composition based on business goals. We anticipate its application in addressing challenges like ensuring diversity, mitigating bias, and meeting business objectives across various web domains, including e-commerce, online media, and web search.

text: The rapid expansion of computational resources, which has been accelerating since the 1970s, shows no signs of slowing down. This trend suggests that computational power will continue to become more affordable and accessible in the foreseeable future. Researchers have capitalized on this surge in computational capacity to enhance the control of robotic systems, with advancements in both hardware and algorithms paving the way for breakthroughs in various fields. A notable development is model-free reinforcement learning, a machine learning approach that enables an agent to interact with its environment and autonomously optimize a reward function. This technique holds great potential for addressing complex systems that are difficult to model or for which solutions are not readily apparent. Recent advancements in robotics illustrate this potential, such as the control of a 47 DOF humanoid navigating diverse obstacles \cite{heess_emergence_2017}, the dexterous manipulation of objects using a 24 DOF robotic hand \cite{openai_learning_2018}, and the development of a quadruped robot capable of running \cite{hwangbo_learning_2019} and recovering from falls \cite{lee_robust_2019}. In this paper, we focus on the challenging problem of legged locomotion. This domain is notoriously complex, making reinforcement learning a popular method of choice. While hand-crafted, model-based control strategies, like those employed by Boston Dynamics, still lead the field, reinforcement learning has shown promising results. There are instances where learned policies surpass those designed by experts \cite{hwangbo_learning_2019}, and it is anticipated that these learning techniques will continue to enhance performance and usability. However, a significant drawback of these algorithms is their black-box nature. Understanding exactly what an RL agent has learned remains an open question. Even if an agent achieves high rewards, verifying its safety and rationality across all possible states is challenging. Furthermore, assessing the system's stability and robustness is not straightforward. Recent research \citep{Taleledeep} has explored mesh-based tools to address these concerns. Nevertheless, the effectiveness of mesh-based tools is constrained by the curse of dimensionality, limiting their ability to discretize state spaces accurately. These methods can only handle relatively high-dimensional systems if the growth of the reachable space is significantly slower than the exponential increase of the full state space in which the system operates. To extend these methods to more complex systems, strategies must be developed to prevent the volume of visited states from expanding proportionally. One way to measure this growth rate is through various "fractional dimensions" concepts from fractal geometry. In this study, we introduce an efficient meshing algorithm known as box meshing. We demonstrate that this approach enables the feasible calculation of the mesh dimension within reinforcement learning contexts. Additionally, we suggest using alternative notions of fractional dimension from existing literature as proxies for the properties of interest. We then illustrate how reinforcement learning agents can be trained to minimize these measures by adjusting their reward functions. Finally, we present the outcomes of this training and provide a brief analysis of the resulting structures for selected policies.

text: Deep neural networks (DNNs) have recently achieved remarkable breakthroughs across various domains, including computer vision and speech recognition, among others. The capabilities of DNNs have sparked immense interest and exploration. Numerous pivotal and intriguing studies have emerged, focusing on different types of DNNs such as convolutional neural networks (e.g., LeNet \cite{45_lecun1998gradient}, AlexNet \cite{33_krizhevsky2012imagenet}, ResNet \cite{42_he2016deep}) and recurrent neural networks (e.g., LSTM \cite{46_olah2015understanding}). As DNN technology rapidly advances, increasing attention is being directed towards their security. In particular, the development of adversarial examples and methods to defend against adversarial attacks are critical areas within DNN security. Since the discovery of the vulnerability \cite{2_szegedy2013intriguing} of DNNs, it has attracted significant attention. The literature on this topic is extensive, with research primarily categorized into adversarial attacks \cite{2_szegedy2013intriguing,6_goodfellow2014explaining,7_kurakin2016adversarial,8_papernot2016limitations,9_moosavi2016deepfool,10_carlini2017towards,11_chen2017zoo,12_moosavi2017universal,13_su2019one,14_zhao2017generating,15_tabacof2016adversarial} and adversarial defenses \cite{2_szegedy2013intriguing,24_madry2017towards,43_tramer2017ensemble,44_papernot2016distillation,50_huang2015learning,51_cheng2020cat,52_song2018improving,53_zhang2019theoretically}. The aim of adversarial attacks is to generate examples that deceive DNNs, often remaining undetectable by humans. Conversely, adversarial defenses enhance the robustness of DNNs against such examples. This dynamic between attacks and defenses can be likened to a zero-sum game. The conventional definition of adversarial examples describes them as being nearly indistinguishable from natural images yet capable of misleading DNNs \cite{2_szegedy2013intriguing}. Under this framework, adversarial examples are often imperceptible to humans (referred to as imperceptible adversarial examples). However, there are other forms of adversarial examples. For instance, some studies introduce patches to images to deceive DNNs \cite{16_brown2017adversarial,17_liu2018dpatch,18_karmon2018lavan,19_lee2019physical}. These are termed adversarial patches and are noticeable to humans. Additionally, adversarial noise images, deliberately manipulated by humans, can also mislead DNNs \cite{4_nguyen2015deep}. Although these noise images lack meaning for humans, DNNs confidently classify them into specific categories (referred to as unrecognizable adversarial examples). Notably, most research has concentrated on image perturbations that cause incorrect class labeling. In contrast, Sabour et al. \cite{55_DBLP:journals/corr/SabourCFF15} focused on DNN hidden layer representations, proposing a method to create adversarial examples that appear similar to one image but whose hidden layer representation closely resembles another, from a different class. This work prompts further exploration into DNN representations and the nature of adversarial examples. It is crucial to investigate how adversarial disturbances manifest in hidden layers and whether hidden layer information can be leveraged to develop more robust adversarial defense strategies. Building on these foundations, this paper examines the characteristics of various adversarial example types. We observe that regardless of whether a sample is an imperceptible adversarial example, an adversarial patch, or an unrecognizable adversarial example, there exists a level of uncertainty (correct or incorrect) in machine predictions. However, as long as the disturbance does not alter the objective reality, human judgment remains largely accurate. We highlight the significant differences between human and DNN image recognition. Humans interpret images in pixel space, while machines operate in a distinct "vision" space within hidden layers. We propose the hypothesis that, without altering objective reality, the effect of adversarial disturbances on predictions hinges on changes to original semantic characteristics during hidden layer propagation. Based on this hypothesis, we introduce a defense mechanism that utilizes hidden layer representations to bolster model robustness against adversarial attacks. Our defense strategy compresses input information and filters out unnecessary elements, including adversarial perturbations. This proposed method functions as an activation mechanism within the neural network's hidden layers, enhancing adversarial robustness. We provide theoretical validation of this defense's efficacy in a straightforward scenario. Additionally, we offer a specific defensive function and empirically demonstrate our defense mechanism's effectiveness. Notably, our defense model achieves state-of-the-art results. Finally, we explore constructing imperceptible adversarial examples, adversarial patches, and unrecognizable adversarial examples using hidden layer representations. The contributions of this paper are as follows: \begin{enumerate} 	\item We analyze the characteristics of different adversarial example types (imperceptible adversarial examples, adversarial patches, and unrecognizable adversarial examples) and propose that adversarial perturbations manifest differently in hidden layers compared to clean examples. 	\item Based on this hypothesis, we propose an efficient defense method to enhance model robustness against adversarial attacks. Our strategy compresses input information and filters out adversarial perturbations. This defense strategy also functions as an activation mechanism, and we theoretically validate its effectiveness. 	\item Utilizing hidden layer representations, we develop three types of adversarial attacks to generate imperceptible adversarial examples, unrecognizable adversarial examples, and adversarial patches, as illustrated in Fig. \ref{overview_123}. 	\item Our defense method achieves state-of-the-art performance, with $97.09\%$ accuracy against CW on MNIST, $89.03\%$ accuracy against CW on CIFAR10, and $64.38\%$ against CW on ImageNet. \end{enumerate} The remainder of this paper is structured as follows: Section \ref{section2} reviews related literature. Section \ref{section3} discusses three types of adversarial examples and proposes a hypothesis. Section \ref{section4} introduces a defense strategy and a specific defense function (activation function). Section \ref{section5} presents three adversarial attacks to generate the three types of adversarial examples using hidden layer representations. In Section \ref{experiment}, we conduct extensive experiments to validate our methods' effectiveness. Finally, Section \ref{conclusion} concludes the paper.
