text: \noindent Recent years have witnessed the rapid advancement of online recruitment platforms. With the increasing amount of online recruitment data, more and more interview related studies have emerged such as automated interview assessment tools and candidate evaluation systems. These technological advancements have enabled the development of sophisticated algorithms that can process vast amounts of data to derive meaningful insights regarding candidate competencies. The asynchronous video interview (AVI) format, in particular, has gained widespread popularity due to its flexibility for both employers and candidates. In this context, the ability to automatically score candidate responses using ASR transcriptions presents a significant opportunity to enhance the efficiency and fairness of the recruitment process. \subsection{Background and Motivation} The traditional interview process often suffers from subjective biases and inconsistencies across different interviewers and sessions. Automated systems aim to mitigate these issues by providing a standardized assessment framework. The use of ASR technology in AVIs allows for the capture of nuanced information from spoken responses, which can be further analyzed to evaluate competencies such as communication skills, domain knowledge, and problem-solving abilities. The motivation behind this research is to develop a system that leverages modern natural language processing (NLP) and machine learning techniques to provide a robust and scalable solution for competency assessment. By focusing on both linguistic and paralinguistic features, we aim to create a comprehensive model that can accurately reflect a candidate's potential in a professional setting. Previous studies in the field of automated candidate evaluation have explored various aspects of feature extraction and model development. For instance, \cite{smith2019automated} investigated the use of lexical and syntactic features to assess communication proficiency in interview scenarios. Their findings indicate that certain lexical richness metrics, such as type-token ratio, are strong indicators of verbal competence. Similarly, \cite{johnson2020speech} emphasized the importance of paralinguistic cues, demonstrating that speech rate and intonation can significantly influence perceived candidate confidence. These studies underscore the potential of combining multiple feature types to enhance predictive performance. Recent advancements in deep learning have also contributed to this domain. Convolutional neural networks (CNNs) and recurrent neural networks (RNNs), particularly Long Short-Term Memory (LSTM) networks, have been utilized to model sequential data and capture complex dependencies in candidate responses \cite{lee2021deep}. These models have shown promise in improving classification accuracy over traditional machine learning approaches. \subsection{Overview} Our proposed framework for automatic competency scoring in AVIs consists of several interconnected modules: ASR processing, feature extraction, feature selection, model training, and evaluation. Each module is designed to handle specific aspects of the data processing pipeline, ensuring a comprehensive assessment of candidate responses. \subsection{ASR Processing} The first module involves the conversion of audio responses into textual data using state-of-the-art ASR systems. We leverage Google Cloud Speech-to-Text API due to its high accuracy and language support. The transcriptions are then preprocessed to remove filler words and correct any transcription errors, ensuring clean and coherent text for subsequent analysis. \subsection{Feature Extraction} As delineated earlier, we extract a rich set of features encompassing lexical, syntactic, semantic, and paralinguistic dimensions. For lexical features, we compute metrics such as word frequency distribution, lexical diversity, and the presence of domain-specific terminology. Syntactic features are derived from parsing tree structures and analyzing grammatical patterns. Semantic features are extracted using topic modeling techniques like Latent Dirichlet Allocation (LDA) to identify the relevance of the candidate's response to the interview question. Additionally, semantic similarity measures are employed to assess coherence and logical flow within the response. Paralinguistic features are quantified using prosodic analysis tools that measure speech rate, pause length, and pitch variation. These features are indicative of the candidate's expressiveness and engagement during the interview. \subsection{Feature Selection} The high dimensionality of the extracted features necessitates effective dimensionality reduction techniques. We apply Principal Component Analysis (PCA) to capture the most informative components of the feature space. Recursive Feature Elimination (RFE) is further employed to iteratively remove less significant features, optimizing the feature set for training. \subsection{Model Training} We explore several supervised learning algorithms to model the relationship between the selected features and competency scores. Our baseline models include Support Vector Machines (SVMs), Random Forests, and Gradient Boosting Machines. Additionally, we experiment with neural network architectures, such as feedforward neural networks and LSTMs, to capture non-linear patterns and temporal dependencies in the data. The training process involves hyperparameter tuning through cross-validation to ensure optimal model performance. We employ stratified k-fold cross-validation to maintain the class distribution across training and validation sets, preventing overfitting and ensuring generalizability. \subsection{Evaluation} Model evaluation is conducted using standard metrics such as accuracy, precision, recall, and F1-score. We also analyze the receiver operating characteristic (ROC) curve and the area under the curve (AUC) to assess the discriminative power of our models. For a comprehensive assessment, we perform ablation studies to understand the contribution of each feature category to the overall model performance. In our experiments, we observed that combining lexical, syntactic, semantic, and paralinguistic features significantly improved the accuracy of competency prediction models. Among the models tested, gradient boosting machines exhibited the highest performance, closely followed by LSTM networks. The inclusion of paralinguistic features marginally increased the predictive power, highlighting their importance in interpreting candidate responses. Our findings align with previous research, confirming that a multi-faceted approach to feature extraction and model training is essential for capturing the complexities of spoken language in AVIs. The proposed framework demonstrates robustness across various job roles and industries, indicating its potential for wide-scale adoption in online recruitment systems. This study presents a comprehensive framework for automatic competency scoring in asynchronous video interviews, leveraging advanced NLP and machine learning techniques. The integration of diverse feature sets and sophisticated modeling approaches ensures a nuanced evaluation of candidate responses. Future work will focus on expanding the feature set to include additional paralinguistic markers and exploring the use of transformer-based models to further enhance performance. Additionally, we aim to conduct large-scale validations across diverse demographic groups to ensure fairness and bias mitigation in the automated evaluation process. \bibliographystyle{unsrt} \bibliography{references}

Robots must decide in real-time whether to process tasks locally or offload them to edge servers. This decision depends on multiple factors, including the robot's current computational load, the task's complexity, and the network's dynamic conditions. The complexity of this decision-making process necessitates advanced algorithms capable of assessing these factors quickly and accurately. For example, the use of MDPs allows for an optimized approach by modeling the task allocation process as a sequential decision-making problem, where the goal is to maximize the system's overall efficiency \cite{Li2023MDP}. \subsubsection{Resource Management} Resource management in MEC environments is another significant challenge. Efficient use of computational resources across multiple robots and edge servers requires strategic allocation and scheduling. Game-theoretic approaches have been proposed to address this issue, where robots are modeled as players in a game, competing for shared resources. This approach not only optimizes resource usage but also encourages cooperative strategies among robots, leading to improved system performance. Furthermore, incorporating reinforcement learning into these models allows for adaptive strategies that can evolve as the system's operational conditions change \cite{Wang2023Reinforcement}. \subsubsection{Real-Time Communication} The efficacy of MRC systems heavily relies on robust communication protocols. The high data rates and stringent latency requirements pose a significant challenge, particularly in environments with variable network conditions. text: Grouping objects based on the similarity between them is a ubiquitous and important task in machine learning. Grouping objects based on the similarity between them is a ubiquitous and important task in machine learning, with applications ranging from image segmentation \cite{shi2000normalized} and social network analysis \cite{leskovec2010empirical} to bioinformatics \cite{alzate2010multiway} and document clustering \cite{cutting1992scatter}. The Correlation Clustering problem, in particular, provides a powerful framework for unsupervised learning when the relationships between objects can be naturally represented as a graph, with edges indicating pairwise similarities or dissimilarities. This problem is especially relevant in scenarios where the edge labels are derived from noisy data, necessitating robust algorithms that can handle such imperfections. The NP-hard nature of Correlation Clustering implies that exact solutions are computationally infeasible for large instances, thus motivating the development of approximation algorithms. Semidefinite programming (SDP) relaxations have emerged as a particularly effective approach for tackling this problem, offering provable approximation guarantees. The SDP relaxation technique transforms the original combinatorial optimization problem into a convex optimization problem, which can be efficiently solved using polynomial-time interior-point methods \cite{vandenberghe1996semidefinite}. In this paper, we explore advanced SDP relaxation techniques for the Correlation Clustering problem, building on the foundational work of Goemans and Williamson \cite{goemans1995improved} and Bansal et al. \cite{bansal2004correlation}. We aim to enhance the approximation ratios achievable by existing methods and to extend the applicability of these techniques to more complex graph structures, including those with weighted and directed edges. The core idea behind SDP relaxation for Correlation Clustering is to represent each vertex $i$ by a unit vector $\mathbf{v}_i$ in $\mathbb{R}^d$, where $d$ is the dimension of the embedding space. This representation allows us to relax the hard clustering constraints into softer, continuous ones that can be optimized over. The objective function, as described in the SDP formulation, seeks to minimize the misclassification penalty by adjusting the inner products $\langle \mathbf{v}_i, \mathbf{v}_j \rangle$ to align with the edge labels. The SDP relaxation is formally expressed as: \begin{align} \text{minimize} & \quad \sum_{(i,j) \in E} w_{ij} \cdot \frac{1 - \langle \mathbf{v}_i, \mathbf{v}_j \rangle}{2} \\ \text{subject to} & \quad \|\mathbf{v}_i\| = 1 \quad \forall i \in V, \\ & \quad \mathbf{V} \succeq 0, \end{align} where $\mathbf{V}$ is the Gram matrix of the vectors $\{\mathbf{v}_i\}_{i \in V}$, and $\mathbf{V} \succeq 0$ denotes that $\mathbf{V}$ is positive semidefinite. The constraint $\|\mathbf{v}_i\| = 1$ ensures that each vector lies on the unit sphere, which is crucial for maintaining the geometric interpretation of the problem. \subsection{Rounding Techniques} Once an optimal solution to the SDP relaxation is obtained, the next challenge is to convert the vector solution into a discrete clustering. This process, known as rounding, is critical for achieving a good approximation ratio. Several rounding techniques have been proposed in the literature, each with its own strengths and weaknesses. One popular rounding method involves random hyperplane cuts \cite{goemans1995improved}. In this approach, a random hyperplane is chosen, and vertices are partitioned based on the side of the hyperplane on which their corresponding vectors lie. This method is simple and can provide good approximation guarantees, but it may not be suitable for graphs with high edge density. An alternative rounding technique is the use of thresholding methods, where the inner products are directly used to determine the partitioning of vertices. This approach can be more effective for graphs with well-defined clusters but may require careful tuning of the threshold parameter. \subsection{Improved Approximation Ratios} Recent advances in SDP relaxation have focused on improving the approximation ratios for Correlation Clustering. By leveraging tighter relaxations and advanced rounding schemes, it is possible to achieve approximation ratios that are closer to the theoretical lower bounds. For instance, Ankur Moitra et al. \cite{moitra2010approximation} introduced techniques that exploit the structure of the input graph to provide improved guarantees. One promising direction is the incorporation of spectral methods into the SDP framework. Spectral clustering techniques, which utilize the eigenvectors of the graph Laplacian, can be combined with SDP relaxations to capture global graph structure more effectively. This hybrid approach has been shown to provide better approximations in practice, particularly for large-scale problems with complex cluster structures \cite{von2007tutorial}. \subsection{Applications and Extensions} The versatility of the SDP relaxation approach makes it applicable to a wide range of problems beyond standard Correlation Clustering. For instance, variants of the problem where edges have weights reflecting varying degrees of similarity or dissimilarity can be naturally handled within the SDP framework. Additionally, directed graphs, where the relationships are not symmetric, pose unique challenges that can be addressed by modifying the SDP formulation to account for directionality. Furthermore, the integration of additional constraints, such as those arising from prior knowledge or external data sources, can be seamlessly incorporated into the SDP model. This flexibility allows for the customization of the algorithm to specific application domains, such as community detection in social networks or protein interaction networks in bioinformatics. To evaluate the effectiveness of our proposed methods, we conducted extensive experiments on both synthetic and real-world datasets. The performance of the SDP relaxation algorithm was compared against several baseline methods, including traditional graph clustering algorithms and other state-of-the-art approximation algorithms for Correlation Clustering. \subsection{Dataset Description} The datasets used in our experiments were selected to cover a broad spectrum of graph characteristics, including variations in size, density, and the degree of noise in the edge labels. Synthetic datasets were generated using stochastic block models \cite{holland1983stochastic}, which allow precise control over the underlying cluster structure and noise levels. Real-world datasets were sourced from publicly available benchmarks in social network analysis and bioinformatics. \subsection{Evaluation Metrics} The quality of the clustering solutions was assessed using standard metrics, such as the normalized mutual information (NMI) \cite{strehl2002cluster} and the adjusted Rand index (ARI) \cite{hubert1985comparing}. These metrics provide a quantitative measure of the agreement between the computed clusters and the ground truth, allowing for a comprehensive evaluation of algorithm performance. \subsection{Results and Discussion} Our experimental results demonstrate that the SDP relaxation approach consistently outperforms baseline methods across all datasets, achieving higher NMI and ARI scores. The improved approximation ratios are particularly evident in datasets with high levels of noise, where traditional methods struggle to recover the underlying cluster structure. In addition to quantitative metrics, we also conducted qualitative analyses to gain insights into the behavior of the algorithms. Visualizations of the clustering solutions revealed that the SDP-based methods are better at capturing subtle structures in the data, such as overlapping clusters and non-uniform cluster sizes. In this paper, we have presented advanced techniques for solving the Correlation Clustering problem using semidefinite programming relaxations. Our approach not only improves the theoretical approximation guarantees but also demonstrates superior empirical performance on a diverse set of datasets. The flexibility of the SDP framework allows for extensions to more complex problem settings, paving the way for future research in scalable, robust clustering algorithms. Future work could explore the integration of machine learning techniques to automatically tune the parameters of the SDP model, as well as the development of distributed algorithms to handle even larger datasets. Additionally, investigating the theoretical limits of approximation ratios for various graph classes remains an open and intriguing question. \bibliographystyle{plain} \bibliography{references}

text: Interactive media experiences present individual audience members with media that is tailored to their particular context, knowledge, or needs. In this dynamic landscape, there is a growing imperative for media producers to understand and optimize the factors that contribute to effective personalization. This involves not only tailoring content but also considering the mode of delivery and the interface through which users interact with the media. The convergence of data analytics, machine learning, and user interface design forms the backbone of this personalization process, allowing for the creation of adaptive media experiences that respond to real-time feedback \cite{johnson2019adaptive}. \subsection{The Role of Data Analytics in Personalization} Data analytics plays a critical role in the personalization of media experiences by enabling the granular analysis of user behavior. Through the aggregation and analysis of large datasets, patterns and preferences can be discerned, which inform the customization of content. Advanced algorithms can predict user interests based on past interactions, thus facilitating the delivery of content that aligns with user preferences. This approach, however, raises significant challenges in terms of data privacy and ethical considerations, necessitating robust frameworks to ensure user consent and data protection \cite{li2021data}. \subsection{Machine Learning and Adaptive Content} Machine learning algorithms are instrumental in refining the personalization process. These algorithms are designed to learn from user interactions and continuously improve the relevance of the content delivered. For example, recommendation systems, powered by collaborative filtering and content-based approaches, analyze user history and preferences to suggest new content. The effectiveness of such systems hinges on their ability to adaptively learn from evolving user patterns, thereby maintaining engagement over time \cite{zhou2020machine}. \begin{equation} R(u, i) = \mu + b_u + b_i + q_u^T p_i \end{equation} where \( R(u, i) \) is the predicted rating of user \( u \) for item \( i \), \( \mu \) is the global average rating, \( b_u \) and \( b_i \) are the biases of user \( u \) and item \( i \), respectively, and \( q_u \) and \( p_i \) are the latent feature vectors for user \( u \) and item \( i \). \subsection{User Interface Design and Engagement} The design of user interfaces is another critical component in the personalization of media experiences. An intuitive and responsive interface can significantly enhance user engagement by facilitating seamless interaction with content. Designers must consider various factors, such as accessibility, visual appeal, and ease of navigation, to create interfaces that cater to diverse user demographics. The integration of adaptive user interfaces that adjust based on user feedback and interaction patterns is an emerging trend in this domain \cite{martin2020ui}. \subsection{Challenges and Ethical Considerations} While personalization offers numerous benefits, it also presents challenges, particularly concerning user privacy and algorithmic transparency. The collection and analysis of user data must be conducted within ethical boundaries, ensuring that users are informed about how their data is being used and have the option to opt-out. Furthermore, the opacity of machine learning algorithms can lead to issues of bias and fairness, necessitating the development of transparent models that can be audited and understood by users \cite{dastin2018bias}. In this study, we employ a mixed-methods approach to investigate the effectiveness of personalized media experiences. Our methodology comprises three primary components: quantitative analysis of user interaction data, qualitative assessment of user feedback, and experimental testing of adaptive content algorithms. \subsection{Quantitative Analysis} We collect interaction data from a sample of users engaging with a personalized media platform. This data includes metrics such as click-through rates, time spent on content, and engagement duration. Using statistical analysis techniques, we identify patterns and correlations that provide insights into user behavior and preferences. \subsection{Qualitative Assessment} To complement the quantitative data, we conduct interviews and surveys to gather user feedback on their experiences with the platform. This qualitative data helps to contextualize the quantitative findings, offering a deeper understanding of user satisfaction and areas for improvement. \subsection{Experimental Testing} We implement a series of experiments to test the effectiveness of different personalization algorithms. These experiments involve modifying algorithm parameters and measuring the impact on user engagement metrics. This iterative process allows us to refine the algorithms and enhance their predictive accuracy. The results of our study highlight the significant impact of personalization on user engagement. Quantitative analysis reveals a strong correlation between personalized content and increased engagement metrics, such as longer session durations and higher content consumption rates. Qualitative feedback indicates that users appreciate the relevance and convenience of personalized experiences, although concerns about privacy and data use remain prevalent. Our experimental testing demonstrates that adaptive algorithms significantly outperform static models in maintaining user interest over time. Users are more likely to engage with content that is dynamically tailored to their evolving preferences, underscoring the importance of continuous learning in personalization systems. In conclusion, the integration of data analytics, machine learning, and user interface design is essential for the development of effective personalized media experiences. While personalization offers substantial benefits in terms of user engagement, it also necessitates careful consideration of ethical issues and user privacy. This technique has garnered significant attention within the field of remote sensing due to its ability to penetrate dense foliage and generate high-resolution images of the underlying terrain. Traditionally, AOS relies heavily on precise drone navigation and accurate pose estimation to synthesize coherent images from multiple aerial passes. However, dense environments pose substantial challenges to conventional navigation systems, primarily due to signal occlusion and multipath effects that degrade GPS accuracy. \subsection{Challenges in Pose Estimation} Pose estimation in dense forest environments is fraught with difficulties. The Global Positioning System (GPS), while a cornerstone of modern navigation, suffers from significant accuracy degradation in environments with substantial canopy cover. This issue is exacerbated by the multipath phenomenon, where GPS signals reflect off various surfaces before reaching the receiver, leading to erroneous position readings. Inertial measurement units (IMUs), which provide data on acceleration and angular velocity, can partially compensate for these inaccuracies. However, they are prone to drift over time, particularly when subjected to the dynamic motions inherent in drone flights. Visual odometry, which estimates the motion of the camera in relation to its environment by analyzing sequential images, offers an additional layer of data. Yet, it too is not without limitations, as it can be affected by rapid movements and low-texture scenes, which are common in forested areas. \subsection{Proposed Approach} To address these challenges, our approach integrates GPS, IMU, and visual odometry data through an extended Kalman filter (EKF). The EKF serves as an optimal estimator that fuses these diverse data streams, leveraging their complementary strengths while mitigating their individual weaknesses. By doing so, we achieve a more accurate and robust estimation of the drone's pose, which is critical for the effective application of AOS. The integration process begins with the initialization of the EKF using GPS data, which provides an initial estimate of the drone's position and velocity. Concurrently, IMU data supplies high-rate accelerometer and gyroscope measurements, which are used to predict the drone's state in between GPS updates. text: Historically, recommendation algorithms were developed to maximize the accuracy of the delivered recommendations to the users. However, the singular focus on accuracy has been increasingly scrutinized as researchers and practitioners recognize the multifaceted nature of recommendation quality. Beyond accuracy, dimensions such as diversity, fairness, and novelty have emerged as critical factors in evaluating the effectiveness of recommender systems. The complexity of user preferences and the diversity of item catalogs necessitate a more holistic approach to recommendation, where these additional dimensions are given due consideration. \subsection{Challenges in Recommender Systems} Recommender systems face several challenges that go beyond the traditional accuracy-oriented paradigm. One of the foremost challenges is the trade-off between accuracy and diversity. While accuracy measures how well the recommended items match user preferences, diversity ensures a broader spectrum of items is presented, thereby reducing the likelihood of user fatigue and increasing engagement \cite{mcnee2006being}. Achieving a balance between these two dimensions is non-trivial, as enhancing diversity may sometimes come at the cost of reduced accuracy. Another significant challenge is the incorporation of fairness in recommendations. Fairness can be viewed from multiple perspectives, including user fairness—ensuring that all users receive equal attention—and item fairness—guaranteeing that all items, regardless of their popularity, have a fair chance of being recommended. The notion of fairness is particularly relevant in domains where certain items or categories are systematically underrepresented. Algorithms that prioritize fairness must navigate the tension between serving user interests and promoting equitable exposure across the item space \cite{ekstrand2018all}. Moreover, the novelty of recommendations is a crucial aspect that influences user satisfaction and system effectiveness. Novel recommendations introduce users to items they have not previously encountered, enhancing the discovery experience and potentially leading to more satisfied and loyal users. However, recommending overly novel items might risk user dissatisfaction if the items are perceived as irrelevant or of low quality \cite{vargas2011rank}. \subsection{Mitigation Strategies} To address these challenges, various mitigation strategies have been proposed, each with its strengths and limitations. A common strategy involves the integration of diversity-promoting mechanisms within the recommendation algorithm. Techniques such as re-ranking, where the initial list of recommendations is adjusted to include a more diverse set of items, have shown promise in enhancing diversity without significantly compromising accuracy \cite{zhang2008avoiding}. Hybrid recommendation models also play a pivotal role in mitigating popularity bias and enhancing diversity. By combining collaborative filtering with content-based approaches, these models leverage both user interaction data and item attributes, thereby enriching the recommendation process. Such hybrid systems can highlight less popular items that might align with user preferences based on content similarities \cite{burke2002hybrid}. Fairness-aware recommender systems represent another innovative approach. These systems incorporate fairness constraints into the recommendation process, ensuring a more equitable distribution of exposure among items. Techniques such as adversarial training and constraint-based optimization have been explored to enforce fairness, thereby promoting underrepresented items and mitigating the impact of popularity bias \cite{beutel2019fairness}. \subsection{Recent Advances} Recent advances in machine learning, particularly in deep learning and reinforcement learning, have opened new avenues for addressing the limitations of traditional recommender systems. Deep learning models, with their ability to capture complex patterns in data, have been employed to enhance personalization while simultaneously promoting diversity and fairness \cite{zhang2019deep}. Reinforcement learning, on the other hand, offers a framework for optimizing long-term user engagement. By modeling the recommendation process as a sequential decision-making problem, reinforcement learning algorithms can dynamically adjust recommendations based on user feedback, potentially balancing accuracy, diversity, and fairness over time \cite{zhao2017deep}. Moreover, context-aware recommender systems have emerged as a promising direction, incorporating contextual information such as time, location, and social factors into the recommendation process. This additional layer of context can help tailor recommendations more precisely to the user's current situation, thus enhancing the relevance and novelty of the recommendations \cite{adomavicius2011context}. In this section, we outline the methodology employed to assess the impact of various mitigation strategies on the performance of recommender systems. Our approach is structured around a comprehensive evaluation framework that considers multiple dimensions of recommendation quality, including accuracy, diversity, fairness, and novelty. \subsection{Dataset and Preprocessing} The evaluation was conducted using a publicly available dataset, which contains user-item interaction data across several categories. The dataset was preprocessed to ensure consistency and accuracy in the evaluation. This involved steps such as data cleaning, normalization, and the handling of missing values. Additionally, we employed stratified sampling to create training and test sets that reflect the distribution of interactions in the original dataset, ensuring a robust evaluation of the algorithms. \subsection{Evaluation Metrics} To comprehensively evaluate the performance of the recommender systems, we utilized a diverse set of metrics. For accuracy, we employed standard metrics such as Precision@K and Recall@K, which measure the proportion of relevant items among the top-K recommendations. Diversity was assessed using metrics like the Intra-list Diversity and the Long-tail Coverage, which quantify the variety of items in the recommendation list and the representation of less popular items, respectively \cite{adomavicius2011improving}. Fairness was evaluated using exposure-based metrics, which measure the distribution of recommendation exposure across different item categories. Specifically, we calculated the Gini coefficient of item exposure to assess the equity of exposure distribution. Novelty was measured using metrics such as the Average Novelty, which calculates the average unfamiliarity of recommended items based on user history \cite{vargas2014diversity}. \subsection{Algorithm Implementation} We implemented several recommendation algorithms, each incorporating different mitigation strategies. These included a baseline collaborative filtering algorithm, a hybrid model combining collaborative filtering and content-based approaches, and a fairness-aware algorithm designed to promote equitable exposure. For the fairness-aware algorithm, we employed an adversarial training approach, where a discriminator was used to penalize item exposure imbalances. This adversarial component was trained alongside the recommender model to ensure that the final recommendations adhered to predefined fairness constraints \cite{beutel2019fairness}. \subsection{Experimental Setup} The experiments were conducted in a controlled environment, with each algorithm evaluated under identical conditions to ensure comparability. The evaluation process involved repeated trials with different random seeds to account for variability in the results. Hyperparameters for each algorithm were tuned using grid search, optimizing for a balanced performance across all evaluation metrics. The results of our evaluation provide insights into the effectiveness of various mitigation strategies in addressing popularity bias and enhancing recommendation quality. The baseline collaborative filtering algorithm, while achieving high accuracy, exhibited significant popularity bias, with a skewed exposure distribution favoring popular items. In contrast, the hybrid model demonstrated improved diversity and novelty, as evidenced by higher Intra-list Diversity and Average Novelty scores. This improvement can be attributed to the model's ability to leverage item attributes, thereby highlighting less popular items that align with user preferences. The fairness-aware algorithm achieved the most equitable exposure distribution, with a substantially lower Gini coefficient compared to the other models. This indicates the effectiveness of adversarial training in enforcing fairness constraints, promoting a more balanced representation of items across the recommendation spectrum. Interestingly, the improved diversity and fairness of the hybrid and fairness-aware algorithms did not come at a significant cost to accuracy. Both models maintained competitive Precision@K and Recall@K scores, suggesting that these dimensions of recommendation quality can be enhanced without severely compromising accuracy. These findings underscore the potential of advanced mitigation strategies in overcoming the limitations of traditional recommender systems. By integrating diversity-promoting mechanisms, hybrid approaches, and fairness-aware techniques, it is possible to develop recommender systems that provide a more balanced and equitable user experience. In this study, we explored the challenges of popularity bias in recommender systems and evaluated several strategies for mitigating its impact. Our results demonstrate that diversity, fairness, and novelty can be effectively integrated into recommendation algorithms, enhancing the overall quality of recommendations. Future research directions include the exploration of more sophisticated machine learning models, such as graph neural networks, which can capture complex relationships within user-item interactions. Additionally, the development of user-centric evaluation frameworks that incorporate user feedback and perceptions of recommendation quality could provide further insights into the effectiveness of mitigation strategies. Ultimately, the goal is to create recommender systems that not only deliver accurate recommendations but also promote a diverse, fair, and engaging user experience. As the field of recommender systems continues to evolve, it is imperative to adopt a holistic approach that considers the multiple dimensions of recommendation quality, ensuring that all users and items are treated equitably. \bibliographystyle{plain} \bibliography{recommender_systems}

text: Reinforcement learning for control has achieved great success in a wide variety of challenging sensory-motor control tasks, including agile drone flight~\cite{Kaufmann2018drone,Kaufmann2020drone,Loquercio2021drone}, deformable object manipulation~\cite{Wu2019deformable}, and quadruped locomotion~\cite{Hwangbo2019agile,Miki2022wild,Lee2020terrain,margonlis2022rapid}. Sensor fusion is a critical aspect of modern robotics, providing a pathway to enhance perceptual capabilities by integrating data from multiple sensors. By leveraging complementary information from different sensory modalities, robots can achieve more robust and reliable perception, which is crucial for operating in dynamic and unpredictable environments. For instance, combining visual and inertial data allows for improved pose estimation in autonomous vehicles \cite{leutenegger2015keyframe}, while fusing tactile and visual inputs can enhance object manipulation tasks \cite{lee2019touch}. \subsection{Multi-Modal Fusion Techniques} The effectiveness of sensor fusion largely depends on the techniques used to integrate and process the sensory data. Traditional approaches often rely on probabilistic frameworks, such as the Kalman filter and its variants, which provide a mathematical means to estimate the state of a system by optimally combining noisy measurements \cite{thrun2005probabilistic}. More recently, deep learning-based methods have been employed to learn fusion strategies directly from data \cite{baltrusaitis2018multimodal}. These methods can capture complex, non-linear relationships between sensor modalities, offering significant improvements over classical techniques. \subsection{Challenges in Sensor Fusion} Despite its advantages, sensor fusion presents several challenges. One significant issue is the synchronization of data from different sensors, which often have varying sampling rates and latencies. Misalignment in sensor data can lead to inaccurate estimations and degraded system performance \cite{castro2019synchronization}. Additionally, sensor fusion systems must be robust to sensor failure or degradation, necessitating strategies for fault detection and recovery \cite{Khaleghi2013multisensor}. To further enhance the adaptability of robotic systems, it is essential to consider the role of adaptive domain adaptation. Unlike traditional domain adaptation, which typically involves a static transfer of knowledge, adaptive domain adaptation continuously updates the model parameters as the robot encounters new environments. This approach is particularly beneficial in non-stationary environments where the distribution of input data may shift over time \cite{wang2019characterizing}. \subsection{Techniques for Adaptive Domain Adaptation} Several techniques have been proposed to facilitate adaptive domain adaptation. One approach involves online fine-tuning, where the model is continuously updated using a small stream of labeled or pseudo-labeled data from the target domain \cite{li2020online}. Another strategy employs meta-learning, where the model is trained to quickly adapt to new tasks with minimal data \cite{finn2017model}. These methods can be combined with unsupervised domain adaptation techniques, such as generative adversarial networks (GANs), to create a more flexible and responsive adaptation process \cite{tzeng2017adversarial}. \subsection{Applications and Implications} The application of adaptive domain adaptation in robotics holds promise for a range of tasks, including autonomous navigation, where robots must adapt to changing terrain and lighting conditions \cite{loquercio2019deep}. In industrial settings, adaptive models can help robots adjust to variations in assembly line configurations or material properties, improving efficiency and reducing downtime \cite{schwarz2018nimbro}. Continual learning, or lifelong learning, is a paradigm that enables robots to learn continuously from a stream of data, retaining previously acquired knowledge while integrating new information. This capability is essential for developing autonomous systems that can operate over extended periods without human intervention \cite{parisi2019continual}. \subsection{Mechanisms to Mitigate Catastrophic Forgetting} A significant challenge in continual learning is catastrophic forgetting, where the model's performance on previously learned tasks deteriorates as new tasks are learned. To address this, various strategies have been proposed, including regularization-based methods, which introduce constraints to preserve important model parameters \cite{kirkpatrick2017overcoming}, and replay-based methods, which maintain a buffer of past experiences to retrain the model periodically \cite{rebuffi2017icarl}. \subsection{Integration with Robotic Systems} Integrating continual learning into robotic systems requires careful consideration of computational constraints and real-time processing requirements. Techniques such as model compression and hardware acceleration can help manage the increased computational load associated with continual learning \cite{deng2020model}. Moreover, the development of efficient algorithms for task recognition and prioritization is crucial to ensure that robots focus on learning the most relevant information \cite{van2019three}. In conclusion, the integration of sensor fusion, adaptive domain adaptation, and continual learning represents a significant advancement in the development of autonomous robotic systems. These technologies collectively enhance a robot's ability to perceive, adapt, and learn in complex, real-world environments. As research continues to progress in these areas, we anticipate the emergence of more capable and intelligent robotic systems that can operate autonomously across diverse applications and settings. The continued exploration and integration of these approaches will be pivotal in driving the next generation of robotic innovations. \bibliographystyle{IEEEtran} \bibliography{references}

text: Ground-truth labels for health data are both difficult and expensive to acquire. Lack of access to labelers (e.g. physicians) poses significant challenges in developing robust predictive models for healthcare applications. This scarcity of labeled data necessitates the exploration of alternative strategies, such as self-supervised learning (SSL), to leverage the vast amounts of unlabeled data available in electronic health records (EHRs) and medical imaging repositories. Self-supervised learning has emerged as a promising approach to address these challenges by learning useful data representations without requiring manual labeling. In the context of healthcare, SSL can facilitate the extraction of meaningful patterns from unlabeled data, which can subsequently improve model performance on various downstream tasks, including disease diagnosis, patient outcome prediction, and treatment recommendation. Despite its potential, the application of SSL in healthcare is not straightforward. A critical issue is the selection of appropriate self-supervised objectives that align well with the characteristics of medical data and the specific requirements of the target tasks. The diversity and complexity of healthcare data, ranging from structured EHRs to unstructured clinical notes and high-dimensional medical images, further complicate this selection process. In this paper, we systematically explore the efficacy of different SSL objectives tailored to healthcare data. We propose a novel meta-learning-based framework that automatically selects the most suitable SSL objectives based on the target task characteristics and the nature of the input data. Our framework draws inspiration from the Model-Agnostic Meta-Learning (MAML) algorithm \cite{finn2017model}, which is designed to quickly adapt models to new tasks with minimal adjustments. The intersection of self-supervised learning and healthcare has garnered increasing attention in recent years. Several studies have demonstrated the potential of SSL in improving model performance in medical imaging by utilizing tasks like image inpainting, jigsaw puzzle solving, and contrastive learning \cite{azizi2021big}. These methods exploit the inherent structure in medical images to train models that generate robust feature representations. In the realm of EHRs, SSL techniques such as masked language modeling and autoencoder-based approaches have been employed to learn representations that capture temporal dynamics and clinical semantics \cite{choi2016learning}. These representations have shown promise in enhancing predictive performance for tasks like patient trajectory prediction and risk stratification. Despite these advancements, a principled method for selecting SSL objectives that generalize across diverse healthcare datasets remains elusive. Our work addresses this gap by integrating meta-learning with SSL to dynamically select objectives that maximize transferability and performance on downstream healthcare tasks. Our proposed framework consists of three main components: (1) a library of self-supervised tasks, (2) a meta-learning algorithm for task selection, and (3) an evaluation protocol for assessing transferability. \subsection{Self-Supervised Task Library} We construct a comprehensive library of self-supervised tasks tailored to different types of healthcare data. For medical imaging, tasks such as patch-based contrastive learning and rotation prediction are included. For EHR data, we incorporate tasks like masked record modeling and sequence prediction. Each task in the library is designed to exploit specific data characteristics, aiming to produce representations that are both informative and transferrable. \subsection{Meta-Learning-Based Selection}

text: Adversarial example is a well-known severe security vulnerability of classifiers. Specifically, given a classifier $f$ and a testing input $\mathbf{x}$, an attacker can carefully craft a human-imperceptible perturbation $\delta$ such that the perturbed input $\mathbf{x}' = \mathbf{x} + \delta$ leads the classifier to output an incorrect prediction, i.e., $f(\mathbf{x}') \neq f(\mathbf{x})$. This phenomenon poses significant challenges to the deployment of machine learning models in security-sensitive applications, where robustness and reliability are paramount \cite{Szegedy2014}. The study of adversarial examples has garnered substantial attention within the machine learning community, prompting the development of numerous defense mechanisms. These defenses can be broadly categorized into two approaches: input transformation methods and model enhancement strategies. Input transformation methods aim to preprocess inputs to remove adversarial perturbations before they are fed to the classifier. Techniques such as input denoising, feature squeezing, and adversarial training fall under this category \cite{Gu2014}. On the other hand, model enhancement strategies focus on modifying the classifier itself to be inherently more robust against adversarial attacks. This can be achieved through regularization techniques, robust optimization frameworks, or by designing architectures that are resilient to input perturbations. For example, recent work has explored the integration of adversarial training into the learning process, where the model is explicitly trained on adversarial examples \cite{Madry2018}. Despite these advancements, the adversarial vulnerability of classifiers remains a critical concern, particularly in domains where decision accuracy is crucial. For instance, in autonomous driving systems, misclassifications due to adversarial attacks could lead to catastrophic outcomes. Similarly, in the healthcare sector, erroneous predictions in medical diagnostics could have life-threatening implications. Therefore, understanding and mitigating the risks posed by adversarial examples is essential for the safe and effective deployment of machine learning technologies in these fields. The exploration of adversarial examples traces back to the seminal work by Szegedy et al. \cite{Szegedy2014}, who first highlighted the existence of these inputs and their implications for neural networks. Following this, Goodfellow et al. \cite{Goodfellow2015} proposed the Fast Gradient Sign Method (FGSM) as an efficient approach to generate adversarial examples. FGSM leverages the gradients of the loss function with respect to the input to craft perturbations that maximize the model's prediction error. Subsequent research has introduced more sophisticated attack algorithms, including the Basic Iterative Method (BIM) and the Carlini & Wagner attack, both of which iteratively refine adversarial perturbations to evade detection \cite{Kurakin2017,Carlini2017}. These methods underscore the persistent challenge adversaries pose, as they are capable of generating highly effective perturbations that remain imperceptible to humans. In response, a variety of defense strategies have been proposed. Adversarial training, which augments the training dataset with adversarial examples, has emerged as one of the most promising techniques for enhancing model robustness \cite{Madry2018}. However, it is computationally expensive and may not generalize well across different types of attacks. Other notable defenses include defensive distillation \cite{Papernot2016}, which modifies the training process to make models less sensitive to small input perturbations, and the use of randomized smoothing, which transforms a classifier into a robust one by averaging its predictions over random perturbations of the input \cite{Cohen2019}. Although these methods provide varying degrees of protection, no single defense has proven to be completely effective against all forms of adversarial attacks. Consequently, the pursuit of new approaches that can deliver comprehensive security guarantees remains an active area of research. To rigorously analyze the robustness of classifiers against adversarial attacks, we adopt a theoretical framework grounded in the concepts of adversarial risk and robust optimization. Let $\mathcal{D}$ denote the data distribution, and let $\mathcal{L}(f(\mathbf{x}), y)$ represent the loss incurred by the classifier $f$ when predicting the label $y$ for input $\mathbf{x}$. The standard risk, $\mathbb{E}_{(\mathbf{x}, y) \sim \mathcal{D}} [\mathcal{L}(f(\mathbf{x}), y)]$, measures the expected performance of the classifier over the data distribution. In contrast, the adversarial risk considers the worst-case loss over a set of allowed perturbations. Formally, it is defined as: \[ \mathbb{E}_{(\mathbf{x}, y) \sim \mathcal{D}} \left[ \max_{\delta \in \Delta} \mathcal{L}(f(\mathbf{x} + \delta), y) \right], \] where $\Delta$ represents the set of perturbations constrained by a norm, such as the $\ell_p$ norm. The goal of robust optimization is to minimize this adversarial risk, thus ensuring that the classifier performs well even when subject to adversarial perturbations. Several optimization techniques have been explored to address this challenge. One approach involves reformulating the training objective to incorporate the adversarial risk, effectively guiding the learning process to favor weight configurations that are less susceptible to adversarial influences \cite{Madry2018}. Another strategy leverages gradient regularization to directly penalize changes in the loss function with respect to input perturbations, thereby encouraging smoother decision boundaries \cite{Ross2018}. To empirically validate the effectiveness of various defense mechanisms, we conduct a comprehensive set of experiments on benchmark datasets, including MNIST, CIFAR-10, and ImageNet. These datasets provide a diverse range of challenges in terms of complexity and scale, making them ideal for assessing the robustness of classifiers. Our evaluation focuses on several key metrics: accuracy on clean data, accuracy under adversarial attack, and computational efficiency. For adversarial attacks, we implement FGSM, BIM, and the Carlini & Wagner attack, each with varying perturbation constraints to simulate different threat models. The results indicate that while adversarial training significantly improves robustness against single-step attacks like FGSM, it exhibits diminished efficacy against more sophisticated attacks such as the Carlini & Wagner method. Defensive distillation offers moderate improvements but is often outperformed by randomized smoothing techniques, which provide a probabilistic robustness guarantee \cite{Cohen2019}. Furthermore, we observe that combining multiple defense strategies can lead to synergistic effects, enhancing overall robustness beyond that achievable by individual methods. This suggests that a holistic approach, incorporating diverse defensive mechanisms, may be necessary to counter the evolving landscape of adversarial threats. The enduring challenge of adversarial examples in machine learning underscores the necessity for continued innovation in defense strategies. While progress has been made in developing robust models and effective countermeasures, the adversarial arms race persists, driven by the ingenuity of attack methodologies. As machine learning systems are increasingly integrated into critical sectors, the imperative for reliable and secure models becomes ever more pressing. Future research directions include the exploration of adaptive defenses that can dynamically respond to new attack vectors, the establishment of standardized benchmarks for robustness evaluation, and the development of theoretical frameworks that provide formal robustness guarantees. By advancing our understanding and capabilities in these areas, we can pave the way for more secure and trustworthy machine learning applications across a myriad of domains.

text: The individualization-refinement (IR) framework is a general backtracking technique employed by algorithms solving tasks related to the computation of symmetries of combinatorial objects~\cite{McKay201494}. Within this framework, the treatment of graph symmetries is a notable application, where the primary objective is to determine the automorphism group of a graph. This group consists of all permutations of the graph's vertices that preserve its edge structure. The IR method is particularly robust and versatile, allowing it to be applied to a diverse range of combinatorial structures beyond graphs, such as hypergraphs, incidence structures, and block designs. The IR algorithm's core principle involves recursively partitioning the vertex set of a graph into cells, which are refined iteratively to become smaller and more homogeneous. This refinement process is guided by the graph's adjacency relations, aiming to achieve a balanced search tree with minimal depth, thus optimizing the algorithm's performance. The refinement procedure can extensively leverage domain-specific properties, resulting in significant computational savings. Recent advances in IR algorithms have focused on several key areas: (i) the development of more sophisticated heuristics for vertex selection during individualization, (ii) the optimization of partition refinement strategies, and (iii) the efficient management of search trees using data structures that minimize redundancy and support rapid backtracking. These enhancements have been pivotal in scaling the IR approach to tackle larger graphs, which was previously infeasible. The methodology of IR algorithms revolves around the strategic interplay between individualization and refinement. Here, we outline the primary components of an IR algorithm and how they interact to compute graph symmetries efficiently. \subsection{Vertex Individualization} Vertex individualization is the process of selecting a vertex and treating it as distinguished, effectively reducing the symmetry of the problem at each step. The choice of which vertex to individualize is crucial, as it impacts the balance and size of the search tree. Several heuristic strategies have been developed to guide this choice, such as selecting vertices with high degrees or those that maximize the entropy of the partition refinement. \subsection{Partition Refinement} Once a vertex is individualized, the partition refinement process updates the partition of the vertex set, aiming to further distinguish vertices based on the graph's connectivity properties. The refinement process typically involves coloring vertices based on their adjacency to previously individualized vertices, effectively refining the partition into smaller cells. An efficient refinement routine is crucial, as it directly influences the depth and breadth of the search tree. \subsection{Search Tree Exploration} The search tree is explored in a depth-first manner, where each node corresponds to a specific partial permutation of the graph's vertices. As the tree is traversed, the algorithm checks for automorphism candidates by verifying whether the current permutation stabilizes the graph. If a complete automorphism is found, it is recorded, and the search continues until all possible permutations have been explored or pruned. \subsection{Pruning Techniques} To enhance efficiency, various pruning techniques are employed to eliminate redundant branches in the search tree. These techniques are based on symmetry properties observed during earlier stages of the search, allowing the algorithm to disregard certain branches without explicit exploration. For example, isomorphism pruning leverages previously discovered automorphisms to avoid redundant computations. Recent research has led to several performance improvements in IR algorithms, particularly in the context of large and dense graphs. Innovations include the integration of probabilistic methods to estimate the size of the automorphism group and the use of parallel computing architectures to distribute the search process. \subsection{Heuristic Enhancements} Improved heuristics for vertex selection and refinement have been developed, allowing the algorithm to adapt dynamically to the graph's structure. These heuristics utilize machine learning techniques to predict the most promising individualization choices based on historical data from similar graphs. \subsection{Data Structures for Efficiency} The adoption of advanced data structures, such as balanced trees and hash tables, has facilitated faster partition refinement and search tree management. These structures support rapid insertion and deletion operations, which are critical during backtracking. \subsection{Parallelization Strategies} Parallelization strategies have been explored to distribute the computational load across multiple processors. This approach takes advantage of the inherent parallelizability of the search process, where different subtrees can be explored independently. Load balancing algorithms ensure that each processor contributes effectively to the overall computation. The versatility of IR algorithms has led to their application across various domains beyond graph theory. In chemical informatics, for instance, they are used to identify molecular symmetries, which play a crucial role in the study of chemical compounds and reactions. In network analysis, IR algorithms assist in detecting symmetrical structures that may suggest underlying regularities or redundancies. \subsection{Chemical Informatics} In the field of chemical informatics, graph-based representations of molecules are analyzed to determine symmetry properties that can influence chemical behavior. The automorphism group of a molecular graph can reveal insights into the molecule's stability, reactivity, and spectral properties. \subsection{Network Analysis} In network analysis, identifying symmetries can help uncover repeating patterns or motifs, which may indicate functional modules within a complex network. By understanding these symmetrical structures, researchers can draw conclusions about the network's robustness and vulnerability to perturbations. The individualization-refinement framework remains a cornerstone in the study of graph symmetries and related combinatorial problems. Continued advancements in algorithmic strategies and computational techniques promise to further extend the applicability and efficiency of IR algorithms. As the complexity and scale of problems increase, these algorithms will remain essential tools in both theoretical research and practical applications across diverse scientific domains. \section*{Acknowledgements} The authors would like to thank the contributions of the computational mathematics community, whose innovations and insights have significantly advanced the field of graph algorithms. Special thanks to the developers of benchmarking tools and datasets that facilitate the evaluation of algorithmic performance. \bibliographystyle{plain} \bibliography{references} \end{document}

This approach has demonstrated success across various applications, from natural language processing to computer vision tasks, where it often reduces the amount of labeled data required for effective model training \cite{Yosinski2014}. Despite the promise shown by these methods, challenges remain in optimizing their performance in low-data regimes. For instance, the effectiveness of transfer learning is highly contingent upon the similarity between the source and target domains. A significant domain shift or covariate shift can lead to suboptimal model performance, necessitating domain adaptation techniques to mitigate these effects \cite{Pan2010}. In this section, we review the principal methodologies that have been developed to address the limitations imposed by scarce annotated data. These include, but are not limited to, semi-supervised learning, few-shot learning, and transfer learning. \subsection{Semi-Supervised Learning} Semi-supervised learning (SSL) is a paradigm that seeks to leverage both labeled and unlabeled data to improve learning outcomes. The fundamental assumption in SSL is that the unlabeled data, when used appropriately, can help in constructing a better decision boundary. Various SSL techniques have been proposed, including: \begin{itemize} \item \textbf{Pseudo-Labeling:} This approach involves assigning labels to unlabeled data using the model's current predictions, which are then treated as true labels in subsequent training iterations. While simple, this method can be effective if the initial model predictions are reasonably accurate \cite{Lee2013}. \item \textbf{Consistency Regularization:} This strategy enforces that the model's predictions remain consistent under small perturbations of the input data. Techniques such as MixMatch \cite{Berthelot2019} and FixMatch \cite{Sohn2020} have demonstrated significant improvements in model accuracy by applying consistency constraints. \item \textbf{Graph-Based SSL:} This method constructs a graph where nodes represent data points, and edges encode relationships based on feature similarities. Label information propagates through the graph, allowing unlabeled nodes to be influenced by labeled ones \cite{Zhu2003}. \end{itemize} \subsection{Few-Shot Learning} Few-shot learning (FSL) addresses the challenge of learning from a limited number of examples. The core idea is to design algorithms that can quickly adapt to new tasks with minimal supervision. Notable approaches include: \begin{itemize} \item \textbf{Meta-Learning:} Often referred to as "learning to learn," meta-learning involves training a model on a variety of tasks such that it can rapidly adjust to new tasks using only a few examples. Model-Agnostic Meta-Learning (MAML) \cite{Finn2017} is a popular algorithm in this category, optimizing for model parameters that are easily fine-tunable with few samples. \item \textbf{Siamese Networks:} These networks learn to differentiate between pairs of input samples and are particularly useful in one-shot learning scenarios. By measuring similarity, the model can classify new instances based on their proximity to known examples \cite{Koch2015}. \item \textbf{Prototypical Networks:} These networks represent each class by a prototype, typically the mean of the embedded support points for that class. Classification is performed by finding the nearest prototype to the query sample \cite{Snell2017}. \end{itemize} \subsection{Transfer Learning} Transfer learning has gained prominence due to its ability to utilize pre-trained networks as a starting point for new tasks. This method is especially beneficial in domains with limited data, as it reduces the need for extensive labeled datasets for training from scratch. Key techniques include: \begin{itemize} \item \textbf{Fine-Tuning:} This involves adapting a pre-trained model to a new task by training it further on a smaller, task-specific dataset. The initial layers are often frozen to retain learned features, while the later layers are adjusted to the new domain \cite{Howard2018}. \item \textbf{Domain Adaptation:} When there is a domain shift between the source and target data, domain adaptation techniques can be employed to minimize discrepancies. Methods such as adversarial training and domain discrepancy minimization have been proposed to address this issue \cite{Ganin2016}. \item \textbf{Multi-Task Learning:} This approach involves training a single model to perform multiple related tasks simultaneously, thereby encouraging the model to learn more generalized features that are beneficial across tasks \cite{Ruder2017}. \end{itemize} The methodologies described have found applications across a range of specialized domains, each presenting unique challenges due to limited data availability. \subsection{Medical Imaging} In medical imaging, acquiring large labeled datasets is often impractical due to privacy concerns and the need for expert annotations. SSL and FSL have been particularly useful in this domain. For example, SSL has been applied to enhance the segmentation of medical images by utilizing unlabeled data to improve model robustness \cite{Cheplygina2019}. Similarly, FSL techniques have facilitated the classification of rare diseases by effectively leveraging small, annotated datasets \cite{Wang2020}. \subsection{Ecology and Wildlife Conservation} In ecology, the classification of rare species poses a significant challenge due to the scarcity of labeled images. Transfer learning, combined with FSL, has enabled the development of models that can recognize endangered species with limited examples \cite{Norouzzadeh2018}. These models are critical for conservation efforts, allowing for automated monitoring of wildlife populations. \subsection{Robotics and Autonomous Systems} Robotics and autonomous systems often operate in environments where real-time data collection and labeling are limited. Here, SSL and transfer learning have been used to enhance object detection and navigation capabilities. By leveraging synthetic data and simulations, these methods enable robots to adapt to new tasks with minimal real-world data \cite{James2019}. While progress has been made, several challenges remain in learning with limited data. One key issue is the potential for model bias due to the small size and possible imbalance of datasets. Techniques such as data augmentation and synthetic data generation hold promise for mitigating these issues by artificially expanding the training set \cite{Shorten2019}. Moreover, the integration of unsupervised learning methods, which do not rely on labeled data, could further enhance the capabilities of models in low-data regimes. Future research should focus on developing hybrid approaches that combine the strengths of SSL, FSL, and transfer learning to create robust models capable of generalizing from minimal data. Additionally, interpretability and explainability of models trained on limited data must be prioritized to ensure their reliability, especially in critical domains such as healthcare and autonomous driving \cite{Doshi-Velez2017}. text: Cancer is becoming the leading cause of death and the most significant obstacle to increase life expectancy in many countries~\cite{world2020report}. , accounting for millions of deaths each year. Lung cancer, in particular, remains one of the most prevalent and deadly forms of cancer, largely due to its often late diagnosis and the complexity of treatment. Early and accurate detection is crucial for improving patient outcomes, making the development of advanced diagnostic tools a research priority \cite{bray2018global}. The integration of artificial intelligence (AI) into diagnostic practices, particularly through the use of convolutional neural networks (CNNs), has shown promise in enhancing the accuracy and efficiency of lung cancer detection and segmentation. These networks, by leveraging deep learning techniques, can process vast amounts of imaging data, identifying patterns and features that may be imperceptible to the human eye \cite{shen2017deep}. \subsection{Challenges in Lung Tumor Segmentation} The segmentation of lung tumors presents several challenges, primarily due to the heterogeneous nature of tumor morphology and the variability in imaging modalities. Tumors can vary significantly in size, shape, and texture, and may be obscured by surrounding anatomical structures or artifacts in the imaging data \cite{armato2011lung}. Furthermore, the presence of overlapping organs and tissues in thoracic CT scans complicates the task of isolating tumor boundaries \cite{depeursinge2015lung}. Traditional image processing techniques, which often rely on thresholding and region-growing methods, may struggle to adapt to such variability, necessitating the development of more flexible and robust methods. CNNs address these limitations by learning complex feature hierarchies that capture both high-level and low-level information, thus adapting to the intricate properties of medical images \cite{cicek2016full}. \subsection{Advancements in Deep Learning for Medical Imaging} Recent advancements in deep learning have significantly impacted the field of medical imaging, with CNNs leading the forefront of research and application \cite{litjens2017survey}. Architectures such as U-Net and its variants have been specifically designed to tackle the challenges of medical image segmentation by incorporating skip connections and multi-scale feature extraction \cite{ronneberger2015u}. This approach allows for the effective combination of spatial and contextual information, crucial for accurate tumor localization. Moreover, the concept of transfer learning has gained traction, enabling models pre-trained on large, general datasets, such as ImageNet, to be fine-tuned for specific medical imaging tasks \cite{tajbakhsh2016convolutional}. This method not only reduces the computational burden of training from scratch but also enhances performance by leveraging learned representations that generalize well across different domains. The methodology for lung tumor segmentation using CNNs involves several key steps, starting from data acquisition to model evaluation. This section outlines the approach employed in this study, highlighting the importance of each phase in the overall workflow. \subsection{Data Acquisition and Preprocessing} High-quality annotated datasets are crucial for training deep learning models. For this study, we utilized publicly available datasets, such as the Lung Image Database Consortium (LIDC) and Image Database Resource Initiative (IDRI) database \cite{armato2011lung}. These datasets provide a comprehensive collection of thoracic CT scans with expert-annotated tumor regions, serving as a reliable benchmark for model training and validation. Preprocessing steps are essential to ensure data consistency and enhance model performance. These steps include normalization of pixel intensities, resizing images to a consistent scale, and augmentation techniques such as rotation, flipping, and contrast adjustment to increase data diversity \cite{shorten2019survey}. \subsection{Model Architecture} The core architecture employed in this study is based on the U-Net model, with modifications to accommodate the specific characteristics of lung CT images. The encoder-decoder structure of U-Net is augmented with residual blocks and attention mechanisms to refine feature extraction and improve segmentation accuracy \cite{oktay2018attention}. Residual connections help mitigate the vanishing gradient problem, while attention gates enhance the model's focus on relevant features. \subsection{Training and Optimization} Training the CNN model involves optimizing a loss function that quantifies the discrepancy between predicted and true segmentations. In this study, we employed a combination of cross-entropy loss and Dice coefficient loss to balance the precision and recall of tumor boundary predictions \cite{milletari2016v}. The Adam optimizer, known for its adaptability and efficiency, was used to adjust the model weights during training \cite{kingma2014adam}. To prevent overfitting, regularization techniques such as dropout and early stopping were implemented. Dropout randomly deactivates neurons during training, promoting model generalization, while early stopping monitors validation loss to halt training when performance plateaus \cite{srivastava2014dropout}. The performance of the proposed CNN model was evaluated on a test set, distinct from the training and validation datasets, ensuring an unbiased assessment of model generalizability. Metrics such as Dice similarity coefficient (DSC), precision, and recall were calculated to quantify segmentation accuracy \cite{zhuang2019evaluation}. Our model achieved a mean DSC of 0.85, indicating a high degree of overlap between predicted and true tumor regions. This performance is comparable to, or exceeds, results from recent studies employing similar methodologies \cite{isensee2021nnu}. The incorporation of attention mechanisms and residual connections was found to significantly enhance boundary delineation, particularly in complex cases with irregular tumor shapes. \subsection{Comparison with Traditional Methods} Compared to traditional segmentation methods, our CNN-based approach demonstrated superior robustness and adaptability to diverse tumor presentations. Handcrafted methods often require extensive tuning and domain knowledge, whereas our model autonomously learned features that generalized well across different patient scans \cite{van2019deep}. \subsection{Limitations and Future Work} Despite promising results, this study acknowledges certain limitations. The reliance on annotated datasets restricts model applicability to scenarios where such data is available. Additionally, the computational demands of training deep networks necessitate access to significant processing power, potentially limiting accessibility in resource

As the prevalence of robotic automation increases, understanding the dynamics of human-robot interaction (HRI) becomes paramount. The design of these interactions must prioritize not only efficiency and productivity but also safety and user comfort. One of the critical aspects of HRI is the development of intuitive interfaces that allow human operators to easily communicate their intentions to robots. Adaptive algorithms enable robots to modify their behavior based on real-time feedback from the environment and human partners. For instance, by employing reinforcement learning techniques, robots can dynamically adjust their task execution strategies in response to human input or changes in the environment \cite{argall2009survey}. Moreover, the ethical and social implications of robots in shared environments must be considered. As robots assume more roles traditionally occupied by humans, questions regarding job displacement, data privacy, and ethical decision-making arise. It is imperative that robotic systems are designed with transparency and accountability in mind, ensuring that they operate within the bounds of societal norms and ethical standards \cite{winfield2014robot}.
