text: With the proliferation of mobile and edge devices, federated learning~\cite{konevcny2016federatedlearning, mcmahan2017communication} has emerged as a framework for training machine learning models over geographically distributed and heterogeneous devices. diverse network environments. Unlike traditional centralized learning paradigms, federated learning allows models to be trained locally on devices, thereby preserving data privacy and reducing the dependency on centralized data storage. However, this decentralized nature also introduces unique challenges, particularly in terms of communication overhead and system heterogeneity. In federated learning, communication between client devices and a central server is a critical bottleneck due to limited bandwidth and high latency. Each participating device typically computes local updates based on its private data and periodically communicates these updates to the server. The server aggregates the received updates to refine the global model, which is then disseminated back to the clients. This iterative process necessitates frequent exchanges of model parameters or gradients, which can be prohibitively expensive, especially in networks with constrained resources. The heterogeneity among client devices poses additional challenges. Devices may vary significantly in terms of computational capabilities, power constraints, and data distribution. Such variability can lead to imbalanced contributions to the global model, with some devices dominating the learning process due to their superior resources or richer data. This heterogeneity not only affects the convergence speed but can also compromise the fairness and generalization of the learned model~\cite{zhao2018federated}. To mitigate these challenges, recent research has focused on communication-efficient federated learning algorithms that leverage compression techniques, adaptive communication strategies, and client selection protocols. Communication compression, as previously discussed, reduces the volume of data exchanged during model updates, thereby alleviating network congestion. Adaptive communication strategies adjust the frequency of communication based on the state of the training process, reducing unnecessary updates and conserving bandwidth. Client selection protocols aim to balance the contributions of heterogeneous devices, ensuring fair and equitable participation in the federated learning process. In this paper, we present a comprehensive study of state-of-the-art techniques in communication-efficient federated learning. We systematically analyze various compression methods, their integration with federated learning frameworks, and their impact on model performance and convergence. Furthermore, we explore adaptive strategies that optimize communication schedules and client selection mechanisms that enhance the robustness and fairness of the learning process. Through extensive empirical evaluations on benchmark datasets and real-world scenarios, we demonstrate the efficacy of these techniques in overcoming the inherent challenges of federated learning. The development of communication-efficient algorithms for federated learning has been an active area of research, with numerous approaches proposed to tackle the communication bottleneck. This section reviews key contributions in the field, focusing on gradient and model compression techniques, adaptive communication strategies, and client selection mechanisms. \subsection{Gradient and Model Compression} Gradient compression techniques, such as quantization and sparsification, have been extensively studied in the context of distributed learning. Quantization methods like QSGD~\cite{alistarh2017qsgd} allow gradients to be represented with fewer bits, significantly reducing communication costs. Sparsification strategies, on the other hand, transmit only a fraction of the gradient elements, focusing on those with the highest magnitude~\cite{aji2017sparse}. These methods are often complemented by error-feedback mechanisms~\cite{karimireddy2019error}, which help maintain convergence by compensating for the information lost during compression. Model compression techniques, including pruning~\cite{han2015deep} and knowledge distillation~\cite{hinton2015distilling}, have also been adapted to federated learning. Pruning reduces the size of the neural network by eliminating redundant parameters, thereby decreasing the amount of data exchanged during model updates. Knowledge distillation transfers the knowledge of a larger model to a smaller one, maintaining performance while reducing computational and communication demands. \subsection{Adaptive Communication Strategies} Adaptive communication strategies dynamically adjust the communication frequency and granularity during the training process. Deep Gradient Compression (DGC)~\cite{lin2017deep} and AdaComm~\cite{chen2018adacomm} are notable examples that exploit the redundancy in neural network updates to reduce unnecessary data transmission. These methods typically involve monitoring the training progress and selectively synchronizing model parameters based on predefined thresholds or heuristic rules. Such strategies are particularly beneficial in federated learning, where network conditions can vary significantly across devices. By tailoring communication schedules to the state of the training process, these approaches help conserve bandwidth and accelerate convergence. \subsection{Client Selection Mechanisms} Client selection mechanisms aim to address the heterogeneity among participating devices in federated learning. By intelligently selecting a subset of clients to participate in each training round, these mechanisms ensure balanced contributions and improve the overall robustness of the learned model. Strategies like FedCS~\cite{nishio2019client} and Oort~\cite{lai2021oort} leverage information about device capabilities and data distribution to optimize client selection. These approaches consider factors such as computational power, network connectivity, and data diversity, striking a balance between model accuracy, fairness, and resource utilization. By promoting equitable participation, client selection mechanisms enhance the generalization and fairness of federated learning systems. In this paper, we propose a novel framework for communication-efficient federated learning that integrates advanced compression techniques with adaptive communication and client selection strategies. Our methodology is designed to optimize the trade-off between communication costs and model accuracy, addressing the challenges of bandwidth constraints and device heterogeneity. \subsection{Compression Techniques} We employ a hybrid compression strategy that combines quantization and sparsification to minimize communication overhead while preserving model convergence. Our approach leverages stochastic quantization to reduce the precision of gradient updates, complemented by top-k sparsification to prune insignificant elements. This dual compression method is augmented with an error-feedback mechanism that accumulates and corrects compression errors over successive iterations. \subsection{Adaptive Communication Protocol} Our adaptive communication protocol dynamically adjusts the communication frequency in response to the training progress and network conditions. By monitoring the convergence rate and model accuracy, the protocol selectively triggers communication events to synchronize model updates. This approach enables efficient use of network resources, minimizing redundant data exchanges and accommodating varying device capabilities. \subsection{Client Selection Strategy} We introduce a client selection strategy that prioritizes devices based on a multi-objective optimization criterion, considering factors such as data quality, computational power, and network latency. Our strategy employs a weighted scoring system to evaluate potential clients, ensuring a diverse and representative sample of the population in each training round. By promoting balanced participation, our approach enhances the fairness and robustness of the federated learning process. To evaluate the effectiveness of our proposed framework, we conduct extensive experiments on a range of benchmark datasets, including CIFAR-10, MNIST, and a real-world federated learning scenario involving edge devices. Our experimental setup includes simulations of varying network conditions, device heterogeneity, and data distributions to comprehensively assess the performance of our method. \subsection{Experimental Setup} We implement our framework using a federated learning simulation environment, configuring a set of client devices with diverse computational resources and data characteristics. Each device performs local training using its private dataset and periodically communicates updates to a central server. The server aggregates these updates to refine the global model, following the federated averaging protocol~\cite{mcmahan2017communication}. We benchmark our method against state-of-the-art communication-efficient federated learning algorithms, including QSGD~\cite{alistarh2017qsgd}, DGC~\cite{lin2017deep}, and FedCS~\cite{nishio2019client}. Performance metrics include model accuracy, convergence speed, communication cost, and fairness, measured across diverse experimental conditions. \subsection{Results and Discussion} Our results demonstrate that the proposed framework achieves significant reductions in communication costs while maintaining or improving model accuracy compared to baseline methods. The hybrid compression strategy effectively reduces data transmission without compromising convergence, and the adaptive communication protocol optimizes synchronization frequency, leading to faster convergence rates. text: Recently, modern voice-controlled devices with virtual assistants like Alexa, Siri, and Google Assistant, have been working their way into every activity of our daily life from playing a song to managing smart home devices. These systems rely heavily on Spoken Language Understanding (SLU), which involves interpreting user utterances into actionable data. Despite significant advancements in SLU for major languages, there remains a substantial challenge in extending these capabilities to less-resourced languages. This is primarily due to the scarcity of annotated datasets and the inherent linguistic diversity that exists across languages. Cross-lingual transfer learning, particularly using models like BERT \cite{devlin2018bert}, has emerged as a promising approach to mitigate these challenges. BERT, a transformer-based model, has shown exceptional performance in various Natural Language Processing (NLP) tasks by leveraging a massive amount of unlabeled text data for pre-training. Its multilingual variant, mBERT, pre-trained on 104 languages, provides a solid foundation for cross-lingual applications by encoding shared linguistic information. This paper explores the extent to which a multilingual BERT-based model can transfer knowledge across languages in SLU tasks. Specifically, we focus on intent classification and entity recognition, as these are critical components in the functionality of voice-activated systems. Intent classification involves categorizing user queries into predefined intents, while entity recognition identifies and classifies key information within the text. Cross-lingual learning has gained significant attention in the NLP community, with many studies investigating the transferability of multilingual models. Prior research has indicated that models like mBERT can perform zero-shot transfer, where a model trained on one language is applied to another without additional training data \cite{wu2019zero}. However, the effectiveness of such transfers varies and is often contingent on linguistic similarities. Models such as XLM-R \cite{conneau2019xlmr} have further enhanced the ability to generalize across languages by training on more extensive datasets. These models benefit from the shared representation space, allowing them to perform well in languages with limited resources. However, the degree of transfer remains inconsistent, particularly for languages with unique syntactic and morphological features. Our approach involves training a multilingual BERT model on intent classification and entity recognition tasks using the XNLI dataset \cite{conneau2018xnli} as a starting point. We then fine-tune the model on a subset of languages and evaluate its performance on both seen and unseen languages. \subsection{Data Collection} We utilize the XNLI dataset for initial training due to its extensive multilingual coverage. This dataset provides a rich source of aligned text across multiple languages, facilitating the learning of cross-lingual representations. For fine-tuning, we select datasets specific to intent classification and entity recognition for languages such as English, Spanish, Arabic, and Chinese. These datasets include the ATIS corpus \cite{hemphill1990atis} and the MIT Movie Corpus \cite{liu2012movie} for intent classification, as well as CoNLL-2003 \cite{sang2003conll} for entity recognition. \subsection{Model Training} The model training process involves two phases: pre-training and fine-tuning. Initially, we pre-train the multilingual BERT model on the XNLI dataset to capture general linguistic features. This is followed by fine-tuning on specific SLU tasks using the aforementioned datasets. Hyperparameters such as learning rate, batch size, and epochs are optimized to ensure robust performance across languages. To assess the model's cross-lingual transfer capabilities, we conduct comprehensive evaluations on both intent classification and entity recognition tasks. We measure performance using standard metrics such as accuracy, precision, recall, and F1-score. \subsection{Intent Classification} We evaluate the model's ability to classify intents across different languages. The results demonstrate that languages with similar syntactic structures, such as Spanish and Italian, show higher transfer accuracy compared to morphologically rich languages like Arabic. \subsection{Entity Recognition} For entity recognition, we observe that the model performs well on languages with ample training data, such as English and Spanish. However, for languages such as Chinese, the model struggles with the identification of entities due to its distinct character-based writing system, which differs significantly from the alphabetic systems of other languages. The findings indicate that while multilingual BERT models exhibit a notable degree of cross-lingual transfer, the effectiveness is highly dependent on the linguistic characteristics of the target language. Shared syntactic and morphological features enhance transferability, whereas unique linguistic properties pose challenges. The availability of parallel corpora also significantly impacts performance. Languages with rich parallel datasets benefit more from the pre-trained multilingual representations, highlighting the importance of data availability in cross-lingual applications. Future research should focus on enhancing model architectures to better handle linguistic diversity, potentially through the integration of language-specific modules or leveraging unsupervised machine translation methods to augment data for low-resource languages. This study underscores the potential of multilingual BERT models in facilitating cross-lingual SLU, while also highlighting the limitations posed by linguistic diversity and data scarcity. By advancing these models and addressing the current challenges, we can move towards more inclusive and effective language understanding technologies. \bibliographystyle{plain} \bibliography{references}

text: During the recent years, micro-blogging become a source of current and topical news. Twitter\footnote{www.twitter.com} has emerged as a pivotal platform in this realm, providing real-time updates and facilitating rapid communication across the globe. The brevity and immediacy of tweets make Twitter a unique and valuable data source for those interested in studying social dynamics and information dissemination. However, this same brevity poses significant analytical challenges, particularly in extracting nuanced meaning from limited textual content. The process of collecting data from Twitter involves interacting with its API to retrieve tweets relevant to specific research questions or topics. Researchers must carefully design their queries to maximize the relevance and quality of the data collected. Commonly used parameters include hashtags, keywords, geolocation, and time frames. Once collected, the raw data is often noisy, necessitating a comprehensive preprocessing phase. Preprocessing typically includes steps such as tokenization, stop-word removal, stemming, and lemmatization. Tokenization involves breaking down the tweet text into individual words or tokens, which are more manageable for computational analysis. Stop-word removal eliminates common words that do not contribute significantly to the meaning of the text, such as "and," "the," and "is." Stemming and lemmatization reduce words to their root forms, aiding in the normalization of the text and improving the performance of NLP models. Furthermore, handling non-standard language features such as emojis, hashtags, and mentions requires special attention. Emojis, for instance, can convey sentiment and should be converted to their descriptive form or included in analysis as features. Hashtags, often serving as thematic markers, can be analyzed to understand trends and topics of interest. Sentiment analysis on Twitter data can be approached using various methodologies. Lexicon-based approaches rely on pre-defined dictionaries of words associated with particular sentiments. These methods are straightforward but may struggle with context and idiomatic expressions. Machine learning approaches, on the other hand, involve training classifiers such as Support Vector Machines (SVM), Random Forests, or deep learning models using labeled datasets. These models can capture complex patterns and contextual nuances but require a substantial amount of labeled data for training. Recent advancements in deep learning, particularly the development of transformer-based models like BERT (Bidirectional Encoder Representations from Transformers), have significantly enhanced sentiment analysis capabilities \cite{devlin2018bert}. BERT's ability to capture context and semantic relationships between words in a sentence makes it particularly well-suited for analyzing the nuanced and context-dependent nature of tweets. The study of information diffusion on Twitter focuses on understanding how information spreads within and across social networks. Network analysis techniques are essential in this domain, enabling researchers to model and visualize the complex web of interactions among users. Key metrics such as centrality, clustering coefficient, and path length help identify influential users and information hubs within the network. Simulation models like the Independent Cascade Model (ICM) and Linear Threshold Model (LTM) provide frameworks for studying diffusion processes. The ICM assumes that each user has a probability of influencing their neighbors, while the LTM considers the cumulative influence of a user's connections. These models can be used to simulate the spread of information and to identify strategies for maximizing or minimizing its reach. Despite the advancements in Twitter data analysis, several challenges remain. The dynamic nature of language, the evolving structure of social networks, and the presence of bots and fake accounts complicate analyses. Moreover, ethical considerations, such as privacy concerns and data misuse, must be addressed. Future research may focus on improving model robustness to handle the continuously changing linguistic and social landscape of Twitter. Integrating multimodal data, such as images and videos accompanying tweets, could provide richer context and enhance analytical precision. Additionally, the development of more sophisticated algorithms for bot detection and sentiment analysis could further improve the reliability of insights drawn from Twitter data. In conclusion,

text: Clinicians currently spend more time documenting information in electronic health records (EHRs) than they do interacting with patients, which can impede the quality of care and increase burnout \cite{Shanafelt2016}. The cumbersome nature of EHRs, often necessitating extensive manual entry, is a significant contributor to this issue. The integration of intelligent systems that assist in the documentation process can potentially alleviate this burden. In this paper, we introduce an advanced clinical documentation system that employs a sophisticated autocompletion mechanism, aimed at streamlining the documentation workflow and enhancing overall efficiency. The use of natural language processing (NLP) in healthcare has been extensively explored, with applications ranging from information extraction \cite{Jonnalagadda2015} to predictive analytics \cite{Miotto2016}. Autocompletion technologies, while common in general text editing software, have seen limited application in clinical documentation. Previous studies have demonstrated the potential for NLP-based systems to assist in generating structured clinical summaries \cite{Pivovarov2015}; however, these systems often lack the adaptability required for diverse clinical scenarios. Our approach builds upon these foundations by integrating a domain-specific knowledge base with machine learning techniques to provide real-time, context-aware suggestions. This hybrid model ensures that the system is not only responsive but also capable of evolving with continual usage, thereby maintaining its clinical relevance. \subsection{Data Collection} The training dataset comprises a vast collection of de-identified clinical notes sourced from multiple healthcare institutions. These notes encompass a wide range of specialties, ensuring that the model is exposed to a diverse set of clinical terminologies and documentation styles. Prior to use, the data underwent rigorous preprocessing, including tokenization, normalization, and anonymization, to ensure patient privacy and compliance with ethical standards \cite{McMurry2016}. \subsection{Model Architecture} The core of the autocompletion system is a recurrent neural network (RNN) designed to capture the sequential nature of clinical text. The RNN is enhanced with an attention mechanism, allowing it to focus on relevant parts of the input when generating suggestions. This architecture is augmented by a domain-specific knowledge base, which provides additional context for the suggestions and helps resolve ambiguities inherent in medical language \cite{Bahdanau2015}. \subsection{Feedback Loop and Continuous Learning} To ensure the system remains accurate and contextually relevant, we implemented a feedback loop where user interactions—such as accepting, modifying, or rejecting suggestions—are logged and analyzed. This data is used to fine-tune the model, allowing it to learn from real-world usage patterns and user preferences. Such continuous learning mechanisms are crucial for maintaining the system's efficacy over time \cite{Settles2012}. \subsection{Experimental Setup} We conducted a series of experiments to evaluate the performance of our system, focusing on metrics such as suggestion relevance, acceptance rate, and documentation time reduction. Participants included a cohort of clinicians across various specialties, ensuring that the evaluation metrics were representative of real-world clinical settings. \subsection{Results} The results demonstrated that our autocompletion system significantly improves documentation efficiency. On average, the system was able to reduce documentation time by 30\%, corroborating initial findings. Moreover, the suggestion acceptance rate was notably high, with clinicians choosing to accept the system's suggestions in over 70\% of cases. This high acceptance rate underscores the contextual accuracy and clinical relevance of the proposed system. Additionally, the system's ability to suggest less common but contextually appropriate phrases was highlighted as a key strength. This feature not only enhances the quality of documentation but also assists in clinical decision-making by reminding clinicians of pertinent, albeit atypical, considerations \cite{Weng2017}. The integration of NLP-based autocompletion into clinical documentation represents a significant advancement in healthcare technology. By reducing the time burden of EHRs, clinicians can allocate more resources to direct patient care, potentially enhancing patient outcomes and satisfaction. Furthermore, the system's adaptability and continuous learning capabilities ensure that it remains a valuable tool in the ever-evolving landscape of clinical practice. Future work will focus on expanding the system's capabilities to include voice recognition and multilingual support, further broadening its applicability. Additionally, we aim to explore the integration of this system with existing EHR platforms to provide a seamless user experience. In conclusion, the proposed autocompletion system offers a promising solution to the challenges of clinical documentation. By leveraging advanced NLP techniques and a robust feedback mechanism, the system not only streamlines the documentation process but also enhances the quality of clinical notes. As healthcare continues to embrace digital technologies, such innovations hold the potential to transform clinical practice, ultimately benefiting both clinicians and patients alike. \bibliographystyle{plain} \bibliography{references} \end{document}

Hand dexterity is fundamental to daily human activities, requiring complex and precise control of finger movements. This intricate coordination is achieved through the integration of sensory feedback and motor commands, enabling humans to manipulate objects with remarkable precision and adaptability. Mimicking such capabilities in robotic systems remains a formidable challenge due to the intricate interplay between perception, control, and actuation required for dexterous manipulation. Despite significant progress in robotic manipulation, current approaches often fall short when confronted with the diversity and unpredictability of real-world environments. Traditional robotic systems tend to rely on pre-programmed sequences and rigid control algorithms, which lack the flexibility and adaptability seen in human actions. To overcome these limitations, the field has gradually shifted towards data-driven methods, leveraging vast datasets and computational resources to train robots in a manner analogous to human learning processes. Reinforcement learning (RL) has emerged as a powerful framework for developing autonomous agents capable of learning complex manipulation tasks through trial and error \cite{Sutton2018}. However, RL's applicability is often constrained by the extensive computational resources required for training and the difficulty in generalizing learned policies to new tasks and environments. This has prompted researchers to explore hybrid approaches that combine model-free and model-based strategies, allowing robots to benefit from both the exploratory power of RL and the structured guidance of predictive models \cite{Chua2018}. Parallel to RL, imitation learning has gained traction by providing a mechanism for robots to acquire skills by observing human demonstrations. Techniques such as Behavioral Cloning (BC) and Inverse Reinforcement Learning (IRL) allow robots to infer the underlying intentions and strategies of human actions, thereby facilitating the transfer of complex skills \cite{Ziebart2008}. By incorporating demonstrations into the learning pipeline, robots can reduce the exploration burden and improve the efficiency of skill acquisition. In addition to algorithmic advancements, the integration of multimodal sensory feedback has become a critical component of modern robotic manipulation systems. Vision and tactile sensors provide complementary information that can significantly enhance the decision-making capabilities of robots. Vision systems offer global context and object recognition capabilities, while tactile sensors deliver detailed information about object properties and contact dynamics \cite{Yuan2017}. Together, these sensory modalities enable robots to perceive and adapt to their environment with human-like perceptual richness. Moreover, the development of novel hardware, such as anthropomorphic robotic hands with increased degrees of freedom, has expanded the scope of achievable manipulation tasks. These advanced robotic platforms, combined with sophisticated control algorithms, are paving the way for robots capable of performing intricate manipulation tasks with precision akin to human hands \cite{Kumar2016}. Despite these advancements, several challenges remain in achieving human-level dexterity in robotic systems. One significant hurdle is the development of robust control strategies that can handle the high-dimensional action spaces characteristic of dexterous manipulation. Additionally, ensuring the transferability of learned skills across different tasks and environments continues to be a major research focus. In conclusion, the quest for achieving human-like dexterity in robotic manipulation is inherently multidisciplinary, requiring advances in machine learning, sensory integration, and robotic hardware. By drawing inspiration from human capabilities and leveraging cutting-edge technologies, researchers are gradually bridging the gap between robotic and human manipulation skills. The ongoing integration of reinforcement learning, imitation learning, and multimodal sensory feedback holds promise for the development of robotic systems that can seamlessly interact with complex and dynamic environments, ultimately achieving the goal of truly autonomous dexterous manipulation. text: The task of image captioning aims to generate human-readable descriptive text from an image. The task of image captioning aims to generate human-readable descriptive text from an image. This involves understanding and interpreting the visual content, identifying salient objects, actions, and scenes, and expressing them linguistically. Image captioning is a complex problem at the intersection of computer vision and natural language processing, requiring models to bridge the semantic gap between visual data and textual descriptions. Traditionally, image captioning models have relied heavily on convolutional neural networks (CNNs) for feature extraction and recurrent neural networks (RNNs) for language generation. However, these approaches often require extensive preprocessing, such as object detection and region proposal, which can be computationally intensive and may not capture global image contexts effectively \cite{karpathy2015deep, vinyals2015show}. Recent advances in transformer-based architectures have revolutionized the field by leveraging self-attention mechanisms to process entire images and their corresponding text concurrently. This has led to the development of more sophisticated models that do not rely on predefined object regions, allowing for end-to-end learning of visual and linguistic features. The Vision Transformer (ViT) \cite{dosovitskiy2021an}, for example, has demonstrated that transformers can be effectively applied to image data, capturing complex dependencies across image patches. The evolution of image captioning models can be traced through several key developments. Early models predominantly employed CNNs for image feature extraction, followed by LSTMs or GRUs for sequence generation \cite{vinyals2015show, xu2015show}. These models were limited by their reliance on object detectors and region-based features, which constrained their ability to generate contextually rich captions. The introduction of attention mechanisms marked a significant turning point, allowing models to focus on relevant parts of the image while generating corresponding words in the caption. This approach was pioneered by the work of Xu et al. \cite{xu2015show}, who integrated spatial attention into the captioning pipeline, enabling dynamic weighting of image features. More recently, the adoption of transformers has further enhanced model capabilities by eliminating the need for recurrent structures. The self-attention mechanism inherent in transformers facilitates the simultaneous consideration of all input elements, making them particularly well-suited for tasks that require global context understanding \cite{vaswani2017attention}. The Vision-Language Pre-training (VLP) paradigm \cite{li2019visualbert} extends this concept by jointly pre-training models on both image and text data, leading to improved alignment between modalities. \subsection{Model Architecture} Our proposed model builds upon the ViT framework, integrating it with a transformer-based language model to form a unified vision-language transformer. The architecture consists of several key components: \begin{itemize} \item \textbf{Image Encoder:} A modified Vision Transformer that processes the image as a sequence of non-overlapping patches. Each patch is linearly embedded and augmented with positional encodings, facilitating the model's ability to capture spatial hierarchies. \item \textbf{Text Decoder:} A transformer decoder that generates captions by attending to the encoded image features. This component is initialized with a pre-trained language model, allowing it to leverage rich linguistic representations. \item \textbf{Cross-Attention Layers:} These layers enable interaction between the visual and textual streams, allowing the model to focus on relevant image regions while generating specific words in the caption. \end{itemize} \subsection{Training Objectives} To train our model, we employ a combination of objectives that encourage effective cross-modal learning: \begin{itemize} \item \textbf{Masked Language Modeling (MLM):} Inspired by BERT \cite{devlin2019bert}, we randomly mask words in the caption and task the model with predicting them based on the image context, promoting robust language understanding. \item \textbf{Image Reconstruction:} We incorporate an auxiliary task where the model attempts to reconstruct masked image patches, enhancing its ability to capture detailed visual features. \item \textbf{Contrastive Loss:} To improve the alignment between image and text modalities, we utilize a contrastive loss that minimizes the distance between corresponding image-caption pairs while maximizing the distance from non-corresponding pairs. \end{itemize} \subsection{Datasets} We evaluate our model on several benchmark datasets, including MS COCO \cite{lin2014microsoft} and Flickr30k \cite{plummer2015flickr30k}. These datasets provide a diverse range of images and captions, serving as a comprehensive testbed for assessing model performance. \subsection{Evaluation Metrics} To measure the effectiveness of our approach, we employ standard evaluation metrics such as BLEU, METEOR, and CIDEr \cite{vedantam2015cider}. These metrics evaluate the quality of generated captions based on n-gram overlaps, semantic similarity, and consensus with human-annotated references. \subsection{Results} Our experiments demonstrate that the proposed model outperforms existing state-of-the-art approaches across all evaluation metrics. The integration of self-attention and cross-attention mechanisms allows our model to generate more coherent and contextually accurate captions. Notably, our model exhibits improved performance in capturing fine-grained details and complex interactions between objects, as evidenced by higher CIDEr scores. The success of transformer-based models in image captioning highlights the importance of joint vision-language modeling. By moving away from traditional region-based approaches, these models can better capture global contexts and nuanced relationships within the image. However, challenges remain in ensuring model robustness and fairness. The tendency to overfit to frequent patterns and biases in the training data can lead to less diverse and informative captions. Future work should explore strategies for mitigating these biases, such as incorporating adversarial training or using more diverse and representative datasets. text: Environmental sound provides rich perspectives on the physical world. For example, if we hear: \emph{joyful laughing, a playful scream, and a splash;} Environmental sound provides rich perspectives on the physical world. For example, if we hear: \emph{joyful laughing, a playful scream, and a splash; we might infer the presence of children playing by a pool.} Such soundscapes not only convey the activities taking place but also evoke contextual information about the setting, such as the time of day or the environment. This auditory context is invaluable for a variety of applications, including surveillance, wildlife monitoring, and immersive virtual environments. Despite the potential applications, automatically interpreting these soundscapes remains a challenging task due to the vast diversity and complexity of natural sounds. The current advancements in machine learning, particularly in the domains of unsupervised and self-supervised learning, offer promising solutions to these challenges. These approaches can leverage large datasets of unlabelled audio recordings, extracting meaningful patterns and representations without the need for extensive manual annotation \cite{schneider2019wav2vec}. This is crucial given the impracticality of collecting and annotating comprehensive datasets for every possible environmental sound. Self-supervised learning has gained traction as an effective strategy for learning representations in the absence of labelled data. This paradigm involves designing a pretext task that exploits the inherent structure in the data. A popular method in the audio domain is contrastive learning, wherein the model is trained to differentiate between similar and dissimilar audio segments. This can be achieved by using contrastive loss functions that encourage representations of similar sound events to be closer in the feature space than those of differing events \cite{oord2018representation}. More specifically, models like Contrastive Predictive Coding (CPC) have shown effectiveness in capturing temporal dependencies in audio sequences. By predicting future audio slices based on past context, CPC models can encode information that captures both local and global structure in audio streams. These representations can then be fine-tuned for downstream tasks, such as audio tagging, with minimal labelled data, thus enhancing the model's utility in real-world applications \cite{oord2018representation}. The intersection of sound and language processing is a burgeoning field that benefits greatly from cross-modal learning frameworks. By developing models that jointly process audio and text, it is possible to create systems that not only recognize sounds but can also describe them in natural language. Transformer architectures, originally designed for NLP tasks, have been adapted to process audio inputs, allowing for the joint embedding of audio and text data \cite{vaswani2017attention}. These models can be trained using paired audio-text datasets, where the task is to align spoken descriptions with corresponding audio events. This alignment can be further refined using techniques such as cross-modal attention, which enables the model to focus on relevant portions of the audio when generating textual descriptions. Such multimodal representations are powerful, as they can be applied to diverse tasks ranging from automatic captioning of environmental soundscapes to enhancing accessibility for the visually impaired \cite{deselaers2010cross}. To further improve the performance and interpretability of models interpreting environmental sounds, it is crucial to incorporate domain-specific knowledge. This can be achieved by integrating ontologies and knowledge graphs into the learning process. Ontologies provide a structured format for representing sound categories and their interrelations, which can guide the model in understanding the hierarchical and contextual nature of sound events \cite{niles2001ontology}. For instance, a model equipped with an understanding of animal sound ontologies can more accurately distinguish between similar sounds by leveraging knowledge about species-specific vocalizations and their typical contexts. Knowledge graphs can also support reasoning tasks, enabling models to make inferences about unobserved events based on observed audio cues and their known relationships. This integration of symbolic knowledge with data-driven learning approaches represents a promising direction for enhancing model robustness and applicability across domains \cite{bollacker2008freebase}. Despite the progress, several challenges remain in the development of systems that can fully understand and describe environmental soundscapes. One significant challenge is the inherent variability in natural sounds, which can be influenced by factors such as environmental acoustics, the presence of background noise, and the fidelity of recording equipment. Robust models must be capable of generalizing across these variations to provide reliable interpretations. Additionally, the ethical implications of deploying sound recognition systems in public or private spaces must be carefully considered. Privacy concerns arise when audio data is collected and processed, necessitating the development of privacy-preserving techniques that anonymize or obfuscate sensitive information while retaining the utility of the sound data \cite{dwork2014algorithmic}. Future research should focus on enhancing the generalization capabilities of audio models, possibly through the application of domain adaptation techniques that transfer knowledge across different environments. Moreover, the integration of causal inference methods could further improve the interpretability of models by allowing them to distinguish between correlation and causation in complex soundscapes. In summary, while significant strides have been made in the automatic interpretation of environmental soundscapes, continued innovation in learning methodologies, cross-modal integration, and knowledge incorporation is essential. These efforts will pave the way for more sophisticated systems capable of interacting with and understanding the acoustic environment as naturally as humans do. \bibliographystyle{plain} \bibliography{references}

The release of large pre-trained language models like BERT~\cite{devlin2019bert} has shaken up Natural Language Processing (NLP) and Information Retrieval (IR). By providing rich contextual embeddings, these models have significantly enhanced the ability to understand and process language at a deeper semantic level. In the context of IR, BERT and its variants have been pivotal in advancing the capabilities of dense retrieval systems, where the objective is to effectively capture the nuanced meanings of queries and documents to improve retrieval accuracy. Dense retrieval models, which rely heavily on these pre-trained representations, have been shown to outperform traditional TF-IDF and BM25-based methods in numerous benchmarks \cite{nogueira2019passage}. Yet, their success is not without challenges. One major hurdle is the computational overhead associated with training and deploying these models at scale. Dense vectors, though powerful, necessitate sophisticated infrastructure capable of handling large-scale vector computations, particularly in the deployment phase where latency is a critical factor. Moreover, while dense retrieval models excel at capturing semantic similarities, they often require considerable fine-tuning on domain-specific data to achieve optimal performance \cite{hofstatter2021improving}. This need for domain-specific adaptation stems from the variability in language use across different fields, which can cause models trained on general corpora to exhibit reduced effectiveness when applied to specialized datasets. Techniques such as domain adaptation and transfer learning are being actively researched to mitigate these limitations and enhance model robustness across diverse information domains \cite{gururangan2020don}. Another pressing issue is the interpretability of dense models. Unlike sparse models, where the contribution of each term to the retrieval score is explicit, dense models encode information in a way that is not easily interpretable. Understanding how these models derive relevance scores from dense embeddings is crucial for debugging and improving system transparency \cite{wallace2021interpreting}. Current efforts in this area involve developing explainable AI techniques that can offer insights into the decision-making processes of dense retrieval systems, thereby increasing user trust and system accountability. Recent advancements in hybrid models, which combine dense and sparse retrieval approaches, have shown promise in addressing some of these issues. By leveraging the strengths of both methodologies, hybrid systems can achieve superior performance across a variety of retrieval tasks \cite{lin2021hybrid}. This synergy has led to improved retrieval outcomes, especially in cases where queries involve complex, nuanced language. text: Data sets and statistics about groups of individuals are increasingly collected and released, feeding many optimization and learning algorithms. in diverse domains such as healthcare, finance, and social sciences. However, the granularity of these data sets often contains sensitive information about individuals, raising substantial privacy concerns. Differential privacy has emerged as a gold standard for privacy-preserving data analysis, providing robust guarantees that mitigate the risk of exposing individual data points while still allowing meaningful insights to be extracted from the data. The primary goal of differential privacy is to ensure that the inclusion or exclusion of a single individual's data does not significantly affect the outcome of any analysis. This is achieved by adding carefully calibrated noise to the results of queries on the data set. The parameter $\epsilon$, known as the privacy budget, controls the trade-off between privacy and accuracy: a smaller $\epsilon$ provides stronger privacy but at the cost of reduced accuracy, and vice versa. In this paper, we explore the implications of differential privacy in data-intensive applications, emphasizing its applicability in modern machine learning pipelines. We review the theoretical foundations of differential privacy and illustrate its practical implementation in various contexts, highlighting its strengths and limitations. Our discussion extends to the challenges and opportunities in integrating differential privacy with emerging techniques such as federated learning and deep learning. Differential privacy is formally defined as follows: a randomized mechanism $\mathcal{M}$ provides $\epsilon$-differential privacy if for all data sets $D_1$ and $D_2$ differing on at most one element, and for all subsets of outputs $S \subseteq \text{Range}(\mathcal{M})$, \begin{equation} \Pr[\mathcal{M}(D_1) \in S] \leq e^{\epsilon} \Pr[\mathcal{M}(D_2) \in S]. \end{equation} This definition ensures that the presence or absence of a single individual's data in the data set $D$ does not significantly change the probability of any particular output, thereby protecting individual privacy. The parameter $\epsilon$ dictates the level of privacy: smaller values of $\epsilon$ correspond to stronger privacy guarantees. \subsection{Mechanisms for Achieving Differential Privacy} Several mechanisms have been developed to achieve differential privacy, with the Laplace and Gaussian mechanisms being the most prominent. The Laplace mechanism adds noise drawn from the Laplace distribution, which is centered at zero with a scale proportional to the sensitivity of the query function. The sensitivity of a function $f$, denoted $\Delta f$, is defined as the maximum amount by which $f$ can change by altering a single data point in the data set. For a query function $f: D \rightarrow \mathbb{R}$, the Laplace mechanism $\mathcal{M}_L$ is given by: \begin{equation} \mathcal{M}_L(D) = f(D) + \text{Laplace}\left(\frac{\Delta f}{\epsilon}\right). \end{equation} Similarly, the Gaussian mechanism adds noise drawn from a Gaussian distribution, which is particularly useful when dealing with high-dimensional data or when $\delta$-approximate differential privacy is permissible. \subsection{Composition and Privacy Amplification} One of the key properties of differential privacy is its behavior under composition. When multiple differentially private mechanisms are applied to the same data set, the overall privacy loss can be bounded by the composition theorem. Specifically, if $\mathcal{M}_1$ and $\mathcal{M}_2$ are $\epsilon_1$- and $\epsilon_2$-differentially private, respectively, their sequential composition is $(\epsilon_1 + \epsilon_2)$-differentially private. Privacy amplification occurs when random sampling is involved. By sampling a subset of the data set and applying a differentially private mechanism, the effective privacy cost can be reduced, offering a more favorable privacy-utility trade-off. Incorporating differential privacy into machine learning models is critical for developing responsible AI systems that respect user privacy. Techniques have been developed to train models with differential privacy guarantees, such as differentially private stochastic gradient descent (DP-SGD). In DP-SGD, noise is added to the gradients during training, ensuring that the learned model does not overfit to the specifics of any individual data point. Moreover, differential privacy is increasingly applied in federated learning, where multiple clients collaboratively train a model without sharing their raw data. In this setting, differential privacy helps ensure that updates from individual clients do not leak private information

text: This work considers a perimeter defense problem in a conical environment in which a single mobile vehicle seeks to intercept mobile intruders before they enter a specified region (referred to as the protected boundary). The defense strategy involves optimizing the vehicle's path and speed to effectively intercept multiple intruders whose trajectories are predetermined and linear. The conical nature of the environment imposes additional geometric constraints on the vehicle's movement, necessitating sophisticated control strategies to ensure successful interception within minimal time. The perimeter defense problem is of significant interest in various fields, including military operations, robotics, and security systems, where the need to protect critical assets from unauthorized access is paramount. In military applications, this scenario can be likened to an anti-missile system designed to intercept incoming threats. In robotics, it relates to automated surveillance systems tasked with monitoring and responding to intrusions within a defined space. \subsection{Problem Definition} The problem is formally defined within a two-dimensional plane, where the conical sector is characterized by an angle \(\alpha\) and a radial distance \(r\). The center of the conical sector is located at the origin of the coordinate system. The vehicle, positioned initially at a known location within the cone, is tasked with intercepting intruders that enter the sector at various angles and velocities. Each intruder's path is defined by a line \(y = m_i x + c_i\), where \(m_i\) and \(c_i\) are constants specific to the \(i\)-th intruder, and the direction of travel is towards the origin. The objective of the vehicle is to minimize the interception time, \(T\), which is the time taken to intercept all intruders before any reach the protected boundary. This objective is subject to the vehicle's dynamic constraints and the requirement that it remains within the conical boundary throughout its mission. \subsection{Mathematical Formulation} The problem can be expressed as an optimal control problem with state variables \(x(t)\), \(y(t)\), control inputs \(v(t)\), \(\theta(t)\), and the following constraints: 1. **Kinematic Constraints**: Governed by the equations \[ \begin{align*} \dot{x}(t) &= v(t) \cos(\theta(t)), \\ \dot{y}(t) &= v(t) \sin(\theta(t)). \end{align*} \] 2. **Velocity Constraint**: The vehicle's speed is bounded by a maximum velocity \(v_{\max}\), i.e., \(0 \leq v(t) \leq v_{\max}\). 3. **Angular Constraint**: The rate of change of the heading angle is limited by the vehicle's maneuverability, \(|\dot{\theta}(t)| \leq \omega_{\max}\). 4. **Geometric Constraint**: The vehicle must remain within the conical sector, which imposes the following inequality: \[ |y| \leq x \tan(\frac{\alpha}{2}). \] 5. **Capture Condition**: An intruder is considered intercepted if the vehicle comes within a capture radius \(R\) of the intruder's trajectory. The problem is to find the control inputs \(v(t)\) and \(\theta(t)\) that minimize \(T\), the total time required to intercept all intruders, subject to the above constraints. \subsection{Related Work} Several studies have addressed the perimeter defense problem under various assumptions and environments. Early work by Isaacs \cite{isaacs1965differential} laid the foundation for differential game theory, which has been extensively applied to pursuit-evasion scenarios. More recent approaches have focused on algorithmic strategies for single and multiple pursuer scenarios in diverse environments, ranging from simple geometries to complex terrains \cite{li2016survey, shishika2018localization}. In the context of conical environments, previous research has primarily addressed static perimeters or simplified dynamic models \cite{guo2017optimal}. However, the incorporation of realistic vehicle dynamics and constraints remains an area requiring further exploration. Recent advancements in control theory and computational methods have opened new avenues for addressing such complex optimal control problems \cite{bryson1975applied}. The methodology employed in this study involves the formulation of the perimeter defense problem as a time-optimal control problem. We utilize Pontryagin's Maximum Principle \cite{pontryagin1962mathematical} to derive necessary conditions for optimality, which guide the selection of control strategies for the vehicle. The approach begins with the establishment of a Hamiltonian function, \(H\), which incorporates the state dynamics and control inputs. The Hamiltonian is given by: \[ H = \lambda_x \dot{x} + \lambda_y \dot{y} + \mu \left( v(t) - v_{\max} \right), \] where \(\lambda_x\) and \(\lambda_y\) are costate variables, and \(\mu\) is a Lagrange multiplier associated with the velocity constraint. Applying Pontryagin's Maximum Principle, we derive the necessary conditions: \[ \begin{align*} \dot{\lambda}_x &= -\frac{\partial H}{\partial x}, \\ \dot{\lambda}_y &= -\frac{\partial H}{\partial y}, \\ \frac{\partial H}{\partial v} &= 0, \\ \frac{\partial H}{\partial \theta} &= 0. \end{align*} \] These conditions yield a system of differential equations that describe the optimal control trajectory. Numerical methods, such as the shooting method or collocation techniques \cite{betts2010practical}, are employed to solve the resulting boundary value problem. The proposed methodology is evaluated through simulation studies that demonstrate the effectiveness of the control strategy in minimizing interception time. Various scenarios are tested, including different initial positions, intruder entry angles, and velocities, to assess the robustness of the solution. Simulation results indicate that the optimal control strategy successfully intercepts all intruders within the conical sector, adhering to the dynamic and geometric constraints. The time-to-interception is significantly reduced compared to heuristic approaches, highlighting the benefits of the optimal control framework. This study presents a comprehensive approach to solving the perimeter defense problem in a conical environment using optimal control theory. The formulation as a time-optimal control problem, along with the application of Pontryagin's Maximum Principle, provides a robust framework for designing efficient interception strategies. Future work will explore the extension of this methodology to multi-vehicle scenarios and the incorporation of stochastic elements to account for uncertainty in intruder trajectories. Semi-VOS tracks an object of interest across all the frames in a video given the ground truth mask of the initial frame. This task poses significant challenges due to the inherent complexity of video data, including occlusions, appearance variations, and intricate motion patterns. The primary objective is to maintain accurate object segmentation throughout the video sequence while minimizing computational overhead. A critical component of Semi-VOS is the ability to generalize well to new frames, leveraging the initial ground truth and any previously acquired knowledge efficiently. Traditional methods have relied heavily on handcrafted features and heuristic-based motion models, which often struggle to adapt to diverse and unseen environments. However, the advent of deep learning has revolutionized this domain, allowing for more robust and flexible models that can learn directly from data \cite{jain2017fusionseg}. Recent contributions have focused on enhancing the capacity of neural networks to comprehend both spatial and temporal dynamics. For instance, Long Short-Term Memory (LSTM) networks and Gated Recurrent Units (GRUs) have been utilized to capture long-range dependencies across frames, effectively modeling temporal context \cite{xiao2020memory}. Moreover, Transformer models, initially designed for natural language processing tasks, have shown promise in capturing global dependencies in video data, providing a complementary approach to CNNs for feature extraction \cite{liu2021swin}. The integration of attention mechanisms has further bolstered the performance of Semi-VOS models. By allowing the network to focus selectively on pertinent regions of the input, attention-based models can enhance segmentation accuracy, especially in cluttered scenes \cite{vaswani2017attention}. This mechanism is particularly beneficial in scenarios where the object of interest undergoes substantial changes in appearance or is partially occluded. Another critical aspect of Semi-VOS is addressing the scarcity of labeled data. Annotating video data is labor-intensive and costly, thus motivating the use of semi-supervised learning strategies. Self-supervised learning, which exploits the temporal continuity of video data, has gained traction as a means to pre-train models on vast unlabeled datasets, thus improving their generalization capabilities \cite{wang2020self}. Techniques such as predicting future frames or reconstructing inputs from corrupted versions have demonstrated effectiveness in learning robust representations \cite{doersch2015unsupervised}. Moreover, generative models like Generative Adversarial Networks (GANs) have been employed to synthesize realistic video sequences, providing additional training data for Semi-VOS models. These synthetic data augmentations can help bridge the gap between labeled and unlabeled datasets, offering a richer learning environment \cite{chan2019everybody}. In addition to model-specific innovations, there has been a surge in developing novel loss functions that better capture the nuances of video data. Losses that account for temporal consistency, such as temporal smoothness loss, encourage the model to produce coherent segmentations across consecutive frames \cite{mahadevan2020making}. Furthermore, incorporating perceptual losses, which compare high-level feature representations rather than pixel-wise differences, has shown to enhance segmentation quality by focusing on semantic rather than superficial similarities \cite{johnson2016perceptual}. Despite these advancements, challenges remain in making Semi-VOS models scalable and efficient for real-time applications. The high computational cost associated with deep learning models poses a barrier to deployment in resource-constrained environments. Efforts to address these issues include model compression techniques such as pruning and quantization, which aim to reduce model size and inference time without sacrificing performance \cite{han2015deep}. text: Query attribute value extraction is the joint task of detecting named entities in the search queries as the diverse surface form attribute values and normalizing them into a canonical representation. This task is integral to natural language processing (NLP) applications, particularly in improving search engines, automated assistants, and other systems that rely on understanding user intent. As users interact with these systems through queries, accurately extracting and representing the semantic content of these queries is essential for delivering relevant results and enhancing user experience. The complexity of this task arises from several factors. Firstly, user queries are often short, contextually ambiguous, and lack grammatical structure, making it difficult to apply traditional NLP techniques designed for well-formed text. Secondly, named entities in queries can appear in numerous surface forms, requiring robust methods to recognize and normalize them into a standard representation. Thirdly, the diversity of entities across different domains and languages further complicates the extraction and normalization process. Our approach addresses these challenges by combining deep learning techniques with external knowledge resources. The use of BiLSTM networks allows us to effectively capture the sequential dependencies and context within queries, which is crucial for identifying potential attribute values. The addition of a CRF layer helps refine these predictions by considering the dependencies between labels, thereby enhancing the precision of the sequence labeling process. Moreover, the integration of knowledge graph embeddings, such as TransE, enriches the model's ability to semantically interpret and disambiguate entities. By embedding both query entities and knowledge graph entities into a shared vector space, our model benefits from the rich semantic relationships encoded within knowledge graphs. This allows the model to align diverse surface forms with their canonical representations more accurately, thereby improving the overall extraction process. The task of attribute value extraction has been explored through various methodologies in the literature. Early approaches primarily relied on rule-based systems and lexical databases such as WordNet \cite{miller1995wordnet}. However, these methods often struggled with scalability and adaptability to new domains. With the advent of machine learning, statistical models such as Hidden Markov Models (HMMs) and Conditional Random Fields (CRFs) became popular for sequence labeling tasks \cite{lafferty2001conditional}. These models, however, rely heavily on feature engineering and often require large amounts of labeled data, which may not always be available. Recent advancements in deep learning have revolutionized the field of NLP, leading to the development of models that can learn representations directly from data. Neural networks such as LSTMs \cite{hochreiter1997long} and their bidirectional variants (BiLSTMs) have shown significant success in capturing contextual information for sequence labeling tasks \cite{huang2015bidirectional}. The integration of external knowledge through embeddings has further enhanced the capabilities of these models. Knowledge graph embeddings, such as TransE \cite{bordes2013translating}, have been effectively used to incorporate structured knowledge into deep learning models, improving their ability to understand and process semantic information. Our work builds on these advancements by combining BiLSTM-CRF architectures with knowledge graph embeddings, resulting in a model that leverages both contextual and semantic information for query attribute value extraction. The architecture of our proposed model consists of three main components: the BiLSTM network, the CRF layer, and the knowledge graph embedding integration. This section details each component and their roles in the extraction process. \subsection{BiLSTM Network} The BiLSTM network is tasked with capturing the contextual dependencies within the query. By processing the query sequence in both forward and backward directions, the BiLSTM can effectively utilize information from the entire sequence to make predictions about each token. The output of the BiLSTM serves as a set of dense representations that encode the contextual information necessary for identifying potential attribute values. \subsection{CRF Layer} Following the BiLSTM, a Conditional Random Field layer is employed to refine the predictions. The CRF considers the dependencies between adjacent labels, which is particularly useful for sequence labeling tasks where the context of surrounding tokens can influence the label of a given token. This layer enhances the model's ability to produce coherent and accurate label sequences, thereby improving the precision and recall of entity extraction. \subsection{Knowledge Graph Embeddings} To incorporate semantic information, we integrate knowledge graph embeddings into the model. We employ TransE embeddings to map entities from both the query and the knowledge graph into a shared vector space. This mapping allows the model to utilize the rich relational information encoded in the knowledge graph, aiding in the disambiguation and normalization of extracted entities. The embeddings are used to augment the BiLSTM output, providing additional semantic context that enhances the model's ability to correctly identify and categorize attribute values. By doing so, our model benefits from both the contextual strength of the BiLSTM-CRF architecture and the semantic richness of the knowledge graph embeddings. We conducted a series of experiments to evaluate the performance of our proposed model on query attribute value extraction. This section describes the dataset, evaluation metrics, and baseline methods used for comparison. \subsection{Dataset} Our experiments were conducted on a publicly available dataset composed of user queries annotated with named entity labels. The dataset spans multiple domains, providing a diverse set of queries that test the model's ability to generalize across different contexts and entity types. \subsection{Evaluation Metrics} We use standard metrics for sequence labeling tasks to evaluate our model: precision, recall, and F1-score. Precision measures the accuracy of the extracted entities, recall assesses the model's ability to identify all relevant entities, and the F1-score provides a balanced measure of both precision and recall. \subsection{Baselines} To demonstrate the efficacy of our approach, we compare it against several baseline methods, including traditional CRF models, BiLSTM networks without knowledge graph integration, and state-of-the-art transformer-based models such as BERT \cite{devlin2018bert}. These comparisons highlight the advantages of integrating knowledge graph embeddings with deep learning architectures for enhanced semantic understanding. The results of our experiments indicate that our proposed model significantly outperforms baseline methods across all evaluation metrics. The integration of knowledge graph embeddings contributes to substantial improvements, particularly in recall and F1-score, demonstrating the model's superior ability to disambiguate and normalize attribute values. Our analysis reveals that the semantic information provided by the knowledge graph embeddings plays a crucial role in the model's performance. By aligning query entities with their counterparts in the knowledge graph, the model effectively reduces ambiguity and improves the accuracy of entity extraction. Furthermore, our experiments show that the BiLSTM-CRF architecture is well-suited for capturing the complex contextual information inherent in user queries. The CRF layer, in particular, enhances the coherence of the predicted label sequences, leading to more precise and accurate extraction results. In this study, we have presented a novel approach to query attribute value extraction that combines the strengths of deep learning and knowledge graph embeddings. Our method leverages the contextual capabilities of BiLSTM-CRF networks and the semantic richness of knowledge graphs to improve the accuracy and reliability of entity extraction from user queries. The promising results of our experiments suggest that this approach is a viable solution for enhancing the semantic understanding of queries in NLP applications. Future work may explore the integration of additional types of embeddings, such as contextual embeddings from pre-trained language models, to further improve the model's performance. Additionally, expanding the model's applicability to a wider range of domains and languages will be an important step in making this approach broadly useful. Ultimately, our research contributes to the ongoing efforts in NLP to bridge the gap between unstructured user input and structured data representations, thereby enabling more intelligent and responsive information retrieval systems.

Our analysis shows that the semantic information provided by the knowledge graph is essential for the performance of the model. This demonstrates the value of combining deep learning with knowledge graphs to enhance semantic understanding. We have presented a novel approach for query attribute value extraction that combines the advantages of deep learning and knowledge graph embeddings. By associating query entities with their counterparts in the knowledge graph, the model effectively reduces ambiguity and improves the accuracy of entity extraction. The integration of knowledge graph embeddings is accompanied by significant improvements, especially in terms of recall and F1-score, thereby demonstrating the model's improved ability to disambiguate and normalize attributes. The encouraging results of our experiments show that this method is a promising method for recognizing the semantics of natural language. Moreover, our experiments show that the BiLSTM-CRF network is very well suited to capturing the complex information inherent in the context of queries, especially the CRF layer, which effectively combines the prediction of the sequence of labeled features and thus produces more accurate and precise results. This work will help to close the gap between unstructured text and structured representations. It will contribute to more intelligent and effective information retrieval systems. Furthermore, expanding the model to other languages and domains will be an important step towards the expansion of its usefulness.

text: Manipulation aims to achieve a relative arrangement of objects, often with a desired set of contacts between them. Achieving a reliable manipulation task necessitates an understanding of the forces and motions involved at each contact point. These interactions are inherently complex due to the variability in object shapes, material properties, and the dynamic nature of the task environment. The primary challenge lies in accurately predicting and controlling these interactions to ensure that the desired outcome is achieved without causing damage to the objects or the robotic manipulator. \subsection{Challenges in Contact-Rich Manipulation} One of the significant challenges in contact-rich manipulation is the dynamic and often unpredictable nature of contact transitions. These transitions occur when the contact state changes, such as when a grasped object slips or when a new contact point is established. Such events are typically characterized by rapid changes in force and torque measurements, necessitating high sampling rates and precise sensor calibration. The complexity of these tasks is further compounded by the need to handle uncertainties in the environment. These may arise from sensor noise, variations in object properties, or unmodeled dynamics. Robust algorithms capable of operating under such uncertainties are essential for reliable manipulation. This has led to increased interest in probabilistic approaches, which model the uncertainty explicitly and use it to guide decision-making processes. \subsection{Role of Machine Learning} Machine learning techniques have emerged as powerful tools for addressing the challenges in contact-rich manipulation. By leveraging large datasets of sensory information, machine learning models can learn complex patterns and relationships that are difficult to capture with traditional analytical methods. Deep learning, in particular, has shown promise in tasks such as object recognition, grasp synthesis, and force estimation. Consider a neural network model $g(\mathbf{x}; \boldsymbol{\phi})$, where $\mathbf{x}$ is the input feature vector and $\boldsymbol{\phi}$ represents the network parameters. This model can be trained using supervised learning techniques to predict the contact state or the likelihood of a successful grasp. The training process involves minimizing a loss function $\mathcal{L}(\mathbf{y}, g(\mathbf{x}; \boldsymbol{\phi}))$, where $\mathbf{y}$ is the true contact state label. This optimization is typically performed using gradient-based methods such as stochastic gradient descent (SGD). \subsection{Sensor Fusion for Enhanced Perception} The integration of multiple sensor modalities provides a more comprehensive view of the manipulation environment. For example, combining visual data with tactile feedback allows for more accurate estimation of object poses and contact forces. This multimodal fusion can be achieved through algorithms that align and integrate data streams from different sensors, often using techniques such as Kalman filtering or particle filtering. Let $\mathbf{z}_\text{tactile}$ and $\mathbf{z}_\text{visual}$ represent the sensor outputs from tactile and visual modalities, respectively. A fusion algorithm $h(\mathbf{z}_\text{tactile}, \mathbf{z}_\text{visual}; \boldsymbol{\psi})$ can be designed to produce a joint representation $\mathbf{z}_\text{fused}$ that is more informative than either sensor output alone. This joint representation can then be used to improve the accuracy of contact detection and state estimation. In this section, we outline our approach for contact detection and manipulation using a combination of machine learning and sensor fusion techniques. Our methodology consists of three main components: data collection, model training, and real-time implementation. \subsection{Data Collection} Data collection involves capturing a diverse set of contact interactions using a robotic manipulator equipped with multiple sensors. The dataset includes variations in object types, contact scenarios, and environmental conditions to ensure the robustness of the trained model. Each data sample consists of synchronized sensor readings, including force/torque measurements, tactile pressure maps, and visual images. \subsection{Model Training} The training phase involves developing models that can accurately classify contact states and predict future interactions. We employ a convolutional neural network (CNN) architecture for processing visual data, while a recurrent neural network (RNN) is used to capture temporal dependencies in the tactile data. The models are trained jointly using a multi-task learning framework, optimizing a loss function that combines classification error with regression error for force prediction. \subsection{Real-Time Implementation} For real-time implementation, the trained models are deployed on a robotic platform. The system continuously processes incoming sensor data and updates the estimated contact state. An adaptive control strategy is employed to adjust the manipulator's actions based on the predicted contact state, ensuring robust and responsive manipulation. We evaluate our approach on a series of benchmark manipulation tasks, including assembly, sorting, and dexterous object handling. The performance metrics include contact detection accuracy, task completion time, and robustness to perturbations. Our results demonstrate significant improvements over baseline methods, highlighting the effectiveness of integrating machine learning with sensor fusion for contact-rich manipulation. In summary, our work presents a comprehensive framework for enhancing contact-rich manipulation through advanced sensing and machine learning techniques. By leveraging the strengths of multiple sensor modalities and data-driven models, we achieve higher accuracy and robustness in complex manipulation tasks. Future work will explore the integration of additional sensory inputs, such as auditory signals, to further improve the system's capabilities. \bibliographystyle{IEEEtran} \bibliography{refs} \end{document}
