text: Object counting has become increasingly important due to its wide range of applications such as crowd surveillance, traffic monitoring, wildlife conservation and inventory management. Our proposed framework for one-shot object counting integrates several sophisticated components designed to work in tandem to achieve high accuracy in counting novel object instances. Below, we detail each component of our framework, elucidating the role it plays and the innovations introduced to tackle the task's inherent challenges. \subsection{Feature Extraction} The feature extraction component is a pivotal part of our framework, tasked with transforming raw images into meaningful feature representations. We employ a convolutional neural network (CNN), specifically a variant of the ResNet architecture \cite{he2016deep}, due to its proven effectiveness in capturing hierarchical features across different levels of abstraction. The CNN is pre-trained on a large-scale dataset such as ImageNet \cite{deng2009imagenet} and fine-tuned on task-specific data to ensure adaptability to novel categories. The exemplar and query images are passed through this shared network, producing high-dimensional feature maps. These feature maps serve as the input to the subsequent similarity estimation component. The fine-tuning process involves optimizing the network to enhance its ability to generalize to previously unseen object categories, ensuring that the learned representations maintain robustness across varied visual appearances. \subsection{Similarity Estimation} The similarity estimator is designed to measure the congruence between the exemplar and regions within the query image. For this purpose, we utilize a metric-based learning approach, inspired by the success of Siamese networks \cite{koch2015siamese}. The core idea is to learn a metric space where visually similar objects are mapped closer together, and dissimilar ones are positioned further apart. The similarity score is computed using a cosine similarity metric, which is defined as follows: \begin{equation} \text{Similarity}(\mathbf{f}_e, \mathbf{f}_q) = \frac{\mathbf{f}_e \cdot \mathbf{f}_q}{\|\mathbf{f}_e\| \|\mathbf{f}_q\|} \end{equation} where $\mathbf{f}_e$ and $\mathbf{f}_q$ represent the feature vectors of the exemplar and a candidate region in the query image, respectively. This metric is chosen for its ability to provide a bounded score that is invariant to the scale of the feature vectors. Regions in the query image with high similarity scores are identified as potential instances of the target object class. \subsection{Counting Module} The counting module is responsible for aggregating the similarity information to produce the final count of objects. Unlike traditional counting methods that rely on explicit object detection, our method employs a regression-based approach. This decision is motivated by the observation that regression models can effectively handle scenarios with high object density, where individual detection becomes infeasible. We implement a fully connected neural network layer that takes as input the similarity scores from the entire query image and outputs an integer count. The network is trained to minimize the difference between the predicted count and the ground truth using a mean squared error loss. Additionally, we incorporate a spatial attention mechanism \cite{jetley2018learn} that weighs the contributions of different regions in the query image, focusing the model's attention on areas that are more likely to contain instances of the target object. \subsection{Training and Optimization} The training process for our framework involves several stages. Initially, the CNN is trained to produce discriminative features, followed by the fine-tuning of the similarity estimator to sharpen its ability to discern subtle variations between object classes. The counting module is subsequently trained using a combination of synthetic and real-world datasets, ensuring a diverse exposure to various object categories and counting scenarios. We employ data augmentation techniques such as random cropping, scaling, and rotation to bolster the model's ability to generalize across different viewing angles and object scales. Moreover, a curriculum learning strategy \cite{bengio2009curriculum} is adopted, gradually increasing the complexity of the training samples, which aids in stabilizing the learning process. To validate the efficacy of our proposed framework, we conducted a series of experiments on several benchmark datasets, including the FSC-147 \cite{ranjan2021learning} and a newly curated dataset comprising categories from the COCO dataset \cite{lin2014microsoft}. text: Recommendation systems have been extensively applied in online platforms nowadays, e.g., Amazon \cite{amazon}, Google \cite{youtube_dnn,youtube1,NIS} and Facebook~\cite{ebr}. Interpretability has become a significant focus in the development of sequential recommendation systems. As these systems are increasingly integrated into critical applications, understanding the decision-making process behind the recommendations is vital for user trust and system transparency \cite{lipton2018mythos}. Deep learning models, especially those utilizing complex architectures like Transformers, are often criticized for being "black boxes" due to their lack of transparency in how input data is transformed into outputs \cite{doshi2017towards}. Several approaches to improving interpretability in sequential recommendation systems have been proposed. One common method involves attention visualization in Transformer models. By examining the attention weights across different layers and heads, researchers can gain insights into which parts of the input sequence are most influential for the final recommendation \cite{cheng2016wide}. This method aligns well with the self-attention mechanism, which inherently provides a potential path toward interpretability \cite{ghosh2020explainable}. Another approach to enhancing interpretability is through the integration of explainable AI techniques. These techniques involve developing surrogate models that approximate the behavior of complex models with simpler, more interpretable models \cite{ribeiro2016should}. For instance, using decision trees or rule-based systems as interpretative layers can provide clearer insights into the decision logic of the recommendation process. Despite these efforts, balancing the trade-off between model accuracy and interpretability remains a challenge. Highly interpretable models often sacrifice performance, while high-performing models tend to be less interpretable. Therefore, an ongoing research direction is to design models that can maintain high accuracy while offering interpretable insights into their mechanisms. The cold-start problem continues to be a significant challenge in the field of recommendation systems \cite{schein2002methods}. It refers to the difficulty of providing recommendations when there is insufficient data about users or items. This issue is particularly prevalent in sequential recommendation systems where the reliance on historical sequence data is paramount. To address the cold-start problem, various strategies have been explored. One effective approach is to incorporate rich side information about users and items. Such information can include demographic data, social network connections, or item attributes \cite{schein2002methods, liang2016factorization}. By leveraging these additional data sources, recommendation systems can formulate initial predictions even in the absence of extensive interaction history. Moreover, transfer learning techniques have shown promise in mitigating the cold-start issue. By transferring learned knowledge from domains where data is abundant to domains where data is scarce, systems can make more informed predictions \cite{pan2010survey}. For example, a model trained on a comprehensive dataset from one domain can be fine-tuned on a smaller dataset from a related domain, thus improving recommendation quality. Hybrid models, which combine collaborative filtering and content-based methods, also offer a viable solution to the cold-start problem. By integrating multiple data types and leveraging both historical interactions and content features, hybrid models can better handle scenarios with limited data \cite{burke2002hybrid}. The field of sequential recommendation systems is rapidly evolving, with several promising avenues for future research. One key area is the exploration of novel architectures that can further enhance the efficiency and effectiveness of recommendation models. While Transformer models have advanced the state-of-the-art, there is room for innovation in creating models that require less computational power while maintaining accuracy. Additionally, fairness and bias mitigation are becoming increasingly important in recommendation systems \cite{beutel2019fairness}. Ensuring that recommendations do not propagate existing biases present in the data is crucial for ethical AI deployments. Techniques such as fairness-aware learning and bias correction algorithms are being developed to address these concerns. Another exciting direction is the integration of reinforcement learning with sequential recommendation systems. Reinforcement learning offers the potential to model dynamic user interactions more effectively, allowing systems to adapt to users' changing preferences \cite{zheng2018drn}. By framing recommendation as a sequential decision-making problem, reinforcement learning methods can refine recommendations based on user feedback. Finally, exploring cross-domain recommendation is a burgeoning area of interest. By leveraging data from multiple domains, systems can provide better recommendations even in domains where data is sparse \cite{elkahky2015multi}. Cross-domain recommendation involves challenges such as data heterogeneity and domain adaptation, but it holds the promise of significantly enhancing recommendation system capabilities. Sequential recommendation systems are crucial for modern recommender systems, providing personalized and timely suggestions to users based on their interaction history. While significant advancements have been made in this field, challenges such as interpretability, the cold-start problem, and bias remain areas of active research. Future developments will likely focus on creating more efficient models, integrating novel machine learning techniques, and ensuring ethical AI practices. As these systems continue to evolve, they will play an increasingly vital role in shaping user experiences across various digital platforms. \bibliographystyle{plain} \bibliography{references} \end{document}

text: Security researchers regularly find serious security flaws in critical components, even those with years of scrutiny and widespread deployment. Security researchers regularly find serious security flaws in critical components, even those with years of scrutiny and widespread deployment. These vulnerabilities can lead to severe repercussions, including unauthorized data access, system crashes, and financial losses. As systems grow in complexity and interconnectivity, the challenge of ensuring their security and correctness becomes increasingly formidable. Formal verification offers a promising approach to address these issues by providing rigorous guarantees about system behavior. Formal verification, through its various methodologies, aims to tackle the inherent limitations of traditional testing and debugging. While testing can only evaluate a finite number of scenarios, formal verification seeks to prove properties for all possible execution paths. This distinction is crucial as it allows developers to uncover and rectify flaws that might remain hidden under conventional testing paradigms. \subsection{Challenges in Applying Formal Verification} Despite its potential, the application of formal verification in industrial settings is fraught with challenges. The process of formalizing specifications is non-trivial and requires a deep understanding of both the system and its intended behavior. Capturing all relevant properties in a formal specification is difficult, and omissions can lead to verification of incorrect or incomplete system aspects \cite{Rushby1993}. Moreover, the scalability of formal verification techniques remains a pressing issue. As systems increase in size and complexity, the computational resources required to perform verification grow exponentially. For example, model checking, while effective for small-scale systems, faces the state explosion problem as the number of system states increases exponentially with the number of components \cite{Clarke1999}. Theorem proving, although more flexible, demands considerable effort from skilled practitioners to construct proofs manually. This dependency on expert intervention limits the widespread adoption of theorem proving in commercial software development, where time-to-market pressures are intense. \subsection{Advancements in Verification Techniques} To mitigate these challenges, recent advancements have focused on improving the automation and efficiency of formal verification processes. One promising direction is the development of hybrid approaches that combine different verification techniques to leverage their respective strengths. For instance, tools that integrate model checking with theorem proving can utilize model checking to handle finite-state components efficiently, while employing theorem proving to address the infinite-state aspects \cite{Ball2001}. Additionally, the incorporation of machine learning into formal verification workflows shows potential for reducing the manual effort needed in proof development. Machine learning algorithms can be trained to identify patterns and heuristics that aid in automated theorem proving, thus reducing the burden on human experts \cite{Gao2013}. \subsection{Integration into Software Development} Integrating formal verification into the software development lifecycle is crucial for its practical adoption. Continuous integration pipelines that incorporate formal methods can help ensure that verification is performed regularly, rather than as an afterthought. This integration requires tool support that can seamlessly fit into existing development environments and allow for incremental verification as code evolves \cite{Gunter2000}. Efforts to develop domain-specific languages (DSLs) that facilitate the specification of formal properties in a manner accessible to software engineers are also underway. These DSLs aim to bridge the gap between high-level system requirements and the low-level formal models required for verification \cite{Hudak1996}. The successful application of formal verification in various domains underscores its potential to enhance system reliability. In the aerospace industry, formal methods have been employed to verify critical systems such as flight control software, where safety requirements are stringent \cite{Rushby1995}. These applications demonstrate the feasibility of formal verification in high-assurance systems where failure is not an option. In the realm of hardware design, formal verification has become an indispensable tool. Modern processors undergo rigorous formal checks to ensure that their specifications are met, preventing costly errors that could arise post-manufacture \cite{Bryant1986}. The use of formal methods in hardware design highlights their effectiveness in domains where precision is paramount. \subsection{Emerging Domains} As technology evolves, new domains are emerging where formal verification can play a vital role. Autonomous systems, including self-driving cars and drones, represent a growing field where formal guarantees can significantly enhance safety and reliability. These systems operate in dynamic environments, requiring robust verification to handle a multitude of scenarios and interactions \cite{Koopman2017}. Blockchain technology and smart contracts are another area where formal verification is gaining traction. Given the immutable nature of blockchain transactions, the correctness of smart contract code is critical to prevent vulnerabilities that could lead to significant financial losses \cite{Bhargavan2016}. Formal methods provide the necessary tools to ensure that smart contract implementations adhere to their intended logic. Formal verification represents a powerful approach to ensuring the correctness and reliability of complex systems. However, its widespread adoption faces challenges related to scalability, expertise requirements, and integration into existing development processes. Continued research and innovation are essential to address these challenges and unlock the full potential of formal methods. Future directions may include the development of more intuitive specification languages, enhanced automation through artificial intelligence, and the creation of more efficient verification algorithms. As these advancements unfold, the hope is to make formal verification a routine part of software and hardware development, leading to more secure and dependable systems across diverse domains. \bibliographystyle{plain} \bibliography{references}

text: Robots are increasingly operating in environments where they must interact with humans, such as collaborative grasping~\cite{strabala2013toward,dragan2013legibility} and autonomous driving~\cite{montemerlo2008junior,levinson2011towards,sadigh2016planning,sadigh2016information}. and update their control strategies to ensure compliance with safety constraints. This dynamic adaptation is crucial for maintaining safety in unpredictable and rapidly changing environments, such as those encountered in shared human-robot workspaces. The interaction between humans and robots introduces unique challenges to safety assurance. Traditional safety measures, such as physical barriers or emergency stop mechanisms, are often insufficient in environments where close and continuous interaction is required. Instead, the field has seen a shift towards more sophisticated approaches that incorporate real-time sensing and decision-making capabilities. \subsection{Real-Time Sensing and Perception} Real-time sensing is pivotal in ensuring the safety of human-robot interactions. Advanced perception systems, which include a combination of cameras, LiDAR, and other sensor modalities, provide the robot with a comprehensive understanding of its surroundings \cite{chen2017lidar}. These systems enable the detection of humans and other dynamic obstacles, allowing the robot to anticipate potential collisions and adjust its path or behavior accordingly. The integration of machine learning techniques in perception systems has further enhanced their capability to interpret complex scenes \cite{redmon2016you}. Deep learning models can be trained to recognize human gestures and predict intentions, enabling more intuitive and safe interactions \cite{huang2017arx}. However, ensuring the robustness of these models in diverse real-world conditions remains an ongoing research challenge. \subsection{Task Planning and Safety} Task planning in human-robot interaction scenarios must consider both the robot's objectives and the safety of human users. This dual focus often requires the development of planning algorithms that can optimize for multiple criteria, balancing efficiency with safety \cite{garrett2020integrated}. The use of multi-objective optimization techniques allows for the formulation of planning problems where safety-related constraints are explicitly included. For instance, trajectory planning for mobile robots can be approached using methods that ensure a minimum safe distance from humans at all times, while still achieving task goals \cite{lu2020safety}. Furthermore, the incorporation of human-aware planning frameworks has been shown to improve the safety and acceptance of robots in shared environments. These frameworks take into account human psychology and social norms, adjusting the robot's behavior to align with expected human responses \cite{sisbot2007human}. \subsection{Control Strategies for Safety} Control strategies play a crucial role in ensuring the real-time safety of robots interacting with humans. Traditional control methods, such as PID control, can be augmented with advanced techniques like model predictive control (MPC) to better handle the dynamic and uncertain nature of human environments \cite{mayne2014model}. MPC allows for the prediction of future states and the proactive adjustment of control inputs, thereby providing a mechanism to anticipate and mitigate potential safety violations. Recent advancements in fast solvers and computational hardware have made real-time MPC feasible for complex robotic systems \cite{wang2018fast}. In addition, the application of safety barriers, such as control barrier functions (CBFs), ensures that the robot's control actions remain within safe bounds. These functions can be seamlessly integrated with existing control laws, providing a layer of safety without compromising performance \cite{ames2016control}. Despite significant advancements, several challenges remain in the pursuit of safe human-robot interaction. One of the primary issues is the trade-off between safety and performance. As robots become more capable, the expectation for them to operate efficiently in human environments increases, often at the expense of conservative safety measures. Another challenge lies in the verification and validation of safety systems. While formal methods offer rigorous assurances, their scalability to complex, high-dimensional systems is limited. Research into more scalable formal verification techniques is essential for the widespread deployment of safety-critical robotic systems \cite{clarke2018model}. Moreover, the ethical implications of safety decisions made by autonomous systems require careful consideration. As robots gain more autonomy, the responsibility for safety decisions becomes a shared burden between the system designers and the robots themselves. This necessitates the development of ethical frameworks that guide decision-making processes in safety-critical situations \cite{gonzalez2016ethical}. Looking forward, advances in artificial intelligence and machine learning hold promise for further improving the safety of human-robot interactions. Reinforcement learning, for example, is being explored as a means to enable robots to learn safe behaviors through trial and error, within controlled environments \cite{silver2016mastering}. However, ensuring the transferability of these learned behaviors to real-world scenarios remains a significant hurdle. In conclusion, ensuring the safety of human-interactive robotics demands a multi-faceted approach that combines robust sensing, intelligent planning, and adaptive control strategies. By addressing the current challenges and leveraging emerging technologies, the field can move closer to realizing robots that safely and effectively coexist with humans in a variety of settings.

text: The Gaussian mechanism is the workhorse for a multitude of differentially private learning algorithms \cite{song2013stochastic, bassily2014private, abadi2016deep}. The Gaussian mechanism is the workhorse for a multitude of differentially private learning algorithms \cite{song2013stochastic, bassily2014private, abadi2016deep}. It operates by perturbing data with noise drawn from a Gaussian distribution, which provides strong privacy guarantees under the framework of $(\epsilon, \delta)$-differential privacy. However, in practice, the Gaussian mechanism is often implemented in continuous domains, which can lead to challenges when applied to inherently discrete data. To address these challenges, researchers have explored alternative mechanisms tailored for discrete data. One such mechanism is the Skellam mechanism, which is particularly suited for scenarios where the data naturally consists of counts or other integer-valued quantities. The Skellam distribution, being the difference of two independent Poisson-distributed random variables, offers a natural framework for differential privacy in discrete settings. The multi-dimensional Skellam mechanism extends the conventional Skellam distribution to higher dimensions, allowing for simultaneous perturbation of multiple correlated counts. Consider a vector of counts \(\mathbf{X} = (X_1, X_2, \ldots, X_d)\), where each \(X_i\) follows a Poisson distribution with parameter \(\lambda_i\). The multi-dimensional Skellam mechanism generates noise \(\mathbf{Z} = (Z_1, Z_2, \ldots, Z_d)\), where each component \(Z_i = X_i - Y_i\) is the difference of two independently drawn Poisson variables with the same parameter \(\lambda_i\). The moment generating function (MGF) of the Skellam distribution facilitates the derivation of privacy guarantees in the Rényi differential privacy (RDP) framework. text: Given that machine learning has achieved super-human performance in image classification~\citep{Ciresan_Schmidhuber_12,Krizhevsky_Hinton_12} and games \citep{Mnih_Hassabis_15,Silver_Hassabis_16}, the question arises why we do not see similar results in robotics. in robotics. Unlike the static nature of image classification tasks or the well-defined rules of games, robotic tasks are inherently dynamic and involve high-dimensional continuous action spaces, complex sensorimotor loops, and non-stationary environments. The physical presence of robots in the real world adds layers of uncertainty and variability that are absent in virtual environments or controlled simulations. These challenges necessitate advanced algorithms capable of generalizing across diverse conditions, handling noise, and adapting to unforeseen environmental changes. The sim-to-real transfer problem is particularly pronounced due to what is known as the "simulation optimization bias" \cite{sim_opt_bias}. This bias arises when models are optimized in a simulation environment that does not perfectly replicate the real world, leading to overfitting to the simulated conditions and poor performance when deployed in reality. Addressing this bias is crucial for the successful application of deep learning methods in real-world robotics. Domain randomization has emerged as a potent technique to mitigate the reality gap by training models under a wide range of simulated variations. By randomizing various parameters such as lighting, textures, and physical properties, domain randomization aims to prevent overfitting to the specific conditions of the simulation \cite{domain_randomization}. This results in models that are more robust and generalizable when faced with the inherent variability of the real world. In addition to domain randomization, domain adaptation techniques focus on aligning the feature distributions of the simulated and real environments. This can be achieved through adversarial training methods, where a discriminator learns to distinguish between features extracted from the simulation and those from the real world. The goal is to train the feature extractor to produce domain-invariant features that minimize the discrepancy between the two domains \cite{domain_adaptation}. Such approaches have shown promise in reducing the reality gap and improving the transferability of policies learned in simulation. Meta-learning, or "learning to learn," provides a framework for enhancing the adaptability of models by training them on a distribution of tasks. The core idea is to enable the model to rapidly adapt to new tasks with minimal additional data \cite{meta_learning}. In the context of sim-to-real transfer, meta-learning can be particularly beneficial as it equips models with the ability to quickly adjust their parameters when deployed in novel real-world scenarios. One popular meta-learning algorithm is Model-Agnostic Meta-Learning (MAML), which optimizes for initial parameters that can be fine-tuned efficiently for new tasks \cite{Finn_Abbeel_Levine_17}. By training on a variety of simulated tasks, MAML can prepare models with a strong prior that facilitates rapid adaptation to the complexities of the real environment. This approach addresses the variability and unpredictability that robotic systems encounter beyond the confines of controlled simulations. Reinforcement learning (RL) strategies tailored for sim-to-real transfer often incorporate aspects of both domain adaptation and meta-learning. For instance, multi-task learning frameworks can be employed to jointly train on multiple simulated environments, providing a richer set of experiences from which the agent can generalize \cite{multi_task_rl}. Additionally, incorporating human demonstrations or expert guidance can bootstrap the learning process, offering a template of desirable behaviors that can be refined through RL \cite{human_in_loop}. Moreover, hierarchical reinforcement learning (HRL) decomposes complex tasks into simpler sub-tasks, enabling agents to learn high-level strategies while delegating low-level actions to specialized sub-policies \cite{HRL}. This hierarchical approach not only simplifies the learning problem but also enhances the agent's ability to transfer learned skills across different domains. Despite advancements, several challenges remain in achieving robust sim-to-real transfer. One major hurdle is the computational cost associated with training complex models across diverse simulated environments. Efficient training strategies and the development of more realistic simulation platforms are essential to alleviate this bottleneck. Furthermore, the integration of real-time feedback from the physical environment into the learning loop could enhance model robustness and adaptability. Techniques such as online learning and continual learning have the potential to improve the agent's performance by allowing it to update its knowledge based on real-world experiences continuously \cite{continual_learning}. In addition, exploring the synergy between model-based and model-free RL approaches could yield new insights into optimizing sim-to-real transfer. Model-based methods, which leverage a learned model of the environment to plan and predict, can complement model-free methods that optimize policies through direct interaction \cite{model_based_vs_free}. The sim-to-real transfer remains a pivotal challenge in the deployment of robotic systems in real-world applications. By leveraging domain randomization, meta-learning, and advanced RL strategies, researchers are gradually narrowing the reality gap. Continuous innovation and interdisciplinary collaboration will be key to unlocking the full potential of robotics in complex, dynamic environments, paving the way for truly autonomous and intelligent robotic systems. As these methodologies advance, the vision of seamless integration of robots into everyday life becomes increasingly attainable.

text: We aim to solve a fundamental problem in statistical inference---mean estimation---under minimal assumptions. Formally, we seek the tightest confidence interval (up to constants) on the mean of a heavy-tailed distribution using robust estimators that account for the absence of finite variance. In traditional settings where the data is light-tailed and variance exists, classical methods such as the sample mean and variance-based confidence intervals suffice. However, in heavy-tailed settings, these methods can perform poorly due to the undue influence of extreme values, which are more prevalent and impactful compared to light-tailed distributions. Our objective is to develop robust estimation techniques that maintain high efficiency across a wide range of distributions, particularly focusing on those scenarios where only minimal assumptions can be made about the underlying distribution. This is achieved by employing concentration inequalities and robust statistical methods that are resilient to deviations from standard distributional assumptions. The problem of estimating the mean of a heavy-tailed distribution has garnered significant attention in recent years, particularly in the realms of robust statistics and machine learning. Traditional approaches, such as the sample mean, become unreliable due to their sensitivity to outliers and extreme observations. Hence, alternative estimators have been developed to address these limitations. \subsection{Trimmed Mean} The trimmed mean estimator is a classical approach to mitigate the effects of outliers by discarding a certain proportion of the largest and smallest observations. This involves selecting a trimming proportion $\alpha \in [0, 0.5)$ and computing the mean of the remaining data points. The effectiveness of the trimmed mean heavily depends on the choice of $\alpha$, which requires careful consideration. An inappropriate choice can lead to either excessive bias or insufficient robustness. \subsection{Median-of-Means Estimator} The Median-of-Means (MoM) estimator, introduced by Nemirovsky and Yudin \cite{nemirovsky1983problem}, offers a compelling alternative by dividing the sample into several equally sized blocks and computing the mean of each block. The median of these block means is then used as the estimator for the overall mean. The MoM estimator is particularly advantageous due to its simplicity and its strong theoretical guarantees, even in the absence of finite variance. \subsection{Recent Advances} Recent works have extended the MoM framework to more general settings, incorporating techniques such as bootstrapping and subsampling to enhance robustness. For instance, Lugosi and Mendelson \cite{lugosi2019mean} proposed novel variants of the MoM estimator that adaptively choose the number of blocks based on the sample size and desired confidence level, thereby optimizing the trade-off between bias and variance. In this section, we outline our proposed methodology for robust mean estimation. Our approach builds on the strengths of existing estimators while introducing novel modifications to improve performance in heavy-tailed environments. \subsection{Adaptive Median-of-Means} We propose an adaptive version of the MoM estimator that dynamically adjusts the number of blocks $k$ based on the sample characteristics. This adaptability is crucial for balancing the estimator's robustness and efficiency across various distributional settings. Let $n$ be the sample size, and define $k = f(n)$ where $f$ is a non-decreasing function that ensures $k \to \infty$ as $n \to \infty$ but grows slower than $n$. The choice of $f$ is pivotal, as it dictates the granularity of partitioning and directly impacts the estimator's variance. \subsection{Concentration Inequalities} To theoretically justify the performance of the adaptive MoM estimator, we leverage concentration inequalities that provide probabilistic bounds on the deviation of the estimator from the true mean. Specifically, we utilize the Bernstein inequality, which is suitable for sums of independent but not necessarily identically distributed random variables with bounded moments. This allows us to establish confidence intervals for the mean that are both tight and reliable under heavy-tailed conditions. \subsection{Algorithmic Implementation} The algorithm for the adaptive MoM estimator proceeds as follows: 1. **Input:** Sample $\mathbf{X} = (X_1, X_2, \ldots, X_n)$, function $f(n)$ for determining $k$. 2. **Partition:** Divide $\mathbf{X}$ into $k = f(n)$ blocks of approximately equal size. 3. **Compute Block Means:** Calculate the mean of each block, resulting in $\overline{X}_1, \overline{X}_2, \ldots, \overline{X}_k$. 4. **Median Calculation:** Determine the median of these block means. 5. **Output:** Return the median as the estimate of the mean. In this section, we provide a rigorous analysis of the proposed adaptive MoM estimator. Our analysis focuses on establishing the estimator's asymptotic properties and its robustness to heavy-tailed distributions. \subsection{Asymptotic Normality} Under certain conditions, the adaptive MoM estimator exhibits asymptotic normality, which is crucial for deriving confidence intervals. We prove that as the sample size $n$ increases, the distribution of the estimator approaches a normal distribution centered around the true mean with a variance that decreases with $n$. This result is formalized in the following theorem: \begin{theorem} Let $\mathbf{X} = (X_1, X_2, \ldots, X_n)$ be a sample from a distribution $F$ with mean $\mu$. If $k = f(n)$ such that $k \to \infty$ and $k/n \to 0$ as $n \to \infty$, then the adaptive MoM estimator $\text{MoM}(\mathbf{X})$ is asymptotically normal with mean $\mu$. \end{theorem} \begin{proof} The proof involves showing that the variance of the block means decreases as the number of blocks increases, and applying the Central Limit Theorem to the distribution of block means. Detailed steps are provided in Appendix A. \end{proof} \subsection{Robustness to Heavy Tails} The robustness of the adaptive MoM estimator is characterized by its resilience to deviations from the assumptions of finite variance. We demonstrate this by establishing bounds on the estimator's bias and variance that remain valid even when the underlying distribution has infinite variance. These bounds are derived using robust statistical techniques and are corroborated by empirical simulations. To validate the theoretical properties of our proposed estimator, we conduct extensive simulations and empirical studies. Our experiments compare the adaptive MoM estimator with traditional methods such as the sample mean, trimmed mean, and conventional MoM estimator across a range of distributions, including Cauchy and Pareto. \subsection{Simulation Setup} We simulate samples from heavy-tailed distributions with varying tail indices and sample sizes. For each scenario, we compute the bias, variance, and mean squared error (MSE) of each estimator. Additionally, we analyze the coverage probability of confidence intervals derived from each method. \subsection{Results and Discussion} The results indicate that the adaptive MoM estimator consistently outperforms the traditional sample mean and trimmed mean in terms of robustness and efficiency. It achieves lower bias and variance, particularly in settings with extreme tail behavior. Furthermore, the confidence intervals constructed using our estimator maintain the nominal coverage probability, affirming the theoretical guarantees. In conclusion, the adaptive Median-of-Means estimator provides a powerful tool for mean estimation in heavy-tailed settings. Its robustness and adaptability make it suitable for a wide range of applications where traditional estimators fall short. Future work includes extending this approach to multivariate and high-dimensional data, where the challenges of heavy-tailed distributions are even more pronounced. \bibliographystyle{plain} \bibliography{references}

text: Machine learning (ML) is increasingly used to make predictions on privacy-sensitive data. in a wide range of applications, including healthcare, finance, and social networks. The integration of ML in these domains has demonstrated significant potential in improving decision-making processes by uncovering patterns and insights from complex datasets. However, the deployment of ML models in environments where data privacy is paramount introduces a myriad of challenges that must be addressed to prevent unauthorized access to sensitive information. The susceptibility of ML models to various privacy attacks, such as model inversion, membership inference \cite{shokri2017membership}, and adversarial attacks \cite{goodfellow2015explaining}, has prompted a surge of research into privacy-preserving techniques. Membership inference attacks, for instance, aim to determine whether a particular data point was part of the model's training set, posing a significant risk to data confidentiality. These threats necessitate robust solutions that can guard against privacy breaches while maintaining the utility of the ML models. In light of these challenges, this paper explores the landscape of privacy considerations in machine learning, focusing on both the vulnerabilities of existing models and the emerging techniques that aim to protect against such threats. We delve into the mechanisms of model inversion attacks, examining how they exploit model parameters to infer sensitive information and the conditions under which these attacks are most effective. Furthermore, we evaluate the effectiveness of various countermeasures, such as differential privacy and federated learning, in safeguarding sensitive data. Model inversion attacks exploit the predictive capabilities of a trained ML model to deduce sensitive attributes of input data, potentially revealing confidential information. These attacks typically involve an adversary who has access to the model's outputs and leverages this information to reconstruct the inputs. The process can be likened to solving an inverse problem, where the goal is to determine the causes (inputs) from the observed effects (outputs). The threat posed by model inversion attacks is particularly pronounced in models trained on datasets containing highly sensitive information. For instance, in healthcare, a model designed to predict the likelihood of a disease based on patient data could be manipulated to infer specific patient conditions or genetic information. Similarly, in financial applications, an adversary could extract details about an individual's financial status or transactions. To conduct a model inversion attack, the adversary often employs optimization techniques that iteratively adjust guesses about the input until the model's output closely matches the observed output. This process is facilitated by the gradients of the model, which provide directional information on how to adjust the inputs to achieve the desired output. The effectiveness of the attack depends on several factors, including the architecture of the model, the nature of the data, and the level of access the adversary has to the model's internals. Given the potential impact of model inversion attacks, various strategies have been developed to enhance the privacy of ML models. These strategies aim to either prevent the inference of sensitive attributes or limit the amount of information that can be extracted from the model. Two prominent approaches in this domain are differential privacy and federated learning. \subsection{Differential Privacy} Differential privacy provides a mathematically rigorous framework for ensuring that the inclusion or exclusion of a single data point in a dataset does not significantly alter the output of a computation. By introducing controlled noise to the output, differential privacy makes it difficult for an adversary to draw precise conclusions about any individual data point. The privacy guarantees offered by differential privacy can be tailored by adjusting the noise level, allowing for a trade-off between privacy and utility. In the context of ML, differential privacy can be applied during the training process to protect the privacy of the training data. Techniques such as differentially private stochastic gradient descent (DP-SGD) \cite{abadi2016deep} have been proposed to incorporate noise into the gradients used for model updates, thus limiting the information leakage about the training data. This approach has been shown to be effective in mitigating model inversion attacks, though it may introduce challenges related to model accuracy and training efficiency. \subsection{Federated Learning} Federated learning presents an alternative paradigm for training ML models while preserving data privacy. In federated learning, the model is trained collaboratively across multiple devices, each holding its own local dataset. Instead of sharing raw data, only model updates, such as gradients or weight changes, are communicated to a central server for aggregation. This decentralized approach significantly reduces the risk of data exposure, as the raw data never leaves the local devices. Furthermore, by ensuring that data remains distributed, federated learning inherently provides a level of privacy protection against model inversion attacks. However, federated learning also introduces new challenges, such as communication overhead, system heterogeneity, and the potential for adversarial participants to corrupt the model updates. As machine learning continues to permeate domains with sensitive data, the importance of robust privacy-preserving techniques cannot be overstated. Model inversion attacks exemplify the vulnerabilities inherent in ML models, necessitating the development and implementation of effective countermeasures. Differential privacy and federated learning represent promising avenues for enhancing the privacy of ML models, each with its own strengths and limitations. Future research must focus on refining these techniques to balance privacy and utility, ensuring that ML models can be deployed safely in privacy-sensitive environments. Additionally, the exploration of novel approaches, such as homomorphic encryption and secure multi-party computation, may offer further advancements in the quest to protect sensitive data from unauthorized access. text: As the adoption of autonomous robotic systems increases around us, there is a need for the controllers driving them to exhibit the level of sophistication required to operate in complex and dynamic environments. Reinforcement learning (RL) has emerged as a powerful paradigm for developing such controllers, enabling robots to learn complex policies through trial and error. However, the transition from controlled, simulated environments to the variability and unpredictability of the real world remains a significant challenge. The reality gap, which represents the divergence between simulation and reality, is primarily attributed to several factors. These include inaccuracies in the dynamics model used during simulation, discrepancies in sensor readings due to noise, and the presence of unanticipated environmental conditions not accounted for during training. Addressing these challenges is essential for ensuring that RL-trained agents can operate reliably and safely in real-world settings. \subsection{Bridging the Reality Gap} To address the reality gap, researchers have explored various methodologies aimed at enhancing the generalization capabilities of RL agents. Among these, domain adaptation techniques have gained significant traction. Domain randomization and adversarial domain adaptation are two prominent strategies that have been extensively studied. \subsubsection{Domain Randomization} Domain randomization involves training RL agents in a multitude of simulated environments, each with randomly varied parameters such as friction coefficients, lighting conditions, and object textures. This approach, as demonstrated by Tobin et al. \cite{tobin2017domain}, encourages the agent to learn robust policies that are less sensitive to specific environmental configurations. By encountering a wide spectrum of scenarios during training, the agent is better prepared to handle unexpected variations in real-world deployments. \subsubsection{Adversarial Domain Adaptation} Adversarial domain adaptation leverages generative adversarial networks (GANs) to minimize the difference between the feature distributions of the source (simulated) and target (real) domains. This is achieved by introducing a discriminator network that distinguishes between features from the two domains while the agent's policy network learns to generate features indistinguishable to the discriminator \cite{ganin2016domain}. This technique effectively reduces the domain discrepancy, facilitating smoother transfer of learned behaviors from simulation to reality. \subsection{Model-Based Reinforcement Learning} In addition to domain adaptation techniques, model-based reinforcement learning (MBRL) offers another promising avenue for improving the adaptability of RL agents. MBRL incorporates explicit models of the environment dynamics into the learning process, allowing agents to simulate future states and evaluate potential actions before they are executed. This predictive capability enhances decision-making under uncertainty and enables agents to better cope with discrepancies between the simulated and real-world dynamics. \subsubsection{Integration with Domain Adaptation} The integration of MBRL with domain adaptation strategies can yield synergistic benefits. By leveraging a model of the environment, agents can generate synthetic experiences that further enrich the domain randomization process. Moreover, model-based predictions can be used to refine adversarial domain adaptation by providing a more informed basis for aligning feature distributions across domains. The proposed methodology for bridging the reality gap and enhancing the deployment of RL agents in real-world environments involves a multi-faceted approach. This includes the application of advanced domain adaptation techniques, the incorporation of model-based strategies, and the iterative refinement of agent policies. \subsection{Experimental Setup} To evaluate the efficacy of the proposed methods, we conduct experiments using a set of benchmark tasks representative of common robotic challenges. These tasks include object manipulation, navigation, and dynamic interaction scenarios. Each task is initially trained in a high-fidelity simulation environment before being transferred to a real-world setting. \subsubsection{Simulation Environment} The simulation environment is designed to closely mimic the dynamics of the real-world setting, with parameters adjustable to test various domain adaptation strategies. The environment is equipped with high-resolution sensors and actuators to capture realistic interactions and feedback. \subsection{Training Procedure} The training procedure involves a phased approach, beginning with domain randomization to expose the agent to a diverse range of simulated conditions. Subsequently, adversarial domain adaptation is employed to refine the agent's policy by aligning the feature distributions between the simulated and real-world environments. \subsection{Performance Metrics} The performance of the RL agents is evaluated based on a set of quantitative metrics, including task completion rate, policy robustness, and adaptability

text: With the growing popularity of open-access academic article repositories, such as arXiv or bioRxiv, disseminating new research findings has become nearly effortless. The ease of access to these repositories has democratized the availability of cutting-edge research, allowing researchers, practitioners, and the general public to access a vast array of scholarly articles. However, this abundance of information brings the challenge of information overload, where researchers struggle to identify and assimilate relevant literature efficiently. This challenge underscores the necessity for advanced tools and methodologies that can streamline the process of literature review, synthesis, and knowledge extraction. In this paper, we address this need by presenting SciSummarizer, a tool that not only offers high-quality summaries but also facilitates the categorization of articles based on thematic areas. Our methodology combines state-of-the-art natural language processing (NLP) techniques with domain-specific adaptations to enhance the extraction and summarization of scientific content. By leveraging machine learning, SciSummarizer is capable of parsing complex scientific texts and distilling them into clear, concise summaries that retain the essence of the original works. The task of automatic summarization has been extensively studied, with numerous approaches proposed over the past decades. Early methods predominantly relied on extractive techniques, which select sentences or phrases directly from the source text based on predefined importance criteria \cite{edmundson1969new}. More recent advancements have shifted towards abstractive summarization, wherein models generate novel sentences that paraphrase the content \cite{rush2015neural}. Transformer-based architectures, such as BERT \cite{devlin2019bert} and its successors, have shown considerable promise in abstractive summary generation due to their contextual understanding and ability to capture semantic nuances. In the realm of scientific literature, specialized models like SciBERT \cite{beltagy2019scibert} have been developed to accommodate the unique linguistic patterns found in academic texts. These models are pre-trained on large corpora of scientific articles, enabling them to better understand and generate summaries in this domain. Additionally, topic modeling techniques, such as LDA, have been employed to aid in the thematic analysis of documents, providing insights into the prevalent topics within a corpus \cite{blei2003latent}. Despite these advancements, challenges remain in creating summaries that are not only accurate and informative but also align with the specific interests of the reader. Our work builds upon these foundations by integrating citation analysis and topic modeling with advanced summarization techniques to deliver a tool that is both robust and adaptable to the needs of researchers across various fields. The architecture of SciSummarizer is designed to efficiently process and summarize scientific texts. It comprises several core components that work in concert to achieve high-quality summarization and categorization: \subsection{Pre-processing Module} The pre-processing module is responsible for preparing the input text for analysis. This involves cleaning the text by removing unnecessary elements such as footnotes, references, and figures, which are not relevant to the summarization task. The module also tokenizes the text into sentences and words, which are then fed into the summarization model. \subsection{Summarization Model} Our summarization model is based on a transformer architecture fine-tuned specifically for scientific texts. The model is trained using a supervised learning approach on a dataset of annotated academic papers. During training, the model learns to identify key sentences and generate summaries that capture the main contributions and findings of the articles. The integration of LDA allows the model to focus on content that is aligned with the primary topics of the document. \subsection{Citation Network Analysis} To assess the impact of an article, the citation network analysis module examines the network of references within the article. By analyzing citation patterns, this module identifies influential papers and seminal works that are frequently cited, enhancing the relevance of the generated summaries. This analysis not only provides context but also helps in understanding the relationship between different research contributions. \subsection{Post-processing and User Interface} Once the summaries are generated, they are subjected to a post-processing step where coherence and readability are improved. The final summaries are presented to the user via an intuitive interface, which allows for easy exploration of the summarized content. Users can filter summaries based on topics or citation impact, tailoring the information to their specific research interests. \label

text: Advances in deep neural networks over the past decade has allowed models to begin solving new tasks requiring information from more than modality. Advances in deep neural networks over the past decade have allowed models to begin solving new tasks requiring information from more than one modality. These tasks, known as multimodal learning problems, involve the integration of data from different sources, such as images, text, and audio, to achieve a comprehensive understanding of the content. Among these tasks, Visual Question Answering (VQA) has emerged as a prominent challenge, necessitating the development of sophisticated techniques to bridge the gap between visual and textual data. Multimodal learning leverages the complementary nature of different data types to enhance model performance. In the context of VQA, the model must not only recognize objects and scenes depicted in images but also comprehend and process natural language questions to provide accurate answers. This dual requirement has led to extensive research aimed at improving the fusion and interaction of distinct feature sets extracted from each modality. Bilinear pooling, as discussed previously, plays a crucial role in this endeavor by facilitating a richer coupling of visual and textual features through pairwise multiplicative interactions. However, the computational costs associated with bilinear pooling have motivated the development of efficient approximations such as Multimodal Compact Bilinear Pooling (MCB) and Factorized Bilinear Pooling (FBP). These methods reduce the resource demands while striving to retain the expressive capabilities required for effective feature fusion. The incorporation of attention mechanisms into bilinear pooling frameworks marks another significant advancement. Attention mechanisms enable models to dynamically weigh the importance of different features from each modality, focusing on the most pertinent aspects of the input data. This selective emphasis not only improves interpretability but also enhances the overall accuracy of the model by directing computational resources towards the most informative features. The integration of multimodal data for VQA and related tasks has been a subject of active research, spawning a variety of techniques designed to improve feature fusion and interaction. Early approaches relied on simple concatenation or addition of feature vectors, but such methods often failed to capture the complex relationships inherent in multimodal data. The introduction of bilinear pooling marked a significant shift towards more sophisticated fusion techniques. By leveraging the outer product to capture interactions between all combinations of feature elements, bilinear pooling offered a means to exploit the full potential of multimodal data. However, computational inefficiencies prompted the exploration of alternative strategies. Multimodal Compact Bilinear Pooling (MCB) \cite{gao2016compact} emerged as a practical solution by employing a count sketch technique to approximate the outer product. This approach reduced the dimensionality of the resulting feature space, making the computation feasible for real-time applications. Factorized Bilinear Pooling (FBP) \cite{kim2017hadamard} further optimized this process by decomposing the interaction into lower-dimensional components, leveraging tensor decomposition methods to maintain high expressiveness with reduced complexity. Attention mechanisms have further refined the bilinear pooling paradigm. By allowing the model to focus selectively on critical features, attention-based methods enhance both the interpretability and the efficacy of the feature fusion process. These mechanisms dynamically adjust the importance of different feature interactions, thus enabling models to better align with the underlying semantics of the data. Moreover, recent studies have explored the integration of graph-based methods with bilinear pooling to model relationships not only between individual features but also among groups of features. This approach is particularly suited to tasks like scene graph generation and semantic role labeling, where understanding the relational structure is crucial. Our approach builds upon these foundational techniques by introducing a novel attention-enhanced bilinear pooling framework. This framework incorporates both the efficiency of compact bilinear pooling and the dynamic adaptability of attention mechanisms, resulting in a robust system capable of handling high-dimensional multimodal data. The core innovation lies in a hierarchical attention mechanism that operates at multiple levels of the feature extraction process. Initially, a pre-attention layer filters and enhances salient features from each modality, reducing noise and irrelevant information. This is followed by a bilinear pooling layer that computes the outer product interactions between the refined feature sets. To maintain computational efficiency, we employ a sketch-based approximation similar to MCB, ensuring that the dimensionality remains manageable without compromising on the richness of the feature interactions. The final stage involves a post-attention layer that further refines the bilinear pooled features by emphasizing interactions that are contextually relevant to the task at hand. The hierarchical nature of the attention mechanisms allows for a comprehensive analysis of both local and global feature relationships, providing a detailed and nuanced understanding of the multimodal inputs. This structured approach not only enhances the model's performance but also facilitates easier interpretation of the decision-making process, as the attention weights can be visualized to reveal the model's focus during inference. To evaluate the efficacy of our proposed framework, we conducted extensive experiments on several benchmark datasets commonly used in the VQA community. These datasets include the VQA v2.0 \cite{antol2015vqa} and the CLEVR dataset \cite{johnson2017clevr}, which are designed to test the model's ability to reason about visual data in response to natural language questions. Our evaluation metrics focused on accuracy and computational efficiency, comparing our approach to existing state-of-the-art methods. The results demonstrate that our attention-enhanced bilinear pooling framework achieves superior performance, particularly in scenarios requiring complex reasoning and feature interaction. In addition to quantitative analysis, we performed qualitative assessments to gain insights into the model's decision-making process. By visualizing the attention weights at different stages of the framework, we observed that the model consistently highlighted relevant features and interactions, corroborating the effectiveness of the hierarchical attention design. In conclusion, the integration of attention mechanisms into bilinear pooling frameworks represents a significant advancement in the field of multimodal learning. Our proposed methodology not only addresses the computational challenges associated with bilinear pooling but also enhances the interpretability and performance of VQA models. Future work will explore the application of this framework to other multimodal tasks, including video analysis and audio-visual scene understanding, to further validate its versatility and generalizability. \bibliographystyle{plain} \bibliography{references}

Bilinear pooling, as discussed above, plays a central role in this, since it allows a more complex combination of features from different modalities through multiplicative interactions. Another important advance is the integration of attention mechanisms into the framework of bilinear pooling. Attention mechanisms make the model dynamically evaluate the importance of features in each modality, and focus on the most relevant features of the input. However, the high computational cost of bilinear pooling has led to the development of more efficient methods such as multimodal compact bilinear pooling (MCB) and factorized bilinear pooling (FBP). The fusion of the data of a task has long been the subject of a lively research which has given rise to a number of techniques for improving the fusion and the interplay of features. The simplest approaches, such as the simple concatenation or addition of feature vectors, failed to make use of the complex relationships in the data. These methods reduce the resource requirements while striving to retain the expressive power needed for a good feature fusion. Bilinear pooling was a great step towards more sophisticated fusion. By using the outer product to measure the interaction of all the possible combinations of the elements, it gave the opportunity to exploit all the resources of the multimodal data. This selective emphasis not only increases the interpretability of the model but also improves the accuracy of the model by directing the computation to the most informative features. Having been prompted by the difficulty of the computation, a more effective method was sought. Multimodal Compact Bilinear Pooling (MCB) has been proposed as a practical solution by a count sketch method to approximate the outer product, reducing the dimensionality of the resulting feature space, and enabling the computation to be feasible for real-time applications. Bilinear pooling can be combined with graph-based methods to capture not only the relationship between features, but also the relationships between groups of features. Attention mechanisms have further refined the bilinear pooling method. By enabling the model to selectively focus on critical features, attention-based methods enhance both the interpretability and the efficiency of the feature fusion process. A pre-attentional layer, which is the first to be encountered in this model, filters and accentuates the most significant features of each dimension, reducing noise and irrelevant information. This is particularly useful in tasks such as graph generation or semantic role labeling, where an understanding of the relational structure is essential. This framework combines the efficiency of compact bilinear pooling with the dynamic adaptability of attentional mechanisms, thus producing a robust system which can cope with very high dimensional data. In order to maintain the computational efficiency, a sketch-based approximation like MCB reduces the dimensionality of the interactions, without sacrificing the richness of the feature interactions. Finally, a bilinear pooling layer calculates the outer product of the interactions between the filtered feature sets. A post-attention layer further refines the bilinear pooled features by focusing on the interactions that are context-sensitive. To evaluate the efficiency of our proposed framework, we have conducted extensive experiments on several common VQ datasets. The hierarchical attention mechanism not only improves the performance of the model, but also makes the model’s decision easier to interpret, as the weights of the attention mechanism can be directly observed and viewed. The hierarchical attention mechanism can be used to study the relationship between local and global features, which provides a detailed and nuanced understanding of the multimodal inputs. Our evaluation metrics were accuracy and efficiency. We compared our method to existing state-of-the-art methods. Our results demonstrate that our attention-augmented bilinear pooling framework is superior to the existing state-of-the-art methods, especially in complex reasoning and feature interaction scenarios. In addition to a quantitative analysis, we also made a qualitative analysis in order to understand the model's decision-making process. By visualizing the weights of attention in the different stages of the framework, we observed that the model is consistent in highlighting the relevant features and their interactions, which is in line with the effectiveness of hierarchical attention. In conclusion, attention mechanisms in combination with the bilinear frameworks constitute a significant advance in the field of multi-modal learning. The next step would be to apply this framework to other multimodal tasks, such as the analysis of visual and acoustic scenes, in order to further demonstrate its generalizability and versatility. This method not only addresses the computational problems associated with bilinear pooling, but also improves the interpretability and performance of VQ models.

text: The task of question answering has benefited largely from the advancements in deep learning, especially from the pre-trained language models(LM)~\cite{radford2019language,devlin2018bert}. These models have demonstrated remarkable capabilities in understanding and generating human-like text. However, their application in narrative QA poses unique challenges that are not thoroughly addressed by existing models. These challenges stem from the need for a deeper understanding of narrative techniques, such as irony, foreshadowing, and unreliable narration, which are prevalent in literary texts. \subsection{Challenges in Narrative QA} Narrative QA involves several intrinsic challenges that differentiate it from other QA tasks. Firstly, narratives often require an understanding of temporal sequences and causal relationships. Unlike factual QA, where questions typically pertain to isolated facts, narrative questions may span across chapters or even the entire book, demanding models to maintain a long-term memory of the text \cite{das2019chains}. Secondly, character dynamics play a crucial role in narrative comprehension. Characters evolve, form relationships, and undergo emotional and psychological changes that influence the story's progression. Accurately answering questions about these aspects requires models to engage in character reasoning and personality inference \cite{bruner1986actual}. Thirdly, thematic elements and moral undertones often underpin narrative structures, requiring models to grasp abstract concepts that are not explicitly stated. This necessitates a sophisticated level of inference, often drawing from world knowledge and cultural context \cite{graesser1994constructing}. \subsection{Existing Approaches} While there has been significant research on QA systems, most methodologies are optimized for non-narrative tasks. Traditional QA systems leverage information retrieval systems and knowledge bases to retrieve factual information \cite{chen2017reading}. However, these approaches fall short in narrative contexts where the information is less structured and often implicit. Transformer-based models, such as BERT \cite{devlin2018bert} and GPT \cite{radford2019language}, have been adapted for QA tasks with considerable success. These models utilize attention mechanisms to capture dependencies between words over long distances, which is beneficial for understanding narrative text. Despite their success, these models still struggle with the nuanced understanding required for narrative QA due to limitations in their ability to model time, causality, and deep contextual understanding. \subsection{Recent Advancements} Recent studies have started to address these challenges by extending transformer architectures with mechanisms specifically designed for narrative understanding. For instance, narrative-focused models have incorporated memory networks to better handle long-range dependencies and track character evolution throughout the storyline \cite{weston2015memory}. Additionally, efforts to integrate commonsense reasoning into language models have shown promise in improving their ability to infer implicit narrative information \cite{talmor2018commonsenseqa}. Another promising direction is the use of pre-trained models fine-tuned on narrative-specific datasets. These datasets are designed to capture the intricacies of narrative texts, providing models with a more robust understanding of storytelling elements \cite{koehn2017six}. \subsection{Our Contribution} In this paper, we propose a novel approach to narrative QA that leverages a hybrid model combining transformer architectures with a narrative-aware component. This component is designed to enhance the model's ability to understand and process narrative elements by incorporating character arcs and thematic developments as part of the input features. Furthermore, we introduce a new dataset specifically curated for narrative QA, which includes a diverse range of literary works. This dataset is annotated with questions that target various narrative aspects, including character motivations, plot developments, and thematic interpretations. By training our model on this dataset, we aim to improve its capability to handle complex narrative questions

text: Drones have great potential for transforming urban logistics services. By enabling quick, flexible, and efficient delivery, they can help address the rapidly growing logistics and e-commerce needs of modern cities. However, drones are constrained by limited battery life and range, which limits their ability to handle long-distance deliveries independently. To address these limitations, integrating drones with traditional delivery vehicles such as trucks presents a promising solution. This hybrid approach harnesses the advantages of both modes of transportation: trucks provide extended range and capacity, while drones offer speed and circumvent traffic congestion. This study proposes a novel framework for optimizing the routing of a mixed fleet of drones and trucks across urban environments. The primary focus is on minimizing total operational costs while ensuring timely and effective delivery. Our approach leverages a Mixed-Integer Linear Programming (MILP) model to capture the complexity of the problem, considering both the continuous and discrete nature of the decision variables involved. The integration of drones into logistics has been explored in various studies. \cite{murray2015flying} introduced the concept of the Flying Sidekick Traveling Salesman Problem, where drones work in tandem with a delivery truck. Similarly, \cite{otto2018optimization} examined the optimization of routes for drones launched from trucks. These studies highlight the potential cost savings and efficiency gains of integrating drones into traditional delivery systems. However, they often assume simplified environments or ignore the complex energy dynamics of drones. Our MILP model is designed to optimize the routing of trucks and drones. We define our model on the graph \( G = (V, E) \), where vertices \( V \) represent locations such as delivery points and truck depots, and edges \( E \) represent possible travel paths. \subsection{Objective Function} The objective is to minimize the total cost, which is a combination of the truck travel cost and the drone energy cost. The formulation is: \[ \min \sum_{t \in T} \sum_{(i,j) \in E} \sum_{k \in R_t} c_{ijk} x_{ijk} + \sum_{d \in D} \sum_{(i,j) \in E} e_{ij} y_{ij} \] where \( c_{ijk} \) is the cost of truck \( t \) traveling from node \( i \) to node \( j \) along route \( k \), and \( e_{ij} \) is the energy cost for drone \( d \) traveling directly from node \( i \) to node \( j \). \subsection{Constraints} The model incorporates constraints to ensure feasible solutions: 1. **Flow Conservation:** Ensures that the flow of trucks and drones is maintained across the network. 2. **Capacity Constraints:** Limit the number of drones a truck can carry. 3. **Energy Constraints:** Ensure that drones do not exceed their energy capacities. 4. **Route Validity:** Restrict trucks to predefined routes, ensuring operational feasibility. To solve the MILP efficiently, we employ a branch-and-bound algorithm enhanced with cutting-plane methods. This approach is well-suited for handling the combinatorial nature of the problem and can effectively navigate the large solution space. \subsection{Heuristic Initialization} We begin with a heuristic approach to generate an initial feasible solution. This step involves a greedy algorithm that prioritizes short-distance deliveries for drones while using trucks for longer hauls. The initial solution provides a baseline for the branch-and-bound process. \subsection{Branch-and-Bound Enhancements} The branch-and-bound algorithm is enhanced with cutting planes derived from valid inequalities, which tighten the relaxation of the MILP. These cuts help in eliminating infeasible solutions early in the search process, improving computational efficiency. To evaluate the performance of the proposed model and solution approach, we conduct computational experiments on synthetic and real-world datasets. These experiments assess the scalability and efficiency of the MILP model and the solution algorithms. \subsection{Dataset Description} The synthetic datasets are generated based on typical urban environments, with varying numbers of delivery points, truck depots, and road networks. Real-world datasets are sourced from publicly available urban logistics data, providing a realistic testbed for our model. \subsection{Results and Discussion} The results indicate that our model effectively reduces operational costs while ensuring timely delivery. The integration of drones and trucks significantly enhances delivery speed and reduces energy consumption. The branch-and-bound algorithm, with heuristic initialization and cutting-plane enhancements, demonstrates robust performance across different scenarios. This study presents a comprehensive framework for the optimization of hybrid drone-truck delivery systems in urban environments. By leveraging the strengths of both transportation modes, our approach addresses the limitations of drones and enhances the overall efficiency of urban logistics operations. Future work can explore dynamic routing strategies and real-time adjustments based on traffic and weather conditions, further improving the adaptability and resilience of the system. \section*{Acknowledgments} The authors would like to thank the anonymous reviewers for their valuable comments and suggestions, which have significantly improved the quality of this paper. This research was supported in part by the Urban Logistics Innovation Grant. \bibliographystyle{plain} \bibliography{references} \end{document}
