text: Precise box estimation is indispensable for a successful tracker. Early trackers usually solve this problem by multi-scale search~\cite{SiameseFC,ECO,DRT,unveiling} employing a sliding window approach to evaluate different scales and aspect ratios of the target object. However, this method is computationally expensive and often fails to capture rapid changes in the object's appearance or scale. Contemporary approaches leverage deep learning to achieve more efficient and accurate bounding box regression. For instance, Region Proposal Networks (RPNs) have been adapted to the tracking domain to generate candidate bounding boxes that are refined iteratively \cite{Ren2015}. In recent years, the integration of Transformer architectures into the tracking pipeline has gained momentum. Transformers, initially designed for sequential data tasks such as language modeling \cite{Vaswani2017}, have shown great potential in vision tasks due to their ability to capture long-range dependencies and contextual relationships. In the context of object tracking, Transformers can be employed to model the temporal and spatial coherence of the target across frames, thereby enhancing the tracker's robustness to occlusions and abrupt motion changes. The self-attention mechanism, a core component of Transformers, enables the model to dynamically weigh the importance of different regions in the input sequence, facilitating more precise target localization. Despite these advancements, the development of robust trackers that can operate under challenging conditions remains an active area of research. One of the major hurdles is achieving a balance between accuracy and efficiency, especially in resource-constrained environments such as mobile and edge devices. Techniques such as model compression and knowledge distillation have been explored to reduce the computational burden of deep learning models without significant loss in performance \cite{Hinton2015}. These methods involve training a smaller, compact model (student) to mimic the behavior of a large, complex model (teacher), thus retaining the performance benefits of the teacher while gaining the efficiency of the student. Moreover, the role of unsupervised and semi-supervised learning in visual object tracking has been increasingly recognized. These paradigms allow for the utilization of vast amounts of unlabeled data, which is particularly advantageous given the scarcity of annotated video datasets. Methods that incorporate self-supervised learning signals, such as temporal consistency and cycle consistency constraints, have shown promise in enhancing the robustness and generalization capability of trackers \cite{Wang2019}. By leveraging inherent structures within the data, these techniques enable the model to learn useful representations without extensive manual labeling. Furthermore, domain adaptation techniques are being developed to mitigate the domain shift problem, where a tracker trained on a specific dataset may perform poorly when applied to a different dataset with varying characteristics such as lighting, background, and object types. Domain adaptation strategies, such as adversarial training and feature alignment, aim to bridge the gap between the source and target domains by aligning feature distributions and ensuring that the tracker generalizes well across diverse conditions \cite{Ganin2016}. In summary, the landscape of visual object tracking is rapidly evolving with the integration of advanced learning paradigms and architectural innovations. While deep learning-based approaches have already made significant strides in improving tracking accuracy and robustness, ongoing research continues to push the boundaries of what is possible. By addressing current limitations through innovations in model design, learning strategies, and computational efficiency, the field is poised to achieve even greater advancements in the coming years. The continued exploration of these areas promises to unlock new applications and enhance existing systems in dynamic environments, ultimately paving the way for more intelligent and autonomous visual systems. In this section, we detail the methodological framework underlying our proposed visual object tracking approach. Our methodology builds on the aforementioned advancements by integrating a novel combination of deep learning architectures, including CNNs and Transformers, alongside innovative training strategies to enhance both the accuracy and efficiency of the tracking system. \subsection{Network Architecture} The backbone of our tracking system is a hybrid architecture that synergizes the feature extraction capabilities of CNNs with the contextual modeling strength of Transformers. The CNN component is responsible for extracting fine-grained, spatially localized features from the input frames. We employ a ResNet-based architecture \cite{He2016} due to its proven efficacy in capturing hierarchical feature representations. These features are then fed into a Transformer module, which is tasked with modeling temporal dependencies and capturing global contextual information across multiple frames. The Transformer module utilizes a series of multi-head self-attention layers, allowing the model to focus on different parts of the input sequence dynamically. This mechanism is particularly beneficial for handling scenarios with occlusions or fast-moving objects, as it enables the network to maintain a coherent representation of the target across the temporal domain. \subsection{Training Strategy} Our training pipeline incorporates a multi-faceted strategy designed to enhance the robustness and generalization of the tracker. text: Learned index structures have emerged as an alternative to traditional database indexes in the recent years since their potential was demonstrated by Kraska et al. \cite{originalLearnedIndex}. The robustness of learned indexes under dynamic data updates remains a critical area of research. Traditional indexes, such as B-trees, are designed to handle insertions, deletions, and updates efficiently. However, learned indexes, which often rely on static models trained on a snapshot of the data, may need to be retrained or adapted as the underlying data changes. This has prompted the exploration of incremental learning techniques and adaptive model architectures that can efficiently accommodate data modifications without necessitating a complete retraining of the model \cite{incrementalLearning}. Another challenge faced by learned index structures is managing the trade-offs between model training time and query execution speed. While more complex models can capture intricate data distributions and provide better query accuracy, they also require longer training times and more extensive computational resources. This is particularly problematic in scenarios where the data distribution changes rapidly, necessitating frequent model updates. Researchers are investigating the use of transfer learning and online learning techniques to reduce the training overhead while maintaining high query performance \cite{transferLearning}. Moreover, the generalization capability of learned indexes across different data distributions is an ongoing concern. A model trained on one dataset may not perform optimally on another dataset with a different distribution. This lack of generalization can limit the applicability of learned indexes in environments where data characteristics are diverse or unknown a priori. Approaches such as ensemble methods, where multiple models are combined to enhance generalization, are being explored to address this issue \cite{ensembleMethods}. Despite these challenges, the opportunities presented by learned index structures are substantial. The ability to customize index models for specific data distributions and query workloads enables more efficient data access patterns compared to one-size-fits-all traditional index structures. For example, in read-heavy workloads, learned indexes can significantly reduce the number of disk I/O operations, thereby improving system throughput and reducing latency \cite{readHeavyWorkloads}. Furthermore, as machine learning techniques continue to evolve, the integration of advanced models such as deep neural networks and reinforcement learning into index structures holds the promise of further performance gains. These models can potentially learn complex query patterns and data relationships that static models cannot capture, leading to even more efficient data retrieval mechanisms \cite{deepRLforIndexes}. Learned index structures have been successfully applied in various domains, demonstrating their versatility and effectiveness. In the realm of spatial databases, for instance, learned indexes have been utilized to enhance the performance of geographic information systems (GIS). By learning the spatial distribution of data points, these indexes can expedite range queries and nearest neighbor searches, which are common operations in GIS applications \cite{spatialDatabases}. In financial services, learned indexes have been employed to manage large volumes of transactional data. The ability of these indexes to quickly adapt to changing data patterns makes them ideal for environments where data is continuously updated, such as stock trading platforms and real-time fraud detection systems \cite{financialServices}. Moreover, cloud storage solutions have started incorporating learned indexes to optimize data retrieval and storage efficiency. Cloud providers like Amazon Web Services and Google Cloud are exploring the use of machine learning-based indexing to reduce latency and improve the scalability of their storage solutions. This has significant implications for big data analytics, where the speed of data access is often a bottleneck \cite{cloudStorage}. The future of learned index structures is promising, with several exciting research directions on the horizon. One such direction is the exploration of hybrid indexing systems that seamlessly integrate learned indexes with traditional index types. These hybrid systems aim to leverage the strengths of both approaches, offering robust performance across varied data and query types \cite{hybridIndexing}. Another potential area of research is the development of self-optimizing database systems that autonomously select and configure the optimal index structures based on current workloads and data characteristics. Such systems could employ machine learning models to continuously monitor performance metrics and adjust index configurations in real time, thereby optimizing query performance without manual intervention \cite{selfOptimizingDB}. Additionally, as privacy concerns and data regulations become increasingly important, the incorporation of privacy-preserving techniques in learned index structures is gaining attention. Techniques such as differential privacy and federated learning could be integrated into learned indexes to ensure that sensitive data is protected while still benefiting from the performance enhancements these indexes provide \cite{privacyPreserving}. In conclusion, learned index structures represent a significant shift in how databases can be optimized for modern data workloads. While there are challenges to overcome, the potential benefits in terms of performance and flexibility make this an exciting and rapidly evolving field of research. As we continue to explore and develop these techniques, it is likely that learned indexes will become a staple in the next generation of database systems. \bibliographystyle{plain} \bibliography{references}

text: Hardware advances in the last decade have brought multicore parallel machines to the mainstream. These advances necessitate new approaches in algorithm design and software development to fully exploit the computational power available. The shift from single-core to multicore architectures has led to a paradigm shift in how computations are approached, with parallelism becoming an intrinsic component of modern software engineering. The Randomized Work-Stealing (RWS) scheduler has emerged as a pivotal mechanism in this context, providing a robust framework for task scheduling in parallel environments. Its ability to dynamically balance loads among processors not only optimizes performance but also simplifies the programming model by abstracting the complexities of parallel task management from the developer. The relevance of RWS is underscored by its application across various domains where task parallelism is prevalent, including scientific computing, real-time data processing, and high-performance computing. This paper explores the latest advancements in the RWS scheduler, focusing on its theoretical foundations, practical implementations, and adaptations to modern computational challenges. We begin by reviewing the fundamental principles that underpin the RWS scheduler, followed by an examination of its implementation in contemporary software systems. Furthermore, we discuss the scheduler's adaptability to heterogeneous and distributed computing environments, highlighting recent modifications that enhance its applicability in these contexts. The theoretical underpinnings of the RWS scheduler are grounded in the concept of probabilistic load balancing. The scheduler's effectiveness is largely attributed to its ability to minimize the variance in processor loads through stochastic task redistribution. Blumofe and Leiserson's seminal work \cite{blumofe1999scheduling} provides a comprehensive analysis of this process, demonstrating that the expected execution time of a multithreaded computation is bounded by $O(W/P + S)$, where $W$ represents the total work and $S$ the critical path length or span. The mechanism of work-stealing involves processors maintaining local deques (double-ended queues) of tasks. When a processor becomes idle, it selects another processor at random and attempts to "steal" a task from the tail of the victim's deque. This randomized approach ensures that the system remains balanced, as the probability of multiple processors targeting the same victim is low, thus reducing contention and overhead. The probabilistic analysis of work-stealing is supported by the Chernoff bound, which indicates that the likelihood of substantial load imbalance decreases exponentially with the number of processors. This property is crucial for ensuring scalability, as it implies that the RWS scheduler can efficiently handle large-scale parallel computations. Implementing the RWS scheduler in real-world systems involves addressing several practical considerations. Key among these is the design of efficient data structures and algorithms to support task deque operations. The deque must allow constant-time access and modification at both ends to facilitate the rapid scheduling decisions necessary in parallel environments. One popular implementation of the RWS scheduler is found in the Cilk programming language \cite{frigo1998implementation}. Cilk's runtime system incorporates an optimized work-stealing scheduler that employs lock-free deques, leveraging atomic operations to ensure thread safety and minimize synchronization overhead. This implementation demonstrates the efficacy of RWS in delivering high performance with minimal programmer intervention. The increasing prevalence of heterogeneous and distributed computing architectures presents new challenges for the RWS scheduler. In heterogeneous systems, processors may have varying capabilities, necessitating an adaptation of the stealing strategy to account for differences in execution speed and task suitability. Agrawal et al. \cite{agrawal2006work} proposed modifications to the standard RWS approach to handle such environments. Their strategy involves dynamically adjusting the priority and granularity of tasks based on processor characteristics, thereby optimizing the overall throughput of the system. This adaptive approach requires a careful balancing of task sizes and priorities to ensure efficient resource utilization without introducing excessive scheduling overhead. In distributed systems, the communication latency between nodes can significantly impact the performance of work-stealing. To address this, Dinan et al. \cite{dinan2009} introduced a hierarchical work-stealing model that organizes processors into clusters. Within each cluster, work-stealing operates as usual, but inter-cluster stealing is governed by a more conservative strategy to mitigate the impact of network delays. As computational demands continue to evolve, the RWS scheduler must adapt to address emerging challenges. One potential avenue for future research is the integration of machine learning techniques to enhance the scheduler's decision-making capabilities. By leveraging historical data and predictive models, the scheduler could dynamically adjust its strategies to better match the workload characteristics and hardware configurations. Moreover, the rise of exascale computing necessitates the development of even more scalable work-stealing algorithms. This will likely involve innovations in both the theoretical modeling of load balancing and the practical design of distributed task management systems. In conclusion, the RWS scheduler remains a cornerstone of parallel computing, offering a versatile and efficient solution for load balancing in a wide array of computational environments. Its continued evolution will be essential to meet the demands of future high-performance computing applications, ensuring that it remains at the forefront of parallel algorithm design. The randomized work-stealing scheduler has proven to be an invaluable tool in the realm of parallel computing, providing robust performance guarantees and adaptability across diverse computational platforms. Its probabilistic approach to load balancing not only minimizes processor idle time but also simplifies the development of parallel applications. As the landscape of computing continues to shift towards increasingly complex architectures, the ongoing refinement and adaptation of the RWS scheduler will be crucial for harnessing the full potential of modern hardware. Through continued research and innovation, work-stealing is poised to remain a key player in the advancement of scalable and efficient parallel computing solutions. \bibliographystyle{plain} \bibliography{references}

In heterogeneous systems, the capabilities of the different processing elements can vary, and this requires the stealing strategy to be adapted to the differences in execution speed and task suitability. Their strategy consists in adjusting the priority and the grain of the tasks according to the characteristics of the nodes, thus obtaining an overall throughput for the system. Taking these two limitations into account, Dinan et al. (2009) developed a hierarchical work-stealing mechanism which groups processors into clusters. This approach requires a precise balance between the size of the tasks and their priorities to optimize the use of resources without introducing an excessive overhead. The requirements of the RWS system will continue to evolve, and the scheduler must continue to adapt to meet them. Work-stealing within a cluster is subject to the usual protocol, but work-stealing between clusters is subject to a more conservative strategy which seeks to minimize the effect of network delay. One potential avenue for future research is to integrate machine learning into the scheduler to enhance its decision-making capability. In conclusion, the RRW scheduler remains a cornerstone of parallel computing, providing a flexible and efficient solution to load balancing in a wide variety of situations. Its probabilistic load-balancing not only reduces the idle time of the machines but also simplifies the parallelization of the program. It has proven to be stable and adaptable to many platforms. text: When healthcare professionals (HCPs) use a treatment search engine to find treatment options for their patients, they need to gain a certain trust in the system. The trustworthiness of a treatment search engine is paramount, as it directly influences the decision-making process of HCPs and, consequently, patient outcomes. This trust is predicated on several key factors: the relevance and accuracy of search results, the timeliness of information, and the transparency of the search engine's algorithms. Relevance and accuracy are critical because they ensure that the search engine provides pertinent clinical trial options that align with the specific needs of individual patients. To achieve this, advanced algorithms must be capable of parsing complex medical datasets and understanding nuanced medical terminologies. This is where machine learning and NLP become indispensable, as they enable the system to learn from vast datasets and improve over time by recognizing patterns and drawing inferences that a simple keyword-based search might overlook \cite{Johnson2019}. Timeliness of information is another critical aspect, as it ensures that HCPs are making decisions based on the most recent data. Real-time updates from clinical trial databases and registries are essential to reflect the latest developments in treatment options. This requires robust data integration frameworks that can seamlessly incorporate new information from disparate sources without significant delays. The implementation of such frameworks often involves leveraging cloud computing technologies that provide scalable storage and computational power needed for processing large volumes of data in real time \cite{Brown2020}. Transparency in the functioning of search algorithms helps build trust by allowing HCPs to understand how recommendations are generated. Explainable AI (XAI) approaches can be integrated into these systems to provide insights into the decision-making process of the algorithms. By offering explanations that are comprehensible to non-experts, XAI can demystify the "black box" nature of many AI models, thereby fostering greater confidence among users \cite{Gilpin2018}. Integrating heterogeneous data sources remains a formidable challenge in the development of effective treatment search engines. Clinical trial data, electronic health records (EHRs), and medical literature are often stored in different formats, making interoperability a significant concern. The lack of standardized data formats across these sources complicates the process of data aggregation and analysis. One promising approach to overcome these challenges is the adoption of ontologies and standardized vocabularies, such as SNOMED CT and LOINC, which facilitate semantic interoperability by providing a common language for medical concepts. By employing these standardized terminologies, search engines can more accurately map and interpret data from diverse sources, thereby enhancing the precision of search results \cite{Cimino2006}. Furthermore, the use of data harmonization techniques, such as data normalization and cleansing, is essential to ensure consistency and accuracy in the data being integrated. These techniques help eliminate discrepancies and redundancies in the data, which can otherwise lead to incorrect or misleading search results \cite{Friedman2017}. While the backend capabilities of a treatment search engine are crucial, the user interface (UI) plays an equally important role in its overall effectiveness. A user-centric design approach ensures that the UI is intuitive and easy to navigate, enabling HCPs to efficiently locate and interpret relevant information. Customizable filters and search parameters allow users to tailor their queries to their specific needs, thereby increasing the relevance of search results. For example, HCPs might want to filter clinical trials based on criteria such as patient demographics, geographical location, or trial phase. Providing such options requires a flexible UI that adapts to the varying needs of different users \cite{Nielsen1993}. Additionally, incorporating feedback mechanisms within the UI can significantly enhance user satisfaction. By allowing HCPs to provide feedback on the relevance and usefulness of search results, developers can continually refine and improve the system. This iterative process of feedback and enhancement is critical for maintaining the system's reliability and user trust over time. In summary, the development of a reliable and efficient treatment search engine for healthcare professionals hinges on advancements in machine learning, NLP, and data integration technologies. By addressing the challenges of data heterogeneity and fostering user trust through explainable AI and user-centric design, these systems can significantly enhance the decision-making capabilities of HCPs. As technology continues to evolve, ongoing research and development will be essential to further refine these systems, ensuring they remain a valuable resource in the ever-changing landscape of clinical research and patient care. Future work should focus on expanding the scope of data sources, improving algorithmic transparency, and enhancing the adaptability of these systems to meet the diverse needs of healthcare professionals worldwide.

text: Semantic segmentation targets to group an image into segments with semantic categories. Although remarkable progress has been made~\cite{FCN,Deeplab,Deeplabv3Plus,pspnet,ocrnet,segformer}, current semantic segmentation models are mostly trained in a supervised learning paradigm, relying heavily on large-scale annotated datasets. This dependency on annotated data presents a significant limitation, particularly when considering the vast number of potential categories that exist in the real world. The cost and effort required to label such extensive datasets are prohibitive, motivating the exploration of zero-shot learning paradigms in semantic segmentation. Zero-shot learning (ZSL) \cite{larochelle2008zero, xian2017zero} emerges as a promising solution to address this limitation by enabling models to recognize and segment unseen categories without direct supervision. In the context of zero-shot semantic segmentation (ZS3), the objective is to accurately segment unseen classes by transferring knowledge from seen classes using semantic information. This necessitates a robust mapping between visual features and a semantic space that encompasses both seen and unseen classes. Traditional ZSL approaches have predominantly focused on image-level recognition tasks. However, the pixel-level nature of semantic segmentation introduces additional complexity. Each pixel must be individually classified, which requires the model to possess a nuanced understanding of the spatial and contextual relationships within the image. This challenge is compounded by the need to generalize from seen to unseen categories, where the visual features may exhibit significant variability. Recent advances in ZS3 leverage deep learning techniques to bridge the semantic gap between visual and linguistic modalities. For instance, embedding-based methods map visual features to a shared semantic space, typically using embeddings derived from pre-trained language models. Word embeddings, such as those produced by Word2Vec \cite{mikolov2013efficient} and GloVe \cite{pennington2014glove}, capture rich semantic relationships between categories, serving as a valuable resource for zero-shot transfer. \subsection{Challenges in Zero-shot Semantic Segmentation} Despite these advances, several challenges persist in the domain of ZS3. One of the primary hurdles is the semantic gap between the visual and linguistic domains. Visual features are often high-dimensional and may contain noise, whereas semantic embeddings are more abstract, representing conceptual similarities between categories. Effectively aligning these disparate representations is crucial for successful zero-shot transfer. Moreover, the diversity of visual appearances within a category further complicates the task. For instance, an "unseen" animal class may exhibit varying colors, shapes, and textures across different instances. Traditional feature extraction methods may fail to capture this variability, resulting in suboptimal segmentation performance. This challenge is exacerbated by the lack of annotated examples for unseen classes, which precludes the use of conventional supervised learning techniques. To address these issues, recent research has focused on enhancing feature representation and semantic alignment through various strategies. Generative models, such as VAEs and GANs, have been employed to synthesize plausible features for unseen categories \cite{xian2018feature}. These models generate diverse training samples, enabling the classifier to become more robust to variations in the semantic space. Attention mechanisms have also been integrated into ZS3 frameworks to improve the focus on discriminative regions of the image \cite{vaswani2017attention}. By selectively attending to informative parts of the input, these models can better differentiate between visually similar classes. This capability is particularly valuable in distinguishing subtle differences that may be crucial for accurate segmentation. Additionally, metric learning approaches have gained traction as a means to enhance semantic alignment. By optimizing distance metrics within the semantic space, models can more effectively capture relational information between categories \cite{snell2017prototypical}. Such techniques facilitate the clustering of semantically similar classes, thereby aiding in the zero-shot transfer process. \subsection{Contributions and Organization} In this work, we propose a novel framework for zero-shot semantic segmentation that leverages advances in deep learning and semantic embedding techniques. Our approach integrates feature synthesis, attention mechanisms, and metric learning to address the challenges outlined above. Specifically, we make the following contributions: 1. We introduce a feature synthesis module that utilizes generative models to create diverse and representative samples for unseen categories. This module enhances the robustness of the classifier by enriching the training set with synthetic features. 2. We incorporate attention mechanisms to refine feature extraction, enabling the model to focus on discriminative regions of the image. This attention module improves the model's ability to distinguish between visually similar categories. 3. We employ metric learning techniques to optimize the semantic alignment between visual features and semantic embeddings. By learning a distance metric in the semantic space, our model achieves better clustering of related categories, facilitating more accurate segmentation. 4. We conduct extensive experiments on benchmark datasets to evaluate the performance of our framework. Our results demonstrate significant improvements over state-of-the-art methods in zero-shot semantic segmentation, highlighting the effectiveness of our approach. Section \ref{sec:methodology} details our proposed framework, including the feature synthesis, attention, and metric learning components. Section \ref{sec:experiments} presents experimental results and analysis, followed by a discussion in Section \ref{sec:discussion}. Finally, Section \ref{sec:conclusion} concludes the paper and outlines directions for future research. In this section, we review relevant literature on zero-shot learning and semantic segmentation, highlighting key developments and methodologies that have informed our approach. We divide our discussion into two primary areas: zero-shot learning techniques and advances in semantic segmentation. \subsection{Zero-shot Learning Techniques} Zero-shot learning (ZSL) has gained significant attention in recent years as a means to address the scalability issues inherent in supervised learning. The core idea of ZSL is to enable models to recognize categories that were not present during training by leveraging auxiliary information, typically in the form of semantic embeddings. Early approaches to ZSL focused on attribute-based methods, where each category is described by a set of human-defined attributes \cite{lampert2009learning}. These attributes serve as an intermediary representation, facilitating the transfer of knowledge from seen to unseen classes. However, the reliance on manually curated attributes limits the scalability and flexibility of these methods. To overcome these limitations, embedding-based approaches have been proposed, where both visual and semantic data are projected into a common embedding space. Word embeddings, such as Word2Vec \cite{mikolov2013efficient} and GloVe \cite{pennington2014glove}, have been widely used in this context, capturing semantic relationships between categories that can be exploited for zero-shot transfer. Recent advances have focused on improving the alignment between visual features and semantic embeddings. Generative models, including VAEs and GANs, have been utilized to synthesize features for unseen classes, thereby augmenting the training set and enhancing model robustness \cite{xian2018feature}. Moreover, attention mechanisms have been integrated into ZSL frameworks to improve feature discrimination and focus on informative regions of the input \cite{vaswani2017attention}. \subsection{Advances in Semantic Segmentation} Semantic segmentation has witnessed remarkable progress with the advent of deep learning. Convolutional Neural Networks (CNNs) have become the cornerstone of modern semantic segmentation methods, enabling models to learn rich hierarchical features from images. Early CNN-based methods, such as Fully Convolutional Networks (FCNs) \cite{FCN}, laid the foundation for end-to-end semantic segmentation by replacing fully connected layers with convolutional layers. Subsequent works have built upon this foundation, introducing architectural enhancements and optimization techniques to improve segmentation accuracy. Deeplab \cite{Deeplab} introduced atrous convolution to capture multi-scale contextual information, while PSPNet \cite{pspnet} utilized pyramid pooling to aggregate global context. More recent approaches, such as SegFormer \cite{segformer}, have focused on transformer-based architectures, leveraging self-attention mechanisms to enhance feature representation and spatial understanding. Despite these advances, the reliance on annotated data for training remains a significant challenge, motivating the exploration of zero-shot learning paradigms in semantic segmentation. By integrating zero-shot learning techniques with state-of-the-art segmentation models, researchers aim to develop systems capable of generalizing to unseen categories without direct supervision. text: \vspace{-8pt} Over the recent eight years, deep generative models have demonstrated stunning performance in generating photorealistic images, considerably boosted by the revolutionary technique of generative adversarial networks (GANs)~\citep{gan14nips,radford2015dcgan,gulrajani2017wgan,miyato2018spectral,brock2018BigGAN,karras2017ProGAN,karras2019StyleGAN,karras2019StyleGAN2}. \noindent The advancements in deep generative models are not limited to image synthesis. These models have been successfully applied across a range of domains including text generation, music composition, drug discovery, and even protein folding \cite{brown2020language,huang2020music,stokes2020deep}. The underlying principle of these models is to learn the distribution of the training data and subsequently generate new instances that resemble the original data distribution. As the field continues to evolve, it is essential to address the multifaceted challenges that arise, particularly concerning model robustness, interpretability, and ethical deployment. \subsection{Robustness of Generative Models} Robustness in generative models pertains to their ability to maintain performance under various conditions, including the presence of adversarial perturbations and shifts in data distribution. Adversarial attacks, which are small, often imperceptible modifications to the input data, can severely affect the output of generative models, leading to inaccurate or harmful results \cite{madry2017towards}. Techniques such as adversarial training and robust optimization have been proposed to mitigate these vulnerabilities \cite{kurakin2016adversarial, goodfellow2014explaining}. However, achieving a balance between robustness and model generalization remains an open research question. \subsection{Interpretability and Transparency} The interpretability of deep generative models is critical for their adoption in sensitive applications where understanding model decisions is paramount. Traditional interpretability methods, such as saliency maps and feature visualization, have been adapted to suit generative models \cite{olah2017feature,selvaraju2017grad}. Recent approaches focus on disentangling the latent representations within models like VAEs, aiming to isolate factors of variation that contribute to different aspects of the generated outputs \cite{burgess2018understanding}. Despite these efforts, the "black-box" nature of many deep learning models continues to challenge researchers \cite{lipton2018mythos}. \subsection{Ethical Considerations and Societal Impact} The ethical deployment of generative models is a subject of intense debate. The creation of deep fakes and the potential for misinformation are significant concerns \cite{chesney2019deep}. To address these issues, a combination of technical solutions and policy measures is necessary. Researchers are exploring methods for watermarking generated content and developing algorithms capable of detecting synthetic media \cite{yu2019attributing,zhang2019detecting}. Additionally, ethical guidelines are being proposed to govern the responsible usage of these technologies \cite{floridi2018ai4people}. The architecture of generative models has seen remarkable innovations aimed at improving quality, efficiency, and scalability. GANs, for example, have evolved from their original form to more sophisticated variants such as Deep Convolutional GANs (DCGANs), Wasserstein GANs (WGANs), and StyleGANs, each introducing novel mechanisms to stabilize training and enhance output fidelity \cite{radford2015dcgan,gulrajani2017wgan,karras2019StyleGAN}. The introduction of spectral normalization in GANs has been pivotal in controlling the Lipschitz constant of the discriminator, thereby addressing issues of mode collapse and training instability \cite{miyato2018spectral}. Furthermore, the progressive growing technique, employed in ProGAN and extended in StyleGAN2, allows for high-resolution image synthesis by gradually increasing the resolution of generated images during training \cite{karras2017ProGAN,karras2019StyleGAN2}. In the realm of VAEs, advancements have focused on improving the expressiveness of the latent space and the flexibility of the posterior distribution. Approaches such as the importance-weighted autoencoder (IWAE) and hierarchical VAEs represent significant strides in this direction \cite{burda2015importance,sonderby2016ladder}. Transformers, originally designed for sequence modeling tasks, have also been adapted for generative purposes, particularly in text and image generation \cite{vaswani2017attention,dosovitskiy2020image}. Their self-attention mechanism allows for capturing long-range dependencies, facilitating the generation of coherent and contextually relevant outputs. The impact of deep generative models spans diverse fields, each with its own set of challenges and opportunities. In healthcare, generative models are used to simulate medical data for research and training purposes, while in the field of autonomous vehicles, they aid in generating realistic driving scenarios for testing \cite{chen2019medgan,grigorescu2020survey}. Looking forward, several promising directions for research include the development of hybrid models that combine generative and discriminative approaches, the integration of generative models with reinforcement learning for dynamic environment simulation, and the exploration of biologically inspired architectures to enhance model efficiency and robustness \cite{lee2020stochastic,wang2019generative}. Ultimately, the continued evolution of deep generative models will hinge on interdisciplinary collaboration, bridging the gap between technical advancements and societal needs. As these models become increasingly integrated into various aspects of life, the emphasis on ethical frameworks, interpretability, and robustness will ensure that their impact remains positive and beneficial. In summary, deep generative models have revolutionized the way data is synthesized and utilized across numerous domains. While tremendous progress has been made, ongoing research is essential to address the challenges of robustness, interpretability, and ethics. By fostering a deeper understanding of these models and their implications, the academic community can pave the way for innovative solutions that maximize the benefits of generative technologies while mitigating potential risks. Future work will likely focus on refining model architectures, enhancing transparency, and developing comprehensive guidelines for ethical use, ensuring that generative models continue to contribute positively to society. \bibliographystyle{plain} \bibliography{references} \end{document}

text: Deep Packet Inspection (DPI) middleboxes are widely deployed as part of modern network security infrastructures \cite{xu2016survey}. \subsection{Semantic Ambiguities} Semantic ambiguities arise when packets are constructed in such a way that they possess multiple valid interpretations due to differences in protocol handling by various systems. Attackers exploit these ambiguities to cause inconsistent packet processing between DPI middleboxes and end hosts. For example, by carefully crafting HTTP headers or using non-canonical character encodings, attackers can introduce variations that a DPI might overlook, yet are processed as intended by the end host \cite{ptacek1998insertion}. 3. **Timing and Sequence Manipulation**: This vector involves altering the timing and sequence of packet delivery to exploit asynchronous processing in DPI systems. Techniques such as packet reordering or intentional delays can lead to parts of the traffic being misinterpreted or ignored by the DPI, thus facilitating evasion \cite{handley2001network}. \subsection{Experimental Setup} The testbed for our experiments was designed to replicate a wide array of network configurations and DPI system architectures. We included popular open-source DPI solutions such as Snort and Suricata, as well as proprietary systems, ensuring a comprehensive evaluation across different implementations \cite{roesch1999snort, deraison1998nessus}. Each DPI was configured using default security policies to mirror real-world deployment scenarios. Traffic was generated using a mixture of benign and malicious payloads, with the latter crafted to exploit the aforementioned attack vectors. Network conditions such as bandwidth limitations, latency variations, and packet loss were simulated to assess the robustness of each DPI under diverse operational environments \cite{floyd2003tcp}. Our findings indicate significant variability in the effectiveness of DPI systems when confronted with evasion techniques. Notably, protocol noncompliance attacks were most successful against systems with rigid protocol parsers, which failed to recognize non-standard packet structures. Conversely, systems with more flexible parsers showed resilience against such attacks but were more vulnerable to semantic ambiguities \cite{paxson1998bro}. Semantic ambiguity attacks resulted in a high rate of evasion, particularly in DPIs that relied on strict pattern matching algorithms. These systems often failed to account for variations in packet encoding and format, leading to high false-negative rates. Our results suggest that incorporating machine learning-based anomaly detection could potentially mitigate these vulnerabilities by adapting to non-standard packet behaviors in real-time \cite{wang2020machine}. Timing and sequence manipulation attacks demonstrated that many DPI systems lack sufficient temporal awareness to handle asynchronous packet flows effectively. Systems with stateful inspection capabilities performed better, though they were not immune to sophisticated reordering attacks that subtly adjusted packet timing within acceptable protocol limits \cite{handley2001network}. \subsection{Limitations and Future Work} While our study provides valuable insights into DPI evasion techniques, it is not without limitations. The diversity of DPI implementations means that results may not fully generalize across all systems. Further research is needed to explore the impact of evolving network protocols and encryption standards on DPI effectiveness, as well as the potential for integrating advanced detection mechanisms such as deep learning \cite{shah2019deep}. Future work will also focus on developing standardized benchmarks for evaluating DPI systems, facilitating more consistent assessments across different research efforts. Additionally, we aim to investigate the potential for collaborative filtering among multiple DPI systems to enhance detection rates by leveraging shared intelligence and threat data \cite{zhao2017collaborative}. Deep Packet Inspection systems play a vital role in modern network security by scrutinizing traffic flows to enforce policies and detect threats. However, as our study demonstrates, these systems are not infallible and remain susceptible to sophisticated evasion techniques that exploit protocol discrepancies and implementation weaknesses. By understanding the limitations of current DPI technologies, security practitioners can better anticipate potential threats and implement more robust defenses. Our research highlights the need for continuous innovation in DPI methodologies, including the adoption of adaptive algorithms and cross-system collaboration to address the dynamic nature of network threats effectively. \section*{Acknowledgements} We would like to thank the institutions and industry partners that provided access to DPI technologies and the necessary infrastructure for conducting this research. Special thanks go to the anonymous reviewers for their insightful feedback and suggestions that greatly improved the quality of this paper. \bibliographystyle{IEEEtran} \bibliography{dpiresearch} \appendix In this appendix, we provide a comprehensive overview of the experimental configurations used in our study. Each DPI system was deployed in a virtualized environment, ensuring isolation and control over network parameters. The traffic generator tool employed was capable of simulating complex attack scenarios, providing a robust platform for testing DPI resilience. \subsection{Configuration Parameters} - **Snort**: Version 3.0 with default community rules. Custom rules were added to test specific protocol noncompliance scenarios. - **Suricata**: Version 6.0 configured with the Emerging Threats ruleset to enhance detection capabilities for known evasion techniques. - **Proprietary DPI Systems**: Tested under vendor-recommended configurations, with custom logging enabled to capture detailed packet inspection logs for analysis. - **Network Topology**: Simulated a typical enterprise network with multiple subnets, incorporating NAT, firewalls, and load balancers to replicate real-world complexities. \subsection{Traffic Generation} Traffic was generated using the D-ITG tool, enabling precise control over packet characteristics and timing. Attack traffic incorporated a mix of known vulnerability exploits and novel packet crafting techniques to assess DPI adaptability and detection accuracy. By providing this detailed insight into our experimental setup, we aim to facilitate reproducibility and encourage further exploration of DPI evasion challenges in future research endeavors.

text: The current status in data privacy could be categorized as the post-privacy area due to the unintended consequences of the big data revolution. The current status in data privacy could be categorized as the post-privacy era due to the unintended consequences of the big data revolution. The pervasive collection and analysis of vast amounts of data have fundamentally altered how privacy is perceived and managed. In this context, blockchain technology emerges as a double-edged sword: while it offers unprecedented opportunities for decentralization and transparency, it simultaneously challenges conventional privacy paradigms \cite{Narayanan2016}. Blockchain's intrinsic properties, such as immutability and transparency, directly conflict with traditional privacy mechanisms that rely on data alteration and access restrictions. Despite these challenges, the potential of blockchain to enhance data security and integrity cannot be overlooked, particularly in sectors where data authenticity and traceability are paramount, such as healthcare, finance, and supply chain management \cite{Swan2015}. The application of blockchain in healthcare presents both opportunities and challenges. The secure and decentralized nature of blockchain could facilitate improved patient data management, interoperability, and trust among stakeholders. However, the sensitive nature of health data demands rigorous privacy controls. The GDPR, which enforces stringent data protection rules, highlights the importance of ensuring that blockchain solutions are compliant with privacy regulations \cite{Zyskind2015}. A promising approach to reconciling these issues involves the use of cryptographic primitives. Zero-knowledge proofs allow for the verification of data authenticity without revealing the data itself, thus preserving privacy while maintaining transparency \cite{Ben2018}. Similarly, secure multi-party computation enables collaborative data processing without exposing individual data points, aligning with privacy requirements \cite{Yao1982}. To enable privacy-preserving blockchain solutions, several methodologies have been proposed. One such method is the deployment of hybrid blockchain architectures, which combine public and private blockchain elements. This approach allows for the segregation of sensitive data onto private chains while maintaining a public ledger for transactional integrity \cite{Xu2019}. Additionally, the use of advanced encryption techniques, such as homomorphic encryption, further enhances data confidentiality by allowing computations to be performed on encrypted data \cite{Gentry2009}. The implementation of permissioned blockchains, wherein access to read or write data is restricted to authorized participants, is another viable strategy. This model not only aligns with the privacy requirements of healthcare data management but also ensures compliance with regulatory standards like HIPAA and GDPR \cite{Zhang2020}. Furthermore, smart contracts can be employed to automate complex data sharing agreements, ensuring that data is only accessed under predefined conditions, thus enhancing both security and operational efficiency. In conclusion, while blockchain presents certain inherent challenges to privacy, particularly in sectors involving sensitive data, it also offers innovative solutions that can be harnessed to enhance data security, integrity, and transparency. By integrating advanced cryptographic techniques and exploring hybrid and permissioned blockchain models, it is possible to develop systems that uphold both the decentralized ethos of blockchain and the stringent privacy requirements dictated by modern regulations. Future research should focus on refining these models and developing standardized frameworks that facilitate the seamless integration of blockchain technology into privacy-sensitive domains. \bibliographystyle{IEEEtran} \bibliography

text: The brain is one of the most complicated and mysterious tissues, controlling the motion, perception, and emotion of animals (including us humans). The field of connectomics aims to map the intricate web of neural connections within the brain, providing insights into its structure and function. Advances in imaging techniques, such as electron microscopy (EM) and light microscopy (LM), have enabled the acquisition of high-resolution volumetric datasets. However, the manual annotation of these massive datasets is labor-intensive and prone to errors. This challenge has led to the increasing application of deep learning-based segmentation techniques, which can automate and enhance the accuracy of neuronal reconstruction. Within this context, PyTorch Connectomics (PyTC) emerges as a pivotal tool for researchers working on connectomics. Its design philosophy centers around accessibility, performance, and flexibility, making it suitable for both novice users and expert practitioners. The framework is particularly advantageous in the realm of volumetric image analysis, where it facilitates the segmentation of neurons and synapses, critical tasks for understanding neural circuitry. The architecture of PyTC is composed of several key components that together form a robust pipeline for segmentation tasks. These components include data processing modules, neural network configurations, and training utilities. Each component is designed to be easily interchangeable, promoting experimentation and rapid prototyping. \subsection{Data Processing} Data processing in PyTC is streamlined through a series of pre-defined pipelines that handle data loading, augmentation, and normalization. Volumetric data often requires extensive preprocessing to enhance contrast and mitigate noise, tasks that are automated within PyTC. The framework supports a variety of data formats, ensuring compatibility with common imaging outputs. Augmentation techniques are crucial for improving the generalization of deep learning models. PyTC provides an array of augmentation strategies, such as random rotations, flips, and intensity variations, which are applied on-the-fly during training. These strategies are implemented to simulate different imaging conditions and enhance the robustness of the models. \subsection{Neural Network Configurations} PyTC supports a wide range of neural network architectures, catering to the diverse needs of connectomics research. The U-Net architecture \cite{ronneberger2015u}, known for its efficacy in biomedical image segmentation, serves as a foundational model within PyTC. Users can also leverage more complex models such as ResNet \cite{he2016deep} and Mask R-CNN \cite{he2017mask}, each offering unique benefits in terms of feature extraction and instance segmentation. The modularity of PyTC allows for the easy integration of novel layers and mechanisms. For instance, attention layers, which have shown promise in enhancing model focus on salient features, can be seamlessly incorporated into existing architectures. This flexibility empowers researchers to push the boundaries of current methodologies and explore new paradigms in neural network design. \subsection{Training Utilities} To facilitate efficient model training, PyTC includes a comprehensive suite of training utilities. These utilities encompass loss functions tailored for segmentation tasks, such as cross-entropy loss and dice loss, which are crucial for optimizing model performance. Additionally, PyTC supports advanced optimization algorithms, like Adam \cite{kingma2014adam} and stochastic gradient descent (SGD), allowing users to experiment with different training strategies. PyTC is optimized for high-performance computing environments, supporting both single-machine and distributed training setups. This scalability is essential for handling the large volumetric datasets typical of connectomics studies. By leveraging parallel processing capabilities, PyTC reduces training times and enables the handling of more complex models. The versatility of PyTC is demonstrated through its successful application to various connectomics datasets. In this section, we highlight several case studies that underscore the framework's capabilities. \subsection{Electron Microscopy Datasets} One of the primary applications of PyTC is the segmentation of EM datasets, which are characterized by their high resolution and large size. In a recent study, PyTC was employed to segment a dataset from the Open Connectome project \cite{openconnectome}, achieving state-of-the-art results in neuronal segmentation accuracy. The ability to accurately delineate neuronal boundaries in EM images is critical for constructing detailed neural maps. \subsection{Light Microscopy Datasets} PyTC has also been applied to LM datasets, which offer different challenges due to their lower resolution and varying contrast levels. In collaboration with a leading neuroscience lab, PyTC was used to segment neurons in a light sheet fluorescence microscopy dataset. The framework's robust data augmentation and normalization techniques were instrumental in overcoming the variability inherent in LM data, leading to improved segmentation performance. PyTorch Connectomics represents a significant advancement in the toolkit available to researchers in the field of connectomics. Its emphasis on modularity, ease of use, and high performance makes it an invaluable resource for automating the segmentation of complex volumetric datasets. As the field continues to evolve, PyTC is well-positioned to incorporate emerging deep learning techniques and support the next generation of discoveries in neural mapping. Future work will focus on expanding the framework's capabilities, including the integration of additional neural network architectures and the development of more sophisticated data augmentation strategies. By continuing to enhance its functionality, PyTC will remain at the forefront of connectomics research, empowering scientists to unravel the mysteries of the brain's intricate networks. \bibliographystyle{unsrt} \bibliography{references} \end{document}

text: Assessing the structure of the brain is critical to better understanding its normal and abnormal functioning. Advances in electron microscopy (EM) now allow three-dimensional (3D) imaging of neural tissues at nanometer-scale resolution, providing unprecedented insights into the intricate architecture of neuronal circuits. This capability is indispensable for exploring the complex connectivity and functionality of the brain's micro- and macro-scale networks. As researchers endeavor to map the human connectome, the integration of high-resolution EM data with functional imaging modalities becomes increasingly vital. The present study aims to elucidate the structural organization of neuronal circuits within the mammalian cortex using state-of-the-art 3D EM techniques. By focusing on the cortical regions of adult mice, we seek to unravel the synaptic architectures and interconnections that underpin neural processing. The identification and characterization of synaptic motifs can illuminate the principles of signal integration and plasticity, potentially uncovering novel pathways that contribute to cognitive functions and dysfunctions. \subsection{Sample Preparation} Adult C57BL/6J mice were used for this study. All procedures were conducted in compliance with institutional animal care guidelines. Mice were anesthetized and perfused transcardially with a fixative solution containing 2.5\% glutaraldehyde and 2\% paraformaldehyde in 0.1M phosphate buffer (pH 7.4). The brains were extracted, and cortical regions were dissected and post-fixed overnight in the same fixative at 4°C. Subsequently, tissues were rinsed in phosphate buffer and stained en bloc with 1\% osmium tetroxide and 1.5\% potassium ferrocyanide, followed by 1\% uranyl acetate staining. Samples were dehydrated through a graded ethanol series and embedded in epoxy resin. Ultrathin sections (70 nm) were cut using an ultramicrotome and collected on copper grids for imaging. \subsection{Imaging and Data Acquisition} Serial block-face scanning electron microscopy (SBF-SEM) was employed to acquire volumetric datasets. The imaging was conducted using a Gatan 3View system integrated with a Zeiss Sigma VP SEM. The automated imaging process involved iterative slicing and imaging of the sample block face, yielding high-resolution 3D reconstructions with voxel dimensions of approximately 5 nm × 5 nm × 70 nm. \subsection{Image Processing and Analysis} Following image acquisition, datasets were processed using a custom pipeline developed in Python. Image stacks were aligned using a cross-correlation algorithm to correct for drift and distortion. Neuronal structures were segmented using a combination of thresholding, watershed transformation, and supervised machine learning models, particularly convolutional neural networks (CNNs). Manual annotations served as ground truth for training and validating the neural network models. Synaptic junctions were identified based on morphological criteria and validated against synaptic marker immunolabeling. Dendritic spines were automatically detected and classified using a CNN trained on manually annotated spines, achieving a precision and recall rate exceeding 90\%. \subsection{Statistical Analysis} Quantitative analyses of synaptic density, spine morphology, and connectivity patterns were performed using MATLAB and R. Data were analyzed using standard statistical tests, including ANOVA for comparing means across multiple groups and t-tests for pairwise comparisons. Correlations between structural features and functional connectivity were explored using Pearson's correlation coefficient. Our analysis revealed a heterogeneous distribution of synaptic connections across cortical layers, with layer-specific synaptic densities and motifs. Notably, layer 2/3 exhibited the highest density of dendritic spines and synaptic boutons, consistent with its role in intracortical communication. Several novel synaptic motifs were identified, including triadic synapses involving astrocytic processes, which may play roles in synaptic modulation and plasticity. Quantitative analysis showed significant variability in spine morphology, indicating diverse roles in synaptic strength and plasticity. Furthermore, the data suggest a non-uniform distribution of inhibitory and excitatory synapses, with clusters of inhibitory synapses observed proximal to the soma and major dendritic branches, potentially contributing to local circuit dynamics and oscillatory activity. The comprehensive mapping of synaptic landscapes presented in this study enhances our understanding of cortical microcircuitry. The identification of unique synaptic motifs and their spatial distributions provides insights into the principles of neural computation and information processing. Our findings highlight the significance of astrocytic processes in synaptic regulation, supporting the tripartite synapse model where glial cells actively participate in synaptic transmission and plasticity. This involvement of astrocytes may have implications for neurodegenerative diseases, where glial dysfunction is a hallmark. The non-uniform distribution of synaptic types and their strategic positioning suggest mechanisms for balancing excitation and inhibition within cortical circuits, crucial for maintaining neural network stability and preventing pathological overexcitation, such as in epilepsy. Future work will focus on integrating these structural insights with functional imaging techniques, such as calcium imaging and optogenetics, to correlate structural motifs with dynamic neural activity. Moreover, expanding this research to include disease models could reveal alterations in synaptic architecture associated with neurological disorders, offering potential targets for therapeutic intervention. This study demonstrates the power of 3D electron microscopy in uncovering the detailed architecture of neuronal circuits. By leveraging advanced imaging and analysis techniques, we have delineated complex synaptic networks within the mammalian cortex, providing a foundation for future explorations into brain function and pathology. Such high-resolution structural insights are indispensable for advancing our understanding of the intricate workings of the brain and for developing interventions for neurological diseases. \bibliographystyle{plain} \bibliography{references}

text: Recent advances on Supervised Re-Identification (re-ID) have led to excellent performance on widely used public re-ID datasets (\cite{ye2021deep,ni2021adaptive}). by leveraging large-scale labeled data. However, such labeled data is often expensive and time-consuming to obtain, especially for domain-specific applications where the visual appearance of objects may vary significantly across different domains. This challenge has spurred interest in Unsupervised Domain Adaptation (UDA) techniques, which aim to transfer knowledge from a labeled source domain to an unlabeled target domain, thereby reducing the reliance on labeled data in the target domain. One of the most promising approaches in the realm of UDA for re-ID is the use of pseudo-labels. As outlined earlier, pseudo-labeling involves generating artificial labels for the unlabeled target domain data based on the model's predictions. These pseudo-labels are then used to iteratively adapt the model, which is initially trained on the source domain, to better generalize to the target domain. The pseudo-labeling process typically begins with training a model on the source domain dataset $\mathcal{D}_s$. The trained model $\theta_0$ is then used to infer pseudo-labels for the target domain dataset $\mathcal{D}_t$. The confidence of these predictions is crucial, as incorrect pseudo-labels can introduce noise, subsequently deteriorating the model's performance. To address this issue, confidence-based filtering strategies are employed, where only samples with prediction confidence above a certain threshold are assigned pseudo-labels. Subsequent iterations involve retraining the model using both the source domain data and the pseudo-labeled target domain data. The model is iteratively refined, where in each iteration, the pseudo-labels are updated based on the improved model $\theta_i$. This iterative refinement process aims to gradually reduce the domain discrepancy by aligning the feature distributions of the source and target domains. \subsection{Clustering-Based Pseudo-Label Generation} Clustering-based methods have emerged as an effective strategy for pseudo-label generation in UDA re-ID tasks. This paper describes a policy learning approach that leverages task-and-motion planning (TAMP) to train robot manipulation policies for long-horizon tasks. Our methodology integrates the strengths of symbolic planning and continuous motion optimization, aiming to address the limitations inherent in conventional reinforcement learning approaches, particularly in complex and unstructured environments. The core challenge in robotic manipulation for long-horizon tasks lies in efficiently managing the combinatorial explosion of possible action sequences needed to achieve a given goal. Traditional reinforcement learning methods often require an extensive amount of exploration, which is computationally prohibitive and impractical in real-world settings. By contrast, TAMP provides a structured framework that facilitates the decomposition of complex tasks into manageable sub-goals, which can be systematically solved using domain knowledge encoded in symbolic representations. Our approach involves a two-phase learning process. Initially, we employ a symbolic planner to generate a high-level task sequence based on a given goal. This sequence is then used to guide a motion planner that operates in the continuous domain, refining the symbolic actions into executable trajectories. This hierarchical structure not only reduces the search space but also allows for the incorporation of probabilistic models to handle uncertainties encountered in dynamic environments. To effectively integrate learning into this TAMP framework, we adopt a model-based strategy that uses a learned transition model to predict the outcomes of actions in uncertain environments. This model is trained using deep neural networks, which have shown great promise in capturing complex patterns and correlations from raw sensory data \cite{lecun2015deep}. By leveraging these capabilities, our approach can dynamically adapt to changes in the environment and improve policy robustness over time. The integration of learning with planning has been a vibrant area of research. Early work by \cite{kaelbling2011hierarchical} laid the groundwork for hierarchical planning approaches that combine symbolic and geometric reasoning. More recent efforts have focused on enhancing the adaptability of these systems through learning-based methods. For instance, \cite{silver2016mastering} demonstrated the power of deep reinforcement learning in solving complex decision-making problems, albeit with significant computational resources. In the context of TAMP, \cite{garrett2020online} introduced an online replanning mechanism that incorporates feedback from the environment to adjust plans in real-time. This approach is particularly relevant for dynamic tasks where static planning models may fail due to unforeseen changes. Our work builds on these foundations by integrating probabilistic reasoning directly into the planning loop, thus enabling more robust handling of uncertainties. Additionally, \cite{schulman2015trust} presented trust region methods for policy optimization that improve stability and performance in reinforcement learning. Inspired by these techniques, we incorporate trust region constraints into our motion planning phase to ensure safe and reliable execution of learned policies. Our proposed method begins with a symbolic planner generating a sequence of high-level actions. This planner utilizes domain-specific knowledge encoded in a task graph, which specifies the preconditions and effects of each action in a symbolic form. The task graph serves as a blueprint for the motion planner, which operates in a continuous space to translate symbolic actions into precise trajectories. To manage environmental uncertainties, we integrate a probabilistic framework using Partially Observable Markov Decision Processes (POMDPs). This allows the system to maintain a belief state—a probabilistic representation of the environment that accounts for uncertainties in perception and action outcomes. By continuously updating this belief state, the planner can make informed decisions that maximize expected reward while minimizing risk. The motion planner utilizes a sampling-based approach, specifically Rapidly-exploring Random Trees (RRTs), to efficiently explore the continuous space. This method is coupled with a neural network-based model that predicts the feasibility and safety of candidate trajectories, refining the search process and improving convergence rates. We evaluate our approach on a set of benchmark tasks designed to test the efficacy of TAMP in long-horizon and dynamic environments. These tasks involve complex manipulation scenarios requiring the coordination of multiple robotic arms, each tasked with achieving distinct yet interdependent sub-goals. Our results demonstrate that the proposed method significantly outperforms baseline reinforcement learning algorithms in terms of both efficiency and success rate. The integration of symbolic planning with motion optimization enables the system to generate feasible solutions with fewer iterations, while the probabilistic reasoning framework enhances adaptability to environmental changes. Self-supervised learning, especially self-trained learning, has been gaining ground as a way of coping with large amounts of unlabeled data. [17, 51] Triplet networks extend this idea to a triplet of examples, a positive, a negative, and a reference. [17, 51] Siamese networks with pairwise loss functions have been developed for learning embeddings that minimize the distance between matching points and maximize the distance between non-matching points. These methods allow the model to learn by instance discrimination, in which the task is to discriminate the different instances of the data. Despite their success, these methods are sensitive to the choice of pairs and triplets, which can lead to suboptimal training. Our work builds on these advances by introducing a dynamic margin into the loss function, which is specifically tuned to deal with the variances in multimodal data. Sub-chapter Face The face is a convolutional neural network that receives a static facial image as input. It uses the ResNet-50 architecture, which has been shown to be effective for extracting features from images. The voice is a convolutional neural network that receives a speech signal as input. Inspired by the work on speaker recognition, the network architecture is based on a modified VGG network (cf. Nagrani, voxceleb, 2012) and produces a fixed-dimensional representation of the voice. The voice branch processes the waveforms through a series of one-dimensional convolutional layers, followed by a temporal pooling mechanism. The network is pre-trained on a large-scale face recognition dataset, which provides a good initial representation, and is then further tuned to our specific task to optimize the representation for voice matching. Our experiments focus on two main tasks: pairwise verification and retrieval. For face images, we perform the standard preprocessing steps, including landmarking and face normalization. Signals are resampled to a common frequency and normalized to ensure uniformity between samples. Edge-aware filters are among the most commonly used image processing operators in a wide range of computational photography applications. Also called \emph{edge-preserving smoothing} techniques, these filters are designed to smooth images while maintaining significant edges, thus avoiding the blurring of key structural information. The primary goal of edge-aware filters is to enhance image quality by selectively processing regions of interest without degrading important features. Two prominent types of edge-aware filters are bilateral filters and anisotropic diffusion. The bilateral filter, introduced by Tomasi and Manduchi \cite{Tomasi1998}, operates by performing a weighted average of nearby pixels, where the weights are determined by both spatial distance and intensity difference. The bilateral filter's strength lies in its ability to perform non-linear smoothing, which effectively reduces noise while preserving edges. The mathematical formulation of the bilateral filter is given by:  egin{equation} I_{filtered}(x) =  rac{1}{W_p} \sum_{x_i \in \Omega} I(x_i) \cdot f_r(\|I(x_i) - I(x)\|) \cdot f_s(\|x_i - x\|), \end{equation} where \(I_{filtered}(x)\) is the intensity of the filtered image at pixel \(x\), \(I(x_i)\) is the intensity of a nearby pixel \(x_i\), \(\Omega\) is the neighborhood of the pixel, and \(W_p\) is the normalization factor. The functions \(f_r\) and \(f_s\) are the range and spatial kernels, respectively, which typically follow Gaussian distributions. Anisotropic diffusion, introduced by Perona and Malik \cite{Perona1990}, is another edge-preserving smoothing technique inspired by heat diffusion processes. It modifies the traditional isotropic heat conduction equation to allow for differential smoothing across an image. The diffusion process is governed by a diffusion coefficient that varies spatially, allowing the algorithm to smooth homogeneous regions while preserving edge information. The function \(c(x, t)\) is typically chosen to decrease at edges, thereby reducing the smoothing effect in these regions. Edge-aware filters have found widespread application in various domains within computational photography and beyond. Some notable applications include: \subsection{Detail Enhancement} In detail enhancement, edge-aware filters are employed to amplify fine details within an image while retaining the overall structure. This is particularly useful in high dynamic range (HDR) imaging, where detail enhancement can lead to more visually appealing images \cite{Fattal2002}. By applying an edge-preserving filter, one can enhance textures and details without introducing artifacts such as halos around edges. \subsection{Image Abstraction} Image abstraction aims to create visually simplified representations of images by removing unnecessary details while highlighting essential features. Edge-aware filters are integral to this process, as they allow for the selective removal of fine textures and noise, leaving behind a stylized version of the original image. This technique is widely used in artistic rendering and non-photorealistic rendering applications \cite{Winnemoller2006}. \subsection{Texture Removal} Texture removal is another critical application of edge-preserving filters, particularly in tasks such as image segmentation and stylization. By effectively smoothing out textures while preserving edges, these filters facilitate the isolation of key image components, aiding in accurate segmentation and the creation of visually distinct styles \cite{Paris2008}. Despite their widespread application and utility, edge-aware filters face several challenges. One of the primary issues is computational complexity, particularly for real-time applications. The quadratic complexity of naive implementations of bilateral filters, for instance, can be prohibitive for large images.
